We demonstrate that incorporating explicit negative examples to regularize the model substantially boosts performance, surpassing the state-of-the-art results by Fu et al. (2014) across three datasets spanning different languages.

We introduce a methodology for deriving concepts within a target domain from extensive Linked Open Data (LOD) resources to facilitate the development of domain ontologies that encapsulate field-specific knowledge and definitions. This approach identifies search entities by connecting LOD vocabularies with technical terminology relevant to the target domain. These entities serve as the foundation for retrieving upper-level concepts within the LOD, where we analyze the frequency of common upper-level entities and their chain-of-path relationships to map the extent of conceptual connections in the target domain. Furthermore, a technical dictionary index combined with natural language processing is employed to assess the coverage of the extracted concepts. Using Wikidata as a case study, we demonstrated the extraction of a class hierarchy to build a domain ontology for polymer materials and their physical properties. This method is applicable to general datasets featuring class hierarchies and enables ontology developers to establish an initial model of a domain ontology tailored to their specific needs.

We propose a novel conceptual framework wherein inflationary Cosmology is formulated through quantum mechanics, utilizing the Hilbert space representation of the crossed product. This construction involves the type $III$ factor linked to the algebra of local operators within the de Sitter static patch and the automorphism governing translations in the emergent conformal time. Within this formalism, scalar curvature fluctuations arise from the gravitational potential generated by the quantum variance of the generator associated with the conformal time automorphisms. By selecting the effective vacuum state for each mode and conformal time as a representative within the Hilbert space of the crossed product, we compute the quantum variance and the resulting scalar curvature fluctuations. This approach yields a model-independent characterization of inflationary parameters, specifically $(1-n_s) \sim 0.0318$ and $\epsilon \sim 0.0027$, which align well with Planck experimental data. Furthermore, in this formal structure, inflation extends the algebra of observables in a primordial de Sitter expanding universe, rendering time evolution an inner automorphism where conjugated energy fluctuations appear as observable scalar curvature fluctuations.

We have developed and trained a convolutional neural network, named APOGEE Net, to derive effective temperature ($T_\mathrm{eff}$), surface gravity ($\log g$), and, where applicable, metallicity ([Fe/H]) from APOGEE spectra. This represents the inaugural pipeline tailored to these data that estimates these stellar parameters in a self-consistent framework, covering not only low-mass stars—such as main sequence dwarfs, pre-main sequence stars, and red giants—but also high-mass stars with $T_\mathrm{eff}$ exceeding 50,000 K, including hot dwarfs and blue supergiants. The catalog of approximately 650,000 stars introduced in this paper facilitates a comprehensive analysis of the star formation histories of both the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds. By enabling the cleaner selection of various object types tracing different galactic regions through their unique positions in the $T_\mathrm{eff}$-$\log g$ parameter space, this work offers improvements over previous APOGEE catalogs generated by alternative pipelines.

Reference \cite{butman1976} employs a linear coding scheme defined by $X_t = g_t\Big(\Theta - {\bf E}\Big\{\Theta\Big|Y^{t-1}, V_0=v_0\Big\}\Big)$ for $t=2,\ldots,n$ and $X_1=g_1\Theta$, where $\Theta$ is a Gaussian random variable. This approach is used to establish a lower bound on the feedback rate for additive Gaussian noise (AGN) channels, described by $Y_t=X_t+V_t$ with $V_t$ representing Gaussian autoregressive (AR) noise, under a total transmitter power constraint $\kappa \in [0,\infty)$. Specifically, for unit memory AR noise characterized by parameters $(c, K_W)$, where $c\in [-1,1]$ is the pole and $K_W$ is the noise variance, the derived lower bound is $C^{L,B} =\frac{1}{2} \log \chi^2$. Here, $\chi =\lim_{n\longrightarrow \infty} \chi_n$ denotes the positive root of the equation $\chi^2=1+\Big(1+ \frac{|c|}{\chi}\Big)^2 \frac{\kappa}{K_W}$, with the sequence $\chi_n \triangleq \Big|\frac{g_n}{g_{n-1}}\Big|$ satisfying a specific recursion. The authors of \cite{butman1976} conjectured that $C^{L,B}$ represents the feedback capacity. In this correspondence, it is noted that the nontrivial lower bound $C^{L,B}=\frac{1}{2} \log \chi^2$, where $\chi >1$, necessitates that the feedback code scaling coefficients $g_n$ become unbounded, meaning $\lim_{n\longrightarrow\infty}|g_n| =+\infty$. This unbounded growth of $g_n$ is deduced from the ratio limit theorem for real sequences and confirmed via simulations. Consequently, these linear codes are deemed impractical and highly sensitive to discrepancies between the theoretical channel model and actual channel statistics. Specifically, even a minute perturbation error $\epsilon_n>0$ results in the term $g_n \epsilon_n$ diverging to infinity as $n \longrightarrow \infty$, causing $X_n$ to be dominated by the error amplification.

Deep learning has emerged as a natural, data-driven approach for analyzing modern astronomical datasets. This study employs a deep convolutional neural network to derive fundamental stellar parameters, including effective temperature ($T_{\rm eff}$), surface gravity (log g), metallicity ([M/H] and [Fe/H]), alpha-element enhancement ([$\alpha$/M]), and nine specific elemental abundances ([C/Fe], [N/Fe], [O/Fe], [Mg/Fe], [Al/Fe], [Si/Fe], [Ca/Fe], [Mn/Fe], [Ni/Fe]). The model was trained on common stars shared between the APOGEE and LAMOST surveys, utilizing low-resolution LAMOST spectra as input and APOGEE measurements as ground truth labels. For the test set, where the signal-to-noise ratio in the g-band exceeds 10, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 29 K for $T_{\rm eff}$, 0.07 dex for log g, 0.03 dex for both [Fe/H] and [M/H], and 0.02 dex for [$\alpha$/M]. The MAE for the majority of individual elements falls between 0.02 and 0.04 dex. The trained network was applied to a sample of 1,210,145 giants and sub-giants from LAMOST DR8, covering stellar parameters of 3500 K < $T_{\rm eff}$ < 5500 K, 0.0 dex < log g < 4.0 dex, and -2.5 dex < [Fe/H] < 0.5 dex. The resulting chemical distributions align closely with APOGEE labels, and the derived stellar parameters agree well with external high-resolution data from GALAH. These findings facilitate further investigations using LAMOST data and enhance our comprehension of the Milky Way's accretion and evolutionary history. The electronic version of the value-added catalog is accessible at http://www.lamost.org/dr8/v1.1/doc/vac.

Envelope models can significantly lower the computational resources required for Particle in Cell (PIC) simulations of Laser Wakefield Acceleration (LWA) in many relevant scenarios. However, integrating tunneling ionization into this time-averaged framework is challenging because the statistical characteristics of ionization-generated electron beams must be accurately captured without explicitly resolving high-frequency laser oscillations. To address this, the study proposes an extension of an existing envelope ionization method, applicable to higher-intensity laser pulses. This approach involves imparting an initial longitudinal drift to newly created electrons within the ionizing laser pulse. The method's accuracy is validated using both linear and circular polarization in a simple benchmark involving nitrogen slab ionization by a laser, as well as in a more complex nonlinear regime scenario featuring ionization injection during laser-plasma acceleration. By incorporating this enhancement into the envelope ionization algorithm, key phase space properties of bunches injected into plasma wakefields—such as charge, mean energy, energy spread, root-mean-square sizes, and normalized emittance—can be estimated with precision comparable to full non-envelope simulations, albeit with substantially reduced computational costs, even in cylindrical geometries. Consequently, this extended algorithm facilitates preliminary investigations into ionization injection for LWA, making such studies feasible even on standard laptop computers.

The local well-posedness of the initial value problem for the two-dimensional Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation on a periodic domain is established within the cylinder for the range 9/10 < s < 1. This result is demonstrated through the application of bilinear estimates, with the spatial variables analyzed separately.

By utilizing vast quantities of product data gathered from hundreds of active e-commerce platforms, we established 1,000 distinct classification tasks featuring similarly structured inputs that combine text and images. These tasks are designed to learn the product hierarchies of various sites, resulting in significant correlations among them. We addressed these challenges collectively using a multi-modal transformer model through multi-task learning (MTL). Extensive experiments conducted on an initial dataset of 100 tasks uncovered best practices for "large-scale MTL" (involving over 100 tasks). These findings culminated in a unified methodology integrating established best practices with novel proposals, such as DyPa—a straightforward heuristic for automatically assigning task-specific parameters to tasks requiring additional capacity. Applying this large-scale MTL framework, we successfully trained a single model across all 1,000 tasks with minimal task-specific parameters, demonstrating that MTL can be scaled several orders of magnitude beyond current efforts.

We conducted a comprehensive analysis of the dynamic stability of the recently predicted BaSiH$_8$ phase [Lucrezi $\textit{et al.}$, npj Comp. Mat. 8, 119 (2022)]. Our findings indicate that incorporating quantum ionic effects, anharmonicity, and phonon-phonon interactions using the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation (SSCHA) raises the critical dynamical pressure to $20\,\text{GPa}$, a significant increase from the $5\,\text{GPa}$ threshold observed in purely harmonic treatments of classical nuclei. We attribute this rise primarily to structural changes driven by quantum ionic effects, a phenomenon that can already be explained at the harmonic level through zero-point energy corrections to the total electronic energy. Crucially, the previously established critical pressure for kinetic stability ($p_\text{kin} = 30\,\text{GPa}$) remains the more stringent constraint on the synthesizability of BaSiH$_8$ and analogous hydrides, offering a more rigorous and accurate prediction of their experimental feasibility. Regarding our methodology, we showcase the application of highly precise machine-learned interatomic potentials to simulate significantly larger supercell sizes and population numbers, thereby facilitating faster and more thoroughly converged SSCHA calculations.

This paper investigates the asymmetric Ramsey properties of the random graph $G_{n,p}$. For a natural number $r$ and graphs $H_1, \ldots, H_r$, the notation $G_{n,p} \to (H_1, \ldots, H_r)$ signifies that any edge coloring of $G_{n,p}$ using colors from $[r] = \{1, \ldots, r\}$ guarantees a monochromatic copy of $H_i$ in color $i$ for some $i \in [r]$. Significant research has focused on identifying the asymptotic threshold function for this property. While Rödl and Ruciński established the threshold for the symmetric case where $H_1 = \cdots = H_r$, a conjecture by Kohayakawa and Kreuter would completely solve the asymmetric version. The first part of this conjecture was recently verified by Mousset, Nenadov, and Samotij. Extending the work of Marciniszyn, Skokan, Spöhel, and Steger, we reduce the second part (the 0-statement) of the Kohayakawa and Kreuter conjecture to a specific deterministic subproblem. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by proving the subproblem holds for almost all pairs of regular graphs, thereby settling the 0-statement for all such pairs.

Artificial neural networks and other universal function approximators can arbitrarily well learn diverse target functions with enough training data, though this adaptability sacrifices parametric inference capabilities. To bridge this divide, we propose a general framework grounded in the Shapley-Taylor decomposition of a model. By conducting surrogate parametric regression within the space defined by the Shapley value expansion, this method enables the testing of standard hypotheses. Simultaneously, it offers new perspectives on statistical learning processes by leveraging the consistency and bias characteristics of nonparametric estimators. We demonstrate the framework's utility in estimating heterogeneous treatment effects across both simulated and real-world randomized trials. Furthermore, we introduce an explicit treatment function utilizing higher-order Shapley-Taylor indices to uncover complex treatment pathways and facilitate the generalization of experimental findings. Ultimately, this approach promotes the standardized application and communication of results derived from machine learning models.

To fully grasp the capabilities and constraints of quantum computing, one must develop efficient techniques to characterize and benchmark the error channels inherent in these systems. This paper introduces MATEN, a method that faithfully reconstructs a marginal (local) approximation of the effective noise channel, which functions as a single layer at the circuit's conclusion. We begin by establishing a dual map framework that enables the analytical derivation of observable expectation values for noisy circuits. Numerical simulations of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) validate these findings and demonstrate the robustness of MATEN, even when non-local errors occur during execution. Finally, we apply this method to QAOA circuits with up to six qubits on Rigetti's Aspen-9 quantum processor, successfully predicting the majority of observed measurements across the qubits.

The study of adversarial examples, which emerge when training deep neural networks on pixel-grid images, has inspired a new approach. Drawing inspiration from human ability to reconstruct abstract concepts, we propose encoding input bitmap images into a set of compact, interpretable components to prevent manipulation by adversarial structures. This work initiates that direction by testing image vectorization as an input transformation technique designed to map adversarial instances back onto the natural manifold of MNIST handwritten digits. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art input transformations and analyze the trade-offs between using hand-crafted versus learned transformation defenses.

The deployment of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) relies on channel state information (CSI), yet rapid channel variations often impede progress due to the substantial overhead associated with training, estimation, and feedback. To address this, the paper introduces a novel two-timescale beamforming framework designed to maximize the average achievable rate (AAR) in IRS-assisted MIMO systems. In this approach, the IRS configuration is adjusted infrequently using statistical CSI (S-CSI), while the base station's precoder and power allocation are updated frequently based on instantaneous CSI (I-CSI), even if the data is somewhat outdated. The core methodology first identifies that the optimal small-timescale power allocation under outdated I-CSI follows a water-filling pattern. Building on this optimal power distribution, a new mini-batch sampling (mbs) particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm is proposed to optimize large-timescale IRS settings with fewer channel samples. Furthermore, a model-driven PSO algorithm is developed to maximize a lower bound of the AAR using only S-CSI, thereby removing the dependency on channel samples; this model-driven approach acts as a reliable benchmark for the mbs-PSO. Simulation results validate the superiority of this two-timescale strategy over existing alternatives, demonstrating enhanced AAR and efficiency while highlighting the advantages of IRS technology.

Optical spectroscopy of ultra-thin materials has greatly advanced our comprehension of collective excitations in low-dimensional semiconductors, a field notably enriched by the complex physics of excitons in atomically thin crystals. This unique behavior stems from the interaction of strong Coulomb correlations, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and lattice geometry. In this work, we expand upon this domain by demonstrating the existence of room-temperature excitons in a material possessing non-trivial global topology. We investigated the fundamental optical excitation spectrum of a single layer of bismuth atoms epitaxially grown on a SiC substrate (bismuthene or Bi/SiC), a system recognized as a large-gap, two-dimensional (2D) quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulator. Our experiments reveal well-defined optical resonances near the direct band gap at the K and K' points of the Brillouin zone, signifying the creation of bound excitons with significant oscillator strength. These experimental results are supported by *ab-initio* GW and Bethe-Salpeter equation calculations, which validate the nature and energy scale of the excitonic resonances and confirm pronounced Coulomb interaction effects. Our findings present the first proof of room-temperature excitons in a 2D QSH insulator, where both excitonic and topological phenomena originate from the same underlying electronic structure.

The cross-section of an implosion for a symplectic manifold constitutes a stratified space that facilitates the abelianization of its symplectic reduction. Following a review of the fundamentals of symplectic and Poisson reduction alongside the basics of symplectic implosion, we establish a cross-section theorem for Poisson manifolds. This result extends the Guillemin-Sternberg theorem originally formulated for symplectic manifolds, marking a preliminary step toward the development of Poisson implosion. During this process, we locate and correct an error in the original proof of the Guillemin-Sternberg theorem and demonstrate that Poisson transversals serve as the appropriate analogue to symplectic submanifolds within this framework.

We examine the quasi-Hopf twist of the quantum toroidal algebra associated with $\mathfrak{gl}_1$, interpreting it as an elliptic deformation. Although the algebraic structure remains unchanged under this twist, the coproduct undergoes deformation, with the twist parameter $p$ corresponding to the elliptic modulus. By calculating the twisted $R$ matrix, we reveal its connection to the elliptic lift of the Nekrasov factor used in instanton counting for quiver gauge theories on $\mathbb{R}^4 \times T^2$. Furthermore, this $R$ matrix governs the commutation relations of intertwiners, leading to an elliptic quantum Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation for their trace. Finally, we demonstrate that the solution to this equation factorizes into a product of elliptic Nekrasov factors and the triple elliptic gamma function.

This study establishes the global existence of a unique, non-negative mild solution for the Cauchy problem associated with the cutoff Boltzmann equation under the soft potential model ($-1 \leq \gamma < 0$) in three-dimensional space, assuming small initial data. Consequently, this work rectifies a previous gap concerning the $\gamma = -1$ case in three dimensions, where an improper estimation of the loss term had occurred. Additionally, the earlier gap for $\gamma = 0$ in two dimensions has recently been addressed by Chen, Denlinger, and Pavlović. The initial data $f_0$ is non-negative, small in weighted $L^{3}_{x,v}$, and finite in weighted $L^{15/8}_{x,v}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solution exhibits scattering relative to the kinetic transport operator. The primary innovation of this research stems from investigating the symmetric property of the gain term within weighted estimates, which serves as the crucial element for resolving the model for $-1 < \gamma < 0$ when utilizing Strichartz estimates.

Independent component selection (ICS), as introduced by Tyler et al. (2009, JRSS B), serves as an effective method for identifying promising projections within multivariate datasets. However, certain ICS-generated projections may appear near highly significant structures, yet minor deviations can obscure these features—such as clusters—that would otherwise be distinct. To address this limitation, we propose an automated, localized variant of projection pursuit (PP), referencing Huber (1985, Ann. Statist.). Specifically, our approach utilizes a local search strategy grounded in gradient descent, optimizing the estimated differential entropy with respect to the projection matrix.

Machine learning models perform essential tasks, such as distinguishing between high-risk and low-risk loan applicants. These models are typically trained on the premise that both the training dataset and real-world operational data originate from the same unknown distribution. However, this assumption frequently fails in practice. Detecting such violations is crucial to mitigating their adverse effects on model performance. We propose a novel method for detecting distributional shifts by discovering polynomial relationships among data features. The significance of each relationship is quantified using its R-square value. Strong polynomial relations reflect key data characteristics that should remain consistent if the underlying distribution is stable. Consequently, we employ a collection of learned, high-strength polynomial relations to detect drift. For relations exceeding a specific strength threshold, we quantify the observed drift by computing the Bayes Factor comparing the likelihood of the polynomial relation under baseline versus field data. We validate this approach empirically by simulating various distributional changes and identifying drift through the Bayes Factor of the resulting likelihood variations.

This paper investigates seismic data inversion via multi-objective optimization using the NSGA II algorithm. The inversion process aims to determine subsurface rock slowness by analyzing wave travel times between seismic transmitters and receivers. Employing a multi-objective approach, the method balances the misfit functional against a stabilizing constraint, specifically the classic first-order Tikhonov regularization. The study utilizes a synthetic model featuring inclined layers, yielding satisfactory results. Analysis of cumulative error graphs confirms the optimization method's effectiveness in generating acceptable solutions while resolving the inherent instability of the inverse problem. Furthermore, the generation of a convergence curve on the Pareto frontier represents a significant outcome with potential for future research.

Training agents to execute new tasks via natural language is often obstructed by interpretative ambiguities. Specifically, when a teacher describes an object's features to a learner, the learner may misinterpret the intended meaning if those features are referenced ambiguously; this is known as referential ambiguity. This study explores how two cognitive science concepts—pedagogy (choosing optimal instructions) and pragmatism (inferring another agent's preferences through inductive reasoning)—can mitigate such ambiguities. These principles are applied within a teacher-learner framework involving two artificial agents performing a simulated block-stacking task. The results demonstrate that incorporating these concepts enhances the sample efficiency required to train the learner.

This study introduces a microscopic imaging method utilizing variable-angle illumination to retrieve complex polarimetric properties of a sample with high resolution across an extensive field of view. Building upon Fourier ptychography—a synthetic aperture technique that enhances resolution from phaseless measurements—the proposed approach incorporates the vectorial characteristics of light. Following data acquisition with a standard microscope equipped with an LED array and dual polarizers, the developed vectorial Fourier Ptychography (vFP) algorithm computes the complex 2x2 Jones matrix for the anisotropic specimen at every resolved spatial point. Furthermore, we present a novel sequential Gauss-Newton solver that simultaneously corrects for polarization-dependent aberrations within the imaging system. The efficacy of vFP is validated through the generation of large-area (29 mm²) and high-resolution (1.24 μm full-pitch) reconstructions of absorption, phase, orientation, diattenuation, and retardance for diverse calibration standards and biological samples.

For a Hilbertian field $k$ and a finite collection $\mathcal{S}$ of Krull valuations, we demonstrate that any finite split embedding problem $G \rightarrow {\rm{Gal}}(L/k)$ with an abelian kernel admits a solution ${\rm{Gal}(F/k)} \rightarrow G$ where each $v \in \mathcal{S}$ splits completely in $F/L$. We present two applications of this result. First, we address a non-constant version of the Beckmann--Black problem for solvable groups: given a field $k$ and a non-trivial finite solvable group $G$, every Galois extension $F/k$ with group $G$ can be realized as the specialization at some $t_0 \in k$ of a Galois extension $E/k(T)$ of group $G$, where $E \not\subseteq \overline{k}(T)$. Second, we advance inverse Galois theory over division rings by proving that for any division ring $H$ and automorphism $\sigma$ of $H$ with finite order, all finite semiabelian groups appear as Galois groups over the skew field of fractions $H(T, \sigma)$ of the twisted polynomial ring $H[T, \sigma]$.

The uncertainties arising from infrared renormalons in the (color dipole) gluon distribution are evaluated. It is demonstrated that non-linear saturation effects at small-$x$ displace the first IR pole in the Borel plane from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$. Consequently, the estimated uncertainty is determined to be ${\cal O}\left(\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2\right)$ rather than ${\cal O}\left(\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4\right)$.

Hand segmentation plays a vital role in first-person vision systems. Because first-person imagery often displays significant appearance variations across different environments, adapting pre-trained segmentation models to new domains is essential. This work specifically addresses appearance discrepancies in both hand regions and backgrounds. We introduce two key components: (i) foreground-aware image stylization and (ii) consensus pseudo-labeling for domain adaptation. Our approach involves stylizing source images independently for the foreground and background by adopting the style of target images. To mitigate remaining domain shifts caused by stylization, we implement careful pseudo-labeling that aggregates predictions from models trained on both the original and stylized source data. We evaluated our method on adapting hand segmentation between real-world and simulated images, achieving state-of-the-art results in both scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrated promising outcomes in challenging multi-target domain adaptation and domain generalization tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ut-vision/FgSty-CPL.

Quantum process tomography is essential for constructing quantum computers, developing quantum networks, and analyzing quantum sensors. Similar to quantum state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel via process tomography typically demands a number of measurements that grows exponentially with the count of affected qubits. Nevertheless, the emerging field of shadow tomography, originally applied to quantum states, has shown the capacity to extract vital state information using only polynomially many measurements. In this study, we extend the principles of shadow state tomography to the problem of characterizing quantum processes. By leveraging the Choi isomorphism, we directly apply rigorous bounds established for shadow state tomography to the domain of shadow process tomography, while also deriving unique measurement bounds specific to processes. Our findings, which encompass algorithms for executing shadow process tomography, facilitate new methodologies such as assessing channel concatenation and applying channels to quantum state shadows. These advancements offer a significant enhancement for comprehending large-scale quantum systems.

The OpenFlexure Microscope is a low-cost, 3D-printed device that enables automated image capture via a motorized translation stage and a Raspberry Pi imaging setup. This automation supports research and healthcare applications, particularly in aiding malaria diagnosis within resource-limited environments. Since the Plasmodium parasites responsible for malaria require high magnification and exhibit a shallow depth of field, an accurate and precise autofocus mechanism is essential. This paper outlines techniques for determining the focal plane and establishes protocols for reliably acquiring focused image stacks on systems prone to backlash and drift. Additionally, we introduce and evaluate a method for verifying autofocus success during scanning. Each approach is assessed regarding its speed, reliability, and precision, with limitations discussed in the context of end-user needs.

We demonstrate the existence of an oblivious routing scheme that achieves $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$-competitiveness regarding the combined metric of $(congestion + dilation)$, thereby solving a longstanding open problem in oblivious routing. Specifically, in an undirected network where each packet has a designated source and destination, the goal is to assign a path to every packet such that the sum of dilation and congestion is minimized. Dilation is defined as the maximum number of hops in any path, while congestion is the maximum number of paths traversing any single edge. Our scheme randomly and obliviously selects a path for each packet without knowledge of other packets; despite this lack of coordination, the resulting paths yield a $(congestion + dilation)$ value within a $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ factor of the optimal. More precisely, for any integer hop-bound $h$, the scheme selects paths with lengths no greater than $h \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ and maintains $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$-competitiveness in terms of congestion compared to the best possible congestion achievable using paths limited to $h$ hops. These paths can be sampled in polynomial time. This achievement serves as an analogue to the celebrated oblivious routing results by R\"{a}cke [FOCS 2002, STOC 2008], which are $O(\log n)$-competitive in terms of congestion but fail to offer competitiveness regarding dilation.

Drawing inspiration from the side-by-side swimming and mid-swim synchronization shifts of red-nose tetra fish, this study utilized numerical simulations to investigate how abrupt phase angle changes affect the unsteady wake dynamics of two pitching foils. The analysis focused on a Reynolds number of 4,000 and a Strouhal number of 0.50. Four hybrid kinematic modes were evaluated: two involved an abrupt $\pi$ phase shift during the 20th cycle, while the other two simulated a burst-and-coast pattern featuring a brief (two oscillation periods) pause in oscillation prior to the phase change. In all scenarios, the foils transitioned from out-of-phase to in-phase pitching, initiating either with the upstroke or downstroke. This kinematic shift generated a secondary vortex street between the primary ones, sustaining a split wake configuration. Additionally, the phase switching equalized pressure levels on the upper and lower surfaces of both foils, thereby reducing side-force. Notably, the growth rate of the secondary vortex street remained constant across all four hybrid modes.

This study examines a generalization of a definite integral containing the Bessel function of the first kind, demonstrating that it can be represented using the Fox-Wright function ${}_p\Psi_q(z)$ with a single variable. By selecting specific parameters, we investigate the implications of this representation and derive two closed-form evaluations for infinite series involving the Fox-Wright function.

Stick-breaking priors are frequently utilized in Bayesian nonparametric mixture models to construct mixing weights, particularly when covariates affect cluster sizes, allowing these models to employ binary regression techniques to simplify posterior computation. Conventional stick-breaking priors generally operate by repeatedly breaking a single remaining segment of a unit stick. We show that this "single-piece" approach can lead to three highly problematic behaviors, which our proposed model resolves by continuously breaking off all remaining segments of the unit stick while maintaining nearly identical computational efficiency. Specifically, the new framework offers greater flexibility in defining prior correlations across covariates among the resulting random measures, reduces the complications of component label switching during Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation, and eliminates the artificial decay of posterior uncertainty regarding mixing weights based on their order of generation. Distinct from prior research on covariate-dependent mixtures that emphasizes estimating dependent distributions, our work concentrates on inferring the specific impact of individual covariates on mixture weights akin to classical regression, and introduces a novel class of posterior predictive checks for summarizing these covariate effects.

Deep learning has significantly transformed robotics, with deep reinforcement learning algorithms proving particularly effective at creating neural-network controllers for diverse tasks. Despite this empirical success, these controllers currently lack theoretical performance guarantees, such as Lyapunov stability, which ensures that all closed-loop system trajectories converge to a goal state under the policy. This stands in sharp contrast to traditional model-based design, where methods like LQR can generate stable controllers with provable guarantees. To bridge this gap, we introduce a general method for synthesizing a Lyapunov-stable neural-network controller alongside a neural-network Lyapunov function that jointly certifies its stability. We formulate the verification of the Lyapunov condition as a mixed-integer linear program (MIP). Our MIP-based verifier either confirms the Lyapunov condition or produces counter-examples to refine the candidate controller and Lyapunov function. Additionally, we present an optimization program to calculate an inner approximation of the closed-loop system's region of attraction. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on robots such as an inverted pendulum and both 2D and 3D quadrotors, showing that our neural-network controller surpasses a baseline LQR controller. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/StanfordASL/neural-network-lyapunov}.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become a dominant method for image synthesis, with StyleGAN standing out as a particularly compelling example due to its exceptional visual fidelity and versatility in downstream applications. This comprehensive report examines the StyleGAN architecture, its evolution since inception, and its significant constraints. It serves as a resource for both novices seeking foundational knowledge and experienced researchers interested in current trends and available tools. A key feature of StyleGAN is its learned latent space, which, despite being trained without supervision, exhibits remarkable disentanglement and stability. Coupled with its high-quality image generation, these attributes have enabled unprecedented editing capabilities. However, StyleGAN's control is restricted to its own generated distribution, limiting its direct application to real-world images. To address this, research into GAN inversion and latent space embedding has surged in popularity, offering insights into the model's internal mechanics and limitations. This analysis traces StyleGAN's development through these investigations, highlighting the factors that established it as the preferred generator. Additionally, we explore the visual priors constructed by StyleGAN and their utility in discriminative tasks. Finally, we outline the model's shortcomings and speculate on future research directions, including task-specific and target-specific fine-tuning.

As the number of frogs per site increases, the frog model on a rooted d-ary tree shifts from a transient to a recurrent state. We demonstrate that the threshold for this transition scales proportionally with the tree's degree.

This study investigates three-dimensional (3D) visible light positioning (VLP) utilizing smartphone cameras within indoor environments. Grounded in a quantized pixel-domain positioning model, we characterize the 3D normalized positioning error metric (NPEM) by analyzing the partial derivatives of the positioning function, specifically assessing NPEM for both horizontal and non-horizontal camera orientations. Furthermore, focusing on horizontal receiver terminals, we examine the correlation between NPEM and LED cell configurations, derive an approximation linking NPEM to the count of LEDs captured by the camera, and validate this approximation's accuracy using simulated positioning errors. Leveraging these findings, we optimize the LED transmitter cell layout to minimize NPEM, assuming structured square arrangements with defined distance parameters.

End-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) models strive to learn generalized speech representations; however, few tools exist to examine their internal mechanisms or the impact of hierarchical dependencies within their architectures. Understanding correlations between layer-wise representations is vital for gaining insights into the link between neural structures and performance. While prior correlation analyses have not been applied to End-to-End ASR models, this study investigates the internal dynamics across CNN, LSTM, and Transformer architectures during training using Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) and Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). Results indicate that CNN layers display hierarchical correlation dependencies that strengthen with depth, though this is primarily evident when representations are closely related. In contrast, LSTM architectures do not show this pattern but instead exhibit a bottom-up progression throughout training, whereas Transformer encoder layers demonstrate irregular correlation coefficients as depth increases. Collectively, these findings offer new perspectives on how neural architectures influence speech recognition performance and can serve as metrics for developing more effective models.

Recently, reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) have gained significant interest because their adjustable scattering elements can steer electromagnetic waves toward desired paths. While RISs and relays share certain traits, fundamental distinctions affect their performance. This paper introduces a multi-user communication framework where a relay and an RIS collaborate to enhance energy efficiency. By employing singular value decomposition (SVD), semidefinite programming (SDP), and function approximations, we develop various strategies to optimize beamforming matrices at the base station and relay, as well as RIS phase shifts, aiming to minimize total transmit power while satisfying quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. These solutions address scenarios involving half-duplex and full-duplex relaying, as well as continuous and discrete phase shifts. Simulation results compare system performance with and without the RIS or relay across both duplex modes under different optimization schemes. Generally, the configuration combining a full-duplex relay with an RIS yields superior performance, with the full-duplex relay contributing more significantly than the RIS. However, when high QoS is required, an RIS outperforms a half-duplex relay. Furthermore, simulations indicate that adding more RIS reflecting elements boosts performance more effectively when a relay is present compared to when it is absent.

This paper utilizes Joung's (2009) publication to establish a stability outcome for the second-order linear functional equation $f(x) = pf(x-1)-qf(x-2)$, valid for all $x\in\mathbb R$, where $f$ maps $\mathbb R$ into the induced random space of a Banach space. We extend Jung's (2009) findings to arbitrary random normed spaces equipped with the minimum $t$-norm by relaxing the lower bound assumption, though this requires the distribution to be monotonic. Leveraging the characteristics of normal distributions, our primary result becomes applicable.

This work extends the concept of divisibility from dynamical maps to quantum channels by examining channel simulability via these maps. Specifically, it addresses Lindblad, completely positive, and positive divisibility. Leveraging findings by Wolf et al. (2008), the paper characterizes and visualizes the corresponding L-divisible, CP-divisible, and P-divisible subsets of qubit channels. It analyzes general inclusions among these sets and demonstrates several equivalences specific to qubits. Additionally, conditions for L-divisibility in finite-dimensional channels are investigated, particularly regarding negative eigenvalues, thereby extending and completing previous results from Phys. Rev. Lett. (2008). The study confirms that transitions between any two defined divisibility sets are possible and explores specific dynamical map examples to compare these concepts. Finally, it establishes that every divisible but non-infinitesimally divisible qubit channel (under positive maps) is entanglement breaking, while raising the question of whether a similar phenomenon occurs in higher dimensions.

By employing a simple fully quantum model within an effective exciton framework that incorporates system-environment interactions, we investigate the various regimes present in a microcavity-quantum dot setup. Our numerical analysis of emission linewidth, energy, integrated intensity, and second- and third-order correlation functions demonstrates strong qualitative alignment with existing experimental data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the shift from a polariton-laser to a photon-laser regime can be characterized by the critical points of both the steady-state negativity and linear entropy.

Understanding the superconducting (SC) mechanism relies heavily on examining how the transition temperature ($T_{\rm c}$) varies with pressure. This study presents such an investigation for CaSb$_2$, a nonmagnetic topological line-nodal material, utilizing electric resistance and alternating current magnetic susceptibility measurements. The results show that $T_{\rm c}$ rises with pressure until reaching a maximum of approximately 3.1~GPa. Beyond this point, $T_{\rm c}$ declines and vanishes entirely by 5.9~GPa. Given the absence of normal-state phase or Lifshitz transitions, the unique peak in $T_{\rm c}$ indicates that CaSb$_2$ exhibits unconventional superconducting behavior.

Although emergent communication has advanced significantly, existing research has largely concentrated on protocols mimicking human language. In contrast, natural multi-agent cooperation generates a diverse array of communication structures and complexities. This study acknowledges the entire spectrum of natural communication by focusing on lower-level, emergent implicit signaling within decentralized multi-agent learning, specifically in challenging environments with sparse rewards. To address the difficulty of coordinating under these conditions, we introduce a curriculum-driven approach that integrates (i) velocity-based environment shaping adapted to the team's skill level, and (ii) a behavioral curriculum that teaches successful single-agent strategies before advancing to multi-agent behaviors. Experiments on pursuit-evasion tasks demonstrate that our method achieves superior coordination compared to both sophisticated analytical and learned baseline policies. Notably, our approach successfully completes the task even when pursuers move at half the evader's speed, whereas the best-performing baseline fails when pursuers reach 80% of that speed. Furthermore, we investigate implicit signaling through position-based social influence, revealing that pursuers trained with our strategy exchange more than twice the amount of information (measured in bits) compared to baseline methods, confirming that the system learns to rely heavily on implicit signal exchange.

Rapid population expansion and urbanization have made traffic congestion an unavoidable challenge, particularly in major metropolitan areas. While various strategies to alleviate congestion have been suggested historically—from expanding road networks to managing transportation demand—congestion pricing has notably served as a punitive measure for traffic control. This project investigates an alternative method that provides positive incentives to encourage drivers to select alternative routes. Specifically, we introduce an algorithm designed to enhance routing efficiency and reduce congestion by delivering personalized incentives to motorists. Leveraging the widespread availability of smart devices, we established a communication channel with drivers and created an incentive mechanism that accounts for individual preferences alongside aggregate traffic data. These incentives are determined after solving a large-scale optimization problem aimed at minimizing total travel time or other network cost functions, such as carbon emissions. Given the need to solve this massive optimization problem continuously across the network, we developed a distributed computational approach. Under mild assumptions verified with real-world data, this proposed distributed algorithm is guaranteed to converge. We assessed the algorithm's effectiveness using traffic data from the Los Angeles region, with experiments demonstrating a congestion reduction of up to 11% on arterial roads and highways.

We extend the nonnegativity result for Brown-York mass established by Y. Shi and L.-F. Tam \cite{ShiTam} by examining nonnegative scalar curvature (NNSC) fill-ins that are required only to be complete, rather than compact. Furthermore, these NNSC fill-ins do not need to be complete, provided that any incompleteness is "shielded" by a region possessing positive scalar curvature and is situated sufficiently distant. This achievement involves generalizing P.~Miao's~\cite{Miao02} positive mass theorem with corners to apply to asymptotically flat manifolds that may possess additional complete ends, or incomplete ends that are suitably shielded. We can likewise extend various other findings regarding the compact NNSC fill-in problem to accommodate complete (or shielded) NNSC fill-ins. Specifically, we demonstrate the following extension of a theorem by Miao~\cite{Miao20}: For any metric $\gamma$ defined on a closed manifold $\Sigma^{n-1}$, there exists a constant $\lambda$ such that for every complete (or shielded) NNSC fill-in $(\Omega^n, g)$ of $(\Sigma^{n-1},\gamma)$, the inequality $\min_\Sigma H \le \lambda$ holds, where $H$ represents the mean curvature of $\Sigma$ relative to $g$.

We present Bayesian Bits, a practical approach for jointly optimizing mixed-precision quantization and pruning using gradient-based methods. This technique utilizes a unique decomposition of the quantization process that iteratively doubles the bit width. At each stage, the difference between the full-precision value and the previously rounded approximation is quantized; we then determine whether to include this quantized residual to achieve a higher effective bit width and reduced noise. By initiating with a power-of-two bit width, this method inherently generates hardware-compatible configurations, while an added 0-bit option unifies pruning and quantization under a single framework. Furthermore, Bayesian Bits incorporates learnable stochastic gates that regulate the bit width of individual tensors. Consequently, approximate inference over these gates, guided by priors that favor deactivation, yields low-bit solutions. Experimental results across various benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method successfully learns pruned, mixed-precision networks that outperform static bit-width counterparts in balancing accuracy and efficiency.

In safety-critical domains, practitioners often hesitate to rely on neural networks lacking interpretable justifications. While existing methods typically focus on pixel-level attributions or established concepts, this paper introduces a novel approach to uncover provably identified, high-level, previously unknown ground-truth concepts. We present CLAP (Concept Learning and Prediction), a VAE-based classifier that leverages visually interpretable concepts as predictors for a downstream classifier. Under the assumption of a generative model for these true concepts, we demonstrate that CLAP can successfully identify them while achieving optimal classification performance. Experiments on synthetic data confirm the method's ability to detect distinct ground-truth concepts, and tests on the medical Chest X-Ray dataset show promising results.

Magnetic cataclysmic variables (CVs) are bright Galactic X-ray sources that have historically been elusive in optical surveys because they typically do not exhibit outbursts. The eROSITA telescope, part of the Spektr-RG (SRG) mission, is currently performing an all-sky X-ray survey and has recently made the eROSITA Final Equatorial Depth Survey (eFEDS) catalog available to the public. By cross-referencing this catalog with photometric data from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), we identified two new magnetic CVs. High-cadence optical photometry and phase-resolved spectroscopy were conducted for both candidates, confirming them as polars. One discovery, ZTFJ0850+0443, is an eclipsing polar with an orbital period of $P_\textrm{orb} = 1.72$ hours, a white dwarf mass of $M_\textrm{WD} = 0.81 \pm 0.08 M_\odot$, and an accretion rate of $\dot{M} \sim 10^{-11} M_\odot$/yr; we propose it is a polar with a relatively low magnetic field strength, where $B_\textrm{WD} \lesssim 10$ MG. Additionally, we found a non-eclipsing polar, ZTFJ0926+0105, characterized by an orbital period of $P_\textrm{orb} = 1.48$ hours, a strong magnetic field of $B_\textrm{WD} \gtrsim 26$ MG, and an accretion rate of $\dot{M} \sim 10^{-12} M_\odot$/yr.

We introduce a tight-binding model analysis of a two-terminal graphene nanopore system designed for the sequential identification of DNA bases. Employing Green's function methodology, we examine how the insertion of various nucleotides into a nanopore within a zigzag graphene nanoribbon alters the device's electronic transport characteristics. Our approach first establishes the device's static behavior before advancing to sequencing applications by applying a specific bias voltage and capturing the resulting current signatures for each translocating nucleotide. These findings suggest that graphene nanopores hold significant potential as highly efficient and dependable tools for future sequencing technologies.

Tunable two-qubit couplers provide a pathway to reduce errors in multi-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Nevertheless, the majority of existing couplers function within a restricted frequency range and are designed for particular interactions, such as the unwanted $ZZ$ coupling. We present a superconducting coupler that overcomes these constraints by eliminating all two-qubit interactions with an exponentially high on-off ratio, all without requiring precise fine-tuning. This method relies on a bus mode augmented by an ancillary nonlinear resonator mode. By driving the ancillary mode, we induce a field displacement in the resonator that depends on the coupler state, which subsequently causes an exponential reduction of both real and virtual two-qubit interactions relative to the drive power. Furthermore, we demonstrate a superconducting circuit realization that supports this proposed mechanism.

Although one-sided t-tests are frequently employed in neuroimaging, two-sided tests ought to be the standard approach unless there is a compelling justification for a one-sided alternative. This study expands on our prior investigation into cluster false positive rates—which originally utilized one-sided tests—by applying the analysis to two-sided tests. Our findings indicate that parametric methods exhibit inferior performance with two-sided t-tests, whereas non-parametric methods maintain equivalent efficacy regardless of whether one-sided or two-sided tests are used.

With the growing prevalence of large-scale graphs, processing, extracting, and analyzing this data presents substantial computational hurdles. Graph coarsening is a widely adopted technique to shrink graph size while retaining key characteristics. Although the literature on graph coarsening is extensive, data-driven approaches remain underexplored. This study harnesses recent advances in graph deep learning to address coarsening. We introduce a framework for evaluating coarsening quality, demonstrating that the choice of Laplace operator, along with associated projection and lift operators, on the coarse graph must be carefully aligned with specific objectives. Noting that existing edge weight assignments for coarse graphs are often sub-optimal, we parametrize the weight assignment map using graph neural networks and train it unsupervised to enhance coarsening quality. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world networks reveal that our method significantly outperforms standard coarsening techniques across various metrics, reduction ratios, graph sizes, and types. Furthermore, the approach generalizes to graphs up to 25 times larger than those used for training, adapts to both differentiable and non-differentiable loss functions, and scales to much larger graphs than prior work.

The integration of self-supervised pre-training models like HuBERT and wav2vec 2.0 has substantially advanced automatic speech recognition (ASR). Nevertheless, achieving top-tier performance with these architectures often entails high computational costs, which hampers inference speed. To enhance efficiency, we introduce HuBERT-EE, an early exit strategy for ASR that enables dynamic termination of inference. This approach incorporates multiple early exit branches at intermediate layers, each evaluating whether an early prediction is feasible. Experiments on the LibriSpeech dataset demonstrate that HuBERT-EE accelerates the inference of large-scale HuBERT models while effectively balancing the trade-off between word error rate (WER) and latency.

**Objective:** This study experimentally examined whether FLASH irradiation depletes oxygen in water across various radiation modalities, including photons, protons, and carbon ions.

**Methods:** Oxygen consumption was measured in sealed, 3D-printed water phantoms during exposure to X-rays, protons, and carbon ions at dose rates ranging up to 340 Gy/s. Non-invasive optical sensors were utilized to monitor these changes.

**Results:** Oxygen depletion in water was determined to be a function of the administered dose, dose rate, and linear energy transfer (LET). Specifically, oxygen levels dropped by 0.04–0.18 % atm per 10 Gy for 225 kV photons, 0.04–0.25 % atm for 224 MeV protons, and 0.09–0.17 % atm for carbon ions. Consumption followed an inverse power law relative to dose rate, saturating at higher rates due to radical self-interactions; consequently, higher dose rates resulted in reduced oxygen consumption. However, total oxygen depletion was not observed for clinical doses.

**Conclusions:** While FLASH irradiation does consume oxygen, it is insufficient to exhaust all available oxygen. Higher dose rates led to lower oxygen consumption compared to standard radiotherapy rates. Furthermore, complete oxygen depletion was not achieved for any radiation type analyzed when delivering a 10 Gy dose via FLASH.

The well-known yet somewhat esoteric Mach principle proposes a purely relational framework for physical theories, eliminating any reliance on the concept of "absolute space." When applied to classical mechanics through an extended symmetry group, this approach yields equations of motion featuring inertial-like forces generated by the system's own mass distribution. This paper adopts a similar strategy to reformulate the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation in a fully Machian manner. Consistent with its classical analogue, the resulting quantum theory relies entirely on the relational positions and momenta of the constituent bodies, thereby excluding the notion of absolute space.

Recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in creating realistic images; however, they frequently fail to capture complex underlying modalities within datasets, leading to subpar image quality. To address this limitation, we introduce Mixture of Experts GAN (MEGAN), a novel ensemble framework utilizing multiple generator networks. In MEGAN, each generator specializes in producing images from a specific subset of modalities, such as a particular image class. Unlike methods requiring manual clustering of modalities, our model employs end-to-end training where gating networks automatically select the appropriate generator for a given condition. We utilize the categorical reparameterization trick to facilitate this generator selection while preserving gradient flow. Our results show that individual generators successfully learn distinct and significant subparts of the data, achieving a Multiscale Structural Similarity (MS-SSIM) score of 0.2470 on CelebA and a competitive unsupervised Inception Score of 8.33 on CIFAR-10.

This study employs progressive growth-based Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to create the Clarkson Fingerprint Generator (CFG). We show that the CFG successfully produces realistic, high-fidelity, full, plain impression fingerprints at a resolution of $512\times512$ pixels. Our findings indicate that the CFG-generated fingerprints are unique and diverse, mirroring the training dataset's minutiae configuration and quality without exposing the identities of the original data. Additionally, we have made the pre-trained CFG model and the synthetic dataset publicly accessible at https://github.com/keivanB/Clarkson_Finger_Gen.

The cosmographic approach, utilizing a Taylor expansion of the Hubble function, serves as a model-independent technique for studying cosmic evolution against observational data. However, beyond potential technical constraints such as the radius of convergence, significant debates persist regarding tensions that arise when analyzing high-redshift cosmological data. This study evaluates the strengths and limitations of the cosmographic method by applying it to two standard datasets: the Pantheon sample of Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) and Hubble constant data. To facilitate this comparison, we derive the evolution of cosmographic parameters using the cosmographic method alongside two other established model-independent techniques: Gaussian processes and genetic algorithms. Furthermore, we adopt the $\Lambda$CDM model as the concordance benchmark to contrast these results. Our findings suggest that cosmography yields less precise outcomes compared to the alternative methods. Specifically, when examining the less certain Hubble data, the cosmographically derived parameters $q_0$ and $j_0$ exhibit a tension exceeding $3\sigma$ relative to the optimal $\Lambda$CDM predictions. By integrating both datasets across the different methodologies, we conclude that the cosmographic approach is suboptimal for reconstructing cosmographic functions, particularly at higher redshifts, due to its tendency to produce biased results.

Online Transient Stability Assessment (TSA) is critical for ensuring the security and stability of power systems. The proliferation of Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) generates vast amounts of data that can significantly improve online TSA. Nevertheless, traditional data-driven approaches demand extensive transient datasets to accurately evaluate system stability. This paper introduces a novel data-driven TSA methodology capable of performing assessments with fewer data points than conventional techniques. By employing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to learn dynamic patterns from historical transient data, the method facilitates data reduction. These learned insights are utilized online to forecast voltage time series following a transient event. Furthermore, a classifier integrated within the generative network utilizes the predicted post-contingency data to determine system stability after a fault. The proposed GAN-based approach maintains the spatial and temporal correlations inherent in multivariate PMU time series. Consequently, compared to state-of-the-art TSA methods, it achieves superior assessment accuracy using just a single data sample and offers a faster response time. Case studies on the IEEE 118-bus system confirm the method's enhanced performance relative to traditional data-driven techniques.

We investigate problems involving a central planner tasked with choosing a subset of agents, each characterized by distinct quality levels and costs. The objective is to maximize utility while maintaining an average quality above a specified threshold. In scenarios where agent qualities are known, we model the issue as an Integer Linear Program (ILP) and introduce the deterministic \dpss algorithm, which yields an exact solution. Conversely, when qualities are unknown, we frame the challenge as a Multi-Arm Bandit (MAB) problem and propose \newalgo\ to learn these qualities across multiple rounds. We demonstrate that after a specific number of rounds, $\tau$, \newalgo\ selects a subset satisfying the average quality constraint with high probability. Furthermore, we establish bounds for $\tau$ and prove that the algorithm achieves a regret of $O(\ln T)$ after $\tau$ rounds, where $T$ represents the total number of rounds, with efficacy validated through simulations. Finally, to address the computational constraints of \dpss, we develop a polynomial-time greedy approach, \greedy, offering an approximate solution to the ILP, and we evaluate the comparative performance of both \dpss\ and \greedy\ via experiments.

This research addresses the challenge of inferring 3D human poses for multiple individuals across several calibrated camera perspectives. Adhering to a top-down framework, the problem is split into two phases: person localization and pose estimation, both executed using coarse-to-fine strategies. To facilitate efficient message passing, we introduce three specialized graph neural networks. For 3D localization, the Multi-view Matching Graph Module (MMG) establishes cross-view associations to generate initial human proposals, which are then refined by the Center Refinement Graph Module (CRG) through flexible point-based prediction. In the pose estimation phase, the Pose Regression Graph Module (PRG) captures both multi-view geometric constraints and the structural relationships among body joints. Our method attains state-of-the-art results on the CMU Panoptic and Shelf datasets while maintaining significantly reduced computational complexity.

Individuals express their intent and stance via the linguistic style of their writing. This research examines word usage across different styles through two perspectives: human perception and machine-assessed word significance, acknowledging that words vary in the strength of their stylistic signals. To gather human perception labels, we developed a new dataset called Hummingbird, building upon existing style benchmarks. Crowd workers were tasked with identifying key words that signal specific styles, including politeness, sentiment, offensiveness, and five distinct emotion categories. We subsequently compared these human-selected words with importance scores derived from a widely used fine-tuned style classifier, such as BERT. Our findings indicate that BERT frequently prioritizes content words unrelated to the target style for prediction, whereas humans do not perceive them as significant in the same way. However, there is notable overlap between human and machine-identified words for certain styles, such as positive sentiment and joy.

This research addresses low-energy collision avoidance and formation maintenance within autonomous drone swarms. It tackles two primary challenges: 1) preventing collisions by temporarily disrupting the formation, known as collision-avoidance reformation, and 2) optimizing this reformation process to minimize deviation, thereby reducing total time and energy consumption. To solve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based approach identifies an efficient obstacle-avoiding formation that minimizes time and energy costs. For the second challenge, a temperature function reduction technique, originally developed for point set registration, is applied to achieve near-optimal swarm reformation following successful collision avoidance. The objective of this reformation is to eliminate disturbance while minimizing the time to reach the destination and the associated energy usage. The level of formation disturbance is quantified by measuring the deviation of the swarm's centroid, drawing inspiration from the center of mass concept in classical mechanics. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the proposed technique's efficiency regarding both performance and energy consumption.

Conversational interfaces are gaining significant traction, with an increasing number of applications adopting chat-like interactions to enhance user experience and boost acceptability. Similarly, in the realm of questionnaire design and administration, interaction design is becoming a crucial component of digital solutions. Consequently, we created and built a conversational survey tool that delivers questionnaires through a colloquial, chat-based web interface. This paper details the evaluation of our approach, examining it from both the user perspective—specifically regarding acceptance and preferences for the survey compilation experience—and the survey design perspective, which compares the effectiveness of conversational surveys against traditional ones. Our findings indicate that users distinctly favor the conversational format over traditional methods and that, in terms of data collection, the conversational approach demonstrates equal reliability while yielding higher response quality.

We report on deep X-ray and radio monitoring of the Fast Blue Optical Transient (FBOT) AT2020xnd/ZTF20acigmel at a redshift of $z=0.2433$, conducted between 13 and 269 days post-explosion. This optically bright FBOT shares characteristics with the prototype event AT2018cow. Its radio emission was highly luminous, peaking at $L_{\nu}\approx8\times10^{29}$ergs$^{-1}$Hz$^{-1}$ at 20 GHz around 75 days after the explosion, while it exhibited bright, rapidly declining soft X-rays with a peak luminosity of $L_{X}\approx6\times10^{42}$ergs$^{-1}$. Modeling the radio data as synchrotron radiation from the shock interacting with the environment suggests AT2020xnd ejected a high-speed outflow ($v\sim$0.1-0.2$c$) into a dense circumstellar medium, characterized by a mass-loss rate of $\approx10^{-3}M_{\rm{sol}}$yr$^{-1}$ assuming a wind speed of 1000 km/s. Consistent with AT2018cow, the observed X-rays exceed the extrapolated synchrotron spectrum, indicating a distinct emission component likely driven by accretion onto a newly formed compact object such as a black hole or neutron star. These findings identify AT2020xnd as a high-redshift counterpart to AT2018cow and confirm it as the fourth known optically luminous FBOT possessing luminous multi-wavelength signatures.

We provide an example of a complete Riemannian plane containing exactly two injective geodesics, considered up to reparameterization. This example is derived from perturbing a surface of revolution that features a contracting end. The final section addresses open problems.

This paper introduces Slurk, a lightweight interaction server designed for configuring dialog datasets and conducting experiments. It supports diverse interaction modes, including text, speech, and video exchanges between multiple humans or humans and bots, alongside a multimodal display area for sharing or isolating interactive context. Built with Python and an adaptable HTML/JS frontend, the software allows for easy customization to specific requirements. Additionally, it facilitates participant pairing on crowdworking platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk and includes example bot scripts for typical interaction scenarios.

This work investigates the spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix $S$ for connected chain graphs. We demonstrate that $-1$ is invariably an eigenvalue of $S$, with all remaining eigenvalues having a multiplicity of no more than two. Furthermore, we determine the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, establish the minimum count of distinct eigenvalues, derive eigenvalue bounds, formulate the characteristic polynomial, and calculate both lower and upper bounds for the Seidel energy of these graphs. Our results indicate that the derived energy bounds surpass those conjectured by Haemers. Additionally, we compute the minimal Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$ and present several open problems.

This study investigates modern robust classification techniques designed to mitigate class-dependent label noise, specifically examining Forward, Importance Re-weighting, and T-revision methods. Models are trained on datasets corrupted by class-conditional random label noise but evaluated on clean test data. We introduce strategies for estimating the transition matrix to enhance classifier performance under noisy conditions. Furthermore, we apply deep learning approaches to three distinct datasets, conducting a novel end-to-end analysis on the CIFAR dataset with unknown noise levels. Finally, we assess the effectiveness and robustness of these classifiers by comparing their top-1 accuracy across all experiments.

This study explores the relationship between neutrino mass origins and dark matter candidate characteristics within gauge extensions of the Standard Model. We examine minimal gauge frameworks for neutrino masses, predicting that neutrinos exist as either Dirac or Majorana fermions. Our analysis reveals that limits on the effective number of relativistic species impose significant constraints on scenarios involving Dirac neutrinos. Furthermore, in models where lepton number acts as a local gauge symmetry spontaneously broken at a low energy scale, anomaly cancellation necessitates the existence of dark matter. By applying cosmological constraints on dark matter relic density, we determine an upper limit for the symmetry breaking scale, placing it in the multi-TeV range. These findings suggest that simple gauge theories for neutrino masses are testable using current or upcoming experimental facilities.

This paper introduces a federated deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework designed to address a multi-objective optimization challenge for IoT devices, specifically aiming to reduce both expected long-term task completion delays and energy usage. The approach optimizes transmit power, computation resource allocation, and offloading decisions. Given that the problem constitutes a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) issue, we formulate it as a multi-agent distributed DRL task and solve it using a double deep Q-network (DDQN), with offloading decisions serving as the actions. The immediate cost for each agent is derived by solving either the local computation or transmit power optimization sub-problem, contingent upon the chosen offloading action. To accelerate the learning process for IoT devices (agents), we integrate federated learning (FDL) at the conclusion of each episode. This integration boosts the scalability of the DRL framework, fosters agent cooperation, and mitigates privacy risks. Numerical results validate the proposed federated DDQN framework's superior learning speed compared to non-federated DDQN and federated DQN algorithms. Furthermore, we examine how batch size, network layers, and the frequency of DDQN target network updates influence the learning efficiency of the FDL system.

Contemporary spin-based technologies frequently utilize the spin-orbit interaction, a phenomenon that exhibits significant variation based on the host semiconductor heterostructure, crystal orientation, and asymmetries arising from both crystal structure (Dresselhaus) and quantum confinement (Rashba). One-dimensional quantum point contacts serve as an effective instrument for examining the energy and directional dependencies of this interaction via their influence on the hole $g$-factor. This study examines how cubic crystal asymmetry induces oscillations in the in-plane hole $g$-factor anisotropy as the quantum point contact is rotated relative to the crystal axes, successfully isolating contributions from Rashba and cubic crystal asymmetry spin-orbit interactions within the Zeeman Hamiltonian. We observe that the in-plane $g$-factor is remarkably orientation-dependent, shifting by a factor of five upon a $45^{\circ}$ rotation. Such pronounced crystal lattice anisotropy in in-plane Zeeman splitting defies explanation by axially symmetric theoretical models. Conversely, theoretical modeling utilizing the combined Luttinger, Rashba, and Dresselhaus Hamiltonians uncovers novel spin-orbit contributions to the in-plane hole $g$-factor and demonstrates strong consistency with the experimental findings.

The rise of multi-agent applications, including federated learning, networked sensing, IoT, and autonomous systems, necessitates decentralized algorithms for finite-sum optimization that are efficient in both computation and communication. This paper addresses a scenario where agents collaborate to minimize the sum of local loss functions by exchanging information only with their neighbors within a fixed network topology. We introduce DESTRESS (DEcentralized STochastic REcurSive gradient methodS), a novel algorithm designed for nonconvex finite-sum optimization. DESTRESS achieves the optimal incremental first-order oracle (IFO) complexity for locating first-order stationary points comparable to centralized algorithms, all while preserving communication efficiency. Both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments confirm that DESTRESS surpasses previous decentralized methods in resource efficiency across diverse parameter settings. Key innovations driving these improvements include randomly activated stochastic recursive gradient updates using mini-batches for local processing, gradient tracking enhanced with extra mixing (multiple gossip rounds) for communication, and strategic hyper-parameter selection supported by new analytical frameworks to ensure an optimal computation-communication balance.

Although most deep learning set prediction models employ set-equivariant operations, they functionally process multisets. We demonstrate that set-equivariant functions fail to represent specific multiset functions, necessitating the introduction of multiset-equivariance. We establish that the existing Deep Set Prediction Network (DSPN) can be adapted to satisfy multiset-equivariance without the constraints of set-equivariance. By enhancing it with approximate implicit differentiation, we enable faster optimization with reduced memory usage. Our toy experiments confirm the advantages of the multiset-equivariance perspective, showing that our DSPN modifications yield superior results in most scenarios. Furthermore, on the CLEVR object property prediction task, we significantly outperform the state-of-the-art Slot Attention method, improving results from 8% to 77% on one of the most stringent evaluation metrics, thanks to the benefits provided by implicit differentiation.

This paper establishes the homological domination principle for random multi-parameter simplicial complexes, asserting that the Betti number in a specific dimension—explicitly defined by the probability parameters—overwhelmingly surpasses Betti numbers in all other dimensions. Furthermore, we present and analyze evidence supporting two intriguing conjectures that would suggest a stronger form of this principle: namely, that the homology of a random simplicial complex generically matches that of a wedge of $k$-dimensional spheres. These conjectures imply that, under an additional condition outlined in the paper, a random simplicial complex collapses to a $k$-dimensional complex that is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of $k$-dimensional spheres.

We offer a straightforward approach for identifying Bailey--Borwein--Plouffe formulas, complete with a dedicated algorithm and an implementation in \texttt{sage}. While the method has rediscovered several existing formulas, it was instrumental in uncovering a new BBP-type formula for $\sqrt{3}\pi$. Furthermore, the implementation is highly flexible, enabling the search for BBP-type formulas with integer coefficients in irrational bases. For instance, by exploring various Pisot bases, we discovered a formula for $\pi$ in base $1 + \sqrt{3}$, as well as several others.

This report examines the primary theories regarding baryon and lepton number violation within physics extending beyond the Standard Model. We outline theoretical forecasts for rare phenomena, including neutrinoless double beta decay, proton decay, and neutron-antineutron oscillation, while surveying the prospects for their discovery in the near term. The report details the potential to detect baryon and lepton violating signals at existing and future colliders, through precision studies of other rare processes, and by testing various baryogenesis mechanisms. A robust and diverse experimental program targeting proton decay, neutrinoless double beta decay, and neutron-antineutron oscillation is vital for advancing this field. These investigations are conducted at numerous facilities domestically and internationally, utilizing instrumentation that spans traditional High Energy Physics/Nuclear Physics boundaries. Furthermore, experiments like those at the Large Hadron Collider may reveal exotic signatures of baryon and/or lepton number violation linked to low-scale neutrino mass theories, supersymmetric models with R-parity violation, new gauge theories, or other mechanisms for beyond-Standard Model physics. The landscape outlined in this report could be pivotal in uncovering the fundamental origin of neutrino masses and the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Personalized federated learning aims to develop machine learning models for diverse clients, each possessing unique data distributions. The objective involves collaboratively training personalized models that address inter-client data disparities and minimize communication expenses. We introduce a novel solution leveraging hypernetworks, designated as pFedHN (personalized Federated HyperNetworks).
