When the system interfaces with zero-temperature baths at both ends, this results in a subdiffusive conductance scaling with system size (exponent $2$) provided the bath chemical potentials align with the band edges. Furthermore, tuning the chemical potential across any band edge reveals a dissipative quantum phase transition, a phenomenon strikingly similar to the transition across a mobility edge in quasi-periodic systems. This behavior is universal, independent of the specific periodic potential details or the number of lattice bands, yet it does not occur in the absence of the baths.

A pivotal discovery in particle physics is the confirmation of nonzero neutrino masses, indicating that the Standard Model (SM) is incomplete. Additionally, recent evidence of lepton flavor universality violation (LFUV) suggests the existence of physics beyond the SM. Scalar leptoquarks at the TeV scale are currently the primary candidates for addressing flavor anomalies in semileptonic charged and neutral current B-decays, as well as anomalies in the muon and electron magnetic dipole moments, which may also contribute to neutrino mass generation. This study posits that neutrino masses and LFUV share a common origin in new physics, proposing a novel two-loop neutrino mass model capable of resolving certain flavor anomalies through leptoquarks while offering extensive phenomenological possibilities. Following the derivation of the neutrino mass formula for this model, we conduct a comprehensive numerical analysis focused on neutrino and charged lepton flavor violation, with the latter imposing strict constraints on Yukawa couplings and leptoquark masses. Finally, we examine current and future limits on the model's parameter space using representative benchmark scenarios.

The visual dialog task aims to train an agent to respond to multi-turn questions based on an image, necessitating a deep comprehension of the interplay between the visual content and the conversation history. While current research often relies on modality-specific modules to model these interactions, such approaches can be cumbersome. To address this limitation, we introduce VU-BERT, a unified framework for joint image-text embedding, which utilizes patch projection to generate vision embeddings early in the visual dialog pipeline, thereby streamlining the model architecture. The system is trained on two objectives: masked language modeling and next utterance retrieval. These tasks facilitate the learning of visual concepts, dependencies between utterances, and the relationships linking the two modalities. Ultimately, our VU-BERT achieves competitive performance, attaining an NDCG score of 0.7287 on the VisDial v1.0 dataset.

This study investigates a standard extension of k-medoids and k-median clustering applied to a two-dimensional Pareto front produced by bi-objective optimization methods. The paper provides a characterization of optimal clusters, enabling the solution of these optimization problems to optimality in polynomial time via a shared dynamic programming approach. Specifically, when clustering $N$ points into $K$ subsets, the algorithm achieves $O(N^3)$ time complexity and $O(K \cdot N)$ memory usage for $K \geqslant 3$, while requiring $O(N^2)$ time for the $K=2$ case. Additionally, the dynamic programming process can be accelerated by eliminating redundant computations, offering practical speed improvements without altering the theoretical complexity. The discussion also addresses parallelization strategies to enhance practical execution speed.

Marking the 450th anniversary of its discovery, Tycho Brahe's supernova (SN 1572) can now be understood using modern classifications for Type Ia supernovae. By compiling observation records from 1572–1574 and assessing their uncertainties, researchers have reconstructed the event's light curve and color evolution. These findings indicate that, among Type Ia supernovae, this event exhibited a standard rate of decline. Furthermore, the recovered data on color evolution confirms previous conclusions that SN 1572 was a normal Type Ia supernova. Since 2004, searches for its progenitor have tentatively pointed toward a single-degenerate binary system as the explosion mechanism, though this remains unconfirmed. Meanwhile, X-ray spectroscopy analyses of the entire remnant suggest the explosion resulted from a delayed detonation of a Chandrasekhar-mass white dwarf. As the first supernova ever studied by astronomers, SN 1572 continues to be a focus of active research.

This study addresses the difficult challenge of simultaneously tracking hand object poses and reconstructing their shapes from depth point cloud sequences in uncontrolled environments, provided with initial poses at frame zero. For the first time, we introduce HandTrackNet, a point cloud-based network designed to estimate inter-frame hand joint motion. HandTrackNet incorporates a novel hand pose canonicalization module to simplify the tracking process, resulting in accurate and robust joint estimation. Subsequently, the system reconstructs the complete hand by mapping predicted joints to a template-based parametric model, MANO. For object tracking, we develop a straightforward yet effective module that derives the object Signed Distance Field (SDF) from the initial frame and utilizes optimization-based tracking. Furthermore, a joint optimization step is employed to reason about both the hand and object simultaneously, mitigating ambiguity caused by occlusion and further refining the hand pose. During training, the entire pipeline relies exclusively on synthetic data generated with diverse variations and depth simulations to facilitate generalization. The method is designed to bridge generalization gaps, enabling direct transfer to real-world in-the-wild data without finetuning. Evaluations on two real-world hand-object interaction datasets, HO3D and DexYCB, demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses previous state-of-the-art depth-based methods for hand and object pose estimation and tracking, achieving a frame rate of 9 FPS.

Singular boundary value problems (SBVPs) appear across diverse domains in mathematics, engineering, and physics, including boundary layer theory, gas dynamics, nuclear physics, and nonlinear optics. This monograph focuses on systems of SBVPs involving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), presenting existence theories for problems characterized by unbounded nonlinearities within the regions of interest. The primary objective is to demonstrate the existence of positive solutions, utilizing methods grounded in regularization and sequential procedures. The initial chapter outlines the motivation behind studying SBVPs and reviews relevant findings from functional analysis and fixed point theory. Subsequent chapters draw upon results from the author's PhD thesis at the National University of Sciences and Technology in Islamabad, Pakistan. These findings establish the existence of positive solutions for various systems of SBVPs that exhibit singularities with respect to the independent and/or dependent variables, as well as the first derivatives of the dependent variables.

We examine the conditions required for an isolated quantum system to reach a microcanonical equilibrium state. A central element is the eigenstate thermalisation hypothesis, which asserts that every energy eigenstate exhibits thermal properties. We propose a less stringent variant of this condition, restricting it to the average distinguishability between eigenstates and the thermal state, and then assess whether this criterion is both necessary and sufficient for thermalisation.

Could we exist within a computer simulation? I will outline an argument demonstrating that the outcome of a specific experiment provides empirical proof that we do not inhabit at least one particular type of simulation. While the simulation this reasoning excludes is quite narrow, this limitation may simply be the necessary trade-off to achieve any form of Popperian scientific advancement.

Utilizing Reinforcement Learning (RL) after Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pre-training is a flexible approach for boosting Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Nevertheless, recent studies suggest that RL's benefits in NMT largely stem from reinforcing tokens that were already highly probable during pre-training. We propose that the extensive action space is a primary barrier to RL's efficacy in machine translation and validate this hypothesis through two experimental series. First, we observe that shrinking the vocabulary size enhances RL performance. Second, we demonstrate that effectively lowering the action space dimensionality without altering the vocabulary also leads to significant gains, as measured by BLEU scores, semantic similarity, and human assessment. Specifically, initializing the network's final fully connected layer—which maps internal dimensions to the vocabulary—with a layer designed to generalize across similar actions results in a substantial performance boost, averaging 1.5 BLEU points.

Let $\psi$ be a continuous, decreasing function defined for all sufficiently large positive real numbers. A real $m \times n$ matrix $A$ is termed $\psi$-Dirichlet if, for every large enough real $t$, there exist vectors $\boldsymbol{p} \in \mathbb{Z}^m$ and $\boldsymbol{q} \in \mathbb{Z}^n \smallsetminus \{\boldsymbol{0}\}$ such that $\|A\boldsymbol{q}-\boldsymbol{p}\|^m < \psi(t)$ and $\|\boldsymbol{q}\|^n < t$. This concept, introduced by Kleinbock and Wadleigh in 2018, extends the notion of Dirichlet improvability originally established by Davenport and Schmidt in 1969. In this paper, we establish sufficient conditions on $\psi$ that guarantee the set of $\psi$-Dirichlet matrices possesses either zero or full Lebesgue measure. Our approach is dynamical, utilizing the effective equidistribution and doubly mixing properties of specific expanding horospheres within the space of lattices. Additionally, our proof incorporates an asymptotic measure estimate for compact neighborhoods of the critical locus (under the supremum norm) in the space of lattices. Furthermore, our methodology applies to the corresponding weighted problem, where the relevant supremum norms are substituted with specific weighted quasi-norms.

Current cosmic ray research primarily examines the most energetic particles entering the atmosphere to generate single Extensive Air Showers (EAS). However, certain models suggest that high-energy particle interactions can produce Cosmic-Ray Ensembles (CRE) far from Earth, potentially observable as multiple correlated air showers of relatively low energy spread across vast regions. The Cosmic Ray Extremely Distributed Observatory (CREDO) aims to detect these CREs by utilizing data from all available detectors and observatories, including numerous small-scale instruments distributed over large areas. Interpreting these measurements necessitates precise knowledge of EAS properties across a broad energy spectrum. Low-energy EAS are analyzed using events from CORSIKA, a simulation program for air showers, covering a primary cosmic ray energy range from 1 TeV to 4000 TeV. The study focuses on secondary particles at ground level to determine density fluctuations and spatial correlations. While observed multiplicity distribution fluctuations align with random expectations, a detailed analysis indicates that the density of particles near a specific one is higher than would be expected without correlations. These findings could prove valuable for future calculations, such as estimating the probability of EAS detection without requiring specialized simulations.

We introduce general expressions for the oblique-correction parameters $S$, $T$, $U$, $V$, $W$, and $X$ within an extended Standard Model framework. This framework accommodates any number of singlet, doublet, and triplet quarks carrying electric charges of $-4/3$, $-1/3$, $2/3$, and $5/3$, which are allowed to mix with standard quarks of identical charge.

Building on a recent study by Lucas and Das Sarma regarding solvable models of collective modes in 2D metals within the hydrodynamic regime, this work extends hydrodynamic theory to 3D metals, enabling an explicit calculation of sound modes in a strongly-coupled quantum Coulomb plasma. The central inquiry addresses the relationship between the standard linearly dispersing hydrodynamic sound mode and the established gapped 3D plasmon mode under long-range Coulomb interactions. We demonstrate analytically that in three dimensions, both the collisionless zero sound and the hydrodynamic first sound acquire a finite mass gap due to these long-range interactions, with their damping rates scaling quadratically with momentum. Additionally, we examine other long-range potentials and their corresponding effects on sound mode dispersion. Our general findings indicate that the leading-order hydrodynamic sound mode corresponds to the leading-order plasmon frequency in the presence of long-range Coulomb interaction, although the next-to-leading-order dispersion corrections differ between the hydrodynamic and collisionless regimes.

Driven by the rapidly expanding volume of image-text pairs and the increasing variety of Vision-and-Language (V&L) tasks, researchers have developed a vast array of deep learning models within this field. Recently, transfer learning has demonstrated remarkable success in Computer Vision (e.g., Image Classification, Object Detection) and Natural Language Processing (e.g., Question Answering, Machine Translation). Embracing this paradigm, V&L research has adopted multiple pretraining strategies on large-scale datasets to improve downstream task performance. This article aims to offer a comprehensive review of current V&L pretraining models. Specifically, we classify and detail various pretraining methods, summarize state-of-the-art vision-and-language pretrained models, and provide a curated list of training datasets and downstream tasks to deepen the understanding of V&L pretraining. Finally, we explore several promising directions for future research.

We demonstrate that the bounded cohomology of lamplighter groups vanishes across a broad spectrum of coefficient systems. Consequently, this vanishing property extends to various groups exhibiting self-similarity, including Thompson's group F, rendering them boundedly acyclic. Our approach utilizes ergodic theory, proving effective for extensive transformation groups where the Mather-Matsumoto-Morita technique may be insufficient due to the absence of standard acyclicity.

The $H$-theorem asserts that entropy production is nonnegative, implying that the entropy of a closed system must change monotonically over time. In the context of information processing, this principle holds as positive entropy production occurs during the random transformation of signals, a concept known as the information processing lemma. Initially, both the $H$-theorem and the information processing lemma were established for the classical Boltzmann-Gibbs-Shannon entropy and its associated relative entropy. Over recent decades, numerous new entropy measures and divergences have emerged, necessitating a verification of the $H$-theorem for each. This note introduces a straightforward, general criterion to determine the validity of the $H$-theorem for any convex divergence $H$, demonstrating that certain widely used divergences fail to satisfy it. We examine systems comprising $n$ states $A_i$ governed by first-order kinetics described by a master equation. We prove that a convex function $H$ serves as a Lyapunov function for all master equations with a specified equilibrium if and only if its conditional minima accurately reflect the equilibria of pairwise transitions $A_i \rightleftharpoons A_j$. This theorem remains independent of the principle of detailed balance and applies to general Markov kinetics. Elementary analysis of pair equilibria reveals that popular Bregman divergences, such as the Euclidean distance or Itakura-Saito distance within the space of distributions, cannot act as universal Lyapunov functions for first-order kinetics and may increase during Markov processes. Consequently, these measures violate the second law and the information processing lemma; specifically, for these information metrics, random data manipulation can actually increase the information within the data. The primary findings are further extended to nonlinear generalized mass action law kinetic equations. Finally, the Appendix presents a new family of universal Lyapunov functions tailored for generalized mass action law kinetics.

We examine linear spectral statistics of the form $\mathrm{tr} (\varphi(H))$, where $\varphi$ represents test functions with low regularity and $H$ denotes Wigner matrices featuring smooth entry distributions. Our results demonstrate that for functions $\varphi$ belonging to the Sobolev space $H^{1/2+\varepsilon}$ or the Hölder space $C^{1/2+\varepsilon}$, and which are supported within the spectral bulk of the semicircle law, these statistics exhibit asymptotic Gaussian fluctuations. Furthermore, the variance matches that of the Central Limit Theorem applicable to functions of higher regularity, holding for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs), characterized by non-analyticities in the logarithm of the Loschmidt echo, have been proposed as a framework to categorize diverse phenomena in closed quantum systems far from equilibrium. This study presents an analytical examination of the Loschmidt echo within nonequilibrium $s$-wave and topological $p_x+ip_y$ fermionic superfluids. We demonstrate that the occurrence of these non-analyticities lacks invariance under global rotations of the superfluid phase. To address this limitation, we propose a broader definition of the grand canonical Loschmidt echo. Our findings indicate that DQPTs are ineffective indicators for the long-term dynamics of interacting systems; specifically, they fail to distinguish between different dynamical phases in quenched BCS superconductors. However, DQPTs can effectively signal topology changes resulting from a quench and track the emergence of solitons from unstable stationary states in BCS superconductors.

Measurements of the Hubble constant ($H_0$), cosmological mass density ($\Omega_M$), and dark energy equation-of-state parameter ($w$) using Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) depend on extensive surveys utilizing diverse photometric systems over thirty years. This study evaluates how potential systematics in the relative photometric zeropoint calibration among the 17 surveys comprising the Pantheon+ data set affect upcoming SH0ES+Pantheon+ constraints on $H_0$, $\Omega_M$, and $w$. By varying these zeropoints simultaneously with cosmological parameters, we find that while the SH0ES+Pantheon+ determination of $H_0$ remains robust against inter-survey photometric miscalibration, the derived values for $\Omega_M$ and $w$ are sensitive to such errors. Specifically, miscalibration introduces an uncertainty in $H_0$ of no more than $0.2$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, which is insufficient to explain the $7$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ "Hubble Tension" between SH0ES and Planck $\Lambda$CDM inferences. However, $\Omega_M$ and $w$ shift significantly—by approximately $0.04$ and $-0.17$, respectively, for every $25$ mmag of calibration uncertainty—highlighting the critical importance of cross-calibration for accurate parameter estimation. Given that the Pantheon+ collection includes multiple surveys sharing low-redshift Hubble Flow and Cepheid-paired SNe, the joint SH0ES+Pantheon+ constraint on $H_0$ is resilient to inter-survey photometric errors, ensuring that such systematics do not hinder the goal of measuring $H_0$ to 1% accuracy using this combined dataset.

I develop a Generative Adversarial Network to generate realistic seismic wave speed models. By embedding the generator within seismic Full-Waveform Inversion, I decrease the parameter count and constrain the inversion to plausible models only. When applied to a 2D slice of the SEAM model, the approach yields more credible outcomes than traditional Full-Waveform Inversion.

Synchrophasor devices are essential for ensuring real-time monitoring and operational visibility within the smart grid. However, their extensive deployment has introduced substantial challenges, particularly regarding communication, data integrity, and cybersecurity. While current literature often addresses these issues in isolation, they actually exist in a complex, interconnected relationship. This paper provides a comprehensive review of quality and cybersecurity challenges associated with synchrophasors, highlighting the interdependencies between them. It further summarizes various methods for evaluating these dependencies and examines how quality assessment techniques can be leveraged to identify potential cyber-attacks. Ultimately, this work serves as a foundational resource for researchers new to the domains of synchrophasor data analytics and security.

Brown dwarfs serve as natural timekeepers, gradually cooling and fading because they lack sufficient core fusion. Their abundance and presence across nearly all Galactic environments make them promising chronometers for diverse Galactic research. However, realizing this potential demands precise and accurate age determinations for individual objects, a challenge hindered by the complex atmospheres and spectra of cool brown dwarfs, the degeneracy among mass, age, and luminosity, and the absence of reliable age indicators in magnetic activity and rotation. This paper reviews five distinct methods for uniquely determining brown dwarf ages, examines their applicability and constraints, and reports current empirical precision levels.

This paper establishes regularity results regarding the behavior of weak and very weak solutions to the degenerate wave equation near the boundary. While corresponding results for the nondegenerate case were originally derived by Fabre and Puel (J. of Diff. Eq. 106, 1993), findings of this nature are closely tied to the exact boundary controllability of the wave equation, which serves as the limit of internal controllability.

The spectrum $\omega(G)$ of a finite group $G$ is defined as the collection of the orders of its elements. This paper establishes a sufficient condition for nonsolvability: if a group $G$ has four distinct prime divisors such that $\omega(G)$ includes every pairwise product of these primes but excludes the product of any three, then $G$ is nonsolvable. Applying this theorem, we demonstrate that for $q \geqslant 8$ and $q \neq 32$, the direct square $Sz(q) \times Sz(q)$ of the simple exceptional Suzuki group is uniquely determined by its spectrum within the class of finite groups. However, for the case of $Sz(32) \times Sz(32)$, exactly four finite groups share the same spectrum.

Let $q$ be a nondegenerate quadratic form on a vector space $V$. Suppose $X$ is a subset of $V$ that remains invariant under the action of a Lie group $G$ within $SO(V,q)$. For any vector $f \in V$, we define a function $d_f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ by $d_f(x) = q(f-x)$. We demonstrate that the critical points of $d_f$ are contained within the subspace orthogonal to ${\mathfrak g}\cdot f$, which we refer to as the critical space. Consequently, every point in $X$ closest to $f$ resides in this critical space. This framework is applicable to singular t-ples of tensors and flag varieties, extending a prior result by Draisma, Tocino, and the author. Furthermore, we utilize this approach to calculate the Euclidean Distance degree of a complete flag variety.

Occlusion, encompassing self-occlusions, object-human interactions, and inter-person blockages, represents a primary hurdle in human pose and shape estimation. This challenge is exacerbated by the scarcity of diverse, accurate training data, particularly for real-world scenarios involving occlusions. This paper addresses the estimation of human pose and shape specifically under inter-person occlusions, while simultaneously managing object-human and self-occlusions. We introduce a novel framework that synthesizes occlusion-aware 2D keypoints and silhouettes to directly regress SMPL parameters. By leveraging a neural 3D mesh renderer for on-the-fly silhouette supervision, we achieve significant enhancements in shape estimation. Furthermore, we generate panoramic viewpoint data driven by keypoints and silhouettes to address the limited viewpoint diversity found in current datasets. Experimental evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art pose estimation performance on the 3DPW and 3DPW-Crowd benchmarks. In terms of shape estimation, our method surpasses Mesh Transformer, 3DCrowdNet, and ROMP, while also achieving top-tier results on the SSP-3D dataset for shape prediction. The demonstration and source code are accessible at https://igame-lab.github.io/LASOR/.

Computer Tomography (CT) imaging has become increasingly vital for disease diagnosis; however, the extensive data within CT scan slices often exceeds the limits of human visual inspection in terms of speed and precision. To address this, a computer-assisted expert system for classifying skull fractures is required to support physicians. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as the leading deep learning models for image categorization, frequently surpassing other approaches in accuracy and performance. Various CNN architectures were developed and evaluated, with a hybrid model demonstrating superior results. This approach combined ResNet50 for feature extraction with a gradient-boosted decision tree as the classifier to categorize skull fractures from brain CT scans into three distinct groups. This configuration achieved the highest overall performance metrics, including an F1-score of 96%, a Hamming Score of 95%, a Balanced Accuracy Score of 94%, and an ROC AUC of 96%.

Recent literature has introduced various copula-based methods to assess independence among multiple random variables; however, these existing tests lack invariance under monotone transformations and often struggle when variable dependence is highly non-monotone. This article introduces a novel copula-based dependency measure to develop new distribution-free tests of independence. Both the proposed measure and the resulting tests are invariant under permutations and monotone transformations of the variables. The dependency measure utilizes a Gaussian kernel function within a multi-scale framework, aggregating results across several bandwidth parameter choices. Under suitable regularity conditions, we derive the large-sample properties of both the measure and the tests. Finally, we analyze multiple simulated and real datasets to evaluate the performance of the proposed tests against established methods found in the literature.

In this study, we introduce a deep learning algorithm designed to solve Principal-Agent (PA) mean field games subject to market-clearing constraints—a previously unexplored problem class that challenges conventional numerical techniques. Our methodology employs an actor-critic optimization framework wherein agents derive a Nash equilibrium based on the principal's penalty function, which the principal subsequently evaluates. To address the inner problem, we utilize a modified variant of the deep backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE) method tailored for McKean-Vlasov forward-backward SDEs, incorporating dependencies on the distributions of both forward and backward processes. Furthermore, the outer problem's loss is approximated via a neural network through sampling across the space of penalty functions. We demonstrate the algorithm's application to a stylized PA scenario within Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) markets, where participants can lease clean energy capacity, trade RECs, and scale long-term infrastructure to maximize profits. Numerical experiments validate the algorithm's effectiveness and yield significant insights into optimal PA interactions within the mean-field limit of such markets.

This study addresses a boundary value problem involving a fully fourth-order nonlinear functional differential equation that incorporates all lower derivatives with proportional delay arguments. By reducing the problem to an operator equation regarding the nonlinear function on the right-hand side, we prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution and develop iterative methods at both continuous and discrete levels to solve it. Furthermore, we derive a comprehensive error estimate for the discrete iterative solution. Numerous examples are provided to validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical approach.

This study employs modular reduction on the rank 4 Coxeter group defined by a star diagram with labels 5, 3, and $k \in \{3, 4, 5, 6\}$. Using odd primes within the quadratic integer ring $\mathbb{Z}[\tau]$ (where $\tau = \frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$ represents the golden ratio) as moduli, we categorize each resulting reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reduced group maintains the C-group property irrespective of the specific prime chosen for the reduction.

Safeguarding human rights remains one of the most critical global challenges. This study introduces a dataset addressing a prominent recent contradiction affecting worldwide: the George Floyd incident. We present a labeled collection of 17 million tweets, gathered between May 25 and August 21, 2020, spanning 89 days from the event's onset. The data was annotated by tracking the most prevalent news topics from both international and local newspapers. Additionally, we establish two baseline models, TF-IDF and LDA, and evaluate their performance across three k-values using precision, recall, and F1-score metrics. The complete dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/MeysamAsgariC/BLMT.

The 2048 puzzle features tiles with powers of two that combine to create larger powers, a mechanic shared by variants using different numerical values. We investigate the highest possible scores in these games by demonstrating a min-max theorem: in a generalized version of 2048 permitting all original moves, the maximum score equals the minimum number of coins required by a greedy change-making algorithm to reach a specific sum. A popular 2048 strategy keeps tiles reflecting the move count in binary, while the Fibonacci variant (987) employs the Zeckendorf representation to sum the fewest Fibonacci numbers; our analysis reveals that the viability of these strategies depends directly on the optimality of greedy change-making for binary and Fibonacci coin systems. Conversely, for variants where greedy change-making is suboptimal, the game's duration is dictated by the greedy approach rather than the optimal tile sum representation. Specifically, the game inevitably ends if the sequence of allowed tile values contains arbitrarily large gaps between consecutive numbers.

As social media participation among the general public grows, policymakers and journalists frequently utilize online polls to gauge the political leanings of specific demographics. However, a significant limitation exists: only influential figures can conduct such polls at a mass scale, leading to uncontrollable and potentially biased voter distributions. Conversely, analyzing publicly available social media data allows for controllable insights into survey populations, significantly reduces costs, and avoids direct involvement with the subjects. To achieve this, we propose a self-attentive semi-supervised framework for detecting political inclination. Our model's primary advantage is its ability to operate without requiring massive training datasets or storing social network parameters. It achieves an accuracy of 93.7% even with zero annotated data and delivers competitive results with only a few examples per class. Furthermore, the model demonstrates high efficiency in resource-constrained environments, and its predictions align well with manual survey outcomes across various real-world scenarios.

Advancements in adversarial learning have facilitated the creation of highly realistic synthetic visual media. While various detection methods have been developed to differentiate between real and fake content, their effectiveness often declines drastically when test data originates from a different distribution than the training data. This limitation has spurred research aimed at enhancing the generalization capabilities of fake detectors. Given that existing generation techniques fail to accurately replicate the frequency spectrum of natural images, we identified that the frequency domain of synthetic data possesses unique discriminative traits useful for detection. Furthermore, we noted that the information embedded in the frequency spectrum differs from that in the spatial domain. Leveraging these findings, we introduced TwoStreamNet, a two-stream convolutional neural network that integrates both frequency and spatial domain features. Our results demonstrate that this two-stream architecture achieves superior generalization across unseen generation models, datasets, and techniques. Compared to current state-of-the-art detectors, our proposed method shows significant performance gains, with the fusion of frequency and spatial streams further boosting the detector's generalization.

We have derived a system of Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) equations that describe the exact WKB periods within one-dimensional Quantum Mechanics featuring arbitrary polynomial potentials. These equations extend the ODE/IM correspondence and can be interpreted as the solution to a Riemann-Hilbert problem in the context of resurgent Quantum Mechanics as formulated by Voros. Our approach relies on solving analogous Riemann-Hilbert problems previously utilized in investigating BPS spectra in $\mathcal{N}=2$ gauge theories and minimal surfaces in AdS. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining our TBA equations with exact quantization conditions offers a robust technique for resolving spectral problems in Quantum Mechanics. We substantiate this general framework through an in-depth examination of PT-symmetric cubic and quartic oscillators.

The ground state $B_{c}^{\ast}$ meson remains experimentally undiscovered to date. Beyond its primary electromagnetic decay channels, nonleptonic weak decays offer an alternative avenue for detecting these elusive $B_{c}^{\ast}$ mesons. Motivated by the promising prospects of observing $B_{c}^{\ast}$ mesons at future high-luminosity colliders, researchers have investigated nonleptonic weak decays of $B_{c}^{\ast}$ induced by bottom and charm quark transitions within the Standard Model using a naive factorization framework. The analysis indicates that for decay modes including $B_{c}^{\ast} \to B_{s,d}\pi$, $B_{s,d}^{\ast}\pi$, $B_{s,d}\rho$, $B_{s}K$, $B_{s}^{\ast}K$, $B_{s}K^{\ast}$, ${\eta}_{c}(1S,2S)\pi$, ${\eta}_{c}(1S,2S)\rho$, and ${\psi}(1S,2S)\pi$, yields ranging from a few hundred to several thousand events could be observable in experiments at CEPC, FCC-ee, and LHCb@HL-LHC.

This study investigates the optimal performance of Bayesian learning within generative frameworks by introducing and upper-bounding the Minimum Excess Risk (MER), defined as the disparity between the lowest expected loss achievable through data-driven learning and the lowest possible loss if the true model were known. The MER concept offers a rigorous framework for characterizing various forms of uncertainty in Bayesian inference, specifically aleatoric and minimum epistemic uncertainty. We present two approaches to deriving upper bounds for the MER. The first approach, applicable to Bayesian learning with parametric generative models, bounds the MER using the conditional mutual information between model parameters and the target quantity given observed data; this enables the quantification of the MER's decay rate as data volume increases and, under realizable conditions, links the MER to the generative class's complexity, such as the VC dimension in binary classification. The second approach, tailored for Bayesian learning with parametric predictive models, connects the MER to the minimum estimation error of model parameters derived from data, explicitly illustrating how parameter estimation uncertainty propagates into the MER and final prediction uncertainty. Furthermore, we extend the MER definition and analysis to scenarios involving multiple model families and nonparametric models. Throughout this discussion, we compare the MER in Bayesian learning with excess risk in frequentist learning.

Scaling relationships between city characteristics and population are fundamental yet complex aspects of urban development. Quantifying these patterns and grasping their theoretical underpinnings remains challenging due to difficulties in delineating city borders and insufficient historical records to track urban dynamics across time and space. To overcome these obstacles, we examined scaling between city infrastructure and population across 857 U.S. metropolitan regions over an exceptional 115-year span. Our approach utilized dasymetrically refined historical population data, archival road network records, and multi-temporal settlement information to establish dynamic city boundaries based on settlement density. We provide robust evidence that urban scaling exponents align closely with theoretical models over a century when cities are defined as dense settlement clusters. Conversely, when cities are aggregated into administratively defined metropolitan areas—a common method in prior studies—the results diverge significantly from theory and fluctuate over time. Although our findings show strong quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions, empirical scaling relations unexpectedly vary geographically, a trend corroborated by global scaling analyses. Furthermore, our analysis of scaling coefficients indicates that a city in 2015 with a population comparable to one in 1900 utilizes more developed land and road kilometers, suggesting cities may have become increasingly detrimental to the local environment. Ultimately, our work highlights both the strengths and limitations of existing theoretical models and introduces a novel framework for studying urban systems using historical data.

Simple random coverage models, which are well-established in Euclidean space, can be extended to any general compact metric space. Drawing parallels with geometric models, the discrete coupon collector's problem, and cover times in finite Markov chains, it is anticipated that a "weak concentration" bound applies to the distribution of cover times under minimal assumptions. This paper presents two such results: one regarding random fixed-radius balls and another concerning sequentially arriving balls with random centers and deterministic growth. The first result is a direct application of a broader bound covering coverage by i.i.d. random sets with arbitrary distributions, while the second applies to hitting times in Markov chains possessing a strong monotonicity property. The growth model appears generally more manageable, leading the authors to document several fundamental findings and open questions specific to it.

The standard thermoelectric figure of merit and power factor fail to adequately assess thin film quality, as conversion efficiency relies on film dimensions. To address this, we introduce an effective thermoelectric figure of merit and an effective Seebeck coefficient that account for film size, ensuring that maximum energy conversion efficiency rises with the effective figure of merit. We also define an effective power factor. Using typical properties for Bi$_2$Te$_3$ and PEDOT, we examine how film thickness influences these effective parameters.

This study investigates alternative news media ecosystems that reportedly shaped opinions and beliefs through false or biased reporting during the 2016 US Presidential Elections. By analyzing a substantial, professionally curated dataset of 668 hyper-partisan websites and their associated Facebook pages, we identified key characteristics governing traffic flow within this network. Our findings reveal a pattern where new websites launch just before the elections but are subsequently abandoned, forming an interconnected ecosystem through internal website links and mutual Facebook page endorsements. These mechanisms effectively direct user traffic within the ecosystem in a highly partisan manner: right-leaning sites link to and endorse other right-leaning sites, while left-leaning sites do the same, creating a filter bubble among news producers comparable to those observed among consumers. Although activity exists on both sides, right-leaning sites are more developed, accounting for a disproportionate share of abandoned sites and internal partisan links. Furthermore, an examination of consumer demographics indicates that certain populous groups in the US are more likely to consume right-leaning hyper-partisan content.

Detecting parity-violating phenomena like cosmic birefringence (CB) through the polarization of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) demands precise management of instrumental errors. A primary source of such errors arises from imperfections in the half-wave plate (HWP), which serves as the polarization modulator. We investigate how these non-idealities affect CMB angular power spectra, noting that their effects partially overlap with those of CB and polarization angle miscalibration. Our approach involves generating mock, noiseless time-ordered data via full-sky beam convolution simulations that incorporate the HWP; this data is then processed using a bin-averaging map-maker to compute power spectra, including $TB$ and $EB$ correlations. Additionally, we develop analytical expressions that accurately reproduce the observed spectra. For the HWP parameters considered, the resulting instrumental rotation spans several degrees, a magnitude that could be erroneously attributed to CB. Consequently, precise characterization of the HWP is essential to avoid this confusion. Both our simulations and derived formulae will assist in establishing the necessary calibration accuracy standards for HWPs.

This article investigates $f(\bar{R},T)$-gravity within the framework of dark energy, employing the {\bf K-}essence model to analyze dark energy effects in cosmological scenarios. In this context, $\bar{R}$ denotes the Ricci scalar of the {\bf K-}essence geometry, while $T$ represents the trace of its energy-momentum tensor. We utilize a Dirac-Born-Infeld type non-canonical Lagrangian to derive the {\bf K-}essence emergent gravity metric $(\bar{G}_{\mu\nu})$, which is not conformally equivalent to the standard gravitational metric $(g_{\mu\nu})$. The resulting modified field equations and corresponding Friedmann equations for $f(\bar{R},T)$-gravity differ from those of standard $f(R,T)$-gravity, assuming a flat Friedmann-Robertson-Walker background metric. To determine the equation of state (EoS) parameter $(\omega)$, we solved the Friedmann equations under the assumption that $f(\bar{R},T) \equiv f(\bar{R}) + f(T) = f(\bar{R}) + \lambda T$, where $\lambda$ is a model parameter. By selecting various forms for $f(\bar{R})$, we established the relationship between $\omega$ and time, treating the dark energy density ($\dot{\phi}^{2}$) as a time-dependent variable that adheres to specific constraints. Analysis of the EoS parameter versus time plots demonstrates that our model aligns with observational data derived from SNIa+BAO+H(z) observations within a specific temporal range.

A conjecture by Kac, now established as a theorem, states that the Kac polynomial—which enumerates the isomorphism classes of absolutely indecomposable representations of a quiver over a finite field for a given dimension vector—possesses exclusively non-negative integer coefficients. In this work, we demonstrate that for quivers containing sufficient loops, any Kac polynomial can be decomposed into a sum of refined Kac polynomials, indexed by tuples of partitions, which also feature only non-negative integer coefficients. Furthermore, a closed-form expression for these refined Kac polynomials is provided.

Animals rapidly acquire knowledge of event timing within fixed intervals, a learning rate that remains independent of the interval's duration. Conversely, recurrent neural networks employing gradient-based learning struggle to predict the timing of events influenced by distant past stimuli. This paper introduces the latent time-adaptive drift-diffusion model (LTDDM), an extension of the time-adaptive drift-diffusion model (TDDM), which replicates the behavioral characteristics of animal timing learning observed in experimental data. We evaluate the LTDDM against a state-of-the-art long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network across three distinct timing tasks. The discussion highlights performance disparities between the two models, demonstrating that the LTDDM can learn these temporal sequences orders of magnitude faster than recurrent neural networks.

Given a directed graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a starting node $u_{\sf start}$, the goal is to approximately sample an $L$-step random walk using minimal space and few passes over the edges. This task has numerous applications, such as estimating webpage PageRank. While a single-pass algorithm requires $\tilde{\Theta}(n \cdot L)$ space, previous work only achieved better space complexity with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{L})$ passes. This paper resolves the space complexity for two-pass streaming algorithms by establishing almost matching upper and lower bounds of $\tilde{\Theta}(n \cdot \sqrt{L})$. Furthermore, the lower bound proof generalizes to any constant number of passes $p$, demonstrating that any $p$-pass algorithm necessitates $\tilde{\Omega}(n \cdot L^{1/p})$ space. Finally, we prove a similar $\tilde{\Theta}(n \cdot \sqrt{L})$ space complexity bound for algorithms (regardless of pass count) tasked with sampling an $L$-step random walk from every vertex in the graph.

Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) utilizes a thin sheet of light to optically section and image transparent organisms or tissues in a living state, offering benefits such as rapid imaging and minimal phototoxicity. In this study, we applied LSFM to examine how polarization affects fluorescence emission from zebrafish neurons by altering the electric oscillation orientation of the excitation light. The resulting fluorescence intensity from the excited zebrafish larvae adheres to a cosine squared function relative to the excitation light's polarization state, showing a 40% increase in emission when the polarization is orthogonal to both the illumination and detection axes. By registering and subtracting fluorescence images captured under varying polarization conditions, we demonstrated that the majority of the enhanced signals originate from nerve cells rather than extracellular substances. This approach enables the distinction of cell boundaries and the observation of organismal structures with enhanced contrast and resolution.

Imitation learning aims to derive an expert policy from observed demonstrations, yet in practical settings, identifying a flawless expert is often challenging, making the prevention of hazardous actions critical for safety. We introduce the concept of \textit{learning to avoid}, an objective that functions as a counterpoint to imitation learning, wherein an agent learns to evade a demonstrator's policy within a specific environment. We define avoidance learning as the optimization of an agent's reward while simultaneously steering clear of dangerous behaviors exhibited by the demonstrator. In this study, we establish a framework for avoidance learning by proposing an objective function that incorporates the \emph{distance} between the state occupancy distributions of the expert and the demonstrator policies. By utilizing density estimates for state occupancy measures, we apply this calculated distance as a reward bonus to encourage avoidance of the demonstrator. We validate our theoretical approach through experiments across a diverse range of partially observable environments. The results demonstrate that our method enhances sample efficiency during training when compared to current state-of-the-art policy optimization and safety techniques.

Recently, next-generation neural mass models have garnered significant interest from researchers in mathematical neuroscience. Their capacity to quantify synchrony within neural populations has proven valuable across various applications, including the modeling of brain rhythms, working memory, and spatio-temporal activity patterns. In this Letter, we investigate how finite network size influences the collective behavior of neural networks and demonstrate that these effects can be represented by suitably adjusted neural mass models. Specifically, the finite size of a network gives rise to shot noise, which manifests as a stochastic component within the model. We compute the power spectrum of this shot noise and reveal that it can exhibit distinct peaks at frequencies comparable to the mean firing rate. While shot noise remains weak in large, massively connected networks, its influence on collective dynamics may be substantial due to resonance phenomena.

Domain adaptation aims to bridge the gap between training on a \emph{source} domain and evaluating on a \emph{target} domain. While most adaptation techniques depend on source data through joint optimization of both source and target datasets, source-free approaches substitute the source data with a pre-trained source model, fine-tuning it on the target. Regardless of the method, the majority of parameter updates for both the model representation and classifier originate from the source rather than the target. Since the ultimate objective is target accuracy, we advocate for maximizing optimization on target data. We demonstrate substantial gains through on-target adaptation, which derives representations exclusively from target data while using only source predictions for supervision. Furthermore, within the long-tailed classification setting, we achieve additional improvements by learning the on-target class distribution, capturing the (im)balance of classes directly from the target data.

A metric space is defined as strongly rigid when no positive distance occurs more than once within its metric. In 1972, Janos demonstrated that a separable metrizable space admits a strongly rigid metric if and only if it is zero-dimensional. This paper extends that finding to the theory of metric spaces. Specifically, we prove that for any strongly zero-dimensional metrizable space, the collection of all strongly rigid metrics is dense within the space of metrics. Furthermore, if the space consists of a union of countable compact subspaces, this collection becomes comeager. As a consequence, we establish that for a strongly zero-dimensional metrizable space, the set of metrics that lack any nontrivial bijective self-isometry is comeager in the space of metrics.

The identification of changing-look active galactic nuclei (CLAGNs)—characterized by dramatic shifts in optical broad emission lines and/or substantial fluctuations in line-of-sight column densities—poses a challenge to the orientation-based AGN unification framework. Utilizing data from the {\it Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer} ({\it WISE}) archive, we investigated the mid-infrared (mid-IR) characteristics of 57 optical CLAGNs and 11 X-ray CLAGNs. Our results indicate that the Eddington-scaled mid-IR luminosities for both subtypes fall within the range typical of low-luminosity AGNs (LLAGNs) and luminous QSOs. Specifically, the mean Eddington-scaled mid-IR luminosities are approximately 0.4% for optical CLAGNs and 0.5% for X-ray CLAGNs, values that align closely with the bolometric luminosity marking the transition between radiatively inefficient accretion flows (RIAFs) and Shakura-Sunyaev disks (SSDs). Furthermore, by estimating mid-IR time lags relative to optical variations for 13 CLAGNs exhibiting strong mid-IR variability, we observed that the correlation between time lag and bolometric luminosity ($\tau - L$) for these objects closely mirrors that seen in luminous QSOs.

This paper introduces a model explaining the plant stem morphogenesis phenomenon observed by Cesar Gomez-Campo in 1970. By examining a simplified auxin dynamics model, we demonstrate that once the initial primordium forms, varying a single parameter—the diffusion rate—can account for random, distichous, and spiral leaf arrangements. This analysis further applies to the $n$-jugate scenario, where $n$ primordia initiate simultaneously at each plastochrone. After validating the model, we explore its ability to replicate the Gomez-Campo phenomenon, specifically how a stem exhibiting spiral phyllotaxis can generate branches with either matching or opposing chirality. Finally, we examine how this relationship shifts from discordant to concordant throughout the growing season.

This paper introduces a novel approach to solving the core challenge of learning optimal Q-functions by formulating them as saddle points of a nonlinear Lagrangian derived from the classic Bellman optimality equation. The study demonstrates that this Lagrangian exhibits strong duality despite its nonlinearity, establishing a foundation for a general Lagrangian framework for Q-function learning. As a practical demonstration, the authors develop an imitation learning algorithm grounded in this duality theory and apply it to a leading machine translation benchmark. Furthermore, the paper investigates a symmetry breaking phenomenon related to the optimality of Lagrangian saddle points, thereby validating an often-overlooked avenue for advancing the Lagrangian method.

This work examines a square lattice system of strongly interacting spinor bosons under isotropic Rashba spin-orbit coupling ($\alpha=\beta$). The system exhibits several distinct phases: a collinear spin-bond correlated Y-x magnetic phase, a gapped in-commensurate co-planar IC-XY-y phase, and a non-coplanar commensurate $3 \times 3$ Skyrmion crystal (SkX) phase. At the Abelian point where $\alpha=\beta=\pi/2$, the state corresponds to an antiferromagnetic (AFM) configuration in a rotated basis. Deviating slightly from this point reveals a spurious $U(1)$ symmetry. We introduce a novel non-perturbative approach to compute both the energy gap and the excitation spectrum arising from the order-from-quantum-disorder (OFQD) mechanism. Furthermore, we construct a symmetry-based effective action to analyze the quantum Lifshitz transition between the Y-x and IC-XY-y states, linking the phenomenological parameters of the action to those derived from microscopic non-perturbative OFQD analysis in the large $S$ limit. Finally, we discuss potential experimental realizations in cold atom systems and specific 4d or 5d Kitaev materials.

Measurements of the bremsstrahlung flux-averaged cross-sections $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle$ were conducted for the photonuclear reactions ${^{65}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,n)^{64}\rm{Cu}$, ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,n)^{62}\rm{Cu}$, ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,2n)^{61}\rm{Cu}$, and ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,3n)^{60}\rm{Cu}$ across bremsstrahlung end-point energies ranging from 35 to 94 MeV. These experiments utilized an electron beam from the NSC KIPT LUE-40 linear accelerator, employing activation and off-line $\gamma$-ray spectrometric methods. Theoretical flux-average cross-sections $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle_{\rm{th}}$ were computed using $\sigma(E)$ data from the TALYS1.95 code with default settings. Results indicate that experimental average cross-sections for the ${^{65}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,n)^{64}\rm{Cu}$, ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,n)^{62}\rm{Cu}$, and ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,2n)^{61}\rm{Cu}$ reactions consistently exceed TALYS1.95 predictions. The new $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle$ data enhance existing laboratory records for $(\gamma,n)$ and $(\gamma,2n)$ reactions, while the measurement of $\langle{\sigma(E_{\rm{\gamma max}})}\rangle$ for the ${^{63}\rm{Cu}}(\gamma,3n)^{60}\rm{Cu}$ reaction represents a first-time observation.

We present an optimal measurement strategy for a specific class of noisy channels, known as spreading channels, which simplify to the identity channel at a particular parameter value. A physically significant application involves estimating the absolute displacement magnitude under phase-randomizing noise; notably, this noise does not diminish the efficacy of the optimal measurement. For small displacements, a squeezed vacuum probe field emerges as the optimal strategy within the set of methods sharing the same average energy. While a squeezer combined with photodetection achieves the quantum Fisher information, standard homodyne detection fails in the limit of small displacements, a limitation analogous to Rayleigh's curse in optical superresolution. Furthermore, a quantum advantage is demonstrated: utilizing squeezed or Fock states with $N$ average photons enables asymptotic parameter estimation with a $\sqrt{N}$ improvement in precision compared to classical states of equivalent energy.

This paper demonstrates that the dynamics of the MBO scheme for data clustering converge to a viscosity solution of the mean curvature flow. The proof relies on two key components: (i) a novel abstract convergence theorem grounded in quantitative estimates for heat operators, and (ii) the establishment of these estimates within the framework of random geometric graphs. For practical implementation, two critical parameters are the number of eigenvalues used to compute the heat operator and the scheme's step size. The findings in this study provide theoretical support for selecting these parameters based on sample size and interaction width.

Although polar codes are theoretically capable of achieving highly competitive Frame Error Rates, their practical performance relies heavily on the decoding method and the broader communication system parameters. Consequently, designing optimized polar codes for specific scenarios can be a complex task. This paper presents a methodology that trains deep neural networks to estimate the Frame Error Rate of polar codes using their frozen bit construction sequences. We further introduce an algorithm utilizing Projected Gradient Descent, which employs the neural network's gradients to generate promising frozen bit sequences. Our experiments on synthetic datasets demonstrate that this approach can produce codes superior to those used for training the neural networks, even when the training set includes some of the most efficient codes available.

Power iteration serves as a foundational technique in data analysis, designed to identify the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue of a matrix. It is widely utilized in various domains, including recommendation systems, ranking algorithms, and principal component analysis (PCA). This paper presents Multiplication-Avoiding Power Iteration (MAPI), a variant that substitutes the standard $\ell_2$-inner products of regular power iteration (RPI) with multiplication-free vector products based on Mercer-type kernels related to the $\ell_1$ norm. Specifically, for an $n \times n$ matrix, MAPI requires only $n$ multiplications per iteration compared to the $n^2$ needed by RPI. This substantial decrease in multiplication operations is particularly beneficial given their high energy consumption. The study applies MAPI to PCA-driven image reconstruction and graph-based ranking tasks. Compared to RPI, MAPI demonstrates superior performance and typically achieves convergence much more rapidly.

This work presents an exact, analytic solution for a straightforward electrostatic model relevant to biomolecular recognition. The model consists of a variable-thickness layer of high-dielectric material (simulating solvent or water) positioned between two regions of low-dielectric material (representing proteins, DNA, or RNA), each containing an embedded point charge. For identical charges, the screening layer invariably reduces the energy relative to an infinite low-dielectric medium. Surprisingly, it also lowers the energy compared to an infinite high-dielectric medium when the layer is sufficiently thick. In contrast, for oppositely charged pairs, the screening layer always decreases the energy compared to either infinite medium. This energy behavior results in a significantly enhanced repulsive force between like charges. Conversely, the attractive force between opposite charges is weaker than in a low-dielectric infinite medium but stronger than in a high-dielectric one. This phenomenon, termed asymmetric screening, observed in this simple system validates the broader behavior previously identified in more complex systems involving arbitrary numbers of charged dielectric spheres in an infinite solvent.

This study reports a search for high-mass resonances appearing as dielectron or dimuon pairs within the mass interval of 250 GeV to 6 TeV. Utilizing data from the ATLAS experiment collected during Run 2 of the Large Hadron Collider in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=$13 TeV, the analysis covers an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. Background contributions are modeled by fitting a functional form to the dilepton invariant-mass spectrum, while a generic signal shape assesses the significance of any deviations from this background prediction. No significant anomalies were found; consequently, 95% confidence level upper limits on the fiducial cross-section times branching ratio were established for various resonance width scenarios. These constraints apply to spin-0, spin-1, and spin-2 hypotheses. When translated into lower bounds on resonance mass for specific benchmark models, the analysis reaches up to 4.5 TeV for the E6-motivated $Z^\prime_\psi$ boson, and additional limits on the couplings of the Heavy Vector Triplet model are also provided.

This study examines the scaling relationships between star formation rates (SFR) and molecular gas masses, analyzing both local Galactic clouds and a sample of external galaxies. We focus on the connections between SFR and measurements of both total and dense molecular gas masses. Our findings suggest a fundamental empirical scaling relation that directly links the local star formation process with global galactic processes. Specifically, the total SFR in either a molecular cloud or a galaxy is linearly proportional to the mass of dense gas present within it. This straightforward relationship, previously noted in earlier research, spans nearly nine orders of magnitude, indicating that the star formation rate is directly governed by the quantity of dense molecular gas available within a star-forming complex. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SFRs and total molecular gas masses, across both local clouds and galaxies, exhibit correlations over similarly extensive mass ranges and can be described by a family of linear scaling laws parameterized by $f_{DG}$, the fraction of dense gas. Essentially, the underlying star formation scaling law remains linear for clouds and galaxies sharing the same dense gas fraction. These insights offer a unified framework to reconcile the standard non-linear Schmidt-Kennicutt scaling law (typically derived from CO observations) with the linear scaling law derived from HCN observations of dense gas.

Public sharing of scientific datasets and analysis pipelines is growing to support open science, yet reliable methods for determining which resources are compatible remain absent. This gap jeopardizes the findability and reusability of these assets as their numbers increase. We assess the viability of a collaborative filtering system that suggests pipelines and datasets by analyzing provenance records from past executions. Using resources from the Canadian Open Neuroscience Platform, a national open neuroscience initiative, we evaluated our system. The results (AUC=0.83) were significantly better than random chance and surpassed recommendations based on domain expert knowledge or textual descriptions (AUC=0.63). Notably, experts often overlook low-level technical interactions, such as preprocessing levels, which our provenance-based approach captures effectively. We conclude that recommending pipelines and datasets through provenance analysis is both feasible and advantageous for enhancing open-science resource sharing. Future efforts will prioritize gathering more extensive provenance data and moving the system into production.

Solar eruptive events frequently cause sudden fluctuations in the geomagnetic field, which, through induced electric currents, impact human infrastructure, particularly electric power transmission systems. Previous research indicates that exposure to strong geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) can elevate the frequency of power-grid anomalies. This study investigates the rapid response of devices within the Czech electric distribution grid during days of heightened geomagnetic activity. These disturbed days are characterized by specific indices: the cumulative storm-time $Dst$ or $d(\textit{SYM-H})/dt$ low-latitude indices (reflecting ring current changes), the cumulative $AE$ high-latitude index (measuring substorm-related auroral currents), and the cumulative $ap$ mid-latitude index (capturing both ring and auroral current variations). Using superposed epoch analysis, we aimed to detect potential spikes in anomaly rates occurring during and following these events. Our findings reveal that when power lines exhibit a high frequency of anomalies, the anomaly rate rises significantly within one day of a geomagnetic storm's onset. Conversely, for transformers, this increase is typically delayed by two to three days. Additionally, we observed that transformers and certain substations appear sensitive to extended substorm exposure, resulting in delayed anomaly increases. Overall, our data shows an approximately 5--10\% rise in recorded anomalies in the Czech power grid within five days of geomagnetic activity onset, suggesting this fraction is likely attributable to GIC exposure.

Conventional extrinsic calibration methods depend on fiducial markers, whereas learning-based techniques typically rely on simulated data. This study introduces a learning-based, markerless extrinsic calibration system utilizing a depth camera that operates without simulation data. Models for end-effector (EE) segmentation, single-frame rotation prediction, and keypoint detection are trained using automatically generated real-world datasets. To derive EE pose estimates, we employ a transformation trick applied to rotation predictions and a matching algorithm applied to keypoint predictions. Additionally, we enhance calibration robustness by integrating the iterative closest point algorithm, multi-frame analysis, filtering, and outlier detection. Evaluations using training data from various camera poses and test data from unseen poses demonstrate sub-centimeter and sub-deciradian average errors in both calibration and pose estimation. Furthermore, we show that a single, carefully selected training pose yields comparable performance.

Faraday and resonant density waves arise in Bose-Einstein condensates through harmonic driving, representing nonlinear excitations generated by the parametric resonance of coupled collective oscillation modes induced by interactions. Employing both a mean-field variational method and comprehensive numerical simulations, we investigated density waves in zero-temperature dipolar condensates, where the symmetry breaking caused by the anisotropy of the dipole-dipole interaction (DDI) is significant. We formulated variational equations of motion for driven dipolar systems to identify the most unstable modes corresponding to Faraday and resonant waves, subsequently deriving analytical expressions for their spatial periods as functions of contact and DDI strengths. Our variational findings were compared with extensive 3D numerical solutions of the dipolar Gross-Pitaevskii equation, revealing excellent agreement.

Earlier research demonstrated that discrete-time coined quantum walks can facilitate (almost) perfect state transfer on complete bipartite graphs when the sender and receiver reside either within the same partition or in opposite partitions of equal size. By modifying the coin operator, this study analyzes the state transfer problem and establishes that high-fidelity transfer remains achievable even when the sender and receiver occupy partitions of differing sizes. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that an active switching strategy utilizing lackadaisical quantum walks—where the marked vertex alternates between the sender and receiver throughout the process—is also a viable approach.

We introduce a tomographic protocol designed to characterize multi-qubit quantum channels. We examine a specific class of input states where the Pauli measurements performed on the channel's output directly correspond to the components of the Pauli transfer matrix. Comparing our approach to standard quantum process tomography reveals an exponential decrease in the number of distinct experimental configurations needed to extract a single matrix element, while maintaining the same number of measurement shots. This advancement facilitates more efficient experimental realizations whenever selective knowledge of the Pauli transfer matrix is required. We support these findings with various examples and simulations.

The advancement of AI-driven systems has permeated daily life, influencing decisions with profound consequences for individuals and society. Given the explosive expansion of online data, commonly known as the Online Infosphere, it is critical to monitor this domain to safeguard social well-being, as AI decisions rely heavily upon it. This survey aims to offer a thorough examination of key research areas concerning the infosphere, highlighting technical hurdles and prospective solutions, while also outlining future research trajectories. We commence by exploring collaborative systems within the infosphere, with a specific emphasis on Wikipedia. Subsequently, we illustrate how the infosphere has catalyzed the growth of scientific citations and collaborations, thereby fostering interdisciplinary research. Finally, we address governance challenges within the infosphere, including the mitigation of rising hate speech and abusive conduct, as well as the elimination of bias and discrimination across various online platforms and news outlets.

Fluid temperature plays a critical role in thermal hydraulics heat transfer analysis, yet accurately measuring or estimating it in multiphase flows remains a significant challenge. This difficulty arises because thermocouple signals combine temperature data from all phases and are subject to substantial noise. To address this, the study introduces a novel method for estimating local fluid temperature in multiphase environments using experimental time-series data. By treating the thermocouple signal as a sequence with Markov properties and applying the particle filter method to extract the fluid temperature, this approach offers a new solution. The article provides a comprehensive description of this methodology.

Minimizing prediction latency in time-sensitive domains like healthcare and finance has driven extensive research into early time series classification. The core objective of these methods is to classify incomplete sequences as quickly as possible while maintaining a target accuracy. In recent years, numerous approaches have emerged to address this challenge. Given that existing solutions tackle the problem from various angles, a comprehensive review is essential to understand the field's current landscape. These methods have shown promising results across diverse applications, such as human activity recognition, gene expression-based diagnostics, and industrial monitoring. This paper offers a systematic review of literature on early classification for both univariate and multivariate time series. We categorize existing strategies into four distinct groups: prefix-based, shapelet-based, model-based, and miscellaneous approaches. Furthermore, we explore applications in areas including industrial monitoring, intelligent transportation, and medicine, concluding with a concise summary of current literature and suggested future research directions.

Random forests remain the preferred model for applied statisticians and data scientists due to their proven efficacy as pre-built predictors. However, until recently, the specific mechanisms driving their performance were poorly understood. Recently, two competing hypotheses have arisen to explain this success: one rooted in interpolation and the other in regularization. This study supports the regularization hypothesis by re-evaluating the long-standing debate on pruning individual trees within an ensemble through a regularization lens. Although default implementations in most software packages utilize trees of near-maximum depth, we present compelling evidence that tree depth functions as a natural form of regularization throughout the entire process. Specifically, our findings indicate that random forests employing shallow trees are beneficial in scenarios with a low signal-to-noise ratio. Furthermore, while constructing this argument, we critique the emerging concept of "double descent" in random forests by drawing comparisons to U-statistics; we argue that observed fluctuations in accuracy stem from simple averaging rather than interpolation.

Pulsars are renowned for their exceptional rotational stability, yet they gradually lose energy through braking mechanisms that remain a subject of intense scientific inquiry. Typically modeled as highly magnetized neutron stars emitting radiation from their magnetic poles, it is logical to attribute this energy loss to a magnetic brake. However, a purely magnetic braking model fails to accurately explain the observed spindown rates. Consequently, numerous alternative mechanisms have been proposed, including the pulsar wind model, wherein a stream of particles originating from the pulsar transports a portion of its rotational kinetic energy. This mechanism relies critically on three parameters: the dipole magnetic field strength ($B$), the angle between the magnetic and rotation axes ($\phi$), and the density of primary particles ($\zeta$) within the magnetosphere. Unlike previous studies on this topic, this work presents, for the first time, a statistical framework that integrates both dipole magnetic and wind braking effects. This approach enables the constraining of the aforementioned parameters, specifically for the Crab and Vela pulsars.

This article pursues three primary objectives. First, it provides a pedagogical overview of Noether's two theorems and their consequences for energy conservation within general relativity, a topic central to the historical debates involving Einstein, Hilbert, Klein, and Noether. Second, it presents and contrasts two distinct proposals for defining gravitational energy and momentum—both of which, to the author's knowledge, remain unexamined in philosophical discourse, with one being highly influential in physics. Third, it evaluates these proposals against the backdrop of recent philosophical inquiries into energy and momentum conservation in general relativity.

Following a brief review of the historical controversies surrounding energy conservation among the aforementioned physicists, the paper explicates Noether's theorems. It demonstrates that Einstein's gravitational energy-momentum pseudo-tensor, along with its superpotential, is determined by boundary terms in the action via Noether's theorem. Specifically, the liberty to incorporate an arbitrary superpotential into the pseudo-tensor mirrors the freedom to add boundary terms to the action without altering the equations of motion, a constraint that applies equally to both scenarios. The text also surveys two specific proposals for energy and momentum in general relativity: one serving as a quasi-local alternative to local formulations, and the other extending Einstein's local pseudo-tensor methodology. Finally, the paper examines recent philosophical literature on GR energy and momentum conservation, assessing and comparing the two proposals through the lens of issues regarding diffeomorphism invariance and background independence.

We show that time-reversal (T) invariance can be broken even if the Pontecorvo--Maki--Nakagawa--Sakata (PMNS) lepton mixing matrix is real. We establish a sufficient condition for T violation in neutrino oscillations occurring within both matter and electromagnetic fields. Using a two-flavor model, we derive the spin-flavor transition probabilities associated with T violation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transition probabilities for neutrinos in a moving medium under an electromagnetic field differ from those of antineutrinos in a medium composed of antiparticles and an electromagnetic field solely by the sign of the T-violating term.

Achieving precise optical path difference (OPD) control in the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) was essential for characterizing the Galactic center's black hole, a breakthrough that contributed to the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics. Current initiatives aim to push these OPD limits further, specifically targeting 100nm OPD RMS on the 8m unit telescopes (UTs) to enhance contrast and sensitivity. This study calculated the theoretical atmospheric OPD limit for the VLTI to be 5nm and 15nm RMS, whereas current operational levels under bright targets and favorable atmospheric conditions stand at approximately 200nm RMS for UTs and 100nm RMS for the 1.8m auxiliary telescopes (ATs). Experimental results support the theoretically predicted $f^{-17/3}$ power law for ATs caused by telescope filtering, a phenomenon not yet observed in UTs. By modeling vibrating mirrors as damped harmonic oscillators, we successfully fitted the UT OPD power spectral density (PSD) of the Gravity fringe tracker to less than 1nm/$\sqrt{Hz}$ RMSE up to 100Hz, potentially explaining a hidden $f^{-17/3}$ power law on the UTs. Analysis revealed that vibration frequencies between 60-90Hz and 40-50Hz generally dominate the closed-loop OPD residuals in Gravity. Cross-correlating accelerometer data with Gravity observations indicated that the 40-50Hz range is strongly influenced by M1-M3 mirrors, while the 60-100Hz power is likely attributable to components between M4-M10. Furthermore, the vibrating mirror model demonstrates that achieving sub-100nm OPD RMS for specific baselines (currently around 200nm RMS) necessitates the removal of nearly all vibration sources below 100Hz.

We report a measurement of atmospheric tau neutrino appearance resulting from oscillations, utilizing three years of data from the DeepCore sub-array of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. This study examines atmospheric neutrinos across the full sky within reconstructed energy ranges of 5.6 to 56 GeV to identify a statistical surplus of cascade-like events, indicative of tau neutrino interactions. For both CC+NC and CC-only interaction channels, we determine the tau neutrino normalization to be $0.73^{+0.30}_{-0.24}$ and $0.57^{+0.36}_{-0.30}$, respectively.
