These findings rule out the non-existence of tau neutrino oscillations with significances of 3.2 sigma and 2.0 sigma. The outcomes align with and match the precision of a concurrent confirmatory IceCube analysis, as well as results from other experimental efforts.

As spectrum resources dwindle, wireless communication systems increasingly rely on large antenna arrays to leverage spatial degrees of freedom, utilizing technologies like millimeter wave massive MIMO, reconfigurable intelligent surface-assisted communications, and cell-free massive MIMO. In these architectures, acquiring precise channel state information (CSI) remains challenging and acts as a critical bottleneck for communication links. This article introduces channel extrapolation, a concept that infers the majority of channel parameters from a limited subset. Since this process essentially involves mapping one parameter subspace to another, deep learning (DL) serves as a robust architecture to approximate this mapping function. We begin by examining the requirements, conditions, and challenges inherent to channel extrapolation. Subsequently, we detail three common extrapolation approaches spanning the antenna, frequency, and physical terminal dimensions, outlining their underlying principles, design hurdles, and specific DL strategies. It becomes evident that channel extrapolation can significantly lower transmission overhead and improve performance relative to traditional methods. Finally, we outline several promising research directions for channel extrapolation within future intelligent communication systems.

Knowledge graph (KG) embedding techniques, which map entities and relations into unique vectors, have demonstrated significant success in various reasoning tasks. However, assigning a uniform embedding dimension to both dense and sparse entities leads to over-parameterization for sparse entities or underfitting for dense ones. While increasing the dimension often improves performance, inference time scales log-linearly with the total number of entities due to the traversal and comparison of all candidates. Consequently, both parameter count and inference speed pose substantial challenges when dealing with massive entity sets. To address this, we introduce PIE, a **p**arameter and **i**nference **e**fficient approach. Drawing inspiration from tensor decomposition, we decompose the entity embedding matrix into low-rank components, reducing parameters by more than half while retaining comparable performance. To accelerate inference, we propose a self-supervised auxiliary task resembling fine-grained entity typing; by randomly masking and reconstructing connected relations, the model learns entity-relation co-occurrence patterns. Leveraging this fine-grained typing allows us to filter out irrelevant entities during inference, achieving targets with potentially sub-linear time complexity. Experiments on link prediction benchmarks validate these core capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution on the Open Graph Benchmark's large-scale WikiKG90Mv2 dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results.

A position-sensitive thin gap chamber has been constructed, with its position resolution evaluated using cosmic muons. This paper details the detector's structure, the methodology employed for measuring position resolution, and the resulting data.

Multi-source domain adaptation has received significant research attention, yet the inherent feature distribution shifts across specific domains often lead to negative transfer, which diminishes a model's ability to generalize to unseen tasks. In Federated Learning (FL), global model parameters are shared to synthesize knowledge from client models trained on distinct data domains; however, FL's strict data confidentiality limits the efficacy of conventional domain adaptation techniques that rely on access to raw domain data. To address this, we introduce Federated Knowledge Alignment (FedKA), a novel federated domain generalization approach. FedKA utilizes feature distribution matching within a global workspace to enable the global model to learn domain-invariant client features without requiring knowledge of the client data. Furthermore, FedKA incorporates a federated voting mechanism that produces target domain pseudo-labels through client consensus to support global model fine-tuning. We conducted extensive experiments, including ablation studies, to assess FedKA's performance on image and text classification tasks using various architectures. Empirical results indicate that FedKA achieves performance improvements of 8.8% and 3.5% on the Digit-Five and Office-Caltech10 datasets, respectively, and a 0.7% gain on the Amazon Review dataset under conditions of extremely limited training data. Additionally, we evaluated FedKA's capacity to mitigate FL negative transfer using a new metric termed "Group Effect." Our findings demonstrate that FedKA reduces negative transfer, thereby enhancing performance gains through model aggregation by a factor of four.

Accelerating the reconstruction of magnetic resonance images (MRI) presents a difficult ill-posed inverse problem, largely caused by aggressive under-sampling in k-space. This paper introduces ReconFormer, a recurrent transformer model designed to iteratively recover high-fidelity MR images from highly under-sampled k-space data. The architecture relies on Recurrent Pyramid Transformer Layers (RPTL), which simultaneously leverage intrinsic multi-scale information within each unit and capture deep feature correlations through recurrent states. Additionally, ReconFormer is lightweight, utilizing a recurrent structure to enhance parameter efficiency. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness across multiple datasets and varying MRI sequences, showing it outperforms state-of-the-art methods with superior efficiency. The implementation code will be accessible at https://github.com/guopengf/ReconFormer.

In recent years, determining the precise locations of street objects from images has become a significant area of focus. We introduce a method to enhance the geolocation of assets captured in street view imagery by leveraging Structure from Motion to improve the quality of associated metadata. Furthermore, we refine the predicted object positions by integrating contextual geographic data derived from OpenStreetMap. We validate our proposed pipeline through experiments comparing its performance against current state-of-the-art geotagging techniques specifically for traffic lights.

Although theoretical research in waveguide quantum electrodynamics predominantly focuses on single- and two-photon Fock state inputs, experimental investigations mainly utilize faint coherent light. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze and distinguish between linear and nonlinear light scattering by two-level or three-level emitters situated within open waveguides, accommodating both Fock and coherent state inputs. We establish criteria for comparing light transport characteristics, as well as the Kerr and cross-Kerr nonlinearities of the medium under these two input conditions. Furthermore, we formulate a generalized description of the Kerr and cross-Kerr effects applicable to various input types, enabling a comparison of Kerr and cross-Kerr nonlinearities between photons within these models.

Driven by the growing demand for blockchain to enable secure, auditable, and decentralized applications, several associated challenges must be overcome. This letter specifically addresses the latency inherent in Proof-of-Work (PoW) networks, where participants validate new data for the distributed ledger through consensus to confirm transactions. We introduce a novel end-to-end latency model grounded in batch-service queuing theory, which uniquely characterizes timers and forks. Additionally, we analytically derive an estimate for the optimal block size. Supported by simulation results, we demonstrate that this optimal block size approximation is a consistent approach that yields near-optimal performance by substantially reducing the overheads of blockchain applications.

We present a comprehensive framework that explicitly realizes edge modes in classical gauge field theory as dynamical reference frames, an interpretation frequently proposed but rarely made fully explicit. Focusing on a bounded region $M$ with a codimension-one time-like boundary $\Gamma$ embedded in a global spacetime, we derive consistent variational principles and boundary actions for the subregion starting from a global variational principle. This approach employs a post-selection procedure on $\Gamma$ to isolate the subsector of the global theory compatible with arbitrary gauge-invariant boundary conditions in $M$. These conditions link configuration fields on $\Gamma$ to a dynamical frame field encoding information about the spacetime outside $M$, allowing them to be interpreted as relational or frame-dressed observables. Generally, this external frame field leaves an imprint on the dynamics within $M$, manifesting as a local field on $\Gamma$ known as an edge mode. We identify boundary symmetries as frame reorientations and demonstrate that they categorize into three types based on boundary conditions, each influencing the physical nature of the edge modes differently. Built upon the covariant phase space formalism, this construction is broadly applicable to any gauge field theory. We validate the method with three standard examples: Maxwell, Abelian Chern-Simons, and non-Abelian Yang-Mills theories. Additionally, we examine a mechanical toy model to align our findings with recent research on (quantum) reference frames.

Multiple instances have demonstrated that the module category of a vertex operator algebra (VOA) corresponds to a representation category of a specific quantum group. This article focuses on establishing such a duality for the Virasoro VOA at a generic central charge, an object that is arguably the simplest VOA yet possesses significant structural complexity. Rather than examining the entirety of the generic Virasoro VOA's modules, we restrict our analysis to the infinitely many modules located in the first row of the Kac table. Leveraging an explicit quantum group approach based on Coulomb gas integrals, we provide a novel proof of the fusion rules, demonstrate the analyticity of compositions of intertwining operators, and establish that conformal blocks are entirely dictated by the quantum group method. Most importantly, we prove the associativity of intertwining operators within the first-row modules, revealing that this associativity is controlled by the quantum group's $6j$-symbols. These findings establish a concrete duality between a VOA and a quantum group, providing the essential tools required to prove the equivalence between the first-row subcategory of the generic Virasoro VOA modules and the category of (type-1) finite-dimensional representations of $\mathcal{U}_{q}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2})$.

Current Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) methods typically prioritize either result quality by processing entire videos offline or processing speed by analyzing frames sequentially, often at the expense of performance. This paper presents an online approach that matches the quality of offline methods. We introduce a message-passing graph neural network that represents objects and tracks their relationships across time, alongside a new module designed to fuse features from a feature pyramid network with residual connections. Trained end-to-end, our model achieves state-of-the-art results on the YouTube-VIS dataset among online methods. Additional experiments on the DAVIS dataset confirm the model's ability to generalize to video object segmentation tasks. The source code is accessible at: \url{https://github.com/caganselim/TLTM}

This paper introduces a neural architecture designed for identifying Slavic languages within speech signals, extending the application of deep neural networks beyond general spoken language recognition to specific multilingual tasks. We examine the model's emergent representations to determine if they align with objective metrics of linguistic relatedness or with non-expert perceptions of language similarity. Our findings indicate that while the learned representation space largely captures language relatedness, the strongest predictor of similarity within this space is the degree of perceptual confusability between languages.

We define (multiplicative) Hom-Lie-Yamaguti superalgebras, which extend both Hom-Lie supertriple systems (and, by extension, ternary multiplicative Hom-Nambu superalgebras) and Hom-Lie superalgebras in a manner analogous to how Lie-Yamaguti superalgebras generalize Lie supertriple systems and Lie superalgebras. We demonstrate that the category of (multiplicative) Hom-Lie-Yamaguti superalgebras remains closed under twisting by self-morphisms and provide several illustrative examples. Furthermore, we extend the concept of $n^{th}$-derived binary Hom-superalgebras to $n^{th}$-derived binary-ternary Hom-superalgebras, proving that the category of Hom-Lie-Yamaguti superalgebras is closed under the formation of these derived structures.

For discrete-time dynamical systems that are $C^1$-smooth and strongly monotone, it is demonstrated that converging to linearly stable cycles is a prevalent asymptotic behavior from a measure-theoretic perspective. These findings are subsequently applied to specific classes of time-periodic parabolic equations, yielding new insights into the prevalence of convergence toward periodic solutions. Specifically, for equations featuring Neumann boundary conditions on convex domains, we establish that the set of initial conditions leading to solutions converging to spatially homogeneous periodic solutions is prevalent. Conversely, for equations defined on radially symmetric domains, we prove the prevalence of initial values resulting in solutions that asymptotically approach radially symmetric periodic solutions.

This study examines how noise affects the training of object detection networks within the medical field and explores mitigation strategies through enhanced training protocols. Since annotating extensive medical datasets for data-intensive deep learning models is costly and laborious, utilizing existing clinical data such as text reports, bookmarks, or lesion measurements could significantly lower these expenses. However, automatically extracting precise lesion bounding boxes remains challenging. We present a quantitative assessment of how noise in bounding box coordinates influences Faster R-CNN network performance specifically for breast mass detection. By randomly altering bounding boxes to simulate varying noise levels—up to six times the original size in our experiments—we evaluate the impact on the CBIS-DDSM public mammography dataset, which offers accurate lesion locations. Our findings demonstrate that noise propagates during training due to imperfect alignment between ground truth and network proposals, thereby diminishing the network's capacity to distinguish lesions from background tissue. Using the standard Intersection over Union criterion, the area under the FROC curve drops by as much as 9%. To address this, we propose a new matching criterion designed to increase tolerance to noise.

In reinforcement learning, the graph Laplacian has served as a powerful asset in task-agnostic scenarios, facilitating applications such as reward shaping and skill discovery. Recent efforts have attempted to address computational constraints in large or continuous state spaces by framing Laplacian learning as the optimization of a temporally-contrastive objective; however, this method assumes uniform access to all states, thereby neglecting the inherent exploration challenges. This work introduces an alternative approach capable of recovering the expressiveness and key properties of the Laplacian representation within a non-uniform prior setting. By integrating representation learning with a skill-based covering policy, we generate a superior training distribution to refine and expand the representation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that augmenting the representation objective with learned temporal abstractions enhances dynamics awareness and aids exploration. Our results indicate that this method effectively replaces the Laplacian in non-uniform contexts and scales to demanding continuous control tasks. Additionally, despite not being explicitly optimized for skill discovery, the acquired skills successfully tackle difficult continuous navigation problems with sparse rewards, a scenario where conventional skill discovery techniques often fail.

Word translation or bilingual lexicon induction (BLI) represents a fundamental cross-lingual objective designed to overcome lexical disparities across languages. This study introduces a robust, two-stage contrastive learning framework for BLI. In Stage C1, we refine standard cross-lingual linear mappings between static word embeddings (WEs) using a contrastive learning goal, further enhancing these maps through an integrated self-learning process. Stage C2 focuses on contrastive fine-tuning of mBERT specifically for BLI, thereby activating its word translation potential. Additionally, we demonstrate that static WEs generated from the mBERT model after Stage C2 complement those produced in Stage C1. Extensive experiments across standard BLI datasets for various languages and configurations reveal significant performance improvements from our framework. While Stage C1 alone surpasses all state-of-the-art BLI methods in our comparisons, the complete two-stage approach delivers even stronger results: we achieve gains across all 112 BLI setups, covering 28 language pairs.

We derive novel equitightness and $C([0,T];L^p(\mathbb{R}^N))$-convergence theorems for finite-difference schemes applied to generalized porous medium equations given by $\partial_tu-\mathfrak{L}[\varphi(u)]=g$ in $\mathbb{R}^N\times(0,T)$, where $\varphi$ is a continuous, nondecreasing function and $\mathfrak{L}$ represents either a local or nonlocal diffusion operator. These findings encompass scenarios involving slow diffusion, strongly degenerate Stefan problems, and fast diffusion exceeding a critical threshold. Furthermore, our work enhances prior results by the authors regarding $C([0,T];L_{\text{loc}}^p(\mathbb{R}^N))$-convergence. Achieving both equitightness and global $L^p(\mathbb{R}^N)$-convergence requires specific constraints on $\mathfrak{L}$ and $\varphi$; however, standard symmetric operators such as the Laplacian, fractional Laplacians, and generators of symmetric Lévy processes with fractional moments remain applicable. Additionally, we explore extensions to nonlinear, possibly strongly degenerate convection-diffusion equations.

Annotation ambiguity represents a primary challenge in Facial Expression Recognition (FER), stemming from subjective labeling and the inherent similarity between different facial expressions. To tackle this issue, we introduce DMUE, a solution that addresses ambiguity through two distinct approaches: latent distribution mining and pairwise uncertainty estimation. First, an auxiliary multi-branch learning framework is employed to effectively mine and characterize the latent distribution within the label space. Second, the pairwise semantic relationships among instances are fully leveraged to estimate the degree of ambiguity in the instance space. The proposed method is backbone-agnostic and incurs no additional computational cost during inference. Evaluated on both standard real-world benchmarks and synthetic noisy datasets, DMUE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

This study investigates the intriguing effects resulting from coupling a clean non-Hermitian chain exhibiting skin localization with a delocalized chain of equal length across different boundary conditions (BCs). We find that in ladders with weak rung coupling, non-Hermitian skin localization can generate a pseudo mobility edge within the complex energy plane, distinguishing between extended and localized states while facilitating unidirectional signal transport. Furthermore, under standard open BCs, we show that increasing the rung coupling leads to a gradual dominance of the non-Hermitian skin effect throughout the system. When the non-Hermitian chain is subject to open BCs while the other follows periodic BCs, a quantized winding number defined under periodic conditions characterizes the transition from the pseudo mobility edge to trivial extended phases, thereby establishing a "bulk-defect correspondence" in this quasi-1D non-Hermitian framework. Consequently, this work reveals deeper characteristics of non-Hermitian skin effects and clarifies the topological nature of non-Hermitian localized modes near systems with distinct localization behaviors.

The rising trends in Internet-of-Vehicles (IoV) necessitate centralized servers to gather and process sensitive data, as individual vehicles possess limited computational capacity. This centralization creates a critical need for robust privacy safeguards. While Differential Privacy (DP) is a widely used paradigm that ensures strong privacy by introducing noise, its direct application to IoV presents significant hurdles regarding data utility and effective protection. We identify that the primary challenge in DP-enabled IoV protection lies in synergizing DP with the unique characteristics of IoV, specifically the formation of unbalanced query batches resulting from frequent interactions between edge vehicles and central servers. To address this, we introduce HUT, a novel algorithm designed to achieve High UTility for DP protection within IoV. Our core insight leverages the inherent nature of unbalanced batches in IoV; by aggregating local batches and applying Order Constraints, we mitigate information loss caused by DP noise. Evaluations against state-of-the-art DP mechanisms demonstrate that HUT reduces information loss by 95.69% while simultaneously providing strong, mathematically guaranteed protection for sensitive data.

This study determines the optimal stroke sequences for a finite-sized swimming predator pursuing either a non-motile point or finite-sized prey within a low Reynolds number environment. We employ optimal control theory to find globally optimal solutions for point prey scenarios and utilize reinforcement learning (RL) for more general cases. The predator is modeled as a squirmer capable of forward and lateral translation, rotation, and stresslet flow generation. We identify specific squirming patterns that achieve time-optimal (TO) and efficiency-optimal (EO) predation. For point prey, the TO strategy involves translational motion along a two-fold L-shaped trajectory that leverages disturbance flows for acceleration. In contrast, utilizing a stresslet mode significantly enhances EO predation, enabling faster capture with reduced energy expenditure and higher efficiency by sucking the prey toward the predator. While a purely translating predator is less time-efficient than one combining translation and rotation, the latter occasionally achieves TO predation by retreating to advance. Furthermore, RL successfully replicates the globally optimal strategy for point prey, qualitatively capturing the essential two-fold characteristics of the TO path. By simulating an RL environment, we investigate how prey size influences the optimal predatory trajectory. These findings offer valuable insights for designing synthetic microswimmers, such as *in vivo* medical micro-robots, capable of capturing and approaching objects in viscous flows.

The incommensurate magnetism of CrB$_2$ is investigated using a spin model derived from density functional theory calculations. Comparing Heisenberg exchange interactions obtained via the disordered local moment (DLM) approach in the paramagnetic phase against those derived from a ferromagnetic treatment reveals substantial differences; the DLM method provides a notably more realistic description. The study identifies strong ferromagnetic coupling between Cr planes but largely frustrated interactions within them. While the ground state ordering vector proves sensitive to exchange interactions across many neighbor shells, the theory successfully reproduces the $q$-vector of the incommensurate spin spiral state ($0.213$ versus the experimental value of $0.285\times (2\pi)/(a/2)$ along $\Gamma-{\rm K}$). Furthermore, the strong geometric frustration inherent in these exchange interactions results in a relatively low Néel temperature of approximately 97 K, which aligns well with experimental findings.

We employed Density Functional Theory (DFT) to determine the core structures of $a_0[100](010)$ and $a_0[100](011)$ edge dislocations, as well as $a_0/2[\bar{1}\bar{1}1](1\bar{1}0)$ and $a_0/2[111](1\bar{1}0)$ $71^{\circ}$ mixed dislocations in body-centered cubic (bcc) iron. These calculations utilized Flexible Boundary Conditions (FBC), enabling isolated defect relaxation by coupling the dislocation core to an infinite harmonic lattice via the Lattice Green Function (LGF). Unlike prior FBC studies that relied on bulk crystal LGFs, our approach uses LGFs specific to dislocated geometries, thereby accounting for topological changes within the core and strain throughout the lattice. While a bulk-like approximation for force constants successfully optimized the cores of the $a_0[100](010)$ edge, $a_0[100](011)$ edge, and $a_0/2[111](1\bar{1}0)$ $71^{\circ}$ mixed dislocations, it proved insufficient for the $a_0/2[\bar{1}\bar{1}1](1\bar{1}0)$ dislocation; consequently, we derived its LGF using accurate force constants from a Gaussian approximation potential. The widths of the dislocation cores were quantified by the standard deviations of their Nye tensor distributions, revealing compact relaxed cores where magnetic moments on Fe atoms closely track volumetric strain distributions. Additionally, we computed these core structures using eight distinct classical interatomic potentials and assessed symmetry differences via the Fourier coefficients of their Nye tensor distributions. Most classical potential results aligned well with the DFT findings. These DFT geometries serve as benchmarks for classical potential investigations into work-hardening, as well as for calculating substitutional and interstitial sites to evaluate solute-dislocation interactions. These interactions provide essential inputs for mesoscale modeling of solute strengthening and diffusion near dislocations.

We report measurements of the branching fractions for the Cabibbo-favored $\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}\pi^{-}$ and the Cabibbo-suppressed $\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}K^{-}$ decay modes. The results are $\mathcal{B}(\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}\pi^{-}) = (2.48 \pm 0.01 \pm 0.09 \pm 0.04) \times 10^{-3}$ and $\mathcal{B}(\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}K^{-}) = (2.03 \pm 0.05 \pm 0.07 \pm 0.03) \times 10^{-4}$, where the uncertainties correspond respectively to statistical, systematic, and those arising from the $D^{+} \rightarrow K^{-}\pi^{+}\pi^{+}$ branching fraction. The ratio of these branching fractions, $R^{D} = \mathcal{B}(\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}K^{-}) / \mathcal{B}(\overline{B}{}^0\rightarrow D^{+}\pi^{-})$, is determined to be $[8.19 \pm 0.20(\rm stat) \pm 0.23(\rm syst)] \times 10^{-2}$. These analyses utilize the complete Belle data set, comprising $772 \times 10^{6} B\overline{B} $ pairs.

The conifold serves as a fundamental instance of a noncompact Calabi-Yau threefold featuring a simple flop; within M-theory, this configuration produces a 5d hypermultiplet at low energies, manifested by an M2-brane wrapping the vanishing sphere. We introduce a new gauge-theoretic approach to generate novel examples that extend the simple flop to length $l=1,\dots,6$. This technique enables the direct determination of Gopakumar-Vafa invariants. While these threefolds exhibit properties akin to the conifold, they are anticipated to support M2-bound states of higher degree, a prediction confirmed by our invariant calculations. Additionally, we comprehensively describe the corresponding Higgs branches by calculating their dimensions and flavor groups. Finally, our methods allow for the extraction of refined data, including the charges of the hypermultiplets under the flavor symmetry.

This study employs an autoethnographic case study of a Latinx high school student from a California agricultural community to demonstrate how AI is acquired beyond the classroom and how her personal background shaped her social-justice-driven applications of AI. Utilizing the concept of learning pathways from learning sciences, we contend that redesigning AI education to be more inclusive regarding socioeconomic status, ethnoracial identity, and gender is crucial for developing computational projects that tackle social injustice. Furthermore, we explore the roles of institutions, power structures, and community within her learning and application journey. Ultimately, the future of AI, its capacity to address social injustices, and its ability to mitigate negative consequences will rely on the participation and voices of students from the most vulnerable communities.

We introduce a treatment interference framework in which a unit's response is determined solely by its own treatment assignment and the assignments of units within its K-neighborhood. While existing detection approaches rely on meticulously designed randomized experiments and conditional randomization tests applied to specific focal units, we provide strategic guidance for selecting these focal units under our proposed model. Furthermore, a simulation study assesses the performance of current methods for identifying network interference. Our results demonstrate that the recommended selection of focal units yields highly powerful tests for treatment interference that surpass the effectiveness of existing experimental techniques.

This work examines Wick-rotations applied to left-invariant metrics on Lie groups by leveraging findings from real geometric invariant theory (references 1–3). We introduce an invariant specifically for such rotations and delineate the conditions under which a pseudo-Riemannian Lie group can be transformed into a Riemannian one. Furthermore, we establish a generalized theorem applicable to arbitrary Lie algebras that confirms the existence and conjugacy of Cartan involutions, extending $\acute{E}$. Cartan's original result.

Recent years have underscored the critical role of telemedicine, which facilitates remote diagnosis and treatment. Within this domain, Computational Paralinguistics, a specialized branch of speech processing, plays a vital role by extracting speaker-related information. This study concentrates on two specific paralinguistic challenges: detecting mask usage and predicting breathing states. Effective solutions for these tasks could significantly aid in monitoring and curbing the spread of viruses such as COVID-19. Current state-of-the-art approaches rely on deep neural network ensembles, such as ResNets, combined with feature engineering. While these methods achieve high accuracy, their large size and heavy computational demands limit portability to resource-constrained devices. Consequently, their dimensions and processing speeds render them impractical for telemedicine deployment. Conversely, lighter, feature-engineered alternatives are often labor-intensive and complex, hindering rapid system deployment. To address these issues, this work introduces an ensemble-based automatic feature selection technique designed to create fast, memory-efficient systems. Specifically, we propose an output-gradient-based approach to identify key features using large, high-performing ensembles prior to training a smaller model. Experimental results demonstrate that utilizing neural network ensembles with output-gradient-based features reduces inference times by 25% to 32%. This method provides a straightforward pathway to accelerate system performance for real-time application while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to larger ensembles utilizing all spectral features.

Combinatorial research frequently investigates the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP), a model inspired by statistical mechanics where particles of fixed species move across a lattice. While traditional ASEP allows movement without species transformation, this paper introduces a new combinatorial framework known as the doubly asymmetric simple exclusion process (DASEP). Motivated by biological systems, the DASEP distinguishes itself by permitting particles to change species in addition to moving. The study examines the combinatorics of DASEP on a one-dimensional lattice, including its associated generating function, and analyzes its stationary probabilities. Furthermore, the paper establishes proven relationships between these stationary probabilities and those of the simpler ASEP.

A pixelated silicon detector, initially designed for particle physics, was employed to measure the beam profile of a Co-60 irradiator within a water phantom, with results compared against those from a pinpoint ionization chamber. The relative profiles from both detectors differed by approximately 0.02, but after applying correction factors derived from Monte Carlo simulations to the pixel detector data, this discrepancy was reduced to nearly 0.005. Additionally, the detector's pulse-height measurement capability was utilized to record an electron pulse-height spectrum in water under the Co-60 beam, yielding results that aligned well with simulation predictions.

**Objective:** In laparoscopic liver surgery (LLS), pre-operative data can be superimposed onto the intra-operative view by aligning a 3D pre-operative model with a partial surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. To facilitate this, we investigate learning-based feature descriptors, a method previously unexplored for laparoscopic liver registration. Additionally, no existing dataset supports the training or evaluation of these descriptors.

**Approach:** We introduce the LiverMatch dataset, comprising 16 pre-operative models paired with their simulated intra-operative 3D surfaces. We also propose the LiverMatch network, specifically designed for this application, which generates per-point feature descriptors, visibility scores, and corresponding matched points.

**Findings:** We evaluated the LiverMatch network against a similar network and a histogram-based 3D descriptor using the LiverMatch dataset's testing split, which contained two unseen pre-operative models and 1,400 intra-operative surfaces. Results indicate that the LiverMatch network produces more accurate and dense matches than the alternative methods and can be effectively integrated with a RANSAC-ICP-based algorithm to ensure precise initial alignment.

**Conclusion:** Applying learning-based feature descriptors in laparoscopic liver registration shows great promise for achieving accurate initial rigid alignment, which acts as a crucial starting point for subsequent non-rigid registration. The dataset and code will be made available upon acceptance.

A tree $t$-spanner of a graph $G$ is a spanning tree $T$ where the distance between any two adjacent vertices in $G$ does not exceed $t$. The minimum such $t$ is defined as the tree stretch index. The $t$-admissibility problem involves determining whether the tree stretch index is at most $t$. In its optimization form, the minimal $t$ making $G$ $t$-admissible is referred to as the stretch index of $G$, denoted $\sigma_T(G)$. For a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, checking $2$-admissibility is solvable in $O(n+m)$ time, while determining $t$-admissibility is NP-complete for $t \geq 4$, with the case for $t = 3$ remaining an open problem for over two decades. Since understanding the structure of specific graph classes is crucial for resolving the complexity of $3$-admissibility, this paper introduces simpler and more efficient algorithms to verify $2$ and $3$-admissibility for families of graphs containing few $P_4$'s and $(k,\ell)$-graphs. Additionally, for $(0,\ell)$-graphs, we establish lower and upper bounds for the stretch index and characterize those graphs that achieve the proposed upper bound. Finally, we demonstrate that $t$-admissibility remains NP-complete even when restricted to line graphs of subdivided graphs.

We investigate light-front dynamical quantum electrodynamics (QED) through the lens of null-plane causal perturbation theory. By demonstrating equivalence with instant dynamics for scattering processes, we derive the normalization required to construct the instantaneous terms within the standard null-plane QED Lagrangian density. Furthermore, we analyze vacuum polarization by examining its insertion into Møller scattering; this normalization yields the complete photon propagator, which aligns with the instant dynamics result only when gauge invariance is properly incorporated.

We examine how surface states affect the nonlinear Hall response in time-reversal invariant, non-centrosymmetric Weyl semimetals. Utilizing a minimal two-band model, we conduct a tomography of the Berry curvature dipole within a slab system. Our findings indicate that in the type-I phase, the nonlinear Hall response remains largely unaffected by Fermi arcs or other trivial surface states. Conversely, in the type-II phase, these surface states significantly enhance the Berry curvature dipole, resulting in a pronounced dependence on slab thickness. This behavior varies with the specific nature of the surface states and the chosen slab geometry. To validate these findings for realistic materials, we carried out first-principles calculations of the Berry curvature dipole on WTe$_2$, confirming the substantial impact of surface states for certain slab configurations. Our results imply that surface states—regardless of whether they are topological or not—can contribute far more efficiently to the nonlinear Hall response than bulk states. This insight extends beyond topological semimetals to topologically trivial non-centrosymmetric materials and heterostructures, offering new avenues for the interfacial engineering of the nonlinear Hall effect.

The STAR experiment at RHIC is executing an extensive high-energy spin physics program designed to elucidate the proton's internal structure and dynamics through polarized proton-proton collisions at center-of-mass energies of $\sqrt{s} = 200$ GeV and $\sqrt{s} = 500/510$ GeV. With nearly complete azimuthal coverage, STAR can reconstruct leptons, hadrons, and jets within the mid-rapidity region ($|\eta|<1$). Data from the 2009 RHIC run regarding inclusive jet longitudinal double spin asymmetries reveal the first non-zero gluon contribution ($\Delta g(x,Q^{2}) / g(x,Q^{2})$) to the proton spin across the Bjorken-x range of $0.05<x<1$. Furthermore, recent measurements of longitudinal single-spin asymmetries for $W^{+/-}$ bosons at $\sqrt{s} = 500/510$ GeV offer a direct investigation into polarized anti-u and anti-d quark distributions ($\Delta \bar{u}(x,Q^{2})$, $\Delta \bar{d}(x,Q^{2})$). These findings refine constraints on the proton's polarized gluon and sea quark distributions within the kinematic region accessible to RHIC. Looking ahead, future high-energy polarized proton-proton runs, supported by detector upgrades, will investigate the gluonic contribution to proton spin over an expanded kinematic range.

This study investigates the near-threshold inclusive photoproduction of $\Xi^-$ hyperons from $^{12}$C and $^{184}$W targets using a first-collision model based on the nuclear spectral function. The framework incorporates incoherent $\Xi^-$ production via direct elementary ${\gamma}p \to K^+{K^+}\Xi^-$ and ${\gamma}n \to K^+{K^0}\Xi^-$ reactions, accounting for the effects of nuclear effective scalar potentials ($K^+$, $K^0$, $\Xi^-$) alongside Coulomb interactions. It further considers the absorption of final $\Xi^-$ hyperons within nuclear matter, nucleon binding energies, and Fermi motion. Absolute differential cross sections and their ratios for $\Xi^-$ production at laboratory polar angles up to 45$^{\circ}$ are calculated for photon energies of 2.5 and 3.0 GeV, both with and without phase space constraints on the $\Xi^-$ emission angle in the respective ${\gamma}p$ center-of-mass frames. Additionally, the momentum dependence of the transparency ratio for the $^{184}$W/$^{12}$W pair is evaluated at these energies. The results demonstrate that, unlike the transparency ratio, the absolute and relative $\Xi^-$ momentum distributions exhibit distinct sensitivity to variations in the scalar $\Xi^-$ nuclear mean-field potential at saturation density ($\rho_0$) within the low-momentum range of 0.1--0.8 GeV/c. Consequently, precise measurements of these distributions in a dedicated experiment at the CEBAF facility would yield valuable insights into $\Xi^-$ in-medium properties, complementing data obtained from ($K^-$,$K^+$) reactions at initial momenta of 1.6--1.8 GeV/c.

Hybrid probabilistic logic programs leverage the enhanced expressivity of logic programming—augmented with facts modeling both discrete and continuous distributions—to capture multiple scenarios. Establishing the semantics for these programs is vital, as it guarantees that a probability value can be assigned to every query. In this work, we present a specific syntax based on a recent semantic proposal and examine the syntactic constraints necessary to maintain well-definedness.

This study examines the drift-implicit (backward) Euler numerical method applied to stochastic differential equations featuring unbounded drifts driven by arbitrary $\lambda$-Hölder continuous processes where $\lambda\in(0,1)$. Under mild moment conditions on the noise's Hölder constant, we establish that the $L^r(\Omega;L^\infty([0,T]))$-rate of convergence equals $\lambda$. As illustrations, we apply these schemes to the generalized Cox--Ingersoll-Ross and Tsallis--Stariolo--Borland models, with findings supported by simulation results.

A quantum lattice algorithm (QLA) has been formulated to solve Maxwell's equations within scalar dielectric media, employing the Riemann-Silberstein representation. For spatial inhomogeneities varying along the x or y axes, the algorithm necessitates 8 qubits per lattice site; this is possible because the associated Pauli spin matrices contain off-diagonal elements that enable collisional entanglement between two qubits. Conversely, inhomogeneities dependent on the z-axis demand 16 qubits per site, as the $\sigma_z$ Pauli spin matrix is diagonal. Simulations were conducted to model the time evolution of an initial electromagnetic pulse traveling normally toward a boundary layer separating two media with distinct refractive indices. The results demonstrated excellent consistency across all three representations and strong alignment with standard plane wave boundary condition outcomes regarding reflection and transmission at a dielectric discontinuity. Notably, the QLA simulation achieved these results without imposing explicit boundary conditions at the continuous yet sharply increasing boundary layer.

Optimal sensor selection policies are crucial for numerous engineering fields, including event detection and autonomous navigation. This study addresses the synthesis of such policies over an infinite horizon using a discounted cost framework. The problem is modeled via value iteration across the continuous space of covariance matrices. To ensure computational feasibility, we develop an approximate sensor selection approach that utilizes point-based value iteration over a finite mesh of covariance matrices, constrained by a user-defined bounded trace. We offer theoretical bounds on the suboptimality of the resulting policies and include numerical examples that compare these findings against established results.

The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (KHI) represents a nonlinear, shear-driven phenomenon occurring at the boundaries of plasma shear flows. Although previously inferred in various astrophysical plasmas and observed both in situ at planetary magnetospheres and remotely at coronal mass ejection boundaries, direct and unambiguous detection of KHI within the solar wind remained elusive. This study reports the first in-situ observations of active KHI in the solar wind, captured by the Solar Orbiter during its cruise phase. The instability was identified within a shear layer of the slow solar wind near the Heliospheric Current Sheet, exhibiting characteristics consistent with linear theoretical predictions for its growth. We conducted an analysis to determine the local configuration of the KHI and established a 2-D MHD simulation using empirical parameters to validate the shear layer's stability. Furthermore, magnetic spectra associated with the KHI event were examined. Our findings confirm that the observed conditions meet the KHI onset criteria derived from linear theory, a conclusion reinforced by the simulation results. Geometric analyses of the current sheet further align with KHI development. Additionally, we document an ion jet consistent with magnetic reconnection at a compressed current sheet occurring within the KHI interval. The KHI is shown to generate magnetic and velocity fluctuations displaying power-law scalings of approximately $k^{-5/3}$ in the inertial range and $k^{-2.8}$ in the dissipation range. These results provide strong evidence for KHI development in the solar wind, offering new insights into shear-driven turbulence mediated by KHI and its role in driving solar wind fluctuations.

Various techniques exist for assessing the dynamical state of galaxy clusters using observational data, with morphological image analysis being particularly effective. This study introduces a novel approach that analytically models cluster images using Zernike polynomials (ZPs), a set of orthogonal functions. The method was validated against mock high-resolution Compton parameter maps of synthetic galaxy clusters from THE THREE HUNDRED project. To characterize morphology, we defined a single parameter, $\mathcal{C}$, derived from specific ZP contributions within the model. We confirmed that $\mathcal{C}$ exhibits a linear correlation with both standard morphological parameter combinations and a dedicated 3D dynamical-state indicator available for the synthetic clusters. Furthermore, we present initial findings from applying Zernike modelling to Compton parameter maps of local clusters ($z < 0.1$) observed by the $\textit{Planck}$ satellite, along with preliminary results from similar morphological analyses on mock X-ray maps of THE THREE HUNDRED clusters.

This research investigates a higher-dimensional analogue of Marstrand's circle packing problem concerning curves. Specifically, we examine families of curves formed by translating and dilating a base curve $\gamma$ in $\mathbb R^d$, defined as $x + t\gamma$ where $(x,t) \in \mathbb R^d \times (0,\infty)$. For any Borel set $F$ within $\mathbb R^d \times (0,\infty)$, we demonstrate that the union of these curves, $\bigcup_{(x,t) \in F} (x + t\gamma)$, possesses a Hausdorff dimension of at least $\alpha+1$ provided the dimension of $F$ exceeds $\alpha$, assuming $\alpha \in (0, d-1)$. Additionally, we derive findings regarding unions of curves produced by multi-parameter dilations of $\gamma$. A key component of our approach is a local smoothing estimate applied to averages over curves with respect to fractal measures.

A well-known theorem regarding character degrees establishes that any finite group with fewer than four distinct character degrees must be solvable. We demonstrate an analogous result for character values, proving that if a finite group possesses fewer than eight character values in its character table, the group is necessarily solvable. This finding validates a conjecture proposed by T. Sakurai. Additionally, we provide a classification of non-solvable groups that contain exactly eight character values.

This study addresses leader-following formation control for heterogeneous, second-order, uncertain, input-affine nonlinear multi-agent systems represented by directed graphs. A tunable three-layer neural network (NN), comprising an input layer, two hidden layers, and an output layer, is introduced to approximate unknown nonlinearities. Unlike traditional methods that rely on trial and error to determine neuron counts, this approach utilizes \textit{a priori} knowledge to define the number of neurons per layer. Weight tuning laws are established via Lyapunov theory. The proposed solution combines robust integral of the sign of the error (RISE) feedback with NN-based control to solve the formation and leader-following challenges. The RISE component handles unknown leader dynamics and bounded disturbances, while the NN term addresses unknown nonlinearities in the system dynamics. Semi-global asymptotic tracking is rigorously demonstrated using Lyapunov stability analysis. Finally, the proposed method's efficiency and performance are evaluated by comparing results against two prior studies.

We investigate a two-dimensional quantum memory consisting of qubits arranged on a torus that implement an extended Fibonacci string-net code, developing error-correction strategies against depolarizing noise. Leveraging tube algebras, we design a collection of measurements and quantum gates capable of mapping arbitrary qubit errors into the string-net subspace and characterizing the resulting error syndromes using doubled Fibonacci anyons. Through tensor network methods, we quantitatively analyze the impact of Pauli noise on this subspace. Monte Carlo simulations of error correction within this Fibonacci code are conducted to evaluate various decoders. Under a fixed-rate sampling depolarizing noise model, we identify an error correction threshold of 4.7% when employing a clustering decoder. To our knowledge, this marks the first estimation of a threshold for a two-dimensional error-correcting code that supports universal quantum computation via anyon braiding within its code space.

We provide a description of the formal neighborhoods of the boundary divisor components within the Deligne-Mumford moduli stack $\overline{{\mathcal M}}_g$ of stable curves, utilizing an extended clutching construction we define. This construction serves as a formal analogue to the analytic plumbing process. The benefit of our approach lies in the ability to regulate the impact of altering formal parameters at the marked points involved in the gluing. As a primary application, we demonstrate that the first infinitesimal neighborhood of the boundary component $\Delta_{1,g-1}$ is canonically isomorphic to the corresponding first infinitesimal neighborhood in the normal bundle, specifically near the locus ${\mathcal M}_{1,1}\times {\mathcal M}_{g-1,1}\subset \Delta_{1,g-1}$ representing pairs of smooth curves with marked points. Furthermore, we illustrate how the extended clutching construction's coordinates facilitate the analysis of the period map in proximity to the boundary components $\Delta_{g_1,g_2}$.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) has seen significant research in recent years, typically focusing on four core components: aspect categories, aspect terms, opinion terms, and sentiment polarity. While previous studies often focus on identifying only some of these elements rather than predicting all four simultaneously, this work introduces the Aspect Sentiment Quad Prediction (ASQP) task. ASQP aims to jointly detect all sentiment elements as structured quads for opinionated sentences, offering a more thorough and complete representation of aspect-level sentiment. To achieve this, we propose a novel \textsc{Paraphrase} modeling paradigm that reframes the ASQP task as a paraphrase generation process. This generative approach enables an end-to-end solution for ASQP, thereby reducing error propagation common in sequential pipeline methods. Additionally, learning to generate these elements in natural language allows for the full utilization of their semantic information. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and the potential for cross-task transfer within the proposed unified \textsc{Paraphrase} framework.

Various exactly solvable spin models, such as the two- and three-dimensional Kitaev toric codes and the three-dimensional X-cube model, can be connected to their parent lattice gauge theories (LGTs) via the mathematical mechanism of 'Higgsing.' Building on the symmetries of these parent LGTs, one can subsequently construct field theories describing the low-energy excitations of the spin models. Recently, two of the authors introduced a variant of the three-dimensional toric code termed the F3 model; its elementary excitations combine the freeons and fluxons of the 3D toric code with the fractons of the X-cube model. In this study, we identify the parent LGT for the F3 model as a hybrid rank-1 and rank-2 U(1) LGT and derive the associated field theory. The resulting Lagrangian describes a three-dimensional toric code augmented by an additional term that couples the dynamics of fractons to those of fluxons. Furthermore, by rigorously maintaining the gauge invariance of the F3 model, we derive the matter component of the effective action. We also obtain the hydrodynamic equations of motion for the quasiparticles, accurately capturing their constrained dynamics, and finally, we present a tight-binding model for quasiparticle motion within the F3 framework.

As machine learning evolves, individual servers can no longer handle the entire dataset, necessitating a shift from centralized to distributed processing across multiple machines. However, privacy concerns persist within this distributed framework. Multi-key homomorphic encryption over torus (MKTFHE) emerges as a promising solution to address these privacy issues. Nevertheless, MKTFHE faces challenges regarding decryption security risks and functional limitations; recent advancements only support Boolean and linear operations, preventing direct computation of non-linear functions like Sigmoid. Consequently, high-performance implementation of common machine learning tasks, such as logistic regression and neural networks, remains difficult.

This paper introduces a novel distributed decryption protocol for MKTFHE by integrating secret sharing, designs an activation function specifically optimized for MKTFHE, and applies these innovations to execute logistic regression and neural network training within the MKTFHE framework. We establish the correctness and security of our decryption protocol and conduct a comparative analysis of efficiency and accuracy between our proposed activation function and the use of Sigmoid's Taylor polynomials. Experimental results demonstrate that our function achieves a 10-fold improvement in efficiency compared to directly using 7th-order Taylor polynomials, while maintaining training model accuracy comparable to high-order polynomial schemes.

As machine learning models improve in accuracy, they often grow more complex and opaque to human understanding. This "black-box" nature hinders their practical adoption, particularly in high-stakes fields like healthcare and defense where failures can be catastrophic. Offering interpretable and meaningful insights into model predictions can enhance user trust. Drawing on the well-established strategy of example-based reasoning—utilizing past experiences with similar tasks to justify decisions—this work introduces LEAFAGE, a novel explanation extraction method applicable to any black-box ML model. LEAFAGE generates explanations by visualizing similar training examples alongside feature importance scores, while also providing contrastive explanations tailored to user expectations. The method was evaluated for its fidelity to the underlying model and its practical utility. Results indicate that LEAFAGE outperforms the current state-of-the-art, LIME, in fidelity, specifically for models with non-linear decision boundaries. A user study further compared example-based explanations against feature importance-based ones, revealing that the former significantly surpassed the latter in perceived transparency, information sufficiency, competence, and confidence. Surprisingly, when assessing actual knowledge retention, participants demonstrated that feature importance explanations were less effective than no explanation at all; users found these explanations vague and difficult to generalize to new instances.

Delay and Age-of-Information (AoI) serve as vital performance indicators for emerging time-sensitive applications within the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). To achieve peak performance, it is essential to investigate the complex relationship between these two metrics in non-trivial scenarios. This study examines a heterogeneous Device-to-Device (D2D) IIoT network accommodating two traffic categories: those focused on AoI and those focused on delay. We propose a distributed, backlog-aware random access protocol enabling AoI-centric nodes to opportunistically utilize the channel by monitoring the queue status of delay-centric nodes. Furthermore, we construct an analytical framework to assess average delay and average AoI, formulating an optimization problem aimed at minimizing AoI while adhering to specific delay constraints. Finally, numerical results are presented to illustrate how various network parameters influence average delay and AoI, alongside the calculation of optimal parameters that minimize AoI under the given delay constraint.

The #MyBodyMyChoice hashtag, initially established to champion women's rights and bodily autonomy—particularly regarding abortion—was later co-opted during the Covid-19 pandemic by groups opposing containment measures like mask mandates and vaccination campaigns to assert their own autonomy. This paper examines how the discourse surrounding #MyBodyMyChoice on Twitter evolved post-outbreak, identifying two primary shifts. Semantically, the hashtag drifted toward Covid-19 topics, specifically within content resisting public health restrictions. Furthermore, while pre-pandemic usage featured content from experts and authorities, post-pandemic attention shifted toward individual voices.

We determine the mass of the vector meson within a vacuum where chiral symmetry is restored. This process involves decomposing the four-quark operators present in both vector and axial vector meson sum rules into components that are either chiral symmetric or symmetry-breaking, based on the contribution of fermion zero modes. By fitting the resulting vector and axial vector meson masses, we isolate each component. Assuming the symmetry-breaking part vanishes while the symmetric operator retains its vacuum expectation value, we derive a symmetric mass range for both vector and axial vector mesons of 550 to 600 MeV. This indicates that although chiral symmetry breaking generates the mass splitting between chiral partners, it contributes only a minor fraction to the overall symmetric mass.

We introduce two primary contributions that facilitate the application of graphon theory to model evolutionary processes. First, we propose a generative model for digraphons constructed from a finite subgraph basis, which effectively represents biological networks evolving through duplication. Second, we present a straightforward Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation for this Bayesian non-parametric model, utilizing a Dirichlet Chinese restaurant process framework and a Gibbs sampling algorithm to infer the prior. Subsequently, we demonstrate an efficient method for simulating finite basis segmentations of digraphons. This approach supports rapid evolutionary simulations via a compact 2-D representation of digraphons based on dynamic segment trees with square-root decomposition. Furthermore, we illustrate the flexibility of this representation in accommodating changes in graph nodes and modeling dynamic digraphons; by employing an amortized update strategy, we achieve an efficient time complexity of $O(\sqrt{|V|}\log{|V|})$ for updates.

Probabilistic quantum error correction is a method that employs postselection to verify whether encoded data has been successfully recovered. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of this probabilistic approach under general noise conditions. We extend the Knill-Laflamme conditions to accommodate errors correctable with probability. Our findings indicate that for certain noise channels, encoding information into a mixed state maximizes the likelihood of successful correction. Furthermore, we examine a key advantage of probabilistic correction over deterministic methods: by accepting a lower success probability, the procedure can correct errors arising from a wider variety of noise channels. Notably, when errors result from unitary interactions with an auxiliary qubit system, a qubit state can be probabilistically restored using just one additional physical qubit.
We derive results characterizing how rotation generators act on polynomials defined over a commutative ring, and we investigate harmonic polynomials within a strictly algebraic framework.

This study investigates the instabilities of quadratic band crossing systems toward Chern insulating states and uncorrelated disorder. We mapped the phase diagram across the topological mass and disorder strength, analyzing spectral, localization, and topological characteristics. In the absence of disorder, the system exhibits two gapped Chern insulating phases with Chern numbers $C=\pm2$ alongside a trivial phase with $C=0$. However, at finite disorder, the quadratic band crossing points become unstable, giving rise to emergent gapless Chern insulating phases with $C=\pm1$, which do not exist in the clean limit. These phases dominate a significant portion of the phase diagram at intermediate disorder levels and display traits of topological Anderson insulators, as they can be accessed via disorder-induced transitions from trivial states.

Space-time parity offers a solution to the strong CP problem and induces a spontaneously broken $SU(2)_R$ gauge symmetry. We explore baryogenesis mechanisms driven by a first-order $SU(2)_R$ phase transition, analogous to electroweak baryogenesis. The model employs minimal Higgs content, resolving the strong CP issue without requiring additional symmetries beyond parity. While parity symmetry appears to prohibit the $SU(2)_R$ anomaly associated with $B-L$, the specific arrangement of fermion masses enables $SU(2)_R$ sphalerons to generate a non-zero $B-L$ asymmetry in Standard Model particles, thereby evading washout by $SU(2)_L$ sphalerons. This framework predicts a new hyper-charged fermion whose mass correlates with both the $SU(2)_R$ symmetry breaking scale and the mass of the $SU(2)_R$ gauge boson; depending on the source of CP violation, this mass also relates to the electron electric dipole moment. Furthermore, in scenarios where a singlet scalar field facilitates both CP violation and the first-order phase transition, this singlet could be detected at future colliders.

The task of inharmonious region localization involves identifying areas within a synthetic image that clash with their surrounding background. This conflict primarily stems from color and lighting inconsistencies introduced by image editing. In this study, we propose converting the input image into a different color space to amplify the domain discrepancy between the inharmonious region and the background, thereby facilitating easier detection by the model. To achieve this, we introduce a new framework comprising a color mapping module and an inharmonious region localization network; the former utilizes a novel domain discrepancy magnification loss, while the latter can be any arbitrary localization network. Extensive experiments on an image harmonization dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/bcmi/MadisNet-Inharmonious-Region-Localization.

We develop supercharacter theories for finite groups formed via parabolic construction from simple groups of Lie types $A, B, C,$ and $D$. By analyzing rook placements within the root systems, we categorize both the supercharacters and the superclasses.

Despite the success of numerical Monte Carlo simulations, strong coupling expansions have not been systematically employed in lattice QCD thermodynamics for an extended period. However, the enduring sign problem at finite baryo-chemical potential has spurred interest in these approaches, either independently or alongside numerical methods, to explore finite density physics. This review outlines strategies that have yielded significant qualitative insights, including the emergence of the hadron resonance gas and the identification of the transition onset to baryon matter within specific regions of the QCD parameter space. Furthermore, in the simpler context of Yang-Mills theory, the deconfinement transition can be determined quantitatively even in the scaling region, suggesting promising avenues for continuum physics.

This study investigates the breakup dynamics of a capillary bridge situated on a hydrophobic stripe flanked by two hydrophilic stripes through both experimental observation and numerical direct simulations. The bridge originates from an evaporating water droplet wetting three adjacent stripes on a chemically patterned surface. By analyzing the breakup process within a phase space framework, researchers can assess the dynamics without relying on the uncertain determination of a specific breakup time. The simulations utilize the Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) method within the Free Surface 3D (FS3D) code, while the Surface Evolver tool generates physically accurate initial configurations consistent with experimental data. To mitigate numerical instabilities at the contact line, a novel discretization of the Navier-slip boundary condition is applied on staggered grids. The results indicate that the capillary bridge's breakup does not follow a single scaling law; rather, distinct scaling exponents apply at various stages, accompanied by qualitative structural changes. Ultimately, in the final breakup stage, the bridge forms a liquid thread that disintegrates in accordance with the Rayleigh-Plateau instability.

The emergent universe model offers a solution to the Big Bang singularity issue inherent in standard Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker cosmology by proposing that the Universe begins from a nonsingular static configuration. This study examines the feasibility of such a nonsingular state within the Kantowski-Sachs framework. By analyzing four and five-dimensional models (both with and without branes), we demonstrate that the existence and stability of this nonsingular state are contingent upon the spacetime dimensions and the characteristics of the fluid sustaining the geometry.

This paper introduces an attentional neural network designed for classifying folk songs. We propose the concept of musical motif embedding and demonstrate that by leveraging melodic local context, monophonic folk song motifs can be effectively modeled using the skipgram variant of the word2vec algorithm. These motif embeddings represent folk songs from Germany, China, and Sweden, which are then classified by an attentional neural network capable of identifying relevant motifs within a song. Our results indicate that the network achieves state-of-the-art accuracy through a fully unsupervised process, while the motif embeddings generate high-quality representations of folk songs. Furthermore, we discuss the benefits of this representation approach for large symbolic music corpora and its potential utility in the musicological analysis of folk song collections across diverse cultures and regions.

Federated learning (FL) was introduced to safeguard data privacy and virtually unify isolated data silos by enabling cooperative model training across organizations without compromising security or privacy. Nevertheless, FL encounters heterogeneity stemming from data space, statistical, and system dimensions. For instance, collaborating entities from diverse fields often possess data within different feature spaces, and participants may require personalized local models to accommodate non-IID and imbalanced data distributions alongside varying resource constraints on their devices. Consequently, heterogeneous FL has emerged to address these challenges. This survey provides a comprehensive examination of heterogeneous FL across data space, statistical, system, and model heterogeneity. It begins with an overview of FL, covering its definition and classifications. Subsequently, a precise taxonomy of heterogeneous FL settings is proposed for each heterogeneity type based on problem settings and learning objectives. The survey also explores transfer learning methods used to mitigate heterogeneity in FL, presents relevant applications, and concludes by highlighting current challenges and opportunities while envisioning future research directions focused on novel framework designs and trustworthy approaches.

We forecast rapid domain wall (DW) movement driven by a thermal gradient within a nanoscopic ferromagnetic MnBi stripe, propelled by exchange torque generated from magnon accumulation at the DWs. Depending on the sample's thickness, DWs can migrate in either a hot-to-cold or cold-to-hot direction. This discovery reveals an energy-efficient method for controlling DWs, which are crucial components in magnetic data processing technologies like racetrack memory.

To create highly efficient solar cells without requiring inhomogeneous doping, it is desirable to maximize the shift component of the bulk photovoltaic current in noncentric semiconductors featuring wide band gaps. I have demonstrated this maximization for a novel class of topological insulators, where the band topology permits only polar crystal symmetries. In these materials, the $\boldsymbol{k}$-dependent electron-hole dipole moment (or "shift vector") cannot be continuously adjusted to zero across the entire Brillouin zone. Instead, averaging this shift vector over all high-symmetry cross-sections yields a rational multiple of a Bravais lattice vector oriented parallel to the polar axis. Despite possessing wide band gaps, the frequency-integrated shift conductivity of these intrinsically polar insulators surpasses $e^3/h^2$ and is at least three orders of magnitude greater than that of the prototypical ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$, thereby contradicting the common belief that small band gaps are essential for large shift currents in topological materials. Furthermore, as a topological phase transition approaches, the integrated conductivity diverges following a $|E_g|^{-1/2}$ dependence on the band gap $E_g$, indicating potential applications in ultrafast infrared detection.

We introduce NeRF-SR, a method designed for generating high-resolution (HR) novel views from predominantly low-resolution (LR) inputs. Built on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), which utilize multi-layer perceptrons to predict per-point density and color, our approach addresses the limitation where standard NeRF struggles to render resolutions exceeding those of the observed images. Our core insight is that NeRF leverages 3D consistency, allowing an observed pixel to integrate information from neighboring viewpoints. We initially harness this by employing a supersampling technique that casts multiple rays per pixel, thereby enforcing multi-view constraints at a sub-pixel level. Furthermore, we demonstrate that NeRF-SR can enhance supersampling performance through a refinement network that uses available depth estimates to hallucinate details from related patches on a single HR reference image. Experimental results confirm that NeRF-SR produces high-quality novel view synthesis at HR on both synthetic and real-world datasets without requiring any external information.

We bridge concepts from geometric group theory and homotopy theory via their underlying combinatorics. For a flag simplicial complex $K$, we establish a necessary and sufficient combinatorial criterion for the commutator subgroup $RC_K'$ of a right-angled Coxeter group—which serves as the fundamental group of the real moment-angle complex $\mathcal{R}_K$—to constitute a one-relator group. Additionally, we define a corresponding condition for the Pontryagin algebra $H_*(\Omega \mathcal{Z}_K)$ of the moment-angle complex to be a one-relator algebra. Furthermore, we provide homological characterizations for these properties: for $RC_K'$, the condition relies on the homology group $H_2(\mathcal{R}_K)$, while for $H_*(\Omega \mathcal{Z}_K)$, it is formulated in terms of the bigrading of the homology groups of $\mathcal{Z}_K$.

Using the Dyson-Schwinger equations (DSE), we investigate the quark condensate, magnetic moment, polarization, and susceptibility under strong external magnetic fields. Our findings indicate that these quantities rise with increasing field strength in the small-field regime but remain nearly constant in the large-field limit. Additionally, quark spin polarization is found to be roughly proportional to the magnetic field's magnitude. For context, we also examine nucleon magnetic moments and susceptibility within the constituent quark model framework, where both properties increase as the magnetic field intensifies.

This paper investigates elliptic and parabolic issues associated with the singular elliptic operators defined as \begin{equation*} \mathcal L =y^{\alpha_1}\Delta_{x}
+y^{\alpha_2}\left(D_{yy}+\frac{c}{y}D_y -\frac{b}{y^2}\right), \qquad\alpha_1,
\alpha_2 \in\mathbb R \end{equation*} within the domain of the half-space $\mathbb
R^{N+1}_+=\{(x,y): x \in \mathbb R^N, y>0\}$.

We extend the temporally encoded spectral shifting (TESS) analysis, originally developed for plasma wakefield measurements via spectral interferometry, to accommodate dissimilar probe pulses with arbitrary spectral profiles and to characterize nonlinear wakefields. Our findings show that the Gaussian approximation previously employed leads to significant errors in wakefield amplitude calculations, with discrepancies reaching a factor of two. We propose an extended TESS method capable of accurately measuring higher-amplitude quasilinear and nonlinear wakefields, while also defining the limits of its precision in these regimes. These enhancements highlight the technique's potential for rapid and precise on-shot diagnostics of plasma wakefields, even under conditions of low plasma density.

Dam reservoirs are crucial for achieving sustainable development objectives and global climate goals, yet there is a significant lack of consistent geographical data, especially concerning small dams. To bridge this gap, we propose using automated extraction from globally accessible remote sensing imagery. This process is a fine-grained task involving the identification of water areas and their subsequent classification as either dam reservoirs or natural water bodies. We introduce a novel deep neural network (DNN) pipeline that splits this extraction into two stages: water body segmentation and dam reservoir recognition. First, a segmentation model isolates water bodies from the background land, enhanced by point-level metric learning with triplets across images to resolve contour ambiguities between water and land. Second, a classification model determines whether each water body is a dam or natural, utilizing prior-guided metric learning with cluster-based triplets to refine the image embedding space at a fine-grained level. To support future research, we have created a benchmark dataset featuring earth imagery and human-labeled reservoirs from river basins in West Africa and India. Extensive experiments on this benchmark demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in water body segmentation, dam reservoir recognition, and the combined extraction task.

This research investigates holographic models featuring closed FRW cosmologies on a constant-tension brane situated within a Schwarzschild-AdS black hole. For dimensions d>2, the requirement of a smooth Euclidean solution without self-intersection restricts the brane tension to T<T_*, thereby precluding a separation of scales between the brane and the bulk curvature. We demonstrate that incorporating interface branes into this framework fails to alleviate the constraint on the brane tension.

In February 2017, the blazar OJ287, a leading candidate for a supermassive binary black hole system, was first observed at very high energies (VHEs; E>100 GeV) by the ground-based VERITAS gamma-ray observatory. Since VHE gamma rays are believed to originate near the central engine of active galactic nuclei, we aimed to characterize the physical mechanisms behind the observed TeV flare by analyzing parsec-scale source properties using high-resolution very long baseline interferometry (VLBI). Our study combines Global Millimeter-VLBI Array (GMVA) data at 86 GHz from 2015 to 2017 with multi-frequency radio monitoring data. By modeling the brightness distribution with two-dimensional Gaussian components in the visibility plane, we analyzed the source structure. In the GMVA epoch following the VHE activity, we identified a new jet feature (K) approximately 0.2 mas from the core, situated between two quasi-stationary components (S1 and S2). Enhanced activity was detected at various radio frequencies before and during the VHE flare. Based on these findings, we propose that the VHE emission in early 2017 was triggered by the passage of the new jet feature through a recollimation shock (modeled as component S1) within the jet at a de-projected distance of roughly 10 pc from the radio core.

Continuum mechanics traditionally characterizes compressive failure as a standard bifurcation, where uniform damage initially spreads throughout a material before localizing into a narrow band upon failure. However, experimental data capturing acoustic signals prior to this localization reveal power-law distributed precursors of increasing magnitude, implying that compressive failure might instead be a critical phenomenon. This study investigates the apparent conflict by analyzing the spatial arrangement and temporal evolution of damage activity during the compression of two-dimensional cellular solids. Our experimental measurements of intermittent damage evolution align well with a non-stationary depinning equation derived from damage mechanics, which resembles models of critical phenomena. In this framework, precursors are identified as damage cascades arising from the interaction between material disorder and long-range stress redistributions triggered by individual damage events. Nevertheless, the observed divergence in the characteristic size of these precursors near failure does not indicate a transition toward criticality. Instead, the system maintains a constant distance from the critical point throughout the damage evolution. The divergence is actually caused by the progressive loss of stability as the material approaches localization. Consequently, this research demonstrates that compressive failure remains a standard bifurcation where material disorder plays only a marginal role.
