Furthermore, it establishes that precursory activity acts as a by-product of the localization process, offering a basis for developing predictive methods to estimate the residual lifetime of structures.

This work numerically investigates the temporal development of the Misner-Sharp mass and apparent horizon during the gravitational collapse of a massless scalar field within $AdS_{5}$ spacetime, considering both narrow and broad wave configurations by solving the Einstein equations coupled to the scalar field. The analysis incorporates the complete collapse dynamics, specifically utilizing the framework of dynamical horizons. Results indicate that the Misner-Sharp mass remains constant throughout, undergoing a rapid transition only across a thin shell determined by the collapsing wave's density profile. Furthermore, tracking the apparent horizon's evolution reveals the black hole formation timeline and the asymptotic emergence of an event horizon. Additionally, the study examines how the thermalization time varies with the initial radius of the black hole's event horizon.

Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) have been suggested as a mechanism for identifying and authenticating electronic hardware, with recent proposals extending this concept to quantum devices. Some of these approaches utilize single-qubit gates to generate a secure fingerprint for the quantum system. In this study, we formally define the class of Classical Readout Quantum PUFs (CR-QPUFs) within the statistical query (SQ) framework and explicitly demonstrate that CR-QPUFs relying on single-qubit rotation gates lack sufficient security when the adversary possesses SQ access. We illustrate how an attacker can exploit this vulnerability to learn the device's characteristics and forge signatures through a modeling attack that employs simple regression of low-degree polynomials. This modeling attack was successfully executed in a real-world setting on actual IBM Q quantum computers. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive discussion regarding the opportunities and challenges associated with using quantum device imperfections as a secure fingerprint in CR-QPUFs.

This study employs convolutional neural networks to reconstruct images that have been optically down-sampled by a factor of 6.7 via coherent aperture synthesis across a 16-camera array. Unlike conventional ptychography, which depends on scanning and oversampling, we utilize decompressive neural estimation to retrieve full-resolution images from a single snapshot, though simulations indicate that multiple snapshots can enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. By training directly on experimental data, we eliminate the necessity for direct system calibration. Additionally, we provide simulations of various array camera sampling strategies to investigate potential optimizations for snapshot compressive systems.

This paper explores near-perfect numbers across several distinct categories. Specifically, we examine whether near-perfect numbers exist within the Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, investigate near-perfect values generated by integer polynomials, and analyze near-perfect repdigits.

To address the tenfold rise in integrated luminosity at the High-Luminosity LHC, scheduled to begin in 2027, the CMS detector is set for substantial upgrades. This initiative features a brand-new calorimeter for the CMS endcap regions, designed to endure radiation fluences as high as 10^16 n_eq /cm^2. The High Granularity Calorimeter (HGCAL) will introduce unparalleled segmentation in both transverse and longitudinal readout and trigger systems, supporting the particle-flow method for reconstructing electromagnetic and hadronic showers and measuring their energies. In low-radiation areas, the active material will consist of small plastic scintillator tiles linked to on-tile silicon photomultipliers, whereas silicon is selected for high-radiation zones due to its inherent radiation tolerance. These hexagonal silicon sensors will come in three nominal thicknesses—120 μm, 200 μm, and 300 μm—tailored to varying radiation environments. Each sensor will be divided into hundreds of individually readout hexagonal cells, ranging from 0.5 to 1.1 cm^2. Currently, a comprehensive effort is underway to finalize optimal sensor design parameters, including bulk doping, layouts, and manufacturing techniques. The text presents findings from full electrical characterizations of various sensors alongside initial results from an irradiation test of large-area silicon devices.

This paper introduces a novel approach for multirotor navigation in dynamic settings, utilizing a temporal occupancy grid to model both current and predicted obstacle states. Building on existing research regarding Safe Corridor generation and multirotor planning for both static and moving obstacles, the method first computes a global path to the target without considering dynamic constraints. Subsequently, it employs temporal Safe Corridors to define safe spatial regions available at discrete future time steps. Finally, these corridors are integrated into an optimization framework that incorporates multirotor dynamics and obstacle avoidance to produce an executable trajectory, with simulation results demonstrating the method's effectiveness.

Recovering bandlimited signals that possess a high dynamic range is a critical topic in current sampling research. Unlimited sampling theory extends the operational range of conventional analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) without limit by folding the signal into a lower dynamic range measurement, thereby preventing saturation. This study investigates the unlimited sampling of high-dynamic-range, non-bandlimited signals within the Fourier domain (FD) utilizing the fractional Fourier transform (FRFT). First, modular nonlinear folding is executed in the fractional Fourier domain (FRFD) to facilitate modular arithmetic. Subsequently, the fractional spectrum is estimated for any folding interval using annihilation filtering. Finally, a new unlimited sampling algorithm within the FRFD is developed. The findings demonstrate that non-bandlimited signals can be reconstructed in the FD based on the FRFT without being influenced by ADC thresholds.

Four years after their initial conceptualization five decades ago, the first resolved, multiply imaged Type Ia supernova, iPTF16geu, was detected. These unique systems offer significant potential for investigating galaxy structure and cosmological parameters, yet this inaugural case posed several challenges for modelers. While stellar microlensing was deemed necessary to account for image fluxes, accommodating its magnitude required a shallow density slope ($\rho_{2D} \propto r^{-0.7}$) in the elliptical power law lens model. Additionally, the mass center needed to be offset from the light center by approximately 0.1 kpc, and the position angles of mass and light distributions were misaligned by roughly 40 degrees. This paper introduces mass models that address the first two issues and propose a solution for the third. Drawing on observations of local ellipticals and recent analyses of galaxy-scale lenses, our models feature two offset baryonic mass components. The resulting distributions possess a single centroid but are asymmetric, with isodensity contours that deviate from pure ellipses and lack self-similarity across radii. In many of these models, microlensing requirements are reduced, and the extended host galaxy's ring closely matches the observed structure.

Although natural language processing (NLP) algorithms have achieved significant success, they often fail when encountering out-of-distribution instances. To address this domain adaptation (DA) challenge, we introduce a controllable generation method called DoCoGen. This algorithm takes an input text and produces a domain-counterfactual example (D-con) that retains the original task label and semantic meaning while shifting the domain to a target setting. Notably, DoCoGen is trained exclusively on unlabeled data from various domains, eliminating the need for task labels or parallel domain-counterfactual pairs. We demonstrate that DoCoGen can create coherent, multi-sentence counterfactuals. These D-cons are used to augment sentiment and multi-label intent classifiers across 20 and 78 DA scenarios respectively, particularly where labeled source-domain data is limited. Our model surpasses strong baselines and enhances the performance of a leading unsupervised DA algorithm.

The deterministic membership problem for timed automata investigates whether a nondeterministic timed automaton's recognized timed language can also be recognized by a deterministic timed automaton. We demonstrate that this problem is decidable specifically when the input automaton is a one-clock nondeterministic timed automaton lacking epsilon transitions, and the number of clocks in the deterministic timed automaton is fixed. Conversely, we establish that the problem is undecidable in all other scenarios: either if the input nondeterministic timed automaton possesses two or more clocks, if it utilizes epsilon transitions, or if the number of clocks in the output deterministic automaton is not fixed.

This work classifies every non-invertible Kramers-Wannier duality defect within the $E_8$ lattice Vertex Operator Algebra (specifically the chiral $(E_8)_1$ WZW model) that arises from $\mathbb{Z}_m$ symmetries. We demonstrate the systematic derivation of these defects as $\mathbb{Z}_2$ twists of invariant sub-VOAs, calculate their partition functions for small values of $m$, and cross-check our findings with alternative methods. Our approach emphasizes a physical viewpoint, clarifying the key components of the computations. We utilize Kac's theorem regarding finite automorphisms of Lie algebras alongside modern findings on holomorphic VOAs. Furthermore, we offer insights from the perspective of (2+1)d Topological Field Theory and present a rigorous proof confirming that all associated Tambara-Yamagami actions on holomorphic VOAs can be constructed this way. Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research.

This paper introduces the notions of quasi-finitely separating maps and quasi-approximate identities, which serve as the foundation for defining QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. The study investigates the properties and characterizations of QFS-spaces, yielding the following key results: (1) Every QFS-space is a quasicontinuous space; (2) QFS-spaces are preserved under closed subspaces and quasicontinuous projection spaces; (3) Continuous retracts of QFS-spaces remain QFS-spaces, with a specific construction of such retracts provided; and (4) The upper powerspaces of continuous QFS-spaces are FS-spaces.

Using the 8-meter Gemini telescopes, we have captured new, high-resolution images of the extensively studied HR 4796A dust ring at wavelengths of 18 and 25 microns. These observations validate the spatial dimensions previously detected in near-IR, optical, and mid-IR data. We identify brightness and temperature asymmetries, noting that the dust on the northeast side is warmer and brighter compared to the southwest. Our findings demonstrate that models of "pericenter glow" successfully explain these asymmetries, thereby confirming and expanding upon our earlier work. In this framework, the ring's center is displaced from the star because gravitational interactions with an eccentric body have induced a forced eccentricity in the dust orbits. Models incorporating 2-micron silicate particles and a forced eccentricity of 0.06 provide a simultaneous fit for observations at both wavelengths. Furthermore, we establish that the parameters defining the disk's thermal-emission characteristics are also sufficient to explain the asymmetries seen in shorter-wavelength scattered-light images.

This study investigates the potential for detecting circumstellar absorption lines of Na I D$_{1,2}$ and Ca II H,K in type IIP supernovae spectra during the photospheric phase. Modeling indicates that Na I doublet lines from circumstellar material would remain undetectable in type IIP supernovae with moderate wind densities, such as those seen in SN 1999em, while Ca II lines exhibiting a P Cygni profile should be clearly observable. The same modeling approach was applied to SN 1998S, a type IIL supernova characterized by a dense wind, to account for its observed Na I and Ca II circumstellar lines. We demonstrate that the line intensities in SN 1998S are accurately reproduced by assuming an ultraviolet excess, primarily driven by the Comptonization of supernova radiation within the shock wave.

Blockchain technology initially emerged from cryptocurrencies, leading most implementations to assume a fast and stable network environment. However, in certain blockchain applications, such as supply chain management systems, some IoT nodes must operate under low-quality network conditions to reach consensus. Consequently, it is essential to assess the suitability of current consensus algorithms in such scenarios. This research conducted a systematic mapping study to evaluate and contrast the ability of existing mechanisms to ensure integrity and security across varying network properties. The study analyzed 25 state-of-the-art consensus algorithms drawn from published and preprint literature, categorizing and comparing them qualitatively based on standard performance metrics, integrity measures, and recognized blockchain security vulnerabilities. The findings indicate that consensus algorithms dependent on synchronous networks for correctness fail to deliver the expected level of integrity. Furthermore, these synchronous algorithms may be susceptible to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) and routing attacks due to constrained network throughput. In contrast, asynchronous consensus algorithms, such as Honey-Badger-BFT, are considered more resilient against various attacks and capable of maintaining high integrity even during asynchronous events.

For every non-negative integer $m$, triangular numbers are defined as $\mathbf{T}(m)=\frac{m(m+1)}{2}$. Sun Zhi-Wei proposed a conjecture asserting that for any $n>2$, the integer $2^n\pm n$ cannot be a triangular number. This study aims to verify that conjecture.

Halo Models serve as essential instruments for phenomenologically analyzing matter clustering across the Universe. Although these models construct cosmic structures by superimposing haloes, defining their density profiles in the outer regions—beyond virial radii—becomes increasingly problematic due to the difficulty of uniquely assigning matter to individual haloes. This study addresses this challenge by employing numerical N-body simulations to establish a systematic definition of mean halo profiles applicable to large radii. These profiles are compensated and form the fundamental components for calculating cosmological correlation functions within the Amended Halo Model. Previously introduced in our work (arXiv:1912.04872), this model offers a more physically rigorous description of nonlinear structure formation that adheres to conservation laws on large scales. In this paper, we extend the model from the matter auto-power spectrum to halo-matter cross-power spectra using N-body simulations. Our results indicate that the dimensionless compensated halo profile, defined as $r^3 \times \rho(r)/M_{200c}$, exhibits a near-universal peak within the narrow range of $0.03-0.04$ near the virial radius ($r \simeq r_{\rm 200c}$), regardless of halo mass. Furthermore, the profiles transition into negative values in the halo outskirts beyond 2-3 times $r_{\rm 200c}$, aligning with our prior findings. We also present preliminary fitting functions for compensated Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) profiles, enabling the computation of more physically accurate observables within the Amended Halo Model of large-scale structure.

Previous research on islands and double holography has primarily centered on codimension-one branes. In contrast, this study investigates islands situated on codimension-two branes within the AdS/dCFT framework. Unlike codimension-one branes, codimension-two branes are intrinsically linked to conical singularities. Our analysis of the graviton mass spectrum on these branes reveals an inverse relationship between brane tension and gravitational mass: as tension increases, the mass decreases. Furthermore, massless modes are prohibited by boundary or normalization constraints. We demonstrate that the first massive gravitational mode is localized on the codimension-two brane, with higher tension enhancing this localization. This behavior parallels that of codimension-one branes and establishes a robust physical basis for examining black hole evolution on codimension-two branes. Additionally, we show that the Page curve for eternal black holes can be successfully recovered when the island terminates on the codimension-two brane. A novel feature of this scenario is that, in the no-island phase, the extremal surface crossing the horizon becomes undefined after a finite duration. However, this anomaly does not impact the Page curve, as it occurs subsequent to the Page time.

We investigate the discontinuous first-order transition from superfluid $^3$He A to B near the polycritical point (2.232 mK and 21.22 bar). Our findings reveal path-dependent behavior: while cooling at constant pressure defines a clear transition line in the temperature-pressure plane, this line can be reliably crossed by reducing pressure at nearly constant temperature after surpassing $T_{\rm c}$ at a higher pressure. This observed path dependence contradicts all standard B-phase nucleation mechanisms described in existing literature. Consequently, this symmetry-breaking transition serves as a potential analog for first-order phase transitions in the early universe.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer significant advantages for brain neuroimaging by leveraging graphical network perspectives. However, most current GNN-based approaches treat the brain connectome as a homogeneous graph, utilizing only single node and edge types. Conversely, recent research highlights the critical importance of heterogeneity in human brain activity, particularly distinguishing between the two cerebral hemispheres. Consequently, homogeneous graph methods fall short in modeling complex cerebral states. To address this limitation, this paper introduces HebrainGNN, a heterogeneous graph neural network designed for multimodal brain neuroimaging fusion. First, we represent the brain network as a heterogeneous graph featuring multitype nodes (left and right hemispheres) and multitype edges (intra- and interhemispheric connections). Second, we develop a self-supervised pretraining strategy grounded in this heterogeneous network to mitigate overfitting arising from the disparity between large model parameters and limited medical data. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing methods in predicting brain-related diseases. Furthermore, ablation studies reveal that our approach prioritizes hemispheric connections often overlooked by homogeneous models due to their lower strength. Additional experiments confirm that the proposed pretraining strategy effectively tackles the challenge of scarce labeled data, resulting in substantial accuracy improvements.

This paper introduces a novel \emph{multiple-correction method} designed to expedite the convergence rate. Specifically, we develop sequences that approximate the Euler-Mascheroni and Landau constants, achieving superior speed compared to traditional approximations found in existing literature.

Predicting the type of a location (POI) from social media posts is a key task for computational social science fields like sociolinguistics, geosemiotics, and cultural geography, as well as for geosocial technologies such as recommendation and visualization systems. While previous research has relied exclusively on textual data, real-world social media communication is shaped by diverse modalities and their interrelationships. This study introduces a multimodal approach to POI type prediction that integrates both text and images available at the time of posting. We enhanced an existing dataset by incorporating accompanying images and developed a method that extracts relevant features from each modality to effectively model text-image interactions. Our approach achieved a macro F1 score of 47.21 across eight categories, significantly surpassing state-of-the-art text-only methods. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of cross-modal interactions and the limitations of our best-performing model.

Thunderstorm hazard forecasting is essential for various sectors, including aviation, infrastructure management, and first responders. To meet this demand, we introduce a flexible deep learning model capable of adapting to diverse hazard types. This model integrates multiple data streams, including digital elevation models, numerical weather predictions, satellite visible/infrared imagery, lightning detection, and weather radar. It is designed to function with any combination of these inputs, ensuring predictions remain possible even if certain data sources become unavailable. We demonstrate the model's capacity to probabilistically forecast lightning, hail, and heavy precipitation on a 1 km grid with a 5-minute time resolution and lead times extending up to 60 minutes. Furthermore, Shapley values reveal the relative importance of each data source, identifying weather radar products as the most critical predictors across all three hazard categories.

Drawing on the high critical temperature of yttrium superhydrides and the low stabilized pressure of superconducting cerium superhydrides, we performed four independent syntheses of yttrium-cerium alloy hydrides. Raman scattering and x-ray diffraction were used to characterize the resulting phases. Superconductivity was confirmed via the zero-resistance state, occurring between 97 and 140 K at pressures from 114 to 120±4 GPa. These hydrides exhibit a maximum critical temperature exceeding that of previously reported cerium hydrides, while requiring significantly lower pressures than superconducting yttrium hydrides. Structural analysis and theoretical calculations identify the Y$_{0.5}$Ce$_{0.5}$H$_9$ phase as belonging to the $P6_3/mmc$ space group, with a predicted critical temperature of 119 K that aligns well with experimental findings. These results demonstrate that alloying superhydrides can indeed sustain relatively high critical temperatures at modest pressures accessible to many laboratories.

This study significantly enhances AI-generated solar farside magnetograms by integrating datasets from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). We have refined our prior deep learning architecture and input configurations to produce more realistic magnetograms. Our updated model, Pix2PixCC, incorporates novel objective functions that evaluate correlation coefficients (CCs) between actual and generated data. Additionally, we constructed input datasets pairing solar farside STEREO extreme ultraviolet (EUV) observations with corresponding frontside SDO EUV observations and magnetograms; we anticipate that these frontside pairs provide historical context regarding magnetic field polarity distributions. Our results demonstrate that the generated magnetic field distributions align more closely with real data across multiple metrics. Specifically, the averaged pixel-to-pixel CC for full-disk, active, and quiet regions (using 8x8 binning) between real and AI-generated magnetograms reached 0.88, 0.91, and 0.70, respectively. Furthermore, the total unsigned and net magnetic fluxes in the AI-generated outputs match those of the real data for test sets. Notably, the farside magnetograms exhibit consistent polar field strengths and polarities with nearby frontside observations during solar cycles 24 and 25. Consequently, researchers can now monitor the temporal evolution of active regions by combining frontside and farside magnetograms produced by this model. Our AI-generated Solar Farside Magnetograms (AISFMs) are now publicly accessible via the Korean Data Center (KDC) for SDO.

Label shift occurs when the prior class probability $p(y)$ varies between training and test distributions, even though the conditional probability $p(x|y)$ remains constant. This issue is common in medical diagnosis, where a model trained to predict disease from symptoms must adjust to different baseline disease prevalences. Saerens et al. introduced an efficient maximum likelihood algorithm to correct label shift without retraining, relying on the assumption that $p(y|x)$ is calibrated—a condition often unmet by modern neural networks. Recently, Black Box Shift Learning (BBSL) and Regularized Learning under Label Shifts (RLLS) have become state-of-the-art solutions for uncalibrated classifiers, yet both require retraining with importance weights and lack benchmarking against maximum likelihood. This work demonstrates that: (1) combining maximum likelihood with bias-corrected calibration surpasses both BBSL and RLLS across various datasets and shifts; (2) the maximum likelihood objective is mathematically concave; and (3) a principled strategy for estimating source-domain priors enhances robustness against poor calibration. Consequently, maximum likelihood paired with proper calibration stands as a powerful and efficient baseline for label shift adaptation. Experimental notebooks are available at https://github.com/kundajelab/labelshiftexperiments.

We examine Vaughan's approximation for the count of primes within arithmetic progressions. Rather than averaging the anticipated error term across all residue classes for moduli within a specified range, we focus exclusively on subsets of these progressions that adhere to extra congruence constraints and derive corresponding asymptotic approximations.

The sex industry operates along a spectrum defined by the level of labor autonomy, ranging from independent workers with significant agency to individuals subjected to human trafficking with minimal control. Across North America, organizations provide outreach to this population, offering services like healthcare, housing, and financial aid, alongside spiritual support and intervention. Technology is increasingly employed to locate trafficking victims or deliver these services; for instance, algorithms scrape and parse advertisements to compile contact databases for outreach groups. However, the effectiveness of such anti-trafficking technologies remains unclear, as does the potential risk they pose to the highly stigmatized and marginalized sex industry workforce. This study examines the usage, context, advantages, and drawbacks of an anti-trafficking technology platform through qualitative interviews with six developers, seventeen organization users, and twenty-four sex industry workers. Our results reveal a significant disconnect between developers, platform users, and the workers they intend to help. Currently, these tools are ineffective and, at best, function as spam mechanisms, while at worst, they amplify harm against the very communities they aim to support. We conclude by proposing best practices for technology-driven outreach that can efficiently deliver necessary services while minimizing risks and harm to sex industry workers.

Autonomous robots and vehicles are poised to become a fundamental component of our surroundings, yet significant barriers remain, including poor interaction with current road users, suboptimal performance in mixed-traffic scenarios, and a lack of transparent decision-making. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a physics-informed neural network that integrates a social force model augmented with group forces (SFMG) and a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). This hybrid framework predicts pedestrian paths while accounting for interactions with static obstacles, individual pedestrians, and groups. We assess the model's realistic accuracy, predictive performance, and interpretability through both quantitative and qualitative analysis. Preliminary findings indicate that, even when trained exclusively on synthetic data, the model generates realistic and interpretable trajectories that surpass state-of-the-art accuracy.

This work presents positive solutions to the challenge of equipping dynamical systems with a Hamiltonian formulation within the geometric context of Poisson structures. Focusing on orientable manifolds and utilizing decomposable Poisson structures, we first demonstrate that a Hamiltonian formulation exists when certain topological obstructions vanish, thereby refining a result by Gao. Second, we employ a variation of the Hojman construction to resolve the issue for vector fields possessing a transversally invariant metric, specifically addressing infinitesimal generators of proper actions. Finally, we examine the hamiltonization of Lie group actions, providing solutions for the specific scenario where the acting Lie group is a low-dimensional torus.

Creating synthetic surveys of fluxes and redshifts (representing distances) for astrophysical populations is a common procedure. The \texttt{popsynth} library offers a flexible, object-oriented framework capable of generating these surveys from diverse distributions and luminosity functions, applying selection criteria to observed variables, and saving the results in a portable HDF5 format. Users can build population synthesis workflows either through Python classes or via serializable YAML files, ensuring both adaptability and portability. Beyond sampling luminosity and distance, the tool allows for the creation of auxiliary distributions with arbitrarily complex inter-parameter dependencies. Consequently, researchers can simulate intricate astrophysical populations to either calibrate analysis pipelines or rapidly evaluate new hypotheses.

PCMSolver serves as an open-source library designed for continuum electrostatic solvation, capable of integration with any quantum chemistry package through a minimal interface that significantly cuts down on coding requirements. To function, it requires only the molecular geometry to construct the cavity and compute the expected electrostatic potential on its surface, subsequently returning the solvent polarization to the host application. The system is engineered for versatility and efficiency, incurring negligible performance overhead, with implementing a standard single-point self-consistent field calculation demanding no more than two days of effort. The documentation includes a concise theoretical introduction, two tutorials—one for developers seeking to interface their software with PCMSolver and another for library contributors—and concludes with demonstrations of past and current projects, highlighting the library's capabilities alongside various quantum chemistry programs.

Generating images from text descriptions via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has emerged as a prominent research field, with recent successes producing visually compelling results. Motivated by this progress, we explored the creation of artistic imagery using a dataset characterized by large variance, encompassing differences in shape, color, and content. These variations are crucial for achieving the originality that defines artistic essence. A key feature of our approach is the use of keywords rather than full sentences to describe images. We introduced a sequential GAN architecture where the initial stage processes word vectors to generate a base image, while subsequent stages refine this into high-resolution artistic outputs without reprocessing the textual data. To address the inherent instability of GANs, we combined several techniques, including Wasserstein loss, spectral normalization, and minibatch discrimination. Consequently, we successfully produced paintings across a diverse range of styles. Our evaluation relied on the Fréchet Inception Distance metric and a user study involving 186 participants.

We introduce DLKoopman, a software suite implementing Koopman theory that leverages deep learning to map nonlinear dynamical systems into linear spaces while concurrently learning the linear dynamics. Unlike prior approaches that either constrained encoding capabilities or were tailored for specific systems, DLKoopman serves as a generalized tool for data-driven learning and optimization applicable to any dynamical system. It supports two training modes: learning from individual state snapshots to predict unknown states, or learning from system trajectories to forecast new trajectories from different initial conditions. Available on PyPI as 'dlkoopman', the package offers comprehensive documentation and tutorials. Furthermore, it features a novel performance metric known as Average Normalized Absolute Error and an integrated hyperparameter search module to facilitate optimization.

Non-Hermitian systems have garnered significant attention for modeling open and dissipative quantum environments. A prominent feature of these systems is the non-Hermitian skin effect, an anomalous accumulation of bulk states at boundaries caused by asymmetric hopping amplitudes. This phenomenon has been extensively explored theoretically and experimentally through the lens of the Hatano-Nelson model and topological exceptional points. However, other forms of non-Hermiticity and their associated properties remain poorly understood. This study examines a non-Hermitian system characterized by non-reciprocal hopping phases and investigates the resulting evolution of quantum state localization. We highlight that non-Hermiticity embedded within the hopping phase factor induces state delocalization, standing in contrast to the localization typical of the skin effect. Moreover, by employing the inverse participation ratio and fractal dimension to quantify spectral localization, we demonstrate that non-Hermitian hopping phases enable precise control over the localization characteristics of quantum states. Our findings introduce novel classes of non-Hermitian systems capable of manipulating wave localization, and we conclude by discussing potential experimental applications.

Progresses in machine learning have introduced versatile tools with wide-ranging utility in scientific inquiry. These methods are now utilized across the full spectrum of nuclear physics, driving breakthroughs that will enhance both scientific discovery and societal impact. This review offers a comprehensive overview of how machine learning has fundamentally reshaped research within the field of nuclear physics.

Driven by recent irregularities in $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions, we investigate a minimal $Z^\prime$ model where the boson exhibits flavour-changing couplings to charm and top quarks alongside flavour-conserving interactions with muons. Our analysis demonstrates that such a $Z^\prime$ can account for the observed $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ anomalies while remaining consistent with other flavour and collider constraints. The boson's mass could be as low as a few hundred GeV; under these conditions, $t \to c \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays and associated $tZ^\prime$ production at the LHC offer promising avenues for detection. A distinctive aspect of this model is that $Z^\prime$ contributions to all rare $B$- and $K$-meson processes are governed by a single parameter, generating intriguing correlations that could yield deeper insights. Furthermore, we examine an extended scenario where the $Z^\prime$ couples to $SU(2)_L$ fermion doublets with analogous interactions to those in the minimal case.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) has primarily been researched within the domain of written text. However, NER plays a crucial role in the de-identification (de-ID) of medical records, many of which consist of recorded doctor-patient dialogues. In these audio files, segments containing personal information must be redacted, mirroring the process of removing sensitive character spans in written de-ID tasks. The application of NER to audio de-identification remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we define the task of audio de-ID, which involves detecting audio spans containing entity mentions. We subsequently present a pipeline for this task comprising Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), NER performed on the transcribed text, and text-to-audio alignment. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric for evaluating audio de-ID and establish a novel benchmark using a substantial labeled portion of the Switchboard and Fisher audio datasets, detailing the performance of our pipeline on this benchmark.

Decoherence is an unavoidable aspect of quantum computing operations, making dynamic suppression methods—such as dynamical decoupling and quantum error correction codes (QECC)—essential for accurately implementing both established and emerging quantum algorithms. Although this active noise mitigation aligns with future expectations for quantum computing, we have, given current limitations, developed self-protected quantum algorithms for over 15 years based on an alternative "living-with-noise" strategy. In this work, we introduce self-protected quantum simulations that are robust against a broad spectrum of classical noise. Furthermore, we extend the conventional quantum phase estimation method to an enhanced version capable of operating effectively in the presence of classical noise for readout purposes.

Cut-cell finite element methods are gaining prominence due to their superiority over body-fitted mesh formulations for handling moving interfaces. In these approaches, cells intersected by domain boundaries require specialized integration techniques to ensure accurate interfacial fluxes and optimal convergence. Among available methods, recursive subdivision (adaptive integration) is favored for complex three-dimensional geometries because it avoids the limitations of tessellation. While this technique imposes no constraints on immersed solid representation, relying solely on point location algorithms, it can be computationally costly to achieve optimal convergence. This study provides a thorough evaluation of adaptive integration for computational fluid dynamics and fluid-structure interaction (FSI). By analyzing examples in both 2D and 3D, we examine how integration accuracy influences velocity and pressure convergence, as well as forces and displacements in FSI scenarios. Balancing computational expense against the accuracy of forces and displacements, we find that acceptable results for laminar flow FSI problems can be achieved with reduced refinement levels. Specifically, we demonstrate that three levels of adaptive refinement are adequate to obtain accurate force and displacement values for laminar fluid-structure interaction.

This study introduces and examines a diffuse interface framework for inductionless magnetohydrodynamic fluids. The framework integrates a convective Cahn-Hilliard equation to track interface evolution, the Navier-Stokes equations to describe fluid dynamics, and the Poisson equation for electrostatics. Derived systematically from Onsager's variational principle and conservation laws, the work employs formal matched asymptotic expansions to construct various sharp interface models as the interfacial thickness approaches zero. The analysis demonstrates that the sharp interface limit of these models yields the standard incompressible inductionless magnetohydrodynamic equations, each coupled with distinct interface conditions dependent on specific mobility choices. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm the convergence of the diffuse interface model across different mobility parameters.

This paper introduces a sequence of results from Complex Analysis that, while appearing disconnected, are unified through a novel proof strategy based on Errett Bishop's work regarding volumes and limits of analytic varieties. We begin by establishing Chow's theorem using a method originally proposed in Gabriel Stolzenberg's seminal book, an approach we consider both accessible for students and novices and uniquely connected to mathematical areas rarely linked to Chow's result. Furthermore, Bishop's findings directly yield both Chow's and Remmert-Stein's theorems, rendering this perspective as profound and streamlined as the latter's original proof. Subsequently, we provide a comparative table demonstrating how Bishop's theorems extend classical results from one complex variable to several, and we utilize these techniques to prove Montel's compactness theorem. Finally, we offer an alternative demonstration of a theorem by Edwards, Millet, and Sullivan concerning foliations with compact leaves, specifically addressing complex foliations within Kähler manifolds.

By employing gauge/string duality, we simulate a heavy quark-antiquark pair in a color singlet configuration traversing a cold medium to investigate how temperature and velocity influence string breaking. Our findings indicate that the distance at which the string breaks changes gradually with temperature and velocity as one moves away from the critical line, but may decrease significantly near it.

The study investigates coherent photoproduction of heavy quarkonia on nuclear targets using the QCD color dipole formalism, incorporating four key phenomena: i) the correlation between the collision impact parameter $\vec b$ and dipole orientation $\vec r$; ii) higher-twist nuclear shadowing associated with the $\bar QQ$ Fock state of the photon; iii) leading-twist gluon shadowing linked to higher Fock components of the photon containing gluons; and iv) diminished quantum coherence effects within the widely used Balitsky-Kovchegov equation compared to standard literature calculations. Our computed differential cross sections align well with recent ALICE data regarding charmonium production in ultra-peripheral nuclear collisions. Additionally, we provide predictions for the coherent photoproduction of other quarkonium states ($\psi^{\,\prime}$(2S), $\Upsilon$(1S), and $\Upsilon^{\,\prime}$(2S)), which can be tested by future LHC measurements.

Recent contrastive learning-based image translation techniques have been introduced to improve spatial correspondence by contrasting different spatial locations. However, these approaches frequently overlook diverse semantic relationships within images. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Semantic Relation Consistency (SRC) regularization combined with decoupled contrastive learning, which leverages diverse semantics by focusing on heterogeneous semantics among image patches within a single image. Furthermore, we introduce a hard negative mining strategy that exploits semantic relations to enhance performance. We validated our method across three tasks: single-modal and multi-modal image translation, as well as GAN compression for image translation. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in all three tasks.

The study examines the hadronic characteristics of $\rho$ mesons generated in inclusive photonuclear reactions, assuming the fundamental process within the nucleus is $\gamma N \to \rho^0 N$. As the $\rho$ meson traverses the nucleus, it interacts with nuclear constituents, leading to potential modifications of its properties. Given its short lifetime, the $\rho$ meson decays into various elementary particles, including $e^+e^-$ and $\pi^+\pi^-$. To determine the $\rho$ meson's mass and width parameters within the nuclear medium, the distribution spectra of the $e^+e^-$ invariant mass (corresponding to the $\rho$ meson mass) were computed. These calculated results were then compared with experimental data from Jefferson Laboratory.

The Standard Model of Particle Physics anticipates double-$\beta$ decay in specific nuclei accompanied by the emission of two active neutrinos. In this letter, we contend that double-$\beta$ decay experiments can investigate theories involving light exotic fermions by searching for spectral anomalies in the electron energy distribution relative to Standard Model predictions. We examine two specific scenarios: models featuring light sterile neutrinos produced singly during the decay, and models containing a light $Z_2$-odd fermion generated in pairs via $Z_2$ symmetry. By evaluating the discovery reach of various double-$\beta$ decay experiments, we conclude that upcoming searches will, for the first time, explore a new region of the parameter space at the MeV mass scale.

We investigate inflationary dynamics and the potential for generating an increased abundance of primordial black holes (PBHs) and gravitational waves (GWs) within a string-motivated framework featuring two axion fields coupled to Chern-Simons gravity, which yields a running-vacuum-model inflation. This model accounts for scale-invariant fluctuations consistent with cosmological observations through world-sheet (non-perturbative) instanton terms in the axion field, originating from string compactification. These modulations drive a heightened production of PBHs and GWs, potentially creating observable signatures in the GW spectrum during the radiation-dominated era. Furthermore, we show that PBHs could constitute a substantial fraction of the universe's Dark Matter. For context, we also examine a conventional two-stage inflation model based on string-inspired axion monodromy, also involving two axion fields. The distinct modifications these two model classes imprint on the GW spectrum could, in principle, be differentiated by future interferometers. We analyze scenarios ranging from nearly instantaneous to prolonged reheating periods, noting that extended reheating can further amplify the power spectrum and consequently increase the fraction of PBHs serving as Dark Matter.

Identifying recurrent fragments, also known as spatial motifs or substructures, represents one of the most potent methods for analyzing protein structures, utilizing these patterns to characterize specific proteins. A growing trend involves representing the three-dimensional (3D) architecture of proteins as graphs of amino acids, thereby framing the search for spatial motifs as a frequent subgraph discovery task. Although numerous efficient algorithms for this task have been developed, the resulting set of frequent subgraphs is often excessively large for effective analysis or further exploration. This paper introduces a novel pattern selection strategy designed to reduce this volume by identifying representative subgraphs. Unlike existing methods that ignore domain-specific knowledge, our approach integrates evolutionary information derived from amino acid substitution matrices to select these representative patterns. Experimental results on real datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, showing that it significantly reduces the number of motifs while simultaneously increasing their interestingness.

The Pierre Auger Observatory stands as the world's largest extensive air shower detector. Operating on a hybrid detection system, the experiment analyzes both the longitudinal development of air showers and the particles reaching the ground. This setup enables the derivation of proton-air cross-sections at energies far exceeding those reachable by existing colliders. Furthermore, hadronic interaction models can be tested by examining correlations among various shower observables, such as the depth of shower maximum and ground-level muon counts, including their fluctuations. Additionally, the low-energy extension of the observatory allows researchers to investigate the muon deficit in air shower simulations across nearly three decades of the highest energy range.

In five-cyclidic coordinates within three-dimensional Euclidean space, we obtain eigenfunction expansions for a fundamental solution to Laplace's equation. These expansions consist of three distinct series based on internal and external harmonics of the first, second, and third kinds. Both sets of harmonics are defined as solutions to a Fuchsian differential equation featuring five regular singular points.

This study details the creation of a rapid neutron detector utilizing a liquid scintillator enhanced with enriched Li-6. The lithium was incorporated as an aqueous LiCl micro-emulsion within a di-isopropylnaphthalene-based scintillator matrix, achieving a Li-6 concentration of 0.15% by weight. A 125 mL glass vessel containing this mixture was irradiated with neutrons from a fission source. In this setup, fast neutrons generate recoil protons, while neutrons that thermalize within the detector are captured by Li-6. Neutron energy is derived from the light output of recoiling protons, and the delayed capture of thermal neutrons helps suppress background noise. The paper covers the development of this 6Li-loaded scintillator, its operational demonstration, and a comparison of its efficiency and capture lifetime against Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, data from a boron-loaded plastic scintillator were collected for comparative analysis. We also introduce a pulse-shape discrimination technique to distinguish between electronic and nuclear recoil events by calculating the Matusita distance between normalized observed waveforms and specific templates for nuclear and electronic recoils. The report concludes with a discussion of measurement specifics, data analysis procedures, and their alignment with Monte Carlo simulation results.

We examine order-preserving $C^3$ circle maps featuring a flat segment, an irrational rotation number, and critical exponents $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$. We observe a shift in the system's geometry: it is degenerate for $(\ell_1, \ell_2) \in [1,2]^2$ but becomes bounded for $(\ell_1, \ell_2) \in [2,\infty)^2 \setminus \{(2,2)\}$. Specifically, when the rotation number follows the pattern $[abab\cdots]$ with $a,b\in\mathbb{N}^*$, the geometry is bounded for $(\ell_1, \ell_2)$ values lying above a specific curve defined on $]1, +\infty [^2$. Consequently, we estimate the Hausdorff dimension of the non-wandering set $K_f= \mathcal{S}^1 \setminus \bigcup_{i=0}^\infty f^{-i}(U)$. In the degenerate case, this dimension is zero, whereas it is strictly positive when the geometry is bounded.

Numerical representations of chemical systems for electronic structure calculations often employ basis functions localized in real space (atomic orbitals), momentum space (plane waves), or a combination of both within phase space. While wavelets, as phase-space localized functions, have long been utilized in this field, this paper focuses on a specific phase-space basis set originally proposed by K. G. Wilson, offering the first comprehensive study of its numerical implementation. To determine electronic energies for various small molecules and states, we employ the sum-of-products approach combined with Gaussian quadratures and develop techniques for selecting sample points from a grid of Wilson basis functions. We detail both full configuration interaction and Hartree-Fock implementations. Recognizing that grid-based methods struggle to describe both tightly bound and diffuse orbitals, we explore augmenting the Wilson basis with projected Slater-type orbitals. Additionally, we compare the Wilson basis against recently introduced wavelet-transformed Gaussians (gausslets). Throughout the discussion, we provide implementation insights and use small atoms and molecules to demonstrate the convergence characteristics of the Wilson basis.

This study identifies key components of successful machine learning datasets within the field of astronomy and offers recommendations for their development. As machine learning becomes an indispensable tool for processing the vast influx of astronomical data, robust datasets are essential for both training and testing models. However, creating such datasets presents significant challenges because astronomical instruments are primarily designed to address traditional scientific inquiries rather than machine learning tasks. Consequently, raw or even processed data often fails to be in a format suitable for machine learning applications. We examine the process of constructing these datasets and investigate the defining characteristics of effectiveness. Specifically, we define an effective astronomical machine learning dataset as one composed of clearly defined data points, organized structure, and comprehensive metadata. We discuss the importance of these elements for astronomical applications and provide practical strategies for their implementation. Furthermore, we argue that these qualities not only render the data appropriate for machine learning but also promote science practices that are usable, reusable, and replicable.

We confirm a conjecture by Goncharov, demonstrating that any multiple polylogarithm can be represented using polylogarithms of depth no greater than half the weight. An explicit formula for this representation is provided, featuring a summation over trees that reflect the decomposition of a polygon into quadrangles. Additionally, we present a formula for the volume of hyperbolic orthoschemes, extending Lobachevsky's three-dimensional result to arbitrary dimensions. We uncover a remarkable connection between two results, stemming from the fact that hyperbolic orthoschemes are parameterized by point configurations on $\mathbb{P}^1$. Specifically, we derive both formulas from their shared generalization.

Recently discovered high-spin $d^7$ Co(II) compounds have emerged as promising candidates for implementing the highly anisotropic and bond-dependent interactions characteristic of quantum-compass models, notably the Kitaev model. To assess their viability, we analyzed all symmetry-allowed contributions to magnetic exchange within ideal edge-sharing bonds. Despite employing a combination of *ab initio* and cluster many-body calculations, our findings indicate that in actual materials, bond-dependent couplings are typically suppressed, with Heisenberg exchange dominating. We further examine the implications of these results for several key materials, such as Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$ and BaCo$_2$(AsO$_4$)$_2$.

This paper investigates a class of flows for closed, star-shaped hypersurfaces in hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^{n+1}$ evolving with a speed given by $(\sinh r)^{{\alpha}/{\beta}}\sigma_{k}^{{1}/{\beta}}$, where $\sigma_{k}$ denotes the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial of the principal curvatures, $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are positive constants, and $r$ represents the distance from points on the hypersurface to the origin. We establish convergence results under specific conditions on $k$, $\alpha$, and $\beta$. Specifically, when $k=1$, $\alpha > 1+\beta$, and the initial hypersurface is mean convex, we demonstrate that the mean convex solution exists globally in time and converges smoothly to a sphere. Furthermore, for $1 \leq k \leq n$, $\alpha > k+\beta$, and a uniformly convex initial hypersurface, we prove that the uniformly convex solution exists for all time and also converges smoothly to a sphere. These findings extend Li-Sheng-Wang's results from Euclidean space to the setting of hyperbolic space.

The majority of atomic nuclei exhibit deformation characterized by a quadrupole shape defined by the strength parameter $\beta_2$ and the triaxiality angle $\gamma$. In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, this deformation can be probed by analyzing how the collective flow of the resulting quark-gluon plasma responds to the initial-state eccentricity $\varepsilon_2$ and the transverse density gradient $d_{\perp}$. Based on analytical estimates and a Glauber model, I demonstrate that the variances, $\langle\varepsilon_2^2\rangle$ or $\langle(\delta d_{\perp}/d_{\perp})^2\rangle$, and skewnesses, $\langle\varepsilon_2^2\delta d_{\perp}/d_{\perp}\rangle$ or $\langle(\delta d_{\perp}/d_{\perp})^3\rangle$, follow simple analytical forms given by $a'+b'\beta_2^2$ and $a'+(b'+c'\cos(3\gamma))\beta_2^3$, respectively. Utilizing these relations, I developed several normalized skewnesses to disentangle the $\gamma$ dependence from the $\beta_2$ dependence, proving that the correlations between any normalized skewness and any variance can simultaneously constrain both $\beta_2$ and $\gamma$. Assuming a linear relationship with the elliptic flow $v_2$ and the mean transverse momentum $[p_{\mathrm{T}}]$ of final-state particles, similar conclusions apply to the variances and skewnesses of these observables. These findings encourage a dedicated system scan of high-energy heavy-ion collisions to measure nuclear triaxiality. This approach is optimized by first colliding prolate nuclei ($\cos(3\gamma)=1$) and oblate nuclei ($\cos(3\gamma)=-1$) with well-known $\beta_2$ values to calibrate the coefficients $b'$ and $c'$, followed by collisions of nuclei of interest that have known $\beta_2$ but unknown $\gamma$. Ultimately, these results highlight the unique potential of high-energy collisions to facilitate interdisciplinary studies in nuclear physics.

This paper investigates the time decay properties of the transport-diffusion equation featuring inhomogeneous localized damping within a multi-dimensional torus. The system involves a drift driven by an autonomous Lipschitz vector field and diffusion modeled by the standard heat equation with a small viscosity coefficient $
u$. The initial section addresses the inviscid scenario, demonstrating energy decay results that heavily rely on the ergodicity and unique ergodicity of the flow induced by the drift. The subsequent part examines the problem with small viscosity, yielding analogous results regarding exponential decay that remain uniform with respect to $
u$ over a specific logarithmic time scale, defined as $t \in [0,C_0\ln(1/
u)]$.

This work investigates the local well-posedness of the two-dimensional inviscid Boussinesq system where vorticity is defined by a singular patch. We significantly enhance the results of \cite{Hassainia-Hmidi} by substituting their density compatibility requirement with a condition regarding the degree of flatness on the singular set. A second major contribution addresses the partial viscous Boussinesq system, establishing a uniform local well-posedness theory as conductivity approaches zero. This problem is notably more complex than the inviscid scenario due to diffusion effects that can disrupt local structures; consequently, deriving weak a priori estimates requires sophisticated analysis of transport-diffusion equations under logarithmic singular potentials. Furthermore, we manage the challenges posed by commutators affecting co-normal regularity by leveraging the maximal smoothing properties of the transport-diffusion equation, which is advected by a velocity field scaling just below the Lipschitz class.

This study investigates heavy, long-lived charged particles using 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data recorded at $\sqrt{s}$= 7 and 8 TeV with the LHCb detector. The analysis primarily relies on ring imaging Cherenkov detector responses to differentiate these slow-moving heavy particles from muons. No evidence for the production of such long-lived states was observed. Consequently, the results are presented as upper limits on Drell-Yan pair production where both particles fall within the LHCb pseudorapidity acceptance range of $1.8 < \eta < 4.9$. The derived mass-dependent cross-section limits lie between 2 and 4 fb (at 95% CL) for masses ranging from 124 to 309 GeV/c$^2$.

Yang et al. recently demonstrated that every 2-positive map from $\mathcal{M}_3(\mathbb{C})$ to itself is decomposable, a result equivalent to the assertion that all PPT states on $\mathbb{C}^3\otimes\mathbb{C}^3$ possess a Schmidt number of at most 2. This finding extends the Perez-Horodecki criterion, which establishes that PPT states on $\mathbb{C}^2\otimes\mathbb{C}^2$ or $\mathbb{C}^2\otimes\mathbb{C}^3$ have Schmidt rank 1, meaning they are separable. A natural inquiry is whether Yang et al.'s result holds for PPT states defined on $\mathbb{C}^3\otimes\mathbb{C}^4$, an issue that also extends to higher dimensions. In this work, we construct a positive map suspected to serve as a counterexample. More broadly, we present a class of positive maps between matrix algebras whose $k$-positivity characteristics can be readily manipulated.

Driven by recent breakthroughs in deep learning, interest in sensorimotor learning has surged to new heights. This paper introduces an open-source framework designed to gather extensive, time-synchronized synthetic data across diverse sensory modalities—including audio, video, and proprioception—to facilitate robot manipulation learning. We illustrate the system's capability by training a humanoid drumming robot to produce original motion sequences from target audio inputs, leveraging cross-modal mappings. Our evaluation assesses the system's performance through cross-modal retrieval quality, specifically its ability to generate appropriate motion sequences that align with desired, previously unseen audio or video data.

Let $p$ be a prime. We demonstrate that specific amalgamated free pro-$p$ products of Demushkin groups with pro-$p$-cyclic amalgams cannot form a 1-cyclotomic oriented pro-$p$ group, and consequently, they do not appear as maximal pro-$p$ Galois groups for fields containing a $p$-th root of unity. Furthermore, we observe that other cohomological obstructions typically employed to identify pro-$p$ groups that are not maximal pro-$p$ Galois groups—specifically, the quadraticity of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$-cohomology and the vanishing of Massey products—are ineffective for these particular groups. Finally, we establish that the Mina\v{c}-T\^an pro-$p$ group also fails to yield a 1-cyclotomic oriented pro-$p$ group, and we conjecture that all 1-cyclotomic oriented pro-$p$ groups satisfy the strong $n$-Massey vanishing property for $n=3,4$.

We demonstrate that the cross section for the diffractive dissociation of a small onium by a large nucleus, characterized by a total rapidity $Y$ and a minimum rapidity gap $Y_{\text{gap}}$, corresponds to a specific classical observable within a stochastic process describing the onium's evolution via color dipole branchings as rapidity increases. In a well-defined parametric limit, this quantity formally equals twice the probability that an even number of dipoles effectively participate in the scattering, evaluated in a frame where the onium has evolved to rapidity $Y - Y_{\text{gap}}$. Consequently, determining asymptotic solutions to the Kovchegov-Levin equation, which governs the $Y$-dependence of the diffractive cross section, reduces to solving a probabilistic problem. This framework enables the derivation of a parameter-free analytical expression for the gap distribution. Notably, events involving the simultaneous interaction of many dipoles are significant, as the distribution of the number $k$ of participating dipoles is found to be proportional to $1/[k(k-1)]$.

We demonstrate that for a multigraph $G$ with $n$ vertices, the number of edges is bounded by $O(n^2\log n)$, assuming that any two edges intersect at most once, parallel edges do not cross, and the lens formed by every pair of parallel edges contains at least one vertex. Consequently, we establish an extension of the Crossing Lemma by Ajtai, Chvátal, Newborn, Szemerédi, and Leighton: if $G$ possesses $e \geq 4n$ edges, any drawing of $G$ satisfying these conditions yields at least $\Omega\left(\frac{e^3}{n^2\log(e/n)}\right)$ crossings. This result resolves a query posed by Kaufmann et al. and is tight aside from the logarithmic factor.

The growing volume and highly volatile nature of indicators of compromise (IoCs) present significant processing challenges. After compromised systems are remediated, adversaries typically shift to new targets or alter their tactics. To streamline IoC evaluation and leverage collective analytical power, threat intelligence sharing platforms have been developed to promote community collaboration. This paper utilizes the open-source platform MISP to demonstrate a generic scoring model designed to manage the decay of shared IoCs across communities with diverse objectives. By incorporating existing metadata alongside the indicators, the model assists automated systems in assessing the validity of shared IoCs. Finally, the model is tested against common scenarios typically encountered during incident response.

Although learning policies through preference-based reward learning has become a popular approach for tailoring agent behavior, it is anecdotally known to be vulnerable to spurious correlations and reward hacking. While previous research has largely addressed causal confusion within reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning, this study investigates the phenomenon specifically in reward learning. We conducted sensitivity and ablation analyses across three benchmark domains, revealing that while preferences can yield minimal test error, the learned rewards often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution states, leading to suboptimal policy performance upon optimization. Our results indicate that non-causal distractor features, noise in stated preferences, partial state observability, and increased model capacity can all intensify causal confusion. Furthermore, we propose methods to interpret causally confused rewards by observing that optimizing such rewards pushes the policy off its training distribution, creating a scenario where predicted rewards remain high while true rewards drop. These findings highlight the susceptibility of reward learning to causal confusion, particularly in high-dimensional environments, demonstrating that overlooking even a single factor—such as data coverage or state definition—can rapidly lead to unexpected and undesirable behaviors.

We introduce a renormalization group (RG) framework designed to elucidate the localization characteristics of one-dimensional quasiperiodic lattice systems. This RG evolution arises from expanding the unit cell of successive commensurate approximants, where fixed points represent exactly solvable models identifiable by their most basic commensurate approximant. This methodology not only reformulates numerous existing exact solutions for 1D quasiperiodic systems but also facilitates the discovery of novel families of exactly solvable models. While generic models produce complex RG flows and intricate phase diagrams, analyzing relevant and irrelevant perturbations allows us to determine phase boundaries with exponential precision relative to the approximant unit cell size. Consequently, our results offer a unified perspective on diverse classes of 1D quasiperiodic systems, enabling a complete characterization of the localization phase diagram—including extended, localized, and critical phases along with their transitions—and providing clear guidance on constructing exactly solvable quasiperiodic models.

The study examines electron-positron pair production within spatially inhomogeneous electric fields characterized by high or low central frequencies and sinusoidal phase modulation. Results indicate that the momentum spectrum, representing the reduced particle number, exhibits heightened sensitivity to variations in the phase's modulated amplitude and frequency. As modulation parameters increase, the interference effects within the momentum spectrum become more pronounced. Specifically, in fields with high central frequencies, an exceptionally symmetric momentum spectrum emerges, which is significantly disrupted by large modulated amplitudes. Additionally, the reduced particle number can be substantially amplified by modulation factors, ranging from a few times to an order of magnitude. A detailed analysis of spatial scales reveals that the reduced particle number rises rapidly at small scales but stabilizes at larger scales. Two notable characteristics of the reduced particle number are identified: the existence of optimal modulation parameters and the ability to achieve identical particle numbers through different parameter sets. This latter finding is significant as it allows for alternative phase modulation strategies to attain specific pair production targets, even under optimal conditions.

While it is established that Bloch domain walls in anisotropic ferromagnets are transparent to spin waves when dipolar interactions are approximated as effective anisotropy, this paper investigates scattering by incorporating the full complexity of dipolar interactions within the distorted wave Born approximation. Although implementing this approach is challenging due to the specific nature of dipolar forces, the study overcomes these hurdles by decomposing the dipolar contribution to the spin wave operator into two parts: a term commuting with the non-dipolar spin wave operator and a local term suitable for perturbative treatment. Analysis of the resulting scattering parameters reveals that, in general, the reflection coefficient does not vanish and transmitted waves experience a lateral shift even at normal incidence. This shift can be significantly amplified by routing spin waves through an array of widely spaced domain walls. Notably, at normal incidence, the reflection coefficient becomes zero, meaning the outgoing spin wave suffers no attenuation from scattering at the walls. This phenomenon holds considerable promise for controlling spin waves in magnonic devices.

We introduce a data-driven approach for synthesizing strategies in partially-known switched stochastic systems. System properties are defined using linear temporal logic over finite traces (LTLf), which matches the expressiveness of standard LTL while specifically accommodating finite behaviors. The framework initially estimates unknown dynamics through Gaussian process regression. Subsequently, it constructs a formal abstraction of the switched system as an uncertain Markov model, specifically an Interval Markov Decision Process (IMDP), by integrating the system's stochastic nature with uncertainties arising from the learning phase. A strategy is then synthesized on this IMDP to maximize the probability of satisfying the LTLf specification while ensuring robustness against all abstraction uncertainties. This strategy is subsequently refined into a switching policy for the original stochastic system. We demonstrate that this approach yields a near-optimal strategy and establish a bound on the error relative to the optimal solution. Finally, we validate the framework through experiments on diverse case studies, encompassing both linear and non-linear switched stochastic systems.

This study details the search for the Standard Model Higgs Boson in its two-photon decay channel using data collected by the CMS experiment during the 2010 and 2011 LHC runs, which operated at a center-of-mass collision energy of 7 TeV.

We suggest modeling both $n$-qubits and the quantum gates operating on them as elements within the complex Clifford algebra defined over a complex vector space of dimension $2n$. Within this framework, the Dirac formalism can be implemented directly. We validate this method by executing quantum computations using several standard quantum gates. Furthermore, we contrast our approach with representations based on real geometric algebras.

We define and examine sequences of Bernstein-type linear operators applied to bivariate functions over the unit disk. This involves analyzing Bernstein-type operators following a domain transformation, investigating bivariate Bernstein-Stancu operators, and introducing Bernstein-type operators on disk quadrants through continuously differentiable function transformations. We establish convergence theorems for continuous functions and determine the rate of convergence. Additionally, we present numerical examples that compare approximations derived from shifted Bernstein-Stancu operators versus those using the Bernstein-type operator on disk quadrants.

The correlated probabilistic framework introduced and analyzed by Hanel et al. (2009) relies on a self-dual transformation of the index $q$, which defines a broad extension of Boltzmann-Gibbs statistical mechanics known as nonextensive statistical mechanics. In the thermodynamic limit ($N\to\infty$), this approach produces a $Q$-Gaussian distribution for any selected $Q \in [1,3)$. This study demonstrates that by appropriately extending this self-dual transformation, one can derive a comprehensive family of such probabilistic models, each converging to a $Q_c$-Gaussian ($Q_c \ge 1$) as $N\to\infty$. This newly identified family is isomorphic to the model proposed by Hanel et al. via a specific monotonic mapping $Q_c(Q)$. Furthermore, following the methodology of Tirnakli et al. (2022), we provide numerical evidence that this family of correlated probabilistic models reinforces the validity of a $q$-generalized Large Deviation Theory (LDT), aligning with the Legendre structure inherent in thermodynamics. This analysis enhances our comprehension of complex systems characterized by global correlations among their components, bolstering the conjecture that generic models where the attractors of sums of $N$ strongly-correlated random variables are $Q$-Gaussians are invariably linked to $q$-exponentials within the framework of LDT.

The fundamental concepts of quantum mechanics are defined using separable, infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}$. Within the Hilbert lattice $\mathcal{L}$, comprising the closed linear subspaces of $\mathcal{H}$, states and observables can be expressed as specific types of measures, as detailed in [21]. This paper aims to demonstrate the existence of a robust notion of computability for these data structures according to Weihrauch's Type Two Effectivity (TTE) [26]. Rather than explicitly defining admissible representations for the relevant data types, we prove that they reside within the category $\mathbf{QCB}_0$, which is equivalent to $\mathbf{AdmRep}$, the category of admissible representations and continuously realizable maps between them. To achieve this, particularly for observables, we substitute measures with valuations, enabling the proof of an effective version of von Neumann's Spectral Theorem.

Davis recently began investigating an $n$-dimensional generalization of the Klein bottle, which serves as a moduli space for planar polygons under specific side length constraints. Having already established numerous topological invariants and manifold properties for this space, the primary objective of this brief note is to demonstrate that the $n$-Klein bottle constitutes a real Bott manifold and to identify its associated Bott matrix. Furthermore, we characterize two additional classes of polygon spaces as total spaces of iterated $S^1$ bundles. For all these instances, we calculate the Betti numbers by applying a formula attributed to Suciu and Trevisan.

This paper addresses resource allocation in wireless interference channels subject to link outage constraints. Because the associated optimization problem is non-convex, traditional methods for determining optimal power allocation are computationally demanding and often impractical. Recently, deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising solution for such non-convex problems due to its lower complexity. This correspondence employs a deep Q-learning (DQL) framework that interacts with the wireless environment to learn optimal power allocation strategies for an interference channel, aiming to maximize the total system sum-rate while ensuring the reliability of individual links. To mitigate inherent instability in the learning process, two distinct deep Q-networks are utilized. Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed DQL method surpasses existing geometric programming-based solutions.

Solid polycrystalline materials experiencing diffusion creep are typically modeled using Cauchy continuum frameworks featuring a Newtonian viscous rheology that varies with grain size. However, these standard continua omit the rotational degrees of freedom necessary to account for grain rotation. This study presents a broader continuum framework for diffusion creep that incorporates grain rotation by equating material deformation to that of a micropolar (Cosserat) fluid. We derive the micropolar constitutive tensors through the homogenization of physics governing a discrete set of rigid grains, ensuring equivalent dissipation between the discrete and continuum formulations. General constitutive laws are established for both Nabarro-Herring (volume diffusion) and Coble (grain-boundary diffusion) creep mechanisms. Detailed computations for a two-dimensional arrangement of irregular hexagonal grains demonstrate a possible coupling between rotational and translational degrees of freedom. Furthermore, if material addition or removal at grain boundaries is the sole consideration, the constitutive laws become degenerate, failing to resist deformation modes involving pure tangential motion at these boundaries. This degeneracy is resolved by incorporating resistance to grain-boundary sliding or by applying additional constraints to the deformation.

This study analyzes the degrees of freedom (DoF) regions for the multi-user vector broadcast channel under periodic channel state information (CSI) feedback. As part of this analysis, we introduce a novel transmission strategy termed space-time interference alignment, which leverages both current and historical CSI. Employing this alignment method, we derive an inner bound for the sum-DoF region as a function of the normalized CSI feedback frequency, which quantifies the speed of feedback relative to channel variations. A key finding is that the sum-DoF gain improves substantially when users transmit both current and outdated CSI compared to scenarios involving only current CSI. Furthermore, we characterize the trade-off between CSI feedback delay and sum-DoF gain for the multi-user vector broadcast channel using a normalized delay metric that reflects CSI obsolescence relative to the channel coherence time. A critical insight emerges: optimal DoF gain is attainable provided the feedback delay remains below a specific fraction of the channel coherence time, thereby mathematically validating the intuition that minimal delays have negligible impact.

Amid growing concerns about AI's societal impact, this article examines how AI and automation may ignite a new social struggle between existing capitalist elites and a rising "creative class" (including R&D scientists, engineers, and business developers), potentially reshaping social tensions and urban landscapes. Drawing parallels to the 17th–18th century European conflict between the aristocracy and the emerging bourgeoisie, and incorporating lessons from historical urban changes and contemporary urban geography trends, the piece outlines potential future transformations in cities driven by shifting production and consumption economies.

While statistical analysis of multiple networks is increasingly prevalent, most existing approaches assume networks share a common set of labeled vertices. This study addresses the challenge of reconstructing a parent network from noisy, unlabeled samples.
