We pinpoint a specific regime within noisy network literature where recovery is both asymptotically unbiased and computationally feasible, achieved through a three-stage process: first, aligning networks using sequential pairwise graph matching; second, calculating the sample average of these aligned networks; and third, estimating the parent network by thresholding that average. In contrast, prior research on multiple unlabeled networks is limited to trivial cases due to the prohibitive complexity of brute-force methods.

This paper introduces the concept of firm non-expansive mappings within weak metric spaces, thereby broadening earlier results established for Banach and specific geodesic spaces. We demonstrate that for these mappings, the minimal displacement, linear rate of escape, and asymptotic step size are identical, thus generalizing a theorem by Reich and Shafrir.

Studying how interlocutors cooperate is fundamental to understanding dialogue pragmatics. Models assuming only cooperative agents cannot adequately explain the dynamics of strategic conversations. Therefore, this work examines agents' capacity to detect non-cooperative partners while simultaneously performing a visual-dialogue task. In this novel framework, we evaluate the optimality of communication strategies aimed at achieving this multi-task goal. Utilizing learning theory, we construct a theoretical model for identifying non-cooperative interlocutors and apply it to analyze various communication approaches. Furthermore, we present a new corpus of non-cooperative conversations regarding images within the GuessWhat?! dataset (De Vries et al., 2017). We employ reinforcement learning to implement multiple communication strategies in this context, with empirical results confirming our theoretical predictions.

Over the last few years, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have yielded substantial advancements in speech enhancement (SE), though their training remains challenging. This study presents several refinements to GAN training protocols applicable to the majority of GAN-based SE architectures. We introduce consistency loss functions designed to address discrepancies between the time and time-frequency domains arising from Fourier and Inverse Fourier Transforms. Additionally, we propose a self-correcting optimization strategy for training GAN discriminators in SE contexts, which mitigates detrimental training trajectories within specific components of the discriminator loss. Our proposed methods were evaluated across multiple state-of-the-art GAN-based SE models, yielding consistent performance gains, including new record-breaking results on the Voice Bank+DEMAND dataset.

Traditional derivations of the (generalized) Mass Action Law (MAL) rely on two conditions for the intermediate transition state (i): a short lifetime and partial equilibrium with the initial reactants of the elementary reaction. This partial equilibrium assumption (ii) implies that the reverse decomposition of intermediates occurs much more rapidly than their progression through other channels to form products. In this study, we show how eliminating this partial equilibrium assumption alters reaction rates. This kinetic refinement of transition state theory yields an effective "entanglement" of rates, where they manifest as linear combinations of various MAL expressions.

The independent set polynomial holds significant importance across various fields. For any integer $\Delta \geq 2$, the Shearer threshold is defined as $\lambda^*(\Delta)=(\Delta-1)^{\Delta-1}/\Delta^{\Delta}$. It is established that when $\lambda < -\lambda^*(\Delta)$, there exist graphs with maximum degree $\Delta$ such that their independent set polynomial evaluated at $\lambda$ is non-positive; conversely, no such graphs exist for any $\lambda > -\lambda^*(\Delta)$. This study is driven by the computational challenge of approximating the independent set polynomial in the regime where $\lambda < -\lambda^*(\Delta)$. The central complexity issue revolves around "implementation." Informally, an implementation of a real number $\lambda'$ refers to a graph whose hard-core partition function, at parameter $\lambda$, mimics a vertex weight of $\lambda'$, meaning $\lambda'$ represents the ratio of the partition function's contribution from independent sets containing a specific vertex versus those excluding it. These implementations form the foundation of intractability results for approximating the independent set polynomial. Our primary finding demonstrates that for any $\lambda < -\lambda^*(\Delta)$, one can implement a set of values that is dense within the real numbers. This result is tight because implementing a dense set of real values becomes impossible for any $\lambda > -\lambda^*(\Delta)$. This discovery has already been applied in a joint paper with \bezakova{} (STOC 2018) to prove that approximating the independent set polynomial evaluation is \#P-hard for graphs with degree at most $\Delta$ at any $\lambda < -\lambda^*(\Delta)$. Additionally, the appendix presents an extra inapproximability result that is incomparable to the main theorem, strengthening the inapproximability bound to an exponential factor while reducing the hardness classification to NP-hardness.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) frequently reveal heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs), making the identification of patient subgroups with comparable responses crucial for advancing precision medicine. While RCTs often measure multiple clinical outcomes, each potentially exhibiting distinct heterogeneity, existing tools have primarily focused on single-outcome scenarios rather than multi-outcome settings. This study introduces a framework designed to partition the covariate space and identify subgroups across several outcomes simultaneously by leveraging joint confidence intervals. Validated using both synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets involving two outcomes, our algorithm successfully captures heterogeneous treatment effects for all outcomes at once.

As energy consumption by data centers and computing systems escalates, integrating energy efficiency into scheduling algorithm design is essential. Machine learning offers a practical solution by forecasting system load using historical data, yet its efficacy relies heavily on prediction accuracy, often yielding suboptimal results when forecasts are poor. Conversely, traditional online algorithms provide worst-case guarantees but tend to be overly pessimistic for many real-world scenarios. Addressing these limitations, this paper adopts the principles of machine learning-augmented algorithms to optimize the classical, deadline-based, online speed-scaling problem. By introducing a novel prediction framework, we propose algorithms that achieve provably low energy consumption when predictions are accurate, remain robust against poor forecasts, and exhibit smooth performance degradation as prediction errors increase.

Utilizing 330-meter baselines to achieve an angular resolution as fine as 0.1–0.2 milliseconds of arc and operating within the 600–900 nm spectral range, the CHARA Array is optimally positioned to determine precise fundamental stellar parameters. The CHARA/SPICA (Stellar Parameters and Images with a Cophased Array) project is designed to conduct an extensive survey of stars across the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. This initiative will also investigate how various surface structures and variability types impact the accuracy of derived fundamental parameters. Furthermore, the survey aims to establish new surface-brightness-colour relations to facilitate distance measurements and the characterization of faint stars. SPICA consists of a visible-light 6T fibered instrument and a near-infrared fringe sensor. This paper outlines the scientific objectives and primary specifications of SPICA-VIS, concluding with a presentation of the initial performance metrics achieved during the commissioning phase.

This study establishes finite-blocklength achievability bounds for the Gaussian multiple access channel (MAC) and random access channel (RAC) subject to average-error and maximal-power constraints. By employing random codewords uniformly distributed on a sphere alongside a maximum likelihood decoder, the derived MAC rate bound for each transmitter aligns with the MolavianJazi-Laneman bound (2015) regarding its first- and second-order terms, while refining the remaining terms to $\frac12\frac{\log n}{n}+O \left(\frac 1 n \right)$ bits per channel use. These findings are subsequently extended to a RAC framework where neither the encoders nor the decoder identifies which of the $K$ potential transmitters are active. Utilizing a rateless coding approach, decoding takes place at a time $n_t$ contingent upon the decoder's estimate $t$ of the active transmitter count $k$. At each potential decoding instant $n_i$ (where $i \leq t$), single-bit feedback from the decoder to all encoders signals when transmission should cease. For this RAC scenario, the proposed code attains the same first-, second-, and third-order performance as the leading known results for the Gaussian MAC.

Singular spectrum analysis has been applied to examine the evolution of mean sea-level atmospheric pressure since 1850, revealing striking symmetries of orders 3 and 4 in the main trend components. In the Northern Hemisphere (NH), three positive features form an almost perfect equilateral triangle, whereas the Southern Hemisphere (SH) exhibits three positive features arranged in an isosceles triangle, potentially including a fourth, weaker feature. This geometric pattern can be modeled as Taylor-Couette flow of mode 3 for the NH and mode 4 for the SH. Notably, the NH's triskelion displays remarkable regularity and order-three symmetry despite the absence of cylindrical symmetry in northern continents. The SH features are characterized by greater intensity and size, which correlates with the annular AAO. Beyond the dominant trends, the analysis identifies quasi-periodic components corresponding to the Jose, Gleissberg, Hale, and Schwabe cycles, along with periods of 130, 90, 50, 22, 15, 4, 1.8, 1, 0.5, 0.33, and 0.25 years, representing the annual cycle and its first three harmonics.

Leveraging the robust expressive power of graphs, graph-based methods have become widely adopted for processing multi-modal medical data, yielding remarkable results across diverse biomedical domains. In disease prediction, most current graph-based approaches manually construct graphs based on specific modalities, such as demographic data, before integrating additional modalities via Graph Representation Learning (GRL) to derive patient representations. However, manually designing an appropriate graph is a challenging task, and these methods often overlook the intricate correlations between modalities. Consequently, these limitations hinder the provision of comprehensive patient condition information necessary for reliable diagnosis. To address this, we introduce MMGL, an end-to-end Multi-modal Graph Learning framework for multi-modal disease prediction. To fully harness rich information across modalities related to diseases, we propose a modality-aware representation learning strategy that aggregates features by exploiting both the correlation and complementarity among modalities. Moreover, rather than relying on manual graph construction, MMGL captures latent graph structures through adaptive graph learning. This process is jointly optimized with the prediction model to uncover intrinsic connections among samples. Additionally, the model supports inductive learning for unseen data. Extensive experiments on two disease prediction tasks demonstrate that MMGL outperforms existing methods, with the code available at \url{https://github.com/SsGood/MMGL}.

Open-domain question answering relies on retrieving evidence from extensive corpora to address queries. While current leading neural methods depend on intermediate evidence annotations for training, these labels are costly and prevent adaptation to scenarios where only question-answer pairs exist. This study explores whether models can autonomously locate evidence within large corpora using solely distant supervision from answer labels, thereby eliminating additional annotation expenses. We propose DistDR, a novel framework that iteratively refines a weak retriever by alternating between identifying evidence using the current model and guiding the model toward the most probable evidence. DistDR achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised state-of-the-art methods on both single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks without utilizing any evidence labels. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that DistDR progressively identifies more accurate evidence through iterations, directly driving model performance improvements.

This research investigates novel facets of twin prime distribution, with a particular emphasis on how prime pairs are arranged within arithmetic progressions based on the residues of their initial members. We identify a modified totient function as pivotal to this inquiry, analyzing it to develop a fresh heuristic for the twin prime conjecture. Additionally, we examine a sieve method analogous to Eratosthenes' sieve and present a formula resembling Legendre's approach to the prime counting function, both applied specifically to twin primes. The study concludes with an analysis of three distinct biases affecting twin prime distribution, offering comparisons with corresponding patterns in the distribution of standard primes wherever feasible.

This work examines limitations on the power spectrum of primordial tensor perturbations by synthesizing data from Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations with direct gravitational wave detections from LIGO/Virgo and DECIGO. The analysis highlights two key findings: (1) Although inflation forecasts an approximately power-law shape for the primordial tensor spectrum, it does not specify its amplitude. Since neither Planck nor LIGO/Virgo has yet observed primordial tensor modes, it is unsurprising that current data cannot yield any model-independent constraints on the spectrum's slope. (2) The disparity between CMB and LIGO/Virgo scales exceeds 19 orders of magnitude, with DECIGO differing by 16. I demonstrate that extrapolating a power law from CMB frequencies to direct detection ranges can overestimate the amplitude of primordial tensor modes by up to two orders of magnitude compared to realistic single-field inflation models. Furthermore, the tensor amplitude at direct detection scales is largely uncorrelated with the spectral index at CMB scales, meaning any resulting constraints rely heavily on the specific form of the inflationary potential.

This work investigates inflation driven by a fermionic field with non-minimal gravitational coupling, utilizing the constant-roll framework. We analyze a specific coupling form and conduct the corresponding inflationary study. By comparing our results with Planck CMB anisotropy data, we derive observational constraints on the model's parameter space and its predictions. Our findings indicate that for $|\xi|=0.1$ and $N=60$, the predicted values of $r$ and $n_{s}$ align well with observations within the range $-1.5<\beta\leq-0.9$.

This study examines information-theoretic security for satellite-to-ground links. While Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) offers robust security based on quantum physics laws, its application in space is hindered by extremely low key rates and the inability to operate during the day. Conversely, eavesdropping on free-space channels appears difficult due to orbital mechanics constraints. By assuming an eavesdropper cannot be present within a specific exclusion zone around the transmitter and receiver, we can limit their access to only a fraction of the optical signal. In this scenario, quantum-keyless private (direct) communication, modeled as a wiretap channel, serves as a viable alternative for achieving information-theoretic security. Similar to QKD, legitimate users are constrained by current technology, whereas the eavesdropper is limited only by physical laws, specifically the Helstrom detector for measurements and the Holevo bound for quantum electrodynamics. We demonstrate that positive keyless private capacity exists over a classical-quantum wiretap channel using on-off-keying of coherent states. Numerical results for a setup comparable to recent Micius satellite experiments are compared against the fundamental limits of QKD secret key rates. Our findings show significantly higher rates than QKD when the exclusion area is less than 13 meters for Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. Furthermore, we illustrate that wiretap channel-based quantum keyless privacy is far less susceptible to noise and signal dynamics, enabling daytime operation.

We present a class of stochastic maps, specifically certain Markov kernels defined on compact Hausdorff spaces, and develop a stochastic counterpart to the Gelfand spectrum functor. This work establishes a stochastic version of the commutative Gelfand-Naimark Theorem, thereby bridging concepts from algebra and operator theory with those from topology and probability. To ensure completeness, we provide a review of stochastic matrices, their connection to positive maps on commutative $C^*$-algebras, and the original Gelfand-Naimark Theorem. The material requires no prior knowledge of probability theory or $C^*$-algebras and includes several examples drawn from physics.

In passive linear systems, the conservation of energy prohibits the total merging of power from multiple input wave channels into one output channel. However, we show that both coherent and incoherent plane waves can be fully combined using metasurfaces with spatiotemporal variations. This structure directs waves of identical frequency but different incident angles into a single direction. By shifting the frequencies of the output waves, the metasurface ensures perfect incoherent power combining. This general concept is applicable across electromagnetic spectra, ranging from microwaves to optics, and can extend to other physical wave types.

Graph signal processing (GSP) has emerged as a vital instrument in image processing due to its capacity to uncover inherent data structures. However, numerous real-world multimedia datasets display heterogeneous structures across different frames. Multilayer graphs (MLG) offer a superior representation for such data, including videos and hyperspectral images, compared to traditional single-layer graphs. To extend GSP to multilayer graph models and enable multilayer analysis for image processing, this study introduces a tensor-based framework for multilayer graph signal processing (M-GSP) and presents practical M-GSP tools. Furthermore, we provide guidelines for applying M-GSP in image processing and demonstrate several applications, such as RGB image compression, edge detection, and hyperspectral image segmentation. Successful experimental outcomes highlight the effectiveness and potential future of M-GSP within the field of image processing.

This study introduces COCONUT, a novel implicit unstructured coronal code designed to deliver rapid and precise inputs for space weather forecasting, serving as an alternative to empirical models. The research utilizes all 20 available solar photospheric magnetic maps from July 2, 2019—the date of a solar eclipse—and applies uniform pre-processing and MHD simulation parameters to each. Performance is evaluated against three remote-sensing metrics: white-light eclipse imagery for streamer edges, EUV synoptic maps for coronal holes, and white-light coronagraph data for the heliospheric current sheet. Results indicate that the selection of input magnetic maps significantly influences forecast accuracy, yielding success rates of 24% to 85% for streamer edges, 24% to 88% for coronal hole boundaries, and a mean angular deviation of 4 to 12 degrees for the heliospheric current sheet. Overall, HMI data provided the best performance across all indicators, followed by GONG-ADAPT. Specifically, HMI excelled at streamer edges, while GONG-ADAPT performed best for polar coronal holes; HMI synchronous data was superior for equatorial coronal holes and the streamer belt. The study emphasizes the critical importance of filling the solar poles, demonstrating that they must be considered even for predictions focused on the ecliptic plane.

Low-power computer vision on embedded systems offers numerous applications, and this paper introduces an efficient technique for object re-identification (reID), which involves matching a query image against a gallery of known images. While current state-of-the-art methods depend on large, computationally demanding Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), we propose a novel hierarchical DNN architecture that leverages attribute labels from the training data to achieve efficient reID. In this hierarchy, each node employs a small DNN to identify a specific attribute of the query image. The DNN at each leaf node specializes in re-identifying only a subset of the gallery—specifically those images matching the attributes identified along the path from the root to that leaf. Consequently, accurate re-identification is achieved by processing the query through only a few small DNNs. When compared to existing state-of-the-art reID techniques, our method incurs a 4% accuracy reduction but delivers substantial resource efficiency: it reduces memory usage by 74%, operations by 72%, query latency by 67%, and energy consumption by 65%.

The Kochen-Specker theorem, a cornerstone of quantum foundations, has generated significant interest since its introduction. We demonstrate that within every Kochen-Specker graph, there exist intriguing subgraphs called $01$-gadgets that encapsulate the core contradiction required to establish the theorem. Specifically, every Kochen-Specker graph contains a $01$-gadget, and conversely, any $01$-gadget suffices to construct a proof of the Kochen-Specker theorem. Furthermore, we establish that $01$-gadgets serve as a fundamental primitive for formulating both state-independent and state-dependent statistical Kochen-Specker arguments, as well as providing straightforward constructive proofs for an "extended" Kochen-Specker theorem originally proposed by Pitowsky.

Providing explanations for AI model predictions is vital for cybersecurity decision-making, particularly when erroneous predictions risk severe damage or loss of life and critical assets. Despite their high performance, most current AI models fail to offer such explanations. This work introduces PhilaeX, a novel explainable AI method that heuristically identifies an optimized subset of features to generate comprehensive explanations. PhilaeX isolates features responsible for borderline predictions and extracts those with positive individual contributions, quantifying these attributions via Ridge regression optimization. Two experiments validate the method's fidelity: first, by assessing its ability to correctly identify activated features in Android malware adversarial samples using PhilaeX's attribution values; second, through deduction and augmentation tests. Results demonstrate that PhilaeX correctly explains various classifiers with higher fidelity than state-of-the-art methods like LIME and SHAP.

This paper examines housing markets as defined by Shapley and Scarf (1974), focusing on the computational complexity of questions concerning an agent $a$'s situation within a market $H$. We demonstrate that determining whether there exists a core allocation where (i) $a$ receives a specific house, (ii) $a$ does not receive a specific house, or (iii) $a$ receives a house different from her own is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard. Furthermore, we establish that the core of housing markets adheres to an improvement property: if an agent $a$ currently holds a house $h$ in a core allocation and the value of that house increases, then the modified market admits a core allocation where $a$ receives either $h$ or a house she prefers to $h$, and such an allocation can be computed efficiently. Finally, we extend this finding to the Stable Roommates setting, proving that stable matchings in one-sided markets also satisfy an analogous improvement property.

The study demonstrates that dynamical quantum phase transitions, characterized by singularities in the Loschmidt rate, closely mirror standard Rabi oscillations typical of two-level system dynamics. In certain many-body systems, this analogy extends further, allowing the behavior of models like the transverse Ising chain to be directly mapped onto such simple dynamics. Additionally, the work elucidates why a direct connection is proposed between Loschmidt echo singularities and quantum scars.

This study explores applying a retrospective approximation framework to effectively address risk-averse optimization problems through importance sampling (IS). Although IS is a leading method for managing the extensive sample sizes required to estimate tail risk metrics like Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), its application in CVaR-driven optimization is hindered by the necessity of customizing the IS measure change for each iteration and the resulting circular dependency. The proposed algorithm resolves these issues by utilizing a univariate IS transformation that ensures consistent variance reduction within a retrospective approximation process, facilitating the tuning of IS parameters. Consequently, the resulting simulation-based approximation scheme combines the computational efficiency of retrospective approximation with the logarithmically efficient variance reduction provided by importance sampling.

This work introduces KDF, a novel framework for addressing kinodynamic motion planning by combining sampling-based planning with funnel-based feedback control. Designed for systems governed by intricate, nonlinear, and uncertain dynamics (differential constraints), the approach operates in two stages: first, a geometric planner generates a high-level safe trajectory within a user-defined free space; second, a low-level funnel control algorithm ensures the system tracks this path safely. Notably, neither the planner nor the controller requires knowledge of the specific system dynamics, rendering the scheme highly adaptable across diverse systems and scenarios. Intuitively, the funnel control module implicitly handles dynamic variations, enabling the use of purely geometric planners. The effectiveness of this method is confirmed through extensive simulations and experiments involving a 6-DOF robotic arm.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have revolutionized machine learning, becoming integral to applications in image, video, speech, and natural language processing. While Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) and specialized accelerators have traditionally met the rising computational needs of DNNs, the expanding model sizes now expose limitations in von Neumann architectures, which demand excessive memory bandwidth to fully utilize processing elements as data remains primarily in main memory. To address this "memory wall," processing-in-memory (PIM) has emerged as a viable solution for machine learning workloads. This study introduces a novel DRAM-based PIM multiplication primitive combined with intra-bank acceleration to speed up matrix-vector operations. The proposed primitive incurs less than 1% area overhead and requires no modifications to existing DRAM peripherals, ensuring seamless adoption in standard DRAM chips. Building on this, we designed a comprehensive DRAM-based PIM architecture, including a specific data mapping scheme and dataflow tailored for executing DNNs directly within DRAM. System evaluations on architectures such as AlexNet, VGG16, and ResNet18 demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves up to 19.5x speedup compared to an NVIDIA Titan Xp GPU, underscoring the critical necessity of overcoming memory bottlenecks in future DNN hardware.

This research examines fairness in Machine Learning (FairML) by analyzing attribute-based explanations produced by ML models, operating under the hypothesis that biased models generate biased explanations. To validate this, we first reinterpret established statistical definitions of group fairness through the framework of model explanations. Subsequently, we introduce a new method for detecting fairness or unfairness in any black-box model. We further investigate post-processing techniques for fairness, exploring how explanations can enhance the individual fairness of bias mitigation strategies. Finally, we present a novel post-processing mitigation approach that improves individual fairness in recourse scenarios while preserving group-level fairness.

This work presents an integration-by-parts reduction method grounded in Gröbner bases. We define the supporting noncommutative rational double-shift algebra, within which the integration-by-parts relations constitute a left ideal. Using the one-loop massless box as a detailed case study, we demonstrate the complete reduction to master integrals via the Gröbner basis technique and evaluate the implementation's performance. Furthermore, we pinpoint potential performance bottlenecks in more complex scenarios and outline promising avenues for future research.

Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), supported by specialized neuromorphic hardware, offer a path toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence. By integrating SNNs with deep reinforcement learning (RL), a viable solution for realistic control tasks emerges. However, current SNN-based RL approaches are scarce; most either struggle with generalization or rely on Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to estimate value functions. The former requires extensive hyper-parameter tuning for every scenario, while the latter constrains the variety of applicable RL algorithms and overlooks the significant energy costs associated with training. To address these challenges and create a robust spike-based RL framework, we were inspired by non-spiking interneurons in insects to develop the Deep Spiking Q-network (DSQN). This method utilizes the membrane voltage of non-spiking neurons to represent Q-values, enabling the direct learning of robust policies from high-dimensional sensory inputs through end-to-end RL. Testing across 17 Atari games reveals that DSQN outperforms the ANN-based Deep Q-network (DQN) in the majority of cases. Furthermore, results indicate that DSQN exhibits superior learning stability and greater resilience against adversarial attacks.

While algorithms are a central topic, there is no consensus on their definition; for instance, Gurevich defines them as abstract state machines, whereas others describe them as recursors. We advocate for a third perspective that synthesizes these two distinct viewpoints. Grounded in computability logic, this approach defines an algorithm as $A(I,O)$, where $I$ represents a set of input services and $O$ an output service. This framework yields the following modern definition: {\it An algorithm $A$ is a (tree of) sequence of legal moves for providing $O$ using $I$. } In this formulation, $A$ is expressed in an imperative language or abstract state machine, while $I$ and $O$ are formulated using recursors and logical specifications.

Accurate optical flow estimation is vital for numerous video analysis and restoration techniques utilized across sectors such as media, industrial inspection, and automotive applications. This study examines the qualitative performance of optical flow algorithms when embedded within a state-of-the-art video denoising framework. We evaluate both traditional methods (e.g., TV-L1) and modern deep learning-based approaches (such as RAFT or BMBC). Rather than relying on standard benchmarks common in literature, our qualitative assessment utilizes realistic, challenging content featuring noise and significant motion.

In 1975, P. Erd\H{o}s posed the problem of finding the maximum number of edges, denoted as $f(n)$, in a graph with $n$ vertices such that all cycles have distinct lengths. Specifically, $f^{\ast}(n)$ represents the maximum edge count for simple graphs on $n$ vertices satisfying this cycle-length uniqueness condition. The set $M_n$ consists of all such simple graphs on $n$ vertices that possess exactly $f^{\ast}(n)$ edges, and $mc(n)$ denotes the maximum cycle length among graphs in $M_n$. This paper establishes that for sufficiently large $n$, $mc(n) \leq \frac{15}{16}n$. Furthermore, we propose the following conjecture:
$$\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} {mc(n)\over n}= 0.$$

The LHCb collaboration has recently refined its analysis of the resonant $J/\psi\, p$ mass spectrum within the $\Lambda_b^0 \to J/\psi\, p\, K^-$ decay channel, utilizing combined data from Run~1 and Run~2. This updated study identifies three narrow states: $P_c (4312)^+$, $P_c (4440)^+$, and $P_c (4457)^+$, though their spin-parity configurations remain undetermined. We propose that these narrow resonances correspond to compact hidden-charm pentaquarks composed of a diquark-diquark-antiquark structure. By employing an effective Hamiltonian grounded in constituent quarks and diquarks, we computed the pentaquark mass spectrum for the full set of $SU (3)_F$ lowest $S$- and $P$-wave multiplets, incorporating key spin-spin, spin-orbit, orbital, and tensor interactions. This calculation yields a rich spectrum, allowing us to determine the quark flavor compositions, masses, and $J^P$ quantum numbers for these pentaquarks. However, heavy quark symmetry limits which of these states are observable in $\Lambda_b$-baryons, as well as in the weak decays of other $b$-baryons like $\Xi_b$ and $\Omega_b$. Furthermore, certain pentaquark states are predicted to lie below the $J/\psi\, p$ threshold in $\Lambda_b$ decays (and analogous thresholds in $\Xi_b$ and $\Omega_b$ decays). These states are expected to decay via $c \bar c$ annihilation into light hadrons or dilepton pairs, likely exhibiting narrower widths than the observed $P_c$ states. We anticipate the discovery of these states, along with other pentaquarks in the spectrum, at the LHC and potentially in the future at a Tera-$Z$ factory.

Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) molecular simulations represent a promising avenue for emerging noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers. The successful execution of these simulations relies heavily on developing accurate molecular ansatzes that are both easy to optimize and executable via shallow quantum circuits. While ansatzes are typically built from sequences of fermionic-excitation evolutions, this work demonstrates the efficacy of an alternative approach using "qubit-excitation evolutions," which adhere to qubit commutation relations rather than fermionic ones. Although qubit excitation evolutions lack certain physical attributes found in their fermionic counterparts, they successfully generate accurate ansatzes while demanding asymptotically fewer gates. Leveraging this method, we propose the Qubit-Excitation-Based Adaptive (QEB-ADAPT)-VQE protocol. This protocol adapts the ADAPT-VQE framework to perform molecular simulations with a problem-specific ansatz that is iteratively expanded by appending qubit excitation operator evolutions. Through classical numerical simulations on small molecules, we benchmark QEB-ADAPT-VQE against both the standard fermionic-ADAPT-VQE and qubit-ADAPT-VQE. Our results indicate that QEB-ADAPT-VQE surpasses qubit-ADAPT-VQE—which, to our knowledge, was previously the most circuit-efficient scalable VQE protocol for molecular simulations—in both circuit efficiency and convergence speed.

Using proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 5 $fb^{-1}$ gathered by the LHCb experiment from 2011 to 2016, the branching fraction for the $B_s^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0$ decay has been measured. The result is BR($B_s^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0$) = [8.3 $\pm$ 1.6 (stat) $\pm$ 0.9 (syst) $\pm$ 0.8 (norm) $\pm$ 0.3 ($f_s/f_d$)] $\times 10^{-6}$, where the uncertainties correspond to statistical effects, systematic errors, the normalization mode $B^0 \to \phi K_S^0$, and the hadronization fraction ratio $f_s/f_d$, respectively. This represents the most precise determination of this branching fraction to date. Additionally, the ratio of the branching fractions for $B^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0$ and $B_s^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0$ was measured relative to the latter, yielding $\frac{BR(B^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0)}{BR(B_s^0 \to K_S^0 K_S^0)}$ = [7.5 $\pm$ 3.1 (stat) $\pm$ 0.5 (syst) $\pm$ 0.3 ($f_s/f_d$)] $\times 10^{-2}$.

Using the post-Newtonian approximation, the energy of Schwarzschild spacetime is derived via the Weinberg prescription. In the first post-Newtonian approximation, the energy $E^{(1)} = m$ recovers the Newtonian treatment. However, the second post-Newtonian approximation reveals that $E^{(1)}$ is supplemented by additional terms, $E^{(2)}$, which comprise the configuration energy ($E_{\rm config}$), the energy within the gravitational field ($E_{\rm field}$), and a surface integral term. These extra terms provide the necessary post-Newtonian corrections to the Newtonian framework.

This study addresses a discounted optimal control problem involving partially observed forward-backward stochastic systems with jumps over an infinite horizon. It features a convex control domain and introduces a specific type of infinite horizon observation equation. The paper establishes the unique solvability of infinite horizon forward and backward stochastic differential equations with jumps, providing extended analysis, particularly for the backward case. New estimates for the critical variational inequality are derived and proven. Subsequently, an ergodic maximum principle is formulated through the introduction of infinite horizon adjoint equations, whose unique solvability is ensured. Finally, comparisons are drawn between the proposed systems and two representative types of infinite horizon stochastic systems along with their associated optimal controls.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), designed to extract representations from graph-structured data, are inherently well-suited for modeling molecular systems. This review explores GNNs and their diverse applications in the context of small organic molecules. Utilizing a versatile yet potent message-passing framework, GNNs iteratively refine node features. Numerous studies have developed GNN architectures capable of capturing both the topological details of 2D molecular graphs and the geometric properties of 3D molecular structures. These networks have been applied across a broad spectrum of molecular tasks, such as property prediction, scoring and docking, optimization and de novo generation, and molecular dynamics simulation. Furthermore, the review examines recent advancements in applying self-supervised learning techniques to molecules using GNNs.

This study details the experimental detection of multiple dispersive waves generated within the anomalous dispersion regime of an optical fiber by a sequence of dark solitons. Utilizing phase-matching criteria that account for higher-order dispersion and soliton velocity, each individual dispersive wave is linked to a specific dark soliton in the sequence. When the number of dark solitons exceeds ten, a continuum emerges due to the highly efficient emission of these dispersive waves.

Traditional financial market analysis has concentrated on deriving signals from hard numerical data, such as P&L statements, stock prices, and earnings per share reports. However, decision-makers frequently rely on soft, text-based documents that interpret this hard data. Recent advancements in computational methods for analyzing unstructured text at scale present opportunities to better understand financial market dynamics, thereby enhancing investments and market equity. Earnings calls represent a critical and ubiquitous form of this soft data; these periodic (typically quarterly) statements, often delivered by CEOs, aim to shape investor expectations regarding a company's past and future performance. This study examines the statistical relationships between earnings calls, corporate sales, stock performance, and analyst recommendations. The research encompasses a decade of data, analyzing approximately 100,000 earnings call transcripts from 6,300 public companies between January 2010 and December 2019. We report three novel findings: first, analyst buy, sell, and hold recommendations issued prior to earnings exhibit low correlation with subsequent stock price movements; second, utilizing a graph neural network approach to process the semantic features of earnings calls, we can reliably and accurately forecast stock price movements across five major economic sectors; third, the semantic features found within these transcripts are more predictive of stock price movements than traditional hard data, such as sales figures and earnings per share, in most instances.

The interior and exterior polynomials serve as generalizations of valuations on $(1/\xi,1)$ and $(1,1/\eta)$, respectively, extending the Tutte polynomial $T_G(x,y)$ of graphs to hypergraphs. For a connected bipartite graph, the pair of induced hypergraphs acts as abstract duals; they share the same interior polynomial, though their exterior polynomials may differ. In the case of a special alternating link, the top of the HOMFLY polynomial aligns with the interior polynomial derived from the pair of hypergraphs induced by the link's Seifert graph. Let $G=(V\cup E, \varepsilon)$ represent a connected bipartite graph. This paper focuses on the coefficients of these polynomials. We establish that the interior polynomial for a connected bipartite graph is interpolating and enhance existing results regarding its degree, specifically for graphs with 2-vertex cuts in $V$ or $E$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that interior polynomials for certain balanced bipartite graph families are monic and show that the interior polynomial of any connected bipartite graph can be expressed as a linear combination of those from connected balanced bipartite graphs. Similarly, we prove that exterior polynomials for hypergraphs are interpolating. While it is established that the linear term coefficient of the interior polynomial equals the nullity of the bipartite graph, we derive a dual result for the exterior polynomial: if $G-e$ remains connected for every edge $e\in E$, then the linear term coefficient of the exterior polynomial is $|V|-1$. Finally, we compute the interior and exterior polynomials for various families of bipartite graphs.

Research into higher-order finite element methods has gained significant momentum. Among the techniques for mesh generation, the deformation method has proven valuable for mesh adaptation by successfully enforcing a constraint of a prescribed positive Jacobian determinant. This study integrates the deformation method with local refinement to produce higher-order meshes. Numerical examples in both 2D and 3D, utilizing an element order of p=3, illustrate the efficacy of the proposed algorithm.

The increasing diversity of action categories presents a significant hurdle for video understanding, propelling Zero-Shot Action Recognition (ZSAR) as a promising research avenue. ZSAR seeks to identify unseen actions without specific training data by utilizing semantic representations to connect known and unknown classes. Nevertheless, the inherent complexity and variety of actions make it difficult to create effective semantic representations and transfer knowledge from observed to unseen data. This study introduces an ER-enhanced ZSAR model, inspired by the human memory technique of Elaborative Rehearsal (ER), which involves expanding new concepts by linking them to existing ones. Specifically, we represent each action class with an Elaborative Description (ED) sentence, offering better discriminative power than simple class names while avoiding the high cost of manually defined attributes. Beyond aligning class semantics with video content, we integrate objects present in the video as Elaborative Concepts (EC) to enhance video semantics and facilitate generalization from seen to unseen actions. Our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance on three established benchmarks. Additionally, we introduce a new evaluation protocol for the Kinetics dataset to address current benchmark limitations, demonstrating the first instance where ZSAR performance rivals few-shot learning baselines in this more realistic scenario. Our code and collected EDs will be made available at https://github.com/DeLightCMU/ElaborativeRehearsal.

It is demonstrated that the collection of all homogeneous continua within the hyperspace of every finite-dimensional Euclidean cube or the Hilbert cube constitutes an analytic subspace. This subspace includes a closed topological copy of the linear space $c_0=\{(x_k)\in \mathbb R^\omega: \lim x_k=0\}$.

We examine the Hartle-Hawking wavefunction of the universe, formulated as a Euclidean path integral adhering to the "no-boundary proposal," within the simplest minisuperspace framework consisting of a single scale factor and a positive cosmological constant. This system is interpreted as a non-linear $\sigma$-model with a line-segment base. By reducing the path integral over the lapse function to an integral over the base's proper length and employing diffeomorphism-invariant measures for both the scale factor and the ghosts, we ensure that the gauge-fixed path integral remains independent of the specific gauge choice. However, we note that various field redefinitions of the scale factor generate distinct gauge-invariant path-integral measures. Computing the wavefunction at the semi-classical level for each prescription yields different outcomes, which we resolve by addressing the ambiguity in the Wheeler-DeWitt equation at this approximation. By requiring that the Hamiltonians for these potentially distinct quantum theories be Hermitian, we determine the corresponding Hilbert space inner products and discover a universal norm, at least in the semi-classical regime. Consequently, quantum predictions are independent of the chosen prescription at this level of approximation. Finally, all wavefunctions within the Hilbert spaces of this minisuperspace model, including the no-boundary states, are found to be non-normalizable.

We calculate the full two-loop electroweak corrections for the Higgsstrahlung process $e^+e^-\rightarrow HZ$ at the future Higgs factory. The Feynman integrals are broken down into linear combinations of a minimal set of master integrals, utilizing recent advancements in integral reduction methods. These master integrals are subsequently evaluated using differential equations, with boundary conditions derived via the auxiliary mass flow method. Our final result, expressed for a specific $\sqrt{s}$, takes the form of a piecewise function composed of several highly expanded power series, offering high precision and allowing for efficient manipulation. This calculation represents the first instance of complete two-loop electroweak corrections for a process involving four external particles.

Named entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE) are fundamental components of information extraction and retrieval (IE \& IR). While recent studies show that joint learning of these tasks is advantageous—mitigating error propagation common in pipeline approaches and enhancing overall performance—current state-of-the-art joint models often depend on external NLP tools like dependency parsers. This reliance restricts their applicability to specific domains, such as news, where such tools are effective. Although some neural, end-to-end models exist, they are typically trained almost entirely from scratch. This paper introduces a neural, end-to-end framework for jointly extracting entities and relations that avoids external NLP dependencies and incorporates a large pre-trained language model. By leveraging pre-trained parameters and replacing recurrence with self-attention, our model achieves rapid training. Evaluated across five datasets spanning three domains, it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance, occasionally by a significant margin.

The role of social media in spreading vital information regarding health, politics, and the economy is undeniable. However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, anti-vaxxers exploited these platforms to circulate misinformation and anxiety-inducing content about vaccines, posing a threat to public well-being. This study examines the psycho-linguistic characteristics of anti-vaxxers within the Twitter network. By gathering COVID-19 related tweets from February 2020 to June 2021, we analyzed vaccination stances, linguistic patterns, and social network structures. Our findings reveal that, in contrast to pro-vaxxers, anti-vaxxers exhibit higher levels of negative emotion, narrative-oriented thinking, and poorer moral reasoning. Ultimately, this research enhances our comprehension of the online anti-vaccination movement and offers critical insights for managing social media and formulating policies during and following the pandemic.

The GeMSE facility, located in a Swiss underground laboratory with 620 meters of water equivalent rock overburden, utilizes a low-background HPGe crystal optimized for continuous remote operation. Its background rate has been reduced by 33% to (164±2) counts/day within the 100-2700 keV range over five years, thanks to multi-layer passive shielding, a muon veto, and a nitrogen purge system inside the measurement cavity. This reduction aligns with predictions regarding the decay of short-lived isotopes. Analysis indicates that the background is now dominated by muons, based on a fit to known components using a precise detector simulation. Additionally, improvements to the detection efficiency calculation include a precise determination of the crystal's outer dead-layer thickness, allowing for easy efficiency calculations across various sample geometries. This capability is demonstrated by accurately determining the $^{40}$K content in a complex-shaped object: a banana.

We investigate the asymptotic properties of the expected maximum within a specific assignment process characterized by constant or i.i.d. coefficients, demonstrating how these expectations are influenced by the distribution of the coefficients.

Mirai and its subsequent malware variants introduced a significant innovation: the use of self-contained loaders to infect IoT devices and enroll them into botnets. These loaders operate independently from other botnet components and are not embedded within the payload, rendering them inaccessible to traditional analysis methods that depend on honeypots for sample capture. Consequently, novel approaches are required to investigate the evolution of these loaders and establish their genealogy. Addressing the lack of understanding regarding loader lineages in current research, this paper presents a semantic-aware methodology designed to measure, categorize, and compare various loader servers, thereby isolating their evolution from that of the payload. By utilizing behavior-based metrics to cluster discovered loaders, we identified eight distinct families to map their genealogy and establish homology. Our findings indicate that the Mirai source code is continuously evolving, generating new botnets with enhanced capabilities on both client and server sides. Ultimately, gaining deeper insights into infection loaders can empower the cybersecurity community to develop more effective detection and prevention mechanisms.

A cylindrically symmetric inhomogeneous cosmological model featuring a bulk viscous fluid and an electromagnetic field has been derived, where the magnetic field originates from an electric current flowing along the z-axis. The non-zero component of the electromagnetic field tensor is denoted as $F_{12}$. To achieve a deterministic solution, the model assumes a proportionality between the expansion scalar $\theta$ and the shear scalar $\sigma$. The resulting cosmological constant values are determined to be small and positive at late times, aligning with recent observations from Type Ia supernovae. Additionally, the physical and geometric characteristics of these models are analyzed both with and without the presence of a magnetic field.

Axion-like particles (ALPs), which arise in theories extending beyond the Standard Model, may influence the transparency of the Universe to gamma rays when magnetic fields are present. This study utilizes 80 months of data from the ${\it Fermi}$ Large Area Telescope to search for ALP signatures by comparing the energy distributions of high-energy photons from sources at redshifts $z \geq 0.1$ against theoretical models incorporating ALPs. Our analysis yields no evidence for enhanced gamma-ray transparency caused by ALPs; consequently, we establish constraints on ALP parameters assuming an intergalactic magnetic field strength of 1 nG. We exclude photon-ALP couplings exceeding $10^{-11}$ GeV$^{-1}$ for ALP masses $m_{a} \lesssim 3.0$ neV. These new limits rule out a region of parameter space unexplored by other gamma-ray observatories and remain consistent with restrictions derived from other experiments.

Nanodiamonds with nitrogen vacancy centers, suspended in a high vacuum, serve as a promising platform for exploring fundamental physics. Previously, these experiments were restricted to low vacuum conditions because optical absorption from the trapping laser caused heating. We demonstrate that milling pure diamond produces nanodiamonds that remain cool even when optical intensity exceeds 700 GW/m² at pressures under 5 mbar. Consequently, the vacuum limits for nanodiamonds in optical dipole traps are no longer constrained by temperature.

The study investigates magneto-intersubband resistance oscillations (MISO) in highly mobile two-dimensional electrons within symmetric GaAs quantum wells containing two populated subbands, using magnetic fields tilted relative to the 2D electron layer across various temperatures ($T$). A reduction in MISO amplitude with rising temperature is noted. At moderate tilts, this temperature-dependent amplitude decline aligns with a decrease in the Dingle factor, attributed to shortened quantum electron lifetimes at higher temperatures. Conversely, large tilts reveal a new regime characterized by strong temperature-induced suppression of MISO. The proposed model links this suppression to magnetic entanglement between subbands, which induces beating in the oscillating density of states. This model predicts a corresponding temperature damping factor: $A_{MISO}(T)=X/\sinh(X)$, where $X=2\pi^2kT\delta f$ and $\delta f$ represents the frequency difference of density of states oscillations between the two subbands. This theoretical factor matches experimental observations, and the study also notes Fermi liquid enhancement of the MISO amplitude.

The $	au$ lepton is identified via a final state containing three charged pions. A new technique leverages the distinct vertex characteristics of signal events versus backgrounds to achieve high-purity samples of semitauonic $b$-hadron decays. u_{\mu})$. This result aligns with both the Standard Model prediction and earlier experimental measurements.

This paper introduces a practical algorithm for constructing an explicit basis of the space of regular differential forms on the nonsingular projective model of any specified plane algebraic curve. We illustrate the algorithm using concrete examples, with an implementation performed in the computer algebra system Magma. Furthermore, as an application, we detail the Cartier-Manin matrix for the nonsingular projective curve relative to the basis generated by our method.

We introduce a broadened version of the Leggett-Garg inequalities applicable to macrorealistic systems. This approach substitutes the traditional assumption of non-invasive measurability with the principle of information retrievability. Consequently, our framework encompasses a strictly wider range of hidden variable theories compared to those constrained by macrorealism. A key advantage is that, unlike standard quantum mechanical tests of macrorealism which necessitate optimizing over all possible state updates, our retrievability-based method only requires the fundamental Lüders state update inherent in every quantum measurement. Furthermore, in qubit systems, the optimal retrieval protocols are linked to the fundamental precision limits of quantum theory, specifically the Busch-Lahti-Werner error-disturbance uncertainty relations. We demonstrate this by implementing an optimal protocol in a photonic setup, successfully reporting an experimental violation of the proposed generalization of macrorealism.

This study investigates heterogeneous wireless sensor networks (WSNs) and establishes the necessary conditions for optimal sensor placement. Consistent with homogeneous WSNs, this condition dictates that each sensor's location must align with the centroid of its corresponding optimal sensing region. Furthermore, we examine dynamic sensor deployment strategies for both homogeneous and heterogeneous networks under constrained communication ranges. The primary objective of deployment is to enhance sensing performance, specifically regarding distortion and coverage. We formulate the deployment challenge as a source coding problem where distortion signifies sensing accuracy. While coverage traditionally refers to the area monitored by sensors, limited communication ranges can fragment a WSN into disconnected sub-graphs. In such fragmented scenarios, neither standard distortion nor coverage accurately reflects performance, as data from isolated sub-graphs cannot reach the access point. To address this, we introduce a novel distortion metric and propose the Restrained Lloyd (RL) and Deterministic Annealing (DA) algorithms to optimize deployment in both network types. Simulation results demonstrate that both the DA and RL algorithms surpass the conventional Lloyd algorithm in performance when communication ranges are restricted.

Acquiring predictive models in new domains with limited training data presents an increasing challenge in contemporary supervised learning. This necessity drives the development of domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge from known source domains to target domains with distinct probability distributions. The task becomes particularly difficult when the source and target domains exist in heterogeneous feature spaces, a scenario known as heterogeneous domain adaptation (HDA). Although most HDA approaches rely on mathematical optimization to map data into a shared space, they often exhibit poor transferability. While neural representations offer superior transferability, they are currently tailored primarily for homogeneous settings. Building upon domain adaptation theory, we introduce Heterogeneous Adversarial Neural Domain Adaptation (HANDA), a novel framework designed to maximize transferability within heterogeneous environments. HANDA performs feature and distribution alignment within a unified neural architecture, achieving domain invariance via adversarial kernel learning. Three experiments were carried out to benchmark HANDA against state-of-the-art HDA methods on prominent image and text e-commerce datasets, demonstrating statistically significant gains in predictive performance. Furthermore, the framework's practical utility was validated in real-world dark web online markets, marking a significant advancement toward effective domain adaptation in e-commerce applications.

We perform a local classification of all 4-dimensional pseudo-Finsler Berwald structures that remain invariant under SO(3). These geometries represent the Finslerian analogues most closely resembling (spatially or SO(3)-spherically symmetric) pseudo-Riemannian ones, serving as essential ansätze for deriving solutions to Finsler gravity equations that extend the Einstein equations. Our results identify six distinct classes of non-pseudo-Riemannian (specifically, non-quadratic in velocity) SO(3)-spherically symmetric pseudo-Finsler Berwald functions, characterized by either power-law or exponential dependencies, or by a functional dependence on either one or two velocity variables.

The switching of ferroelectric domains in c-axis-oriented epitaxial Pb(Zr$_{0.2}$Ti$_{0.8}$)O$_3$ thin films was investigated using biased scanning probe microscopy. Although it is established that domain size exhibits linear and logarithmic relationships with tip bias and writing time, respectively, we demonstrate an additional linear correlation with relative humidity between 28% and 65%. We characterize the switched domain size across varying tip biases and pulse durations, identifying a growth-limited regime for brief pulses and a nucleation-limited regime at low biases. By employing "interrupted-switching" techniques with subcritical pulses to examine the nucleation regime, we detected an unexpectedly long relaxation time of approximately 100 ms, attributing this phenomenon to ionic redistribution occurring both on the surface and throughout the thin film.

The Grundy domination number, denoted as ${\gamma_{\rm gr}}(G)$, represents the maximum length of a vertex sequence $(v_1,v_2,\ldots, v_k)$ in a graph $G$ where, for each $i \in \{2,\ldots, k\}$, the closed neighborhood $N[v_i]$ includes a vertex not present in any preceding closed neighborhood $N[v_j]$ with $j<i$. It is established that for any graph $G$, the Grundy domination number is at least the upper domination number $\Gamma(G)$, which itself is at least the independence number $\alpha(G)$. This paper begins an investigation into graphs satisfying $\Gamma(G)={\gamma_{\rm gr}}(G)$, with a specific focus on the subclass where $\alpha(G)={\gamma_{\rm gr}}(G)$. We provide a characterization of these graphs within the realm of twin-free, connected graphs and establish several of their properties. Furthermore, we outline multiple necessary conditions for graphs where $\Gamma(G)={\gamma_{\rm gr}}(G)$ and introduce extensive families of such graphs.

We developed the APOGEE-GALEX-Gaia catalog specifically to investigate white dwarf binaries. This database seeks to construct a minimally biased collection of WD binary systems by integrating data from APOGEE, Gaia, and GALEX, thereby expanding the count of WD binaries with known orbital parameters and chemical compositions. We identified 3,414 WD binary candidates featuring nondegenerate companions ranging from F to M spectral types, encompassing main sequence stars, binaries, subgiants, sub-subgiants, red giants, and red clump stars. Key findings include: (a) 1,806 systems with inferred WD radii smaller than 25 Earth radii, forming a more reliable subset; (b) a distinct difference in the metallicity distribution function between WD candidates and a control sample of the most luminous giants ($M_H < -3.0$); (c) the confirmation of a sub-subgiant population hosting WD companions; (d) indications of shorter periods in WD-containing binaries versus those without, derived from cumulative APOGEE radial velocity shift distributions; (e) signs of systemic orbital evolution in 252 WD binaries with measured periods, revealed by comparing period distributions across different companion types (red clump, main sequence binary, sub-subgiant versus main sequence or red giant); and (f) proof of chemical enrichment during common envelope evolution, evidenced by lower metallicities in wide WD candidates ($P > 100$ days) relative to post-common envelope systems ($P < 100$ days).

Circuit quantum electrodynamics stands out as a leading platform for efficient quantum computation and simulation. Recent breakthroughs have leveraged the adaptability of superconducting microwave resonators to construct hyperbolic lattices, effectively modeling quantum phenomena within negatively curved spaces. This study explores practical experimental configurations where a small number of superconducting qubits interact with a photon bath distributed across such a hyperbolic lattice. Our numerical simulations for finite lattices are contrasted with analytical predictions for continuous hyperbolic space defined on the Poincaré disk, revealing strong consistency between the two approaches in the long-wavelength limit. We demonstrate that photon-qubit bound states possess a size constrained by curvature. Furthermore, we suggest employing a qubit as a localized sensor of the hyperbolic environment, such as by monitoring its relaxation dynamics. While boundary effects significantly alter the photonic density of states, the spectral density remains well-approximated by continuum theory. Additionally, we illustrate that qubit interactions are mediated by photons traveling along geodesics. Finally, we show that the photonic bath can generate geometrically frustrated hyperbolic quantum spin models featuring either finite-range or exponentially decaying interactions.

Gradient Boosting Machines (GBMs) have emerged as highly effective function approximators widely applied across diverse domains. However, their sequential training requirements for individual base learners make parallelization for acceleration impossible. Furthermore, in online or incremental learning contexts, GBMs often yield sub-optimal results because previously trained base learners cannot adapt to changing environments. To address these limitations, this paper introduces the Soft Gradient Boosting Machine (sGBM), which integrates multiple differentiable base learners by incorporating both local and global objectives inspired by gradient boosting. This architecture allows for the joint optimization of all base learners, achieving linear speed-ups. When utilizing differentiable soft decision trees as base learners, sGBM serves as an enhanced alternative to traditional hard gradient boosting decision trees. Empirical results demonstrate that sGBM delivers superior time efficiency and improved accuracy compared to standard methods in both online and offline settings, given identical base learners.

The refined de Sitter derivative conjecture imposes restrictions on potentials within low-energy effective theories of quantum gravity, offering direct constraints on inflationary models and helping distinguish between the Landscape and the Swampland. This framework applies to all inflationary scenarios, including non-minimally coupled scalar field theories. By examining the Palatini Higgs inflation scenario under these conjectural conditions and incorporating recent cosmological data from Planck 2018, BICEP2+Keck, along with limits on the non-minimal coupling parameter $\xi$, we find that the model likely resides in the Swampland. Specifically, if the refined de Sitter conjecture holds, the Palatini Higgs inflation model fails to qualify as a consistent low-energy effective theory of quantum gravity because its parameters $c_1$ and $c_2$ are significantly smaller than order 1, thereby violating the conjecture.

We introduce a new randomized block coordinate descent primal-dual algorithm designed for a specific class of non-smooth, ill-posed convex optimization problems. This method bridges the gap between the renowned Chambolle-Pock primal-dual approach and Tseng's accelerated proximal gradient technique. We demonstrate global convergence of the final iterate, achieving optimal complexity rates of $O(1/k)$ for convex scenarios and $O(1/k^2)$ for strongly convex scenarios, where $k$ represents the number of iterations. Inspired by distributed and data-driven control applications in power systems, we evaluate the algorithm using a second-order cone relaxation of an AC-OPF problem. Within this optimization framework, distributed control is realized through distributed locational marginal prices (DLMPs), which serve as the dual variables.

This study introduces a new numerical analysis of free-boundary dynamics in viscoelastic liquid membranes. The governing equations model linear momentum balance, incorporating viscoelastic stresses of the Maxwell type in response to deformation. To ensure near-incompressibility within the viscoelastic medium, a penalty method is employed, where the penalty constant scales with the fluid's viscosity. The finite element method is applied using linear three-node triangular elements under plane stress conditions to discretize the slender geometry of the membrane. Two specific applications are examined within this numerical framework: shear flow and extensional flow associated with drawing processes.

UNIONS represents an active collaboration aimed at delivering the most extensive deep photometric survey of the Northern sky to date, covering four optical bands. Within this framework, the CFIS instrument collects $r$-band data with a mean seeing of 0.65 arcsec, achieving completeness up to magnitude 24.5, making it highly suitable for weak-lensing research. This study presents the inaugural weak-lensing analysis of CFIS $r$-band data across 1700 deg$^2$, generating a catalog of galaxy shapes for 40 million objects with an effective density of 6.8 galaxies per square arcminute, while demonstrating minimal systematic biases. These results lay the groundwork for future cosmological investigations using the full 4800 deg$^2$ UNIONS survey upon completion. We introduce ShapePipe, a newly developed weak-lensing pipeline that leverages advanced techniques like Ngmix for precise galaxy shape measurement and employs metacalibration for shear calibration. Extensive validation tests were conducted on the Point Spread Function (PSF) and galaxy shapes, supplemented by realistic image simulations to verify shear estimates. We confirmed the high accuracy of the PSF model, showing that systematics, as indicated by PSF residuals, are negligible and have a sub-dominant impact on the shear two-point correlation function for angular scales smaller than 100 arcmin. The additive shear bias remains below $5 \times 10^{-4}$, while the residual multiplicative shear bias does not exceed $10^{-3}$ based on image simulations. Using COSEBIs, we found no significant B-modes in second-order shear statistics. Additionally, we generated convergence maps that reveal clear correlations between E-modes and known cluster locations. Finally, we measured stacked tangential shear profiles around Planck clusters with a significance exceeding $4\sigma$.

We investigate the connection between the Square Root Problem for a non-negative measure $\mu$ possessing $p$ atoms and the subnormality of ${\tilde W_\mu}$, the Aluthge transform of the corresponding unilateral weighted shift. Our methodology relies on uniquely representable elements within the support of $\mu*\mu$. We initially establish that if ${\tilde W_\mu}$ is subnormal, the cardinality of the support of $\mu*\mu$ must satisfy $2p-1\le card(supp(\mu*\mu))\le [\frac{(p-1)^2+6}{2}]$. Furthermore, we restate several existing findings for finitely atomic measures with no more than five atoms and provide a comprehensive solution for the case involving six atoms.

The beacon chain serves as the foundation for Ethereum's transition into a scalable, proof-of-stake network. Beacon clients are the software applications that implement the necessary services to run the beacon chain, including validators, beacon nodes, and slashers. Vulnerabilities within these clients can result in fund loss, breaches of consensus rules, network congestion, and other operational issues. We have reported over 35 findings to beacon client developers, covering various security enhancements, specification discrepancies, absent security checks, and exposures to known vulnerabilities. Notably, none of our discoveries reached high severity levels. Our analysis spanned the four primary beacon clients: Lighthouse (Rust), Nimbus (Nim), Prysm (Go), and Teku (Java). Over a three-month period, following an initial review of BLS signature code, we scrutinized the logic and implementation of critical security components, including BLS signatures, slashing mechanisms, networking protocols, and APIs. We prioritized Lighthouse and Prysm as the most popular and high-value targets. Additionally, we identified protocol-level flaws such as replay attacks and incomplete forward secrecy. We also examined the network fingerprints of beacon clients to determine information accessible through passive and active reconnaissance, and assessed supply chain risks associated with third-party dependencies, offering indicators and recommendations to mitigate the threat of backdoors and unpatchable vulnerabilities. Our findings indicate that despite rigorous scrutiny by security auditors and independent researchers, the complexity and continuous evolution of a platform like Ethereum necessitate regular expert reviews and robust SSDLC practices.

Alfalfa serves as a globally vital livestock feed, making the development of efficient planting and harvesting methods crucial, particularly as climate change renders traditional techniques less reliable. While recent machine learning (ML) initiatives have shown potential in predicting yields for alfalfa and other crops by utilizing remote sensing, weather, soil, and planting data, these models often demand extensive datasets and cannot forecast results until the harvest season commences. Leveraging weather and planting data from variety trials in Kentucky and Georgia, our prior research compared feature selection methods to identify optimal configurations. In this study, we trained diverse ML models using cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning to predict biomass yields, achieving superior accuracy compared to similar studies that utilized more complex methodologies. Our top-performing individual model was a random forest, which recorded a mean absolute error of 0.081 tons/acre and an R² of 0.941. We subsequently expanded the dataset to include Wisconsin and Mississippi, repeating the experiments to achieve a peak R² of 0.982 using a regression tree. Finally, we segmented testing datasets by state to investigate the problem's suitability for domain adaptation (DA), training on multiple source states while testing on single target states. This Trivial DA (TDA) approach indicates significant potential for improvement through the exploration of more sophisticated DA techniques in future work.

A notable outcome from Veech over half a century ago concerns the parity, or modulo 2, variant of the Kronecker–Weyl equidistribution theorem regarding the irrational rotation sequence $\{q\alpha\}$ for $q=0,1,2,3,\ldots$. Specifically, if $\alpha$ is badly approximable and $b\in(0,1)$ is chosen such that $b\ne\{m\alpha\}$ for any integer $m$, then the parities of the cardinalities of the sets $\{1\le q\le N:\{q\alpha\}\in[0,b)\}$ exhibit even distribution as $N$ approaches infinity.

First, we address a question posed by Veech by proving a stronger version of his result for the modulo $n$ analog (Theorem 3.1). Additionally, for irrational $\alpha$ where $b=\{m\alpha\}$ for some natural number $m$, we provide a concise and exact characterization of the conditions under which even distribution occurs (Theorem 2.1). We also derive a time-quantitative description of significant deviations from uniformity; this section is deeply rooted in number theory, utilizing Ostrowski representations of positive integers and $\alpha$-expansions of real numbers (Theorem 3.4).

The Veech discrete 2-circle problem can be viewed as an issue concerning 1-direction geodesic flow on a surface formed by altering a pair of adjacent squares through the addition of symmetric barriers and gates on vertical edges, along with corresponding adjustments to vertical edge identifications. We demonstrate a substantial generalization of this scenario to cases involving 1-direction geodesic flow on surfaces derived from finite square-tiled translation surfaces by applying analogous, though not necessarily symmetric, modifications (Theorem 3.2).

This paper proposes a paradigm shift in the variational approach to brittle fracture, treating both dynamics and statics within a unified framework. Unlike conventional incremental methods, the study employs a space-time principle that encompasses the entire loading history and crack evolution. The focus lies on modeling crack propagation through internal variable formalism and a dissipation potential similar to those used in plasticity, diverging from Griffith's original surface-area-based approach. This new formulation is presented as more conducive to generalization compared to standard theories.

This study addresses cardinality-constrained optimization problems and introduces a novel sequential optimality condition for the recently popular continuous relaxation reformulation. This new condition is strictly stronger than current results and remains a first-order necessity for cardinality-constrained problems without requiring additional assumptions. Additionally, we present a specialized, weaker constraint qualification that ensures the new sequential conditions yield Mordukhovich-type stationary points. We also enhance the theoretical foundations of the augmented Lagrangian algorithm; under conditions identical to existing literature, we demonstrate that any feasible accumulation point of the algorithm's iterative sequence satisfies the proposed sequential optimality condition. Moreover, when the problem-specific constraint qualification holds, the algorithm converges to a Mordukhovich-type (essentially strong) stationary point.

Although significant recent efforts have been made, identifying out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and adversarial attacks (AA) for computer vision models continues to be difficult. This paper presents DAAIN, a new unified method designed to detect both OOD inputs and AA specifically for image segmentation. Our method tracks the internal operations of a neural network and trains a density estimator to model the distribution of activations. By attaching a classification head to this estimator, we can distinguish between normal and anomalous inputs. To manage the high-dimensional activation space common in segmentation networks, we employ subsampling to achieve uniform coverage across layers and spatial dimensions. The subsampling pattern is selected once for each monitored model and remains constant for all inputs. Because adversaries lack access to both the detection model and the sampling key, they cannot backpropagate attacks through the detector, thereby increasing the difficulty of compromising the segmentation network. We validated our approach using an ESPNet segmentation model trained on the Cityscapes dataset, an affine Normalizing Flow for density estimation, and blue noise to guarantee homogeneous sampling. Furthermore, the model can be trained on a single GPU, offering computational efficiency and deployability without the need for specialized hardware accelerators.

The shift between ergodic and many-body localized phases is anticipated to proceed through an avalanche mechanism, where local fluctuations generate \emph{ergodic bubbles} that thermalize their environment and drive delocalization, a process that only halts if disorder is strong enough to prevent it. We introduce a neural network-based algorithm capable of identifying these ergodic bubbles via experimentally accessible two-site correlation functions. By analyzing the system's time evolution, we find that ergodic bubbles grow logarithmically in time within the MBL regime.
