Furthermore, the distribution of bubble sizes stabilizes over time to an exponentially decaying form in the MBL regime and a power-law distribution with a thermal peak in the critical regime, thereby validating the avalanche-driven delocalization scenario. Our method enables the precise differentiation of time evolution between systems with random and quasiperiodic potentials and allows for the detection of rare (Griffiths) events. These findings establish new avenues for investigating thermalization mechanisms in disordered many-body systems and related fields.

Two-dimensional topological insulators (2DTIs), characterized by the quantum spin Hall (QSH) effect, represent a critical class of materials for future spintronic applications. Although experimental confirmation of the QSH effect remains limited to a select few substances, identifying new 2DTIs is a primary focus in physical and materials research. This study presents experimental verification of a 2DTI in the van der Waals compound Ta$_2$Pd$_3$Te$_5$. First-principles modeling indicates that individual monolayers of Ta$_2$Pd$_3$Te$_5$ exhibit 2DTI properties with minimal interlayer coupling. Furthermore, integrated transport data, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy validate the presence of a band gap at the Fermi level and topological edge states within this gap. These findings establish Ta$_2$Pd$_3$Te$_5$ as a viable candidate for constructing spintronic devices leveraging the QSH effect.

Dynamic early exiting accelerates the inference of pre-trained language models (PLMs) by generating predictions from internal layers rather than processing the full model. However, our empirical analysis reveals that this approach encounters a performance ceiling at high acceleration rates. Specifically, shallow-layer representations often lack the necessary high-level semantic details for accurate forecasting, while internal classifiers produce unreliable exit decisions that lead to premature and incorrect predictions. To address these limitations, we introduce CascadeBERT, a novel framework that accelerates PLM inference by dynamically selecting complete, appropriately sized models in a cascading structure to ensure comprehensive representation. Additionally, we develop a difficulty-aware objective function that guides the model to output class probabilities reflecting the actual difficulty of each instance, thereby enhancing the reliability of the cascading mechanism. Experiments demonstrate that CascadeBERT achieves a 15% overall improvement under a 4$\times$ speed-up ratio compared to existing dynamic early exiting methods across six classification tasks, resulting in more accurate and well-calibrated predictions.

This study presents a streamlined approach for managing communication resources in dense wireless environments where all nodes target a single common destination. By clustering nodes according to their proximity to the destination, the method establishes a structured multi-hop topology that enables each group to relay data for its neighbors. It leverages the high density of active radio nodes and their unified communication direction to enhance spatial reuse of limited spectrum resources across separated groups. Furthermore, spectrum allocation constraints between these groups are integrated into a unified routing and resource allocation framework designed to optimize both paths and resource distribution. The proposed solution achieves superior performance compared to conventional decoupled-layer approaches by coordinating lower layers within the wireless protocol stack. Additionally, the problem's inherent structure is utilized to develop a semi-distributed optimization algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), allowing each node to independently optimize its resources using only local channel information.

This study utilizes high-resolution Submillimeter Array data to investigate the massive star-forming complex G9.62+0.19, revealing three sub-mm cores with masses of 13, 30, and 165 M$_{\sun}$ in the northern, middle, and southern regions, respectively. Infall motions detected via HCN (4-3) and CS (7-6) lines are centered on the middle core (G9.62+0.19 E), yielding an infall rate of $4.3\times10^{-3}~M_{\odot}\cdot$yr$^{-1}$. Conversely, the southern core exhibits a bipolar outflow identified through SO ($8_{7}-7_{7}$) line wing emission, characterized by a total mass of approximately 26 M$_{\sun}$ and a mass-loss rate of $3.6\times10^{-5}~M_{\odot}\cdot$yr$^{-1}$. While CS (7-6) and HCN (4-3) lines trace higher-velocity gas compared to SO, G9.62+0.19 F is confirmed as the driving source of this outflow. Additionally, an analysis of CS, SO, and HCN abundances along the redshifted outflow lobes shows that their mass-velocity diagrams align well with a single power law. The evolutionary sequence of the cm/mm cores in this area further indicates that UC~H{\sc ii} regions display a greater blue excess than their precursor stages.

To address the anticipated rise in intensity for fixed-target beams within the CERN accelerator complex, a barrier-bucket method was devised to mitigate beam loss during the Multi-Turn Extraction (MTE), a five-turn process transferring particles from the PS to the SPS. This scheme requires the low-level RF system to align the barrier phase precisely with the PS extraction and SPS injection kickers to minimize particle losses occurring during their field rise times. Since the RF voltage in the wide-band cavity creating the barrier bucket is insufficient for standard synchronization, a hybrid approach combining feedforward cogging manipulation with real-time barrier phase control was developed and validated. Additionally, a deterministic frequency bump was introduced to correct for the imperfect circumference ratio between the PS and SPS. This work outlines the concept and practical implementation of the synchronized barrier-bucket transfer, with high-intensity beam measurements confirming the feasibility of the proposed scheme.

We construct a sequence-based calculus by establishing definitions for equivalence, fundamental operations, derivatives, and integrals within the domain of sequences. Subsequently, we introduce sequence analogues for identity, power, exponential, hyperbolic, and trigonometric functions, deriving their corresponding Maclaurin series. Notably, the sequence versions of the exponential function incorporate divergent series, such as Grandi's series. Leveraging this framework, we derive sequence counterparts to the binomial theorem and Euler's identity. Furthermore, we develop novel formalisms for the Fibonacci sequence and its generalizations. Finally, we propose a sequence dual of the factorial and Bell numbers, identifying sequence duals of their respective modular properties related to prime numbers, specifically Wilson's theorem for factorials and a similar property for Bell numbers.

We investigate the crystallization kinetics of deeply supercooled liquid silicon through computer simulations utilizing the Stillinger-Weber three-body potential. Free energy barriers for crystallization are calculated via umbrella sampling Monte Carlo simulations and, at specific low-temperature, zero-pressure conditions, through unconstrained molecular dynamics simulations that reconstruct free energy using mean first passage time formulations. Our analysis targets state points identified in prior research [Sastry and Angell, Nature Mater., 2, 739, 2003] as lying near a first-order liquid-liquid phase transition (LLPT) between two metastable liquid phases. Subsequent arguments [Ricci et al., Mol. Phys., 117, 3254, 2019] suggest this apparent transition actually results from the loss of the liquid's metastability relative to the globally stable crystalline state. Consequently, determining whether a crystallization barrier exists at these points is crucial, particularly considering potential ambiguities linked to order parameter selection. We detail our chosen order parameters and methodologies for computing free energy at deep supercooling levels. Our findings reveal a distinct free energy barrier to crystallization, demonstrating quantitative agreement between both umbrella sampling and mean first passage time approaches. These results strongly indicate that liquids near the reported LLPT do not undergo slow, spontaneous crystallization, though they do not confirm or deny the existence of an LLPT itself. Furthermore, we calculate crystallization free energy barriers across a wide range of temperatures and pressures at other state points, examining how variations in the microscopic structure of the metastable liquid influence barrier heights.

SN 2020cxd belongs to the class of underluminous, low-energy Type IIP supernovae, a group recently characterized by Yang et al. (2021). This study re-analyzes observational data for this event using a 3D, fully self-consistent hydrodynamic simulation of a neutrino-driven explosion in a 9 M_sun red supergiant with an 8.75 M_sun iron core. We computed multi-band light curves and photospheric velocities during the plateau phase using the STELLA radiation-hydrodynamics code, applying it to both spherically averaged and direction-specific radial profiles from the 3D model. Our model successfully reproduces the bolometric light curve evolution, plateau duration, and multi-band emission characteristics with an explosion energy of only 0.7x10^50 erg and an ejecta mass of 7.4 M_sun. These figures are significantly lower than previously reported values but align well with requirements to explain the prototype low-luminosity SN 2005cs. Given the strong agreement between our modeled photospheric velocities and those observed for SN 2005cs, we conclude that the line velocities of SN 2020cxd may be overestimated by a factor of approximately three. Furthermore, comparing the line velocity evolution of SN 2005cs against photospheric velocities across different explosion directions suggests the presence of intrinsic asymmetries in the supernova ejecta.

Previous studies have established the small-$x$ quark helicity evolution equations at double-logarithmic order, characterized by a kernel proportional to $\alpha_s\ln^2(1/x)$. This paper derives the corresponding single-logarithmic corrections, specifically to order $\alpha_s\ln(1/x)$ within the evolution kernel. These updated equations incorporate effects from the running coupling and unpolarized small-$x$ evolution, both of which are parametrically important at this order. We also calculate the large-$N_c$ and large-$N_c\& N_f$ approximations (where $N_c$ and $N_f$ denote the number of quark colors and flavors, respectively). Solving these equations will yield more accurate estimates of the quark helicity distribution at small $x$, aiding in the solution of the proton spin puzzle.

Continuum-armed bandits, also known as black-box or $0^{th}$-order optimization, focuses on minimizing the number of queries required to optimize an unknown objective function via an evaluation oracle. While existing literature primarily addresses the case where the objective function is Lipschitz continuous, establishing minimax rates for both simple and cumulative regrets in noiseless and noisy environments, this paper extends the analysis to more general smoothness conditions defined by Besov spaces. We derive minimax rates for both regret types under these broader assumptions. Our findings demonstrate that the minimax rates for functions within a Besov space are equivalent to those for functions in the smallest Hölder space that contains the Besov space.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have effectively pinpointed numerous genetic variants linked to various traits and diseases; however, deciphering the functional mechanisms behind many of these variants remains difficult, particularly for those shared across multiple phenotypes. To overcome this limitation, we introduce GGPA 2.0, a new statistical framework designed to unify GWAS data from multiple phenotypes while integrating functional annotations. Simulation studies demonstrated that GGPA 2.0 not only enhances the detection of disease-associated variants but also reveals more precise relationships among diseases. We applied this method to five autoimmune diseases and five psychiatric disorders, utilizing functional annotations from GenoSkyline and GenoSkyline-Plus alongside a prior disease graph constructed via biomedical literature mining. In the autoimmune analyses, GGPA 2.0 highlighted enrichment in blood components, specifically B cells and regulatory T cells, across several conditions. For psychiatric disorders, the method identified brain enrichment, notably in the prefrontal cortex for bipolar disorder (BIP) and the inferior temporal lobe for schizophrenia (SCZ). Furthermore, GGPA 2.0 successfully uncovered the pleiotropic relationship between BIP and SCZ. These findings illustrate that GGPA 2.0 serves as a robust tool for identifying both phenotype-specific and shared genetic variants, thereby advancing our understanding of the functional mechanisms underlying them.

Direct characterization of planet formation is facilitated by accreting protoplanets. Within a high-contrast imaging survey for accreting planets conducted with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Wide Field Camera 3, we report H$\alpha$ observations of AB Aurigae (AB Aur), a Herbig Ae/Be star possessing a transition disk. Using the F656N narrow-band filter, we obtained direct-imaging data across two epochs. Following the subtraction of the primary star's point spread function, we detected a point-like source positioned at a position angle of $182.5^{\circ}\pm1.4^{\circ}$ and a separation of $600\pm22$~mas from the host star, a location consistent with the previously identified protoplanet candidate AB Aur b. This source appeared in both epochs, which were separated by approximately 50 days, with consistent H$\alpha$ intensities. The measured H$\alpha$ flux density is $F_{\nu}=1.5\pm0.4$~mJy, representing $3.2\pm0.9$ times the optical continuum derived from published HST/STIS photometry. Compared to PDS 70 b and c, the H$\alpha$ excess emission is notably weak. The central star exhibits accretion, and its stellar H$\alpha$ emission displays a line-to-continuum ratio similar to that observed in AB Aur b. Consequently, both planetary accretion and scattered stellar light remain viable origins for the detected H$\alpha$ emission; thus, the H$\alpha$ detection alone cannot confirm AB Aur b as an accreting protoplanet. Resolving the source of this emission is essential for investigating planet formation within the AB Aur disk.

This study addresses the computation of approximate pure Nash equilibria in weighted congestion games, a problem established as PLS-complete. Leveraging $\hat{\Psi}$-games and approximate potential functions, we introduce two algorithms grounded in best response dynamics. We demonstrate that these algorithms efficiently derive $\frac{\rho}{1-\epsilon}$-approximate pure Nash equilibria for $\rho = d!$ and $\rho = \frac{2\cdot W\cdot(d+1)}{2\cdot W+d+1}\le {d + 1}$, respectively. These results hold when the weighted congestion game features polynomial latency functions of degree at most $d \ge 1$ and player weights are capped by a constant $W \ge 1$. This advancement surpasses recent findings by Feldotto et al. [2017] and Giannakopoulos et al. [2022], which established efficient methods for computing $d^{d+o(d)}$-approximate pure Nash equilibria.

Although compelling data, such as recent observations of hadronic gamma-ray signatures from two supernova remnants (SNRs), suggest that these objects produce Galactic cosmic rays (CRs), their collective role as the ultimate source remains unclear. This study tackles the enduring mystery of CR nuclei origins by utilizing a statistically robust sample of GeV-emitting SNRs to quantify their direct contribution to observed CRs. By analyzing the GeV photons generated through pion decay when CRs interact with surrounding gas near SNRs, we provide an *in situ* method to trace CR populations that are otherwise measured directly by satellite and balloon experiments near Earth. While the Fermi LAT SNR Catalog currently identifies over 50 SNRs and potential associations across diverse property classes, all are considered viable accelerators. We examine both GeV and multiwavelength emission from these remnants to limit their maximum possible contribution to the observed Galactic CR flux. Our findings indicate that simple models previously deemed adequate for describing GeV and multiwavelength emission from these objects require significant refinement.

The Continuous Spontaneous Localization (CSL) model offers an alternative to standard quantum mechanics by incorporating a non-linear noise term coupled to the wave function to explain its collapse. This study examines the impact of CSL on quantum computers utilizing superconducting transmon qubits. While CSL directly diminishes quantum superpositions of computational basis states, this reduction is demonstrated to be negligible. Conversely, an indirect effect arises where CSL-induced noise generates additional quasiparticles, causing transmon qubits to decohere. Given that the decoherence rate of transmon qubits is contingent upon quasiparticle density, calculating the CSL-induced generation rate allows us to estimate this density and determine the performance limits imposed by CSL on transmon quantum computers. Our findings indicate that CSL could potentially disrupt the execution of practical algorithms on large-scale devices. Additionally, we investigate the feasibility of testing CSL effects using superconducting hardware.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven highly effective for pulmonary nodule detection; however, current CNN-based methods struggle to capture long-range dependencies essential for extracting global information. Although non-local operations are common in computer vision, their computational cost is prohibitive for 3D computed tomography (CT) images. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Long Short Slice-Aware Network (LSSANet) for pulmonary nodule detection. Specifically, we propose a novel non-local mechanism called Long Short Slice Grouping (LSSG), which divides compact non-local embeddings into short-distance and long-distance slice groups. This approach significantly reduces computational overhead while maintaining long-range dependencies across all elements within slices and the entire feature map. The LSSG module is user-friendly and can be integrated into various pulmonary nodule detection architectures. We validated LSSANet by comparing it against several recent and competitive 2D/3D CNN-based detection methods. Promising results on the large-scale PN9 dataset confirm the method's effectiveness. The source code is available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/LSSANet.

Adaptive techniques lack a direct extension to manifolds because their adaptive components are not invariant, while momentum-based approaches on manifolds encounter efficiency hurdles due to curvature. We propose a framework for extending both adaptive and momentum methods to arbitrary manifolds by leveraging the fact that every differentiable manifold is covered by a radially convex open set that is nearly exhaustive. Since such a set is radially convex, it is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$, offering a natural way to generalize any adaptive or momentum-based algorithm to this covering set. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to adapt these methods for gradient descent using a retraction. For practical implementation, we utilize a matrix exponential approximation requiring only five matrix multiplications, which enhances efficiency on GPUs. Empirically, this family of algorithms bridges the numerical gap caused by the improper application of momentum and adaptive methods on manifolds. Additionally, we find that the most efficient algorithm within this family involves pulling the problem back to the tangent space at the initial point via the exponential map.

Contemporary software systems depend on extracting insights from business-critical data hosted in public clouds, yet data breaches typically result in substantial financial losses for commercial entities. Fundamentally, cloud security hinges on Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, which require IT administrators to configure and regularly update them accurately. However, security lapses and human mistakes frequently lead to IAM misconfigurations, potentially creating backdoors for adversaries. To tackle these issues, we first introduce a novel framework that employs constraint programming (CP) to generate optimal IAM policies, using the reduction of "dark permissions" (unnecessary data access rights) as a key optimality metric. Second, to enhance policy interpretability, we apply graph representation learning to historical user access patterns, integrating similarity constraints into our CP model so that analogous users are grouped and assigned common policies. Third, we outline various attack scenarios and demonstrate, using real-world data from eight commercial organizations alongside synthetic instances, that our optimized IAM policies significantly mitigate the impact of security threats.

Users increasingly rely on vast, heterogeneous entity graphs across diverse applications. However, selecting the appropriate graph for a specific task remains difficult due to the abundance of datasets from various sources and the frequent lack of detailed information about them. To address this, we introduce methods that generate preview tables, offering a compact representation of key entity types and relationships. These tables enable users to obtain a rapid, preliminary overview of the data within limited display areas, facilitating exploration before committing time and resources to retrieve and analyze the full dataset. We formulate several optimization problems aimed at producing previews with the highest scores based on intuitive quality metrics, subject to constraints on preview size and the distance between tables. While the optimization problem involving distance constraints is proven to be NP-hard, we have developed both a dynamic-programming approach and an Apriori-style algorithm to identify optimal previews. Experimental results, comparisons with existing work, and user studies confirm the accuracy of our scoring measures and the efficiency of the proposed discovery algorithms.

Deep generative models are defined by a representation space, its associated distribution, and a neural network that maps representations to a distribution over feature vectors. While common techniques like Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) utilize variational inference for training, optimizing them remains challenging. The inclusion of an encoder increases model complexity, creates an amortization gap, and leaves the quality of the variational approximation uncertain. Furthermore, the performance of these models is heavily dependent on balancing the loss terms within the objective function. Consequently, we propose investigating a simpler approximation that determines representations and their distributions by maximizing model likelihood through back-propagation. This approach eliminates the need for an encoder, leading us to name it the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD). Experiments on the CIFAR10 dataset demonstrate that DGD is more efficient and faster to optimize than VAEs, yields more consistent low reconstruction errors on test data, and resolves the difficulty of balancing reconstruction and distribution loss terms. Although the basic DGD model does not match state-of-the-art image generation capabilities, it achieves superior generation scores compared to variational methods on CIFAR10. Additionally, using MNIST data, we illustrate how incorporating Gaussian mixture priors enables clear class separation in a 2D representation space and how DGD can be adapted with labels for supervised representation learning.

In this study, we investigate the surface electronic structure of 1T-VSe2 using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and identify a dispersionless emission near the Fermi level. Its crystal momentum dependence indicates that this feature occupies extensive regions of the Brillouin zone where no bulk bands are anticipated. When the system undergoes electron doping via the deposition of rubidium atoms, it exhibits unexpected evolution. Beyond the anticipated downward shift of the bands, we observe a splitting of both the bulk states and the dispersionless emission. This unusual behavior strongly implies an intrinsic origin for this emission, making its characterization crucial for a more profound understanding of the physics governing transition metal dichalcogenides.

We present a new category of polytopes termed "chainlink polytopes," which enable the creation of infinite sets of non-isomorphic rational polytopes sharing an identical Ehrhart quasi-polynomial. This approach relies on circular fence posets, which possess a subtle yet non-trivial symmetry within their rank sequences that manifests at the polytope level. We also define a corresponding class of chainlink posets and demonstrate that they display analogous symmetry characteristics. Additionally, we provide a proof for a significant conjecture regarding the unimodality of circular rank polynomials.

This study introduces an image-to-painting translation framework capable of producing vivid, realistic artworks with controllable stylistic variations. Unlike prior image-to-image approaches that rely on pixel-wise prediction, our method operates within a vectorized environment, generating a sequence of physically interpretable stroke parameters suitable for rendering. Addressing the non-differentiability of standard vector renders, we developed a specialized neural renderer that mimics vector rendering behavior, framing stroke prediction as a parameter search aimed at maximizing the similarity between the rendered output and the input image. To resolve the zero-gradient issues inherent in this parameter search, we propose an optimal transportation-based solution. Furthermore, we identify parameter coupling limitations in existing neural renderers and redesign the network using separate rasterization and shading components to effectively disentangle shape and color. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves high fidelity in both global appearance and local textures. Additionally, the approach supports joint optimization with neural style transfer to incorporate visual styles from external images. The project's code and animated demonstrations are accessible at \url{https://jiupinjia.github.io/neuralpainter/}.

This paper examines the evolution of autoencoders close to their initialization phase. Specifically, we analyze the eigenvalue distributions of the Jacobian matrices for autoencoders trained on the MNIST dataset during the early stages of training. Our findings reveal that untrained autoencoders exhibit eigenvalue distributions that differ qualitatively from those of models trained for extended periods (over 100 epochs). Furthermore, we observe that even at early epochs, these eigenvalue distributions rapidly converge to become qualitatively similar to those of fully trained autoencoders. Additionally, we compare the eigenvalues at initialization with relevant theoretical research concerning the eigenvalues of random matrices and their products.

This paper introduces novel binary quantum code constructions derived from quaternary linear Hermitian self-dual codes. These constructions rely primarily on nearly self-orthogonal cyclic or duadic codes defined over F_4. We provide an infinite family of 0-dimensional binary quantum codes and establish lower bounds for their minimum distances based on the minimum distances of the underlying linear codes. Additionally, we present new findings regarding the minimum distance of linear cyclic codes through the analysis of their fixed subcodes. Finally, we compile a list of numerous new record-breaking quantum codes generated by these methods.

Differentially Private Stochastic Convex Optimization (DP-SCO) stands as a foundational challenge in machine learning, statistics, and differential privacy, attracting significant research attention recently. However, prior studies have largely been limited to low-dimensional settings involving either regular or irregular data distributions. To address the complexities introduced by irregular distributions, this paper presents the inaugural investigation into DP-SCO with heavy-tailed data in high-dimensional spaces. Initially, we examine the problem under polytope constraints, such as the $\ell_1$-norm ball. We demonstrate that when the loss function is smooth with a gradient possessing a bounded second-order moment, a high-probability error bound (excess population risk) of $\tilde{O}(\frac{\log d}{(n\epsilon)^\frac{1}{3}})$ can be achieved within the $\epsilon$-DP framework, where $n$ denotes sample size and $d$ represents dimensionality. Subsequently, for LASSO problems where the data distribution has bounded fourth-order moments, we enhance this bound to $\tilde{O}(\frac{\log d}{(n\epsilon)^\frac{2}{5}})$ under the $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP model. The second section explores sparse learning with heavy-tailed data. We begin by revisiting the sparse linear model, introducing a truncated DP-IHT method that yields an error of $\tilde{O}(\frac{s^{*2}\log d}{n\epsilon})$, with $s^*$ indicating the true parameter sparsity. We then address a more general problem involving $\ell_0$-norm constraints, proving that an error of $\tilde{O}(\frac{s^{*\frac{3}{2}}\log d}{n\epsilon})$ is attainable when the loss function is smooth and strongly convex; this result is nearly optimal, up to a factor of $\tilde{O}{(\sqrt{s^*})}$.

We introduce a system for generating contrapuntal music grounded in a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) framework, specifically targeting Baroque counterpoint. This approach models the interaction between two musical parts as a mapping from source material to a corresponding target, where the source imposes constraints but does not fully dictate the outcome, mirroring the translation process. We curated and refined a specialized dataset of Baroque compositions to train an attention-based neural network, evaluating the results through both BLEU scores and musicological analysis. Our findings indicate that the model successfully reproduces idiomatic features like imitation and proper rhythmic alignment; however, it struggles to master stylistically accurate contrapuntal motion, such as avoiding parallel fifths, and fails to adhere to stricter imitative structures like canons.

The classical shadows protocol, recently proposed by Huang, Kueng, and Preskill [Nat. Phys. 16, 1050 (2020)], serves as a quantum-classical framework for estimating properties of unknown quantum states. Unlike full quantum state tomography, this method is suitable for near-term quantum hardware, enabling numerous high-probability predictions with minimal quantum measurements. This paper investigates the impact of noise on the classical shadows protocol, specifically analyzing scenarios where the involved quantum circuits undergo various known noise channels. We derive an analytical upper bound for sample complexity, expressed via a shadow seminorm, applicable to both local and global noise. Furthermore, by adapting the classical post-processing stage of the noiseless protocol, we introduce a new estimator that maintains unbiasedness despite the presence of noise. As practical applications, we demonstrate that our findings establish rigorous sample complexity upper bounds for cases involving depolarizing noise and amplitude damping.

Hawkes processes are point processes designed to model clustered events driven by the self-exciting nature of their intensity functions. We examine a multivariate framework where multiple dimensions interact, with an intensity function capable of capturing both excitation and inhibition effects within and across dimensions. We outline the implementation of this model and address estimation challenges arising from potentially negative intensity values. Additionally, we propose a novel, stronger stability condition that subsumes existing literature-based approaches. Finally, we analyze the total number of offsprings to facilitate model reparametrization, applying Normal and sparsity-inducing priors within a Bayesian estimation procedure on simulated datasets.

The recent NANOGrav discovery of a common-spectrum process has prompted interpretations suggesting it could be evidence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) stronger than standard inflation plus ΛCDM predicts. Such an SGWB would introduce an additional radiation component to the early Universe, potentially influencing its expansion history and offering a novel link between gravitational waves and cosmology that could help resolve the Hubble tension. We explore this possibility using a cosmological model based on "standard inflation plus stiff amplification," which adds a stiff component (w=1) and the primordial SGWB to the ΛCDM framework. In previous work, we demonstrated that under standard inflation, an SGWB amplified by a hypothetical early stiff era following reheating could be detectable by high-frequency laser interferometers. However, models amplifying the SGWB enough to cause significant backreaction must still maintain the well-measured radiation-matter equality required by precision cosmology. To address this, we calculated the fully coupled evolution of the SGWB and expansion history, sampling key parameters including the tensor-to-scalar ratio, reheating temperature, and the temperature at stiff-to-radiation equality. We subsequently conducted a joint analysis incorporating NANOGrav data with the latest constraints from Planck, big bang nucleosynthesis, and Advanced LIGO-Virgo to constrain the model. Our results indicate that the resulting blue-tilted, stiff-amplified SGWB remains too weak to account for the NANOGrav findings. Nevertheless, if Advanced LIGO-Virgo eventually detects the SGWB, our model could explain it within the framework of standard inflation without necessitating an initial blue tilt. Furthermore, this model could reduce the Hubble tension, bringing high-redshift measurements within 3.4 sigma of SH0ES low-redshift results (down from 4.4 sigma) and within 2.6 sigma of H0LiCOW measurements (down from 3.1 sigma).

Causal consistency is a prevalent weak consistency model that ensures high availability even during network partitions, with numerous research prototypes and industrial implementations existing. However, to our knowledge, no existing solutions address Byzantine faults except for Byz-RCM by Tseng et al. Byz-RCM provides causal consistency in a client-server architecture using $3f + 1$ servers, tolerating up to $f$ Byzantine servers, but it assumes clients are non-Byzantine. This paper introduces Byz-GentleRain, the first causal consistency protocol capable of handling up to $f$ Byzantine servers within each partition of a $3f + 1$ server group, alongside any number of Byzantine clients. Inspired by the stabilization mechanism of GentleRain, Byz-GentleRain leverages PBFT to achieve consensus on a sequence of global stable times and server updates. Consequently, only updates with timestamps less than or equal to these agreed-upon global stable times are visible to clients. We demonstrate that Byz-GentleRain achieves Byz-CC, the variant of causal consistency resilient to Byzantine faults. Preliminary evaluations on Aliyun indicate that Byz-GentleRain remains efficient under typical workloads.

George Box famously noted that "All models are wrong, but some are useful." To enhance model utility, we quantify the inaccuracy between a model and the system it represents, leveraging this metric to aid in controller synthesis and verification. Specifically, we introduce a method to identify a sim2real gap that holds with a minimum probability. By augmenting the nominal model with this identified gap, we create an uncertain model proven to accurately represent system behavior. We utilize this uncertain model to synthesize and verify controllers in simulation via a probabilistic approach. This pipeline yields controllers with an arbitrarily high probability of achieving safe desired behaviors on physical hardware, eliminating the need for hardware testing except for the specific steps required to identify the sim2real gap. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this procedure on two hardware platforms: the Robotarium and a quadruped.

Clinical metabolomics research frequently suffers from insufficient data management. To address this, we developed LabPipe, a customizable, guided solution designed for study-specific sample collection. The system operates via a local client that orchestrates the workflow and transmits local data to a remote server through a secure, access-controlled web API. LabPipe supports diverse sampling methodologies across various sites and studies, serving as a vital component for local study management at the EPSRC/MRC funded East Midlands Breathomics Pathology Node. The software is freely available for non-commercial use under the NPOSL 3.0 license, accompanied by documentation and installation guides at http://labpipe.org. For inquiries, please contact rob.free@le.ac.uk.

This paper establishes a matrix Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality for the Green function on complete Kähler manifolds featuring nonnegative holomorphic bisectional curvature. Such an estimate serves as an elliptic counterpart to the matrix estimate derived by Cao and Ni for the heat equation on Kähler manifolds, and it also represents the complex analogue of the prior estimate for Riemannian manifolds obtained by the author.

We report the discovery of CWISE J203546.35-493611.0, an unusual M8 companion to the M4.5 star APMPM J2036-4936, identified via the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 citizen science initiative. With proper motion ($\mu_{\alpha}$, $\mu_{\delta}$) = ($-$126$\pm$22, $-$478$\pm$23) and an angular separation of 34.2$''$ from APMPM 2036-4936, we determine a chance alignment probability of $1.15 \times 10^{-6}$. Both components of this system exhibit underluminosity, and the spectrum of CWISE J203546.35-493611.0 reveals a triangular H band, indicating that further investigation is necessary to elucidate these anomalies.

This study presents an angular analysis of the $B_s^0 \rightarrow K^{*0}\bar{K}{}^{*0}$ decay based on $pp$ collision data with an integrated luminosity of $1.0$ ${fb}^{-1}$ recorded by the LHCb experiment at $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV. By employing a combined angular and mass analysis, six helicity amplitudes are disentangled, yielding a longitudinal polarisation fraction of $f_L = 0.201 \pm 0.057 {(stat.)} \pm 0.040{(syst.)}$ for the $B_s^0 \rightarrow K^*(892)^0 \bar{K}{}^*(892)^0$ channel. The observation of significant scalar contributions from the $K^{*}_{0}(1430)$ and $K^{*}_{0}(800)$ resonances enables the extraction of further $CP$ asymmetries. Both triple product and direct $CP$ asymmetries are found to be consistent with Standard Model predictions. Additionally, the branching fraction for $B_s^0 \rightarrow K^*(892)^0 \bar{K}{}^*(892)^0$ is measured as $(10.8 \pm 2.1 {\ \rm (stat.)} \pm 1.4 {\ \rm (syst.)} \pm 0.6 \ (f_d/f_s) ) \times 10^{-6}$.

Inspired by investigations into small-amplitude non-linear waves in Anti-de-Sitter spacetime, particularly the conjecture of time-periodic solutions to the Einstein equations, we construct families of arbitrarily small time-periodic solutions for the conformal cubic wave equation and spherically-symmetric Yang-Mills equations on the Einstein cylinder $\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{S}^3$. Regarding the conformal cubic wave equation, we examine both spherically-symmetric configurations and complex-valued aspherical solutions utilizing an ansatz based on the Hopf fibration of the 3-sphere. In each scenario, the governing equations simplify to $1+1$ semi-linear wave equations. Our methodology depends on a theorem by Bambusi and Paleari, which requires a seed solution defined as a non-degenerate zero of a non-linear operator linked to the resonant system. For our specific problems, these seed solutions correspond to the mode solutions of the linearized equations. Assuming the Fourier coefficients are computable, verifying the non-degeneracy conditions reduces to solving infinite-dimensional linear systems. Since the eigenfunctions for all three cases involve Jacobi polynomials, we derive the respective Fourier and resonant systems through linearization, connection formulas, and integral transformations of these polynomials. In the Yang-Mills context, the original Bambusi-Paleari theorem does not apply because the lowest-degree non-linearity is non-resonant; consequently, resonant terms arise from higher-order non-linearities, accompanied by corrections due to backreaction from the smallest-degree non-linearity, for which we establish an analogous theorem.

Multiple studies indicate a robust correlation between various cancer types and the relative levels of short, circulating RNA sequences known as miRNA. However, detecting miRNA is challenging due to their small size and low abundance. Conventional techniques like RT-PCR necessitate both a reverse transcription step and subsequent PCR amplification. In this study, we explore DNA nanopores as a method for identifying short oligonucleotide sequences at the single-molecule level. These nanostructures exhibit two distinct conformations contingent on the presence of DNA analogues mimicking miRNA sequences. By measuring the current flow across a lipid bilayer, we demonstrate that this conformational shift results in varying conductivity levels.

This work demonstrates that local complete intersections with k-rational singularities are k-Du Bois. In the specific case of hypersurfaces, we define k-rationality using the minimal exponent. Additionally, we prove several local vanishing theorems concerning both k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities; certain findings of this nature were also derived independently in [FL2].

This study extends our prior development of double tensor integrals (DTI) to parametrization double tensor integrals (PDTI) by leveraging integral kernel transform bounds to establish an upper limit for the PDTI norm and deriving a novel perturbation formula. Additionally, we examine the convergence characteristics of random PDTIs and apply these findings to define the relationship between the original derivative tensor and the action of PDTI on that tensor. These methodologies enable the derivation of new tail bounds for random tensors based on broader operator inequalities, such as the Heinz and Birman-Koplienko-Solomyak inequalities. Furthermore, we obtain additional tail bounds for random tensors by utilizing our newly formulated perturbation expression alongside integral kernel transform constraints.

Questions inherently reveal the questioner's uncertainties. This paper introduces a novel method enabling a learning agent to identify and query the aspects it finds most difficult to predict while generating a final output. By examining the timing and content of these queries, we enhance the model's transparency and interpretability. Initially, we established a general framework for deep neural networks capable of asking questions, termed "asking networks." We then designed a specific architecture and training protocol for an asking network applied to colorization, a one-to-many exemplar task where inquiry improves accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that the model learns to formulate meaningful questions, prioritizes challenging ones, and leverages hints more effectively than baseline models. Ultimately, we conclude that this asking framework allows learning agents to expose their weaknesses, offering a promising avenue for developing interpretable and interactive models.

Assessing the similarity of multiple dose-response curves in interlaboratory regulatory toxicology studies is a critical aspect of assay validation. This study illustrates the application of dose-by-laboratory interaction contrasts, specifically Williams-type contrasts against the total mean. Using the open-source R software and the CRAN packages `statint` and `multcomp`, calculating adjusted p-values or simultaneous confidence intervals is straightforward. However, interpreting these results as global or partial equivalence remains challenging due to the lack of predefined thresholds. The methodology is illustrated using selected in-vitro Ames MPF assay data.

Sports analytics has emerged as a growing area of interest for both academic institutions and professional sports organizations. Driven by the increasing availability of athlete data, the main objective of this analysis is to enhance athletic performance in a quantifiable way. This research specifically targets the difficulties associated with gathering sufficient swimming data. Previous studies have demonstrated that detecting and tracking swimmers is possible, though it faces significant hurdles, such as accurately localizing the pool and determining swimmers' positions relative to it. This work offers two contributions to address these issues: first, it introduces a pool model featuring invariant key-points essential for swimming analytics; second, it examines the detectability of these key-points in images with partial pool views, a challenging yet common scenario in swimming race footage.

This study presents a game-theoretic framework designed to evaluate the efficiency losses resulting from decentralized control or local management of global epidemics. In this model, each player represents a region or country that selects control actions to balance socioeconomic factors against health outcomes. We perform a Nash equilibrium analysis of this game, providing sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of equilibria given the analytical complexity. Furthermore, we quantify the efficiency loss due to decentralization using numerical results expressed through the Price of Anarchy (PoA) and Price of Connectedness (PoC). These findings enable the clear identification of scenarios where decentralization is either viable or detrimental based on global efficiency metrics.

JLab has recently reported signs suggesting the possible presence of a $\Sigma NN$ resonance with parameters $(3.14 \pm 0.84) - i (2.28 \pm 1.2)$ MeV. Historically, models leveraging symmetry between the strangeness-free and strangeness-containing two-baryon sectors have been employed to derive hyperon-nucleon interactions that align with experimental data in the strangeness $-1$ regime. Utilizing these interactions, we revisit current Faddeev investigations of the $\Lambda NN$-$\Sigma NN$ system, which provide theoretical support for a $(I,J^P)=(1,1/2^+)$ $\Sigma NN$ quasibound state situated near the threshold. Our calculations place the pole at 2.92$-i\,$2.17 MeV, showing reasonable consistency with the experimental results.

We examine a stochastic model describing the evolution of a discrete population characterized by traits located on a finite grid of a torus, subject to mutation and selection. Traits are passed vertically unless mutated and affect birth and death rates. We analyze a specific parameter regime featuring a large population, infrequent yet non-rare individual mutations, and a trait grid mesh significantly finer than mutation steps. Over long time scales, small sub-populations can significantly impact the dynamics. Our primary result quantifies the asymptotic behavior of sub-population sizes on a logarithmic scale. We demonstrate that, under this scaling, the appropriately normalized logarithm of the stochastic population size process converges to the unique viscosity solution of a Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Such equations have previously been derived from parabolic integro-differential equations and are extensively used in studying the adaptation of quantitative traits. This work offers a direct justification of this framework starting from a stochastic individual-based model, thereby enhancing the understanding of results previously obtained within this approach. The proof relies on almost sure maximum principles and precise control of martingale components.

Liquid crystal elastomers exhibit reversible contraction along their director axis upon heating and expansion upon cooling, presenting significant promise for use as artificial muscles and actuators. When a flat sheet is patterned with a spatially varying director orientation, it transforms into a curved surface, enabling functions such as lifting or grasping. This study focuses on programmed annular sheets; their central hole allows them to bypass typical constraints regarding area and orientation. We systematically identify the range of developable surfaces achievable through axisymmetric director patterns and reveal several novel actuation modes, including cylinders, iris-like mechanisms, and everted surfaces where the inner boundary becomes the outer boundary after deformation. These designs are validated through a combination of numerical simulations and experiments. Furthermore, many of these actuators can return to their original inner or outer radii after actuation, making them highly advantageous for applications involving fixed frames or pipes, as they minimize potentially damaging stresses during operation.

Stellar streams originating from dwarf galaxies offer direct proof of the Milky Way's hierarchical formation. In this work, we introduce the first comprehensive analysis of the "LMS-1" stream, identified by searching the Gaia EDR3 dataset for wide streams using the STREAMFINDER algorithm, a discovery initially reported by Yuan et al. (2020). We characterize LMS-1 as a 60-degree-long structure located north of the Galactic bulge at a distance of approximately 20 kpc from the Sun, alongside additional components indicating the stream fully encircles the inner Galaxy. Spectroscopic data from LAMOST, SDSS, and APOGEE reveal that the stream is highly metal-poor ($\langle \text{[Fe/H]} \rangle = -2.1$) with substantial metallicity dispersion ($\sigma_{\text{[Fe/H]}} = 0.4$) and a large radial velocity dispersion ($\sigma_v = 20 \pm 4 \, \text{km s}^{-1}$). These properties confirm LMS-1 as a dwarf galaxy stream. Its orbit is nearly polar, inclined at $75^\circ$ to the Galactic plane. The stream's orbit and metallicity closely resemble those of globular clusters NGC 5053 and NGC 5024, as well as the "Indus" stellar stream. Consequently, LMS-1 represents a significant addition to the stellar population of the inner Milky Way halo.

This review examines techniques for detecting explosive bubbles within time series data. It comprehensively covers numerous recently developed testing methodologies under diverse assumptions regarding error innovations. Additionally, the paper addresses methods for dating explosive bubble periods, with particular focus on time-varying volatility in errors. Furthermore, it explores the modeling of potential relationships between time series exhibiting explosive regimes.

This research investigates the self-similarity evolution of advection-dominated accretion flows (ADAF) under the influence of a toroidal magnetic field. Assuming that angular momentum transport is driven by viscous turbulence, the study employs the $\alpha$-prescription to define the kinematic viscosity coefficient. To resolve the integrated equations governing the flow's dynamics, a self-similar approach was utilized. The results reveal that physical quantities in a dynamical ADAF behave differently compared to steady-state accretion flows and polytropic disks. Furthermore, a transonic point exists within the accretion flow for all chosen advection parameters. Increasing both the magnetic field strength and the advection degree leads to a reduction in the disk's radial thickness, effectively compressing it. Finally, the model suggests that the flow exhibits differential rotation, remaining sub-Keplerian at small radii while becoming super-Keplerian at larger distances.

The Fermi Large Area Telescope has identified more than 260 gamma-ray pulsars, approximately 25% of which are classified as radio-quiet. Within the subset of nonrecycled gamma-ray pulsars, this fraction rises to roughly 50%. Traditional radio surveys of these pulsars typically operate between 300 MHz and 2 GHz. However, because radio flux increases significantly at lower frequencies and radio beams often widen in this regime, some pulsars undetected above 300 MHz might still be observable at lower frequencies. Our objective was to test this hypothesis using low-frequency radio observations. We conducted single-station observations of 27 Fermi-discovered gamma-ray pulsars using the LOFAR FR606 station in its High Band Antenna (HBA) configuration (110–190 MHz). After filtering out affected data, we averaged 9 hours of observation per target, achieving a pulse-averaged flux sensitivity of approximately 1–10 mJy. We detected no radio pulsations from any of the 27 sources and established stringent upper limits on their low-frequency radio fluxes. These non-detections align with upper limits previously derived from observations at other frequencies. By analyzing gamma-ray profiles to determine pulsar geometry, we identified which sources were expected to have their low-frequency radio beams intersect Earth. This study provides the most restrictive upper limits on flux density at 150 MHz for 27 radio-quiet gamma-ray pulsars. Despite the anticipated beam widening at low frequencies, most non-detections are attributable to unfavorable viewing geometries; for the remaining cases, particularly those involving pulsars detected at higher frequencies, the lack of detection is consistent with insufficient sensitivity.

This study details the inaugural survey of molecular emissions from cometary volatiles utilizing standalone Atacama Compact Array (ACA) observations of the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) directed at comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS). Conducted on April 11 and 15, 2017, shortly following the comet's April 4 outburst, these observations targeted HCN, CS, CH$_3$OH, H$_2$CO, and HNC, alongside dust continuum emission. Probing the inner coma, the data revealed asymmetric outgassing and successfully distinguished between parent and daughter or distributed source species. The analysis provides spectrally integrated flux maps, autocorrelation spectra, production rates, and parent scale lengths for each molecule, along with a strict upper limit for CO. While HCN appears consistent with direct release from the nucleus, CS, H$_2$CO, HNC, and potentially CH$_3$OH are linked to distributed sources within the coma. Applying a Haser model, the derived parent scale lengths for H$_2$CO ($\sim$2200 km) and HNC ($\sim$3300 km) align with prior comet studies; however, CS indicates significant extended source production ($\sim$2000 km), implying generation from an unknown parent in the coma. The continuum emission exhibits a point-source distribution with a flux density suggesting an unrealistically large nucleus, inconsistent with other size estimates. This is best explained by thermal radiation from slowly moving outburst ejecta, with a total mass between 5 and 8 $\times$ 10$^{10}$ kg. These findings highlight the ACA's capability to uncover the abundances, spatial distributions, and production locations of volatiles in moderately bright comets like C/2015 ER61.

Numerical relativity simulations represent the sole method for computing precise gravitational waveforms from binary neutron star mergers and for constructing necessary templates for gravitational-wave astronomy. The precision of these calculations is vital for quantifying tidal effects near the merger, which remain a primary source of uncertainty in current waveform models. This study investigates an entropy-based flux-limiting scheme designed for high-order, convergent simulations of neutron star spacetimes. By utilizing the residual of the entropy equation to track the stellar surface and physical shocks, this approach enables the application of unlimited central flux schemes in regions of smooth flow. We present the first neutron star merger simulations utilizing this technique, demonstrating up to fourth-order convergence in the gravitational waveform phase. Compared to state-of-the-art high-order characteristic schemes, this method reduces phase error by a factor of five and is suitable for generating accurate tidal waveforms for gravitational-wave modeling.

Recommender systems aim to predict user preferences across numerous items for all users using limited observations. A key challenge lies in exploiting three-way interactions—specifically user-item-stage dependencies along a monotonic sequence of events—to improve prediction accuracy. Such sequences occur, for example, in article-sharing contexts where a "follow" action necessitates a "like," which in turn requires a "view." This paper introduces a multistage recommender system that leverages a two-level monotonic property inherent in these event chains for personalized prediction. Specifically, we propose a large-margin classifier grounded in a nonnegative additive latent factor model, designed to handle high rates of missing data between stages. This approach reduces the parameter count for personalized prediction while ensuring consistency. Building on this, we formulate a regularized cost function to capture user-specific behaviors across stages, connecting decision functions with both numerical and categorical covariates to model user-item-stage interactions. Computationally, we employ a blockwise coordinate descent algorithm. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the two-level monotonic property yields superior learning accuracy compared to standard methods that treat stages independently or ordinal methods relying on single-level monotonicity. Finally, experimental results on simulations and an article-sharing dataset show that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches.

We demonstrate that each tetrahedron T contains a simple, closed quasigeodesic intersecting three of its vertices. This result is equivalent to stating that for every T, there exists at least one face where all exterior angles do not exceed π.

This paper computes late-time correlation functions within three-dimensional de Sitter spacetime for a higher-spin gravity theory. To achieve this, we refine the formulation to derive the universe's wave functional from a dual conformal field theory, facilitating the calculation of these correlators. We posit a connection between this approach and direct bulk Feynman diagram computations using the in-in formalism. Additionally, we outline a precise method for constructing higher-spin dS$_3$ holography by analytically continuing the Gaberdiel-Gopakumar duality applicable to AdS$_3$. While some findings were previously announced in a letter, this work provides detailed derivations and extends the analysis to broader scenarios. Building on prior examinations of two-, three-, and simple four-point functions at leading order in the Newton constant, we now evaluate more intricate four-point correlators. Furthermore, we investigate late-time correlators in an alternative dS$_3$/CFT$_2$ limit involving critical level cosets, such as two-point functions on conical defect geometries, and analyze one-loop corrections to two-point correlators on dS$_3$.

Political polarization is escalating, as evidenced by voting trends, emotional responses to opposing parties, and online content consumption. While previous studies have examined the internet's role in driving this divide, the current research investigates specific factors by analyzing the browsing histories of tens of thousands of users alongside their time spent on various news outlets. The findings reveal a polarized pattern in news consumption, where individuals spend significantly more time on sites aligning with their political views compared to those of opposing factions. These preferences exist both at the individual and population levels, resulting in distinct partisan communities of news domains when browsing patterns are aggregated. Furthermore, the study addresses whether users merely follow available links or actively intensify polarization by seeking out like-minded content. By comparing browsing habits with the underlying hyperlink structure of news domains, the research demonstrates strong evidence that partisan browsing habits exceed what can be attributed to the web's link structure alone, indicating active user choice in driving polarization.

In functional programming, generalized algebraic data types (GADTs) prove highly valuable because they eliminate redundant pattern matching through the failure of type argument unification. Within dependent type systems, these are known as indexed types and are especially beneficial for representing the identity type as a specific instance. However, matching over indexed types is inherently complex due to the necessity of general term unification. This paper examines a streamlined variant termed "simpler indexed types," in which constructor selection is explicitly defined, while analyzing its expressive power, constraints, and theoretical properties.

Numerous ordinal regression models found in existing literature function by minimizing a convex surrogate of the zero-one, absolute, or squared loss functions. A fundamental property enabling the analysis of these approximations is Fisher consistency, which ensures that if the true data-generating distribution were known, optimizing the surrogate would yield the optimal model. This paper characterizes the Fisher consistency of a broad class of surrogate losses applicable to ordinal regression, such as support vector ordinal regression, ORBoosting, and least absolute deviation. We demonstrate that for a family of surrogates encompassing support vector ordinal regression and ORBoosting, consistency can be fully described by the derivative of a real-valued function at zero, mirroring the behavior of convex margin-based surrogates in binary classification. Additionally, we derive excess risk bounds for an absolute error surrogate that extend current risk bounds from binary classification. Our analysis also proposes a new surrogate for squared error loss. Empirical evaluations across nine datasets reveal that our method is highly competitive, surpassing the least squares loss in seven out of nine cases.

For a complex $n\times n$ matrix $C$, the $C$-numerical range of a bounded linear operator $T$ on a Hilbert space of dimension $\ge n$ is defined as the set of values ${\rm tr}(CX^*TX)$, where $X$ is a partial isometry such that $X^*X = I_n$. It is demonstrated that the equality $${\bf cl}(W_C(T)) = \cap \{{\bf cl}(W_C(U)): U \hbox{ is a unitary dilation of } T\}$$ holds for any contraction $T$ if and only if $C$ is a rank one normal matrix.

This study represents a significant step forward in practical continuous-variable quantum optical technologies by demonstrating the feasibility of experiments where non-Gaussian state generation depends solely on plug-and-play components from guided-wave optics. The approach is experimentally validated through the heralded creation of low-amplitude Schrödinger cat states via single-photon subtraction from a squeezed vacuum, with every stage utilizing standard off-the-shelf fiber components. This results in a stable, compact, and easily reconfigurable system that is fully compatible with current fiber networks and broader future applications outside the laboratory.

Neuromorphic computers emulate the human brain to execute computations with minimal power consumption, positioning them as essential for future energy-efficient computing. Although currently dominant in spiking neural network applications, these systems are Turing-complete and capable of general-purpose computation. However, unlocking their full potential requires efficient number encoding mechanisms, as existing methods often lack the versatility needed for broad computational tasks. This paper introduces the "virtual neuron" as a solution for encoding integers and rational numbers. Evaluations on both physical and simulated neuromorphic hardware demonstrate that the virtual neuron can perform addition with an average energy consumption of 23 nJ on a mixed-signal memristor-based processor. Furthermore, its utility in general-purpose computation is illustrated through its application in mu-recursive functions, which serve as foundational building blocks for such systems.

We present a Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) for calculating the count of matchings of size $k$ in a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and maximum degree $\Delta$, valid for all $k \leq (1-\delta)m^*(G)$, where $\delta>0$ is a fixed constant and $m^*(G)$ denotes the matching number. Additionally, we provide an FPTAS for the number of independent sets of size $k \leq (1-\delta) \alpha_c(\Delta) n$, with $\alpha_c(\Delta)$ representing the NP-hardness threshold for this problem. We also introduce randomized algorithms running in quasi-linear time to approximately sample from the uniform distribution over matchings of size $k \leq (1-\delta)m^*(G)$ and independent sets of size $k \leq (1-\delta)\alpha_c(\Delta)n$. These advancements rely on a novel framework that leverages local central limit theorems as an algorithmic instrument. By combining Fourier inversion, probabilistic estimates, and deterministic approximations of partition functions at complex activities, we extract estimates for the partition function's coefficients. Specifically regarding independent sets, we establish a new local central limit theorem for the hard-core model that holds for all fugacities below $\lambda_c(\Delta)$, the uniqueness threshold on the infinite $\Delta$-regular tree.

This study examines Lehnert and Schweitzer's proof regarding the co-context-free nature of the word problem for the Thompson group V, demonstrating that this problem corresponds to the complement of the cyclic closure of a union of reverse deterministic context-free languages. For specific finite generating sets, the word problem is identified as the complement of the cyclic closure of a union of four deterministic context-free languages. Consequently, the deterministic time complexity of the word problem for $V$ is bounded by at most quadratic.

In clinical trials, appropriately adjusting statistical analyses for baseline variables, known as covariate adjustment, can enhance precision and decrease the necessary sample size. Although regulatory bodies recommend this practice, its underutilization results in inefficient studies. This work tackles two barriers to its adoption: the incompatibility of many covariate-adjusted estimators with standard boundaries in group sequential designs (GSDs), and the uncertainty regarding precision gains at the design phase. We introduce a method that adapts the original estimator to align with GSDs while maintaining or improving precision. This approach accommodates any asymptotically linear estimator, encompassing most used in randomized trials. Furthermore, we propose an information adaptive design that continues the trial until a target information level is met; this strategy adjusts to actual precision gains, enabling faster and more efficient trials without compromising validity or power. Finally, we assess estimator performance through simulations reflecting a completed stroke trial.

Recent investigations indicate that high-precision velocity measurements of very wide binary stars obtained by GAIA offer a promising avenue for testing modified-gravity theories designed to mimic dark matter. Specifically, MOND-like frameworks incorporating the external field effect predict that wide binaries (separations exceeding $\sim 7$ kAU) should orbit approximately $15\%$ faster than Newtonian expectations for equivalent orbital parameters; this deviation is theoretically detectable within the 9,000 candidate systems identified by Pittordis and Sutherland (2022) from the GAIA EDR3 dataset. The primary current limitation is the presence of a "fat tail" among candidates exhibiting velocity differences of $\sim 1.5 - 6 \times$ the circular velocity. These systems cannot be pure binaries and are likely dominated by triple or quadruple systems with unresolved or undetected companions.

Although this tail can be modeled and subtracted, constructing an accurate model of the triple population is essential for a robust test of modified gravity. This study examines the feasibility of observationally constraining such triples by simulating a hierarchical triple population observed under random epochs and viewing angles, similar to the PS22 sample. Various detection strategies are evaluated, including GAIA astrometry, radial velocity drift, and imaging techniques from the Rubin Observatory, speckle imaging, and coronagraphy. The results are encouraging, with approximately 90% of triple systems in critical parameter regions being detectable. However, a moderate "dead zone" exists for cool brown-dwarf companions at $\sim 25-100$ AU separations, which remain undetectable using current baseline methods. A large yet feasible observing campaign could clarify the nature of the triple/quadruple population and render the gravity test conclusive.

Yes—This research examines how standard lossy image compression affects face recognition algorithms, specifically concerning the racial characteristics of the subjects. We utilize a recently developed methodology based on racial phenotypes to assess the effects of varying compression levels across different phenotype groups. Furthermore, we analyze the connection between chroma subsampling and race-related phenotypes in the context of recognition performance. While previous studies have explored the impact of lossy JPEG compression on modern face recognition, a gap remains regarding how this impact differs across intersectional racial groups and the underlying causes. Through an extensive experimental framework, we show that common lossy compression techniques negatively affect facial recognition more severely for specific racial phenotype categories, such as darker skin tones (by up to 34.55%). Additionally, eliminating chroma subsampling during compression reduces the false matching rate by up to 15.95% across all affected phenotype categories, including those with darker skin tones, wide noses, prominent lips, and monolid eyes. Finally, we outline the specific characteristics that likely serve as the root causes of these phenomena within lossy compression algorithms like JPEG.

We introduce a quantum eigenstate filtering method grounded in quantum signal processing (QSP) and minimax polynomials. This approach enables the efficient preparation of a specific Hamiltonian's target eigenstate, provided an initial state exists with non-negligible overlap to that target and a reasonable lower bound on the spectral gap is known. Applying this framework to the quantum linear system problem (QLSP), we propose two distinct algorithms utilizing quantum adiabatic computing (AQC) and the quantum Zeno effect. Both methods yield the final solution as a pure state and attain the near-optimal query complexity of $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(d\kappa\log(1/\epsilon))$ for a $d$-sparse matrix, where $\kappa$ denotes the condition number and $\epsilon$ represents the required precision. Importantly, neither algorithm relies on phase estimation or amplitude amplification.

We present and investigate a fermionization method applied to the cohomological Hall algebra $\mathcal{H}_{\Pi_Q}$ associated with representations of a preprojective algebra. This approach selectively alters the cohomological parity of the BPS Lie algebra, transitioning it from even to odd. This is achieved by computing the cohomological Donaldson--Thomas invariants for central extensions of preprojective algebras—previously examined by Etingof and Rains—using deformed dimensional reduction. Employing identical techniques, we also calculate the Borel-Moore homology of the stack of representations for the $\mu$-deformed preprojective algebra introduced by Crawley-Boevey and Holland across all dimension vectors. This work offers a unified generalization of Crawley-Boevey and Van den Bergh's findings on the cohomology of smooth moduli schemes for deformed preprojective algebras, as well as my prior results concerning the Borel-Moore homology of the representation stack for the undeformed preprojective algebra.

Domain randomisation has become a widely adopted technique for sim-to-real transfer in robotics, valued for its simplicity and capacity to enable transfer without requiring any real-world images. However, achieving optimal transfer necessitates careful selection of specific design parameters. This paper presents an extensive benchmarking study of these choices, evaluated through two key experiments focused on a real-world object pose estimation task. First, our analysis of rendering quality reveals that a limited set of high-quality images outperforms a larger collection of low-quality ones. Second, regarding the type of randomisation, we find that incorporating both distractors and textures is crucial for generalizing to new environments.

This study establishes explicit bilipschitz bounds regarding the metric variation between the thick sections of a cusped hyperbolic 3-manifold $N$ and those of its long Dehn fillings. By specifying a bilipschitz constant $J > 1$ and a thickness threshold $\epsilon > 0$, we determine the necessary length of a Dehn filling to ensure a $J$-bilipschitz map on the $\epsilon$-thick components. While Brock and Bromberg previously demonstrated a similar qualitative result using Hodgson and Kerckhoff's cone deformation theory, our work introduces quantitative precision by bounding the analytic factors that govern infinitesimal metric changes during these deformations.

These quantitative findings yield two primary applications. First, we connect the Margulis number of $N$ with those of its Dehn fillings; specifically, we provide a lower bound for the systole of any closed 3-manifold with a Margulis number under 0.29. When paired with Shalen's upper bound on the volume of such manifolds, this yields an algorithm to enumerate the finite set of 3-manifolds possessing Margulis numbers below 0.29. Second, we apply these results to the cosmetic surgery conjecture. Given the systole of a one-cusped hyperbolic manifold $N$, we derive an explicit upper limit for the slope length involved in a cosmetic surgery on $N$, thereby reducing the conjecture for $N$ to a verifiable finite search.

Although extensive theoretical and experimental research over the last ten years has failed to explain extragalactic radio background observations below 10 GHz across multiple frequencies using known radio sources, these anomalies may indicate new physics. This Letter introduces a novel class of dark sector models featuring feebly interacting particles, specifically where dark photons oscillate into standard photons to contribute to the radio background. Our proposed scenario accounts for both the magnitude and spectral index of the radio background while remaining consistent with existing cosmological and astrophysical constraints. Furthermore, these models predict the emergence of new relativistic degrees of freedom and spectral distortions in the cosmic microwave background, which upcoming experiments might detect.

We present a unified demonstration of H\"{o}lder regularity for weak solutions to mixed local and nonlocal parabolic equations of $p$-Laplace type, covering the complete exponent range $1<p<\infty$. This approach relies on the expansion of positivity, energy estimates, and a De Giorgi type lemma.

This study derives Born's rule within the de Broglie-Bohm pilot-wave framework. Utilizing a toy model where a particle interacts with an environment composed of "qubits" (interpreted as Bohmian pointers), we demonstrate that the combination of entanglement and deterministic chaos drives a rapid relaxation of any initial statistical distribution $\rho(x)$ for a particle's position to the Born probability law $|\Psi(x)|^2$. Situating this model alongside Boltzmann's kinetic theory, we establish an H theorem that characterizes the system's relaxation toward quantum equilibrium.

Bilingual Lexicon Induction (BLI) seeks to align words across languages, typically by learning linear projections to map monolingual word representation spaces. While both static word embeddings and contextual representations have been investigated for BLI, no prior research has attempted to integrate them. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective method to merge static embeddings with contextual representations, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. We evaluate this mechanism across diverse language pairs under both supervised and unsupervised BLI benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms robust BLI baselines across all language pairs, achieving an average improvement of 3.2 points in the supervised setting and 3.1 points in the unsupervised setting.

Federated learning (FL), which trains deep models on decentralized data while preventing privacy breaches, has recently gained significant traction. However, its performance is constrained by two prevalent challenges: data heterogeneity from a local viewpoint and class imbalance from a global perspective. These coupled issues remain insufficiently explored, and current research often fails to realistically model data distributions found in practical environments, such as healthcare. A key observation is that global class distributions are frequently skewed (e.g., common versus rare diseases), and data tends to cluster among more advanced clients, a phenomenon known as the data agglomeration effect that existing frameworks cannot adequately capture. Drawing inspiration from real-world medical imaging datasets, we define a novel and more realistic distribution termed the L2 distribution, characterized by highly imbalanced global classes and client-level imbalances that exhibit specific degrees of data agglomeration. To address effective FL under this distribution, we introduce FedIIC, a new privacy-preserving framework designed to mitigate bias arising from imbalanced training. To refine the feature extractor, we employ intra-client contrastive learning with an adjusted similarity metric and inter-client contrastive learning guided by shared global prototypes to achieve a uniform embedding distribution across all classes and clients. For the classification heads, we develop a softmax cross-entropy loss incorporating difficulty-aware logit adjustment to ensure balanced decision boundaries for every class. Experimental results on public datasets confirm that FedIIC outperforms existing methods in handling both this proposed realistic distribution and traditional models of these coupled problems.

Overcoming the next decade and beyond, extensive high-intensity searches will sensitively investigate new light mediator particles that interact via minimal renormalizable vector, Higgs, and neutrino portals, as well as higher-dimension axion-like portals.
