Furthermore, while a recent trend in multilingual modeling involves using a single bridge language (e.g., English) rather than training on all parallel language pairs, we observe that this approach degrades zero-shot translation. Specifically, it triggers a failure mode where the model disregards language tags and defaults to generating English output for zero-shot directions. We demonstrate that this bias toward English can be effectively mitigated by incorporating even a small volume of parallel data for certain non-English language pairs.

Citation recommendation aims to support researchers in identifying relevant references for a given input. Current test sets for this task suffer from noise and unreliability due to their automatic generation from parsed PDFs. This paper introduces our ongoing development of a publicly accessible, manually annotated benchmark for citation recommendation. We also perform experiments to assess the performance of content-based baseline models on this new dataset, offering results to guide future improvements. The test collection and code for reproducing these experiments can be found at https://github.com/boudinfl/acm-cr.

For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $A_p=\{0,1,...,p-1\}$ to rational values. The image of this function is denoted by $N_{p/q}$. While $N_{p/q}$ encompasses all nonnegative integers, existing literature typically concentrates on the subset of words evaluating to these integers; this set forms a chaotic, non-context-free language. In contrast, this work examines subsets of $(N_{p/q})^d$ that are $p/q$-recognisable, meaning they can be recognized by finite automata operating over $(A_p)^d$. First, we provide a characterization of these sets as those definable within a specific first-order logic, drawing a parallel to the B\"uchi-Bruy\`ere Theorem for integer-based numeration systems. Second, we demonstrate that neither the natural ordering relation nor the modulo-$q$ operator are $p/q$-recognisable.

In 2007, Andrews and Paule released the eleventh installment of their series on MacMahon's partition analysis, centering on broken $k$-diamond partitions. Along this path, they developed the concept of $k$-elongated partition diamonds. More recently, Andrews and Paule returned to this subject, utilizing partition analysis and the Omega operator to demonstrate that the generating function for the partition numbers $d_k(n)$—derived from summing the links of $k$-elongated plane partition diamonds of length $n$—is $\frac{(q^2;q^2)_\infty^k}{(q;q)_\infty^{3k+1}}$ for all $k\geq 1.$ A major component of their recent study involves establishing various congruence properties for $d_1, d_2,$ and $d_3$ using modular forms as the primary method. The objective of this paper is to broaden the findings of Andrews and Paule by proving infinitely many congruences for the functions $d_k$ across an infinite range of $k$ values. Our approach relies entirely on elementary techniques, specifically generating function manipulations and classical $q$-series results.

At the Tien Shan mountain station (3340m elevation) in Northern Tien Shan, researchers are monitoring near-surface atmospheric radiation, gamma rays, borehole geoacoustic emissions and temperature (at 40m depth), and Doppler sounding on low-inclined radio passes to identify precursory seismogenic effects before earthquakes. Gamma ray flux in the borehole shows negligible daily variation and remains unaffected by precipitation, yet characteristic bay-like drops lasting 2 to 8 days were observed prior to M5.0–M6.2 earthquakes. During a M4.2 event located 5.3 km away, anomalies in gamma ray flux, geoacoustic emission, and temperature were detected 7 to 10 days in advance. Concurrently, disturbances in the Doppler shift of ionospheric signals were recorded. Retrospective analysis of Doppler shift data following underground nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk similarly revealed ionospheric disturbances triggered by increased near-surface atmospheric radioactivity. These findings are analyzed within the framework of the lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere coupling concept.

This document details our first-place submission to the Real Robot Challenge (https://real-robot-challenge.com), a three-stage dexterous manipulation competition utilizing the TriFinger Platform to handle various rectangular objects. Our methodology integrates motion planning with multiple motion primitives for object manipulation. For Phases 1 and 2, we further trained a residual policy in simulation to execute corrective actions alongside our primary controller. This approach secured first place in both Phase 2 and Phase 3. Competing under the anonymous handle `ardentstork` on the leaderboard (https://real-robot-challenge.com/leader-board), our videos and code are available at https://github.com/ripl-ttic/real-robot-challenge.

The Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) serves as a powerful approach for point set registration, though its original design for pairwise alignment struggles when extended to multi-view scenarios. Addressing this limitation, this paper introduces 3DMNDT, a novel multi-view registration framework within the NDT paradigm that combines K-means clustering with a Lie algebra solver. Specifically, the multi-view registration task is framed as a maximum likelihood estimation problem. The K-means algorithm partitions data points into clusters, allowing a normal distribution to model the measurement probability for points within each cluster locally. The registration problem is then defined using an NDT-based likelihood function, which is maximized by a developed Lie algebra solver that sequentially optimizes each rigid transformation. The proposed method iteratively performs data clustering, NDT computation, and likelihood maximization until optimal registration is achieved. Experimental evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that 3DMNDT attains state-of-the-art performance in multi-view registration.

This study introduces a probabilistic framework for iterative techniques used to approximate the solution $\mathbf{x}_* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ of a nonsingular linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}_* = \mathbf{b}$. The proposed approach elevates a conventional iterative method operating on $\mathbb{R}^d$ to function within the space of probability distributions, $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. While traditional methods generate a sequence of approximations $\mathbf{x}_m$ converging to $\mathbf{x}_*$, the methods developed here yield a sequence of probability distributions $\mu_m \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. These distributions serve a dual purpose: they offer a "best estimate" for $\mathbf{x}_*$, such as through the mean of $\mu_m$, and simultaneously provide probabilistic uncertainty quantification when the exact solution remains undetermined. Theoretical analysis is conducted for the prototypical scenario of a stationary linear iterative method, characterizing both the contraction rate of $\mu_m$ toward an atomic measure at $\mathbf{x}_*$ and the characteristics of the resulting uncertainty quantification. The paper concludes with an empirical demonstration that underscores the insights regarding solution uncertainty achievable through probabilistic iterative approaches.

Oscillating propulsors are capable of generating both propulsive and maneuvering forces for underwater vehicles; given that they operate within the same area, the magnitude of maneuvering forces can match that of the propulsive forces. This study examines a flexible beam configured as an oscillating propulsor, which is attached to a vehicle via a pin joint and driven by a motor. It is demonstrated that by utilizing feedback from the propulsor's state, the flexible beam can be induced into post-flutter limit cycle oscillations. These oscillations create traveling waves that produce thrust. Furthermore, using the propulsor's elastic strain for feedback reveals that adjusting the strain measurement location yields a diverse range of stability transitions, where each transition corresponds to a distinct flutter-based propulsion mode characterized by unique thrust and efficiency profiles.

We present a rotation sensor utilizing the intrinsic $^{14}$N nuclear spins found within nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color centers in diamond. This device relies on optical polarization and readout of the nuclei, coupled with a radio-frequency double-quantum pulse sequence to track $^{14}$N nuclear spin precession. The measurement technique mitigates sensitivity to temperature fluctuations in the $^{14}$N quadrupole splitting and eliminates the need for microwave pulses resonant with NV electron spin transitions. Testing on a rotation platform revealed a sensitivity of 4.7 $^{\circ}/\sqrt{\rm{s}}$ (13 mHz/$\sqrt{\rm{Hz}}$) and a bias stability of 0.4 $^{\circ}$/s (1.1 mHz).

Curved beams serve as fundamental elements in Nano-Electro-Mechanical Systems (NEMS), necessitating models that accurately capture scale effects. This study examines the size-dependent static behavior of curved elastic nano-beams using stress-driven nonlocal continuum mechanics. In this framework, axial strain and flexural curvature are defined as integral convolutions involving equilibrated axial force and bending moment fields alongside an averaging kernel. The proposed nonlocal integral method extends the approach previously applied only to straight beams to include curved geometries. Additionally, the associated nonlocal differential formulation, which incorporates non-standard boundary conditions, is presented and demonstrated to yield mathematically well-posed problems for nano-engineering. The theoretical results, which reveal stiffening nonlocal effects, are well-suited for modeling a broad spectrum of nanotechnological devices. Finally, the nonlocal methodology is applied analytically to determine the size-dependent responses of curved elastic nano-sensors and nano-actuators, driven by the characteristic small-scale parameter.

This study addresses blind image super-resolution (SR) by introducing a reformulated degradation model alongside two innovative modules. Aligning with standard blind SR approaches, our framework aims to enhance both kernel estimation and subsequent high-resolution image restoration based on that kernel. Specifically, we redefine the degradation model to shift deblurring kernel estimation into the low-resolution domain. Building on this, we propose a dynamic deep linear filter module that adaptively generates deblurring kernel weights conditioned on the input image, rather than relying on a fixed kernel, thereby producing more robust estimations. Next, a deep constrained least squares filtering module utilizes this reformulation and estimated kernel to derive clean features. These deblurred features, combined with features from the low-resolution input, are processed by a dual-path structured SR network to recover the final high-resolution image. We validated our approach on multiple benchmarks, including Gaussian8 and DIV2KRK. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both quantitative accuracy and visual quality.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective in recommender systems by modeling users and items through their interaction histories. Nevertheless, the susceptibility of GNNs to exposure bias remains largely overlooked; because users encounter only a restricted set of items, the system develops a skewed understanding of preferences, leading to suboptimal recommendations. While inverse propensity weighting (IPW) can mitigate exposure bias at the model output level, it often fails to address bias introduced during the neighbor aggregation phase within GNNs. To address this, we introduce Neighbor Aggregation via Inverse Propensity (Navip), a straightforward yet powerful method for GNNs. Our approach involves calculating the propensity score for every user-item interaction within a bipartite graph and then applying the inverse of these scores, combined with Laplacian normalization, to debias the neighbor aggregation process. Extensive experiments on two public datasets and the Amazon Alexa dataset demonstrate the method's efficacy, yielding performance improvements of up to 14.2%.

A central question in fault-tolerant quantum computation is determining the fundamental resource costs required to execute a universal set of logical gates on encoded qubits with arbitrary precision. This work examines qubits encoded with constant space overhead (finite encoding rate) as the code distance $d$ approaches infinity, utilizing topological codes linked to triangulations of hyperbolic surfaces. We present explicit protocols showing that Dehn twists of these hyperbolic surfaces can be realized via constant-depth unitary circuits without increasing space overhead. Each circuit for a Dehn twist involves a permutation of physical qubits followed by a constant-depth local unitary circuit, where locality is defined by the hyperbolic metric governing the code. Applying these findings to the hyperbolic Fibonacci Turaev-Viro code suggests that universal logical gate sets can be applied to encoded qubits using constant-depth unitary circuits and constant space overhead. These circuits are intrinsically error-protected because they map local operators to local operators, altering their support size by at most a constant factor. In the presence of noisy syndrome measurements, our results indicate the feasibility of universal fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant space overhead and a time overhead scaling as $\mathcal{O}(d/\log d)$. For quantum circuits permitting parallel gate operations, this achieves the optimal space-time overhead scaling known to date.

Recent advancements in Vision-Language (V&L) joint research have yielded impressive outcomes across various text-driven applications. Notably, high-quality Text-to-Video (T2V) generation, once deemed infeasible, has recently become achievable with promising results. However, these generated videos frequently suffer from undesirable artifacts due to the purely data-driven nature of current systems, which lack adherence to physical laws. To address this limitation and enhance the physical realism of T2V, we introduce an autonomous data generation method and a corresponding dataset designed to bridge the gap with extensive multi-modal, 3D Text-to-Video/Simulation (T2V/S) resources. This dataset features high-resolution 3D physical simulations of both solids and fluids, accompanied by textual descriptions of the underlying physical phenomena. Leveraging state-of-the-art simulation techniques, specifically Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) and the Material Point Method (MPM), we simulate a wide range of scenarios such as elastic deformations, material fractures, collisions, and turbulence. Furthermore, we provide high-quality, multi-view rendered videos to support T2V, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), and other research communities. This project marks the initial step toward fully automated Text-to-Video/Simulation (T2V/S). Live demonstrations and further details are available at https://sites.google.com/view/tpa-net.

We present closed-form expressions for nonlinear forecasts and impulse response functions (IRFs) within Mixed Causal-Noncausal (Structural) Vector Autoregressive (SVAR) frameworks. Furthermore, we examine the identification of nonlinear causal innovations to which these shocks are applied. This methodology is demonstrated through a simulation study and an empirical application analyzing a bivariate system comprising Bitcoin/USD and Ethereum/USD exchange rates.

This paper introduces the notions of an $n$-minimal Auslander--Gorenstein category and an $n$-precluster tilting subcategory. Using these concepts, we establish an analogue of the higher Auslander--Solberg correspondence (arXiv:1608.04179) specifically for exact categories. Our methodology relies on the recent extension of the (higher) Auslander correspondence to the realm of exact categories (arXiv:2011.15107, arXiv:2108.13645).

Reinforcement Learning (RL) stands as a highly active field within Game AI and AI generally, frequently utilizing diverse games as primary testbeds. However, this domain faces a replicability crisis common to much algorithmic AI research, highlighting the need for verifiable benchmarking results. While environments like Atari serve as standard benchmarks for comparing algorithmic performance, reviewers often struggle to trust reported figures due to the difficulty of reproducing exact training curves. To address this, we propose granting access to original experimental data for result validation. Our solution leverages "minimal traces," which facilitate the re-simulation of action sequences in deterministic RL settings. This enables reviewers to verify, reuse, and manually inspect results without requiring access to large compute clusters. Furthermore, this method supports the validation of reward graphs, individual episode analysis, and the reuse of baseline data for comparative studies in subsequent research. We provide plug-and-play code compatible with Gym, ensuring seamless integration into the existing RL reproducibility ecosystem. Our approach is free, user-friendly, and incurs minimal overhead, achieving a data compression ratio of up to approximately 10,000:1 (reducing an 8MB Atari Pong MDP trace to 94GB of standard data). The paper demonstrates these proof-of-concept capabilities across various games.

The growing integration of converter-interfaced distributed energy resources necessitates decentralized criteria to guarantee small-signal stability in interconnected systems. Passivity of the D-Q admittance or impedance represents a viable solution, leveraging the inherent passivity of an electrical network's D-Q impedance. Nevertheless, these passivity conditions are often overly restrictive and difficult to satisfy in the low-frequency range for D-Q admittances governed by standard power control strategies. Despite this, it does not necessarily indicate system instability. Consequently, this paper explores alternative formulations utilizing polar variables—specifically voltage magnitude and phase angle, along with real and reactive power injection—rather than D-Q voltage and current components. The study presents analytical results and illustrative examples to demonstrate the passivity characteristics of the electrical network under these varied formulations.

Currently, digital agriculture has accumulated a vast amount of knowledge. Since this information originates from diverse sources, the challenge lies in organizing it for efficient utilization. While existing methods such as ontologies, rule-based expert systems, and data-mining-derived knowledge models can represent agricultural practices, scalability remains a significant hurdle. This study introduces a new knowledge representation model known as an ontology-based knowledge map. Designed to aggregate knowledge from multiple origins, store it, and facilitate direct use by stakeholders or serve as input for data mining, the model operates in two phases: first, constructing an ontology to serve as a domain-specific knowledge base incorporating data mining concepts, and second, developing the ontology-based knowledge map to represent and store mined knowledge from crop datasets. A framework implementing this model within the agriculture sector has been created. It proves to be both efficient and scalable, functioning effectively as a knowledge repository for digital agriculture.

Beam Intercepting Devices (BIDs) serve as critical safety components within the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) complex. The LHC Target Dump Injection (TDI) acts as the primary BID for the injection system, designed to safeguard LHC equipment should the injection kicker magnets fail during the transfer of beam from the SPS to the LHC. Operational challenges arose with the TDI, primarily stemming from outgassing caused by electron cloud effects in its core components. This phenomenon restricted injector intensity and consequently affected LHC availability. Generally, the absorbing cores of BIDs must withstand severe thermo-mechanical stresses generated by high-intensity particle beams. Furthermore, devices like the TDI, where absorbers are positioned near the beam, significantly contribute to the accelerator's impedance budget. To mitigate this impedance, absorbing materials are typically coated with high-conductivity metals. Consequently, beam impact testing is a vital development step to verify the proper functioning of these coated absorbers. At CERN's HiRadMat facility, researchers investigated the behavior of various metal-coated absorbers under high-energy, high-intensity proton beams. The study tested different configurations using copper and molybdenum coatings on absorbing materials including isostatic graphite, Carbon Fibre Composite (CfC), and Silicon Carbide reinforced with Silicon Carbide fibres (SiC-SiC). These experiments aimed to evaluate TDI performance and gather data applicable to other BIDs utilizing similar materials. The research combined beam impact tests with a comprehensive Post Irradiation Examination (PIE) campaign and extensive numerical simulations.

The paper establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the boundedness of Hausdorff operators acting on generalized Hardy spaces $H^p_E(G)$, the real Hardy space $H^1_{\mathbb{R}}(G)$, $BMO(G)$, and $BMOA(G)$ over a compact Abelian group $G$. Remarkably, these conditions prove to be identical across all the groups and function spaces examined. The study further explores applications to Dirichlet series and investigates the case involving the space of continuous functions on $G$, including specific examples.

Superconducting qubits have risen as a promising foundational technology for solving computational problems that are currently intractable for classical systems. Although recent progress has enabled multiqubit designs with coherence lifetimes reaching hundreds of microseconds, device performance remains limited by material quality and interfacial structures. Specifically, when niobium serves as the superconducting material, two-level system defects within the thin films and neighboring dielectric layers generate stochastic noise and dissipate electromagnetic energy at cryogenic temperatures. This study employs time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) to investigate how specific fabrication protocols contribute to these dissipation mechanisms in complex architectures. We analyzed Nb thin films and transmon qubits produced by Rigetti Computing and the National Institute of Standards and Technology, varying processing and vacuum conditions slightly. Our findings reveal that sputtering Nb onto silicon substrates creates oxide and silicide regions at various interfaces, while subsequent lithographic patterning incorporates impurity species such as niobium hydrides and carbides into the niobium layer. These resistive compounds likely degrade the superconducting properties of the films. Furthermore, halogen species were detected distributed throughout the patterned thin films. We conclude by hypothesizing the origins of these impurities to guide the intelligent fabrication of superconducting qubits and extend coherence times in future developments.

Interactions with the environment are a cornerstone of any controlled quantum system. Although coupling to a dissipative bath often causes decoherence, it can also generate beneficial emergent phenomena, such as induced spin-spin correlations. This study demonstrates that under broad conditions, a dissipative bosonic bath can trigger a long-range ordered phase even in the absence of direct spin-spin interactions. By employing a quantum-to-classical mapping and classical Monte Carlo simulations, we examine the $T=0$ quantum phase transition of an Ising chain coupled to a bosonic bath with Ohmic dissipation. Our findings reveal that the quantum critical point is continuous, Lorentz invariant, and characterized by a dynamical critical exponent $z=1.07(9)$, a correlation length exponent $\nu=0.80(5)$, and an anomalous exponent $\eta=1.02(6)$. These parameters indicate a universality class distinct from previously examined limiting cases. Finally, we discuss the relevance of these results for experiments involving ultracold atomic mixtures and qubit chains operating in dissipative settings.

Interstellar dust significantly degrades most stellar observations, making its correction essential for accurately determining stellar physical properties. We represent dust distribution as a spatially varying latent field modeled by a Gaussian process (GP), creating a likelihood model and inference method capable of scaling to millions of astronomical data points. This modeling task faces two primary challenges: first, the nature of integrated observations, where Earth-based data represent line-of-sight integrals of an unobserved function, leading to a complex likelihood and inference difficulty greater than in classical GP scenarios; second, the massive scale of stellar catalogs containing millions of entries. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce "ziggy," a scalable GP inference approach for integrated observations utilizing stochastic variational inference. We evaluate ziggy using synthetic data and the Ananke dataset, a high-fidelity mechanistic Milky Way model comprising millions of stars. Results demonstrate that ziggy reliably reconstructs the spatial dust map with well-calibrated posterior uncertainties.

We employ a Convolutional Denoising Autoencoder to clean synthetic images from advanced radio telescopes, aiming to reveal faint, diffuse radio sources expected to define the cosmic web. This denoising process targets both random instrumental noise and spurious artifacts, such as sidelobes generated by aperture synthesis. We evaluate the method's accuracy, effectiveness, and computational efficiency across various corrupted image types. To ensure realistic training data, we utilized outputs from cosmological numerical simulations to create mock observations mimicking 8 hours of LOFAR HBA data at 150 MHz. Our autoencoder successfully denoises complex images, isolating faint objects near the instrument's sensitivity limits. The approach scales efficiently to large datasets using high-performance computing in a fully automated manner, requiring no human oversight post-training. Furthermore, it performs precise image segmentation to identify the low-brightness edges of diffuse sources, demonstrating its viability for detecting challenging extended objects obscured by noise in radio observations.

By extending the Standard Model to include three right-handed neutrinos alongside a straightforward QCD axion sector, one can simultaneously explain neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry, while resolving the strong CP problem, stabilizing the electroweak vacuum, and enabling critical Higgs inflation consistent with all current observational constraints. In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of dark matter within this framework, termed the $a\nu$MSM. Despite the presence of a (quasi) inflection point in the inflaton potential characteristic of critical Higgs inflation, we demonstrate that primordial black holes do not contribute to the dark matter abundance in the $a\nu$MSM. Consequently, dark matter emerges as a multicomponent mixture of axions and sterile neutrinos, allowing for correlations between axion parameters, such as the decay constant, and neutrino parameters. Our study incorporates various production mechanisms, including axion generation through misalignment and the decay of topological defects, sterile neutrino production via both resonant and non-resonant channels, and production within the recently proposed CPT-symmetric universe.

Knowledge Graph Embeddings (KGEs) have demonstrated strong performance in link prediction by projecting entities and relations into a geometric vector space. The validity of predicted links is assessed through scoring functions applied to these learned vectors. Consequently, the ability to maintain critical graph features, such as semantics and structure, relies heavily on the KGE's design and the geometric properties it inherits. Many existing models utilize flat geometry, which limits their capacity to capture complex structures and often leads to erroneous inferences. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a neuro-differential KGE that positions knowledge graph nodes along the trajectories of Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs). In this framework, each relation is modeled as a vector field on a smooth Riemannian manifold. We parameterize these ODEs using neural networks to represent diverse, complex manifold shapes and vector fields. This approach enables the embedding space to adopt various geometric forms, effectively encoding the complexity of subgraph structures and their distinct motifs. Experimental results on synthetic data, benchmark datasets, and social network knowledge graphs confirm that ODE trajectories enhance structural preservation and prevent incorrect inferences, outperforming current state-of-the-art KGE models.

This study enhances the runtime efficiency of recent classical algorithms designed for the strong simulation of quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The enhancement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the stabilizer rank of $m$ copies of the magic state $|T\rangle=\sqrt{2}^{-1}(|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle)$ as $m$ becomes large. Specifically, we demonstrate that $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$ can be precisely represented as a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states, with $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, thereby surpassing the previous best-known bound of $\alpha \leq 0.463$. Leveraging established methods, this result yields a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of an $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuit $U$ containing $m$ T gates to within a specified inverse polynomial relative error, achieving a runtime of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Additionally, we present tighter upper bounds on the stabilizer rank for general symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$; consequently, we develop a strong simulation algorithm for circuits utilizing Clifford gates and $m$ instances of any fixed single-qubit $Z$-rotation gate, with a runtime of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. Finally, we propose a strategy to further refine these upper bounds by constructing linear codes possessing specific characteristics.

Determining which brain areas are linked to specific neurological conditions is crucial for developing biomarkers and diagnostic tools. This study introduces an interpretable Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) framework designed to identify and classify Alzheimer's disease (AD) using multi-modal brain imaging data. We adapted the Gradient Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) method to quantify the most discriminative features derived by the GCN from brain connectivity patterns. These features were then used to pinpoint signature regions of interest (ROIs) by analyzing feature differences across healthy control (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD cohorts. Experiments conducted on the ADNI database, utilizing three imaging modalities—VBM-MRI, FDG-PET, and AV45-PET—demonstrated that the ROI features learned by our approach effectively enhanced both clinical score prediction and disease status identification. Furthermore, the method successfully identified biomarkers associated with AD and MCI.

The growing popularity of open-source software has spurred the creation of extensive, language-specific repositories for reusable libraries, exemplified by npm and RubyGems. These packages can harbor vulnerabilities that compromise dependent projects through their declared dependencies. Leveraging Snyk's vulnerability database, this study empirically examines security flaws within npm and RubyGems, analyzing their disclosure and remediation timelines as well as trends in prevalence over time. Furthermore, the research investigates how vulnerable packages expose both direct and indirect dependents to risk, distinguishing between packages hosted on package managers and external GitHub projects relying on npm. The findings indicate that while npm experiences a rising number of vulnerabilities that are disclosed more rapidly than those in RubyGems, the time required to disclose vulnerabilities is lengthening for both ecosystems. Regarding impact, a single npm vulnerability affects a median of 30 package releases, compared to 59 for RubyGems. Additionally, a significant portion of external GitHub projects are exposed to risks via direct or indirect dependencies. Notably, 33% of vulnerabilities affecting packages and 40% affecting projects are mitigated by fixes in newer releases within the same major version range of the dependency. These results underscore the urgent need for enhanced security measures within open-source package distributions.

Whole-cell computational models seek to forecast cellular phenotypes from genotypes by simulating the complete genome, the structure and concentration of every molecular species, all molecular interactions, and the extracellular environment. These models hold immense promise to revolutionize bioscience, bioengineering, and medicine. Despite this potential, significant hurdles remain before fully realized whole-cell models can be achieved. However, scientists are now utilizing advancements in measurement technologies, bioinformatics, data sharing, rule-based modeling, and multi-algorithmic simulations to construct the initial whole-cell models. We expect that continued development of scalable whole-cell modeling tools will facilitate the creation of far more comprehensive and accurate models, including those for human cells.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) accretion disks represent a compelling environment for the gravitational wave (GW) mergers of compact objects. Because these mergers occur within a dense, baryon-rich setting, they constitute the sole GW channel requiring an electromagnetic (EM) counterpart, regardless of its detectability. Focusing on AGN exhibiting unusual flaring activity identified by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF), we conducted a search for EM counterparts to binary black hole (BBH) mergers detected by LIGO/Virgo during the O3 run. Following the removal of likely false positives, we identified nine candidate counterparts (seven from O3a and two from O3b) with a $p$-value of 0.019. Based on ZTF sky coverage and the geometric constraints of both AGN and merger events, we anticipate approximately $3(N_{\rm BBH}/83)(f_{\rm AGN}/0.5)$ potentially detectable EM counterparts from O3, where $N_{\rm BBH}$ denotes the total observed BBH mergers and $f_{\rm AGN}$ represents the fraction originating in AGN. Further modeling of flaring and breakout phenomena within AGN disks is necessary to lower the false positive rate. Notably, two of these events correspond to mergers with total masses exceeding $100M_\odot$, aligning with the expected rate for O3 if hierarchical mergers occur within the AGN channel. Future GW observing runs could better constrain candidate EM counterparts by improving Southern sky coverage and implementing spectral monitoring of unusual AGN flaring events within LIGO/Virgo alert volumes. Ultimately, a robust set of confirmed AGN EM counterparts to BBH mergers would provide an independent method for measuring the cosmic expansion rate ($H_0$) across various redshifts.

To enhance patient safety in deep learning-based diagnostic image classification, we assessed two approaches for incorporating prediction uncertainty. The first approach utilizes Monte Carlo sampling with dropout during testing to derive a posterior distribution of class labels, known as Bayesian ResNet. The second approach adapts ResNet into a probabilistic framework by predicting posterior distribution parameters and sampling the final outcome, termed Variational ResNet. In both cases, posterior variance serves as the uncertainty metric. The models were trained on optical coherence tomography scans depicting four distinct retinal conditions. Our findings indicate a strong correlation between incorrect classifications and elevated uncertainty levels; specifically, the mean uncertainty for misdiagnosed cases was 4.6 to 8.1 times greater than that for correctly diagnosed ones. Consequently, modeling prediction uncertainty in computer-aided diagnosis via deep learning produces more reliable outcomes and is expected to improve patient safety.

Driven by the need for demand-side management in smart grids, this work introduces a decentralized controlled Markov chain model to represent a homogeneous group of users characterized by binary demands (on/off), a scenario common in scheduling tasks like plug-in hybrid vehicle management. Typically, an Independent Service Operator (ISO) has limited choices when supplying electricity, including various incentives, generation sources, and pricing structures. The ISO's goal is to determine the optimal combination of these options to align the aggregate demand distribution with a time-varying target while minimizing prices for users. A Bellman equation is formulated to derive a globally team-optimal strategy that ensures fairness among all users and safeguards their privacy. Additionally, the computational complexity of this strategy scales linearly with the number of users rather than exponentially. A numerical case study involving 100 users is provided to demonstrate the approach for peak-load management.

The evolution of magnetic domains in FePd alloy thin films, tracked via magneto-optic Kerr effect (MOKE) microscopy, reveals noncollinear magnetic anisotropy induced by hydrogenation. MOKE imaging exposes complex interactions between various magnetic anisotropies as hydrogen permeates the film. Notably, the study identifies an enhanced hydrogen diffusion rate when an initial exchange bias, created by a high magnetic field, is present. This finding suggests new avenues for controlling magnetic metal hydrides, highlighting their potential as advanced materials for hydrogen storage and sensing applications.

A recent surge of interest in the spectroscopy of radioactive compounds has emerged following the successful application of the novel ISOL/CRIS technique to the optical spectroscopy of radium monofluoride molecules. This development offers significant potential for investigating phenomena linked to "new physics," specifically those indicating deviations from the physical laws defined by the Standard Model of elementary particles. The search for such effects would benefit greatly from the ability to trap working molecules, their capacity for laser cooling, the existence of co-magnetometer molecular states, and the availability of various accessible nuclear isotopes within the molecule that possess different nuclear multipole moments. Laser-coolable polyatomic molecular ions containing radium nuclei satisfy these criteria; consequently, this article examines several prospective molecular ions and calculates their electronic structures and molecular properties.

Using the Gamow shell model, we have computed nuclear observables for the $^{26-31}$Ne isotopes, which are located near the neutron drip line and exhibit a one-neutron halo structure. This method effectively incorporates both many-body correlations and continuum coupling, allowing for a proper analysis of halo properties. Our calculations yield accurate descriptions of these nuclei, particularly regarding the asymptotic behavior essential to their structure. We have also determined the one-body density, neutron root-mean-square radii for $^{26-31}$Ne, and one-neutron overlap functions for $^{29,31}$Ne. These findings confirm the existence of a one-neutron \textit{p}-wave halo in $^{31}$Ne, a feature previously identified experimentally. A comparable scenario exists in the ground state of $^{29}$Ne, which consists primarily of a \textit{p}-wave valence neutron coupled to an inner $^{28}$Ne \textit{core}. Additionally, we examined the $3/2^+$ excited state of $^{29}$Ne, which is dominated by a \textit{d}-wave valence neutron. Comparisons reveal that the ground state of $^{29}$Ne possesses a larger radius and a more extended wave function than its $3/2^+$ first excited state. Consequently, our results indicate that $^{29}$Ne is a promising candidate for a one-neutron \textit{p}-wave halo within the medium-mass region.

This study establishes a geometric finding concerning composite materials within the context of elliptic and parabolic partial differential equations. While classical works by Li and Vogelius (2000) and Li and Nirenberg (2003) postulated that a suitable coordinate system exists—rendering the boundaries of individual material components as $C^{1,\gamma}$-graphs at any scale and location—we demonstrate that such a system indeed exists whenever the individual components possess $C^{1,\gamma}$-boundaries. Consequently, we derive results regarding gradient boundedness and piecewise gradient Hölder continuity for linear elliptic systems associated with these composite materials.

We introduce a finitary variant of Moss' coalgebraic logic tailored for $T$-coalgebras, where $T$ denotes a locally monotone endofunctor acting on the category of posets and monotone maps. This logic employs a single cover modality, with its arity determined by the least finitary subfunctor of the dual of the coalgebra functor $T_\omega^\partial$, and its semantics are grounded in relation lifting. For this semantic framework to function, $T$ must preserve exact squares, while the finitary requirement necessitates that $T_\omega^\partial$ preserves finite intersections. We establish a concept of a base for subobjects within $T_\omega X$, which facilitates the discussion of the finite poset of subformulas associated with any given formula. This notion of a base is defined broadly for categories endowed with an appropriate factorization system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting logic satisfies the Hennessy-Milner property regarding similarity, which is derived from relation lifting. Finally, we construct a sequent proof system for the logic and prove its completeness.

Collective phenomena arising from light interacting with groups of identical scatterers are crucial across various physics disciplines. Nevertheless, the designation "identical" is frequently inaccurate because hyperfine fields generate inhomogeneous transition shifts and splittings. This study introduces a formalism utilizing the Green function method to model the linear response of such inhomogeneous ensembles within one-dimensional waveguides. We derive a concise expression for the collective spectrum, which reveals deviations from the uniform frequency shifts and broadening typically anticipated for two-level systems. Specifically, when the coherent component of the collective coupling is significant, the impact of inhomogeneous broadening can be mitigated, causing the linewidth to converge toward the superradiant limit. We further apply this framework to characterize collective effects in x-ray scattering from thin-film waveguides featuring inhomogeneous hyperfine parameters.

Utilizing advanced deep learning models on embedded hardware to address practical issues remains difficult with current technology due to privacy concerns, data scarcity, connectivity constraints, and the requirement for rapid model adaptation, rendering existing edge solutions inadequate for real-time on-device training. Google is addressing these hurdles by integrating an experimental transfer learning API into TensorFlow Lite. This paper demonstrates that while transfer learning offers a viable starting point for on-device training, it is prone to catastrophic forgetting in realistic scenarios. We illustrate this limitation by evaluating a basic transfer learning model against the CORe50 benchmark and through a custom Android application. Furthermore, we enhance the TensorFlow Lite library by incorporating a simple replay mechanism into the transfer learning framework to enable continual learning. Testing on the CORe50 benchmark confirms that our approach mitigates catastrophic forgetting, while our Android app validates its capacity for continuous learning under suboptimal conditions. Finally, we release the source code for our Android application to assist developers in implementing continual learning within their smartphone apps and to support ongoing advancements in the TensorFlow Lite ecosystem.

Angiogenesis refers to the formation of new blood vessels from existing ones, a critical mechanism in biological functions such as embryogenesis and wound repair, as well as in pathologies like cancer and rheumatoid arthritis. The efficacy of these vessel networks in supplying nutrients and clearing metabolic waste depends on their structural organization. This study simulates the Anderson-Chaplain angiogenesis model across various parameter settings and quantifies the resulting vessel architectures. We introduce a topological data analysis (TDA) pipeline designed for the systematic examination of this model. As a burgeoning area in computational mathematics focused on data geometry, TDA allows us to calculate both standard and topological descriptors from simulations driven by different parameters. Our findings demonstrate that applying TDA to model outputs effectively partitions the parameter space into regions characterized by similar vessel morphologies. The methods presented here hold broad applicability for analyzing both synthetic and experimental datasets in contexts ranging from wound healing and development to plant biology.

This study examines Huber loss, its asymmetric forms, and the resulting Huber functionals within the frameworks of point forecasting and forecast evaluation. Defined as the set of minimizers for the expected (asymmetric) Huber loss, each Huber functional serves as a bridge between quantiles and expectiles and is rooted in M-estimation theory. Under mild regularity conditions regarding probability distributions, these functionals are elicitable, meaning they uniquely correspond to the minimizers of an expected score, and possess a comprehensive characterization of consistent scoring functions. These scoring functions can be expressed as a weighted mixture of elementary scores, each representing the relative economic loss incurred when a specific forecast is applied to a range of investment decisions with capped profits and losses. Additionally, the paper explores the implications of this theoretical framework for the comparative assessment of weather forecasts.

We introduce the moiré bilayer as a system capable of stabilizing and electrically detecting exotic quantum phases. This structure comprises two distinct moiré superlattice layers linked by inter-layer Coulomb repulsion. At short distances, the real spin and layer pseudospin combine to form an SU(4) spin. As a specific case, we examine an SU(4) spin model on a triangular lattice within the fundamental representation. By adjusting a three-site ring exchange term proportional to $K\sim \frac{t^3}{U^2}$, we identify an SU(4) symmetric crystallized phase and an SU(4)$_1$ chiral spin liquid (CSL) at balanced filling. Furthermore, we predict two distinct exciton supersolid phases exhibiting inter-layer coherence under displacement fields at imbalanced fillings. Notably, the system can emulate an SU(2) Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) by introducing inter-layer excitons into a magnetically ordered Mott insulator at the layer-polarized limit. Definitive evidence for these phases can be acquired through measurements of pseudo-spin transport in the counter-flow channel.

We introduce Deep Global Registration, a differentiable framework designed for the pairwise registration of real-world 3D scans. This system comprises three core components: a six-dimensional convolutional network that predicts correspondence confidence, a differentiable Weighted Procrustes algorithm for closed-form pose estimation, and a robust gradient-based SE(3) optimizer for refining the pose. Experimental results show that our method surpasses both classical and learning-based state-of-the-art approaches when applied to real-world data.

We compute the unpolarized and polarized gluonic massive operator matrix elements, denoted as $A_{gg,Q}(x,\mu^2)$ and $\Delta A_{gg,Q}(x,\mu^2)$, respectively, at the three-loop level for a single mass. These components are essential for matching the gluon distribution within the variable flavor number scheme. Specifically, the polarized element is evaluated using the Larin scheme. In Mellin $N$-space, these matrix elements involve finite binomial and inverse binomial sums, while in momentum fraction $x$-space, they consist of iterated integrals over alphabets with square-root values. We establish the required analytic relations to continue these quantities from even or odd Mellin moments into the complex plane, provide explicit analytic expressions in $x$-space, and generate numerical results. Consequently, these findings finalize the three-loop calculation of gluon transition matrix elements for both single- and double-mass variable flavor number schemes.

During the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, a primary challenge is managing the high noise levels inherent in physical qubits. While quantum error correction is a viable solution, it demands an extensive number of physical qubits—often over 1,000—to synthesize a single "perfect" qubit, surpassing the capabilities of current hardware. This paper addresses the noise problem from a different perspective: rather than striving for perfect qubits for general algorithms, we explore noise mitigation strategies tailored to specific applications. Specifically, focusing on quantum neural networks (QNNs), we propose learning errors during the training phase to produce models resilient to noise. Consequently, implementing these QNNs requires little to no additional physical qubits, making them more feasible for near-term quantum computers. Achieving this necessitates an application-specific compiler; the mapping from logical to physical qubits must be deterministic to allow error learning, and the compiler must be efficient enough to complete the lengthy training process within a reasonable timeframe. Using the QuantumFlow framework as a case study, we demonstrate that this approach optimizes QNN models against various qubit errors, yielding up to a 28% accuracy improvement compared to error-agnostic training.

A mixed graph is defined as \textit{integral} when every eigenvalue of its Hermitian adjacency matrix is an integer. The \textit{mixed circulant graph} $Circ(\mathbb{Z}_n,\mathcal{C})$ consists of a vertex set $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and an edge set $\{ (a,b): b-a\in \mathcal{C} \}$, with the condition that $0\not\in \mathcal{C}$. When $\mathcal{C}$ is closed under inverses, the graph is termed a \textit{circulant graph}. We derive expressions for the eigenvalues of $Circ(\mathbb{Z}_n,\mathcal{C})$ using primitive $n$-th roots of unity and establish a sufficient condition for their integrality. Specifically for cases where $n\equiv 0 \Mod 4$, we decompose the cyclotomic polynomial into two irreducible factors over $\mathbb{Q}(i)$. Leveraging this decomposition, we characterize integral mixed circulant graphs based on their symbol sets. Furthermore, we formulate the integer eigenvalues of integral oriented circulant graphs using a Ramanujan-type sum and explore several of their properties.

A graph is defined as Helly if every collection of mutually intersecting balls shares a nonempty common intersection. This class serves as the discrete counterpart to hyperconvex metric spaces and holds significant importance in Metric Graph Theory, as every graph can be isometrically embedded within a Helly graph. This paper investigates the computation of diameter, radius, and all eccentricities within Helly graphs. Based on reasonable complexity assumptions, it is established that neither the diameter nor the radius can be calculated in truly subquadratic time for general graphs. Conversely, recent research demonstrated that for an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge Helly graph $G$, the radius and diameter can be determined with high probability in $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(m\sqrt{n})$ time, achieving subquadratic performance relative to $n+m$. We enhance this finding by introducing a deterministic $\mathcal{O}(m\sqrt{n})$ algorithm capable of computing the radius, diameter, and all vertex eccentricities in a Helly graph. Additionally, we propose a parameterized linear-time algorithm where the parameter is the Gromov hyperbolicity $\delta$. Specifically, for an $m$-edge $\delta$-hyperbolic Helly graph $G$, we show that the radius and a central vertex can be found in $\mathcal{O}(\delta m)$ time, while all vertex eccentricities can be computed in $\mathcal{O}(\delta^2 m)$ time. These broader results rely heavily on novel structural properties we have derived for Helly graphs.

The heat pulse (flash) technique is a standard and widely recognized approach for determining a material's thermal diffusivity. Recently, however, studies have shown that the thermal response of heterogeneous materials—such as metal foam inclusions, layered composites, or porous and cracked rocks—often deviates from classical Fourier predictions, necessitating additional thermal parameters for accurate identification. While the Guyer-Krumhansl equation has been successfully applied to these cases, its evaluation typically demands computationally expensive numerical fitting procedures, even with manually derived initial parameter estimates. This paper introduces a Galerkin-type discretization of the Guyer-Krumhansl equation, which facilitates a relatively simple analytical solution for time-dependent boundary conditions. By leveraging this analytical framework, we have developed a novel evaluation method capable of instantly estimating all required thermal parameters directly from measured temperature histories.

The radiative characteristics of ice-free clouds are governed by the spatial distribution of their liquid water, representing a major source of uncertainty in weather and climate modeling. While evaporation and turbulent mixing induce substantial fluctuations in droplet number density with only minor changes in droplet size [Beals et al. (2015)], direct numerical simulations of these combined processes near cloud edges predict markedly different outcomes, leaving a discrepancy with experimental data that remains unresolved. Inferring the historical dynamics of mixing and evaporation from observational snapshots is difficult due to the transient nature of clouds. Consequently, we developed a statistical model that accurately represents the evaporation-mixing process observed in direct numerical simulations. This model enables the deduction of critical aspects of droplet population histories, identifies the primary underlying mechanisms, and clarifies the divergences between observational findings and simulation results.

Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) enhance downstream tasks by estimating image transformations that focus on relevant regions, but they are difficult to train and highly sensitive to prediction errors. To address these issues, we introduce a probabilistic extension that generates stochastic transformations instead of deterministic ones. By marginalizing these transformations, the model evaluates images from multiple poses, which simplifies localization and strengthens training robustness. Furthermore, these stochastic transformations function as localized, learned data augmentation, further boosting downstream performance. Experiments on standard benchmarks and a difficult real-world dataset demonstrate that these features improve classification accuracy, robustness, and model calibration. Additionally, the method extends to non-visual domains, enhancing performance on time-series data.

This work addresses the Stechkin problem concerning the approximation of generally unbounded hypersingular integral operators by bounded ones. As part of the proof, we resolve several related and independently significant problems. Specifically, we derive sharp Landau-Kolmogorov type inequalities in both additive and multiplicative forms for hypersingular integral operators and establish a sharp Ostrowski type inequality for multivariate Sobolev classes. Furthermore, we explore applications of these findings, including an analysis of the modulus of continuity for hypersingular integral operators and the solution to the optimal recovery problem for the value of such an operator based on data with a known error.

Drawing inspiration from recent experimental findings on $^{173}$Yb atoms [N. Darkwah Oppong \textit{et al.}, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{122}, 193604 (2019)], we investigate the repulsive Fermi polaron within a two-component, two-dimensional system of fermionic atoms. Employing the diffusion Monte Carlo technique, we calculate key observables, including the polaron energy and quasi-particle residue, which align with experimental measurements. To further elucidate the quasi-particle nature of the system, we also present data on the effective mass. Our findings demonstrate that accurately reproducing experimental results requires incorporating both the scattering length and the effective range. By utilizing various model potentials for the interaction between the impurity and the Fermi sea, we identify a universal regime defined by these two parameters that encompasses the entire experimental range. This underscores the critical role of quantum fluctuations and beyond mean-field effects in providing a correct description of the Fermi polaron problem.

We have tested the gauge/gravity duality between the matrix model and type IIA string theory at low temperatures with unprecedented precision. This was achieved by conducting lattice Monte Carlo simulations of the Berenstein-Maldacena-Nastase (BMN) matrix model—a one-parameter deformation of the Banks-Fischler-Shenker-Susskind (BFSS) model—while simultaneously taking the large $N$ and continuum limits. We utilized the property that sufficiently small flux parameters in the BMN model stabilize flat directions with negligible effects on system energy, thereby enabling simulations at smaller $N$ values than feasible for the BFSS model. Consequently, we performed a high-precision measurement of the large $N$ continuum energy at the lowest temperatures recorded to date. The resulting energy values align perfectly with supergravity predictions, including prior estimates of $\alpha'$-corrections. At the lowest efficiently simulatable temperature ($T=0.25\lambda^{1/3}$, where $\lambda$ denotes the 't Hooft coupling), the deviation from the pure supergravity prediction remains under 10%. Additionally, we successfully extracted the coefficient of the $1/N^4$ corrections at a fixed temperature with high accuracy, a value that was previously inaccessible.

A point is defined as "bad" for a positive semidefinite real polynomial $f$ if every representation of $f$ as a sum of squares of rational functions exhibits a pole at that location. We demonstrate that quartic polynomials in three variables do not possess such bad points. Furthermore, we provide examples of positive semidefinite polynomials with a bad point at the origin that are still expressible as sums of squares of formal power series, thereby resolving a question posed by Brumfiel. Additionally, we present an example of a positive semidefinite polynomial in three variables featuring a complex bad point that is not real, which answers a question raised by Scheiderer.

Dowling defined the lattice Qn(G) for any finite set of n elements and any finite multiplicative group G of order m, establishing it as a finite geometric lattice. He also introduced Whitney numbers of the first and second kinds for such lattices. For the specific case of Qn(G), these are denoted as Vm(n,k) and Wm(n,k) respectively, and they follow Stirling-number-like formulas. This paper introduces degenerate versions of both the first and second kind Whitney numbers by adapting these relations, and examines their generating functions, recurrence relations, and explicit expressions. Additionally, the study extends these concepts further by exploring degenerate r-Whitney numbers of both kinds.

Teaching a deep reinforcement learning (RL) agent to adhere to instructions within multi-task settings presents a significant challenge. In our approach, users define each task using a linear temporal logic (LTL) formula. However, in complex environments, certain causal dependencies may remain unknown to the user beforehand, meaning the robot cannot merely execute the provided instructions to succeed. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework where a symbolic transition model is learned to generate efficient high-level plans that guide the agent in solving diverse tasks. Specifically, inductive logic programming (ILP) is employed to train this symbolic model, capturing the underlying logic rules of state transitions. By planning over the product of this model and the automaton derived from the LTL specification, the agent can identify and resolve causal dependencies, decomposing complex problems into sequences of simpler low-level sub-tasks. We validate the proposed framework across three environments in both discrete and continuous domains, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing representative methods.

Packing problems aim to determine whether a specific set of pieces can be arranged within a designated container. These problems are characterized by the types of pieces and containers involved, as well as the permitted movements for the pieces. Crucially, the pieces must be positioned such that they are pairwise interior-disjoint. We present a framework demonstrating that for numerous combinations of pieces, containers, and allowed motions, the resulting problem is $\exists \mathbb{R}$-complete. This classification indicates that the problem is polynomial-time equivalent to determining if a system of polynomial equations and inequalities with integer coefficients admits a real solution.

We analyze scenarios where only translations are permitted, as well as cases allowing arbitrary rigid motions, including both translations and rotations. When rotations are included, we prove that deciding whether a set of convex polygons, each with at most seven vertices, can be packed into a square is an $\exists \mathbb{R}$-complete problem. In the context of translation-only constraints, we establish $\exists \mathbb{R}$-completeness for two specific cases: (i) packing pieces bounded by segments and hyperbolic curves into a square, and (ii) packing convex polygons into a container whose boundary consists of segments and hyperbolic curves.

The efficiency of main memory column stores relies heavily on scan and lookup operations performed on base column layouts. Current column stores utilize a uniform layout for all columns, which results in sub-optimal performance on real-world workloads because distinct columns exhibit varying data characteristics. This paper introduces ByteStore, a column store that employs diverse storage layouts tailored to specific columns. First, we propose a novel, data-aware layout called PP-VBS (Prefix-Preserving Variable Byte Slice), which leverages data skew to accelerate scans while maintaining lookup efficiency. Second, we develop an experiment-driven advisor to determine the optimal individual column layout for a given workload. Extensive experiments using real data demonstrate that ByteStore surpasses homogeneous storage engines by up to 5.2X.

This paper employs a Tsallis holographic dark energy model in both interacting and non-interacting forms to derive parameters for the equation of state regarding the energy density within an FRW universe, specifically focusing on the complex quintessence framework. We investigate the cosmology of complex quintessence by revising the potential and analyzing scalar field dynamics. Subsequently, we examine the ($\omega-\omega'$) plot and stability across both non-interacting and interacting scenarios. We assess the viability of these models for describing the real universe by calculating the fractional energy density $\Omega_{D}$, taking into account the effects of both the complex and real components of the quintessence field, with the latter treated as a slow-roll field. Notably, we identify that regions where $\Omega_{D} > 1$ fail to represent a physical universe. Furthermore, we define an interacting coupling parameter $b^{2}$ dependent on the Tsallis model constant $\delta$ relative to the fractional energy density value of $0.73$. In contrast to the independence observed in standard real quintessence models, our theory establishes a specific relationship among these parameters. Finally, through graphical analysis, we characterize the features of ($\omega-\omega'$) and ($\nu_{s}^{2}$) in both cases and compare the resulting outcomes.

Determining the position and orientation changes of a mobile platform using two successive point clouds from a high-resolution sensor is a fundamental challenge in autonomous navigation. Specifically, scan matching algorithms seek the translation and rotation required to align these point clouds. A core difficulty in this process is associating measurements between the first and second point clouds. Traditional methods rely on non-probabilistic data association, assuming only a single hypothesis, which results in overconfident pose estimates and lower accuracy in ambiguous settings. In contrast, our probabilistic scan matching approach accounts for all association hypotheses weighted by their likelihoods. We model the combined problem of data association and pose estimation as a holistic Bayesian framework, represented by a joint factor graph. By applying iterative message passing to this graph, we derive near-optimum maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates for the sensor pose. Numerical evaluations demonstrate that our method outperforms existing non-probabilistic techniques based on Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) and Implicit Moving Least Squares (IMLS).

The topological quantum field-effect transition in buckled 2D-Xenes offers the potential for engineering sub-thermionic transistor operation with dissipationless conduction in the ON state. Achieving this requires device design strategies grounded in an understanding of the physics governing the transition between the band insulator phase and the dissipationless topological phase. Our investigation of viable device architectures reveals fundamental sub-threshold constraints imposed by the gating mechanism driving this transition, highlighting the necessity for material and structural innovations. By detailing the intricate band translation physics associated with the quantum spin Hall effect phase transition, we demonstrate that while gating strategies can overcome the thermionic limit, they may compromise the dissipationless nature of the ON state. Furthermore, we show that introducing an out-of-plane antiferromagnetic exchange via proximity coupling can trigger transitions between the quantum spin-valley Hall and spin quantum anomalous Hall phases. This approach ensures the topological robustness of the ON state while exceeding the thermionic limit. Consequently, our work establishes the operational criteria for constructing topological transistors using quantum materials that surmount Boltzmann's tyranny without sacrificing topological robustness.

The growing reliance on easily accessible text data in social science, such as from Twitter, has inadvertently disadvantaged research requiring sensitive, hard-to-share information like interview transcripts, police reports, and electronic health records. To resolve this conflict, we present Textwash, an open-source software for text anonymization. This paper empirically evaluates Textwash using the TILD framework, which assesses technical accuracy, information loss, and resistance to de-anonymization by humans. Results indicate that Textwash matches the performance of leading entity recognition models while introducing a minimal information loss of 0.84%. In the de-anonymization phase, human participants attempted to identify individuals from crowdsourced descriptions of famous, semi-famous, and non-existent people; the de-anonymization rate for realistic use cases ranged between 1.01% and 2.01%. These findings were replicated in a second study, confirming that Textwash effectively removes sensitive details, rendering detailed person descriptions practically anonymous.

This study investigates the acoustic scattering characteristics of a phononic crystal engineered to function as a gradient index lens within water, utilizing both experimental and theoretical methods. The lens, constructed from a square lattice of stainless-steel cylinders, is designed using a multiple scattering approach under the homogenization limit. Experimental results confirm that the lens adheres to graded index equations derived for optics by analyzing the pressure intensity from a spherical source at 20 kHz. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between these experimental findings and theoretical predictions based on multiple scattering theory.

Under non-resonant laser pumping within an annular trapping potential, concentric ring exciton polariton condensates sustain persistent circular polariton currents. This potential arises from a cylindrical micropillar etched into a semiconductor microcavity containing embedded quantum wells, alongside a repulsive cloud of optically excited excitons located beneath the pump spot. The potential's symmetry can be externally regulated by adjusting its pump-induced component. This manuscript presents the excitation of concentric ring polariton current states with specific, predetermined vorticity, tracked via interferometry using a spherical reference wave. Furthermore, we observe the polariton condensate dynamically altering its vorticity during observation; this manifests as pairs of fork-like dislocations on the time-averaged interferogram, coexisting with an azimuthally homogeneous photoluminescence distribution within the micropillar.

By applying a Wigner-Weyl transformation to the Born-Oppenheimer decomposition of the Wheeler-DeWitt equation for a matter-gravity system in quantum cosmology, we derived equations describing a Wigner function associated with the scale factor and its conjugate momentum. This approach enables a more detailed investigation of how the classical limit of gravity emerges and how time arises within that framework. At the lowest order, our results recover the Friedmann equation and the prior equation governing matter evolution, while also providing expressions for higher-order corrections to the semi-classical regime.

Opinion dynamics models have been created to analyze and forecast the evolution of public sentiment. Extensive research has focused on these models, particularly examining various rules and network topologies, which serve as two key degrees of freedom. This paper introduces a third degree of freedom. Since opinions cannot be directly accessed without measurement, researchers must select a method to convert real-world stances (e.g., anti-Trump views) into numerical values. However, the literature on opinion dynamics rarely addresses the properties of this transformation. Fundamental questions remain, such as whether this conversion must be unique or if multiple scales are viable, and how the selected scale influences model dynamics.

This article investigates these issues by applying principles from psychometrics, a field dedicated to quantifying psychological constructs like opinions for over a century. We begin by illustrating this phenomenon with a simple opinion dynamics example, followed by an introduction to the necessary mathematical framework and an analysis of three models proposed by Hegselmann and Krause. Finally, we validate these models through agent-based simulations under both idealized conditions (infinite precision) and realistic scenarios (real-world scales).

Both theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate that the choice of scale can profoundly alter model dynamics, even with perfect accuracy and precision. Specifically, selecting a different scale can: (1) yield a different number of final opinion clusters, (2) shift the mean value of the final opinion distribution by up to ±100%, and (3) effectively transform one model into another.

We present a new set of observables describing angular distribution asymmetries, which generalize the Forward-Backward Asymmetry and serve as an effective method for detecting $C\!P$ violation in the decays of bottom and charmed baryons. We suggest investigating these $C\!P$ asymmetries in processes involving $\Lambda^0$, $\Sigma^\pm$, or $\Lambda_c^+$, such as $\Lambda_b\to \Lambda^0 D$ and $\Lambda_b\to\Lambda^0\rho^0(770)$. Furthermore, we propose examining three-body decays of bottom baryons that include intermediate resonances with opposite parity, with typical examples being $\Xi_b^-\to p K^- K^-$, $\Lambda_b^0\to p K_S\pi^-$, and $\Lambda_b^0\to \Lambda^0\pi^+\pi^-$.

This paper demonstrates how to optimally incorporate indirect or prior information to build prediction regions that achieve a specific frequentist coverage rate. When such information is accurate, the resulting region typically has a smaller average volume compared to other regions with the same coverage. Even if the information is inaccurate, the method guarantees the target coverage rate is maintained. These regions can be constructed for models possessing a complete sufficient statistic, encompassing many common parametric and nonparametric frameworks. Specific instances include a Bayes-optimal conformal prediction approach that ensures constant coverage across distributions in nonparametric settings, and a procedure for normal linear regression that leverages a regularizing prior while preserving frequentist coverage rates that remain constant regardless of model parameters or explanatory variables. Crucially, no findings in this article depend on asymptotic approximations.

Following the deaths of Berni Alder [1] and Francis Ree [2], Douglas Henderson became the third of Bill's California colleagues from the 1960s to pass away in 2020. Inspired by Doug's passing, we sought a deeper understanding of Lyapunov instability and time symmetry breaking within both continuum and atomistic simulations. This study extends our investigation into two specific nonequilibrium systems: steady shockwaves and unsteady rarefaction waves. By simulating collisions between pairs of mirror-image projectiles, we remove the necessity for boundary potentials. The resulting structures represent the compression and expansion of simple fluids, where shockwaves maintain a steady form while rarefaction fans continuously widen during free expansion. We model these phenomena using classical molecular dynamics and Eulerian fluid mechanics in two dimensions. Although molecular dynamics equations are time-reversible, reversing a simulation of a steady shockwave compression quickly produces an unsteady rarefaction fan; this violates microscopic time symmetry yet aligns with macroscopic Navier-Stokes predictions. These outcomes arise from an interplay of two irreversible instabilities: Lyapunov and Navier-Stokes.

Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in various real-world scenarios, particularly within mechanical engineering. To effectively approximate the Pareto front for these challenges, we introduce a general hybrid methodology combining Multi-Criteria Branch-and-Bound (MCBB) with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm 2 (NSGA-II). Our study includes a computational experiment utilizing statistical evaluation to assess the performance of the proposed BnB-NSGAII algorithm against standard NSGA-II using established metrics. Additionally, we introduce a novel metric called the Investment Ratio (IR), which evaluates the relationship between solution quality and computational effort. The experiment involves five practical mechanical engineering cases alongside two mathematical test problems. Results demonstrate that BnB-NSGAII serves as a competitive alternative for addressing MO-MINLPs.

This study utilizes Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithms for Gaussian processes [1] to reconstruct the growth and evolution of cosmic structure within the Universe. We assess the discrepancy between reconstructions derived from maximizing kernel hyperparameters and those resulting from a comprehensive exploration of the parameter space, finding the difference to be approximately $1\%$. Additionally, when comparing our findings with the Planck Collaboration 2018 results under a $\Lambda$CDM framework, no statistically significant difference is observed in the redshift range where $f\sigma_{8}$ reconstructions were performed.

We establish global well-posedness for the half-wave map targeting $S^2$ given small initial data in the $\dot{H}^{\frac{n}{2}} \times \dot{H}^{\frac{n}{2}-1}$ space. Furthermore, we demonstrate global well-posedness for the equation with $\mathbb{H}^2$ as the target, assuming small smooth initial data belonging to the $\dot{B}^{\frac{n}{2}}_{2,1} \times \dot{B}^{\frac{n}{2}-1}_{2,1}$ class.

The rapid advancement of internet technology has led to the frequent occurrence of dirty data in diverse real-world scenarios, primarily due to unreliable sensor readings and the transmission and collection of information from heterogeneous sources. To mitigate the adverse impacts of such data on downstream applications, data cleaning approaches have been developed to preprocess these issues before application execution. Most existing methods operate on the principle of identifying or correcting erroneous values by referencing neighboring data points that share similar information. However, data sparsity and heterogeneity often limit the number of neighbors identifiable through strict equality, particularly when values exhibit variance. To address this, distance-based data cleaning approaches utilize similarity based on value proximity rather than exact matches. By tolerating minor variations, these methods can identify a richer set of similar neighbors for cleaning tasks. Furthermore, the distance relationships between tuples offer valuable guidance for data cleaning by encompassing more information than simple equality checks. Consequently, distance-based technology is pivotal in the field of data cleaning, and it is anticipated to garner increasing attention in future preprocessing research. This survey categorizes four primary data cleaning tasks—rule profiling, error detection, data repair, and data imputation—and provides a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art techniques for each category.

If a bulk gravitational path integral corresponds to an average of partition functions across an ensemble of boundary quantum theories, the associated moment problem becomes solvable. We examine the conditions for existence and uniqueness within the Stieltjes moment problem, which rely on an infinite series of positivity requirements.
