When $f \geq 0.4$, the reaction efficiency remains unity within the operative temperature range of 12–30 K. Conversely, if $f$ is lower, the efficiency drops drastically; for instance, at $f = 0.3$, it never exceeds 0.01. Furthermore, acetaldehyde production is consistently competing with the formation of CO + CH$_4$.

Amidst an information-rich environment, safeguarding specific data from adversaries has become increasingly critical. The recent surge in research within lightweight cryptography is evident from the numerous stream and block ciphers proposed in recent years. This paper concentrates exclusively on lightweight block ciphers. We introduce Marvin, a novel 256-bit lightweight block cipher that falls under the Extended LS design family.

In Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC), configuration space sampling relies on walkers performing random movements. Previous research on the Hubbard model [Assaraf et al. Phys. Rev. B 60, 2299 (1999)] demonstrated that the probability of a walker remaining in a specific state follows a Poisson distribution, allowing the on-state dynamics to be integrated out exactly to produce an effective dynamics restricted to transitions between distinct states. This study extends that concept to the broader scenario of walkers confined within domains of arbitrary geometry and dimensions. We derive the equations governing this resulting effective stochastic dynamics. Results indicate that as the average trapping time within these domains increases, the reduction in statistical fluctuations becomes more pronounced. A numerical implementation for the Hubbard model is provided. While this work details the method for finite linear spaces, it can be extended to continuous configuration spaces without encountering fundamental obstacles.

Let $p$ be a prime number. This work examines pro-$p$ groups of $p$-absolute Galois type, a concept introduced by Lam, Liu, Sharifi, Wake, and Wang. We demonstrate that the pro-$p$ completion of a right-angled Artin group, where the defining simplicial graph is chordal, possesses $p$-absolute Galois type and fulfills a robust form of the Massey vanishing property. Additionally, we establish that Demushkin groups also exhibit $p$-absolute Galois type. Furthermore, we show that the free pro-$p$ product of two such groups satisfying the Massey vanishing property—and, under specific conditions, their direct product—remains a pro-$p$ group of $p$-absolute Galois type with the same vanishing property. As a result, we identify a vast array of pro-$p$ groups with these characteristics that do not arise as absolute Galois groups.

This study investigates the extent and morphology of ice formation within a differentially heated water-filled cavity using both experimental and numerical methods. Our findings indicate that the primary mechanism driving ice shaping is a cold upward convective current, which arises due to water's unique equation of state—specifically, its non-monotonic density-temperature relationship. The specific configuration of the ice front is determined by several factors, notably the temperature gradient driving the convection and the wall's inclination relative to the vertical axis, both of which are examined here. Furthermore, we introduce a boundary-layer model and a buoyancy-intensity model that capture the essential characteristics of the resulting ice morphology.

It is demonstrated that a non-decreasing self-similar stochastic process $T$ with independent increments possesses a range forming a Poisson point process with $\sigma$-finite intensity if and only if the distribution of $T(1)$ in one dimension follows the gamma type. This conclusion arises from a general hold-jump characterization of such processes $T$ and confirms the established finding that the spacings between consecutive points of a scale-invariant Poisson point process, characterized by intensity $\theta x^{-1} dx$, constitute the points of another scale-invariant Poisson point process with identical intensity.

Eliminating atmospheric and instrumental noise is critical for submillimeter spectroscopy using ground-based single-dish telescopes. To address this, we introduce a novel data-science-based method centered on statistical matrix decomposition. This technique automatically isolates astronomical emission line signals from drift noise within fast-sampled (1–10 Hz) time-series spectra acquired via position-switching (PSW) observations. Unlike traditional approaches that subtract noisy on-source and off-source data, our method avoids such subtraction, enhancing observation sensitivity by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. Additionally, it suppresses artificial artifacts like baseline ripples, further boosting effective sensitivity. We validated these gains using spectroscopic data of high-redshift galaxy emission lines collected with a 2-mm receiver on the 50-m Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT). Since the method operates offline without requiring extra measurements, it provides immediate improvements to previously reduced spectra. Furthermore, it facilitates efficient deep spectroscopy for future 50-meter class submillimeter single-dish telescopes, where achieving fast PSW through mechanical antenna or mirror movement remains challenging.

Bondi-Hoyle accretion configurations arise whenever a gravitating object moves through an ambient medium at a supersonic relative speed. This regime has been observed repeatedly across various systems, ranging from wind-accreting X-ray binaries to runaway neutron stars, and is thought to explain shock formation, though analytical derivation of their properties remains limited. This paper introduces the first numerical characterization of the stationary flow structure in Bondi-Hoyle accretion onto a compact object, spanning from the large-scale accretion radius down to the immediate vicinity of the body. By examining bow shocks across different Mach numbers, the simulations confirm the analytical predictions made by Foglizzo & Ruffert (1996) regarding the topology of the inner sonic surface for an adiabatic index of 5/3. Furthermore, these results allow for the derivation of mass accretion rates, bow shock position and temperature, as well as transverse density and temperature profiles in the wake, all as functions of the flow parameters.

When an optical beam encounters an interface along its path, it undergoes polarization-dependent deflections both longitudinally and transversely relative to the plane of incidence. The underlying physics of these beam shifts links to deep universal wave phenomena driven by the fine interference of wave packets, thereby enabling new metrological applications. In this work, we demonstrate the intrinsic non-separability of longitudinal and transverse beam shifts by examining a simple scenario involving a partially reflecting Gaussian laser beam at a dielectric boundary. This non-separability becomes significant within specific regions of the parameter space. Furthermore, we illustrate that this phenomenon manifests as a position-position classically entangled state of light, where the tunability of experimental parameters allows for control over the entanglement degree. Revealing this inherent non-separability is anticipated to deepen the physical understanding of this fundamental effect, influence the interpretation of numerous analogous phenomena, and potentially yield practical applications by leveraging position-position-polarization classical entanglement within a fundamental Gaussian beam.

Cryptocurrencies have recently gained significant attention due to their transformative potential and reports of exceptional returns. Concurrently, scholars are increasingly recognizing the predictive capabilities of social media across various domains, particularly within finance and economics. This study utilizes sentiment data from Twitter and Reddit, alongside Google Trends metrics for search volume and interest, to forecast the log returns of ten specific cryptocurrencies: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, Binance Coin, Litecoin, Enjin Coin, Horizen, Namecoin, Peercoin, and Feathercoin. Using daily data spanning from January 2018 to January 2022, we assess the efficacy of the LASSO-VAR model. In a 30-day recursive forecasting framework, the model successfully predicts the direction of actual returns more than 50% of the time. When compared to primary benchmarks, this approach yields a 10% enhancement in Mean Directional Accuracy (MDA). While incorporating sentiment and attention variables substantially boosts forecast accuracy regarding MDA, it does not significantly reduce Root Mean Squared Errors (RMSE). Furthermore, Granger causality tests conducted with post-double LASSO selection for high-dimensional VARs indicate no causal relationship from social media sentiment to cryptocurrency returns.

A version of Connes' Integration Formula is presented, offering concrete asymptotics for eigenvalues and significantly broadening the range of quantum-integrable functions defined on compact Riemannian manifolds.

Building on recent observations of late afterglows resulting from compact object mergers or the core-collapse of massive stars, this study investigates the evolution of afterglows generated by off-axis top-hat jets interacting with surrounding media. The medium is modeled using a power-law density profile, $n(r)\propto r^{-k}$, where $k$ represents the stratification parameter, covering scenarios of constant density ($k=0$) and wind-like distributions ($k=2$). We constructed an analytical synchrotron forward-shock model for off-axis viewing in a stratified environment. By applying this model to X-ray data from extensive satellite and ground-based campaigns, we successfully fitted the X-ray spectrum of the GRB afterglow associated with SN 2020bvc using standard parameters. Our results indicate that the circumburst medium for this event is best described by a power law with a stratification parameter of $k=1.5$.

The Lax-Wendroff approach functions as a single-step technique for advancing time-dependent solutions to partial differential equations, distinguishing itself from Runge-Kutta methods which require multiple stages per time step. This work presents a flux reconstruction variant of the method, integrated with a Jacobian-free Lax-Wendroff procedure suitable for general hyperbolic conservation laws. Designed as a collocation-based scheme, the method eliminates the need for quadrature and relies on matrix and vector operations. Particular emphasis is placed on constructing numerical fluxes, including for non-linear scenarios, which achieves higher CFL numbers compared to current approaches. This improvement is validated through Fourier analysis and demonstrates consistent performance across all orders of accuracy. Numerical experiments showcasing up to fifth-order precision for both linear and non-linear problems illustrate the method's effectiveness and accuracy.

We present a geometric dynamical system in which iteration consists of cycling through a finite set of geometric maps acting on a space comprising three or more lines within $\mathbb{R}^2$. Inspired by the dynamics of iterated function systems and billiards with altered reflection rules, we establish conditions ensuring the generation of periodic orbits. Leveraging this finding, we demonstrate the existence of closed nonsmooth curves over $\mathbb{R}^2$ that adhere to specific structural requirements relative to a configuration of intersecting lines in the plane.

This study extends Resta's theory of electronic polarization to non-Hermitian systems subject to periodic boundary conditions. We define electronic polarization as the expectation value of the exponential of the position operator within a biorthogonal basis. Our findings reveal a finite region of zero polarization situated between two topologically distinct phases, alongside a one-to-one mapping between polarization and the winding number, which assumes both integer and half-odd integer values. We validate these conclusions using the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.

In recent years, k-Nearest-Neighbor Machine Translation (kNN-MT) has emerged as a significant area of research within Neural Machine Translation (NMT). Its core concept involves retrieving relevant key-value pairs from an external datastore to adjust translations without retraining the NMT model. However, the presence of noisy retrieved pairs can severely degrade model performance. This paper presents a preliminary investigation revealing that this issue stems from underutilizing the NMT model's predictions. To mitigate the adverse effects of noise, we propose a confidence-enhanced kNN-MT framework featuring robust training. Specifically, we incorporate NMT confidence scores to refine the modeling of two critical kNN-MT components: the kNN distribution and the interpolation weight. Additionally, we introduce two types of perturbations into the retrieved pairs to facilitate robust training. Experiments across four benchmark datasets show that our model not only outperforms existing kNN-MT approaches significantly but also demonstrates superior robustness. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepLearnXMU/Robust-knn-mt.

It is a well-established result that for any commutative unitary ring $\mathbf{R}$, the Serre conjecture ring $\mathbf{R}\langle X \rangle$—defined as the localization of the univariate polynomial ring $\mathbf{R}[X]$ at monic polynomials—is a Bézout domain with Krull dimension at most 1, provided that $\mathbf{R}$ itself satisfies these conditions. By induction, defining $\mathbf{R}\langle X_1,\ldots,X_n \rangle$ recursively as the Serre ring over the previous stage, it follows that the multivariate version $\mathbf{R}\langle X_1,\ldots,X_n \rangle$ is also a Bézout domain of Krull dimension $\leq 1$ whenever $\mathbf{R}$ is. This property, specifically when $\mathbf{R}$ is a valuation domain of Krull dimension $\leq 1$, served as the foundation for Brewer and Costa's theorem, which asserts that if $\mathbf{R}$ is a one-dimensional arithmetical ring, then finitely generated projective modules over $\mathbf{R}[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ are extended. Furthermore, this fact is central to proving the Gröbner Ring Conjecture for lexicographic order: for any valuation domain $\mathbf{R}$ of Krull dimension $\leq 1$, any positive integer $n$, and any finitely generated ideal $I$ in $\mathbf{R}[X_1, \dots, X_n]$, the ideal $\operatorname{LT}(I)$ generated by the leading terms of $I$'s elements under the lexicographic monomial order ($X_1<X_2<\cdots<X_n$) is finitely generated. Given that $\mathbf{R}\langle X_1,\ldots,X_n\rangle$ can equivalently be defined as the localization of $\mathbf{R}[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ at polynomials whose leading coefficients in the lexicographic order are 1, we propose extending the result that $\mathbf{R}\langle X_1,\ldots,X_n\rangle$ is a Bézout domain of Krull dimension $\leq 1$ (when $\mathbf{R}$ is) to any rational monomial order. This generalization aims to strengthen the evidence supporting the Gröbner Ring Conjecture in the rational case.

The excited-state population of individual solid-state emitters undergoes energy fluctuations around equilibrium, driven by the surrounding bath and relaxation via phonon or photon emission. Investigating the associated spectral dynamics simultaneously demands a technique offering high spectral and temporal resolution alongside a large temporal dynamic range. We introduce a pulsed excitation-laser analog of Photon-Correlation Fourier Spectroscopy (PCFS) that extracts the lineshape and spectral diffusion dynamics along the emitter's emission lifetime trajectory, effectively distinguishing spectral dynamics from relaxation and bath-induced fluctuations. This lifetime-resolved PCFS correlates photon pairs at the output of a Michelson interferometer based on two time delays: the interval between laser excitation and photon detection, and the interval between the two photons. We suggest applying this technique to systems where the relative contributions to emission from multiple states vary, such as quantum emitters displaying phonon-mediated exchange between different fine-structure states.

Recent years have established the electronic Berry curvature (BC) as a fundamental concept for understanding and predicting the physical properties of crystalline materials. This phenomenon drives a variety of Hall-type responses in charge, spin, and heat transport, including the anomalous Hall effect in magnetic systems and diverse nonlinear Hall and Nernst effects in non-magnetic systems lacking inversion symmetry. However, for the most prevalent class of materials—non-magnetic systems with inversion symmetry—the bulk electronic BC is strictly zero. This study demonstrates that despite the absence of bulk BC, finite values can emerge at the surfaces and interfaces of these materials, thereby activating specific surface regions to generate Hall-type transport responses. We validate this through first-principles calculations of BC at the surfaces of bismuth, mercury-telluride (HgTe), and rhodium across various symmetries, revealing surface Berry curvature dipoles and associated quantum nonlinear Hall effects in several cases. These findings open numerous materials for exploring and utilizing physical effects arising from electronic Berry curvature that exists exclusively at their boundaries.

Complex-domain deep learning models are favored for their robust representation capabilities; however, many are limited to the first quadrant of the complex plane or force a projection into the real domain, resulting in data loss. This paper argues that performing operations entirely within the complex domain enhances the performance of complex-valued models. To support this, we introduce a novel, fully complex-valued training framework for a Fully Complex-valued Convolutional Neural Network (FC-CNN), utilizing a new complex-valued loss function and training strategy. Evaluated on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and CIFAR-100, FC-CNN demonstrates a 4–10% performance improvement over real-valued counterparts without increasing model complexity. Furthermore, it matches the accuracy of state-of-the-art complex-valued models on CIFAR-10 and SVHN while using fewer parameters, and it achieves state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-100 with 25% fewer parameters. Additionally, FC-CNN exhibits superior training efficiency and significantly faster convergence compared to other models.

A straightforward geometric mechanism, defined as "the locus of intersections of perpendicular bisectors and normal lines," frequently appears in various forms within Nonlinear Sciences. This paper introduces a novel application of this mechanism, demonstrating that it simultaneously resolves all four fundamental issues concerning envelopes generated by hyperplane families: the existence problem, the representation problem, the equivalence of definitions, and the uniqueness problem.

We present findings from an analysis of galactic outflows in 45 low-redshift starburst galaxies from the COS Legacy Archive Spectroscopic SurveY (CLASSY), supplemented by five additional similar starbursts observed with COS. These outflows are identified through blueshifted metal absorption lines covering a broad spectrum of ionization potentials. The superior quality and extensive spectral range of CLASSY data allow us to distinguish absorption caused by the static interstellar medium from that produced by outflows. By analyzing various line multiplets and doublets, we derived the covering fraction, column density, and ionization state as functions of velocity for each outflow. We measured the mean velocity and velocity width of the outflows, discovering a highly significant correlation with star-formation rate, galaxy mass, and circular velocity across ranges spanning four orders of magnitude for the first two parameters. Additionally, we calculated outflow rates for metals, mass, momentum, and kinetic energy. Our results indicate that at most only ~20% of silicon produced and expelled by supernovae in starbursts is found in the warm phase we observe. The mass-loading factor of the outflows rises steeply and inversely with both circular and outflow velocities (log-log slope $\sim$ -1.6), reaching approximately 10 in dwarf galaxies. Furthermore, we found that outflows typically transport 10 to 100% of the momentum injected by massive stars and 1 to 20% of the kinetic energy. These findings provide valuable constraints and novel insights for models and simulations of galactic winds.

We generalize core concepts from the established extension of Lie theory involving Lie groupoids by recasting them within a well-adapted synthetic differential geometry model. Specifically, we introduce internal versions of source path and source simply connected groupoid definitions, as well as the integration of $A$-paths. Our primary findings demonstrate that when a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid meets a standard connectedness condition, it necessarily satisfies its corresponding internal counterpart.

Satellite cameras enable the acquisition of data across vast terrestrial regions, offering insights far beyond human visual range from the ground. This capability facilitates the detection and monitoring of physical attributes such as land-use patterns, atmospheric states, and forest coverage, alongside numerous other factors. These images serve not only to track ongoing natural processes but are also vital in addressing the global crisis of deforestation, particularly within the Amazon basin, which experiences the highest annual loss. Effective data analysis is essential for mitigating negative impacts on ecosystems and biodiversity while fostering a sustainable atmosphere. This report focuses on classifying satellite image segments of the Amazon rainforest into atmospheric and land-use categories using advanced machine learning and deep learning techniques. Performance is evaluated using the F2 metric, with both sigmoid and softmax cross-entropy employed as loss functions. Machine learning classifiers receive input via extracted features from pre-trained ImageNet architectures, whereas deep learning models utilize ensembles of fine-tuned, pre-trained ImageNet models through transfer learning. The highest F2 metric score achieved to date is 0.927.

The worsening gas shortage in the EU necessitates urgent political and regulatory measures to enhance energy security. Currently, member states are focused on filling their own reservoirs independently, yet the practical application of future solidarity remains uncertain, specifically regarding how accumulated reserves might be redistributed to assist those in need. This paper proposes a formalized game-theoretic model to capture the essential aspects of this issue, accounting for uncertainties in future reservoir levels and potential transmission constraints. We introduce a voluntary cooperation mechanism designed to improve the efficiency of storage capacity utilization, should it be implemented later. By applying this framework to a simple example, we demonstrate that under conditions of risk aversion, the concept holds significant potential.

Textures and edges provide distinct data for image recognition tasks. While edges and boundaries capture shape details, textures represent regional appearance. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved significant success in computer vision and medical imaging, they primarily learn texture abstractions, frequently resulting in inaccurate boundary definitions. In medical contexts, expert manual segmentation typically depends on organ boundaries; for instance, when segmenting a liver, a practitioner usually locates edges before filling in the mask. Driven by these insights, we introduce a plug-and-play module called Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), designed to integrate with standard encoder-decoder frameworks to handle both edge and texture data. The EG-CNN enhances edges within the encoder, predicts sharp boundaries through auxiliary supervision, and merges these results with the original CNN output. We assessed the EG-CNN's efficacy across various mainstream CNNs using two public datasets, BraTS 19 and KiTS 19, for brain tumor and kidney segmentation. Our results demonstrate that incorporating EG-CNNs consistently boosts segmentation accuracy and generalization capabilities.

Recent studies have shown that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial patches, which create localized yet perceptible alterations in input images. However, while methods for generating such patches on static images are well-established, their application to video remains underexplored. Attacking videos presents a significantly greater challenge than attacking images because it requires accounting for both spatial and temporal cues. To address this gap, this paper introduces a novel adversarial technique called the bullet-screen comment (BSC) attack, designed to compromise video recognition models using BSCs. Adversarial BSCs are generated through a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework where the target model serves as the environment and the agent determines the optimal position and transparency for each comment. By iteratively querying the target model and incorporating its feedback, the agent refines its selection strategy to maximize the fooling rate using non-overlapping BSCs. Since BSCs represent meaningful content, inserting them into clean videos does not hinder human comprehension or raise suspicion. Extensive experiments on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 datasets demonstrate the method's efficacy: our BSC attack achieves approximately a 90% fooling rate against three leading video recognition models while occluding less than 8% of the video area. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/kay-ck/BSC-attack.

In the metric $f(R)$ gravity framework, the scalaron can serve as dark matter provided its mass falls within the range $4\,\text{meV} \lesssim m \lesssim 1\,\text{MeV}$. This paper provides an overview of such a theory minimally coupled to the Standard Model. Like other scalar-field-based dark matter models, this approach faces challenges regarding initial conditions. First, the scalaron's initial state must be finely tuned to yield the observed dark matter density. Second, primordial spatial inhomogeneities in the field must remain sufficiently small, as they induce entropy (or isocurvature) perturbations that are observationally constrained. We address these issues in the current study. Presumably arising during inflation, the initial conditions for the scalaron present a significant hurdle: the homogeneous component of the initial value is largely unpredictable due to quantum diffusion. Consequently, explaining the observed dark matter abundance requires invoking anthropic arguments. Furthermore, observational limits on the scalaron's primordial spatial inhomogeneity translate into upper bounds on the inflationary energy scale; these bounds are relatively low but not overly restrictive.

This study focuses on developing reduced-order observers for robotic manipulators. Using Lyapunov analysis, stability criteria are established, and the observer is further improved by incorporating a hybrid approach capable of adjusting gains to handle potentially unbounded joint velocities. Consequently, this hybrid strategy ensures accurate performance whether the robot is controlled via open-loop or output feedback methods. Numerical simulations demonstrate the observer's effectiveness across various scenarios, including a comparative analysis against the performance of a traditional full-order observer.

This paper presents and justifies the investigation of Quantum Weyl Gravity, also referred to as Conformal Gravity. We highlight attractive characteristics of this framework at both classical and quantum levels. The construction of the quantum theory is detailed up to the one-loop approximation. To streamline calculations, we employ exclusively physical degrees of freedom, identified via the York decomposition. At the one-loop level, we calculate the partition function on a general Einstein space. Subsequently, we examine the functional renormalization group flow for the couplings within Quantum Weyl Gravity. Our analysis fully reproduces prior findings derived from maximally symmetric and Ricci-flat backgrounds. Finally, we discuss potential future research avenues and address the matter of the conformal anomaly.

For every irreducible module of the symmetric group acting on $N$ objects, there exists a collection of parametrized nonsymmetric Jack polynomials defined in $N$ variables that map into that module. These polynomials serve as simultaneous eigenfunctions for a commutative family of operators that are self-adjoint under specific Hermitian forms. The author and J.-G. Luque previously investigated these polynomials using a Yang-Baxter graph approach. This work develops a matrix-valued measure on the $N$-torus for which the polynomials exhibit mutual orthogonality, employing Fourier analysis methods in the process. The paper derives recursion relations for the Fourier-Stieltjes coefficients of this measure to determine parameter values where the construction breaks down. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the absolutely continuous component of the measure obeys a first-order system of differential equations.

The Dynaswap project is developing a comprehensive, trustworthy, and coherently integrated security architecture designed to protect workflows within cyberinfrastructures, specifically for virtual machines hosted via CI services like JetStream. JetStream provides a user-friendly cloud platform that grants researchers on-demand access to interactive computing and data analysis tools. The Dynaswap architecture manages roles, role hierarchies, and data hierarchies, enabling dynamic adjustments to these structures within scientific infrastructure. It merges state-of-the-art security frameworks—such as Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA), Multi-Factor Authentication, Secure Digital Provenance, and Blockchain—with advanced security mechanisms including Biometric-Capsules, Cryptography-based Hierarchical Access Control, and Dual-level Key Management. Currently, this cyberinfrastructure is being validated in life-science research and within Health Informatics educational programs.

This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the optical model framework for nucleon-nucleus scattering and reactions, grounded in fundamental nuclear two-body and many-body forces. It starts with a historical perspective before examining various theoretical methods used to derive nucleon-nucleus optical potentials that incorporate antisymmetry, Pauli blocking, and multiple scattering effects. Subsequently, it summarizes ongoing efforts to establish microscopic nuclear forces aligned with the fundamental theory of strong interactions, quantum chromodynamics, and their application in building microscopic optical potentials. Additionally, the chapter outlines the dispersive optical potential approach, which, although largely phenomenological, stems from formal Green's function theory. Finally, it compares results from modern optical potentials against experimental data.

Consider a complete, connected, non-compact Riemannian manifold $M$ where the Ricci curvature is bounded below by a negative constant. We establish a sufficient condition for open, connected subsets $D \subset M$ such that the associated Dirichlet heat semigroup exhibits intrinsic ultracontractivity. This condition relies on the concept of capacitary width. Furthermore, when the capacitary width of $D$ is sufficiently small, it is demonstrated that the square of this width is comparable to both the reciprocal of the bottom of the spectrum of the Dirichlet Laplacian on $L^2(D)$ and the supremum of the torsion function for $D$. The proof hinges on technical elements including the volume doubling property, the Poincaré inequality, and the Li-Yau Gaussian estimate for the Dirichlet heat kernel at finite scales.

We present recent analyses of various datasets that demonstrate Geometrical Scaling (GS) and its breakdown. As a result of an intermediate energy scale known as saturation momentum, GS enables the correlation of data across different energies, system types, and varying multiplicities or centralities.

We present a novel approach for two-sample testing of high-dimensional linear regression coefficients that does not require individual coefficient estimability. This method operates by projecting covariate matrices and response vectors along directions with complementary signs within a subset of coordinates, a technique termed 'complementary sketching.' These projections are then aggregated to generate two test statistics, which demonstrate essentially optimal asymptotic power under a Gaussian design for both sparse and dense differences in regression coefficients. Simulations validate the method's effectiveness across various settings, while an application to a large single-cell RNA sequencing dataset illustrates its practical utility.

This study examines a Bolza-type optimal control problem formulated as:
\begin{equation}\min J_{t}(y,u):=\int_t^T\Lambda(s,y(s),
u(s))\,ds+g(y(T))\tag{P$_{t,x}$}\end{equation}
Subject to the constraints:
\begin{equation}\label{tag:admissible}\tag{D}\begin{cases} y\in
AC([t,T];\mathbb R^n)\\y'=b(y)u\text{ a.e. } s\in [t,T], \,y(t)=x\\u(s)\in
\mathcal U\text{ a.e. } s\in [t,T],\, y(s)\in \mathcal S\,\,\forall s\in [t,T],
\end{cases} \end{equation}
In this framework, the function $\Lambda(s,y,u)$ is locally Lipschitz with respect to $s$ and merely Borel measurable regarding $(y,u)$; the function $b$ exhibits at most linear growth, and both the Lagrangian $\Lambda$ and the terminal cost $g$ are permitted to assume the value $+\infty$. When $b$ is identically $1$ and $g$ is identically $0$, problem (P$_{t,x}$) reduces to the classical calculus of variations problem. We assume a slow growth condition on $u$, as proposed by Clarke in 1993, which encompasses Lagrangians such as $\Lambda(s,y,u)=\sqrt{1+|u|^2}$ and $\Lambda(s,y,u)=|u|-\sqrt{|u|}$, as well as superlinear cases. If $\Lambda$ is real-valued, any family of optimal pairs $(y_*, u_*)$ for (P$_{t,x}$) with energy $J_t(y_*, u_*)$ that remains equi-bounded as $(t,x)$ varies over a compact set possesses $L^\infty$-equi-bounded optimal controls. In the case where $\Lambda$ is extended-valued, this conclusion remains valid provided an additional lower semicontinuity assumption is imposed on the mapping $(s,u)\mapsto\Lambda(s,y,u)$ and on the structure of its effective domain. No convexity or local Lipschitz continuity is required with respect to the variables $(y,u)$. As a practical application, we derive the local Lipschitz continuity of the value function under these slow growth assumptions.

To facilitate the comparison between lattice field theory outcomes and the high-energy continuum limit, we compute the Green's function featuring a tensor quark bilinear operator inserted at zero momentum within a quark two-point function, applicable to any covariant gauge. These calculations are performed to four-loop order in both the MSbar and RI' schemes. Furthermore, the anomalous dimension of the tensor current is determined to four loops in both schemes for an arbitrary color group.

The bandwidth theorem, established in *Mathematische Annalen* (343(1):175--205, 2009), asserts that every $n$-vertex graph $G$ possessing a minimum degree of $\big(\tfrac{k-1}{k}+o(1)\big)n$ includes all $n$-vertex $k$-colourable graphs $H$ that have bounded maximum degree and bandwidth $o(n)$. This work extends these findings to sparse analogues within random and pseudorandom graphs. Specifically, it demonstrates that for $p\gg \big(\tfrac{\log n}{n}\big)^{1/\Delta}$, a spanning subgraph $G$ of $G(n,p)$ with minimum degree $\big(\tfrac{k-1}{k}+o(1)\big)pn$ asymptotically almost surely contains all $n$-vertex $k$-colourable graphs $H$ characterized by maximum degree $\Delta$, bandwidth $o(n)$, and at least $C p^{-2}$ vertices not participating in any triangle. A comparable result is derived for sufficiently bijumbled graphs, representing, to the authors' knowledge, the first resilience outcome in pseudorandom graphs for a broad class of spanning subgraphs. Furthermore, the study offers enhanced results for graphs $H$ with low degeneracy, which notably imply a resilience result in $G(n,p)$ regarding the containment of spanning bounded degree trees when $p\gg \big(\tfrac{\log n}{n}\big)^{1/3}$.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment polarity of specific aspects within product reviews. We observe that approximately 30% of reviews lack explicit opinion words yet still convey clear human-aware sentiment orientation, a phenomenon known as implicit sentiment. However, recent neural network-based methods have largely overlooked implicit sentiment embedded in these reviews. To address this limitation, we implement Supervised Contrastive Pre-training using large-scale sentiment-annotated corpora sourced from in-domain language resources. By aligning the representations of implicit sentiment expressions with those sharing the same sentiment label, our pre-training process enhances the model's ability to capture both implicit and explicit sentiment orientations regarding aspects in reviews. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on SemEval2014 benchmarks, and comprehensive analysis confirms its efficacy in learning implicit sentiment.

Studying biomass compounds adsorbed on surfaces presents significant challenges because of the vast number of potential species and adsorption geometries. This study investigates possible intermediates of erythrose, glyceraldehyde, glycerol, and propionic acid on the Rh(111) surface. These intermediates and elementary reactions were generated using the first two iterations of a recursive bond-breaking algorithm. These structures served as input for an unsupervised Mol2Vec algorithm to create vector descriptors. A data-driven approach was developed to classify reactions and predict adsorption energies. Our model achieved a lowest mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.39 eV for adsorption energy predictions, with relatively accurate relative ordering of different surface adsorption geometries. We demonstrate that integrating geometries from density functional tight-binding (DFTB) calculations with machine-learning-derived energies offers a novel workflow for rapidly evaluating the stability of various molecular geometries on the Rh(111) surface.

In computational physics, it is conventional to model continuum systems using discretized frameworks. This work examines a particular discretization of the continuum complex Hilbert space in quantum mechanics, characterized by rational squared amplitudes and complex phases. The resolution of this discretization is governed by a finite prime parameter, $p$. Unlike standard computational approaches, as $p \rightarrow \infty$, this model does not converge smoothly to the continuum; rather, the continuum limit of quantum mechanics emerges as a singular state of the discretized model at $p=\infty$. Leveraging number-theoretic properties of trigonometric functions, we demonstrate that for sufficiently large $p$, the discretized Hilbert space accurately captures ensemble representations of quantum systems within an inherently superdeterministic framework that formally violates the Statistical Independence assumption of Bell's theorem. Consequently, this model accounts for the violation of Bell inequalities without resorting to nonlocality or indefinite reality. Furthermore, the framework is shown to be non-conspiratorial, as it is not fine-tuned relative to its natural $p$-adic metric. Aligning with Michael Berry's observation that established physical theories often represent singular limits of newer ones (as a parameter approaches zero or infinity), we address Scott Aaronson's critique of superdeterminism by explaining when a major physical theory like quantum mechanics is merely "grudgingly accommodated" by a successor theory rather than "gloriously explained" by it. In this context, the proposed superdeterministic theory of physics based on discretized Hilbert space serves as such a successor.

Accurate time synchronization in wireless networks relies heavily on compensating for clock skew. However, current estimation techniques struggle because they depend on imprecise transmission time measurements. To address this, this study introduces a novel maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach with a unique implementation designed to reduce delay-induced skew errors within a one-way broadcast synchronization framework. The research develops a multiple one-way broadcast model for observation and data collection, analyzing the distribution of actual delays. A Gaussian delay-based clock skew MLE is proposed, along with its Cramer-Rao lower bound. Notably, this method operates independently of clock offset estimation and achieves accurate results using only two synchronization periods. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed MLE outperforms the methods commonly employed in existing time synchronization protocols.

Since the 20th century, the rising prevalence of suicide has inflicted profound emotional harm on individuals, families, and communities alike. Despite the gravity of this epidemic, no reliable or systematic method currently exists to assess an individual's intent to commit suicide. While recent efforts to automate mental illness diagnosis have increasingly focused on verbal and acoustic behaviors as biomarkers, the role of eyelids, gaze, and head pose in evaluating suicide risk has been largely overlooked. This study investigates statistical analysis, feature selection, and machine learning classification as tools for suicide risk assessment and the interpretation of nonverbal behavior. By applying these techniques to eye and head signals derived from a unique dataset, the research reveals that individuals at high risk of suicide exhibit psycho-motor retardation alongside anxiety and depression symptoms, specifically manifested through avoidance of eye contact, slower blinking rates, and downward gaze. Comparisons across various classification methods indicate that these features can consistently and accurately distinguish between different levels of suicide risk with accuracy exceeding 98%. These findings align with existing psychological studies and demonstrate the significant potential of a systematic approach to suicide risk evaluation that is viable for both healthcare professionals and lay observers.

Magnetic impurities embedded in a superconducting substrate generate in-gap Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states; their complex spatial configurations are vital for designing collective impurity systems. Using a saddle-point approximation, we examine the scattering mechanisms that produce YSR states within gapped two-dimensional superconductors. Additionally, we construct a theoretical framework that connects the spatial characteristics of YSR states to the energy dispersion of normal electrons in a two-dimensional host via a straightforward analytical formula. Specifically, we demonstrate that regions of the Fermi surface with low curvature and high Fermi velocity amplify the local density of states (LDOS) near the impurity. This analytical approach yields quantitative results consistent with tight-binding simulations across diverse lattices and Fermi surface geometries, enabling predictions regarding the morphology and orientation of YSR states detected in scanning tunneling spectroscopy. We validate these findings using a model of $\mathrm{NbSe}_2$.

Current transient gravitational wave detection and analysis methods operate under the assumption that detector data contains no more than a single signal at any given moment; however, as detector sensitivity increases, this assumption becomes untenable. This paper investigates the performance of existing transient search techniques when faced with multiple simultaneous signals. We analyze data sets featuring time-overlapping compact binary coalescences using two pipelines employed by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration: the modelled, matched-filter search PyCBC and the unmodelled coherent search cWB. Our results indicate that both pipelines successfully identify both signals when they are sufficiently separated in merger time ($|\Delta t_c| \geq 1$ second), with PyCBC losing only 1% of overlapping binary black hole merger signals. While both pipelines can detect signal pairings within the $|\Delta t_c| < 1$ second window, internal clustering routines typically recover only one of the two signals, thereby reducing overall efficiency. Notably, within this tighter time window, cWB is capable of identifying both signals. Furthermore, we demonstrate that matched filter searches can be adapted to yield accurate parameter estimates for each individual signal.

Precision flavor experiments offer a complementary approach to standard axion helio- and haloscopes for detecting the QCD axion, enabling tests of Peccei-Quinn (PQ) breaking scales up to $10^{12} \, {\rm GeV}$. These searches probe flavor-violating axion interactions, which are naturally expected to be significant whenever Standard Model fermions possess flavor non-universal PQ charges. A notably predictive framework emerges when the PQ symmetry corresponds to the simplest Froggatt-Nielsen (FN) flavor symmetry; in this case, all flavor-violating axion couplings are linked to Yukawa hierarchies, modulo ${\cal O}(1)$ coefficients.

We detect a collective suppression of optical pumping between hyperfine ground states that scales with density within an array of submicrometer-sized clouds of cold rubidium atoms. This reduced Raman transition rate is attributed to strong resonant dipole-dipole interactions, which intensify as atom density rises. These findings align with stochastic electrodynamics simulations that model nonlinear population transfer through internal atomic levels within a coupled-dipole framework.

Identifying IoT devices is crucial for enhancing their security and operational performance. Unlike traditional non-IoT devices, IoT systems present distinct challenges and opportunities for device classification. Building on prior insights regarding the network traffic patterns of IoT devices, this paper introduces iotID, a machine-learning-based identification framework. The iotID system extracts 70 TCP flow features across three dimensions: remote server and port information, packet-level metrics like inter-arrival times, and flow-level metrics such as duration. A key distinction from existing approaches is that iotID addresses the inherent class imbalance in network traffic during both training and evaluation phases. Performance evaluations conducted in a typical smart home environment containing both IoT and non-IoT devices demonstrate that iotID achieves a balanced accuracy exceeding 99%.

Large-scale multilingual models trained on numerous languages have shown significant promise across various tasks due to their cross-lingual learning abilities. Adapting these models to specific languages, particularly those absent from the pre-training data, is crucial for expanding the reach of language technology. This study demonstrates how leveraging language phylogenetic information can enhance cross-lingual transfer by utilizing closely related languages in a structured, linguistically informed approach. By conducting adapter-based training on languages spanning diverse families—such as Germanic, Uralic, Tupian, and Uto-Aztecan—and evaluating performance on both syntactic and semantic tasks, we achieve over 20% relative improvements compared to strong common baselines, with notable gains on languages unseen during pre-training.

Understanding human behavior is a central focus in computer science, driving research into Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) and Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC). Psychologically, emotions represent short-term affective expressions, whereas sentiments denote longer-held feelings. Despite this distinction, current studies often treat them in isolation, failing to leverage their complementary insights. This paper introduces UniMSE, a multimodal framework for sentiment knowledge sharing that integrates MSA and ERC across features, labels, and models. By performing modality fusion at both syntactic and semantic levels, and employing contrastive learning between modalities and samples, the method effectively captures the nuances and consistencies between sentiments and emotions. Evaluations on four public benchmarks—MOSI, MOSEI, MELD, and IEMOCAP—confirm the approach's efficacy, yielding consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art techniques.

This work provides both analytical and simulated findings regarding the impact of acceleration gradients within velocity bunching, a beam compression technique utilizing a traveling wave accelerator. Our analysis demonstrates that employing a low acceleration gradient enhances tolerance to phase jitter and yields a more effective compression, resulting in an electron beam with a symmetrical longitudinal profile and reduced energy spread. Additionally, we introduce a transverse emittance compensation method designed to mitigate emittance growth driven by escalating space charge forces during compression, offering a flexible solution adaptable to various compression factors.

Supernova (SN) rates provide a crucial test for star-formation models and initial mass functions. However, near-infrared, ground-based surveys with seeing-limited resolution typically identify only one-third to one-tenth of the SNe predicted by far-infrared (FIR) luminosities. This shortfall stems from sensitivity constraints caused by variable point-spread functions (PSFs) and significant dust extinction in the cores of star-forming galaxies. Such discrepancies may impact our comprehension of star-formation rates and massive-star evolution, especially at higher redshifts where these galaxies are prevalent. To address this gap, effective local SN surveys require longer wavelengths and space-based platforms offering stable PSFs, thereby minimizing the need for subtraction algorithms and reducing residuals. This study presents a two-year Spitzer/IRAC 3.6 µm survey targeting dust-obscured SNe in the nuclei of forty luminous infrared galaxies (LIRGs) within 200 Mpc. Due to the asymmetric Spitzer PSF, standard template subtraction yielded worse-than-expected residuals; however, employing forward-modeling techniques enhanced sensitivity by approximately 1.5 magnitudes. We identified nine SNe, five of which had eluded optical surveys. After adjusting predicted rates for our survey's sensitivity, the detection count aligns with theoretical models. Although this effort was constrained by the challenging-to-model PSF and Spitzer's limited resolution, future missions like the Roman Space Telescope and JWST, offering superior resolution and more symmetric PSFs, will greatly benefit from this approach.

We provide the source code along with a 121 GB dataset comprising 96 long-term N-body simulations of the Solar System. This dataset can be analyzed independently to investigate Solar System dynamics. Furthermore, these simulations can serve as a foundation for future research exploring alternative initial conditions or additional physical effects. They can also function as a benchmark and comparison tool for new numerical algorithms.

We compute the Abraham and Aharonov-Casher forces generated by the electromagnetic quantum vacuum acting on alkaline atoms in highly excited, long-lived Rydberg states. Due to their substantial polarizability and extended lifetimes, these atoms serve as ideal candidates for detecting such forces.

We demonstrate that the presence of a specific, well-known class of ideals on a regular cardinal $\lambda$ entails a compactness result regarding the specialisability of a branchless tree of height $\lambda$. Furthermore, utilizing Neeman's technique of side conditions, we establish that the existence of such ideals remains consistent with the presence of stationarily many suitable guessing models. These entities allow us to generalize the principal theorem from \cite{mhpr_spe}: it is possible to generically specialise any tree of height $\kappa^{++}$ lacking cofinal branches, provided the forcing is ${<}\kappa$-closed, $\kappa^{+}$-proper, $\kappa^{++}$-preserving, and possesses the $\kappa^+$-approximation property.

Recent advances in unsupervised deep learning have demonstrated significant potential for disease detection across diverse medical imaging types. Although earlier generative models effectively identified anomalies by learning the distribution of healthy 2D slices, they treated each slice in isolation, neglecting the inherent correlations present within 3D volumes. We demonstrate that integrating 3D context and analyzing entire-body MRI (wbMRI) volumes enhances the ability to differentiate anomalies from benign findings. Our study introduces a multi-channel sliding window generative model specifically designed for lesion detection in wbMRI. Experimental results indicate that our approach substantially outperforms methods processing images independently, with ablation studies confirming the critical role of 3D reasoning. Furthermore, we found that incorporating additional patient-specific features further improves anomaly detection performance in pediatric scans.

The delayed response characteristic of slow passage through a Hopf bifurcation is a common feature in multiple-timescale dynamical systems, where a gradually changing variable replaces a fixed parameter, causing solutions in slow-fast systems to experience the bifurcation with a lag. While this behavior is well-established in smooth slow-fast systems, this work presents the first investigation of such phenomena in piecewise linear (PWL) slow-fast systems. This specific class of systems replicates all characteristics of their smooth equivalents yet facilitates more rigorous quantitative analysis and simplification, largely due to the presence of canonical (linear) slow manifolds. We establish the criteria under which a PWL slow-fast system displays a slow passage through a Hopf-like bifurcation, relating these conditions to the number of linear regions and potential interactions between attracting and repelling canonical slow manifolds. Through this analysis, we completely characterize the associated way-in/way-out functions. Furthermore, we apply these findings to the Doi-Kumagai model, a neuronal PWL system known for exhibiting elliptic bursting oscillations, to examine the slow passage effect.

We demonstrate that investigating neutrino capture on tritium for non-relativistic neutrinos enables the differentiation between various neutrino models, potentially confirming quantum field theory condensation effects and testing the hypothesis that flavor vacuum energy contributes to the universe's dark matter. Specifically, we show that the capture rate varies according to the chosen neutrino model and carries an imprint of the flavor vacuum condensate. Consequently, experiments such as PTOLEMY, which aim to detect the cosmic neutrino background, may provide evidence for the dark matter component arising from neutrino mixing.

Crowdsourcing effectively gathers data by leveraging a distributed human workforce, where researchers implement reward mechanisms to encourage accurate reporting. This paper specifically examines Peer-Based Mechanisms (PBMs), highlighting a critical issue: these systems can be unfair, denying diligent and truthful agents their deserved rewards. Such inequity risks deterring participation. Consequently, this study proposes a general framework designed to ensure fairness within PBMs in temporal contexts, where early submissions are prioritized. We define two fairness concepts—gamma-fairness and qualitative fairness—and address them by granting trustworthy agents additional pairing opportunities. To measure this trustworthiness across tasks, we introduce the Temporal Reputation Model (TERM). Serving as the core component, our iterative framework, REFORM, can integrate the reward structures of any existing PBM. We validate REFORM's effectiveness by applying it to the RPTSC reward scheme, demonstrating that it significantly enhances fairness while simultaneously incentivizing truthful and early reporting. Both theoretical proofs and synthetic simulations confirm that REFORM outperforms RPTSC in terms of fairness.

This progress report outlines the computation of the connected hadronic contribution to the muon g-2 utilizing C* boundary conditions. The analysis employs a QCD gauge ensemble featuring 3+1 flavors, alongside two QCD+QED gauge ensembles with 1+2+1 dynamical quark flavors, all generated by the RC* collaboration. Furthermore, we provide a detailed account of the vector mass calculation and discuss both statistical and systematic uncertainties.

The optimal choice between discrete-variable (DV) and continuous-variable (CV) quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols for a thermal-loss channel remains unclear. This study examines standard DV-QKD and CV-QKD schemes, specifically BB84 and squeezed-state protocols, within a thermal-loss environment assuming ideal sources and detectors. Our results indicate that in an intermediate-noise regime, the BB84 protocol achieves higher positive key rates than any known CV protocol. Conversely, the squeezed-state protocol surpasses BB84 in high thermal noise conditions. This analysis determines which QKD platform and protocol perform best across varying thermal-loss channel parameters under ideal operational conditions.

The recently identified superconductor UTe$_2$, characterized by a critical temperature ($T_c$) ranging from 1.5~K to 2~K, has garnered significant interest due to strong indications of spin-triplet and topological superconductivity. Notably, its behavior under magnetic fields is exceptional, featuring both field-reinforced and field-induced superconducting phases. In this study, we present the first comprehensive thermodynamic mapping of the phase diagram for magnetic fields applied along the three principal crystallographic axes. Experiments were conducted up to 36~T along the hard magnetization $b$~axis, allowing us to track the superconducting transition up to the metamagnetic point at $H_{m} = 34.75$~T. These findings uncover a phase transition line within the superconducting regime and highlight profound differences between the resulting phases. Rigorous analysis indicates a distinct spin state across these phases, suggesting a rare transition from a low-field spin-triplet to a high-field spin-singlet state—a unique phenomenon among superconductors that offers valuable insights into the mechanisms driving spin-triplet superconductivity.
The Monitor of All-sky X-ray Image (MAXI) is a Japanese all-sky X-ray observatory located on the International Space Station (ISS).

We showcase the spatial mapping of local and nano-scale structures in thin-film objects through spatially resolved pair distribution function (PDF) analysis of synchrotron x-ray diffraction data. This approach is applied to a lab-on-chip combinatorial array of sample spots featuring catalytically relevant nanoparticles, which were deposited from liquid precursors via an ink-jet liquid handling system. We introduce a software implementation of the entire workflow, including an automated data acquisition and analysis strategy based on the PDF method. The protocol software manages semi-automated data reduction, normalization, and modeling, utilizing user-defined recipes to generate extensive metadata and analysis outputs. By applying built-in functions to slice the resulting data collection, we constructed 2D images of the object using varying contrast parameters, thereby enabling the creation of spatial maps that reflect different aspects of the local structure across the array.

Solar magnetic activity dictates the conditions surrounding Earth, generating space weather phenomena that significantly impact both ground-based and space-based technologies. Among the key solar magnetic structures driving this space weather is the solar wind, which emanates from coronal holes (CHs). Consequently, accurately identifying CHs on the Sun is vital for developing predictive capabilities. This study employed an unsupervised machine learning approach, specifically $k$-means clustering, to analyze pixel-by-pixel passband images of the Sun captured by the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on the {\it Solar Dynamics Observatory} (SDO) across 171 \AA, 193 \AA, and 211 \AA wavelengths in various combinations. Our findings indicate that pixel-wise $k$-means clustering, when combined with systematic pre- and post-processing, yields results consistent with those produced by sophisticated methods like convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Crucially, this research highlights the necessity for a consensus-based CH database established by independent observers. Such a database would serve as a "ground truth" reference for supervised learning applications or for evaluating model performance.

The violation of the null energy condition is significant in both general relativity and quantum field theory within curved spacetimes. Historical analysis indicates that such violations often result in causality breaches and instability. In the context of quantum field theory, whether the energy condition is violated depends not only on spacetime geometry but also on the specific quantum states involved, highlighting the critical role of quantum effects. This study demonstrates that the collection of all coherent states does not violate the null energy condition. However, under specific circumstances, violations can occur with either pure or mixed states. Additionally, the paper examines the dynamic violation of the null energy condition arising from quantum states.

Feature selection involves identifying an optimal subset of features for a machine learning model to maximize performance within a given resource budget. While existing approaches for neural networks—such as those utilizing $\ell_1$ regularization, attention, or stochastic gates—typically evaluate all features in a single pass and overlook the residual value (i.e., the marginal contribution of a feature given previously selected ones), we introduce Sequential Attention. This algorithm achieves state-of-the-art empirical performance by implementing an efficient greedy forward selection process that leverages attention weights at each step to approximate marginal feature importance. Theoretically, we demonstrate that for linear regression, an adaptation of our method is equivalent to the classical Orthogonal Matching Pursuit algorithm [PRK1993], thereby inheriting its provable guarantees. Furthermore, our combined theoretical and empirical analyses offer novel insights into the efficacy of attention mechanisms and their relationship to overparameterization, findings that may hold independent interest.

Given the significant commercial value of deep neural networks (DNNs) trained at the production level, there is a growing need to safeguard these models from unauthorized access and copyright violations. While existing protection techniques have primarily targeted image classification, they have not yet been applied to semantic segmentation, despite its expanding applications. This paper introduces a novel approach to securing semantic segmentation models by employing block-wise transformations secured with a secret key for the first time. These protected models are trained using transformed images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method enables authorized users with the correct key to access the model's full capabilities while significantly degrading performance for unauthorized users. However, the protected models exhibit a slight reduction in segmentation accuracy compared to their unprotected counterparts.

This work presents a concise overview of the string percolation model and its findings, alongside a comparison with experimental data. It begins with an introduction to the quark-gluon phase diagram and lattice QCD results regarding confinement and the percolation of center domains. The interaction of strings generated in proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus collisions is examined to illustrate the emergence of string percolation. Key implications of this phenomenon, specifically concerning energy and centrality dependencies on particle multiplicities and mean transverse momentum, are derived by matching theoretical predictions with experimental observations. The non-abelian nature of the color fields within the formed strings is highlighted as essential for explaining the increase in transverse momentum with multiplicity and the relative suppression of multiplicities. Various observables are analyzed, including multiplicity and transverse momentum distributions, their interdependencies, forward-backward correlations, Bose-Einstein correlation strengths, the multiplicity dependence of $J/\Psi$ production and its potential suppression in high-multiplicity pp collisions, strangeness enhancement, elliptic flow, and the ridge structure. The data comparison demonstrates overall agreement. Furthermore, the thermodynamic properties of the extended clusters created in collisions are investigated by calculating energy and entropy densities, the ratio of shear viscosity to entropy density, bulk viscosity, sound speed, and the trace anomaly as functions of temperature, revealing remarkable consistency with lattice QCD calculations. Ultimately, the string percolation model is positioned as an initial framework capable of describing the collective behavior observed in both AA and pp collisions.

We construct a spatially real-analytic solution for the 2D and 3D stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, driven by spatially real-analytic multiplicative and transport noise, starting from an initial condition that merely requires bounded enstrophy. Assuming the solution exists globally in time, we further demonstrate that the finite-dimensional Galerkin approximation exhibits exponential decay relative to its wavenumber, converging to the strong pathwise solution of the stochastic Navier-Stokes equation. This decay remains uniform over time, independent of the initial enstrophy, and invariant with respect to the noise coefficients.

This paper aims to explore applications of umbral calculus through the use of extended fermionic p-adic q-integrals over Zp. Based on these applications, we establish several novel and intriguing properties regarding a new family of Euler numbers and polynomials. Furthermore, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of Sheffer sequences in relation to the generating functions of weighted Euler polynomials.

Modern spintronic device development necessitates materials with distinct magnetic properties. This study examines a magnetization reversal process in a [Co/Pdx]7/CoO/[Co/Pdy]7 thin-film composite, where an antiferromagnet is positioned between ferromagnetic layers of differing coercivities. The interfaces between the antiferromagnet and ferromagnets generate the exchange bias effect. The combination of soft and hard ferromagnetic films induces exchange-spring-like behavior, while the specific Co/Pd multilayer configuration yields significant out-of-plane magnetic anisotropy. Our findings indicate that both the magnitude and polarity of the exchange bias anisotropy field depend on the magnetic moment arrangement within the antiferromagnetic layer. This specific ordering is driven by the spin orientation in adjacent ferromagnetic films, which itself varies according to the external magnetic field's direction and intensity.

The electronic properties of rhombohedral sp2-hybridized boron nitride (r-BN) were investigated using X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy. Data collected at the boron and nitrogen K-edges (1s) were analyzed through first-principles density functional theory calculations that incorporate final state effects via core-hole application. The study demonstrates that distinct 2D planar polytypes—specifically rhombohedral, twinned rhombohedral, hexagonal, and turbostratic BN—can be differentiated based on their chemical shifts. Notably, the chemical shift at the boron 1s-edge is particularly pronounced in the turbostratic form. These findings suggest that the band gap can be modulated through the superposition of various polytypes and the stacking of lattice planes.

This study introduces a method for producing Co-Cu alloys with soft magnetic characteristics using high-pressure torsion. Deforming these alloys, which originate from initial powder mixtures containing over 70 wt.% Co, yields nanocrystalline, supersaturated single-phase microstructures. Isochronal annealing up to 400°C demonstrates exceptional microstructural stability; decomposition into two fcc-phases occurs only at 600°C. SQUID measurements indicate that coercivity remains significantly lower than that of bulk-Co across all examined conditions. To elucidate the magnetic behavior, magnetic force microscopy was employed for a quantitative analysis of the magnetic microstructure, correlating structural changes with coercivity variations. The findings reveal that the increase in coercivity is attributable to a magnetic hardening effect associated with spinodal decomposition.

This paper investigates a mobile molecular communication (MC) system comprising two mobile nanomachines—a transmitter and a receiver—driven by Brownian motion and a positive drift velocity within a realistic blood-vessel-like flow environment. To address the nonlinear dynamics of the nanomachines, an extended Kalman filter is utilized to estimate the transmitter-receiver distance. Subsequently, to maintain a stable count of received molecules for bit 1, a power control strategy is implemented, adjusting the number of transmitted molecules based on the estimated distance and residual channel molecules from prior transmissions. The optimal detection threshold is derived by minimizing the error probability. Simulations confirm that a fixed optimal detection threshold is effective for this power control scheme in mobile MC, and the bit error rate (BER) performance of the proposed approach is validated through simulation results.

Videos are susceptible to tampering attacks that distort their meaning and mislead viewers. While prior forgery detection methods identify minute indicators to pinpoint altered regions, adversaries can bypass these defenses by erasing such clues through compression or blurring. This study introduces a video watermarking network designed for tampering localization. We concurrently train a 3D-UNet-based watermark embedding model and a decoder that forecasts the tampering mask, ensuring that the embedding perturbations remain nearly imperceptible. Given the lack of an off-the-shelf differentiable video codec simulator, we approximate video compression by combining simulation results from other common attacks, such as JPEG compression and blurring. Experimental findings show that our approach produces watermarked videos with high imperceptibility while robustly and accurately detecting tampered areas even after they have been attacked.

Achieving wearable, unobtrusive monitoring and prediction of epileptic seizures could greatly enhance patient quality of life, yet this remains an unattained objective due to hurdles in wearable device design and real-time detection. While Hyperdimensional (HD) computing has emerged as a promising machine learning paradigm for wearable applications, standard HD methods currently fall short compared to state-of-the-art algorithms in epilepsy detection. This underperformance likely stems from the inherent complexity of seizure signatures across biosignals like EEG, their high personalization, and the severe imbalance between seizure and non-seizure instances. Although various strategies to enhance HD learning—such as iterative (multi-pass) learning, multi-centroid learning, and weighted sample learning ("OnlineHD")—have been proposed in literature, few have been evaluated on the specific challenge of epileptic seizure detection. Consequently, it remains uncertain if these approaches can elevate HD performance to match current benchmarks like random forests. In this study, we implement and evaluate various learning strategies, individually and in combination, focusing on detection accuracy alongside memory and computational efficiency. Our results demonstrate that a hybrid approach combining multi-centroid and multi-pass learning successfully achieves random forest-level performance on a highly unbalanced dataset simulating real-world seizure detection scenarios.

The J-PARC Hadron Experimental Facility was built to investigate the origins and evolution of cosmic matter using high-intensity particle beams. Over the last ten years, the facility has yielded numerous significant findings in particle and nuclear physics. To extend research into previously uncharted territories, the extension of the Hadron Experimental Facility has been the subject of extensive discussion. This white paper outlines the physics behind this expansion, focusing on addressing key questions in strangeness nuclear physics, hadron physics, and flavor physics.

Scoring rules assess the quality of predictions expressed as probability distributions. A scoring rule is considered strictly proper when its expected value reaches a unique minimum at the true probability distribution. The logarithmic scoring rule is one of the most recognized and frequently applied strictly proper scoring rules. This paper introduces an adaptation of the logarithmic scoring rule tailored for competing risks data and demonstrates that it retains strict propriety under non-informative censoring.

Detecting heads in indoor video feeds is a critical step for monitoring building occupancy. Although deep learning models have made significant strides in general object detection, they often struggle within the complexities of indoor environments. These surveillance videos typically feature cluttered backgrounds where heads appear at small scales and exhibit varied poses. This paper introduces the Motion-aware Pseudo Siamese Network (MPSN), an end-to-end solution that utilizes head motion cues to guide deep models in extracting effective features for indoor scenarios. By incorporating the pixel-wise difference between consecutive frames as an auxiliary input, MPSN effectively amplifies human head motion signals while filtering out irrelevant background elements. Compared to previous approaches, MPSN delivers superior performance on two indoor video datasets. Experimental results indicate that the method successfully suppresses static background objects and emphasizes moving targets, particularly human heads. We further compare various techniques for capturing head motion, highlighting the simplicity and flexibility of MPSN. To verify robustness, we performed adversarial experiments using mathematical small perturbations for robust model selection. Finally, to demonstrate its applicability in building control systems, we applied MPSN to occupancy counting tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/pl-share/MPSN.

First-person wearable cameras continuously record unscripted interactions between users and their surroundings, including objects, people, and scenes, which reveal personal and relational patterns. Among these, interactions involving food events are a notable preference. Since regulating food intake and its timing is crucial for disease prevention, this study proposes a smart model designed to identify a person's visits to food locations throughout the day. Built upon a deep end-to-end framework for automatic recognition of dining venues, the model analyzes egocentric photo streams. Specifically, we employ multi-scale Atrous convolution networks to extract key features related to food places from input images. The proposed system is evaluated using a proprietary in-house dataset named "EgoFoodPlaces," and experimental results demonstrate promising performance in classifying food locations within egocentric photo streams.

Spatio-temporally modulated impedance surfaces represent promising candidates for generating radiating waves with arbitrary eigenstates by violating momentum and energy conservation laws. This work introduces a theoretical framework utilizing the holographic technique and generalized Floquet-wave expansion to analyze these modulated surfaces. The holographic approach determines the necessary impedance distribution to attain specific momentum targets, while temporal modulation shifts eigenvalues and alters the radiation frequency. The proposed analytical model enables accurate calculation of eigenvalues under combined spatial and temporal modulations, thereby allowing for the prediction of propagation mechanisms for both bounded and radiative states. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that temporal modulation induces a Doppler shift and nonreciprocal behavior within the hologram. System nonreciprocity is verified by plotting the antenna dispersion diagram and observing the asymmetric displacement of the dispersion curve resulting from temporal modulation. Finally, the beam scanning capabilities of these structures were also examined.

This study introduces an Eulerian-Lagrangian (EL) Runge-Kutta (RK) discontinuous Galerkin (DG) approach for solving wave equations. Built upon the ELDG framework developed for transport problems [J. Comput. Phys. 446: 110632, 2021], the method tracks solutions along characteristic approximations within the DG setting, thereby enabling significantly larger time steps while maintaining stability. Since the wave equation can be expressed as a first-order hyperbolic system, a direct application of ELDG would involve converting to characteristic variables, evolving them across characteristic-specific space-time regions, and then reverting to the original variables. However, such a direct approach fails to guarantee mass conservation in general scenarios. To address this, we develop a mass-conserving semi-discrete ELDG scheme by decomposing each variable into two components linked to distinct characteristic families. Consequently, four separate quantities are evolved using the EL method and subsequently recombined to update the solution. The fully discrete scheme is constructed using method-of-lines RK techniques, where intermediate RK solutions are updated on the background mesh. Numerical experiments on 1D and 2D wave equations demonstrate the method's efficacy, highlighting its high-order spatial and temporal accuracy, stability with large time steps, and adherence to mass conservation.

This study examines few-boson systems confined within finite one-dimensional multi-well traps, spanning the entire interaction range from uncorrelated to fermionized states. Ground state characteristics are analyzed using the numerically exact Multi-Configurational Time-Dependent Hartree method. In cases of commensurate filling, we identify signatures of localization across various observables—including reduced density matrices, fluctuations, and momentum distribution—as interaction strength grows.
