We have derived a revised energy formalism that incorporates this effect and examined its implications for neutron star binary formation and the engulfment of planets and brown dwarfs by host stars. This new framework indicates that the companion mass needed to eject the envelope can be up to 50% lower, significantly altering common-envelope evolution outcomes. Furthermore, energy deposition in the outer envelope—which influences transient luminosity and duration—can be approximately seven times greater. Thus, common-envelope efficiency values exceeding unity, often deemed unphysical, may actually reflect an incomplete description of energy deposition rather than a physical impossibility. This updated formalism offers enhanced insights for interpreting stellar merger events and common-envelope observations and simulations.

Topological magnons represent emergent quantum spin excitations characterized by linearly crossing magnon bands at specific points known as nodes, mirroring the behavior of fermions in topological electronic systems. Although experimental confirmation of three-dimensional topological magnons has remained elusive, we present direct spectroscopic evidence of their existence in the 3D antiferromagnet Cu$_{3}$TeO$_{6}$. Through inelastic neutron scattering measurements of spin excitations, we demonstrate the coexistence of symmetry-protected Dirac nodes and triply degenerate nodes, the latter arising from three-component magnons that extend beyond the standard Dirac-Weyl framework. Theoretical calculations indicate that the observed topological magnon band structure aligns well with linear-spin-wave theory derived from a Hamiltonian primarily governed by the nearest-neighbour exchange interaction $J_1$. Consequently, Cu$_{3}$TeO$_{6}$ is established as a model system for the simultaneous occurrence of Dirac and triply degenerate magnonic nodal excitations, illustrating an exotic topological state of matter and offering a new platform for investigating topological properties in quantum materials.

We investigate a free field realization of the elliptic quantum algebra $U_{q,p}(sl_3^)$ valid for any level $k$. Specifically, we construct the free field representation of the elliptic analogue of the Drinfeld current corresponding to this algebra at arbitrary level $k$. Furthermore, in the limit where $p \to 0$ and $q \to 1$, our realization recovers the Wakimoto realization for the affine Lie algebra $sl_3^$.

Focusing on stratified case-control designs involving a binary primary variable, we derive the formula for sampling-induced distortion affecting the logistic model parameters of a secondary variable. This approach is especially pertinent for mediation analysis—potentially within a causal framework—using stratified case-control data where both the outcome and mediator are binary. Our identification findings facilitate the application of M-estimation and Maximum Likelihood estimation. Subsequently, a simulation study demonstrates the efficiency gains of these estimators for both outcome and mediator parameters compared to existing weighting-based methods. As an illustrative application, we reanalyze a German case-control dataset to examine whether the impact of reduced immunocompetency on listeriosis onset is mediated by gastric acid suppressor intake.

Although many existing speech technology systems function effectively in environments with multiple active speakers, they typically rely on the assumption that the count of concurrent speakers is known, a constraint that often does not hold in real-world scenarios. This study introduces a real-time, single-channel attention-guided Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) designed to estimate the number of active speakers during overlapping speech. The system utilizes a CNN to extract high-level features from the speech spectrum, after which an attention mechanism condenses these features into a compact vector while retaining essential data. A fully connected network then performs the classification of active speakers. Experiments conducted on simulated overlapping speech from the WSJ corpus demonstrate that the attention-based approach improves performance by nearly 3% absolute compared to conventional temporal average pooling. The proposed Attention-guided CNN achieves 76.15% Weighted Accuracy and average Recall, along with 75.80% Precision, even on speech segments as brief as 20 frames (200 ms). Furthermore, in offline scenarios involving input signals longer than 100 frames (1 second), all classification metrics for the attention-guided model surpass 92%.

The dynamics of wetting and dewetting are primarily governed by the velocity field in the vicinity of contact lines. Observations on water droplets indicate that adding surfactants reduces the dynamic receding contact angle, even at concentrations well below the critical micelle concentration (CMC). To elucidate why surfactants exert such a profound influence on drop dynamics, we developed a specialized setup using an inverted microscope, where a stationary aqueous drop is subjected to horizontal motion of a transparent substrate. By employing astigmatism particle tracking velocimetry, we tracked the three-dimensional displacement of tracer particles within the flow. Our study examines how surfactants modify flow dynamics near the receding contact line of a moving drop at capillary numbers around $10^{-6}$. We find that even at surfactant concentrations $c$ significantly lower than the CMC ($c \ll$ CMC), Marangoni stresses drastically alter the flow. Initially, we discuss our findings using a 2D model that accounts for advective and diffusive surfactant transport, deriving estimates for the magnitude and scaling of the Marangoni stress. Both modeling and experimental results confirm that a minute surface tension gradient of a few $\mu N \, m^{-1}$ is sufficient to significantly change the flow profile. The variation of Marangoni stress with distance from the contact line implies that the 2D advection-diffusion model must be expanded into a comprehensive 3D model. This phenomenon is ubiquitous, as surfactants are present in numerous technical and natural dewetting processes, either intentionally or as contaminants.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) provide an efficient solution for image-to-image translation, unlocking new potential in medical imaging by converting images between different modalities cost-effectively. While cycle loss is the primary mechanism for handling unpaired datasets, it can sometimes create a mismatch between input and output distributions despite its ability to capture underlying data patterns. This study explores the hypothesis that image quality can be predicted by analyzing the latent representations within the GAN bottleneck. By introducing noise into the latent space to generate multiple outputs, we measure representation strength based on the variance of the resulting images: a robust representation yields minimal changes even when corrupted. Our findings indicate that this approach can i) forecast uncertain regions in synthesized images and ii) flag samples unsuitable for downstream applications, such as liver segmentation.

We have created two hybrid quantum-classical classifier models designed for the $t\bar{t}H(b\bar{b})$ classification task, specifically tailored for Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Together with existing research, our findings demonstrate that Quantum Machine Learning (QML) can match or surpass conventional machine learning methods in scenarios with limited training data, even when constrained by the small number of qubits currently available. To address hardware limitations in both simulations and physical quantum processors, we explored various feature reduction techniques and evaluated their effects on the performance of both classical and quantum models. Furthermore, we examined two distinct implementations of QML models that represent the primary supervised learning approaches today: a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM), which is kernel-based, and a Variational Quantum Circuit (VQC), which employs a variational strategy.

We construct a formal model to analyze how varying policymaking contexts influence the reform choices and execution of officials driven by career concerns. When such concerns are intense, officials may inefficiently launch reforms merely to signal alignment with the central government. To enhance the quality of reform policymaking, the central government must hold officials accountable for policy results. We show that this accountability can be achieved by mandating the public disclosure of policy outcomes while keeping implementation details confidential. Under these conditions, officials can only signal their congruence through successful policy results, creating a strong incentive to execute reforms effectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that outcome-based accountability is not feasible in alternative policymaking environments. Finally, we apply these findings to China's recent approach to decentralized reform policymaking.

Existing multi-object trackers typically prioritize short-term tracking and rely on complex deep learning systems that often fail to meet real-time requirements, rendering them unsuitable for video surveillance. This paper introduces a long-term, multi-face tracking architecture designed for crowded environments where faces are frequently the only visible body parts. Leveraging recent advancements in face detection and recognition, our system achieves robust long-term tracking while remaining highly resilient to occlusions and varied motion. Operating on a tracking-by-detection framework, it integrates a rapid short-term visual tracker with a new online tracklet reconnection strategy based on rank-based face verification. This rank-based constraint maximizes inter-class distance between tracklets and minimizes error propagation from incorrect reconnections. Furthermore, a correction module is incorporated to rectify past assignments without incurring additional computational overhead. We introduce specialized metrics for evaluating long-term tracking performance and publicly release a dataset comprising 10 manually annotated videos totaling 8 minutes and 54 seconds. Experimental results confirm the robustness of our proposed modules and demonstrate that, in such challenging scenarios, our approach produces tracks up to 50% longer than current state-of-the-art deep learning trackers.

This project introduces the use of Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks (CycleGANs) to create vivid, personalized visualizations of climate change impacts. By training our model on street-level imagery of homes before and after extreme weather events—such as floods and forest fires—we establish a mapping that can be applied to locations that have not yet faced such disasters. This visual transformation is combined with long-term climate model projections (spanning 50 years) to estimate the likelihood and nature of future climate events, thereby making the future more tangible for viewers. Ultimately, our goal is to empower individuals to make better-informed decisions regarding their climate future by fostering a visceral understanding of these effects while upholding scientific credibility through the integration of established climate projections.

Let $D$ be a weighted oriented graph with edge ideal $I(D)$. We demonstrate that if $D$ contains an induced odd cycle of length $2n+1$ and satisfies specific conditions, then the $(n+1)$-th symbolic power of $I(D)$ is distinct from its $(n+1)$-th ordinary power. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the equality of ordinary and symbolic powers for the edge ideal of a weighted oriented graph where every edge belongs to an induced odd cycle. We also characterize weighted naturally oriented unicyclic graphs featuring a unique odd cycle, as well as those with even cycles, regarding the equality of their ordinary and symbolic powers. Additionally, by defining $D^{\prime}$ as the graph derived from $D$ by assigning trivial weights to sinks with non-trivial weights, we prove that the symbolic powers of $I(D)$ and $I(D^{\prime})$ exhibit analogous behavior. Finally, for any weighted oriented star graph $D$, we show that the $s$-th symbolic power equals the $s$-th ordinary power for all integers $s \geq 2$.

The widespread use of offensive language on social networks has negatively impacted society, particularly by fostering abusive online behavior, making the urgent detection and containment of such content essential. Although prior research indicates that incorporating community structure features enhances offensive language detection performance, existing models often treat these structures in isolation, which significantly hinders their effectiveness. This paper introduces CT-OLD, an end-to-end detection framework that integrates both community structure and text features. Specifically, community structure is directly extracted via a graph attention network layer, while text embeddings are sourced from BERT's final hidden layer; these are fused using attention mechanisms and position encoding. Additionally, user features are represented by incorporating user opinions derived from historical behavior, which proves superior to text-based representations. Furthermore, addressing the class imbalance between users and tweets prevalent in common datasets—which restricts model generalization—we have constructed and released a new dataset with a balanced user distribution. Our approach surpasses baseline methods, achieving an F1 score of 89.94%. These findings demonstrate that the end-to-end model effectively captures latent information from both community structures and text, confirming that user historical behavior is the optimal metric for representing user opinions.

Ensembles are a widely adopted technique for enhancing the performance of discriminative CNNs, where combining multiple networks trained with distinct initializations yields significant improvements. This paper explores the application of GAN ensembles, noting that the unique characteristics of GANs enable novel ensemble construction strategies. The first approach leverages the dynamic nature of the generator in the GAN minimax game; even after reaching optimality, the generator continues to evolve. Consequently, ensembles can be formed from the same initial network by selecting models trained for varying numbers of iterations. These "self-ensembles" offer a faster training process compared to traditional methods. The second strategy, known as cascade GANs, diverts data poorly modeled by the initial GAN to a subsequent network. Experiments on the CIFAR10 dataset demonstrate that GAN ensembles produce probability distributions that better approximate the underlying data distribution. Furthermore, these performance gains are achieved with minimal additional computational overhead.

Determining the adequacy of clusters and identifying the optimal cluster count remain challenging tasks. To evaluate cluster homogeneity, the study proposes utilizing a membership matrix alongside a degree of membership matrix. Additionally, optimizing the cluster number involves maximizing the ratio of the overall degree of membership at a cluster lag of 1, while a threshold factor applied to the degree of membership further ensures homogeneous clusters. Simulation results compare the proposed approach against established methods, demonstrating its applicability to outputs from both hierarchical and k-means clustering algorithms.

Previous work by Dosi and a recent article by the author demonstrated that for nilpotent Lie algebras, there exists a sheaf of Frech\'et-Arens-Michael algebras defined on the character space, corresponding to "non-commutative holomorphic functions" in the complex setting and "non-commutative smooth" functions in the real setting. Extending this result, we construct analogous sheaves for the Lie algebra of the group of affine transformations of the line—the simplest non-nilpotent solvable Lie algebra—over a specific set of representations, covering both the holomorphic and smooth cases.

Driven by the growing intricacy of configuring and optimizing machine learning models, the field of automated machine learning (AutoML) has developed significantly over the last ten years. Nevertheless, existing tools like Auto-WEKA and Auto-sklearn primarily address traditional ML tasks, such as classification and regression. This work represents the inaugural effort to provide a unified AutoML framework for the majority of scenarios encompassed by multi-target prediction (MTP), including multi-label classification, multivariate regression, multi-task learning, dyadic prediction, matrix completion, and zero-shot learning. By integrating DeepMTP, a versatile deep learning architecture for MTP, with established hyperparameter optimization (HPO) techniques, we achieve automated problem selection and model tuning. Comprehensive benchmarking across various datasets and MTP configurations reveals instances where certain HPO methods surpass others in performance.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks, and various defense strategies have been developed to enhance their robustness, with adversarial training proving particularly effective. Despite existing preliminary insights, the specific architectural configurations that maximize robustness remain unclear. This paper bridges that gap by thoroughly examining how network width and depth influence the robustness of adversarially trained DNNs. Our key findings include: 1) increased model capacity does not guarantee improved robustness; 2) reducing capacity in the network's final stages can enhance robustness; and 3) given a fixed parameter budget, there is an optimal architectural setup for maximizing robustness. Furthermore, we offer a theoretical explanation for why these configurations are beneficial. These insights can guide the design of more robust DNNs. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/HanxunH/RobustWRN}.

In the context of multichannel speech enhancement, this letter introduces a robust maximum likelihood distortionless response (MLDR) beamformer, termed the CGGD-MLDR beamformer. This approach models speech sparse priors using a complex generalized Gaussian distribution. The proposed method can be viewed as an extension of the minimum power distortionless response (MPDR) beamformer and its enhanced variants. Furthermore, for narrowband scenarios, the beamformer simplifies to the minimum dispersion distortionless response beamformer, originally derived via $\ell_p$-norm minimization. The mechanisms underlying the beamformer's enhanced robustness are explicitly explained, and experimental outcomes demonstrate its superior performance in improving PESQ scores.

We establish a semantic sufficient condition ensuring that every finite-satisfiable formula within a specific PCTL fragment admits a model containing at most a doubly exponential number of states; this implies that the finite satisfiability problem for the fragment resides within 2-EXPSPACE. This condition mandates a particular type of "progress" within non-bottom strongly connected components (SCCs) that contribute to the formula's satisfaction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this condition applies to PCTL fragments that exceed the capabilities of current methodologies.

The Affine (Jump) Diffusion (AD) class has achieved widespread adoption among researchers and practitioners thanks to its closed-form characteristic function. Nevertheless, a linear constraint proves inadequate for accurate and consistent option pricing. Any non-affine model must satisfy the rigorous demand for rapid calibration, a task that is frequently difficult. This work concentrates on Randomized AD (RAnD) models, which incorporate exogenous stochasticity into model parameters. Since randomization operates outside the standard affine framework, it generalizes the approach by loosening affinity constraints. This generic method can be applied to any model parameter and depends on the existence of moments for the associated randomizer. RAnD offers flexibility while retaining the benefits of fast calibration and established large-step Monte Carlo simulations typically available for AD processes. The article explores both theoretical and practical dimensions of the RAnD method, including characteristic function derivations, simulation techniques, and sensitivity computations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of randomized stochastic volatility models in consistently pricing options on the S&P 500 and VIX.

We establish the existence of a martingale $f\in H_p$ for which the subsequence $\{L_{2^n}f\}$ of Nörlund logarithmic means, relative to the Walsh system, fails to remain bounded in the weak-$L_p$ Lebesgue space when $0<p<1$. Additionally, we demonstrate that for every $f\in L_p(G)$ with $p\geq 1$, the sequence $L_{2^n}f$ converges to $f$ at each Lebesgue point $x$. Furthermore, several novel related inequalities are obtained.

This work establishes the mathematical framework for the predictive accuracy index and defines the integral average transform. We demonstrate the connection between our definition and two-variable kernels, $K({\bf y},{\bf x})$. As an illustrative application, we show that solving the Poisson equation via integration against the fundamental solution of the Laplace operator can be reinterpreted as integrating averages of the forcing term over balls. Consequently, we derive a new integral representation for the solution to the Poisson equation. This research is motivated by the necessity to achieve a deeper mathematical understanding of the prediction accuracy index, which is employed to detect hot spots in predictive security and related fields.

Quantum samplers are thought to be able to efficiently sample from distributions that are intractable for classical computers. We examine a sampler based on the classical Ising model, which is nonadaptive and thus suitable for experimental implementation. Under a reasonable conjecture, achieving classical sampling of this model up to additive errors is known to be difficult. We introduce a trap-based verification protocol for quantum supremacy that requires the verifier to prepare only single-qubit states. This verification occurs on the same square-lattice model as the original sampler, incurring only constant overhead. Subsequently, we refine the verification scheme in two distinct ways using fault tolerance while maintaining nonadaptivity. The first approach utilizes error correction with a lower overhead and the same threshold as universal quantum computation. The second employs error detection, resulting in a higher overhead but an improved threshold of 1.97%. We demonstrate that classically sampling up to additive errors remains likely hard in both scenarios. Our findings are relevant to other sampling tasks, such as the Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) model, and should aid both near-term and long-term efforts to experimentally demonstrate quantum supremacy.

Current neural vocoders produce high-fidelity speech when ample training data exists. While speaker-dependent (SD) models typically surpass speaker-independent (SI) models in performance, gathering extensive data for a specific target speaker is often unfeasible in practical scenarios. To address this data scarcity, this paper introduces a data augmentation technique leveraging speaker representations and similarity metrics derived from speaker verification. This approach identifies utterances from an external corpus that share a similar speaker identity with the target and merges them with the limited available target data to facilitate SD vocoder adaptation. Evaluation results demonstrate that, compared to adaptation using only restricted target data, the vocoder trained with augmented data achieves superior synthesis quality and speaker similarity.

Quantum computing leverages the principles of quantum physics to transform information processing and computation. Although the final stages of computation may involve non-unitary measurements, quantum computers fundamentally operate using physical quantum gates that process information unitarily. Their applications span a wide range, from established quantum algorithms to quantum machine learning and neural networks, with the latter being especially significant due to its connection to artificial intelligence. However, developing quantum neural networks presents substantial technological hurdles, as emulating neuronal behavior necessitates non-unitary operations. In classical neural networks, the breakthrough of the memristor—a passive circuit element that retains a memory of its history through resistive hysteresis, enabling nonlinear gate operations—was pivotal. While several proposals for a quantum memristor have emerged, they all currently face significant practical limitations. This study introduces and experimentally validates a new quantum-optical memristor built on integrated photonics and designed to operate on single photons. We characterize its memristive properties and demonstrate its practical utility by numerically simulating quantum reservoir computing tasks, where our device shows a distinct advantage over classical architectures. Building on recent advances in photonic circuits for neural networks, this device has the potential to serve as a foundational component for immediate and near-term quantum neuromorphic systems.

This study examines secure multiuser communication systems enhanced by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) that are affected by hardware impairments (HIs). The goal is to jointly optimize the base station's (BS) beamforming vectors and the RIS's reflecting element phase shifts to maximize the weighted minimum secrecy rate (WMSR), adhering to BS transmission power limits and RIS unit-modulus constraints. To solve this optimization challenge, the problem is decomposed into two manageable subproblems, which are then addressed alternately using the block coordinate descent (BCD) technique. Two distinct approaches are introduced for resolving these subproblems: the first converts them into second-order cone programming (SOCP) problems solvable via CVX, while the second employs the Minorization-Maximization (MM) algorithm. Under the MM approach, a concave approximation serving as a lower bound for the original objective is derived, transforming the subproblems into simpler surrogate forms with closed-form solutions. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed robust transmission strategy outperforms existing nonrobust designs, and the MM algorithm demonstrates significantly lower computational complexity compared to the SOCP-based method.

A primary challenge in image processing involves approximating images degraded by blurring, a task categorized into non-blind and blind deconvolution problems. Blind deconvolution is computationally more demanding than its non-blind counterpart because it requires estimating both the original image and the point spread function (PSF). This paper introduces a coarse-to-fine iterative algorithm utilizing $l_0-\alpha l_1$ regularization and framelet transforms to estimate the PSF. The framelet transform enhances the restored kernel by decomposing it across various frequencies, while the proposed model replaces the standard gradient operator with a fractional gradient operator. Evaluated on diverse image types, including text, faces, and natural scenes, the results demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in addressing blind deconvolution issues.

We derive the few-shot continual learning task from fundamental principles, proposing that executive function evolved as a contrastive value policy. This mechanism resamples and relabels perceptual data through hindsight summarization to reduce attended prediction error, functioning similarly to online prompt engineering. Enabled by a memory policy and a pretrained network with inductive biases for a grammar of learning, the system is trained to maximize evolutionary survival. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this model of executive function can implement hypothesis testing as a stream of consciousness, potentially explaining both human few-shot learning capabilities and neuroanatomical observations.

It is now widely recognized that Dirac fermions interacting with non-Abelian gauge theories can experience an Anderson-type localization transition. This phenomenon impacts eigenmodes within the lowest segment of the Dirac spectrum, which are most critical for the low-energy dynamics of these systems. In this review, we examine various facets of this behavior, primarily utilizing lattice gauge theory methods. Specifically, we explore the relationship between the localization transition and finite-temperature transitions responsible for fermion deconfinement, as well as the restoration of chiral symmetry that is spontaneously broken at low temperatures. We also address the universality of the transition, its link to topological gauge field excitations (instantons) and their associated fermionic zero modes. Although the primary emphasis is on Quantum Chromodynamics, we further analyze how the localization transition manifests in other related models featuring varying fermionic configurations (including the quenched approximation), distinct gauge groups, and different space-time dimensions. Finally, we propose speculations regarding the physical significance of this localization transition within these theoretical frameworks.

Utilizing a substantial spectroscopic dataset of approximately 4,300 RR Lyrae stars, which includes measurements of metallicity, systemic radial velocity, and distance, we conduct a comprehensive examination of the chemical and kinematic characteristics of the Galactic halo. This analysis yields the metallicity distribution function (MDF) relative to radius $r$ and the velocity anisotropy parameter $\beta$ profiles across various metallicity groups. Both the chemical and kinematic findings indicate that the Galactic halo consists of two distinct components: an inner halo and an outer halo. The transition radius at approximately 30 kpc aligns with the previously identified break in the stellar halo's density distribution. The inner region is dominated by a metal-rich population exhibiting extreme radial anisotropy ($\beta \sim 0.9$), a signature consistent with the ``{\it Gaia}-Enceladus-Sausage'' (GES) event; consequently, we attribute this inner component primarily to stars deposited by this ancient merger. Our results suggest that GES possessed a slightly negative metallicity gradient. Conversely, metal-poor populations within the inner halo display a long tail in the MDF and an anisotropy of $\beta \sim 0.5$, matching the outer halo's profile. The outer halo's MDF is notably broad, featuring multiple weak peaks, with a $\beta$ value near 0.5 across all metallicities.

A k-queue layout is a specific linear arrangement of a graph where the vertex order avoids (k+1)-rainbows, defined as k+1 independent edges that form pairwise nested pairs. The primary objective is to find the queue number of a graph, which corresponds to the smallest k allowing for a feasible k-queue layout. In 2020, Dujmović et al. [J. ACM, 67(4), 22:1-38] proved that the queue number for planar graphs does not exceed 49, thereby confirming a longstanding conjecture by Heath, Leighton, and Rosenberg. Their breakthrough relied on three distinct methods: (i) an algorithm generating straight-line drawings of outerplanar graphs where the y-distance between any two adjacent vertices is 1 or 2, (ii) an algorithm creating 5-queue layouts for planar 3-trees, and (iii) a decomposition of planar graphs into tripods. Building upon these techniques, the current work achieves the first non-trivial reduction in the upper bound, improving it from 49 to 42.

This study examines ejection mechanisms for two types of steady jets: those from black hole binaries in the low/hard state and those from SS433. For jets to extend to infinity, the specific energy of the ejected gas must be positive, whereas the accreted gas is typically assumed to have negative specific energy at the outer boundary of the accretion flow. To resolve this discrepancy in energy signs, we propose a model featuring two layers within the accretion flow, where one layer transfers sufficient energy to the other to render its specific energy positive. In the low/hard state scenario, the outer accretion ring is modeled as a two-layer system comprising a geometrically thick ADAF surrounding a geometrically thin disk, with the thin disk transitioning into an ADAF inwardly. Energy transfer is anticipated via turbulent mixing between these layers, with the upper layer expected to possess positive specific energy sufficient to achieve a terminal velocity of approximately 0.1$c$. Regarding SS433's steady jets, a slim disk is hypothesized to stratify into two layers due to photon diffusion perpendicular to the equatorial plane under advection-dominated conditions. In this configuration, the upper layer's specific energy is predicted to be positive, yielding a terminal velocity exceeding 0.2$c$. Finally, the jet ejection process near the black hole is analyzed for both two-layer scenarios, predicting a jet opening angle as narrow as 2°.

CLIC is a proposed linear $e^{+}e^{-}$ collider capable of reaching center-of-mass energies up to $3\,\textrm{TeV}$. Its primary scientific goals include precise measurements of the top quark and Higgs boson, alongside searches for physics beyond the Standard Model. Achieving these objectives necessitates that the vertex and tracking detectors possess spatial resolutions in the few-micrometer range and minimal material budgets, complemented by timing precision of a few nanoseconds to effectively suppress beam-induced backgrounds. Various hybrid silicon detector technologies are being investigated for the vertex detector, including dedicated readout ASICs, small-pitch active edge sensors, and capacitively coupled High-Voltage CMOS sensors. For the tracking detector, monolithic sensors are under consideration, with a prototype currently being designed using a CMOS process featuring a high-resistivity epitaxial layer. Additionally, designs based on a silicon-on-insulator process are being explored for both detector systems. All prototypes undergo evaluation through laboratory and beam tests, while newly developed simulation tools that integrate Geant4 and TCAD are employed to assess and optimize performance. This contribution provides an overview of the R&D program for the CLIC vertex and tracking detectors, emphasizing recent findings from these prototypes.

This work investigates generalized Hermite polynomials featuring rectangular matrix arguments, which play a significant role in multivariate statistical analysis and zonal polynomial theory. We demonstrate that these polynomials are ideal for formulating the Wiener-Ito chaos expansion of functionals linked to the spectral measure of Gaussian matrices. Specifically, we derive the Wiener chaos expansion for Gaussian determinants such as $\det(XX^T)^{1/2}$. Furthermore, we establish that when the rows of $X$ consist of i.i.d. centred Gaussian vectors with a specified covariance matrix, the projection coefficients of these determinants possess a geometric interpretation via the intrinsic volumes of ellipsoids. This result extends the findings of Kabluchko and Zaporozhets (2012) to arbitrary chaotic projection coefficients. Our proofs rely fundamentally on a key relationship between generalized Hermite and generalized Laguerre polynomials. In a subsequent section, we introduce a matrix extension of the classical Mehler's formula for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup and demonstrate that matrix-variate Hermite polynomials serve as eigenfunctions for these operators. Consequently, we derive an orthogonality relation for Hermite polynomials evaluated at correlated Gaussian matrices. Finally, we apply these findings to vectors of independent arithmetic random waves on the three-torus, notably proving a Central Limit Theorem within the high-energy regime for a generalized concept of total variation across the entire torus.

Deep Learning models exhibit two critical characteristics that render their real-world deployment risky: poor generalization beyond their training distribution and a tendency to display high confidence even when generating nonsensical outputs. Despite their immense capability in addressing complex, high-dimensional tasks, these combined traits undermine trust in their practical applications. To address this, the field has defined Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) Detection, a task aimed at identifying when a model encounters inputs outside its training scope. This paper presents DOODLER, a novel OOD Detection framework that directly exploits the very traits necessitating its existence. By training a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) alongside a Deep Learning model on identical data, the VAE learns to accurately reconstruct In-Distribution (ID) inputs while failing to reconstruct OOD inputs, thereby utilizing this failure mode for detection. Distinct from existing approaches, DOODLER relies on minimal assumptions regarding the availability of OOD datasets, facilitating more realistic application scenarios. Furthermore, it enables pixel-wise segmentation of input images based on OOD likelihood, with experimental results demonstrating that it matches or exceeds the performance of other methods operating under similar constraints.

When a software bug is reported, developers collaborate through discussion to find a solution, yet the answer often gets lost within extensive text, hindering understanding and slowing implementation. To accelerate resolution, we propose synthesizing a concise natural language summary of the solution from the discussion, which includes both text and source code. We constructed a corpus for this task using a new method to derive noisy supervision from repository changes associated with bug reports, thereby creating benchmarks. Additionally, we developed two systems capable of generating a description in real-time during an active discussion by detecting when sufficient context has accumulated. Through both automated and human evaluations, we determined that this task serves as an excellent testbed for complex reasoning within long, bimodal dialogue contexts.

Utilizing stellar mass density profiles derived from stacked HSC images of satellite galaxies relative to isolated central galaxies (ICGs) selected from SDSS/DR7 spectroscopic data at $z\sim0.1$, we analyze their distribution as a function of projected distance ($r_p$). We further quantify the projected stellar mass density profiles for ICGs and their stellar halos, while total mass distributions are determined through HSC weak lensing signals. ICGs account for the majority of mass within approximately $0.15R_{200}$. As $r_p$ increases up to $\sim0.15R_{200}$, the fractions of stellar mass to total mass decline; beyond this radius, these fractions remain nearly constant at less than 1%, suggesting that satellite radial distributions trace dark matter. For ICGs with masses exceeding $10^{10.5}M_\odot$, the total satellite stellar mass scales linearly with the host halo's virial mass ($M_{\ast,\mathrm{sat}} \propto M_{200}$), whereas the combined stellar mass of ICGs and diffuse halos follows a relation closer to $M_{\ast,\mathrm{ICG+diffuse}}\propto M_{200}^{1/2}$. Below $10^{10.5}M_\odot$, variations in $M_{200}$ occur more slowly as $M_{\ast,\mathrm{ICG+diffuse}}$ decreases. At a fixed stellar mass, red ICGs reside in more massive dark matter halos and host a greater number of satellites. Around $M_{200}\sim10^{12.7}M_\odot$, both the satellite stellar mass and the satellite mass fraction ($f_\mathrm{sat}$) are marginally higher for blue ICGs, potentially indicating their later formation. Furthermore, $f_\mathrm{sat}$ rises with increasing $M_{\ast,\mathrm{ICG+diffuse}}$ and $M_{200}$, exhibiting a stronger linear correlation with $M_{200}$. We present best-fitting formulas for these scaling relations, distinguishing between red and blue ICG populations.

Emerging advancements in AI-composed music facilitate novel avenues for collaborative creation and creativity. We introduce Artificial.fm, a proof-of-concept casual creator platform that integrates AI music generation, subjective user ratings, and personalized recommendations to manage the creation and curation of AI-generated tracks. Listeners can evaluate emerging songs to influence the trajectory of future musical output and tailor their preferences to explore the creative landscape more effectively. Functioning as a "slow creator" involving numerous human participants, Artificial.fm demonstrates how casual creators can harness large-scale human curation to collectively navigate possibility spaces. Furthermore, it serves as a case study for examining ownership considerations in such environments. This paper details the design and development of Artificial.fm and includes a legal analysis regarding the ownership of artifacts produced on the platform.

Since major search engines have relaxed exact-match requirements for sponsored search to include synonymous matches, retrieving synonymous keywords has emerged as a critical challenge. Given the scarcity of synonymous relationships between queries and keywords, traditional information retrieval methods are often inefficient. To address this, we introduce a novel retrieval framework based on quotient spaces. By treating keyword synonymy as a mathematical equivalence relation, we compress synonymous keywords into single representatives, thereby significantly reducing the size of the keyword repository. Retrieval is then performed directly between queries and these representatives using embedding techniques. To bridge the semantic gap inherent in this quotient space approach, we employ a single semantic Siamese network to identify both keyword-keyword and query-keyword synonymous relationships. Experimental results demonstrate that our quotient space-based method substantially improves synonymous keyword retrieval in terms of memory efficiency and recall. This approach has been successfully deployed in Baidu's online sponsored search system, resulting in significant revenue growth.

Since every household and individual has unique preferences, future domestic robots must be capable of reasoning about the sequential steps of daily tasks and adapting to specific user habits. To address this, we introduce the Transformer Task Planner (TTP), a system that derives high-level actions from demonstrations by utilizing object attribute-based representations. The TTP is pre-trained on diverse preferences, enabling it to generalize to unseen scenarios using just a single demonstration as a prompt within a simulated dishwasher loading scenario. Additionally, we showcase real-world dish rearrangement achieved with the TTP and a Franka Panda robotic arm, guided by a single human demonstration.

In recent years, agent-based and activity-based models for transportation simulation have garnered considerable interest, yet few studies offer a detailed representation of active travel modes like walking and cycling at a city-wide scale, where motorized transport often takes precedence. This paper introduces an open workflow for developing a multi-modal agent-based and activity-based transport simulation focused on Greater Melbourne, specifically detailing the calibration process for mode choice across driving, public transit, cycling, and walking. The simulation utilizes a synthetic population derived from the 2016 Census to represent Melbourne, with daily activities and trips informed by Victoria's 2016–18 travel survey data. The underlying road network encompasses all public roads accessible through the included travel modes. By comparing model outputs with real-world observations regarding mode share, road volume, travel time, and distance, this study demonstrates the model's suitability for analyzing traveler mode choice and road usage behavior.

Run-and-tumble particles, commonly used to model bacterial movement, also arise naturally in non-biological contexts, such as generating waves in the telegraph process. In this work, we employ a wave function to govern both their propulsion and tumbling. This quantum-active motion mimics the jittery behavior of Dirac electrons, known as Zitterbewegung, where the electron acts as a run-and-tumble particle with tumbling events occurring between chiralities. We visualize the resulting trajectories within diffraction and double-slit experiments for electrons, specifically deriving the time-of-arrival statistics at the detection screen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even without pure quantum guidance, run-and-tumble particles equipped with appropriate spacetime-dependent parameters can generate interference patterns.

Current state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) struggle to scale effectively with growing graph and model dimensions. In large-scale graphs, increasing model depth frequently triggers an exponential expansion of the receptive field. Beyond a shallow layer count, two primary obstacles arise: reduced expressivity caused by oversmoothing and prohibitive computational costs stemming from neighborhood explosion. We introduce a design principle that decouples depth from scope in GNNs: to represent a target entity (node or edge), we first isolate a bounded subgraph containing only critical neighbors, then apply a GNN of any depth to this localized structure. This approach prevents the global graph from degrading into "white noise" by smoothing the local neighborhood into informative representations instead. Theoretically, separating depth and scope enhances GNN expressivity across graph signal processing (GCN), function approximation (GraphSAGE), and topological learning (GIN) frameworks. Empirically, testing on seven graphs containing up to 110 million nodes across six backbone architectures demonstrates that this method yields substantial accuracy gains while reducing computational and hardware requirements by orders of magnitude.

For instance, the traditional Ljung-Box test evaluates only the autocorrelation function (ACF). However, time series may exhibit heteroscedasticity and thus fail to be i.i.d., yet still qualify as white noise since their ACF remains zero. A typical example of heteroscedasticity involves financial time series, where periods of high variance (financial crises) alternate with periods of low variance (calm markets). In such cases, the absolute values of the series terms do not constitute white noise. One approach involves conducting separate white noise tests for both the original and absolute values, such as applying Ljung-Box tests to each. This article introduces an omnibus test that integrates these two assessments and establishes a general framework for developing various i.i.d. tests. The proposed methods are applied to simulated data, encompassing both autoregressive linear and heteroscedastic scenarios.

For an MSO formula $\phi$ with free variables $x_1, \dots, x_k$, we can define a function $\# \phi$ that maps a word $w$ to the count of valuations satisfying $\phi$ within $w$. This paper introduces the class of $\mathbb{Z}$-linear combinations of these functions, termed $\mathbb{Z}$-polyregular functions, which exhibit a close relationship to the established class of polyregular functions. The primary contributions address two fundamental decision problems for this class: first, determining the minimal number $k \ge 0$ of free variables required to represent a function; and second, deciding whether a function can be defined via first-order formulas by generalizing the concept of residual automata and offering a novel semantic characterization grounded in aperiodicity. Additionally, the paper establishes connections between this class of functions and $\mathbb{Z}$-rational series.

The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) holds the title of the most sensitive ground-based, single-dish radio telescope globally. However, the initial HI spectra generated by FAST suffer from standing wave interference. To fully leverage FAST's capabilities for high-sensitivity observations, we developed an algorithm that integrates fast Fourier transforms with extreme envelope curves to automatically correct baseline distortions and eliminate standing waves. This method suppresses the amplified noise resulting from standing waves to near-ideal levels, ensuring no signal loss or the introduction of false signals. Consequently, the root mean square of the average baseline achieves approximately 8 mK, which is close to the theoretical sensitivity of ~6 mK for an HI spectrum acquired by FAST over an integration time of 335 minutes.

Social media serves as a crucial decentralized space for exchanging information and forming opinions, yet it often traps users in echo chambers where they encounter only content reinforcing their existing views, thereby excluding opposing perspectives. This study investigates these dynamics by examining the social network structures of contentious Twitter debates on climate change during 2019, utilizing unsupervised methods that require minimal computational resources. Focusing on retweet networks during a period of significant climate activism, we identified distinct echo chambers comprising both climate believers and skeptics based exclusively on user retweeting behaviors. Specifically, we analyzed the information sources consumed by the audiences of leading figures in the conversation. We observed that users sharing similar (or contrasting) ideologies exhibited significantly high (or low) overlap in their information chambers, creating a bimodal distribution. Furthermore, we were able to infer the ideological stance of previously unknown high-impact users by analyzing the composition of their audiences within these echo chambers. Our analysis revealed the ideological alignment of over half the retweeting population as either pro-climate or skeptical, while noting that cross-group communication remains limited. Although the structural patterns of these echo chambers remained consistent throughout the year, the specific users within them changed weekly, indicating that they are a stable emergent feature of the Twitter ecosystem. Notably, we detected a marked reduction in polarization and a substantial rise in the number of climate skeptics coinciding with the major #FridaysForFuture strikes in September 2019.

We introduce an optimization technique for automatically designing approximate multipliers that minimizes average error based on operand distributions. This multiplier delivers up to 50.24% greater accuracy than the best reproduced approximate multiplier in DNNs, while offering a 15.76% reduction in area, a 25.05% decrease in power consumption, and a 3.50% improvement in delay. In comparison to an exact multiplier, our design achieves 44.94%, 47.63%, and 16.78% reductions in area, power consumption, and delay, respectively, with negligible accuracy trade-offs. Furthermore, DNN accelerator modules utilizing our multiplier demonstrate up to 18.70% smaller area and 9.99% lower power consumption compared to the original implementations.

Medical image analysis utilizing machine learning relies heavily on data, yet biases within these datasets can be absorbed by models, thereby undermining their generalizability. While research into debiased models exists, practitioners and researchers struggle to detect implicit biases, resulting in a scarcity of reliable test sets for validating unbiased models. To address this, we introduce the concept of "data intrinsic bias" and propose a novel framework for identifying biases in medical image datasets. This framework consists of two primary components: KlotskiNet, which constructs a mapping to differentiate positive and negative samples based on background features, and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis (bdda), which offers a theoretical approach to determining bias attributes. Experiments across three datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the bias attributes identified by this framework.

Giorgi, Jim\'enez, and Novo (J Optim Theory Appl 171:70--89, 2016) recently proposed the approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (AKKT) condition for smooth multiobjective optimization, deriving both necessary and sufficient AKKT-type conditions for weak efficiency. This note extends those optimality results to locally Lipschitz multiobjective optimization via Mordukhovich subdifferentials. Additionally, we demonstrate that, under appropriate supplementary conditions, an AKKT condition implies a KKT condition.

This study presents a search for narrow, low-mass resonances decaying into quark-antiquark pairs, utilizing proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis employs a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ from 2016, focusing on scenarios where the resonance possesses high transverse momentum induced by the initial-state radiation of a hard photon. In this approach, the resonance decay products are reconstructed as a single large-radius jet exhibiting two-pronged substructure, with the signal manifesting as a localized excess in the jet invariant mass distribution. No evidence for such a resonance was found within the 10 to 125 GeV mass range, leading to the establishment of 95% confidence level upper limits on the coupling strengths of resonances decaying to quark pairs. Notably, these results, derived from a photon trigger strategy, constitute the first direct constraints on quark-antiquark resonance masses below 50 GeV achieved at a hadron collider.

The BESIII Collaboration has recently identified three resonances: $X(2232)$ with a mass of $2232 \pm 19 \pm 27$ MeV and a width of $93 \pm 53 \pm 20$ MeV, $X(2200)$ with a mass of $2200 \pm 11 \pm 17$ MeV and a width of $74 \pm 20 \pm 24$ MeV, and $X(2222)$ with a mass of $2222 \pm 7 \pm 2$ MeV and a width of $59 \pm 30 \pm 6$ MeV. Using the modified Godfrey-Isgur model to analyze the $\omega$ meson family's mass spectrum, we examined the two-body strong decays of these three states via two distinct $^3P_0$ model approaches. Our findings suggest that $X(2232)$, $X(2200)$, and $X(2222)$ are likely the same particle, specifically the $\omega(3D)$ state. This discovery holds significant value for completing the spectrum of $\omega$ mesons.

We establish a universal quantum exchange fluctuation theorem for multipartite systems with arbitrary coupling strengths by incorporating the informational impact of quantum measurement back-action. The resulting second law of thermodynamics, governing net entropy production, is constrained more tightly by the quantum mutual information of the conditional thermal state—a thermal state defined by the initial energy measurement. These findings clarify the significance of quantum correlations in heat exchange among multiple subsystems interacting with arbitrary coupling strengths.

Audio-Text retrieval systems use natural language queries to locate relevant audio files within a database, whereas Text-Audio retrieval uses an audio file to find corresponding textual descriptions. Although most existing research trains these systems on a single audio captioning dataset, the advantages of utilizing multiple datasets remain underexplored. Additionally, these systems must learn to align detailed sentences of variable length, spanning from a few seconds to several minutes. This study introduces a new framework and a curated dataset of approximately five thousand web-derived audio-text pairs named WavText5K. When used for training, WavText5K yields superior performance compared to other audio captioning datasets. Our proposed framework employs a text encoder, two audio encoders, and a contrastive learning objective to establish connections between language and audio; the dual audio encoders specifically facilitate the processing of variable-length audio. These contributions achieve state-of-the-art results, improving Text-Audio retrieval by 2% and 16% on the AudioCaps and Clotho datasets, respectively, and boosting Audio-Text retrieval by 6% and 23%.

A weight normalization technique, referred to as "pushing," is presented for weighted tree automata (wta) operating over commutative semifields. While this normalization maintains the recognized weighted tree language even for nondeterministic wta, it is particularly beneficial for bottom-up deterministic wta, facilitating both minimization and equivalence testing. In these contexts, strategically selecting weights for redistribution prior to normalization reduces general problems to their counterparts for bottom-up deterministic unweighted tree automata. This methodology mirrors the successful approach employed by Mohri and Eisner for minimizing deterministic weighted string automata. Furthermore, the proposed equivalence test for two wta, $M$ and $M'$, operates in $\mathcal O((\lvert M \rvert + \lvert M'\rvert) \cdot \log {(\lvert Q\rvert + \lvert Q'\rvert)})$ time, where $Q$ and $Q'$ denote the state sets of $M$ and $M'$, respectively, thereby enhancing the prior best complexity of $\mathcal O(\lvert M \rvert \cdot \lvert M'\rvert)$.

Recent investigations into networks spanning complex systems, from neural structures to social graphs, have uncovered a higher-order architecture characterized by aggregates of simplexes, including triangles, tetrahedrons, and larger cliques. Contemporary efforts focus on quantifying these concealed geometries through algebraic topology and advanced graph theory, alongside analyzing dynamic processes on simplicial complexes. In this work, we employ a recently developed model for the geometrical self-assembly of cliques to construct nano-networks of triangles, specifically examining field-driven spin reversal dynamics on these structures. Featuring antiferromagnetic interactions between Ising spins at the nodes, this assembly inherently supports geometric frustration, a phenomenon known to drive novel effects in condensed matter physics. Our dynamical model incorporates a parameter that gradually shifts the interaction regime from pairwise to triangle-based. Consequently, local spin frustration within individual triangles evolves into mesoscopic ordering dictated by the intricate arrangement of these triangles. We demonstrate how the equilibrium between these interaction types alters the hysteresis loop's shape. Furthermore, fluctuations in the associated Barkhausen noise serve as robust markers of self-organized criticality, a state triggered solely by the network's geometry in the absence of magnetic disorder.

This paper investigates the dynamical properties of non-autonomous stochastic hybrid systems featuring delays. Utilizing a generalized Krylov-Bogolyubov approach, we establish sufficient conditions for the existence of an evolution system of measures for such non-autonomous stochastic systems, alongside several easily verifiable criteria. We subsequently demonstrate a sufficient condition ensuring the convergence of these evolution systems of measures as the delay diminishes toward zero. Applying this abstract framework, we first prove the existence of evolution systems of measures for stochastic systems with time-varying delays arising from feedback control problems based on discrete-time state observations. Moreover, as the observation interval approaches zero, we show that every limit point of the sequence of evolution systems of measures for the non-autonomous stochastic system corresponds to an evolution system of measures for the limiting system.

Given the success of the Energy Mover's Distance in characterizing collider events, we investigate the broader domain of unbalanced optimal transport distances, with the Energy Mover's Distance serving as a specific instance. Both geometric and computational factors point toward the Hellinger-Kantorovich distance as the optimal choice; its Riemannian structure facilitates efficient linearization. Consequently, we introduce the particle linearized unbalanced Optimal Transport (pluOT) framework for collider events, built upon the linearized Hellinger-Kantorovich distance. Our results demonstrate its effectiveness in boosted jet tagging, establishing a flexible and computationally efficient optimal transport approach ideally tailored for collider physics.

Measurements from coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering (CE$
u$NS) experiments now offer a pathway to constrain neutrino physics beyond the standard model. Additionally, analyzing neutrino-electron scattering in the keV range enables the establishment of further limits on new physics. This work presents constraints on beyond standard model (BSM) phenomena—including tensor and vector non-standard interactions (NSIs) in the neutrino-quark sector, as well as light vector and scalar mediators—derived from CONUS germanium data. Leveraging the CONUS experiment's exceptionally low background levels at ionization energies below 1 keV, we have established the world's strongest limits on tensor NSIs from CE$
u$NS, constraining the associated new physics scale to exceed 360 GeV. Regarding vector NSIs, the derived limits are highly sensitive to the assumed ionization quenching factor in the detector material; smaller quenching factors significantly suppress potential signals for both the standard model CE$
u$NS process and vector NSIs. Moreover, competitive limits on scalar and vector mediators are achieved via the CE$
u$NS channel at reactor sites, probing coupling constants as low as $5\cdot10^{-5}$ for low-mass mediators under the currently favored quenching regime. Finally, incorporating neutrino-electron scattering yields even tighter constraints on mediator masses below $\sim1$ MeV and $\sim10$ MeV for scalar and vector mediators, respectively.

Anomalous Radiative Transfer (ART) theory extends classical radiative transfer principles. This tutorial demonstrates the implementation of Monte Carlo (MC) codes for simulating photon transport within anomalous media. The core methodology involves characterizing photon steps in a "non-classical" way, specifically when originating from fixed light sources or boundaries between regions with varying optical properties. Numerical examples illustrate that this approach is crucial for maintaining the invariance property of light propagation, thereby clarifying the significance of these specific step lengths. Furthermore, a notable advantage of applying the MC method to ART is the simplification of the architecture typically found in classical MC codes used in biomedical optics.

To address scalability challenges in high-class industrial applications, Metric Learning has garnered significant attention from both academic and non-academic sectors. However, these applications often rely on large-scale web-generated datasets that frequently contain noisy labels. Since existing literature primarily focuses on manually annotated data and neglects noise sensitivity, current Metric Learning systems struggle with such imperfections. This work introduces a novel Smooth Proxy-Anchor Loss designed to mitigate the impact of noisy labels. We propose a two-phase architecture: first, a confidence module calculates class probabilities for each sample, and second, these probabilities weight the samples' influence during embedding training, yielding robust representations. When evaluated on datasets with noisy labels against current state-of-the-art proxy-based and pair-based losses, our method achieved Recall@1 improvements of 2.63 and 3.29 over MultiSimilarity and Proxy-Anchor Loss, respectively, demonstrating superior performance in noisy labeling scenarios.

$\tau$ Sco, a magnetic B-type star within the Upper Sco association known for its well-documented nature, exhibits several unexpected traits. It displays a notably slow rotation rate alongside nitrogen enrichment, and its surface magnetic field is significantly more intricate than a simple dipole, a rarity among magnetic massive stars. Utilizing the CMFGEN radiative transfer code, we derived the star's fundamental parameters and surface abundances of CNO and helium. Subsequently, we applied MESA and GENEC stellar evolution models that incorporate surface magnetic field effects. To align $\tau$ Sco's observed properties with single-star models, rotational mixing efficiency must increase by a factor of 3 to 10, and magnetic braking efficiency by a factor of 10. While a decaying magnetic field scenario could account for the spin-down, the concurrent chemical enrichment contradicts the single-star hypothesis. Although prior studies have proposed a stellar merger origin, this scenario similarly struggles to explain the combination of slow rotation and nitrogen excess. Ultimately, the single-star pathway appears less viable for resolving these inconsistencies, whereas the merger hypothesis and other binary-evolution mechanisms necessitate further evaluation to determine if they can self-consistently account for $\tau$ Sco's observables.

We examine two algorithmic advancements that facilitate more reliable quantum simulations of model systems in high-energy physics and related fields using noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. The first approach involves the dimensional expressivity analysis of quantum circuits, enabling the creation of circuits that are both minimal in size and maximally expressive. The second approach focuses on efficiently mitigating readout errors inherent to quantum hardware. Together, these methods offer substantial enhancements for quantum simulations, particularly when employing variational quantum eigensolvers.

Understanding the environments of dwarf galaxies, such as the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), is gaining critical importance as upcoming surveys enhance sensitivity to low-mass systems at cosmological distances. Using zoom-in simulations from the Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) project, we investigated how LMC-mass halos ($M_{200m} \sim 10^{11}$ M$_\odot$) influence their satellite populations ($M_\star \geq 10^4$ M$_\odot$). Our results predict the presence of substantial hot coronas with temperatures around $10^5$ K and gas masses of approximately $10^{9.5}$ M$_\odot$. We detect clear signs of environmental quenching in dwarf satellites, especially those of intermediate mass ($M_\star = 10^{6-7}$ M$_\odot$). The gas properties of these objects point to ram pressure as the primary quenching mechanism, occasionally supplemented by star formation feedback. Satellites orbiting LMC-mass hosts mirror the stellar mass trend in quiescent fractions seen in Milky Way-mass hosts, where lower stellar mass correlates with a higher quiescent fraction. Furthermore, while nearby central galaxies exhibit a strongly bi-modal distribution of quenching times, satellites of LMC-mass hosts display a broader range of quenching timescales. Finally, we found significant tidal stellar structures around four of our six LMC analogs, indicating that stellar streams are likely common; these features stem from satellites on close orbits, stretch up to ~80 kpc from the host, and contain roughly $10^{6-7}$ M$_\odot$ of stars.

Using hybrid-kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, we investigate the time-dependent formation and evolution of a current sheet (CS) within a magnetized, collisionless, high-beta plasma. An initially tearing-stable Harris sheet is embedded in a continuously driven incompressible flow, causing its characteristic thickness to diminish over time. As the CS thins, the reconnecting field strengthens, and adiabatic invariance in the inflowing fluid generates a field-aligned pressure anisotropy characterized by excess perpendicular pressure. In high-beta conditions, this anisotropy triggers the mirror instability, which distorts the reconnecting field at ion-Larmor scales and significantly reduces the CS's effective thickness. Consequently, tearing modes with wavelengths comparable to the mirror scale become unstable, initiating reconnection on smaller scales and earlier than if the CS had maintained its original Harris profile. We introduce a novel technique for identifying and tracking X-points, revealing initial separations intermediate between the upstream perpendicular and parallel mirror wavelengths. Ultimately, these mirror-stimulated tearing modes grow and merge to create island widths similar to the CS thickness, a result verified across various CS formation timescales and initial widths. Our findings may have immediate relevance to the tearing disruption of magnetic folds produced by turbulent dynamos in weakly collisional, high-beta astrophysical plasmas.

We introduce a Bayesian framework designed to estimate proportions within finite populations for small areas. This methodology enhances conventional sample survey techniques by leveraging strength from multiple data sources, a capability absent in traditional approaches. Unlike existing small-area Bayesian methods that typically apply hierarchical models to every unit in the population, our approach restricts such modeling only to units with observed outcomes. This distinction is crucial because models for observed units can be validated using standard statistical tools, whereas modeling unobserved units presents significant challenges due to the lack of outcome data for validation. To address this, we propose dividing each small area into numerous cells based on factors likely to influence the binary outcome of interest. This strategy aims to ensure homogeneity within cells and among cells sharing identical factor level combinations across different small areas. Rather than modeling true probabilities for individual unobserved units, we assume that population means for cells with the same factor levels are consistent across areas, and that the population mean of true probabilities for a cell matches the mean of true values observed within that cell. We demonstrate the utility of this methodology by applying it to a real-world COVID-19 survey, integrating disparate data sources to estimate vaccine hesitancy rates for 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. Furthermore, we outline practical model selection techniques applicable to a broader class of models in similar contexts, benefiting a wide range of scientific inquiries.

Cyberattacks have increasingly targeted Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) networks, prompting the adoption of powerful Machine Learning (ML) models for Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) to ensure protection. To effectively train these models, selecting an optimal set of data features is crucial for maximizing both detection accuracy and computational efficiency. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of feature importance and predictive power regarding network attacks. It employs three selection algorithms—chi-square, information gain, and correlation—to identify and rank features. These features are then evaluated using two ML classifiers, deep feed-forward and random forest, to assess their impact on attack detection accuracy. The experimental assessment utilizes three NIDS datasets (UNSW-NB15, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, and ToN-IoT) in both proprietary flow and NetFlow formats. Furthermore, the research investigates the marginal gains of incrementally adding features. Results indicate that while detection accuracy rises sharply with the inclusion of additional features, it quickly converges to a maximum threshold. Consequently, this approach offers significant potential to reduce the computational and storage costs of NIDS while maintaining near-optimal detection performance, a critical advantage for resource-constrained IIoT systems.

The CPU stands as the most critical resource within a computer system. However, recent developments in system architecture and software have heightened processing complexity, particularly as computing has evolved to become distributed and parallel. CloudSim captures the intricacies of an application by defining its computational needs. As a comprehensive solution for simulating cloud computing environments and establishing testbeds for provisioning algorithms [9], this paper examines and assesses the performance of cloud environment modeling via CloudSim. We outline the CloudSim architecture and subsequently explore the novel models and techniques it employs.

This study investigates fermionic dark matter (DM) within a left-right symmetric framework by incorporating a pair of vector-like doublets into the particle spectrum. DM stability is maintained via an unbroken $\mathcal{Z}_2$ symmetry. We analyze the model's parameter space to ensure compatibility with observed relic density and both direct and indirect detection cross-sections. The existence of charged dark fermions suggests a viable signal for doubly charged Higgs bosons at the LHC and ILC. Furthermore, we examine the signature of doubly charged scalars decaying into the dark sector across multilepton final states, using several representative parameter sets that align with current DM observational constraints.

We establish that the derived parabolic induction functor, acting on the unbounded derived category of smooth mod $p$ representations of a $p$-adic reductive group, possesses a left adjoint denoted by $\mathrm{L}(U,-)$. Through a detailed examination of the cohomology functors $\mathrm{H}^i\circ \mathrm{L}(U,-)$, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{L}(U,-)$ maintains bounded complexes and global admissibility according to the Schneider--Sorensen framework. Leveraging $\mathrm{L}(U,-)$, we introduce a derived Satake homomorphism and show that it captures the mod $p$ Satake homomorphisms explicitly constructed by Herzig.

Nature has driven numerous transformative technological advancements across fields including aerospace engineering, robotics, and medical device manufacturing. Nevertheless, extracting insights from scientific biology literature remains a challenging and time-intensive endeavor that demands specialized domain expertise. Enhancing accessibility for external researchers could significantly benefit interdisciplinary initiatives such as Nature-Inspired Engineering. This study introduces a dataset comprising 1,500 manually annotated sentences that identify domain-independent relationships—such as trade-offs and correlations—between core concepts in biological texts. The arguments within these relations, which can include multi-word expressions, are annotated with modifying phrases to create non-projective graph structures. Consequently, this dataset facilitates the training and assessment of relation extraction algorithms designed for coarse-grained typing of scientific biological documents, thereby providing engineers with an effective high-level filtering mechanism.

Although Cycle-consistent generative adversarial networks (CycleGAN) demonstrate promising capabilities for speech enhancement (SE), they suffer from a critical limitation: noise components persist throughout the cycle and cannot be fully removed. Furthermore, traditional CycleGAN-based SE approaches typically estimate only spectral magnitude, leaving the phase unchanged. Driven by multi-stage learning principles, this paper introduces a novel two-stage denoising framework that integrates a CycleGAN-based magnitude estimator with a subsequent complex spectral refinement network. In the first stage, the CycleGAN model estimates magnitude, which is then combined with the original noisy phase to generate a coarsely enhanced complex spectrum. The second stage employs a complex spectral mapping network—a pure complex-valued architecture utilizing complex 2D convolution/deconvolution and complex temporal-frequency attention blocks—to further suppress residual noise and accurately estimate the clean phase. Experiments on two public datasets show that this proposed method consistently outperforms existing one-stage CycleGANs and other state-of-the-art SE systems across various metrics, with particular superiority in background noise suppression.

This tutorial presents the framework of macroscopic QED, deriving a Hamiltonian that describes the interaction between the electromagnetic field and a dispersive, dissipative medium. Beginning with a one-dimensional model as a foundation, we construct the more complex three-dimensional theory. We then extend this framework to moving materials, accounting for Doppler shifts and the coupling between electric and magnetic responses, which naturally yields the theory of quantum electromagnetic forces. Finally, we apply macroscopic QED to derive Pendry's formula for the quantum friction force arising between sliding plates.

Meeting or surpassing the fault-tolerance threshold remains a primary objective in quantum computing research, with randomized benchmarking now providing routine measurements of error rates. Nevertheless, directly comparing these measured values to thresholds is difficult because benchmarking yields average error rates, whereas thresholds depend on worst-case scenarios that occur when gates operate within large-scale computations; in the relevant regime, these two metrics can diverge by orders of magnitude. This work bridges the gap between experimentally accessible average errors and the worst-case quantities required by current threshold theorems by establishing relationships between them for various physical noise models. Our findings demonstrate that coherent errors are responsible for a massive discrepancy between average and worst-case values, and we quantify the level of control needed over these errors to ensure a fair comparison between average error probabilities and fault-tolerance thresholds.

Addressing class imbalance remains a critical and difficult challenge within data mining and machine learning, where traditional classifiers often struggle due to issues like class overlap, noise, and skewed distributions. Originally designed solely for data cleaning, the Tomek-Link algorithm has recently been integrated with sampling techniques. This hybrid approach effectively mitigates class overlap and eliminates hard-to-distinguish majority instances, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. However, the standard Tomek-Links under-sampling method focuses exclusively on globally nearest neighbor boundary instances, overlooking potential local overlaps. Consequently, when minority classes are scarce, the under-sampling efficacy is limited, yielding minimal performance gains. To overcome these limitations, a multi-granularity relabeled under-sampling algorithm (MGR) has been developed based on Tomek-Link principles. By incorporating local information within subspace granularity, MGR identifies local overlapping instances and removes redundant majority samples using a global relabeled index. This strategy significantly broadens the detection scope of Tomek-Links. Experimental results demonstrate that when the optimal global relabeled index is applied, the proposed algorithm achieves superior classification accuracy and generalization performance compared to other baseline methods.

Simulating complex physical systems with high fidelity is prohibitively costly and often inaccessible across various spatiotemporal scales.
