In terms of performance, the high-energy integrated luminosity is roughly one-fifth, and the peak differential luminosity is about one-quarter of the values observed for a $\approx 250$ GeV photon collider.

To explore the soliton resolution phenomenon, we examine a characteristic initial boundary value problem for the 4$d$ equivariant Yang-Mills equation in the region exterior to a ball. Our primary aim is to demonstrate the benefits of using outgoing null (or asymptotically null) foliations for studying energy relaxation caused by radiative dispersal. Specifically, this framework reveals that the long-term evolution must be non-radiative, characterized by zero energy flux at future null infinity. In this simplified model, such non-radiative states consist of a static solution (the half-kink) combined with an alternating sequence of $N$ decoupled kink-antikink pairs. Numerical analysis shows that the cases $N=0$ (the static half-kink) and $N=1$ (a superposition of the static half-kink and a receding antikink) act as generic attractors, with a codimension-one boundary separating their respective basins of attraction. Furthermore, we provide a detailed examination of the convergence rates toward these attractors.

MXenes, which are transition-metal carbides and nitrides, are increasingly valued for energy storage, particularly as pseudocapacitive electrodes capable of rapid electrochemical energy conversion. Employing voltage-dependent cluster expansion models, we forecast the charge storage capabilities of MXene pseudocapacitors across various electrode compositions. Electrodes composed of $M_3C_2O_2$ with group-VI transition metals demonstrate up to 80% higher areal energy densities compared to standard titanium-based MXenes like $Ti_3C_2O_2$. This enhanced pseudocapacitance stems from the broader Faradaic voltage windows of group-VI MXenes, which are predicted to be 1.2 to 1.8 times wider than those of titanium counterparts. The magnitude of this pseudocapacitive voltage window correlates with the accessible range of oxidation states for the transition metals. Similarly, the coexistence of multiple solvent ions (Li$^+$ and H$^+$) induces abrupt shifts in transition-metal oxidation states, substantially boosting the charge capacity of MXene pseudocapacitors.

Recent advancements have made Virtual Reality (VR) accessible and affordable for home use by ordinary people. A critical aspect of interacting with immersive VR is navigating virtual environments (VEs), for which direct control interfaces are considered the most effective solution. Among these, natural walking (NW) offers the most enjoyable user experience. However, existing techniques supporting direct control often face limitations that hinder their use in the confined spaces typical of homes, as NW demands ample, unobstructed room. To address this, we introduce a novel virtual locomotion method called Combined Walking in Place (CWIP). CWIP enables users to leverage their limited physical space while utilizing NW for virtual navigation. For traversing longer distances, we incorporate Walking in Place (WIP) to allow movement beyond the constraints of a small real-world room. Nevertheless, roaming in immersive alternate realities while confined within cluttered environments poses a risk of stumbling and falling. To mitigate this, we developed Augmented Virtual Reality (AVR), which alerts users to real-world hazards like chairs, drawers, and walls through virtual proxies and signs. Consequently, we propose CWIP-AVR as a safe method for exploring VR within the cramped confines of a home. To our knowledge, this represents the first approach to combining different locomotion modalities safely. We validated this system through a user study involving 20 participants, assessing their ability to navigate a virtual world while walking in a restricted and cluttered real space. Our findings demonstrate that CWIP-AVR enables safe VR navigation, allowing users to flexibly switch between locomotion modes while maintaining high immersion.

This paper examines the connected power domination number ($\gamma_{P,c}$) across three standard graph products. We derive the exact value of $\gamma_{P,c}(G\circ H)$ for any pair of non-trivial graphs $G$ and $H$. Additionally, we establish tight upper bounds for the connected power domination number of the Cartesian product of two graphs, $G$ and $H$, which allows us to determine the exact value for several standard graphs. Finally, we address the connected power domination number of the tensor product of graphs.

Inverse problems are pervasive across natural phenomena, appearing in nearly every domain of science and engineering, from geophysics and climate studies to astrophysics and biomechanics. A primary hurdle in addressing these problems is their ill-posed nature. Bayesian inference offers a rigorous solution by casting the inverse problem within a statistical framework. However, applying this method becomes difficult when dealing with high-dimensional discrete fields (the "curse of dimensionality") or when prior knowledge is limited to previously obtained solutions. This paper introduces a new approach for efficient and precise Bayesian inversion using deep generative models. Specifically, we show that employing the approximate distribution learned by a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) as a prior within a Bayesian update, and reformulating the inference in the GAN's low-dimensional latent space, allows for the effective resolution of large-scale Bayesian inverse problems. Our statistical framework maintains underlying physical principles and delivers accurate results with trustworthy uncertainty quantification, even without knowledge of the noise model—a notable limitation of many current techniques. We validate the proposed method across various inverse problems, utilizing both synthetic and experimentally derived data.

Classification challenges frequently arise from the presence of vast quantities of irrelevant features. Feature selection addresses this by identifying key variables, reducing dimensionality, and enhancing model interpretability. Within support vector machine research, this is typically handled via $\ell_1$ penalties, which are convex relaxations that heavily bias parameter estimates toward zero and often retain excessive irrelevant features. This paper introduces an alternative approach that substitutes penalties with sparse-set constraints. While penalties remain, they serve a distinct role. The proximal distance principle constructs an objective function by combining a loss function $L(\boldsymbol{\beta})$ with a penalty term, $\frac{\rho}{2}\mathrm{dist}(\boldsymbol{\beta}, S_k)^2$, representing the squared Euclidean distance between the parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and a sparsity set $S_k$ (where no more than $k$ components of $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ are nonzero). If $\boldsymbol{\beta}_\rho$ minimizes $f_\rho(\boldsymbol{\beta})=L(\boldsymbol{\beta})+\frac{\rho}{2}\mathrm{dist}(\boldsymbol{\beta}, S_k)^2$, it converges to the constrained minimum of $L(\boldsymbol{\beta})$ over $S_k$ as $\rho$ approaches infinity. We develop two closely related algorithms to implement this strategy. Both simulated and real-world examples illustrate that these algorithms achieve significantly improved sparsity without sacrificing classification performance.

We provide a comprehensive proof of the theorem by P.S. Green and T. Hübsch, which establishes that all complete intersection Calabi--Yau 3-folds residing in a product of projective spaces are linked via projective conifold transitions, forming what is termed the standard web. Additionally, we define a specific subset of small transitions, designated as primitive small transitions, and investigate this category. Specifically, for a Calabi--Yau 3-fold $X$ with a small projective resolution $\pi : \widehat{X} \rightarrow X$, we demonstrate that if the natural closed immersion $Def(\widehat{X}) \hookrightarrow Def(X)$ constitutes an isomorphism, then $X$ possesses only ordinary double points (ODPs) as its singularities.

Gaseous time projection chambers (TPCs) featuring high readout segmentation can reconstruct detailed three-dimensional ionization patterns of nuclear recoils caused by elastic neutron scattering. Utilizing a configuration of six compact TPCs equipped with pixel ASIC readout and filled with a 70:30 He:CO$_2$ gas mixture, we present the initial directional analysis of beam-induced neutron backgrounds within the tunnel areas surrounding the Belle II detector at the SuperKEKB $e^+e^-$ collider. Through 3D recoil tracking, we demonstrate that these TPCs sustain nearly 100% nuclear recoil purity down to reconstructed ionization energies ($E_\text{reco}$) of 5 $\mathrm{keV_\text{ee}}$. By analyzing a substantial dataset of simulated $^4$He, $^{12}$C, and $^{16}$O recoil tracks, we observed agreement between predicted and measured recoil energy spectra in five of the six TPCs, offering valuable validation of the modeled neutron production mechanisms. When restricting the dataset to $^4$He recoils with $E_\text{reco}>40$ $\mathrm{keV_\text{ee}}$, we achieved axial angular resolutions better than $8^{\circ}$ and developed a method that correctly assigns vector direction to 91% of simulated $^4$He recoils under appropriate conditions. Applying this method to measured $^4$He recoil tracks revealed consistency between the angular distributions of observed and simulated recoils, providing the first experimental confirmation of localized neutron "hotspots" in the accelerator tunnel. Furthermore, the observed nuclear recoil rates in these TPCs indicate that simulations currently overestimate the neutron flux emanating from these hotspots.

In recent research published in *Pure Appl. Anal.* (2020), the first author and J. Zhang established a link between the regularity theory of optimal transport and the curvature of Kähler manifolds. Specifically, they demonstrated that the MTW tensor for a cost function $c(x,y)=\Psi(x-y)$ corresponds to the anti-bisectional curvature of a related Kähler metric defined on a tube domain, where the anti-bisectional curvature is given by $R(\mathcal{X}, \overline{ \mathcal{Y}},\mathcal{X}, \overline{ \mathcal{Y}})$ for polarized $(1,0)$ vectors $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$. This relationship allows the anti-bisectional curvature to be meaningfully assigned a sign (positive or negative). In this study, we examine how the anti-bisectional curvature evolves under Kähler-Ricci flow. We prove that non-positive anti-bisectional curvature is preserved during the flow. Furthermore, in complex dimension two, we show that non-negative orthogonal anti-bisectional curvature (the MTW(0) condition) is also preserved. These findings have several applications across complex geometry, optimal transport, and affine geometry.

While Bloch oscillations—nontrivial current density oscillations under a constant electric field with a finite amplitude even as system size grows—are well-documented in nearly noninteracting systems and observed experimentally, this study revisits their behavior in strongly interacting regimes. By examining the spin-1/2 XXZ chain, which maps to spinless electrons, we find that at specific anisotropy values $\Delta=-\cos(\pi/p)$ ($p=3,4,5,\cdots$) within the ferromagnetic gapless regime, the current density exhibits qualitative similarity to the noninteracting case ($\Delta=0$), even under weak electric fields. However, when $\Delta$ deviates from these points, the oscillation amplitude in a weak field is suppressed by a factor proportional to the system size. Finally, we utilize the Landau--Zener formula to estimate the requisite electric field strength for observing this phenomenon.

By applying Hamiltonian reduction to three-dimensional Einstein gravity with a negative cosmological constant under near horizon boundary conditions, the theory simplifies to a Floreanini-Jackiw scalar field theory on the horizon. In this framework, scalar zero modes represent global black hole charges, and the near horizon Hamiltonian takes the form of a total derivative, accounting for the softness of all scalar field oscillator modes. Additionally, we identify a modified hierarchy of Korteweg-de Vries boundary conditions that resolves the degeneracy of soft hair excitations on the horizon.

This study explores $H$-recurrence, characterized by the relation $H(n) = H(n-H(n-2)) + H(n-H(n-3))$, utilizing a recent methodology applicable to specific recurrences like the Conway and Hofstadter $Q$ recursions.

Kostka-Foulkes polynomials serve as Lusztig's $q$-analogues for the weight multiplicities of irreducible representations within semisimple Lie algebras, and their coefficients are known to be non-negative. While a combinatorial formula demonstrating this non-negativity in type $A$ was established using a statistic on semistandard Young tableaux known as \textit{charge}, extending this charge definition to other types has remained a persistent challenge. This work introduces a novel methodology rooted in defining Kostka-Foulkes polynomials as an alternating sum over Kostant partitions, which can be viewed as formal sums of positive roots. By employing a sign-reversing involution, we derive a positive expansion where the pertinent statistic corresponds directly to the count of parts in these Kostant partitions. We anticipate that the inherent simplicity of this new crystal-like model will facilitate its extension to other classical types.

Within two decades, the internet has shifted from a hopeful promise to democratize knowledge and foster global understanding into a source of daily terror. We are now flooded with disinformation—including lies, conspiracies, and nonsense—that carries severe real-world consequences, such as human rights abuses, threats to democracy, and risks to public health. Despite the internet's vastness, those spreading this misinformation seem to operate on a more localized scale. Consequently, we present a domain-level analysis designed to predict whether a specific domain is involved in distributing or amplifying disinformation by examining its underlying content and hyperlink connectivity. These findings also apply to an investigation of disinformation on Telegram and Twitter. Based on these insights, we propose that search engines and social media recommendation algorithms can systematically identify and demote the most egregious offenders, thereby restoring some trust and sanity to our online communities.

Addressing bias in natural language processing necessitates measuring it, a process typically reliant on lexicons composed of seed terms that define stereotypes or specific dimensions. This reproducibility study examines the original authors' central assertion: the logic behind constructing these lexicons must be rigorously vetted before application, since the seed words themselves may harbor biases. The research evaluates the reproducibility of both the quantitative and qualitative findings and conclusions from the source paper. We successfully replicated most results supporting the original authors' broad claim, confirming that seed sets frequently contain biases that compromise their utility as baselines for bias metrics. Our outcomes generally align with those of the original paper; while minor discrepancies exist in specific instances, they do not detract from the paper's primary objective of demonstrating the inherent fragility of seed sets.

To endow robots with dexterous capabilities, a robust strategy involves initially transferring skills through Learning from Demonstration (LfD) followed by refinement via self-exploration using Reinforcement Learning (RL). This paper introduces a new LfD+RL framework called Adaptive Conditional Neural Movement Primitives (ACNMP), designed to facilitate efficient policy adaptation in unfamiliar environments and effective skill transfer across different agents. This capability leverages the latent representations learned by a Conditional Neural Process (CNP) model and combines simultaneous supervised learning (SL) for mastering demonstrated trajectories with RL for discovering new ones. Simulation results demonstrate that (i) ACNMP allows the system to generalize to scenarios where pure LfD fails; (ii) concurrent SL and RL training maintains the integrity of demonstrations while adapting to novel contexts through shared representations; (iii) ACNMP achieves order-of-magnitude improvements in sample efficiency for extrapolating reaching tasks compared to existing methods; and (iv) the framework supports skill transfer between robots with varying morphologies, offering competitive learning speeds and fewer assumptions than state-of-the-art solutions. Furthermore, real-world experiments involving obstacle avoidance, pick-and-place, and pouring tasks confirm the practical applicability of ACNMPs.

This study reports a search for exclusive two-photon production through photon exchange in proton-proton collisions ($pp \to p\gamma\gamma p$), where protons remain intact. The analysis utilizes data from 2016 with an integrated luminosity of 9.4 fb$^{-1}$, gathered by the CMS and TOTEM detectors at the LHC's center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. To minimize backgrounds from strong interactions, events are filtered to have a diphoton invariant mass exceeding 350 GeV and intact protons in the final state. The selected events require consistency between the invariant mass and rapidity derived from the momentum loss of the forward protons and those calculated from the central two-photon system. No events meeting these criteria were observed. By interpreting these findings within an effective dimension-8 extension of the Standard Model, this work establishes the first constraints on two anomalous four-photon coupling parameters. Assuming the other parameter adheres to its Standard Model value, the 95% confidence level limits are determined to be $|\zeta_1| < 2.9 \times 10^{-13}$ GeV$^{-4}$ and $|\zeta_2| < 6.0 \times 10^{-13}$ GeV$^{-4}$.

Overcrowding in Emergency Departments (EDs) is a globally acknowledged issue with repercussions ranging from extended patient wait times to life-threatening outcomes. To mitigate these delays and enhance service quality, the international community is increasingly focusing on analyzing this phenomenon. Within this context, we introduce a Discrete Event Simulation (DES) model designed to examine patient flow in a medium-sized ED in Central Italy, an area recently affected by a major earthquake. Specifically, our objective is to simulate atypical ED conditions triggered by critical events, such as natural disasters, which result in a sharp surge in patient arrivals. Thanks to access to detailed operational data, we constructed a precise DES model capable of conducting comprehensive scenario analyses. Consequently, the model serves as a robust decision support tool for ED administrators, particularly in formulating specific emergency response plans for mass casualty incidents.

Identifying statistical interactions among input features remains a critical yet difficult challenge. Recent progress shows that trained neural networks can be mined to reveal these learned interactions, with observations indicating that interacting features invariably maintain strongly weighted connections to shared hidden units. Inspired by this insight, we approach the interaction detection problem from a fresh topological standpoint by examining network connectivity. Specifically, we introduce a novel metric for quantifying interaction strength grounded in the established theory of persistent homology. Leveraging this metric, we developed the Persistence Interaction Detection (PID) algorithm, designed for efficient interaction identification. We evaluated PID across various tasks using multiple synthetic and real-world datasets under diverse hyperparameters. Experimental findings confirm that the PID algorithm surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines.

Structural node embeddings, which encode local connectivity details for graph nodes, are widely utilized in machine learning and data mining tasks such as node classification, clustering, anomaly detection, and network alignment. For directed graphs—including social, communication, and transaction networks—the ability to capture directional information alongside scalability is crucial. However, most current approaches are limited to undirected graphs. To address this, we introduce Digraphwave, a scalable algorithm designed to extract structural embeddings specifically for directed graphs. These embeddings utilize compressed diffusion pattern signatures that are enhanced twice to boost discriminative power. By establishing a lower bound on local heat diffusion, we derive theoretically grounded diffusion timescales, resulting in an algorithm with only two interpretable hyperparameters: embedding dimension and neighborhood resolution. Experimental results demonstrate that our two enhancement techniques, transposition and aggregation, significantly improve macro F1 scores in automorphic identity classification, outperforming all structural embedding baselines. Furthermore, on real-world datasets, Digraphwave either surpasses or matches existing methods, showing particularly strong gains in network alignment tasks. It also scales efficiently to graphs containing millions of nodes and edges, operating up to 30 times faster than prior diffusion-based methods while consuming significantly less memory.

Given the lack of effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease (AD), preventing the condition through lifestyle modifications has become increasingly vital. Analyzing electronic health records (EHR) offers a pathway to better comprehend how lifestyle influences AD, yet such information is often embedded within unstructured clinical narratives. Consequently, this study aimed to validate the feasibility of using natural language processing (NLP) to classify lifestyle factors, such as physical activity and poor diet, from clinical text. To create training data, we employed a rule-based NLP algorithm to automatically generate labels. We then applied weak supervision techniques to various pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) models, including BERT base, PubMedBERT (both full text and abstracts only), UMLS BERT, Bio BERT, and Bio-clinical BERT. Two case studies focusing on physical activity and excessive diet were conducted to assess the models' efficacy in identifying these factors for AD. Performance was evaluated against a developed Gold Standard Corpus (GSC). The PubMedBERT(Abs) model yielded the highest results for physical activity, achieving precision, recall, and F-1 scores of 0.96 each. For classifying excessive diet, Bio BERT demonstrated superior performance with perfect scores across all metrics. This approach, which leverages weak supervision, can substantially expand the dataset size necessary for training deep learning models. Furthermore, the study confirms the effectiveness of BERT models in extracting lifestyle-related information from clinical notes concerning Alzheimer's disease.

Numerous metallic transition-metal oxides become insulating when synthesized as films just a few unit cells thick, yet the microscopic mechanisms driving these thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transitions remain contentious. In this study, we simulate the extreme scenario of a monolayer of the correlated metal strontium vanadate (SrVO$_3$) grown on a SrTiO$_3$ substrate. Notably, our system allows for two distinct vacuum terminations: either a SrO or a VO$_2$ top layer. Although both configurations result in Mott insulating behavior at nominal stoichiometry, the phase diagrams generated by doping—whether chemical or via an applied gate voltage—exhibit qualitatively different characteristics. Our many-body simulations uncover a wide array of nonlocal fluctuations linked to (in)commensurate antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic states, as well as stripe and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By recognizing that these two geometries induce crystal-field splittings with opposite signs, we clarify the resulting phases through the perspective of orbital degrees of freedom. Broadly, this work underscores that interface and surface reconstructions, along with the distortion or breaking of coordination polyhedra in ultra-thin films, generate rich physical properties that starkly contrast with the material's bulk behavior.

Atmospheric turbulence degrades visual imagery, hindering information interpretation for both humans and machines. While most established correction techniques rely on models, their high computational demands and memory requirements make real-time operation unfeasible. Although deep learning methods have gained prominence, they currently function effectively only on static scenes. This paper introduces a novel learning-based framework designed to handle dynamic scenes through short temporal spanning. We utilize complex-valued convolutions because they capture phase information altered by turbulence more effectively than standard real-valued convolutions. The proposed architecture consists of two concatenated modules: the first addresses geometric distortions, while the second refines micro-details in videos, provided sufficient memory is available. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework efficiently mitigates atmospheric turbulence distortion and significantly surpasses existing methods.
We will address the most critical open problem in real phase retrieval via projections by demonstrating that a minimum of $2n-2$ projections are necessary for phase retrieval in $\RR^n$.

We suggest investigating $P$- and $CP$-symmetries through the reaction $e^+e^- \to J/\psi \to \Lambda\bar \Lambda$. The general angular distribution for this process is derived, and multiple observables are introduced to facilitate the proposed tests. These observables enable the distinction between $P$-violations occurring in the production of $J/\psi$ versus those in its decay into a $\Lambda \bar \Lambda$ pair. Numerical estimates for $P$-violating asymmetries arising from $Z$ exchange within the Standard Model (SM) are provided. Our findings indicate that BESIII has achieved the necessary sensitivity to detect these effects. Furthermore, a proposed super-tau-charm factory, equipped with significantly higher luminosity, will allow for high-precision tests of SM predictions. The $CP$-violating effect in $J/\psi \to \Lambda \bar \Lambda$ is also testable; notably, current BESIII data already possess the sensitivity to confirm $CP$ violation given the existing upper limits on the $\Lambda$ electric dipole moment. At the super-tau-charm factory, this upper limit could be improved by an order of magnitude.

In the tropical sandpile model, relaxation involves deforming a tropical hypersurface into a finite set of points. We demonstrate that in the one-dimensional scenario, this relaxation concludes after a finite number of steps. Additionally, we provide experimental evidence indicating that the count of these steps follows a power law.

This paper establishes the existence and multiplicity of solutions for a broad range of quasilinear problems within a nonreflexive Orlicz-Sobolev space. The approach relies on Szulkin's variational techniques alongside specific characteristics of the weak$^*$ topology.

We demonstrate that string moduli possess an axion-philic character due to model-independent derivative interactions derived from the Kaehler potential. Consequently, the decay of a modulus into stringy axions proceeds without suppression from the final states' masses. Remarkably, this behavior extends generally to any modulus, not merely the scalar partner of the stringy axion. Furthermore, decays into (pseudo) Nambu-Goldstone bosons (NGBs) similarly evade mass suppression when the modulus mass is comparable to or less than that of the NGB's scalar partner. This intrinsic axion-philicity renders string moduli a natural origin for significant dark radiation in string compactifications featuring ultralight stringy axions, as well as in Standard Model extensions containing cosmologically stable NGBs like the QCD axion. In the latter scenario, the fermionic superpartner of the NGB may additionally contribute to dark matter as a feebly interacting massive particle.

Leveraging general symmetry principles and a many-body invariant, we propose a novel phase of matter characterized as a topological SO(5) superfluid. This discovery relies on an exactly solvable model that exhibits parallels to the minimal model of superfluid $^3$He. Upon analyzing its quantum phase diagram and correlations, we identify exotic superfluid and metallic phases within the repulsive sector. At the critical boundary between trivial and nontrivial superfluid states, our Hamiltonian simplifies to the globally SO(5)-symmetric Gaudin model, featuring a degenerate ground manifold that encompasses quartet states. Crucially, the exact solution reveals a unique non-pair-breaking mechanism for superfluids exposed to external magnetic fields. Furthermore, introducing nonintegrable modifications to our model yields a strong-coupling limit of the metallic phase, characterized by a ground-state manifold with extensive entropy.

This study introduces a Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach integrated with Model Predictive Control (MPC) to determine the optimal control policy for a multi-agent battery storage network. The framework incorporates time-varying power price forecasts and uncertainties in production and demand. The primary goal is to minimize economic costs while preventing battery degradation caused by extreme states of charge (SoC). Additionally, the model accounts for grid power limits and individual agent constraints regarding power input and SoC. By employing a parametrized MPC scheme as a function approximator for deterministic policy gradients, RL optimizes closed-loop performance through parameter updates. Simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed method successfully manages these constraints and yields an optimal policy.

This paper aims to link different subclasses of analytic univalent functions by utilizing a specific convolution operator that incorporates Touchard polynomials. Specifically, we examine these relationships within the context of analytic univalent functions possessing positive coefficients defined in the open unit disk U.

The Fisher market serves as a foundational model in economic theory for resource allocation, where agents utilize currency budgets to purchase goods for utility maximization, and producers sell capacity-limited items for payment. However, the classical model's reliance on only two constraint types—individual budgets and good capacities—limits its applicability in scenarios where agents face additional linear constraints, such as knapsack or proportionality rules. This study introduces a modified Fisher market that incorporates these extra linear constraints, demonstrating that this change fundamentally reshapes market equilibrium properties and optimal allocation outcomes. These new characteristics motivate the formulation of a Budget Perturbed Social Optimization Problem (BP-SOP), with prices derived from the dual variables associated with its capacity constraints. To calculate budget perturbations, we propose a fixed-point iterative scheme and confirm its convergence via numerical simulations.

Given that this fixed-point approach requires solving a centralized problem at every iteration, we introduce a novel class of distributed algorithms for computing equilibrium prices. Specifically, we develop an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm with robust convergence guarantees for both Fisher markets featuring homogeneous linear constraints and classical Fisher markets. Within this framework, prices are adjusted using the tatonnement process with a step size that remains entirely independent of individual agent utilities. Consequently, our mechanism addresses a core limitation of classical Fisher markets—which consider only capacity and budget constraints—offering both theoretical and computational advantages.

This paper examines the Bohr phenomenon for the class of analytic functions defined on the simply connected domain $\Omega_{\gamma}=\bigg\{z\in\mathbb{C} : \bigg|z+\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\bigg|<\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\bigg\}\;\; \text{for}\;\; 0\leq \gamma<1$. We investigate the improved Bohr radius, Bohr-Rogosinski radius, and refined Bohr radius for functions analytic within $\Omega_{\gamma}$, deriving multiple sharp results.

While it is frequently asserted that the entropy of a network's degree distribution serves as an indicator of robustness, this study clarifies that relationship. We demonstrate that for randomly configured networks without specified additional characteristics, degree distribution entropy only establishes a lower bound for giant component robustness against node removal. Furthermore, when comparing networks with a fixed expected degree and identical distribution forms, degree distribution entropy fails to predict robustness. In contrast, we find a positive monotonic correlation between remaining degree entropy and robustness, providing an analytical formula for the remaining degree entropy of log-normal distributions. Additionally, we show that degree-degree correlations alone do not reliably indicate robustness in real-world networks. Finally, we propose a modified method for measuring mutual information that more effectively captures structural properties associated with robustness.

We have evaluated the performance of a new 250 $\mu$m thick, fully-depleted Skipper CCD specifically for its potential in astronomical use, focusing on its response to visible and near-infrared light. By analyzing charge in each pixel through 400 non-destructive reads, we attained stable single-electron resolution with a readout noise of $\sigma \sim 0.18$ e$^{-}$ rms/pix. Our results confirm that the gain obtained from photon transfer curves matches the gain calculated from the quantized charge of individual electrons to within 1%. Additionally, we conducted relative quantum efficiency tests, showing high efficiency at optical and near-infrared wavelengths, which aligns with expectations for a thick, fully depleted device. Furthermore, we demonstrated the capability to execute multiple non-destructive measurements and achieve sub-electron readout noise across configurable detector subregions. This study represents the initial phase in establishing the utility of Skipper CCDs for future astronomical and cosmological endeavors.

Human activity recognition (HAR) utilizing IMU sensors, specifically accelerometers and gyroscopes, holds significant potential for smart homes, healthcare, and human-machine interfaces. However, real-world IMU-based HAR systems often face challenges such as sensor degradation, environmental factors, noise, and the presence of unknown activities. To address these practical deployment issues, analyzing statistical confidence regarding activity class scores is crucial. This paper introduces XAI-BayesHAR, an integrated Bayesian framework that enhances IMU-based HAR classification accuracy by recursively tracking feature embedding vectors and their associated uncertainties using a Kalman filter. Furthermore, XAI-BayesHAR functions as an out-of-distribution (OOD) detector by leveraging predictive uncertainty to identify alien input data distributions. Finally, the framework's performance is assessed using Shapley values to determine the significance of the feature embedding vectors, facilitating subsequent model compression.

Touchscreens have become a dominant interaction method due to their widespread availability; however, existing technologies are constrained by the need for specialized hardware and are often impaired by surface contaminants such as water. To address these limitations, we introduce MagSurface, a system that leverages magnetic field sensing to track fingers on ordinary surfaces with minimal instrumentation. This approach transforms everyday materials into interactive touch media, significantly expanding the range of usable surfaces. We evaluated the system by measuring its 2D localization accuracy across three different material types to assess practical applicability. Additionally, a qualitative user study gathered feedback on usability and comfort. Our results demonstrate a localization error of just a few millimeters.

The latest Fermilab measurement of the muon $g$-2 validates the earlier findings from Brookhaven. The dominant hadronic vacuum polarization (HVP) contribution to the muon $g$-2 is essential for determining whether the Standard Model prediction deviates from experimental data. A recent lattice QCD calculation by the BMW collaboration exhibits a discrepancy with the low-energy $e^+e^- \to \text{hadrons}$ data currently utilized to compute the HVP contribution; we term this inconsistency the new muon $g$-2 puzzle. In this Letter, we examine whether new physics could influence the $e^+e^- \to \text{hadrons}$ cross-section, a scenario that might theoretically resolve the puzzle. However, we demonstrate that this hypothesis is ruled out by various experimental constraints.

Advancements in micropixel avalanche photodiode (MAPD) technology have recently made these devices highly attractive as sensors for scintillation detectors. Since the performance of scintillation detectors is closely linked to the physical characteristics of the MAPD, this study examines three specific types—MAPD-3NK, MAPD-3NM, and MAPD-3NM-II—for potential application in such detectors. The investigated avalanche photodiodes feature key parameters including a low operating voltage (90V < U < 50V), high pixel density (4000 pixels/mm²), high photodetection efficiency (40%), and high gain (6×10⁴). The gamma-ray detection capabilities of the MAPD-based scintillation detector were evaluated using various gamma rays. The results confirm that this type of scintillation detector is suitable for use in next-generation medical PET cameras.

Over the past few years, evaluating researcher performance has become increasingly burdensome due to the sheer volume of scholarly output. Consequently, evaluators frequently depend on specific metrics, such as the h-index. However, an excessive focus on these indicators can perpetuate questionable research behaviors and neglect critical elements of a researcher's career, including their specific contributions to individual works or other academic activities like dataset creation and peer review. To address this, several initiatives have emerged to establish guidelines for more equitable research assessment frameworks. This paper introduces BIP! Scholar, a web-based platform that enables researchers to create comprehensive career profiles aligned with these fair assessment standards, thereby assisting evaluators in adhering to these practices.

Offshore wind energy is gaining traction as a preferred power source due to its reduced environmental footprint. To enhance its competitiveness against traditional energy sources, it is essential to implement effective operation and maintenance strategies that maximize generation availability and minimize production costs. Condition monitoring systems play a vital role in managing the health of offshore wind farms to achieve these operational goals. Furthermore, reliability assessments are increasingly utilized to support maintenance processes and boost farm availability. However, much of the existing reliability analysis relies on offline statistical data. This article introduces a drone-assisted monitoring method designed for the online reliability evaluation of wind turbines, using a wind turbine blade system as a case study to illustrate the proposed approach.

What drives biased predictions, and how can we stop them? We analyzed 8.2 million algorithmic forecasts of mathematical ability generated by approximately 400 AI engineers, who each built an algorithm under a randomly assigned experimental condition. Our treatment groups altered programmers' incentives, training datasets, awareness, and/or technical understanding of AI ethics. Subsequently, we evaluated out-of-sample predictions from these algorithms using randomized audit manipulations of inputs and ground-truth math performance for 20,000 subjects. Our findings indicate that biased predictions are primarily the result of biased training data. However, one-third of the advantage provided by superior training data stems from a novel economic mechanism: engineers demonstrate increased effort and responsiveness to incentives when equipped with better training data. We also examined how performance varies based on programmers' demographic traits and their scores on an implicit bias (IAT) psychological test regarding gender and careers. We found no evidence that female, minority, or low-IAT engineers produce less biased or discriminatory code. Nevertheless, we observed that prediction errors are correlated within demographic groups, which enables performance gains through cross-demographic averaging. Finally, we quantified the advantages and trade-offs of practical managerial or policy interventions—including technical guidance, simple reminders, and enhanced incentives—to reduce algorithmic bias.

When microlenses have sufficiently low mass, the angular size of the source star can significantly exceed the angular Einstein radius of the lens. In these extreme finite source effect (EFSE) scenarios, finite source effects govern the entire event duration. This work demonstrates and investigates a continuous degeneracy involving multiple parameters of such EFSE events. The first aspect of this degeneracy stems from the fact that the directly observable peak flux change relies on both the ratio of the angular source radius to the angular Einstein radius and the fraction of the baseline flux contributed by the lensed star. The second aspect arises because the observable event duration depends on both the impact parameter and the relative proper motion between the lens and the source. When the detailed light curve morphology is analyzed, particularly by incorporating a limb-darkening profile, these two pairwise degeneracies become coupled. We derive these degeneracies mathematically using analytic approximations and further examine them numerically without approximations. Additionally, we explore the physical conditions under which these mathematical degeneracies might occur and potentially be resolved. As microlensing surveys achieve higher precision and cadence, detecting an increasing number of low-mass lensing events with shrinking Einstein radii, the discovery of EFSE events is expected to rise. Specifically, the Roman Space Telescope's Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey could lead to a dramatic increase in the detection of EFSE microlensing events.

High-order Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is emerging as a promising industrial tool, with Flux Reconstruction (FR) representing a key methodology. However, for FR to replace existing lower-order techniques in handling complex geometries, it must be capable of operating on stretched and warped meshes. Consequently, this study investigates the analytical and numerical performance of FR on deformed grids for both the 1D linear advection equation and the 2D Euler equations. The analytical framework relies on a modified von Neumann analysis tailored for linearly deformed grids. Both analytical and numerical explorations determine temporal stability limits for linear advection on these grids, establishing CFL constraints for various Runge-Kutta schemes. The primary finding indicates that contracting mesh regions result in higher CFL limits, while expansion reduces them. Finally, FR benchmarks are compared against finite difference and finite volume schemes commonly used in industry; these comparisons demonstrate FR's superior wave propagation capabilities on warped and stretched meshes, highlighting its enhanced resilience to mesh deformation.

Face recognition, widely utilized in intelligence, law enforcement, surveillance, and consumer sectors, has recently been integrated into smartphones and body-worn cameras (BWC). In the context of BWCs, this technology supports surveillance, situational awareness, and officer safety. Despite these applications, academic research on BWC-based face recognition remains limited. While a recent study introduced the BWCFace dataset and assessed the ResNet-50 model, the constraints of real-time inference on resource-limited devices and privacy concerns necessitate on-device solutions. Consequently, this study evaluates lightweight architectures—MobileNet-V2, EfficientNet-B0, LightCNN-9, and LightCNN-29—using the publicly available BWCface dataset. Performance was tested across three mobile devices, with comparative analysis against heavy-weight models like VGG-16 and ResNet-50, as well as six hand-crafted features, to balance accuracy and model size. Results indicate that the LightCNN-29 model achieves a maximum rank-1 accuracy 1.85% lower than the best-performing ResNet-50 but reduces parameter count by 23.49M. Most deep learning models exhibited similar performance at rank-5 and rank-10, while LightCNN inference was 2.1 times faster on mobile hardware than other models. At rank-1, the performance gap between LightCNN-29 and the Local Phase Quantization (LPQ) descriptor was only 14%. Across most experimental configurations, the lightweight LightCNN models provided the optimal trade-off between accuracy and model size.

This paper presents a unified investigation into $L_1$ over $L_2$ sparsity-promoting models, which are extensively utilized within coherent dictionaries to recover both nonnegative and arbitrary sparse signals. First, we derive exact recovery conditions for both constrained and unconstrained variants across a broad spectrum of signals. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of solutions for these $L_1/L_2$ models under the assumption that the measurement matrix's null space satisfies the $s$-spherical section property. By obtaining an analytical expression for the proximal operator of the nonnegative-constrained $L_1/L_2$ norm, we propose a novel alternating direction method of multipliers approach, termed ADMM$_p^+$, to address the unconstrained model. We prove that this algorithm converges globally to a $d$-stationary (the sharpest form of stationary) solution and achieves local linear convergence under specific conditions. Numerical experiments on two distinct applications validate the superiority of ADMM$_p^+$ over state-of-the-art sparse recovery techniques. Specifically, when tackling the wavelength misalignment problem, ADMM$_p^+$ reduces computational time by approximately $95\%$ to $99\%$ while delivering significantly higher accuracy compared to the commonly employed scaled gradient projection method.

Using a covariant perturbative field-theoretic framework, the wave-packet-modified neutrino propagator is formulated as an asymptotic series in powers of dimensionless Lorentz- and rotation-invariant quantities. This expansion applies at high energies and over short yet macroscopic space-time intervals separating the vertices of the proper Feynman macrodiagram. Leveraging the duality between the propagator and the effective neutrino wave packet, neutrinos are characterized as deeply virtual and moving quasiclassically at short times and distances. In the lowest-order approximation, this yields a classical inverse-square relationship for the modulus squared of the flavor transition amplitude and the associated neutrino-induced event rate with respect to the distance $L$ between source and detector. The aforementioned asymptotics introduce corrections to this classical behavior in powers of $L^2$. This contrasts with the long-baseline regime, where similar corrections arise from an asymptotic expansion in inverse powers of $L^2$. Nevertheless, in both short- and long-baseline scenarios, the primary corrections result in a reduction of the number of observed neutrino events.

Event-based sampling has been introduced as a broad method to reduce average communication rates in remote state estimation, a strategy particularly valuable when network bandwidth or sensor energy is limited. Recently, there has been a renewed focus on using particle filters for event-based state estimation, driven by the need to address nonlinear and non-Gaussian challenges, as well as the absence of analytic solutions for linear-Gaussian systems under event-based protocols. However, few practical considerations have been addressed regarding the application of particle filtering in this context. This paper fills that gap by (i) highlighting the significant risk of sample degeneracy at new events and proposing the auxiliary particle filter as an intuitive remedy, (ii) presenting a novel alternative to the local predictor approach that relies on precomputed state estimates to better handle observer-to-sensor communication in closed-loop triggering for complex systems, and (iii) examining the computational challenges associated with the increased processing load required when implementing particle filters under event-based sampling.

Recent focus has intensified on algorithmic fairness within socially sensitive fields. Although substantial research exists regarding mean fairness, studies on quantile fairness are limited yet crucial. To address this gap and highlight the importance of quantile fairness, we introduce a new framework for learning a real-valued quantile function that satisfies Demographic Parity constraints across sensitive attributes like race or gender, enabling the derivation of trustworthy fair prediction intervals. Leveraging optimal transport and functional synchronization methods, we provide theoretical assurances of distribution-free coverage and precise fairness for the resulting intervals. We also present a practical pipeline that integrates flexible quantile regression with an efficient post-processing step for fairness adjustment. Empirical evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate the method's superior performance, revealing the model's capacity to elucidate the mechanisms behind the fairness-accuracy trade-off across various societal and medical contexts.

This study addresses secret communication over a two-receiver multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) Gaussian broadcast channel, where the transmitter possesses a common message for both receivers and two independent confidential messages, each destined for a specific receiver while remaining perfectly hidden from the other. The paper demonstrates that the secrecy capacity region can be achieved by a natural scheme integrating secret dirty-paper coding with Gaussian superposition coding. The proof of this result relies on a channel-enhancement technique and an extremal entropy inequality proposed by Weingarten et al.

This paper addresses linear ill-posed problems defined by the system $A_i x = y_i$ for $i = 1, \dots, p$, where each $A_i$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space $X$ to a Hilbert space $Y_i$. When $p$ is very large, traditional iterative regularization methods that utilize all data at every iteration become computationally prohibitive due to high memory requirements and excessive processing costs. To tackle these large-scale systems efficiently, we propose a stochastic mirror descent algorithm that randomly selects a subset of equations at each step and integrates convex regularization. This approach ensures excellent scalability with problem size while effectively capturing the characteristics of the desired solution. The method's convergence is heavily influenced by step-size selection; we examine various selection strategies and derive convergence guarantees under *a priori* early stopping criteria. Specifically, adopting the principles of the discrepancy principle, we introduce a step-size rule designed to mitigate iterate oscillations and minimize semi-convergence effects. Additionally, we prove an order-optimal convergence rate provided the true solution satisfies a standard source condition. Finally, numerical experiments are presented to validate the method's performance.

STIT (sees to it that) semantics stands as a leading framework in the modal logic of agency, widely adopted by both philosophers and researchers in responsible AI. This logic examines the properties of agents ensuring specific states of affairs occur without detailing the concrete actions taken to guarantee them. Compared to other multi-agent modal logics, the primary strength of STIT theories lies in their expressive capacity. Unlike variations of Coalition Logic or Propositional Dynamic Logic, which focus solely on an agent's ability to perform actions, STIT logic also investigates the choices agents make and the outcomes they effectively achieve. However, in certain contexts, such high expressivity may be superfluous. This paper explores a specific fragment of classical STIT logic that utilizes only a strategic modal operator, representing an agent's ability to see to it that a particular state of affairs holds. It presents a neighbourhood semantics for this fragment, along with proofs of soundness, canonicity, and strong completeness. Additionally, the paper offers preliminary considerations regarding the epistemic extension of this fragment.

Network states arise from the interaction between a system's structure and its dynamics. These states can be described using network density matrices, where von Neumann entropy quantifies the count of distinct microstates consistent with a specific topology and dynamical evolution. This Letter introduces a maximum entropy principle to define network states in systems featuring heterogeneous, correlated connectivity patterns and complex dynamics. We examine three specific coalescence processes common in empirical interconnected systems, analyzing their entropy and the transitions between different dynamical regimes across various time scales. Our framework enables the study of the statistical physics of systems that either aggregate—such as transportation networks covering the same region—or correlate, including inter-brain synchrony in socially interacting organisms and the collective behavior of swarming or synchronizing active matter.

Although planning-based sequence modeling has demonstrated significant promise for continuous control, extending these methods to high-dimensional state-action sequences remains an unresolved challenge due to computational demands and the inherent difficulties of planning in such spaces. We introduce the Trajectory Autoencoding Planner (TAP), a reinforcement learning approach that overcomes these limitations by scaling to high dimensionalities. Leveraging a state-conditional Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE), TAP models the conditional distribution of trajectories relative to the current state. When acting as an RL agent, TAP bypasses the need for step-by-step planning in a high-dimensional continuous action space; instead, it identifies optimal latent code sequences through beam search. Unlike the Trajectory Transformer, which suffers from $O(D^3)$ complexity, TAP achieves a constant $O(C)$ computational complexity with respect to state-action dimensionality $D$. Empirical results further demonstrate that TAP's performance improves as dimensionality increases. In Adroit robotic hand manipulation tasks characterized by high state and action dimensions, TAP significantly outperforms existing model-based methods, such as the Trajectory Transformer, and also surpasses strong model-free actor-critic baselines.

This paper investigates several findings regarding almost semi-invariant submanifolds of generalized Sasakian-space-forms, as discussed in \cite{ALEGRE3}, specifically in relation to semisymmetric metric and non-metric connections, as well as the Schouten-van Kampen and Tanaka-Webster connections.

Cell membranes act as barriers between the intracellular space and the external world, composed of diverse lipids whose makeup governs protein dynamics and cellular adaptability. While model membranes provide insights into lipid interactions and general mechanics, the properties of native membranes remain poorly understood. To bridge the gap between topological and nanomechanical analyses of native membranes, I developed a method to examine plasma membranes isolated from various single cells. By testing five distinct cell types, I observed a 20% variation in membrane thickness. Furthermore, by assessing the resistance of these isolated membranes to indentation, I determined their line tension and spreading pressure. These findings indicate that neuronal membranes are stiffer and exhibit lower diffusivity compared to those from brain cancer cells, offering direct quantitative insights into the mechanics of native cell membranes.

We introduce Hyper-pool, an analytical, offline, and utility-focused ride-pooling algorithm designed to consolidate individual trip requests into high-occupancy shared rides. Building upon our existing ExMAS algorithm, which aggregates single trips into efficient door-to-door journeys, we develop two novel demand-side strategies to further cluster individual requests into more compact groups. First, we create stop-to-stop rides featuring a single, optimal pickup and drop-off point for all passengers. Second, we bundle these rides again to produce hyper-pooled rides that closely mimic public transport efficiency. Our bottom-up framework gradually increases the pooling degree of identified rides, ensuring attractiveness at every aggregation stage. The Hyper-pool method generates a set of appealing pooled rides for various service variants based on specific travel demand. The algorithms are publicly accessible and reproducible, capable of handling real-world demand datasets while unlocking new potential for ride-pooling. In an Amsterdam case study, we successfully pooled over 220 travelers into 40 hyper-pooled rides, achieving an average occupancy of 5.8 passengers per vehicle.

High-resolution spectroscopy has significantly enhanced our ability to characterize exoplanet atmospheres, particularly for non-transiting planets, thereby expanding the pool of observable targets. Among these, hot Jupiters represent prime candidates due to their substantial spatial variability in temperature, winds, and clouds, rendering viewing geometry a critical factor. While three-dimensional models have traditionally simulated hot Jupiter observations under edge-on assumptions, ignoring non-transiting systems, this study pioneers the analysis of orbital inclination effects on high-resolution emission spectra. Utilizing a General Circulation Model, we simulate the atmospheric structure of Upsilon Andromedae b, a non-transiting hot Jupiter. To accurately model cloud scattering, we incorporated a generalized two-stream radiative transfer routine designed for inhomogeneous multiple scattering. Comparisons between cloudy and clear-sky models reveal that cloud coverage amplifies spatial variations, leading to increased net Doppler shifts and greater fluctuations in continuum flux amplitude throughout the orbit. Furthermore, as orbital inclination decreases, four specific features diminish in both clear and cloudy scenarios: (1) mean continuum flux levels, (2) the amplitude of continuum variation with orbital phase, (3) net Doppler shifts of spectral lines, and (4) spectral Doppler broadening. Ultimately, models that account for heterogeneous cloud coverage and diverse viewing angles are essential for interpreting high-resolution emission spectra, opening new pathways to explore these extreme atmospheric environments.

This paper reports findings from the Alexa speech teams regarding semi-supervised learning (SSL) for acoustic models, based on experiments utilizing over 3,000 hours of GPU compute, establishing one of the most extensive studies in this domain. We examine SSL within a constrained model footprint, demonstrating that a compact model trained on one million hours of unsupervised data can surpass a supervised baseline by reducing word error rate (WERR) by 14.3%. However, when supervised data increases seven-fold, these gains decrease to a 7.1% WERR reduction. To enhance SSL efficiency at larger supervised data scales, we apply step-wise distillation into a smaller model, achieving a WERR of 14.4%. Subsequently, we investigate SSL with larger student models in low-data scenarios; although unsupervised learning efficiency improves, student models can outperform teacher models in this context. We also propose a theoretical framework to elucidate this phenomenon.

The primary goal of this paper is to present and analyze the function $_pR_q(A, B; z)$ featuring matrix parameters, along with an examination of its convergence. We derive contiguous relations, differential formulas, and an integral representation for this matrix function. Additionally, we explore specific properties of $_pR_q(A, B; z)$ through the lens of fractional calculus. The study concludes by highlighting special cases, including the generalized matrix $M$-series, the Mittag-Leffler matrix function and its extensions, as well as certain matrix polynomials.

Diffusion is a widespread phenomenon in natural physical systems, grounded in the universality of the central limit theorem. Over a century ago, researchers discovered that this framework could be extended to "anomalous" diffusion, characterized by distributions with heavy, power-law tails. Laser-cooled atomic ensembles serve as an ideal experimental platform for studying such dynamics due to the distinct nature of their momentum-dependent dissipative friction. The interaction between laser cooling and anomalous behavior offers profound predictive insights into fundamental concepts within both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical physics. The precise control afforded by cold-atom experiments enables the tuning of friction force parameters, thereby exposing transitions in the system's dynamical properties. Rare events occurring in both spatial and momentum distributions are modeled using non-normalized states derived from infinite ergodic theory. This approach has yielded significant new theoretical and experimental findings that clarify the diverse characteristics of these systems.

We demonstrate that the position operator with commuting components, initially proposed by M. Hawton [M. Hawton, Phys. Rev. A {\bf 59}, 954 (1999)] and further developed in later works, lacks the essential characteristics of a photon position operator. Depending on the precise interpretation of these findings, the operator either describes a triplet of massless spin-zero particles instead of a photon, or fails to exhibit the necessary covariance properties under spatial rotations.

Numerous machine learning tasks involve optimizing objectives subject to noisy measurements. The standard approach employs first-order stochastic gradient descent, utilizing one or more Monte Carlo (MC) samples per iteration. However, in scenarios characterized by ill-conditioning, second-order methods like L-BFGS often prove superior. This work examines the application of randomized quasi-Monte Carlo (RQMC) sampling in these contexts. While standard MC sampling typically yields a root mean squared error (RMSE) of $O(n^{-1/2})$, RQMC achieves an RMSE of $o(n^{-1/2})$, potentially approaching $O(n^{-3/2})$ under favorable conditions. We demonstrate that this enhanced sampling precision directly correlates with improved optimization outcomes. Empirical studies on variational Bayes reveal that integrating RQMC with stochastic L-BFGS significantly accelerates optimization and occasionally results in superior parameter estimates compared to traditional MC methods.

For any contractive iterated function system (IFS, encompassing Moran systems), we demonstrate the existence of a natural hyperbolic graph within the symbolic space, establishing a H\"{o}lder equivalence between the hyperbolic boundary and the IFS's invariant set. This work extends prior research (\cite{[Ka]}, \cite{[LW1]}, \cite{[W]}) by removing unnecessary constraints and accommodating a broader range of sets, such as Moran sets. Furthermore, we establish that the bounded degree property of the graph serves as a characterization for specific separation conditions in the IFS, including the open set condition and weak separation condition; this property is especially critical when analyzing random walks on these graphs. Additional applications, including the Lipschitz equivalence of self-similar sets, will also be addressed.

Over recent years, Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) have advanced significantly, transforming sectors like smart manufacturing, healthcare, and transportation to boost national economies. Despite this progress, CPS security remains a critical barrier to widespread adoption due to the proliferation of internet-connected devices and the inadequacy of traditional security measures against sophisticated, application-specific threats. This paper proposes a programmable device network layer architecture designed to mitigate attacks and enable efficient monitoring within heterogeneous CPS environments. By leveraging Industrial Control Systems (ICS), the study examines current challenges and underscores the necessity of an advanced network layer for CPS. Furthermore, it introduces the Programmable Data Plane Language (P4) to effectively detect well-known HELLO Flood attacks with minimal network-level overhead, demonstrating its potential as a robust security solution.

Identifying parameters in marine ecosystem models is crucial for validating and assessing these models against observational data. Surrogate-based optimization (SBO) offers a computationally efficient strategy for optimizing complex systems by substituting a high-fidelity, expensive model with a surrogate derived from a low-fidelity, cheaper model, enhanced by a correction method to boost accuracy. To develop such a cost-effective low-fidelity model, we evaluated three methods for approximating the annual periodic solution (steady annual cycle) of a marine ecosystem model: reducing spin-up iterations from millennia to decades, utilizing an artificial neural network (ANN) to approximate the cycle, and combining both techniques. Results showed that, except for the ANN-only low-fidelity model, SBO produced solutions near the target while drastically reducing computational costs. Consequently, if a suitable ANN approximating a marine ecosystem model exists, employing SBO with this ANN as the low-fidelity component represents a promising and highly efficient approach for model validation.

This text offers a self-contained introduction to finite extensive games with perfect information. In these games, players take turns, each having a finite set of moves at every stage, with every play eventually concluding and all players possessing full knowledge of prior moves. While nearly all presented results are well-established, they are often not formulated in their most optimal manner. Furthermore, as these results typically appear in literature targeting economists or mathematicians, their algorithmic and logical dimensions are frequently overlooked.

This article establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for the validity of Huygens' principle regarding the Dirac operator within non-constant curvature spacetimes characterized by Friedmann-Lema\^itre-Robertson-Walker cosmological models. The analysis of Huygens' principle covers both massless particles ($m=0$) and massive spin-1/2 fields, accounting for the redshift in wavelength that occurs as the universe expands.

Inspired by finite volume schemes, we introduce a neural network approach grounded in cell averages and the integral or weak formulations of partial differential equations. This simple feed-forward network is trained offline via supervised learning to approximate the evolution of solution averages between consecutive time steps, thereby defining a unique finite-volume-like method. Once optimized, the network functions as a finite volume scheme, inheriting mesh dependence. Unlike conventional numerical techniques, this approach bypasses the explicit scheme's CFL stability constraint, allowing for flexible time step selection. In the case of the heat equation, the method achieves first-order convergence, where errors depend on spatial discretization but remain independent of temporal mesh size. Furthermore, the cell-average based neural network effectively resolves contact discontinuities with negligible numerical diffusion and accurately captures shock and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws.

This paper presents a summary of the LHCb collaboration's initial observation of CP violation within the Charm sector, reviews various theoretical models that account for this finding, and explores future experimental possibilities for further measurements.

We show that non-equilibrium steady states within the dissipative Rabi model exhibit pronounced peaks in transport rates across specific, narrow parameter intervals. Comparable outcomes are observed in the Holstein and Dicke models. This phenomenon arises from avoided energy level crossings in the associated closed systems and aligns with spikes in the entanglement entropy of relevant eigenstates, indicating robust mixing and resonance among the system's degrees of freedom. Additionally, comparing the Rabi model to the Jaynes-Cummings model suggests that this behavior is linked to quantum integrability.

This brief note examines the QED extension of the nucleon spin sum rule. To achieve this, we calculate the leading-order (LO) QED evolution kernels for quark/gluon helicity and orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) distributions, alongside the novel introduction and calculation of LO evolution kernels for lepton and photon analogue distributions in both QCD and QED frameworks. Collectively, these results confirm that the nucleon spin sum rule remains scale-invariant within QCD$\times$QED, as anticipated, thereby validating the new findings. This theoretical advancement will enable future quantification of lepton and photon contributions to nucleon spin and provide more precise control over associated uncertainties.

Despite the high accuracy of current object detection and classification models, they are typically limited by fixed training sets, making them inflexible when encountering new, unseen categories. Additionally, these models usually process single frames, which can lead to errors when viewpoints are ambiguous. This paper introduces an active inference agent capable of actively collecting evidence for classifications and learning new object categories over time. Inspired by the human brain, we develop object-centric generative models featuring two distinct information streams: a "what-stream" that determines object categories and a "where-stream" that represents objects within an internal 3D reference frame. Our results demonstrate that the agent can (i) learn representations for numerous object categories in an unsupervised manner, (ii) achieve state-of-the-art classification accuracy while actively resolving ambiguity, and (iii) identify novel object categories. Furthermore, we validate the system end-to-end, showing the agent can locate an object at a specific pose from pixel-based rendering. We consider this a foundational step toward creating modular, intelligent systems capable of handling diverse tasks involving three-dimensional objects.

The challenge of transporting non-thermal particles across large-scale magnetic fields amidst magnetized turbulence remains a significant topic in high-energy astrophysics, particularly regarding how parallel ($\lambda_{\parallel}$) and perpendicular ($\lambda_{\perp}$) mean free paths depend on rigidity $\mathcal{R}$. Addressing this with applications ranging from Galactic cosmic ray transport to shock acceleration, we conducted test particle simulations within synthetic, isotropic Kolmogorov turbulence. These simulations reached unprecedentedly low reduced rigidities ($r_g/L_c \simeq 10^{-4}$), equivalent to $\mathcal{R} \simeq 10 \, \text{TV}$ given a turbulent magnetic field of $B_{rms} = 4 \, \mu\text{G}$ and a correlation length $L_c = 30 \, \text{pc}$. By determining the asymptotic mean free paths, we confirmed that $\lambda_{\parallel} \propto (r_g/L_c)^{1/3}$, consistent with Kolmogorov theory. Conversely, $\lambda_{\perp}$ exhibits a steeper dependence on $r_g/L_c$ within the range $10^{-2} \lesssim r_g/L_c \lesssim 1$, yet reverts to $\lambda_{\perp} \propto (r_g/L_c)^{1/3}$ when $r_g/L_c \ll 10^{-2}$. These findings carry significant implications for understanding Galactic cosmic ray transport.

Nontrivial topology serves as a fundamental driver for numerous phenomena in physical systems, necessitating that matter phases be categorized by their topological characteristics. Systems exhibiting topological order (TO), exemplified by the fractional quantum Hall effect (QHE), host anyonic excitations governed by fractional statistics, offering promising avenues for topological quantum computing. Conversely, states without intrinsic TO can still occupy topological phases when specific symmetries are enforced; while these symmetry-protected phases lack anyons, they may exhibit other distinct properties, such as protected boundary states. This thesis details research on various nontrivial systems. Initially, we examine light propagation through valley modes in inversion-symmetry-broken honeycomb lattices, discovering that the nontrivial topology of these valleys induces a rotating spiral pattern in the beam's intensity profile, known as Zitterbewegung. Subsequently, we provide numerical evidence of dynamical topological phase transitions within soliton SSH lattices, driven by the nonlinearity of the photonic medium. These transitions, characterized by the emergence of topological edge states within the band gap, result from a configuration that allows continuous variation of intracell and intercell soliton couplings. Finally, we propose a method for generating and manipulating synthetic anyons in a noninteracting system using specially designed localized probes. Since noninteracting systems lack the intrinsic TO required for native anyons, we utilize an external magnetic field setup starting with a 2DEG in an integer QHE state, introducing thin solenoids carrying fractional magnetic flux. We identify a viable ground state and demonstrate fractional braiding statistics relative to the solenoid coordinates.
We extend the investigation of Schroder quasigroups and Schroder T-quasigroups.

Debris disc structures offer exoplanetary scientists vital insights into planet formation and evolution, specifically by constraining the masses of perturbing bodies, whether visible or hidden. This is especially relevant to the HD 106906 disc, where early Hubble Space Telescope data and subsequent polarimetric studies revealed asymmetries and needle-like features attributed to a massive, distant planetary companion orbiting outside the disc. In this study, we re-examine the long-term secular dynamical evolution of the HD 106906 disc, incorporating the combined gravitational influence of both the external planetary companion and the inner stellar binary that binds the system, a factor previously overlooked in dedicated models. Utilizing Laplace's foundational principles, recently adapted for wide eccentric perturbers such as Planet 9, we demonstrate that, within orbital uncertainties, the disc transitions from being dominated by the inner binary to being significantly influenced by it, rarely extending beyond the binary's reach. Our analysis predicts a rounded, mildly warped disc architecture consistent with recent ALMA observations, a model that can be further refined through dialogue with these new data. Additionally, we apply our findings to establish dynamical constraints on the orbit of the planetary companion.

The ALICE Collaboration has finished upgrading its detector and is currently commissioning it for data collection at the start of LHC Run 3. Concurrently, R&D efforts and simulations are underway to plan the experiment's evolution beyond Run 3. Two major upgrades are scheduled for the upcoming Long Shutdown 3 (LS3). The initial upgrade involves replacing the three innermost tracking layers nearest to the beam with a new vertex detector made of curved, wafer-scale ultra-thin silicon sensors in precise cylindrical configurations. This aims to enhance impact parameter resolution and greatly expand physics potential for studying heavy-flavor production and low-mass dielectrons. The second LS3 upgrade will add a Forward Calorimeter at large rapidity, featuring a Si-W electromagnetic calorimeter with pad and pixel readout, granting the experiment unique abilities to measure small-x gluon distributions through prompt photon production. Additionally, a proposal for a next-generation heavy-ion experiment for LHC Run 5 is being prepared. This initiative seeks novel measurements of electromagnetic and hadronic probes of the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP), such as multiply-charmed baryons, which have previously been out of reach due to detector limitations and luminosity constraints. The proposed apparatus design emphasizes extensive use of thin silicon sensors for tracking and a modern particle identification system that integrates a silicon-based time-of-flight detector, a RICH detector, an electromagnetic calorimeter, and a muon system.

We conduct General Relativity (GR) tests using gravitational waves (GWs) from compact binary inspirals within a theory-independent framework that applies generic phase corrections to each multipole of a frequency-domain GR waveform model. Previously validated on LIGO-Virgo data, this approach yields tight constraints on post-Newtonian inspiral predictions and evaluates potential systematic biases in parameterized tests. In this work, we outline the framework's structure for aligned-spin waveform models and investigate how higher modes influence GR tests by analyzing two unequal-mass simulated signals analogous to GW190412 and GW190814. Our results demonstrate that incorporating higher modes enhances both the precision and accuracy of deviation parameter measurements. Additionally, the framework permits varying the baseline GR waveform model and the frequency at which non-GR corrections are tapered; we conclude that optimizing GR tests for high-mass binaries requires comprehensive studies to identify the optimal tapering frequency based on binary properties. Furthermore, we analyze the binary neutron-star event GW170817 to constrain the coupling constant $\alpha_0$ in Jordan-Fierz-Brans-Dicke gravity. Employing two strategies—a \emph{theory-agnostic} method yielding $\alpha_0 \lesssim 2\times 10^{-1}$ and a \emph{theory-specific} method yielding $\alpha_0 \lesssim 4\times 10^{-1}$, both at the $68\%$ credible level—we attribute these discrepancies primarily to the differing statistical hypotheses employed.

I highlight two phenomenological approaches to quantum gravity that appear highly promising. Furthermore, I contend that significant empirical data already exists and should guide future research in this field.
