Furthermore, we examine the real-space eigenmodes, analyzing their spatial characteristics and temperature dependence within the random phase approximation.

Cells within an epithelial monolayer synchronize their movements with adjacent cells, forming collective groups that span multiple cell diameters. However, the physical mechanism governing the size of these groups remains undefined. One proposed mechanism suggests that if cell-substrate traction forces maintain their direction over a sufficient time scale, large collective packs will form. To evaluate this hypothesis, researchers measured both the velocity and net traction of individual cells. The results revealed that, alongside temporal persistence, tractions exhibit spatial correlations, indicating that cells coordinate to apply forces in the same direction as their neighbors. Using chemical inhibitors and activators of actomyosin contraction, the study examined how altering traction persistence and alignment affects these dynamics. Numerical simulations based on a self-propelled Voronoi model, which incorporated both traction persistence and alignment and were calibrated to experimental data, successfully reproduced the observed pack sizes. The model demonstrated that without alignment of traction between neighboring cells, the resulting collective packs would be significantly smaller than those observed experimentally. By integrating experimental findings with a simple mechanical model, this study validates the established concept of traction persistence and introduces traction alignment between neighbors as a critical factor. Ultimately, both persistence and alignment are identified as key determinants of the size of collectively moving cell packs.

Infectious disease and climate modeling often employ multi-model ensembles where independent teams generate projections across various future scenarios, typically defined by the presence or absence of specific decisions, such as vaccination programs. While these models provide probabilistic forecasts for each scenario, deriving a confidence interval for the impact of a decision—such as the number of lives saved—remains challenging because the joint probability distribution is unknown and difficult to reconstruct due to computational and logistical constraints. This work proposes a method to estimate meaningful bounds on the outcomes of decision variables without requiring additional simulations from the models. We first demonstrate, under a specific assumption, how to calculate an $\alpha$-confidence interval for the difference between scenarios using only prediction quantiles, and then extend this to cases where the assumption is relaxed. Finally, we apply this approach to estimate confidence intervals regarding reductions in cases, deaths, and hospitalizations resulting from vaccinations, utilizing data from the US Scenario Modeling Hub.

Dialogue disentanglement involves organizing utterances from lengthy, multi-turn conversations into distinct threads, a process beneficial for discourse analysis and downstream tasks like response selection, where it helps build clean context-response pairs. However, manually labeling all \emph{reply-to} relationships is computationally expensive, scaling quadratically with the number of utterances, as annotators must examine every preceding statement to find the one being replied to. This paper introduces the first \textbf{zero-shot} approach to dialogue disentanglement. We initially train a model on a large, unannotated web-derived dataset of multi-participant responses and subsequently apply it for zero-shot disentanglement. Even without any labeled data, our model achieves a cluster F1 score of 25. Additionally, we explore fine-tuning the model with varying amounts of labeled data. Results indicate that utilizing just 10\% of the labeled data yields performance nearly equivalent to using the complete dataset\footnote{Code is available at \url{https://github.com/chijames/zero_shot_dialogue_disentanglement}}.

This paper derives a formula for estimating the number of primes within a specific interval based on prime distribution characteristics. For any prime pairs $p>5$ and $q>5$, an infinite sequence of disjoint sets $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_i, \ldots$ is constructed such that the count of prime pairs $(p_i, q_i)$ with a constant difference $p_i-q_i = p-q$ within each set $A_i$ grows progressively as $i>0$. This construction is presented as proof for the truth of the twin prime conjecture. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that for every even integer $m>2700$, there are more than 10 prime pairs $(p,q)$ satisfying $p+q=m$, thereby confirming the Goldbach conjecture.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to various simulated real-world scenarios, including sensor coordination, traffic light management, and on-demand mobility services. However, actual deployments remain uncommon because RL agents struggle with the dynamic nature of real-world environments, often requiring substantial time to learn tasks and adapt to changing conditions. Transfer Learning (TL) offers a solution by reducing these adaptation periods. Specifically, TL holds significant promise for multi-agent RL systems, enabling agents to share knowledge both among themselves and with newly joined agents. To maximize the benefits of inter-agent transfer, it is crucial to dynamically select transfer roles (identifying source and target agents) and relevant content parameters (such as transfer volume) for each specific situation. As an initial step toward fully dynamic transfers, this paper examines the effect of TL transfer parameters when source and target roles are fixed. We annotate every agent-environment interaction with the agent's epistemic confidence and filter shared examples using different threshold levels and sample sizes. Finally, we evaluate the impact of these parameters in two scenarios: a standard predator-prey RL benchmark and a ride-sharing simulation involving 200 vehicle agents and 10,000 ride requests.

Color symmetry extends symmetry principles from isometric transformations by assigning colors to geometrical objects based on their inherent symmetry properties. This concept ensures that the coloring of objects permutes consistently with their symmetry groups. We apply this framework to bio-inspired generative art, interpreting geometrical objects as motifs that repeat with symmetry-consistent coloring. These motifs are derived from stigmergy-based design principles. The discussion includes a proposed design procedure alongside visual examples of the results.

Grain growth, a sophisticated process during the annealing of polycrystalline materials, poses significant challenges for numerical modeling, particularly when accounting for anisotropy factors like grain orientation and boundary inclination. This paper applies the front-tracking method, ToRealMotion, previously detailed in earlier studies, to simulate anisotropic grain boundary dynamics at the mesoscopic level. The proposed boundary migration formulation accommodates various anisotropy sources, including those at grain boundaries and multiple junctions (MJs)—points where three or more boundaries intersect. A key focus is the decomposition of high-order MJs using a new algorithm grounded in local grain boundary energy minimization. The study presents numerical tests on highly heterogeneous configurations and compares results with a recently developed Finite-Element Level-Set (FE-LS) method. Additionally, the model's computational efficiency is evaluated by comparing CPU times between the anisotropic implementation and an isotropic version of the same model.

Recent studies indicate that deep vision models often rely excessively on low-level "texture" features, which hampers their generalization capabilities. To address this texture bias in deep neural networks (DNNs), various data augmentation methods have been suggested. We introduce a simple, lightweight adversarial augmentation approach designed to explicitly encourage the network to learn holistic shapes for accurate object classification. Our method superimposes edge maps from one image onto another image containing shuffled patches, applying a randomly determined mixing ratio while retaining the label of the source edge map. To classify these augmented images, the model must not only identify and attend to edges but also differentiate between relevant and spurious ones. We demonstrate that our augmentations significantly boost classification accuracy and robustness across multiple datasets and neural architectures. For instance, using ViT-S, we achieved absolute accuracy improvements of up to 6%. Furthermore, we observed gains of up to 28% on natural adversarial datasets (ImageNet-A for ViT-B) and 8.5% on out-of-distribution datasets (ImageNet-R for ViT-S). Probe dataset analysis reveals a marked increase in shape sensitivity within our trained models, accounting for the observed enhancements in both robustness and accuracy.

Recent years have seen significant interest in counting BPS states within four-dimensional ${\cal N}=1$ theories. In superconformal contexts, these states map bijectively to local operators residing in various short representations. The generating function for this enumeration exhibits branch cuts, yielding multiple Cardy-like limits that mirror high-temperature regimes. Of particular note is the second sheet, which has been demonstrated to encode the microstates and phases of supersymmetric black holes in AdS$_5$. This work introduces a three-dimensional Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework to analyze the high-temperature limit on the second sheet. Utilizing this EFT, we derive the index's behavior at orders $\beta^{-2}, \beta^{-1},$ and $\beta^0$. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture for the $O(\beta)$ term, arguing that the series truncates up to exponentially suppressed corrections. A crucial aspect involves vector multiplet zero modes existing without accompanying massless matter fields. While the Affleck-Harvey-Witten runaway is averted by a non-perturbative confinement mechanism, this same mechanism ensures the robustness of our findings.
This paper presents two results regarding the mean value problem, comprehensively resolving Smale's mean value problem.

Reducing gradient norms remains a core challenge in first-order optimization, lacking unified and straightforward convergence proofs that have traditionally been applied only to criteria like closing the optimality gap. We propose a new potential function-based framework to analyze the convergence of standard techniques for minimizing gradients within smooth convex and convex-concave min-max settings. This intuitive approach offers a perspective that frames these algorithms as balancing the reduction of gradient norms against a specific measure of the optimality gap. Regarding lower bounds, we examine the tightness of our convergence findings for convex problems and introduce a novel lower bound for minimizing the norm of cocoercive operators, which supports arguments about the optimality of methods in min-max scenarios.

The Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) provides significant benefits, particularly in resource efficiency and circuit approximation, for executing arithmetic on quantum computers, potentially establishing a new numerical quantum-computational framework. This paper employs efficient methods to realize QFT-based integer addition and multiplication, operations essential for diverse quantum applications such as Shor's algorithm, weighted sum optimization in data processing and machine learning, and algorithms involving inner products. We evaluate the performance of these implementations on IBM's superconducting qubit architecture across various compatible noise models. Our analysis isolates the sensitivity of component circuits to one- and two-qubit gate error rates as well as the number of superposed integer states in the operands. We determine the most effective approximation depths for quantum adders and multipliers within this context, observing a strong dependence of the optimal depth on machine noise levels and the number of superposed states in specific regimes. Furthermore, we discuss algorithmic challenges related to signed, unsigned, modular, and non-modular variants that apply to current QFT-based implementations of subtraction, division, exponentiation, and their potential tensor extensions. Finally, we examine performance trends in our findings and speculate on future developments within this computational paradigm.

This study introduces HST photometric data for 17 Cepheids within open clusters, accompanied by mean parallaxes derived from Gaia EDR3. These cluster-averaged parallaxes offer superior precision compared to individual parallaxes from fainter Cepheids (G<8 mag) previously utilized for Hubble constant measurements, as they result from averaging over more than 300 stars per cluster. Furthermore, the smaller systematic uncertainties in these cluster parallaxes stem from the fact that their constituent stars fall within the G>13 mag range, where Gaia's parallax calibration is most robust. The Cepheid photometry used to establish the period-luminosity relation was obtained using the same WFC3 instrument and filters (F555W, F814W, F160W) as those employed for extragalactic Cepheids in SNIa host galaxies. No residual parallax offset was detected in this magnitude range (zp=-3+/-4 muas), aligning with Lindegren:2021b and most prior research. The Cepheid luminosity (for P=10d and solar metallicity) in the HST near-infrared Wesenheit system, derived from the cluster sample, yields values of M_{H,1}^W=-5.902+/-0.025 and -5.890+/-0.018 mag when accounting for or excluding a simultaneous parallax offset, respectively. These findings mirror measurements from field Cepheids, validating the accuracy of Gaia parallaxes across a wide magnitude spectrum. When the SH0ES distance ladder is calibrated exclusively using this sample, it produces H_0=72.8+/-1.3 and H_0=73.2+/-1.1 km/s/Mpc with or without offset marginalization; incorporating all anchors results in H_0=73.01+/-0.99 and 73.15+/-0.97, respectively. This represents a 5% or 7% reduction in uncertainty and a 5.3 sigma Hubble Tension relative to the Planck+LambdaCDM model. Consequently, reconciling two of the most precisely measured cosmic scales—Gaia parallaxes and the CMB's acoustic angular size—appears increasingly challenging under the simplest LambdaCDM framework.

This research utilizes Monte Carlo simulations via the GEANT4 code to validate the effectiveness of dual-parameter muon tomography for inspecting nuclear waste barrels. The experimental configuration involves a hodoscope with three top and three bottom 0.4 cm thick polyvinyl toluene scintillators. The simulated target is a cylindrical waste drum (96 cm high, 29.6 cm radius) featuring a 3.2 cm thick stainless steel shell and ordinary concrete filling containing 20$\times$20$\times$20 cm$^{3}$ nuclear materials. Simulations employ a narrow 1$\times$1 cm$^{2}$ planar muon beam across a uniform energy range of 0.1 to 8 GeV. We analyzed the variation in average scattering angles and their standard deviations using 0.5-GeV energy bins, counted scattering angles with 1-mrad resolution, and tracked absorption events for five common nuclear elements ranging from cobalt to plutonium. The study demonstrates that duo-parametric analysis, combining scattering angle and absorption data, makes nuclear materials within waste barrels numerically distinguishable from concrete-filled drums lacking such materials. Furthermore, muon tomography can differentiate between specific nuclear materials by correlating scattering and absorption information, even when individual parameters show similar values for certain isotopes.

This study investigates the spin-dependent transport characteristics of a spin valve constructed from a double quantum dot system. In this configuration, each quantum dot is strongly connected to its respective ferromagnetic lead, while the inter-dot coupling remains relatively weak. We calculate the system's current using perturbation theory applied to the hopping interaction between dots, and determine the spectrum of the quantum dot-ferromagnetic lead subsystem via the numerical renormalization group method. Spin-dependent charge fluctuations occurring between the ferromagnets and the quantum dots produce an effective exchange field that splits the double dot energy levels. This field can be independently adjusted for each dot through gate voltages or by altering the magnetic configuration of the external leads. We demonstrate that this double quantum dot spin valve setup exhibits enhanced magnetoresistive properties, encompassing both normal and inverse tunnel magnetoresistance. Furthermore, we show that the system can generate highly spin-polarized currents controllable via purely electrical means. Consequently, this double quantum dot structure with ferromagnetic contacts functions as an efficient, voltage-tunable spin valve with superior output parameters.

We examine variations in Spitzer/IRAC photometry at 3.6 and 4.5 microns that arise from different observing strategies. By analyzing archival calibration data for ten stars observed under all possible strategies, we quantify differences in measured flux densities based on three factors: 1) array mode (full versus subarray), 2) exposure time, and 3) dithering versus staring. Our results show that median fluxes for full-array observations are 1.6% and 1% lower than those from subarray observations at [3.6] and [4.5], respectively. Furthermore, flux measurements depend on exposure time; for [3.6] bands, long frame times yield fluxes that are 3.4% (full array) and 2.9% (subarray) lower than short frame times, while for [4.5] bands, the reductions are 0.6% and 1.5% for full and subarray modes, respectively. These minor variations may only impact science users requiring high-precision photometry across multiple modes. No statistically significant difference was found between dithered and staring modes. Additionally, across the entire sample, the fractional well depth of the pixel correlates with observed flux differences, suggesting a cause in small non-linearities at low well depths where linearity was previously assumed to be negligible.

Recent studies have developed Lindblad-type master equations to model the dynamics of quarkonium states within the quark-gluon plasma. Due to the significant computational difficulty of solving these equations in three dimensions, they are frequently simplified to one dimension. Central to these equations is a complex potential that characterizes both the binding of heavy quark-antiquark pairs and their interactions with the surrounding medium. In this study, we introduce a one-dimensional complex potential designed to optimally match two critical features of a three-dimensional lattice QCD-inspired potential: the temperature-dependent masses of the eigenstates and their decay widths. We subsequently calculate the spectral decompositions of these potentials to verify their consistency with the positivity requirements of the master equations.

We demonstrate that for a semisimple Lie algebra over a discrete valuation ring with fraction field $K$, every primitive ideal possessing a rational central character within the affinoid enveloping algebra $\widehat{U(\mathfrak{g})_{K}}$ serves as the annihilator of an affinoid highest weight module.

Let $K$ be a field with characteristic $p > 0$ and let $\omega$ denote an $r$-form in $K^n$. Unlike in characteristic zero, the standard Poincaré Lemma fails in this setting, as there exist closed $r$-forms that are not exact. This work introduces the definition of $p$-closed $r$-forms and establishes a version of the Poincaré Lemma applicable to $p$-closed polynomial or rational $r$-forms on $K^n$. Consequently, the de Rham cohomology modules of $K^n$ are found to be non-trivial.

This paper introduces a learning framework where system acquisition is steered by physical principles. Specifically, we address the two-point boundary optimal control challenge for linear time-varying systems with unknown dynamics by employing reinforcement learning. By adapting methods from singular perturbation theory, we decompose the time-varying optimal control task into a set of time-invariant subproblems. This decomposition enables the use of an off-policy iteration approach to derive controller gains. We demonstrate that the performance of our learned controller closely mirrors that of a model-based optimal controller, with approximation accuracy enhancing as the control time horizon expands. Furthermore, we present a simulation study to validate these findings.

For a finite group $G$, we examine the properties of four invariants, $\text{MaxDim}(G)$, $\text{MinDim}(G)$, $\text{MaxInt}(G)$, and $\text{MinInt}(G)$, which quantify the width and height of the lattice $\mathcal M(G)$ formed by the intersections of $G$'s maximal subgroups.

This research investigates the dynamics of open quantum many-body systems driven through a critical point by varying a Hamiltonian parameter at a specific speed. We establish general scaling laws describing the density of excitations and energy generated during the quench as functions of the quench velocity and bath temperature. These laws, along with their respective regimes of validity, are confirmed using the XY spin chain locally coupled to bosonic environments. Furthermore, a comprehensive derivation and analysis of the problem's kinetic equation are provided.

Directly alerting users is not always an effective strategy, particularly when they lack the motivation to comply. For instance, in video-based learning, distracted learners often ignore prompts urging them to pay attention. Drawing inspiration from the concept of Mindless Computing, we introduce a new intervention called Mindless Attractor. This approach utilizes the inherent characteristics of human speech to help learners regain focus without depending on their conscious motivation. Specifically, it subtly alters the voice in the video to guide attention while bypassing conscious awareness. Our experiments validated the effectiveness of this method and highlighted its benefits when paired with a machine learning-based sensing system. Notably, the system avoids frustrating users even if the intervention triggers on false-positive detections of their attentional state. Ultimately, this intervention offers a dependable method for inducing behavioral change within human-AI symbiotic environments.

Weak measurements on superconducting qubits yield noisy voltage signals that only weakly correlate with the qubit's state. Conventional techniques to extract individual quantum trajectories from this noise rely on slow qubit dynamics and extensive prior knowledge gained from calibration experiments; monitoring rapid dynamics, such as those occurring during quantum gates, necessitates even more complex approaches with higher information demands. In this work, we experimentally present an alternative approach for accurately tracking rapidly driven superconducting qubit trajectories using a Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) artificial neural network that requires minimal prior information. Despite making few training assumptions, the LSTM successfully generates trajectories that incorporate qubit-readout resonator correlations arising from finite detection bandwidth. Beyond revealing rotated measurement eigenstates and a reduced measurement rate consistent with theoretical predictions for a fixed drive, the trained LSTM also correctly reconstructs the evolution of an unknown drive featuring rapid modulation. This research facilitates new applications of weak measurements in scenarios involving faster or initially uncertain qubit dynamics, including the diagnosis of coherent errors in quantum gates.

Recent progress in attention mechanisms has significantly boosted performance across various machine learning domains by facilitating the dynamic modeling of temporal sequences. Video action recognition in computer vision stands to gain substantially from integrating these mechanisms. However, existing research predominantly focuses on spatial and temporal attention, which often fail to leverage the inherent motion present in videos. Addressing this gap, we introduce Motion Aware Attention (M2A), a novel mechanism designed to explicitly incorporate motion characteristics. Specifically, M2A extracts motion data between consecutive frames and employs attention to highlight motion patterns across frames, thereby enhancing action recognition accuracy. The proposed M2A is straightforward to implement and can be seamlessly integrated into any neural network backbone. Our results demonstrate that combining motion mechanisms with attention via M2A improves top-1 accuracy by 15% to 26% across various backbones, with only a minor increase in computational cost. Furthermore, comparisons against state-of-the-art motion and attention mechanisms on the Something-Something V1 benchmark reveal that M2A yields additional gains when paired with other temporal mechanisms and outperforms motion-only or attention-only approaches by up to 60% in top-1 accuracy for certain classes.

This study derives an exact formula for determining the fourth-moment tensor from the second-moment tensor within the context of the three-dimensional Jeffery's equation. Although this method belongs to the class of moment tensor closures, it avoids the approximations—whether analytic or curve-fitted—that characterize prior closures. The resulting closure is orthotropic, as defined by \cite{cintra:95}, or alternatively, a natural closure according to \cite{verleye:93}. While the existence of such explicit formulas has been hypothesized before, their specific forms have not previously been published. These expressions utilize elliptic integrals and remain valid provided the fiber orientation was isotropic at some prior time. Furthermore, the paper introduces the Fast Exact Closure (FEC), an efficient and theoretically exact approach to solving Jeffery's equation that eliminates the need for approximate closures or the computation of elliptic integrals.

Solving adjoint problems for inversion and PDE-constrained optimization is essential for computing objective function gradients, yet this process demands substantial memory storage for intermediate data, thereby restricting the scale of solvable problems. Checkpointing mitigates this by recomputing specific segments rather than retaining all intermediate results. The Revolve algorithm provides an optimal schedule balancing computational overhead against reduced memory usage. However, embedding Revolve into modern Python high-performance computing environments alongside code generation remains complex. This work introduces an API enabling checkpointing access within a DSL-based code generation framework, accompanied by preliminary performance metrics tailored for seismic applications.

We examine the linearized Vlasov and Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equations under weakly collisional conditions within a uniform magnetic field, assuming periodic confinement and Maxwellian (or near-Maxwellian) initial distributions. In the collisionless regime, transverse modes are decomposed precisely into a countable set of standing waves, referred to as Bernstein modes in physics; this decomposition does not follow immediately from known theoretical arguments. While these specific modes remain stable, other modes exhibit Landau damping. When collisions are introduced with a frequency $
u \ll 1$, the Bernstein modes experience uniform-in-$
u$ Landau damping and accelerated collisional relaxation on an $O(
u^{-1/3})$ timescale. Conversely, transverse modes remain uniformly stable and thermalize exponentially over an $O(
u^{-1})$ timescale. The majority of these findings are established through Laplace transform analysis of the related Volterra equations, while stability in the collisional scenario is demonstrated using a simplified version of Yan Guo's energy method for the hypocoercivity of collision operators.

This study examines three-dimensional bow shocks within a highly collisional, magnetized aluminum plasma created during the ablation phase of an exploding wire array on the MAGPIE facility (1.4 MA, 240 ns). Plasma ablation from the wire array produces radially expanding, supersonic ($M_S \sim 7$), super-Alfv\'enic ($M_A > 1$), magnetized flows characterized by frozen-in magnetic flux ($R_M \gg 1$). These flows impact an inductive probe serving as both the obstacle generating the magnetized bow shock and the diagnostic for the advected magnetic field. Line-integrated electron density is measured via laser interferometry along two orthogonal sightlines. A detached bow shock forms ahead of the probe, exhibiting a wider opening angle in the plane parallel to the magnetic field compared to the plane normal to it. Because the plasma's resistive diffusion length is comparable to the probe's size, the magnetic field decouples from the ion fluid at the shock front, resulting in a hydrodynamic shock whose structure depends on the sonic Mach number rather than the flow's magnetosonic Mach number. Resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations using the GORGON code validate this scenario but underestimate the anisotropy observed in the experimental shock shape, indicating that non-MHD mechanisms may play a significant role in modifying the shock structure.

Identifying anatomical landmarks for 2D echocardiographic measurements is a standard component of clinical workflows for diagnosing cardiac conditions. Automating this process is highly sought after to streamline operations and minimize interobserver variability. However, developing a machine learning framework for this task is challenging due to the scarcity of gold-standard labels, as only a small fraction of frames in cardiac cine series are typically manually annotated. To address this, we introduce a novel end-to-end reciprocal detection and tracking model specifically tailored for the sparse labeling inherent in echocardiography. This model leverages a limited set of annotated frames across the entire sequence to ensure consistent landmark detection and tracking, employing adversarial training to maximize the utility of these scarce annotations. The proposed reciprocal model's superiority is validated through a series of experiments.

Entanglement transitions represent a new category of phase transitions occurring in non-equilibrium quantum dynamics. When a many-body quantum system evolves unitarily punctuated by monitored random measurements, its steady state can undergo a transition between volume-law and area-law entanglement regimes. There exists a correspondence between measurement-induced transitions in non-unitary quantum circuits of $d$ spatial dimensions and classical statistical mechanical models in $d+1$ dimensions. While these models can map to percolation in specific limits, analytical and numerical evidence suggests that away from these limits, the universality class is generally distinct from percolation. Interestingly, numerical studies on 1D qubit circuits reveal bulk exponents closely resembling those of 2D percolation, despite potential differences in surface behavior. The first part of this work investigates the critical properties of 2D Clifford circuits. In the bulk, we observe properties consistent with the percolation picture, including matching bulk exponents and an inverse power-law for critical entanglement growth, $S(t,L) \sim L(1 - a/t)$, which saturates to an area-law. Subsequently, we employ a graph-state based algorithm to analyze critical entanglement cluster properties in both 1D and 2D settings. We demonstrate that in a model with a straightforward geometric mapping to percolation, specifically the projective transverse field Ising model, entanglement clusters are governed by percolation surface exponents. Conversely, in Clifford models, we identify significant deviations in cluster exponents from surface percolation values, indicating the failure of any simple geometric mapping to percolation. Given this evidence of deviations from the percolation universality class, our findings prompt the question of why many bulk properties nonetheless exhibit behavior similar to percolation.

Facial expressions serve as an excellent channel for conveying emotions and intentions. This review examines both the recognition of human facial expressions and the generation of robotic facial expressions. Regarding human recognition, it addresses techniques applied to predefined datasets as well as real-time scenarios. For robotic generation, it covers both hand-coded approaches and automated methods, where machine learning techniques are used to manipulate robotic features like the eyes and mouth to produce expressions. While existing studies demonstrate high accuracy for recognizing emotions on fixed datasets, real-time recognition accuracy remains comparatively lower. Similarly, although many robots can produce basic facial expressions, few studies focus on enabling automatic expression generation. This overview synthesizes current state-of-the-art research on facial emotions within human-robot interaction, identifying potential avenues for future investigation.

Fortran stands as the oldest high-level programming language still in active use and remains a dominant choice for compute-heavy scientific and engineering tasks. Nevertheless, it has failed to align with contemporary software development methodologies and internet-era tooling, leading to a decline in the developer experience. This downturn is specifically attributed to the absence of a robust general-purpose library ecosystem, modern utilities for constructing and packaging applications, and accessible online educational materials, which hinders the language's ability to recruit and keep new users. To counter these challenges, an open-source community launched on GitHub in 2019 to develop foundational tools, including a standard library, a build system, a package manager, and a community-maintained website dedicated to Fortran. This paper details the progress achieved so far and proposes the subsequent steps for the project.

We offer explicit parametrisations for every Darboux transform of Delaunay surfaces. By applying the Darboux transformation to a multiple cover, we generate new closed constant mean curvature (CMC) surfaces featuring dihedral symmetry. These surfaces serve as the foundation for constructing closed same-lobed CMC multibubbletons through the application of Bianchi permutability.

Wave propagation issues are prevalent in physics and engineering, where stochastic effects are crucial for accurate modeling due to media uncertainties. This study examines and analyzes a fully discrete finite element approach for a specific class of nonlinear stochastic wave equations, characterized by a globally Lipschitz continuous diffusion term and a drift term that meets only the weaker conditions outlined in [11]. The paper's contributions are threefold. First, direct error estimation is unattainable using a primal-form numerical scheme; consequently, a mixed-form scheme is introduced alongside proofs of several Hölder continuity properties for the strong solution, enabling error estimates in both $L^2$ and energy norms. Second, two distinct discretization methods for the nonlinear term are proposed to ensure $L^2$ and energy stability of the discrete solutions. These methods, combined with specific test functions, address challenges related to stochastic time scaling and nonlinear interactions, with these stability results being essential for demonstrating that the probability of the error estimates holding approaches unity. Third, higher-order moment stability of the discrete solutions is established through energy arguments and the method's inherent energy decay properties. Finally, numerical experiments are provided to validate the stability of the discrete solutions and to illustrate convergence rates across various norms.

Recent years have seen Neural Machine Translation (NMT) emerge as a promising tool for automatic source code editing. However, standard NMT-based editors typically input only the specific code requiring modification and return a ranked list of patches, where the optimal solution is not always ranked first. Although these systems produce a wide range of plausible fixes, the most appropriate patch often relies on developer intent and the specific application context. Consequently, NMT models can improve by incorporating developer hints in natural language or additional patch context. As a proof of concept, this research leverages three information modalities—edit location, surrounding code context, and commit messages (serving as natural language hints)—to drive NMT-based edit generation. This approach led to the development of MODIT, a multi-modal NMT code editing engine. Through comprehensive analysis, we demonstrate that including developer hints as an input modality narrows the patch search space and surpasses state-of-the-art models by placing the correct patch in the top-1 position.

This article introduces a linear differential operator $P$ defined on a domain $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and considers a second-order stochastic process $U = (U_x)_{x \in \mathcal{D}}$. In the first section, we establish a novel necessary and sufficient condition ensuring that all trajectories of $U$ satisfy the partial differential equation (PDE) $T(U) = 0$. This condition is expressed through the covariance kernel of $U$. Unlike prior results, our approach interprets the equality $T(U) = 0$ within the *sense of distributions*, a framework particularly significant for PDEs. This theorem serves as a foundation for the second section, which applies "physically informed" machine learning to the homogeneous three-dimensional free-space wave equation. We employ Gaussian process regression (GPR) using pointwise observations of the solution by propagating Gaussian process (GP) priors from the initial conditions through the wave equation. We derive explicit formulas for the covariance kernel of the propagated GP, facilitating GPR. We further examine specific scenarios involving radial symmetry and point sources. For radial symmetry, we develop GPR formulas that avoid convolution operations; for point sources, we demonstrate a direct connection between GPR and the classical triangulation method utilized in GPS for point source localization. Moreover, this Bayesian framework offers a solution to the ill-posed inverse problem of reconstructing initial conditions for the wave equation using a limited number of sensors while simultaneously enabling the inference of physical parameters from the data. Finally, we validate this physically informed GPR approach through several practical examples.

Studying the significant achievements and milestones of public figures typically demands a laborious and time-intensive close reading of extensive biographical or encyclopedic texts. While structured semantic resources like the EventKG knowledge graph offer relevant facts, they frequently contain hundreds of events and temporal relationships for specific entities. This paper introduces EventKG+BT, a timeline generation system that leverages distant supervision to derive concise, interactive spatio-temporal biographical representations directly from a knowledge graph.

This study establishes a collection of two-dimensional variational inequalities designed to represent the displacement of a linearly elastic flexural shell under confinement, where all points of the admissible deformed states are constrained to a specific half-space, and frictional effects are disregarded.

We introduce a straightforward, purely data-driven approach to determine new energy levels in quantum many-body systems using only observed spectral line wavelengths. The method calculates every possible combination derived from known energy levels and the wavelengths of unidentified lines. Since each excited state generates numerous transition lines to various lower levels, the correct energy levels will coincidentally emerge from multiple combinations of these lines, whereas incorrect combinations will scatter randomly. This statistical coincidence allows for easy detection. We validate this statistical technique by identifying new levels across different atomic and nuclear systems using publicly available lists of unidentified lines.

It is established that the right and left keys of a Kashiwara-Nakashima tableau in type $C$ can be determined via the Lecouvey-Sheats symplectic jeu de taquin. Inspired by Willis' direct approach for computing type $A$ keys, we also present a method for calculating symplectic right and left keys that does not rely on the symplectic jeu de taquin.

This paper investigates a specific subset of non-convex quadratic programs featuring two potentially indefinite quadratic constraints, provided their constraint function level sets are not positioned alternatively. We demonstrate that these problems satisfy strong duality via a tight semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation, even in the absence of primal or dual Slater conditions. Our findings encompass Ye and Zhang's 2003 work and the generalized trust region subproblems (GTRS) as particular instances. By utilizing a new geometric perspective and illustrative examples, we clarify why the problem difficulty escalates significantly when the constraint level sets are indeed arranged alternatively.

Building interactive machine learning systems traditionally resembles a teacher-learner dynamic, where human instructors train machine models. This study investigates employing a conversational interface to examine the interaction between human teachers and interactive learners. Specifically, we assess whether teachable AI agents can effectively acquire knowledge from humans through dialogue and compare this approach with conventional supervised learning methods. The findings confirm the viability of teachable conversational agents and identify key factors essential for developing machine learning systems designed to learn via conversation.

SOXS represents the new spectrograph for the ESO NTT telescope, capable of spanning optical and near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths through two distinct arms: UV-VIS (350–850 nm) and NIR (800–2000 nm). This article details the final design of the visible camera cryostats, the facilities used for CCD characterization testing, and initial results obtained with the scientific detector. The UV-VIS system utilizes an e2v CCD 44-82, paired with a custom detector head, the ESO Continuous Flowing Cryostat (CFC) cooling mechanism, and the New General Detector Controller (NGC) developed by ESO. Laboratory testing is conducted on an optical bench featuring a Xenon lamp, filter wheels for wavelength selection, an integrating sphere, and a calibrated diode for flux measurement. This paper outlines the visible camera cryostat design, the CCD characterization test setup, and preliminary results from laboratory tests as well as post-integration performance within the instrument.

Building climate control accounts for a major share of global energy use, positioning groundwater heat pumps as a viable alternative. To mitigate potential adverse interactions between these systems within urban areas, future city planning must optimize their spatial arrangement. We introduce a new data-driven method to create small-scale surrogates for modeling the thermal plumes produced by groundwater heat pumps in the surrounding subsurface. Utilizing a dataset derived from 2D numerical simulations, we trained a convolutional neural network to predict steady-state subsurface temperature fields based on given subsurface velocity fields. Our results demonstrate that, compared to existing models, this approach captures more complex dynamics with faster computation times. Consequently, the resulting surrogate is ideally suited for interactive design tools used by city planners.

In a finite undirected graph $G$, a vertex set $D$ constitutes an {\em efficient dominating set} (abbreviated as e.d.s.) if every vertex in $G$ is dominated by precisely one member of $D$. The \emph{Efficient Domination} (ED) problem, which determines the existence of such a set, has been established as \NP-complete for chordal bipartite graphs, $P_7$-free graphs, and even specific restricted $H$-free bipartite subclasses, including $K_{1,4}$-free and $C_4$-free bipartite graphs. Conversely, polynomial-time algorithms exist for ED in $P_8$-free, $S_{1,3,3}$-free, and $S_{1,1,5}$-free bipartite graphs. This work demonstrates that the ED problem is also solvable in polynomial time for $(S_{1,2,5},S_{3,3,3})$-free chordal bipartite graphs.

A {\em quasi-kernel} in a digraph $D$ refers to an independent set $Q\subseteq V(D)$ where every vertex $v$ outside $Q$ can reach a vertex $u$ in $Q$ via a directed path of length one or two. Chv\'{a}tal and Lov\'{a}sz established in 1974 that all digraphs possess a quasi-kernel. Subsequently, Erd\H{o}s and S\'zekely proposed in 1976 that every sink-free digraph $D=(V(D),A(D))$ contains a quasi-kernel with a size no greater than $|V(D)|/2$. This paper introduces a novel approach to demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for a broader class of anti-claw-free digraphs. Specifically, for any sink-free one-way split digraph $D$ with order $n$ (where $n\geq 3$), we prove a tighter bound, showing that the quasi-kernel size is at most $\frac{n+3}{2} - \sqrt{n}$, and we confirm that this bound is sharp.

This study explores an extension of the Kuramoto model incorporating run-and-tumble dynamics, a form of self-propelled motion. Unlike the original model where individual particle angular velocity remains constant, this extended version allows angular velocity to fluctuate sporadically, with new velocities sampled from a distribution g(w). Since the Kuramoto model exhibits a phase transition, it serves as an ideal framework for examining phase transitions within systems composed of self-propelled particles.

Using ensemble theory and a recently developed method with *ab initio* accuracy, this study examines the structural phase behaviors of pure zirconium metal under compression up to 160 GPa at room temperature. The Gibbs free energy derived from this approach serves as the primary criterion for identifying phase transitions. The calculated transition pressures for the $\alpha\rightarrow\omega$ and $\omega\rightarrow\beta$ transformations are 6.93 GPa and 24.83 GPa, respectively; notably, the former value currently represents the sole theoretical prediction that aligns with multiple experimental findings. The parameter-free equation of state obtained shows deviations of less than 1.5% compared to recent experimental data across the entire pressure range, shrinking to within 0.7% for pressures exceeding 40 GPa. This close agreement supports the conclusion that the previously hypothesized anharmonicity-driven isostructural phase transition does not occur in the $\beta$-phase, despite our quantitative comparisons confirming that thermal effects at room temperature significantly influence phase stability relative to 0 K results.

Standard Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for training multi-layer Graph Convolution Networks (GCN) suffers from poor scalability because every descent step requires updating node embeddings across a significant portion of the graph. Previous solutions attempt to mitigate this by sub-sampling the graph, which lowers computational costs but often increases variance and leads to suboptimal results. This paper presents IGLU, a method that caches intermediate computations at various GCN layers to facilitate lazy updates, thereby substantially reducing the computational expense of descent steps. Although IGLU introduces bounded bias into the gradients, it still converges to a first-order saddle point under standard assumptions like objective smoothness. Experimental benchmarks demonstrate that IGLU achieves up to 1.2% higher accuracy while consuming up to 88% less compute.

Predicting cognitive tasks from electroencephalography (EEG) signals using Machine Learning and Deep Learning is a rapidly evolving area within Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCI). Unlike computer vision and natural language processing, BCI trials currently suffer from a scarcity of data. To address this challenge, we developed a PC-based machine learning approach designed to engage non-expert end-users. We introduced a novel algorithm named Time Majority Voting (TMV), which outperformed state-of-the-art methods in our experiments. TMV operates efficiently on personal computers for BCI classification tasks, and its interpretable results have enhanced the understanding of EEG experiments for both researchers and users.

The behavior of precipitation and its reaction to external forcings constitute a critical component of the planetary climate system. This study investigates precipitation intensity across experiments with varying atmospheric masses and their sensitivity to surface warming, utilizing three global atmospheric general circulation models (GCMs) alongside one regional cloud-resolving model (CRM). Our findings indicate that for a specific surface temperature, precipitation is less intense when the atmospheric mass is greater. Additionally, the rate at which precipitation increases with rising surface temperature is lower under conditions of larger atmospheric mass compared to smaller mass. These patterns can be explained through atmospheric and surface energy balance principles, as atmospheric mass affects Rayleigh scattering, multiple scattering, pressure broadening, and the lapse rate, thereby influencing precipitation strength. Consequently, these results hold significant implications for understanding the climate and habitability of early Earth, early Mars, and ocean-bearing exoplanets.

This study introduces a unified approach to multimodal pretraining designed to eliminate the need for complex, task- or modality-specific customization. We present OFA, a framework that is both task-agnostic and modality-agnostic, supporting comprehensive task coverage. OFA consolidates a wide range of cross-modal and unimodal tasks—including image generation, visual grounding, captioning, classification, and language modeling—into a streamlined sequence-to-sequence learning architecture. By adhering to instruction-based learning throughout both pretraining and fine-tuning phases, OFA requires no additional task-specific layers for downstream applications. Unlike recent state-of-the-art vision-language models that depend on massive cross-modal datasets, OFA is pretrained on just 20M publicly available image-text pairs. Despite its simplicity and smaller training scale, OFA establishes new state-of-the-art results across various cross-modal tasks and achieves highly competitive performance on unimodal tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that OFA effectively transfers to unseen tasks and domains. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/OFA-Sys/OFA.

We have determined stellar parameters and abundances (referred to as "stellar labels") for 40,034 late-B and A-type main-sequence stars selected from the LAMOST Medium Resolution Survey (LAMOST-MRS). Our early-type sample, primarily chosen from LAMOST Data Release 7 using spectral line indices, was analyzed using the Stellar LAbel Machine (SLAM). This method relies on Kurucz spectral synthesis models covering effective temperatures ($T_\mathrm{eff}$) between 6000 K and 15,000 K and metallicities ([M/H]) ranging from -1 to 1 dex. For a signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 60, the cross-validated uncertainties are roughly 75 K, 0.06 dex, 0.05 dex, and 3.5 km/s for $T_\mathrm{eff}$, $\log g$, [M/H], and $v\sin i$, respectively. Comparisons with stars having previously known labels demonstrate strong agreement across all parameters, with the exception of $\log g$. While this discrepancy is an inherent limitation due to the narrow wavelength coverage of the MRS, it minimally impacts rotation rate estimates thanks to the survey's decent spectral resolution and the profile-fitting technique used. Consequently, masses and ages for these early-type stars were estimated using non-rotating stellar evolution models, facilitating an investigation into how stellar rotation distributions vary with mass and age.

While SAT provers are potent instruments for tackling real-world logical challenges, their utilization demands extensive programming expertise, often feeling as cumbersome as assembly language for general programmers. There was a lack of a high-level language to make these tools more accessible to a broader audience. \textsc{TouIST} was developed to bridge this gap, focusing on propositional logic with two primary objectives: first, to provide a high-level language for concisely expressing complex formulas (such as those governing Sudoku or planning tasks), and second, to automatically generate models for these formulas using powerful underlying provers that remain hidden from the user. This system offers a user-friendly interface with various syntactic features, connecting to robust provers capable of resolving large, difficult instances like scheduling problems or puzzles. \textsc{TouIST} supports interaction with both pure SAT solvers and SMT provers (incorporating theories like linear arithmetic), making it suitable for beginners exploring propositional logic, graduate students, and researchers addressing complex planning problems with extensive fluents and numerical constraints.

We investigate mass-deformed theories possessing ${\cal N}\geq2$ supersymmetry defined on both round and squashed three-spheres. By embedding these supersymmetric backgrounds into extended supergravity, we demonstrate that supersymmetry is enhanced on squashed spheres at specific mass deformation values. When the three-dimensional partition function arises as a limit of a four-dimensional index, we further show that for these special masses, only states annihilated by additional supercharges contribute to the index. Leveraging an equivalence between partition functions on squashed spheres and ellipsoids, we clarify the recently noted independence of the mass-deformed ABJ(M) theory partition function on squashing when evaluated on the ellipsoid. Additionally, we offer further instances of such simplifications across various three-dimensional supersymmetric theories.

This work introduces a technique for directly extracting Wilson coefficients associated with rare $b\to s$ transitions via $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, employing an unbinned maximum likelihood fit. Compared to the standard approach of deriving these coefficients from angular observables binned in $q^2$ (the squared dimuon mass), this method offers distinct benefits by optimally utilizing all available experimental data and inherently managing experimental correlations. Through pseudoexperiments, we illustrate the enhanced sensitivity of this proposed approach for determining the Wilson coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate the method's viability when applied to the combined Run 1 and 2 dataset from the LHCb experiment.

PSZ2 G091.83+26.11 is a massive galaxy cluster characterized by a mass of M500 = 7.43 x 10^14 Msun at a redshift of z = 0.822. Although this system displays a complex morphology with distinct bimodality in X-ray data, it was previously identified and analyzed within the Planck survey as a single, spherical cluster adhering to a universal profile [1]. Such an oversimplified model can result in erroneous thermodynamic calculations, particularly regarding the pressure profile. Given that upcoming multiwavelength experiments will increasingly detect high-redshift objects—where merging clusters are expected to be more prevalent—it is essential to quantify this systematic bias. To address this, we employ high-resolution NIKA2 observations of PSZ2 G091.83+26.11 to incorporate the cluster's morphological features into our modeling framework. This approach involves fitting a two-halo model to the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect image and reconstructing the corresponding projected pressure profile, which is then compared against results derived from a spherical assumption.

We designed and experimentally realized a two-qubit quantum correlated SWAP heat engine that surpasses the standard Carnot efficiency limit and enhances extractable work within a broader range of qubit energy-gap ratios compared to cycles lacking initial correlations. This efficiency boost results from balancing entropy production against the consumption of quantum correlations throughout the thermodynamic cycle. Furthermore, we established a generalized second-law limit and experimentally verified the engine's performance improvement by adjusting the qubits' effective energy gaps and temperatures using an IBM quantum processor.

Precise extraction of gravitational wave (GW) signal waveforms is crucial for confirming detections and investigating the astrophysics of their sources. However, achieving this in realistic conditions is challenging due to non-stationary, non-Gaussian noise contaminating signals from current GW detectors. Although existing waveform extraction methods are optimal in performance, their computational speed is insufficient for online applications required by multi-messenger astronomy. This paper demonstrates that a deep learning architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks and bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory components can extract binary black hole (BBH) GW waveforms from realistic noise within a few milliseconds. We systematically tested our network on injected GW signals with component masses uniformly distributed between 10 and 80 solar masses, using both Gaussian and LIGO detector noise. Our results show that the model extracts waveforms with overlaps exceeding 0.95 with pure Numerical Relativity templates for signals with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) greater than six, while remaining robust against interfering glitches. Furthermore, applying our model to all ten detected BBH events from the first (O1) and second (O2) observing runs yielded overlaps greater than 0.97 with the corresponding pure templates for every waveform. We discuss the implications of these findings and their potential future applications in GW localization and mass estimation.

We introduce an \emph{ab-initio} investigation determining the primary electron-phonon scattering pathways in $n$-type PbTe. We construct an electronic transport model grounded in the Boltzmann transport equation under the transport relaxation time approximation, entirely parameterized by first-principles calculations that precisely capture the dispersion of electronic bands near the band gap. The calculated electronic mobility, varying with temperature and carrier concentration, aligns well with experimental data. We demonstrate that longitudinal optical phonon scattering governs electronic transport in $n$-type PbTe, whereas acoustic phonon scattering is comparatively minor. Furthermore, we identify that scattering from soft transverse optical phonons is the least significant mechanism, resulting from symmetry-forbidden interactions between conduction band minima and zone-center soft modes. Consequently, soft phonons are pivotal to the high thermoelectric figure of merit in $n$-type PbTe: they strongly inhibit lattice thermal conductivity without degrading electronic transport. These findings imply that materials featuring soft modes with weak coupling to the electronic states critical for transport could be promising candidates for high-efficiency thermoelectrics.

While nucleation studies typically center on critical cluster properties, crystal lattice defects ensure that nuclei evolve through a distribution of pre-critical clusters with varying structural disorder before stabilizing. To explore the role of these pre-critical clusters, we constructed a simplified thermodynamic model relating cluster size and order, enabling us to modify the formation energy of pre-critical clusters independently of critical cluster characteristics. We numerically analyzed both steady-state and transient nucleation behaviors across various microscopic ordering kinetics. Our results reveal a generic order-disorder transition within pre-critical clusters. Regardless of the specific ordering kinetics, greater accessibility to disordered pre-critical clusters reduces both the steady-state nucleation rate and the nucleation lag time. Additionally, the interaction between the free energy landscape and microscopic ordering kinetics generates three distinct nucleation pathways.

Over the past few years, visual forgeries have become so advanced that they evade human detection, presenting a serious risk to information security. This has fueled a proliferation of harmful uses, including the dissemination of fake news, defamation and blackmail of public figures, political impersonation, and rumor-mongering designed to generate engagement. Consequently, a vast array of visual forensic methods has been developed to combat this growing threat. This paper introduces a benchmark offering deep insights into visual forgery and forensics through a comprehensive, empirical methodology. Specifically, we have constructed an independent framework that unifies leading counterfeit generators and detectors, evaluating their performance across multiple metrics. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis of these benchmarking results to identify the key characteristics of the methods that serve as a reliable comparative standard in the ongoing struggle between detection techniques and forgery tools.

The significant discrepancy between the time symmetry inherent in fundamental microscopic laws and the time asymmetry observed in macroscopic processes presents a difficult physical challenge. This issue is examined within a comprehensive information framework, focusing on the unitary evolution of a general physical system as perceived by an idealized observer whose recording and processing capabilities are time-neutral. In the macroscopic limit, a contradiction emerges between observations and predictions made at different times. This contradiction suggests that an observer is unable to access records generated during periods when the system's entropy is higher.

Modeling living systems at a collective level presents significant difficulties, primarily because individual components are complex and their interactions are not entirely understood. However, the availability of high-throughput experiments and big data has spurred the growth of data-driven approaches to address these hurdles. To reveal the fundamental physical principles, we introduce a data-driven technique for calculating phase-space density, allowing the stochastic dynamic equation for active matter to emerge naturally and enabling the straightforward extraction of time and space-dependent physical order parameters. For systems near a steady state, we demonstrate how to construct a field theory to generate physical predictions. We first develop the method analytically and then calibrate it using simulated data. Subsequently, we apply this approach to an experimental system involving particles driven by a *Serratia marcescens* bacterial swarm under spatially localized UV light. The analysis reveals that the particles remain in a steady state both before and after the UV exposure, adhering to a Gaussian field theory with a spatially varying "mass." This surprising simplicity is notable given the complex dynamics of the swarm. In response to the UV light, we observe a net particle flow away from the light source and an increase in particle entropy away from it. We conclude by discussing further potential applications of our data-driven method, particularly in scenarios where the internal structure of individual constituents changes dynamically, thereby altering the governing stochastic dynamic equation.

This study presents the initial successful deployment of a differentiable architecture search (DARTS) method for detecting deepfakes and spoofing. As a form of neural architecture search, DARTS functions within a continuous, differentiable space, allowing both network architecture and parameters to be refined through gradient descent. By employing partially-connected DARTS with random channel masking, the search space is optimized to reduce GPU consumption while automatically discovering complex structures built from convolutional layers and residual blocks. Although these networks are trained rapidly with minimal human intervention, their performance rivals the most advanced systems in existing literature. Furthermore, certain models exhibit significantly reduced complexity, featuring 85% fewer parameters than a Res2Net alternative.

(Pre-)transitional disks feature gaps and cavities indicative of active planet formation. Theoretical models suggest that young, embedded planets accrete material from both circumplanetary and circumstellar disks, making them detectable via accretion tracers such as the H$_{\alpha}$ emission line. This study presents SPHERE/ZIMPOL AO-assisted spectral angular differential imaging observations of five (pre-)transitional disks at the Very Large Telescope (VLT), captured in both the H$_{\alpha}$ line and adjacent continuum. By combining spectral and angular differential imaging techniques, we enhanced contrast in the innermost regions near the stars to search for signatures of young, accreting protoplanets. However, the processed images revealed no clear H$_{\alpha}$ point sources around any of the targets. Faint H$_{\alpha}$ emissions were reported for TW Hya and HD163296; while the former is likely an artifact caused by a spike, the origin of the latter remains ambiguous. The differential images achieved contrasts of 6--8 magnitudes at separations of approximately 100 mas from the central stars, except for LkCa15, which showed values of roughly 3 mag. We calculated upper limits for the accretion luminosity of potential protoplanets, finding that planetary models yield an average value of $L_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{-4}$ $L_{\odot}$ at 200 mas. This is approximately two orders of magnitude higher than the $L_{\rm acc}$ derived from extrapolating the stellar $L_{H_{\alpha}}$ - $L_{acc}$ relationship. We attribute the non-detection of protoplanets to a combination of factors, including episodic accretion, extinction from circumstellar and circumplanetary disks, and/or the prevalence of low-mass, low-accreting planets.

The inherent antisymmetry of identical fermions creates the notorious fermion sign problem, characterized by massive cancellations between positive and negative terms in the partition function. This phenomenon renders simulation techniques that directly sample the partition function exponentially challenging to converge. In this study, we utilize path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) and leverage the recently identified fictitious particle model to explore the fermion sign problem in greater depth. We examine the specific conditions under which the parametrized path integral formulation of the partition function, combined with extrapolation techniques, is either valid or invalid for circumventing this issue. Within the valid operational range, our simulations demonstrate the ability to accurately predict energies for large fermion systems, a feat far surpassing the capabilities of traditional direct sampling methods. Notably, we identify and confirm a simple universal relationship applicable to high-temperature noninteracting particles as well as strongly repulsive interacting particles at low temperatures.

The magnetic, dielectric, and structural characteristics of the type-I multiferroic material KNiPO$_4$ were examined using neutron powder diffraction, magnetization, dielectric measurements, and high-temperature synchrotron X-ray diffraction. Below the Néel temperature ($T_\mathrm{N}$ = 25 K), KNiPO$_4$ exhibits a weakly non-collinear antiferromagnetic (AFM) arrangement where Ni$^{2+}$ magnetic moments are primarily oriented along the $a$ axis. At room temperature, the compound crystallizes in the polar orthorhombic $Pna2_1$ space group. A second-order structural phase transition, marking the emergence of ferroelectricity, occurs near $T_\mathrm{C}\sim$ 594(3)$^\circ$C; above this temperature, the crystal structure becomes centrosymmetric, adopting the $Pnma$ space group. Additionally, a first-order structural phase transition is observed at $T_\mathrm{0}\sim$ 469 -- 488$^\circ$C, caused by the rearrangement of oxygen ligands, which alters the nickel ion coordination from four to five.

Recent theoretical models accurately describe experimental data for ternary fission, reinforcing the conclusion that the primary cluster formation mechanism involves highly neutron-rich, low-density, chemically equilibrated nucleonic matter. An expanded comparative analysis of these approaches applied to thermal neutron-induced $^{241}$Pu($n_{\rm th}$,f) fission yields has been conducted to better characterize the source matter. By incorporating in-medium effects on binding energies, the resonance gas approximation was refined. The study identifies a temperature of 1.29 MeV, a density of $6.7 \times 10^{-5}$ nucleons/fm$^3$, and a proton fraction $Y_p$ of 0.035 as parameters that effectively reproduce the yields of ternary light particles and clusters, with specific results detailed for $Z=1$ and $Z=2$ isotopes. Furthermore, isotopes with higher $Z$ are examined to illustrate the significance of medium and continuum effects, even at such low densities.

During the early stages of a pandemic, limited vaccine supplies necessitate the prioritization of specific population groups, making the evaluation of allocation strategies a critical component of the response. This study develops a model to retrospectively assess age-dependent counterfactual vaccine distribution strategies during the COVID-19 pandemic. To estimate the impact of allocation on expected severe case incidence, we utilize a simulation-assisted causal modeling framework that integrates a compartmental infection-dynamics simulation, a coarse-grained, data-driven causal model, and literature-based estimates for immunity waning. We compare Israel's 2021 vaccine allocation strategy against counterfactual approaches, including no prioritization, prioritization of younger demographics, and a strict risk-ranked method; our analysis confirms that Israel's implemented strategy was highly effective. Additionally, we examine the marginal benefits of increasing vaccine uptake within specific age groups, finding that boosting vaccination rates among the elderly is most effective at preventing severe cases, while increasing vaccinations in middle-aged groups is most effective at reducing infections. Given its modular design, our model can be readily adapted to study future pandemics. We illustrate this versatility by analyzing vaccine allocation strategies for a pandemic resembling the Spanish Flu. Consequently, our approach facilitates the evaluation of vaccination strategies amidst the complex interplay of core epidemic factors, such as age-dependent risk profiles, immunity waning, vaccine availability, and transmission rates.

The study focuses on a solid ionic conductor exhibiting cation conductivity within the interelectrode region, where large anions are treated as immobile, creating a uniform neutralizing electric background; this framework effectively models ceramic conductors. To address the statistical mechanics of such systems, characterized by short-range Van der Waals and long-range Coulomb forces, the research employs a hybrid approach integrating the collective variables method with the method of mean cell potentials. While this formalism was previously applied to homogeneous states by Bokun et al. (2019), the current work extends it to inhomogeneous conditions driven by an external electric field. Consequently, mean cell potentials are derived as functionals of the density field, governed by a closed system of integral equations. The problem is solved using the lattice approximation to analyze charge and electric field distributions in the interelectrode region as a function of electrode charges, followed by the calculation and discussion of the differential electric capacitance.

Semantic scene segmentation is vital for numerous robotics tasks, such as autonomous navigation, yet these tasks face strict computational constraints, including the need for rapid performance on low-power GPUs with high-resolution inputs. While existing state-of-the-art models are typically evaluated on high-power hardware, this paper examines the deployment speed of leading segmentation models across diverse setups (various GPUs and input sizes) relevant to robotics. The objective is to conduct a comparative analysis of current top-tier models to identify those that best align with the specific requirements of robotic applications.

C. Thomassen (Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 42 (1981), 231-251) established a characterization for strongly connected non-Hamiltonian digraphs of order $p \geq 3$ with a minimum degree of $p-1$. This paper presents a corresponding characterization for strongly connected non-Hamiltonian digraphs satisfying a Meyniel-type condition, where the sum of degrees for any pair of non-adjacent vertices $x$ and $y$ is at least $2p-2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such digraphs $D$ possess cycles of every length $k$, where $2 \leq k \leq m$, and $m$ denotes the length of the longest cycle in $D$.

This study tackles the persistent challenge of extracting dynamical information from noisy acoustic emission signals generated by an adhesive tape being peeled under a constant traction velocity. By applying a phase space reconstruction method, we confirm deterministic chaotic dynamics through the identification of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent within a specific range of traction speeds. These findings are interpreted using a model that underscores the deterministic nature of acoustic emissions by linking them to stick-slip dynamics.

The growing integration of Distributed Energy Resources (DER) into distribution networks introduces new operational challenges for both transmission and distribution systems. Conversely, the controllability of converter-interfaced devices (CIG) offers opportunities for flexible operation and the provision of ancillary services, whether or not economic incentives are present. The primary objective of this study is to develop a framework for calculating the operational flexibility of an Active Distribution Network, which is then utilized by the Transmission System Operator to solve a centralized Optimal Power Flow problem, specifically focusing on maximizing Voltage Stability Margins. Two distinct methods are proposed to determine the Flexibility Region (FR) within the PQ plane, and the centralized optimization is evaluated using both simple and complex transmission test systems as well as various feeder configurations.

This paper investigates self-dual gravity using the Newman-Penrose formalism. We define the space of self-dual solutions by starting with Newman-Unti solutions. We demonstrate that the asymptotic symmetries of self-dual gravity remain the (extended) BMS symmetries. Additionally, we convert the self-dual Taub-NUT solution into the Newman-Unti gauge, providing its analytical form.

This paper demonstrates that several prominent uncertainty principles associated with the Fourier transform—including the Heisenberg, Donoho--Stark, and Meshulam's non-abelian principles—rely minimally on the specific structure of the Fourier transform itself. Instead, these results stem from very weak, shared properties of the Fourier transform (and many other linear operators): specifically, that it is bounded from $L^1$ to $L^\infty$ and that it is unitary. By applying a single, straightforward proof template based solely on these (or even weaker) conditions, we derive new proofs and extensive generalizations of these fundamental uncertainty principles, extending them to novel operators and settings in a fully unified manner. Alongside our comprehensive overview, this work also functions as a survey of the diverse aspects of the phenomenon known as uncertainty principles.

Smart buildings have become essential due to rising demand-supply imbalances and the need to generate substantial power. In modern non-industrial infrastructure, these needs primarily involve thermostatically controlled loads (TCLs)—such as air conditioners, heaters, and refrigerators—which are ubiquitous and can be adjusted to regulate aggregate power. By managing the operating times of these devices, utilities can achieve specific power targets, enabling load management and providing ancillary services (AS) to the grid. This study employs a distributed averaging protocol utilizing steady-state desynchronization to meet the power aggregates set by the utility. The approach was validated through computer simulations involving both homogeneous and heterogeneous TCL populations, as well as a load-following scenario using utility signals as a reference. Beyond delivering significant ancillary services, the proposed method also mitigates power system oscillations caused by TCLs. Hardware-based experiments confirmed the feasibility of real-time implementation, and the study further extends this concept to a data-driven framework with comparative analysis.

Precise and comprehensive terrain maps are essential for enhancing autonomous robot situational awareness and facilitating safe, optimal navigation. However, rocks and complex topography frequently cause occlusions, resulting in gaps within Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs). Current strategies for handling these gaps involve either completely avoiding occluded zones during motion planning or filling missing elevation data using conventional methods like interpolation, diffusion, or patch-matching. These existing techniques fail to utilize high-level terrain features and the line-of-sight geometric constraints that humans intuitively employ to predict occluded regions. This paper introduces a self-supervised learning framework capable of reconstructing occluded DEM areas using real-world data without requiring ground-truth labels. The method involves artificially creating occlusions in elevation maps generated by a real robot through ray casting. We initially validate a supervised learning approach on synthetic data with complete ground truth before applying the model to various real-world datasets. These datasets were collected during the exploration of both structured and unstructured terrains by a legged robot, as well as in a planetary simulation on lunar analogue terrain. Our approach demonstrates significant performance improvements over baseline methods across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the neural network operates in real-time on both CPU and GPU architectures at sampling rates suitable for autonomous ground robots. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of reconstructing elevation map occlusions through preliminary motion planning experiments.

This paper investigates the fundamental efficiency of delimited control. We demonstrate that effect handlers can yield an asymptotic improvement in runtime complexity for a specific class of functions.
