Focusing on the generic count problem, we analyze a pure PCF-like base language, $\lambda_b$, alongside its extension with effect handlers, $\lambda_h$. Our findings indicate that $\lambda_h$ supports an asymptotically more efficient implementation of generic count than any possible implementation within $\lambda_b$. Furthermore, we establish that this performance gap persists even when $\lambda_b$ is augmented with mutable state. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first such result concerning control operators.

Grasping cascading dynamics within complex network structures is essential for modeling the propagation of diseases, information, misinformation, and other media. This study expands upon the multi-type branching process framework introduced by Keating et al. (2022), moving beyond homogeneous network assumptions to address a broader category of clustered networks. By employing a socially-inspired complex contagion model, we derive insights not only regarding the average behavior of cascades but also concerning their full property distributions. We propose a novel technique for inverting probability generating functions to reconstruct their underlying distributions, a method that inherently generalizes to higher dimensions. Integrating this inversion approach with the multi-type branching process allows us to calculate both univariate and bivariate distributions of cascade characteristics. Finally, utilizing clique cover techniques, we apply this methodology to both synthetic and real-world networks, contrasting the theoretical predictions for cascade sizes against results from extensive numerical simulations.

In the 1970s, Nicolas established that the partition function $p(n)$ is log-concave for $n > 25$. Later, the conjecture regarding the log-concavity of the plane partition function $\func{pp}(n)$ for $n > 11$ was formulated in \cite{HNT21} and subsequently proved by Ono, Pujahari, and Rolen. This paper offers a broader framework by associating polynomials $\{P_n^{g_d}(x)\}_{d,n}$ to double sequences $\{g_d(n)\}_{d,n}$ satisfying $g_d(1)=1$ and the inequality $0 \leq g_{d}\left( n\right) - n^{d}\leq g_{1}\left( n\right) \left( n-1\right) ^{d-1}$. These polynomials are defined by the generating function \begin{equation*} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} P_n^{g_d}(x) \, q^n := \func{exp}\left( x \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} g_d(n) \frac{q^n}{n} \right) =\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( 1 - q^n \right)^{-x f_d(n)}. \end{equation*} Specifically, $ p(n)$ corresponds to $P_n^{\sigma_1}(1)$ and $\func{pp}\left( n\right)$ to $P_n^{\sigma_2}(1)$, where $\sigma_d (n):= \sum_{\ell \mid n} \ell^d$ and $f_d(n)= n^{d-1}$. For $n \geq 6$, the sequence $\{P_n^{\sigma_d}(1)\}_d$ exhibits log-concavity for almost all $d$ if and only if $3$ divides $n$. When $\func{id}(n)=n$, the polynomial becomes $P_n^{\func{id}}(x) = \frac{x}{n} L_{n-1}^{(1)}(-x)$, with $L_{n}^{\left( \alpha \right) }\left( x\right) $ representing the $\alpha$-associated Laguerre polynomial. The study focuses on Turán inequalities \begin{equation*} \Delta_{n}^{g_d}(x) := \left( P_n^{g_d}(x) \right)^2 - P_{n-1}^{g_d}(x) \, P_{n+1}^{g_d}(x) \geq 0. \end{equation*} If $n \geq 6$ and $0 \leq x < 2 - \frac{12}{n+4}$, then $n$ is a multiple of $3$ precisely when $\Delta_{n}^{g_d}(x) \geq 0$ holds for almost all $d$. Furthermore, if $n \geq 6$ and $n \not\equiv 2 \pmod{3}$, the constraint on $x$ simplifies to $x \geq 0$, allowing for the determination of explicit bounds. Analogous to Nicolas' finding, it is shown that for $g_1= \func{id}$, the inequality $\Delta_{n}^{\func{id}}(x) \geq 0$ holds for all $x \geq 0$ and all $n$.

Over the last few years, autonomous robots have become integral to both research and everyday life. While public datasets are crucial for advancing this field by eliminating the need for substantial initial hardware and labor investments, there remains a notable scarcity of comparable public data for autonomous aerial systems, unlike the abundant resources available for ground robots and autonomous driving. To address this gap, we have executed a data collection campaign using an aerial platform outfitted with a comprehensive and distinctive sensor array, including two 3D LiDARs, two hardware-synchronized global-shutter cameras, multiple IMUs, and notably, several Ultra-wideband (UWB) ranging units. This extensive suite mirrors the configuration of an autonomous vehicle but is adapted to the unique and demanding nature of aerial operations. We have recorded multiple datasets across various challenging indoor and outdoor environments, with each package containing calibration data and ground truth derived from a high-precision laser tracker. All materials are available for access at https://ntu-aris.github.io/ntu_viral_dataset.

We introduce a Bayesian hierarchical framework designed to analyze photometric galaxy survey data using stellar population synthesis (SPS) models. This method integrates robust modeling of spectral energy distributions with both population and noise models to characterize the statistical properties of galaxy populations and observational data, respectively. By self-consistently inferring all model parameters—from high-level hyperparameters to individual galaxy SPS parameters—the framework effectively distinguishes between data biases and uncertainties. We validate the approach's flexibility and strength by deriving accurate photometric redshifts for spectroscopically confirmed galaxies in the COSMOS field, utilizing 26-band photometry and spectroscopic redshifts, achieving performance comparable to existing public catalogs based on the same data. Previously, this approach was computationally impractical due to the heavy load of SPS model calls; we resolve this using neural emulators. Our analysis reveals that the largest photometric residuals stem from poor calibration of emission line luminosities, prompting the development of a framework to mitigate these effects. This synergy of physics-based modeling accelerated by machine learning establishes a pathway to meet the stringent accuracy requirements for photometric redshift estimation in upcoming cosmological surveys, while also offering potential new connections between cosmology and galaxy evolution through the analysis of photometric datasets.

This paper investigates the hydrodynamic limits of three specific one-dimensional stochastic log-gas models: Dyson's Brownian motion, its chiral variant, and the Bru-Wishart process from dynamical random matrix theory. We construct measure-valued processes whose Cauchy transforms satisfy complex Burgers-type equations. By applying the method of characteristic curves to these partial differential equations, we derive functional equations that link the Cauchy transforms of the measures at any given time to their initial states. These functional equations for Cauchy transforms are then converted into corresponding equations for the $R$-transforms and $S$-transforms, which are fundamental in free probability theory. The resulting equations for the $R$- and $S$-transforms are more tractable than those for the Cauchy transforms and facilitate explicit computations, such as determining free cumulant sequences. Additionally, some findings are established using the concept of free convolutions.

This study addresses the optimization deployment of multistatic radar systems (MSRS) by optimizing antenna placement and transmitted power allocation to achieve two objectives: maximizing the surveillance coverage ratio and ensuring an even distribution of signal energy across the region. For the two typical operational modes of MSRS, we define corresponding objective functions for each goal. To overcome the primary challenges of applying multi-objective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) to this problem, we propose a novel deployment algorithm utilizing multi-objective particle swarm optimization with non-dominated relative crowding distance (MOPSO-NRCD). Specifically, we introduce a new selection method based on non-dominated relative crowding distance to address value differences, and we incorporate a multi-swarm structure to handle particle allocation issues. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness and validity of the proposed algorithm, showing that MOPSO-NRCD outperforms traditional MOPSO with crowding distance (MOPSO-CD) in optimization performance when using an equivalent number of particles.

We present WiCluster, a novel machine learning (ML) framework designed for passive indoor localization using radio frequency (RF) channel state information (CSI). Unlike existing methods, WiCluster can determine both zone-level and precise 2D or 3D locations without relying on exact position labels during the training phase. Previous CSI-based positioning techniques have primarily depended on non-parametric digital signal-processing (DSP) methods or, more recently, parametric fully supervised ML approaches. However, these traditional methods struggle with the intricacies of real-world environments and fail to satisfy the demands of large-scale commercial deployment: DSP accuracy drops sharply in non-line-of-sight scenarios, while supervised ML requires extensive, difficult-to-obtain centimeter-level position labels. In contrast, WiCluster offers high precision, functions effectively under non-line-of-sight conditions, and operates with weaker label requirements that are easily gathered. Our first contribution introduces a new dimensionality reduction technique for charting that integrates triplet-loss with multi-scale clustering-loss to project high-dimensional CSI data into a 2D/3D latent space. Second, we propose two weakly supervised losses that translate this latent space into a Cartesian map, achieving meter-level accuracy. These losses rely only on simple priors, including a floorplan sketch, approximate access-point locations, and a small set of CSI packets labeled with their corresponding zones. Finally, we provide experimental results and a robustness analysis for 2D positioning in two single-floor office buildings and 3D positioning in a two-story residential home.

The study examines and discusses the relationship between the chemical depiction of an isolated molecule and the one derived from the eigenfunctions of the Schrödinger Coulomb Hamiltonian for that same isolated molecule.

Let $ F $ denote a finite field, and let $ UT_n $ represent the algebra of $ n\times n $ upper triangular matrices over $ F $. Reference [1] established that every $ G $-grading on this algebra is elementary. Subsequently, [2] provided a classification of all nonisomorphic elementary $ G $-gradings and characterized the set of $ G $-graded polynomial identities for $ UT_n $ under the condition that $ F $ is infinite. In [3], the complete set of $ G $-graded polynomial identities for $ UT_n $ was described specifically when $ F $ is finite. This paper focuses on the scenario where $ G = \mathbb{Z}_2 $, $ n $ equals 2 or 3, and $ F $ is a finite field.

The discovery of a strong correlation between dynamical and baryonic radial acceleration in galaxies, known as the radial acceleration relation (RAR), has been interpreted as indirect evidence for modified gravity theories. Yet, it remains debated whether this relation applies to galaxy clusters. This paper derives an analytic RAR for the central regions of galaxy clusters and analyzes data from several large clusters. Our findings reveal that the resulting relation exhibits significant scatter. Furthermore, while the cluster RAR aligns with the galactic version within a specific range of baryonic radial acceleration, their functional forms differ. These discrepancies suggest that the radial acceleration relation may not be universal across all cosmic structures.

The theory of motives aims to enhance the (co)homology groups of varieties by introducing the additional structure known as a motive. A longstanding challenge involves applying similar enrichment to the topological fundamental group. For instance, Hain demonstrated in [arXiv:alg-geom/9607019] that under specific conditions, a variation of Hodge structures endows the Malcev completion of the fundamental group (relative to its associated monodromy representation) with a canonical mixed Hodge structure. Our primary contribution presents a motivic analogue of Hain's theorem: specifically, for a "motivic local system" defined on the generic point of a smooth variety in characteristic zero, we establish that the Malcev completion of the fundamental group (relative to its monodromy representation) is canonically a (Nori) motive.

Furthermore, we establish a stronger result: the homomorphism mapping the topological fundamental group to the motivic fundamental group is itself Malcev complete, meaning it is isomorphic to its own Malcev completion. Our principal instrument is an abstract criterion determining when homomorphisms between affine group schemes are Malcev complete, with the majority of our efforts dedicated to proving this criterion. Additionally, we demonstrate how this criterion offers a novel proof of the central theorem in [arXiv:2009.14170]—which asserts that the homomorphism from the topological fundamental group to the Hodge fundamental group is Malcev complete—and shows how this leads to a strengthened version of Hain's theorem applicable to all admissible variations of mixed Hodge structures.

Using first-principles calculations, we examine the electronic structure of the emerging family of kagome metals AV$_{3}$Sb$_{5}$ (where A = K, Rb, Cs). Our analysis systematically tracks the evolution of van Hove singularities (vHss) across this series under applied pressure and hole doping, with specific attention to the two vHss nearest to the Fermi energy. As pressure increases, these two saddle points move further away from the Fermi level. Concurrently, the Fermi surface experiences significant reconstruction involving the Sb bands, whereas the V bands remain relatively stable, highlighting the critical influence of Sb atoms on the electronic properties of these materials. In contrast, hole doping induces an opposing effect, causing the saddle points to approach the Fermi level as doping increases. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that both pressure and doping serve as effective mechanisms for tuning the position of the two vHss closest to the Fermi level, thereby enabling the control of various Fermi surface instabilities and their associated ordered states.

This study experimentally examines the stochastic phase dynamics of planar Josephson junctions (JJs) and superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) fabricated within epitaxial InAs/Al heterostructures, which exhibit a high ratio of Josephson energy to charging energy. We identify a transition from macroscopic quantum tunneling to phase diffusion as temperature varies, where the critical temperature $T^{*}$ can be controlled via a gate. The observed switching probability distributions align with models featuring small shunt capacitance and moderate damping, yielding a switching current that constitutes only a minor fraction of the critical current. Furthermore, phase locking between two JJs creates a discrepancy in switching currents when comparing an isolated JJ to one embedded in an asymmetric SQUID loop; notably, for the loop configuration, $T^*$ is also modulated by magnetic flux.

It is well-established that the spread and concurrent interaction of narratives—defined here as enduring point-of-view messaging—play a significant role in shaping political discourse and public opinion. This study introduces a methodology utilizing Multi-Variate Hawkes Processes and our newly developed Process Influence Measures to quantify and evaluate how these narratives mutually influence (Granger-cause) one another. This approach can assist social scientists in better understanding socio-geopolitical phenomena as they emerge and develop within social media environments. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply our method to Twitter narratives surrounding the 2019 Venezuelan presidential crisis. Our analysis reveals a complex, evolving influence structure among eight distinct narratives, some of which can be attributed to key historical events.

This paper investigates eigenvalues associated with periodic cycles of post-critically finite endomorphisms on $\mathbb{CP}^n$ in dimensions greater than one. For the case $n=1$, it is a well-established fact that these eigenvalues are either zero or have a modulus strictly greater than 1. A conjecture proposed by Van Tu Le in 2020 suggests this property extends to all $n \geq 2$. In this work, we confirm the conjecture for the class of weakly post-critically finite all-the-way-down maps, a category introduced by Astorg in 2020. This category encompasses the well-known class of post-critically finite maps developed by Koch in 2013. Consequently, our results validate the conjecture specifically for Koch maps.

The celebrated Oseledets theorem \cite{O}, extending foundational contributions by Furstenberg and Kesten regarding random matrix products and random variables on non-compact semisimple Lie groups \cite{FK,Furstenberg}, guarantees that the Lyapunov exponents of $\mathrm{SL}(d,\mathbb R)$-cocycles ($d\geqslant 2$) over the shift are well-defined for all points within a set of full measure for any invariant probability. Focusing on a locally constant $\mathrm{SL}(d,\mathbb R)$-valued cocycle, we investigate two specific sets: the collection of points in the shift space where certain Lyapunov exponents are undefined, and the set of directions in the projective space $\mathbf P \mathbb R^d$ where no well-defined exponential growth rate exists for specific matrix products. We demonstrate that if the semigroup generated by a finite set of matrices in $\mathrm{SL}(d,\mathbb R)$ is non-compact and strongly projectively accessible, then there exists a dense set of directions in $\mathbf P \mathbb R^d$ along which the Lyapunov exponent for a typical product of these matrices fails to be well-defined. Consequently, we conclude that Lyapunov non-typical behavior is prevalent among hyperbolic $\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb R)$-valued cocycles. These findings stem from a broader characterization of non-typical points regarding Ces\`aro averages of continuous observables and infinite paths within finitely generated semigroup actions by homeomorphisms on a compact metric space $X$, provided a mild hitting times condition is met.

This study illustrates that the quantum paraelectric ground state of SrTiO$_3$ can be reached through a microscopic *ab initio* method grounded in density functional theory. At low temperatures, intense quantum fluctuations stabilize the paraelectric phase, overriding the ferroelectric phase predicted by classical models. We determine that incorporating quantum lattice fluctuations and the robust coupling between the ferroelectric soft mode and lattice elongation is essential to match the experimental frequency of the soft mode quantitatively. Furthermore, the proposed microscopic framework successfully reproduces the temperature-dependent properties of SrTiO$_3$.

This study introduces a probabilistic framework for translating parametric uncertainty into output state uncertainty within first-order hyperbolic conservation laws. Specifically, we examine nonlinear immiscible two-phase transport in heterogeneous porous media subjected to a stochastic velocity field, where uncertainty in total velocity stems from incomplete knowledge of the porosity field, injection flux, or both. Consequently, the total-velocity uncertainty induces spatiotemporal variability in the saturation field. By utilizing the method of distributions and incorporating spatial/temporal statistics of correlated heterogeneity, we derive deterministic equations governing the evolution of the single-point cumulative distribution function (CDF) for saturation. Distinct from the Buckley-Leverett equation, our derived equation for the raw CDF is linear with respect to space and time. This approach offers a pathway to bypass the high computational costs associated with Monte Carlo simulations while still capturing the full statistical description of saturation. Through a series of numerical experiments, we compare saturation statistics generated by the method of distributions against those from statistical moment equations and kernel density estimation applied to high-resolution Monte Carlo results. These comparisons reveal that the CDF-based equations maintain accuracy across a broad spectrum of statistical properties, including varying standard deviations and correlation lengths of the underlying random fields. In contrast, low-order statistical moment equations diverge significantly from Monte Carlo benchmarks unless the standard deviation and correlation length are extremely small.

Recent research introduces computational justification for broadening the range of proper cones supported by conic optimization solvers, enabling simpler and more natural formulations. We define an "exotic cone" as a proper cone equipped with a small set of tractable oracles—specifically those that are fast, numerically stable, and analytic—for a logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier or its dual. Our extensible, open-source solver, Hypatia, supports modeling and solving conic optimization problems over Cartesian products of these exotic cones. This paper details Hypatia's interior point algorithm, which generalizes the approach by Skajaa and Ye [2015] to handle exotic cones lacking tractable primal oracles. To enhance practical iteration counts and solve times, we propose four improvements to the stepping procedure of Skajaa and Ye [2015]: (1) relaxing the central path proximity condition, (2) refining directions via a third-order directional derivative barrier oracle, (3) conducting backtracking searches along a curve, and (4) integrating prediction and centering directions. We have implemented 23 useful exotic cones within Hypatia, summarizing their oracle complexities and demonstrating that the new third-order oracle does not create bottlenecks while providing efficient, stable implementations. Additionally, we created a diverse benchmark of 379 conic problems drawn from 37 applied examples. Computational results indicate that each enhancement reduces both iteration counts and solve times, collectively lowering the shifted geometric means of these metrics by over 80% and 70%, respectively.

The study calculates the relic gravitational wave background arising from tensor linear perturbations produced during Higgs inflation. The analysis examines both the Standard Model and a well-motivated phenomenological extension that incorporates all experimentally verified evidence of new physics. The research centers on critical Higgs inflation, which offers improvements over the non-critical variant by amplifying tensor fluctuations. This amplification suggests that future space-based interferometers, including DECIGO, BBO, and ALIA, could detect these primordial gravitational waves.

Quantum dimer and loop models have garnered significant interest due to their role in elucidating novel phases and transitions within constrained prototypical systems, as well as their direct relevance to ongoing experiments on Rydberg atom arrays where blockade mechanisms enforce local constraints. Utilizing the sweeping cluster quantum Monte Carlo method, we map the complete ground-state phase diagram of the fully packed quantum loop model on a square lattice. Our results identify a resonating plaquette (RP) phase, characterized by off-diagonal translational symmetry breaking, situated between the lattice nematic (LN) phase (dominated by strong dimer attraction) and the staggered phase (SP) (dominated by strong dimer repulsion). The RP phase is separated from the LN phase by a first-order transition and from the SP phase at the renowned Rokhsar-Kivelson point. Furthermore, our renormalization group analysis confirms distinct flow directions, which align perfectly with order parameter histograms derived from Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we propose the potential realization and implications of this phase diagram for Rydberg experiments.

We introduce an efficient approach for leveraging pretrained language models by learning selective binary masks for their weights, serving as an alternative to traditional finetuning. Comprehensive evaluations across various NLP tasks using masked BERT and RoBERTa demonstrate that this strategy achieves performance on par with finetuning while significantly reducing memory usage during simultaneous multi-task inference. Intrinsic assessments reveal that representations from these masked models retain the essential information required for downstream tasks. Furthermore, an analysis of the loss landscape indicates that both masking and finetuning result in models located at minima that are linearly connected with nearly constant test accuracy, confirming masking as a viable and efficient substitute for finetuning.

Galactic evolution is influenced by environmental factors, prompting this study to investigate active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity across four distinct settings: voids, isolated regions, groups, and brightest group galaxies (BGGs). Comparisons of optical and radio AGN fractions reveal that void galaxies exhibit significantly lower stellar ages, concentrations, colors, and surface mass densities compared to isolated or grouped galaxies, alongside a higher frequency of one-on-one interactions. To isolate pure environmental effects, the analysis controlled for biases related to stellar mass and galaxy type using the 4000$\AA$ break strength. Results indicate no environmental dependence for optical AGN in blue galaxies and only marginal significance in green ones; however, massive red galaxies in voids display a higher fraction of optical AGN than their counterparts in dense environments. This discrepancy may stem from increased one-on-one interactions in voids or reflect fundamental differences in host properties or void environments. Conversely, radio-mode AGN activity rises in dense environments for red galaxies, while the fraction of radio-loud AGN remains unchanged for blue and green galaxies, suggesting that cold gas presence mitigates environmental effects on AGN activity. Finally, the study explores whether gas accretion efficiency varies based on host galaxy characteristics.

This paper generalizes earlier findings on quantum vacuum or Casimir energy—previously studied for either non-interacting rotating systems or interacting non-rotating ones—to a scenario encompassing both rotation and interactions. Specifically, we first revisit the non-interacting rotating scalar field theory, introducing a streamlined approach to calculate Casimir energy utilizing the replica trick and the Coleman-Weinberg effective potential. Subsequently, we analyze the combined influence of rotation and interactions, accounting for explicit rotational symmetry breaking, and implement a numerical zeta-function regularization scheme. Our findings recover prior results as limiting cases and demonstrate that incorporating both rotation and interactions yields significant modifications to the quantum vacuum energy. Beyond anticipated trends, such as the increase in angular momentum with angular velocity for a fixed interaction strength and ring size, we find that the interplay between rotation and the coupling constant intensifies the interaction strength. Furthermore, we observe a deviation from standard massless behavior, where the Casimir energy is no longer inversely proportional to the ring's size.

This paper introduces RefVAE, a novel reference-based image super-resolution method utilizing a Variational AutoEncoder. Unlike current state-of-the-art techniques that primarily target single-image super-resolution and struggle with high upsampling factors like 8×, our approach leverages any arbitrary image as a reference. RefVAE effectively transfers knowledge from the reference—even if it is a random map or the low-resolution input itself—to enhance the super-resolved output. By varying the reference, the method generates diverse versions of the restored image from a latent super-resolution space. In addition to standard evaluations using PSNR and SSIM across various datasets, we participated in the NTIRE2021 SR Space challenge to assess our method's randomness. Compared to other leading approaches, our technique achieves superior diversity scores.

This work investigates active flows surrounding isolated defects and the self-propulsion speed of $+1/2$ defects within an active nematic film subjected to both viscous dissipation (viscosity $\eta$) and substrate friction (damping $\Gamma$). The interaction between these dissipation mechanisms is governed by the hydrodynamic screening length $\ell_d=\sqrt{\eta/\Gamma}$. For an isolated defect, the spatial extent of the surrounding vortical flow is limited by the system size $R$ when no screening occurs. However, when friction introduces a finite $\ell_d$, the vorticity field diminishes to zero at scales exceeding $\ell_d$. Our findings indicate that the self-propulsion velocity of $+1/2$ defects increases with $R$ in small systems where $R<\ell_d$, but saturates to a constant value determined by $\ell_d$ in the limit of an infinite system or when $R\gg \ell_d$.

In 2021, the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory organized an internal competition to create AI agents capable of excelling at the collaborative card game Hanabi. Participants were assessed on their ability to collaborate with unfamiliar human players. This paper outlines the creation of the winning agent, which achieved a human-play average score of 16.5, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art for human-bot performance in Hanabi. The development process involved observing and accurately modeling the author's decision-making in the game, followed by training using a behavioral clone of the author. Significantly, the agent discovered a human-complementary play style by first mimicking human decisions and then exploring variations of this human-like strategy that resulted in higher simulated scores. This research provides a detailed examination of the design and implementation of this human-compatible teammate, alongside an analysis of the existence and implications of human-complementary strategies for enhancing AI applications in human-machine teams.

This article explores fixed point results based on a novel generalized $\Delta$-implicit contractive condition within ordered complete multiplicative $\mathbf{G}_\mathcal{M}$-metric spaces. Additionally, the study introduces new definitions and fixed point theorems for this specific space. To support these findings, several nontrivial and illustrative examples are provided.

This study utilizes the theory of infinitesimal transformations to investigate a family of previously proposed 1+1 fifth-order partial differential equations, which model multiple kink solutions. Our analysis includes a comprehensive classification of the Lie symmetries and the corresponding one-dimensional optimal system. These findings are employed to derive similarity solutions, specifically identifying travel-wave and scaling solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that existing kink solutions can be reconstructed using Lie symmetries, while also generating new solutions.

In Phys. Rev. A 101, 022117 (2020), it was contended that Bell inequalities stem from classical rather than quantum physics, meaning their experimental violation does not substantiate the purported existence of nonlocal or superluminal influences in the real quantum world. This Reply to Lambare's Comment, published in Phys. Rev. A 104, 066201 (2021), aims to clarify issues regarding the proper application of Hilbert space quantum mechanics to determine the microscopic origins of macroscopic measurement results. This aspect was inadequately addressed by Bell, who substituted classical hidden variables for the Hilbert subspaces (or their projectors) utilized by von Neumann in his *Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics*.

We examine a system modeling self-gravitating dust balls within an expanding universe, showing that one can specify data at infinity and evolve it backward in time without generating shocks or singularities. The resulting solution to the Einstein-lambda-dust equations persists indefinitely in the asymptotic region of spacetime. Additionally, we demonstrate that when the density is negligible relative to the cosmological constant, cosmological solutions to the Einstein constraint equations can be constructed on a standard Cauchy hypersurface for self-gravitating dust balls. If the density is further assumed to be sufficiently small, this initial data yields a future geodesically complete solution to the Einstein-lambda-dust equations that admits a smooth conformal extension at infinity, interpretable as a perturbation of de Sitter spacetime. The primary technical instrument in this analysis is the Friedrichs conformal Einstein field equations for the Einstein-lambda-dust system, formulated in a gauge where dust flow lines are represented as conformal geodesics.

A compatible $L_\infty$-algebra consists of a graded vector space equipped with two compatible $L_\infty$-algebra structures. For any given graded vector space, we construct an associated graded Lie algebra where the Maurer-Cartan elements correspond exactly to compatible $L_\infty$-algebra structures on that space. We present examples of such algebras derived from Nijenhuis operators, compatible $V$-data, and compatible Courant algebroids. Furthermore, we define the cohomology of a compatible $L_\infty$-algebra and apply this definition to investigate formal deformations. Subsequently, we classify 'strict' and 'skeletal' compatible $L_\infty$-algebras using crossed modules and the cohomology of compatible Lie algebras. Finally, we introduce compatible Lie $2$-algebras and establish their relationship with compatible $L_\infty$-algebras.

This paper investigates gossip algorithms within communication models reflecting the peer-to-peer networking capabilities found in most mainstream smartphone operating systems. We introduce and analyze a novel synchronous gossip algorithm for this environment, which offers both reduced round complexity and simpler operations compared to the best existing solutions. Furthermore, we establish a new lower bound on the rounds necessary to solve the gossip problem, thereby resolving a minor open issue by demonstrating that current synchronous approaches are within logarithmic factors of optimality. We subsequently adapt this synchronous algorithm to create a new gossip strategy for an asynchronous model that directly mirrors the interface of standard smartphone peer-to-peer networking libraries, allowing algorithms in this model to be readily implemented on actual devices. Employing fresh analytical techniques, we demonstrate that this asynchronous strategy efficiently resolves the gossip problem, marking the first known efficient asynchronous information dissemination result for the smartphone peer-to-peer context. We contend that our proposed strategy can facilitate effective information spreading subroutines in real-world smartphone peer-to-peer applications, and that the analytical tools developed for it can be utilized to generate other broadly useful algorithmic strategies for this increasingly significant domain.

The two-dimensional cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation models the propagation of high-intensity laser beams through Kerr-nonlinear media, whereas the coupled two-dimensional version describes electromagnetic wave interactions involving different polarizations in nonlinear optics. This study derives more comprehensive families of exact solutions for these equations by applying quadratic constraints to the associated argument functions and leveraging their symmetry transformations. Notably, many well-known solutions, including solitons, emerge as specific instances within these newly obtained solution families.

The non-Markovian master equation for open quantum systems is derived by extending the standard Zwanzig-Nakajima (ZN) projection method. This involves formulating a set of coupled equations for the reduced density matrices of the system, $\varrho_{S}(t)$, and the bath, $\varrho_{B}(t)$. By formally solving the equation for $\varrho_{B}(t)$ up to the second order in interaction, an additional term emerges that reflects intrinsic bath dynamics. This term is nonlinear with respect to $\varrho_{S}(t)$ and disappears in the Markovian limit. To validate the consistency and robustness of this generalized ZN projection scheme, it is applied to a simple dephasing model. The resulting kinetic equation is analyzed both within the Markovian approximation and beyond it (specifically regarding the intrinsic bath dynamics term), with the outcomes compared against exact solutions.

This study employs a high-order accurate numerical framework that integrates an implicit two-derivative deferred correction time discretization with the discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method for spatial discretization, targeting the solution of (non-)linear partial differential equations. Since the proposed scheme accounts for two time derivatives, spatial operators must be defined for each, leading to an extended system matrix. We investigate potential simplifications of this matrix and develop efficient strategies for solving the resulting (non-)linear systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that a tailored preconditioner combined with a matrix-free approach enables an efficient implementation and application of the new method. The scheme achieves up to eighth-order temporal accuracy for both linear advection and compressible Euler equations, and its capability to approximate solutions for compressible Navier-Stokes equations is also illustrated.

To ensure stable power grid operation, fluctuations arising from unpredictable renewable sources, consumer behavior, and trading activities must be balanced. Conventional smart grid approaches that rely on centralized data collection to address significant frequency deviations often raise security and privacy issues. Additionally, fluctuation control is frequently evaluated using Gaussian perturbations. This study demonstrates that power grid frequency variations are typically non-Gaussian, meaning large deviations occur more frequently than Gaussian models predict. We analyze real-world frequency data from Continental Europe, contrasting it with stochastic models and predictions derived from Fokker-Planck equations. Moreover, we examine a decentralized smart grid control strategy designed to limit these fluctuations. Specifically, we establish a scaling law describing how decentralized actions diminish the amplitude of frequency variations and validate these theoretical findings using a test grid. Overall, our results indicate that decentralized smart grid control can effectively reduce frequency excursions caused by both Gaussian and non-Gaussian fluctuations, providing a viable alternative for mitigating risks associated with grid variability.

The LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA Collaboration's direct detection of gravitational waves (GWs) from merging compact binaries offers a unique chance to investigate the fundamental theory of gravity governing coalescence in strong, highly dynamic regimes. This study examines how spatial covariant gravities influence GW propagation within a cosmological setting, aiming to establish observational limits on the coupling coefficients within the corresponding gravitational action. Initially, GWs are decomposed into left- and right-handed circular polarization modes to derive how spatial covariant gravities alter the propagation equations. Our analysis identifies three distinct classes of these effects: (1) frequency-independent modifications to GW speed and friction, (2) parity-violating amplitude and velocity birefringences, and (3) Lorentz-violating damping rates and dispersion. Utilizing these findings, we compute the resulting modified waveforms for GWs from compact binary coalescences. By comparing these theoretical effects with existing posterior samples and results from various gravity tests using LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA data found in the literature, we derive stringent observational constraints on the coupling coefficients of spatial covariant gravities. These findings currently represent the most comprehensive constraints on such gravities available.

Recent state-of-the-art image super-resolution (SR) techniques have demonstrated remarkable results by leveraging deep neural networks (DNNs), specifically those utilizing deep residual networks with dense skip connections. Although these models excel on benchmark datasets where low-resolution (LR) images are synthetically generated from high-resolution (HR) references with known blur kernels, real-world SR remains more difficult when both LR and HR images are captured by actual cameras. Building upon existing dense residual networks, this work employs a Gaussian process-based neural architecture search (GP-NAS) to explore a vast design space by adjusting the quantity of dense residual blocks, block dimensions, and feature counts. A collection of heterogeneous models with varied structures and hyperparameters is curated for ensemble learning, yielding exceptional performance in real image SR. Consequently, the proposed method secured first place across all three tracks of the AIM 2020 Real Image Super-Resolution Challenge.
This article describes the creation and certain characteristics of the Kochawave curve, an uncomplicated and asymmetrical variation of the Koch curve.

Predictions for galactic dark matter (DM) signals frequently depend on assumptions regarding the DM phase-space distribution function (DF) within halos. This reliance extends to both microscopic candidates, such as those involving $p$-wave suppressed or Sommerfeld-enhanced annihilation and atomic scattering, and macroscopic ones like primordial black holes detected via microlensing. As experimental precision increases, accurately quantifying theoretical uncertainties becomes crucial for establishing robust constraints on DM candidates or identifying credible detection signals. The most dependable DF predictions typically involve solving the steady-state collisionless Boltzmann equation—using methods like Eddington inversions or action-angle techniques—in agreement with observational data. This process often begins with maximal symmetries and a minimal set of degrees of freedom, gradually introducing complexity. Critical questions arise regarding whether this added complexity, which demands significant computational resources, yields better predictions, and if so, determining the optimal stopping point. Insights can be derived from zoomed-in hydrodynamical cosmological simulations, which provide access to true coarse-grained phase-space data. In this work, we evaluate an axisymmetric extension of the Eddington inversion to determine the full DM DF from a system's density profile and total gravitational potential. This approach surpasses spherical symmetry and is theoretically well-suited for spiral galaxies. However, we demonstrate that axisymmetry does not inherently outperform spherical symmetry, as the angular momentum of the DM halo is not generally aligned with that of the baryonic component. Consequently, theoretical uncertainties remain comparable to those of standard Eddington inversions, typically ranging between 10% and 20% for velocity-dependent predictions relevant to particle DM searches in spiral galaxies. We provide a detailed description of this methodology and discuss the resulting findings.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have created new business avenues for companies through automated user interactions and enhanced data analysis. However, developing sophisticated NLP applications involves modern machine learning technologies, which often hinders enterprises from launching successful projects. Our experience with applied NLP research demonstrates that continuously integrating research prototypes into production-like environments with rigorous quality assurance fosters trust in the software and highlights its utility for business objectives. We present STAMP 4 NLP, an iterative and incremental process model designed for NLP application development. By merging software engineering principles with data science best practices, this model enables the efficient creation of prototypes using templates, conventions, and existing implementations, allowing developers and data scientists to concentrate on business goals. Thanks to its iterative-incremental nature, organizations can deploy improved versions of prototypes into their software environments after each iteration, maximizing early business value and trust while avoiding the costs associated with successful experiments that remain undeployed.

Hedin's scheme is resolved by incorporating the vertex function ($GW\Gamma$) for various small molecules. This computational framework consistently integrates the vertex within both the self-energy and the polarizability. Diagrammatic analysis confirms that the self-energy constructed using this four-point vertex avoids double-counting diagrams, specifically those categorized as direct "bubbles" and exchange diagrams. By excluding the exchange diagrams from the self-energy, a more streamlined approximation known as $GW^{\rm{tc-tc}}$ is derived. Both approximations yield excellent agreement with costly wavefunction-based methods.

Machine-learned black-box policies are widely used for nonlinear control tasks, often accompanied by crude model information derived from linear approximations of nonlinear dynamics. This study addresses the challenge of integrating model-based guidance with black-box policies along a single trajectory. We first demonstrate that a straightforward convex combination of a stabilizing black-box policy and a stabilizing linear model-based policy can result in instability. Subsequently, we introduce an adaptive $\lambda$-confident policy, where the parameter $\lambda$ reflects confidence in the black-box approach, and establish its stability. Furthermore, under conditions of bounded nonlinearity, we prove that this adaptive policy achieves a bounded competitive ratio when the black-box policy is near-optimal. Finally, we develop an online learning framework to implement this policy and validate its effectiveness through case studies involving the CartPole problem and a real-world electric vehicle (EV) charging scenario characterized by data bias resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.

An in-house optical method, grounded in light-matter interactions, has been developed to identify thermo-acoustic disturbances occurring during the ignition and propagation of a premixed flame front within a half-open channel. This approach works by directing polarized laser light through a medium where density or refractive index fluctuations—caused by acoustic waves and/or the flame front—result in leaked depolarized light, which is subsequently captured by a photo-detector using an analyser. The technique was utilized to study a combustor featuring premixed flame propagation and tulip inversion. By comparing oscilloscope data with high-speed photography of the flow field, researchers distinguished between thermo-acoustic signals and the flame front, revealing that acoustic waves intercept flame propagation at various axial positions and specific time intervals.

Malware family labels suffer from inconsistency and act as black boxes because they fail to reflect actual malware capabilities. Current state-of-the-art approaches for assessing these capabilities rely primarily on manual methods, which are impractical given the rapidly growing volume of discovered malware samples. To address this, we introduce MalPaCA, a novel unsupervised machine learning framework that automates capability assessment by clustering the temporal behavior found in malware network traces. MalPaCA generates meaningful behavioral clusters using just 20 packet headers, creating behavioral profiles based on the cluster membership of these traces. Furthermore, a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) illustrates the relationships between malwares through their overlapping behaviors, offering a more insightful characterization than traditional family designations. We also propose a visualization-based evaluation method to help practitioners interpret the clustering results. Applied to a dataset of 1,100 real-world financial malware samples containing 3.6 million packets, our experiments demonstrate that: (i) MalPaCA successfully identifies specific capabilities, such as port scanning and Command and Control server reuse; (ii) it reveals multiple discrepancies between behavioral clusters and existing family labels; and (iii) it validates the effectiveness of using temporal features for clustering, achieving an error rate of 8.3% compared to 57.5% when using statistical features.

This article continues a series investigating the renormalization of field theories interacting with gravity within the effective field theory framework. While prior studies in this series examined the universality of electric charge and the two-loop beta function in Einstein-QED, this work applies the same methodology to non-Abelian gauge theories coupled with fermions and gravity. We demonstrate that, despite certain counterterms depending on gravitational couplings, the renormalized coupling constant and its associated beta function remain uncorrected by gravity at the one-loop level. Furthermore, we explicitly verify that Slavnov-Taylor identities hold at this order. The paper concludes by contextualizing these findings alongside results from earlier studies in the series.

Access to higher education is vital for minority and emergent bilingual populations, yet higher education institutions often communicate with prospective students using overly complex language. Specifically, many U.S. institutions publish admissions instructions that exceed the average reading level of a typical high school graduate, often reaching the 13th or 14th grade level, thereby creating an unnecessary barrier to access. This project addresses this issue through text simplification by introducing PSAT (Professionally Simplified Admissions Texts), a dataset comprising 112 admissions instructions randomly selected from universities across the United States. These texts were professionally simplified and validated by subject-matter experts who are full-time admissions staff at various institutions. Furthermore, PSAT includes manual alignments of 1,883 sentence pairs linking the original and simplified versions. This creates a unique corpus for evaluating and fine-tuning text simplification systems within a high-stakes domain distinct from current resources.

Serverless computing, particularly Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), is establishing a transformative paradigm expected to underpin the next generation of cloud infrastructure. Its growing prominence stems from its highly transparent architecture, which allows applications to scale with the granularity of individual functions. Because these typically small, single-purpose functions execute on shared backend resources, they present significant opportunities for computational reuse and approximate computing. Harnessing these opportunities could markedly enhance the efficiency of serverless systems, benefiting both user quality of service and system metrics such as energy consumption and costs. Consequently, this survey aims to first elucidate the internal mechanics of serverless computing and second, investigate efficiency potentials by examining function reuse and approximation strategies, including their respective advantages and limitations. Furthermore, the study outlines prospective research directions that could either expand use cases or further optimize the paradigm.

This study investigates the reconstruction capabilities of a novel Molecular Breast Imaging (MBI) system designed for early breast cancer detection using Limited Angle Tomography (LAT). The system employs two asymmetric detector heads equipped with distinct collimators, positioned in an anti-parallel orientation to face each other. By applying mild compression to a breast phantom, this configuration successfully reconstructs internal tumors using a limited set of projections, facilitated by a specialized maximum-likelihood expectation maximization (ML-EM) algorithm. The paper provides brief descriptions of the phantoms, the MBI hardware, and a Monte Carlo simulator based on Geant 4 Application for Tomographic Emission (GATE) software. Furthermore, an MBI system model implemented in IDL (Interactive Data Visualization) was utilized to assess optimal LAT configurations and reconstruction performance across varying tumor sizes, depths, and uptake levels. The discussion covers both real and simulated LAT setups, details the ML-EM methodology, and presents preliminary reconstruction outcomes.

This study addresses an initial value problem defined by generalized Rayleigh-Stokes equations, where the nonlinearity relies on historical states and maps into Hilbert scales of negative order. Through fixed point techniques and embeddings within fractional Sobolev spaces, we establish both the solvability and Hölder regularity of the solutions. Additionally, we provide an application to a corresponding inverse source problem.

In machine learning, we leverage the fact that model parameters often outnumber data points within a single batch for large-scale nonlinear least squares loss functions. This condition induces a low-rank structure in the loss function's Hessian, facilitating efficient computation of search directions. Building on this insight, we introduce two algorithms for estimating Jacobian matrices that demonstrate performance competitive with current state-of-the-art approaches.

The surge in artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly boosted the popularity of generative art, which now spans from painting creation to the development of novel artistic styles. Despite these diverse applications, the ethical implications of AI-driven generative art remain largely overlooked. This study examines biases inherent in the generative art AI pipeline, ranging from issues stemming from flawed problem formulation to those arising in algorithm design. Adopting an art history perspective, we explore the socio-cultural consequences of these biases. By utilizing causal models, we demonstrate how current methodologies fail to accurately capture the art creation process, thereby contributing to various forms of bias. We substantiate these findings through case studies, particularly focusing on style transfer. To our knowledge, this represents the first comprehensive analysis of biases in the generative art AI pipeline through the lens of art history. Ultimately, we aim to stimulate interdisciplinary dialogue regarding the accountability of generative art.

Joint contributions by the Pierre Auger Collaboration and the Telescope Array Collaboration presented at the 34th International Cosmic Ray Conference, held from July 30 to August 6, 2015, in The Hague, Netherlands.

This paper presents two main contributions. First, we outline the methodological prerequisites for a risk framework governing custodial operations and demonstrate its value as a complement to cryptographic and blockchain security models. Second, we introduce a risk model implemented as a library of attack trees specific to Revault, an open-source custody protocol. This model serves as a risk quantification framework that organizations can employ to conduct comprehensive security analyses within their unique deployment contexts. Furthermore, our work illustrates an adaptable approach applicable to any custody protocol, including those that are complex, involve multiple stakeholders, and feature active defense infrastructure.

By employing gravitational potential and source multipole moments that are bilinear in spins, first calculated to next-to-leading order (NLO) in the post-Newtonian (PN) expansion using the effective field theory (EFT) framework, we finalize the derivation of dynamical invariants and flux-balance equations, encompassing both energy and angular momentum. Leveraging these findings, we compute spin-spin contributions to the orbital frequency and accumulated phase at NLO for circular trajectories. Furthermore, we derive the linear momentum and center-of-mass fluxes, along with the corresponding kick velocity, up to the highest pertinent PN order. We explicitly confirm the equivalence between quadratic-in-spin source multipoles derived via the EFT formalism and those rederived using conventional methods, resulting in perfect agreement for spin-spin radiative observables at NLO across both approaches.

$PSP$ and $SolO$ data are employed to study magnetic field intermittency in the solar wind (SW). While methods based on higher-order moments ($SF_q$, $SDK$) reveal that small-scale intermittency ($20-100d_{i}$) strengthens radially, no distinct trend appears at larger scales. Conversely, lower-order moment techniques, such as PVI, are better suited for analyzing the evolution of the majority of Coherent Structures (CSs) where $PVI \ge 3$. Application of the PVI index shows a scale-dependent change in the fraction of the dataset containing CSs ($f_{PVI \ge 3}$). Specifically, irrespective of SW velocity, a slight rise in $f_{PVI \ge 3}$ occurs at $\ell = 20 d_i$, contrasting with a more significant radial increase observed at larger scales. When examining intermittency alongside plasma parameters, slower SW intervals show elevated $f_{PVI \geq 6}$ values and higher kurtosis peaks, yet no statistical variation exists for $f_{PVI \geq 3}$. Furthermore, highly Alfv\'enic periods exhibit reduced intermittency. Analysis of anisotropy relative to the angle between the magnetic field and SW flow ($\Theta_{VB}$) indicates that intermittency is weaker near $\Theta_{VB} \approx 0^{\circ}$ and intensifies at larger angles. Holding the alignment angle constant, intermittency weakens as the advection time of the SW increases. These findings suggest that the radial strengthening of intermittency in the inner heliosphere is caused by an increasing sampling of relatively high-intermittency perpendicular intervals by the probes as distance grows, an effect directly linked to the evolution of the Parker spiral.

This work investigates, both theoretically and numerically, terahertz auto-oscillations in thin-film metallic non-collinear coplanar antiferromagnets (AFMs), specifically $\mathrm{Mn_{3}Sn}$ and $\mathrm{Mn_{3}Ir}$, driven by anti-damping spin-torque with spin polarization perpendicular to the film plane. To capture the order parameter dynamics, we solve three coupled Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equations incorporating exchange interactions, accounting for both single- and multi-domain (micromagnetic) behaviors. Under strong exchange interaction limits, the oscillatory dynamics of these AFMs—which exhibit opposite chiralities—can be mapped to a linear damped-driven pendulum for $\mathrm{Mn_{3}Sn}$ and a non-linear damped-driven pendulum for $\mathrm{Mn_{3}Ir}$. This theoretical framework enables the determination of input current thresholds as a function of material and geometric parameters to induce oscillatory responses. Furthermore, we derive a closed-form approximate solution for the oscillation frequency at large input currents for both materials. Our analytical predictions for threshold currents and frequencies align closely with numerical simulations, offering compact models for designing and optimizing auto-oscillators. Utilizing a circuit model grounded in tunnel anisotropic magnetoresistance, we detail the output power and efficiency profiles relative to oscillation frequency. Finally, we examine the spiking dynamics of two coupled AFM oscillators, considering both unidirectional and bidirectional configurations, using non-linear damped-driven pendulum equations.

We introduce a machine learning model designed to predict market correlation structures by leveraging financial network features derived from both nodes and links. In this approach, market structure is represented as a dynamic asset network, capturing the time-dependent co-movement of price returns among constituents of major global indices. We substantiate our findings empirically using three distinct network filtering techniques: the Dynamic Asset Graph (DAG), Dynamic Minimal Spanning Tree (DMST), and Dynamic Threshold Networks (DTN). Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high predictive accuracy, outperforming static correlation-based benchmarks by up to 40%. Furthermore, we find that non-pair-wise correlation features are crucial compared to traditional pair-wise measures across all studied markets, especially for long-term stock market structure forecasting. The study covers constituents of the DAX30, EUROSTOXX50, FTSE100, HANGSENG50, NASDAQ100, and NIFTY50 indices. These insights hold significant value for enhancing portfolio selection and risk management strategies, which often depend on backward-looking covariance matrices to assess portfolio risk.

Supporters of Distributed Morphology suggest a two-tiered structure for morphological word formation: a lower tier yielding loose semantic connections between input and output, and an upper tier producing tight ones. This study investigates the validity of that hypothesis using Hebrew word embeddings. Should the two-level theory hold true, we anticipate that advanced Hebrew embeddings will represent a noun (1), its upper-level denominal derivative (2), and its lower-level related verb (3) in a specific geometric configuration: the denominal (2) must be semantically closer to the noun (1) than the verb (3) is. Our findings confirm this hypothesis across four Hebrew embedding models—fastText, GloVe, Word2Vec, and AlephBERT—demonstrating that these models successfully capture complex, fine-grained semantic features driven by morphology.

Distributed learning frequently encounters Byzantine failures, prompting numerous studies on distributed stochastic optimization in such environments. However, existing approaches, which rely on only a subset of workers to compute stochastic gradients per iteration, often suffer from either sub-optimal convergence rates or excessive computational costs. To address these limitations, we introduce BrSGD, a novel Byzantine-resilient stochastic gradient descent algorithm proven to be robust against Byzantine failures. BrSGD simultaneously achieves optimal statistical performance and computational efficiency; specifically, it attains an order-optimal statistical error rate for strongly convex loss functions. Furthermore, the algorithm's computational complexity is O(md), where d represents the model dimension and m denotes the number of machines. Experimental findings demonstrate that BrSGD yields competitive effectiveness and convergence rates compared to systems without Byzantine failures.

This work investigates the generalization characteristics of weakly supervised learning, a scenario where a small set of "strong" labels (the true prediction targets) coexist with a larger pool of "weak" labels. We demonstrate that access to these weak labels can substantially boost the learning rate for the strong task, accelerating it to a fast rate of $\mathcal{O}(\nicefrac1n)$, where $n$ represents the count of strongly labeled instances. This improvement occurs even when the strongly labeled data alone would only permit the slower $\mathcal{O}(\nicefrac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$ convergence. The degree of acceleration varies continuously based on the quantity of available weak labels and the relationship between the two tasks. Our theoretical findings are corroborated empirically across various tasks, highlighting how weak labels expedite learning on the primary objective.

Automatic portrait video matting remains an under-constrained challenge, as most leading approaches rely solely on semantic data and treat frames in isolation, which hampers performance by ignoring temporal relationships. To address this, we introduce the Context Motion Network, which simultaneously utilizes semantic and motion cues. By estimating optical flow and implementing a context-motion updating operator that recurrently integrates features across frames, our method effectively captures motion dynamics. Experimental results on the Video240K SD dataset demonstrate that our network significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art matting techniques.

This paper proposes an alternative approach to achieving topological superfluidity (TS) that does not rely on spin-orbit coupling or external magnetic fields. By introducing an experimentally viable technique known as on-site rotation (OSR) into p-band honeycomb optical lattices for spinless Fermi gases, and treating charge density waves (CDW) and pairing equally, we examine how OSR influences superfluidity. Our findings indicate that once OSR exceeds a critical threshold—causing the CDW to disappear—the system transitions from a normal superfluid (NS) characterized by a zero TKNN number to a TS marked by a non-zero TKNN number. Furthermore, transitions between distinct TS phases are also feasible.

Current debates in the first-principles modeling of conduction within molecular devices focus on defining current accurately when non-local potentials are present. Although the physical current density ${ f j}=(-ie\hbar/2m)(\Psi^* 
abla \Psi- \Psi 
abla \Psi^*)$ fails to satisfy local conservation and requires adjustment via a non-local term, it remains unclear which current represents the physical reality. We demonstrate that the extended Maxwell equations proposed by Aharonov and Bohm uniquely determine the electromagnetic fields generated by such currents. For an oscillating dipole, we show that the radiated electric field includes a longitudinal component proportional to $ \omega \hat{P}$, where $\hat{P}$ denotes the anomalous moment $\int \hat{I}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{x} d^3x$ and $\hat{I}$ represents the spatially varying part of the anomaly $I=\partial_t ho+
abla \cdot \mathbf{j}$. Furthermore, in stationary currents within molecular devices, the violation of local current conservation leads to a "missing field" effect that may be experimentally detectable, particularly when its magnitude depends on the total current.

This study reports the inaugural polarimetric space-based VLBI observations of OJ 287, conducted using RadioAstron at 22 GHz during a perigee pass on April 4, 2014, alongside five near-simultaneous snapshots and concurrent ground-based VLBI data at 15, 43, and 86 GHz. Ground-space interferometric fringes were achieved with a projected baseline of up to 3.9 Earth diameters during the perigee session and a record 15.1 Earth diameters during the snapshot sessions, enabling the imaging of the innermost jet at an angular resolution of approximately 50 microarcseconds—the highest resolution ever attained at 22 GHz for this source. Comparisons with ground-only VLBI data reveal progressive jet bending as angular resolution increases, a finding consistent with supermassive binary black hole models, though alternative models remain viable. Spectral analysis indicates that the VLBI core's emission is dominated by the internal energy of particles during the onset of a multi-wavelength flare, whereas the parsec-scale jet appears to be in equipartition between particles and magnetic fields. Minimum brightness temperatures, derived from visibility amplitudes, exhibit a continuous rise with increasing baseline length, reaching $10^{13}$ K; this is reconciled with the inverse Compton limit via Doppler boosting for a jet closely aligned with the line of sight. Furthermore, the observed electric vector position angle suggests a predominantly toroidal magnetic field in the innermost jet, and marginal evidence of a rotation measure gradient across the jet width implies that the VLBI core is threaded by a helical magnetic field, aligning with current jet formation theories.

Recent studies utilizing Gaia data have uncovered diffuse stellar populations encircling nearby open clusters. It is crucial to confirm that these structures, referred to as "halos," "tails," and "strings," share the same ages and chemical compositions as the dense central regions. This work presents an analysis of NGC 2516 (approximately 150 Myr old), which features a classical tidal radius of 10 pc but an apparent halo extending 500 pc ($20^\circ$ across the sky). By integrating Gaia photometry, TESS rotation periods, and lithium abundance data from Gaia-ESO and GALAH, we demonstrate that NGC 2516's halo matches the age of its core. Specifically, two-thirds of the kinematically selected halo members within 250 pc of the center exhibit rotation periods consistent with a gyrochronological age of 150 Myr, a trend absent in a comparison sample of field stars. Halo stars also display lithium abundances higher than those of field stars, correlating with stellar rotation rates and binarity fractions, a pattern observed in other young open clusters. Overall, this study supports a new paradigm suggesting that open cluster halos are frequently more populous than their cores. We further discuss the implications for spectroscopic survey targeting, open cluster dispersal, and planet searches around young stars.

The unconventional strange metal phase observed in high-$T_c$ cuprates defies standard condensed-matter theories, particularly Fermi liquid theory, posing a significant theoretical challenge. Precise experimental measurements of the electronic self-energy offer a rigorous test for strange metal models, a capability achievable via angle-resolved photoemission across variations in frequency, momentum, temperature, and doping. We demonstrate that constant energy slices of the nodal spectral function in (Pb,Bi)$_{2}$Sr$_{2-x}$La$_x$CuO$_{6+\delta}$ exhibit a non-Lorentzian profile, indicating that the nodal self-energy depends on momentum ($k$). Furthermore, the experimental data are exceptionally well-fitted by a power law featuring a $k$-dependent scaling exponent that transitions smoothly with doping; this framework arises naturally from AdS/CFT-based semi-holography. These findings highlight the potential of holographic approaches for quantitatively modeling strongly interacting quantum materials, such as strange metals in cuprates.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to perform spatial image transformation with the specific objective of reducing the bit depth required for image storage. The core technique relies on the modulus operator, transforming the entire image into multiples of a predefined integer; dividing the image by this integer ensures the resulting file size is smaller than the original. Although the k-Modulus Method cannot function as a standalone image compression transform due to its exceptionally high compression ratio, it serves effectively as an embedded scheme within other image processing domains, particularly compression. Given its high PSNR value, this method can be integrated with other techniques to enhance redundancy reduction.

This paper introduces a low-power processor designed for fast Fourier transform (FFT) calculations that utilizes a transport triggering template. The processor is software-programmable and maintains energy efficiency comparable to fixed-function alternatives. Power savings are achieved by compressing the computation kernel into a single instruction word, which is stored in an instruction loop buffer that consumes less power than standard instruction memory. The processor supports all power-of-two FFT sizes ranging from 64 to 16384; with 1 mJ of energy, it can perform 20,916 transforms of size 1024.

Although Weighted Finite Automata (WFA) can effectively model functions over strings, they are fundamentally linear. Given the recent triumphs of nonlinear models in machine learning, it seems logical to explore whether extending WFA into the nonlinear domain would yield advantages. This paper introduces a new neural network-based nonlinear WFA (NL-WFA) model and a corresponding learning algorithm. Drawing inspiration from spectral learning methods for WFA, our approach utilizes an auto-encoder network to perform a nonlinear decomposition of the Hankel matrix. We evaluate the expressive capabilities of NL-WFA and the proposed learning algorithm using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that NL-WFA can achieve smaller model sizes and successfully infer complex grammatical structures from data.

The monogamy, or unextendibility, of entangled states represents a fundamental characteristic of quantum entanglement. Departing from traditional methods that rely on entanglement measure inequalities to express this concept, we propose a state-dependent set of free states to quantify the unextendibility of bipartite quantum systems. Initially, we define a class of entanglement metrics termed *unextendible entanglement*. For a given bipartite state $\rho_{AB}$, these measures are derived by minimizing the divergence between $\rho_{AB}$ and any potential reduced state $\rho_{AB'}$ obtained from an extension $\rho_{ABB'}$ of the original state. This approach is grounded in the intuitive principle that increased entanglement between two parties restricts their ability to share entanglement with a third party. Furthermore, we demonstrate that unextendible entanglement acts as an entanglement monotone under two-extendible operations, a category that encompasses local operations and one-way classical communication as a specific instance. These measures also exhibit other advantageous traits, such as normalization and faithfulness. In terms of practical utility, we illustrate that unextendible entanglement offers efficiently calculable benchmarks for determining the rates of exact secret key and entanglement distillation, as well as the overhead associated with probabilistic distillation protocols.

We assess how well upcoming experiments will probe the existence of neutrinoless double-beta decay driven by light neutrinos with inverted mass ordering. Although comparing results from different isotopes remains challenging, our analysis indicates that a global, multi-isotope effort will completely validate the inverted ordering scenario. Furthermore, these future searches will investigate alternative mechanisms responsible for the decay, including exploring a vast, previously uncharted region of parameter space under the assumption of normal mass ordering.

This study investigates the breakdown of inviscid, incompressible flows along a rigid body under slipping boundary conditions. Although the flow itself is inviscid, the slipping condition introduces compressibility, which serves as the primary driver for the singularity in the gradient of the velocity component parallel to the rigid boundary. Analytically, these slipping flows are examined using two- and three-dimensional inviscid Prandtl equations, yielding criteria for gradient catastrophe in both dimensions. In the 2D case, breaking occurs for both the parallel velocity along the boundary and the vorticity gradient. For 3D flows, breaking—defined as the formation of a fold within finite time—affects both the symmetric part of the velocity gradient tensor and the antisymmetric part, representing vorticity. Additionally, numerical analysis of velocity gradient formation between two parallel plates is conducted using the two-dimensional Euler equations. Results indicate that the maximum velocity gradient increases exponentially over time on a rigid boundary, accompanied by a double exponential rise in the vorticity gradient. Detailed analysis reveals that this phenomenon constitutes folding, characterized by a power-law relationship between the maximum velocity gradient and its width: $\max|u_x| \propto \ell^{-2/3}$.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly attracting researchers in quantitative finance because its agent-environment interaction framework aligns well with decision-making processes in various business scenarios. While most existing financial applications rely on model-free RL methods that struggle with stability and adaptivity, the maturation of model-based RL (MBRL) in fields like robotics and video games has inspired a new approach. This method incorporates resistance and support (RS) levels as regularization terms for actions within MBRL to enhance both efficiency and stability. Experimental results demonstrate that utilizing RS levels as a market timing technique improves pure MBRL models across multiple metrics, yielding higher profits with reduced risk. Notably, the proposed method effectively mitigates significant drawdowns during the unpredictable market crisis of the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, numerical experiments investigating the loss of actor-critic networks and prediction errors of transition dynamic models reveal why controlling RS levels boosts MBRL performance. These findings indicate that RS indicators facilitate faster convergence during the initial training stages and result in lower critic loss as training episodes accumulate.

Accurate sleep staging using electroencealogram (EEG) data is vital for the clinical diagnosis and management of sleep disorders. To reduce the burden of manual labeling by human experts, recent efforts have utilized deep neural networks to build automated staging systems. However, these networks often lose significant detailed information during signal propagation, which degrades the quality of deep feature representation. To overcome this limitation, we introduce MRNet, a data-driven framework that combines a multi-scale feature fusion model with a Markov-based sequential correction algorithm. Built upon a residual block-based backbone network for feature extraction, the proposed fusion model creates a feature pyramid by concatenating outputs from various network depths, enabling the system to better interpret signals across different scales. Additionally, the Markov-based algorithm mitigates output jitter from the classifier by leveraging prior stage distributions and sleep stage transition rules within a Markov chain. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves competitive performance in terms of both accuracy and F1 score, recording 85.14% accuracy and 78.91% F1 score on the Sleep-EDFx dataset, and 87.59% accuracy with 79.62% F1 score on the Sleep-EDF dataset.

To implement few-body quantum gates, we examine three-body resonant interactions among Rydberg atoms. Previous resonances identified in cesium or rubidium depended on an adjacent two-body resonance that vanishes for principal quantum numbers exceeding $n \simeq 40$. Recently, we introduced a novel class of three-body interaction resonances in alkali-metal Rydberg atoms [P. Cheinet \textit{et al.}, Quant. Elect. \textbf{50}, 213 (2020)] that overcomes this constraint. This study compares the strength of this new three-body resonance against quasi-forbidden two-body resonances in rubidium and cesium. Finally, we determine the optimal conditions for detecting and utilizing this three-body interaction.

Melanoma represents a primary cause of skin cancer-related fatalities, making its early and accurate detection a critical priority.
