Existing automated diagnostic methods typically rely on pattern recognition or analytical frameworks such as the ABCDE criteria (asymmetry, border, color, diameter, and evolving). However, clinical practice often employs a differential approach that identifies outliers, known as the "ugly duckling" sign, to assess nevi and lesions. While integrating this differential recognition into Computer Aided Diagnosis (CAD) systems remains underexplored, it offers significant value by providing clinical rationale for diagnostic decisions. This study introduces a methodology for identifying and quantifying ugly ducklings through Intra-Patient Comparative Analysis (IPCA) of adjacent nevi, which is integrated into a CAD system designed for melanoma detection. The proposed design maintains flexibility to manage scenarios where IPCA cannot be performed. Experimental results on a public dataset demonstrate that incorporating outlier information enhances detection sensitivity by at least 4.1%, while improving specificity by 4.0% to 8.9%, contingent upon whether a robust (EfficientNet) or moderately robust (VGG or ResNet) classifier is utilized.

Active galactic nucleus (AGN) accretion disks are thought to host various transient events, including supernovae, compact object mergers, and tidal disruptions, which emit detectable electromagnetic signals; these are collectively termed "AGN disk transients." Shortly after ejecta shocks exit the disk, inelastic hadronuclear ($pp$) collisions between shock-accelerated cosmic rays and disk matter can generate high-energy neutrinos. However, assuming a standard Gaussian density profile for stable, gas-dominated disks leads to a rapid decline in neutrino production efficiency. Conversely, AGN accretion disks frequently exhibit outflows and winds. This paper demonstrates that the surrounding circum-disk medium can absorb additional shock kinetic energy, thereby significantly boosting the production of high-energy neutrinos, particularly in the $\sim$TeV–PeV range of interest to IceCube. Due to the presence of this circum-disk environment, neutrino generation is markedly enhanced, contributing substantially to the diffuse neutrino background. Optimistically, AGN disk transients could account for approximately 20% of the diffuse neutrino background.

While the correctness of reactive systems is well-established, their efficiency has garnered less attention, even though multiple correct systems can vary in fitness. We introduce a novel, highly general framework that assigns comparable fitness scores to these systems. By intentionally separating the framework's parameters from the systems being evaluated, we enhance the interpretability of the scores and reduce the user burden compared to existing methods that require manual numerical annotation. We define the computational problem of assessing a system within this framework and present a method for calculating fitness scores for finite labeled transition systems. Finally, we demonstrate our approach by comparing two versions of a simple communication protocol and four variants of the Alternating Bit Protocol.

We demonstrate that for fixed finitely generated subgroups $A$ and $B$ within a free group $F$, the count of conjugacy classes arising from intersections $A\cap B^g$ is bounded by the ranks of $A$ and $B$. This finding validates an intuition proposed by Walter Neumann. Previously, such a result was established solely when either $A$ or $B$ was cyclic, based on the $w$-cycles theorem by Helfer and Wise and independently by Louder and Wilton. To establish our primary theorem, we develop novel insights into the structure of fibre products of finite graphs. By employing a generalized definition of graph immersions, our findings extend to the theory of regular languages; notably, we present a new algorithm for determining the non-emptiness of the intersection of two regular languages.

We provide a combinatorial definition of the "$D_{2n}$ planar algebra" using generators and relations. We detail the interaction between these generators and Temperley-Lieb braiding, demonstrating that the known braiding on the even component extends to a "braiding up to sign" across the entire algebra. Leveraging this property, we offer a direct proof of the consistency of our relations, deliver a full description of the corresponding tensor category and principal graph, and establish the planar algebra's positive definiteness. These results enable us to confirm that our combinatorial construction corresponds to the standard invariant of the $D_{2n}$ subfactor.

While numerous studies address the stability of nonlinear positive systems with time delays, the majority assume constant delays. This work examines systems with time-varying, potentially unbounded delays, establishing asymptotic stability and determining decay rate bounds for a broad class of nonlinear positive systems that encompasses positive linear systems as a subset. Specifically, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for delay-independent stability in continuous-time positive systems characterized by cooperative and homogeneous vector fields, demonstrating that their global asymptotic stability remains unaffected by the magnitude or variation of time delays. Furthermore, we provide explicit expressions to quantify decay rates for various delay types and present corresponding results for discrete-time positive systems with non-decreasing and homogeneous vector fields.

Although pretrained large generative language models excel at numerous tasks, they often struggle with compositional generalization. However, scaling these models enhances their performance across various NLP tasks, even when conditioned on few-shot examples without fine-tuning, a technique known as in-context learning. This study investigates the disparity between in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance in semantic parsing tasks utilizing in-context learning. Specifically, ID settings involve demonstrations drawn from the same data split used for evaluation, whereas OOD settings use demonstrations from the alternate split. We analyze how the relative generalization gap in in-context learning changes as model size increases. By evaluating four model families—OPT, BLOOM, CodeGen, and Codex—across three semantic parsing datasets (CFQ, SCAN, and GeoQuery) with varying numbers of exemplars, we observe a trend where the relative generalization gap diminishes as models scale up.

Effort estimation models serve as essential instruments in software management, providing forecasts for resources, constraints, and costs linked to development. In the context of Free/Open Source Software (FOSS) projects, this estimation is particularly challenging due to the collaboration between professional and occasional volunteer developers, making the calculation of total effort (measured in person-months) difficult. The primary goal of this research is to create a straightforward effort estimation model for FOSS projects grounded in historical developer data, with accuracy ensured through direct developer feedback. By analyzing personal development profiles of thousands of contributors across six major FOSS projects, we surveyed participants to assess whether they should be classified as full-time. This feedback was utilized to refine an effort threshold that defines full-time status. Utilizing over 1,000 completed questionnaires, we identified specific commit thresholds for each sampled project that effectively distinguish between full-time and non-full-time contributors while minimizing both type I and type II errors. Finally, we provide guidelines and a tool for applying this model to FOSS projects utilizing version control systems.

We demonstrate that orthogonal arrays $OA(16 \lambda, 11, 2,4)$ do not exist for $\lambda=6$ and $\lambda=7$, thereby resolving an open problem from the NSUCRYPTO Olympiad 2018. This finding enables the determination of minimum weights for specific higher-order correlation-immune Boolean functions.

We advocate for a model-centric Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) approach to generate meaningful explanations of trained model behaviors that differ from and complement the insights provided by popular data-centric tools like LIME and SHAP. By comparing these methodologies, we demonstrate that data-centric approaches can produce fragile explanations with limited practical value. In contrast, the model-centric framework provides actionable insights into the risks associated with deploying AI models. For critical AI applications requiring split-second decisions, robust explanations that remain invariant to data properties—capabilities unique to model-centric frameworks—are essential for informed decision-making.

We introduce a natural extension of irreducibility within order lattices equipped with arbitrary metrics, examining specific instances involving valuation metrics as well as broader metric types for lattices. This work is primarily derived from a section of the author's doctoral thesis, though it also addresses several supplementary inquiries.

Finite element methods have effectively predicted the macro-scale behavior of heterogeneous materials like composites, multicomponent alloys, and polycrystals in industrial settings. However, these methods require mesh sizes smaller than the material's microstructural heterogeneities, resulting in computationally intensive and time-consuming simulations. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning-based image super-resolution (SR) offer a potential solution by allowing the enhancement of spatio-temporal resolution from coarse mesh data. Despite this promise, significant technical hurdles remain in creating high-fidelity SR models for computational solid mechanics, particularly for materials experiencing large deformations. This study introduces PhySRNet, a physics-informed deep learning framework that reconstructs high-resolution deformation fields (displacement and stress) from low-resolution inputs without needing high-resolution labeled datasets. A synthetic case study demonstrates the framework's efficacy, showing that the super-resolved fields achieve accuracy comparable to an advanced numerical solver running at 400 times the coarse resolution while adhering to highly nonlinear governing laws. This approach facilitates the synergistic use of machine learning and traditional numerical methods to reduce computational costs, thereby accelerating scientific discovery and engineering design.

Gravitational waves resulting from the mergers of binary black holes and neutron stars are now routinely observed. By 2021, the LIGO and Virgo observatories had confidently identified ninety such events. Efforts are underway to enhance detector sensitivity for the fourth observing run, featuring the installation of A+ upgrades aimed at reducing fundamental noise that currently constrains gravitational wave detection capabilities. This review examines the operational principles of LIGO detectors, including their optical setup and lock acquisition process, analyzes their fundamental and technical noise limits relative to present sensitivity levels, and details the A+ upgrades currently being implemented.

The persistent search for definitive signatures of topological superconductivity and Majorana modes in magnet-superconductor hybrids has generated a strong need for appropriate superconducting substrates. Ideal candidates would combine $s$-wave superconductivity with a broad energy gap, robust spin-orbit coupling, and superior surface quality, thereby allowing for the precise, atom-by-atom fabrication of magnetic nanostructures via scanning tunneling microscope tips. Because single materials seldom meet all these criteria, we propose and demonstrate the growth of thin Ir films—a high-Z metal—on the surface of elemental Nb, which possesses the largest energy gap among superconductors. Our results reveal that films one to two atomic layers thick form a strained Ir(110)/Nb(110) superlattice, whereas 10-atom-thick films transition into a compressed Ir(111) surface. Tunneling spectroscopy confirms proximity-induced superconductivity in the thicker Ir(111) films, exhibiting a hard gap $\Delta$ equal to $85.3\%$ of the gap found in bare Nb(110).

This study introduces an integration framework enabling a 6-DoF collaborative robot to manipulate pipettes for liquid dispensing. The technical development consists of three main components: first, the design of an end-effector capable of gripping and actuating manual pipettes; second, the utilization of a collaborative robot to identify laboratory equipment orientations and generate corresponding motion plans; and third, the creation of vision-based classifiers to forecast and rectify positioning errors, ensuring precise attachment of pipettes to disposable tips. Experimental results and analysis demonstrate that the proposed system, particularly its planning and visual recognition capabilities, facilitates high-precision and flexible liquid dispensing. The system is well-suited for low-frequency, high-repetition biochemical dispensing tasks. Furthermore, it is anticipated to advance the adoption of collaborative robots in laboratory automation, thereby enhancing experimental efficiency with minimal customization of the laboratory environment.

Solar flares and coronal mass ejections draw their energy from magnetic fields stored within coronal electric currents. This study investigates the characteristics of these coronal currents in both observed and modeled active regions (ARs) by analyzing their signatures in photospheric vector magnetograms. Utilizing the recently introduced Gauss separation method in solar physics, we decompose the photospheric magnetic field into three distinct parts originating from separate sources: (i) currents crossing the photosphere, (ii) currents situated beneath it, and (iii) currents located above it. We designate the third component as the photospheric imprint of coronal currents. In active regions 10930 and 11158, these imprints reveal large-scale, spatially coherent structures aligned with the central, sheared polarity inversion lines (PILs), indicating horizontal coronal currents flowing above the PILs, a result consistent with recent observations of AR 12673 by Schuck et al. (2022). Similar imprints were identified in a simplified model of a non-potential AR with defined currents. Regarding AR 11158, we observed that flare-related changes in photospheric imprints align with previous reports of near-PIL fields becoming more horizontal, supporting the "implosion" scenario. We propose that this evolution effectively shortens current-carrying coronal fields overall, thereby reducing the inductive energy (DIE) within the coronal field. Additionally, we hypothesize that in the hours leading up to flares, portions of the coronal field gradually expand through a process termed coronal inflation (CI), which is essentially the inverse of implosion. Both hypotheses can be tested using non-potential coronal field extrapolations.

The study examines Yang-Mills-aether theory, focusing on the implications of a non-abelian, aether-like term that induces Lorentz symmetry violation within a thermal quantum field theory framework. By employing the Thermofield Dynamics formalism to account for temperature and spatial compactification, the analysis calculates corrections arising from this non-abelian term to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, as well as to the Casimir energy and pressure at both zero and finite temperatures.

Sparse coding is celebrated for its ability to represent data parsimoniously by exploiting low-dimensional structures. However, inferring these codes usually depends on optimization methods that scale poorly in high-dimensional settings. For instance, applying sparse inference to the representations found in the deep intermediary layers of neural networks necessitates iterative minimization at every training iteration. Consequently, recent variational inference techniques have been developed to infer sparse codes by learning a code distribution via a deep neural network. This paper introduces a novel variational sparse coding approach that learns sparse distributions through sample thresholding, thereby circumventing problematic relaxations. We first assess and analyze this method by training a linear generator, demonstrating its superior performance, statistical efficiency, and gradient estimation relative to other sparse distributions. Subsequently, we compare our approach against a standard variational autoencoder utilizing a DNN generator on the Fashion MNIST and CelebA datasets.

Considering a valued field $(K,v)$ and its completion $(\widehat{K},v)$, we investigate the collection of all possible extensions of $v$ to $\widehat{K}(X)$. We demonstrate that every such extension is intimately linked to the underlying subextension $(K(X)|K,v)$. These relationships are analyzed using minimal pairs, key polynomials, pseudo-Cauchy sequences, and implicit constant fields. Consequently, we derive significant ramification theoretic properties of $(\widehat{K},v)$. Furthermore, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for $(K(X),v)$ to be dense within $(\widehat{K}(X),v)$.

This study introduces a mode-in-state contribution factor for specific nonlinear dynamical systems by leveraging the spectral characteristics of the Koopman operator alongside sensitivity analysis. By employing Koopman eigenfunctions to analyze a target nonlinear system, the authors demonstrate that the relative influence of modes versus state variables can be quantified even beyond linear regimes, effectively accounting for system nonlinearity. The proposed factor is utilized to examine large-signal simulations within an interconnected AC/multi-terminal DC power system.

**Context.** Detecting Earth-like planets via the radial velocity (RV) technique is primarily hindered by stellar activity and instrumental artifacts. Recent research suggests that analyzing the spectra directly, instead of relying solely on RV time series and limited activity indicators, offers a path to mitigate these disturbances. **Aims.** This study aims to demonstrate that applying principal component analysis (PCA) to the "shell" time series—defined as the projection of a spectrum onto space-normalized flux versus flux gradient—can significantly enhance RV precision. **Methods.** Decomposing the shell time series via PCA yields a basis set of first-order spectral variations uncorrelated with Keplerian motion. The temporal coefficients linked to this basis are then utilized to correct RV data for non-Dopplerian signatures. **Results.** We tested this method on post-processed spectra from HD10700 and HD128621 using the YARARA pipeline. For HD10700, signal injection tests confirmed that the approach effectively separates genuine Doppler signals from instrumental systematics. Regarding HD128621, the methodology rendered the prominent stellar activity signal (observed at the rotational period and one-year aliases) insignificant in periodogram analysis, reducing the five-year RV root mean square from 2.44 m/s to 1.73 m/s. While this technique strongly mitigates stellar activity, noise injection tests indicate that a high signal-to-noise ratio (S/N > 250) is necessary to correct the observed activity in HD128621.

We investigate a Zee model incorporating modular $A_4$ symmetry, constructing the lepton sector with the minimal possible modular weight. Using a $\Delta \chi^2$ analysis, we present our predictions for neutrino masses and phases. Our results indicate a preference for normal hierarchy, with the parameter $\tau$ localized near $2.3i$, which approximates the fixed point $i \times \infty$. In this limit, the neutrino mass matrix reduces to a two-zero texture known as the $B_1$ pattern. We demonstrate that our predicted phases align well with those of the $B_1$ texture.

Quantitatively analyzing the conversion of sensory inputs into motor outputs imposes valuable constraints on brain functionality and illuminates its fundamental computational mechanisms. This study examines the mechanosensory responses of the nematode *C. elegans* through a high-throughput optogenetic assay combined with automated behavioral quantification. While the established view suggests that behavior is dictated by specific neuronal activation and stimulus intensity, our findings indicate that responses are instead calibrated to the temporal characteristics of mechanosensory signals, such as their integral and derivative, spanning several seconds. Even within the same neurons, mechanosensory inputs can be modulated to trigger distinct behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, the animal's reaction is contingent upon its behavioral context; most notably, the organism disregards all tested mechanosensory stimuli during turning maneuvers. Finally, we introduce a linear-nonlinear model capable of predicting the animal's behavioral response to a given stimulus.

By merging newly established intersection theory for non-reductive geometric invariant theoretic quotients with equivariant localization, we derive a formula for the Thom polynomials associated with Morin singularities. These expressions rely exclusively on the toric combinatorics of specific partition polyhedra, and our novel method bypasses the inadequately understood Borel geometry inherent in current models.

We illustrate the derivation of integrable outcomes for Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) utilizing Liouville conformal field theory (LCFT) and the mating-of-trees framework within Liouville quantum gravity (LQG). Specifically, we establish an exact formula for the distribution of the conformal derivative associated with a classical variant of SLE, denoted as $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa(\rho_-;\rho_+)$. Our demonstration rests on two pivotal links between SLE, LCFT, and mating-of-trees. First, LCFT and mating-of-trees offer equivalent yet complementary approaches to characterizing natural random surfaces in LQG; by employing a new instrument termed the uniform embedding of an LQG surface, we broaden previous equivalence findings to accommodate fewer marked points and more general singularities. Second, the conformal welding of these random surfaces yields SLE curves as their boundaries. This second point specifically leverages the conformal welding results established in our companion paper [AHS20]. This work constitutes a vital component of an ongoing initiative to prove integrability results for SLE, LCFT, and mating-of-trees, grounded in these two fundamental connections.

This paper addresses exact community recovery within the symmetric stochastic block model, involving a graph of $n$ vertices partitioned into $K \ge 2$ equal-sized communities, with edge probabilities determined by community membership. Despite the maximum-likelihood approach being discrete and non-convex, we propose solving it directly via projected power iterations initialized with a partial recovery guarantee, achievable through various existing techniques. We demonstrate that in the logarithmic degree regime, this method achieves exact community recovery at the information-theoretic limit. Furthermore, with a suitable initialization, the algorithm operates in $\mathcal{O}(n\log^2n/\log\log n)$ time, matching the efficiency of current state-of-the-art approaches. Finally, we provide numerical experiments to validate and extend our theoretical findings.

Extensive research indicates that machine learning systems used for medical diagnosis often exhibit bias toward specific subgroups, prompting the development of numerous algorithms designed to mitigate such unfairness. However, evaluating the effectiveness of these methods in medical imaging remains challenging due to two main factors: a lack of consensus on fairness assessment criteria and the heterogeneous nature of existing algorithms, which are trained on varying datasets, model backbones, selection strategies, and metrics, rendering direct comparisons impossible. To address this, we present MEDFAIR, a comprehensive framework for benchmarking fairness in machine learning models for medical imaging. This framework evaluates eleven algorithms across diverse categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Our extensive experiments reveal that the often-overlooked issue of model selection criteria can significantly influence fairness outcomes. Conversely, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not substantially outperform empirical risk minimization (ERM) in either in-distribution or out-of-distribution scenarios. By assessing fairness from multiple angles, we offer recommendations tailored to different medical applications requiring distinct ethical principles. MEDFAIR serves as a reproducible and accessible platform for developing and evaluating future bias mitigation techniques in deep learning, with code available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

It has been demonstrated that two permutation classes—the X-class and subpermutations of the increasing oscillation—display an exponential Wilf-collapse. This phenomenon indicates that the count of distinct enumerations for principal subclasses within each class increases at a significantly slower rate than the class itself, despite no prior expectation of such behavior based solely on the class's symmetries. The root cause of this collapse in both instances is the application of a specific type of local symmetry; when combined with a greedy algorithm for pattern detection, this results in a Wilf-collapse.

A "transplantable pair" refers to a set of gluing diagrams utilized to construct pairs of plane domains that share identical spectra for the Laplace operator. We introduce a variety of such pairs, which were developed by John Conway through his theory of quilts.

Recently, associative $n$-categories have been introduced as a strictly associative and unital framework for higher category theory. This approach holds promise as a foundation for proof assistants, offering the potential to formalize complex high-dimensional algebraic structures with relative simplicity. Nevertheless, the original theory depends on an implicit term normalization process to identify valid composites, lacking a recursive method for its computation. In this work, we present a novel normalization strategy for associative $n$-categories utilizing the categorical zigzag construction. This method significantly streamlines the theory and provides a recursive normalization algorithm, the correctness of which we establish. By leveraging categorical lifting properties, we achieve efficient proofs of our findings. Furthermore, this normalization algorithm serves as a fundamental component of the proof assistant homotopy.io, a capability we demonstrate through detailed worked examples.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technologies are increasingly utilized across a wide array of industrial sectors. Because domain-specific models outperform generic ones when evaluated within their specific context, there is a clear demand for domain adaptation methods that are efficient in terms of memory and computation. This is especially true when adapting large, parameter-intensive transformer-based language models used for rescoring ASR hypotheses. This study addresses this challenge through prompt-tuning, a technique that trains only a small set of domain-specific token embeddings to align a transformer-based language model with a particular domain. By adding just a few parameters per domain, we achieve significantly lower perplexity scores compared to the baseline of using an unadapted model. Although highly parameter-efficient, these gains are comparable to those of fully fine-tuned models containing hundreds of millions of parameters. We further validate these results by translating the improved perplexity metrics into reduced Word Error Rates within a domain-specific ASR system.

Deep learning systems are vulnerable to imperceptible disturbances known as adversarial attacks. This research investigates how Test-time Transformation Ensembling (TTE) can serve as an effective defense mechanism. Although applying data transformations during both training and inference is recognized for boosting performance, its influence on adversarial robustness remains underexplored. We conduct a thorough empirical analysis of how common image transforms, implemented via TTE, affect robustness. Our findings demonstrate that TTE consistently strengthens model resilience against diverse, sophisticated attacks without requiring retraining, and it achieves this with negligible impact on accuracy for clean inputs. Furthermore, we show that these advantages extend to certified robustness, where TTE delivers substantial and reliable enhancements.

It is established that helical magnetic fields exhibit an inverse cascade in classical ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), where magnetic helicity conservation causes the correlation length to increase. However, at energies exceeding approximately 10 MeV, classical MHD must be replaced by chiral MHD. In this regime, the conserved quantity becomes $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle + 2 \langle\mu_5\rangle / \lambda$, where $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ represents the mean magnetic helicity, $\langle\mu_5\rangle$ denotes the mean chiral chemical potential of charged fermions, and $\lambda$ is a phenomenological chiral feedback parameter. This paper investigates the evolution of a chiral MHD system initialized with nonzero $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ but zero $\mu_5$. We provide analytic expressions for the time evolution of both $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ and $\langle\mu_5\rangle$ and compare them with laminar and turbulent three-dimensional direct numerical simulations. Our results indicate that the late-time behavior of $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ is governed by the magnetic and kinetic Reynolds numbers, ${\rm Re}_{_\mathrm{M}}$ and ${\rm Re}_{_\mathrm{K}}$. In the high Reynolds number regime where turbulence dominates, $\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle$ evolves similarly to classical ideal MHD, with the inverse correlation length of the helical magnetic field scaling as $k_\mathrm{p} \propto t^{-2/3}$. Conversely, at low Reynolds numbers where the velocity field is negligible, the scaling shifts to $k_\mathrm{p} \propto t^{-1/2}\mathrm{ln}\left(t/t_\mathrm{log}\right)$. Following rapid generation, $\langle\mu_5\rangle$ consistently decays in tandem with $k_\mathrm{p}$, approximately following $\langle\mu_5\rangle \approx k_\mathrm{p}$, with its specific time evolution contingent upon whether the system operates under low or high Reynolds number conditions.

This paper introduces and investigates multiple concepts of independence among sets, defined relative to generalized information measures parametrized by submodular functions, along with their interconnections. Given that entropy can also serve as a parameter for these measures, we establish significant independence characteristics regarding the entropy of sets of random variables. Additionally, we examine multi-set independence and its associated properties. Finally, we outline optimization algorithms designed to identify a set independent of a given set and explore the implications and applications of combinatorial independence.

Let $a > 1$. We establish that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $a^n < n!$. We demonstrate that the minimal such $n$ is either uniquely determined or belongs to a specific pair of candidates, and we provide a method to compute it. Our arguments rely centrally on three distinct numerical sequences. This work builds upon Robbins' refinement of Stirling's approximation for factorials \cite{Robbins} as well as findings from \cite{Radford}.

An extended Bose-Hubbard model (EBHM) incorporating three- and four-body interactions is viable for cold atoms within an optical lattice. Numerical simulations with appropriate parameters and filling factors reveal a complex phase diagram featuring numerous symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases. These SPT phases are identified using the Berry phase as a local topological order parameter and by analyzing the entanglement spectrum structure. Due to the existence of multiple topological phases separated by gapless boundaries, the EBHM supports various bosonic topological pumps. These pumps are formed by linking distinct SPT phases without requiring a gap closure. In the bulk, these pumps display plateau transitions defined by many-body Chern numbers. For systems with boundaries, the center of mass (CoM) within the grand canonical ensemble highlights the role of multiple edge states and uncovers the system's topology. Ultimately, we show that interacting bosonic pumps adhere to the bulk-edge correspondence.

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) released the first image of the supermassive black hole Sgr A*, revealing a shadow with a diameter of $\theta_{sh}= 48.7 \pm 7\,\mu$as. This measurement exhibits a fractional deviation from the Schwarzschild prediction of $\delta = -0.08^{+0.09}_{-0.09}~\text{(VLTI)}, -0.04^{+0.09}_{-0.10}~\text{(Keck)}$. Since the Sgr A* shadow size aligns within approximately $10\%$ of Kerr predictions, it offers a new avenue for exploring strong-field gravity. This study utilizes Sgr A* shadow observables to constrain four independent, well-motivated rotating regular spacetimes that differ parametrically from Kerr geometry, along with their associated no-horizon counterparts. Specifically, we derive limits on the deviation parameter $g$ for rotating regular black holes. Using the $1\sigma$ range for the shadow angular diameter $\theta_{sh}$, we bound the parameters $a$ and $g$. Combining these findings with existing EHT constraints on $\theta_{sh}$ and $\delta$ for Sgr A*, our analysis demonstrates that the three rotating regular black holes—the Bardeen, Hayward, and Simpson-Visser types, and their corresponding no-horizon spacetimes—are consistent with EHT observations. Consequently, these rotating regular spacetimes are indistinguishable from Kerr black holes within certain parameter ranges, meaning they cannot be excluded as viable candidates for astrophysical black holes.

The study investigates the source of nonlocal adiabatic response in an interacting Anderson insulator by utilizing optically induced nonequilibrium phonon distributions. Applying weak infrared radiation to the system effectively mitigates the long-range effects typically seen in field-effect experiments, with minimal heating and negligible impact on conductance. These observations align with the quantum characteristics of the phenomenon, indicating that such effects are unique to disordered systems exhibiting quantum coherence.

Despite its widely recognized limitations and frequent calls for abandonment, the infamous h-index remains prevalent in grant allocations, hiring, and promotion decisions. To remedy this, I developed an improved index designed to factor in individual author contributions and significantly mitigate scientific literature pollution. Ultimately, I propose a strategy that is guaranteed to be optimal for all researchers.

Contemporary digital platforms enable users to engage in diverse activities, including content creation, social networking, and commerce. As these services expand rapidly, constructing data-driven models of user behavior has become essential for delivering personalized experiences. Recently, neural networks trained on extensive interaction datasets have made representation learning a powerful approach for user modeling. However, a significant hurdle remains: the widespread issue of data sparsity, affecting ground-truth labels and entity-level interactions, particularly for cold-start users, long-tail items, and transient groups. This dissertation introduces generalizable neural frameworks for modeling user behavior that tackle various sparsity challenges across different applications. These frameworks address both transductive scenarios, which model entities observed during training, and inductive scenarios, which target entities encountered only at inference time. By utilizing diverse aspects of user behavior data—such as social network connectivity, temporal dynamics, and attributed interactions—the proposed models facilitate personalized inference at scale. Furthermore, these models complement recent advancements in neural architecture and remain adaptable to the swift emergence of new applications within online platforms.

This study investigates the inherent dynamics of spherical shells within a fluid near their buckled configuration using both experiments and 3D axisymmetric simulations. A theoretical framework, which models the buckled shell as a two-variable oscillator, substantiates these findings. We quantify the effective "softening" of shells beyond the buckling threshold, a phenomenon noted in recent experiments involving encapsulated microbubbles and acoustic waves. Furthermore, the primary dissipation mechanism occurring in the adjacent fluid is identified.

Ground-state cooling of mechanical motion through coupling to a driven optical cavity has been realized in numerous optomechanical systems. Our study presents a previously absent thermodynamic performance analysis of optomechanical sideband cooling, modeled as a heat valve. We evaluate performance metrics beyond the minimum achievable effective temperature (phonon number), specifically including evacuated heat flow as a proxy for cooling power and relevant thermodynamic efficiencies; all these parameters can be experimentally derived from measurements of the cavity's output light field. Significantly, we extend our investigation beyond the standard coherent-light setup to two recent alternative configurations: one utilizing squeezed light instead of a coherent laser drive, and another employing a cavity with a frequency-dependent (Fano) mirror. We analyze the dynamics of these configurations both within and outside the weak-coupling regime, providing concrete examples grounded in the parameters of current experimental systems. By applying this thermodynamic framework, we obtain detailed insights into these three distinct optomechanical cooling schemes, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the underlying thermodynamic mechanisms.

Automated driving systems require persuasive arguments and robust evidence to convince regulatory bodies and the public that they are safe for public roads, a process typically organized within a safety case. While reviews and testing are standard approaches for verifying automotive systems, they cannot exhaustively cover the infinite range of possible behaviors. Conversely, formal methods offer exhaustive mathematical proofs of model correctness, demonstrating that formalized functional safety requirements are met by system component models. This paper illustrates how formal methods can substantiate the decomposition of functional safety requirements into components within feedback loops and how this evidence integrates into the broader safety case. When a proof is established, the formal models serve as definitive requirements for the components. This structured safety argumentation can reduce the reliance on traditional reviews and tests to verify the decomposition, thereby conserving both data collection resources and verification time.

A viable model for coronal loops must account for several observed characteristics of warm (~ 1 MK) structures: elevated density, a flat temperature profile, a scale height exceeding hydrostatic predictions, a uniform intensity profile, and lifetimes ranging from 1000 to 5000 seconds. We investigated if thermal nonequilibrium could match these observations through hydrodynamic simulations utilizing steady coronal heating that decays exponentially with altitude, analyzing both monolithic and multi-stranded loop configurations. While the simulations successfully replicated certain features, such as excess density, each approach failed in at least one critical aspect. Monolithic models exhibited excessive intensity structuring, whereas multi-strand models were either overly structured or lasted too long. These findings suggest that heating which is highly concentrated in the lower corona and steady or quasi-steady is unlikely to be widespread, as active regions would look significantly different under such conditions. Nevertheless, thermal nonequilibrium might still be significant for prominences and catastrophic cooling events like coronal rain, which occupy a small portion of the coronal volume. However, discrepancies between these models and observations regarding cooling events remain unexplained.

Although many efforts have sought to simultaneously parse syntax and semantics, achieving high accuracy in one area often compromises performance in the other. This compromise conflicts with extensive research highlighting the profound interactions at the syntax-semantics interface. We examine various model architectures designed to leverage the abundant syntactic and semantic annotations within the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset, enabling the joint parsing of Universal Dependencies and UDS to achieve state-of-the-art outcomes in both frameworks. Furthermore, we analyze the behavior of a joint syntax-semantics model, identifying patterns that align with linguistic theory at this interface. Finally, we assess the extent to which joint modeling generalizes across a multilingual context, observing consistent trends across eight languages.

The rapid rise of automatic faithfulness metrics for summarization has created a demand for new benchmarks to assess them. Although current benchmarks evaluate how well these metrics correlate with human judgments of faithfulness in model-generated summaries, they fall short in diagnosing three critical aspects: 1) consistency (whether metrics decrease as errors are added), 2) effectiveness on human-written texts, and 3) sensitivity to various error types (since summaries may contain multiple errors). To meet these needs, we introduce BUMP (Benchmark of Unfaithful Minimal Pairs), a dataset comprising 889 human-written, minimally different summary pairs. In this dataset, a single error drawn from an ontology of seven types is inserted into summaries from the CNN/DailyMail dataset to create unfaithful versions. Our findings indicate that BUMP complements existing benchmarks in several ways: 1) the summaries are more challenging to distinguish and less probable under state-of-the-art summarization models; 2) BUMP allows for the measurement of metric consistency, revealing that the most discriminative metrics are often the least consistent; and 3) BUMP facilitates the evaluation of metrics across individual error types, identifying specific weaknesses for future research.

Halo models describing the Universe's large-scale structure are rigorously reviewed, specifically addressing the conceptualization of halos as smooth cold dark matter distributions. This perspective largely stems from cosmological N-body simulations. Through a meticulous evaluation of the standard premises underlying both halo models and these simulations, alongside prior research on the self-similarity of the cosmic web, we determine that N-body simulations lack full reliability at the scales where halos manifest. Consequently, to establish a consistent definition of halos, one must either characterize them as entities of arbitrary size possessing a granular rather than smooth composition, or define their extent based on small-scale baryonic physics.

Millimeter wave (mmWave) radars are becoming viable substitutes for cameras in pervasive, contactless monitoring of industrial spaces, facilitating close human-machine interaction. However, commercial mmWave radars face limitations in range (typically 6–8 meters) and are prone to occlusion, which can be a major hindrance in large industrial areas filled with machinery and obstacles. Consequently, monitoring extensive indoor environments necessitates deploying multiple radars with known relative positions and orientations, requiring algorithms to integrate their data. This paper introduces ORACLE, an autonomous system that (i) automatically estimates the relative position and orientation of multiple radar units by analyzing the trajectories of people moving within their overlapping fields of view, and (ii) fuses tracking data from these radars to achieve unified tracking across all sensors. Experimental results show that ORACLE achieves median errors of 0.18 m and 2.86° for radar location and orientation, respectively. Furthermore, the fused tracking approach improves mean accuracy by 6% compared to single-sensor tracking, reducing the mean tracking error to as low as 0.14 m. Additionally, ORACLE demonstrates robustness against relative time synchronization mismatches ranging from -20% to +50%.

This study introduces the first accurate third-order homoclinic predictors for $n$-dimensional ordinary differential equations near a generic Bogdanov-Takens bifurcation. Achieving this requires higher-order time approximations for the nonlinear time transformation within the Lindstedt-Poincar\'e method, as well as a precise transformation linking solutions in the normal form to those on the parameter-dependent center manifold. The paper conducts a thorough comparison of various approaches, including different normal forms (smooth versus orbital), phase conditions, and perturbation techniques (regular and Lindstedt-Poincar\'e) for approximating homoclinic solutions near Bogdanov-Takens points. Validity is demonstrated through specific examples, and the newly developed predictors have been integrated into the open-source MATLAB/GNU Octave continuation software, MatCont.

We examine the achievements and constraints of statistical sampling across a series of models within lattice QCD, highlighting the necessity for novel techniques to address finite-density and real-time dynamics. We demonstrate that these lattice models can be recast using tensorial approaches, wherein path-integral field integrations are substituted with discrete sums. These formulations leverage diverse dualities and yield exact coarse-graining equations that, when paired with truncations, facilitate practical applications of the Wilson renormalization group. Being inherently discrete, these tensor-based structures offer tractable transfer matrices. By merging truncations with the time continuum limit, we construct Hamiltonians amenable to quantum simulation via cold atoms or current quantum computing platforms. We also survey recent advancements in tensor field theory regarding non-compact scalar models, supersymmetric systems, efficient four-dimensional algorithms, noise-resistant Gauss's law enforcement, symmetry-conserving truncations, and topological aspects, alongside connections to other tensor network methodologies.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a significant approach in deep representation learning, demonstrating robust generalization and competitive results even with limited labeled data. The SimCLR framework introduces the NT-Xent loss for contrastive representation learning, aiming to maximize agreement and similarity among sampled positive pairs. This short paper derives and proposes an upper bound for both the loss and average similarity. However, an analysis of the implications is not included; we strongly encourage researchers in the field to undertake this analysis.

Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE)—how treatments impact individual units—is crucial for policy and decision-making. The surge in data availability across fields like healthcare and e-commerce has spurred interest in data-driven algorithms for deriving HTE from both observational and experimental sources. However, many existing approaches rely on strong assumptions regarding observed features while neglecting the underlying causal model structure, often resulting in biased HTE estimates. Simultaneously, incorporating causal structure is challenging because the true mechanisms generating real-world data are typically unknown. To overcome this, we propose a feature selection method that evaluates each feature's utility for HTE estimation and learns pertinent causal structures directly from data. We offer robust empirical evidence demonstrating that our approach outperforms current data-driven HTE methods across various underlying causal structures. Experiments on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world datasets confirm that our algorithm significantly reduces HTE estimation error.

We examine a broad category of non-diffusive active scalar equations featuring constitutive laws defined by an operator $\mathbf{T}$ that is singular of order $r_0\in[0,2]$. For the range $r_0\in(0,1]$, we establish well-posedness within Gevrey spaces $G^s$ where $s\in[1,\frac{1}{r_0})$, whereas for $r_0\in[1,2]$ under additional constraints on $\mathbf{T}$, we demonstrate ill-posedness in $G^s$ for appropriate values of $s$. These findings regarding ill- and well-posedness are subsequently applied to various specific non-diffusive active scalar equations, such as the magnetogeostrophic equation, the incompressible porous media equation, and the singular incompressible porous media equation.

Speakers' referential choices frequently deviate from optimal communicative strategies, offering valuable insights into pragmatic language use. In particular, patterns of overmodification—where redundant modifiers are employed despite the speaker's goals—provide significant illumination on this topic. These patterns appear to be influenced by the speaker's environment through complex mechanisms. However, systematically manipulating such environmental factors during human language acquisition is unfeasible. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes utilizing neural networks as learning agents. By varying the training environments for these agents while maintaining a constant network architecture, we demonstrate that overmodification increases in likelihood when environmental features are either infrequent or salient. Furthermore, these results arise naturally within a probabilistic framework of pragmatic communication.

We present a method for deriving function definitions from input/output equations within a term-rewriting framework. By restricting the scope to structurally recursive definitions, we achieve a relatively efficient learning algorithm that frequently produces results aligned with intuitive expectations. We offer a Prolog-based prototype implementation of this approach and highlight several open issues warranting further research.

Although numerous safety issues remain unresolved, the widespread adoption of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) seems imminent. A major hurdle to accepting this technology is the lack of universally accepted Verification and Validation (VV) frameworks that can guarantee absolute safety. Uncertainties inherent in dynamic environments and the unpredictable behavior of traffic participants induce stochastic responses in advanced autonomous systems. Furthermore, integrating machine learning algorithms and probabilistic techniques significantly complicates real-world testing compared to traditional approaches. Current research primarily focuses on generating difficult concrete scenarios or test cases to assess system performance by analyzing the frequency distribution of parameters extracted from real-world data; these methods typically rely on Monte-Carlo simulations and importance sampling to produce critical cases. This paper introduces an efficient falsification method for evaluating the System Under Test. The proposed approach frames the task as a parameter optimization problem designed to identify challenging scenarios with the highest return. By employing a policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm, the method facilitates this learning process. Scenario riskiness is quantified using established metrics such as RSS safety distance, Euclidean distance, and collision instances. We demonstrate that this proposed method enables a more efficient search for challenging scenarios capable of causing system failure, thereby ensuring safety requirements are met.

Intrinsic alignment (IA) of galaxies poses a significant challenge for extracting cosmological constraints from weak lensing surveys. To examine this phenomenon, we assign intrinsic shapes and orientations to galaxies within the MICE simulation's light-cone output, covering approximately 5000 deg² up to a redshift of z=1.4. This assignment utilizes a 'semi-analytic' IA model that incorporates galaxy photometric properties alongside the spin and shape of their host halos. Building upon prior research, our model features more realistic galaxy shape distributions and a luminosity-dependent galaxy-halo alignment. The model parameters are calibrated using COSMOS and BOSS LOWZ observational data, with random orientations assigned to blue galaxies to reflect the null detection of IA in such populations. We compare two-point alignment statistics from the simulation against predictions from the analytical NLA and TATT models across various scales, redshifts, and luminosities, analyzing red and blue galaxies separately. Our results indicate that both models align well with measurements at scales larger than 8 h⁻¹ Mpc, though TATT performs better at smaller scales. The IA parameters derived from these fits broadly match diverse observational constraints regarding red galaxies. Finally, we construct a realistic source sample simulating DES Year 3 observations to estimate IA contamination in shear statistics. Our findings suggest this contamination lies within measurement uncertainties, potentially due to the random alignment of blue galaxies in the simulation.

This study examines a comprehensive dataset of monthly new-car sales in Spain spanning ten years (January 2007 to January 2017), covering over 6,500 distinct model configurations and 10 million units sold. Our findings indicate that for model configurations with a monthly market share exceeding 0.1%, sales follow Gibrat's law of proportional growth under logistic dynamics. Notably, the distribution of total sales aligns with the Maximum Entropy Principle for systems undergoing proportional growth in dynamical equilibrium. Furthermore, the associated dynamics are non-Markovian, characterized by a decaying memory or inertia of approximately five years, which implies that car sales are predictable within specific timeframes. We demonstrate that the primary features of these dynamics can be modeled using a framework based on the Langevin equation, a construct that encapsulates the fundamental principles any predictive model for car sales must adhere to.

A compact binary merger generating a neutrino-cooled accretion flow around a rotating black hole presents a viable mechanism for creating jets and magnetically driven outflows. Supported by the LIGO and Virgo detection of GW170817 and its subsequent electromagnetic signals, this framework elucidates the central engine behind short gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and kilonova emissions. Utilizing the open-source GRMHD HARM-COOL code, we simulated various 2D magnetized accretion disk-black hole systems with realistic equations of state within a fixed curved spacetime. By employing particle tracer techniques, we assessed the characteristics of the resulting outflows, initializing disk and black hole parameters to reflect diverse post-merger scenarios. Our simulations reveal a robust link between black hole spin and ejected mass, indicating that rapidly spinning black holes accompanied by massive disks produce the most powerful outflows. The generated winds exhibit moderate velocities ($v/c \sim 0.1-0.2$) and a wide spectrum of electron fractions. Leveraging these findings, we estimated the luminosity and light curves of potential radioactively powered transients from such systems, finding peak luminosities between $10^{40}$ and $10^{42}$ erg/s, consistent with prior research on disk wind outflows.

The Karlsruhe Tritium Neutrino experiment (KATRIN) seeks to determine the effective mass of electron anti-neutrinos with a sensitivity of $0.2\,\mathrm{eV}/\mathrm{c}^2$ by analyzing $\beta$-electrons produced in tritium decay. These electrons are steered by superconducting magnets through a vacuum beamline, moving from a windowless gaseous tritium source, through differential and cryogenic pumping stages, to a high-resolution spectrometer and a segmented silicon pin detector. Crucially, the pumping sections must reduce tritium gas flow by over 14 orders of magnitude to prevent contamination of the spectrometer. This paper details the measurement of the differential pumping section's reduction factor using high-purity tritium gas during the experiment's initial campaigns. The obtained results are evaluated against prior simulations and the strict requirements imposed by the KATRIN experiment.

Gaussian boson sampling (GBS) offers a pathway to demonstrating quantum supremacy using modest experimental resources, including squeezed light sources, linear optics, and photon detection. However, in practical settings, factors such as loss, partial photon distinguishability, and the use of threshold detectors rather than photon-counting devices can alter the sampling's complexity. This paper examines GBS with partial distinguishability by employing an approach grounded in virtual modes and indistinguishability efficiency. We construct a model utilizing these concepts to derive measurement probabilities for specific output patterns in both lossy and partially distinguishable GBS scenarios, covering both threshold and photon-counting detectors. For threshold detectors, the probability derived from the Torontonian emerges as a specific instance within our framework. By analyzing these probability expressions, we propose an efficient auxiliary classical simulation algorithm. Our model and algorithm establish a foundation for an approximation method that supports simulation strategies compatible with current state-of-the-art ideal GBS algorithms while reducing their computational complexity exponentially based on the level of indistinguishability. Finally, using this approximation method and the proposed simulation algorithms, we demonstrate how partial distinguishability can extend the boundaries of quantum supremacy in GBS.

Video paragraph captioning involves creating multi-sentence descriptions for untrimmed videos that pinpoint specific temporal events within a coherent narrative. Emulating human perception, which decomposes scenes into visual elements (e.g., humans, animals) and non-visual components (e.g., actions, relationships) through the interplay of vision and language, we introduce a novel Visual-Linguistic (VL) feature. This feature models scenes across three modalities: (i) the global visual environment, (ii) local visual main agents, and (iii) linguistic scene elements. Furthermore, we employ an autoregressive Transformer-in-Transformer (TinT) architecture to simultaneously capture semantic coherence among both intra- and inter-event contents. Additionally, a new VL contrastive loss function is proposed to ensure that learned embedding features align semantically with the generated captions. Extensive experiments and ablation studies on the ActivityNet Captions and YouCookII datasets demonstrate that our proposed Visual-Linguistic Transformer-in-Transform (VLTinT) surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both accuracy and diversity.

This research calculates the anticipated liquidity expenses incurred during the delta hedging of a European option. It models this cost through an integral formula incorporating European option prices and a specific function of the delta process. The study first establishes a unit liquidity cost, demonstrating that the total cost equals the product of this unit cost, the stock price, a supply curve parameter, and the square of the option quantity. Leveraging this formula allows for a significantly faster computation of expected pre-hedging liquidity costs compared to Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, numerical distributions of these costs for specific scenarios are presented.

Recent observational breakthroughs over the past ten years have facilitated high-resolution interferometric analyses of developing multiple systems, statistical examinations of multiplicity within star-forming regions, and novel understandings of disk evolution and planetary structures. This review synthesizes findings from both observational and theoretical research concerning stellar multiplicity. We outline population statistics covering the evolution of systems from the protostellar stage to the main sequence, while assessing the role of the local environment. Essentially, although the majority of stars originate in multiple systems and most main-sequence stars belong to such systems, the majority of star systems are actually single. We present current models regarding the genesis of stellar multiplicity, examine the scope of numerical simulations, and evaluate their alignment with observational data. Additionally, we discuss disk characteristics and the effects of multiplicity on planet formation and system architectures. Finally, we highlight outstanding questions and outline the technical necessities for advancing future observational and theoretical efforts.

The core challenge in sparse recovery and compressive sensing lies in achieving stable sparse recovery: identifying a distribution of $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ such that, for any $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, an algorithm can recover $x^*$ from $Ax$ with probability at least $2/3$ satisfying $\|x^* - x\|_p \le C \min_{k\text{-sparse } x'} \|x - x'\|_p$ for some constant $C > 1$ and norm $p$. While the measurement complexity for constant $C > 1$ is well-established, obtaining $C = 1 + \epsilon$ for small $\epsilon > 0$ is crucial for various applications yet remains poorly understood. We address the dependence on $\epsilon$ in the measurement count for $k$-sparse recovery, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the primary cases of $p=1$ and $p=2$. Specifically, we present new algorithms and lower bounds demonstrating that the required measurements scale as $(1/\epsilon^{p/2})k \cdot \text{polylog}(n)$. For $p=2$, our bound of $(1/\epsilon)k \log(n/k)$ is tight up to constant factors. Furthermore, we provide matching bounds for scenarios requiring a $k$-sparse output, achieving $(1/\epsilon^p)k \cdot \text{polylog}(n)$, thereby highlighting a fundamental distinction between the complexities of sparse versus non-sparse outputs.

Binomial coefficients, which have been applied across many disciplines for centuries and possess numerous definitions, are redefined in this paper as repeated sums of ones. To validate this new definition, we demonstrate a wide array of binomial coefficient identities. Leveraging this approach, we streamline specific summations, including repeated Harmonic and repeated Binomial-Harmonic sums. Furthermore, we develop formulas to simplify general repeated sums and a variant involving binomial coefficients. Finally, we examine the $m$-th difference of a sequence and illustrate how sequences with a constant $m$-th difference relate to binomial coefficients.

For every linear inequality in three variables, $\mathcal{L}$, we identify (when possible) the minimal integer $R(\mathcal{L}, \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})$ with the property that any mapping $\chi :[1,n] \to \{0,1,2\}$ where $n\geq R(\mathcal{L}, \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})$ guarantees a solution $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in [1,n]^3$ to $\mathcal{L}$ satisfying $\chi(x_1)+\chi(x_2)+\chi(x_3)\equiv 0$ (mod $3$). Furthermore, we demonstrate that $R(\mathcal{L}, \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})=R(\mathcal{L}, 2)$, where $R(\mathcal{L}, 2)$ represents the standard $2$-color Rado number—the smallest integer ensuring a monochromatic solution to $\mathcal{L}$ in any $2$-coloring of $[1,n]$. Consequently, we establish an Erd\H{o}s-Ginzburg-Ziv type generalization for all linear inequalities in three variables that possess solutions in positive integers. Additionally, we present several families of linear equations in three variables for which this generalization fails, specifically where $R(\mathcal{L}, \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})\neq R(\mathcal{L}, 2)$. The paper concludes with a set of open questions.

Denoising diffusion models (DDMs) have recently garnered significant interest due to their high sample quality and diversity. Despite their impressive performance, these models function as black boxes, necessitating further investigation to advance the field. Motivated by this gap, we examine the architecture of conventional U-shaped diffusion models, specifically analyzing their self-attention modules through rigorous experimentation to uncover their characteristics. Furthermore, building on research validating guidance schemes, we introduce Self-Attention Guidance (SAG), a plug-and-play technique that significantly enhances existing diffusion models. SAG operates by extracting intermediate attention maps at each iteration, masking and blurring tokens that exceed a specific attention threshold to generate a partially obscured input. The method then calculates the discrepancy between noise predictions from the blurred versus original inputs, utilizing this difference as a guidance signal. Our approach yields substantial improvements across various models, including ADM, IDDPM, and Stable Diffusion, with additional gains observed when combined with standard guidance methods. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate our design choices.

Although self-supervised learning advancements have substantially lowered the transcribed audio needed for training, most existing research concentrates on read speech. This study investigates limited supervision within conversational speech contexts. Assuming scarce in-domain data, we enhance the model using open-source read speech datasets. Given the XLS-R model's strong performance with limited adaptation data, it serves as a robust baseline. We employ untranscribed data for both self-supervised learning and semi-supervised training within an autoregressive encoder-decoder framework. Our results show that leveraging the XLS-R model for pseudotranscription enables a significantly smaller autoregressive model to surpass a fine-tuned XLS-R model when in-domain transcribed data is scarce, achieving up to an 8% absolute reduction in Word Error Rate (WER).

Offensive language is widespread on social media, where individuals often exploit the perceived anonymity of digital communication to engage in behaviors they might avoid in person. Automatically detecting such content online has become a critical and increasingly studied task. This process is typically framed as a supervised classification problem, where systems are trained on datasets annotated for various forms of abusive or offensive material. The aim of this study is to describe a classification system developed for SemEval-2019 Task 6: OffensEval. This system determines whether a tweet is offensive (Sub-task A) and, if so, categorizes the type of offense (Sub-tasks B & C). To achieve optimal results, we employed machine learning and deep learning models alongside data preprocessing and sampling techniques. The models examined include Naive Bayes, SVM, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and LSTM.

Cerebral microbleeds appear as small hypointense lesions on MRI scans utilizing gradient echo, T2*, or susceptibility-weighted (SWI) sequences. Traditionally, these are evaluated through visual inspection, but the last ten years have witnessed the development of semi-automatic aids, followed more recently by fully automated detection systems. This study investigates the application of nnU-Net as a fully automated solution for microbleed segmentation, utilizing data from the MICCAI 2021 "Where is VALDO?" challenge. The implemented method employs nnU-Net in a "3D full resolution U-Net" configuration, trained on the complete dataset (fold = `all`) without any post-processing steps. Self-assessment on the training data yielded an estimated Dice coefficient of 0.80, a false discovery rate of 0.16, and a false negative rate of 0.15. Evaluation on the VALDO challenge test set is currently pending. Visual analysis of the outputs suggests that many identified false positives likely represent genuine microbleeds that were overlooked during manual rating. The source code is hosted at https://github.com/hjkuijf/MixMicrobleedNet, and the corresponding Docker container, hjkuijf/mixmicrobleednet, can be accessed via https://hub.docker.com/r/hjkuijf/mixmicrobleednet.

This paper constructs a framework for oscillatory integrals featuring complex phases. For a function $f:{\mathbb C}^n \to {\mathbb C}$, we apply this phase to the fundamental character ${\rm e}(z) := e^{2\pi i x} e^{2\pi i y}$ of ${\mathbb C} \simeq {\mathbb R}^2$ (where $z = x+iy \in {\mathbb C}$ or $z = (x,y) \in {\mathbb R}^2$) to examine integrals of the form $$ I \ = \ \int_{{\mathbb C}^n} {\rm e}(f({\underline{z}})) \, \phi({\underline{z}}) \, d{\underline{z}} $$ with $\phi \in C^{\infty}_c({\mathbb C}^n)$. Regrettably, fundamental scale-invariant estimates for these integrals $I$ fail to hold in the same generality as they do in real-valued contexts. Consequently, our primary objective is to establish a viewpoint and provide arguments that identify scale-invariant bounds within a necessarily more restricted setting than typically assumed in real analysis.

Millisecond pulsars serve as ideal settings for investigating matter-geometry coupling and its physical consequences, particularly in light of recent data from the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER). This study applies Rastall field equations, which feature nonminimal coupling between matter and geometry, to the Krori-Barua interior spacetime, assuming an anisotropic fluid as the matter source. We demonstrate that all internal physical quantities can be defined using Rastall parameter $\epsilon$, compactness $C=2GM/Rc^2$, and other relevant parameters. By utilizing NICER and X-ray Multi-Mirror constraints on the mass and radius of PSR J0740+6620, we constrain the Rastall parameter to $\epsilon \leq 0.041$ within the positive range. The resulting solution describes a stable compact object where the squared sound speed satisfies the conjectured limit $c_s^2 \leq c^2/3$, a condition not always met in general relativity. Importantly, no specific equation of state is assumed, though the model aligns well with linear patterns involving bag constants. Generally, for $\epsilon > 0$, the theory predicts a slightly larger stellar radius compared to general relativity for the same mass. This effect is attributed to an additional force arising from matter-geometry coupling in the hydrodynamic equilibrium equation, which partially counteracts gravitational attraction. Consequently, the maximum compactness permitted by the strong energy condition is calculated as $C = 0.735$, approximately 2% higher than the general relativistic prediction. Furthermore, at a surface density corresponding to saturation nuclear density ($\rho_{\text{nuc}} = 2.7\times 10^{14}$ g/cm$^3$), we estimate a maximum mass of $M=4 M_\odot$ with a radius of 16 km.

Tayal and Zatsarinny [Astrophys. J. 850 (2017) 147] presented computed values for energy levels, radiative rates (A-values), lifetimes, and effective collision strengths ($\Upsilon$) for 202 levels of C-like O~III. Utilizing the multi-configuration Hartree-Fock (MCHF) code for energy levels and A-values, and the B-spline $R$-matrix (BSR) code for $\Upsilon$, they provided data covering a significantly broader range of levels and transitions than typically found in existing literature, with their energy levels and A-values appearing accurate. Nevertheless, the magnitude and behavior of $\Upsilon$ seem incorrect for several transitions. We substantiate this discrepancy through independent calculations performed with the flexible atomic code (FAC) and recommend that a new calculation be conducted for this critical ion.

Analyzing transport phenomena in intricate nanoscale environments, such as ionic conductivity in nanofluidic systems or heat flow in low-dimensional solids, necessitates investigating current fluctuations within nonequilibrium steady states and linking them to nonlinear or anomalous responses. We have established a systematic methodology for calculating the distributions of time-integrated currents in molecular models and connecting the cumulants of these distributions to nonlinear transport coefficients. This perspective builds upon the theory of dynamical large deviations, leverages significant prior formal advancements, and has been demonstrated through multiple applications. The framework offers a microscopic foundation for extending traditional hydrodynamics in scenarios where local equilibrium assumptions fail, a condition that is common at the nanoscale.

Using variational methods, we establish a limiting description for a specific class of integral functionals subject to linear differential constraints. These functionals model the energy of high-contrast composites, which are heterogeneous materials featuring a periodically perforated matrix at the microscale, where the voids are filled with a substance possessing significantly different physical properties. Our primary finding presents a $\Gamma$-convergence analysis as the periodicity vanishes, demonstrating that the variational limit comprises two distinct components: energy stored within the matrix and energy stored within the inclusions. Due to the inherent high-contrast nature of the structure, the study encounters a lack of coercivity under standard $L^p$ topologies, an issue we address using two-scale convergence techniques. Furthermore, to manage the differential constraints, we derive new results concerning the existence of potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators for linear, homogeneous, constant-coefficient differential operators of order $k$ with constant rank.

Zener-Klein (ZK) interband tunneling within graphene layers (GLs) featuring lateral n-i-n and p-i-n junctions generates nonlinear current-voltage (I-V) characteristics, facilitating the rectification and detection of terahertz (THz) signals. The transit time delays experienced by tunneling electrons and holes in depletion regions induce a phase shift between the THz voltage and current, producing negative dynamic conductance across specific frequencies and triggering transit-time (TT) instability. By integrating ZK tunneling with this TT-induced negative dynamic conductance, it becomes possible to achieve resonant THz detection alongside the amplification and generation of THz radiation. This study proposes and assesses THz devices constructed from periodic cascades of GL p-i-n structures that exhibit TT resonances, termed GPIN-TTDs. These architectures function effectively as THz amplifiers and, when integrated with Fabry-Perot cavities, THz antennas, or ring oscillator configurations, serve as THz radiation sources.

This research investigates the log-concavity of the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the Laplacian within convex domains. We demonstrate that for positively curved surfaces meeting specific criteria regarding curvature and its second derivative, the first eigenfunction exhibits strong log-concavity. While log-concavity for such eigenfunctions was previously established only for convex domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{S}^n$, our findings extend this result. Leveraging these estimates, we derive lower bounds for the fundamental gap in these regions. Additionally, we examine how these estimates evolve under Ricci flow and other metric deformations.

Learning arguments holds significant importance within explainable artificial intelligence, representing a class of symbolic machine learning methods renowned for their high interpretability. These techniques generate a set of arguments as an intermediate representation, where arguments function as small, exception-based rules that can be chained together to facilitate predictions or decisions. This study examines the acquisition of arguments, specifically focusing on the 'case model' introduced by Verheij [34]. In Verheij's framework, these models consist of cases or scenarios derived from legal contexts, which typically involve a relatively small number of instances. Consequently, we explore the applicability of Verheij's approach for learning arguments from diverse datasets characterized by a substantially larger volume of data points. Furthermore, we compare the efficacy of learning arguments from a case model against the HeRO algorithm [15] and decision tree learning.

This study investigates localized direct CP violation in the hadronic decays $B^\pm\rightarrow \rho^0 (\omega)\pi^\pm\rightarrow\pi^+ \pi^-\pi^\pm$, specifically accounting for a mechanism driven by charge symmetry violating mixing between $\rho^0$ and $\omega$. We compute the localized integrated direct CP violation when the low invariant mass of the $\pi^+\pi^-$ pair, $m(\pi^+\pi^-)_{low}$, approaches the $\rho^0(770)$ resonance. Across five investigated form factor models, the localized integrated direct CP violation ranges from -0.0170 to -0.0860 within the parameter space of our model for $0.750<m(\pi^+\pi^-)_{low}<0.800$\,GeV. This result, particularly its negative sign, aligns with experimental observations and remains independent of the specific form factor models used. Recent experimental data indicates that the signs of the localized integrated CP asymmetries are positive in the region $0.470<m(\pi^+\pi^-)_{low}<0.770$\,GeV and negative in the region $0.770<m(\pi^+\pi^-)_{low}<0.920$\,GeV. We demonstrate that $\rho$-$\omega$ mixing drives the localized integrated CP asymmetry toward negative values, thereby facilitating the observed sign change across these two regions, a behavior that is also model independent. Furthermore, we calculated the localized integrated direct CP violating asymmetries for the aforementioned regions and found agreement with experimental data in certain form factor models.

High-order and factorial cumulants of conserved charges are proposed as tools for investigating critical dynamics in heavy ion collisions. This study employs a parametric representation of the three-dimensional Ising model to analyze and compare the sign distribution across the phase diagram, as well as the temperature dependence of both cumulants and factorial cumulants. Near the critical point, these two types of quantities are indistinguishable; however, far from this point, factorial cumulants exhibit sign changes relative to their corresponding higher-order cumulants. The underlying reasons for these sign variations are examined, and it is suggested that such differences could serve as a metric for determining the distance to the critical point.

Distance Metric Learning (DML) aims to derive a discriminative embedding where similar instances are proximate and dissimilar ones are distant. This paper tackles Semi-Supervised DML (SSDML), which involves learning a metric from a small set of labeled examples alongside a vast amount of unlabeled data. SSDML is crucial because manually annotating every sample in large datasets is impractical. Notably, aside from a few classical methods focusing on linear Mahalanobis metrics, recent years have seen little research on SSDML, particularly within deep learning contexts.
