To address this gap, we revitalize SSDML through a deep learning lens by introducing a stochastic, graph-based framework. This approach propagates affinity relationships from labeled pairs to unlabeled ones, utilizing these propagated affinities to mine triplet-based constraints for metric learning. Furthermore, we enforce an orthogonality constraint on the metric parameters to enhance performance and prevent model collapse.

This paper examines the state estimation of continuous-time nonlinear systems where an attacker can maliciously manipulate a subset of sensor outputs by injecting potentially unbounded additive signals. Drawing parallels to our previous work on continuous-time linear systems \cite{chong2015observability}, we define the convergence of state estimates to true values despite sensor attacks as "$M$-attack observability," where $M$ denotes the number of compromised sensors. Unlike the linear scenario, we establish only a sufficient condition for a nonlinear system to remain observable under $M$ attacks. This condition necessitates the existence of asymptotic observers that exhibit input-to-state stability with respect to the attack signals. We demonstrate that an algorithm capable of selecting a consistent state estimate from a bank of observers ensures asymptotic state reconstruction. Furthermore, we offer a constructive approach for designing robust state observers for a specific class of nonlinear systems. The practical significance of this research is demonstrated through the monitoring of safe operations in a power distribution network.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have significantly propelled general salient object detection (SOD). Conversely, task-aware SOD remains largely unexplored due to the scarcity of specialized datasets. To address this, we introduce a novel driving task-oriented dataset featuring pixel-level annotations of salient objects. Our analysis reveals that cross-domain knowledge discrepancies and task-specific scene variations are the primary challenges in identifying salient objects within driving contexts. Guided by these insights, we propose a baseline model for driving task-aware SOD utilizing a knowledge transfer convolutional neural network. This architecture incorporates an attention-based knowledge transfer module to mitigate knowledge gaps and an efficient boundary-aware feature decoding module to refine feature extraction in complex, task-specific environments. The network integrates these components progressively. Experimental results demonstrate that our dataset presents a significant challenge, and our method surpasses 12 state-of-the-art approaches, thereby advancing the field of task-aware SOD.

This work applies PAC-Bayes theory to the field of learning-to-optimize, introducing, to our knowledge, the inaugural framework for acquiring optimization algorithms with provable generalization guarantees (PAC-bounds) and an explicit trade-off between high-probability convergence and rapid convergence speed. Even under ideal conditions where convergence is assured, our learned algorithms demonstrably outperform related methods grounded in deterministic worst-case analysis. Our findings depend on PAC-Bayes bounds tailored for general, unbounded loss functions within exponential families. By extending existing concepts, we recast the learning process as a one-dimensional minimization problem and investigate the feasibility of locating a global minimum, thereby enabling the practical implementation of the procedure. As a proof-of-concept, we train hyperparameters for standard optimization algorithms to empirically validate our theoretical contributions.

This paper introduces a novel generalized reference kernel designed to enhance the original base kernel through the utilization of reference vectors. Our formulation exhibits characteristics akin to approximate kernels, random mappings, and the Non-linear Projection Trick, contingent upon the chosen reference vectors. By concentrating on small-scale one-class classification, our analysis and experimental findings demonstrate that this new approach enables the regularization, rank adjustment, and integration of supplementary information directly into the kernel, ultimately boosting one-class classification accuracy.

This paper introduces the Blind Speech Separation and Dereverberation (BSSD) network, a unified neural architecture capable of simultaneously executing speaker separation, dereverberation, and speaker identification. Speaker separation is steered by predefined spatial cues, dereverberation is achieved through neural beamforming, and speaker identification is enhanced via embedding vectors and triplet mining. The study presents both a frequency-domain model utilizing complex-valued neural networks and a time-domain variant that performs beamforming within latent space. Additionally, we propose a block-online mode designed to handle extended audio recordings typical of meeting environments. Our system's performance is evaluated using Scale Independent Signal to Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), Word Error Rate (WER), and Equal Error Rate (EER).

The paper [L. Fei et al., JHEP 09 (2015) 076] introduced a cubic field theory involving a scalar field $\sigma$ and two anticommuting scalar fields, $\theta$ and $\bar\theta$. In $6-\epsilon$ dimensions, this model exhibits a weakly coupled fixed point characterized by imaginary cubic couplings and an enhanced symmetry to the supergroup OSp$(1|2)$. This theory serves as a "UV completion" for the non-linear sigma model with a hyperbolic target space H$^{0|2}$ (defined by a pair of intrinsic anticommuting coordinates) in the range $2<d<6$. Furthermore, it corresponds to the $q\rightarrow 0$ limit of the critical $q$-state Potts model, which represents the statistical mechanics of spanning forests on a graph. This letter extends those findings to a broader class of OSp$(1|2M)$ symmetric field theories, where the upper critical dimensions are given by $d_c(M) = 2 \frac{2M+1}{2M-1}$. These theories comprise one commuting scalar field and $2M$ anticommuting scalar fields, $\theta^i, \bar \theta^i$, interacting via $g\left (\sigma^2+ 2\theta^i \bar \theta^i \right )^{(2M+1)/2}$. At $d_c(M)-\epsilon$ dimensions, we identify a weakly coupled infrared fixed point at an imaginary coupling $g$. We propose that these critical theories act as UV completions for sigma models featuring fermionic hyperbolic target spaces H$^{0|2M}$. Of special relevance is the quintic field theory possessing OSp$(1|4)$ symmetry, which has an upper critical dimension of $10/3$. Leveraging this theory, we offer a prediction regarding the critical behavior of the OSp$(1|4)$ lattice system in three dimensions.

This study outlines a systematic framework leveraging channel state information (CSI) for authentication and secret key generation within physical layer security (PLS). By employing signal processing techniques and popular machine learning (ML) methods, the approach separates large-scale fading, utilized as a source of uniqueness, from small-scale fading, which serves as a source of shared entropy for secret key generation (SKG). The proposed ML techniques are fully unsupervised, thereby eliminating the need for extensive measurement campaigns. Furthermore, we introduce the use of the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (HSIC); simulation outcomes confirm that the extracted stochastic components of CSI vectors exhibit statistical independence.

Languages utilizing algebraic effects typically monitor computational effects through type-and-effect systems. In this work, we suggest treating an algebraic effect theory as a variable context, proposing instead that algebraic effects be tracked via *contextual modal types*. We introduce ECMTT, a new calculus that monitors algebraic effects using a contextualized version of the modal $\Box$ (necessity) operator, derived from Contextual Modal Type Theory (CMTT). Unlike traditional type-and-effect systems, which overlay effect annotations onto existing languages, ECMTT integrates these annotations intrinsically; they are governed by programming constructs that mirror the logical introduction and elimination rules for the $\Box$ modality. Consequently, the type-and-effect system of ECMTT functions essentially as a standard type system. Our design ensures local soundness and completeness, deriving operational semantics exclusively through $\beta$-reduction, consistent with other logic-based calculi. In this framework, effect handlers emerge naturally as evidence that one context (algebraic theory) can be reached from another, extending the concept of explicit substitutions from CMTT. To our knowledge, ECMTT represents the first system to connect algebraic effects with modal types. We also regard it as a progression toward establishing a Curry-Howard style correspondence, potentially enabling the transfer of numerous results from modal logic and modal type theory to the domain of algebraic effects.

This study introduces a new inverse kinematics (IK) solver designed for path planning in articulated robotic systems. While IK is a fundamental yet conventional challenge in robot manipulation, recent data-driven approaches have emerged to address it efficiently by leveraging GPUs to process numerous requests simultaneously. Despite these advantages, existing models suffer from low accuracy and demand extensive training times. To overcome these limitations, we present an IK solver that enhances both accuracy and memory efficiency by exploiting the continuous hidden dynamics inherent in Neural ODEs. The proposed method's performance is evaluated across multiple robotic platforms.

This study details the field research, design, and comparative deployment of a multimodal medical imaging user interface tailored for breast screening. The work presents three primary contributions: 1) the development of an advanced visual interface for multimodal breast cancer diagnosis named BreastScreening; 2) findings from a field-based comparison of single versus multimodal screening involving 31 clinicians and 566 images; and 3) the visualization of two principal breast lesion types across three modalities: MammoGraphy (MG) in Craniocaudal (CC) and Mediolateral oblique (MLO) views, UltraSound (US), and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). The paper concludes with radiologist recommendations to guide the future design of medical imaging interfaces.

Stellar dust grains are primarily made of anorganic mineral material that forms within the circumstellar envelopes of oxygen-rich AGB stars, yet the initial nucleation phase of this synthesis remains poorly understood, particularly regarding the chemical identity of the molecular clusters involved in nucleation. This study utilized density functional theory to calculate the vertical and adiabatic ionization energies of four distinct metal-oxide clusters—magnesia (MgO)$_n$, silicon monoxide (SiO)$_n$, alumina (Al$_2$O$_3$)$_n$, and titania (TiO$_2$)$_n$—across stoichiometric sizes ranging from $n$=1 to $n$=8. Results indicated that magnesias, aluminas, and titanias exhibited minimal variation in ionization energy relative to cluster size, with ranges of 7.1–8.2 eV, 8.9–10.0 eV, and 9.3–10.5 eV, respectively. Conversely, the ionization energies of (SiO)$_n$ clusters declined as size increased, dropping from 11.5 eV at $n$=1 to 6.6 eV at $n$=8. Consequently, these findings establish constraints on the stability limits required for neutral metal-oxide clusters to maintain ionization under radiation or high-temperature conditions, thereby enabling nucleation through neutral-neutral reactions.

We present the Activity Graph Transformer, an end-to-end learnable framework designed for temporal action localization that accepts video input and directly outputs a set of detected action instances. Accurately detecting and localizing actions within untrimmed videos demands reasoning across multiple instances. While prevailing approaches in the literature process videos sequentially to either propose regions or generate frame-level detections, this linear method struggles when actions exhibit non-sequential dependencies or non-linear temporal ordering, such as overlapping events or re-occurrences throughout the clip. To address this, our work models the non-linear temporal structure by treating videos as non-sequential entities represented as graphs. We assess the model on rigorous benchmarks including THUMOS14, Charades, and EPIC-Kitchens-100. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents a recently completed indoor-to-outdoor measurement campaign designed to study the propagation characteristics of an $8 \times 8$ virtual MIMO-based wireless sensor network (WSN). The study was conducted in a windowless instrumentation room populated with various noisy electrical and measuring equipment. Channel impulse responses were recorded using a 20 MHz wide signal transmitted at 2.53 GHz, with data collected across 15 distinct spatial configurations of the transmit antennas. Following the analysis of this data, the system capacity and achievable transmission rates were computed for each scenario. These metrics were then used to identify the optimal sensor placement configuration for maximizing overall network throughput. The results indicate that distributing sensors across all four walls of the room yields the highest possible information rate.

We examine bounded composition operators generated by linear fractional self-maps of the right half-plane $\mathbb{C}_+$ acting on the Hardy space $H^2(\mathbb{C}_+)$. Our work fully characterizes the conditions under which these operators are cohyponormal and identifies conjugations for the linear fractional composition operators that exhibit complex symmetry.

This observational study examines the dark matter fraction in 225 rotationally supported, star-forming galaxies at a redshift of approximately $z \approx 0.9$. The sample spans stellar masses between $9.0 \leq \log(M_*/\mathrm{M_\odot}) \leq 11.0$ and star formation rates (SFR) ranging from $0.49 \leq \log(\mathrm{SFR}/[\mathrm{M_\odot}\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}]) \leq 1.77$. As a subset of the KMOS Redshift One Spectroscopic Survey (KROSS), previously analyzed by \citet{GS20}, these galaxies had their stellar masses estimated via mass-to-light ratios derived from spectral energy distribution fitting, while their SFRs were calculated using H$_\alpha$ luminosities. Total gas masses ($M_{gas}$) were derived by applying scaling relations for atomic and molecular gas \citep{Tacconi2018, Lagos2011}, respectively. Dynamical masses ($M_{dyn}$) were computed directly from rotation curves at various scale lengths (effective radius $R_e$, $\sim 2 R_e$, and $\sim 3 R_e$), enabling the calculation of dark matter fractions ($f_{DM} = 1 - M_{bar}/M_{dyn}$) at these radii. Our findings indicate that at $z \sim 1$, only a minor portion ($\sim 5\%$) of the sample exhibits a low dark matter fraction ($< 20\%$) within $\sim 2\text{--}3 R_e$. Conversely, the majority ($> 72\%$) of star-forming galaxies possess dark matter-dominated outer disks ($\sim 5\text{--}10$ kpc), consistent with local populations. Furthermore, we observe significant scatter in dark matter fractions at fixed stellar mass or circular velocity compared to local star-forming galaxies, implying that galaxies at $z \sim 1$ a) occupy a broad spectrum of stellar disk formation stages and b) display diverse dark matter halo properties interacting with baryonic matter.

Leveraging the success of neural architecture search (NAS) in designing feature pyramid networks (FPNs) for visual object detection, we introduce OPANAS, a novel One-Shot Path Aggregation Network Architecture Search algorithm that enhances both search efficiency and detection performance. Our approach begins by defining a search space comprising six heterogeneous information paths: top-down, bottom-up, fusing-splitting, scale-equalizing, skip-connect, and none. We then construct a new FPN search space where candidates are modeled as densely connected directed acyclic graphs, with nodes representing feature pyramids and edges corresponding to the six defined paths. To identify the optimal architecture efficiently, we employ a one-shot search strategy involving the training of a super-net followed by an evolutionary algorithm to select the best candidate. Experimental findings confirm OPANAS's superiority: it outperforms state-of-the-art methods like NAS-FPN and Auto-FPN with a drastically reduced search cost (e.g., 4 GPU days on MS-COCO). Furthermore, the architectures discovered by OPANAS boost the performance of mainstream detectors such as RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, and Cascade R-CNN by 2.3–3.2% mAP over their standard FPN versions. Additionally, OPANAS achieves a new state-of-the-art balance between accuracy and speed (52.2% mAP at 7.6 FPS) with lower training costs than comparable methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/OPANAS.

Test-time adaptation represents a specific scenario within unsupervised domain adaptation, requiring a model trained on a source domain to adjust to a target domain without access to the source data. We introduce a novel approach that combines self-supervised contrastive learning to enhance target feature learning with an online pseudo-labeling framework that includes a refinement process to substantially reduce label noise. This contrastive learning task operates in conjunction with pseudo-labeling, contrasting positive and negative pairs constructed similarly to MoCo, yet utilizing a source-initialized encoder and excluding same-class negative pairs identified by the pseudo labels. Additionally, we generate pseudo labels dynamically and refine them through soft voting among their nearest neighbors in the target feature space, a process facilitated by a memory queue. Our method, AdaContrast, achieves state-of-the-art results on key benchmarks and offers several advantageous characteristics over existing methods, such as memory efficiency, reduced sensitivity to hyper-parameters, and improved model calibration. Project page: sites.google.com/view/adacontrast.

Probing the nucleon's spin structure in the domain where the strong interaction is dominant presents a significant challenge for both theoretical models and experimental investigations. Below the nucleon mass scale of approximately 1 GeV, the intense interplay among quarks and gluons within the nucleon creates high correlations. This coherent behavior gives rise to effective degrees of freedom, necessitating the use of non-perturbative methods like chiral effective field theory. In this study, we report measurements of the neutron's generalized spin-polarizabilities, which characterize its spin precession under electromagnetic fields at very low momentum transfer squared, extending down to 0.035 GeV$^2$. Within this regime, chiral effective field theory calculations are anticipated to be valid. However, our results reveal a substantial deviation from these predictions, challenging the current understanding of the neutron's spin characteristics.

We introduce a novel dark matter freeze-out mechanism in which particle annihilation is catalyzed. We examine in detail the scenario where dark matter depletion occurs through $2\chi \to 2A'$ and $3A' \to 2\chi$ reactions, with $\chi$ representing dark matter and $A'$ the catalyst. In this framework, the dark matter number density decreases polynomially instead of exponentially (as seen in Boltzmann suppression typical of classic WIMPs and SIMPs). This paradigm is applicable to a secluded weakly interacting dark sector containing dark matter with masses ranging from MeV to TeV. Furthermore, the catalyzed annihilation model remains consistent with CMB and BBN constraints while predicting enhanced signals for indirect detection.

Our objective is source-free domain adaptation, involving the deployment of a model initially trained on source data to target domains. The primary challenges arise from the distribution shift between these domains, compounded by the lack of access to source data and labeled target data for optimization. Instead of adapting through parameter fine-tuning, we propose perturbing the source model to facilitate target domain adaptation. We introduce these perturbations into the model parameters using variational Bayesian inference within a probabilistic framework. This approach allows for effective adaptation to the target domain while largely maintaining the model's discriminative capabilities. Significantly, we establish a theoretical link to Bayesian neural networks, validating the generalizability of the perturbed model to target domains. To enhance optimization efficiency, we implement a parameter sharing strategy that drastically reduces the number of learnable parameters compared to a fully Bayesian neural network. Our method offers a novel probabilistic approach to domain adaptation, enabling efficient target domain adaptation while maximally retaining knowledge from the source model. Experiments conducted across various source-free benchmarks under three distinct evaluation settings confirm the efficacy of the proposed variational model perturbation for source-free domain adaptation.

Utilizing the JETSCAPE framework, we examine jet-medium interactions across different scales within high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Through multiple jet and high-$p_{\mathrm{T}}$ particle observables, we analyze the multi-stage modeling physics and high-virtuality coherence effects by comparing our results with experimental data. Additionally, we explore the jet-medium interactions occurring during the hadronization process.

We introduce a new federated learning framework designed to capture data heterogeneity across diverse clients in multi-centric research. This approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian latent variable model, where client-specific parameters are treated as samples drawn from a global distribution estimated at the master level to address data bias and variability. We demonstrate that the framework can be efficiently optimized using expectation maximization (EM) over the latent master distribution and client parameters. Additionally, we incorporate formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees that are compatible with our EM optimization process. Our method was evaluated on multi-modal medical imaging data and clinical scores from distributed datasets of Alzheimer's disease patients. Results show that the approach remains robust under both independent and identically distributed (iid) and non-iid data conditions, even when local parameter perturbations are applied for DP. Furthermore, our method enables interpretable quantification of data, view, and center variability while ensuring high-quality data reconstruction, outperforming state-of-the-art autoencoding models and federated learning schemes. The source code is accessible at https://gitlab.inria.fr/epione/federated-multi-views-ppca.

We construct complete Kähler-Einstein metrics with negative scalar curvature in the vicinity of an isolated log canonical (non-log terminal) singularity, provided the ambient space has complex dimension 2 or the singularity is smoothable. In the two-dimensional complex case, we demonstrate that any such complete metric near an isolated log canonical (non-log terminal) singularity is smoothly asymptotically close to a model metric developed by Kobayashi and Nakamura, which originates from hyperbolic geometry.

This numerical study examines the yielding transition of a two-dimensional model glass under athermal quasi-static cyclic shear, focusing on how the degree of annealing—dictated by the preparation protocol—affects yielding behavior. We identify two distinct annealing regimes separated by a threshold energy. In poorly annealed glasses, the system gradually evolves toward this threshold energy as strain amplitude increases toward the yield point. Conversely, well-annealed glasses with initial energies below the threshold display stable behavior, showing negligible energy changes with increasing strain until yielding occurs. Both energy and stress discontinuities at yielding increase with the level of annealing, aligning with recent three-dimensional findings. We observe significant structural changes correlated with strain amplitude that mirror fluctuations in energy and stress. Furthermore, we analyze groups of particles participating in plastic rearrangements, investigating distributions of avalanche sizes, clusters of connected rearranging particles, and related metrics using finite-size scaling. We confirm previously established relations between exponents characterizing these distributions and validate a newly proposed relationship between exponents describing avalanche and cluster size distributions.

Cochran's $Q$ statistic is commonly employed to assess heterogeneity in meta-analysis, with its expected value also utilized for estimating the between-study variance, $\tau^2$. However, because $Q$ (specifically $Q_{IV}$) relies on estimated inverse-variance weights, deriving its distribution is complex. As an alternative, this study investigates a new statistic, $Q_F$, which employs constant weights derived solely from the effective sample sizes of the studies. Focusing on the standardized mean difference as the effect measure, simulations are conducted to approximate the distributions of both $Q_{IV}$ and $Q_F$ for use in heterogeneity testing and for developing new point and interval estimators of $\tau^2$. These developments include novel DerSimonian-Kacker (2007)-type moment estimators based on the first moment of $Q_F$, as well as new median-unbiased estimators for $\tau^2$.

Although data is fundamental to machine learning, current research and tools predominantly address systems built upon existing data rather than the interpretation and manipulation of data itself. This paper introduces DataLab, a unified, data-centric platform that enables interactive analysis of data characteristics alongside a standardized interface for various data processing operations. Addressing the rapid growth of datasets, \toolname also offers dataset recommendation and global vision analysis capabilities to enhance researchers' understanding of the data ecosystem. To date, DataLab encompasses 1,715 datasets and 3,583 transformed versions (such as hyponym replacements), with 728 datasets supporting diverse analyses—including gender bias detection—leveraging 140 million samples annotated by 318 feature functions. Actively developed and supported for the future, DataLab is available via a web platform, web API, Python SDK, PyPI package, and online documentation, aiming to satisfy the varied needs of researchers.

Knowledge Graph (KG) completion is a vital task that significantly aids knowledge discovery across various domains, such as biomedical research. Recently, learning KG embeddings to address this task has garnered substantial interest. Although KG embedding methods have proven successful, they largely rely on negative sampling, which leads to higher computational complexity and biased predictions stemming from the closed world assumption. To address these drawbacks, we introduce **KG-NSF**, a negative sampling-free framework for learning KG embeddings that utilizes the cross-correlation matrices of embedding vectors. Results demonstrate that this approach achieves link prediction performance comparable to negative sampling-based methods while converging significantly faster.

Advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) have enabled algorithms to excel in highly complex yet largely static environments, whereas biological learning prioritizes efficient adaptation to a perpetually changing world. This work extends a recently proposed neuronal learning rule, which posits that neurons optimize their energy balance by forecasting their own future activity. This assumption yields a learning mechanism where presynaptic inputs modulate prediction errors. We contend that an analogous RL framework would employ action probabilities to adjust reward prediction errors. This modulation enhances an agent's sensitivity to adverse experiences and fosters greater caution in preference formation. When integrated into both tabular and deep Q-network RL architectures, the proposed rule surpasses conventional methods in simple, highly dynamic tasks. We propose that this new rule embodies a fundamental principle of biological intelligence, offering a crucial mechanism for enabling algorithms to adapt to change in a manner reminiscent of human cognition.

Melody harmonization has historically been closely linked to Johann Sebastian Bach's chorales. Earlier research seldom prioritized generating chorales conditioned on chord progressions, nor did it focus on assistive compositional tools. In this study, we introduce a novel music representation that encodes chord symbols to enable chord conditioning, and present DeepChoir, a system capable of generating four-part chorales for a given melody based on a specific chord progression. Featuring controllable harmonicity, the system allows users to regulate the degree of harmonicity in the output. Experimental outcomes demonstrate both the efficacy of the proposed music representation and the controllability of DeepChoir.

This paper introduces a model designed to examine how a single student appropriates knowledge within a non-collaborative online learning environment. We develop a stochastic framework grounded in the teacher's instructional quality and the student's affinity for grasping the material, operating under the premise that prior sessions influence comprehension of subsequent ones. Consequently, this dynamic renders the process non-Markovian, a scenario characteristic of seminars and multi-session courses. We derive recursive formulas for the distribution of the number of sessions a student understands, and we further investigate the convergence of this distribution, including the rate of convergence, through numerical simulations.

We establish concentration inequalities for both the hidden layer outputs and the final output of a stochastic deep neural network (SDNN). These findings enable the definition of an expected classifier (EC) and provide a probabilistic upper bound on the EC's classification error. Furthermore, we determine the optimal number of layers for the SDNN using an optimal stopping procedure. Finally, we apply this theoretical analysis to a stochastic feedforward neural network featuring ReLU activation functions.

High-performance machine learning models increasingly rely on access to vast amounts of high-quality training data. To facilitate this, central bodies like governments have proposed that various data providers pool their resources to train a unified predictive model, which typically yields superior performance. However, since these providers are often motivated by profit, they will only engage in data sharing if the process is perceived as both equitable and financially beneficial. Given the scarcity of existing research, it remains uncertain whether fair and stable outcomes are achievable in such scenarios. Consequently, this study investigates the potential results of these situations and examines whether providers would initially agree to collaborate. By applying concepts from cooperative game theory, we introduce a novel class of cooperative games for data sharing among agents, featuring redefined metrics for stability and fairness. Leveraging these new definitions, we theoretically analyze optimal and suboptimal outcomes and their sensitivity to perturbations. Finally, through experimental validation, we provide intuitive insights into these theoretical findings and explore various methods for reasonably valuing data.

Estimating 3D poses from a single image is difficult primarily because of depth ambiguity. Existing methods generally fall into two categories: those that lift 2D joints—detected externally—into 3D space, thereby ignoring rich contextual image cues essential for accurate estimation; and those that predict joints directly from monocular images using a 2.5D representation ($P^{2.5D} = (u,v,z^{r})$), where spatial coordinates are 2D but depth is root-relative. The latter approach relies on ground-truth root depth to convert outputs to full 3D space, restricting its practical utility. This paper introduces a novel end-to-end framework that leverages contextual information and generates direct 3D outputs through a cascaded dimension-lifting strategy. The task is decomposed into three sequentially supervised sub-tasks: estimating kinematic skeletons and 2D joints, predicting root-relative depth, and lifting the pose to 3D space, all guided by contextual features. Extensive experiments on the Human3.6M and MuPoTS-3D datasets demonstrate that this framework achieves state-of-the-art performance.

The total graph is constructed by connecting a graph to its line graph through their incidences. We propose an analogous construction for signed graphs. Based on two parallel definitions of the line signed graph, we define the total signed graph and demonstrate its stability under switching. We examine balance, the frustration index, the frustration number, and the largest eigenvalue. In the regular case, we calculate the spectrum of the adjacency matrix for the total graph, as well as the spectra of specific compositions, and identify those possessing exactly two main eigenvalues.

The function $r_N$ enumerates the count of irreducible representations for simple complex Lie groups with dimension $N$. Although an explicit formula for this function remains unknown, prior research has established bounds for the cumulative sum $R_N=\sum_{i=1}^Nr_i$. This paper refines those existing bounds by demonstrating that $R_N=O(N)$.

This study examines how a standing linear sausage fast magnetoacoustic wave modulates the intensity of microwave emissions from a flaring loop, utilizing a model of a straight plasma slab with a perpendicular Epstein density profile and an embedded magnetic field. The emissions are of the gyrosynchrotron (GS) type, generated by mildly relativistic electrons confined to a specific layer within the oscillating slab, meaning the emitting and oscillating volumes are distinct. The analysis reveals that the microwave response to the linear sausage wave is highly non-linear. The degree of this non-linearity, expressed as the ratio of the second harmonic's Fourier power to that of the principal harmonic, varies based on the combination of the GS source width and the viewing angle, differing between the optically thick and thin regions of the microwave spectrum. Consequently, this phenomenon may serve as a diagnostic tool for determining the transverse scales of the regions populated by accelerated electrons.

We re-examine laser intensity noise within the framework of Stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS), a technique that has recently emerged as a vital method for generating label-free images of chemical bonds in biological and medical specimens. Unlike most microscopy approaches that rely on detecting weak photon fluxes from light-matter interactions, SRS operates as a pump-probe scheme in a high-flux regime, manifesting as a minute modulation ($10^{-4}-10^{-6}$) within a powerful laser field. Consequently, laser noise constitutes a critical challenge in SRS detection. This practical tutorial equips experimentalists with the necessary tools to evaluate noise levels and determine the ultimate detection limits of a standard lock-in-based SRS system. We begin by defining the parameters pertinent to intensity noise, demonstrating them via a conventional photodiode detection model. Next, we introduce lock-in-based SRS and adapt the model to this specific context. Key metrics, including Power Spectral Density (PSD), Relative Intensity Noise (RIN), Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and system sensitivity, are derived and analyzed. Furthermore, two complementary methods for measuring RIN and assessing SRS system performance are presented, illustrated using two commercial laser platforms. The discussion concludes with an analysis of noise consequences in SRS and suggestions for future advancements. The material is designed to be accessible to undergraduates, graduates, and newcomers to SRS and, more broadly, to pump-probe methodologies.

Although a substitution's matrix does not fully define its associated dynamics—even in basic scenarios—because numerous words share the same abelianization, this paper investigates the intersection of canonical broken lines linked to two distinct Pisot irreducible substitutions, $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, that possess identical incidence matrices. We demonstrate that if 0 lies within the interior of the Rauzy fractal corresponding to $\sigma_1$, these shared points can be produced by applying a substitution to an alphabet composed of "balanced blocks."

The minimal integral Mahler measure of a number field $K$, denoted $M(\mathcal{O}_K)$, represents the smallest Mahler measure among non-torsion primitive elements within $\mathcal{O}_K$. Established upper and lower bounds for this measure are functions of the discriminant. This work demonstrates that for cubic fields, the lower bounds accurately reflect the growth rate with respect to the discriminant. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm capable of calculating $M(\mathcal{O}_K)$ for all cubic fields where the absolute value of the discriminant does not exceed $N$.

This study addresses the challenge of developing prediction models for spatiotemporal physical processes governed by unknown partial differential equations (PDEs). We introduce a deep learning framework capable of inferring underlying dynamics and forecasting their evolution using data collected from sparsely distributed locations. While deep learning has recently demonstrated significant potential in modeling physical dynamics, existing approaches for unknown governing PDEs typically rely on dense grid data. Our approach, by contrast, is designed specifically to learn from sparsely observed data for unknown PDE-driven systems. The method is both spatially dimension-independent and geometrically adaptable. We validate its performance by forecasting the two-dimensional wave equation and the Burgers-Fisher equation across various geometries and boundary conditions, as well as the ten-dimensional heat equation.

A core challenge in mathematics and network analysis involves identifying the conditions necessary to partition a graph into smaller components. The primary instrument for this task is the Fiedler vector, often linked to the discrete Cheeger inequality. These concepts establish a connection between the graph spectrum—specifically the eigenvalues of the normalized adjacency matrix—and the capacity to divide a graph into two parts by removing a minimal number of edges. This body of work has given rise to the distinct field of spectral graph theory. However, these established results fail to account for the complex community structures prevalent in real-world networks, which typically feature many densely clustered blocks containing a substantial proportion of edges. Drawing inspiration from the characteristics of such networks, we have identified a novel spectral condition that associates eigenvalue powers with a decomposition of a network into densely clustered blocks, which we term the *spectral triadic decomposition*. Our findings precisely predict the presence of community structures frequently observed in actual network data. Furthermore, our proof yields an efficient algorithm for generating this spectral triadic decomposition. Empirical analysis across various social, coauthorship, and citation networks demonstrates that these decompositions exhibit a strong correlation with semantically meaningful communities.

This study examines the extended two-temperature model (eTTM), a framework designed to capture electronic non-equilibrium states and their impact on energy dissipation in metals following ultrashort laser excitation. We derive and analyze enhancements to this model relative to previously published versions [E. Carpena, Phys. Rev. B 2006, 74, 024301; G. Tsibidis, Appl. Phys. A 2018, 124, 311]. Comparing eTTM outcomes with those of the standard two-temperature model (TTM) reveals that the eTTM predicts a delayed rise in electronic temperature. Furthermore, our findings align well with kinetic descriptions incorporating a Boltzmann collision term regarding the non-equilibrium energy distribution post-photon absorption. The eTTM serves as an efficient instrument for rapidly computing non-equilibrium electron characteristics. Specifically, we analyze the dynamics of high-energy electrons detectable via photo-electron spectroscopy, illustrating the superior performance of the eTTM compared to the conventional two-temperature model.

This study demonstrates that gauge theoretic structures emerge naturally within a non-commutative calculus. Key elements of gauge theory, Hamiltonian mechanics, and quantum mechanics arise organically from the mathematical framework of non-commutative calculus and differential geometry. Specifically, we derive a covariant version of the Levi-Civita connection inherent to this commutator-based approach. This connection adheres to the formula $$\Gamma_{kij} + \Gamma_{ikj} = \nabla_{j}g_{ik} = \partial_{j} g_{ik} + [g_{ik}, A_j]$$, making it a precise generalization of the connection originally formulated by Hermann Weyl in his foundational gauge theory. In the non-commutative realm $\cal N$, the metric exhibits a broader variability compared to classical metrics, extending even to angular holonomy. Since Weyl proposed working with such expanded metric variability, the current formalism offers a novel context for his original concept.

Automated essay scoring stands as a pivotal challenge within Natural Language Processing. Despite years of investigation, the issue remains only partially resolved, offering both practical value for economics and education and significant avenues for research. While transfer learning has proven advantageous in NLP and data augmentation techniques have contributed to building state-of-the-art models for this task, previous efforts have largely relied on architectures such as RNNs and LSTMs. This study investigates transformer-based models, including BERT and RoBERTa. We empirically validate the efficacy of combining transformer models with data augmentation for automated essay grading across diverse topics using a unified model.

We introduce a statistical investigation into tidal structures surrounding massive early-type galaxies (ETGs). By employing automated methods on imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP), we quantified the tidal flux fraction ($f_{\rm tidal}$) for 2649 ETGs possessing stellar masses $M_* > 10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and redshifts $0.05 < z < 0.15$. The $i$-band sensitivity of the HSC-SSP Wide-layer extends to approximately 28.5 mag arcsec$^{-2}$. Below this surface brightness threshold, roughly 28% of these galaxies exhibit significant tidal features where $f_{\rm tidal} > 1\%$. The frequency of ETGs with prominent tidal features declines exponentially with increasing $f_{\rm tidal}$, characterized by a logarithmic slope of about 100. Within the observed stellar mass range, $f_{\rm tidal}$ doubles as the mass increases from $M_* \approx 10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $M_* \approx 10^{12}M_{\odot}$. Furthermore, we conducted pair-count analysis to derive the merger rates for these massive ETGs. By integrating these merger rates with the measured $f_{\rm tidal}$ values, we estimated that the typical lifespan of tidal features is approximately 3 Gyr, a finding that aligns with prior research.

We apply rank-one constraints to the marginalizations of a tensor defined over a simplicial complex. Building on the research of Kirkup and Sullivant, we demonstrate that these marginal independence models can be transformed into toric varieties through a linear coordinate change. Our investigation focuses on their associated toric ideals, specifically highlighting random graph models and the independent set polytopes of matroids. Furthermore, we establish the numerical algebra required for parameter estimation via both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood methods, and we provide an extensive database of small-scale models.

A well-scaled critical Galton-Watson process approaches a continuous-state critical branching process, $\xi(\cdot)$, as the initial population size grows without bound. This study expands upon that classical finding by accommodating overlapping generations and examining a broad spectrum of population metrics. The primary contribution demonstrates the convergence of finite-dimensional distributions for a scaled vector comprising multiple population counts. These limiting distributions are effectively characterized by integrals of the form $(\int_0^y\xi(y-u)du^\gamma, y\ge0)$, where $\gamma\ge0$ is a specific parameter.

The quantum steering ellipsoid associated with a two-qubit state represents the collection of Bloch vectors to which Bob can collapse Alice's qubit by performing any possible measurement on his own qubit. We offer a straightforward method to construct this ellipsoid for any state, compute its volume, and clarify how to ensure this geometric depiction remains faithful. This approach yields several novel findings and reveals new phenomena, including the presence of "incomplete steering" even within separable states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that entanglement can be characterized by three specific geometric attributes of the ellipsoid and prove that a state is separable if and only if it satisfies a "nested tetrahedron" condition.

As graph data increasingly permeates diverse applications, there is a growing necessity to continuously analyze structural trends within dynamic graphs. Shortest cycles represent a foundational pattern in graph analytics. This paper examines the challenge of counting shortest cycles for a specific vertex in dynamic graphs, highlighting their utility in scenarios like fraud detection. To handle these queries efficiently, we introduce a 2-hop labeling algorithm named Counting Shortest Cycle (CSC), alongside methods for dynamically updating the CSC index. Extensive experiments validate the method's efficiency and effectiveness; specifically, CSC facilitates query evaluation in under a few hundred microseconds for graphs containing millions of edges, representing a two-order-of-magnitude improvement over baseline solutions. Furthermore, the update algorithm effectively manages both edge insertions and deletions.

We present a successful validation of a novel approach for generating intense ion beams, which utilizes an extraction process driven by an inhomogeneous electric field. This method's primary advantage lies in the unique geometry of its extraction electrodes, designed to enhance the rate of ion acceleration. Because it is compatible with any ion source configuration, it holds potential for optimizing the performance of various plasma devices. The concept was experimentally verified using the high-current electron-cyclotron resonance ion source SMIS 37, which demonstrated highly efficient extraction and proton beam formation, achieving a record-breaking current density of up to 1.1 A cm-2.

Although momentum acceleration is a common component in numerous optimization algorithms, the theoretical impact of momentum on generalization remains unexplained. This paper addresses this gap by investigating the implicit regularization inherent in momentum-based methods. We demonstrate that for linear classification tasks involving separable data and exponentially tailed losses, Gradient Descent with Momentum (GDM) converges to the L2 max-margin solution, identical to that achieved by vanilla gradient descent. Consequently, momentum-accelerated descent continues to yield low-complexity models, thereby ensuring strong generalization capabilities. Furthermore, we examine stochastic and adaptive variations of GDM, specifically Stochastic GDM (SGDM) and deterministic Adam, proving that they too converge to the L2 max-margin solution. Methodologically, to address the challenge of error accumulation associated with momentum, we develop novel potential functions to measure the discrepancy between model parameters and the max-margin solution. Numerical experiments corroborate these theoretical findings.

Drug discovery involves a multi-stage workflow dominated by two expensive phases: pre-clinical research and clinical trials. Notably, lead optimization alone accounts for over half of the pre-clinical budget. We introduce an automated, *in silico* approach that integrates machine learning with molecular modeling to streamline this process. The workflow begins by gathering initial data through physics-based molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, from which contact matrices are derived as preliminary features. To capture temporal dynamics inherent in the simulations, we augment these matrices with a representation of temporal dynamism, which is then processed using an unsupervised convolutional variational autoencoder (CVAE). We subsequently compare conventional clustering techniques against our CVAE-based method using specific metrics to rank submolecular structures and identify promising candidates for optimization. Crucially, this method operates without requiring extensive structure-activity relationship databases, offering novel insights into drug modification hotspots that can enhance efficacy. By replacing labor-intensive, months- or years-long conventional processes with our efficient workflow, we aim to reduce lead optimization turnaround times to days, thereby providing a valuable asset for medical researchers.

A primary challenge in optimizing orbit transfers is identifying the count, timing, orientation, and size of velocity impulses required to minimize total impulse. Although T. N. Edelbaum formulated this problem in 1967, a rigorous solution for multi-revolution maneuvers has remained elusive for more than fifty years despite significant progress. This study revisits Edelbaum's inquiry using a bottom-up methodology to construct a minimum-fuel switching surface. By analyzing time profiles of the minimum-fuel switching function across increasing thrust magnitudes, particularly in the high-thrust limit, we observe that the continuous thrust switching surface exposes the $N$-impulse solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a *fundamental* minimum-thrust solution is essential for determining the optimal minimum-fuel maneuver across all thrust levels. Our findings indicate that Edelbaum's question does not generally yield a unique answer; instead, it often results in a set of equal-$\Delta v$ extremals. However, when the question is refined to determine the number of finite-duration thrust arcs for a specific rocket engine, a unique extremal is typically identified. Numerical examples illustrate these concepts and their applicability to various interplanetary and Earth-bound optimal transfers involving up to eleven impulses or short thrust arcs for finite thrust. Additionally, this paper offers a significant unification in astrodynamics by linking impulsive and continuous-thrust trajectories through the concept of *optimal switching surfaces*.

Harsh conditions present distinct obstacles for networking strategies, yet the impact of these environments on network resources and the consequences of long-term unattended maintenance remain poorly understood. To tackle these issues, we introduce a flexible and adaptive resource management framework that integrates environment-aware capabilities. Specifically, we propose a novel network architecture that augments traditional components with new functionalities. Key innovations in this architecture include a deep-learning-based module for predicting environmental resources and a self-organized service management module. First, the prediction module estimates available network resources across varying environmental conditions. Subsequently, an environment-centric resource allocation method is developed based on these predictions to maximize system utility. To validate the efficacy and efficiency of these new functionalities, we conduct experiments within a case study. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for extending resource management strategies in harsh environments beyond the scope of this work.

We examine the relationship between the observed turbulent pressure in molecular gas ($P_\mathrm{turb}$) and the equilibrium pressure required for interstellar gas within a galaxy's gravitational potential ($P_\mathrm{DE}$). By integrating high-resolution CO observations from PHANGS-ALMA with multi-wavelength data tracing atomic gas, stellar structures, and star formation rates (SFR) across 28 nearby star-forming galaxies, we analyze this balance. Our results indicate that while $P_\mathrm{turb}$ correlates with $P_\mathrm{DE}$ on kiloparsec scales, it nearly always exceeds the latter, suggesting molecular gas is over-pressurized relative to the large-scale environment. We demonstrate that this discrepancy arises from the clumpy nature of molecular gas; when $P_\mathrm{DE}$ is recalculated on cloud scales to include molecular self-gravity, external gravity, and ambient pressure, it aligns closely with observed $P_\mathrm{turb}$. Additionally, we find that molecular gas in our sample where cloud-scale $P_\mathrm{turb} \approx P_\mathrm{DE} \gtrsim 10^5\,k_\mathrm{B}\,\mathrm{K\,cm^{-3}}$ is more prone to self-gravity, whereas lower-pressure gas appears dominated by ambient pressure and/or external forces. We further show that the ratio of $P_\mathrm{turb}$ to the observed SFR surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$) generally supports stellar feedback-driven momentum injection, though some regions may exhibit turbulence from other sources. The correlation between $\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$ and kpc-scale $P_\mathrm{DE}$ in galaxy disks aligns with predictions from self-regulated star formation models. Finally, we validate the previously reported empirical link between the molecular-to-atomic gas ratio and kpc-scale $P_\mathrm{DE}$.

A three-atom molecule consisting of two identical bosons (A) and one distinct particle (B) is analyzed through coupled channels near a Feshbach resonance. The model assumes the AB subsystem has one channel, while the AA subsystem possesses two channels—an open and a closed one separated by an energy gap. Using Feshbach projection operators for these channels, an induced three-body interaction within a single-channel framework is derived. In the limit where the trap is tuned to vanishing scattering lengths, an effective three-body interaction emerges. Corresponding homogeneous coupled Faddeev integral equations are established in the unitarity limit. The s-wave transition matrix for the AA subsystem is calculated using a zero-range potential via a subtractive renormalization scheme that introduces two finite parameters alongside the energy gap. The coupling between channels in the coupled equations is identified with the energy gap, which acts as an ultraviolet scale competing with the van der Waals radius to define the short-range physics of the open channel. This competition at short distances demonstrates the violation of "van der Waals universality" for narrow Feshbach resonances in cold atomic systems, highlighting the energy gap's active role in governing short-range three-body dynamics.

The exceptional precision of contemporary Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems is driving their rapid adoption as mainstream technology. Essential for applications ranging from voice assistants and dictation tools to real-time translation, ASR faces a significant hurdle: high accuracy demands immense computational resources, often requiring billions of arithmetic operations per second of audio. This intensity clashes with the increasing desire to deploy ASR on edge devices, where hardware acceleration is critical for viable performance. However, because ASR is a rapidly evolving and complex domain, designing overly specialized accelerators risks quick obsolescence. To address these issues, this paper introduces ASRPU, a programmable accelerator designed for edge-based ASR. ASRPU utilizes a pool of general-purpose cores to execute small, parallel code segments, where each program handles a specific portion of the decoder, such as a neural network layer. The system automates select decoder components to streamline programming while maintaining flexibility. An analysis of a modern ASR system running on ASRPU demonstrates that this architecture supports real-time decoding within a minimal power budget.

The Flow Decomposition problem, defined as identifying the minimal set of weighted paths required to represent a flow on a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), has recently become a critical computational component in transcript assembly. We demonstrate that this problem belongs to the class of Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) problems when parameterized by the number of paths, providing a practical linear-time FPT algorithm. Building on this, we developed and optimized a Flow Decomposition solver based on our algorithm and assessed its efficacy using RNA-sequence data. Notably, our solver delivers exact solutions with runtimes that rival those of current state-of-the-art heuristics. Furthermore, we justify our design decisions by presenting two hardness results concerning preprocessing and weight recovery: under standard complexity assumptions, $k$-Flow Decomposition does not admit polynomial kernels, and the associated task of assigning known weights to a predefined set of paths is NP-hard.

Low rank approximation is a fundamental issue across various scientific fields. Historically, this challenge has been addressed using unitary invariant norms, such as the Frobenius or spectral norms, because efficient methods exist for constructing approximations under these metrics. Nevertheless, recent findings highlight the utility of low rank approximations within the Chebyshev norm, a measure that frequently emerges in practical applications. This paper addresses the task of generating optimal rank-1 approximations specifically under the Chebyshev norm. We examine the characteristics of the alternating minimization algorithm for constructing such approximations and illustrate its application in deriving optimal rank-1 solutions. Consequently, we present an algorithm capable of producing optimal rank-1 approximations in the Chebyshev norm for matrices of small dimensions.

Multilayer diffusion issues have become critically important due to their prevalence in various industrial, environmental, and medical applications involving heat and mass transfer. This article investigates the solvability of a one-dimensional nonhomogeneous multilayer diffusion problem. We employ a novel generalized integral transform, the $ \bb M_{\rho,m} -$transform [Srivastava et al., https://doi.org/10.1016/S0252-9602(15)30061-8]. Initially, the nonhomogeneous multilayer problem is decomposed into a sequence of one-layer diffusion problems featuring time-varying functions, which are then solved using the $ \bb M_{\rho,m} -$transform. Consequently, a system of renewal equations is established through general interface conditions. Ultimately, the $ \bb M_{\rho,m} -$transform and its analytic inverse are applied to derive an explicit solution for this renewal equations' system. These findings extend the results presented in [Rodrigo and Worthy, http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/ j.jmaa.2016.06.042].

We examine a variant of the sine-Gordon model where the cosine potential's strength varies periodically with time. This system represents the continuum limit of a many-body extension of the Kapitza pendulum. Utilizing the perturbed Conformal Field Theory (CFT) framework, we apply the Truncated Conformal Space Approach (TCSA) to study the Floquet quasienergy spectrum. Our analysis emphasizes the effective behavior at high driving frequencies, a result we also derive analytically. Depending on the specific driving protocol, the system can revert to the standard sine-Gordon model or evolve into its two-frequency counterpart. The complex structure of the two-frequency model suggests that periodic driving can disrupt integrability, introduce new spectral states, or induce phase transitions. Furthermore, our methodology is generalizable to any periodically driven perturbed conformal field theories.

Manipulating composite objects that combine rigid and deformable components with varying stiffness remains a difficult yet practically significant challenge that has not been adequately addressed in existing literature despite recent advancements. This paper introduces a novel visual servoing method capable of handling this diverse range of objects—from soft to rigid—using a unified adaptive strategy. To characterize the object's infinite-dimensional configuration, the proposed approach calculates a concise feedback vector derived from 2D contour moment features. A sliding mode control scheme is subsequently developed to guarantee finite-time convergence for both the shape error feedback and the model estimation error. Using Lyapunov theory, the stability of the entire framework, including the boundedness of all signals, is rigorously demonstrated. Detailed simulations and experimental results validate the efficacy of this method. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this represents the first application of contour moments combined with finite-time control to resolve this complex manipulation problem.

This thesis aims to identify integrable and superintegrable systems within magnetic fields. We derive the quantum mechanical equations governing second-order integrals of motion in cylindrical coordinates to determine all quadratically integrable systems of this type. From this set, we seek those possessing additional integrals of motion, specifically finding all systems with an extra first-order integral in both classical and quantum frameworks. Results indicate that all such systems were previously known, with no new discoveries in this category. Furthermore, we identify all systems featuring an additional integral of the form $L^2+\ldots$ or $L_y p_y-L_x p_y+\ldots$, most of which are novel to the literature. All identified superintegrable systems share the first-order integral $L_z$, and we solve their Hamilton-Jacobi and Schrödinger equations via separation of variables in cylindrical coordinates, as well as for first-order systems in Cartesian coordinates.

We provide the inaugural complete analytic computation of the scattering amplitude for the process $q {\bar q} \to Q {\bar Q}$ up to two-loop order in Quantum Chromodynamics, involving a massless quark flavor $q$ and a massive quark flavor $Q$. The interference between the Born amplitude and both the one- and two-loop amplitudes is calculated analytically after decomposing them into gauge-invariant form factors that account for color and flavor structures. These results retain full dependence on the squared center-of-mass energy, squared momentum transfer, and the heavy-quark mass, expressed as Laurent series around four space-time dimensions with coefficients comprising generalized polylogarithms and transcendental constants up to weight four. Our findings confirm existing purely numerical determinations of the squared amplitude and expand analytic understanding from a partial set of form factors to the complete set derived from both planar and non-planar diagrams, covering corrections up to the second order in the strong coupling constant.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) are widely recognized as a powerful tool for addressing diverse challenges in machine learning and computer vision. This paper presents a novel deep learning architecture, the Inception-Recurrent Convolutional Neural Network (IRCNN), which integrates the capabilities of inception networks with recurrent layers within a DCNN framework. The proposed model's recognition performance was empirically assessed across several benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Experimental findings indicate that the IRCNN achieves recognition accuracy comparable to or superior to many popular DCNNs, including RCNNs. Additionally, we compared the IRCNN against standard Inception Networks and Inception-Residual Networks using the CIFAR-100 dataset. On the augmented CIFAR-100 dataset, the IRCNN demonstrated improvements in classification accuracy of approximately 3.5% over RCNN, 3.47% over equivalent Inception Networks, and 2.54% over Inception-Residual Networks.

Differential equations are essential to engineering and, by extension, innovation. Recently, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising approach for solving these equations. PINNs offer advantages such as being meshless, scalable, and capable of intelligently transferring knowledge between different differential equations. However, research in this area has primarily focused on linear-elasticity and crack propagation issues. This study applies PINNs to address coupled thermo-mechanical problems in functionally graded materials. It involves a detailed analysis of the PINN framework, examining training datasets, model architectures, and loss functions. The effectiveness of the PINN models is evaluated by comparing their solutions against analytical results or those derived from the finite element method. While the model achieved an R² score exceeding 99% for primary variables like displacement and temperature fields, predicting secondary variables such as stress proved more difficult. This research marks the first implementation of the PINN framework for coupled thermo-mechanical problems in composite materials. It aims to deepen the understanding of this novel framework and serve as a foundational reference for future PINN research.

This study investigates decoherence effects influencing active neutrino propagation, arising from non-forward scattering within a medium of electrons and nucleons. We compute the imaginary component of the neutrino self-energy resulting from these scattering events. Because the initial neutrino state is depleted without vanishing—transitioning instead into a different flavor rather than decaying—these processes necessitate a description of decoherence that extends beyond the coherent evolution of the state vector. Leveraging the formalism established in our prior work regarding non-forward scattering and stochastic state evolution, we define the jump operators utilized in master or Lindblad equations based on our calculation of the self-energy's imaginary part. To facilitate the estimation of decoherence in practical scenarios, we provide explicit formulas for decoherence terms under various background conditions, highlighting key features such as neutrino energy dependence. To connect with previous approaches that treat decoherence terms phenomenologically, we solve the evolution equation for a two-generation system. We offer formulas for estimating decoherence impacts across different environments, including the matter-dominated conditions typical of long-baseline experiments. In these contexts, the effects appear minimal, suggesting that any significant decoherence observed would likely stem from non-standard contributions to the decoherence terms.

Over the past few years, COVID-19 has emerged as a critical global issue, causing widespread harm and resulting in billions of dollars in lost business capital. To address the complex spatial and temporal dependencies inherent in this pandemic's time series data, we introduce a novel Spatial-Temporal Synchronous Graph Transformer network (STSGT) designed to predict the pandemic's future trajectory. By integrating graph convolution networks (GCN) with transformer self-attention mechanisms on a synchronous spatial-temporal graph, the STSGT layers effectively model the dynamic patterns of the data. This synchronous graph architecture captures both spatial and temporal relationships between graph vertices across current and future time steps, thereby accounting for time series heterogeneity and enhancing forecasting precision. Extensive experiments on two real-world COVID-19 datasets demonstrate that STSGT significantly surpasses existing state-of-the-art spatial-temporal forecasting algorithms. Specifically, over a 12-day horizon, it achieves an average improvement of 12.19% and 3.42% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) compared to the next best algorithm when forecasting daily infections and deaths, respectively, across 50 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. Furthermore, the model excels in state-level county-level infection forecasting, such as for Michigan. The code and models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/soumbane/STSGT.

This study demonstrates that the Temperley-Lieb algebra is built from the generators of the transverse-field Ising-type bond algebra. Additionally, it is established that applying the representation of these generators to the one-dimensional transverse-field Ising model transforms the Temperley-Lieb algebra, formed by three consecutive bond generators, into the XXZ model. Moreover, by utilizing other representations for the bond generators, we derive several additional integrable spin systems.

Neutron scattering has been pivotal in clarifying the pairing mechanism and the symmetry of the superconducting energy gap in iron arsenide materials. While neutron data on phonon density of states aligns well with ab initio calculations—once iron magnetism is included—the predicted transition temperatures remain below 1 K, ruling out conventional phonon-mediated superconductivity. Investigations into spin dynamics within the spin density wave phase of parent compounds reveal strongly dispersive spin waves with exchange interactions matching the observed magnetic order. Although antiferromagnetic fluctuations persist in the normal phase of superconducting samples but appear more diffuse, evidence below the critical temperature (Tc) indicates these fluctuations condense into a resonant spin excitation at the antiferromagnetic wavevector. This excitation possesses energy scaling with Tc, supporting a model of unconventional superconductivity with extended s± wave symmetry.

Counting the homomorphisms of a pattern graph $H$ within a large input graph $G$ is a foundational issue in computer science, with widespread applications across databases, graph algorithms, and network science. Frequently, the total count is insufficient; particularly in large-scale network analysis, it is necessary to determine, for every vertex $v$ in $G$, how many $H$-homomorphisms include that vertex. This specific task is known as homomorphism orbit counting, reflecting the relationship between vertex orbits in $H$ under its automorphisms.

Motivated by the demand for efficient solutions, this study investigates the conditions under which near-linear time algorithms are feasible. A key constraint involves assuming the input graph $G$ has bounded degeneracy, a trait common in modern massive networks. The central question is to identify which patterns $H$ allow for linear-time orbit counting.

We establish a dichotomy theorem that answers this question. For a given pattern $H$, let $l$ represent the length of the longest induced path connecting any two vertices within the same automorphism orbit of $H$. If $l \le 5$, then $H$-homomorphism orbit counting is solvable in linear time for graphs with bounded degeneracy. Conversely, if $l > 5$, then, under fine-grained complexity conjectures, no near-linear time algorithm exists for this problem. Building upon prior dichotomy results for total homomorphism counting, we notably identify and characterize specific patterns $H$ where the total homomorphism count can be computed in linear time, yet the corresponding orbit counting problem remains intractable even in near-linear time.

Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL) aims to recognize concepts without any labeled training data. Distinct from conventional classification or detection tasks, ZSL evaluates performance on classes completely unseen during training, making it a challenging yet promising area for unsupervised concept learning, domain adaptation, and dataset drift detection. Recent ZSL approaches include enhanced metric learning, transfer learning, semantic-image fusion via word vectors, and generative models to map the latent space of known classes for identifying unknown ones. However, many of these methods rely heavily on training augmentation using attributes or features that are often unavailable or vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This work proposes adapting techniques from the person re-identification task for ZSL, with specific modifications to boost performance without requiring feature or dataset augmentation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the CUB200 and Cars196 datasets, yielding an NMI of 63.27 and top-1 accuracy of 61.04 for CUB200, and an NMI of 66.03 with 82.75% top-1 accuracy for Cars196. Furthermore, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in Generalized Zero-Shot Learning (GZSL), achieving a Harmonic Mean R-1 of 66.14% on CUB200.

This study presents results from a search for new physics conducted using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, focusing on events characterized by large missing transverse momentum and two Higgs bosons decaying into bottom-antibottom quark pairs. The analysis utilizes a 2016 CMS dataset with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 inverse femtobarns. The investigation is driven by gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking models, which forecast the electroweak production of a higgsino pair; each higgsino is expected to decay through a cascade into a Higgs boson and an invisible lightest supersymmetric particle. The observed event counts in the signal regions align with standard model background predictions derived from data control regions. Consequently, higgsinos with masses between 230 and 770 GeV are excluded at the 95% confidence level within the framework of a simplified model describing the production and decay of nearly degenerate higgsinos.

We introduce a newly discovered monolayer borophene allotrope, designated as super-B, which exhibits a flat configuration confirmed by ab initio calculations. Compared to other typical borophenes, super-B demonstrates superior thermal, dynamical, and mechanical stability. Its unique chemical bonding environment features standard $sp$ and $sp^2$ hybridizations alongside a delocalized five-center three-electron $\pi$ bond, termed $\pi$(5c-3e), an electronic structure critical for its chemical stabilization. Through additional doping, pristine super-B can be converted into a Dirac material. Similar to graphene, it maintains structural integrity under tensile strains below 24%, showcasing exceptional flexibility. Furthermore, driven by its low atomic mass and high density of states at the Fermi level, super-B achieves the highest critical temperature ($T_c$) of 25.3 K among single-element superconductors at ambient conditions. This elevated $T_c$ is attributed to the pronounced anharmonicity of two linear acoustic phonon branches and an exceptionally low-frequency optic phonon mode. These findings offer new perspectives on the chemistry of low-dimensional boron nanostructures and underscore the potential for developing flexible devices and high-$T_c$ superconductors.

The swift evolution of sensor technology and artificial intelligence is opening fresh avenues for improving traffic safety. Dashcams are now extensively used in both human-driven and autonomous vehicles. Developing a computational intelligence model capable of swiftly and accurately predicting accidents from dashcam footage would significantly improve readiness for accident prevention. However, the complex spatial-temporal interactions among traffic participants, combined with the deeply embedded visual cues for future accidents within dashcam data, make early anticipation a significant challenge. Drawing inspiration from human visual attention mechanisms regarding accident risk perception, this paper introduces a Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Attention (DSTA) network for early accident prediction from dashcam videos. This network utilizes a Dynamic Temporal Attention (DTA) module to identify discriminative temporal segments within video sequences and a Dynamic Spatial Attention (DSA) module to focus on informative spatial regions in frames. A Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) is jointly trained with these attention modules to forecast the probability of future accidents. Evaluation on two benchmark datasets demonstrates that the DSTA-network outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, a comprehensive ablation study at the component level elucidates how the network achieves these results. Finally, the paper proposes a method to fuse prediction scores from two complementary models, verifying that this approach effectively enhances the performance of early accident anticipation.

The magnetic characteristics of A2BB'O6 double perovskites, where A represents rare or alkaline earth ions and B, B' denote transition metal ions, hold significant promise for spintronic technologies. Of particular note is the zero field cooled exchange bias (ZEB) phenomenon detected in hole-doped polycrystalline La2-xAxCoMnO6 samples. This study employs the floating zone technique to grow single crystals of La2CoMnO6, La1.5Ca0.5CoMnO6, and La1.5Sr0.5CoMnO6 to investigate their magnetic properties. All three compounds exhibit ferromagnetism. Unexpectedly, neither conventional nor zero-field exchange bias effects were found in the Ca and Sr doped single crystals, a result that starkly contrasts with the behavior of polycrystalline counterparts. This discrepancy suggests that the absence of grain boundaries and spin-glass-like dynamics—which are missing in these single crystals—may be essential factors driving the spontaneous exchange bias observed in polycrystalline materials.

Classical mechanics relies on position and momentum variables that must be selected as specific coordinates to be promoted into appropriate quantum operators. Since these variables are not unique, only a single, distinguished set should be chosen. We will demonstrate how selecting these preferred variables and their corresponding quantum operators ensures a genuinely valid quantization. Mistaking an invalid quantization for a valid one can result in erroneous physical predictions. In addition to particle systems, we provide a brief overview applicable to fields and gravity.

The performance of machine learning models is heavily influenced by dataset size and feature quality, as the presence of redundant or irrelevant features can drastically impair results. This study introduces IGRF-RFE, a hybrid feature selection approach designed for multi-class network anomaly detection utilizing a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). IGRF-RFE integrates both filter and wrapper methods for feature reduction. Specifically, the filter stage combines Information Gain and Random Forest Importance to narrow the feature search space, followed by the application of Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) as a wrapper method to recursively remove redundant features from the reduced subsets.
