A primary inconsistency emerged between the spectroscopically measured gas outflow velocity along the line of sight and the proper motion expansion of the dust across the sky plane. This puzzling behavior originates at the wind base of the central, spatially unresolved Wolf-Rayet binary. This study presents an updated proper motion analysis based on a two-year baseline, revealing that the dust plume expands four times slower than the spectroscopic wind speed, thereby validating and reinforcing earlier results. Additionally, high-angular-resolution near-infrared imaging of the system's core identifies a close binary consistent with a Wolf-Rayet colliding-wind system. Leveraging these new observational constraints, we propose an enhanced geometric model that aligns closely with the data, refining the orbital parameters of the Wolf-Rayet binary and providing further evidence for the anisotropic wind model.

The LHCb experiment initiated its physics run with 37/pb of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, provided by the LHC in 2010. The experiment's capabilities, designed for precision measurements within the heavy flavor sector, are demonstrated through initial results from its core program. A comprehensive set of production studies offers precise tests of QCD and electroweak theories in the unique high-rapidity region accessible to LHCb. Notably, the results regarding W and Z production are highly promising for establishing constraints on parton distribution functions.

Pulmonary hypertension is a cardiovascular condition characterized by high arterial blood pressure alongside stiffening and thickening of vessel walls, resulting from changes in collagen, elastin, and smooth muscle cells. Type 3 pulmonary hypertension, driven by hypoxia, can be modeled in animals subjected to prolonged low-oxygen environments, which induce biomechanical changes in vessel wall architecture. This research develops and systematically simplifies a nonlinear elastic structural model for a large pulmonary artery, creating a new pressure-area relationship that accounts for remodeling in type 3 hypertension. The model was calibrated using *ex vivo* data on vessel diameter and wall thickness variations under controlled flow in isolated left pulmonary arteries from both control and hypertensive mice. Utilizing the Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden framework, a two-layer, hyperelastic, anisotropic model incorporating residual stresses was formulated. Complex equations predicting vessel area and wall thickness as functions of increasing blood pressure were derived and fitted to the experimental data. Through sensitivity analysis, parameter estimation, and subset selection, the original 16-parameter model was reduced to a version estimating only a smaller subset of identifiable parameters via an inverse problem. The final reduced model comprises a single set of three elastic moduli. Analysis of the estimated parameter ranges reveals that nonlinear stiffening is primarily driven by elastin in control subjects but by collagen in the hypertensive group. The novel pressure-area relation established in this study holds potential for improving one-dimensional fluid network models of vessel wall remodeling in cardiovascular disease.

Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) have demonstrated significant success in realistic image classification, achieving accuracy comparable to full-precision models optimized for edge devices. Due to their reliance on 1-bit inputs and weights, BNNs offer minimal storage needs, and their computations, primarily based on XOR and population count operations, are highly efficient with simple hardware. However, efficiently supporting BNNs on mobile CPUs remains challenging due to frequent memory accesses required for loading weights and inputs. In BNNs, bits are packed into sequences to enhance storage and computational efficiency. This work observes that the number of unique sequences representing a set of weights is typically low, and during BNN layer evaluation, a small subset of these sequences is used far more frequently than others. Leveraging this insight, we propose using Huffman Encoding to compress bit sequences and an indirection table for decoding during evaluation. Additionally, we introduce a clustering scheme to identify the most frequent bit sequences and replace less common ones with similar common sequences, thereby reducing storage requirements and memory accesses by encoding common sequences with fewer bits. We extended a mobile CPU with a specialized hardware structure capable of efficiently caching and decoding these compressed sequences. Evaluations using the ReAacNet model on the ImageNet dataset demonstrate that our approach reduces memory requirements by 1.32x and improves performance by 1.35x.

Domain adaptation enables generative language models to overcome specific issues arising from domain shifts in their target applications. However, traditional approaches involving further training on domain-specific data often degrade the model's generalization capabilities to other domains, increasing the risk of errors in open-ended deployments. This study introduces new training objectives based on the semantic similarity between predicted tokens and reference tokens. Our findings demonstrate that (1) moving away from the assumption of a single correct prediction by utilizing token-level semantic similarity for training targets can alleviate catastrophic forgetting during adaptation, (2) while maintaining high adaptation quality, and (3) with minimal increases in computational costs. From a broader perspective, these objectives, rooted in soft token alignment, bridge the gap between efficient yet simplistic exact-match token-level methods and highly expressive but resource-heavy sequential objectives.

Inspired by inflationary magnetogenesis scenarios where a homogeneous magnetic field emerges, we examine the magnetohydrodynamic evolution of primordial plasma under two distinct initial conditions: (i) a spatially uniform field with infinite correlation length, and (ii) a zero flux, scale-invariant, statistically homogeneous magnetic field. For a brief initial period, we impose monochromatic forcing at a specific wave number in both cases, ensuring a finite correlation length that remains significantly smaller than the typical turbulence scale. Specifically, we analyze the decay rates of both nonhelical and helical hydromagnetic turbulence. Our findings indicate that when a homogeneous magnetic field is present, both helical and nonhelical small-scale fields can decay rapidly. This behavior is unique to systems with a perfectly homogeneous field, often treated as a local approximation for a slowly varying background; in this context, the field remains immutable and acts as an external constraint. This stands in stark contrast to the case of a statistically homogeneous field, where we observe conventional decay characteristics: a significantly slower reduction in magnetic energy coupled with a more rapid increase in correlation length, particularly when magnetic helicity is present. These results imply that a homogeneous magnetic field generated during inflation should remain stable against the influence of small-scale fields and may serve as the source of the universe's large-scale magnetic field.

The Future Circular Collider operating in an $\mathrm{e^{+}e^{-}}$ mode presents a unique chance to markedly enhance Standard Model measurements through specialized runs at the Z-pole, WW threshold, ZH (240 GeV), and $\mathrm{t}\bar{\mathrm{t}}$ threshold. Benefiting from roughly $10^{5}$ times more statistics at the Z-pole and $10^{4}$ times more at the WW threshold compared to LEP, FCC-ee will allow for the determination of the strong coupling $\alpha_{s}$ with per-mille precision. Investigations into parton showering, utilizing the pure gluon sample from $\mathrm{ZH}({\rightarrow} \mathrm{gg})$, will substantially advance our comprehension of gluon radiation and fragmentation, thereby directly influencing quark versus gluon discrimination efforts. Additional opportunities encompass precision studies of hadronization and color reconnection at the WW threshold. Selected aspects of FCC-ee's comprehensive precision QCD agenda are detailed below.

Consider $u$ as a solution to the Fisher-KPP equation $\partial_t u=\Delta u+f(u)$ for $t>0$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$. We investigate whether $u$ approaches a locally planar state as $t\to+\infty$. Specifically, does the sequence $u(t_n,x_n+\cdot)$ converge locally uniformly, possibly after extracting a subsequence, to a one-dimensional function for any sequence $((t_n,x_n))$ where $t_n\to+\infty$? This inquiry aligns with De Giorgi's conjecture regarding stationary solutions of the Allen-Cahn equation. The validity of this convergence relies on the initial datum $u_0$. It is established that the answer is positive if the support of $u_0$ is bounded or contained between two parallel half-spaces, but negative if the support has a "V-shaped" configuration. In this work, we demonstrate that $u$ becomes asymptotically locally planar when the support of $u_0$ is a convex set (subject to a uniform interior ball condition) or, more broadly, lies at a finite Hausdorff distance from a convex set. We further establish this result under an even more general geometric condition on the support, thereby encompassing previously known results. Additionally, we identify the specific directions in which $u$ exhibits asymptotic local planarity and prove that the resulting asymptotic profiles are monotone. These findings are particularly applicable when the support of $u_0$ corresponds to the subgraph of a function with a vanishing global mean.

Composite fermions (CFs) are exotic quasi-particles arising in interacting electron systems under high magnetic fields, created by binding an electron with an even number of magnetic flux quanta. These particles account for various many-body phases, including the fractional quantum Hall state (FQHS). The effective mass of CFs ($m_{CF}$) is inversely proportional to the energy gap, a fundamental characteristic of the FQHS. This study reports experimental determinations of $m_{CF}$ in ultra-high-quality GaAs quantum wells of varying thickness. Measuring $m_{CF}$ offers a distinct advantage over gap measurements because mass values are less susceptible to disorder, making them particularly suitable for validating theoretical models, especially regarding high-order FQHS. Our findings indicate that $m_{CF}$ rises as the well width increases, corresponding to a reduction in the energy gap as the electron layer thickens and in-plane Coulomb interactions weaken. When comparing our experimental mass data with existing theoretical predictions, we observe substantial quantitative differences, underscoring the necessity for more precise and rigorous calculations to align with the observed phenomena.

Brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars constitute a substantial portion of the galaxy's stellar population, serving as valuable environments for studying planet formation under extreme conditions of low density and temperature. Furthermore, the radial drift of dust particles presents a particularly formidable obstacle to early planet formation in these systems. High-angular resolution ALMA observations of several protoplanetary disks surrounding brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars have revealed substructures similar to those found around Sun-like stars. These findings imply that embedded giant planets are the most probable cause of such features. However, since confirmed giant exoplanets around all stars account for less than 2% of known cases, and current core accretion models (whether involving pebbles or planetesimals) struggle to explain their formation, the situation remains puzzling. Future dedicated deep observations using ALMA and JWST focused on disks around brown dwarfs and very low-mass stars will significantly advance our understanding of key disk properties, such as mass and size. This knowledge is essential for identifying the physical mechanisms governing disk evolution and assessing the potential for planet formation in these unique environments.

Although melody is fundamental to music perception, reliably identifying melodic notes within arbitrary recordings remains a significant challenge in music information retrieval. A primary difficulty in melody transcription is developing methods that effectively process diverse audio containing various instrument ensembles and musical styles, as current strategies often excel with specific instruments or genres but fail elsewhere. To address this, we utilize representations from Jukebox (Dhariwal et al. 2020), a generative model for broad music audio, which improves melody transcription performance by 20% compared to traditional spectrogram features. Additionally, addressing the scarcity of training data, we created a new dataset comprising 50 hours of melody transcriptions derived from crowdsourced annotations of varied music. Combining generative pre-training with this novel dataset yields a 77% performance improvement in melody transcription over the strongest existing baseline. By integrating our transcription method with solutions for beat detection, key estimation, and chord recognition, we developed Sheet Sage, a system that generates human-readable lead sheets directly from audio. Audio examples are available at https://chrisdonahue.com/sheetsage, and the code can be found at https://github.com/chrisdonahue/sheetsage.

Twisting bilayers induces structural chirality, creating two enantiomers—left- and right-handed structures—based on the orientation of the twist angle. The interaction between this global chirality and other degrees of freedom, including magnetic ordering and local octahedral chirality derived from bond geometry, can produce remarkable effects. This study examines collinear antiferromagnetic CrI$_3$ twisted homo-bilayers, which exhibit staggered octahedral chirality within each monolayer. Through symmetry analysis, density functional theory, and tight-binding model calculations, we demonstrate that twisting reduces both structural and magnetic point-group symmetries. This symmetry breaking activates pyroelectricity and the magneto-optical Kerr effect, properties that are typically absent in untwisted antiferromagnetic homo-bilayers. Notably, both electric polarization and the Kerr angle are tunable via the twist angle, with their signs flipping when transitioning between left- and right-twisted configurations. Furthermore, we reveal the emergence of unconventional vortices featuring spin textures with alternating chiralities in momentum space. These results highlight that the synergy between twisting and octahedral chirality in magnetic bilayers and related van der Waals heterostructures offers a powerful avenue for engineering physical properties for spintronic and optoelectronic applications.

Recent work by the second author alongside D\'{i}az Garc\'{i}a, Krutov, Somberg, and Strung established that every relative line module over an irreducible quantum flag manifold $\mathcal{O}_q(G/L_S)$ possesses a unique $\mathcal{O}_q(G)$-covariant connection defined via the Heckenberger-Kolb differential calculus $\Omega^1_q(G/L_S)$. This paper demonstrates that such connections are bimodule connections featuring an invertible associated bimodule map. The proof utilizes general findings by Beggs and Majid concerning principal connections for quantum principal bundles, applied to the quantum principal bundle formulation of Heckenberger-Kolb calculi recently developed by the authors and D\'{i}az Garc\'{i}a. Explicit forms of the associated bimodule maps are provided sequentially using generalised quantum determinants, the FRT presentation of the algebra $\mathcal{O}_q(G)$, and Takeuchi's categorical equivalence for relative Hopf modules.

The smart grid is essential for developing a smart and future carbon-neutral society, making autonomous fault detection vital for system awareness, maintenance, and operation. This paper examines fault monitoring within smart grids, addressing inherent technical challenges and their solutions. It begins by outlining the fundamental principles of fault detection, followed by an analysis of the new requirements for autonomy, associated technical hurdles, and potential remedies. A case study is presented as a preliminary exploration of autonomous fault detection, and the paper concludes by highlighting key directions for future research.

The elevated interstellar abundances of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and their size distribution stem from intricate chemical processes involving dust, ultraviolet (UV) radiation, and primary gaseous species (H, C+, and O). These mechanisms must account for the high concentration of relatively small PAHs in the diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) and suggest the ongoing formation of PAHs small enough (with carbon counts $N_C \lesssim 35\text{--}50$) to be fully dehydrogenated by interstellar UV. The resulting carbon clusters ($C_n$) are perpetually subjected to UV photons ranging from ~10–13.6 eV, which facilitates isomerization and promotes the creation of the most stable isomers, potentially leading to irregular carbon cages. Frequent collisions with interstellar $C^+$ ions may drive further cage isomerization, a process known in laboratory studies of $C_{60}$, possibly generating highly stable fullerenes such as $C_{40}$, $C_{44}$, and $C_{50}$. These fullerenes are anticipated to be exceptionally stable in the diffuse ISM because $C_2$ ejection requires rare two-photon absorption rather than single-photon absorption. It is plausible that at least one of these fullerenes or its cation reaches an abundance comparable to $C_{60}$ or $C_{60}^+$ in the diffuse ISM, although this abundance is constrained by the absence of corresponding features in observed mid-infrared spectra. B3LYP calculations of visible spectra for various fullerene isomers with $40 \lesssim N_C \lesssim 50$ indicate they typically possess a few spectral bands in the visible range with oscillator strengths ($f$-values) in the range of a few $10^{-2}$. This suggests that such fullerenes could be promising candidates for the carriers of certain diffuse interstellar bands.

This study reports measurements of Higgs boson production resulting in decays to a pair of $\tau$ leptons, utilizing a dataset of proton-proton collisions from the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 138 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis comprises three distinct approaches: two targeting gluon fusion and vector boson fusion, which employ a neural network and an event categorization optimized for the signal-to-background ratio, respectively; and a third focusing on vector boson-associated Higgs production. Results are expressed as signal strengths relative to Standard Model predictions and as cross-section times branching fraction products across up to 16 kinematic regions. When combining the neural network analysis with the vector boson-associated production analysis, the measured signal strengths are $0.82 \pm 0.11$ for inclusive Higgs production, $0.67 \pm 0.19$ (and $0.81 \pm 0.17$) for production dominated by gluon fusion (vector boson fusion), and $1.79 \pm 0.45$ for vector boson-associated Higgs production.

Baryon acoustic oscillations (BAOs) serve as a robust tool for studying the expansion history of the universe, typically analyzed through the two-point statistics of galaxy surveys in either configuration or Fourier space. This study presents the first BAO measurement derived from a joint fit of power spectrum and correlation function multipoles. Validation using 1,000 mock catalogs demonstrates that this approach reduces biases in BAO parameters compared to individually fitting power spectra or correlation functions, or combining them via Gaussian approximation. While our estimated uncertainties are marginally larger than those from the Gaussian approximation—potentially due to noise in the sample covariance matrix, an increased number of nuisance parameters, or the avoidance of Gaussian likelihood assumptions for BAO parameters—we contend that our results are more reliable. This reliability stems from fewer underlying assumptions and the method's incorporation of correlations between Fourier and configuration space at the two-point statistic level. Applying this technique to the luminous red galaxy sample from the eBOSS data release 16, we obtained $D_H/r_d = 19.27 \pm 0.48$ and $D_M/r_d = 17.77 \pm 0.37$, which align closely with the official eBOSS consensus BAO-only results of $D_H/r_d = 19.33 \pm 0.53$ and $D_M/r_d = 17.86 \pm 0.33$.

The Standard Model of elementary particles relies on over twenty parameters, whose connection to deeper underlying principles remains unknown. Efforts to refine this theory often inadvertently generate even more parameters rather than reducing them. However, at distance scales comparable to the Planck length, gravity suggests a clear necessity for new physical principles. A major obstacle is quantum mechanics, which mandates the superposition of physical states; when integrated with general relativity, this implies that space and time themselves may require novel formalisms to serve as primary frameworks for describing events. In prior work, the author suggested reformulating quantum mechanics for elementary particles as arising from a synthesis of deterministic evolution laws and discreteness at the Planck scale. This perspective could profoundly impact symmetry structures and algebras. Since local, discrete, and continuous symmetries do not arise without cause, we propose that these symmetries can reveal insights into fundamental constants, particularly the Higgs mass, which stands out as the most unique and difficult to explain.

This paper proves a central limit theorem (CLT) for linear spectral statistics (LSS) of large-dimensional sample covariance matrices under the condition that population covariance matrices are not uniformly bounded. This represents a significant extension of the Bai-Silverstein theorem (BST) from 2004, which has greatly advanced high-dimensional statistics and the application of random matrix theory. However, the uniform boundedness assumption in BST is a major constraint on its practical utility. Our objective is to eliminate these limitations. The newly established CLT accommodates spiked eigenvalues that can exist and grow indefinitely. Notably, the theorem reveals that either spiked eigenvalues, bulk eigenvalues, or both play a dominant role. Furthermore, simulation studies across various population configurations validate these findings. Finally, we apply the CLT to test the hypothesis that a covariance matrix equals an identity matrix. For this purpose, we derive the asymptotic distributions of the corrected likelihood ratio test (LRT) and Nagao's trace test (NT) under the alternative hypothesis and propose their asymptotic power under specific alternatives.

In cytoplasmic streaming, molecular motors transport cargo along microtubule networks while dragging the surrounding fluid. The piconewton forces exerted by single motors can deform long microtubules, as can the collective fluid flows resulting from many motors. Research on streaming during fruit fly ($D.~melanogaster$) oocyte development reveals a shift from a spatially disordered cytoskeleton, which supports flows with only short-range correlations, to an ordered state characterized by a cell-spanning vortical flow. To test the hypothesis that fluid-structure interactions drive this transition, we examine a discrete-filament model and a coarse-grained continuum theory of motors moving on a deformable cytoskeleton. Both models demonstrate a $swirling~instability$ that leads to the spontaneous large-scale rotational motion observed in nature.

This research investigates the recovery of a joint piece-wise linear trend from time series data using the L1 regularization method known as L1 trend filtering (Kim, Koh, and Boyd, 2009). We establish sufficient conditions ensuring that the L1 trend filter performs reliably in mean estimation and change point detection. Our findings are twofold: regarding mean estimation, we achieve an almost optimal consistent rate, and concerning change point detection, the direction of slope changes can be recovered with high probability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak irrepresentable condition, which is essential for LASSO model sign consistency (Zhao and Yu, 2006), is not required for consistent change point detection. Finally, the efficacy of the L1 trend filter is assessed through finite sample simulation studies.

This study examines an inertial active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle self-propelling within a saw-tooth ratchet potential. Employing both Langevin simulations and the matrix continued fraction method, we analyze transport properties, steady-state diffusion, and transport coherence across the ratchet. Our findings identify spatial asymmetry as the essential condition for directed transport. Notably, simulated trajectories and associated position and velocity distribution functions indicate that the system undergoes an activity-induced transition, shifting from a running phase to a locked phase as the self-propulsion duration varies. Mean square displacement (MSD) calculations corroborate this, showing that MSD is suppressed as activity persistence increases, eventually approaching zero for large self-propulsion times; this reflects a trapping mechanism where the ratchet confines the particle during prolonged periods of activity. Furthermore, the non-monotonic behavior of particle current and the Peclet number with respect to self-propulsion time demonstrates that both transport efficiency and coherence can be modulated by adjusting the persistent duration of activity. Additionally, for intermediate ranges of self-propulsion time and particle mass, the particle current exhibits a significant peak with increasing mass, yet the Peclet number declines rather than increases, indicating a reduction in transport coherence. Finally, analytical results show that in a highly viscous medium where inertial effects are negligible, the particle current converges to that of the overdamped regime.

Aligning with the growing number of gravitational wave detections, researchers are exploring new dimensions of compact star interiors. Of particular interest is a scenario involving a first-order phase transition within these stars, which can generate a third stable branch of "twin stars" alongside white dwarfs and neutron stars. These twin stars share the same mass as standard compact objects but possess significantly different radii. This study investigates hybrid stars undergoing a hadron-to-quark transition near their cores, focusing on how this stable configuration emerges. We analyze the phase transition using both Maxwell and Gibbs construction methods to systematically evaluate gravitational mass, radius, and tidal deformability, comparing these findings with recent LIGO/VIRGO observations of the GW170817 event and existing mass-radius limits to propose robust constraints. Furthermore, we extend this analysis to incorporate rotation effects on twin stars. Motivated by the discovery of the rapidly rotating supermassive pulsar PSR J0952-0607, which drives efforts to constrain the equation of state and test phase transition predictions in dense nuclear matter, we specifically examine whether the properties of PSR J0952-0607 could exclude the existence of twin stars. Finally, we discuss constraints on the mass and radius of the compact object recently observed in the supernova remnant HESS J1731-347; our estimations suggest this object is either the lightest known neutron star or a star governed by a more exotic equation of state.

We re-examine the theoretical framework of ultrastrong light-matter interactions using exactly solvable effective Hamiltonians. By employing a perturbative method grounded in polaronic and spin-dependent squeezing transformations, we derive an effective Hamiltonian for the quantum Rabi model accurate to second order in the expansion parameter. This model incorporates both rotating and counter-rotating terms, thereby surpassing the rotating wave approximation. Analytical and numerical findings indicate that the proposed Hamiltonian outperforms the Bloch-Siegert model in computing operator averages, such as the mean photon number and excitation count. This enhancement stems from a more refined treatment of dressed states within our model. Concerning the frequency shift caused by the qubit-photon interaction, we observe a sign opposite to that predicted by the Bloch-Siegert approach; this distinction non-trivially affects the eigenstate structure and guarantees the accurate determination of excitations for specific dressed states. Finally, as a consistency verification, we demonstrate that the exactly solvable independent boson model emerges as a special limiting case of our perturbative Hamiltonian.

Multi-layer perceptrons (MLP) serve as robust scene encoders when paired with high-dimensional input projections known as *positional encoding*. Nevertheless, scenes exhibiting a broad frequency spectrum pose significant challenges: employing high frequencies for encoding introduces noise in areas with minimal structure, whereas low frequencies fail to capture detailed regions effectively. To overcome this limitation, we introduce progressive positional encoding, which exposes a hierarchical MLP architecture to incremental frequency encodings. This approach enables accurate reconstruction of scenes with wide frequency bands and learns representations at varying levels of detail *without requiring explicit per-level supervision*. The design is modular, where each level generates a continuous implicit representation usable independently at its specific resolution, thereby allowing for smaller networks when coarser reconstructions suffice. Empirical evaluations across multiple 2D and 3D datasets demonstrate enhanced reconstruction accuracy, representational capacity, and training efficiency relative to baseline methods.

This study examines the Shimokawa-Han-Amari (SHA) quantization and binning framework for distributed hypothesis testing. We introduce analytical tools to assess the critical rates achievable under the SHA approach. Furthermore, for binary symmetric double sources with a product distribution, we propose a sequential scheme that outperforms the SHA method.

Significant differences are observed in the collective properties of final-state hadrons produced in high-statistics $^{96}_{44}\text{Ru}+^{96}_{44}\text{Ru}$ and $^{96}_{40}\text{Zr}+^{96}_{40}\text{Zr}$ collisions at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} = 200~\mathrm{GeV}$, suggesting these discrepancies serve as precise indicators of variations in nucleon distributions within isobaric nuclei. This study examines $J/\psi$ production in these isobar collisions using a relativistic transport model. When comparing the systems based on equal centrality and equal multiplicity bins, the $J/\psi$ yield ratio proves sensitive to differences in both the number of binary collisions and medium evolution. Furthermore, the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of $J/\psi$ exhibits qualitative distinctions from those of light hadrons, and the ratio between Ru+Ru and Zr+Zr collisions regarding $v_2$ reflects variations in medium evolution. Consequently, charmonium production offers an independent means to investigate nucleon distributions in the isobar system.

We experimentally verify rapid and high-precision geometric control of a quantum system using the most brachistochrone method on hybrid spin registers within diamond. Leveraging time-optimal universal geometric control, we achieve single geometric gates with fidelities exceeding 99.2% on nitrogen-vacancy center spin states, reducing average operation durations by 74.9% compared to traditional geometric approaches. Furthermore, the fidelity of fast geometric two-qubit gates surpasses 96.5% on hybrid spin registers. Utilizing these high-fidelity, rapid gates, we execute an entanglement-enhanced phase estimation algorithm, achieving the Heisenberg quantum limit at room temperature. Relative to conventional geometric circuits, measurement bandwidth and sensitivity improve by factors of 3.5 and 2.9, respectively. Consequently, our findings indicate that high-fidelity quantum control via a fast geometric pathway serves as a versatile instrument for practical quantum information processing applications.

Recent advancements in high-resolution 3D printing have facilitated the development of various affordable techniques for shaping ultrasonic wave-fronts. Notably, acoustic holograms enable single-element transducers to produce arbitrary, diffraction-limited acoustic fields at MHz frequencies, acting as direct phase-plate equivalents to thin optical holograms. This study demonstrates that multiplexed polymer 3D printing can similarly generate acoustic analogues of 'thick' or volume optical holograms. The work first outlines an analytic method for designing volume holograms that map specific input fields to desired outputs, followed by the introduction of a greedy optimization strategy utilizing random downhill binary search to accommodate fabrication constraints. Finally, an experimental validation using a 2.54 cm planar PZT transducer confirms the approach by diffracting its field into eight distinct patterns based on the incident direction. Field scans of these target outputs verify that multi-polymer printing successfully creates acoustic volume holograms capable of multiplexing different fields according to the angle of incidence.

Although generative models excel at creating high-quality images of concepts derived from vast databases, users frequently desire the ability to synthesize their own specific ideas, such as family members, pets, or personal objects. This raises two key questions: Can a model rapidly learn a new concept from just a few examples, and can it combine multiple new concepts? We introduce Custom Diffusion, an efficient approach for enhancing existing text-to-image models. Our findings indicate that optimizing only a small number of parameters within the text-to-image conditioning mechanism is powerful enough to represent new concepts, allowing for rapid tuning in approximately six minutes. Moreover, we can either jointly train on multiple concepts or merge several fine-tuned models into a single unified model through closed-form constrained optimization. The resulting fine-tuned model produces variations of multiple new concepts and seamlessly integrates them with existing concepts in innovative contexts. Compared to several baselines and concurrent studies, our method achieves superior performance in both qualitative and quantitative assessments while remaining highly efficient in terms of memory usage and computational resources.

This study examines the connection between the e-property and the asymptotic stability of Markov semigroups. Specifically, it demonstrates that any stochastically continuous, asymptotically stable Markov-Feller semigroup possessing an invariant measure with a non-empty support interior must satisfy the e-property. Furthermore, it is established that any stochastically continuous Markov-Feller semigroup exhibiting the eventual e-property also possesses the e-property. However, an example is provided to illustrate that this implication does not necessarily hold if the condition of stochastic continuity is omitted.

Numerous physical systems capable of solving optimization problems through their steady-state dynamical evolution have been proposed as viable alternatives to traditional computing. Among these, oscillator-based architectures—such as coherent Ising and XY machines utilizing lasers, optical parametric oscillators, memristors, and polariton or photon condensates—stand out for their scalability, low energy usage, and ability to operate at room temperature. These systems reach solutions through the bifurcation of a fundamental supermode that globally minimizes either power dissipation or the system Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that canonical Andronov-Hopf networks can effectively model this bifurcation behavior. Moreover, a continuous transformation of variables can map any physical optimizer onto this canonical network, indicating that the performance of physical XY-Ising machines relies chiefly on the precision of network parameter control. Consequently, our research unifies various physical optimizers within a single mathematical framework, facilitating the cross-pollination of concepts across diverse physical platforms.

Let $f(z) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_f(n)q^n$ denote a holomorphic cuspidal newform of even integral weight $k\geq 2$, level $N$, trivial nebentypus, and without complex multiplication. For every prime $p$, there exists an angle $\theta_p\in [0,\pi]$ satisfying $a_f(p) = 2p^{(k-1)/2}\cos \theta_p$. The Sato-Tate conjecture posits that these angles $\theta_p$ become equidistributed according to the measure $\mu_{\textrm{ST}}(I) = \frac{2}{\pi}\int_I \sin^2 \theta \; d\theta$ for any interval $I\subseteq [0,\pi]$. Leveraging recent findings on the automorphy of symmetric-power $L$-functions by Newton and Thorne, we derive an explicit error term bound for the Sato-Tate conjecture in two specific scenarios: when $f$ represents an elliptic curve over $\mathbb{Q}$ with any conductor, or when $f$ possesses a squarefree level. In these instances, defining $\pi_{f,I}(x) := \#\{ p \leq x : p \nmid N, \theta_p\in I\}$ and $\pi(x) := \# \{ p \leq x \}$, we establish the inequality:
$$\left| \frac{\pi_{f,I}(x)}{\pi(x)} - \mu_{\textrm{ST}}(I)\right| \leq 58.1\frac{\log((k-1)N \log{x})}{\sqrt{\log{x}}} \qquad \text{for} \quad x \geq 3.$$ Furthermore, as a practical application, we provide an explicit bound for the count of primes up to $x$ that contradict the Atkin-Serre conjecture for $f$.

We investigate a family of information measures derived from Rényi's $\alpha$-Divergences where $\alpha < 0$. Specifically, we generalize Sibson's $\alpha$-Mutual Information to accommodate negative $\alpha$ values and demonstrate various properties of these constructs. Additionally, we emphasize the connection between this family of measures and functional inequalities, which have applications across diverse fields, such as establishing lower bounds for risk in Bayesian estimation methods.

This submission addresses subtask 4 of the CASE 2021 shared task 1, which focuses on Protest Event Extraction. The EventGraph system utilizes an end-to-end, graph-based semantic parser specifically for extracting event triggers and arguments. We tested various graph configurations, representing events as either "labeled-edge" or "node-centric" graphs. Our findings indicate that the "node-centric" approach delivers superior overall performance across the task's three languages: English, Spanish, and Portuguese. EventGraph secured 3rd place for English and Portuguese, and 4th place for Spanish. The project code is accessible at: https://github.com/huiling-y/eventgraph_at_case

This study examines the modulationally stable Kaup-Boussinesq system, which describes nonlinear wave propagation across diverse physical contexts. We demonstrate that the Whitham modulation equations for this model admit a novel class of solutions characterizing trigonometric shock waves. In the context of the Gurevich-Pitaevskii problem concerning the evolution of an initial discontinuity, these solutions manifest as a non-zero wave excitation on one side of the discontinuity. Our analytical findings are validated through numerical computations.

For a closed four-manifold $X$ possessing an indefinite intersection form, we examine smoothly embedded surfaces within $X \setminus $int$(B^4)$ whose boundaries are knots $K \subset S^3$. We introduce multiple approaches to limit the genus of these surfaces within a specified homology class, utilizing techniques such as adjunction inequalities and the $10/8 + 4$ theorem. Specifically, we derive obstructions for a knot to be H-slice—meaning it bounds a null-homologous disk—in a four-manifold and demonstrate that the collection of H-slice knots can identify exotic smooth structures on closed $4$-manifolds.

We examine a variation of the art gallery problem where guards are restricted to viewing only to the right within a monotone polygon; we refer to these as half-guards. We present a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for point guarding the entire monotone polygon, improving the best known ratio of 40 from [11] to 8. Additionally, we demonstrate that point guarding a monotone polygon using half-guards is NP-hard.

Deriving causal links from observed correlations represents an expanding field within probabilistic reasoning, rooted in the foundational contributions of Pearl and colleagues during the early 1990s. This study introduces a novel perspective grounded in category theory, distinguishing clearly between syntax (represented by string diagrams) and semantics (defined by stochastic matrices), linked through interpretations that act as structure-preserving functors. A central concept for determining causal effects is the intervention, which involves forcibly assigning a variable a specific value regardless of its prior tendencies. We model the impact of such an intervention as an endofunctor that executes "string diagram surgery" within the syntactic framework. This surgical process subsequently generates a new interventional distribution through the interpretation functor. Although computing interventional distributions solely from observed data is generally infeasible, we demonstrate that it is achievable in specific scenarios using a calculational method known as comb disintegration. We apply this approach to a classic example, predicting the causal impact of smoking on cancer while accounting for a confounding common cause. Following this illustration, we establish that the technique offers straightforward sufficient conditions for calculating interventions applicable to numerous contexts found in causal inference literature.

We demonstrate that if probabilistic or deterministic solvers operating in logarithmic or nearly logarithmic space, respectively, for undirected Laplacian matrices can be extended to handle slightly broader subclasses of linear systems, they become capable of solving all linear systems with comparable space constraints. Building on earlier work by Kyng and Zhang regarding similar outcomes in the time complexity domain through reductions between approximate solvers, we establish that their reductions can be executed via constant-depth, polynomial-size threshold circuits.

Typically, the topological corner state in two-dimensional second-order topological insulators (2D SOTIs) is understood as a domain wall state arising from mass inversion between adjacent edges with a $\pi$ phase shift. In this study, we extend beyond this conventional framework by reporting a fractional mass-kink-induced 2D SOTI in monolayer FeSe exhibiting canted checkerboard antiferromagnetic (AFM) order, using both analytical modeling and first-principles calculations. The in-plane Zeeman field generated by the canted spins gaps the quantum spin Hall edge states of FeSe, creating a fractional mass-kink with a $\pi/2$ phase shift at rectangular corners. This results in an in-gap topological corner state possessing a fractional charge of $e/4$. Furthermore, this topological corner state demonstrates robustness against local perturbations, persisting across both naturally and artificially cleaved corners irrespective of edge orientation. Our findings not only identify a material platform for realizing unique 2D AFM SOTIs but also offer a novel approach to engineering higher-order topological states via fractional mass-kinks with arbitrary phase shifts, a development anticipated to attract immediate experimental interest.

Standard BCS superconductors are anticipated to show conductivity with negligible dissipation as temperature drops. Although bulk property measurements classify PdPb$_{2}$ as a conventional superconductor with a critical temperature ($T_c$) of 3.0 K, surface impedance data obtained via microwave cavity perturbation reveal a significant, non-vanishing dissipative component below $T_c$, contradicting conventional superconductivity. We establish PdPb$_2$ as a candidate topological superconductor featuring a fully gapped bulk and a dissipative Majorana fluid on its surface.

This study investigates spiral shocks within a steady, adiabatic, non-axisymmetric accretion disk surrounding a compact star in a binary system. By incorporating the Roche potential and Coriolis forces into the fundamental conservation equations, we account for all binary-induced influences. To streamline the analysis, we assume the spiral shocks are locally self-similar and that the flow maintains vertical hydrostatic equilibrium. Furthermore, we explore mass outflows resulting from shock compression and apply these findings to an accreting white dwarf in a binary. Our results demonstrate that this model offers a significant advantage by eliminating the arbitrary assumption of an optically thick wind typically employed in research on Type Ia supernova progenitors.

Utilizing previously established cluster estimates for spectral projectors, we derive reversed Strichartz estimates for shifted wave equations on non-trapping asymptotically hyperbolic manifolds. These results resolve an unresolved issue from \cite{SSWZ} concerning the endpoint case in the global well-posedness of nonlinear wave equations. Furthermore, we present corresponding estimates for the maximal wave operator within this framework.

This paper introduces a two-factor structural partial differential equation (PDE) framework for pricing puttable bonds incorporating credit risk and derives an analytical pricing formula. Initially, a two-factor structural PDE model for zero-coupon bonds with credit risk is established; under specific conditions regarding default boundaries and recovery rates, the analytical formula is derived, and the strict monotonicity of the bond price function with respect to firm value is demonstrated. Subsequently, a two-factor model for options on credit-risky zero-coupon bonds is presented, yielding an analytical pricing formula under certain exercise price conditions. This is achieved by transforming the two-factor model into a terminal boundary value problem for the Black-Scholes equation with time-dependent coefficients, utilizing the zero-coupon bond as a numeraire. Leveraging this approach, the paper derives pricing formulas for both puttable and callable bonds with credit risk.

Knowledge graph embedding entails deriving representations for entities (graph vertices) and relations (graph edges) so that these representations capture existing factual data, maintain internal consistency, and facilitate the inference of new relations. We demonstrate that knowledge graph embedding can be naturally formulated using the topological and categorical framework of \textit{cellular sheaves}; specifically, learning an embedding is equivalent to learning a \textit{knowledge sheaf} over the graph under specific constraints. Beyond offering a generalized framework for reasoning about these models, this sheaf-theoretic viewpoint allows for the expression of a wide range of prior constraints on embeddings and provides novel inferential abilities. By utilizing recent spectral theory regarding sheaf Laplacians, we analyze the local and global consistency of embeddings and devise new methods for reasoning over composite relations via harmonic extension relative to the sheaf Laplacian. Finally, we apply these concepts to demonstrate the advantages of the extensions arising from this fresh perspective.

Geometry optimization is a fundamental component of computational materials and surface science, serving as the essential route to identifying ground-state atomic structures and reaction mechanisms. These structures enable the prediction of thermodynamic and kinetic characteristics for both molecular and crystalline systems. However, performing this process at the quantum level is time-consuming due to the iterative calculation of forces required by quantum chemical methods like density functional theory (DFT); these methods are computationally intensive and often constrain the efficiency of optimization algorithms. Accelerating this workflow would be highly beneficial, allowing researchers to complete existing tasks faster or undertake more work within the same timeframe. This study introduces a neural network (NN) ensemble-based active learning approach designed to speed up local geometry optimization across multiple configurations at once. We demonstrate this acceleration through several case studies involving bare metal surfaces, surfaces with adsorbates, and nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations for two distinct reactions. In every scenario, the accelerated method reduces the number of required DFT calculations compared to standard techniques. Furthermore, we have developed an ASE-optimizer Python package to simplify the implementation of NN ensemble active learning for geometry optimization.

Recent self-supervised pre-training has achieved significant success on large-scale multimodal datasets, with state-of-the-art contrastive learning approaches typically enforcing feature consistency across cross-modal inputs like video/audio or video/text pairs. Although this cross-modality alignment (CMA) is practical to implement, it offers only weak and noisy supervision because semantic alignment is not guaranteed even when modalities are temporally synchronized. For instance, in instructional videos, speakers may reference objects absent from the current frame, a problem that becomes far more unpredictable with raw internet videos. We hypothesize that these inconsistencies create conflicts and biases among modalities, potentially hindering CMA's ability to scale to larger, more heterogeneous datasets. To test this, we observed that even in the latest VATT pre-training using instructional videos, strong gradient conflicts exist between different CMA losses within the same video, audio, and text triplet, identifying them as a source of noisy supervision. We then propose two techniques to harmonize these gradients: (i) cross-modality gradient realignment, which adjusts CMA loss gradients for each sample triplet to align their directions, and (ii) gradient-based curriculum learning, which uses conflict information as a noise indicator to prioritize training on cleaner samples. Applying these methods to VATT pre-training on the HowTo100M dataset consistently improved performance across various downstream tasks. Furthermore, we successfully scaled VATT pre-training to the more complex, non-narrative Youtube8M dataset, achieving further state-of-the-art improvements.

Modeling the recovery of interdependent critical infrastructure is essential for quantifying and optimizing societal resilience against disruptive events; however, simulating such large-scale systems under random disruptions is computationally intensive. To address this, this paper proposes using Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets) to accelerate the modeling of interdependent system recovery. As DeepONets are machine learning architectures capable of identifying mathematical operators from data, and the operators they detect align closely with the governing equations of interdependent system recovery, we hypothesize that DeepONets can efficiently model these recoveries even with limited training data. We tested this approach on a simplified scenario involving four interdependent systems with sixteen states. Overall, DeepONets performed satisfactorily in predicting the recovery of these systems for out-of-training samples when compared to reference results.

The LHCb detector investigates the production of the $\eta_c (1S)$ state in proton-proton collisions by analyzing its decay into the $p \bar{p}$ final state, specifically within the rapidity interval $2.0 < y < 4.5$ and for transverse momenta exceeding $6.5$ GeV/c. For the first time, the ratio of the prompt $\eta_c (1S)$ cross-section to the prompt $J/\psi$ cross-section is measured at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 7$ TeV using 0.7 fb$^{-1}$ of data, yielding $\sigma_{\eta_c (1S)}/\sigma_{J/\psi} = 1.74 \pm 0.29 \pm 0.28 \pm 0.18 _{B}$. At $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 2.0 fb$^{-1}$, this ratio is found to be $1.60 \pm 0.29 \pm 0.25 \pm 0.17 _{B}$. The listed uncertainties correspond sequentially to statistical, systematic, and the uncertainty regarding the ratio of branching fractions for the decays of $\eta_c (1S)$ and $J/\psi$ to $p \bar{p}$. Additionally, the inclusive branching fraction for $b$-hadron decays into $\eta_c (1S)$ mesons is determined for the first time as $B ( b \rightarrow \eta_c X ) = (4.88 \pm 0.64 \pm 0.29 \pm 0.67 _{B}) \times 10^{-3}$, where the final uncertainty also encompasses the uncertainty in the inclusive $J/\psi$ branching fraction from $b$-hadron decays. Finally, the mass difference between the $\eta_c (1S)$ and $J/\psi$ mesons is established to be $114.7 \pm 1.5 \pm 0.1$ MeV/c$^2$.

We introduce a novel neural network method for separating galaxies in astronomical imagery, built upon a Residual Dense Network (RDN) architecture. The model is trained on synthetic galaxy images that mimic the typical field configurations, incorporating realistic noise and finite point spread functions (PSF). Our approach's primary innovation lies in employing two separate networks: a deblending network that extracts individual galaxy images from composites, and a classifier network that counts the remaining galaxies. The deblending process works iteratively, removing one galaxy at a time until the classifier indicates no further objects remain or other stopping conditions are met. We evaluate deblending quality by analyzing the consistency between the outputs of both networks. Furthermore, we assess flux and shape reconstruction accuracy across various quality tiers and compare our method against the standard SExtractor tool, while also outlining potential future improvements to handle variable PSFs and noise levels.

Formal verification is highly valuable for compilers because errors in them undermine high-level correctness assurances, yet incorporating proof patches can make compiler modifications more laborious. A promising solution involves modeling compilers as collections of algebraic rewrite rules that a generic engine can apply efficiently. This modular approach allows each rule to be verified independently, eliminating the need to re-verify proofs for other compiler sections. We introduce the first implementation of this concept as a framework for the Coq proof assistant. Our new Coq command automatically integrates standard proved theorems into high-performance, verified compilers. We demonstrated the framework's effectiveness by enhancing the Fiat Cryptography toolchain for cryptographic arithmetic, resulting in an extracted command-line compiler that is approximately 1,000 times faster and relies on significantly simpler compiler-specific proofs.

This study introduces deep neural network (DNN) learning algorithms grounded in forward and backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) to solve high-dimensional quasilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), which are linked to FBSDEs via the Pardoux-Peng framework. These methods utilize a training procedure that minimizes the pathwise discrepancy between discrete stochastic processes derived from the time-discretized FBSDEs and the DNN approximations of the PDE solutions. The proposed approach successfully generates DNN solutions for a 100-dimensional Black–Scholes–Barenblatt equation, achieving accuracy within a specific region of the solution space and exhibiting a convergence rate comparable to the Euler–Maruyama discretization employed for the FBSDEs. Consequently, applying Richardson extrapolation across time discretizations can further refine the accuracy of these DNN solutions. Additionally, for time-oscillatory solutions, the implementation of a multiscale DNN enhances the performance of the FBSDE-based DNN when handling high-frequency components.

Recent advancements in Machine Learning (ML) for Natural Language Processing (NLP) have increasingly influenced the creation of superior computer vision algorithms. This study leverages NLP-inspired methodologies to enhance the accuracy, robustness, and generalizability of ML models designed for simulating transient dynamics. By implementing teacher forcing and curriculum learning strategies to model vortical flows, we demonstrate an accuracy improvement of over 50% for ML architectures such as FNO and UNet.

We explore the detection potential of the gravitational-wave background (GWB) generated by the collapse of population III stars. While GWB from younger population I/II stars would manifest in the LIGO/Virgo frequency band during the inspiral phase, signals from population III stars are expected to appear in the later merger and ringdown phases. We demonstrate that a network of third-generation detectors could distinguish between population I/II and population III signals, assuming individual coalescence events can be subtracted. Detecting a population III GWB would provide critical insights, such as the average redshifted total mass.

The emergence of viral outbreaks has compelled the implementation of contact tracing and infection monitoring protocols. Although numerous initiatives have been undertaken, no unified standard currently exists for these practices. Consequently, many countries have devised their own mechanisms to track disease carriers and their contacts. These generalized approaches are implemented either in a distributed framework that grants citizens control over their personal data, or in a centralized system where health authorities collect information on infected individuals. This paper examines some of the most prominent contact tracing strategies adopted globally. Furthermore, it provides a comprehensive review of the key enabling technologies underpinning these infection tracking infrastructures and offers recommendations for developing the most effective practices in this field.

We investigate Edgeworth expansions within limit theorems concerning self-normalized sums. By imposing only minimal moment conditions, we establish non-uniform bounds for expansions in the central limit theorem. This framework also addresses non-integer moments, which result in a diminished remainder term. Additionally, we derive non-uniform bounds for expansions in local limit theorems. The improved tail accuracy of these non-uniform bounds enables the derivation of an Edgeworth-type expansion for the entropic central limit theorem and a central limit theorem in total variation distance for self-normalized sums.

Based on density functional theory, we predict the existence of Weyl points in the rhombohedral, symmorphic structure of PtNiO$_2$. Structural stability is confirmed through formation energy and phonon calculations. The system exhibits a ferromagnetic ground state with an effective magnetic moment of 1.01 $\mu_B$ per unit cell. The electronic structure is primarily driven by Pt-$5d$, Ni-$3d$, and O-$2p$ orbitals, featuring band crossings near the Fermi level. Around 8 eV above the Fermi level, the electronic structure resembles a kagome lattice, dominated by Pt-$s,p$ orbitals, a finding supported by the surface Fermi surface spectral function. We identified 20 pairs of confirmed Weyl nodes aligned along the magnetic easy axis [100]. These findings are anticipated to offer a valuable and engaging platform for investigating magnetic Weyl physics within delafossites.

This study examines robust linear regression in the presence of an oblivious adversary, one who understands the data distribution but remains unaware of specific sample realizations. While this framework has been explored before, prior research relied on stringent conditions: specifically, $\textbf{(i)}$ the requirement that the feature covariance matrix be positive definite, and $\textbf{(ii)}$ the assumption that features possess a zero mean. Furthermore, earlier studies imposed additional restrictive constraints, such as Gaussian distributions for features or symmetric corruption patterns.

Our work extends beyond these limitations by analyzing robust regression under broader conditions: $\textbf{(i)}$ the covariance matrix may be either positive definite or positive semi-definite; $\textbf{(ii)}$ the features need not be centered; and $\textbf{(iii)}$ we impose no further restrictions beyond the boundedness (sub-Gaussianity) of the features and noise. Under these relaxed assumptions, we evaluate a natural variant of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). We demonstrate that when the covariance matrix is positive definite, this method achieves a rapid convergence rate. In the positive semi-definite scenario, we identify two distinct regimes: if the features are centered, a standard convergence rate is attainable; however, if they are not, the adversary can cause any learning algorithm to fail arbitrarily.

We have reconstructed a complete type II superstring field theory possessing L-infinity structure in a symmetric manner with respect to both left- and right-moving sectors. Leveraging this new framework, we demonstrate once more that the tree-level S-matrix aligns with results derived from the first-quantization approach. Beyond offering a straightforward and elegant reconstruction, this method allows the action to be mapped onto that of the WZW-like superstring field theory; this specific mapping had previously been absent, thereby completing the sole missing component of the WZW-like formulation.

Categorization plays a crucial role in numerous decision-making tasks, yet it can sometimes disrupt these outcomes, leading to violations of the law of total probability. To forecast such interference effects, researchers have developed models grounded in quantum probability. This paper introduces a novel Quantum Dynamic Belief (QDB) model. Recognizing that decisions are rarely made with absolute certainty during the process, the model incorporates uncertainty to better simulate actual human cognition. By processing uncertain information, the QDB model successfully predicts the interference caused by categorization. The model was tested on a categorization decision-making experiment to elucidate these interference effects. Compared to existing approaches, the proposed model is notably more concise, and the results demonstrate its validity and effectiveness.

Random Projection (RP) is a foundational technique in machine learning and various other fields, widely utilized for dimensionality reduction, approximate near-neighbor search, and compressed sensing. Essentially, RP offers a straightforward and efficient approach to approximating pairwise inner products and Euclidean distances within massive datasets. Closely linked to RP, Random Fourier Features (RFF) have gained popularity for approximating the Gaussian kernel. RFF employs a specific nonlinear transformation on data projected by random projections. In practical applications, the nonlinear Gaussian kernel often yields superior performance compared to the linear kernel (inner product), largely because of the tuning parameter $\gamma$ inherent to the Gaussian kernel. Consequently, recent research has increasingly focused on analyzing the properties of RFF.

Following random projections, quantization serves as a crucial step for optimizing data storage, computation, and transmission. While quantization for RP has been extensively investigated in existing literature, this paper concentrates on developing quantization algorithms specifically for RFF. This task presents unique challenges due to the $\gamma$ parameter in the Gaussian kernel; for instance, traditional quantizers and their resulting data may be tightly coupled to a specific value of $\gamma$. Our work begins with a key insight: the marginal distribution of RFF is actually independent of the Gaussian kernel parameter $\gamma$. This observation significantly streamlines the design of the Lloyd-Max (LM) quantization scheme for RFF, as it allows for a single LM quantizer applicable regardless of $\gamma$. Additionally, we introduce a variant called the LM$^2$-RFF quantizer, which demonstrates higher accuracy in certain scenarios. Experimental results validate that the proposed quantization schemes perform effectively.

The success of Transformers in natural language processing has inspired the computer vision community to develop Vision Transformers (ViTs). Unlike Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), ViTs possess a larger receptive field that effectively captures long-range dependencies; however, this advantage comes with significant computational costs. To address efficiency, window-based Vision Transformers were introduced, which divide images into local windows and perform self-attention within each. To restore global context, these models rely on complex operations to facilitate communication between windows. This work investigates the necessity of a core component of the Swin Transformer: shifted window partitioning. We find that simple depthwise convolution alone is sufficient for effective cross-window communication. Specifically, the shifted window configuration in Swin Transformer fails to provide additional performance gains when depthwise convolution is present. Consequently, we simplify the Swin Transformer into a plain Window-based (Win) Transformer by removing the complex shifted window mechanism. The resulting Win Transformer is conceptually simpler and easier to implement than Swin Transformer. Furthermore, our Win Transformer consistently outperforms Swin Transformer across various computer vision tasks, including image recognition, semantic segmentation, and object detection.

This study introduces a fully implicit numerical technique grounded in the space-time finite element method to address the Dirac equation across 1+1, 2+1, and 3+1 dimensional spaces. The implementation of the resulting linear systems employs the PETSc/Tao library, leveraging Krylov subspace solvers like GMRES. The proposed method is validated through an examination of various scenarios, including plane wave solutions, Zitterbewegung, and the Klein paradox, alongside an assessment of the parallel performance of the implementation.

This work addresses universal compression for memoryless sources under a fidelity constraint by constructing a dictionary codebook over the reproduction alphabet to parse the source stream. When a source subsequence falls within a specified distortion threshold of a dictionary codeword, the corresponding codeword index is transmitted as the output. Our proposed dictionary comprises coverings of type classes located at the transition boundary between low and high empirical lossy rates. Furthermore, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the $\epsilon$-coding rate, including up to the third-order term, for sufficiently large dictionaries.

In classical cryptography, commitments are equivalent to one-way functions; however, in the quantum realm, while commitments do not necessarily imply one-way functions, all current constructions rely on them. This work investigates whether one-way functions are truly essential for quantum commitments. We demonstrate that non-interactive quantum commitments (for classical messages) featuring computational hiding and statistical binding can exist provided pseudorandom quantum states (PRQS) exist. PRQS are efficiently generatable sets of quantum states whose polynomially many copies are computationally indistinguishable from Haar random states. Notably, PRQS are known to exist even if $\BQP=\QMA$ relative to a quantum oracle, a scenario where no quantum-secure classical cryptographic primitive exists. Consequently, our findings establish that quantum commitments can exist without any quantum-secure classical primitives, including one-way functions. Furthermore, we examine digital signatures, another fundamental cryptographic primitive. We prove that one-time secure digital signatures with quantum public keys also exist under the assumption of PRQS. While classical digital signatures are equivalent to one-way functions, our results indicate that quantum signatures can exist even in the absence of any quantum-secure classical cryptographic primitive, including quantum-secure one-way functions.

It is widely recognized that training deep neural networks yields representations that encapsulate the essential characteristics of input data. Nevertheless, these representations remain poorly understood both theoretically and practically. A key question in supervised learning is whether such representations successfully isolate features relevant for classification while discarding noisy, non-informative ones. To address this, we formalize the issue using a generative framework where each class corresponds to a distinct high-dimensional manifold. In this model, every input is generated from two latent vectors: (i) a "manifold identifier" $\gamma$ and (ii) a "transformation parameter" $\theta$ that adjusts the position of an example along the manifold's surface. For instance, $\gamma$ could denote a standard image of a dog, whereas $\theta$ might account for variations in pose, background, or lighting. We offer both theoretical and empirical evidence demonstrating that neural representations function similarly to Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH), mapping inputs to embeddings determined solely by the informative $\gamma$ and remaining invariant to $\theta$, thereby effectively recovering the manifold identifier. A significant outcome of this mechanism is the ability to perform one-shot learning on previously unseen classes.

Monitoring and responding to unauthorized activities is a cornerstone of security surveillance, yet it is complicated by the vast quantity and diversity of hosts and processes requiring observation, compounded by the absence of precise definitions for normal behavior within each category. Host profiling through stream clustering offers an effective solution for analyzing, categorizing, and flagging anomalous host behaviors; however, unforeseen shifts in behavioral data, known as concept drift, render static profiles unreliable. DenStream, a widely recognized incremental extension of the non-parametric DBSCAN algorithm, is commonly applied to host profiling but has been shown in recent studies to lack robustness against concept drift. This paper introduces DenDrift, a drift-aware host profiling method built upon DenStream that integrates non-negative matrix factorization for dimensionality reduction and the Page-Hinckley test for drift detection. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and industrial datasets confirm that DenDrift effectively withstands abrupt, gradual, and incremental drifts.

Audio source separation models like U-Net and Wave-U-Net are typically specialized for a single task, such as isolating a specific instrument, and often perform worse when trained on multiple tasks simultaneously. This paper introduces the Conditioned-U-Net (C-U-Net), which enhances the standard U-Net with a control mechanism. This allows a single, generic model to handle the separation of various instruments. The C-U-Net determines the target instrument based on a one-hot-encoding input vector, which is then embedded to generate parameters for Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) layers. These layers apply affine transformations to the U-Net's feature maps to isolate the desired instrument. Consequently, the C-U-Net achieves performance levels comparable to dedicated models while handling different instrument separations with a single architecture at a reduced cost.

Inspired by recent advancements regarding the black hole information problem, specifically the holographic triality of the AdS/BCFT framework and the newly proposed "PEE=CFF (component flow flux)" prescription within the bit thread formulation, we investigate the partial entanglement entropy (PEE) in holographic BCFT setups involving entanglement islands. Our work offers a bit thread description of the AdS/BCFT system, elucidating the specific entanglement structures between various system components in the presence of an island and potentially offering deeper insights into the black hole information paradox. Additionally, we demonstrate that within the island context, it is crucial to differentiate between fine-grained PEE and semi-classical PEE. Notably, mirroring the island rule for fine-grained entropy in the semi-classical regime, we also formulate island rules for fine-grained PEE.

For any finite group $G$, we examine the directed graph $\Gamma(G)$, defined with non-hypercentral elements as vertices and an edge from $x$ to $y$ whenever $[x,_ny]=1$ for some natural number $n$. We demonstrate that $\Gamma(G)$ is invariably weakly connected and becomes strongly connected provided that the quotient group $G/Z_{\infty}(G)$ is neither Frobenius nor almost simple.

We analyze mass, momentum, energy, and metal outflow rates in multi-phase galactic winds using a suite of FIRE-2 cosmological "zoom-in" simulations from the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE) project. Our analysis covers low-mass dwarfs, intermediate-mass dwarfs, Milky Way-mass halos, and high-redshift massive halos. Aligning with prior studies, we observe that dwarfs expel approximately 100 times more gas from their interstellar medium (ISM) than they convert into stars, whereas this mass "loading factor" falls below one in massive galaxies. In massive halos, the majority of the mass is transported by the hot phase ($>10^5$ K), while in dwarfs, it is carried by the warm phase ($10^3-10^5$ K); cold outflows ($<10^3$ K) are negligible except in high-redshift dwarfs. Energy, momentum, and metal loading factors from the ISM are roughly unity in dwarfs but significantly lower in more massive halos. Hot outflows possess 2–5 times the specific energy required to escape the gravitational potential of dwarf halos. Specifically, in dwarfs, mass, momentum, and metal outflow rates increase with radius while energy remains roughly conserved, suggesting the sweeping up of halo gas. Burst-averaged mass loading factors are generally higher during intense star formation episodes and when the inner halo is not virialized, yet we detect no effective trend related to the dense ISM gas fraction. Finally, we discuss how these findings can inform future controlled numerical experiments designed to identify the key parameters governing galactic winds and their associated preventative feedback.

This study reports the first observation of the simultaneous production of three massive gauge bosons (VVV, where V represents W or Z) in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The analysis utilizes a data set from the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC, encompassing an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$. Searches for individual WWW, WWZ, WZZ, and ZZZ production were conducted in final states containing three to six leptons (electrons or muons) or in configurations with two same-sign leptons accompanied by one or two jets. The combined VVV signal shows an observed significance of 5.7 standard deviations (with an expected significance of 5.9), and the measured cross section relative to the Standard Model prediction is 1.02 $^{+0.26}_{-0.23}$. Additionally, the individual significances for WWW and WWZ production are determined to be 3.3 and 3.4 standard deviations, respectively, with corresponding measured cross sections for each triboson process also provided.

The 2018 U.S. Farm Bill transitioned industrial hemp cultivation from restricted pilot initiatives into a formal, regulated agricultural framework. Despite this shift, the industrial hemp supply chain (IHSC) encounters significant hurdles, such as high complexity and variability, scarce production expertise, and insufficient data tracking. To address these issues, this study proposes a blockchain-integrated IHSC and establishes a preliminary simulation-based digital twin for the distributed cyber-physical system (CPS) to facilitate process learning and risk management. Specifically, we designed a two-layer blockchain utilizing proof-of-authority smart contracts to track critical data, enhance transparency, and engage local authorities and state regulators for quality control verification. Furthermore, we implemented a stochastic simulation-based digital twin for IHSC risk management, capable of modeling spatial-temporal causal interdependencies and dynamic evolution to support risk mitigation and decision-making. Empirical results demonstrate the promising efficacy of the proposed platform.

We demonstrate that for any closed manifold M with a dimension of 6 or higher, the minimum count of critical points for a function defined on M matches exactly the minimum number of components required in a Singhof-Takens filling of M using smooth balls that have corners.

We present calculations of the cyclotron spin-flip excitation (CSFE) within a spin-polarized quantum Hall system at unit filling. This mode includes a double-exciton component that contributes to the CSFE correlation energy but remains inaccessible through mean field methods. The findings are compared with existing experimental data.

Frequency Containment Reserves may fail to deliver adequate responses during scenarios characterized by significant disturbances and low inertia. To address this, the study evaluates a supplementary droop frequency-based Emergency Power Control (EPC) mechanism utilizing HVDC interconnections within a detailed Nordic Power System model. The analysis centers on EPC allocation strategies and the specific factors influencing HVDC link performance, prioritizing maximum instantaneous frequency deviation and the magnitude of deployed EPC power. Although the methodology is grounded in theoretical observations regarding linearized system representations, the investigated properties—including active and reactive power contributions, their ratios, and the energy impact on total loads and losses—reflect highly nonlinear system dynamics. Ultimately, the study concludes with observations on the practical significance of EPC distribution for mitigating frequency nadirs.

We introduce our submission for the 2021 PhysioNet/CinC challenge, which utilizes a waveform transformer to identify cardiac anomalies within ECG data. Leveraging approximately 88,000 recordings from six distinct datasets, we evaluated the model's performance across various ECG lead configurations. In the official standings, our team, prna, placed between 9th and 15th on 12-, 6-, 4-, 3-, and 2-lead subsets, respectively. The model achieved an average challenge metric of 0.47 on the held-out test set across all lead subsets. Ultimately, our aggregated performance across all leads secured a rank of 11 out of 39 officially ranked teams.

By December 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic had infected more than 75 million individuals, marking it as the most lethal pandemic in modern history.
