This research introduces a new compartmental epidemiological model tailored to SARS-CoV-2, evaluating the impact of standard preventive strategies including vaccination, testing, social distancing, and quarantine. By incorporating the most widespread interventions aimed at curbing viral transmission, the study lays a critical groundwork for future mathematical modeling of COVID-19 and emerging pandemics. The model extends the traditional SIR framework by adding distinct compartments for those in the incubation period, asymptomatic cases, individuals who tested positive, quarantined persons, vaccinated individuals, and the deceased, while also considering variable rates for infection, testing, and mortality. The analysis begins with the outbreak in Santa Clara County, California, before generalizing the results. Findings indicate that while all measures help slow transmission, quarantine and social distancing mandates are the most effective in lowering infection rates, followed by vaccine distribution and public testing. Consequently, governments should prioritize resources toward enforcing quarantine and social distancing policies. Furthermore, the study provides mathematical evidence that the virus's rapid spread is driven significantly by its high asymptomatic rate and extended incubation period.

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers have utilized deep learning to classify pneumonia caused by the virus. However, like many medical imaging tasks, these efforts are often constrained by limited data quantity and quality. This study trains a deep learning model on publicly sourced COVID-19 images and assesses its performance using chest X-rays from a local hospital, which have been carefully reviewed and labeled by two radiologists to ensure high-quality evaluation of the model's generalization. Additionally, we employ a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to create synthetic X-ray images derived from this dataset. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating these synthetic images for data augmentation significantly enhances model performance, suggesting a promising strategy for addressing data scarcity in various domains.

Entanglement serves as a fundamental physical property of quantum systems that underpins the difficulty of simulating them. Although the runtime of specific methods, such as tensor network algorithms, is known to depend directly on entanglement levels, it remains unclear whether entanglement also drives intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic complexity. This study quantitatively links the entanglement in specific quantum systems to the complexity of their simulation and fully characterizes both as functions of a system parameter. Focusing on simulating single-qubit measurements of $k$-regular graph states on $n$ qubits, we demonstrate a sharp transition from an easy, low-entanglement regime to a hard, high-entanglement regime as regularity increases from $1$ to $n-1$. This transition occurs at $k=3$ when moving into the hard regime and reverses at $k=n-3$ when returning to the easy regime. A pivotal technical achievement of this work is the proof of a duality in simulation complexity between low and high regularity for these graph states.

The claim made by Xiangchun Xiao, Guoping Zhao, and Guorong Zhou in [J. Pseudo-Differ. Oper. Appl., (2021) 12:60] is flawed. Furthermore, their work in [2] does not offer a novel characterization of weaving for g-frames. In fact, their interpretation regarding a characterization of weaving g-frames in separable Hilbert spaces is incorrect, as this result was already established by Deepshikha, Vashisht, and Verma in [1].

Observing vortical flow structures at the pore scale within porous media presents a major challenge for numerous natural and industrial applications. The dynamics of these vortices are hypothesized to drive the transition from unsteady laminar to turbulent flow in the porous regime, governed by the pore Reynolds number ($Re_p$). To test this hypothesis, a refractive-index-matched, randomly packed porous medium was developed to measure vortical structure scales during this transition using two-dimensional time-resolved Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV). Planar PIV data spanning $Re_p$ values from 100 to 948 were analyzed to quantify vortex size, strength, and number density using two scaling approaches: (i) macroscopic $Re_p$ and (ii) microscopic $Re_{\langle p\rangle}$. Vortex scales were directly measured via swirl strength, vortex core, and enhanced swirl strength identification techniques, then compared against turbulent integral scales. Results indicated that moderate unsteady laminar conditions ($Re_p < 300$) featured shear-dominant structures, whereas weak turbulent conditions ($Re_p > 500$) exhibited swirl-dominant structures. Macroscopically, increasing $Re_p$ caused vortex sizes to decrease asymptotically to 20% of the global hydraulic diameter, increased vortex strength, and raised average vortex number density. Conversely, at the pore scale, rising $Re_{\langle p\rangle}$ led to a monotonic reduction in vortex size, an increase in strength, and no change in number density. These observations imply a coupling between pore-scale and macro-scale effects regarding vortical flow structure scales during the transition regime.

Multiple research efforts have sought to generalize Witten's cubic open string field theory into a cubic closed string field theory capable of consistently describing Einstein gravity at low energies. This study introduces such a theory by incorporating a double layer to represent the closed string world-sheet, extending the framework of Witten's open string world-sheet. By mapping the closed string world-sheet onto the complex plane—where the lower half is fully covered by the extended string sector—we utilized the Green's function on this plane to evaluate the Polyakov string path integral. This process yielded the Neumann functions and vertex operators, from which we derived the one- and two-string vertices (identities) and ultimately the cubic string vertex operator. Notably, the resulting cubic string scattering amplitude aligns with the cubic graviton interaction of Einstein gravity, confirming that the proposed cubic closed string field theory consistently describes this gravitational framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Kawai-Lewellen-Tye (KLT) relations of first-quantized string theory are explicitly realized within this cubic closed string field theory.

Historically, core Hebrew NLP tasks like segmentation, tagging, and parsing have depended on different versions of the Hebrew Treebank (HTB; Sima'an et al. 2001). Yet, since the HTB is a single-source newswire corpus from over 30 years ago, it fails to capture many facets of modern Hebrew found on the web. This paper introduces a new, freely accessible Universal Dependencies (UD) treebank for Hebrew, derived from diverse topics within Hebrew Wikipedia. Beyond presenting the corpus and assessing annotation quality, we implement automatic validation tools based on grew (Guillaume, 2021) and perform the first cross-domain parsing experiments in Hebrew. Our approach yields new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining the latest language modeling techniques with incremental enhancements to existing transformer-based methods. Additionally, we release an updated version of the UD HTB that aligns with the annotation scheme refined by our new corpus.

Current Human-Object Interaction (HOI) detection approaches predominantly depend on comprehensive annotations involving predefined HOI categories, a strategy that suffers from limited diversity and high scalability costs. This work seeks to advance zero-shot HOI detection to simultaneously identify both familiar and novel interactions. The core difficulties involve uncovering potential human-object pairs and recognizing new HOI categories. To address these issues, we introduce a novel end-to-end zero-shot HOI Detection (EoID) framework utilizing vision-language knowledge distillation. Initially, we develop an Interactive Score module paired with a Two-stage Bipartite Matching algorithm to distinguish human-object interactions in an action-agnostic way. Subsequently, we transfer action probability distributions from a pretrained vision-language teacher and observed ground truth to the HOI model to achieve zero-shot classification. Comprehensive experiments on the HICO-Det dataset confirm that our model successfully identifies potential interactive pairs and recognizes unseen HOIs. Furthermore, our method surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by 8.92% and 10.18% on unseen and overall mAP respectively under the UA setting, and by 6.02% and 9.1% under the UC setting. Additionally, the approach demonstrates generalizability to large-scale object detection data for expanding action sets. The source code will be released at: https://github.com/mrwu-mac/EoID.

To investigate the gas dynamics of typical molecular clouds in numerical simulations, we analyze the Fourier spectra and structure functions of two-dimensional centroid velocity (CV) maps. Our approach incorporates a simplified time-dependent chemical model and accounts for non-isothermal conditions, utilizing a 3D radiative transfer tool in a post-processing stage to simulate CO line emission. Simulations were conducted with three distinct initial mean number densities ($n_0 = 30, 100,$ and $300 \text{ cm}^{-3}$) to cover the range of dense gas conditions found in the solar neighborhood. We calculated the slopes of centroid velocity increment structure functions (CVISF) and Fourier spectra across various chemical components, including total density, $\text{H}_2$ number density, $\text{12CO}$ number density, and the integrated intensity of $\text{12CO}$ ($J=1\text{-}0$) and $\text{13CO}$ ($J=1\text{-}0$). Our results demonstrate that optical depth effects substantially influence CVISF slopes, resulting in distinct scaling behaviors for Fourier spectra. Specifically, the CVISF and Fourier spectrum slopes for $\text{H}_2$ are markedly steeper than those for CO tracers, regardless of density or numerical resolution. This discrepancy arises because $\text{H}_2$ possesses a larger space-filling factor due to its superior ability to self-shield in diffuse regions, which yields a higher fractal co-dimension compared to CO.

We introduce a general approach for addressing nonlinear integro-differential evolution problems subject to periodic boundary conditions, particularly in scenarios lacking direct maximum or minimum principles. This work is driven by recent macroscopic models describing active Brownian particles with repulsive interactions, which involve advection-diffusion dynamics in both particle position and orientation spaces. Specifically, we examine a semilinear parabolic equation featuring a nonlinear active drift term, where velocity relies on particle orientation and an angle-independent global density, resulting in a nonlocal term derived from integrating out the angular variable. The core of our existence analysis leverages a-priori estimates based on (approximate) entropy dissipation. We establish the global existence and uniqueness of weak solutions through a two-step Galerkin approximation that employs suitable cutoffs to ensure nonnegativity, bound the overall density, and maintain these a-priori estimates. Our analysis naturally accommodates finite systems, representing a finite number of directional states. Furthermore, the Duhamel principle is applied to derive additional regularity, specifically time-space continuity. Given the relevance of specific initial data classes for applications, such as perfectly aligned particles, we extend the well-posedness results to very weak solutions capable of handling distributional initial data with low regularity.

In dialogues, an utterance refers to a continuous sequence of sentences generated by a single speaker, varying in length from a brief statement to a post of up to a thousand words. When analyzing dialogues at the utterance level, it is frequent for a single utterance to fulfill multiple functions; for example, "Thank you. It works great." simultaneously conveys gratitude and positive feedback. The presence of multiple dialogue acts (DA) within one utterance creates intricate dependencies across dialogue turns. Consequently, recognizing these acts challenges a model's ability to predict outcomes over long utterances and within complex DA contexts. We define this specific challenge as Concurrent Dialogue Acts (CDA) recognition. Prior research on DA recognition has typically assumed only one DA per utterance or overlooked the sequential characteristics of dialogues. This paper introduces an adapted Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) designed to model interactions between utterances within long-range contexts. Our model demonstrates significant performance improvements over existing approaches in CDA recognition, validated on a technology forum dataset.

The efficacy of word embeddings stems from the linguistic principle that words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts, encapsulated by J.R. Firth's famous assertion, "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." Alongside his American counterpart Zellig Harris, Firth is widely recognized as a pioneer of distributional semantics. Although both scholars are frequently referenced in leading NLP textbooks and seminal research, the nuances and distinctions between their theoretical frameworks are rarely examined. A detailed analysis of their work reveals two fundamentally different and often divergent approaches to meaning: one concentrates solely on the internal mechanics of linguistic structures, whereas the other encourages viewing words within an expanded scope that includes not only other linguistic units but also broader cultural and situational contexts. By contrasting these perspectives against current NLP debates, Firth emerges as a potential guide toward a more culturally situated understanding of semantics. Furthermore, we explore practical strategies for modeling this enriched concept of "context," specifically through comparative stratification and syntagmatic extension.

Historical maps offer unique, detailed geographic insights spanning extended periods—such as 125 years in US topographic records—that are rarely available elsewhere. However, these maps are usually accessible only as scanned images lacking searchable metadata. Current methods for making these maps searchable depend on labor-intensive manual efforts, including crowd-sourcing, to create metadata like geolocations and keywords. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) can reduce manual labor, it typically identifies individual words rather than coherent location phrases (e.g., separating "Black" and "Mountain" instead of recognizing "Black Mountain"). This paper introduces an end-to-end solution to the practical challenge of locating and indexing historical map images. The proposed method automatically extracts text from historical maps and generates metadata linked to extensive external geospatial knowledge bases. By utilizing the Resource Description Framework (RDF) format, this linked metadata enables complex queries, such as retrieving all historical maps depicting mountain peaks exceeding 1,000 meters in California. We have developed a system named mapKurator to implement this approach and evaluated it using historical maps from diverse sources with varying styles, scales, and coverage. The results demonstrate a significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is publicly available as part of the Kartta Labs project modules at https://github.com/kartta-labs/Project.

Based on Hermitian physics, the topological spin-Hall effect drives distinct spins to travel in opposing directions, whereas the non-Hermitian skin effect induces the edge localization of numerous system modes. We introduce a system utilizing exciton-polariton elliptical micropillars that simultaneously exhibit both phenomena. The polarization splitting inherent to these elliptical structures generates the topological spin-Hall effect within a one-dimensional lattice. Furthermore, applying a circularly polarized, incoherent external laser to create an imbalance in the effective decay rates of different spin polarizations shifts the system into a non-Hermitian regime, manifesting the skin effect. These combined effects offer significant implications for robust polariton transport, the deterministic generation of multiply charged vortices, and the maintenance of persistent currents.

Let $G$ be a simple graph where $J(G)$ denotes the vertex cover ideal and $J(G)^{(s)}$ represents the $s$-th symbolic power of $J(G)$. We establish that $\reg(J(C)^{(s)}) = \reg(J(C)^s)$ for every $s \geq 1$ and any odd cycle $C$. For a simplicial complex $\Delta$, we demonstrate that if $I_{\Delta}^{\vee}$ is weakly polymatroidal, then $\Delta$ is vertex decomposable. Furthermore, considering a fully clique-whiskering graph $W = G^{\pi}$, we prove that $J(W)^s$ is weakly polymatroidal for all $s \geq 1$. Finally, we identify a critical flaw in the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.3]{M} and provide a corrected version.

Continual learning (CL) aims to develop models capable of mastering sequential tasks without suffering from catastrophic forgetting. Although numerous CL techniques exist, there is limited insight into how representations acquired from prior tasks aid in learning subsequent tasks. To investigate this, we examine continual representation learning (CRL), which involves evolving representations as new tasks emerge. Focusing on zero-forgetting approaches that embed tasks within subnetworks (such as PackNet), we first present experiments showing that CRL markedly enhances sample efficiency for new tasks. To elucidate this phenomenon, we derive theoretical guarantees for CRL by establishing sample complexity and generalization error bounds for new tasks, formalizing the statistical advantages of pre-learned representations. Our analysis and empirical results also underscore the significance of task learning order. Specifically, we demonstrate that CL performance improves when initial tasks involve large sample sizes and high "representation diversity." Such diversity minimizes representation mismatch upon adding new tasks, allowing them to be learned with few samples and minimal additional non-zero weights. Furthermore, we explore how to maintain inference efficiency for each task subnetwork while preserving representation learning benefits. To this end, we introduce Efficient Sparse PackNet (ESPN), an inference-optimized variant of PackNet utilizing joint channel and weight pruning. ESPN embeds tasks into channel-sparse subnets, reducing computational FLOPs by up to 80% while largely maintaining accuracy and remaining competitive against various baselines. In summary, this work advances data and compute-efficient CL through a representation learning lens. GitHub page: https://github.com/ucr-optml/CtRL

Neural network inference on edge devices is often constrained by limited resources, such as computing power, memory, and bandwidth. Beyond enhancing hardware design and optimizing model efficiency, aggregating the processing capabilities of multiple devices can facilitate machine learning. This paper introduces a novel approach utilizing model parallelism to distribute neural networks across devices for inference. To optimize the trade-off between communication latency, computation latency, and overall performance, we employ neural architecture search (NAS) to identify an optimal transmission policy that minimizes data transfer. Our best-performing model reduces data transmission volume by 86.6% compared to the baseline with negligible performance impact. Experiments under specific device configurations and model settings demonstrate that large-scale neural network inference on edge clusters can be effectively distributed and accelerated, offering a new pathway for deploying intelligent IoT applications.

In numerous developing nations, power generation capacity falls short of total electricity demand. To manage this imbalance, many countries implement routine load shedding, which disconnects entire regions from the grid. This practice causes significant hardship, disproportionately affecting households with higher electricity needs during outages. While Oluwasuji et al. [2020] recently highlighted this issue and proposed heuristic approaches, this study reframes electricity distribution as a fair division problem modeled through cake-cutting literature. We analyze time interval allocations for households across four scenarios: identical demand with uniform or additive utilities, and varying demand with uniform or additive utilities. Solutions are provided for the first two cases, while the latter two are examined through the lens of q-times bin packing and their connection to the consensus k-division problem. The analysis incorporates utilitarian and egalitarian social welfare metrics, aims to minimize the number of cuts, and considers minimizing the maximum utility disparity among agents as a secondary goal.

Population dynamics, a core component of population ecology, examines how organism population sizes fluctuate over time and space. A primary challenge in this field is that experimental costs and measurement limitations often restrict data collection to coarse time intervals at fixed locations. To address this, recent approaches have utilized continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) combined with dynamic optimal transport to infer sample trajectories from fixed-point observations. However, while CNFs produce deterministic sample behaviors, biological populations actually move in a fundamentally random yet directional fashion. Furthermore, transitions between points in dynamical systems typically adhere to the principle of least action, minimizing the corresponding action value. To align with these requirements, we formulate the Lagrangian Schrödinger bridge (LSB) problem and propose an approximate solution using regularized neural stochastic differential equations (SDEs) to model the advection-diffusion process. Additionally, we introduce a model architecture designed to accelerate loss function computation. Experimental results demonstrate that this method efficiently approximates population-level dynamics even in high-dimensional settings and leverages Lagrangian prior knowledge to estimate sample-level dynamics with appropriate stochastic behavior.

We present a detailed analysis of the thermal characteristics and neutral hydrogen (HI) content of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) at redshifts z~3-5, utilizing a new set of cosmological simulations focused on a Mpc-scale intergalactic sheet or "pancake." These simulations achieve unprecedented resolution for such a large volume, covering gas-cell masses spanning nearly three orders of magnitude, from approximately 7.7x10^6 to 1.5x10^4 solar masses. At z~5, a collision between two smaller sheets generates a strong accretion shock around the primary pancake. Subsequent rapid cooling in the post-shock region induces thermal instabilities, resulting in a multiphase medium. Our findings indicate that neither the mass, morphology, nor HI distribution within the WHIM has converged at our highest resolution. Notably, this lack of convergence is particularly pronounced in the less dense, metal-poor intra-pancake medium (IPM) located between filaments and distant from star-forming galaxies. As resolution improves, the IPM evolves into a shattered structure where ~kpc-scale clouds harbor the majority of the HI. Comparing our lowest to highest resolution runs, the covering fraction of metal-poor (Z<10^{-3}Zsun) Lyman-limit systems (NHI>10^{17.2}/cm^2) in the IPM at z~4 rises from 3-15%, while the fraction of Damped Lyman-alpha Absorbers (NHI>10^{20}/cm^2) with similar metallicity triples from 0.2-0.6%, showing no signs of convergence. We determine that resolving the cooling length, lcool=cs*tcool, at T~10^5K is essential for forming a multiphase, shattered structure; without this, gas accumulates at these temperatures, rendering cooling to lower temperatures highly inefficient. Ultimately, we conclude that current state-of-the-art cosmological simulations cannot yet resolve the multi-phase structure of the low-density IGM, a limitation with potentially significant implications.

We demonstrate that the algebra of cylinder functions, generated by a finite, positive Borel measure $\mathfrak{m}$ on the $(p,\mathsf{d})$-Wasserstein space $(\mathcal{P}_p(X,\mathsf{d}), W_{p, \mathsf{d}})$ over a complete and separable metric space $(X,\mathsf{d})$, is dense within the Wasserstein Sobolev space $H^{1,q}(\mathcal{P}_p(X,\mathsf{d}), W_{p, \mathsf{d}}, \mathfrak{m})$ with respect to the energy norm. As an application, we establish that for a separable Banach space $\mathbb{B}$, the corresponding Wasserstein Sobolev space is reflexive (respectively, uniformly convex) provided that $\mathbb{B}$ is reflexive (respectively, if the dual of $\mathbb{B}$ is uniformly convex). Furthermore, we outline sufficient conditions under which Clarkson's type inequalities hold in this Wasserstein Sobolev setting.

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) represents a leading strategy for overcoming the annotation limitations inherent in supervised learning. Modern SSL techniques effectively harness vast amounts of unlabeled data to enhance performance, relying only on a minimal labeled set. However, most existing methods operate under the assumption that labeled and unlabeled data share the same distribution, an assumption that often fails in real-world applications, thereby restricting their utility. This work addresses the more challenging open-world SSL scenario, which does not rely on this distributional assumption. In open-world SSL, the goal involves identifying samples from known classes while simultaneously detecting and clustering samples from novel classes found within the unlabeled data. We introduce OpenLDN, which employs a pairwise similarity loss to identify these new classes. Utilizing a bi-level optimization framework, this loss function leverages information from the labeled set to implicitly cluster novel class instances while recognizing known class samples. Once novel classes are discovered, OpenLDN converts the open-world SSL task into a standard SSL problem, enabling further performance improvements through established SSL methods. Comprehensive experiments show that OpenLDN surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches on several major classification benchmarks, offering a superior balance between accuracy and training time.

Deep reinforcement learning algorithms that estimate state and state-action value functions have proven effective across various challenging domains, including deriving control strategies directly from raw image pixels. However, these algorithms typically assume full state observability and must rely on finite observation histories or recurrent networks to handle partial observations. In this study, we introduce a novel deep reinforcement learning algorithm grounded in counterfactual regret minimization, which iteratively refines an advantage-like function approximation and demonstrates robustness against partially observed states. We show that this new approach significantly outperforms strong baseline methods on several partially observed reinforcement learning tasks, including first-person 3D navigation in Doom and Minecraft, as well as acting amidst partially observed objects in Doom and Pong.

Let $p\in[1,\infty)$, $K\in(0,\infty)$, and $\mu$ be a probability measure. We demonstrate that for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, and elements $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in L_p(\mu)$ satisfying $\big\| \max_{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}} |x_i| \big\|_{L_p(\mu)} \leq K$, there exists a dimension $d\leq \frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$ and vectors $y_1,\ldots, y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that
$$\forall \ i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, \qquad \|x_i-x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)}- \varepsilon \leq \|y_i-y_j\|_{\ell_p^d}^p \leq \|x_i-x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)}+\varepsilon.$$
Furthermore, the proof yields a greedy algorithm capable of generating the set $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^n$ given the input $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$. This result is established by combining a derandomized form of Maurey's empirical method (1981) with Ball's combinatorial approach (1990) and standard factorization theory for $L_p(\mu)$ spaces. Inspired by this embedding, we define the concept of $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension reduction for the unit ball ${\bf B}_E$ of a normed space $(E,\|\cdot\|_E)$ and establish that the unit ball ${\bf B}_{\ell_p}$ cannot be $\varepsilon$-isometrically dimensioned via linear operators for any $p\neq2$.

This paper introduces a technique to estimate the asymptotic phase and amplitude functions of limit-cycle oscillators directly from observed time series data, eliminating the need for prior knowledge of the underlying dynamical equations. By employing polynomial regression, the estimation process is formulated as a convex optimization problem. The method's efficacy is numerically validated using two-dimensional limit-cycle oscillator examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate an application involving data-driven fast entrainment with amplitude suppression, achieved by utilizing an optimal periodic input derived from the estimated phase and amplitude functions.

Ecological systems are inherently dynamic, necessitating that management policies adapt to this variability. However, since adjusting policies can be expensive, closely tracking environmental fluctuations is not always cost-effective. This study investigates how the costs of policy adjustments influence optimal management strategies, using the classic problem of maximizing profits from a stochastically varying fish population with annual quota changes as a case study. Policy adjustment costs—defined here as changes in fishing quotas over time—can vary in form; they might depend on the magnitude of the change or incur a fixed fee whenever a quota is altered. The findings reveal that different cost structures lead to divergent optimal policies. Although it is often assumed that adjustment costs reduce policy volatility, this analysis demonstrates that specific cost frameworks can actually amplify variation over time. Furthermore, neglecting adjustment costs consistently results in poorer economic outcomes compared to scenarios where these costs are correctly accounted for.

This report introduces nine test problems designed for multi-task multi-objective optimization (MTMOO), where each problem involves two concurrent multi-objective optimization tasks. The varying relationships between tasks across these problems are intended to facilitate a comprehensive evaluation of MO-MFO algorithms, with the expectation that these proposed benchmarks will advance MTMOO research.

We examine the evolution of spatial entanglement between two initially independent walkers undergoing discrete-time quantum walks, focusing on symmetric and anti-symmetric initial coin states. By leveraging the system's symmetry and post-selecting the coin states accordingly, we demonstrate that for anti-symmetric initial coin states, the entanglement associated with anti-symmetric outcomes remains constant, whereas the entanglement linked to symmetric outcomes exhibits underdamped-like oscillations with a period ($T$) inversely proportional to the coin operator parameter ($\theta$). Conversely, these behaviors are reversed for symmetric initial coin states. Furthermore, we find that underdamped-like dynamics in spatial entanglement also emerge when post-selected results lack symmetry, regardless of the initial coin state. These findings highlight intriguing connections between symmetry and entanglement dynamics in quantum walks, offering potential utility for quantum communication and related technologies.

The classification of pairs $(\mathcal{D},G)$ is complete, where $\mathcal{D}$ represents a non-trivial $2$-$(k^{2},k,\lambda )$ design satisfying $\lambda \mid k$, and $G$ denotes a flag-transitive automorphism group of affine type acting on $\mathcal{D}$, with the condition that $G$ is not a subgroup of $A \Gamma L_{1}(k^{2})$.

Energy system modellers often opt for low spatial resolutions defined by administrative borders like nations to simplify data gathering and shorten computation times; however, this approach can result in sub-optimal investment strategies for wind and solar power. Specifically, neglecting intra-regional grid bottlenecks tends to underestimate costs, whereas grouping locations with varying wind and solar capacity factors into a single resource class can lead to cost overestimation. This study examines these opposing influences using a high-resolution capacity expansion model for Europe's renewable-heavy power system, leveraging recent data and computing improvements. The analysis interpolates between a 37-node model (based on countries and synchronous zones) and a 1024-node model (based on substation locations). When focusing solely on renewable resource resolution while disregarding network constraints, higher resolution enables optimal placement of wind and solar capacity at sites with superior capacity factors, reducing system costs by up to 10% compared to low-resolution models and shifting investment significantly from offshore to onshore wind. Conversely, introducing grid bottlenecks by increasing network resolution raises costs by up to 23%, as generation must be sourced locally from sites with inferior capacity factors. These dynamics are most evident in scenarios with limited grid expansion, such as those constrained by low local acceptance. Finally, the study demonstrates that permitting grid expansion alleviates some issues associated with low grid resolution and reduces overall costs by approximately 16%.

Drawing from recent breakthroughs in vision transformers for object detection, we introduce Li3DeTr, an end-to-end LiDAR-based 3D Detection Transformer designed for autonomous driving. This model accepts LiDAR point clouds as input and directly regresses 3D bounding boxes. Li3DeTr encodes local and global LiDAR features through sparse convolution and multi-scale deformable attention, respectively. Within the decoder, a novel cross-attention block connects global LiDAR features to 3D predictions by utilizing sparse object queries learned from the data, while object query interactions are managed via multi-head self-attention. The decoder architecture repeats $L_{dec}$ layers to iteratively refine these queries. Following the DETR approach, the network is trained using a set-to-set loss function. Without relying on auxiliary techniques like non-maximum suppression (NMS), Li3DeTr outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the nuScenes dataset, achieving 61.3% mAP and 67.6% NDS, and also demonstrates competitive results on the KITTI dataset. Additionally, we implement knowledge distillation with a teacher-student framework to further slightly enhance the network's performance.

The investigation analyzes orthogonality time across various initial state configurations interacting locally with distinct spin models: $XX$, Ising, and anisotropic. Results indicate that as the number of environment qubits grows, the count of orthogonal states rises, leading to a reduction in orthogonality time. The $XX$ chain model exhibits the minimum orthogonality time, whereas the Ising model yields the maximum. Additionally, an external field increases the number of orthogonal states, while Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interaction reduces the orthogonality time. Furthermore, the combination of initial state settings and the external field significantly influences whether the orthogonality time decreases or increases.

Maintaining the frequency of power grids within narrow limits is essential for their reliable operation, yet various disturbances—such as shifting demand, volatile renewable feed-in, and energy trading—cause fluctuations. This study examines frequency time series from the continental European grid in 2011 and 2017 to isolate the specific impact of trading. The analysis reveals that trading at standard intervals, like full hours, alters the statistical properties of frequency fluctuations. Although the occurrence of particularly large deviations decreased in 2017 compared to 2011, such extreme events became more probable immediately following trading instances. A comparison between the two years suggests that reducing trading intervals could enhance grid stability and frequency quality by significantly dampening large fluctuations. Additionally, the data shows that frequency fluctuation statistics deviate from Gaussian distributions and are better modeled by heavy-tailed, asymmetric distributions, such as Lévy-stable distributions. When comparing periods with and without trading, deviations near trading times exhibit a wider distribution, making extreme events orders of magnitude more likely. Finally, the paper briefly reviews a stochastic framework that enables a quantitative description of power grid frequency fluctuations.

Hardware distortions (HWD) severely degrade communication system performance, yet their recently identified asymmetric characteristics can be effectively counteracted using improper Gaussian signaling (IGS), which offers extra design flexibility. Discrete asymmetric signaling (AS) serves as a practical implementation of IGS by modifying signal geometry or probability distributions. This paper utilizes probabilistic shaping (PS) rather than uniform symbols to address HWD impacts and derives the optimal maximum a posteriori detector. We subsequently design symbol probabilities to minimize error rates while accounting for the improper nature of HWD. Although the resulting design constitutes a non-convex optimization challenge, we simplify it through successive convex programming and propose an iterative algorithm. Furthermore, we introduce a hybrid shaping (HS) scheme to leverage the combined advantages of both PS and geometric shaping (GS). Extensive numerical analysis and Monte-Carlo simulations demonstrate that the proposed PS outperforms conventional uniform constellations and GS. Both PS and HS deliver significant gains over traditional methods, achieving up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in error probability and throughput improvements.

More individuals under the age of 40 succumb to brain tumors than to any other form of cancer. Brain surgery represents the primary and critical intervention for treating these conditions. Although achieving a complete tumor resection is vital, it presents a significant challenge because distinguishing cancerous cells from adjacent healthy white matter is visually difficult. The white matter consists of nerve fiber bundles that possess specific structural anisotropy and birefringence. This birefringence in aligned fibrous tissue is highly responsive to minor pathological changes; specifically, highly aligned anisotropic fibers display greater birefringence compared to disorganized cancerous tissue with weaker alignment. In this study, we conducted experiments on thick coronal slices of a healthy human brain to investigate two objectives: (i) measuring the birefringence of white matter using a polarimetric microscope in a backscattering configuration to enable non-invasive diagnostics, and (ii) correlating these measurements with fiber orientation and alignment levels. This correlation was established by examining the spatial distribution of the degree of polarization in backscattered light and its response to the polarization state of the probing beam. Our findings demonstrate that polarimetry can reliably differentiate between white and gray matter, potentially aiding surgeons in intraoperatively distinguishing between unstructured tumor tissue and organized healthy brain tissue. Furthermore, we show that this technique can sensitively reconstruct local mean nerve fiber orientations, which could guide tumor resections by identifying critical nerve pathways, ultimately improving surgical outcomes.

We examine the nonlinear refraction caused by Rydberg excitons in $\mathrm{Cu_2O}$. By employing a high-precision interferometry imaging method capable of spatially resolving nonlinear phase shifts, we detect substantial shifts at very low laser intensities near exciton resonances. Based on these observations, we calculate the nonlinear index $\mathrm{n_2}$, display its spectral profile for $n\geq 5$, and report $\mathrm{n_2}$ magnitudes on the order of $10^{-3}$ mm$^2$/mW. Additionally, we note a rapid saturation of the Kerr nonlinearity, where the saturation intensity $\mathrm{I_{sat}}$ scales as $n^{-7}$. We attribute this behavior to the Rydberg blockade mechanism; in this scenario, giant Rydberg interactions constrain the exciton density, capping the maximum phase shift at 0.5 rad within our experimental configuration.

This paper addresses the challenge of dynamically adjusting the exploration rate within value-of-information-based exploration frameworks. We achieve this by reformulating value-of-information optimization as an equilibrium-finding problem for a flow dependent on the exploration rate. Subsequently, we propose an efficient path-following algorithm to converge on these equilibria, thereby revealing optimal action-selection policies. This approach automatically tailors the exploration rate based on the agent's accumulated experience, with theoretical guarantees of global convergence.

Initially, we evaluate our exploration-rate adaptation on the Nintendo GameBoy titles *Centipede* and *Millipede*, highlighting key aspects of the search process. Our results demonstrate that this method produces superior policies in fewer episodes compared to conventional strategies that rely on heuristic, annealing-based adjustments. Furthermore, we show that these advantages persist across deep, value-of-information-based agents learning to play ten simple and over forty complex Nintendo GameBoy games. In these scenarios, observed performance reaches levels near or significantly exceeding human play.

The influence of networking games on wireless networks has expanded significantly. This trend highlights the recognition that service providers can achieve substantial scaling benefits by granting mobile devices greater autonomy in decision-making. However, this autonomy may lead to inefficiencies characteristic of non-cooperative game equilibria. Consequently, centralized protocols continue to be evaluated alongside decentralized alternatives. In terms of network architecture, this necessitates the simultaneous operation of network-centric and terminal-centric radio resource management strategies. Rather than aligning with proponents of either extreme, this paper proposes hybrid schemes where the network assists wireless users by broadcasting aggregated load data to inform their decisions. We formulate utilities based on the Quality of Service (QoS) experienced by users and construct a Bayesian framework to determine equilibria. Numerical analysis demonstrates the benefits of this hybrid game framework within an association problem involving networks comprising both HSDPA and 3G LTE systems.

This paper introduces a scalable analysis method that is sensitive to both data dependence and context and path variations. The core strategy involves mitigating the aliasing-path-explosion issue through a sparse, demand-driven, and fused technique that integrates pointer information computation with data dependence resolution. Specifically, the approach divides the computational burden of disjunctive reasoning into two components: first, a context- and semi-path-sensitive analysis that efficiently encapsulates data dependence within symbolic, storeless value-flow graphs; and second, a demand-driven phase that determines transitive data dependence across these graphs. The method has been implemented for thin slicing and value flow analysis. Evaluated on a benchmark suite of 16 programs spanning from 13 KLoC to 8 MLoC, our results demonstrate that this technique outperforms various state-of-the-art analyses in terms of both precision and scalability.

Recent empirical research demonstrates that adversarial topic models (ATM) effectively capture document semantic patterns by distinguishing documents from dissimilar samples. However, this discriminative-generative architecture presents two significant limitations: (1) it fails to link similar documents that share the same distribution of salient words, and (2) it hinders the integration of external information, such as document sentiment, which is known to enhance neural topic model training. To overcome these challenges, we re-examine the adversarial topic architecture through mathematical analysis, propose a new method to reformulate the discriminative objective as an optimization problem, and introduce a novel sampling technique that facilitates the incorporation of external variables. This reformulation promotes the modeling of relationships among similar samples while enforcing constraints on dissimilar ones; meanwhile, the sampling method, grounded in internal inputs and reconstructed outputs, aids the model in identifying salient words that define the primary topic. Experimental results indicate that our framework surpasses other state-of-the-art neural topic models across three diverse benchmark datasets—varying in domain, vocabulary size, and document length—based on topic coherence metrics.

A comparison of volcanic eruption frequencies over the last 270 years against solar activity variations and the summary curve of the solar background magnetic field (SBMF) principal components reveals a 22-year cycle as the most significant period via Morlet wavelet analysis. A strong correlation (0.84) exists between volcanic frequencies and the SBMF summary curve following 1868 across 11 cycles. Volcanic eruption maxima are observed during solar activity cycles characterized by southern magnetic polarity. Consequently, the next predicted volcanic maximum is anticipated during cycle 26, coinciding with a period of southern magnetic polarity in the SBMF.

In 1993, Gromov demonstrated that with high probability, any bounded, reduced van Kampen diagram $D$ within a random group at density $d$ adheres to the isoperimetric inequality $|\partial D|\geq (1-2d-s)|D|\ell$. This article extends Gruber and Mackay's proof regarding random triangular groups by establishing a non-reduced 2-complex variant of this inequality. Furthermore, for any 2-complex $Y$ possessing a specific geometric structure, we identify a phase transition defined by a critical density $d_c$ unique to $Y$: when the density $d$ is less than $d_c$, no reduced van Kampen 2-complex of form $Y$ exists; conversely, if $d$ exceeds $d_c$, such complexes do exist. As a practical application, we demonstrate a phase transition for the $C(p)$ small-cancellation condition: random groups at density $d$ satisfy $C(p)$ when $d < 1/(p+1)$, but fail to satisfy it when $d > 1/(p+1)$.

This work examines the current state of $R$ measurements and low-energy QCD investigations, exploring the potential of a super $\tau$-charm factory operating in the 2–7 GeV range. A high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ collider would eliminate statistical limitations for determining $R$, enabling a precision of 2% or higher. Such accuracy would significantly reduce uncertainties in the hadronic contribution to the QED running coupling constant ($\Delta\alpha_{had}$) and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment ($a_{\mu}$), while also facilitating precise determinations of the strong coupling constant ($\alpha_s$), the charm quark mass, and the parameters of heavy charmonium resonances. Furthermore, the extensive data samples expected in the 2–3 GeV region would allow for the study of excited $\rho$, $\omega$, and $\phi$ states, the exotic $Y(2175)$, the electromagnetic form factors of mesons and baryons, and the fragmentation functions of hadrons.

A defining characteristic of intricate biological systems is their capacity to engage in feedback loops with their surroundings. Reservoir computing serves as a key framework for investigating these dynamics, relying on learning mechanisms that operate through low-dimensional bottlenecks. Although this approach is straightforward, the specific elements that facilitate or impede successful training in reservoir networks remain largely unclear. This study examines non-linear feedback networks designed to produce sinusoidal outputs, focusing on how learning efficacy is influenced by the interaction between internal network dynamics and task characteristics. Through rigorous mathematical analysis of linearized networks, we demonstrate that learning performance peaks when the target frequency is optimal and intermediate, decreasing steadily as the strength of internal reservoir connections increases. At this optimal frequency, the reservoir's representation of the target signal becomes high-dimensional and desynchronized, thereby achieving maximum noise robustness. We confirm that our predictions accurately reflect the qualitative behavior of performance in non-linear networks. Furthermore, we reveal that the link between internal representations and performance can be leveraged in trained non-linear systems to explain phenomena lacking linear equivalents. Our findings suggest that the primary driver of learning success is the quality of the target's internal representation, a quality determined by the interplay between parameters governing the internal network and those defining the task.

We offer a detailed investigation into chiral symmetry breaking minima and baryonic directions within supersymmetric QCD ($SU(N_c)$ with $N_f$ flavors) subjected to Anomaly Mediated Supersymmetry Breaking (AMSB). In the $s$-confining regime where $N_f = N_c + 1$, as well as in the majority of the free-magnetic phase ($N_f \leq 1.43 N_c$), we observe that naive tree-level baryonic runaways are stabilized by loop corrections. However, runaways persist in the upper region of the free-magnetic phase ($N_f \gtrsim 1.43 N_c$) and extend into the conformal window, indicating the presence of incalculable minima at large field values of order $\Lambda$. Despite this, the points of chiral symmetry breaking remain locally stable and are anticipated to connect continuously to QCD vacua for significant SUSY breaking. The scenario where $N_f = N_c$ demands special attention because of the strongly coupled nature of the quantum-modified moduli space; due to the inability to calculate critical Kähler potential terms, the stability of the chiral symmetry breaking point along baryonic directions remains undetermined for this specific case. Excluding this exception, all theories applicable to AMSB ($N_f < 3 N_c$) feature stable chiral symmetry breaking minima, and all theories with $N_f \lesssim 1.43 N_c$ (with the noted exception of $N_f = N_c$) are safeguarded against runaways leading to incalculable minima.

This paper establishes several properties of the $a_{x,y}(.)$-Neumann derivative for the fractional $a_{x,y}(.)$-Laplacian operator and, consequently, proves fundamental characteristics of the associated function spaces. In the second part, utilizing Ekeland's variational principle and a direct variational method, we demonstrate the existence of weak solutions to a nonlocal problem featuring nonhomogeneous Neumann and Robin boundary conditions.

Among the cobalt spinel family ACo$_2$O$_4$ (where A includes Sn, Ti, Ru, Mn, Al, Zn, Fe, etc.), GeCo$_2$O$_4$ stands out as a unique system where magnetic Co ions stabilize on a pyrochlore lattice, creating significant orbital frustration. The intricate low-temperature antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering and extended magnetic exchange interactions have long made the lattice dynamics and magnetic structure of GeCo$_2$O$_4$ enigmatic. To resolve these complexities, this work combines theoretical and experimental analyses of the highly frustrated magnetic structure alongside infrared (IR) and Raman-active phonon modes in GeCo$_2$O$_4$. This material exhibits AFM ordering below a Néel temperature ($T_N$) of approximately 21 K, followed by a structural phase transition from cubic ($Fd{\bar 3}m$) to tetragonal ($I4_{1}/amd$) symmetry at a spin transition temperature ($T_S$) of roughly 16 K. Density-functional theory (DFT+U) calculations indicate that accurately modeling the low-temperature AFM order requires including magnetic-exchange interactions up to the third nearest neighbors. At room temperature, three distinct IR-active modes ($T_{1u}$) are detected at 680, 413, and 325 cm$^{-1}$, accompanied by four Raman-active modes—$A_{1g}$, $T_{2g}(1)$, $T_{2g}(2)$, and $E_{g}$—at 760, 647, 550, and 308 cm$^{-1}$, respectively. These experimental values align reasonably well with our DFT+U predictions. Furthermore, all observed IR and Raman phonon modes display evidence of moderate spin-phonon coupling. The study also examines the temperature dependence of Raman mode parameters, including shifts, widths, and intensities. Significant variations in the Raman line parameters for the $E_{g}$ and $T_{2g}$ modes are noted near $T_N$ and $T_S$, reflecting the modulation of Co-O bonds within CoO$_6$ octahedra during these excitations.

Current trends in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) research increasingly agree that designing AI systems requires actively involving and empowering those impacted by them. Nevertheless, the specific ways stakeholders ought to engage in this design process remain ambiguous. This workshop paper seeks to establish a "participatory turn" in AI design by combining a review of existing literature on participation with empirical insights derived from a survey of recent publications and twelve semi-structured interviews with AI researchers and practitioners. Drawing from this synthesis and empirical data, the paper introduces a conceptual framework for evaluating participatory strategies in AI design and outlines key empirical findings that detail the current state of participatory practices in the field. These results aim to initiate a more structured dialogue regarding the future direction of Participatory Design (PD) for AI across HCI, AI, and related research communities.

Specific simplicial complexes generate a subset $D$ within $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}^m$, which subsequently defines a linear code $C_{D}$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ composed of vectors $(v\cdot d)_{d\in D}$ for $v\in \mathbb{F}_{2^n}^m$. This study focuses on the scenario where $n=3$, resulting in an octanary code. We investigate the relationship between $C_{D}$ and its binary subfield code $C_{D}^{(2)}$ utilizing a generator matrix. A code is defined as distance optimal if, for a specific length and dimension, it achieves the maximum possible distance. Leveraging the Griesmer bound, we derive five infinite families of such distance optimal codes and establish sufficient conditions under which certain linear codes are minimal.

(2+1)-dimensional four-Fermi quantum field theories represent some of the most elementary models in high-energy physics, yet comprehending them demands a non-perturbative lattice approach capable of handling their strongly-coupled fixed points. These lattice frameworks are equally significant in condensed matter physics, serving as an ideal environment to investigate strong correlations within the quantum anomalous Hall (QAH) effect. We provide a comprehensive account of our multidisciplinary strategy for determining the evolution of QAH phases under increasing four-Fermi interactions, integrating strong-coupling and effective-potential methods to reveal a complex phase diagram featuring large-$N$ Chern insulators and Lorentz-breaking fermion condensates. Furthermore, this methodological toolkit can be expanded by incorporating recent developments in quantum information science; specifically, we demonstrate that tensor-network algorithms utilizing projected entangled pairs enhance our grasp of the strong-coupling regime. Additionally, we outline a detailed protocol employing ultra-cold atoms in optical lattices equipped with synthetic spin-orbit coupling to construct quantum simulators for these four-Fermi models. This approach offers a promising alternative for characterizing strongly-coupled fixed points and holds potential for exploring real-time dynamics and finite-fermion densities.

In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed systematically during every fill featuring full-intensity beams under physics production conditions at the Interaction Point (IP) of the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment. This method enables the determination of both emittance and closed orbit parameters at the bunch-by-bunch level. By precisely measuring the beam-beam closed orbit discrepancies, researchers achieved a direct and quantitative observation of long-range beam-beam PACMAN effects, with results that align closely with numerical simulations generated by an enhanced version of the TRAIN code.

We have assembled a database comprising 8,667 transit timing measurements across 382 systems, featuring updated ephemerides for 382 planets. This collection integrates data from the NASA TESS mission with transit times extracted from existing literature using a semi-automated process. The catalog includes approximately 240 TESS-observed hot Jupiters, defined as planets with masses exceeding $0.3M_{\rm Jup}$ and orbital periods under 10 days. These refined ephemerides are valuable for planning follow-up observations and investigating long-term period variations. Notably, WASP-12 stands as the sole system with a securely confirmed period change. We also highlight other intriguing cases, including systems showing suggestive but unconfirmed evidence of period shifts and the identification of a second transiting planet in the NGTS-11 system. The compiled light curves, transit times, ephemerides, timing residuals, and the Python code used for their generation are accessible online at https://transit-timing.github.io.

This study examines the decidability and computational complexity of conservative extensions, along with related concepts such as entailment and inseparability, within Horn description logics (DLs) that incorporate inverse roles. The investigation covers both deductive conservative extensions, which maintain the same entailed concept and role inclusions as well as functionality assertions, and query conservative extensions, which ensure that answers to all conjunctive queries remain unchanged. Establishing upper bounds for query conservative extensions presents significant challenges, as standard approaches relying on unbounded homomorphisms between universal models are ineffective when inverse roles are present. Instead, we utilize a hybrid characterization combining unbounded and bounded homomorphisms, which facilitates a decision procedure integrating tree automata and the mosaic technique. Our primary findings indicate that query conservative extensions are 2ExpTime-complete across all DLs ranging from ELI to Horn-ALCHIF and from Horn-ALC to Horn-ALCHIF, while deductive conservative extensions are 2ExpTime-complete for DLs spanning from ELI to ELHIF_\bot. These complexity results also apply to inseparability and entailment.

This paper begins with a concise overview of Karaji's L-summing technique within the framework of modern algebraic language. Subsequently, we examine Gosper's algorithm, which serves as a decision procedure for computing indefinite sums of hypergeometric terms. Finally, we demonstrate how to apply Gosper's algorithm in conjunction with the L-summing method to derive a specific class of combinatorial identities linked to a given algebraic identity.

In [7], we presented the category of chain bundles, complete with examples, and highlighted its importance. In this work, we define specific categories termed the "category of chains" within the context of chain bundles and examine several notable categorical properties of these chain categories.

The rapid neutron capture process (r-process) serves as a primary mechanism for creating elements heavier than iron and is solely responsible for the natural formation of actinides. Kilonova emissions are predominantly driven by the radioactive decay of species produced through the r-process. Because the r-process occurs far from nuclear stability, unmeasured beta decay rates are critical in determining the process's timescale. To better assess how kilonova models depend on various theoretical global beta-decay descriptions, we integrated these into nucleosynthesis simulations. By comparing the results, we examined variations in kilonova nuclear energy generation and light curve predictions, as well as final abundances and their consequences for nuclear cosmochronometry. Our investigation reveals scenarios where discrepancies in beta decay rates lead to enhanced nuclear heating over days, resulting in significantly higher average bolometric luminosity between 1 and 10 days post-merger. We identified specific nuclei, both measured and unmeasured, whose decay rates directly influence nuclear heating on timescales that shape light curve evolution. Furthermore, we found that uncertainties in beta decay rates substantially affect age estimates derived from cosmochronometry.

End-to-end learning from sensory inputs has yielded encouraging outcomes for autonomous driving. Although integrating numerous sensors improves environmental perception and should enhance vehicle reliability, training and deploying such networks remains difficult, presenting at least two key challenges. First, computational complexity grows as the number of sensing devices increases. Second, networks tend to overfit to the simplest and most informative inputs. We address these issues by introducing a novel multi-modal expert network architecture and a multi-stage training procedure. This network features a gating mechanism that selects the most pertinent input at every inference step using a mixed discrete-continuous policy. We validate the feasibility of this approach on a 1/6 scale truck outfitted with three cameras and one LiDAR sensor.

We have extended the concept of backbending within nearest-neighbor bond percolation by introducing a backbend sequence $\beta : \mathbb{Z}_+ \to \mathbb{Z}_+ \cup \{\infty\}$. A $\beta$-backbend path originating from the origin is defined as one that does not retreat more than $\beta(h)$ levels backward from its current record height $h$. This study examines the connection between the critical probabilities of various percolation processes governed by distinct backbend sequences across half-spaces, full spaces, and half-slabs of the $d$-dimensional ($d \geq 2$) body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions on these sequences that guarantee the absence of percolation at the critical thresholds for processes on both the half-space and full-space of the BCC lattice.

Rosenblatt's initial theorem on the omnipotence of shallow networks asserts that elementary perceptrons can resolve any classification task provided the training set contains no inconsistencies. Conversely, Minsky and Papert examined elementary perceptrons with specific limitations on neural inputs, such as a bounded number of connections or a limited receptive field diameter at the hidden layer. They demonstrated that under these constraints, elementary perceptrons fail to solve certain problems, including image connectivity and pixel parity. In this note, we illustrate Rosenblatt's theorem in practice by showing how an elementary perceptron can solve a variant of the travel maze problem and analyzing the resulting solution's complexity. We also developed a deep network algorithm for the same problem, which proves significantly more efficient. While the shallow network requires an exponentially large number of hidden-layer neurons (Rosenblatt's $A$-elements), the deep network achieves the task with only second-order polynomial complexity. Furthermore, we show that for complex problems of this nature, deep networks can be substantially smaller and provide a heuristic explanation for this efficiency.

This study numerically explores how fully developed plasma turbulence interacts with collisionless shocks using hybrid kinetic simulations. By modeling a turbulent jet colliding with an oblique shock, the research examines the influence of upstream turbulence on plasma transport. A new method based on coarse-graining the Vlasov equation reveals that transport characteristics are heavily dependent on the intensity of upstream turbulence, resulting in patterns modulated by turbulent structures. These findings may contribute to a better understanding of acceleration and heating mechanisms in space plasmas.

We introduce a family of evolutionary models featuring an arbitrary exchangeable breeding mechanism alongside various selection strategies. In these frameworks, a new genome enters the population via the breeding process, while an existing genome is eliminated based on a fitness-dependent selection rule, thereby maintaining a constant population size. The system evolves as a Markov chain; distinct from many other models, its stationary distribution—referred to as the mutation-selection equilibrium—is readily derivable and analyzable. Our primary focus is examining how this stationary distribution behaves as population size grows, for which we establish several phase-transition theorems.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge within a multi-agent system where a subset of agents behaves adversarially. Specifically, these malicious nodes divert the network from the optimal solution by transmitting deceptive data to their neighbors while consuming substantial communication bandwidth. We introduce a distributed gradient-based algorithm wherein benign agents exchange quantized information. We demonstrate that the solution converges to a neighborhood of the optimum and analyze the resulting solutions under communication constraints and the influence of malicious agents. Additionally, numerical simulations are provided to validate these findings.

Utilizing the Gibbons-Hawking ansatz to generate a broad class of circle-invariant hyperkähler 4-manifolds (and consequently Calabi-Yau 2-folds), this work establishes versions of the Thomas conjecture regarding the existence of special Lagrangian representatives within Hamiltonian isotopy classes, as well as the Thomas-Yau conjecture concerning the long-term existence of the Lagrangian mean curvature flow. Additionally, we present observations related to closed geodesics, curve shortening flow, and minimal surfaces.

Dialog serves as a fundamental component of human natural language communication, consisting of multi-party exchanges that transmit information dynamically. Comparing these dialogues is highly valuable for real-world applications, including contact center analytics and virtual agent development. We introduce a new adaptation of the edit distance metric specifically tailored for dialog similarity, incorporating key conversational elements such as utterance meaning, interaction flow, and participant roles. Evaluated on two public datasets, our method is compared against standard document similarity techniques. The findings indicate that our approach surpasses existing methods in capturing conversational flow and aligns more closely with human judgments of similarity.

Induced subgraph classes play a central role in the most significant findings of graph theory and algorithms. A key example involves the concept of {\em perfection}, where the chromatic number of every induced subgraph $H$ of a graph $G$ matches the clique number of $H$. The seminal Strong Perfect Graph Theorem establishes that determining whether $G$ is perfect relies on identifying odd holes within $G$ and its complement. In 2005, Chudnovsky et al. presented an $O(n^9)$ algorithm for recognizing perfect graphs, later optimized by Lai et al. to $O(n^8)$ time using square-matrix multiplication with an exponent $\omega<2.373$. This paper presents further algorithmic improvements:

1.  The feasibility of detecting odd holes remained an open problem for decades until Chudnovsky et al.'s major breakthrough in 2020, which yielded an $O(n^9)$ algorithm. Lai et al. subsequently refined this to $O(n^8)$, establishing the best prior method for perfect graph recognition. Our first contribution is an $O(n^7)$ algorithm for detecting odd holes, which consequently yields an $O(n^7)$ algorithm for recognizing perfect graphs.
2.  In 2021, Chudnovsky et al. extended their 2005 and 2020 algorithms to create the first polynomial-time method for finding a shortest odd hole, with a runtime of $O(n^{14})$. We reduce this runtime to $O(n^{13})$.
3.  Conforti et al. introduced the first polynomial algorithm for detecting even holes in 1997, operating in approximately $O(n^{40})$ time. Subsequent research progressively improved this complexity to $O(n^{31})$, $O(n^{19})$, $O(n^{11})$, and finally $O(n^9)$. Conversely, finding a shortest even hole remained an open challenge for 16 years until Cheong and Lu achieved an $O(n^{31})$ algorithm in 2022. We improve the time complexity for finding a shortest even hole to $O(n^{23})$.

Resolving coreference remains one of the most prominent obstacles in extracting information from biomedical literature. Consequently, this domain has been the second most studied area for coreference resolution after news, and a significant focus within general NLP research. Over recent years, interest in this field has surged, resulting in the creation of extensive datasets, domain-specific contextual language models, and various architectural approaches. This paper reviews the current state-of-the-art in biomedical coreference, with a specific emphasis on these latest advancements.

Accurately localizing mitosis is a vital preliminary step for determining tumor prognosis and grading. However, automated mitosis detection systems utilizing deep learning often struggle with unseen patient data due to inherent domain biases. To address this, we introduce a domain homogenizer designed to mitigate disparities in histology images through adversarial reconstruction. Built upon a U-Net architecture, this homogenizer effectively minimizes the domain variations typical of histological data. We validated the tool's efficacy by demonstrating a significant reduction in domain differences among preprocessed images. When combined with a subsequent RetinaNet object detector, our approach surpassed the baseline methods of the 2021 MIDOG challenge, achieving higher average precision in detecting mitotic figures.

The robustness of voting systems has long been a focal point in computational social choice. Numerous rules, such as plurality, are known to be susceptible to manipulation when attackers target specific voters. However, implementing Local Differential Privacy (LDP) to conceal individual true preferences in pre-election polls could significantly hinder such attacks, as adversaries would only access stochastic data about voter choices. This paper offers a quantitative analysis of how LDP mechanisms impact voting system resilience. We introduce the PoLDP (power of LDP) metric to measure the disparity in an attacker's manipulation cost between LDP-protected and unprotected scenarios; a higher PoLDP indicates greater robustness added by LDP. Furthermore, we fully characterize PoLDP for systems using the plurality rule and offer general guidance on applying LDP mechanisms.

Controllable chiral domain walls in topological magnetic Weyl semimetals offer significant potential for device applications, making the development of effective tuning and manipulation methods crucial. Magnetoelastic coupling presents a viable approach, and the recently identified $R$Al$X$ family ($R$=rare earth, $X$=Si, Ge) serves as a promising platform for this purpose. This study investigates the transport and thermodynamic characteristics of CeAlGe under hydrostatic pressure. Our findings indicate that while pressure strengthens the antiferromagnetic exchange interactions in CeAlGe, it largely preserves the material's magnetic structure. Within the magnetically ordered phase, a substantial topological Hall effect characterized by a distinct loop shape is observed; under pressure, this effect divides into two separate regions. We attribute this anomalous electromagnetic behavior to chiral magnetic domain walls. The unique pressure-induced evolution of these effects, alongside the reemergence of antiferromagnetic order, strongly implies that magnetoelastic coupling can be used to switch this electromagnetic response on and off in noncentrosymmetric magnetic Weyl semimetals.

Parity games are infinite, two-player contests played on directed graphs, with parity game solvers playing a crucial role in formal verification. This paper introduces parametrized parity games and defines an operation called Justify, which identifies a winning strategy for a specific node. By strategically sequencing these Justify steps, we recover three established algorithms from existing literature.

Recent research has demonstrated significant advancements in unsupervised image-to-image (I2I) translation; however, the challenge of learning joint distributions across various domains remains due to data imbalance. While current models can produce realistic target images, they often struggle to preserve the source image's structure. Furthermore, training generative models across multiple domains with extensive data demands considerable time and computational resources. To overcome these issues, we introduce a novel I2I translation approach that fine-tunes a pre-trained StyleGAN2 model to generate target-domain images. StyleGAN2 is particularly well-suited for unsupervised I2I translation on imbalanced datasets because it offers high stability, generates realistic outputs, and effectively learns from limited data using straightforward fine-tuning techniques. Consequently, this paper presents new methods designed to maintain source image structure while creating realistic target images. The code and results are accessible at https://github.com/happy-jihye/Cartoon-StyleGan2.

We introduce LiST, an acronym for Lite Prompted Self-Training, a technique designed for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pre-trained language models (PLMs) to enhance few-shot learning capabilities. LiST surpasses existing prompt-based fine-tuning methods through two primary innovations. First, it employs self-training to harness extensive unlabeled data for prompt-based fine-tuning within few-shot scenarios, combining this with meta-learning to re-weight noisy pseudo-labels. Since self-training is computationally costly due to the need for repetitive full-parameter updates, our second innovation involves lightweight fine-tuning. This approach introduces a minimal set of task-specific parameters for adjustment during self-training while keeping the PLM encoder frozen. Our experiments demonstrate that LiST effectively utilizes unlabeled data to boost few-shot learning performance. Furthermore, the method is highly efficient, updating only a small fraction of parameters and reducing the overall model footprint by allowing multiple tasks to share a common PLM backbone. A comprehensive evaluation across six Natural Language Understanding (NLU) tasks reveals that LiST improves performance by 35% over classic fine-tuning and by 6% over prompt-based fine-tuning. These gains are achieved with a 96% reduction in trainable parameters when using no more than 30 labeled examples per task. Additionally, with just 14 million tunable parameters, LiST outperforms GPT-3's in-context learning by 33% on few-shot NLU tasks.

This research addresses the challenge of assessing the credibility of movie reviews, a task that is difficult for even experts to perform efficiently given the sheer volume of available content. To solve this, we introduce a "historical credibility" metric that evaluates reviews based on a user's past ratings and written feedback. We establish three distinct criteria to categorize reviews as either trusted or distrusted and validate the proposed metric through extensive analysis. Our findings reveal that trusted and distrusted reviews are highly distinguishable across three dimensions: distribution, statistics, and correlation. We then integrate historical credibility into a weakly supervised classification framework. First, we demonstrate significant efficiency; annotating the entire dataset using our predefined criteria takes only 0.093 seconds for 6,400 reviews, accounting for merely 0.55% to 1.88% of the total training time when employing LSTM and SVM models. Second, we show that the historical credibility-based model substantially outperforms models relying solely on textual reviews, achieving up to 11.7% to 13.4% higher classification accuracy. Furthermore, we confirm that the accuracy of our classification model improves as the dataset size grows.

Network-based approaches for identifying topics in extensive text corpora provide an intuitive alternative to probabilistic topic models. We introduce a method specifically tailored to the needs of domain experts. While it utilizes community detection within term co-occurrence graphs like other similar techniques, it is improved by incorporating a resolution parameter to adjust the granularity of targeted topics. Additionally, we implement a term ranking system and employ semantic word embeddings to visualize term communities in a manner that enhances their interpretability. We validate our approach using a standard corpus of general news articles, presenting results from detailed evaluations by social science experts across various resolutions. The study also includes a comparison with topics identified by Latent Dirichlet Allocation and concludes with a discussion on factors affecting topic interpretation.

Sentiment analysis represents a broad field within machine learning, with extensive research currently focused on English datasets. However, Pakistan generates a vast volume of data in Roman Urdu across various social platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and YouTube. This study specifically targets YouTube comments, utilizing a dataset comprised of user feedback on Pakistani dramas and television shows. The data is organized into a multi-class classification scheme, categorizing sentiments as positive, negative, or neutral. Performance evaluation involved a comparative analysis of five supervised learning algorithms: Linear Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Multi-Layer Perceptron, and Naïve Bayes. Metrics including accuracy, recall, precision, and F-measure were employed to assess model effectiveness. The results indicate that SVM achieved the highest accuracy at 64%, outperforming the other algorithms tested.

We introduce a dataset designed for event coreference resolution, constructed from random samples across various languages, nations, and sources. Previous research on gathering event information has failed to quantify the specific impact of event coreference resolution. We curated and examined a representative multilingual corpus to evaluate the performance and utility of current state-of-the-art approaches in this field.
