Our findings reveal that nearly 50% of event mentions in documents appear alongside other related mentions, a fact that inevitably leads to incomplete or inaccurate event data. We demonstrate that event coreference resolution can significantly mitigate this issue. This work highlights a previously neglected or difficult-to-study challenge. Future studies on event information collection can utilize the insights presented here. The project repository is available at https://github.com/emerging-welfare/ECR4-Contentious-Politics.

This paper presents Harmonics Virtual Lights (HVL), a method for modeling indirect light sources in interactive global illumination for dynamic 3D scenes. While Virtual Point Lights (VPL) offer an efficient way to define and evaluate indirect lighting, they often produce disturbing artifacts, particularly with high-frequency materials. Virtual Spherical Lights (VSL) mitigate these artifacts by using spheres instead of points; however, their reliance on Monte Carlo integration for estimating the lighting integral introduces noise. HVL extends VSL within a Spherical Harmonics (SH) framework, providing a closed-form solution for lighting integral evaluation. We propose an efficient SH projection for spherical light contributions that outperforms existing methods. Calculating outgoing luminance requires $\mathcal{O}(n)$ operations for materials with circular symmetric lobes and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ for the general case, where $n$ represents the number of SH bands. HVL works with both parametric and measured BRDFs without additional overhead, allowing users to balance rendering time and image quality by adjusting the SH band limit. This approach is specifically optimized for rendering medium-frequency one-bounce global illumination with arbitrary BRDFs in real-time.

Optimal transport (OT) offers a framework for designing efficient resource allocation strategies within networks comprising multiple sources and targets. This paper introduces a novel application of discrete OT to UAV swarms, facilitating appropriate task assignment and execution. Existing drone swarm deployments across various domains utilize sensors to acquire environmental knowledge [1]. Specific use cases, including chemical and radiation detection alongside thermal and RGB imaging, necessitate an algorithm that accounts for parameters on both the UAV and waypoint levels and permits the matching scheme to evolve as the swarm gathers environmental data. Furthermore, reliance on a centralized planner can be eliminated by employing a distributed algorithm capable of dynamically adjusting to changes within the swarm network or its parameters. To achieve this, we developed a dynamic, distributed OT algorithm that pairs a UAV with an optimal waypoint by considering one parameter from the UAV and another from the waypoint. We demonstrate the algorithm's convergence and allocation capabilities through a case study and evaluate its effectiveness compared to a greedy assignment algorithm in simulation.

We establish bounds regarding the intersection of algebraic varieties within $\mathbb{C}^4$ and Cartesian products of finite sets drawn from $\mathbb{C}^2$, highlighting their relevance to several fundamental theorems in combinatorial geometry. Let $X$ be a variety in $\mathbb{C}^4$ with degree $d$, defined by polynomials that do not all conform to the structure $F(x,y,s,t) = G(x,y)H(x,y,s,t) + K(s,t)L(x,y,s,t)$. Given finite subsets $P$ and $Q$ of $\mathbb{C}^2$, each containing $n$ elements, we demonstrate that if $X$ has dimension one or two, the size of the intersection $|X\cap (P\times Q)|$ is bounded by $O_d(n)$. Conversely, if $X$ is three-dimensional, the intersection size satisfies $|X\cap (P\times Q)| =O_{d,\varepsilon}(n^{4/3+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon>0$. These bounds are optimal within this general framework (aside from the $\varepsilon$ term). They represent distinct generalizations of the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, extending the concept from products of one-dimensional finite sets in $\mathbb{C}$ to products of two-dimensional finite sets in $\mathbb{C}^2$. Specifically, the bound for three-dimensional varieties extends the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem. A central component of our proofs is a two-dimensional adaptation of a specific case of Alon's combinatorial Nullstellensatz. Furthermore, these bounds yield corollaries concerning the number of repeated and distinct values produced by polynomials and polynomial maps acting on pairs of points in $\mathbb{C}^2$, including a characterization of maps where such bounds fail. These findings extend established limits on repeated and distinct Euclidean distances.

This piece serves as a personal recollection of the UC Berkeley Postgres initiative, which was directed by Mike Stonebraker from the mid-1980s through the mid-1990s. Commissioned for Stonebraker's Turing Award book, this account highlights his design philosophy and leadership style. Although Stonebraker was not a programmer himself and deliberately avoided interfering with his development team, the Postgres codebase was crafted by a group of exceptionally talented students and a few university staff members who possessed limited experience and received only marginally higher pay than the students. I had the fortune of joining this team as a student during the project's final years. While I received valuable feedback from senior members of the group, any mistakes or omissions in this write-up are solely my responsibility; please feel free to reach out if you identify any such issues so I can address them.

Demonstrations offer valuable insights into relevant state and action spaces, holding significant promise for enhancing the efficiency and practicality of reinforcement learning agents. This work introduces a method that utilizes demonstration datasets by integrating skill learning with sequence modeling. We begin by establishing a learned joint latent space, within which we independently train a generative model for demonstration sequences and a corresponding low-level policy. The sequence model constructs a latent space prior over plausible demonstration behaviors to speed up the learning of high-level policies. We demonstrate how to derive such priors from state-only motion capture data and investigate various approaches for incorporating them into policy learning for transfer tasks. Our experimental results validate that latent space priors yield substantial improvements in both learning speed and final performance across several challenging sparse-reward environments featuring a complex, simulated humanoid. Videos, source code, and pre-trained models can be accessed at the project website: https://facebookresearch.github.io/latent-space-priors.

Turing's reaction-diffusion theory has proven highly effective in explaining macroscopic patterns in diverse systems, from biological organisms to sand dunes. Yet, this mechanism remained unverified at the atomic level, where quantum mechanical constraints govern the fundamental components. In this study, we present evidence of a Turing pattern forming in a strained monolayer of bismuth assembled on a NbSe$_2$ surface, driven by specific interatomic interactions and kinetics. Numerical analysis reveals that the observed stripe patterns and Y-shaped domain walls arise from a narrow range of microscopic parameters, directly resulting from quantum-mechanically permissible bond lengths and angles. Consequently, this marks the first demonstration of a dynamically generated Turing pattern at the atomic scale.

The long-term effectiveness of targeted cancer treatments is often compromised by therapy-specific limitations and the emergence of drug resistance. Experimental evidence suggests that key drivers of resistance acquisition include cellular heterogeneity, alterations in drug targets, drug inactivation, DNA repair mechanisms, drug efflux, inhibition of cell death, and adaptations within the tumor microenvironment. To address these molecular and pathophysiological barriers and enhance patient survival, combination cancer therapies (CCTs) are utilized; by employing multiple modes of action, CCTs offer a promising strategy to mitigate resistance. Given the substantial costs, time, human resources, and ethical complexities associated with clinical trials and basic research, mathematical modeling and analysis can significantly aid in identifying superior treatment protocols. This article reviews existing mathematical models concerning CCTs for cancer management, highlighting open questions and evaluating plausible therapeutic combinations based on toxicity levels, resistance profiles, survival advantages, preclinical data, and other side effects.

Many applications, such as portfolio optimization, assortment planning, and treatment planning, require the simultaneous enforcement of risk and sparsity constraints. Balancing these often conflicting demands necessitates formulating functional constrained optimization problems with either convex or nonconvex objectives. This paper focuses on projection-free methods capable of generating sparse trajectories to solve these challenging functional constrained optimization problems. In the convex setting, we propose a Level Conditional Gradient (LCG) method, which utilizes a level-set framework to update the optimal value approximation and an inner conditional gradient oracle (CGO) to resolve mini-max subproblems. We demonstrate that this method achieves an iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\big)$ for both smooth and nonsmooth cases, independent of potentially large optimal dual Lagrange multipliers. For the nonconvex setting, we introduce the Level Inexact Proximal Point (IPP-LCG) method and the Direct Nonconvex Conditional Gradient (DNCG) method. The IPP-LCG approach leverages the LCG advantage by transforming the problem into a sequence of convex subproblems, achieving an iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^3}\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}\big)$ to find an ($\epsilon,\epsilon$)-KKT point. The DNCG represents the first single-loop projection-free method, with an iteration complexity bounded by $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\epsilon^4\big)$ for computing an $\epsilon$-Wolfe point. We validate the effectiveness of LCG, IPP-LCG, and DNCG through formulations and numerical experiments on two risk-averse sparse optimization applications: a portfolio selection problem with and without cardinality constraints, and a healthcare radiation therapy planning problem.

Machine learning (ML) is a standard method for enabling personalized services on mobile devices and applications. Federated Learning (FL), a promising technique for executing ML while safeguarding data privacy, generally relies on a vast array of wireless mobile devices to gather training data. However, FL must satisfy strict latency demands despite resource limitations, including wireless bandwidth constraints, power usage, and the computational capabilities of participating devices. Due to practical constraints, FL typically recruits only a subset of devices for model training in each iteration; consequently, efficient resource management and device selection are critical for FL's real-world application. This paper introduces a spectrum allocation optimization mechanism designed to improve FL performance in wireless mobile networks. Specifically, this mechanism minimizes FL time delay while accounting for the energy consumption of individual devices, thereby ensuring that all participants possess adequate resources for local model training. Furthermore, to guarantee rapid FL convergence, a robust device selection strategy is proposed to facilitate swift convergence, particularly in scenarios where local datasets are not independent and identically distributed (non-iid). Experimental findings demonstrate that (1) the proposed spectrum allocation method optimizes time delay while adhering to individual energy constraints, and (2) the proposed device selection approach enables FL to achieve the fastest convergence on non-iid datasets.

Deep learning techniques have been utilized in gravitational-wave astronomy to speed up the creation of surrogate waveforms for the inspiral of spin-aligned black hole binaries, among other uses. We show that the residual error of an artificial neural network modeling the coefficients of a surrogate waveform expansion—particularly the phase coefficients—possesses enough structure to be learned by a secondary network. By incorporating this second network, we reduced the maximum mismatch for validation set waveforms by over an order of magnitude. We also investigated various strategies to enhance surrogate model accuracy, including leveraging waveform similarities, expanding the training set, partitioning the input space, employing dedicated networks for specific output coefficients, and applying output augmentation. While these alternative approaches yielded minor improvements in certain instances, the most substantial gain resulted from adding the second network to model the residual error. Given that residual errors in broader surrogate waveform models (such as those incorporating eccentricity) likely share specific structures, our method is expected to be applicable to scenarios where increased accuracy translates to significant computational efficiency gains.

Learning radiance fields has achieved impressive outcomes in novel view synthesis, yet the training process is typically time-consuming. This has driven recent approaches to accelerate learning by avoiding neural networks or employing more efficient data structures; however, these specialized techniques often fail to apply to most existing radiance field methods. To address this limitation, we propose a general strategy to expedite training across nearly all such methods. Our core concept involves minimizing redundancy by casting significantly fewer rays during the multi-view volume rendering process, which underpins most radiance field techniques. We discovered that directing rays only toward pixels exhibiting drastic color variations substantially lowers the training load while barely compromising the accuracy of the resulting radiance fields. Furthermore, we implement an adaptive quadtree subdivision of each view based on the average rendering error per node, enabling the dynamic allocation of additional rays to complex regions with higher errors. Evaluated against various radiance field methods using standard benchmarks, our approach demonstrates that it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art solutions but with significantly faster training speeds.

Recent years have seen significant research interest in the bulk properties of nodal line materials. This paper investigates their orbital magnetic susceptibility and Hall conductivity by employing thermal Green's functions, revealing characteristic singular behaviors. Specifically, near the gapless nodal line, the orbital magnetic susceptibility exhibits a $\delta$-function singularity, while the Hall conductivity displays a step-function dependence on chemical potential. Additionally, these singularities demonstrate a pronounced dependence on the field angle, which aligns with the nodal line's orientation in momentum space. Such singular behaviors and strong angular dependencies serve as clear signatures for identifying nodal lines and their orientation, offering a viable method for the experimental detection of nodal line materials.

For structureless bosons cooled to low temperatures, electromagnetic wave absorption by their Bose-Einstein condensate is typically prohibited by momentum and energy conservation, as the phase velocity of the condensate's collective modes (bogolons) remains well below the speed of light; consequently, only light scattering occurs. However, this scenario may change for composite bosons or those possessing internal structure. In this work, we construct a microscopic theory describing electromagnetic power absorption in Bose-Einstein condensates of cold atoms across various dimensions, based on the Bogoliubov model of a weakly interacting Bose gas. Specifically, we examine transitions from a collective coherent state of bosons to discrete energy levels associated with the excited internal degrees of freedom of non-condensed individual bosons. We demonstrate that these transitions are facilitated by one- and two-bogolon excitations above the condensate, which exhibit frequency-dependent efficiencies and a strong reliance on condensate density. Furthermore, the impact of density varies according to the system's dimensionality.

Abstractive summarization models are usually pre-trained on extensive generic corpora and subsequently fine-tuned using tens to hundreds of thousands of annotated examples. In the domain of opinion summarization, however, large annotated datasets pairing customer reviews with reference summaries are scarce and costly to produce, necessitating fine-tuning approaches that resist overfitting on limited data. Furthermore, generically pre-trained models often lack familiarity with the nuances of customer reviews, leading to summaries riddled with disfluencies and semantic errors after fine-tuning. To mitigate these issues, we employ an efficient few-shot strategy utilizing adapters. These adapters can readily store domain-specific knowledge without fine-tuning the entire model; instead, we pre-train them on a large collection of unannotated customer reviews using held-out reviews as pseudo-labels, followed by fine-tuning on a small set of human-annotated data. Our results demonstrate that this self-supervised adapter pre-training boosts summary quality by 2.0 and 1.3 ROUGE-L points on the Amazon and Yelp datasets, respectively, compared to standard fine-tuning. Additionally, to enable summary personalization, we condition the model on aspect keyword queries generated from generic datasets. We pre-train the adapters using this query-based approach on customer reviews before fine-tuning them on annotated data, resulting in more coherent and less redundant summary content.

Autoregressive moving average (ARMA) and generalized autoregressive moving average (GARMA) models are frequently employed in statistical analysis. This research adopts these methods because they utilize historical data to forecast current values, a technique particularly valuable for prediction tasks. The study specifically addresses count data, which often exhibits non-normal distribution characteristics. To handle this, time series modeling approaches, including arithmetic series methods, were developed. The primary objective of this study is to identify the optimal model for positive confirmed Covid-19 cases in Indonesia by selecting the model with the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) value.

We define $p$-adic measures that interpolate the special values of reciprocals of $p$-adic $L$-functions for totally real number fields $K$ at negative integers. This construction relies on examining the non-constant component of partial Eisenstein series associated with the Hilbert modular group of $K$.

Semi-supervised medical image segmentation often struggles with limited and imbalanced data, leading to poor performance on specific tail classes. This inadequate training for such classes can introduce noise into pseudo-labels, negatively impacting overall learning. To address this limitation and pinpoint underperforming classes, we propose maintaining a confidence array that tracks class-wise performance throughout training. We introduce a fuzzy fusion technique to adaptively prioritize individual confidence metrics per sample, moving away from traditional ensemble methods that rely on fixed weights for all test cases. Additionally, we implement a robust class-wise sampling method and dynamic stabilization to enhance the training strategy. Our approach dynamically weights all underperforming classes while actively filtering out training noise. Evaluations on two cardiac MRI datasets, ACDC and MMWHS, demonstrate the method's effectiveness and generalizability, showing it outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches in the literature.

We report the initial detection of the [N II] 122 $\mu$m and [O III] 52 $\mu$m spectral lines in a galaxy from the reionisation epoch. Combining these findings with prior measurements of the [C II] 158 $\mu$m and [O III] 88 $\mu$m lines, we derive an electron density of $\lesssim$ 500 cm$^{-3}$ and a gas-phase metallicity of $Z/Z_\odot \sim 1.1 \pm 0.2$ for A1689-zD1. This object is a gravitationally-lensed, dusty galaxy located at $z$ = 7.133. Metallicity estimates from other sources in interstellar media at $z \gtrsim$ 6 are generally an order of magnitude lower. Consequently, A1689-zD1's unusually high metallicity appears inconsistent with the fundamental metallicity relation, though substantial dust obscuration of the stellar mass may partially explain this discrepancy. Assuming solar metallicity, the dust-to-metals ratio is several times lower than anticipated, suggesting that dust formation efficiency might be reduced in galaxies beyond $z \sim$ 7. Furthermore, the inferred nitrogen enrichment relative to oxygen, which underpins the metallicity calculation, implies that star formation in this system began approximately 250 Myr ago, indicating the galaxy's origins date to $z >$ 10.

This study introduces a nonlinear diffusion equation to model thermalization in both fermionic and bosonic systems, supported by analytical solutions. When transport coefficients remain constant, exact time-dependent solutions are obtained via nonlinear transformations, from which local equilibration times are calculated. The stationary solutions of this equation correspond to Fermi-Dirac and Bose-Einstein distributions. The paper illustrates these concepts with applications to the local thermalization of quarks and gluons in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, as well as the thermalization of ultracold atoms, including the time-dependent formation of Bose-Einstein condensates.

This study systematically examines the influence of the Hulthen potential on spin and pseudospin symmetry solutions by solving the Dirac equation using attractive scalar $S(r)$ and repulsive vector $V(r)$ potentials. To incorporate orbital dependencies, including spin-orbit and pseudospin-orbit couplings, the Hulthen-square approximation is applied. This effective method constructs the spin and pseudo-centrifugal kinetic energy terms from the square of the Hulthen potential. Analytical solutions for the Dirac equation, accounting for spin-orbit and pseudospin-orbit couplings within the Hulthen potential framework, are derived using the Nikiforov-Uvarov (NU) method. The resulting energy eigenvalue equations and wave functions for various degenerate states are provided, covering different spin-orbital, pseudospin-orbital, and radial quantum numbers under conditions of spin and pseudospin symmetry. Keywords: Spin and pseudospin symmetry; orbital dependency; Dirac equation; Hulthen potential; Nikiforov-Uvarov Method.

It is important to note that recognizing a specific tensor class as a $P$-tensor guarantees the compactness required to solve the tensor complementarity problem (TCP). This study introduces a new tensor class, the Nekrasov $Z$ tensor, within the framework of the TCP. We demonstrate that the class of $P$-tensors encompasses the class of even-ordered Nekrasov $Z$ tensors with positive diagonal entries. In this context, we propose a method to transform a Nekrasov $Z$ tensor into one that is diagonally dominant.

Keywords: Diagonally dominant tensor, Nekrasov tensors, Nonsingular $H$ tensor, Nekrasov $Z$ tensor, $P$-tensors, Tensor complementarity problem

We investigate agegraphic dark energy models within a braneworld framework that includes energy exchange between the brane and the bulk. Our analysis assumes the adiabatic equation holds for dark matter but is violated for agegraphic dark energy due to this brane-bulk interaction. Our findings indicate that, in the presence of such interactions, the equation of state parameter for agegraphic dark energy on the brane ($w_D$) can evolve from a normal state ($w_D > -1$) into a phantom regime ($w_D < -1$); however, the effective equation of state for dark energy ($w^{\mathrm{eff}}_D$) remains constrained to satisfy $w^{\mathrm{eff}}_D \geq -1$.

This study examines the total cross section for Higgs boson pair production at next-to-next-to-leading order within the large top quark mass limit, calculating four terms in the $1/m_t^2$ expansion. We observe good convergence below the top quark threshold, making our findings a useful resource for approximation methods seeking next-to-next-to-leading order corrections across the full kinematic range. Furthermore, we outline the various stages of our calculation, specifically presenting results for three- and four-particle phase-space master integrals and detailing the assessment of collinear counterterms.

We investigate the Kondo effect involving a localized impurity that transforms under a general symmetry group $G$, termed the $G$-Kondo effect. By deriving a one-dimensional effective model coupled to the impurity, we analyze thermodynamic properties using the boundary conformal field theory framework. Specifically, we examine the impurity entropy at the conformal fixed point, as well as the low-temperature behavior of specific heat and susceptibility. Furthermore, we calculate the Wilson ratio based on these findings and address cases featuring exceptional group symmetry.

Rotating savings and credit associations (roscas) function as informal financial groups prevalent in areas with limited access to formal banking. Within these organizations, a fixed circle of members periodically contributes funds to a collective pool, which is subsequently distributed among them through lottery, auction, or aftermarket mechanisms. While extensively examined in economic literature, roscas pose significant theoretical challenges due to their dynamic characteristics. Conventional economic studies often rely on coarse ordinal welfare comparisons against other credit allocation systems, failing to fully account for the widespread adoption of roscas. This paper adopts an algorithmic approach, leveraging techniques from the price of anarchy field to establish worst-case welfare approximation guarantees. Additionally, we conduct experimental analyses comparing welfare outcomes as various environmental features change. These cardinal welfare assessments provide further justification for the commonality of roscas, and the discussion concludes by highlighting several other promising research directions.

This study examines the inviscid limit of two-dimensional compressible viscoelastic equations on a half-plane subject to no-slip boundary conditions. Assuming the initial deformation tensor is a small perturbation of the identity and the initial density is close to a positive constant, we derive uniform solution estimates within conormal Sobolev spaces. While it is established that the corresponding inviscid limit for compressible Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip conditions typically fails to yield uniform energy estimates due to the emergence of strong boundary layers, our findings indicate that the deformation tensor effect is crucial. Specifically, this effect facilitates the vanishing viscosity process by inhibiting the formation of strong boundary layers. Consequently, we successfully justify the inviscid limit for solutions governed by viscoelastic equations under no-slip conditions, relying on the uniform conormal regularity estimates obtained in this work.

Adversarial attacks expose security weaknesses in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), hindering their use in safety-critical fields. Current attack methods, however, typically require knowledge of the specific GNN model or the target prediction task. Is such information truly essential? Since a single graph often supports multiple downstream tasks unknown to an attacker, it is crucial to evaluate GNN vulnerabilities in a model- and task-agnostic context. This study investigates this issue, demonstrating that GNNs remain susceptible to adversarial perturbations even without knowledge of the downstream task or model. The proposed method, TANDIS (Targeted Attack via Neighborhood DIStortion), proves that distorting node neighborhoods can severely degrade prediction accuracy. Despite neighborhood distortion being an NP-hard problem, TANDIS employs a novel heuristic combining Graph Isomorphism Networks with deep Q-learning to address this efficiently. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets and state-of-the-art models indicate that TANDIS is, on average, up to 50% more effective than existing techniques while operating over 1000 times faster.

Physiological and circadian rhythms are fundamental to both homeostasis and various disease mechanisms, including the infradian and circadian seizure patterns seen in epilepsy. This study investigates a novel implantable stimulator that utilizes chronotherapy as a feedforward mechanism to complement existing open-loop and closed-loop techniques. The integrated algorithm adjusts stimulation to match ultradian, circadian, and infradian patient patterns through gradual temporal modifications of stimulation and algorithm components, while also adapting instantly to immediate physiological demands like breakthrough seizures or posture changes. Embedded sensors within the device can refine the baseline circadian stimulation pattern, acting as a "digital zeitgeber." This methodology was evaluated on a dog with severe, drug-resistant idiopathic generalized epilepsy that followed a diurnal cycle linked to sleep-wake patterns. Before the implant, the animal's cluster seizures progressed to status epilepticus (SE), necessitating emergency medication. The cranially mounted system was fully implanted bilaterally into the centromedian nucleus of the thalamus. Through time-based modulation for thalamocortical rhythm tuning and fast-adaptive modes responsive to activity, the dog has experienced no further SE events since the implantation seven months ago. Notably, no significant cluster seizures have occurred, allowing for a reduction in rescue medication. Employing chronotherapy as a feedforward signal to enhance adaptive neurostimulators may offer a valuable strategy for conditions defined by sensitivity to temporal patterns, introducing a new way to tailor patient-specific therapies.

Ensuring fairness, robustness against confounding biases, and resilience to class imbalance are crucial attributes for autonomous decision-making systems that impact real-world scenarios. While numerous targeted solutions have been developed to tackle these three issues individually, a cohesive framework remains absent. This work introduces a generalized formalization demonstrating that these challenges are merely different manifestations of imbalance. Building on this insight, we propose a unified loss correction method, termed the Fairness, Biases, and Imbalances loss (FBI-loss), to simultaneously address these concerns. We evaluate the efficacy of this approach across three real-world benchmarks—each corresponding to one specific issue—and a suite of synthetic datasets with varying complexities to thoroughly assess its performance. Empirical findings indicate that the flexible design of the FBI-loss achieves competitive results compared to existing specialized literature solutions.

We introduce a novel dark matter stabilization mechanism based on fixed points of modular $A_4$ symmetry, which restores a residual symmetry at specific fixed points ($\tau=\omega,\ i, i\times\infty$). Our analysis demonstrates that a model defined at $\tau =i$ can accurately account for neutrino oscillation data while remaining consistent with dark matter stability.

The field of industry frequently encounters scenarios requiring the automatic colorization of vintage grayscale images, particularly for video platforms and archives. This paper introduces HistoryNet, a framework dedicated to high-fidelity colorization of historical figures' attire through fine-grained semantic analysis and prior knowledge. While colorizing historical persons is both practical and realistic, current methods struggle to perform adequately. To address this, we propose HistoryNet, which comprises three components: classification, fine-grained semantic parsing, and colorization. The classification module categorizes images by era, nationality, and garment type, while the parsing sub-network identifies semantic regions for person contours, clothing, and backgrounds to ensure precise clothing and skin colorization and prevent color bleeding. During training, classification and semantic parsing features are integrated into the coloring generation network to enhance performance. This dual-subnetwork design improves colorization accuracy and clarifies image boundaries. Additionally, we introduce the Modern Historical Movies Dataset (MHMD), a novel resource containing 1,353,166 images with 42 labels covering eras, nationalities, and garment types, sourced from 147 modern historical films and TV series. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art methods, particularly in correctly rendering military uniforms in accordance with historical records.

This study addresses the challenge of Named Entity Recognition (NER) in extremely low-resource languages, where only a few hundred labeled examples are available. As a core component of Natural Language Processing (NLP), NER has traditionally advanced due to large-scale corpora that yield superior results in data-rich languages like English and French; however, its application to low-resource languages remains largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose Mask Augmented Named Entity Recognition (MANER), a novel approach that exploits the distributional properties of pre-trained masked language models (MLMs) for NER tasks. By utilizing the `<mask>` token to capture rich semantic context, MANER repurposes this token for entity prediction by inserting it before every word in a sentence requiring tagging. During training, the method jointly fine-tunes the MLM and a dedicated prediction head connected to each `<mask>` token. Our results demonstrate that MANER is highly effective for low-resource scenarios, improving upon state-of-the-art techniques by an average of 12% and up to 48% in F1 score across 100 languages with as few as 100 training instances. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive analyses and ablation studies to identify the specific contexts where MANER performs optimally.

Symmetries involving complex and Hermitian conjugation, including time-reversal symmetry and pseudo-Hermiticity, significantly influence the eigenvalue spectra of non-Hermitian random matrices. This study demonstrates that these symmetries generate universal level statistics for non-Hermitian random matrices situated on and near the real axis. Through extensive numerical analysis of large random matrices, we derived five distinct universal distributions for the level spacings and spacing ratios of real eigenvalues, with each distribution specific to its respective symmetry class. Additionally, we examined the spacing of real eigenvalues within physical models, such as bosonic many-body systems and disordered, dissipative free fermionic systems. Our findings clarify that level spacings in ergodic (metallic) phases align with the universal distributions of non-Hermitian random matrices belonging to the same symmetry classes, whereas spacings in many-body localized and Anderson localized phases follow Poisson statistics. We further observed that the count of real eigenvalues exhibits distinct scaling behaviors between ergodic and localized phases across these symmetry classes. Consequently, these results provide robust tools for identifying quantum chaos, many-body localization, and real-complex transitions in symmetric non-Hermitian systems.

The T2K experiment investigates muon neutrino disappearance and electron neutrino appearance using accelerator-generated neutrino and antineutrino beams. With an exposure of $14.7(7.6)\times 10^{20}$ protons on target in neutrino (antineutrino) mode, the experiment observed 89 $\nu_e$ candidates and 7 anti-$\nu_e$ candidates, compared to expected values of 67.5 and 9.0 respectively for $\delta_{CP}=0$ under normal mass ordering. The resulting $2\sigma$ confidence interval for the $CP$ violating phase, $\delta_{CP}$, excludes the $CP$-conserving scenarios ($\delta_{CP}=0,\pi$). Additionally, the best-fit values for the other parameters are determined to be $\sin^2\theta_{23} = 0.526^{+0.032}_{-0.036}$ and $\Delta m^2_{32}=2.463^{+0.071}_{-0.070}\times10^{-3} \mathrm{eV}^2/c^4$.

We present a hybrid projection framework that integrates linear Mori projection with conditional Zwanzig projection techniques to derive a Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) applicable to general interacting many-body systems. This derived GLE incorporates three key components: i) the potential of mean force (PMF), which characterizes the equilibrium distribution within the selected reaction coordinate space; ii) a random force term explicitly contingent on the system's initial state; and iii) a memory friction contribution divided into two parts—a component linear in past reaction-coordinate velocities and another generally non-linear in past reaction coordinates but independent of velocities. Consequently, our hybrid approach unifies the advantageous features of both Zwanzig and Mori schemes. We demonstrate that the non-linear memory friction arises from correlations between the reaction-coordinate velocity and the random force. Furthermore, we introduce a numerical method to calculate all GLE parameters, specifically the non-linear memory friction function and the random force distribution, using a trajectory in reaction coordinate space. We apply this method to analyze dihedral-angle dynamics of a butane molecule in water, based on atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, showing that non-linear memory friction exists and that the random force displays significant non-Gaussian corrections. Additionally, we provide a derivation of the GLE for multidimensional reaction coordinates defined as general functions of all phase-space positions, representing a systematic coarse-graining procedure that maintains both the correct equilibrium behavior and the accurate dynamics of the coarse-grained system.

This study examines the collective behavior of self-propelled agents within an obstacle-filled environment where obstacles are anchored to fixed points by springs. The active particles alter this environment by displacing obstacles via repulsive forces, generating feedback loops that produce diverse patterns such as trails, bands, clusters, and honeycomb structures. We begin with a discrete model originally presented in [Aceves2020] and its corresponding continuum PDE formulation. Our first key contribution is a comprehensive analysis of pattern formation in both discrete and continuum frameworks within 2D space; utilizing linear stability analysis, we construct phase diagrams and identify the critical mechanisms driving bifurcations. Consequently, we find that agent-agent repulsion, agent-obstacle repulsion, and obstacle spring stiffness are the primary drivers of pattern emergence, whereas particle alignment forces play a secondary role. Our second major innovation involves developing a novel methodology to compare discrete and continuum models, which we apply to rigorously assess the agreement between the two approaches.

We formulate a nonlinear optimization model incorporating complementarity constraints to manage the time-dependent operation of district heating networks. The underlying physics of heat and water transport within these systems are described by nonlinear, hyperbolic one-dimensional partial differential equations. Furthermore, to account for the blending of varying water temperatures at network junctions, a pooling-type mixing model is necessary; this model can be reformulated using appropriate complementarity conditions. Consequently, the problem becomes a mathematical program with complementarity constraints coupled with nonlinear partial differential equations representing physical laws. To ensure tractability, we implement suitable spatial and temporal discretizations, yielding a finite-dimensional optimization problem with complementarity constraints. For this problem, we devise a specific reformulation that enhances constraint regularity. Additionally, we introduce an instantaneous control strategy for the discretized scenario, examine practically significant penalty formulations, and detail preprocessing methods designed to simplify the nodal mixing model. Finally, we apply these techniques to solve realistic case studies, and our numerical results demonstrate their practical utility.

The LHCb experiment analyzed the angular distribution and differential branching fraction for the $B^{+} \rightarrow K^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ decay using a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $1.0\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. Measurements of the angular distribution, categorized by bins of dimuon invariant mass squared, align with Standard Model predictions. By integrating the differential branching fraction across the complete dimuon invariant mass spectrum, a total branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}(B^{+} \rightarrow K^{+}\mu^{+}\mu^{-}) = (4.36 \pm 0.15 \pm 0.18)\times 10^{-7}$ was determined. These results represent the most precise measurements to date for this specific decay channel.

This study seeks to determine the key physical mechanisms governing the intensity and polarization patterns of the solar K I D lines via spectral synthesis, with a specific focus on the D2 line. Theoretical Stokes profiles were generated by numerically solving the radiative transfer equations for polarized radiation using one-dimensional semi-empirical models of the solar atmosphere. These computations incorporate scattering polarization, partial frequency redistribution (PRD), hyperfine structure (HFS), J- and F-state interference, multiple isotopes, and magnetic fields of varying strength and orientation. Results indicate that intensity and circular polarization profiles for both D lines can be adequately modeled by omitting J-state interference and HFS. Consequently, the magnetograph formula can be utilized on both lines without accounting for HFS to estimate weak longitudinal magnetic fields in the lower chromosphere. In contrast, accurately modeling scattering polarization signals necessitates including HFS. While HFS significantly depolarizes the D2 scattering polarization amplitude, the signal remains detectable. Neglecting PRD effects introduces substantial errors in the scattering polarization profile, and collisions during scattering processes also exert a notable depolarizing influence. Furthermore, the D2 scattering polarization signal is particularly sensitive to magnetic fields of approximately 10 G and their orientation; however, its center-to-limb variation relative to the limb amplitude is largely independent of field strength and orientation. These results underscore the utility of the K I D2 line polarization for diagnosing solar magnetism, demonstrating that the linear and circular polarization signals are primarily sensitive to magnetic fields in the lower chromosphere and upper photosphere, respectively.

The CEGAR loop in software model checking frequently fails to converge if the abstraction refinement process cannot generate a loop invariant. While existing SMT-solver-based refinement methods are limited to analyzing traces—programs stripped of loops—this paper introduces a novel procedure designed to bypass this constraint whenever feasible. By applying abstract interpretation to a program derived from the input trace, we ensure the acquisition of a loop invariant if the program contains one. An SMT solver is invoked solely when abstract interpretation yields an inconclusive result, effectively combining both techniques. Experimental results within the context of trace abstraction demonstrate the practical viability of this approach.

Concerns regarding user and law enforcement privacy in data security are increasingly hindering data sharing between organizations. Data federation offers a solution by enabling inter-organizational cooperation through abstract data interfaces. Concurrently, cloud computing adoption allows organizations to leverage the elasticity and scalability of cloud storage. However, current data placement strategies typically address only a single factor—either execution time or monetary cost—while neglecting data partitioning for hard constraints. This paper introduces a method for cloud-based data processing involving multiple organizations, comprising a federation platform called FedCube and a Lyapunov-based data placement algorithm. FedCube facilitates cloud processing, while the placement algorithm generates plans to partition and store data, optimizing a multi-objective cost model that balances monetary cost and execution time while adhering to specific constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly lowers total costs by up to 69.8% compared to existing methods.

The investigation of complex networks featuring multiple weights has recently become a prominent area of research. While prior work on single-weight networks demonstrates their ability to facilitate synchronization, rigorous analysis confirming that multi-weight networks can achieve synchronization more rapidly has been lacking. This paper addresses complex networks that may be directed, a condition that complicates synchronization analysis involving multiple couplings. By utilizing the normalized left eigenvectors (NLEVec) associated with the zero eigenvalue of the coupling matrices, we establish that if the Chebyshev distance between these vectors remains below a specific allowable deviation bound, synchronization and control will be achieved with sufficiently large coupling strengths, indicating that all coupling matrices accelerate synchronization. Additionally, adaptive rules for the coupling strength are proposed.

Armed conflict has fundamentally defined human history, yet since World War II, low-intensity attacks have overshadowed large-scale interstate wars. These incidents are frequently executed by non-state armed groups (NAGs) backed by host states (HSs). This study examines the global bipartite network connecting NAGs and HSs from 1945 to 2010, revealing structural similarities to ecological systems, including mutualistic and parasitic relationships, as well as nested and modular architectures. The observed nestedness stems from preferential attachment, where highly connected actors are more prone to both acquiring and losing ties. Furthermore, the analysis identifies enduring major modules that reflect regional and trans-regional interests; unlike transient groups, these modules exhibit significant membership turnover. Understanding this network architecture clarifies actor roles and informs more effective intervention strategies.

Semantic search for candidate retrieval represents a critical yet underexplored challenge in retrieval-based chatbots, focusing on efficiently selecting a subset of candidate responses from an extensive database. The current bottleneck lies in designing model architectures that satisfy two key requirements: 1) facilitating rich interactions between queries and responses to generate relevant outputs, and 2) enabling the independent projection of both queries and responses into latent spaces for efficient application during online semantic search. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method termed the Multitask-based Semantic Search Neural Network (MSSNN) for candidate retrieval. This approach achieves query-response interactions through multi-task learning by employing a Seq2Seq modeling task to develop a robust query encoder, followed by a word prediction task to construct response embeddings, and concluding with a simple matching model to compute a dot-product scorer. Experimental results indicate the promising potential of this proposed approach.

This study examines the dynamics of the delay logistic equation featuring complex parameters and arbitrary complex initial conditions, including an analysis of its local stability. Through computational methods, we highlight several distinctive solution characteristics that do not appear when the equation is restricted to positive real parameters and initial conditions. These findings have prompted us to formulate open questions and conjectures concerning chaotic behavior, higher-order periodic solutions, and global asymptotic convergence within the delay logistic framework. We hope these insights into complex difference equations will significantly contribute to current research on rational difference equations by enhancing our understanding of system behavior in the complex domain.

Violations of the positivity assumption, also known as the common support condition, pose significant challenges to health policy research by potentially causing substantial bias, increased variance, and invalid statistical inferences. This paper defines positivity within both single- and multiple-timepoint (longitudinal) health policy evaluation contexts and examines real-world threats to this condition. We present empirical evidence demonstrating practical positivity violations that can occur when estimating the effects of health policies, specifically Naloxone Access Laws. In cases where these violations are severe, an alternative approach is to estimate the impact of a delayed law enactment, which corresponds to a modified treatment policy. This strategy significantly relaxes the required positivity assumption, allowing for the estimation of policy effects even when standard conditions are not met. We apply this method to define and estimate the longitudinal effects of Naloxone Access Laws on opioid overdose rates.

Malware detection typically relies on dynamic analysis, which observes runtime behavior in a controlled setting, or static analysis, which extracts features via reverse engineering. While dynamic analysis struggles with anti-virtualization and evasion techniques, static analysis is hindered by code obfuscation. Previous studies attempted to mitigate these issues by combining both dynamic and static features to leverage their respective strengths. However, merely concatenating these heterogeneous feature vectors often leads to imbalanced contributions, negatively affecting detection performance. Furthermore, dynamic analysis is resource-intensive, requiring secure environments and resulting in significant detection delays and infrastructure costs. This paper introduces a novel approach to constructing aggregated features by concatenating deep learning-derived latent features with dimensions that contribute equally. Additionally, we propose a knowledge distillation method to transfer insights from a teacher model trained on these aggregated features to a student model trained exclusively on static features, enabling the detection of new malware without dynamic analysis. Extensive experiments using a dataset of 86,709 samples (both benign and malicious) demonstrate that the proposed teacher model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to a 2.38% improvement in accuracy. The distilled student model matches the teacher's high performance (97.81% accuracy) while drastically reducing detection time from 70,046.6 ms to 194.9 ms, eliminating the need for dynamic analysis.

We provide a proof demonstrating that the hyperbolic plane cannot be isometrically immersed into Euclidean $3$-space via a $C^\infty$ map. The argument utilizes concepts from various areas of undergraduate mathematics, where the application of moving frames and connection forms streamlines the proof's structure relative to methods employing coordinate patches and Christoffel symbols. The pivotal step involves shifting from representations based on principal directions—which facilitate the calculation of Gaussian curvature—to those based on asymptotic directions, which establish a coordinate system and enable the computation of surface area.

Integrating the complementary data from vast amounts of unlabeled multi-sensor inputs, such as Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and optical imagery, is a pivotal challenge in remote sensing. Although contrastive learning has recently excelled in extracting meaningful representations from multi-view data, it typically concentrates solely on image-level features, which may be insufficient for dense prediction applications like land-cover mapping. To address this, we introduce a self-supervised framework designed for SAR-optical data fusion and land-cover mapping. This framework fuses SAR and optical images through multi-view contrastive loss applied at image-level, super-pixel level, and across early, intermediate, and late stages individually. For the land-cover mapping task, we classify each pixel by combining pre-trained features with the image's intrinsic spectral information. Experimental findings indicate that our approach achieves comparable accuracy while reducing feature dimensionality compared to standard image-level contrastive learning methods. Among the three fusion strategies, the intermediate fusion approach yields the best performance. Furthermore, integrating pixel-level fusion with spectral indices enhances land-cover mapping results relative to image-level fusion, particularly when few pseudo-labels are available.

This study presents an overview of recent jet measurements from pp and Pb-Pb collisions obtained using the ALICE detector. Jets at midrapidity are reconstructed with the anti-$k_{\mathrm{T}}$ algorithm, encompassing both charged particle jets derived from ALICE's tracking detectors and full jets formed by combining the electromagnetic calorimeter with the tracking system. The analysis concentrates on inclusive and semi-inclusive jet measurements, along with jet substructure studies featuring various groomed and ungroomed observables. In pp collisions, these findings validate pQCD methods for $p_{\mathrm{T,\;jet}}<140$ GeV$/c$ within a low pileup setting and help restrict models of non-perturbative effects. Conversely, in Pb-Pb collisions, the data evaluate jet quenching models in the quark-gluon plasma and provide constraints on the characteristics of high-temperature QCD matter.

Deep neural networks often experience substantial performance degradation when facing distribution shifts between training and deployment environments. Domain Generalization (DG) seeks to safely transfer models to unseen target domains using only source domain data. Despite numerous DG approaches, a recent study called DomainBed indicates that many fail to outperform simple Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM). To address this, we introduce a general framework orthogonal to existing DG methods that consistently enhances their performance. Unlike prior DG works that rely on a static source model hoping for universality, our proposed AdaODM adaptively adjusts the source model during testing for various target domains. Specifically, we construct multiple domain-specific classifiers based on a shared domain-generic feature extractor. Trained adversarially, the feature extractor maps inputs to a domain-invariant space while the classifiers learn distinct decision boundaries tied to specific source domains. During testing, differences between target and source distributions are effectively quantified by measuring prediction disagreement among the source classifiers. By fine-tuning source models to minimize this disagreement at test time, target domain features are well-aligned with the invariant feature space. We validated AdaODM on two popular DG methods, ERM and CORAL, across four benchmarks: VLCS, PACS, OfficeHome, and TerraIncognita. Results demonstrate that AdaODM stably improves generalization on unseen domains and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Overdamped Brownian dynamics in harmonic oscillators serve as a fundamental model in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, effectively representing stochastic systems like optically confined colloidal particles. This study designs optimal thermal strategies to minimize the transition duration between equilibrium states of overdamped $d$-dimensional oscillators. Using control theory, we demonstrate that these optimal protocols follow a "bang-bang" pattern, requiring the bath temperature to oscillate between its minimum and maximum permissible limits. Notably, the minimum connection time grows with the dimensionality $d$, even for symmetric oscillators with spherical symmetry; despite the degeneracy of the elastic constant across $d$ directions suggesting a one-dimensional equivalent, a higher dimensional cost is unavoidable. This counterintuitive phenomenon is rigorously analyzed and explained physically. Additionally, the research examines thermodynamic length and its divergence along the brachistochrone using information theory.

Recently, system identification utilizing Koopman operator theory has gained significant traction. The spectral characteristics of the Koopman operator are intrinsically linked to fundamental system properties such as stability, periodicity, and invariant sets. With numerous algorithms developed in recent years, estimating these spectral components has become increasingly accessible. This paper demonstrates the application of one such method, extended dynamic mode decomposition, to data derived from multiple system outputs. These outputs, referred to as observables, may include known state variables or unknown sensor data from biologically relevant systems. To achieve this, we approximate the target observables and their temporal iterates by solving regularized least-squares problems; these problems yield analytic solutions that incorporate heuristic adjustments to ensure expected estimation results.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) remains a difficult task due to two primary obstacles: significant variations in writing styles and a lack of labeled training data. To address these issues, researchers typically rely on synthetic data generation and augmentation to train HTR models; however, this approach often yields encouraging yet still inaccurate transcriptions when applied to real-world text. This paper introduces an unsupervised writer adaptation method capable of automatically tuning a generic recognizer—originally trained on synthetic fonts—to accommodate new writers. Our proposal was experimentally validated across five diverse datasets that present various challenges, including: (i) document sources ranging from modern to historic samples, some affected by paper degradation; (ii) diverse handwriting styles encompassing both single and multi-writer collections; and (iii) linguistic variations involving different character combinations. Results across these demanding datasets demonstrate that our system maintains robust performance, offering a practical and generalized solution for handling new document collections without the need for costly and time-consuming manual annotation.

Let $\sigma$ denote a first-order signature and let $\mathbf{W}_n$ represent the collection of all $\sigma$-structures whose domain is $[n] = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. An inference framework is defined as a class $\mathbf{F}$ consisting of pairs $(\mathbb{P}, L)$, where $\mathbb{P}$ is a sequence $(\mathbb{P}_n : n \geq 1)$ of probability distributions over $\mathbf{W}_n$, and $L$ is a logic with truth values ranging in the unit interval $[0, 1]$. The frameworks under consideration feature pairs where $\mathbb{P}$ is derived from a probabilistic graphical model, and $L$ captures statements regarding (conditional) probabilities or (arithmetic or geometric) averages. We introduce the concept of asymptotic expressivity: a framework $\mathbf{F}'$ is asymptotically at least as expressive as $\mathbf{F}$ if, for every $(\mathbb{P}, L) \in \mathbf{F}$, there exists a $(\mathbb{P}', L') \in \mathbf{F}'$ such that $\mathbb{P}$ is asymptotically total-variation-equivalent to $\mathbb{P}'$, and for every formula $\varphi(\bar{x}) \in L$, there is a corresponding $\varphi'(\bar{x}) \in L'$ that is asymptotically equivalent to $\varphi(\bar{x})$ relative to $\mathbb{P}$. This relationship constitutes a preorder, and we characterize a strict partial order on the equivalence classes of inference frameworks relevant to machine learning and artificial intelligence. Our analysis encompasses Conditional Probability Logic ($CPL$) and Probability Logic with Aggregation functions ($PLA$), previously introduced in our work. Furthermore, we define a sublogic $coPLA$ of $PLA$ wherein aggregation functions adhere to additional continuity constraints, demonstrating that inference frameworks based on $coPLA$ are asymptotically strictly less expressive than those based on $PLA$.

It is established that a positive semi-definite Hamiltonian $H$, possessing a tridiagonal matrix representation in a specific basis, can be expressed as $H = A^\dagger A$, where $A$ acts as a forward shift operator functioning as an annihilation operator. This formulation imparts rich supersymmetric characteristics to $H$, producing results comparable to those derived when treating the Hamiltonian as a differential operator. In this work, we investigate coherent states defined as the eigenstates of $A$ and explicitly determine their expansion coefficients within the specified basis. We further identify a complete set of special coherent states capable of serving as a basis themselves. Using these special states, we demonstrate that any general coherent state follows an expansion structure analogous to a Lagrange interpolation scheme. As an application of this formalism, we analyze examples of systems exhibiting pure discrete, pure continuous, or mixed energy spectra.

In the majority of direct detection experiments, the standard description of free nuclear recoil fails for dark matter masses below approximately 100 MeV or when recoil energies approach several times the typical phonon energy. While single-phonon excitation dominates scattering for dark matter lighter than 1 MeV and has been previously calculated, multiphonon processes prevail in the intermediate mass range or under higher detector thresholds. We present the first calculation of the scattering rate due to multiphonon production across the full keV-to-GeV dark matter mass spectrum, utilizing a harmonic crystal target model. Furthermore, we offer an analytic framework that unifies the single-phonon, multiphonon, and nuclear recoil regimes. These findings are now available within the public $\texttt{DarkELF}$ package.

Recent breakthroughs in visual navigation have enabled intelligent embodied agents to derive meaningful representations from raw RGB images, allowing them to execute diverse tasks that require both structural and semantic reasoning. Nevertheless, the majority of learning-based navigation policies are developed and evaluated exclusively within simulated environments. To achieve practical utility, these policies must be successfully transferred to real-world settings. This paper introduces an unsupervised domain adaptation framework for visual navigation. Our approach translates target domain images into the source domain in a manner that aligns with the representations learned by the navigation policy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses several baselines across two distinct navigation tasks in simulation. Furthermore, we validate that this technique effectively facilitates the transfer of simulation-trained navigation policies to real-world applications.

Inspired by recent experimental findings, we explore the nonreciprocal magnetoelastic coupling between surface acoustic phonons in dielectric, non-magnetic substrates and magnons in adjacent nanomagnets. Rotating forces generated at the nanomagnet's edges by magnetization dynamics drive this nonreciprocal interaction through rotation-momentum locking. This coupling results in nonreciprocal surface phonon transmission and a near-perfect phonon diode effect achievable with multiple (tens of) high-quality (ordinary) magnetic nanowires. Additionally, phase-sensitive microwave transmission exhibits nonreciprocity, enabling the detection of coherent phonon signals excited by magnetization dynamics. Finally, we predict the nonreciprocal pumping of phonons by precessing magnetization using the Landauer-Büttiker formalism.

Magnetic proximity interactions (MPIs) arising from the interface between atomically thin semiconductors and two-dimensional magnets offer a method to tune spin and valley degrees of freedom in nonmagnetic monolayers without requiring external magnetic fields. In these van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures, MPIs stem from nanometer-scale coupling between the spin-dependent electronic wavefunctions of the constituent materials and are typically modeled as an effective magnetic field acting on the semiconductor layer. However, we demonstrate that this conventional view is insufficient: unlike fields applied externally, MPIs in vdW heterostructures can produce markedly asymmetric effects. Valley-resolved optical reflection spectroscopy of MoSe$_{2}$/CrBr$_{3}$ vdW systems reveals pronounced energy shifts in the $K$ and $K'$ valleys of MoSe$_{2}$ driven by the ferromagnetism of the CrBr$_{3}$ layer, with significant asymmetry observed at both A- and B-exciton resonances. Density-functional calculations suggest that valley-asymmetric MPIs rely sensitively on the spin-dependent hybridization of overlapping bands, indicating this phenomenon is likely a universal characteristic of such hybrid vdW structures. Consequently, these findings outline pathways for the selective control of specific spin and valley states in monolayer semiconductors.

The ATLAS experiment relies on electron and photon triggers, effective across transverse energies ranging from 5 GeV to multiple TeV, to capture signals from diverse physics scenarios, including Standard Model processes and new phenomenon searches in both proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions. To manage the fourfold rise in peak LHC luminosity between 2015 and 2018 (Run 2) to 2.1$\times$10$^{34}$cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, alongside a comparable increase in interactions per crossing to approximately 60, trigger algorithms and selection criteria were refined to regulate rates without compromising efficiency for physics studies. In proton-proton collisions, the single-electron trigger efficiency relative to offline selection reaches a minimum of 75% for 31 GeV electrons and climbs to 96% at 60 GeV; similarly, the primary diphoton trigger's 25 GeV leg achieves over 96% efficiency relative to tight offline photon selection for 30 GeV photons. For heavy-ion collisions, primary electron and photon trigger efficiencies, compared to standard offline selections, are at least 84% and 95% respectively at 5 GeV above their respective thresholds.

Mental stress is a widespread condition affecting many individuals and represents a significant health issue. Properly managing mental health can markedly enhance the quality of human life. To address this, we propose a robust method for classifying perceived stress using multimodal data collected from forty subjects across three physiological modalities: electroencephalography (EEG), galvanic skin response (GSR), and photoplethysmography (PPG). Data was recorded for three minutes under open-eyes conditions. Participant stress levels were assessed using a Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) questionnaire to generate two- and three-class stress labels. Feature extraction involved four time-domain features from GSR and PPG signals and four frequency-domain features from EEG. Among the EEG features, a frequency band selection algorithm identified the theta band as optimal, followed by a wrapper-based approach for selecting the best feature set. Stress level classification was conducted using three classifiers fed with a fused set of features from all three modalities. The multilayer perceptron classifier achieved notable accuracy, reaching 95% for two classes and 77.5% for three classes.

This work establishes tight upper bounds for the homogeneous degree-$\ell$ components, $f_\ell$, of bounded functions $f$ defined on the hypercube. Specifically, for a function $f: \{\pm 1\}^n \rightarrow [-1,1]$ with degree $d$, we demonstrate that $\| f_\ell \|_\infty \le d^\ell/\ell!$ and $\| \hat{f}_\ell \|_1 \le d^\ell e^{\binom{\ell+1}{2}} n^{\frac{\ell-1}{2}}$. We explore applications of these results to pseudorandomness and learning theory. Furthermore, employing analogous techniques, we extend the classical Pisier's inequality from convex analysis. Our approach relies on the properties of real-rooted polynomials, which hold potential utility in other contexts.

Unsupervised Graph Representation Learning (UGRL) has gained significant research interest and demonstrated strong performance across various graph analysis tasks. However, current UGRL approaches, which depend on the homophily assumption, typically smooth node representations across all edges, thereby overlooking heterophilic edges that link nodes with differing attributes. Consequently, these methods struggle to generalize on heterophilic graphs where dissimilar nodes are frequently connected and remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce GREET, a novel unsupervised Graph Representation Learning framework that incorporates Edge Heterophily Discrimination. GREET learns representations by simultaneously exploiting both homophilic and heterophilic edges. To differentiate between these edge types, we employ an edge discriminator that infers homophily or heterophily based on feature and structural cues. This discriminator is trained unsupervised by minimizing a crafted pivot-anchored ranking loss, utilizing randomly sampled node pairs as pivots. Node representations are refined by contrasting dual-channel encodings derived from the identified homophilic and heterophilic edges. Furthermore, an effective interplay mechanism ensures that edge discrimination and representation learning mutually enhance each other during training. Extensive experiments across 14 benchmark datasets and various learning scenarios validate the superior performance of GREET.

We investigate the transition from $2d$ relativistic Conformal Field Theories (CFTs) to theories exhibiting Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) or Conformal Carroll symmetries by employing quantum chaos diagnostics. Beginning with an ultrarelativistic limit of a relativistic scalar field theory and advancing to the quantum level via an oscillator representation of states, we demonstrate that the CFT$_2$ vacuum smoothly transforms into a BMS$_3$ vacuum as a squeezed state. Calculating the circuit complexity of this transformation using the covariance matrix method reveals distinct divergences at the BMS point, which corresponds to the target state becoming a boundary state. Additionally, we observe analogous behavior in circuit complexity derived from information geometry techniques. Finally, we examine the system's Hamiltonian evolution and analyze Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) alongside operator growth complexity, finding that both scale polynomially with time at the BMS point.

We have constructed the full integrand, covering both planar and non-planar contributions, for the six-loop four-point amplitude in maximal super-Yang-Mills with $D\le10$. This achievement utilizes novel techniques designed to mitigate the explosion of diagram contributions and state sums encountered when calculating multi-loop unitarity cuts in $D$ dimensions. Specifically, we present two graph-based strategies for evaluating generalized unitarity cuts in $D$ dimensions: the first builds recursively from lower-loop cuts, while the second derives them directly from established higher-loop planar cuts. Importantly, neither approach requires explicit state sums or the sewing of tree-level amplitudes. Both methods rely on identities anticipated to apply across a wide range of theories, such as QCD and Einstein gravity.

The yield ratio of light nuclei serves as a potential probe for critical fluctuations in hot QCD matter. This study examines the \textit{background effects}, or non-critical influences arising from a non-trivial thermal environment, on light-nuclei production using the coalescence model. We specifically evaluate how the equilibrium phase-space distribution of nucleons, $f(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{p})$, affects the light-nuclei yield ratio $N_tN_p/N_d^2$, where $N_t$, $N_p$, and $N_d$ represent the yields of tritons, protons, and deuterons, respectively. By utilizing the characteristic function of the phase-space distribution, we systematically expand the yield of light nuclei composed of $A$ nucleons, $N_A$, in terms of \textit{phase-space cumulants}, $\langle\mathbf{r}^n\mathbf{p}^m\rangle_c$. Our findings indicate that cumulants up to the second order vanish within the generalized ratio $N_p^{B-A} N_B^{A-1}/N_A^{B-1}$. Consequently, dominant background factors—including fireball size, kinetic freeze-out temperature, and coordinate--momentum correlations driven by radial expansion—exert a negligible influence on the yield ratio, thereby reinforcing its utility as a tool for searching the critical point. We also provide qualitative illustrations using various background phase-space distributions. Furthermore, higher-order cumulants, which reflect the non-Gaussian nature of the phase-space profile, significantly impact the variation of the yield ratio, especially in smaller fireballs. Qualitatively, the spatial structure of the background tends to reduce the yield ratio, whereas azimuthal anisotropy $v_n$ increases it, with higher orders of anisotropy producing more pronounced effects. These outcomes underscore the need for comprehensive future investigations into the yield ratio employing sophisticated dynamical models.

The global COVID-19 pandemic necessitated widespread quarantines. To curb the spread of the virus, numerous nations implemented contact tracing systems designed to alert individuals who have interacted with infected persons. These systems are typically delivered via mobile applications that utilize technologies like Bluetooth to track interpersonal interactions. This paper examines various smartphone-based contact tracing applications through the lens of privacy.

Global cooperation is essential for addressing diverse collective action challenges, ranging from network colorings to the tragedy of the commons. Recent empirical evidence indicates that introducing a small number of noisy autonomous agents significantly enhances human performance in networked color coordination games. To gain deeper analytical understanding of behavioral randomness, this study examines myopic artificial agents tackling similar network coloring problems. These agents rely on decision-update rules based solely on local information but incorporate random choices at different stages of their heuristic reasoning. The agents are distributed across a random bipartite network guaranteed to be solvable with two colors. Through agent-based simulations and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the effectiveness of resolving color conflicts depends on the specific implementation of random behavior, including the proportion of noisy agents and the timing of noise introduction within the decision process. Furthermore, behavioral randomness can be precisely calibrated to the underlying population structure, such as network size and average degree, to yield beneficial outcomes in discovering collective coloring solutions. Our findings illustrate that distributed greedy optimization algorithms utilizing local information should be paired with occasional exploratory random choices to escape local minima and achieve global coordination.

The epidemic threshold of a social system is defined as the ratio of infection to recovery rates; exceeding this ratio allows a disease to spread epidemically. Without pharmaceutical measures like vaccines, controlling disease spread relies on non-pharmaceutical interventions, such as social distancing, which shift the system's threshold below the disease-specific level, thereby preventing an epidemic. When modeling disease propagation on a social graph, social distancing corresponds to removing specific links. It is hypothesized that the largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of the modified graph represents the system's epidemic threshold. This study employs a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach to identify link removal strategies that effectively minimize this largest eigenvalue. The method generates samples from a relative canonical network ensemble with a specified expectation value for $\lambda_{max}$, termed the "well-controlling network ensemble" (WCNE). Comparing the WCNE structure to randomly thinned networks with identical link densities reveals that WCNE networks exhibit a more homogeneous degree distribution. Leveraging this insight, we define two ad-hoc removal strategies that also significantly reduce the largest eigenvalue. Furthermore, a targeted removal of 80% of links proves as effective as a random removal of 90%, a difference that results in individuals retaining twice as many contacts.

Using NIRSPEC on the Keck 2 telescope, researchers analyzed the He I 10830 Angstrom line in metal-deficient field giant stars. This spectral line is commonly found in stars with effective temperatures exceeding 4500K and absolute magnitudes fainter than -1.5. Fast outflows were identified in most of these stars, with approximately 40% moving fast enough to allow material to escape both the star and its globular cluster. Neither outflow velocities nor line strengths correlate with metallicity, implying that magnetic and/or hydrodynamic processes drive these winds. While gas outflows are observed in all luminous giants, their absence in some lower-luminosity stars suggests variability. Estimated mass loss rates, derived from the Sobolev approximation, range from 3×10⁻¹⁰ to 6×10⁻⁸ solar masses per year; these values hold evolutionary importance for red giant branch (RGB) and red horizontal branch (RHB) stars. Projections indicate that 0.2 solar masses will be shed during the RGB phase, and the resulting wind torque explains the observed slow rotation of field RHB stars. An additional 0.1–0.2 solar masses are expected to be lost during the RHB phase. This initial empirical assessment of RHB mass loss may help explain the extended horizontal branches seen in globular clusters. Furthermore, these findings address the issue of missing intracluster material. Finally, the study suggests possibilities for dwarf stars to be "wind-smothered" by evolved populations, potentially causing surface pollution in high stellar density regions.

We introduce an unsupervised learning framework utilizing descriptors derived from Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to characterize local atomic-scale structural properties. Relying solely on atomic positions without prior information, our technique enables the autonomous detection of atomic structure clusters via a Gaussian mixture model.
