We have successfully applied this method to analyze elemental Zirconium (Zr) in both crystalline and liquid phases, as well as homogeneous nucleation events occurring under deep undercooling. This approach facilitates more profound and autonomous investigations into complex material phenomena at the atomic level.

We have re-analyzed a collection of observations from 75 bright, unidentified, steep-spectrum polarized radio sources, originally captured by the Green Bank 43-m telescope, in search of previously undetected sub-millisecond pulsars and radio bursts. While Schmidt et al. reported the initial null results from a prior search of this dataset, our reprocessing effort focused on detecting single pulses across dispersion measures (DM) up to 1000 pc cm$^{-3}$, utilizing the Deep Learning classifier FETCH for classification. Additionally, we investigated periodicities over a broader spectrum of DMs and accelerations. This search was designed to identify highly accelerated, rapidly rotating pulsars—such as sub-millisecond pulsars—within compact binary systems, as well as highly dispersed impulsive signals like fast radio bursts. Ultimately, the reprocessing yielded no detections of either pulsars or astrophysical burst signals.

Current robotic harvesters predominantly rely on unimanual systems, where a single arm detaches crops either through a specific movement or by cutting the stem with a specialized end-effector. However, these single-arm approaches are ineffective for sensitive crops and complex environments, such as vineyards, where obstacles can obscure stems and prevent the cutter from being positioned correctly. To address these challenges, a bimanual system is required to visually expose the stem and reposition the grasped fruit, mimicking human harvesting techniques. This study introduces a dual-arm coordinated control method designed to achieve a pre-cut state. In this approach, one arm equipped with a camera and cutter attempts to fully reveal the stem, while the second arm moves the held crop into open space to enable cutting. The proposed methodology was tested on a mock vine setup using a plastic grape cluster, employing two UR5e robotic arms and a RealSense D415 camera.

This work addresses an improper reinforcement learning scenario where a learner receives $M$ base controllers for an unknown Markov decision process (MDP) and aims to optimally combine them into a superior controller. This approach is particularly valuable for tuning controllers trained in mismatched or simulated settings to achieve high performance in a target environment with limited trials. To achieve this, we introduce two algorithms: (1) a Policy Gradient method and (2) a hybrid algorithm that dynamically switches between a simple Actor-Critic (AC) framework and a Natural Actor-Critic (NAC) framework based on available data. Both methods operate within a class of improper mixtures of the provided controllers. We establish convergence rate guarantees for the Policy Gradient approach assuming a gradient oracle. For the AC-based method, we prove convergence to a stationary point in the basic AC setting and to a global optimum in the NAC setting. Numerical experiments on (i) stabilizing a cartpole, a standard control theory benchmark, and (ii) a constrained queueing task demonstrate that our improper policy optimization algorithm can stabilize systems even when the available base policies are unstable.

Observing anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) serves as a fundamental probe in physical cosmology. Due to the faintness of this signal, researchers have developed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experiments that observe the sky across multiple frequencies using thousands of polarization-sensitive detectors. However, the high sensitivity of these instruments means that instrumental systematic effects can become the primary obstacle to fully exploiting their data. This paper introduces s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), a Python package designed to simulate time-domain raw data streams from modern bolometric CMB experiments while injecting realistic instrumental systematics. The package aims to evaluate contamination from these effects in real data, inform the design of future instruments, and enhance the realism of simulated datasets necessary for developing precise data analysis techniques.

We introduce SpectroLab, an open-source, Matlab-based software suite developed in 2018 designed for spectroscopic data analysis. The package includes functionalities for derivative analysis, stacked energy contours, theoretical stacked plots, 3D volumetric visualizations, and core level analysis. Currently optimized for angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) data, it is built with the capability to accommodate other spectroscopic datasets in the future. To demonstrate the program's robustness, we apply it to the HfP2, ZrSiS, and Hf2Te2P systems.

In SU(2) Yang-Mills theory featuring a non-Abelian gauge field sourced by a classical spinor field, we investigate how the mass gap varies with the coupling constant between the gauge and nonlinear spinor fields. The findings demonstrate that the total dimensionless energy of a monopole interacting with these nonlinear spinor fields is determined solely by the dimensionless coupling constant.

Many full-field numerical methods currently address the digital representation of polycrystalline materials and their evolution under thermomechanical processing. Nevertheless, these approaches primarily focus on modeling recrystallization and grain growth in single-phase systems or simulate phase transformations while neglecting recrystallization and associated effects. Consequently, a generalized numerical framework that can predict behavior in multi-phase polycrystalline environments while accounting for the simultaneous operation of various microstructural mechanisms is highly desirable. This study proposes a novel finite element level-set based full-field formulation designed principally to simulate diffusive solid-solid phase transformations at the mesoscopic scale within two-phase metallic alloys. The model incorporates a global kinetic framework capable of handling concomitant mechanisms such as recrystallization and grain growth. The viability of this proposed framework is demonstrated through several illustrative 1D and 2D test cases concerning austenite decomposition in steels, with results compared against ThermoCalc estimations.

The application of deep learning via Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) has significantly enhanced computer vision by enabling direct learning from raw data without manual feature extraction. Currently, there is growing interest in applying ConvNets to interpret and analyze Electroencephalography (EEG) dynamics. This study evaluated various ConvNet architectures designed to predict imagined left and right hand movements on a subject-independent basis using raw EEG signals. The findings indicate that incorporating advanced machine learning techniques—specifically adaptive moments, batch normalization, and dropout strategies—substantially boosts ConvNet predictive performance, surpassing conventional fully-connected neural networks that rely on widely used spectral features.

Google's YouTube platform has generated a lucrative career path that has drawn many users to become content creators. A critical component of this profession is audience feedback via comments, which reflects how well the content is received. However, the sheer volume of comments, combined with spam and a lack of effective classification tools, makes it nearly impossible for creators to manually review every message for constructive insights. Even for established models, automatically classifying these comments is difficult due to their variable lengths and the prevalence of slang, symbols, and abbreviations. The challenge intensifies with multilingual comments, which are often saturated with specific vernacular. This study evaluates top-performing classification models on a dataset mixing English and Malayalam (including mono-lingual and mixed-language combinations). Statistical analysis reveals that Multinomial Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, and Decision Trees achieve comparable accuracy levels. Furthermore, three multilingual transformer-based models (BERT, DISTILBERT, and XLM) were assessed and compared against traditional machine learning techniques. Among the transformers, XLM emerged as the top performer with an accuracy of 67.31. In contrast, the best traditional model was Random Forest paired with a Term Frequency Vectorizer, achieving an accuracy of 63.59.

The Merino-Welsh conjectures propose that, under specific conditions, an inequality exists among the evaluations of the Tutte polynomial $T(M;2,0)$, $T(M;0,2)$, and $T(M;1,1)$. This paper introduces three findings concerning a Merino-Welsh conjecture. While these results appear to be dead ends, they are "inconsequential" in the sense that they do validate a version of the conjecture for numerous matroids.

In 1999, Herzog and Hibi defined the concept of componentwise linear ideals. A homogeneous ideal $I$ qualifies as componentwise linear if, for every non-negative integer $d$, the subideal consisting of its homogeneous elements of degree $d$ admits a linear resolution. In the context of square-free monomial ideals, this property corresponds via Alexander duality to the sequential Cohen-Macaulayness of the associated simplicial complexes. However, componentwise linearity is not generally maintained when taking powers of an ideal. In 2011, Herzog, Hibi, and Ohsugi proposed a conjecture stating that for the cover ideal of a chordal graph, all powers $I^s$ (where $s \geq 1$) are componentwise linear. This overview examines fundamental characteristics of componentwise linear ideals, focuses on recent advancements regarding the Herzog-Hibi-Ohsugi conjecture over the past ten years, and addresses the related inquiry into the componentwise linearity of symbolic powers of cover ideals.

Heavy, doublet-dominated Higgs bosons predicted by Two-Higgs-Doublet-Model extensions of the Standard Model are primary targets for high-energy collider searches, prompting significant current analysis of Large Hadron Collider data. For sufficiently massive states, $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry imposes strict constraints on the decay patterns of these new scalars. In scenarios involving only additional Higgs doublets, fermionic decay channels are anticipated to dominate, though certain bosonic modes could offer cleaner experimental signatures. However, if the Higgs sector is expanded to include singlet states and these singlet-dominated scalars are kinematically accessible, the dynamics shift; in such cases, Higgs-to-Higgs decay widths may become the leading contribution. Consequently, interpreting experimental data within a specific theoretical framework requires precise control over radiative corrections. This paper investigates the bosonic decays of heavy, doublet-dominated Higgs states within the MSSM and NMSSM at full one-loop order, emphasizing the influence of $SU(2)_{\mathrm{L}}$ symmetry and infrared effects, particularly the generation of substantial non-resonant contributions to three-boson final states.

This study employs Gaussian processes to investigate the potential of future gravitational wave (GW) observations in detecting cosmic opacity at high redshifts. This is achieved by comparing opacity-free GW luminosity distances (LD) with opacity-dependent LDs derived from a combination of Type Ia supernovae (SNIa) and gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The datasets used are simulated measurements from the future Einstein Telescope for GWs, the Pantheon compilation for SNIa, and the latest GRB observations compiled by L. Amati et al. A nonparametric approach is introduced to assess the spatial homogeneity of cosmic transparency at high redshifts by contrasting the LDs reconstructed from GW data with those from the Pantheon and GRB datasets. Furthermore, cosmic opacity is evaluated using optical depth parametrizations, yielding constraints that are tighter than previous results. These findings suggest that future GW measurements could serve as a vital instrument for probing cosmic opacity in high-redshift regions.

Demonstrating quantum speedup, or quantum computational supremacy—the capacity of quantum computers to vastly outperform classical systems—represents a pivotal achievement in quantum computing. Although recent experiments are slowly surpassing the limits of classical simulation, they currently lack efficient verification methods and depend on partial validation. In this work, we introduce an efficient verification protocol using single-mode Gaussian measurements to validate the output states of a broad range of continuous-variable quantum circuits that exhibit quantum speedup, such as Boson Sampling. This advancement facilitates a compelling demonstration of quantum speedup via photonic computing. Furthermore, our findings extend beyond this milestone, enabling the efficient and reliable certification of a wide variety of intractable continuous-variable multimode quantum states.

People in developing nations face a higher risk of displacement due to humanitarian crises, where language barriers often prevent aid workers from effectively reaching those affected. To enhance resilience, support services must be adaptable and capable of handling a wide variety of languages. \textit{Tarjimly} addresses this issue by offering a platform that connects bilingual volunteers with aid workers or displaced individuals requiring translation. However, managing a vast pool of translators presents the challenge of identifying the most suitable volunteer for each request. This paper introduces a machine learning system designed to match translation requests with volunteers at scale. We show that a straightforward logistic regression model, utilizing easily calculated features, can accurately predict and rank translator responsiveness. When deployed, this lightweight system successfully matches 82\% of requests with a median response time of 59 seconds, enabling aid workers to more rapidly deliver support to displaced populations.

Driven by recent breakthroughs in machine learning, particularly artificial neural networks (ANNs), data-driven modeling within mechanics is advancing rapidly. As this domain matures, the availability of diverse datasets and models from various research groups creates opportunities for collaborative modeling. However, ANNs face a significant hurdle known as catastrophic forgetting, where learning a new task causes the loss of proficiency in previously learned tasks. This limitation impedes cooperation, as updating a model for a new application degrades its performance on prior tasks developed by others. To address this, the authors introduce a continual learning framework applied for the first time to solid mechanics. Specifically, this method is utilized with recurrent neural networks to forecast history-dependent plasticity, though it remains adaptable to other architectures (such as feedforward or convolutional networks) for predicting various phenomena. The study aims to catalyze future continual learning advancements that will promote cooperative strategies among mechanical engineers to tackle increasingly complex challenges. The results demonstrate that the proposed continual learning approach can sequentially master multiple constitutive laws without forgetting them, while requiring less data to achieve equivalent error rates compared to standard training methods that develop separate models for each law.

Space debris in Earth's orbit presents a major threat to human space endeavors. This population is expanding due to new launches, the shedding of components from spacecraft, and uncontrolled collisions. Consequently, a computationally efficient continuum model describing debris growth and spatial distribution is essential. We introduce a diffusion-collision model to simulate debris density evolution in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) and its sensitivity to launch policies. By parameterizing this model and validating it against public object catalogs, we assess the timescales for uncontrolled expansion. Furthermore, we evaluate viable launch policies and remediation strategies to mitigate future collision risks involving operational satellites and spacecraft.

By detailing recent advancements in Feynman integrals, we utilize intersection theory within twisted de Rham cohomologies to analyze simple integrals of orthogonal polynomials, quantum mechanical operator matrix elements, and field-theoretic Green's functions. We demonstrate that the algebraic identities governing these systems correspond to the decomposition of twisted cocycles in cohomology groups, meaning such identities can be derived through intersection numbers. Our findings propose a broadly applicable algebraic framework for examining higher-order moments of probability distributions, where the dimension of the relevant cohomology groups equals the count of independent moments; consequently, intersection numbers of twisted cocycles yield both linear and quadratic relations among these moments. This research further substantiates the deep connections between physics, geometry, and statistics.

To bypass the sign problem inherent in Lattice QCD, researchers frequently employ Taylor expansions of thermodynamic observables at a finite baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$. However, the computational challenges and precision limitations associated with calculating high-order Taylor coefficients necessitate the development of resummation schemes that reduce costs while ensuring reliable estimates of thermodynamic quantities. Recently, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 128, 2, 022001 (2022) introduced a method to exponentially resum the contributions of the first $N$ charge density correlation functions ($D_1,\dots,D_N$) to all orders in $\mu_B$. Since these correlation functions are computed stochastically using random volume sources, the resummation approach is susceptible to biased estimates. Such biases can severely distort calculations for large $N$ and $\mu$, particularly for higher-order derivatives of the free energy at lower temperatures. This study introduces a cumulant expansion technique to investigate and correct these biased estimates across different orders of $\mu$. We demonstrate that the unbiased estimates derived from the cumulant expansion accurately reflect the genuine higher-order stochastic fluctuations in correlation functions, which were previously suppressed by the exponential resummation. Furthermore, we establish an unbiased formalism for exponential resummation that, when expanded, exactly reproduces the Taylor series up to a specified power of $\mu$. Additionally, we successfully recover the reweighting factor and other crucial properties of the partition function that were otherwise lost during the application of the cumulant expansion scheme.

We examined Chandra X-ray Observatory data for 108 galaxies containing nuclear star clusters (NSCs) to identify evidence of massive black holes (BHs). NSCs represent extremely dense stellar regions where theoretical models suggest massive BHs could form. Recent studies by Stone et al. (2017) indicate that sufficiently dense NSCs are prone to runaway BH growth via tidal captures, reaching massive scales, and propose a velocity dispersion threshold of $40\;\rm{km\;s^{-1}}$ above which massive BH formation is inevitable. To test these hypotheses observationally, we measured X-ray emissions from NSCs and correlated them with their velocity dispersions and tidal capture runaway timescales. Our analysis reveals that NSCs exceeding the $40\;\rm{km\;s^{-1}}$ threshold are detected in X-rays at approximately double the rate of those below it, even after adjusting for contamination from X-ray binaries. These findings support a scenario where dense, high-velocity NSCs can generate massive BHs, offering a formation mechanism independent of high-redshift conditions.

In computer vision, human pose synthesis and transfer involve probabilistically generating images of individuals in novel poses based on existing observations of them. Although recent research has introduced various methods for this task, most approaches derive the target pose directly from a desired image within a specific dataset. This dependency makes the underlying process difficult to apply in real-world settings, as generating the target image is the primary objective. This paper first outlines the limitations of existing pose transfer algorithms and then introduces a novel text-based pose transfer technique to overcome these challenges. We decompose the problem into three independent stages: (a) converting text to pose representation, (b) pose refinement, and (c) pose rendering. To our knowledge, this represents one of the first efforts to create a text-based pose transfer framework; furthermore, we introduce a new dataset, DF-PASS, which adds descriptive pose annotations to the DeepFashion dataset images. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method yields promising results, achieving significant improvements in both qualitative and quantitative metrics.

We report findings regarding the strange quark's contribution to the nucleon's electromagnetic form factors, utilizing CLS ensembles featuring $N_f=2+1$ flavors of $\mathcal{O}(a)$-improved Wilson fermions alongside an $\mathcal{O}(a)$-improved vector current. To assess excited-state contamination, we analyzed multiple source-sink separations. Form factors were determined across six ensembles spanning lattice spacings from $a=0.049$ to $0.086\,\text{fm}$ and pion masses between $m_\pi=200$ and $360\,\text{MeV}$, facilitating a robust chiral and continuum extrapolation. Furthermore, hierarchical probing was implemented as a variance reduction method for calculating quark-disconnected contributions.

This study examines the algebraic and compositional characteristics of abstract multiway rewriting systems, which serve as fundamental structures for the Wolfram model. We establish the presence of higher homotopies within these systems, where homotopical mappings arise from incorporating specific rewriting rules selected from an abstract rulial space encompassing all possible rules. Additionally, we demonstrate that a multiway rewriting system featuring homotopies up to order $n$ can be naturally represented as an $n$-fold category. By including appropriate inverse morphisms through invertible rewriting relations, the infinite limit of this structure forms an ${\infty}$-groupoid. Through Grothendieck's homotopy hypothesis, this ${\infty}$-groupoid acquires the structure of a formal homotopy space. Finally, we discuss potential applications of this computational homotopical framework for establishing formal links to homotopy spaces that could host physics-relevant models.

The properties of the cosmic microwave background offer indirect support for the notion that the early universe's hot, radiation-dominated phase was preceded by an inflationary expansion. This study demonstrates how measuring the stochastic gravitational wave background can illuminate the cosmic timeline and physical conditions during inflation, the subsequent pre- and reheating phases, and the onset of the hot big bang era. We illustrate this using a highly motivated and predictive minimal extension of the Standard Model, which provides a comprehensive framework for particle physics up to the Planck scale and for cosmology back to the inflationary period.

Synthetic Aperture Sonar (SAS) surveys generate images characterized by extensive transitional zones between different seabed types, complicating both the labeling and segmentation processes as well as the subsequent evaluation of those segmentations. Although numerous methods exist for assessing performance in standard crisp segmentation, imposing rigid boundaries on remote sensing imagery that features gradients and uncertainty is unsuitable. Instead, these scenarios require weak labels and a corresponding evaluation framework. This paper introduces a novel labeling strategy alongside a modified Rand index designed for weakly-labeled data to tackle these challenges. The proposed index was tested and compared against conventional segmentation metrics. Experiments conducted on a SAS dataset incorporating must-link and cannot-link constraints demonstrate that the Weakly-Labeled Rand index effectively scores segmentations in alignment with qualitative performance, proving to be more appropriate than traditional quantitative measures for weakly-labeled scenarios.

We tackle active learning within semantic segmentation, demonstrating that self-consistency serves as a potent form of self-supervision, significantly boosting data-driven model performance even with limited labeled data. This approach relies on the principle that semantic segmentation results for a given image must remain consistent under equivariant transformations, such as horizontal flipping (where the output image flips accordingly). This self-supervisory signal is especially valuable in active learning scenarios, where models are susceptible to overfitting due to scarce labeled training samples. Our proposed framework iteratively identifies small image patches requiring labels by selecting those exhibiting high uncertainty (high entropy) under equivariant transformations. We enforce pixel-level self-consistency between the segmentation network's outputs for an image and its horizontally flipped version to leverage rich self-supervisory information and reduce network uncertainty. This strategy allows us to pinpoint image patches where the current model struggles most. Experimental results indicate that by iteratively training on these challenging patches, our active learning method achieves approximately 96% of the performance of a model trained on the full dataset, utilizing only 12% of the data on benchmark semantic segmentation datasets like CamVid and Cityscapes.

This work investigates isometric actions of Lie 2-groups on Riemannian groupoids and highlights their fundamental characteristics. Initially, we establish an existence theorem, characterize equivariant weakly groupoid linearizations, formulate versions of the Slice Theorem and the Equivariant Tubular Neighborhood Theorem, and introduce the concept of orthogonal Lie 2-groups. Additionally, we offer several illustrative examples and applications. Subsequently, we characterize the Lie 2-group of strong (weak) isometries for a Lie groupoid endowed with a 0-metric and derive a model for its Lie 2-algebra of strong (weak) Killing multiplicative vector fields. We demonstrate that the Lie 2-algebra of weak Killing multiplicative vector fields remains invariant under Morita equivalence, thereby providing a robust definition of geometric Killing vector fields on quotient Riemannian stacks.

Over the past ten years, strong-field gravitational lensing has been a subject of intense research. It is established that light rays winding around a black hole's photon sphere generate an infinite series of relativistic Einstein rings, a phenomenon also observed in wormhole lensing. This study examines the Einstein and relativistic Einstein rings produced by both the Schwarzschild black hole and the Ellis wormhole, the latter representing a traversable Morris-Thorne class wormhole. By analyzing the lensing configuration and the radii of these rings, it is theoretically possible to distinguish between a black hole and a wormhole. Our findings suggest that current advanced instruments, such as a 10-meter optical-infrared telescope with a resolution of $10^{-2}$ arcseconds, could detect relativistic Einstein rings from wormholes with throat radii of approximately $a\simeq 0.5$ pc at a galactic center located 10 Mpc away, or $a\simeq 10$ AU within our own galaxy. In contrast, the black holes capable of producing Einstein rings of equivalent size are galactic supermassive black holes, whose relativistic Einstein rings remain too small to measure with present technology. Consequently, future observations of these rings may allow us to test hypotheses regarding astrophysical wormholes.

We establish a general framework to examine detailed balance and investigate its microscopic foundations. Our analysis reveals that two conditions must supplement the standard $T$- or $PT$-invariance of microscopic laws:
1. Equilibrium states must not spontaneously break the pertinent $T$- or $PT$-symmetry.
2. Macroscopic processes must be distinguishable at the microscopic level to ensure the persistence of detailed balance during the reduction from micro- to macrokinetics.
We also briefly address instances where these rules are violated and the resulting breakdown of detailed balance.

Quantum gravity research typically neglects experimental input. This letter addresses that gap by proposing a framework to integrate hypothetical quantum corrections from canonical quantum gravity theories into the derivation of falsifiable modified dispersion relations (MDRs) for particles on deformed Minkowski spacetime. This approach enables the differentiation and potential selection among various quantization schemes through testable, state-of-the-art phenomenological predictions. While specific examples from loop quantum gravity (LQG)—such as regularization methods or gauge group representations—are provided to validate the claim, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to other quantization ambiguities within LQG and similar quantum gravity approaches.

A $\sigma$-ideal $\mathcal{I}$ defined on a Polish group $(X,+)$ is said to possess the Smital Property if, for any dense set $D$ and any Borel set $B$ that is $\mathcal{I}$-positive, their algebraic sum $D+B$ forms a complement of a set belonging to $\mathcal{I}$. This discussion examines various versions of this property and investigates their relationships with the countable chain condition, maximality, and their preservation through Fubini products.

This study investigates Deeply Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) involving nucleons and nuclei using the generalized vector meson dominance (GVMD) framework. Our results show that the GVMD model accurately describes HERA data regarding the proton DVCS cross section's dependence on Q², W (at Q²=4 GeV²), and t. However, at Q² = 8 GeV², the model's soft W-behavior slightly underestimates the DVCS cross section's W-dependence because it lacks hard contributions. We calculate 1/Q² power-suppressed corrections to both the DVCS amplitude and cross section, finding them to be substantial. Additionally, we provide predictions for nuclear DVCS amplitudes and cross sections within the kinematic range of the future Electron-Ion Collider. Our findings indicate significant nuclear shadowing, which aligns closely with leading-twist nuclear shadowing predictions for deep inelastic scattering on nuclei.

This paper examines epidemiological networks used to model how contagious diseases spread through populations. Specifically, we investigate the social sensors problem: identifying a minimal set of nodes within an epidemiological network such that monitoring disease transmission at these points allows us to predict the epidemic's trajectory across the entire population. Despite the significant societal importance of this issue, prior statistical research has been limited; therefore, our goal is to present an overview intended to inspire further interest within the research community. Additionally, by applying established principles from spectral graph theory, we introduce a new approach to selecting social sensors that yields significant performance gains over existing methods in both synthetic and real-world epidemiological networks.

This study examines how superradiant scattering of gravitational perturbations influences the stability of rotating black strings, specifically targeting the six-dimensional equal-spinning Myers-Perry configuration. Our findings indicate that rapidly rotating black strings become unstable to gravitational superradiant modes within a specific, bounded range of string lengths. This instability arises because momentum along the string generates a potential barrier that traps these superradiant modes. Unlike other superradiant systems, however, five-dimensional Myers-Perry black holes lack stable particle orbits; consequently, these black strings remain stable against perturbations with sufficiently high azimuthal mode numbers, resulting in a "finite-$m$" superradiant instability. While this instability can compete with the Gregory-Laflamme instability for certain parameters, it otherwise operates independently. The onset of this phenomenon is degenerate, branching into multiple steady-state solutions. This work serves as the first part of a trilogy; the subsequent papers will detail two distinct families of rotating strings emerging from this superradiant onset, namely "black resonator strings" and "helical black strings." Furthermore, we posit that analogous physics applies to five-dimensional Kerr black strings but does not extend to equal-spinning Myers-Perry black strings in dimensions greater than six.

Text classifiers are frequently deployed as universal, large-scale solutions, yet numerous studies indicate they exhibit bias toward specific languages and dialects. Addressing the gaps revealed when measuring these biases requires answering two key questions: first, whether language, dialect, and topic distribution vary by geographical region; and second, whether such regional differences affect model performance. To tackle these issues, we present GeoOLID, a new dataset comprising over 14,000 examples from 15 geographically and demographically diverse cities. Our comprehensive analysis examines how geographical content influences performance disparities in offensive language detection models. Our findings reveal that current models fail to generalize across different locations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that while offensive language models generate false positives for African American English, their performance does not correlate with the proportion of minority populations in a given city. Warning: This paper contains offensive language.

This study re-examines the two-dimensional spatiotemporal linear stability of slender viscoelastic jets governed by the linear Phan-Thien-Tanner (PTT) constitutive equation, specifically focusing on how finite stresses influence the elasto-capillary stability of Beads-on-a-String (BOAS) structures—characterized by the formation of extremely thin filaments between droplets. We identify regions of topological transition in the advancing jet interface under conditions of low to moderate Ohnesorge numbers ($Oh$) and high Weissenberg numbers ($We$). Utilizing the Briggs method of analytic continuation, previously detailed for the nonaffine response regime by Bansal, Ghosh, and Sircar (Phys. Fluids **33**, 054106 (2021)), we categorize zones of temporal stability, absolute and convective instabilities, and evanescent modes, subsequently comparing these findings with existing experimental data on viscoelastic filaments. The effects of finite stresses manifest through strain-hardening, which leads to reduced absolute growth rates, accelerated drainage, and pinch-off at finite times. Furthermore, the derived phase diagrams highlight the stabilizing roles of (a) capillary forces at infinitesimally small $Oh$ values and (b) inertial forces at significantly larger $Oh$ values.

This study introduces a novel, end-to-end, multi-stage system for generating Knowledge Graphs (KGs) from text, which divides the workflow into two distinct phases. First, pretrained language models are employed to generate graph nodes, followed by a straightforward edge construction module that facilitates efficient KG extraction. Various architectural options are explored for each stage to accommodate different training resource constraints. Evaluation on the WebNLG 2020 Challenge dataset demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in text-to-RDF generation, while tests on the New York Times (NYT) and large-scale TekGen datasets reveal strong overall results that surpass existing baselines. We contend that this proposed system offers a viable alternative to current linearization or sampling-based graph generation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/IBM/Grapher.

Multi-beam LiDAR systems, commonly deployed on autonomous vehicles and mobile robots, generate sequences of 3D range scans known as frames. Because of limited angular resolution and occlusions, individual frames only capture the scene sparsely, which hinders downstream tasks such as semantic segmentation and surface reconstruction. Fortunately, as the sensor traverses, it captures frames from varying viewpoints; accumulating these in a shared coordinate system produces denser sampling and more comprehensive coverage of the 3D environment. However, scenes often contain dynamic objects, and points belonging to them remain misaligned if only the scanner's ego-motion is compensated for. This paper investigates multi-frame point cloud accumulation as a mid-level representation for 3D scan sequences and proposes a method leveraging inductive biases inherent in outdoor street scenes, specifically their geometric structure and object rigidity. Unlike current state-of-the-art scene flow estimators, our approach correctly aligns all 3D points within a common reference frame, ensuring accurate accumulation on individual objects. Our method significantly reduces alignment errors across multiple benchmark datasets, and the resulting accumulated point clouds substantially improve high-level applications like surface reconstruction.

We establish the norm resolvent convergence, as parameters $\epsilon$ and $
u$ approach zero, for a class of one-dimensional Schrödinger operators on the line defined by $S_{\epsilon, 
u} = -D^2 + \alpha\epsilon^{-2}\Phi(\epsilon^{-1}x) +  eta
u^{-1}\Psi(
u^{-1}x)$, where $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are real bounded functions with compact support. This convergence holds provided the ratio $
u/\epsilon$ converges to either a finite value or infinity. The resulting limit operator $S_0$ is determined by the specific forms of $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ and the limiting behavior of the ratio $
u/\epsilon$. Specifically, if the potential $\alpha\Phi$ exhibits a zero-energy resonance, $S_0$ represents a non-trivial point interaction at the origin; otherwise, it decomposes into the direct sum of Dirichlet half-line Schrödinger operators.

Extreme wildfires remain a major driver of human fatalities and biodiversity loss across Mediterranean Basin nations. Recent alarming patterns in fire occurrence and expansion indicate that climate change will profoundly influence wildfire dynamics. To enable effective risk mitigation, it is crucial to pinpoint the primary drivers of extreme fires and evaluate their spatio-temporal evolution to understand global warming's impact. Consequently, this study examines monthly burnt areas from 2001 to 2020 across most of Europe and the Mediterranean Basin, identifying intense fire activity in Portugal, Italy, Algeria, and eastern Europe. We developed a high-dimensional extreme quantile regression model incorporating meteorological, land-cover, and topographical predictors. Utilizing a hybrid statistical deep-learning framework, we isolated the distinct contributions of drought, air temperature, and vapour-pressure deficit (VPD) to fire behavior. Our findings reveal that while VPD, temperature, and drought all significantly influence fire occurrence, only VPD drives extreme fire spread. Finally, by perturbing VPD and temperature based on observed trends to project near-future scenarios, we provide evidence that global warming may induce spatially heterogeneous changes in wildfire activity.

Using Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) data, we examine the orientation of photospheric magnetic fields in the solar polar regions. Within small areas of strong polarization, magnetic field vectors at a $1''$ scale systematically deviate from the radial direction; they predominantly tilt toward the pole and exhibit greater inclination relative to the sky plane than the radial vector. However, these findings are contingent upon the "filling factor" $f$, which describes unresolved magnetic structures. The default, non-informative assumption of $f \equiv 1$ for HMI yields larger inclinations and less radial fields compared to scenarios where $f < 1$. Consequently, the observed trend may reflect a systematic bias arising from limited resolution.

Creating energy-efficient software is a laborious endeavor. Success requires not only recognizing the critical importance of energy efficiency in modern development but also possessing the necessary tools and techniques to assist stakeholders throughout the software development lifecycle. To address this, we introduce the MANAi plugin, an IntelliJ IDE extension that renders the energy consumption of unit tests explicit through visual feedback. Our goal is to elevate software energy usage as a vital non-functional quality metric. Additionally, MANAi facilitates energy-related software experiments for a diverse audience, ranging from academic researchers to industry professionals.

This paper tackles the challenge of determining the optimal policy for a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) via a gradient descent-based method. While prior research indicates that primal-dual approaches yield a global convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for both the optimality gap and constraint violation, we introduce a novel algorithm termed the policy mirror descent-primal dual (PMD-PD). This algorithm theoretically achieves a superior $\mathcal{O}(\log(T)/T)$ convergence rate for both metrics. In its primal (policy) update phase, PMD-PD employs a modified value function to execute natural policy gradient steps, which correspond to mirror descent steps with suitable regularization. Simultaneously, the dual update leverages adjusted Lagrange multipliers to guarantee accelerated convergence. Additionally, we extend this framework to scenarios involving zero constraint violation and sample-based estimation. Empirical evaluations confirm that the PMD-PD algorithm outperforms existing policy gradient-based methods in terms of both convergence speed and overall performance.

Vehicular networks offer capabilities ranging from traffic control and route planning to data exchange and entertainment. However, integrating such large-scale technology necessitates robust security measures, for which blockchain has emerged as a favored solution in numerous studies due to its decentralization, transparency, tamper-proof attributes, and public auditability. This study reviews significant efforts in this domain over recent years, analyzing approximately 75 blockchain-based security schemes for vehicular networks across three dimensions: application, security, and blockchain architecture. The application perspective examines secure implementations in areas like transportation, parking, data trading, and resource sharing, while the security perspective addresses specific requirements and potential attacks. From the blockchain perspective, the analysis covers platforms, types, and consensus mechanisms utilized in these systems. Furthermore, the paper compiles popular simulation tools for both blockchain and vehicular network environments. To provide a comprehensive view of the research landscape, we also explore the role of emerging state-of-the-art technologies in this context. Finally, the survey concludes by outlining common challenges and suggesting future research directions.

We introduce SMURF, an unsupervised optical flow learning method that surpasses state-of-the-art performance on all benchmarks, achieving $36\%$ to $40\%$ gains over the previous best method, UFlow, and even exceeding several supervised techniques like PWC-Net and FlowNet2. Our approach combines architectural enhancements from the supervised RAFT model with novel unsupervised learning strategies, including a sequence-aware self-supervision loss, a mechanism for addressing out-of-frame motion, and a method for effective learning from multi-frame video data that requires only two frames for inference.

This research continues a broader initiative to compare non-smooth optimization problems formulated in abs-normal form with Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints (MPCCs). We examine the general abs-normal nonlinear programming problem, encompassing both equality and inequality constraints, alongside its equivalent MPCC reformulation. Our findings demonstrate that kink qualifications are equivalent to MPCC constraint qualifications of both linear independence and Mangasarian-Fromovitz types. Furthermore, we analyze strong stationarity concepts involving first and second-order optimality conditions, which also prove equivalent across these two problem classes. Throughout this study, we evaluate specific slack reformulations proposed in [9]; while these preserve linear independence-type constraint qualifications, they fail to maintain those of the Mangasarian-Fromovitz type.

This paper investigates the subconvexity problem for both Rankin-Selberg and triple product L-functions, specifically addressing cases with joint ramifications and within the conductor dropping range. Initially, we generalize the Michel-Venkatesh approach to lower L-function bounds by reducing them to local conjectures concerning test vectors. Subsequently, by verifying these local conjectures under specific conditions, we derive new subconvex bounds provided the representations are not entirely related.

Unlike the conventional Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations of Maxwell's theory, which treat the potentials $A^{\mu}$ as the dynamical variables, this paper utilizes the electric field $\vec{E}$ and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ as the fundamental dynamical variables. I derive a Lagrangian that yields the dynamical Maxwell equations, incorporating the constraint equations through Lagrange multipliers. Upon transitioning to the Hamiltonian formalism, the canonical momenta $\vec{\Pi}_E$ and $\vec{\Pi}_B$ are found to be constrained, resulting in 6 second-class constraints per spatial point. Gauss's law and the condition $\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{B}=0$ are subsequently introduced as additional constraints, increasing the total to 8 second-class constraints and reducing the system to 4 phase space degrees of freedom. Finally, the Dirac bracket is constructed and explicitly calculated for the field variables and their conjugate momenta.

Chiral nanostructures enable responses to the vectorial characteristics of light at the nanoscale. Although naturally occurring chiral materials provide a route to scalability, engineered structures allow for wavelength tunability through geometric adjustments. However, neither method currently permits temporal control of chirality. Consequently, the ideal solution involves chiral materials that combine scalability, tailored wavelength responses, and high-speed dynamic control. This study introduces and investigates a novel class of intrinsically chiral phase change nanomaterials (PCNMs) created via a scalable bottom-up fabrication process offering precise three-dimensional control. Optical birefringence and dichroism were characterized using angular-resolved Mueller Matrix and spectroscopic ellipsometry, accompanied by a numerical model to elucidate the source of optical activity. This research successfully demonstrates the critical achievement of high-speed dynamic chirality switching exceeding 50,000 cycles through the underlying PCNM.

This study examines a specific singularly perturbed fractional Kirchhoff equation given by $\Big(\varepsilon^{2s}a+\varepsilon^{4s-N} b{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{N}}}|(-\Delta)^{\frac{s}{2}}u|^2dx\Big)(-\Delta)^su+V(x)u=|u|^{p-2}u$ in $\mathbb{R}^{N}$, under the conditions that $a,b>0$, $2s<N<4s$ with $s\in(0,1)$, $2<p<2^*_s=\frac{2N}{N-2s}$, and $(-\Delta )^s$ denotes the fractional Laplacian. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ and a bounded continuous potential $V$, we derive a local Pohozaev identity using an extension method. Subsequently, leveraging our recent findings on the uniqueness and non-degeneracy of positive solutions to the associated limit problem, we establish the local uniqueness of semiclassical bounded solutions.

The complementarity knapsack problem (CKP) involves real-valued variables subject to complementarity constraints between variable pairs. Building upon the polyhedral analysis of De Farias et al., we introduce three novel families of cutting-planes derived from the combinatorial notion of a "pack." We establish sufficient conditions, utilizing the concept of a maximal switching pack, under which these inequalities define facets. Furthermore, we confirm the conjecture by De Farias et al. regarding the separation complexity of their previously introduced inequalities and develop efficient separation algorithms for the newly proposed cuts.

This study reports a search for resonances decaying into a W boson and a radion, with the radion subsequently decaying into two W bosons. The analysis utilizes 138 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The selection criteria require one isolated charged lepton, missing transverse momentum, and one or two large-radius jets with high mass, which contain the decay products of either one or two W bosons, respectively. No significant excess above the predicted background is observed. These findings are combined with results from a complementary all-hadronic channel detailed in a related publication. Consequently, constraints are placed on the parameters of an extended warped extra-dimensional model. To our knowledge, these constitute the first such searches conducted at the LHC.

While camera trapping is becoming a standard method for wildlife monitoring, it traditionally demands substantial manual data labeling. Although deep learning has recently made significant strides in automating wildlife recognition, existing techniques are limited by their reliance on large, static datasets, which contradicts the dynamic nature of wildlife data and its inherent long-tailed distribution. We propose a hybrid iterative framework that combines automated systems with human-in-the-loop identification to address these challenges. This approach effectively learns from long-tailed wildlife imagery and incorporates self-updating mechanisms to track the community dynamics of rapidly evolving ecosystems. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves approximately 90% accuracy using only about 20% of the human annotations required by current approaches. By fostering a synergistic collaboration between humans and machines, we transform deep learning from a static, post-annotation utility into a dynamic, collaborative annotation system that significantly reduces human workload and enables continuous, efficient model updates.
This article highlights a fluid dynamics video featuring a rectangular cavity with an L/D ratio of 5.67, tested at Mach numbers of 0.7 and 1.5.

Word ordering presents a constrained language generation challenge where the input consists of unsorted words. Although prior research has employed linear models and neural networks for this purpose, the application of pre-trained language models remains unexplored, as does the rationale behind their utility. This study utilizes BART as a case study to demonstrate its efficacy in word ordering. Furthermore, we expand our analysis through probing techniques to empirically determine that syntactic dependency knowledge within BART serves as a robust explanation for its performance. Additionally, we document performance improvements achieved with BART in the related partial tree linearization task, which further validates our findings.

$B$-terms are constructed exclusively from the $B$ combinator, defined as $B \equiv \lambda f g x. f(g~x)$, which serves as a standard function composition operator. This paper examines a notable characteristic of $B$-terms: whether repeatedly applying them to the right results in a cycle. We establish conditions for both the existence and absence of this property using a sound and complete equational axiomatization. Specifically, we provide examples of $B$-terms that exhibit cyclic behavior and demonstrate that infinitely many $B$-terms lack this property. Furthermore, we introduce another significant property regarding the canonical representation of $B$-terms, which aids in detecting cycles or verifying the cyclic property through an efficient algorithm.

Because the sub-6 GHz spectrum fails to satisfy the substantial bandwidth demands of 5G applications, 5G networks extend operations into mmWave bands, which offer multi-GHz capacity. However, utilizing mmWave frequencies introduces significant challenges, specifically high penetration loss and vulnerability to line-of-sight obstructions. To address these issues, transmitters employ beamforming to direct antennas toward receivers, concentrating the signal on the intended target. Furthermore, to prevent connectivity loss caused by blockers or environmental factors like rain, users are linked to multiple base stations (BS). Although beamforming and multi-connectivity alleviate mmWave limitations, determining the optimal user association to sustain minimum rate requirements remains complex. This paper first formulates a throughput-maximizing user association strategy incorporating both beamforming and multi-connectivity, analyzing the optimal solution to develop a simple yet efficient heuristic that avoids the need for global network data. Our proposed method, named "beam-align," relies solely on local base station information and achieves performance nearly equivalent to the optimal solution regarding per-user capacity and user satisfaction, while maintaining polynomial computational complexity. Numerical results demonstrate that beam-align surpasses common association schemes based on SNR. Additionally, we evaluate beam-align across three challenging scenarios: the presence of blockers, varying rain intensities, and clustered user distributions. Simulation outcomes indicate that beam-align exhibits robustness, delivering stable performance across all tested conditions.

Randomized field experiments, such as A/B testing, have traditionally been the benchmark for assessing software modifications. However, in the automotive sector, conducting such randomized trials is often impractical, infeasible, or unethical. To overcome these constraints, we introduce BOAT (Bayesian causal modelling for ObvservAtional Testing), a framework that leverages observational data combined with Bayesian causal inference to analyze the real-world effects of intricate automotive software updates and assist development teams in deriving causal insights. This study outlines three Bayesian causal inference models tailored to address three frequent challenges in automotive software evaluation. Developed in collaboration with an industry partner, the BOAT framework is validated through empirical research on a large vehicle fleet, demonstrating the efficacy of causal inference. Furthermore, we connect causal assumption theories to practical applications, offering a comprehensive guide for implementing these models in automotive software engineering. Specifically, we utilize Bayesian propensity score matching to create balanced control and treatment groups when the full user base is inaccessible, Bayesian regression discontinuity design to detect covariate-dependent treatment assignments and local effects, and Bayesian difference-in-differences to infer treatment effects over time while accounting for unobserved confounders. Each illustrative case reflects a real-world scenario where randomization is not viable. Ultimately, the BOAT framework enables online software evaluation in the automotive industry without requiring fully randomized experiments.

The multi-panel array represents a cutting-edge antenna-in-package solution ideal for millimeter-wave (mmWave) and terahertz (THz) systems, offering both cost-effective deployment and scalable configurations. However, when applied to nonuniform array structures, it results in complex, difficult-to-solve signal processing challenges. Focusing on a base station equipped with such an array, this study proposes a joint active user detection (AUD) and channel estimation (CE) framework utilizing compressive sensing (CS) for massive Internet of Things (IoT) applications. By leveraging the structured sparsity inherent in mmWave/THz massive IoT channels, the problem is first modeled as a multiple measurement vector (MMV) CS task within a multi-panel massive MIMO context. Subsequently, an expectation maximization (EM) algorithm is employed to estimate prior parameters, specifically noise variance and sparsity ratios, leading to the development of an orthogonal approximate message passing (OAMP)-EM-MMV algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves superior AUD and CE performance compared to traditional CS-based methods.

Unit testing involves evaluating the smallest testable code segments, typically classes, in isolation from the broader system. These tests are usually implemented as executable code within a specific framework, such as pytest for Python. Developing unit tests is a labor-intensive task characterized by numerous repetitive and manual steps. To demonstrate how artificial intelligence can assist in this area, this chapter explores search-based unit test generation. This approach models the selection of test inputs as an optimization problem, aiming to discover a set of test cases that satisfy specific, measurable objectives using powerful metaheuristic search algorithms to find the optimal solutions within limited time. Specifically, this chapter presents two algorithms capable of generating pytest-formatted unit tests optimized for source code statement coverage. Finally, the chapter reviews advanced concepts and provides resources for further reading on how AI can aid developers and testers in the unit testing process.

Link prediction (LP) is a pivotal task in graph learning, offering wide-ranging practical utility. A common LP application involves identifying the highest-scoring neighbors for a source node, exemplified by friend recommendation services, which demand high inference scalability to efficiently locate top neighbors among vast candidate pools with minimal latency. Recent LP models primarily employ two decoders for calculating edge scores from node embeddings: HadamardMLP and Dot Product. Following both theoretical and empirical analyses, we observe that HadamardMLP decoders are generally more effective for LP. Nevertheless, HadamardMLP currently lacks scalability for retrieving top neighbors on large graphs, as no existing algorithm can perform this retrieval in sublinear complexity. To address this limitation, we introduce the Flashlight algorithm, which accelerates top neighbor retrieval for HadamardMLP by progressively applying approximate maximum inner product search (MIPS) techniques with adaptively adjusted query embeddings. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Flashlight boosts LP inference speed by over 100x on the large OGBL-CITATION2 dataset without compromising effectiveness. Our work facilitates large-scale LP applications by significantly accelerating the inference of the highly effective HadamardMLP decoders.

The family of rare earth chalcogenides, $ARECh_{2}$ (where A represents alkali or monovalent ions, RE denotes rare earth elements, and Ch stands for O, S, Se, or Te), serves as a compelling platform for investigating quantum spin liquids (QSL). A critical aspect of their low-energy spin dynamics remains elusive. Utilizing muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) and zero-field (ZF) AC susceptibility measurements down to 50 mK, we have identified a gapless QSL in $NaYbSe_{2}$, a representative system with an effective spin-1/2, and probed its anomalous spin behavior. ZF $\mu$SR data definitively exclude spin ordering or freezing in $NaYbSe_{2}$ down to 50 mK, a temperature range two orders of magnitude lower than the exchange coupling energies. Below 0.3 K, the spin relaxation rate, $\lambda$, stabilizes at a constant value, signifying finite spin excitations characteristic of a gapless QSL ground state; this finding is corroborated by our AC susceptibility results. A detailed analysis of longitudinal field (LF) $\mu$SR spectra uncovers both strong spatial and temporal correlations within the spin-disordered ground state, emphasizing the distinctive nature of spin entanglement in the QSL phase. These findings enable the construction of an experimental H-T phase diagram and provide valuable insights into the complex and exotic magnetism exhibited by rare earth compounds.

Addressing mutual exclusion for shared resources in concurrent computation is a core challenge. This paper introduces a new mutual exclusion method tailored for distributed systems that utilizes the widely adopted Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) technology. The proposed approach allows local processes to operate without any RDMA calls, minimizes the RDMA operations needed by remote processes, and ensures both starvation-freedom and fairness.

This study addresses the problem of 2-coloring simple, connected, undirected graphs to avoid monochromatic triangles, where vertices are assigned 'black' or 'white' colors ensuring no three mutually adjacent vertices share the same color. We affirmatively resolve a question from our prior research by demonstrating the existence of a linear-time algorithm capable of solving this triangle-free 2-coloring problem specifically for planar graphs.

This work introduces a technique for directly detecting ultralight scalar field dark matter through its interaction with gravitational-wave interferometers, specifically via modulations of the fine structure constant and electron mass. Such modulations generate an effective strain in solid materials at a frequency tied to the dark matter particle's mass. We evaluate the feasibility of observing this phenomenon in LIGO detectors by utilizing the solid cavity designed for laser frequency pre-stabilization and project corresponding upper limits. These results are contextualized against prior constraints from GEO600, potential bounds from strain effects in LIGO's beamsplitter, and anticipated limits from future missions such as LISA and Cosmic Explorer, as well as from upgraded solid cavity configurations. Our findings indicate that Advanced LIGO's sensitivity allows for competitive upper limits on dark matter coupling, approximately $\left\vert d_{m_e}+d_e\right\vert \sim 0.2$ for $m_\text{DM} \sim 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{eV}/\mathrm{c}^2$, when combining two searches using the solid cavity and beamsplitter; future experiments may lower this limit to roughly $10^{-3}$.

Although unavoidable in deep learning, noisy labels pose significant challenges because models are prone to overfitting them. Label noise manifests in various forms, including symmetric, asymmetric, and instance-dependent noise (IDN); notably, IDN is the only category contingent upon image content. This reliance on visual information renders IDN a crucial area of study, as labeling errors often stem from ambiguous or insufficient details regarding visual classes. To tackle IDN effectively, we introduce InstanceGM, a novel graphical modeling framework that integrates both generative and discriminative models. The primary contributions of InstanceGM are: i) employing a continuous Bernoulli distribution for generative model training, which provides substantial benefits, and ii) leveraging a state-of-the-art noisy-label discriminative classifier to derive clean labels from instance-dependent noisy samples. InstanceGM demonstrates competitiveness against existing noisy-label learning methods, particularly on IDN benchmarks involving both synthetic and real-world datasets, where it frequently outperforms competitors in terms of accuracy.

This work investigates the existence and boundary properties of positive radial solutions to the system:
$$
\left\{ \begin{aligned} \Delta
u&=g(|x|,v(x)) &&\quad\mbox{in}\ \Omega, \\ \Delta v&=f(|x|,|\nabla u(x)|)
&&\quad\mbox{in}\ \Omega, \end{aligned} \right.
$$
where $\Omega$ represents either a ball centered at the origin or the entire space $\mathbb{R}^N$, and the functions $f$ and $g$ belong to $C^{1}([0,\infty)\times [0,\infty))$, are non-negative, and are increasing. Initially, we examine the existence of positive radial solutions within a ball, focusing on their behavior at the boundary. Subsequently, we analyze the existence of such solutions when the system takes the specific forms $g(|x|,v(x)) = |x|^{a} v^p$ and $f(|x|, |\nabla u(x)|) = |x|^{b} h(|\nabla u|)$. Finally, by setting $h(t) = t^s$ with $s>1$ and considering $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^N$, we utilize dynamical system techniques to characterize the behavior at infinity of these positive radial solutions.

We present a universal, language-agnostic approach to gathering a substantial volume of offensive and hateful tweets, irrespective of their subject matter or style. By leveraging extralinguistic data within emojis, we successfully identified a large corpus of such content. Applying this technique to Arabic tweets and contrasting them with English ones, we analyzed significant cultural distinctions. Our observations indicate that these emojis consistently represent offensiveness across various time periods on Twitter. We have manually annotated and publicly released the largest Arabic dataset to date, covering fine-grained hate speech, vulgarity, and violence. Additionally, we benchmarked the dataset for detecting offensiveness and hate speech using diverse transformer architectures, accompanied by a detailed linguistic analysis. To assess generalization, we evaluated our models on external datasets: one Twitter collection gathered via a distinct methodology and a multi-platform set comprising comments from Twitter, YouTube, and Facebook. Competitive performance on these sets suggests that our collection method captures universal traits of offensive language. Our findings also identify frequently used words in offensive communication, common targets of hate speech, specific patterns in violent tweets, and highlight common classification errors stemming from NLP model limitations. We further note that even state-of-the-art transformer models may struggle to incorporate cultural context, background, or nuances found in real-world data, such as sarcasm.

We investigated axion-like resonance states by colliding optical photons within a focused laser environment, utilizing a second laser to stimulate resonance decays and generate frequency-converted signal photons through stimulated photon-photon scattering mediated by these resonances. This quasi-parallel collision system (QPS) in a focused field enables exploration of the sub-eV mass range for such particles. While previous QPS searches simplified the analysis by interpreting scattering rates using a symmetric collision geometry for incident angles and energies—only partially accounting for actual experimental asymmetries—this study presents new results derived from a complete parameterization that fully incorporates asymmetric collision geometries. Specifically, we employed a linearly polarized creation laser alongside a circularly polarized inducing laser to align with this new framework. Experiments utilized a 0.10 mJ / 31 fs Ti:sapphire pulse and a 0.20 mJ / 9 ns Nd:YAG pulse, which were spatiotemporally synchronized via a shared optical axis and focused into a vacuum system. Under conditions where atomic background processes were negligible, no significant scattering signal was detected at a vacuum pressure of $2.6 \times 10^{-5}$ Pa. Consequently, assuming exchanges of scalar and pseudoscalar fields, we established upper limits on the coupling-mass relationship at the 95% confidence level within the sub-eV mass range.

In 1952, Bing introduced a wild involution $I$ on the 3-sphere $S^3$ that is not topologically conjugate to a smooth map. This study investigates the precise analytical wildness of such maps. We demonstrate that any involution $I^h$ topologically conjugate to $I$ must possess a weakly exponential modulus of continuity. Specifically, we establish that there exists a constant $c > 1.167$ such that for certain sequences of $\delta$ approaching zero, there are points $x, y \in S^3$ with $\text{dist}(x,y) < \delta$ satisfying $\text{dist}(I^h(x), I^h(y)) > \epsilon$, where $\delta^{-1} = c^{\sqrt{\epsilon^{-1}}}$. This indicates that $I^h$ distorts distances far more severely than Lipschitz functions ($\delta^{-1} \propto \epsilon^{-1}$) or H\"{o}lder functions ($\delta^{-1} \propto (\epsilon^{-1})^p$ for $1 < p < \infty$). The modulus of continuity for Bing's original construction and known alternatives exceeds $c \sqrt{2}^{\epsilon^{-1}}$, suggesting our result is reasonably tight, as we prove the necessity of a weakly exponential modulus while the true behavior might be fully exponential. Employing the same methodology, we examine a broad class of "ramified" Bing involutions and, as a corollary, show that for any growth function $f: \mathbb{R}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$, there exists a corresponding involution $J$ of $S^3$ such that any topological conjugate $J^h$ of $J$ must have a modulus of continuity growing faster than $f$ near infinity. While literature exists on inherent differentiability, to our knowledge, this is the first exploration of inherent modulus of continuity. This work is dedicated to R.H. Bing's legacy on the 70th anniversary of his involution.

A Local Positioning System (LPS) is introduced, where particles are ejected at specific velocities, and a sensor array tracks their paths within the platform's reference frame. These observations enable the reconstruction of the platform's position and orientation relative to the rotating Earth without relying on traditional navigation equations. Should the platform also include velocimeters, the system can further determine the platform's velocity and rotational angular rate with respect to the Earth. Rather than solving standard navigational equations, the approach requires deriving the classical trajectory of a particle within a rotating gravitational field. By incorporating gravity-gradient, Coriolis, and centrifugal forces, an exact trajectory expression is derived, which holds significant potential for application in atomic interferometry. Additionally, a novel iterative technique for determining platform orientation without gyroscopes is presented. Simulations have established the operational conditions required to achieve an LPS navigation error of approximately 10 meters per hour.

Although non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, which model dissipative systems, and analogue gravity frameworks, which mimic gravitational phenomena, appear distinct, this study explores their intersection. We connect parity-time-symmetric, dissipative Weyl-type Hamiltonians to analogue Schwarzschild black holes that emit Hawking radiation. Our findings reveal that the exceptional points of these Hamiltonians generate tilted cones that emulate the light cone experienced by a radially infalling observer nearing a black hole's horizon. Furthermore, we examine tunneling processes analogous to those in black holes within a specific model, interpreting the resulting non-trivial outcome as the purely thermal component of analogue Hawking radiation in a Schwarzschild context. Assuming our Hamiltonian represents an experimentally viable photonic crystal, we argue that the thermal radiation loss observed at the exceptional cone corresponds to the blackbody contribution to analogue black hole radiation. Consequently, these systems represent promising candidates for modelling black holes.

This paper investigates the algebraic formula complexity of multiplying $d$ $2\times 2$ matrices, represented as $\mathrm{IMM}_{d}$, demonstrating that the standard divide-and-conquer approach cannot be substantially improved at any depth within the multilinear formula framework. Specifically, for every depth $\Delta \leq \log d$, we prove that any multilinear formula with product-depth $\Delta$ computing $\mathrm{IMM}_d$ requires a size of $\exp(\Omega(\Delta d^{1/\Delta}))$. Consequently, any multilinear circuit of product-depth $\Delta$ for this polynomial must also have a size of $\exp(\Omega(d^{1/\Delta}))$. Notably, this implies that any polynomial-sized multilinear formula for $\mathrm{IMM}_d$ necessitates a depth of $\Omega(\log d)$, while any polynomial-sized multilinear circuit requires a depth of $\Omega(\log d/\log \log d)$. Both lower bounds are tight up to constant factors.

1. **Depth-reduction:** A classic result by Brent (JACM 1974) establishes that any formula of size $s$ can be transformed into one of size $s^{O(1)}$ with depth $O(\log s)$, a property that extends to multilinear formulas. However, our lower bound indicates that in the multilinear setting, depth reduction below $o(\log s)$ is impossible without incurring a superpolynomial increase in size.

2. **Separations from general formulas:** Combining our findings with an upper bound for $\mathrm{IMM}_{d}$ derived from Gupta, Kamath, Kayal, and Saptharishi (SICOMP 2016), we show that over fields of characteristic zero, for any size $s$ and product-depth $\Delta = o(\log s)$, general formulas of size $s$ and product-depth $\Delta$ cannot be converted into multilinear formulas of size $s^{\omega(1)}$ and product-depth $\Delta$.

To determine the mechanism behind charge-density wave (CDW) formation in cuprate superconductors, it is essential to distinguish between generic microscopic features and those specific to individual materials. Our findings demonstrate that, at the local scale detected by NMR, long-range CDW order in YBa2Cu3Oy is unidirectional with a commensurate period of three unit cells (lambda = 3b). This indicates that the incommensurability observed in X-ray scattering arises from phase slips, or discommensurations. Additionally, NMR spectra show that the CDW has a predominant oxygen character, featuring an out-of-phase relationship between specific lattice sites, yet they lack any distinct signature of a secondary CDW with lambda = 6b that might correspond to a pair-density wave. These results illuminate universal characteristics of cuprate CDWs, suggesting that their spatial profile generally emerges from the interaction between an incommensurate tendency at large length scales—potentially linked to Fermi surface properties—and local commensuration effects driven by electron-electron interactions or lattice locking.
We explore various constructions of swap polynomials, defined as 2-tensor valued matrix polynomials that are scalar multiples of the swap or switch operator.

Mismatch capacity defines the maximum information rate achievable by a channel under a specific decoding metric, making it a crucial fundamental metric for various practical communication applications. While the generalized mutual information (GMI) is commonly used, the LM rate serves as a tighter lower bound for mismatch capacity. However, calculating the LM rate has historically been challenging because it requires maximizing a function of the channel input; this difficulty escalates with larger input alphabet sizes, and direct numerical techniques, such as interior point methods, demand significant computational and memory resources. Recognizing that the LM rate can also be expressed as a constrained entropy optimization problem, this study reformulates the calculation as an optimal transport (OT) problem with an additional constraint. This transformation enables efficient and accurate computation using the Sinkhorn algorithm, which converges rapidly in just a few iterations because the problem formulation lacks extra regularization terms. Furthermore, the additional constraint is addressed by converting it into a root-finding process for a one-dimensional monotonic function. Numerical experiments confirm that this optimal transport approach is both feasible and efficient for determining the LM rate.

The study demonstrates that a predefined set of occupied or virtual valence and core atomic/fragmental orbitals can be converted into an equivalent set of localized occupied/virtual pre-molecular orbitals (pre-LMOs). These pre-LMOs serve as probes to select the same number of maximally matching localized occupied/virtual Hartree-Fock (HF) or restricted open-shell Hartree-Fock (ROHF) molecular orbitals, which act as the initial local orbitals for the desired complete active space (CAS). During each self-consistent field (SCF) cycle, CASSCF orbitals are localized using a noniterative "top-down least-change" algorithm designed for ROHF orbitals. This process allows for the easy monitoring of maximum matching between orbitals in successive iterations, ultimately yielding converged localized CASSCF orbitals that exhibit the greatest overlap with the initial guess orbitals. This methodology is termed "imposed CASSCF" ($\mathbb{i}$CASSCF or $\mathbb{i}$CAS) for two primary reasons: (1) it imposes a constraint to target only electronic states with the largest projections onto the active space defined by the initially chosen atomic/fragmental orbitals; this assumption is highly applicable in organic and transition metal chemistry where such orbitals are easily identifiable. (2) The selection of both initial and optimized local active orbitals is dictated from the outset by the pre-LMOs, which span the same space as the original atomic/fragmental orbitals. Beyond this imposed automation and localization, $\mathbb{i}$CAS offers an additional advantage: the CAS remains invariant across all geometries because the pre-LMOs maintain their character regardless of geometric changes. The efficacy of $\mathbb{i}$CAS is illustrated through case studies of both organic molecules and transition metal complexes.

It has been established that the wedge product of vectors produces the I-concurrence, a generalized entanglement measure, where the separability of a multiparty qubit system depends on the parallelism of vectors within the subsystems' Hilbert space. This work identifies the geometric criteria for post-measurement vectors that maximize entanglement across bi-partitions, potentially generating distinct sets of maximally entangled states. Specifically, Bell states for two qubits and GHZ-type states (involving a superposition of four components for three qubits) emerge naturally as these maximally entangled configurations. We derive the geometric conditions for maximally entangled two qudit systems, resulting in generalized Bell states characterized by maximally mixed reduced density matrices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the reduced density matrix for any finite-dimensional subsystem of a general qudit state can be constructed from the overlap of post-measurement vectors. Utilizing this framework, we analyze the trade-off between local properties—predictability and coherence—and the global property of entanglement within non-maximally entangled two-qubit states.
