Contemporary approaches to network traffic classification increasingly rely on machine learning (ML); however, this adoption introduces significant hurdles, including a scarcity of high-quality annotated data, data drift leading to model degradation, and the sheer volume of network traffic. This paper contends that traditional ML training and deployment workflows must be enhanced by integrating the Active Learning paradigm into network traffic analysis. To address this, the authors propose a novel Active Learning Framework (ALF) comprising software components designed to establish an active learning loop. This framework enables the continuous, automatic evolution of both datasets and ML models. The resulting solution is suitable for IP flow-based analysis in high-speed (100 Gb/s) networks and facilitates research into various annotation, evaluation, and dataset optimization strategies. Furthermore, the paper outlines key research challenges identified through initial practical experiments with the ALF.

A frequently overlooked hurdle in practical reinforcement learning (RL) is that the real world continues evolving while agents perform learning updates. Since standard simulated environments typically neglect this real-time dynamic, most existing RL implementations handle environment interactions and learning updates sequentially. Consequently, deploying these methods in the real world can result in decisions based on stale observations and a lack of responsiveness. Although asynchronous learning has been suggested to resolve this problem, no systematic comparison between sequential and asynchronous RL has been performed in real-world settings. This study establishes two vision-based robotic arm tasks, implements an asynchronous learning system that builds upon a prior architecture, and evaluates both sequential and asynchronous approaches across varying action cycle times, sensory data dimensions, and mini-batch sizes. Our experiments reveal that as the computational cost of learning updates rises, the action cycle time in sequential implementations can become prohibitively long, whereas asynchronous implementations consistently maintain an appropriate cycle time. Therefore, when learning updates are computationally expensive, sequential learning performance degrades significantly and is substantially outperformed by asynchronous learning. Our system successfully learns in real-time to reach and track visual targets from raw pixels within two hours of experience using real robots, learning entirely from scratch.

Drawing an analogy with the recent resolution of the black hole information paradox, this brief note proposes an order parameter for consciousness grounded in the concepts of the Page curve and Page time. Central to this conjecture are the entanglement between neuronal firing time series and the brain's state, alongside the non-orthogonality of functional connectomes.

This study investigates neutrino propagation and flavor oscillations influenced by gravitational waves (GWs) of arbitrary polarization. We rederive the effective Hamiltonian for a three-flavor neutrino system using perturbation theory and subsequently analyze flavor evolution under stochastic GWs with a general energy density spectrum. The governing equation for the density matrix is derived and solved analytically for three neutrino flavors. As a practical application, we examine the flavor evolution of a neutrino beam generated during a core-collapse supernova. We derive analytical expressions for GW-induced contributions to neutrino fluxes and the damping decrement, which quantifies the attenuation of these fluxes toward their asymptotic limits. Our findings indicate that GWs emitted by merging supermassive black holes exert a dominant influence on neutrino flux evolution compared to those from stellar-mass black holes. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for detecting astrophysical neutrinos using neutrino telescopes.

The recent identification of superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates has become a central subject in condensed-matter physics, sparking intense debate regarding their similarities to and distinctions from cuprates. We investigate the charge excitation spectrum in nickelates from two contrasting perspectives: i) treating them as strongly correlated systems akin to cuprate superconductors and modeling them with the $t$-$J$ Hamiltonian, or ii) assuming that correlation effects are weaker than in cuprates, thereby suggesting that Random Phase Approximation (RPA) calculations suffice to capture the essential physics. Our findings indicate that, regardless of the approach, plasmon excitations occur near the momentum transfer ${\bf q}=(0,0,q_z)$, though these modes exhibit stronger damping in the RPA framework. This damping is particularly pronounced due to the relatively large interlayer hopping anticipated in nickelates. While our results successfully reproduce the experimentally observed optical plasmon at ${\bf q}=(0,0,0)$ in Nd$_{0.8}$Sr$_{0.2}$NiO$_2$, we also predict low-energy plasmons with energy gaps of approximately 360 meV and 560 meV at ${\bf q}=(0,0,q_z)$ for finite $q_z$ under scenarios i) and ii), respectively. Consequently, this study provides a theoretical clue to resolve whether nickelates behave like cuprates and advances the broader understanding of charge dynamics within this material class.

Spatial optimization problems (SOPs) are defined by spatial relationships that dictate their decision variables, objectives, and constraints. This article examines a specific subset known as spatial partitioning, a combinatorial challenge arising from discrete spatial units. Since exact optimization techniques fail to scale effectively with problem size within practical timeframes, we developed population-based metaheuristics to address these SOPs. However, the search operators in these methods are typically tailored for real-parameter continuous optimization. To adapt them for SOPs, we integrated domain knowledge to create spatially-aware search operators that efficiently navigate the discrete search space while maintaining spatial constraints. Consequently, we introduced a simple yet effective algorithm, the swarm-based spatial memetic algorithm (SPATIAL), and evaluated it on the school (re)districting problem. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets assessed SPATIAL's performance, while ablation studies analyzed the contributions of its individual components. Furthermore, we discussed SPATIAL's utility in real-life planning, its versatility across various scenarios, and outlined directions for future research.

This study introduces the notion of harmonically m-convex set-valued functions, a concept derived by integrating definitions of harmonically m-convex functions and set-valued functions. The work establishes various properties and characteristics for these functions and derives a Hermite-Hadamard type inequality applicable to them.

Large Language Models (LLMs) trained on combined text and code data have shown remarkable proficiency in converting natural language into structured code. This paper introduces Code4Struct, a framework that utilizes this text-to-structure translation ability to address structured prediction challenges in NLP. For instance, in Event Argument Extraction (EAE), the goal is to transform text into event-argument structures representable as class objects. By aligning NLP structures with code, we can easily incorporate external knowledge or impose constraints through Programming Language (PL) mechanisms like inheritance and type annotations. Leveraging the analogy between PL and NLP, we apply Code4Struct to EAE via code generation, instructing an LLM to write code that instantiates an event class with predicted arguments based on a natural language sentence. Remarkably, Code4Struct achieves performance comparable to fully-supervised models trained on 4,202 instances using only 50 training examples per event type; under identical 50-shot conditions, it surpasses the current state-of-the-art by an absolute 20.8% in F1 score. Furthermore, when utilizing inheritance for hierarchical event types, Code4Struct can predict arguments for low-resource event types using just 10-shot data from related sibling types, exceeding zero-shot baselines by 12% absolute F1.

To resolve discrepancies identified in one-dimensional analyses, axisymmetric three-dimensional models of the protostellar source B335 have been constructed, heavily constrained by extensive observational data from ALMA, Herschel, and Spitzer. ALMA observations reveal red-shifted absorption against a central continuum in the HCO$^+$ and HCN $J = 4\rightarrow 3$ transitions, signaling infall. When combined with a revised distance estimate, these data tightly constrain three-dimensional radiative transfer simulations that incorporate a rotating, infalling envelope, outflow cavities, and a compact disk. These models indicate an age for the onset of collapse between $3 \times 10^4$ and $4 \times 10^4$ years for both continuum and line features, thereby settling a previous conflict. However, the models fail to fully reproduce the continuum emission detected by ALMA, implying the presence of an additional component, such as a pseudo-disk. Using the best-fitting model, recent variations in the 4.5 $\mu m$ flux over the past few years have been translated into a luminosity variation model, suggesting a factor of 5–7 change over the last 8 years.

We analytically examine the critical properties governing Floquet time crystal formation within the prethermal regime of the periodically driven $O(N)$ model. Our investigation centers on the critical boundary separating a trivial phase—characterized by period-synchronized dynamics and no long-range spatial order—from a non-trivial phase marked by period-doubling and long-range spatial order. By combining dimensional expansion with exact solutions for the $N\to\infty$ limit, we determine three key exponents near this critical line: $\nu$, describing the divergence of the spatial correlation length in equal-time correlation functions; $\beta$, governing the growth of the order-parameter amplitude; and $\theta$, the initial-slip exponent associated with aging dynamics following a quench from the trivial phase to the critical line. Notably, these exponents match those observed in the non-driven system. Furthermore, the functional form of aging varies depending on whether the observation time is short or long relative to the drive period. Finally, the spatial structure of the two-point correlation functions, derived as a linear response to a perturbing potential near the critical line, exhibits algebraic decays that extend further than in the undriven case. Additionally, these correlations are period-doubled and display spatial oscillations at the wave-vector $\omega/(2v)$, where $\omega$ represents the drive frequency and $v$ denotes the quasiparticle velocity.

We have identified a class of planar bipartite graphs where every Lombardi drawing (utilizing circular arcs for edges that intersect at equal angles at vertices) fails to be planar. Additionally, we have discovered families of embedded series-parallel graphs and apex-trees for which no planar Lombardi drawing exists that adheres to the specified embedding.

Although topological quantum computation holds significant promise for fault tolerance, a straightforward demonstration remains elusive. Since Majorana modes serve as the fundamental components, their experimental confirmation across various platforms has yet to be achieved. This study introduces an experimental and theoretical framework designed for the space-resolved detection and exchange of Majorana modes on programmable, noisy quantum hardware. We executed this framework by conducting a series of measurements on a driven Ising-type quantum spin model with adjustable interactions, which validated the presence of topological Majorana modes and differentiated them from trivial ones. Furthermore, we proposed and demonstrated a new method for braiding these modes that yields correct statistics but reduces signal magnitude. This work represents the first reliable observation of Majorana modes on existing quantum hardware.

While multisets contain elements, they differ from sets by tracking the frequency of each element's occurrence. This study examines iterative multisets—constructed recursively from other multisets—within Martin-Löf Type Theory under Voevodsky's Univalence Axiom. Aczel's 1978 model of constructive set theory in type theory relied on a W-type quantifying over a universe and an inductively defined equivalence relation. In contrast, our approach utilizes the identity type on the W-type, which is computable via the Univalence Axiom, proposing that this yields a model for multisets. To validate this, we adapt constructive set theory axioms to the context of multisets and demonstrate their validity within our proposed model.

Column generation serves as an iterative approach for solving various optimization issues by splitting them into a master problem and one or more pricing problems (PP). The overall computational effort is distributed between these two components. In routing and scheduling contexts, which are typically network-based, the PP often involves an NP-hard shortest path problem constrained by resources. This study introduces a novel heuristic pricing algorithm leveraging machine learning. By utilizing data from prior runs, the method aims to shrink the network size and speed up the PP by retaining only arcs with a high probability of inclusion in the linear relaxation solution. The approach was tested on the vehicle and crew scheduling problem for public transit and the vehicle routing problem with time windows, achieving computational time reductions of up to 40%.

A subgroup of a graph $\G$'s automorphism group is defined as {\em half-arc-transitive} if it acts transitively on the vertices and edges of $\G$ but fails to do so for the arcs. While tetravalent graphs with girths 3 and 4 admitting such groups have been previously characterized, this paper investigates the case of girth 5. We demonstrate that, aside from two exceptions, all such graphs possess only directed 5-cycles under the induced edge orientation. Furthermore, we examine these specific examples, analyze their graph-theoretic properties, and establish that their 5-cycles are always consistent cycles relative to the half-arc-transitive group. The study also presents infinite families of examples, classifies tetravalent graphs of girth 5 that are tightly-attached to a half-arc-transitive group, and categorizes tetravalent half-arc-transitive weak metacirculants of girth 5.

While prominent knowledge graphs like DBpedia and YAGO rely exclusively on Wikipedia, numerous other wikis, such as Fandom, host data on long-tail entities. This paper introduces DBkWik++, a fused knowledge graph constructed from thousands of wikis. By adapting the DBpedia framework to each wiki individually, we generate numerous isolated knowledge graphs. We then employ an incremental merge strategy that reuses one-to-one matching systems to address the challenge of multi-source knowledge graph alignment. This process yields a consolidated knowledge graph containing over 15 million instances.

This study examines the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ ($n=1,2,3$) decays by applying a hadronic loop mechanism, identifying the $\Upsilon(10753)$ as a conventional bottomonium state within a $4S$-$3D$ mixing framework. We find that these processes yield significant branching ratios, potentially reaching magnitudes between $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-3}$. Notably, our calculations successfully reproduce the Belle measurements of $\Gamma_{e^+e^-}\times\mathcal{B}[\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-]$, which lends strong support to the $4S$-$3D$ mixing assignment for the $\Upsilon(10753)$. Consequently, testing these predictions represents a promising avenue for the ongoing Belle II experiment.

Flux qubits can engage in strong interactions when capacitively connected to other circuit components. This interaction decomposes into two components: one affecting the qubit subspaces and another mediated by excited states. The first component primarily governs the coupling between a flux qubit and an LC-resonator, resulting in ultrastrong interactions of the form $\sigma^y(a+a^\dagger)$ that complement the standard inductive $\sigma^x i(a^\dagger-a)$ coupling. In contrast, when two flux qubits are capacitively coupled, every term must be considered, yielding a complex non-stoquastic ultrastrong interaction characterized by $\sigma^y\sigma^y$, $\sigma^z\sigma^z$, and $\sigma^x\sigma^x$ terms. Our theoretical framework accounts for these interactions by expressing them through general circuit properties—such as coupling capacitances, qubit energy gaps, and inductive, Josephson, and capacitive energies—that are applicable across a broad spectrum of circuits and flux qubit architectures.

The reward hypothesis suggests that goals and purposes are essentially the maximization of the expected cumulative sum of received scalar signals (rewards). Our objective is to definitively evaluate this hypothesis. Rather than simply affirming or denying it, we aim to precisely delineate the specific implicit conditions regarding goals and purposes necessary for the hypothesis to be valid.

Varieties of minimal degree constitute a fundamental subject in projective algebraic geometry, having been extensively classified and characterized. Similarly, minimal objects exist within the category of higher secant varieties, which exhibit algebraic and geometric structures closely resembling those of varieties of minimal degree. In this paper, we demonstrate that higher secant varieties of minimal degree possess determinantal presentations of two distinct types: the scroll type and the Veronese type. This finding extends the del Pezzo-Bertini classification applicable to varieties of minimal degree. Furthermore, as a direct consequence, we establish that for any smooth projective variety whose higher secant variety is of minimal degree, the associated embedding line bundle decomposes into two line bundles, mirroring the property observed in classic examples such as varieties of minimal degree, smooth del Pezzo varieties, Segre varieties, and 2-Veronese varieties.

The origins and stability of collisionless, self-gravitating systems represent enduring challenges, tracing back to D. Lynden-Bell's research on violent relaxation and extending to the virialization of dark matter (DM) halos. A key outcome of this relaxation process is that spherical equilibrium states can be modeled using a Fermi-Dirac phase-space distribution once coarse-grained entropy is maximized. For DM fermions, the most comprehensive solution features a degenerate, compact core encased by a diffuse halo. Recent findings suggest this halo configuration accounts for galaxy rotation curves, while the DM core effectively simulates a central black hole. However, it remains an open question whether such core-halo structures can actually form and maintain stability over cosmological timescales. To address this, we conducted a thermodynamic stability analysis within the microcanonical ensemble for fixed particle numbers during halo virialization in a cosmological setting. For the first time, we demonstrate that these core-halo DM profiles are stable (representing entropy maxima) and exceptionally long-lived. We identified a critical threshold marking the onset of instability, beyond which the fermion core collapses into a supermassive black hole. Specifically, for particle masses in the keV range, core collapse is only possible when the virial mass exceeds $10^9 M_\odot$ and virialization occurs at approximately $z \approx 10$. These results confirm that DM halos exhibiting a core-halo morphology are a highly plausible outcome of the nonlinear phases of structure formation.

Driven by the growing prevalence of low-energy systems with multiple bands, this study examines transport within the Boltzmann framework for a weakly disordered, noninteracting multiband crystal under a weak electric field. Typically, such multiband structures significantly complicate the Boltzmann equation; even with elastic impurity scattering, calculating dressed velocities for every band and momentum state to account for scattering events remains a demanding numerical challenge. We present a semi-analytical solution that simplifies this task, reducing the computation to determining a small tensor whose size depends only on the number of bands at the Fermi level. This method enables an analysis of how symmetry and disorder interact across various impurity types, including those derived from random-matrix Wigner ensembles. As a specific application, we analyze a 2D isotropic Rashba metal, providing a complete analytical discussion on how different disorder types can violate the relaxation-time approximation, generate transport anisotropy, and reveal the presence of spin-orbit coupling through deviations from Drude conductivity behavior.

This study examines how strong interactions influence the dressed energy levels of two-level emitters. Specifically, strong dipole-dipole interactions generate new sidebands in the fluorescence spectrum, a phenomenon driven by unique couplings among collective dressed levels that vary according to the atoms' spatial arrangement. These couplings primarily determine the frequencies and diversity of the observed sidebands. We outline a general approach for calculating dressed energy levels in systems comprising any number of strongly coupled atoms, applying this method to two distinct spatial configurations of three coupled two-level emitters. Our results demonstrate that both the coupling between dressed levels and the resulting energies and sideband counts differ for each configuration. Consequently, the fluorescence spectrum of strongly interacting atoms encodes information regarding both the number and spatial configuration of the atoms.

Grasping the varied roles individuals play in large-scale information dissemination is crucial for managing online conduct and its potential real-world impacts. While most current research across different fields emphasizes the outsized impact of highly connected "hub" nodes, this study argues that online social media spreading is most accurately understood and predicted by simultaneously identifying two individual-level behavioral traits: influence and susceptibility. We developed a nonlinear network-based algorithm to quantify these traits using data from multiple spreading events. When applied to extensive datasets from Twitter and Weibo, our findings reveal that both influence and susceptibility are essential determinants of peer-to-peer information propagation; omitting either factor results in suboptimal prediction accuracy. Furthermore, accurately identifying information superspreaders requires accounting for both properties, a discovery that challenges prevailing assumptions regarding influential individuals in social networks.

Most current few-shot learning approaches define image relationships using binary labels, yet this binary framework falls short of teaching networks complex real-world relations because it lacks decision smoothness. Additionally, existing models capture similarity solely through relation labels, failing to incorporate class concepts linked to objects; this underutilization of label information likely harms classification performance. Drawing a parallel to how children learn what a tiger is by observing few examples and comparing them to other animals, we hypothesize that effective learning requires simultaneous acquisition of both similarity and class concepts. Based on these insights, we investigate the limitations of simplistic class modeling in current few-shot methods. We re-examine the interplay between class concepts and introduce a novel Absolute-relative Learning paradigm designed to maximize label information, thereby refining image representations and correcting relational understanding in both supervised and unsupervised settings. This proposed approach enhances the performance of several state-of-the-art models across publicly available datasets.

Recent developments in torus manifold theory have introduced partial generalizations of virtual polyhedra theory, often under alternative nomenclature. These newer frameworks differ significantly in appearance from the original virtual polyhedra theory; whereas the latter relies on integration over the Euler characteristic, the former utilizes straightforward arguments from homotopy theory. This paper elucidates the connections between these generalizations and both the classical theory of convex bodies and the original virtual polyhedra theory. The text provides no original proofs, as all demonstrations and details are available in the referenced literature. The work stems from a talk delivered at the 2022 International Conference on Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems in Suzdal, which honored V. I. Arnold's 85th anniversary.

This study establishes that the retract of a consonant (or co-consonant) space retains the property of being consonant (or co-consonant), a finding used to derive several related conclusions. Additionally, we demonstrate that: (1) the co-consonance of the Smyth powerspace entails the co-consonance of the underlying topological space under a necessary condition; (2) the co-consonance of a topological space implies the co-consonance of its Smyth powerspace given certain conditions; (3) if the lower powerspace is co-consonant, then the topological space is necessarily co-consonant; and (4) the co-consonance of the topological space implies the co-consonance of the lower powerspace under specific sufficient conditions.

Globally, possessing sufficient information to guide resource allocation for school improvement is a vital challenge. This study utilizes machine learning and education data mining on large-scale educational datasets to pinpoint the factors driving high school performance in South Africa and Sierra Leone. The primary goal is to construct performance predictors and determine the significance of various community and school-level characteristics. By employing interpretable metrics such as SHAP values for tree-based models and odds ratios from logistic regression, the research uncovers factor interactions to aid policy decisions. Since performance determinants differ between these two nations, the resulting policy implications and resource allocation strategies will also vary.

This paper introduces a proof-theoretic approach to establish uniform Lyndon interpolation for various non-normal modal and conditional logics. The method is applied to demonstrate that logics $\mathsf{E}$, $\mathsf{M}$, $\mathsf{EN}$, $\mathsf{MN}$, $\mathsf{MC}$, $\mathsf{K}$, along with their conditional counterparts $\mathsf{CE}$, $\mathsf{CM}$, $\mathsf{CEN}$, $\mathsf{CMN}$, $\mathsf{CMC}$, $\mathsf{CK}$, and $\mathsf{CKID}$ all possess this property. Consequently, these systems also exhibit uniform interpolation. While uniform interpolation was previously known for some of them, the existence of uniform Lyndon interpolation is a novel finding. Furthermore, the proofs provided are new, offering a constructive means to explicitly calculate the interpolants. Conversely, the study shows that $\mathsf{CKCEM}$ and $\mathsf{CKCEMID}$ have uniform interpolation but lack uniform Lyndon interpolation. Additionally, it is proven that the non-normal modal logics $\mathsf{EC}$ and $\mathsf{ECN}$, as well as their conditional versions $\mathsf{CEC}$ and $\mathsf{CECN}$, do not satisfy Craig interpolation, and therefore cannot have uniform (Lyndon) interpolation.

We demonstrate that the Schnakenberg entropy production rate, as described by a master equation, possesses a lower bound determined by a function of the Markov graph's weight, which is defined as the sum of the absolute values of probability currents across its edges. This finding holds true for time-dependent nonequilibrium entropy production rates. Furthermore, within a broad theoretical framework, we establish a theorem proving that the Kullback-Leibler divergence between distributions $P(s)$ and $P'(s):=P(m(s))$—where $m$ represents an involution satisfying $m(m(s))=s$—is lower bounded by a function of the total variation of both $P$ and $P'$ for any such $m$. This bound is tight and represents an improvement upon Pinsker's inequality in this specific context. Ultimately, this result highlights a significant link between nonequilibrium thermodynamics and graph theory, offering intriguing applications.

Hyperspectral imaging serves as a critical sensing technology with wide-ranging applications in environmental science, meteorology, and geo/space exploration. A key objective in hyperspectral image (HSI) processing involves extracting spectral-spatial features. Building upon recent advancements in graph signal processing over multilayer networks (M-GSP), this study introduces multiple M-GSP-driven approaches for HSI segmentation. To capture joint spectral-spatial data, we first design a customized tensor-based multilayer network (MLN) model for HSI and establish a corresponding MLN singular space for feature extraction. Subsequently, we develop an unsupervised segmentation method by applying MLN-based spectral clustering. By regrouping HSI pixels through MLN clustering, we further propose a semi-supervised classification technique utilizing multi-resolution superpixel fusion. Experimental outcomes highlight the efficacy of M-GSP in HSI processing and the extraction of spectral-spatial information.

Automunge is an open-source Python platform designed to streamline tabular data pre-processing and feature engineering. It automatically handles numerical encoding and missing data imputation, generating tidy datasets tailored to the specific characteristics of columns in a designated training set. This ensures consistent and efficient application across subsequent data pipelines, such as inference, where transformations can be applied to distinct column groups organized in "family tree" structures with generational derivations. The library includes methods for extracting structure from bounded categorical strings via automated parsing; this process compares unique values to identify character subset overlaps, which can be encoded as appended boolean columns or by replacing original strings with identified partition identifiers. Additionally, the library offers string parsing options applicable to unbounded categorical sets, including the extraction of numeric substrings and search functions to detect specific substring patterns. By aggregating these techniques into "family tree" transformation sets, Automunge enables the automatic extraction of structural information from categorical string compositions relative to column entries. This facilitates the preparation of categorical string encodings for machine learning tasks without requiring human intervention.

A sorting network corresponds to a minimal path from the permutation $12\dots n$ to $n\dots 21$ within the Cayley graph of the symmetric group $\mathfrak S_n$, generated by adjacent transpositions. This paper determines the edge local limit of uniformly random sorting networks as $n$ approaches infinity. We derive the asymptotic distribution for the initial appearance of a specific swap $(k,k+1)$ and characterize it as the distribution of the smallest positive eigenvalue of a $2k\times 2k$ aGUE matrix, where entries are purely imaginary, independent Gaussians subject to skew-symmetry. Furthermore, we provide two distinct formal definitions for a "spacing," defined as the temporal distance between successive occurrences of the swap $(k,k+1)$ in a random sorting network. These two definitions yield two separate expressions for the asymptotic laws, both formulated using derivatives of Fredholm determinants.

Quantum walks (QWs) operating on high-dimensional and reconfigurable graphs hold the key to unlocking the full capabilities of quantum simulation and information processing. Yet, experimentally achieving such large-scale, programmable walks remains difficult due to the substantial complexity of current methodologies. We overcome this barrier by demonstrating Grover walks on four-dimensional hypercubes with fidelities exceeding 95%, alongside 400-step quantum walks on circles and finite lines achieving 98% similarity. This success is enabled by a new measurement-based framework for quantum walks, where evolution unitaries are realized through measurements in suitably rotated bases. These findings pave the way for scalable and programmable quantum networks capable of addressing complex applications like Gaussian Boson Sampling.

The flavor ratios $R_K/R_{K^*}$, which exhibit lepton universality violation, suggest the presence of new physics affecting either the $b \to s \mu^+ \mu^-$ or $b \to s e^+ e^-$ transitions, or both. Should the new physics arise exclusively from the $b \to s e^+ e^-$ channel, its associated operators could theoretically possess any Lorentz structure. This study conducts a model-independent analysis of new physics limited to the $b \to se^+e^-$ decay by examining effective operators individually or in pairs of similar types. Our analysis incorporates all existing measurements within the $b \rightarrow se^+e^-$ sector alongside the $R_K/R_{K^*}$ data. We demonstrate that new physics scenarios involving vector or axial-vector operators can explain the $R_K/R_{K^*}$ observations, whereas those involving scalar, pseudoscalar, or tensor operators cannot. Furthermore, we identify the azimuthal angular observable $P_1$ in $B \to K^* e^+ e^-$ decays as the most effective tool for distinguishing between the various viable solutions.

Modern statistical applications frequently involve high-dimensional data, making variable selection methods essential for identifying key features in scientific research. While traditional best subset selection is computationally infeasible with many features, regularization techniques like Lasso and SCAD struggle in ultrahigh-dimensional settings due to instability and inefficiency. Consequently, sure screening methods have gained popularity by first reducing dimensionality via simple metrics, such as marginal correlation, before applying regularization. Although numerous screening approaches exist for various models, none specifically address data with heavy tails—a critical characteristic of contemporary big data. This paper introduces a robust distance correlation (RDC)-based sure screening method designed for ultrahigh-dimensional regression involving heavy-tailed data. The proposed approach retains the favorable model-free properties of standard distance correlation screening while adding the advantage of robustly estimating distance correlation under heavy-tailed conditions, thereby enhancing model selection performance. Extensive simulations across diverse heavy-tailed scenarios demonstrate the superiority of this procedure over existing model-based and model-free methods in terms of feature selection and prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the method was applied to high-dimensional heavy-tailed RNA-seq data from the The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pancreatic cancer cohort, where RDC outperformed other techniques in prioritizing biologically significant and essential genes.

This research investigates the thermodynamics and critical phenomena of higher-dimensional Lovelock black holes featuring non-maximally symmetric horizons within the extended phase space canonical ensemble. We specifically examine third-order Lovelock black holes, analyzing how the non-constant nature of the horizon manifests through two charge-like parameters in thermodynamic quantities. Our findings reveal that Ricci-flat black holes with non-constant curvature horizons exhibit critical behavior, a distinctive feature previously unobserved in either Einstein or Lovelock gravity literature. We analyze how various thermodynamic phenomena—including standard first-order small-large black hole transitions, reentrant transitions, and zeroth-order transitions—occur across Ricci-flat, spherical, and hyperbolic black holes with non-constant curvature horizons, contingent upon the Lovelock coefficients and charge-like parameters. Whereas spherical black holes in third-order Lovelock gravity with constant curvature horizons display phase transitions only within $7 \leq d \leq 11$, our solutions demonstrate criticality and phase transitions in all dimensions. By appropriately selecting free parameters, a large-small-large black hole phase transition is induced, characterized by a finite Gibbs free energy jump known as a zeroth-order phase transition. Additionally, for the case where $\kappa = -1$, we identify a novel behavior allowing for the existence of three critical points.

We utilize both Darmois and $C^3$ matching criteria across three distinct spherically symmetric spacetimes. In these scenarios, the exterior region adheres to the Schwarzschild vacuum solution, while the interior regions utilize various perfect fluid models sharing the same symmetry. Our analysis demonstrates that Darmois conditions hold true for all three instances, whereas $C^3$ conditions fail to be met. We attribute this discrepancy to unphysical pressure behavior at the boundary where the spacetimes match.

A fundamental aspect of mathematical reasoning involves crafting compelling conjectures regarding a specific problem domain. This paper provides a concise overview of QuickSpec, a theory exploration system designed to automatically identify interesting conjectures within a given set of functions. QuickSpec achieves this by integrating term generation with random testing to propose candidate conjectures. This process remains manageable by initiating with small term sizes and restricting consideration to terms that are irreducible with respect to conjectures already discovered. QuickSpec has proven effective in generating lemmas for automated inductive theorem proving and in deriving specifications for functional programs. Furthermore, we outline typical applications of QuickSpec and demonstrate its straightforward integration with any theorem prover of the user's preference.

This study presents a search for physics beyond the Standard Model within final states characterized by two oppositely charged, same-flavor leptons and missing transverse momentum. Utilizing a dataset of proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV with an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC, the analysis investigates three potential new physics signatures: an excess of events featuring a lepton pair with an invariant mass near the Z boson mass, a kinematic edge in the lepton pair's invariant mass distribution, and the nonresonant production of two leptons. The observed event counts align with predictions from Standard Model backgrounds. Consequently, the first search excludes gluino masses up to 1870 GeV, as well as chargino (and neutralino) masses up to 750 (800) GeV. Additionally, the analyses for the other two signatures rule out light-flavor (bottom) squark masses up to 1800 (1600) GeV and slepton masses up to 700 GeV, respectively, at a 95% confidence level under specific supersymmetry models.

This study introduces an all-optical technique for the precise ultrafast rotation of spins, enabling the manipulation of polarization in relativistic beams of leptons or ions. Specifically, dense, ultrashort beams driven by lasers are controlled through a single-shot interaction with a co-propagating laser pulse that exhibits moderate temporal asymmetry, such as frequency chirping or subcycle THz characteristics. Semi-classical numerical simulations indicate that within a temporally asymmetric laser field, a particle's spin rotation can be flexibly regulated by adjusting the phase retardation between its momentum oscillation and spin precession. Consequently, an initial proton beam polarization can be rotated to any target orientation—for instance, shifting from transverse to the highly valuable longitudinal state—with exceptional accuracy (exceeding 99% precision) within tens of femtoseconds using a viable frequency-chirped laser pulse. Furthermore, the rotation process significantly enhances beam quality regarding both energy and angular divergence. This approach holds promise for applications across various fields requiring ultrafast spin control, including laser-plasma interactions, laser-nuclear physics, and high-energy particle research.

Space-based gamma-ray instruments, including the Fermi Large Area Telescope, have relied on single-sided silicon strip detectors to track secondary charged particles generated by primary gamma rays with high precision. However, for the keV-MeV energy range targeted by such telescopes, two-dimensional position data within a single detector is essential for event reconstruction, particularly in the Compton regime. This paper details the creation of AstroPix, a novel monolithic CMOS active pixel silicon sensor technology intended for future gamma-ray telescopes. Drawing upon sensors (ATLASPix) originally developed for the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, AstroPix aims to sustain high performance while minimizing noise and power consumption. These benefits are realized through dual detection and readout functions inherent to each CMOS pixel. The presentation will cover the current status of AstroPix development and testing, along with prospects for future applications and trials.

World knowledge manifests in both structured formats, such as tables and knowledge graphs, and unstructured forms, like text. While recent research has extensively explored integrating these two types, most efforts concentrate on embedding static factual knowledge into pre-trained language models, leaving the enhancement of temporal knowledge graph (tKG) embeddings with textual data largely unaddressed. Current integration methods are ill-suited for tKGs because they typically assume knowledge embeddings remain constant over time. In reality, entity representations in tKG models evolve, creating a challenge to align time-sensitive textual information with these dynamic entities. To address this, we introduce Enhanced Temporal Knowledge Embeddings with Contextualized Language Representations (ECOLA). ECOLA leverages tKG quadruples to implicitly align textual data with time-evolving entity representations and employs a novel knowledge-text prediction task to infuse textual insights into temporal embeddings. By jointly optimizing both the knowledge-text prediction and temporal knowledge embedding objectives, ECOLA fully exploits the synergies between textual and structured knowledge. Given the lack of existing datasets featuring tKGs with aligned textual data, we have developed three new datasets for training and evaluation. Experimental results on temporal knowledge graph completion demonstrate that ECOLA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art tKG embedding models.

Contact binary star systems mark the enduring penultimate stage of binary evolution, where analyzing their physical parameters provides critical insights into evolutionary trajectories and final outcomes. This pilot study examines ten (near-)contact systems within the long-period ($P$>0.5 d) segment of close binaries in the Kepler field, utilizing light curves and new optical spectroscopy. Bayesian probabilities for five key parameters were derived using PHOEBE light curve models, revealing that spectral measurements of mass ratios and third-light contributions align closely with those inferred from light curves. Notably, these systems exhibit extreme mass ratios ($q$<0.32), and the majority are triple systems. A broader analysis of an unbiased sample of 783 (near-)contact binaries with periods between 0.15 d and 2.0 d identified 178 probable contact systems, 114 probable detached systems, and 491 ambiguous systems, for which best-fitting and percentile parameters were reported. Contact systems and those with $q$>0.8 are rare at periods exceeding 0.5 d. An empirical lower mass ratio limit ($q_{min}$($P$)) ranging from approximately 0.05 to 0.15 exists below which contact systems do not occur, a finding that supports new theoretical predictions based on mass and angular momentum conservation during system evolution. Pre-merger systems are expected to reside at long periods near this rising mass ratio limit, which increases from $q$=0.044 at $P$=0.74 d to $q$=0.15 at $P$=2.0 d. These results validate a scenario in which the nuclear evolution of the primary star drives mass transfer, pushing systems toward extreme mass ratios and larger periods until the Darwin instability at $q_{min}$ triggers a merger.

Over the last century, Industry 4.0 within the healthcare sector has undergone significant transformation, continuously advancing through daily innovations in tools and strategies developed by both researchers and clinicians. The convergence of healthcare and technology has been accelerated by the rise of cloud computing and big data. This research investigates the influence of Industry 4.0 on healthcare systems through a systematic literature review of peer-reviewed articles sourced from Scopus and Web of Science (WoS). Guided by the 2015 PRISMA statement, the study initially conducted a bibliometric analysis of 346 articles, examining publication trends, journals, authors, geographical origins, institutions, keywords, and citations. Subsequently, a qualitative analysis was performed on a selected subset of 32 articles, focusing on conceptual frameworks, scheduling challenges, security issues, the impact of COVID-19, digital supply chains, and blockchain technology. Findings indicate that during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, healthcare and Industry 4.0 evolved in tandem to address crises such as data security, resource allocation, and transparency. Industry 4.0 facilitates the use of technologies like IoT, blockchain, big data, cloud computing, machine learning, deep learning, and ICT to manage patient records and mitigate the social transmission of the virus. Ultimately, these insights offer valuable guidance for future researchers and practitioners regarding the integration of healthcare and Industry 4.0.

Driven by the exponential rise in mobile users, demand for cellular data has surged, prompting operators to innovate and boost system capacity. Historically, this has involved spatial reuse of licensed spectrum through the deployment of 4G/LTE small cells, such as femto cells. However, licensed spectrum alone cannot satisfy the continuously escalating data traffic generated by data-heavy applications like augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and high-definition video streaming. Furthermore, applications including AR/VR and online gaming impose extreme data requirements alongside strict latency constraints. To ensure Quality of Service (QoS), operators are increasingly utilizing unlicensed spectrum to coexist with Wi-Fi in the 5 GHz band. The 3GPP standardization body has established guidelines for fair coexistence, including LTE Licensed Assisted Access (LAA), New Radio in unlicensed (NR-U), and NR in Millimeter Wave. The rapid expansion of LAA deployments in developed countries, such as the US, provides a valuable opportunity to analyze unlicensed coexistence networks using real-world data. Consequently, this paper offers a comprehensive overview of the evolution of small cell and unlicensed coexistence technologies from the past through to the future. It also outlines the vision for upcoming research in the newly allocated 6 GHz unlicensed band, where the latest Wi-Fi standard (IEEE 802.11ax) will coexist with the newest cellular technology, 5G New Radio (NR).

A common programming strategy involves implementing the primary execution flow first, followed by addressing alternative scenarios and edge cases. However, unpredictable conditions often arise that trigger atypical behaviors, which are difficult to anticipate in program specifications and consequently remain unimplemented. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying and suggesting these omitted behaviors, a task we term "code sophistication." While prior research on coding assistants typically recommends code snippets based on defined behavioral specifications, code sophistication operates without such specifications, aiming to assist developers in finalizing their program logic by incorporating missing and unspecified behaviors. We detail the research challenges associated with this problem and present preliminary results demonstrating how program logic can be completed by utilizing code structure and insights into input parameter usage.

This paper investigates distributed user association in 5G and beyond millimeter-wave heterogeneous networks through the lens of matching theory. We introduce a novel, efficient distributed matching game named "early acceptance" (EA). In this framework, users apply to their preferred base stations in a distributed manner and are accepted immediately upon appearing in a base station's preference list with available capacity. We compare several EA variants, which incorporate preference list updates and reapplication mechanisms, against the original stability-optimal deferred acceptance (DA) game. The DA approach utilizes waiting lists at each base station, delaying user association until the entire game concludes. Our findings demonstrate that matching stability does not necessarily guarantee optimal performance across other metrics, such as throughput. Both theoretical analysis and simulations reveal that, compared to DA, the proposed EA matching games deliver higher network throughput and a significantly faster association process. Additionally, whether played once or multiple times, the EA games achieve network utility levels closely matching those of centralized user association, yet with substantially lower computational complexity.

Real-world scans often fail to capture complete object geometries due to self-occlusions, external occlusions, and restricted sensor resolution. Point cloud completion seeks to reconstruct full shapes from these incomplete 3D scans. Existing deep learning methods typically depend on large-scale complete shapes sourced from synthetic datasets, a strategy that is ineffective for real-world scans because of the domain gap. To address this, we introduce TraPCC, a self-supervised point cloud completion framework designed for vehicles in actual traffic environments without requiring any complete training data. Leveraging the inherent symmetry and similarity of vehicles, we utilize consecutive point cloud frames to build a vehicle memory bank for reference. Furthermore, we employ a bottom-up mechanism to capture both local geometric details and global shape characteristics of the input. Additionally, a scene graph within the network is designed to highlight missing regions by considering neighboring vehicles. Experimental results demonstrate that TraPCC achieves strong performance on the KITTI and nuScenes traffic datasets for real-scan completion, even in the absence of complete training data. We also present a downstream 3D detection application that benefits from our proposed completion method.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been pivotal in medical imaging applications such as classification and segmentation, often outperforming traditional image processing techniques. Nevertheless, CNNs suffer from high computational demands, a dependency on powerful hardware like GPUs, and their opaque "black-box" characteristics. To address these limitations, this paper introduces quantized, standalone self-attention models as a viable alternative to conventional CNNs. In this approach, convolutional layers are substituted with standalone self-attention layers, and the model parameters are quantized following training. Experimental results on classification and segmentation tasks demonstrate significant improvements, including a 50–80% decrease in model size, 60–80% fewer parameters, 40–85% reduced FLOPs, and 65–80% greater energy efficiency during CPU inference. The source code will be made available at \href{https://github.com/Rakshith2597/Quantised-Self-Attentive-Deep-Neural-Network}{https://github.com/Rakshith2597/Quantised-Self-Attentive-Deep-Neural-Network}.

Entity Typing (ET) involves determining the semantic categories for all entities in a text corpus. Unlike Named Entity Recognition, which assigns zero or one label per token, ET applies one or more labels to each entity mention. Current mention-level ET models face two primary limitations: they fail to utilize recently developed context-dependent embeddings and rely on fixed context windows, making them sensitive to window size choices and incapable of capturing full document context. To address these issues, we propose integrating transformer-based embeddings for mention-level modeling and developing an end-to-end Bi-GRU model to eliminate window size dependencies. An extensive ablation study confirms the benefits of contextualized embeddings for mention-level tasks and demonstrates the competitive performance of our end-to-end approach for entity typing.

Conversational analysis models are frequently trained on noisy human annotations and necessitate substantial preprocessing for multi-modal feature extraction. Relying on such noisy labels within single-task learning heightens the likelihood of overfitting. Introducing auxiliary tasks can enhance the primary task's performance during the same training phase; this strategy effectively bridges transfer learning and multi-task learning (MTL). This paper investigates how preprocessed data utilized for feature engineering can be repurposed as auxiliary tasks to maximize data utility. Our key contributions include: (1) identifying sixteen advantageous auxiliary tasks, (2) analyzing methods for allocating learning capacity between primary and auxiliary tasks, and (3) examining the supervision hierarchy between them. Extensive experiments on the IEMOCAP and SEMAINE datasets confirm that this approach outperforms single-task methods and indicates potential generalizability across various primary tasks.

A primary challenge in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is effectively capturing the significance of neighbor nodes during aggregation for representation learning. A specific category of GNNs, known as implicit GNNs (e.g., Graph Attention Networks), addresses this by learning implicit weights to quantify neighbor importance. These models operate by introducing graph information with unique characteristics, which are then processed by Learnable Transformation Structures (LTS) that encode neighbor importance in a data-driven manner. However, this paper argues that LTS causes the distinctive properties of graph information to vanish during training, rendering such information ineffective for learning node representations. We term this phenomenon Graph Information Vanishing (GIV). Furthermore, we observe that LTS maps diverse graph information into highly similar outputs. To substantiate these claims, we conducted two sets of 70 randomized experiments across five implicit GNN methods and seven benchmark datasets, utilizing a random permutation operator to disrupt graph information order and substitute it with random values. Our findings indicate that randomization did not impact model performance in 93% of cases, with the remaining 7% showing an average accuracy drop of 0.5%. Additionally, the cosine similarity between output results generated by LTS from different graph information exceeded 99%, with an 81% proportion. These experimental results support the existence of GIV in implicit GNNs and suggest that current approaches fail to leverage graph information effectively. Consequently, the relationship between graph information and LTS requires reconsideration to ensure graph information is properly utilized in node representation.

Significant gaps remain in our understanding of the brain's color processing mechanisms, particularly regarding the conversion from cone-opponent signals to perceptual hues, as well as the specific cortical regions responsible for representing unique hues. To address this, we introduce a hierarchical model grounded in neuronal mechanisms that elucidates the roles of various visual cortical areas in hue representation. This local hue encoding strategy relies on progressively increasing nonlinearities starting from cone inputs, incorporating both nonlinear rectifications and multiplicative modulations. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that multiplicative modulations play a crucial role in encoding hues along intermediate axes within the MacLeod-Boynton diagram and that model neurons in area V4 are capable of encoding unique hues. Furthermore, the responses of our model neurons closely mirror those of biological color cells, indicating that this framework offers a novel formulation of the brain's color processing pathway.

Ultimately, global production, understood as a value-creation system, is evolving into a vast and intricate web of value chains that elucidates the transitional frameworks of worldwide trade and economic development. This phenomenon represents a new era of globalization, termed Global Value Chains (GVCs), which establishes a critical nexus connecting firms, laborers, and consumers across the planet. This emerging scenario prompts key questions regarding how economic actors interconnect within the global economy and how they capture value across various dimensions of development. The GVC perspective is essential for comprehending the organization of global industries and corporations, necessitating an analysis of both the static and dynamic roles of diverse participants within this complex production network. Broadly, this concept addresses a spectrum of global issues—from regional to worldwide scales, operating from top-down to bottom-up perspectives—to facilitate policy analysis (Gereffi & Fernandez-Stark 2011). However, as Feenstra (1998) notes, no single computational model can adequately quantify the entire scope of these economic activities; instead, an integrative framework is required to accurately project this dynamic, multidimensional phenomenon.

Ramsey interferometers are extensively utilized across various scientific and engineering fields. While traditional interferometers rely on internal states, those based on external quantum states offer distinct benefits for quantum simulation and high-precision measurements. In this work, we present, for the first time, a Ramsey interferometry scheme utilizing Bloch states within the S- and D-bands of a triangular optical lattice. The successful implementation of this interferometer in a two-dimensionally coupled lattice hinges on employing a shortcut method to generate $\pi/2$ pulses. We successfully observed distinct Ramsey fringes and investigated the underlying decoherence mechanisms. Furthermore, by introducing an echo $\pi$ pulse between the S- and D-bands, we achieved a substantial enhancement in coherence time. This dimensionally coupled lattice interferometer holds promising potential for quantum simulations involving topological physics, frustrated effects, and the manipulation of motional qubits.

This study demonstrates that the interplay between loop and nonlinear Fano resonances generates hybrid resonant states within Mach-Zehnder interferometers, enabling sophisticated phase manipulation. This nonlinear response is significantly amplified, facilitating a low-threshold 100% switching capability. Additionally, we propose a feasible implementation using nonlinear photonic crystal circuits, which are well-suited for optimal all-optical switching.

This article examines multiplier Hermitian-Einstein metrics, a concept introduced by Mabuchi that encompasses Kähler-Einstein metrics, Kähler-Ricci solitons, and Mabuchi solitons as specific instances. Additionally, we analyze KSM-manifolds, originally defined by the first author as toric bundles, to derive an existence criterion for these metrics based on KSM-data. Furthermore, we construct an explicit example of a KSM-manifold that supports a family of multiplier Hermitian-Einstein metrics by utilizing a continuous path linking a Kähler-Ricci soliton with a Mabuchi soliton.

This study investigates the maximum achievable rate of linear subcodes within Reed-Muller (RM) codes that satisfy a runlength-limited (RLL) constraint. Specifically, we focus on the $(d,\infty)$-RLL requirement, which stipulates that any two consecutive $1$s must be separated by a minimum of $d$ $0$s. We examine a sequence of RM codes, $\{{\mathcal{C}_m}\}_{m\geq 1}$, with increasing blocklengths and asymptotic rates approaching $R$. We demonstrate that for any linear $(d,\infty)$-RLL subcode $\hat{\mathcal{C}}_m$ of $\mathcal{C}_m$, its rate cannot exceed $\frac{R}{d+1}$ as the blocklength tends to infinity. Furthermore, we analyze scenarios where RM code coordinates follow non-lexicographic orderings and establish corresponding rate upper bounds for such linear $(d,\infty)$-RLL subcodes. Finally, considering a $(d,\infty)$-RLL input-constrained binary memoryless symmetric (BMS) channel, we propose a novel coding scheme utilizing cosets of RM codes. In the limit of infinite blocklength, this scheme achieves a higher rate than any linear RM subcode in low-noise channel regimes.

A classical parking function of length $n$ consists of a sequence of positive integers $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ such that its nondecreasing rearrangement $b_1 \leq b_2 \leq \cdots \leq b_n$ fulfills $b_i \leq i$. The convex hull of all such functions of length $n$ forms an $n$-dimensional polytope in $\mathbb{R}^n$, known as the classical parking function polytope. Geometric characteristics of this polytope were investigated in (Amanbayeva and Wang 2022) to address a query raised in (Stanley 2020). This study extends that family by analyzing the convex hull of $\mathbf{x}$-parking functions where $\mathbf{x}=(a,b,\dots,b)$, termed $\mathbf{x}$-parking function polytopes, and examines their relationships with the Pitman-Stanley polytope and the partial permutahedra described in (Heuer and Striker 2022). Notably, we derive a closed-form formula for the volume of $\mathbf{x}$-parking function polytopes, which resolves a conjecture by (Behrend et al. 2022) and yields, as a corollary, the first closed-form expression for the volume of the convex hull of classical parking functions.

This study addresses dynamic factor analysis within the context of ARMA processes. To achieve robust estimation of the factor count, we establish a confidence region centered on a finite-sample estimate of the model, ensuring the true model is included with a specified probability. Within this region, the problem—formulated as minimizing the rank of a specific spectral density—is efficiently approximated using a convex relaxation based on the trace norm. We tackle this approximation by applying Lagrange duality theory, which guarantees the existence of solutions. Furthermore, a numerical algorithm for solving the resulting dual problem is introduced. The performance of the proposed estimator is validated through simulation experiments utilizing both synthetic and real-world data.

This paper examines surfaces $S$ that are homeomorphic to either a punctured torus or a pair of pants. The focus is on \emph{\textbf{combinatorial $k$-systoles}}, defined as closed curves with self-intersection numbers exceeding $k$ that possess the minimal combinatorial length. We demonstrate that the maximal intersection number $I^c_k$ for these combinatorial $k$-systoles on $S$ scales linearly with $k$, and that $\underset{k\rightarrow+\infty}{\limsup}(I^c_k-k)=+\infty$. For both the pair of pants and the punctured torus, this finding provides a positive resolution to the combinatorial analogue of the Erlandsson-Parlier conjecture, which was originally posed regarding geometric length.

In numerous survey-based spatial modeling contexts, data are often aggregated across survey regions due to resource constraints, while covariates derived from weather models and satellite imagery are available at various spatial resolutions. This disparity creates a significant pre-processing challenge for spatial modeling tasks. We introduce a Gaussian process regression model that utilizes an additive kernel to flexibly manage multiresolution covariates, enabling efficient aggregation of features across different scales. Unlike existing methods that depend on matching resolutions, our approach preserves distributional information more effectively, resulting in superior performance and interpretability. Empirical evaluations on both simulated data and crop yield datasets demonstrate that our model achieves enhanced predictive accuracy and clarity.

High-throughput screening has emerged as a primary strategy for discovering new functional materials, yet its efficacy is constrained by the limited quantity and diversity of entries in existing repositories like ICSD and OQMD. Recent advancements in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have facilitated a generative approach that learns implicit chemical rules to create chemically valid hypothetical materials with novel compositions and structures. Despite this, current generative models struggle to produce materials that are simultaneously structurally diverse, chemically valid, and stable. To address this, we introduce CubicGAN, a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed for the large-scale generation of novel cubic crystal structures. Trained on a dataset of 375,749 ternary crystal materials from the OQMD database, our model successfully rediscovered most known cubic materials and generated hypothetical candidates featuring new structure prototypes. A total of 506 of these new materials (comprising ternary and quaternary compounds) were confirmed as stable through DFT-based phonon dispersion analysis; several exhibit potential for exceptional functional properties. Given the critical role of cubic materials in applications ranging from solar cells to lithium batteries, our GAN model offers a promising method to significantly expand material repositories, thereby enabling the discovery of new functional materials via screening. The DFT-verified crystal structures are freely available at our Carolina Materials Database (http://www.carolinamatdb.org).

Online controlled experiments are extensively utilized to assess new features within the fast-paced development cycles of web products and mobile apps. While measuring the overall sample is a standard practice for quantifying total treatment effects, segmentation offers a valuable method for conducting a more granular analysis to understand the underlying reasons for these effects. This paper presents a framework for generating and applying user behavioral segments in online experimentation. By leveraging data on how users engage with specific product components as input, this approach defines segments that are directly relevant to the features under evaluation. Through a real-world case study, we demonstrate that analyzing data using these behavioral segments provides profound, actionable insights that effectively guide product decision-making.

This paper provides a positive resolution to two conjectures concerning generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivations and generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan centralizers, originally proposed in works by S. Ali and A. Fo\v{s}ner (Algebra Colloq. 21, 2014) and A. Fo\v{s}ner (Demonstratio Math. 46, 2013). Specifically, for a semiprime ring $R$, and subject to certain torsion constraints, we demonstrate that any nonzero generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan derivation (respectively, a generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan centralizer) is, in fact, a derivation (respectively, a two-sided centralizer).

To achieve high sensitivity in hard X-ray astronomy, it is crucial to comprehend and minimize instrumental backgrounds in orbit. Observational data from the Hard X-ray Imager (HXI) aboard the Hitomi satellite offers valuable insights into these background components, thanks to its multi-layered structure featuring detectors of varying atomic numbers. Specifically, the HXI comprises four stacked silicon (Si, Z = 14) detector layers and one cadmium telluride (CdTe, Z = 48, 52) layer, all enclosed by well-type bismuth germanate (BGO) active shields. Analysis of the observational data indicates that the background sources for the top silicon layer, the three lower silicon layers, and the CdTe layer are primarily dominated by low-energy electrons, albedo neutrons, and proton-induced radioactivation, respectively. Monte Carlo simulations of the in-orbit HXI background successfully replicate the observed spectrum for each layer, quantitatively confirming this hypothesis. Furthermore, we recommend implementing an electron shield to further mitigate background noise.

Most nonrandomized observational studies face challenges where treatment group differences stem not only from the intervention itself but also from confounding variables, making causal inference less direct than in randomized trials. To address confounding from measured covariates, researchers employ various potential outcomes-based methods to estimate average treatment effects. A central requirement is the positivity assumption, which mandates that the probability of receiving treatment remains strictly between zero and one across all confounder combinations. However, techniques for causal inference when this assumption is violated are scarce. This article introduces a novel balance-related condition defined by the convex hulls of treatment groups, termed "relaxed covariate overlap." This concept offers a connection to the margin metric from machine learning. By incorporating relaxed covariate overlap, the proposed approach enables causal inference through a three-step methodology, which is demonstrated using two examples.

**Background:** Describing spontaneous fission at the microscopic level remains one of the most difficult challenges in nuclear physics. Accurately modeling quantum tunneling in spontaneous or low-energy fission requires determining both the collective potential and collective inertia along a fission trajectory. Previous investigations into fission dynamics utilizing nuclear energy density functional (EDF) theory have typically assessed collective inertia using the cranking approximation, which overlooks dynamical residual effects. **Purpose:** The aim is to establish a dependable and efficient approach for incorporating dynamical residual effects into the calculation of collective inertia for fission dynamics. **Methods:** This study employs the local quasiparticle random-phase approximation (LQRPA) to determine collective inertia along a fission path generated by the constrained Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov method using the Skyrme EDF. By applying the finite-amplitude method (FAM) combined with a contour integration technique, we achieve efficient computation of collective inertia within an extensive model space. **Results:** We calculated the FAM-QRPA collective inertia along symmetric fission paths for $^{240}$Pu and $^{256}$Fm. The resulting FAM-QRPA inertia values are substantially higher than those derived from the cranking approximation and exhibit significant peaks near the ground state and fission isomer, a phenomenon attributed to dynamical residual effects. **Conclusions:** To accurately describe spontaneous or low-energy fission, we offer a robust and efficient method for constructing collective inertia that accounts for dynamical residual effects, which have largely been ignored in prior EDF-based studies. Our findings highlight the critical role of these effects on collective inertia. This research serves as a foundation for a systematic investigation of fission dynamics in heavy and superheavy nuclei, enabling the microscopic description of nuclear large-amplitude collective motions.

This Fluid Dynamics Video, submitted to the 31st Gallery of Fluid Motion (an alternative version is available at http://youtu.be/CS0c05WQ_js), demonstrates the unique dynamics of capillary self-propelled Leidenfrost droplets within micrometric ratchets. To enable the propulsion of water droplets approximately 1 mm in size, micro-ratchets were fabricated through direct material ablation using a picosecond pulsed laser. This surface micro-patterning technique allows for the creation of well-controlled topography on various substrates, typically achieving micron-scale resolution. Further details are provided in the referenced materials.

This paper examines convex mutual information, identified as the optimal split point in multilevel coding schemes for additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that achievable communication rates within the convex region are not necessarily bounded below by mutual information, a finding further supported by simulation results.

This paper examines lunisolar resonances driven solely by inclination, which govern the long-term secular dynamics of Medium Earth Orbit (MEO) objects over decades. Building on the framework presented in arXiv:2107.14507, we develop an analytical model that accurately determines the separatrix shapes for major lunisolar resonances within the $(i, e)$ action space (representing inclination and eccentricity) for any specified semi-major axis $a$. Our approach elucidates how this model predicts and explains key structures observed in numerically generated Fast Lyapunov Indicator (FLI) maps. Specifically, we analyze how these maps depend on the initial phases of the object's argument of perigee ($\omega$), its longitude of the ascending node ($\Omega$), and the moon's longitude of the ascending node ($\Omega_L$). Furthermore, based on our model, we investigate the impact of the $\Omega-\Omega_L$ and $2\Omega-\Omega_L$ resonances, which intersect with inclination-only resonances as the semi-major axis $a$ increases, thereby creating extensive regions of chaotic motion. Ultimately, our findings offer a framework for optimizing low-cost satellite deployment and space debris mitigation strategies by leveraging lunisolar resonances to naturally elevate an object's eccentricity until atmospheric drag induces re-entry.

This paper demonstrates that only a finite number of modular curves possess a smooth plane model. Specifically, we establish that no such curves exist if the model's degree is 19 or higher. Regarding modular curves of Shimura type, we prove that none can have a smooth plane model with a degree of 5, 6, or 7. Furthermore, if a Shimura-type modular curve does admit a smooth plane model of degree 8, it must be a twist of one of four specific curves.

Achieving breakthroughs in dynamic whole-body locomotion requires legged robots to possess terrain awareness. Terrain-Aware Locomotion (TAL) enables robots to perceive their environment via sensors and make informed decisions accordingly. This thesis explores TAL strategies through both proprioceptive and exteroceptive lenses, implementing solutions across locomotion planning, control, and state estimation using optimization and learning techniques. The initial section addresses Whole-Body Control (WBC) strategies, introducing a passive WBC (pWBC) framework that stabilizes walking on challenging terrain by accounting for geometric inclinations and friction properties; however, its reliance on rigid contact assumptions limits it to stiff surfaces. To overcome this, we propose Soft Terrain Adaptation aNd Compliance Estimation (STANCE), an algorithm capable of adapting to soft terrains beyond rigid constraints. The second section focuses on vision-based approaches, presenting Vision-Based Terrain-Aware Locomotion (ViTAL), an online planning method that selects footholds based on robot capabilities and poses that maximize the probability of success. ViTAL utilizes a set of robot skills to characterize leg capabilities, including terrain geometry assessment, collision avoidance, and adherence to kinematic limits. Validated through simulations and experiments on HyQ and HyQReal robots, these optimization and learning-driven strategies demonstrate a significant step toward making dynamic legged robots fully autonomous and terrain-aware.

This study examines informational results within a dynamic signaling framework where commitment power diminishes. It demonstrates that, contrary to common assumptions, equilibria featuring informative and payoff-relevant signaling can emerge without relying on implausible off-path beliefs. The paper offers a precise characterization of separating equilibria, establishing that all signaling occurs through attrition, wherein the weakest type randomizes between revealing its type and pooling with stronger types. The model is highly general, requiring only minimal conditions regarding payoff monotonicity and single-crossing. Furthermore, the authors apply the framework to bargaining, monopoly price signaling, and labor market signaling to illustrate the findings in specific scenarios.

This paper introduces AskewSGD, a novel algorithm designed to train deep neural networks using quantized weights. We begin by modeling the training of quantized neural networks (QNNs) as a sequence of smoothed, interval-constrained optimization problems. To address each subproblem, we propose AskewSGD, a new first-order stochastic method. Distinct from approaches relying on active sets or feasible directions, AskewSGD permits infeasible iterates and eliminates the need for projections or optimization over the full feasible set. Its numerical complexity matches that of existing QNN training techniques, including the straight-through gradient estimator in BinaryConnect and state-of-the-art methods like ProxQuant and LUQ. We provide convergence guarantees for AskewSGD under general objective function assumptions. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate that AskewSGD performs as well as or better than current state-of-the-art methods on classical benchmarks.

A common and intriguing characteristic across numerous quantum gravity approaches is the dynamic reduction of the spectral dimension, shifting from $D_s = 4$ at macroscopic scales to approximately $D_s \approx 2$ at microscopic scales. This note examines how this transition influences the energy loss of static, spherically symmetric black holes via Hawking radiation. We show that the drop in spectral dimension ensures a black hole's luminosity remains finite. Although this effect marginally extends the lifespan of low-mass black holes, our analysis indicates that it cannot produce long-lived black hole remnants. We also provide a brief discussion on how these results connect to prior research in the field.

Training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) demands substantial computational throughput and high memory bandwidth. Specifically, convolution layers constitute the bulk of training execution time, leading to the widespread use of GPUs for accelerating these workloads. Optimizing GPU designs for efficient CNN training necessitates precise modeling of performance gains resulting from increased computing and memory resources.
