We introduce DeLTA, the first analytical model capable of accurately estimating traffic across every level of the GPU memory hierarchy while incorporating the intricate reuse patterns inherent in parallel convolution algorithms. Our results demonstrate that the model is both accurate and robust across various CNN types and GPU architectures. Furthermore, we illustrate how this model enables the careful balancing of scaling different GPU resources to achieve improved CNN performance.

We introduce a novel technique for testing antenna arrays that captures radiating electromagnetic (EM) fields using an absorbing material and analyzes the resulting thermal image sequences via an AI-based conditional encoder-decoder model. By utilizing the power and phase of signals supplied to each array element, our trained model reconstructs standard sequences, which are then compared against real-time observations from a thermal camera. These thermograms exhibit only low-level patterns, such as irregular blobs. Consequently, a contour-based anomaly detector maps the reconstruction error matrix to an anomaly score, effectively identifying defective antenna arrays and boosting the classification F-measure by as much as 46%. We validate this approach using time-series thermograms gathered from our antenna testing system. Although variational autoencoders (VAEs) with learned observation noise typically outperform those with constant noise assumptions, we demonstrate that this does not hold for anomaly detection involving such low-level patterns. This conclusion is supported by two factors: first, the baseline reconstruction probability metric, which includes learned observation noise, fails to distinguish anomalous patterns; second, a VAE employing a lower observation noise assumption achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve that is 11.83% higher than that of a VAE with learned noise.

Gaussian quadrature rules serve as a foundational method for numerically approximating integrals involving smooth functions and positive weights. This work derives and explicitly enumerates asymptotic formulas for the nodes and weights of these rules across three broad categories of positive weight functions: analytic functions defined on bounded intervals with algebraic endpoint singularities, analytic weights on the half-line featuring exponential decay at infinity and an algebraic singularity at the finite endpoint, and analytic functions on the entire real line exhibiting exponential decay in both directions. These findings encompass classical orthogonal polynomial rules, such as those for Legendre, Jacobi, Laguerre, and Hermite polynomials, as specific instances. Experimental results demonstrate the number of quadrature points required for these expressions to attain high precision. Furthermore, an algorithm is provided to calculate any number of terms in these expansions for classical cases, and a substantial number of terms for generalized cases, though not necessarily all.

The swift advancement in generating and disseminating ultra-realistic media across social networks necessitates the immediate development of a generalizable deepfake detection method. Observations indicate that existing deepfake generation techniques often leave distinguishable artifacts within the frequency spectrum of forged images and videos. Building on this insight, this paper introduces MD-CSDNetwork, a novel approach that integrates spatial and frequency domain features to extract a shared discriminative representation for deepfake classification. MD-CSDNetwork functions as a cross-stitched architecture featuring two parallel branches that process spatial and frequency information separately. We posit that these multi-domain data streams serve as complementary supervisory signals; supervision from both branches enhances performance and generalization. Additionally, cross-stitch connections are employed between the branches to automatically learn an optimal fusion of domain-specific and shared representations. Extensive experiments were performed on the FaceForensics++ benchmark for forgery classification. Our results demonstrate improvements across all manipulation types in FaceForensics++ and achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in cross-database evaluations on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Datasets.

Bi-partite ribbon graphs play a crucial role in structuring the large $N$ expansion of correlators within random matrix models and in counting observables in random tensor models. An algebra, denoted as $\mathcal{K}(n)$, is defined with a basis consisting of bi-partite ribbon graphs featuring $n$ edges, proving highly valuable for these applications. This algebra exhibits a strong connection to symmetric group algebras and possesses a matrix-block decomposition tied to Clebsch-Gordan multiplicities, or Kronecker coefficients, associated with symmetric group representations. Furthermore, quantum mechanical models utilizing $\mathcal{K}(n)$ as their Hilbert spaces provide combinatorial methods for calculating these Kronecker coefficients.

Although theoretically justified, supersymmetry (SUSY) models featuring a compressed mass spectrum present significant experimental hurdles. This presentation details two recent CMS Collaboration searches focused on leptonic final states indicative of such models. The initial search examines SUSY signatures characterized by two or three low-momentum leptons with opposite signs, while the second explores the parameter space of top squark models where the lightest SUSY particle's mass is nearly equal to that of the top quark. Both analyses utilize the complete Run 2 dataset from the Large Hadron Collider, totaling 137 fb$^{-1}$.

We demonstrate that when the singularity of the quantized gravity propagator scales as $\vert{\bf x}\vert^{-2\gamma}$, the mean value of the fourth power of the distance traversed by a diffusing particle over time $t$ scales as $t^{2(1-\gamma)}$ in the limit of small $t$.

Intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) serve as passive, low-cost, and energy-efficient reflectors capable of significantly enhancing transmission rates by creating a programmable wireless environment. To boost both rate performance and coverage in wireless networks, this work proposes an IRS-aided decode-and-forward (DF) relay network equipped with multiple antennas at the relay station (RS). To maximize the receive rate, an alternately iterative structure (AIS) is introduced to jointly optimize the beamforming vectors at the RS and the phase shifts at the IRS. Addressing the high computational complexity of this approach, two low-complexity schemes are developed: one combining null-space projection (NSP) with maximum ratio combining (MRC), and another utilizing IRS element selection (IRSES) alongside MRC. In the first scheme, NSP isolates the signal reflected by the IRS from the direct source transmission, while MRC merges them at the RS. The second scheme partitions the IRS into M element subsets; by adjusting the phase of elements within each subset, all reflected signals and the direct source signal achieve phase alignment at the corresponding RS antenna. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed three methods substantially outperform existing single-antenna relay networks in terms of rate performance, achieving an 85% rate gain in high signal-to-noise ratio regions. Furthermore, the study confirms that the locations of both the RS and IRS critically influence rate performance, indicating the existence of optimal positions for both nodes.

This paper examines a class of strongly perturbed semilinear wave equations in one spatial dimension featuring a non-characteristic point, accommodating general initial data. Within the framework of similarity variables, Merle and Zaag (in \cite {MZ}) previously derived an explicit stationary solution for the unperturbed case and demonstrated exponential convergence toward this family of solutions. Applying their strategy to our strongly perturbed equation yields only polynomial convergence, a significantly coarser estimate than that of the unperturbed scenario. To refine this approximation, we construct an implicit solution for the perturbed problem that approaches the stationary solutions of the unperturbed case, thereby proving exponential convergence to the specified blow-up profile.

Human annotations are fundamental to machine learning research and development, yet the ethical implications of constructing ML datasets remain underexplored. This paper reviews existing literature to shed light on the ethical dimensions of crowdsourced annotation. By synthesizing these insights, we identify key challenges across two dimensions: the impact of annotators' identities and lived experiences on their work, and the dynamics between annotators and crowdsourcing platforms. Furthermore, we offer a comprehensive set of recommendations and considerations for dataset developers throughout the machine learning data pipeline, covering task design, annotator selection, platform and infrastructure decisions, data analysis and evaluation, as well as documentation and release strategies.

Large, unbiased samples suggest that 10% to 15% of all quasars are radio-loud (RL). Leveraging the Sloan Digital Sky Survey catalog, we demonstrate that the radio-loud fraction (RLF) among high broad line (HBL) quasars—defined by an H$\beta$ full width at half maximum (FWHM) exceeding 15,000 km s$^{-1}$—is approximately 57%. Although our sample shows no significant differences between radio-loud (RL) and radio-quiet (RQ) populations regarding black hole mass, Eddington ratio, or covering fraction (CF), RL quasars exhibit higher optical continuum luminosities. The comparable distribution of CF values suggests our analysis remains unbiased concerning the viewing angles of HBL RL and RQ quasars. Consequently, we conclude that RL quasars in our HBL sample possess higher accretion disc luminosities, implying a link between a brighter disc and a more prominent jet. When compared to non-HBL quasars with broad H$\beta$ emission lines, HBL sources display the lowest Eddington ratios alongside a very high RLF; this aligns with jet formation theories proposing that jets are launched from accreting systems with low Eddington ratios. Furthermore, we observe that the [O III] narrow emission line is stronger in RL than in RQ quasars within our HBL sample, a finding consistent with prior literature and potentially resulting from the interaction between narrow line gas and the jet.

We arrive at conclusions comparable to those of Br\"{u}ck [1] regarding two differential polynomials, which significantly enhance and broaden various established results. Furthermore, numerous examples are provided to demonstrate the necessity and sharpness of specific conditions employed in this study. Finally, we propose an open problem for future investigation.

We investigate the cohomology ring structure of the moduli space of stable 1-dimensional sheaves on $\mathbb{P}^2$ for any given degree. By identifying a minimal collection of tautological generators, we establish an optimal generation result applicable to both the cohomology and Chow rings of this moduli space. This methodology relies on a geometric analysis of tautological relations.

We address the change point problem in ergodic diffusion processes based on discrete data. Building on Tonaki et al. (2020), who introduced adaptive tests to detect shifts in diffusion and drift parameters within ergodic diffusion models, our focus shifts to identifying the precise location of these changes once a shift is detected. Specifically, we propose estimation methods for the change point in two scenarios: when the diffusion parameter changes and when only the drift parameter changes while the diffusion parameter remains constant. Additionally, we derive convergence rates and distributional properties for these estimators and provide illustrative examples along with simulation results.

Following over 25 years of investigation, three even-parity superconducting states—specifically the $d+id$-wave, $d+ig$-wave, and $s+id$-wave configurations—have been identified as the primary contenders for the superconducting behavior of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$. This study introduces a tunneling spectroscopy experiment designed to differentiate between these three states. The central element of our proposal involves analyzing the conductance spectra of normal-metal/Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ junctions across various orientations relative to the crystal axes of the material. Each superconducting state exhibits a distinct angular dependence in these spectra, serving as a unique fingerprint to confirm the pairing symmetry of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$.

While most prior research on random ensembles of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assumes that the degree distributions at both ends of a randomly chosen edge are independent, this paper advances the field by examining ensembles featuring degree-degree correlations. To achieve this, we introduce two methods for constructing such correlated LDPC code ensembles and subsequently derive a system of density evolution equations applicable to these codes over a binary erasure channel (BEC). Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate the impact of degree-degree correlation on LDPC code performance. Our results indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum tolerable erasure probability, and increasing the magnitude of these negative correlations can facilitate superior unequal error protection (UEP) designs.

We analytically model the switching time of magnetization in a biaxial ferromagnet subjected to antidamping-like spin torque. By mapping macrospin dynamics to an energy-flow equation, we employ a rational-function approximation of elliptic integrals—valid for moderate spin currents and small damping—to derive a closed-form expression for the switching time. Variations in the initial magnetization angle yield the corresponding distribution function. This analytical framework aligns with Monte Carlo simulation results across a wide spectrum of material parameters. Consequently, our findings can enhance the design and benchmarking of in-plane spin-torque magnetic memory by eliminating the need for costly numerical computations.

Quantum state measurement represents a central challenge in quantum mechanics. We present a quantum state tomography approach that reconstructs a qubit's state without directly detecting it. This method relies on three key components: (i) utilizing an auxiliary qubit, (ii) aligning the hidden qubit with a known reference state via path identity, and (iii) measuring the auxiliary qubit to infer the state of the undetected one. We both theoretically validate and experimentally verify this technique using photonic polarization states. Furthermore, the core principle of our approach is applicable to quantum systems beyond just photons.

This study examines the global asymptotic stability of an age-structured population model featuring a Ricker-type birth function, formulated as a hyperbolic partial differential equation with a nonlinear, nonlocal boundary condition. We establish a uniform persistence result for the semi-flow associated with this system, demonstrate the existence of global attractors, and prove the global asymptotic stability of the positive equilibrium using an appropriate Lyapunov functional. Additionally, we show that our stability result is sharp, as Hopf bifurcation can occur arbitrarily close to the region of global stability within the parameter space.

Using the ALICE detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), researchers measured the production cross sections of prompt charmed mesons (${\rm D^0}$, ${\rm D^+}$, ${\rm D^{*+}}$, and ${\rm D_s^+}$) at mid-rapidity in proton-proton collisions with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV. The D mesons were identified through their decay channels: ${\rm D}^0 \to {\rm K}^-\pi^+$, ${\rm D}^+\to {\rm K}^-\pi^+\pi^+$, ${\rm D}^{*+} \to {\rm D}^0 \pi^+$, ${\rm D_s^{+}\to \phi\pi^+\to K^-K^+\pi^+}$, along with their corresponding antiparticles. Compared to prior measurements in this rapidity range, this study extends the transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) coverage and reduces uncertainties by approximately a factor of two, thereby enhancing the precision of the estimated total $\rm c\overline c$ production cross section. Finally, the measured $p_{\rm T}$-differential cross sections are contrasted with predictions from three perturbative QCD models.

We establish the groundwork and define the Perfect (Ideal) Hyperfluid. This concept serves as the natural extension of the standard perfect fluid model, incorporating microscopic matter properties such as spin, shear, and dilation. These characteristics source a non-Riemannian spacetime arena, specifically involving torsion and non-metricity within the framework of Metric-Affine Gravity. Following this, we derive the energy tensors associated with this Hyperfluid structure and outline the conservation laws they satisfy. Finally, we explore a cosmological application of the Perfect Hyperfluid and categorize various potential forms of this fluid structure.

Compton backscattering of laser pulses from relativistic electrons generates radiation with high photon energy—ranging from hard x-rays to gamma rays—and high spectral density. This capability stems from the laser's short wavelength compared to classical electromagnetic sources like undulators. This report investigates whether such radiation can be monochromatized using collimation. Two methods for describing the spectral-angular density of Compton radiation were analyzed: one based on classical field theory and the other on quantum electrodynamics. While both approaches yield similar total spectra, their predictions for angular distribution differ, with the classical model forecasting a narrower radiation cone. Additionally, a technique for "electronic" monochromatization is proposed and estimated, which involves the electronic subtraction of images produced by electron beams with slightly varying energies. A "proof-of-principle" experiment to validate this method is suggested for the LUXC facility at KEK in Japan.

Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets) represent a distinct class of neural networks designed to approximate nonlinear operators, such as the solution operator for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs). Despite demonstrating impressive approximation and generalization abilities even with limited training data, DeepONets struggle when the data contains noise, a common practical challenge. To address this, we introduce a training approach based on the Bayesian framework of replica-exchange Langevin diffusion. This method employs two particles to simultaneously explore and exploit the loss landscape of DeepONets. Our results indicate that this dual-capability framework enhances training convergence in noisy environments and provides uncertainty estimates for predicted PDE solutions. Furthermore, compared to standard DeepONets trained with state-of-the-art gradient-based optimizers like Adam, replica-exchange Langevin diffusion notably improves mean prediction accuracy under noisy conditions. To mitigate the high computational costs associated with replica methods, we propose an accelerated training framework that leverages the specific architecture of DeepONets to reduce computational expenses by up to 25% without sacrificing performance. Finally, a series of experiments across four parametric PDE problems demonstrate the efficacy of this proposed Bayesian framework.

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are powerful generative models that leverage deep neural network architectures and Bayesian methods to achieve rich representation capabilities. However, a significant limitation of standard VAEs is their tendency to assign higher likelihoods to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs than to in-distribution (ID) inputs. To overcome this flaw, reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for a deeper analysis of OOD data. This study introduces an Improved Noise Contrastive Prior (INCP) designed to be integrated into VAE encoders, resulting in a model termed INCPVAE. The INCP approach is scalable, trainable, fully compatible with VAEs, and leverages existing advantages for uncertainty estimation. Experimental results across multiple datasets indicate that, compared to conventional VAEs, the proposed model excels in estimating uncertainty for OOD data and demonstrates robustness in anomaly detection tasks. Ultimately, the INCPVAE model provides dependable uncertainty estimation for OOD inputs, effectively resolving the OOD issue inherent in standard VAE architectures.

In the principal-agent framework established by Myerson (1982), agents possess private information regarding their type and make unobservable private decisions. Myerson proposed an elegant solution utilizing the revelation principle, which asserts that, without loss of generality, optimal mechanisms can be designed as truthful and direct. Therefore, when the action and type spaces have finite supports, the problem is solvable via linear programming. This paper extends Myerson's findings to scenarios where the principal's action space may be infinite and subject to further design constraints. This generalized model unifies key design challenges—such as contract design, information design, and Bayesian Stackelberg games—by treating them as special cases. We introduce a revelation principle tailored to this broader model, from which a polynomial-time algorithm is derived to compute the optimal coordination mechanism. This algorithm not only yields new efficient solutions for all the aforementioned specific instances but also substantially streamlines existing methods found in the literature.

The W boson mass ($M_W$) is fundamental for conducting high-precision tests of electroweak theory. By comparing exact theoretical predictions with precisely measured experimental data, researchers achieve high sensitivity to quantum effects arising from loop contributions. This study presents the most accurate current prediction for the W boson mass within the Minimal R-symmetric Supersymmetric Standard Model (MRSSM). Utilizing the on-shell scheme, the analysis integrates all numerically significant Standard Model contributions consistently with complete MRSSM one-loop corrections. Particular attention is given to the triplet scalar vacuum expectation value ($v_T$), which influences the $M_W$ prediction even at the lowest order. The numerical investigation examines the decoupling behavior of supersymmetric loop contributions and compares findings with the MSSM, while highlighting potentially significant numerical impacts from MRSSM-specific $\Lambda$ superpotential couplings. Finally, the results are contextualized by discussing comparisons with existing literature.

Quantifying uncertainty is an essential yet frequently overlooked component of cosmological mass mapping. Existing approaches are often merely approximate or rely heavily on the assumption that the shear field is Gaussian. While probabilistic techniques like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) offer comprehensive and adaptable uncertainty quantification by sampling from probability distributions, they are typically computationally expensive and ill-suited for the high-dimensional parameter spaces common in imaging. This study introduces, for the first time, a trans-dimensional MCMC sampler applied to mass mapping, which enforces sparsity within a wavelet basis. The algorithm dynamically expands the parameter space based on data requirements, capitalizing on the extreme sparsity of mass maps in wavelet space. By organizing wavelet coefficients into a tree-like hierarchy, the method incorporates finer-scale details as the parameter space evolves. Tested on galaxy cluster-scale images where planar modeling holds, the high-resolution experiments yielded naturally parsimonious results, utilizing less than 1% of the maximum possible wavelet coefficients while maintaining a robust fit to the data. Furthermore, when handling noisy data, the trans-dimensional MCMC approach outperformed the standard smoothed Kaiser-Squires method in reconstructing mass maps, with the added benefit of fully quantified uncertainties. This advancement paves the way for novel mass maps and deeper insights into dark matter using upcoming high-resolution data from weak lensing surveys like Euclid.
This paper establishes upper bounds for the volume spectrum of a Riemannian manifold that rely solely on its volume, dimension, and a conformal invariant.

The exact Green's functions for a Dirac particle interacting with a superposition of Aharonov-Bohm and Coulomb fields in (2+1) dimensions are analytically derived using the path integral formalism, covering both global and local representations. This method yields the normalized scattering wavefunctions and their associated continuous energy eigenvalues. Following symmetrization, the intriguing characteristics of the spinors are elucidated. The symmetric formulation of the Green's function demonstrates that equivalence with the Dirac equation is achieved with significant simplicity, and several specific cases are also examined.

This study introduces a time-constrained model predictive control approach for the autonomous rendezvous and docking of a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DOF) deputy spacecraft with an uncontrollable chief spacecraft. Addressing the computational limits imposed by onboard processing capabilities, the method utilizes translational dynamics based on the Clohessy-Wiltshire equations and models angular dynamics resulting from gas jet actuation around the deputy's center of mass. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the docking configuration is successfully achieved under these computational constraints by restricting the number of algorithmic iterations per input calculation. Notably, the research indicates that up to 90% of the computational load in a standard model predictive control framework can be removed without substantially degrading control performance.

This study introduces a new goal-oriented dialogue task focused on automatic symptom detection. We have developed a system capable of engaging with patients in conversation to automatically identify and gather clinical symptoms, thereby reducing the time physicians spend on patient interviews. Initiated by a set of explicit symptoms provided by the patient to start the diagnostic dialogue, the system is trained to query for implicit symptoms, aiming to gather additional data for more accurate diagnoses. Upon receiving patient responses to each inquiry, the system evaluates whether the accumulated information suffices for a human doctor to make a diagnosis. To accomplish this, we present two neural models and a training pipeline designed for multi-step reasoning tasks, alongside a knowledge graph serving as supplementary input to enhance performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly surpasses the baseline by 4%, successfully identifying an average of 67% of implicit symptoms using a limited number of questions.

Scattering amplitudes bridge theoretical frameworks and experimental outcomes, where low-energy terms often factorize from high-energy contributions. Various approaches, including Weinberg's theorem, have been developed to explain this factorization mechanism. It has already been demonstrated that Weinberg's soft factor possesses universal characteristics. In this presentation, we demonstrate that this factor can be calculated independently of the scattering amplitude by utilizing Wigner constraints. Furthermore, we show that these constraints yield a system of partial differential equations, which streamlines the construction of Weinberg's soft factor for scenarios involving one or two particles.

Variations in the pressure of the early Universe plasma influence the mass distribution of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs). Specific phenomena within the standard model of particle physics, including $W^\pm/Z^0$ decoupling, the quark-hadron transition, the non-relativistic transition of muons and pions, and electron-positron annihilation, induce a suppression in the Equation of State parameter. Under conditions of a nearly scale-invariant primordial power spectrum, these events generate distinct peaks in the PBH mass function at approximately $10^{-6}$, $2$, $60$, and $10^6\, M_\odot$. The cumulative effect of unresolved mergers among such PBHs produces a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) spanning a broad frequency spectrum, which is accessible to future gravitational wave (GW) observatories. This study examines how the SGWB's spectral characteristics can reveal insights into inflation, the Universe's thermal evolution, and binary formation dynamics within dense halos, as captured by merger rate formulas. While individual detectors may struggle to distinguish these degenerate physical effects, simultaneous observations of the SGWB across multiple frequencies allow for their separation, underscoring the critical role of multi-frequency GW detection in characterizing PBH physics from the early to the late Universe.

We introduce Styleformer, a style-based generator that replaces the convolutional layers of GANs with a transformer architecture. Our approach demonstrates how transformers can produce high-quality images by addressing the limitation of convolutions in capturing global image features. We adapt the demodulation technique from StyleGAN2 and modify the transformer structure—specifically residual connections and layer normalization—to build a robust, convolution-free generator. By integrating Linformer, we reduce the model's computational weight, allowing Styleformer to generate higher-resolution images more efficiently in terms of speed and memory usage. We evaluate the model on low-resolution datasets like CIFAR-10 and high-resolution datasets such as LSUN-church. On CIFAR-10, Styleformer achieves an FID of 2.82 and an IS of 9.94, matching current state-of-the-art performance while surpassing all existing GAN-based models, including StyleGAN2-ADA, using fewer parameters in an unconditional setting. Additionally, we establish new state-of-the-art results on STL-10 and CelebA with FID scores of 15.17 and 3.66, respectively, and an IS of 11.01. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jeeseung-Park/Styleformer.

Standard quantum mechanics typically models reference frames as abstract, idealized entities with infinite mass that decouple from the rest of the system. However, in reality, all reference frames consist of finite-mass systems governed by quantum laws and must be incorporated into dynamical evolution. Any fundamental physical theory must account for this reality. This paper advances a symmetry-based approach to physics from the viewpoint of quantum reference frames, establishing a unified framework to systematically generate diverse perspective-dependent descriptions and the transformations connecting them. Using a translational-invariant toy model of three free particles, we demonstrate that introducing relative coordinates yields a Hamiltonian structure characterized by two non-commuting constraints. This structure encapsulates all observer perspectives simultaneously, though redundancies initially obscure their operational interpretation. We identify that operationally meaningful descriptions correspond to Darboux coordinates on the constraint surface, with reference frame transformations acting as reparametrizations of this surface. Finally, we construct a quantum perspective-neutral structure that enables the derivation and switching of perspective-dependent descriptions without relying on classical theory. Beyond these physical insights, the study clarifies the relationship between first and second-class constrained systems and their distinct quantization methods.

We introduce a stochastic optimization technique designed to minimize loss functions defined as expected values. This method adaptively adjusts the batch size for gradient approximation and the step size for direction updates, thereby removing the requirement for manual learning rate tuning. By leveraging local curvature data and employing an acute-angle test to guarantee descent directions with high probability, the approach achieves a global linear convergence rate on self-concordant functions. Numerical results indicate that the method effectively selects optimal learning rates and outperforms fine-tuned SGD when training logistic regression models and deep neural networks (DNNs). Additionally, we present an adaptive variant of ADAM that similarly eliminates the need for base learning rate calibration and demonstrates superior performance compared to fine-tuned ADAM on DNN tasks. Our experiments with DNNs revealed that negative curvature along the step direction was rarely observed.

Recent literature has increasingly employed the frameworks and perspectives of quantum information theory to address gravitational issues, sometimes aiming to replace or emulate quantum field theory (QFT), often within the realm of alternative quantum models. This essay identifies three prevalent shortcomings in such approaches. First, we demonstrate that interactions mediated by information channels are not generally equivalent to QFT treatments; when applied to gravity, this conceptualization can result in contradictions with general relativity. Second, we argue that quantum fields cannot simply be substituted with classical stochastic sources, nor can quantum fluctuations be adequately simulated by classical noise, as doing so inevitably omits critical quantum phenomena such as coherence and entanglement. Third, we clarify that under specific conditions, semi-classical and stochastic theories can indeed be derived from their quantum foundations and remain relevant in certain regimes of interest.

This article aims to derive a Markovian approximation for the reduced time dynamics of observables within the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian framework, ensuring precise control over error terms. To achieve this, we introduce a Lindblad operator linked to the associated quantum master equation. In a specific scenario, this approach facilitates the analysis of the transition probability matrix.

As Automated Vehicles (AVs) advance rapidly and the first robotaxi services launch globally, manufacturers must prove to regulatory authorities that their systems are safer than human drivers to achieve mass-deployment certification. This requirement necessitates estimating and modeling the collision rate—or failure rate—of AVs across all potential driving scenarios and error types. Consequently, there is a pressing need for comprehensive Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) models tailored for AVs. This paper presents a generic and scalable model that connects perception system errors to vehicle-level failures (collisions). By utilizing this model, we can determine perception quality requirements based on a target vehicle-level MTBF, or alternatively, calculate an MTBF value given a specific mission profile and perception quality.

Contemporary log file management imposes rigorous regulatory obligations on Internet Service Providers (ISPs) in addition to standard technical challenges. This study examines the intricate relationship between retention policies and timestamping for service providers, noting that this connection can potentially increase operational costs. A novel framework is introduced to reduce reliance on third-party vendors by leveraging cryptographic primitives that are well-established in other IT sectors but remain underutilized in log management. The paper reviews the fundamentals of timestamping and presents cryptographic tools as an effective method to overcome the inefficiencies of legacy schemas while providing enhanced security. These approaches are validated through cost-saving estimates across various ISP scales and supported by essential security considerations.

For every hereditary graph class $\mathcal F$, we develop optimal adjacency labeling schemes for both subgraphs and induced subgraphs derived from Cartesian products of graphs within $\mathcal F$. Consequently, we demonstrate that if $\mathcal F$ supports efficient adjacency labels (or equivalently, small induced-universal graphs) that achieve the information-theoretic lower bound, then the same holds true for the classes of subgraphs and induced subgraphs of Cartesian products of graphs in $\mathcal F$.

This paper introduces "piecewise scalable frames," a novel scaling method that enables the conversion of numerous frames into Parseval frames—a capability unattainable with prior standard scaling techniques. We establish the necessary and sufficient conditions for a frame to be piecewise scalable and demonstrate that this property remains invariant under unitary transformations. Unlike standard scaling, we prove that all frames within $\RR^2$ and $\RR^3$ possess piecewise scalability. Furthermore, we show that frames with vectors that are nearly identical may fail to be piecewise scalable, and we outline several additional properties regarding scaling constants.

Electroosmosis is a captivating phenomenon wherein an applied electric field generates fluid movement. This occurs because counter ions gather near charged surfaces, creating a link between external electric fields and the transport of liquid mass. In nanofluidics, where surface interactions are significantly amplified, electroosmosis becomes a fundamental factor. However, its impact on transport characteristics within both biological and artificial nanopores is complex and nuanced, making a comprehensive understanding difficult but essential for evaluating the underlying mechanisms. This review examines recent advancements in computational methods for analyzing electroosmosis and explores their technological applications, with a specific focus on sensing devices.

We introduce a technique based on contour integration to determine definite integrals and their corresponding infinite sums, which can be represented as special functions. This includes a proof of the fundamental equation alongside illustrative examples. The primary benefit of employing special functions lies in their analytic continuation, which extends the parameter range for which the definite integral formula remains valid. As demonstrations, we apply this method to definite integrals involving logarithmic functions multiplied by trigonometric functions. In several instances, these generalized evaluations result in well-known mathematical constants, including Catalan's constant and $\pi$.

The directed flow's sensitivity to beam energy serves as a crucial probe for the characteristics of strongly interacting matter. Within the relativistic quantum molecular dynamics (RQMD) framework, we investigate various implementations of momentum-dependent hadronic mean fields. Initially, we analyze a Lorentz scalar realization of a Skyrme-type potential, followed by proposing a full Lorentz vector implementation of the same potential. Our findings indicate that the scalar Skyrme force lacks sufficient strength to produce the repulsion required to explain observed sideward flow data at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}<10$ GeV; conversely, the vector implementation yields collective flows consistent with data across a broad energy range of $2.7 <\sqrt{s_{NN}}<20$ GeV. Furthermore, our model successfully reproduces the experimentally observed negative proton directed flow at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}>10$ GeV. We examine the dynamical mechanisms driving directed flow within a standard hadronic mean field context. A positive slope in proton directed flow arises primarily during the compression phase of heavy-ion collisions due to strong repulsive interactions driven by elevated baryon densities. In contrast, during the expansion phase, the tilted expansion and shadowing effects from spectator matter generate a more pronounced negative directed flow. At lower energies ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}<10$ GeV), the positive flow dominates because of an extended compression duration. However, at higher energies ($\sqrt{s_{NN}}>10$ GeV), the negative flow prevails due to a shortened compression time and prolonged expansion time. Consequently, the transition beam energy marking the shift from positive to negative flow is highly sensitive to the interaction strength.

Scientific literature often relies on tables to present critical data concisely. However, extracting both the structure and content from tables embedded in PDF research papers remains a significant challenge due to visual complexities such as spanning cells and content intricacies like mathematical symbols and equations. Most current methods for identifying table structures overlook these specific academic writing characteristics. This paper introduces a transformer-based language modeling approach tailored for scientific table structure and content extraction. Specifically, the proposed model translates tabular images into their corresponding LaTeX source code. In our experiments, we surpassed existing state-of-the-art baselines, achieving exact match accuracies of 70.35% for table structure and 49.69% for content extraction. Further analysis reveals that the proposed models effectively identify the number of rows and columns, alphanumeric characters, LaTeX tokens, and symbols.

This study introduces a systematic framework for modeling and designing controllers for a Commercial-Off-The Shelf (COTS) unmanned rotorcraft, specifically tailored for brick wall construction. Focusing on point-to-point navigation, the system treats commanded velocities along the three UAV axes as inputs and actual velocities as outputs. Leveraging sine and step response data from a Hardware-in-Loop (HiL) simulator, the framework was used to model the system independently for each axis. This model facilitated the design of a sliding mode controller selected to meet application needs such as robustness, flexibility, and precision. Validation using step response data revealed a deviation of merely 9%, while field tests confirmed fine control with an accuracy of up to 8 cm. Additionally, the Sliding Mode Control (SMC) approach was benchmarked against a linear controller developed through iterative experimentation, demonstrating superior performance in accuracy and resilience to parametric variations and wind disturbances.
Building on our earlier calculation of the anomalous magnetic moment, we investigate the proton's electromagnetic form factor by including a non-perturbative term to adjust its $Q^2$ dependence.

Quantum computers are expected to surpass classical supercomputers in handling computationally demanding tasks by leveraging quantum mechanical principles. However, current quantum devices face limitations due to noise and errors, making the implementation of error correction and mitigation techniques essential for the reliable execution of quantum algorithms. This study presents a comparative analysis of three approaches: the [[4,2,2]] quantum error-detecting code (QEC), the duplicate circuit technique, and Bayesian read-out error mitigation (BREM), applied to proof-of-concept implementations of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithm for calculating the ground state energy of an H$_2$ molecule. Experiments conducted on an IBM quantum device reveal that the duplicate circuit method outperforms the QEC method under hardware noise conditions. Additionally, a notable impact of cross-talk noise was observed when multiple mappings of both the duplicate circuit and QEC methods were executed simultaneously, with the duplicate circuit approach again demonstrating superior performance. To further investigate the efficacy of these techniques, quantum simulations were performed on an IBM system with varying levels of depolarizing circuit noise and read-out errors, reinforcing the conclusion that the duplicate circuit offers better error mitigation than QEC. This work provides the first assessment of the duplicate circuit approach for quantum algorithm implementation, offering documented evidence that will facilitate the future scalable application of duplicated circuit techniques for practical, error-mitigated near-term quantum computing.

This work introduces a novel category of non-Markovian processes featuring a countable number of interacting elements, applicable to both discrete and continuous time frameworks. Each element is modeled as a point process that signifies the presence or absence of a spike at specific moments. The system's dynamics are defined such that the probability (in discrete time) or rate (in continuous time) of a spike for any component relies on the complete historical trajectory of the system since that component's last spike. In the discrete-time domain, this framework non-trivially generalizes both the Markovian Spitzer interacting particle systems and Rissanen's stochastic chains with variable-length memory, which possess a finite state space. In continuous time, these models resemble a variable-length memory extension of self-exciting point processes, known as Hawkes processes, but scaled to include infinitely many components. These characteristics render the class particularly suitable for modeling the temporal evolution of spiking neuron networks. This article serves as a critical guide to recent literature on these models across both time domains. It outlines key findings regarding perfect simulation and existence conditions, the de-correlation of successive interspike intervals, the long-term behavior of finite non-excited systems, and chaos propagation within mean field systems.

Given the constraints of limited computational resources, developing lightweight object detectors is crucial, making the generation of redundant features a key factor in minimizing computational costs. This paper introduces a novel Cross-Stage Lightweight (CSL) Convolution module designed to produce redundant features through efficient operations. By substituting Pointwise Convolution with Depthwise Convolution during the intermediate expansion phase, the CSL-Module significantly lowers computational overhead. Experiments on the MS-COCO dataset demonstrate that the proposed module approximates the fitting capability of a 3x3 Convolution. Furthermore, integrating this module into the CSL-YOLO detector yields superior detection performance, achieving only 43% of the FLOPs and 52% of the parameters compared to Tiny-YOLOv4.

Continuum soft robots consist entirely of mechanically deformable components, designed to mimic the mechanics of invertebrates and the soft appendages of vertebrates, such as an elephant's trunk or a monkey's tail. This study introduces a control-theoretic viewpoint to this emerging field of robotics. Our objective is to lower the barriers to entry by synthesizing current findings and future challenges within a coherent framework and a unified terminology. A primary obstacle for newcomers is the significant diversity in scientific backgrounds and inconsistent terminology, which hinders the formation of a comprehensive understanding. Furthermore, it remains difficult to distinguish between limitations caused by immature technology and those intrinsic to the robot class itself. We argue that the latter includes continuum and multi-body dynamics, the influence of non-negligible elastic potential fields, and the variability in sensing and actuation strategies.

We construct a family of six-dimensional block representations of the braid group $B_3$ acting on three strands. We demonstrate that certain representations within this family can detect the invertibility of various known knots, as well as others with 9 and 10 crossings.

Identifying heterogeneous conductivity fields and reconstructing contaminant release histories are critical components of subsurface remediation, yet achieving these objectives with scarce and noisy hydraulic head and concentration data presents significant challenges. These difficulties stem from the complexity of solving inverse problems involving high-dimensional parameters and the substantial computational expenses required for repeated forward modeling. To address this, we employ a convolutional adversarial autoencoder (CAAE) to parameterize the heterogeneous non-Gaussian conductivity field using a compact, low-dimensional latent representation. Furthermore, a three-dimensional dense convolutional encoder-decoder (DenseED) network is trained to act as a forward surrogate for flow and transport processes. By integrating the CAAE with the DenseED surrogate, we utilize the ensemble smoother with multiple data assimilation (ESMDA) algorithm to sample from the Bayesian posterior distribution of the unknown parameters, establishing a CAAE-DenseED-ESMDA inversion framework. This framework was applied to a three-dimensional problem involving the identification of contaminant sources and conductivity fields. A comparison between the CAAE-DenseED-ESMDA results and those from the CAAE-ESMDA approach using a physical flow and transport simulator demonstrates that accurate reconstructions were successfully achieved with significantly improved computational efficiency.

Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) microgels are soft colloidal systems that experience a Volume Phase Transition (VPT) near room temperature. While these materials are extensively utilized for both basic research and practical applications, the structural changes within the microgels during the VPT remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the influence of electrostatic forces. This study investigates, through both experimental and numerical approaches, how incorporating acrylic acid (AAc) as a co-monomer affects the microgel deswelling mechanism. By integrating viscosimetry, light scattering, and electrophoresis, we demonstrate that incrementally adding AAc increases the microgel's mass and inhibits the VPT, thereby shifting the collapse point to higher temperatures. Crucially, this addition significantly amplifies a two-stage deswelling process in these submicron networks, causing the inner core to collapse at temperatures lower than those required for the outer corona's transition. These findings suggest a substantial rise in the charge density difference between the microgel's bulk and its surface. Numerical simulations corroborate this hypothesis and elucidate how charge distribution drives the two-step collapse: mobile counterions effectively screen charges in the inner core while maintaining a higher degree of ionization on the surface. Ultimately, our work clearly demonstrates the pivotal role of electrostatic interactions in governing the behavior of thermosensitive microgels in aqueous environments near their VPT.

The current SPARQL specification lacks clear definitions for correlation and substitution, leading to semantic ambiguities. Consequently, implementations like Fuseki and Virtuoso adopt differing semantic interpretations. This technical report introduces a formal semantics for correlation and substitution grounded in the traditional logical and programming principles found in logic, programming languages, and SQL. We believe this proposal resolves existing ambiguities and issues while establishing a robust formal foundation for future language extensions. This research is part of Daniel Hernandez's ongoing work. These anomalies in the W3C SPARQL 1.1 specification were identified early and reported by 2014, resulting in two registered errata (see https://www.w3.org/2013/sparql-errata#errata-query-8 and https://www.w3.org/2013/sparql-errata#errata-query-10).

We present varbvs, a collection of functions implemented in R and MATLAB designed for performing Bayesian variable selection regression on large-scale datasets. By developing numerical optimization algorithms grounded in variational approximation techniques, we have made it possible to apply Bayesian variable selection to extremely large datasets. Focusing on genome-wide association study examples, we show that varbvs efficiently handles datasets containing hundreds of thousands of variables and thousands of samples, offering features that enable rapid analysis. Additionally, varbvs supports extensive model customization, allowing users to integrate external information into their analyses. We anticipate that the combination of an accessible interface and robust, scalable algorithms for posterior computation will promote wider adoption of Bayesian variable selection in applied statistics and computational biology. The latest source code for R and MATLAB is available on Github (https://github.com/pcarbo/varbvs), and the R package can be installed via CRAN (https://cran.r-project.org/package=varbvs).

In recent years, neural network-based word embeddings have gained significant traction within natural language processing. While prior research has primarily evaluated the quality and utility of embeddings trained on general public corpora like Wikipedia or social media, these studies often overlook the technical and scientific nuances—such as domain-specific terminology, abbreviations, and formulas—essential to academic contexts. This study investigates the performance of word embeddings on a large-scale academic dataset, specifically comparing their quality and efficiency against TF-IDF representations for modeling scientific articles. We utilized a word2vec skip-gram model trained on the titles and abstracts of approximately 70 million scientific papers. Additionally, we established a benchmark to assess content models in a scientific setting, employing a categorization task that aligns articles with journals for roughly 1.3 million publications from 2017. Our findings indicate that while word embedding-based models outperform TF-IDF on titles (short text), TF-IDF is more effective for abstracts (longer text). However, this marginal gain for longer texts requires 3.7 times more memory and up to 184 times more computation time, rendering it potentially inefficient for online applications. Furthermore, we generated a two-dimensional visualization of journals using embeddings to qualitatively analyze the model; this graph offers valuable insights for identifying competitive journals or gaps suitable for new journal proposals.

This study addresses regret minimization within adaptive minimum variance and linear quadratic control frameworks. While existing literature has extensively analyzed the optimal asymptotic regret rates for both domains, this paper offers a novel theoretical and simulation-based investigation. In adaptive minimum variance settings, the optimal asymptotic regret rate of $\log(T)$ is achievable without external excitation. Conversely, adaptive linear quadratic problems typically require external excitation to attain the optimal $\sqrt{T}$ rate. However, we demonstrate that when the control horizon is pre-specified, significantly lower regret can be achieved with either no external excitation or through a new exploration strategy termed "immediate."

The sensor-to-shooter timeline is primarily influenced by two factors: the positioning of satellites and the positioning of assets. Accelerating satellite positioning through increased sensor density or reduced processing time yields significant benefits only when a shooter is already prepared; otherwise, the dominant time constraint is maneuvering the shooter into position. Nevertheless, the intelligence community must strive to maximize both the speed and effectiveness of sensor exploitation. Balancing high effectiveness with rapid response remains a critical trade-off within the sensor-to-shooter framework. This paper examines two core concepts: enhancing the efficacy of satellite imagery via image manipulation and analyzing the impact of on-board processing on the overall timeline. We evaluate these concepts across four scenarios: comparing on-board versus ground station processing through discrete event simulation, assessing information quality after cloud cover removal, evaluating data enhancement via super-resolution, and exploring data reduction through image-to-caption generation. The study demonstrates how techniques such as super-resolution, cloud removal, and image-to-caption not only improve the quality of delivered intelligence but also influence the sensor-to-shooter timeline.

Drawing parallels to successful artificial evolution simulations like Tierra and Avida, this text outlines a method for conducting artificial evolution on a native x86 system. It details the implementation of the artificial chemistry and shares preliminary results from statistical experiments.

Angular dispersion can offset normal group-velocity dispersion (GVD), which extends the wave-vector length within a dispersive medium; by tilting the wave vector, angular dispersion lowers the axial wave number to restore the pre-GVD value. Conversely, angular dispersion cannot counteract anomalous GVD, which shortens the wave-vector length. Consequently, GVD cancellation using angular dispersion has not yet been achieved in the anomalous regime. In this work, we introduce structured femtosecond pulsed beams called "space-time" wave packets. These are engineered to achieve symmetric dispersion cancellation in both normal and anomalous GVD regimes through non-differentiable angular dispersion embedded within the pulsed field. Additionally, we demonstrate GVD inversion, effectively reversing the sign of the GVD experienced by the field relative to the chromatic dispersion of the medium.

We present NetKet 3, the latest iteration of our machine learning toolkit designed for many-body quantum physics. Centered on neural-network quantum states, the platform offers streamlined methods for evaluating and optimizing these states. Built upon JAX, a Python-based framework for differentiable programming and accelerated linear algebra, this update introduces a key capability: defining arbitrary neural network ansätze directly in pure Python using concise machine-learning syntax. This approach enables just-in-time compilation and automatic gradient generation through implicit differentiation. Furthermore, NetKet 3 now supports GPU and TPU accelerators, offers sophisticated handling of discrete symmetry groups, and employs chunking to scale computations to thousands of degrees of freedom. It also includes drivers for quantum dynamics and enhanced modularity, empowering users to leverage specific components as a foundation for custom code.

We apply Hamiltonian reduction to a model coupling 2+1 dimensional gravity with a negative cosmological constant to a cylindrically symmetric dust shell, yielding an action with a finite number of degrees of freedom. The resulting phase space comprises two copies of $ADS^2$, where both momentum and coordinate spaces exhibit curvature. In the Penrose diagram, distinct regions correspond to various patches of the $ADS^2$ momentum space. Quantization in the momentum representation is notably straightforward near the horizon, allowing us to disregard momentum non-commutativity in this vicinity. Using this approximation, we compute the spectrum of the shell radius, which is continuous outside the horizon but becomes discrete inside it, with eigenvalue spacing proportional to the square root of the black hole mass. Furthermore, we numerically evaluate quantum transition amplitudes between different Penrose diagram regions near the horizon. These results indicate a potential for the shell to quantum tunnel into classically forbidden areas, albeit with an exponentially suppressed rate as one moves away from the horizon.

Let $G$ be a graph, and let $g$, $f$, and $f'$ be three positive integer-valued functions defined on $V(G)$ such that $g \le f$. Tokuda, Xu, and Wang (2003) demonstrated that if $G$ possesses a $(g,f)$-factor and a spanning $f'$-tree, it must also contain a connected $(g,f+f'-1)$-factor. In this note, we extend their finding to a tree-connected context by proving that if $G$ contains a $(g,f)$-factor and an $m$-tree-connected $(m,f')$-factor, then $G$ also contains an $m$-tree-connected $(g,f+f'-m)$-factor, assuming $f \ge m$. Furthermore, we establish that $g$ may be nonnegative.

**Context.** Asteroid families serve as records of the violent collisional history within the asteroid belt. Investigating the physical characteristics of family members offers crucial insights into the differentiation state of their parent bodies and their formation processes. Many families in the main belt are dominated by low-albedo, primitive asteroids, which are vital for understanding Solar System formation due to their minimal thermophysical processing and their ability to reveal early planetary conditions.

**Aims.** This study examines the diversity of physical properties across the Themis, Hygiea, Ursula, Veritas, and Lixiaohua families.

**Methods.** We integrate new spectroscopic data with a comprehensive analysis of existing literature, including albedo and rotational data.

**Results.** Our findings indicate that the Themis and Hygiea families, the largest in the region, exhibit comparable levels of hydration. In contrast, the Ursula and Lixiaohua families appear redder than the others and show no evidence of hydrated members in visible spectra. Conversely, the Veritas family contains the highest proportion of hydrated members.

**Conclusions.** This research highlights a diverse range of physical properties among primitive outer-belt families, a scenario potentially linked to the dynamical mixing of asteroid populations and the degree of differentiation of their parent bodies.

This study focuses on developing supervised models for event trigger identification that exhibit improved generalization across different domains. We employ the adversarial domain adaptation (ADA) framework to ensure domain invariance. By utilizing adversarial training, ADA creates representations that effectively identify triggers while remaining uninformative regarding the specific domain of the input data. Since this approach requires no labeled data from the target domain, it operates entirely in an unsupervised manner. Experiments conducted across two domains—English literature and news—demonstrate that ADA yields an average F1 score increase of 3.9 on out-of-domain datasets. Our top-performing model (BERT-A) achieves F1 scores between 44 and 49 across both domains without relying on any labeled target data. Additionally, preliminary results indicate that a strategy combining fine-tuning on 1% labeled data with self-training significantly boosts performance, resulting in F1 scores of 51.5 for literature and 67.2 for news.

Methanol, a fundamental complex organic molecule in the Interstellar Medium (ISM), exists in cold regions like starless cores. This study aims to analyze methanol emission across multiple starless cores to determine the physical conditions necessary for its efficient formation and to understand how the cores' internal structures and external environments influence its spatial distribution. Using the IRAM 30m telescope as part of the GEMS program, we observed methanol and C$^{18}$O emission lines at 3 mm toward 66 positions within 12 starless cores in the Taurus Molecular Cloud. Non-LTE radiative transfer modeling was employed to calculate column densities, followed by the application of advanced chemical models to simulate the observations. We computed N(CH$_3$OH)/N(C$^{18}$O) column density ratios for all offsets, identifying two distinct behaviors: in some cores, the ratio peaks at the dust peak, while in others, it peaks slightly offset by approximately 10,000 AU. We attribute this discrepancy to irradiation from nearby protostars, which drives energetic particles along their outflows. Although chemical models that ignore irradiation variations successfully reproduce the overall methanol column densities, they fail to match the observed radial profiles. These findings confirm the significant impact of the environment on methanol distribution in starless cores. We propose that the clumpy medium created by protostellar outflows enhances the penetration of the interstellar radiation field into molecular clouds, thereby affecting methanol distribution.

We investigate quasilinear wave equations in $(1+3)$ dimensions where the nonlinearity $F(u,u',u")$ may depend on the solution itself, not solely on its derivatives. For scalar cases, Lindblad proved almost global existence under the condition that $(\partial_u^2 F)(0,0,0)=0$. Our goal is to establish a corresponding almost global existence result for coupled systems of these equations. To achieve this, we utilize a modified version of the $r^p$-weighted local energy estimate developed by Dafermos and Rodnianski, incorporating a ghost weight similar to those employed by Alinhac. The necessary decay to close the argument is derived from space-time Klainerman-Sobolev type estimates found in the work of Metcalfe, Tataru, and Tohaneanu.

For any integer $k\ge 2$, consider the $k$-generalized Fibonacci sequence $\{F^{(k)}_{n}\}_{n\ge 2-k}$, defined by starting with $0, \ldots, 0, 1$ (a total of $k$ terms) and generating subsequent terms as the sum of the preceding $k$ terms. This paper identifies all integers $c$ that possess at least two distinct representations as the difference between a $k$-generalized Fibonacci number and a power of $3$. Building upon prior research by the first author concerning standard Fibonacci and Tribonacci numbers, this work extends those findings to the $k$-generalized case.

P/2016 BA$_{14}$ (PanSTARRS), a slow-rotating, nearly dormant comet and probable dynamical counterpart to 252P/LINEAR, exhibits a mid-infrared spectrum distinct from typical comets. Recently selected as a backup target for ESA's \textit{Comet Interceptor}, BA$_{14}$ offers a unique opportunity to refine our knowledge of dormancy mechanisms and support future mission planning. This study presents observations from the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility during BA$_{14}$'s 2016 close approach to Earth, both of which appear to directly sample the nucleus. Although BA$_{14}$'s reflectance spectrum resembles that of 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, it is significantly phase-reddened. We address thermal emission contamination at longer wavelengths using a newly developed Markov Chain Monte Carlo thermal modeling code. Our models indicate a visible geometric albedo of $p_V=0.01-0.03$, aligning with radar data; a beaming parameter typical for Near-Earth Objects in this geometry; and a red, linear reflectance spectrum across the H and K bands. Despite its unusual mid-infrared characteristics, the nucleus appears fundamentally "normal." We propose that the gradual loss of fine grains as activity waned may help explain the conflicting evidence and explore alternative hypotheses. Furthermore, a flyby of this nearly dormant comet could achieve closer proximity to the nucleus than a mission to an active one, prompting a discussion of scientific questions such a visit could address.

This primarily expository article generalizes key properties of the homological duality functor $RHom_{\mathcal H}(-,{\mathcal H})$, originally defined for the Hecke algebra of a reductive $p$-adic group, to the setting of a finite central extension of such a group. Central to this work are the findings that $RHom_{\mathcal H}(-,{\mathcal H})$ operates within a single degree for irreducible representations and induces Schneider--Stuhler duality for Ext groups, a property akin to a Serre functor. Additionally, the paper investigates Grothendieck--Serre duality relative to the Bernstein center and establishes a proof of the well-known result stating that on admissible modules, this functor coincides with contragredient duality. We also identify a necessary and sufficient condition for these three dualities to coincide on finite length modules within a specific block. Notably, we demonstrate that this agreement holds for all cuspidal blocks and, based on Roche's findings, for all blocks possessing a trivial stabilizer in the relative Weyl group.

Optimizing transformer design parameters is essential for enhancing efficiency and reducing material expenses. This study introduces a method for modeling a three-phase transformer and optimizing its design to minimize both volume and losses. Using ANSYS Maxwell 2D, the transformer was modeled and analyzed across various design parameters. A multi-objective differential evolution algorithm was employed to identify the optimal parameters that achieve the lowest volume and loss. Specifically, this paper details the optimal design for a 1 kVA transformer with defined input and output voltage requirements. The resulting transformer was tested under different loading conditions and power factor values. Results indicate that peak efficiency occurs at a 75% load with a unity power factor, while efficiency declines as the power factor drops.

We present the inaugural detection of the 3-cyano propargyl radical (CH2C3N) in interstellar space, observed within the cold dark cloud TMC-1 via the Yebes 40m telescope. Seven rotational transitions corresponding to both ortho- and para-CH2C3N species were identified across the 31.0-50.4 GHz frequency band. Our analysis yields a total column density of (1.6 +/- 0.4)e11 cm-2 and an ortho/para ratio of 2.4 +/- 1.2, suggesting an abundance ratio of CH2C3N/CH3C3N near 0.1. This figure stands in stark contrast to smaller analogues, where the CH2CN/CH3CN ratio is 3, indicating that the chemical behavior of the cyanides CH2C3N and CH3C3N differs significantly from that of CH2CN and CH3CN. Based on our chemical modeling, the primary formation pathways for CH2C3N involve neutral-neutral reactions among C + CH2CHCN, C2 + CH3CN, and CN + CH2CCH, alongside the dissociative recombination of CH3C3NH+ with electrons. While the reaction N + C4H3 could potentially produce CH2C3N, its contribution remains highly uncertain. The presence of this radical may facilitate the synthesis of larger nitrogen-bearing organic molecules, including benzonitrile (c-C6H5CN) and nitrogen heterocycles.

Social media has fundamentally altered the ways users consume and process information, consequently reshaping the trajectory of topic popularity. This study investigates the relationship between the viral spread of contentious subjects, the incitement of intense debates, and the subsequent escalation of user polarization. Through a quantitative analysis of approximately 57 million posts from around 2 million Facebook pages and groups spanning 2018 to 2022, we examined high-engagement themes related to scandals, tragedies, and socio-political matters. By applying logistic functions, we quantified the development of these topics and identified consistent patterns in their engagement dynamics. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the initial burstiness of a topic can forecast future negative user reactions, irrespective of the specific subject matter.

Functional data clustering aims to uncover heterogeneous morphological patterns within the continuous functions that underlie discrete observations. This technique has been widely applied across numerous scientific disciplines, including biology, chemistry, engineering, environmental and medical sciences, psychology, and social sciences. The rapid expansion of its applications highlights an urgent requirement for systematic development of efficient clustering methods and scalable algorithmic implementations. Concurrently, extensive literature exists on clustering time series, trajectories, and spatio-temporal data, all of which are related to functional data; thus, an overarching framework for current functional data clustering methods would facilitate the cross-pollination of ideas across research fields. This paper presents a comprehensive review of original clustering methods for functional data, proposing a systematic taxonomy that examines the connections and distinctions among existing approaches and relates them to conventional multivariate clustering. Built upon three primary attributes of functional data clustering methods, this taxonomy offers greater reliability than previous categorizations. Ultimately, the review seeks to bridge the divide between the functional data analysis and clustering communities while generating new principles for functional data clustering.

We examine the disordered monomer-dimer model on cylinder graphs $\mathcal{G}_n$, constructed as the Cartesian product of a line graph with $n$ vertices and a deterministic graph. These graphs feature independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random weights assigned to both edges and vertices, which may follow different distributions. Based on these weights, a Gibbs measure is defined over the space of monomer-dimer configurations on $\mathcal{G}_n$. We demonstrate that the corresponding free energy converges to a limit and, under appropriate scaling and centering, obeys a central limit theorem. Furthermore, we establish that the count of monomers in a typical configuration satisfies both a law of large numbers and a central limit theorem with suitable adjustments. Finally, regarding a specific height function linked to a matching, we prove convergence to a limiting function and show that, in terms of finite-dimensional distributions, this function exhibits a Brownian motion limit.

Covariant quantization of both QED and QCD necessitates the inclusion of subsidiary gauge-fixing fields and ghost fields, making it essential to comprehend their impact on the energy-momentum tensor as well as the momentum and angular momentum operators. While these matters were examined in \cite{Leader:2011za} and foundational findings from that work informed the comprehensive review of angular momentum presented in \cite{Leader:2013jra}, Damski \cite{Damski:2021feu} has appropriately challenged the correctness of specific equation derivations found in \cite{Leader:2011za}. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the primary results from \cite{Leader:2011za}, which underpin the analysis in \cite{Leader:2013jra}, remain valid despite Damski's objections.

To handle a wide variety of foods, robotic feeding systems must overcome limitations in prior single-arm approaches, such as spoon scooping or fork skewering, which fail with complex or deformable items. For instance, skewering peas can crush them, while open scooping may cause them to scatter. To address this, we introduce a method that uses a second arm to stabilize food during scooping, such as pressing peas against a spoon to prevent dispersion. However, adding this stabilizing arm presents new challenges: it must secure the food without obstructing the scooping motion, a critical constraint for fragile items like tofu that might break between the pusher and spoon, leading to waste. We propose a general bimanual scooping primitive paired with an adaptive stabilization strategy capable of acquiring diverse food geometries and physical properties. Our approach, CARBS (Coordinated Acquisition with Reactive Bimanual Scooping), employs closed-loop visual feedback to identify high-risk foods and stabilize them without hindering task progress. CARBS demonstrates generalization across food shape, size, and deformability, including the ability to manipulate multiple items simultaneously. It achieves an 87.0% success rate on rigid foods, representing a 25.8% improvement over single-arm baselines and a 16.2% reduction in food breakage compared to analytical baselines. Videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/bimanualscoop-corl22/home.

This work examines how different path-wise reflection-at-the-barrier scenarios influence the confining behavior of a standard class of symmetric $\alpha$-stable L\'{e}vy processes, which are kept within a finite interval via two-sided reflection. Depending on the specific reflection mechanism, the resulting jump-type processes exhibit distinct spectral and statistical features, such as relaxation dynamics and the functional forms of their invariant (equilibrium or near-equilibrium) probability density functions. The analysis is performed alongside efforts to define a reflecting L\'{e}vy process by identifying the domain of its motion generator, within which the invariant probability density function (specifically an eigenfunction) resides.

This research investigates the characterization and realization of higher-order topological Anderson insulators (HOTAI) within non-Hermitian systems, where non-Hermitian mechanisms introduce additional symmetries alongside gain and loss disorder. We demonstrate that the quadrupole moment $Q_{xy}$ serves as a real-space topological invariant for non-Hermitian higher-order topological insulators (HOTI). Utilizing biorthogonal bases and non-Hermitian symmetries, we establish that $Q_{xy}$ is quantized to either 0 or 0.5. Examining disorder effects, we identify a disorder-induced phase transition from a normal insulator to a non-Hermitian HOTAI. Moreover, we show that the real-space invariant $Q_{xy}$ remains applicable even in systems exhibiting the non-Hermitian skin effect. This work advances the understanding of the interplay between disorder and non-Hermitian HOTI.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach for spatial homogeneity pursuit tailored to survival data within the proportional hazards framework, aimed at identifying spatial clusters in both baseline hazards and regression coefficients. Specifically, the method assumes that these coefficients and hazards exhibit spatial homogeneity across the study area. To model this structure, we formulate a geographically weighted Chinese restaurant process prior that facilitates the simultaneous estimation of coefficients, baseline hazards, and their associated uncertainties. An efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm is developed to implement this methodology. The proposed approach is validated through simulated datasets and subsequently applied to an empirical analysis of respiratory cancer incidence in Louisiana.

Projections reveal data regarding the dimension, geometric configuration, and size of sets. This can be investigated by examining the energies of measures supported on a set and the energies of their corresponding pushforward measures under projection. For orthogonal projections, quantitative assessments depend on a separation condition, where most points are distinguished by most projections. It appears this concept extends to a wide range of nonlinear projection-type operators that satisfy a \textit{transversality condition}. In this study, we demonstrate that several significant classes of nonlinear projections are indeed transversal. Consequently, we derive quantitative lower bounds on the decay rates for nonlinear versions of Favard length, encompassing the standard Favard curve length, a novel higher-dimensional extension termed Favard surface length, and visibility metrics linked to radial projections. As an application, we offer a streamlined proof of the decay rate for the Favard curve length of the four corner Cantor set's generations, a result originally proven by Cladek, Davey, and Taylor.

Safety filters offer modular methods to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs—such as those from learning-based algorithms or human operators—by ensuring safety through constraint satisfaction. This paper introduces an enhanced model predictive safety filter (MPSF) that integrates system-level synthesis (SLS) techniques.
