Unexpectedly, a statistically significant influence of particle size was observed only in silica nanofluids, where smaller particles facilitate faster heat transfer. However, substantial variability in the experimental data hinders a definitive assessment of these effects. Collectively, the results underscore the need for more comprehensive experimental characterization of nanofluids to accurately evaluate their practical potential.

We introduce a novel collision-free path planning approach using conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) by restricting their latent space to exclusively represent non-collision regions within the robot's joint configuration space. This method generates such a collision-free latent space, enabling any planner to utilize arbitrary optimization criteria for generating optimal paths in real time. The efficacy of this approach was validated through simulations involving a two-link robotic arm.

The rapid advancement of Machine Learning (ML) has spurred the creation of numerous intelligent applications, with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) achieving remarkable success in domains like autonomous driving and medical diagnostics. Despite their widespread use in security-critical areas, DNNs are susceptible to Neural Trojan (NT) attacks, which rely on stealthy triggers for activation and control. This paper proposes a robust, adaptive detection scheme designed to verify whether a pre-trained model has been compromised prior to deployment. Unlike previous methods that ignore the inherent properties of trigger distributions and rely on simple heuristics—such as provoking incorrect outputs to reconstruct patterns—our approach is limited by detection speed and efficacy. Instead, we exploit the spatial dependency characteristic of pixel-based triggers to introduce the first black-box Trojan detection framework based on trigger approximation. This enables a rapid, scalable search for triggers within the input space. Additionally, our method can identify Trojans embedded in the feature space, even when filter transformations are used for activation. Extensive experiments across various datasets and ML models demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, achieving a ROC-AUC score of 0.93 on the public TrojAI dataset. The source code is available at https://github.com/xinqiaozhang/adatrojan.

This paper introduces a novel nonlinear mathematical framework for surface gravity waves in deep water, featuring an analytical approach to classical fluid dynamics equations that operates under less restrictive assumptions than current theories. Notably, this new theory guarantees solution uniqueness without requiring the traditional radiation condition, ensuring the liquid remains stationary at infinity and that energy input from disturbance sources remains finite at all times. Unlike conventional methods relying on spatially infinite harmonic waves, this approach addresses the problem's non-linearity to provide solutions valid from the initial moment to infinity. Furthermore, the author identifies previously unrecognized patterns in wave evolution and validates these findings against experimental data from other researchers.

Driven by the accumulation of big data and advancements in deep learning, research into predicting human emotions in natural settings has gained momentum. We developed a multi-task model utilizing the ABAW dataset to simultaneously predict valence-arousal, facial expressions, and action units based on audio and visual inputs from real-world scenarios. To address incomplete labeling, we employed knowledge distillation, training a student model using soft labels generated by a teacher model trained via supervised learning. This approach yielded a score of 2.40 on the Multi-Task Learning validation dataset.

We introduce an algorithm and implementation for periodic Hartree-Fock (HF) and second-order M{\o}ller-Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) utilizing integral-direct and density-fitted methods. This new code removes previously prohibitive storage constraints, enabling the investigation of systems approximately one order of magnitude larger than previously possible at the periodic MP2 level. We validate this advancement by analyzing the benzene crystal under both thermodynamic and complete basis set limits, predicting an MP2 cohesive energy of $-72.8$ kJ/mol. This value exceeds the magnitude of all prior reported MP2 calculations by about $10$--$15$ kJ/mol. Furthermore, several modified MP2 models approach chemical accuracy relative to the best theoretical literature estimates for the benzene crystal's cohesive energy, suggesting they are promising, cost-effective options for future studies on molecular crystals.

The PageRank algorithm remains a cornerstone in the evolution of the Internet, with its network-theoretic characteristics continuing to attract research. This work introduces findings on the parametric controllability of its centralities and establishes a geometric approach to evaluate the control of its rankings. We apply these techniques to the biplex PageRank scenario, contrasting the two centrality measures through numerical analysis on both real-world and synthetic network datasets.

A highly pixelated sensor was fabricated using a 0.35{\mu}m CMOS industrial standard, designed to directly collect charge through top-mounted metal nodes and generate two-dimensional images of charge cloud distributions. The initial prototype, designated Topmetal-I, incorporates a 64x64 pixel array with an 80{\mu}m pitch. Direct charge calibration indicates an average pixel capacitance of 210fF, while charge collection noise approaches the thermal noise limit. During readout, individual pixel channels demonstrate a most probable equivalent noise charge of 330e-.

Liouville theory characterizes the behavior of surfaces with constant negative curvature, offering a framework to investigate the Weil-Petersson geometry of the moduli space of Riemann surfaces. This approach enables an efficient algorithm for calculating the Weil-Petersson metric with arbitrary precision by utilizing Zamolodchikov's recursion relation for conformal blocks. For instance, we determine the metric on $\mathcal{M}_{0,4}$ with high numerical accuracy by analyzing Liouville theory on a four-punctured sphere. Furthermore, we compute the eigenvalues of the Weil-Petersson Laplacian numerically and observe evidence that they follow the statistical distribution of the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble, characteristic of random matrices.

Galaxy clusters often exhibit a distinct multi-phase structure within their hot intracluster medium (ICM) near the brightest cluster galaxy. While the formation of this central nebula is well-studied, its ultimate fate—specifically after the initial filamentary network fragments into discrete cold clumps—remains less explored. This study utilizes 30 magneto-hydrodynamical simulations of kiloparsec-scale cold clouds, employing parameters consistent with cluster observations, to determine if these clouds eventually mix back into the hot ICM or remain stable. The research examines the impacts of radiative cooling, small-scale heating, magnetic fields, and anisotropic thermal conduction on cloud longevity. Results indicate that filament fragments cool faster than the crushing timescale, lose pressure equilibrium, and shatter into smaller clumplets. These fragments serve as nucleation sites for further condensation and facilitate mixing through Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, effectively doubling the cold gas mass within 75 million years. Cloud expansion relies on density and local heating mechanisms, dictating whether evolution is driven by ablation or shattering. Although magnetic fields delay cloud growth, they do not stop it, and both cold and warm phases remain sensitive to field topology. Surprisingly, anisotropic thermal conduction accelerates cold gas growth compared to non-conductive scenarios, also increasing the warm phase volume. Consequently, dense clumps exceeding 500 pc in scale are significant factors in the long-term cooling flow evolution of galaxy clusters and cannot be disregarded.

In their recent work, Min Ru and Paul Vojta demonstrated the arithmetic component of the so-called general theorem, which serves as an extension of Schmidt's subspace theorem. This note expands upon their findings by substituting divisors with closed subschemes.

This study applies both single- and segregated-network Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to forecast momentum, species, and temperature distributions within a dry air humidification scenario in a simple 2D rectangular domain. The developed PINN models incorporate variable fluid properties alongside species and heat diffusion and convection. Various hyperparameter configurations, including network width and depth, were tested to identify the optimal setup. Results indicate that the segregated-network architecture achieves an average 62% reduction in loss compared to the single-network approach for this specific problem. Additionally, while the single-network variant failed to maintain species mass conservation across various regions of the domain, the segregated method successfully preserved it. Predicted velocity, temperature, and species profiles were benchmarked against OpenFOAM software results under identical boundary conditions. Both PINN architectures yielded accurate temperature and velocity predictions, with average percentage differences relative to CFD data of roughly 7.5% for velocity and 8% for temperature. However, the mean error percentages for species mass fractions were 9% for the single-network model and 1.5% for the segregated-network approach. To demonstrate the utility of PINNs as surrogate models for multi-species problems, a parameterized version of the segregated-network PINN was trained to generate results for varying water vapour inlet velocities. Across three predicted cases, the normalized mean absolute percentage errors relative to OpenFOAM results were approximately 7.5% for velocity and 2.4% for water vapour mass fraction.

**Context.** The Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf galaxy is currently merging with the Milky Way, making the investigation of its globular clusters (GCs) essential for understanding this ongoing interaction's history and results. **Aims.** Our primary objective is to characterize the GC system of the Sgr dwarf galaxy. However, this effort is complicated by significant foreground contamination, primarily from stars in the Galactic bulge. **Methods.** We conducted a targeted GC search to identify new members within the main body of the dwarf galaxy by combining near-infrared data from the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea Extended Survey (VVVX) with optical data from the Gaia Early Data Release 3 (EDR3). **Results.** By applying proper motion cuts to filter out foreground bulge and disk stars, we identified several GC candidates within the main body of the Sgr dwarf galaxy. We selected the most promising candidates based on significant overdensities above the Sgr galaxy's stellar background and color-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) displaying well-defined red giant branches (RGBs) that align with the galaxy's distance and reddening. **Conclusions.** We have discovered eight new GC members of the Sgr galaxy, bringing the total known count to 29. This total indicates that the Sgr dwarf galaxy possesses a relatively rich GC system. Furthermore, most of the newly identified GCs are predominantly metal-rich and exhibit low luminosity. Additionally, we have identified ten other GC candidates that remain uncertain and require further data for confirmation.

We build new complete Calabi-Yau metrics on the complement of an anticanonical divisor $D$ within a Fano manifold of dimension three or higher, provided that $D$ is formed by two transversely intersecting smooth divisors. The resulting asymptotic geometry is described by a generalization of the Calabi ansatz, which is connected to the non-archimedean Monge-Ampère equation.

Generative adversarial networks currently represent the leading method for creating synthetic images through learning. While early achievements were primarily unsupervised, the field has gradually shifted toward techniques utilizing labeled data. These supervised approaches provide superior control over generated images, enhancing both flexibility and stability. However, their primary limitation is the reliance on annotated datasets. This work presents a novel framework that combines adversarial training and representation learning to advance unsupervised conditional GANs. Specifically, our method leverages the latent space structure learned via representation learning to condition the generative model. By doing so, we decouple the traditional link between conditions and labels, replacing the latter with unsupervised latent features. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this technique can generate on-demand samples while maintaining the quality comparable to supervised counterparts.

Quantum spin systems exhibiting topological order have gained significant attention due to their potential for fault-tolerant quantum computation, with Kitaev's toric code serving as a fundamental example. Naaijkens established a mathematically rigorous framework for the toric code on an infinite planar lattice (the thermodynamic limit) through an operator algebraic approach grounded in algebraic quantum field theory. By adapting his methodology, we investigate the toric code featuring gapped boundaries. Specifically, we validate the condensation results outlined by Kitaev and Kong and demonstrate that the boundary theory functions as a module tensor category over the bulk, consistent with theoretical expectations.

Real neurons function as highly intricate computational entities, tasked with converting electrochemical inputs into action potentials, adjusting synaptic weights, managing internal states, and influencing neighboring cells. In fact, one might contend that these biological cells alone display genuine intelligence. It is therefore peculiar that the machine learning field has long operated under the premise that such complexity can be distilled into a mere "sum and fire" mechanism. We propose that enhancing the computational capacity of individual neurons in artificial systems could yield significant benefits. To explore this, we introduce Deep Artificial Neurons (DANs), which are implemented as deep neural networks themselves. Conceptually, DANs are embedded within each node of a conventional neural network, with connections established at multiple synaptic points to vectorize inter-cellular links. We show that a single shared parameter vector, termed a "neuronal phenotype," can be meta-learned to facilitate a specific meta-objective during deployment. Focusing on continual learning as this objective, we demonstrate that an appropriate neuronal phenotype grants a network an innate capacity to update synapses with minimal forgetting. This is achieved using standard backpropagation, without the need for experience replay or distinct wake/sleep phases, and is validated on sequential non-linear regression tasks.

This study introduces the inaugural backdoor attack designed for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Specifically, we present a \emph{subgraph-based backdoor attack} tailored for graph classification tasks. The proposed mechanism ensures that a GNN classifier outputs a target label selected by the attacker whenever a specific subgraph is injected into the input graph. Experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our attack is highly effective while causing minimal degradation to the model's accuracy on clean graphs. Furthermore, we adapt a randomized smoothing-based certified defense to mitigate this threat. Our findings indicate that while this defense works in certain scenarios, it fails in others, underscoring the urgent need for novel defense strategies against such backdoor attacks.

Research into $C\!P$ violation in the decays of beauty- and charm-hadrons serves as a crucial test of Standard Model (SM) predictions and offers a sensitive means to detect phenomena beyond the SM. These proceedings present precision measurements of various observables linked to unitary triangles, which stem from the unitarity constraints on the 3x3 Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix governing quark mixing. Additionally, recent findings on $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadrons are detailed, including an analysis that yields the first evidence of $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and the world's most precise measurement in the charm sector. These analyses rely on proton-proton collision data from 2011 and 2012 (LHC Run 1) gathered by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

Numerous single-field inflationary models align well with recent Planck 2018 observations regarding the spectral index ($n_s$) and tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$). However, despite this observational consistency, certain models contain unregularized potentials that could cause the universe to collapse immediately following inflation. This paper demonstrates that the method used to correct the potential's behavior near the end of inflation significantly alters the model's inflationary predictions, particularly for quartic hilltop and radiatively corrected Higgs inflation scenarios.

Adversarial examples are a significant concern because they undermine the reliability of modern machine learning systems. While effective adversarial examples are typically generated through white-box attacks, they can sometimes be transferred to black-box models, thereby expanding their reach. This study evaluates the transferability of three specific attacks—the Fast Gradient Sign Method, the Basic Iterative Method, and the Carlini & Wagner method—across two model categories: the VGG family (including VGG16, VGG19, and an ensemble of both) and the Inception family (comprising Inception V3, Xception, Inception Resnet V2, and an ensemble of these). Furthermore, the paper identifies flaws in current transferability assessments and proposes solutions by selecting robust attack parameters, employing L-Infinity clipping, and utilizing the SSIM metric to more accurately evaluate attack transferability.

This paper presents a computationally efficient variation of the model-based ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF). The approach incorporates two key modifications: first, the framework is reformulated using precision matrices rather than covariance matrices, accompanied by a novel prior that enforces sparsity on the precision matrix. Second, the state vector is partitioned into multiple blocks, with an approximate updating scheme developed for each block. A simulation study evaluates the resulting gains in computational speed and approximation error. The results demonstrate a significant speedup for high-dimensional state vectors, enabling the application of this filter to much larger problems than the original formulation permits. Furthermore, the simulation indicates that the approximation error introduced by the block updating method is negligible when compared to the Monte Carlo variability present in both the original and proposed procedures.
We provide a concise overview of some of the most striking results achieved by James Maynard, for which he received the Fields Medal.

To tackle the challenges of exploding input and hidden-layer sizes in multi-channel speech enhancement, we introduce a tensor-to-vector regression method. This approach reformulates the traditional deep neural network (DNN) vector-to-vector regression within a tensor-train network (TTN) framework. As a recently developed technique for compactly representing deep models with fully connected layers, TTN retains the expressive capabilities of DNNs while significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters. Moreover, TTN is inherently designed to process multi-dimensional tensor inputs, aligning perfectly with the requirements of multi-channel speech enhancement. We first present a theoretical extension of regression from DNNs to TTNs. Subsequently, we demonstrate that TTN achieves speech enhancement quality comparable to DNNs but with far fewer parameters; for instance, in a single-channel scenario, parameters drop from 27 million to just 5 million. Additionally, TTN improves PESQ scores from 2.86 to 2.96 with a slight increase in parameters. In an 8-channel setting, TTN achieves a PESQ of 3.12 using only 20 million parameters, outperforming a DNN that requires 68 million parameters to reach a PESQ of 3.06. Our implementation is accessible online at https://github.com/uwjunqi/Tensor-Train-Neural-Network.

We demonstrate an application of a subdiffusion equation featuring a Caputo fractional time derivative relative to a function $g$, designed to model subdiffusion within a medium whose structure evolves over time. This framework allows for a continuous transition between subdiffusion and other diffusion types. The process can be viewed as "ordinary" subdiffusion with a constant subdiffusion exponent $\alpha$, where the function $g$ modifies the time scale. Specifically, we examine the shift from "ordinary" subdiffusion to ultraslow diffusion. The function $g$ introduces an additional aging mechanism layered upon the "standard" aging inherent to "ordinary" subdiffusion. We analyze this aging process using the coefficient of relative aging of $g$--subdiffusion compared to "ordinary" subdiffusion and also outline the method for solving the $g$-subdiffusion equation.

Meta Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to automate the creation of RL algorithms capable of generalizing across diverse environments. The framework described in (Anonymous, 2020) tackles this by modeling RL algorithms as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and employing an evolutionary meta-learner to optimize these structures for effective agent update rules. Although the search language in the original paper can represent many established algorithms like DQN and DDQN, it struggles to capture Policy Gradient methods. This work bridges that gap by expanding the search language and introducing DAG representations for five distinct Policy Gradient algorithms: VPG, PPO, DDPG, TD3, and SAC.

In pro-drop languages like Chinese, pronouns are often omitted, which typically creates substantial difficulties for generating complete translations. To date, the issue of dropped pronouns (DPs) has received minimal attention within neural machine translation (NMT). This study introduces a novel reconstruction-based method to mitigate DP translation challenges in NMT. Initially, DPs in every source sentence are automatically annotated using parallel information derived from the bilingual training corpus. Subsequently, these annotated source sentences are reconstructed from the NMT model's hidden representations. Through auxiliary training objectives based on reconstruction scores, the NMT model's parameters are guided to generate enhanced hidden representations that effectively embed the annotated DP information. Experimental results on Chinese-English and Japanese-English dialogue translation tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly and consistently outperforms a robust NMT baseline built directly on DPs-annotated training data.

We introduce Vakyansh, an end-to-end toolkit designed for Speech Recognition across Indic languages. Despite India hosting nearly 121 languages and approximately 1.25 billion speakers, the majority remain under-resourced regarding data and pretrained models. Vakyansh addresses this by providing automated pipelines for data generation, model training, evaluation, and deployment. We have synthesized 14,000 hours of speech data covering 23 Indic languages and trained wav2vec 2.0-based pretrained models. These models are subsequently fine-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art speech recognition performance for 18 Indic languages, complemented by language models and punctuation restoration modules. All resources are open-sourced with the goal of inspiring the speech community to build speech-first applications utilizing these Indic ASR models.

US financial institutions managing over $100 million in assets are required to quarterly report their long positions via the SEC Form 13F-HR. By analyzing fluctuations in holdings across consecutive reporting periods, we calculate the disparity between buying and selling activities for specific assets. A notable profit opportunity exists if an outside investor executes trades that are contrarian to these 13F imbalances. These imbalances reflect the information already incorporated into the market, with associated trades often exacerbated by herding and crowding. Consequently, a profitable strategy involves betting against the direction of these imbalances over a short-term horizon, specifically 21 to 42 trading days (approximately one to two calendar months) following the end of each quarter.

Recently, non-reversible samplers based on simulating piecewise deterministic Markov processes (PDMPs) have demonstrated promise for efficient Bayesian inference. However, guidance on optimal implementation remains scarce; poor execution can cause the computational burden of simulating event times to exceed the statistical benefits of non-reversible dynamics. Drawing from adaptive rejection methods, we introduce the concave-convex adaptive thinning approach (CC-PDMP) for PDMP simulation. This method offers a general framework for constructing bounds to enhance PDMP-based sampling. A primary advantage lies in its additive structure: combining concave-convex decompositions results in a new concave-convex decomposition, which enables flexible prior swapping, straightforward implementation, and computationally efficient thinning. Specifically, the approach is highly effective for local PDMP simulation, leveraging known conditional independence in the target distribution to achieve significant computational gains. We provide an R package implementing CC-PDMP and demonstrate that it surpasses existing event simulation methods in the PDMP literature.

We present a $p_{z}-d$ coupling model Hamiltonian for the $\pi$-graphene/Au bands, which predicts a significantly large intrinsic spin-orbit (SO) coupling consistent with recent experimental and DFT findings. Utilizing the analytical Slater-Koster tight-binding approach, we identified the key overlapping orbitals responsible for enhancing SO coupling in both sublattice symmetric (BC) and ATOP (AC) stacking configurations. Our effective Hamiltonian accurately reproduces the experimental spectra for these two registries and demonstrates that the hollow site configuration (BC), where A/B sites remain symmetric, produces the greater increase in SO coupling. Furthermore, by investigating the Au-diluted case within the BC configuration, we found that it preserves the SO gap with an interaction enhancement similar to the undiluted scenario, albeit with a reduced graphene-gold distance.

This paper resolves a question concerning the probabilistic verification of infinite-state processes, specifically probabilistic pushdown processes. We demonstrate that model checking stateless probabilistic pushdown processes (pBPA) against probabilistic computational tree logic (PCTL) is undecidable.

The unfold/fold method for logic program transformation promotes the development of correct logic programs by applying specific rules to naive ones. This research addresses the challenges of introducing subgoals when synthesizing efficient sorting algorithms from naive sorting programs, utilizing both logic program transformation and abductive reasoning.

We introduce a multi-stage pipeline designed for straightforward gesture recognition. The innovation of our method lies in integrating various technologies, creating the first real-time system capable of simultaneously extracting skeletal structures and identifying gestures on a Pepper robot. To accomplish this, Pepper was enhanced with an embedded GPU to execute deep convolutional neural networks and a fish-eye camera to capture entire scene interactions. This article demonstrates that real-world scenarios present significant challenges, with current state-of-the-art methods struggling to manage unknown human gestures. We propose a solution to effectively address these situations.

This study examines the Noether and Lie point symmetries associated with Vaidya-Bonner geodesics. We classify the one-dimensional subalgebras of these Lie point symmetries, specifically determining the optimal system consisting of all pairwise non-conjugate one-dimensional subalgebras. Additionally, the symmetry analysis is applied to two specific cases of the system to serve as illustrative examples.

The flexibility of ultrasoft colloidal particles causes fluctuations that are vital for their structure and dynamics, yet difficult to measure experimentally. We employed dendrimers as a model system to investigate these fluctuations. By incorporating dynamic polydispersity into our small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) model and accounting for invasive water fluctuations within the contrast mechanism, we determined the fluctuating amplitudes of the size and shape for generation 6 dendrimers at finite concentrations. Our results show that while size fluctuations are suppressed, shape fluctuations increase once the dendrimer weight fraction exceeds 11%. Using neutron spin echo data, we attribute this crossover to the competition between inter- and intra-particle dynamics. Additionally, studying lower-generation samples yielded opposite results, indicating a structural basis for these observed dynamic behaviors.

For an irreducible, end-periodic homeomorphism $f$ acting on a surface $S$ with finitely many ends—where all ends accumulate on genus—the resulting mapping torus forms the interior of a compact, irreducible, atoroidal 3-manifold featuring incompressible boundary. Our primary finding establishes an upper limit for the infimal hyperbolic volume of the compactified mapping torus, expressed via the translation length of $f$ within the pants graph of $S$. This research extends the work of Brock and Agol, which was originally limited to finite-type settings. Furthermore, we define a wide range of examples involving irreducible, end-periodic homeomorphisms to demonstrate that our derived bound is asymptotically optimal.

The geometric formulations for both BRST and anti-BRST structures are fully developed within the context of the Nakanishi-Lautrup field. It is demonstrated that, under the general framework of gauge fixing in the Faddeev-Popov quantization approach, anti-BRST invariance comprehensively embodies the classical symmetries of Yang-Mills theories regarding gauge fixing procedures. Furthermore, the Nakanishi-Lautrup field is explicitly defined and treated as a geometric entity. This formulation facilitates the introduction of two novel topological invariants for quantized Yang-Mills theories, termed the Nakanishi-Lautrup invariants. Additionally, the cohomological structure of anti-BRST symmetry is analyzed, leading to the derivation of the corresponding anti-BRST topological index.

Compiler designers are increasingly turning to machine learning to develop optimization heuristics. The prospect of automating heuristic creation—thereby relieving engineers from navigating the intricate interplay between programs, architectures, and various optimizations—is highly attractive. Nevertheless, the majority of current machine learning approaches fail to emulate even the most basic abstract interpretations of data flow analysis, which are essential for effective optimization. For machine learning to become the prevailing technology in compiler heuristics, this limitation must be overcome. To address this, we introduce ProGraML (Program Graphs for Machine Learning), a portable, language-agnostic representation designed to capture whole-program semantics for deep learning applications. Additionally, to evaluate both existing and emerging learning techniques for compiler analysis, we have released an open dataset comprising 461k LLVM Intermediate Representation (IR) files spanning five source languages and 15.4M associated data flow results. We frame data flow analysis as a Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) task and demonstrate that utilizing ProGraML enables standard analyses to be learned, resulting in enhanced performance for downstream compiler optimization tasks.

Entanglement theory fundamentally relies on characterizing local transformations of pure multipartite states. To begin this characterization, one must determine which states are convertible into one another through local operations with non-zero probability; these groupings are known as SLOCC classes. These classes fall into three mutually exclusive categories: the null-cone, polystable states, and strictly semistable states. While the first two categories are well understood, strictly semistable states remain largely unexplored. This work establishes a criterion for the existence of strictly semistable states, demonstrating that such states exist if and only if there are two polystable states with orbits of differing dimensions. We apply this criterion to tripartite systems involving a qubit, scrutinizing all associated SLOCC classes to provide a complete characterization of their orbit types. Furthermore, we present representatives of strictly semistable classes and identify the polystable states they approach via local regular operators.

This study analyzes the photometric light curve of 1I/'Oumuamua, the inaugural interstellar object detected within the inner Solar System. By comparing observational data with synthetic light curves generated for ellipsoidal bodies across various rotational states and viewing geometries, we identify a discrepancy from prior reports: whereas previous studies noted a periodicity increase in October, our analysis reveals a $\Delta p\simeq0.21$ hour reduction in the spin period between October and November. We examine potential drivers for this evolving period, including outgassing and tidal forces, utilizing a generalized formalism applicable to elongated objects. Although sublimation exerts a stronger influence, tidal deformation can alter the moment of inertia and spin period depending on the object's bulk material properties. We introduce an open-source tool, $\texttt{SAMUS}$, which simulates constant-density, constant-viscosity liquid bodies under tidal forces for diverse viscosity and size parameters. Numerical simulations applied to 'Oumuamua suggest significant tidal deformation may have occurred alongside sublimation; however, synthetic observations incorporating tidal effects indicate that minimal deformation suffices to match the composite light curve. Our findings suggest that a dynamic viscosity of $\mu\geq10^9$ g cm$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, representing a 0.1% shift in moment of inertia, most accurately reproduces the photometric data. Consequently, tidal deformation likely contributed to the rapid spin-down observed in October, while outgassing drove the long-term spin-up.

Adapter Tuning, which involves freezing pretrained language models (PLMs) and fine-tuning only a few additional modules, has emerged as an efficient alternative to full model fine-tuning. While computationally advantageous, recent Adapters often require increasing parameter counts (such as bottleneck dimensions) to match full fine-tuning performance, a trend that contradicts their original goal of efficiency. This study re-evaluates Adapter parameter efficiency through the framework of network pruning, introducing a plug-in concept called \texttt{SparseAdapter}. Our results demonstrate that SparseAdapter achieves comparable or superior performance to standard Adapters when the sparsity ratio reaches up to 80\%. Based on these findings, we propose an effective yet simple configuration termed ``\textit{Large-Sparse}'' to enhance Adapter capacity within the same parameter budget. Experiments across five competitive Adapters and three advanced PLMs indicate that SparseAdapter, utilizing appropriate sparse methods (e.g., SNIP) and ratios (e.g., 40\%), consistently outperforms its counterparts. Notably, employing the \textit{Large-Sparse} setting yields significant gains, sometimes surpassing full fine-tuning by a substantial margin. The code is available at: https://github.com/Shwai-He/SparseAdapter.

This paper introduces a novel static analysis technique tailored for open programs—specifically program fragments containing dynamic pointer-linked data structures, such as lists, that utilize sophisticated low-level pointer operations. The primary objective is to enable the analysis of these programs without requiring analysis harnesses to pre-initialize the involved structures. The methodology leverages a specialized variant of separation logic combined with bi-abduction. The analysis traverses the call tree from the leaves upward, ensuring each function is analyzed exactly once in isolation, free from call context, thereby generating a set of contracts that summarize the functions' behaviors. To accommodate these programs, existing abduction methods from the literature are substantially adapted and expanded. Finally, the approach has been realized in a tool prototype and successfully assessed on complex, albeit not large-scale, programs.

Vision-based deep learning models are typically trained on extensive datasets under the premise that a single universal representation suffices for predicting all samples. While high-complexity models can learn these representations, a mixture of experts (MoE) trained on specific data subsets can infer labels more efficiently. However, implementing MoE introduces two significant challenges: (i) selecting the appropriate expert during inference for unseen samples, and (ii) determining the optimal data partitioning so that experts rely minimally on shared features. Dynamic Routing (DR) proposes an architecture where each layer consists of multiple experts, yet without addressing these challenges, the model tends to revert to using a consistent subset of experts. Our proposed method, Diversified Dynamic Routing (DivDR), explicitly trains the model to resolve the issues of data partitioning and expert assignment in an unsupervised manner. Experimental results on semantic segmentation (Cityscapes), object detection, and instance segmentation (MS-COCO) demonstrate that DivDR outperforms various baselines.

Text classification involves assigning labels to text segments by leveraging global information. While recent research has utilized Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to capture global word co-occurrences within a corpus, existing methods are transductive, meaning they require all nodes (both training and test) to be present during training, which hinders generalization to unseen data. To achieve inductiveness, these models typically rely on additional resources such as pretrained word embeddings; however, high-quality resources are often unavailable, and training them is challenging. This paper addresses the extreme scenario where no extra resources are available and the training set is limited, proposing a solution to learn an inductive, graph-based text classification model. We introduce InducT-GCN (Inductive Graph Convolutional Networks for Text Classification), a novel framework. Unlike transductive models that necessitate test documents during training, our approach constructs a graph solely from training document statistics and represents document vectors as a weighted sum of word vectors. During testing, we perform one-directional GCN propagation. Evaluations across five text classification benchmarks demonstrate that InducT-GCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, whether they are inherently transductive or rely on pretrained resources. Furthermore, scalability tests involving increasing data volumes show that InducT-GCN reduces both time and space complexity. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/usydnlp/InductTGCN.

Recent investigations into complex language models have uncovered valuable insights regarding the linguistic and semantic patterns embedded in their representations. This article focuses specifically on probing BERT to assess the relational knowledge stored within its parameters. While probing for linguistic comprehension typically examines all layers of BERT and fine-tuned variants, such analysis has not yet been applied to factual knowledge. We employ existing knowledge base completion tasks (LAMA) to probe every layer of both pre-trained and fine-tuned BERT models across ranking, question answering, and named entity recognition (NER) tasks. Our results demonstrate that knowledge is not confined solely to BERT's final layers; intermediate layers contribute significantly, accounting for 17% to 60% of the total knowledge. Furthermore, probing these intermediate layers reveals the varying rates at which different knowledge types emerge. We observe that fine-tuning causes relational knowledge to be forgotten, with the degree of forgetting dependent on the fine-tuning objective and training data. Specifically, ranking models exhibit the least forgetting and retain more knowledge in their final layers compared to masked language modeling (MLM) and question-answering models. Conversely, MLM excels at acquiring new knowledge from training data. Regarding fact learning, we identify capacity and fact density as critical factors. We hope this preliminary work encourages further research into the parametric memory of language models and the impact of training objectives on factual knowledge. The code required to replicate these experiments is publicly available on GitHub.

Neural networks frequently struggle to generalize across mismatched domains or distributions. In Natural Language Processing (NLP), this challenge is especially acute when models must generalize compositionally, meaning they need to handle novel combinations of known words and structures. This study explores learning representations that enable transfer learning between different compositional tasks. We strategically train both the model representations and task-specific layers on a pre-finetuning task to ensure robust generalization on mismatched splits requiring compositionality. We evaluate this approach on semantic parsing using three distinct datasets—COGS, GeoQuery, and SCAN—alternating them between pre-finetuning and target roles. Our method yields significant improvements in compositional generalization compared to baselines on the held-out test set of the target task. Furthermore, ablation studies validate the utility of the algorithm's key steps and corroborate our underlying hypothesis.

While the linear and second-order intrinsic anomalous Hall effects (IAHE) have been extensively studied in systems that break time-reversal symmetry, the third-order IAHE has remained unexplored due to a lack of suitable theoretical frameworks, despite prior research on third-order extrinsic AHE using first- and second-order semiclassical models. This work extends the semiclassical theory for Bloch electrons under a uniform electric field to the third order via the wavepacket method, predicting that the third-order IAHE can indeed manifest in time-reversal symmetry-broken systems. Similar to the second-order IAHE, we identify the second-order field-dependent Berry curvature—originating from the field-induced positional shift—as a critical factor in observing this phenomenon. Symmetry analysis further reveals that the third-order IAHE, as the dominant contribution, is permitted in 15 three-dimensional magnetic point groups (MPGs) that break time-reversal symmetry, encompassing a broad range of antiferromagnetic (AFM) materials. To validate the generalized theory, we employ a two-band model guided by these symmetry principles. Additionally, since the generalized third-order semiclassical theory relies solely on Bloch band properties, it can be combined with first-principles calculations to investigate the IAHE in realistic AFM materials.

This research investigates online prediction with sequential side information using logarithmic loss, deriving both general upper and lower bounds on the minimax regret for the predictor. The upper bounds are achieved through the analysis of a probability assignment inspired by mixture distributions in universal compression, whereas the lower bounds are established via a redundancy-capacity theorem. Additionally, the regret is precisely characterized within specific settings.

This paper offers a rigorous examination of a specific class of coupled dynamical systems comprising two distinct component types: excitatory and inhibitory. Although these network models are finite, they can scale to arbitrary sizes. Drawing inspiration from actual biological networks, they incorporate features that serve as idealizations of biological systems. The individual components are modeled using simple, well-established dynamical systems. While the network-level dynamics emerge as complex patterns resulting from the interactions among these subsystems, we utilize established methods from (nonuniform) hyperbolic theory to analyze their Lyapunov exponents and entropy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the long-term network dynamics are controlled by physical measures exhibiting the SRB property.

This paper investigates prime irreducible objects within the Hernandez-Leclerc category for the quantum affine algebra linked to $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$ by employing the dual functional realization of loop algebras. In instances where the HL category serves as a monoidal categorification of a cluster algebra \cite{HL10,HL13}, these representations align exactly with cluster variables, while the frozen variables correspond to minimal affinizations. For every height function, we establish the classical decomposition of these representations relative to the Hopf subalgebra $\mathbf{U}_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1})$ and characterize the graded multiplicities of their graded limits using lattice points within convex polytopes. Integrating these findings with \cite{BCMo15}, we derive the graded decomposition of stable prime Demazure modules occurring in level two integrable highest weight representations of the associated affine Lie algebra.

Separating a speaker's timbre from their style is crucial for enabling style transfer in multi-speaker, multi-style text-to-speech (TTS) systems. Achieving this disentanglement allows TTS models to generate expressive speech for a specific speaker in any style present within the training data. Nevertheless, existing research on timbre and style disentanglement faces significant limitations. Current approaches either depend on single-speaker, multi-style recordings, which are costly and difficult to acquire, or rely on intricate network architectures and training procedures that are hard to reproduce and control. To address these issues and eliminate the need for single-speaker multi-style corpora, this paper introduces a simple yet effective method for disentangling timbre and style. The proposed approach utilizes FastSpeech2 as the backbone network, representing style through explicit duration, pitch, and energy trajectories. By treating each speaker's data as a distinct style, the method incorporates both speaker and style embeddings into FastSpeech2 to learn disentangled representations. Additionally, utterance-level normalization of pitch and energy is applied to enhance the decoupling effect. Experimental results confirm that the proposed model can synthesize speech with high style similarity to any style observed during training, while simultaneously maintaining very high speaker similarity.

This study addresses the global pressure formulation for immiscible, incompressible two-phase flow across heterogeneous rock formations. We introduce two robust numerical schemes leveraging domain decomposition (DD) and operator-splitting. The first approach employs a sequential strategy that fully decouples the global pressure, saturation-advection, and saturation-diffusion components. Each sub-problem is solved independently using distinct DD techniques and numerical solvers, with explicit coupling and no time-marching iterations. To accommodate varying time scales and rock properties, this scheme implements a novel multirate time-stepping strategy: it executes multiple fine time steps for saturation-advection within a single coarse step for pressure and saturation-diffusion, while allowing independent time steps for advection across different rock types. The second scheme revisits the classical Implicit Pressure–Explicit Saturation (IMPES) method, adapted for multirate coupling and nonconforming-in-time DD frameworks. For discretization, the saturation-advection problem utilizes the explicit Euler method in time and a first-order, cell-centered, Godunov-type finite volume method in space. Conversely, the saturation-diffusion problem is solved using the implicit Euler method in time and the mixed finite element method in space, consistent with the pressure treatment. Finally, numerical experiments evaluate the practicality and accuracy-in-time of these schemes, specifically examining the multirate and nonconforming strategies, and compare the convergence behavior of various DD methods within each approach.

A persistent obstacle in scalable optical quantum information processing is maximizing both the collection efficiency ($\varepsilon$) and photon indistinguishability ($\eta$) of single-photon sources toward unity. Recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility of achieving a product $\varepsilon \eta$ arbitrarily close to unity using quantum dot-based sources. This work examines the trade-off between efficiency and indistinguishability under phonon-induced decoherence, demonstrating that the photonic "hourglass" architecture enables $\varepsilon \eta$ to surpass the theoretical maximum predicted for standard micropillar designs under these constraints. This ability to bypass the trade-off stems from controlling spontaneous emission into background radiation modes, underscoring the critical role of engineering background emission in future efforts to achieve near-unity performance in quantum dot single-photon sources.

This letter investigates how external magnetic fields affect the microscopic dynamics of charge transfer (CT) excitons within disordered molecular semiconductors. Such effects arise from the dynamic coupling between the spin and spatial degrees of freedom of electron-hole pairs. To capture this interaction, we developed a numerical framework that integrates a conventional quantum spin dynamics model with a coarse-grained stochastic charge transport model. This hybrid approach offers a versatile and efficient method for simulating magnetic field impacts on CT state dynamics, thereby establishing a foundation for uncovering the microscopic origins of experimentally observed magnetic field effects. We show that simulations based on this model can successfully replicate experimental data and generate theoretical predictions regarding the efficiency of organic electronic materials.

This study employs advanced first-principles calculations to examine the structural, magnetic, vibrational, and electronic characteristics of monolayer aluminum oxide (AlO2). Through total energy optimization and phonon analysis, it is established that single-layer aluminum oxide adopts a distorted octahedral configuration (1T'-AlO2). The research further demonstrates that the surfaces of 1T'-AlO2 exhibit magnetism driven by oxygen atoms. Although the ferromagnetic (FM) state represents the most energetically favorable magnetic ordering, a slight structural distortion can induce a transition to a dynamically stable antiferromagnetic (AFM) state. Additionally, vibrational spectra reveal Raman active modes between 350 and 400 cm^-1, which serve as a distinguishing marker for identifying different magnetic phases. Electronically, both FM and AFM configurations are semiconductors featuring indirect band gaps, enabling the formation of type-III van der Waals heterojunctions with graphene-like ultrathin materials. Furthermore, predictions indicate that oxygen defects, which are unavoidable during synthesis and production, do not compromise the magnetic state, even at high vacancy concentrations. Consequently, ultra-thin 1T'-AlO2, characterized by its stable crystal structure, semiconducting properties, and robust magnetism, emerges as a highly promising candidate for nanoscale device applications.

Bayesian nested sampling relies on a prior sampling technique constrained by likelihood thresholds. To address high-dimensional challenges, various Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods have been suggested. We numerically evaluate ten algorithms derived from slice sampling, hit-and-run, and differential evolution across ellipsoidal, non-ellipsoidal, and non-convex landscapes ranging from 2 to 100 dimensions. Using the nested sampling shrinkage test to assess mixing performance ensures our findings remain robust regardless of posterior tail weight. Under identical step counts, hit-and-run and whitened slice sampling surpass standard slice sampling, whereas whitened hit-and-run yields inferior results. Furthermore, proposing along differential vectors of live point pairs demonstrates the highest efficiency and shows particular promise for multi-modal scenarios. These proposed methods are now integrated into the UltraNest package, facilitating efficient inference for a broad range of practical problems in astronomy, cosmology, particle physics, and related fields across both low and high dimensions.

We present a multi-wavelength investigation of a complex M-class solar eruptive flare characterized by three distinct ribbon configurations: circular, parallel, and remote. Magnetic modeling of active region NOAA 12242 reveals a 3D null-point topology surrounding an inner bipolar region. The event begins with faint circular ribbon signatures and remote brightening during the pre-flare phase, indicating slow but persistent null-point reconnection. Initially, we observed flux cancellation and associated brightening, likely indicative of tether-cutting reconnection constructing a flux rope near the polarity inversion line (PIL) of the inner bipolar area. Subsequently, as the M8.7 flare commenced, the circular ribbon brightened significantly, suggesting an accelerated rate of null-point reconnection. Finally, the eruption of the underlying flux rope triggered "standard flare reconnection" beneath it, causing an abrupt intensification of the parallel ribbons and further enhancing null-point reconnection through external forcing. Our findings show that within the fan dome, the region where the magnetic decay index n exceeds 1.5 borders the null-point quasi-separatrix layer (QSL). Our analysis indicates that both the torus instability and the breakout model contributed to the flare's triggering mechanism. This event serves as a compelling example of the dynamical evolution of a flux rope initially confined within a null-point topology, which subsequently activates and erupts as the circular-to-parallel ribbon flare progresses.

This paper introduces self-supervised, end-to-end systems utilizing speech embeddings to address the stuttering sub-challenge of the ACM Multimedia 2022 ComParE Challenge. Specifically, we leverage pre-trained Wav2Vec2.0 embeddings for stuttering detection (SD) on the KSoF dataset, benchmarking them against various SD methods. Our proposed self-supervised SD system attains Unweighted Average Recall (UAR) scores of 36.9% and 41.0% on the validation and test sets, respectively, outperforming the best challenge baseline (DeepSpectrum) by 31.32% on validation and 1.49% on test data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that concatenating layer embeddings with Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) enhances UAR by 33.81% and 5.45% on validation and test sets, respectively, compared to the baseline. Additionally, aggregating information across all Wav2Vec2.0 layers exceeds the baseline by relative margins of 45.91% and 5.69% on validation and test sets. Grand-challenge: Computational Paralinguistics ChallengE

We introduce a new simulation approach that allows us to pinpoint the critical parameters governing the experimentally observable traits of structural protein tags on dsDNA constructs moving through a dual-nanopore system. Initially, we validated this method computationally by replicating and elucidating the physical basis of experimental dwell time distributions for Streptavidin markers on a 48 kbp dsDNA molecule. These investigations highlighted significant distinctions between protein tag characteristics and dsDNA segment dynamics, offering immediate insights into refining measurement protocols to accurately determine unknown genomic lengths. Of particular significance are the computational studies regarding the electric field's influence inside and outside the pores, which proves essential for distinguishing protein tags based on their effective charges and masses, as revealed by a generic power-law relationship between average dwell time and pore position. The simulation frameworks enable the monitoring of individual monomer dynamics at sub-nanometer scales and explain the varying velocities across different tags using nonequilibrium tension propagation theory—a crucial factor for precise genomic length determination. We further corroborated the model and selected simulation parameters by computing the Peclet number, which aligns closely with experimental data. Our analysis of the coarse-grained model results demonstrates the potential to enhance the accuracy of experimentally derived genomic lengths. Moreover, carefully designed simulation strategies can act as a potent tool to differentiate various neutral and charged tags of diverse origins on dsDNA constructs based on their physical properties, thereby providing insights to boost both the efficiency and accuracy of dual-nanopore experimental setups.

The RowHammer vulnerability in DRAM poses a significant threat to system security. To mitigate this, vendors rely on security-through-obscurity, utilizing undocumented, proprietary on-die defenses known as Target Row Refresh (TRR). While TRR generally functions by detecting and refreshing rows susceptible to RowHammer, its specific implementations remain confidential, making it difficult to verify their security guarantees. To evaluate the security of contemporary DRAM chips, we introduce Uncovering TRR (U-TRR), an experimental framework designed to analyze in-DRAM TRR mechanisms. U-TRR leverages the insight that DRAM data retention failures create a side channel capable of leaking information about how TRR refreshes target rows. This methodology enables us to: (i) map the physical layout of logical DRAM rows within silicon; (ii) investigate undisclosed on-die TRR strategies; and (iii) integrate these insights to assess the RowHammer resilience of modern DRAM. Our results demonstrate that U-TRR facilitates the creation of RowHammer access patterns that bypass the TRR protections in 45 DRAM modules from three leading vendors. Consequently, we discovered that these modules are vulnerable to RowHammer, with bit flips occurring in up to 99.9% of all rows. The source code for U-TRR is publicly available at [106].

Topological shifts within electronic band structures, which generate van Hove singularities in the density of states (DOS), significantly influence ordering phenomena in quantum materials. In two dimensions, standard topological transitions—such as neck formation or collapse—cause the DOS to diverge logarithmically with energy. Beyond these regular singularities, higher-order van Hove singularities (HOVHS) exhibit power-law divergences. Utilizing renormalization group methods, we investigate how density wave phases (specifically spin-density and charge-density waves), which arise from Fermi surface nesting, evolve when a concurrent HOVHS is present. Our results indicate that the emergence of these phases can be substantially enhanced by the singularity, contingent upon specific interaction strengths, potentially raising the critical temperature by several orders of magnitude. We further explore the implications of these findings for experimental systems including Sr$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$ and transition metal dichalcogenides.

We re-examine the constraints on semileptonic operators imposed by mono-$\tau$ high-$p_T$ events in $pp$ collisions at the LHC. Consistent with prior investigations, limits on New Physics couplings derived from CMS data are significantly tighter than those from ATLAS, even though both experiments have collected nearly identical integrated luminosities. We identify that an overlooked systematic uncertainty in $\tau$ lepton reconstruction efficiency can partially account for this discrepancy. Furthermore, we establish updated constraints on New Physics couplings associated with $b\to c\tau\bar{\nu}$ decays, utilizing recent ATLAS data with an integrated luminosity of 139 ${\rm fb}^{-1}$. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating the propagation of the New Physics particle can substantially weaken the bounds obtained when relying solely on an Effective Field Theory framework.

This research details the realization of an all-optical binary logic half adder using triple-core photonic crystal fiber (TPCF). A key finding of this work is that the same TPCF configurations previously shown to perform all-optical logic functions have now been proven capable of executing successful half adder operations. Numerical algorithms were utilized to assess the control signal (CS) power required to define the extinction ratios at the output ports for both symmetric planar and triangular TPCF structures. By adjusting the CS power and input combinations, the system generates logic outputs derived from these extinction ratios to achieve the half adder function. The results highlight the substantial impact of input conditions on the half adder performance across the various TPCF schemes examined. Additionally, TPCF structures filled with chloroform exhibited efficient, low-power half adder operation with a significantly higher figure of merit compared to silica-based counterparts.

arXiv:1705.10172 introduced a string theory-based alternative to gravitational collapse, describing ultra-compact bubbles of AdS space that are $9/8$ times larger than Schwarzschild black holes yet remain nearly indistinguishable from them within the photosphere. Their slowly rotating variants, detailed in arXiv:1712.00511, closely resemble Kerr black holes but possess a distinct quadrupole moment. Recent work in arXiv:2109.09814 analyzed the dynamical stability of stationary black shells against radial perturbations and matter accretion, identifying a two-parameter family of stabilizing fluxes. This paper re-evaluates rotating black shells, applying constraints derived from the non-rotating dynamical analysis. By extrapolating these findings, we demonstrate that rotating shells can sustain themselves at a critical gravitational potential point. Furthermore, the requirement that shells return to their new Buchdahl radius after accretion uniquely determines the fluxes needed for stability; these parameters exhibit a remarkably simple form, satisfying one radial stability constraint perturbatively while exactly saturating the other. Under specific physical assumptions, the resulting preferred quadrupole moment is found to be 7% lower than that of a Kerr black hole.

This study derives the exact eigenstates for a two-dimensional damped harmonic oscillator situated in a time-dependent noncommutative space under the influence of a time-varying external magnetic field. We observe that for particular values of the damping coefficient, alongside specific time-dependent oscillator frequencies and magnetic fields, the noncommutative parameters yield intriguing solutions derived from the Ermakov-Pinney equation. These solutions facilitate the determination of the exact analytic phase connecting the Hamiltonian's eigenstates to those of the Lewis invariant. Subsequently, we calculate the Hamiltonian's expectation value. The results indicate that energy expectation values fluctuate over time, varying according to different Ermakov-Pinney solutions dictated by distinct choices of damping, frequency, and magnetic field parameters. Finally, our findings are compared with previous results obtained in the absence of a magnetic field.

This paper presents an analysis of the B$^+$ $\to$ J$/\psi\overline{\Lambda}$p decay based on proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s} =$ 8 TeV recorded by the CMS experiment at the LHC, with an integrated luminosity of 19.6 fb$^{-1}$. The measured ratio of branching fractions, $\mathcal{B}$(B$^+$ $\to$ J$/\psi\overline{\Lambda}$p ) / $\mathcal{B}$(B$^+$ $\to$ J$/\psi$K$^*$(892)$^+$), is determined to be (1.054 $\pm$ 0.057 (stat) $\pm$ 0.035 (syst) $\pm$ 0.011 ($\mathcal{B}$))%, where the final uncertainty accounts for errors in the world-average branching fractions for the decays of $\overline{\Lambda}$ and K$^*$(892)$^+$ into their observed final states. Investigations into the invariant mass distributions of the J$/\psi\overline{\Lambda}$, J$/\psi$p, and $\overline{\Lambda}$p subsystems reveal inconsistencies with a pure phase space model. Furthermore, a model-independent angular amplitude analysis extends these findings, indicating that the observed mass distributions align with contributions from excited kaons decaying into the $\overline{\Lambda}$p system.

Achieving a device that converts single microwave field quanta into the optical domain is a pivotal goal for linking distant superconducting qubits via quantum interconnects, with additional potential in radio astronomy and classical microwave photonics. Although various optomechanical and electro-optical transduction methods have been proposed and implemented, they have yet to achieve the necessary vanishing added noise and near-unity efficiency. This work introduces a novel transduction scheme capable of theoretically meeting the criteria for quantum-coherent, bidirectional conversion. The proposed method utilizes an intermediary mechanical mode, specifically a high-overtone bulk acoustic resonance (HBAR), to coherently bridge microwave and optical photons via piezoelectric and strain-optical mechanisms. High efficiency is derived from integrating low-loss Si3N4 photonic circuits, which sustain high intracavity photon numbers, with the highly effective microwave-to-mechanical conversion provided by piezoelectrically coupled HBARs. We formulate a quantum theory for this multipartite system by deriving a quantization method for the piezoelectric interaction between microwave and mechanical modes from first principles—a novel approach to date—and connecting it to the conventional Butterworth-Van Dyke model. Furthermore, we couple the HBAR to a pair of hybridized optical modes within coupled ring cavities using the strain-optical effect. By analyzing the device's conversion capabilities through signal flow graphs with realistic experimental parameters, we demonstrate that near-quantum-coherent transduction is achievable.

This work investigates a 3d/2d dimensional degression, a Kaluza-Klein mechanism within AdS$_3$ space foliated by AdS$_2$ hypersurfaces. We demonstrate that a massless AdS$_3$ particle with spin $s=1,2,...,\infty$ degrades into multiple AdS$_2$ particles sharing the same energy $E=s$. While Kaluza-Klein spectra in higher dimensions are typically infinite, we formulate the AdS$_3$/AdS$_2$ degression by analyzing branching rules where AdS$_3$ isometry algebra o$(2,2)$ representations decompose under the AdS$_2$ isometry algebra o$(1,2)$. Our findings show that a massless o$(2,2)$ higher-spin representation, situated on the unitary bound, splits into two equal o$(1,2)$ modules. From a field-theoretic perspective, this phenomenon is explicitly verified for free massless fields of spin-2 and spin-3. Furthermore, a reduction to a finite spectrum is achieved through specific mode expansions, partial diagonalizations, and identities unique to two dimensions.

Radiation therapy treatment planning is a multifaceted challenge due to the conflicting goals of delivering target doses and sparing healthy tissues. To mitigate the time-intensive nature of manual planning and enhance its quality, knowledge-based planning (KBP) has become increasingly essential. This study introduces LENAS, a novel learning-based ensemble framework that combines neural architecture search (NAS) with knowledge distillation to predict 3D radiotherapy doses. The approach begins by exhaustively searching a vast architecture space to identify diverse, high-performing models. To accelerate inference, a teacher-student paradigm is employed, where the aggregated outputs of these diverse networks serve as supervision to train a student model. Furthermore, adversarial learning is utilized to refine the student network, enabling it to recover knowledge from the teacher ensemble. To our knowledge, this marks the first application of NAS and knowledge distillation within ensemble learning specifically for medical image analysis. Evaluated on the OpenKBP and AIMIS datasets, the method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, the study provides in-depth analyses and empirical guidelines for ensemble learning.

The interplay between time-periodic driving fields and non-Hermitian effects can impart unique spectral and transport characteristics to physical systems. This study reveals a novel class of non-Hermitian Floquet matter within one-dimensional quasicrystals, marked by multiple instances of driving-induced ${\cal PT}$-symmetry breaking and restoration, the appearance of mobility edges, and reentrant localization transitions. These discoveries are substantiated through an analysis of spectra, level statistics, inverse participation ratios, and wavepacket dynamics within a periodically quenched nonreciprocal Harper model. Our findings not only expose the complexity of localization phenomena in driven non-Hermitian quasicrystals but also underscore the efficacy of the Floquet approach in creating distinct nonequilibrium phases in open systems.

A previously developed two-tensor-pomeron model, originally designed for low $x$ deep inelastic scattering (DIS), is now utilized to analyze real and virtual Compton scattering on protons. This framework incorporates two tensor pomerons—soft and hard varieties—alongside tensor reggeons, accounting for contributions from both transverse and longitudinal virtual photons. The study demonstrates that the model accurately reproduces experimental data at small Bjorken $x$ for deeply virtual Compton scattering (DVCS) obtained from HERA. Additionally, the reggeon exchange component proves essential for explaining real-photon-proton scattering measurements at lower $\gamma p$ energies taken at FNAL. Two distinct fits are presented, varying slightly in the magnitude of the hard pomeron contribution; however, both indicate that the interference between soft and hard pomeron exchanges is significant. Results show that the soft-pomeron contribution remains substantial in DVCS up to $Q^{2} \sim 20$ GeV$^{2}$. The model facilitates the investigation of the transition from the low-$Q^{2}$ regime, encompassing the photoproduction limit ($Q^{2} = 0$), to the high-$Q^{2}$ DIS regime. Furthermore, the ratio of cross sections for longitudinally and transversely polarized virtual photons in $\gamma^{*} p \to \gamma p$, defined as $\tilde{R}(Q^{2},W^{2},t) = (d\sigma_{\rm L} / dt) / (d\sigma_{\rm T} / dt)$, is examined as a function of $|t|$ and $Q^2$, revealing a strong increase with $t$. These findings could be validated in future low-$x$ lepton-nucleon scattering experiments, such as those planned at the BNL Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) or, should it be implemented, at the LHeC facility at the LHC.

Visual storytelling involves generating engaging and pertinent narratives based on provided image sequences. This study seeks to enhance the variety of these generated stories without compromising the informative details derived from the visuals. To achieve greater diversity and informativeness, we introduce a concept selection module that proposes a range of concept candidates. Subsequently, a large-scale pre-trained model transforms these concepts and images into complete stories. To broaden the pool of candidate concepts, we construct a commonsense knowledge graph for each image sequence. To effectively extract suitable concepts from this graph, we propose two innovative modules that account for correlations among candidate concepts as well as the relationship between images and concepts. Comprehensive evaluations, both automated and conducted by humans, indicate that our model generates reasonable concepts. Consequently, our approach significantly outperforms prior models in terms of story diversity and informativeness while maintaining a strong relevance to the original image sequences.

Recent studies indicate that Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs) significantly lower computational expenses and memory requirements, enabling deployment on devices with limited resources. However, compared to full-precision models, BNNs experience substantial accuracy loss. Existing research addressing this accuracy gap has primarily targeted specific architectures lacking or containing minimal 1x1 convolutional layers, where conventional binarization techniques often fail. Since 1x1 convolutions are integral to modern designs such as GoogleNet, ResNet, and DenseNet, developing an effective binarization method for them is essential for the broader adoption of BNNs. This paper introduces an "Elastic-Link" (EL) module designed to enhance information flow in BNNs by adaptively injecting real-valued input features into subsequent convolutional outputs. The EL module is straightforward to implement and compatible with other BNN optimization strategies. Our results on the large-scale ImageNet dataset demonstrate that incorporating EL yields significant performance gains; for instance, the top-1 accuracy of binarized ResNet26 improves from 57.9% to 64.0%. Additionally, EL accelerates training convergence for binarized MobileNet, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 56.4%. Finally, when combined with ReActNet, the approach achieves a new state-of-the-art top-1 accuracy of 71.9%.

The complex Langevin (CL) method offers a viable solution to the sign problem inherent in real-time quantum field theory formulations. Although stabilization techniques for CL have advanced significantly over the last ten years with notable success in finite density QCD, they remain inadequate for SU($N_c$) gauge theories defined on the Schwinger-Keldysh time contour necessary for real-time dynamics. In this work, we refine the discretization of real-time CL equations and propose a new anisotropic kernel to facilitate CL simulations on discrete time contours. When applied to 3+1 dimensional SU(2) Yang-Mills theory, this approach yields exceptionally stable results, potentially enabling the calculation of real-time observables from first principles.

We demonstrate that for all $r \ge 2$, there exists an $\epsilon_r > 0$ such that any $r$-uniform hypergraph with $m$ edges and a maximum vertex degree of $o(\sqrt{m})$ contains a subset of at most $(\frac{1}{2} - \epsilon_r)m$ edges. Removing this subset partitions the hypergraph into connected components, each containing no more than $m/2$ edges. Leveraging this result, we present an algorithm with a runtime of $d^{(1 - \epsilon_r)m}$ to determine the satisfiability of $(d, k)$-CSPs involving $m$ variables, where each variable participates in at most $r$ constraints; here, $\epsilon_r$ is a function of only $r$ and $k$, with $k \in o(\sqrt{m})$. Additionally, this algorithm addresses the corresponding #CSP-SAT and Max-CSP-SAT problems for these instances. We further establish that unsatisfiable $(2, k)$-CSPs with variable frequency $r$ can be refuted in tree-like resolution using $2^{(1 - \epsilon_r)m}$ steps. Finally, for Tseitin formulas defined on graphs with degree at most $k$ (a class of $(2, k)$-CSPs), we provide a deterministic algorithm capable of generating such refutations.

We demonstrate that a curve qualifies as a soliton solution to the curve shortening flow if and only if its geodesic curvature equals the inner product of its tangent vector field and a constant vector within 3-dimensional Minkowski space. Leveraging this characterization, we conduct a qualitative analysis of these solitons. Specifically, we establish that for any fixed vector, there exists a 2-parameter family of soliton solutions to the curve shortening flow on 2-dimensional hyperbolic space. Furthermore, we prove that each such soliton is defined over the entire real line, is embedded, and exhibits geodesic curvature that converges to a constant value at both ends.

Passwords and the necessity of securing them remain indispensable. Most sites requiring authentication still rely on password-based methods, including high-security platforms like internet banking that utilize two-factor authentication, which inherently depends on passwords as one factor. Despite robust detection efforts, user education, and takedown campaigns, phishing attacks targeting password authentication persist. Currently, no infallible solution exists to prevent even security-focused websites from redirecting users to fraudulent sites for credential theft. This paper conducts a threat analysis of web password login processes, revealing a design flaw in the HTML `<input type="password">` field. Because the web authentication process lacks end-to-end security from the input field to the server, this vulnerability can be exploited for phishing. We define four essential properties required to halt web-based password phishing and propose a secure protocol utilizing a new credential field that adheres to these criteria. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed protocol through abuse-case analysis, address deployment challenges, and present a test implementation to assess its data and execution overheads.

Grazing transits pose unique challenges for exoplanet statistical analysis. Although such orbits are uncommon due to geometric selection biases, a substantial portion of the posterior distribution often aligns with a grazing configuration in low-to-moderate signal-to-noise scenarios. Consequently, failing to accurately model these transits can result in biased inferences, even when the planet is not truly on a grazing path. Given recent improvements in stellar characterization, the primary constraint for many scientific applications has shifted to the quality of transit fits, making it an opportune time to re-examine this problem. This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling exoplanet transits by applying umbrella sampling alongside a geometry-dependent parameter basis designed to minimize covariances among transit parameters. Our technique divides the transit fitting process into separate Monte Carlo sampling runs for grazing, non-grazing, and transition regions, which are subsequently recombined into a unified joint posterior probability distribution using a robust weighting method. The approach is easily parallelized and incurs no additional computational time.
