Most significantly, our method delivers accurate estimates of exoplanet properties for both grazing and non-grazing orbits, producing more reliable results than standard techniques for many typical star-planet configurations.

We provide an overview of rational natural differential invariants applicable to a class of nonlinear differential operators of order $k\ge 2$ defined on a smooth manifold with dimension $n\ge 2$, and we demonstrate their utility in solving the equivalence problem for these operators.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are designed to extract complex feature representations, such as object shapes and textures, to address image recognition challenges. Recent studies suggest that CNNs trained on ImageNet exhibit a bias toward texture-encoding features. While these texture-based features suffice for generalizing to unseen test data from the same distribution, they often fail when applied to out-of-distribution data. Research has demonstrated that augmenting training data with diverse image styles reduces this texture bias in favor of shape bias and simultaneously enhances robustness against common corruptions like noise and blur. This is frequently interpreted as a causal link where increased shape bias drives corruption robustness, yet this relationship remains a hypothesis. This study systematically investigates various input compositions using natural images, explicit edge data, and stylization. Although stylization is crucial for achieving high robustness to corruptions, no clear correlation exists between shape bias and robustness. We conclude that the improvement in corruption robustness stems from the data augmentation provided by style variation, whereas the increased shape bias is merely a secondary effect.

This study introduces a new deep neural network framework for RGB-D salient object detection, which manages message exchange between RGB images and depth maps at the feature level while leveraging long-range semantic and geometric details from both modalities to identify salient objects. To accomplish this, we develop a Dynamic Message Propagation (DMP) module utilizing graph neural networks and deformable convolutions to dynamically acquire context information and automatically generate filter weights and affinity matrices for regulating message propagation. Additionally, this module is integrated into a Siamese architecture to separately process RGB and depth inputs, alongside a Multi-Level Feature Fusion (MFF) module designed to capture cross-level interactions between refined features from both sources. Experimental evaluations against 17 state-of-the-art methods across six benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses all competitors in both quantitative metrics and visual quality.

This study addresses the challenge of precisely aligning points across two 3D point clouds. While traditional approaches typically enhance performance by deriving representative features from individual points using deep learning, they often overlook the correspondence calculation between these features, relying instead on non-trainable algorithms like Sinkhorn. Consequently, extracted features are sometimes forced to conform to these rigid algorithms, and inherent stochastic errors within the features further degrade matching accuracy. In contrast, this paper introduces a differentiable matching network designed for joint optimization with the feature extraction process. The network builds graphs connecting points within each cloud and extracts discriminative edge features through a shared set-encoder and an edge-selective cross-concatenation mechanism. These components facilitate symmetric consideration of both point clouds and the extraction of robust edge features, enabling accurate point correspondence calculation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network significantly enhances point cloud matching performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yanarin/ESFW.

We investigate the connection between monads on a locally presentable enriched category $\mathcal{E}$ and identity-on-objects functors from a small dense full subcategory $\mathcal{A}$ of arities, termed $\mathcal{A}$-pretheories. We demonstrate that the natural mappings linking these structures constitute an adjoint pair. The fixed points of this adjunction are identified as $\mathcal{A}$-nervous monads—those satisfying the conclusions of Weber's nerve theorem—and $\mathcal{A}$-theories, a new concept introduced here. This equivalence between $\mathcal{A}$-nervous monads and $\mathcal{A}$-theories is optimal in a specific sense and generalizes nearly all existing monad-theory correspondences. Furthermore, it establishes entirely new correspondences, notably one capturing the globular theories that define Grothendieck weak $\omega$-groupoids. In addition to proving this general correspondence and demonstrating its scope, we examine favorable properties of $\mathcal{A}$-nervous monads and $\mathcal{A}$-theories that facilitate their recognition and construction. We also compare these entities with the monads and theories equipped with arities previously analyzed by Berger, Melliès, and Weber.

We categorize specific $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded extensions of generalized Haagerup categories by utilizing numerical invariants that satisfy polynomial equations. Specifically, we generate several novel fusion categories, such as $\mathbb{Z}_2$-graded extensions of $\mathbb{Z}_{2n}$ generalized Haagerup categories for all $n \leq 5$, $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$-graded extensions of Asaeda-Haagerup categories, and extensions of the $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2$ generalized Haagerup category by its outer automorphism group $A_4$. This construction relies on the endomorphism categories of operator algebras, notably free products of Cuntz algebras and free group C$^*$-algebras.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework utilizing a novel exponential likelihood function powered by the quadratic Wasserstein metric. In contrast to traditional Bayesian models that rely on Gaussian likelihoods and the $L_2$ norm, this approach offers distinct benefits. Primarily, it avoids dependence on measurement noise distributions, enabling the handling of complex noise patterns like combined additive and multiplicative noise. Second, unlike standard normal likelihoods which often produce multiple local extrema, the Wasserstein-based function typically does not, leading to superior convergence toward accurate posteriors when using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. Third, specifically in signal processing contexts, whereas normal likelihoods assess only amplitude discrepancies between observed and simulated signals, the proposed function captures both amplitude and phase differences. We apply this framework to inverse uncertainty quantification of waveforms, illustrating its superiority over models employing normal likelihood functions.

Abstract: Far-from-equilibrium dynamics driving self-organization are crucial for understanding complex systems across physics, biology, geology, and sociology. However, identifying systems with controllable parameters sufficient for quantitative modeling of emergent properties remains a significant challenge. In this study, we investigate a non-equilibrium phase transition and detect signatures of self-organized criticality within a dilute thermal atomic vapor optically excited to highly interacting Rydberg states. Electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) offers precise control over population dynamics and facilitates high-resolution analysis of driven-dissipative processes, which display phase bistability. Our enhanced sensitivity enables the reconstruction of the complete phase diagram, particularly near the critical point. We find that interaction-induced energy shifts and accelerated decay manifest exclusively in one phase once a critical Rydberg population is exceeded. While this observation restricts the validity of standard mean-field models, a modified approach dependent on a threshold aligns qualitatively with our experimental results. Close to the threshold, we identify self-organized dynamics characterized by population jumps that restore the density to a critical value.

Existing measurements of Standard Model parameters indicate that the electroweak vacuum is metastable, a condition with significant cosmological consequences. Specifically, substantial Higgs field fluctuations during the early universe could precipitate vacuum decay. To prevent this, mechanisms that stabilize the Higgs during inflation—such as inflaton-Higgs interactions or non-minimal gravitational couplings—are generally required. Paradoxically, the post-inflationary preheating dynamics driven by these same interactions can induce vacuum decay, reintroducing the very problem they were meant to solve. This scenario is often considered disastrous for scale-invariant models, as they typically permit unrestricted fluctuation growth. In this study, we analyze "massless preheating" scenarios and demonstrate that the competing risks to metastability can be balanced to ensure model viability. By fully incorporating both backreaction from particle production and perturbative decay effects, we identify numerous distinct "islands of (meta)stability" within the coupling parameter space. Ultimately, the interplay among Higgs-stabilizing interactions drives a sequence of dynamical phases that effectively expand metastable regions to encompass large Higgs-curvature couplings.

We establish equivalence relations for both sequences of point blow-ups on smooth $d$-dimensional projective varieties and their corresponding sequential morphisms, demonstrating a bijection between the equivalence classes of these sequences and the associated morphisms. Furthermore, we highlight distinctions that arise in the broader context of smooth 3-dimensional projective varieties, where blow-up centers can have any dimension.

The emergence of plant phenomics, combined with extensive genotypic data from next-generation sequencing, offers promising new avenues for investigating and improving complex traits. However, these advancements also introduce significant challenges in quantitative genetics, specifically the requirement for robust frameworks capable of handling high-dimensional datasets. This chapter outlines statistical methods for analyzing high-throughput phenotyping (HTP) data to improve the accuracy of genomic selection (GS). Following the Introduction in Section 1, Section 2 examines field-based HTP, covering the application of unmanned aerial vehicles and light detection and ranging (LiDAR), and explains how image data from HTP can boost genetic gain. Section 3 explores extending standard GS models to incorporate HTP data as covariates linked to the primary trait, such as yield, with a specific emphasis on single-trait, multi-trait, and genotype-by-environment interaction models. A distinctive feature of HTP data is its ability to generate large-scale, high-resolution spatial and temporal information that captures dynamic growth, development, and stress responses. Section 4 addresses the application of random regression models for longitudinal genomic selection. The chapter concludes by discussing several ongoing challenges.

Synchronization is a defining characteristic of numerous natural and artificial systems consisting of multiple interacting components, appearing across diverse fields from neuroscience to power grids. These systems synchronize due to intricate coupling mechanisms, which are represented by complex networks. Since the system's dynamics and the network's topology are deeply interconnected, determining the optimal architecture for robust synchronization becomes a critical question. The Master Stability Function (MSF) serves as a widely studied general framework for addressing synchronization issues. Previous applications of this method demonstrated that synchronization in strongly directed networks is resilient to external disturbances for specific models. This paper proposes converting non-autonomous systems of coupled oscillators into autonomous ones to prove that earlier findings are model-independent. Given that many real-world networks are strongly directed and thus potential candidates for optimal synchronization, this work examines the impact of non-normality. Drawing on the observation that highly directed networks are also strongly non-normal, we highlight that conventional techniques like the MSF may fail to accurately predict synchronization stability. These insights reveal a trade-off between non-normality and directedness that must be accounted for in the design of optimal networks to enhance synchronization robustness.

We demonstrate that, with at most two exceptions, every connected subcubic triangle-free graph has a fractional chromatic number no greater than 11/4. This bound is tight unless additional exceptional graphs are ruled out, and it enhances the established limit for the fractional chromatic number of subcubic triangle-free planar graphs.

Accurate labeling of vertebral discs in MRI scans is crucial for diagnosing spinal conditions such as multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, degenerative cervical myelopathy, and cancer. However, automatic disc labeling remains challenging due to the visual similarity between discs and bone, as well as significant variability in spinal geometry and surrounding tissues across individuals and scans (including differences in manufacturer, pulse sequence, contrast, resolution, and artifacts). Previous approaches typically relied on a prior disc detection step, which often fails when localization algorithms produce missed discs or false positives. To address this, we reformulate semantic vertebral disc labeling using pose estimation techniques. We introduce a stacked hourglass network with a multi-level attention mechanism designed to jointly learn intervertebral disc positions and their skeletal structure. By combining the strengths of semantic segmentation and pose estimation, our deep learning model effectively handles missing regions and false detections. Furthermore, we implement a skeleton-based search space to minimize false positives. Evaluated on a generic, multi-center public spine dataset, the proposed method outperforms previous work on both T1w and T2w contrasts. The implementation is available via ivadomed (https://ivadomed.org).

Accurate segmentation of individual teeth on 3D dental models is a critical step in computer-aided orthodontics. While current learning-based approaches depend heavily on costly point-wise labels, we introduce a novel low-cost annotation strategy for 3D tooth instance segmentation that requires labeling only tooth centroids and a subset of teeth per model. To address the challenges posed by such weak supervision, we propose DArch, a dental arch prior-assisted 3D tooth segmentation framework. DArch operates in two phases: first detecting tooth centroids to establish individual tooth locations, and then performing instance segmentation. We leverage dental arch priors to enhance centroid detection. Specifically, we introduce a coarse-to-fine approach for estimating the dental arch, beginning with Bezier curve regression and followed by refinement using a graph-based convolutional network (GCN). Based on this estimated arch, we develop a novel Arch-aware Point Sampling (APS) method to generate tooth centroid proposals. Concurrently, a segmentor is trained independently via a patch-based strategy to isolate tooth instances from 3D patches centered at these centroids. Experiments conducted on 4,773 dental models demonstrate that DArch achieves precise tooth segmentation, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

The pursuit-evasion game within Smart Cities significantly influences the Multi-vehicle Pursuit (MVP) scenario, where police units cooperatively track suspect vehicles. While existing MVP research often assumes evaders move randomly or follow fixed paths, opponent modeling has shown great potential in addressing non-stationarity caused by adversarial agents. However, most current approaches focus on simple two-player games without environmental interference. This paper addresses the Team-to-Team Multi-vehicle Pursuit (T2TMVP) problem in complex urban traffic settings, where evading vehicles employ pre-trained dynamic strategies for intelligent decision-making. To enhance pursuit efficiency in such challenging environments, we introduce OARLM2I2, an opponent-aware reinforcement learning method that maximizes a mutual information indicator. First, we develop a Sequential Encoding-based Opponents Joint Strategy Modeling (SEOJSM) mechanism to generate a joint strategy model for evaders, aiding the multi-agent decision-making process via Deep Q-Networks (DQN). Subsequently, we design a mutual information-united loss function that integrates environmental rewards with the effectiveness of the opponent's joint strategy model to refine the pursuers' decisions. Extensive experiments using SUMO demonstrate that our method reduces pursuit time by an average of 21.48% compared to other baselines. The code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ANT-ITS/OARLM2I2}.

We investigate Mana and Magic measures for quantum states, which are standardly defined via the finite, classically computable Clifford group. We propose modified versions of these measures that retain their classical computability while extending it to additional states. Furthermore, we apply these new definitions to analyze knot states associated with 2-strand knots.

We investigate charge and spin tunneling currents between two Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) superconductors, with one exhibiting a spin-split density of states. Under a significant temperature bias across the junction, we predict the emergence of a spin-polarized thermoelectric current. This thermo-spin effect arises from spontaneous particle-hole symmetry breaking without requiring a polarizing tunnel barrier. When the thermo-active component outweighs the dissipative one, the two spin components moving in opposite directions produce a spin current that exceeds that of the purely polarized case.

We have identified novel hard string scattering amplitudes (HSSA) within the NS sector of 10D open superstring theory, characterized by polarizations perpendicular to the scattering plane. In contrast, the corresponding amplitudes in bosonic string theory appear at a subleading energy order. Furthermore, all discovered HSSA exhibit proportionality to one another, with calculated ratios supporting Gross's 1988 conjecture regarding high-energy string symmetry. Finally, when combined with these new findings, the total count of HSSA at the first massive level of the NS sector aligns perfectly with the recently computed hard polarized fermion string scattering amplitudes (PFSSA) in the R sector.

Given an abelian variety $A$ defined over a field $F$, we investigate the existence of a smooth, projective $F$-variety $X$ whose automorphism group scheme over $F$ is isomorphic to $A$. We demonstrate that such a variety $X$ exists if and only if $A$ possesses a finite number of automorphisms over the algebraic closure of $F$. In the specific case where $F = \mathbb{C}$, this result was previously established by Lombardo and Maffei, while for algebraically closed fields, independent proofs were provided by Blanc and Brion.

This study theoretically examines how tunable magnetic fringe fields, produced by arrays of switchable magnetic junctions (MJs), influence the quantum states within an underlying two-dimensional system in a semiconductor quantum well. The MJ-array creates a magnetic landscape that can be electrically reconfigured at the nanometer scale by altering the magnetic state of individual junctions. Carrier spins interacting with these fringe fields produce effective spin-dependent potentials that function as quantum dots or barriers for carriers with spins parallel or antiparallel to the magnetic texture, respectively. By switching individual MJs, one can modulate the magnetic texture to adjust the position, depth (or height), and coupling between these magnetically induced quantum dots and barriers. This capability facilitates the magnetic control, manipulation, and design of quantum states, their spin characteristics, and transport properties.

Photon echo serves as a key technique for manipulating electromagnetic fields, yet the strong rephasing pulse inherently produces unavoidable spontaneous emission noise. This noise degrades the signal-to-noise ratio and creates a fundamental barrier to applications within the quantum regime. In this study, we introduce a noiseless photon-echo protocol utilizing a four-level atomic system, implemented within a Eu³⁺:Y₂SiO₅ crystal to function as an optical quantum memory. When storing time-bin qubits encoded via single-photon-level coherent pulses, we achieved a storage fidelity of 0.952, significantly surpassing the limits of the classical measure-and-prepare strategy. This demonstrated noiseless photon-echo quantum memory offers spin-wave storage, operational simplicity, and high fidelity, suggesting it can be readily adapted to other physical platforms.

By employing degeneration techniques and Schubert calculus, we investigate the count of linear series with specified degree $d$ and dimension $r$ on a general genus $g$ curve that meet prescribed incidence conditions at $n$ points. We establish complete formulas for arbitrary dimension $r$ when $d$ is large enough, and for all $d$ in the cases where $r=1$ or $n=r+2$. These results extend existing work by Tevelev and Cela-Pandharipande-Schmitt, providing novel proofs for their findings.

This work introduces a universal mechanism explaining strong magnetic-field effects in nonmagnetic organic semiconductors. When the magnetic length is comparable to the distance between molecules and the localization length of electronic states, even a weak magnetic field (under a few hundred mT) can significantly alter the charge carrier hopping coefficient between adjacent organic molecules. Consequently, under illumination or high electric fields, variations in these hopping coefficients modify the polaron density, rendering photocurrent, photoluminescence, electroluminescence, magnetoresistance, and electrically injected currents sensitive to weak magnetic fields. This theoretical framework not only accounts for all observed phenomena but also offers a robust foundation for the empirical fitting formulas commonly used in this field.

This work examines the invertibility and compactness properties of positive Toeplitz operators linked to continuous Parseval frames within a Hilbert space. As practical applications, we establish conditions for the compactness of affine and Weyl-Heisenberg localization operators and derive uncertainty principles applicable to their respective transforms.

Although deep learning is known to be susceptible to adversarial examples, this vulnerability remains under-explored specifically within image caption generation. This study examines adversarial attacks on vision-and-language models, which generally utilize an encoder-decoder architecture comprising a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for image feature extraction and a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) for caption generation. Specifically, we investigate attacks targeting the visual encoder's hidden layers before they are fed into the subsequent recurrent network. Unlike existing methods that either attack the visual encoder's classification layer or back-propagate gradients from the language model, we propose a GAN-based algorithm to craft adversarial examples for neural image captioning. Our approach mimics the internal representations of the CNN, ensuring that the deep features of the input image induce controlled, incorrect caption generation through the recurrent network. This work offers new insights into adversarial attacks on vision systems integrated with language components. To evaluate our method comprehensively, we employ two strategies: first, testing whether the captioning system can be misled into generating targeted captions, and second, analyzing the feasibility of injecting specific keywords into the predicted captions. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively generate adversarial images based on CNN hidden layers to deceive captioning frameworks. Furthermore, we find that the proposed attack exhibits high transferability, leading to significant new implications for the robustness of neural image captioning.

Oxygen-16 ions are scheduled for injection into the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for upcoming runs, with an anticipated day of physics dedicated to O+O collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair ($\sqrt{s_{\rm{NN}}}$) of 7 TeV. Given that the final-state multiplicity in O+O collisions overlaps with that of pp, p+Pb, and Pb+Pb systems, investigating global properties in these collisions could offer deeper insights into heavy-ion-like behavior in small systems and clarify their similarities and differences relative to larger systems like Pb+Pb. This work presents predictions for global properties in O+O collisions at 7 TeV using the multi-phase transport model (AMPT). Reported observables include mid-rapidity charged-particle multiplicity, transverse mass, Bjorken energy density, pseudo-rapidity distributions, squared speed of sound, transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$) spectra, kinetic freeze-out parameters, and $p_{\rm T}$-differential particle ratios across various collision centralities. Additionally, the transverse momentum-dependent elliptic flow of charged particles is analyzed. Results are displayed for both Woods-Saxon and harmonic oscillator nuclear density profiles. Furthermore, comparisons are made with an $\alpha$-clustered structure embedded within the oxygen nucleus. For most central collisions, average charged-particle multiplicity and Bjorken energy density exhibit a significant increase under the harmonic oscillator density profile, whereas other global properties display minimal dependence on the chosen density profile. The $\alpha$-clustered structure yields initial energy densities and final charged-particle multiplicities comparable to those observed with the harmonic oscillator profile.

Although the literature generally agrees on the definition of the estimand and estimator for the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test, determining the most appropriate variance estimator remains less certain. This review examines various proposals for variance estimators that remain consistent under both null and alternative hypotheses. For small sample sizes, alternative approaches—including a t-distribution approximation, a logit transformation, and a permutation method—have been suggested. We also investigated different estimators for degrees of freedom within the t-approximation framework. Simulation studies across multiple scenarios revealed that the performance of variance estimators in controlling Type I error rates is primarily influenced by heteroskedasticity patterns and sample size allocation ratios, rather than the specific underlying distributions. Overall, combining a specific t-approximation with Perme and Manevski's variance estimator proved most effective at maintaining the nominal significance level.

As blockchain technology advances rapidly and integrates across diverse application areas, evaluating performance, optimizing efficiency, and making dynamic decisions have become increasingly critical for developing new blockchain solutions. This paper offers a systematic review of this research domain, with a specific focus on establishing the fundamental theory and mathematical modeling of blockchain systems. Key areas of study include: (a) performance evaluation, utilizing tools such as Markov processes, queuing theory, Markov reward processes, random walks, fluid and diffusion approximations, and martingale theory; (b) performance optimization, employing linear, nonlinear, integer, and multi-objective programming; (c) optimal control and dynamic decision-making, through Markov decision processes and stochastic optimal control; and (d) artificial intelligence, covering machine learning, deep reinforcement learning, and federated learning. Although relatively little research has previously addressed these specific lines of inquiry, we contend that the basic theoretical frameworks, mathematical methods, algorithms, and simulation techniques for blockchain systems presented in this paper will significantly bolster future development and foster continuous innovation in the field.

This paper reexamines existing results in BMS$_3$-invariant field theories through the lens of the Carrollian perspective, building on the isomorphism between the $1+1$D Carrollian conformal algebra and the $1+1$D asymptotic symmetry algebra (BMS$_3$) of $1+2$D asymptotically flat space-time at null infinity. By drawing a direct parallel to covariant transformation laws for Lorentzian tensors, the study defines flat Carrollian multiplets and establishes their conformal transformation properties. Furthermore, it presents a first-principles derivation of Ward identities in a $1+1$D Carrollian conformal field theory (CCFT), introducing complex contour integrals over the spatial variable as a powerful analytical tool. The temporal step-function factors inherent in these identities facilitate a bidirectional translation between operator product expansions (OPEs) and operator commutation relations using a specific contour-integral prescription. Motivated by these step-functions, the paper proposes $i\epsilon$-formulations of the Ward identities and OPEs, which simplify the application of algebraic properties. Finally, employing these computational methods, the authors demonstrate that the modes of the quantum energy-momentum tensor operator generate the centrally extended version of the infinite-dimensional $1+1$D Carrollian conformal algebra.

We introduce and examine an adaptive step-size modification of the Davis-Yin three-operator splitting algorithm. This approach addresses optimization tasks involving a smooth component with a known gradient and an arbitrary number of non-smooth components with available proximal operators. By utilizing local objective information to determine the step-size, the method enables larger steps, necessitates only two additional function evaluations per iteration, and relies solely on an initial step-size estimate rather than other hyperparameters. Our iteration complexity analysis demonstrates performance matching the best-known results for the non-adaptive version, featuring sublinear convergence for general convex functions and linear convergence when the smooth term is strongly convex and one proximal term is smooth. Furthermore, an empirical comparison across six distinct problems highlights the computational benefits of our proposed method.

The Sun releases vast quantities of photons and neutrinos in a roughly spatially uniform manner. Diffuse $\gamma$-rays and ultra-high energy (UHE) neutrinos originating from extragalactic sources can subsequently interact with and annihilate these solar particles. This process generates anisotropies in the cosmic ray background by attenuating the flux of $\gamma$-rays and UHE neutrinos via solar radiation. Consequently, measuring this flux reduction offers a straightforward and potent astrophysical method for probing electroweak interactions. In this letter, we calculate these anisotropies, estimating values of approximately $\simeq 2\times 10^{-3}\,(0.5)\%$ for TeV-scale $\gamma$-rays and $\simeq 1\times 10^{-16}\,(2\times 10^{-14})\%$ for PeV-scale UHE neutrinos at Earth (or the Sun). We also briefly examine promising observational opportunities for facilities such as the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope's Large Area Telescope (Fermi LAT), the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S), the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) detector, and IceCube. Furthermore, we investigate the feasibility of detecting $\gamma$-ray attenuation from other active satellite orbits, including those of the Parker Solar Probe and the James Webb Space Telescope.

Current quantum compilers rely on expert-designed circuit transformations, a method that demands considerable manual effort to adapt to the varying gate sets of different quantum devices and often overlooks optimizations difficult to discover by hand. We introduce Quartz, an automated quantum circuit superoptimizer capable of generating and verifying transformations for any arbitrary gate set. For a specific gate set, Quartz systematically explores small circuits to produce candidate transformations and validates them using an automated theorem prover. The optimization process employs a cost-based backtracking search that applies these verified rules to the target circuit. Evaluation across three widely used gate sets demonstrates that Quartz effectively generates and verifies transformations, covering all those manually created by existing optimizers while also discovering new ones. Consequently, Quartz can optimize a wide variety of circuits for diverse gate sets, achieving performance that equals or surpasses hand-tuned optimizers.

Let $\alpha$ be a real algebraic number with degree $d \geq 3$, and let $\beta \in \mathbb Q(\alpha)$ be an irrational number. Consider a real number $\mu$ satisfying $(d/2) + 1 < \mu < d$ and a positive constant $C_0$. We establish the existence of positive real constants $C_1$ and $C_2$, determined solely by $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\mu$, and $C_0$, such that the following holds: If $x_1/y_1$ and $x_2/y_2$ are reduced rational numbers where $H(x_2, y_2) \geq H(x_1, y_1) \geq C_{1}$, and both satisfy the approximation conditions $\left|\alpha - \frac{x_1}{y_1}\right| < \frac{C_0}{H(x_1, y_1)^\mu}$ and $\left|\beta - \frac{x_2}{y_2}\right| < \frac{C_0}{H(x_2, y_2)^\mu}$, then one of three outcomes must occur: either $H(x_2, y_2) > C_{2}^{-1} H(x_1, y_1)^{\mu - d/2}$; or there exist integers $s, t, u, v$ with $sv - tu \neq 0$ such that $\beta = \frac{s\alpha + t}{u\alpha + v}$ and $\frac{x_2}{y_2} = \frac{s(x_1/y_1) + t}{u(x_1/y_1) + v}$ (or both). In this context, $H(x, y) = \max(|x|, |y|)$ denotes the height of the rational $x/y$. Since the exponent $\mu - d/2$ is strictly greater than one, this theorem implies that unless $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are related by a linear fractional transformation with integer coefficients, the heights of the two rational approximations must differ exponentially. A corresponding result is also proven for the case where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are $p$-adic algebraic numbers.

This paper introduces Poisson mixture approaches for origin-destination (OD) modeling within transportation analysis. We propose covariate-based models that integrate various transport modeling stages and facilitate direct probabilistic inference on link traffic through Bayesian predictions. The study highlights the Poisson-inverse Gaussian distribution as a viable alternative to standard Poisson-gamma and Poisson-lognormal models. We provide a comprehensive Bayesian formulation, demonstrating that the Poisson-inverse Gaussian is especially well-suited for OD analysis owing to its advantageous marginal and hierarchical characteristics. Furthermore, we evaluate the integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) as an alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo, comparing both methodologies under specific modeling assumptions. The case study utilizes 2001 Belgian census data to examine a large, sparsely distributed OD matrix representing trip information for 308 Flemish municipalities.

This paper investigates a single machine scheduling problem aimed at minimizing the total completion time, where jobs are categorized as either short or long. Although the processing times are initially unknown, they can be revealed by querying a processing time oracle, with each query consuming one time unit in the schedule. The algorithm must determine which jobs to test, and the performance of the resulting schedule is evaluated against an optimal schedule that assumes full information. The competitive ratio quantifies the cost incurred by hidden processing times, and the primary goal is to develop an algorithm that minimizes this ratio.

The study examines two distinct models: a non-adaptive model, where the algorithm must pre-determine which jobs to test and which to run untested, and an adaptive model, where decisions can be made dynamically based on test outcomes. In both scenarios, we present optimal polynomial-time algorithms based on a two-phase strategy: a testing phase followed by an oblivious execution phase. Experimental results strongly suggest that optimal algorithms inherently follow this structure, though formally proving this remains an open problem.

In numerous real-world situations characterized by extremely sparse extrinsic rewards, curiosity has proven to be a valuable mechanism for generating intrinsic rewards that facilitate environmental exploration and information gathering. Although current curiosity methods perform well on sparse-reward tasks, they often rely on a holistic perspective of state transitions, failing to provide a structured understanding of specific environmental aspects. This paper proposes a curiosity framework grounded in question answering, where agents are encouraged to query the environment and derive curiosity signals when answers evolve. We demonstrate that formulating natural language questions prompts agents to uncover specific details, such as object physical properties and spatial relationships, which serve as effective intrinsic rewards for solving sparse-reward tasks more efficiently.

Starting with a graph or similarity matrix, we address the challenge of reconstructing the true distances and spatial positions of nodes. This objective is achieved through a two-stage process: first, matrix factorization, and second, nonlinear dimension reduction. This approach is effective because the resulting point cloud from the initial stage resides near a manifold where latent distance corresponds to geodesic distance. Consequently, a nonlinear dimension reduction method capable of approximating geodesic distance can recover the latent positions, subject only to a simple transformation. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the specific combination of spectral embedding followed by Isomap, alongside supportive experimental results for other method pairings.

This research investigates the fundamental \textsc{element-extraction} problem within a query framework that merges two prevalent sublinear algorithmic paradigms: linear measurements for high-dimensional inputs and structured queries for massive datasets. While the former typically relies on non-adaptive methods and the latter on high adaptivity, this work focuses on linear measurements constrained by bounded adaptivity. In \textsc{element-extraction}, the goal is to identify an index $i$ where $z_i = 1$ for a given nonzero vector $\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^n$, using arbitrary linear functions over a specific ring. Although efficient non-adaptive randomized solutions exist via $\ell_0$-sampling and fully adaptive deterministic solutions via binary search, we establish that any deterministic algorithm limited to $k$ rounds of adaptivity must incur $\Omega(k (n^{1/k} -1))$ queries when operating in the ring of integers modulo a fixed $q$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound. Furthermore, for queries utilizing integer arithmetic, we derive a tight $2$-round $\widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$ lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors. These proofs leverage classic combinatorial challenges, drawing upon established results regarding the zero-sum problem and recent enhancements to the sunflower lemma.

This report presents our adaptation of image-text models for long-term action anticipation through the Video + CLIP framework. This approach leverages CLIP, a large-scale pre-trained paired image-text model, alongside a Slowfast video encoder. While CLIP embeddings deliver fine-grained object understanding crucial for actions, the Slowfast network captures temporal dynamics within short video clips. We demonstrate that the features extracted from both encoders are complementary, enabling the framework to surpass baseline performance on the Ego4D dataset for long-term action anticipation. Our code is accessible at github.com/srijandas07/clip_baseline_LTA_Ego4d.

This article explores the structure of singular measures through a microlocal lens. Drawing inspiration from De Philippis-Rindler [10], along with the concepts of the Murat-Tartar wave cone [19,20,26,27] and Denker's polarisation set [9], we define an $L^1$-regularity wave front set applicable to both scalar and vector distributions. Our primary achievement is a precise microlocal characterization of the support for the singular component of tempered Radon measures and their associated polar functions at these locations. The demonstration relies on De Philippis-Rindler's methodology, enhanced by microlocal analysis tools and additional geometric measure theory insights. Consequently, we establish a novel sharp $L^1$ elliptic regularity result for scalar measures that underscores the value of geometric measure theory in harmonic analysis. Specifically, we prove that $\Psi^0 L^1\cap \mathcal M_{loc}\subseteq L^1_{loc}$, yielding implications such as: if $\Delta u\in L^1_{loc}$ and $D^2 u \in \mathcal M_{loc}$, then $D^2 u\in L^1_{loc}$. Furthermore, we derive several consequences, including extensions of [10] that impose constraints on the polar function at singular points for PDE-constrained measures and generalizations of Alberti's rank one theorem. Finally, we highlight the utility of this microlocal framework by presenting a result regarding the propagation of singularities for constrained measures.

This study addresses the automated reconciliation of receivables within non-governmental organizations by employing entity matching techniques. The proposed framework utilizes a base algorithm for initial match ranking, followed by three novel enhancements—score post-processing, a cascade model, and a chain model—to improve accuracy. These contributions advance automated settlement, entity matching, and multilabel classification in open-world settings. Validated using real-world operational data from a settlement service provider, the methods significantly boost recall from 78% (the base model) to over 90% while maintaining 99% precision.

The sampling-based motion planners' testing environment (sbp-env) is a comprehensive framework designed for the rapid evaluation of various sampling-based motion planning algorithms. It emphasizes flexibility by decoupling the core planning elements into two distinct categories: (i) samplers and (ii) planners. Since motion planning research primarily concentrates on (i) enhancing sampling efficiency—through techniques like heuristic or learned distributions—and (ii) the algorithmic construction of connected graphs within the planner, this separation allows researchers to swiftly exchange components to validate innovative concepts.

Utilizing ambient vibrations for energy harvesting through a mechanical oscillator and electrical transducer has emerged as a promising method for supplying power to small wireless sensors. Recently, bistable mechanical oscillators have gained significant research interest due to their ability to harvest energy across a broader frequency range. This manuscript investigates how bistable harvesters respond to various types of ambient vibrations, with a specific focus on harmonic noise. This unique form of noise combines the narrow spectrum of harmonic signals with the stochastic nature of broad-spectrum white noise. Furthermore, the study examines the connections between the responses of bistable harvesters and the phenomena of stochastic and vibrational resonance.

Standard models of disc galaxy formation posit that baryons and dark matter experience identical tidal torques, resulting in comparable initial specific angular momenta. Yet, observations reveal that disc galaxies typically possess only about half the specific angular momentum of their dark matter haloes. We contend that this discrepancy does not necessarily imply such significant angular momentum loss during galaxy formation. Instead, it may suggest that galaxies are most closely linked to the inner regions of their host haloes, a scenario consistent with the early collapse of baryons in these central areas. We examine a limiting case assuming perfect angular momentum conservation to determine the density contrast $\Delta$ (relative to the critical density) required for dark matter haloes to match the average specific angular momentum of their resident galaxies. Assuming galaxies correlate with haloes through characteristic rotation velocities, the necessary $\Delta$ is approximately 600. This value corresponds to an average halo radius and mass that are roughly 60% and 75% of the virial values (defined by $\Delta = 200$), respectively. We designate this radius as the radius of baryonic collapse ($R_{BC}$); under the assumption of perfect conservation, baryons would originate within this boundary. While complex gas physics likely prevents this from being a simple step function, we treat it as an effective radius. In summary, the gap between predicted initial and observed final specific angular momentum in galaxies, traditionally attributed solely to loss, can be more naturally explained by a preference for baryonic collapse within $R_{BC}$, potentially accompanied by some subsequent angular momentum transfer.

Accurate predictions of reservoir inflows are fundamental to optimizing reservoir management, and utilizing real-time forecasts can yield significant economic benefits. However, forecasting inflow is a complex challenge that requires accounting for climate and hydrological shifts. Consequently, this study aims to introduce a novel Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) approach for inflow prediction. These real-time, daily inflow forecasts facilitate efficient water resource management, allowing for the effective monitoring of release variations and enhanced operational reliability. The research proposes a naive anomaly detection baseline grounded in LSTM, serving as a robust reference for flood and drought forecasting within any deep learning framework. The method's practicality was validated using 20 years of observed daily data from the Bhakra Dam in India. Simulation results demonstrate that the LSTM approach outperforms traditional forecasting techniques. Although the experiments utilized data from the Bhakra Dam, the proposed LSTM model and anomaly detection algorithm are general-purpose tools applicable to any basin with minimal modifications. A key practical advantage of this LSTM method is its ability to adequately capture the non-stationarity and non-linearity inherent in historical data.

This research addresses the challenge of compressing a pre-trained deep neural network into a significantly smaller, shallower architecture that maintains its functionality for a specific task. The proposed method is driven by the insight that the pursuit of maximum accuracy across all operational conditions is not always necessary, desirable, or feasible due to data limitations or technical constraints. As a specific application, the study tackles the "backyard dog" problem in face recognition: a lightweight network must identify and distinguish between members of a specific group (a "family") while triggering an alarm for anyone outside that group. To achieve this, a novel shallowing algorithm is introduced. This non-iterative technique, which utilizes Advanced Supervised Principal Component Analysis, accepts a deep learning model as input and generates a streamlined version. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate the method's ability to drastically reduce network depth with only a slight trade-off in performance. Furthermore, the developed approach is a generic, simple, and non-iterative strategy applicable to a wide range of feed-forward networks. It enables the creation of specialized, smaller, and shallower network families optimized for particular tasks and conditions, derived from a single larger, universal legacy model.

This study addresses the unsourced random access problem over a Rayleigh block-fading AWGN channel equipped with multiple receive antennas. We focus on the slow-fading regime, where the coherence block length significantly exceeds the number of active users, allowing message transmission within a single coherence block. Unsourced random access is defined as a grant-free access method in which users are a priori indistinguishable, and the receiver aims to recover a list of transmitted messages regardless of their order. We demonstrate that, provided the coherence block length is sufficiently large, a conventional strategy utilizing non-orthogonal pilot sequences followed by channel estimation and Maximum-Ratio-Combining (MRC) offers a straightforward, energy-efficient solution. The performance of this approach can be accurately approximated using a closed-form expression. For finite block-length simulations, we employ a randomly sub-sampled DFT matrix for pilot design, a low-complexity approximate message passing algorithm for activity detection, and a state-of-the-art polar code with a successive-cancellation-list decoder for single-user error correction. These simulations validate the scalability of the proposed method and confirm the accuracy of the analytical results.

Multi-cluster federation is anticipated to become the next-generation cloud infrastructure, playing a crucial role in enabling concepts like edge and fog computing. Managing applications within these federated settings introduces new challenges to established research areas, including load balancing, auto-scaling, resource allocation, and service migration. Since access to actual multi-cluster infrastructure is restricted, there is a strong need for a test-bed that mimics real system characteristics. To allow researchers to rapidly conduct experiments in a federated cloud setting, we developed the open-source sandbox FedApp. This tool streamlines the deployment of multiple virtual clusters within an OpenStack environment, offering the option to incorporate realistic network attributes between sites. Each cluster is pre-configured with Kubernetes, an open-source, production-ready container orchestrator, alongside federation-wide monitoring via Prometheus/Grafana and simplified inter-cluster microservice communication through Istio.

We investigate the dynamics of a solar-type star orbiting a black hole binary (BHB) within a nearly coplanar configuration. We introduce a new phenomenon that triggers substantial eccentricity oscillations and growth in the stellar orbit upon encountering an "apsidal precession resonance," a state where the precession rates of the outer stellar orbit and the inner BHB align. This eccentricity excitation necessitates a non-zero eccentricity and unequal masses within the inner binary, yet it can also occur in non-coplanar triple systems. We demonstrate that the secular fluctuations in the stellar orbit's apocenter, driven by varying eccentricity, may be detectable by \textit{Gaia}. Such detection is particularly promising for BHBs emitting gravitational waves within the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) frequency band, offering a unique multi-messenger method to identify stellar-mass BHBs in the Milky Way.

This study conducts a multifractal analysis of the homological growth rates associated with oriented geodesics on a hyperbolic surface. The primary finding establishes a formula for the Hausdorff dimension of level sets corresponding to specific growth rates, expressed through a generalized Poincaré exponent of the Fuchsian group. By utilizing Bowen and Series's symbolic dynamics alongside ergodic theory and thermodynamic formalism, we demonstrate the analyticity of both the dimension spectrum and the large deviations rate function.

This study investigates the tunneling of scalar particles near the event horizons of Riemann spacetime, BTZ black holes, and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes by utilizing the Hamilton-Jacobi equation within the framework of Lorentz violation theory in curved spacetime. A modified Hamilton-Jacobi equation is derived from the Klein-Gordon equation for scalar particles under the influence of Lorentz violation. Consequently, the Hawking temperatures for both Riemann spacetime and the BTZ black hole are altered by this effect. Furthermore, the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy near the event horizon of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole is also modified. The results indicate that the adjusted Hawking temperatures and the changes in Bekenstein-Hawking entropy are dependent on the ether-like vectors $u^\alpha$.

Inclusive speech technology development critically requires addressing children's speech recognition, a field that remains largely neglected. The primary obstacle hindering advancement is the scarcity of sufficient child speech data, though recent breakthroughs in self-supervised learning offer a promising solution to this data gap. This study utilizes self-supervised adult speech representations alongside three established child speech corpora to develop recognition models for children. We evaluate fine-tuning performance on both native and non-native speakers, explore the impact of using cross-domain child datasets, and determine the minimal amount of child speech data needed to surpass state-of-the-art adult models. Additionally, we analyze recognition accuracy across different age groups. Our findings reveal that fine-tuning with cross-domain corpora yields relative improvements of up to 46.08% for native speech and 45.53% for non-native speech, with absolute gains of 14.70% and 31.10%, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a child speech recognition system can outperform a state-of-the-art adult model (trained on 960 hours of data) using as little as 5 hours of transcribed child speech.

This paper investigates Bragg resonance, defined as the triad interaction between surface and/or interfacial waves and bottom ripples, under conditions of background flow. We demonstrate that if one wave within the triad possesses negative energy, the amplitudes of all three waves increase exponentially. This behavior contrasts sharply with classic Bragg resonance, where the growth of one wave is driven by the decay of another. The resulting instabilities are "explosive" in nature and differ from standard shear instabilities, as the velocity profiles employed are linearly stable. Our findings may account for the presence of large-amplitude internal waves over periodic seabed topography in the presence of tidal currents, as observed in oceans and estuaries.

We introduce a novel method, termed the functional deep neural network (FDNN), designed for the classification of multi-dimensional functional data. Specifically, this deep neural network is trained using the principal components derived from the training data to forecast the class labels of future functional observations. In contrast to conventional functional discriminant analysis techniques that depend on Gaussian assumptions, the proposed FDNN approach is applicable to general non-Gaussian multi-dimensional functional data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that FDNN attains minimax optimality when the log density ratio exhibits a locally connected functional modular structure. The advantages of our method are validated through experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets.

Building upon previous research that adapted session types to convey behavioral details about Elixir modules, this paper presents a formal validation of the ElixirST type system. Earlier work established ElixirST to statically verify whether functions within an Elixir module adhere to their endpoint specifications, defined as session types, and developed a tool to automate this typechecking process. This study formalizes the system by constructing an LTS-based operational semantics for the specific language fragment supported by ElixirST, which models the runtime behavior observed by the module client. Utilizing this operational semantics, the authors demonstrate the session fidelity of ElixirST.

Controlling complex networks presents a critical challenge across numerous scientific and engineering disciplines, with the potential to drive significant technological advancements. This work tackles the physically significant question of the energy expenditure necessary for control by establishing and verifying scaling laws for both lower and upper energy limits. These bounds offer a pragmatic estimation of the energy costs involved in control mechanisms and mark a pivotal advancement from existing controllability studies toward the ultimate control of complex networked dynamical systems.

The exceptional adaptability and flexibility of both deep learning models and ensemble methods have driven their widespread use in analyzing various physical phenomena. Historically, these two approaches have been applied as separate entities in practice. This study introduces an Optimized Ensemble Deep Learning (OEDL) framework that integrates both techniques to achieve synergistic gains in accuracy, stability, scalability, and reproducibility, thereby catalyzing new applications in dynamic forecasting. Since unpredictability is a defining characteristic of chaotic dynamics, predicting nonlinear systems is a critical scientific challenge, particularly when the focus shifts to forecasting extreme events. In such scenarios, the proposed OEDL model—which combines feed-forward neural networks, reservoir computing, and long short-term memory via an optimal convex combination—plays a pivotal role in improving predictions of dynamics involving extreme events. The resulting framework outperforms both individual deep learners and standard ensemble methods on both simulated and real-world datasets. We demonstrate the OEDL framework's superior performance in forecasting extreme events from a Lienard-type system, as well as in predicting COVID-19 cases in Brazil, dengue cases in San Juan, and sea surface temperatures in the Nino 3.4 region.

Securing HTTPS is notoriously challenging, and flawed server setups have enabled major attacks such as FREAK, Logjam, and POODLE. This study empirically assesses the TLS security status of prominent websites to analyze the configuration choices made by operators. By examining various factors influencing site security—including software defaults, cloud hosting providers, and online guidance—we observe a fragmented web ecosystem. Although most sites maintain secure configurations, this is primarily driven by major cloud providers that enforce secure defaults. Conversely, individually managed servers are frequently insecure, likely because the resources available to individual operators, such as default software settings and configuration guides, often lack security. These results underscore the necessity of distinguishing between SaaS services and self-configured sites in security measurements, as well as the critical need for server software to include secure defaults out of the box.

We describe the custom-developed $\beta$-spectrometer, which features two Si(Li) detectors with sensitive areas exceeding 8~mm in thickness and a $4\pi$-geometry. This full absorption setup enables direct $\beta$-spectrum measurements without requiring corrections for electron backscattering effects from the crystal surface. Additionally, when analyzing $\beta$-spectra from transitions to the excited states of the daughter isotope, a 3" BGO-detector is employed to register $\gamma$-quanta in coincidence with the Si(Li) spectrometers.

This paper examines quantum key distribution protocols and their security under a receiver-device-independent (RDI) framework. While the sender's (Alice's) apparatus is only partially characterized by imposing limits on the overlaps of prepared quantum states, the receiver's (Bob's) device operates as an uncharacterized black box, rendering the protocols resilient against any attacks on Bob, including blinding attempts. We demonstrate that a secret key remains achievable even with arbitrarily low channel transmission rates, provided the RDI protocol utilizes a sufficient number of states. Additionally, we explore the practical application of the bounded-overlap assumption to real-world devices.

This study introduces an observer-based framework designed to address Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) in scenarios where an accurate system model is unavailable. Initially, we suggest employing a Moving Horizon Estimation-Model Predictive Control (MHE-MPC) scheme to generate policies for POMDPs where the full state of the actual process remains unmeasured and unknown. We propose parameterizing both the MPC and MHE formulations, treating specific adjustable parameters as variables for policy tuning. To handle unmodeled and partially observable dynamics, this paper utilizes Reinforcement Learning (RL) to simultaneously optimize the parameters of the MPC and MHE schemes. Unlike traditional approaches focused on model fitting or MHE performance, our method prioritizes the closed-loop performance of the policy as the objective. Demonstrations indicate that the proposed approach effectively enhances the closed-loop control performance of systems defined as POMDPs.

Inspired by recent experimental findings, we conduct a theoretical investigation of a one-dimensional "quantum fluid of light" flowing past an obstacle. This system is resonantly driven and displays bistability. Our analysis reveals that the flow undergoes sudden changes multiple times as either the fluid velocity or the obstacle potential strength increases. Unlike typical fluids or superfluids, these transitions occur between stationary states and fundamentally rely on the fluid's bistability. Notably, at the transition points, the fluid within the obstacle's wake occupies an unstable intermediate density state.

The central density distributions within dwarf galaxy halos are heavily influenced by the characteristics of dark matter. In our recent work (Malhan et al. 2021), we utilized N-body simulations to demonstrate that accreted globular cluster (GC) streams can distinguish between cuspy cold dark matter (CDM) and cored subhalos, as these clusters undergo tidal stripping before joining the Milky Way. Our previous analysis indicated that streams originating from cuspy subhalos exhibit greater physical widths and higher dispersions in line-of-sight velocity and angular momentum compared to those from cored subhalos. In this study, we extend these findings using the same simulations to show that tangential velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{v_\mathrm{Tan}}$) also reflects the central dark matter density profiles of the parent dwarfs; specifically, streams from cuspy subhalos display larger $\sigma_{v_\mathrm{Tan}}$ values than those from cored subhalos. By comparing $\sigma_{v_\mathrm{Tan}}$ measurements from Gaia EDR3 observations of multiple GC streams with our simulations, we find consistency with both an ``in situ'' formation scenario and accretion from cored subhalos of $M\sim 10^{8-9}M_{\odot}$ (or very low-mass cuspy subhalos of $\sim 10^8M_{\odot}$). Despite significant current uncertainties in $\sigma_{v_\mathrm{Tan}}$, the data suggest a low likelihood that any progenitor GCs originated from cuspy subhalos with masses $M_{\rm subhalo}\buildrel > \over \sim$ $10^9 M_{\odot}$. Future reductions in Gaia's tangential velocity measurement errors are expected to provide tighter constraints on subhalo dark matter density profiles.

We present a protocol for generating supersinglets, which are the multipartite extension of angular momentum singlet states. Defined as total spin-zero states composed of $ N $ spin-$ j $ particles, supersinglets exhibit high entanglement and zero spin variance along any axis, making them promising candidates for quantum metrology. Our method relies on projective measurements of the collective spin within the ensemble, followed by a conditional local unitary rotation designed to maximize the likelihood of achieving a spin-zero outcome in subsequent measurements. This iterative process, alternating between the $ z $- and $ x $-bases, continues until the system converges to the supersinglet state. Notably, our approach is independent of the initial state and requires no postselection. Leveraging strong projective measurements, the procedure achieves rapid convergence toward zero spin variance. We illustrate the method with an implementation using quantum nondemolition measurements in atomic ensembles and support our findings with numerical simulations.

This study investigates the empirical likelihood (EL) approach to constructing confidence intervals for linear functionals derived from right-censored lifetime data. Existing literature frequently demonstrates that the log-EL statistic follows a limiting scaled chi-square distribution, where the scale factor depends on an unknown asymptotic variance that must be estimated. This additional estimation step can degrade coverage accuracy, undermining a primary benefit of EL methods for censored data. By incorporating specific influence functions into an estimating equation, we prove that under broad conditions, the log-EL converges weakly to a standard chi-square distribution, removing the necessity for scale parameter estimation. Furthermore, a specialized application of these influence functions simplifies the otherwise computationally intensive procedures associated with EL. Our proposed method achieves a smaller asymptotic variance for the influence function compared to similar approaches by Wang and Jing (2001) and Qin and Zhao (2007). Consequently, simulation results confirm that confidence intervals based on these influence functions provide superior coverage accuracy.

We examine the historical mortality data from the initial phase of the 1871 yellow fever outbreak in Buenos Aires by comparing it against simulations of a stochastic population dynamics model. This model integrates the biology of the urban vector, *Aedes aegypti*, the progression of the disease in humans, and the spatial spread of the epidemic. Following an overview of the historical context and the constraints it imposes on initial conditions and ecological parameters, we analyze the simulation's general characteristics, particularly its sensitivity to initial conditions and available vector breeding sites. We further explore the sensitivity of statistical estimators—including the final death toll, the date of peak cumulative mortality, and normalized daily mortality rates—to free parameters, revealing notable regularities. The model demonstrates sufficient precision and accuracy to evaluate current historical interpretations of the epidemic's causes, indicating that alternative scenarios are more consistent with the historical facts.

This work examines a distributed learning scenario where Alice transmits a compressed representation of training data to Bob, enabling him to optimize a related learning task. We model this scenario as a rate-distortion problem, treating the training set as the source and Bob's cross-entropy loss as the distortion metric. Our analysis covers both batch and sequential data in unsupervised learning contexts. For batch data, the problem aligns with the information bottleneck (IB) framework; we demonstrate that simplified versions of standard IB approaches effectively solve the corresponding rate-distortion issue. Regarding streaming data, we introduce a novel algorithm of potential independent interest that addresses the rate-distortion problem for Gaussian sources. Additionally, we propose a two-pass variant of the iterative algorithm for sequential data to enhance performance. Finally, we analyze the relationship between the required number of samples $k$ and the rate for Gaussian sources, ensuring that cross-entropy loss scales optimally as the training set expands.

Managing the quantum statistical properties of confined light has long been a primary objective in integrated photonics. This study demonstrates that coupling molecular vibrations with the vacuum of a confined mid-infrared cavity allows for the reversible manipulation of photocount and quadrature field statistics over sub-picosecond intervals. The underlying mechanism entails shifting the cavity resonance frequency by modulating the dielectric response of the cavity materials via femtosecond UV pulses. Specifically, in an ultrastrongly coupled system featuring a single anharmonic molecular vibration within an infrared cavity, adiabatic pulsed modulation of the cavity frequency can generate mid-infrared light that is simultaneously sub-Poissonian and quadrature-squeezed, contingent upon the vibrational mode's dipolar characteristics. In strongly coupled vibration-cavity systems, non-adiabatic polariton excitations may arise following the frequency modulation pulse if the system begins in the lower polariton state. We outline design principles for creating mid-infrared quantum light by examining how cavity field statistics depend on the molecule's electric dipole function shape, the cavity detuning at the modulation peak, and the anharmonicity of the Morse potential, while also proposing feasible experimental realizations of this modulation strategy. Ultimately, this research facilitates the advancement of room-temperature, molecule-based mid-infrared quantum optical devices.

The integrability-condition method serves as a mathematical framework for characterizing the symmetry of collective sub-manifolds, utilizing a particle-hole representation. Within conventional time-dependent (TD) self-consistent field (SCF) theory, we define a one-form linearly combining the TD SCF Hamiltonian and the infinitesimal generator derived from the collective-variable differential of a canonical group transformation. Adopting a differential geometric perspective, we apply a Lagrange-like approach, common in fluid dynamics, to model collective coordinate systems. By acknowledging the structure of the coset space SU(m+n)/S(U(m) x U(n)), we formulate a corresponding geometric equation. To develop a perturbative method based on collective variables, we aim to construct a novel fermion SCF theory—essentially renewing the TD Hartree-Fock (TDHF) theory through the application of the canonicity condition, given an invariant subspace within the full HF space. This outcome naturally follows from the maximally decoupled theory, as the invariance principle of the Schrödinger equation ensures the existence of such a subspace. Furthermore, the integrability condition governing the TDHF equation for determining a collective sub-manifold is examined from a differential geometric standpoint. This geometric equation proves effective across a broad spectrum of physics, extending well beyond the random phase approximation.

This study analyzes Call Detail Records (CDRs) from Budapest for June 2016, a period marked by the UEFA European Football Championship. Although no matches were hosted in the city, the event significantly altered local residents' habits. The research evaluates fan behavior during and after Hungarian matches, revealing that mobile network activity mirrors football fans' movements and highlighting the utility of such data for social sensing systems. To refine mobility analysis, the CDRs were enriched with device properties; specifically, Subscriber Identity Modules (SIMs) not associated with cell phones were excluded using Type Allocation Code data to focus solely on human mobility. Furthermore, mobile phone price was assessed as a socioeconomic indicator, showing a correlation with mobility patterns. Additionally, subscriber age and subscription type were found to influence mobility, though neither factor appeared to impact interest in football.

Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) excel in performance, their deployment on low-power devices remains constrained due to high computational costs. A primary source of this complexity is the dense connection between convolutional and fully connected layers, which necessitates a vast number of parameters. To address this, the Bag of Features (BoF) pooling method has recently been introduced, which constructs a histogram representation of input data using a learned dictionary. This paper presents an approach that enhances BoF efficiency by ensuring the learned dictionary contains non-redundant items. We introduce an additional loss term derived from the pairwise correlation of dictionary entries, which supplements the standard loss function to explicitly regularize the model toward a more diverse and rich dictionary. The resulting strategy delivers an efficient BoF variant that improves performance without introducing any extra parameters.

The logistic linear mixed model (LLMM) is a highly prevalent statistical framework. Typically, Bayesian LLMMs rely on Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms to investigate their posterior densities. While Polson, Scott, and Windle (2013) introduced a Polya-Gamma data augmentation technique to build full Gibbs (FG) samplers, this study presents efficient block Gibbs (BG) samplers for Bayesian LLMMs utilizing the same Polya-Gamma method. We evaluate the FG and BG samplers against a real-world dataset, specifically examining scenarios where the correlation between fixed and random effects fluctuates and where design matrix dimensions vary. These numerical results indicate that BG samplers outperform FG samplers. Furthermore, we establish conditions ensuring the geometric ergodicity of the BG Markov chain when improper uniform priors are applied to regression coefficients, alongside proper or improper priors for random effect variance parameters. This theoretical finding holds significant practical value by validating the use of asymptotically correct Monte Carlo standard errors for estimating posterior quantities via Markov chain methods.

Plagiarism involves presenting another author's words, concepts, or ideas as one's own original creation. Within educational settings, definitions of plagiarism can vary by institution. Notable experts on the subject include Rebecca Moore Howard, Susan Blum, Tracey Bretag, and Sarah Elaine Eaton. This act is viewed as a breach of both academic integrity and journalistic ethics, potentially resulting in severe consequences ranging from penalties and suspension to expulsion, heavy fines, and even imprisonment. Recent incidents have highlighted cases of "extreme plagiarism" in academic circles. The modern perception of plagiarism as immoral and originality as a virtue originated in 18th-century Europe, notably during the Romantic era. Although plagiarism is generally not a criminal offense, it can be prosecuted in court alongside fraud if it causes harm through copyright infringement, moral rights violations, or torts. In both academia and industry, it remains a grave ethical violation. While plagiarism and copyright infringement often overlap, they are distinct; many instances of plagiarism do not violate copyright law, which is governed by specific statutes and adjudicated by courts. Cultural perspectives on plagiarism also differ globally; for instance, in countries like India and Poland, it is a criminal act punishable by jail time. Conversely, in some regions, plagiarizing a professional's work may be seen as a compliment rather than dishonesty. Consequently, students relocating from cultures where plagiarism is not stigmatized to Western nations often struggle to adapt to the strict ethical standards regarding originality.

Bayesian optimization (BO) serves as a framework for globally optimizing objective functions that are costly to evaluate. Traditional BO approaches typically treat these functions as black boxes, yet internal details regarding their computation are frequently accessible. For instance, when using simulation to optimize manufacturing throughput, one can observe intermediate metrics like the number of parts waiting at each workstation alongside the final throughput. Recent BO techniques exploit this internal information to significantly enhance performance. We refer to these as "grey-box" BO methods because they view objective computation as partially observable and potentially modifiable, effectively merging black-box strategies with white-box first-principles knowledge. This tutorial examines such methods, with a specific focus on BO for composite objective functions—where individual components contributing to the total objective can be observed and selectively evaluated—and multi-fidelity BO, which involves assessing cheaper approximations of the objective function by adjusting evaluation oracle parameters.

Efficiently leveraging computing resources demands optimizing the performance of large-scale parallel applications. Developers frequently investigate diverse execution parameters—including hardware setups, system software, and application settings—to identify and comprehend performance bottlenecks. These efforts often involve gathering hierarchical performance profiles structured as call graphs, which integrate performance metrics with their respective execution contexts. However, analyzing multiple call graphs simultaneously remains a difficult and laborious task due to substantial structural variations in execution contexts and high variability in performance metrics, such as runtime. This paper introduces an enhanced version of CallFlow designed to facilitate the exploration of call graph ensembles through novel visualizations, analytical methods, graph operations, and features. We propose ensemble-Sankey, a new visual approach that merges the intuitive graphical representation of resource-flow (Sankey) diagrams with box plots overlaid on nodes to illustrate performance variability across the ensemble. Our interactive interface offers linked views to aid in exploring call graph ensembles, specifically by enabling the analysis of structural differences and the identification of similar or distinct graphs. We validate the efficacy and utility of this design through case studies involving large-scale parallel codes.

This study examines the convergence of negative-order Cesàro means for double trigonometric Fourier series associated with functions possessing bounded partial $\Lambda$-variation. Furthermore, sufficient and necessary conditions regarding the sequence $\Lambda = \{\lambda_{n}\}$ are established to ensure the convergence of these Cesàro means for such functions.

Recent attention has focused on applying convolution to irregularly sampled point clouds. Given the distinct nature of point clouds compared to standard raster images, it is crucial to analyze the generalization of convolutional networks, particularly their resilience to variations in scale and rotation. This study evaluates various PointConv architectures to assess their robustness against such transformations. Among the explored variants, two novel approaches yielded substantial performance gains. First, we substituted the multilayer perceptron-based weight function with simpler third-degree polynomials enhanced by Sobolev norm regularization. Second, for 3D data, we introduced a new viewpoint-invariant descriptor that incorporates 3D geometric properties alongside standard coordinates.
