Based on the temperature-dependent trends of these values observed in superconductors, it is hypothesized that minority charge carriers play a decisive role in the emergence of the superconducting state.

We demonstrate that a specific tiling property, which entails the pointwise ergodic theorem, applies to measure-preserving actions of amenable groups along growing Tempelman Følner sequences, thereby offering a concise and combinatorial proof of the theorem.

We build and analyze multiple instances of continuous families of $\mathcal N = 1$ AdS$_4$ solutions within four-dimensional maximal gauged supergravity. These backgrounds serve as holographic duals to conformal manifolds in the associated 3d $\mathcal N = 1$ SCFTs. The investigated solutions can be uplifted to type IIB supergravity, originating from D3-branes wrapping an $S^1$ subject to an S-duality twist. We determine the spectrum of low-lying operators in these 3d SCFTs as a function of the exactly marginal coupling and examine the structure of the relevant superconformal multiplets. Furthermore, employing string theory methods, we explore additional continuous families of $\mathcal N = 1$ AdS$_4$ vacua in both type IIB and massive type IIA supergravity.

Cooperative driving depends on vehicle-to-vehicle communication to establish situational awareness, with Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control (CACC) serving as a key application designed to improve highway safety and capacity. Model-based communication (MBC) represents a flexible paradigm for broadcasting joint predictive behavioral models involving both drivers and vehicles, though the complexity of vehicle dynamics and diverse driving styles complicates this modeling. Gaussian processes (GP), a fully data-driven, non-parametric Bayesian method, offer a suitable solution for MBC. This approach propagates uncertainty by generating local GPs for each vehicle and broadcasting their hyper-parameters to neighbors. Specifically, this study employs GP to model individual speed trajectories, enabling vehicles to anticipate the behavior of predecessors even during communication outages or low-bandwidth conditions. To address safety within vehicle platoons, the system incorporates two operating modes: free following and emergency braking. The research proposes a discrete hybrid stochastic model predictive control framework that integrates these system modes alongside uncertainties captured by the GP models. This control design optimizes vehicle speed trajectories to achieve a safe, efficient platoon with minimal inter-vehicle gaps, thereby reducing dependency on frequent communication. Simulation results confirm the controller's effectiveness under this low-rate, intermittent communication paradigm.

We introduce a robust, efficient, and accurate IMEX solver designed for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations governing non-ideal gases with general equations of state. This approach utilizes an $h$-adaptive Discontinuous Galerkin scheme for spatial discretization and an Additive Runge Kutta IMEX method for time integration, specifically optimized for low Mach number scenarios. It enables the simulation of low Mach regimes at a markedly lower computational cost while retaining full second-order accuracy even in higher Mach number conditions. Implemented within the $deal.II$ numerical library, the method leverages adaptive mesh refinement to boost efficiency, incorporating specialized refinement indicators tailored for real gas phenomena. Numerical experiments on standard compressible flow benchmarks and their extensions to real gases validate the proposed method's performance.

Accurate river flood forecasting within the first 72 hours significantly mitigates damage by granting emergency responders adequate time to mobilize and assist. While such predictive models are already established and effective in many high-income nations, they remain scarce in low-income regions due to insufficient data. This study introduces the first global river flood prediction framework utilizing the recently released Caravan dataset, designed to serve as a benchmark for future research. To substantiate claims of generalizability, we implement custom data evaluation splits. Additionally, we develop and assess a novel two-path LSTM architecture (2P-LSTM) alongside three baseline models. Finally, we test the resulting models on diverse locations across Africa and Asia that were excluded from the Caravan dataset.

In citizen science, particularly within online tasks like image classification, maintaining quality control through replication to achieve consensus remains a persistent challenge. Disagreements among participants often stem from various sources, including poor image quality, interface design nuances, and the inherent complexity of the subject matter. Through a trace ethnography combined with both statistical and qualitative analyses of six Snapshot Safari projects, this research investigates which content characteristics drive uncertainty and low consensus. The study introduces a content categorization framework based on aggregate classifications to quantify image complexity, demonstrating that these categories significantly influence classification efficiency. Additionally, the analysis identifies an inductively derived set of supplementary image quality issues that hinder volunteers' confidence in their classifications. The findings indicate that distinct conceptualizations and metrics for consensus may be necessary for different content types, while aggregate responses provide a mechanism for flagging complex content that requires special handling when complexity cannot be predicted beforehand.

Although self-training has recently yielded notable results in image classification, its application to structured prediction tasks like neural machine translation (NMT) has produced only marginal improvements. This limitation stems primarily from the compositional nature of the target space, which causes distant prediction hypotheses to trigger the well-known reinforced mistake problem. This paper re-examines the use of multiple diverse models and introduces Reciprocal-Supervised Learning (RSL), a straightforward yet powerful method. RSL begins by having individual models generate pseudo-parallel data, which is then used to cooperatively train each model on a combined synthetic corpus. By capitalizing on the distinct inductive biases of different parameterized models, RSL improves accuracy by jointly leveraging agreements among them. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation that relies on a significantly stronger teacher, RSL can enhance a model's performance by incorporating other models that are comparable or even weaker. Additionally, RSL serves as a more efficient alternative to ensemble methods. Comprehensive experiments confirm that RSL achieves superior performance across various benchmarks with substantial margins.

We introduce a hybrid plasmonic-dielectric metasurface designed to control beam propagation. This structure consists of patterned graphene-silicon nano-disks fabricated on a low-index silica substrate. Our findings indicate that this hybrid approach combines the strengths of both graphene-based and dielectric metasurfaces. Specifically, while maintaining the reconfigurability characteristic of graphene systems, it also achieves the low-loss and CMOS-compatible properties typical of dielectric metasurfaces. These unique attributes position the device as a highly promising candidate for efficient optical components. To validate this potential, we demonstrate focusing and anomalous reflection capabilities using the proposed hybrid structure as examples of fundamental optical functions. This research establishes a novel pathway for creating reconfigurable meta-devices with broad real-world applications that exceed the limitations of passive counterparts.

This study examines formal languages defined by formulas utilizing quantifier-free theories of word equations, arithmetic on length constraints, and membership predicates for regular, visibly pushdown, and deterministic context-free languages. We analyze 20 specific theories, focusing on decidability issues regarding language properties like emptiness and universality. First, we evaluate their relative expressive power, identifying a bifurcation into two hierarchies determined by the presence or absence of word equations. Second, we assess the decidability of key problems, noting that emptiness corresponds to satisfiability within the respective theories. Third, we investigate whether a language from one theory can be expressed in another, demonstrating several undecidability results. These findings hold significant relevance for understanding normal forms in both theoretical and practical string solving applications.

Malicious entities may exploit various voice-spoofing techniques to deceive Automated Speaker Verification (ASV) systems or disseminate misinformation, prompting the development of numerous detection countermeasures. Given the substantial research conducted on spoofing detection in ASV over the past six to seven years, it is necessary to categorize these studies and conduct qualitative and quantitative comparisons of state-of-the-art solutions. Currently, no survey paper comprehensively reviews integrated approaches for voice spoofing evaluation and speaker verification, adversarial or anti-forensics attacks targeting spoofing defenses, or unified models capable of detecting multiple attacks simultaneously. Furthermore, there is a lack of standardized, "apples-to-apples" comparisons to assess the generalizability of published countermeasures across different corpora. This study provides a literature review covering spoofing detection methods based on hand-crafted features, deep learning, end-to-end architectures, and universal countermeasures against speech synthesis (SS), voice conversion (VC), and replay attacks. It also examines integrated solutions for spoofing evaluation and speaker verification, along with adversarial and anti-forensics threats to these defenses. The paper outlines the limitations and challenges of existing countermeasures, reports their performance on multiple datasets, and evaluates them across different corpora. Experiments utilize the ASVspoof2019 and VSDC datasets alongside GMM, SVM, CNN, and CNN-GRU classifiers. To ensure reproducibility, the code for the experimental test bed is available in our GitHub Repository.

The photonic lantern (PL) serves as a tapered waveguide designed to efficiently couple light into multiple single-mode optical fibers. These devices are currently under consideration for various applications, such as interfacing telescopes with high-resolution, fiber-fed spectrometers, coherent detection, nulling interferometry, and vortex-fiber nulling (VFN). Beyond these primary functions, PLs are capable of performing low-order focal-plane wavefront sensing simultaneously. This work establishes a mathematical framework for analyzing the photonic lantern wavefront sensor (PLWFS), deriving both linear and higher-order reconstruction models along with metrics to quantify sensing performance across linear and nonlinear regimes. The proposed framework is extensible to incorporate additional optical components, including beam-shaping optics and vortex masks, and is applicable to other wavefront sensing architectures. Furthermore, we offer preliminary numerical validation of these mathematical models through simulations of a 6-port PLWFS. A companion paper will present a more extensive numerical characterization of few-port PLWFSs, exploring methods to control and optimize their sensing properties.

Let $q$ be an odd prime power. Consider the power mappings $F_1(x)=x^{d_1}$ and $F_2(x)=x^{d_2}$ defined over $\mathrm{GF}(q^2)$, where $d_1=q-1$ and $d_2=d_1+\frac{q^2-1}{2}=\frac{(q-1)(q+3)}{2}$. This paper investigates the boomerang uniformity of $F_1$ and $F_2$ by analyzing their differential properties. The results demonstrate that, under specific conditions on $q$, the boomerang uniformity of $F_i$ ($i=1,2$) equals 2.

This paper introduces Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)-aware cross-layer scheduling algorithms designed for multipoint-to-point networks, such as the uplink of an IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) system. Insufficient bandwidth allocation to a TCP flow can trigger timeouts; because the TCP source immediately reduces its congestion window ($cwnd$) following a timeout, this significantly degrades average throughput. Conversely, since the TCP source expands its $cwnd$ only linearly with available bandwidth, assigning excess resources can lead to underutilization. To address these issues, the proposed algorithms allocate resources based on $cwnd$ and TCP timeout events. Focusing on uplink scheduling, the approach assumes that the Base Station ($BS$) receives only flow-level resource requirements rather than per-packet data. Additionally, the schedulers incorporate wireless channel characteristics, making them inherently cross-layer in nature. Extensive simulations reveal that the proposed schedulers achieve superior throughput and fairness compared to the Round Robin (RR) scheduler under various shadowing conditions. Specifically, the results show a throughput gain of 3.5% to 15% and an improvement in channel utilization of 15% to 25% over the RR scheduler.

This paper investigates the minimum income condition order, a mechanism employed in certain day-ahead electricity markets to reflect the production costs of generating units. As a type of complex order, it introduces non-convexities into the market clearing process. Through straightforward numerical examples, we illustrate that an increased presence of such bids can create opportunities for strategic bidding. Specifically, we demonstrate that a strategic agent can manipulate bid parameters to boost its own profits and potentially trigger the rejection of a minimum income condition order that would otherwise be accepted under truthful bidding. Additionally, we show that while adjusting the market clearing objective function based on existing literature can mitigate these strategic behaviors, such modifications introduce other challenges.

We introduce a neural model designed for paraphrasing, specifically trained to produce delexicalized sentences. This is accomplished by constructing a training dataset where every input is associated with multiple reference paraphrases. These references establish a weak form of semantic equivalence grounded in annotated slots and intents. To capture semantics from various slot types beyond simple anonymization, we employ convolutional neural networks (CNNs) before pooling slot values and utilize pointers to identify slots within the generated output. Empirical results demonstrate that the model produces high-quality paraphrases, resulting in a 1.29% increase in exact matches for live utterances. Furthermore, we show that automatically generated paraphrases can enhance natural language understanding (NLU) tasks, including intent classification and named entity recognition, through data augmentation.

This paper proposes employing a set-theoretical interpretation of semantic tableaux as an instructional method for propositional logic. For students possessing foundational knowledge of set theory, this perspective clarifies the functioning of semantic trees by bridging the gap between syntactical and semantical aspects of the process. Furthermore, it may prove beneficial when introducing advanced logical subjects, such as modal logic.

A hallmark of tree-level holography is that a correlator from one theory can generate correlators in another theory possessing reduced continuous symmetry. This principle applies to a specific family of 4d CFTs with eight supercharges, featuring protected operators dual to bulk gluons. Recent members of this family, constructed via S-folds that merge spatial identifications with S-duality group actions in type IIB string theory, exhibit dynamical differences emerging at the one-loop level. To investigate this phenomenon through anomalous dimensions, we employ the AdS unitarity method to bootstrap a one-loop double discontinuity. Unlike prior research, our analysis imposes no constraints on allowable special functions; instead, we iteratively extract Casimir singular and regular terms to transition between successive Regge trajectories. Our findings demonstrate that the presence of an S-fold causes anomalous dimensions to deviate from being rational functions of spin.

Facial recognition (FR) systems are rapidly becoming commonplace, yet significant performance disparities have been observed across various demographics in many popular FR models. A key factor influencing these discrepancies is the subject's skin tone. While prior research has attempted to quantify skin tone using modeling techniques across different lighting conditions or by relying on subjective color labels and demographic data, these approaches often depend heavily on consistent backgrounds and lighting for calibration, or require labeled datasets that are either time-consuming to create or simply unavailable. This study introduces a novel, data-driven method for measuring skin color that accurately captures a subject's skin tone from a single image, eliminating the need for consistent background or illumination. Our approach utilizes the dichromatic reflection model within RGB space to separate skin patches into diffuse and specular components.

The Santa Cruz Extreme AO Lab (SEAL) is a newly established visible-light testbed aimed at pushing the boundaries of wavefront control for high-contrast imaging on large, segmented ground-based telescopes. SEAL offers various methods for simulating atmospheric turbulence, featuring rotating phase plates and a custom Meadowlark spatial light modulator capable of generating phase offsets up to 6π at 635nm. To emulate the W. M. Keck Observatory's segmented primary mirror, a 37-segment IrisAO deformable mirror is utilized. The adaptive optics system integrates a woofer/tweeter deformable mirror configuration, comprising a 97-actuator ALPAO DM and a 1024-actuator Boston Micromachines MEMs DM, alongside four wavefront sensor arms: a high-speed Shack-Hartmann WFS, a reflective pyramid WFS serving as a prototype for Lick Observatory's ShaneAO system, a vector-Zernike WFS, and a Fast Atmospheric Self Coherent Camera Technique (FAST) demonstration arm equipped with a custom focal plane mask and high-speed sCMOS detector. Science capabilities initially include a classical Lyot-style coronagraph and FAST, which functions as both a wavefront sensor and science camera. SEAL's real-time control infrastructure relies on the Compute and Control for Adaptive Optics (CACAO) package, engineered to facilitate efficient software portability between SEAL and the Keck II AO system. This paper provides an overview of SEAL's design and its initial light performance.

Public goods and services—such as housing, medical care, and education—are frequently distributed to people who rank them similarly but hold differing intensities of preference. This analysis characterizes optimal allocation strategies under both known and unknown preference conditions. Key findings indicate that first-best outcomes may require assigning certain agents lotteries between high- and low-ranked options. When preference intensities are private, second-best allocations invariably involve these lotteries and can sometimes align with first-best results. Additionally, second-best scenarios may necessitate the disposal of services. The paper also examines a market-based alternative and highlights its distinctions.

We examine the Universe during its late evolutionary phase within the 150-370 Mpc scale of homogeneity. At these scales, the cosmos is modeled as containing dust-like matter, radiation, and a minimally coupled Galileon field. Employing a mechanical approach, we treat peculiar velocities of inhomogeneities and fluctuations of other perfect fluids as nonrelativistic, assuming these fluids concentrate around the inhomogeneities. We analyze the conditions allowing the physical Galileon field—consistent with recent gravitational wave observations (GW150914, GW151226, GW170104, GW170814, GW170817, and GW170608)—to become coupled. It is established that at the background level, coupled scalar fields act as a two-component perfect fluid: one component mimics a network of frustrated cosmic strings, while the other behaves as an effective cosmological constant. Our findings reveal a correction for the Galileon field, causing it to behave as a matter component.

We examine the reliability and precision of weak-noise (saddle-point or instanton) approximations applied to piecewise-smooth stochastic differential equations (SDEs), using a piecewise-constant SDE as a representative model for Brownian motion subject to solid friction. For this system, we demonstrate that the weak-noise approximation of the path integral accurately yields the known propagator at the lowest order of the noise power and captures the primary characteristics of the exact propagator when higher-order corrections are included, assuming that the path integral's singularity arising from the non-smooth SDE is handled via specific heuristics. Furthermore, we confirm that, consistent with smooth SDEs, the deterministic trajectories of the noiseless system adequately characterize the behavior of the non-smooth SDE in the low-noise regime. Lastly, we explore a smooth regularization of the piecewise-constant SDE to assess how effectively this approach resolves issues related to discontinuous drifts and singularities in SDEs.

This study examines the parameterized complexity of counting matroid bases, as well as trees and forests. We demonstrate that determining the number of trees or forests containing exactly $k$ edges is $\# W[1]$-hard when parameterized by $k$. Building on the recent deterministic matrix truncation algorithm by Lokshtanov et al. (ICALP 2015), our hardness finding for $k$-forests establishes that counting matroid bases is also $\# W[1]$-hard when parameterized by rank or nullity, even for matroids representable over a field of characteristic 2. Conversely, we show that this problem becomes fixed parameter tractable when the matroid is represented over a fixed finite field.

Aligning a sequence to a walk in a labeled graph is a fundamental issue in Computational Biology. For arbitrary graphs with $|E|$ edges, finding a walk that exactly matches a pattern of length $m$ is unlikely to be solved significantly faster than $O(|E|m)$ time under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) [Equi et al., ICALP 2019]. Conversely, specific graph types like de Bruijn graphs allow for exact matching in linear time [Bowe et al., WABI 2012]. Approximate matching presents a more nuanced landscape: it remains solvable in $O(|E|m)$ time if edits are limited to the pattern or if the graph is acyclic. However, allowing edits on arbitrary cyclic graphs renders the problem NP-complete, even for binary alphabets [Jain et al., RECOMB 2019], a result that persists even when restricted to substitutions alone. The complexity of approximate matching on de Bruijn graphs was previously unresolved. This study demonstrates that the efficiency enabling exact matching on de Bruijn graphs does not extend to approximate scenarios, even with only substitutions and an alphabet size of four. We establish that determining the existence of a matching walk in a de Bruijn graph is NP-complete when substitutions are permitted on the graph. Furthermore, we show that no algorithm significantly faster than $O(|E|m)$ is likely for de Bruijn graphs when substitutions are restricted to the pattern. This contrasts sharply with pattern-to-text matching, where exact matching is linear and approximate matching under substitutions achieves subquadratic $O(n\sqrt{m})$ time [Abrahamson, SIAM J. Computing 1987].

This expository article presents an extension of the open Gromov-Witten partition function for Calabi-Yau 3-folds, originally defined via the trace of vertex operators, within the context of topological string theory. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of the relationship between this framework and the Hilbert scheme of points on surfaces. Specifically, we apply an infinite series of twisted Casimir operators to the vertex operator responsible for calculating the amplitude. The scenario involving a finite number of twists has already been extensively explored in both mathematical and physical literature.

Bipolar disorder (BD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) are both chronic psychiatric conditions, yet their shared symptoms and frequent co-occurrence make it difficult for clinicians to differentiate between them during clinical interviews. This study introduces a new multi-modal dataset comprising interviews with individuals diagnosed with either BD or BPD discussing non-clinical subjects. We explore the automatic identification of these disorders and demonstrate that a linear classifier performs well when trained on a refined subset of features derived from various interview aspects, utilizing a novel method for summarizing these features. Furthermore, our findings reveal that distinct feature sets characterize BD and BPD, offering valuable insights into the differences between the automated screening of these two conditions.

Face Image Quality Assessment (FIQA) aims to enhance Face Recognition (FR) performance by supplying data regarding sample quality. Since FIQA methods strive to estimate a sample's utility for FR, it is logical to conclude that they are significantly impacted by the FR system they are paired with. Although contemporary FR systems generally perform well, existing research indicates they frequently suffer from demographic biases; consequently, FIQA techniques likely exhibit similar issues. To examine these biases, this paper offers a comprehensive study utilizing diverse quality assessment approaches—including general-purpose, supervised, and unsupervised face methods—alongside three leading FR models. Analysis of the Balanced Faces in the Wild (BFW) dataset reveals that all evaluated techniques are more adversely affected by racial variations than by sex. While general-purpose image quality assessments demonstrate lower bias regarding these demographics, both supervised and unsupervised face quality methods display pronounced bias, predominantly favoring white individuals regardless of gender. Furthermore, the study found that methods exhibiting less racial bias tend to underperform overall, suggesting that the observed biases in FIQA are substantially linked to the underlying face recognition systems.

We present a general approach for constructing transcendental entire functions of specified small orders, enabling exact control over the magnitude and geometry of the set where the function's minimum modulus is relatively large. This approach relies on a novel technique for establishing an upper bound on the growth of positive harmonic functions within specific multiply connected domains, yielding sharp growth estimates in numerous instances.

Integrable optics represents a novel approach in particle accelerator design that could increase betatron tune spread and suppress collective instabilities. An integrable rapid-cycling synchrotron (RCS) serves as a promising candidate to replace the Fermilab Booster, supporting the high-energy neutrino program's goal of achieving 120 GeV beam power in the multi-MW range. This work presents a sample integrable lattice incorporating modern RCS characteristics, including dispersion-free drifts, a low momentum compaction factor, superperiodicity, chromaticity correction, bounded beta functions, and separate-function magnets.

We examine the influence of thermal fluctuations within the dissipation range of homogeneous, isotropic turbulence using fluctuating hydrodynamics. Simulation results validate theoretical predictions, indicating that the energy spectrum is governed by these fluctuations at scales on the order of the Kolmogorov length. Furthermore, our findings show that the extreme intermittency forecast by Kraichnan in the far-dissipation range is supplanted by Gaussian thermal equipartition.

Recent years have seen the development of numerous unsupervised and self-supervised methods for extracting visual features from extensive unlabeled datasets. However, a primary limitation of these techniques is their inability to recognize visual features when an object is rotated or viewed from different camera perspectives. To address this constraint while leveraging valuable supervisory signals, we utilize video object tracks. Guided by the intuition that patches within a track should share similar representations in a learned feature space, we employ an unsupervised clustering-based strategy that constrains these representations to the same category, assuming they originate from the same object or part. Experimental results on two downstream tasks across various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our Online Deep Clustering with Video Track Consistency (ODCT) approach over prior methods that fail to incorporate temporal information. Furthermore, we show that using an unsupervised, class-agnostic, albeit noisy, track generator achieves higher accuracy than depending on expensive and precise track annotations.

An $s{\operatorname{-}}t$ minimum cut represents the smallest weight set of edges that, when removed, disconnects vertices $s$ and $t$. This problem is a well-known dual to the maximum flow problem. This paper presents a quantum algorithm for solving the minimum $s{\operatorname{-}}t$ cut problem on undirected graphs. For a graph with $n$ vertices, $m$ edges, and integer edge weights limited by $W$, the algorithm determines the weight of the minimum cut with high probability in time $\widetilde O(\sqrt{m} n^{5/6} W^{1/3} + n^{5/3} W^{2/3})$ using adjacency list access. In the case of simple graphs, this complexity simplifies to $\widetilde O(n^{11/6})$, even for dense graphs where $m = \Omega(n^2)$. By comparison, a randomized algorithm requires $\Omega(m)$ queries to the adjacency list of a simple graph merely to determine if $s$ and $t$ are connected.

Smartphone-based earthquake early warning systems (EEWS) are emerging as a complementary alternative to traditional systems that rely on costly scientific-grade instruments. However, smartphone networks feature highly dynamic geometries and produce noisy measurements, creating a critical need to manage both false alarm rates and missed detection probabilities. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a statistical approach utilizing the maximum likelihood method, which enables the near real-time joint estimation of key earthquake parameters such as epicenter and depth. The proposed method was evaluated using data from the Earthquake Network, a global citizen science initiative that operates a smartphone-based EEWS.

Network correctness is frequently evaluated by analyzing the data flow of individual components rather than the system's global behavior. In software-defined networking (SDN), specifying packet behavior is significantly more practical than defining the network's overall state. To address this, we extend Petri nets with transit capabilities and enhance Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) into Flow-LTL, enabling the tracking of token data flows. We introduce AdamMC, the first model checker capable of verifying Petri nets with transits against Flow-LTL specifications. AdamMC automatically encodes concurrent SDN updates into Petri nets with transits and allows for the expression of standard network requirements using Flow-LTL. The tool operates by reducing these problems to circuit model checking; we propose a novel reduction technique that yields substantial performance gains over prior prototypes, enabling AdamMC to verify software-defined networks comprising up to 82 switches.

Household robots require the ability to locate items on shelves, beneath tables, and within cupboards. To operate effectively in these settings, they must perform efficient 3D-scale searches despite constraints such as a limited field of view and the challenge of identifying multiple objects. While Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) are standard for computing search strategies, existing methods typically restrict the search space to 2D. This paper introduces a POMDP formulation designed for multi-object search within a 3D region featuring a frustum-shaped field of view. To solve this complex problem efficiently, we propose a multi-resolution planning algorithm utilizing online Monte-Carlo tree search. This method employs a novel octree-based belief representation to model target uncertainty across varying resolution levels, subsequently deriving abstract POMDPs at lower resolutions that possess significantly reduced state and observation spaces. Evaluations in a simulated 3D environment demonstrate that our approach outperforms baseline methods lacking a resolution hierarchy, achieving higher efficiency and success rates in larger instances under identical computational constraints. Furthermore, we validate the system on a mobile robot tasked with retrieving objects at various heights across two $10\text{m}^2 \times 2\text{m}$ areas by coordinating base movement with torso actuation.

In standard silo discharge, material flow rates are governed by the contact forces among grains. This study presents an investigation into the discharge of a two-dimensional silo containing repelling magnetic grains. Because this non-contact interaction alters the dynamics compared to conventional granular materials, we observed distinct behaviors. Although the flow rate's dependence on aperture size roughly adheres to the $3/2$ power law seen in non-repulsive systems, the resulting density and velocity profiles differ significantly, indicating that new phenomena must be considered. Notably, despite the lack of physical contact, clogging and intermittent flow were still observed for apertures smaller than a critical size defined by the effective radius of the repulsive grains.

The text investigates the extent of explicit guidance required for conditional diffusion. It addresses conditional sampling via an unconditional diffusion model, utilizing restricted explicit guidance—such as a noised classifier or a conditional diffusion model—confined to a few time steps. The authors examine a model predictive control (MPC)-inspired method that approximates guidance by simulating unconditional diffusion forward and backpropagating feedback from explicit guidance. Results indicate that MPC-approximated guides exhibit high cosine similarity to genuine guides, even across extended simulation horizons. Furthermore, incorporating MPC steps enhances generative quality when explicit guidance is constrained to just five time steps.

Current methods for deriving generalization bounds in data-driven optimization and machine learning primarily rely on empirical risk minimization (ERM), which hinges on the functional complexity of the hypothesis class. This paper introduces an alternative pathway to establish these bounds using distributionally robust optimization (DRO), a modern data-driven framework grounded in worst-case analysis and the concept of ambiguity sets to model statistical uncertainty. Unlike ERM, which depends on hypothesis class complexity, our DRO-based bounds are determined by the geometry of the ambiguity set and its alignment with the true loss function. Specifically, when employing statistical distances such as maximum mean discrepancy, Wasserstein distance, or $\phi$-divergence, our analysis yields generalization bounds with the minimal possible dependence on the hypothesis class: the bound relies exclusively on the true loss function, remaining independent of other candidates within the class. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first generalization bound of this nature in the literature, and we anticipate that these results will facilitate a deeper understanding of DRO, particularly regarding its advantages in loss minimization and broader machine learning applications.

The Supix-1 CMOS pixel sensor was engineered for the Circular Electron-Positron Collider (CEPC) silicon tracker. Comprising nine sectors with diverse pixel dimensions, diode sizes, and geometries, the sensor was manufactured using a 180 nm CMOS Image Sensor (CIS) process to investigate the performance of enlarged pixels. This study examines radiation-induced impacts on charge collection under a fluence of $1 \times 10^{13}$ 1 MeV neq/cm², utilizing Fe-55 radioactive sources and Technology Computer Aided Design (TCAD) simulations to meet the required radiation hardness of $6.8 \times 10^{12}$ 1 MeV neq/cm² per year regarding Non-Ionizing Energy Loss (NIEL). Sensor gain calibration was performed via the k-$\alpha$ peak of Fe-55 prior to and following irradiation. Key metrics including pixel-wise equivalent noise charge (ENC), charge collection efficiency (CCE), and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) were assessed, while a custom reconstruction algorithm analyzed radiation effects on cluster properties. TCAD simulations modeled charge collection in $5 \times 5$ pixel matrices for two typical incident particle scenarios, comparing results with and without irradiation. Both experimental data and simulations demonstrate that although enlarged pixels ($21 \, \mu\text{m} \times 84 \, \mu\text{m}$) experience greater performance degradation than smaller ones, they maintain satisfactory noise and charge collection characteristics for particle tracking in future collider detectors post-irradiation.

We applied truncated disc models to multiwavelength (optical/UV/X-ray) observations of the black hole SWIFT J1753.5-0127 during its 2005 hard state outburst. Given the system's high brightness and low interstellar absorption, the dataset offers an ideal opportunity to analyze weak, cool disc emission in this state. By fitting the data with X-ray illuminated disc models, we constrained the inner disc radius across the outburst. Near the peak, the observed soft X-ray component aligns with emission from the inner disc, where intrinsic output is boosted in temperature and luminosity due to reprocessing of hard X-rays within an overlap zone between the disc and corona. This disc emission supplies seed photons for Compton scattering, generating the hard X-ray spectrum, which in turn illuminates the outer disc to produce optical emission via reprocessing.

Conversely, as the outburst fades, the scenario changes significantly. The optical emission likely originates from self-generated cyclotron-synchrotron radiation rather than tracing the outer disc. Similarly, reprocessing limits suggest the soft X-rays do not directly map to the inner disc radius. This is further illustrated by a dim low/hard state spectrum from XTE J1118+480. In that case, the relatively high-temperature soft X-ray component implies a very small emitting area, which contradicts the much larger, cooler UV component well-fit by a truncated disc. Although we speculate on the origin of this component, its presence as a distinct spectral element separate from the truncated disc in XTE J1118+480 indicates it does not trace the inner disc radius and thus cannot be used to constrain truncated disc models.

This study examines the FASER$
u$ detector's sensitivity to new physics arising from non-standard neutrino interactions. Positioned 480 meters downstream from the ATLAS interaction point, FASER$
u$ will uniquely enable the first investigation of multi-TeV neutrino interactions from a controlled source. Our approach, utilizing the Standard Model Effective Theory (SMEFT) and the Weak Effective Field Theory (WEFT) below the electroweak scale, applies to both existing and upcoming neutrino experiments. By deriving coefficients from the WEFT Lagrangian that alter neutrino production in meson decays and detection through deep-inelastic scattering, we represent new physics impacts as modified flavor transition probabilities. For specific coupling configurations, we determine that FASER$
u$ could constrain interactions two to three orders of magnitude weaker than Standard Model weak interactions, suggesting the experiment will indirectly probe new physics at the multi-TeV scale. Furthermore, in certain scenarios, FASER$
u$ constraints will match or surpass current limits—including several derived for the first time in this work—using just $150~$fb${}^{-1}$ of data.

A significant number of experts contend that the future of artificial intelligence hinges on successfully embedding symbolic logical reasoning within deep learning frameworks. SATNet, a recently introduced differentiable MAXSAT solver, marked a breakthrough by demonstrating the ability to integrate with conventional neural networks to tackle visual reasoning tasks, such as learning Sudoku rules solely from image data. However, SATNet ultimately faced a critical hurdle in neurosymbolic systems: the Symbol Grounding Problem, which involves the inability to map visual inputs to symbolic variables without explicit supervision or "label leakage." This study proposes a self-supervised pre-training pipeline designed to overcome this barrier, thereby expanding the range of solvable problems for SATNet to include datasets entirely devoid of intermediary labels. We show that our approach enables SATNet to achieve full accuracy even in challenging scenarios that strictly prevent label leakage. Furthermore, we introduce a proofreading technique that further enhances SATNet's performance, surpassing current state-of-the-art results on Visual Sudoku.

Let $L$ denote the infinitesimal generator of an analytic semigroup on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfying Gaussian kernel bounds, and define the fractional integrals of $L$ as $L^{-\alpha/2}$ for $0<\alpha<n$. For any locally integrable function $b$, the commutators linked to $L^{-\alpha/2}$ are given by $[b,L^{-\alpha/2}](f)(x)=b(x)L^{-\alpha/2}(f)(x)-L^{-\alpha/2}(bf)(x)$. The author establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for the boundedness of these commutators on weighted Morrey spaces, specifically when $b$ belongs to the weighted $BMO$ space $BMO(\omega)$ or the standard $BMO$ space.

This study examines the statistics of alternating words in relation to "possible reflection paths across multiple glass layers." For a vector $v=(v_1,v_2,\cdots,v_n)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$, a path within $n$ glass plates corresponding to $v$ is defined as one where the $i^{\rm{th}}$ plate experiences exactly $v_i$ reflections for all $i\in\{1,2,\cdots,n\}$. We derive a recursion for counting such paths given $v\in\mathbb{Z}^n$ and $\sum_{i\geq 1} v_i=m$. Furthermore, we establish recursions for various statistics concerning the number of paths associated with a specific vector $v\in\mathbb{Z}^n$, provide a closed-form solution for the case $n=3$, and identify an equivalent condition for the existence of a path corresponding to a given vector $v$.

We show that positive frequency modes for a complex scalar field in a constant electric field, known as Schwinger modes, can be expressed as exact Lorentzian worldline path integral amplitudes across three distinct gauges. Despite the mathematical variations in mode functions between these gauges, we establish that a straightforward prescription for the boundary conditions of Lorentzian worldlines unifies the treatment of Schwinger modes in all three cases. Leveraging this formalism, we derive the exact Bogoliubov coefficients and the resulting particle number without relying on the standard connection formulas involving parabolic cylinder functions. This approach is particularly significant given that closed-form solutions are generally unavailable for arbitrary electromagnetic field configurations. We contend that the real-time worldline path integral method offers a promising alternative for such complex scenarios. Furthermore, utilizing Picard-Lefschetz theory, we demonstrate how worldline instantons naturally arise from the relevant complex saddle points.

We demonstrate the existence of extensive $\mathcal C^1$ open sets of area-preserving endomorphisms on the two-torus that lack dominated splitting and exhibit non-uniform hyperbolicity, characterized by Lebesgue-almost-every point possessing both positive and negative Lyapunov exponents. In the $\mathcal C^1$ topology, these integrated exponents vary continuously with the dynamics and can be made arbitrarily distant from zero. By deforming linear endomorphisms, including expanding maps, we derive explicit real-analytic examples. This method applies to nearly every homotopy class, and the resulting examples are stably ergodic (indeed, Bernoulli), assuming the underlying linear map has no eigenvalue with modulus equal to one.

Generating separable representations through representation learning and clustering is essential for analyzing large, unstructured datasets containing only a limited number of labels. These separable representations not only enhance the classification performance of supervised models but also facilitate the generation of new labeled samples. However, most existing unsupervised and semisupervised approaches fail to exploit the small amount of available label information to improve representation quality. This paper introduces a spatiotemporal clustering framework that integrates spatial and temporal features with a constrained loss function to produce highly separable representations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method on ReaLSAT, a newly released dataset tracking surface water dynamics for over 680,000 lakes globally, which is vital for ecological and sustainability research. Using this extensive unlabeled dataset, we first illustrate the superiority of spatiotemporal representations over purely spatial or temporal ones. Subsequently, we show how incorporating a constrained loss with a few labels yields even more effective representations. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach can identify new labeled samples from the unlabeled pool using minimal labels, thereby augmenting supervised methods and improving classification outcomes.

This paper addresses a debonding model for a two-dimensional thin film, coupling the wave equation on a time-varying domain with a flow rule based on Griffith's principle governing the domain's evolution. We introduce a general definition of energy release rate, which is fundamental to formulating Griffith's criterion. Subsequently, using an existence result, we demonstrate that this definition is well-posed for radial solutions; this specific case enables the use of representation formulas characteristic of one-dimensional models.

This work investigates the local boundedness of subsolutions to nonlinear, nonuniformly elliptic equations, exemplified by the prototype $
abla \cdot (\lambda |
abla u|^{p-2}
abla u)=0$. In this model, the variable coefficient $\lambda$ (where $0 \leq \lambda$) and its reciprocal $\lambda^{-1}$ may be unbounded. By imposing specific integrability constraints on $\lambda$ and $\lambda^{-1}$ that depend on $p$ and the spatial dimension, we establish local boundedness. Furthermore, we present counterexamples regarding regularity that demonstrate these integrability conditions are sharp for all $p > 1$.

We outline the quantitative approach from the recent study arXiv:2209.09340 within a simplified framework, supplementing it with a standalone compactness argument omitted from the original paper. Our focus is on the exponential stabilization (spectral gap) of linear kinetic equations featuring degenerate thermalization, where the collision operator becomes zero in specific spatial regions. While the referenced work addresses both scattering and Fokker-Planck operators alongside external potentials and boundary conditions, these notes isolate the fundamental logic, restricting the analysis to the kinetic Fokker-Planck equation on a periodic torus with unit velocities and thermalization degeneracy. This specific case remains unaddressed by prior findings from Bernard and Salvarani (2013), Han-Kwan and Léautaud (2015), and Evans and Moyano (arXiv:1907.12836).

The independence polynomial, which stems from statistical physics as the partition function of the hard-core model, has its complex zeros linked to phase transitions and is crucial for developing efficient algorithms to approximate its evaluations. This paper establishes a direct connection between the positions of these complex zeros and the computational difficulty of approximating the polynomial. Furthermore, we link the zero locations to the chaotic dynamics of a naturally associated family of rational functions known as occupation ratios.

Machine learning increasingly influences nearly every aspect of daily life, spanning critical sectors like healthcare, finance, and energy. As reliance on these technologies grows, it becomes unavoidable that they will drive decisions affecting society at every level, from individual choices to global policies. Consequently, it is essential to prevent both intentional and unintentional biases within machine learning algorithms, particularly when their outputs carry significant, unintended consequences. While algorithmic fairness has gained significant attention in the research community, with numerous metrics and methods proposed to evaluate and ensure fairness in data and models, this paper focuses on supervised learning. We investigate the implications of optimizing classifiers for the Equal Opportunity metric, revealing that such optimization can inadvertently increase false positive rates across sensitive groups. To address this, we propose a straightforward method to mitigate such bias. We provide a rigorous analysis of our approach and validate its effectiveness using multiple real-world datasets.

What drives quantum measurement to breach Bell inequalities? We propose that even without measurement, a spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ particle (qubit) can possess a definite, continuous real-valued spin variable. Furthermore, we assume measurement maps these continuous values to the standard binary quantum outcomes ($\pm 1$) while maintaining bipartite correlations. We demonstrate that such continuous-valued spin variables can indeed be constructed. In this framework, it is the necessity of conserving correlations that forces quantum measurement to violate Bell inequalities for entangled states. We subsequently examine a statistical game modeling this process, where two parties must independently map an ensemble of real-number pairs to binary pairs ($\pm 1$) while preserving correlation. This requirement of correlation conservation ensures the game adheres to Bell's theorem, meaning no classical (local and deterministic) strategy can succeed. Conversely, a quantum strategy utilizing entangled spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ particles and local measurement circuits can win the game.

Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations explore how protostellar jets are driven within various star-forming cores, varying magnetic field strength and mass accretion rate. In strongly magnetized clouds, powerful, high-velocity jets emerge when the mass accretion rate is low ($\dot{M} \lesssim 10^{-3}\,{\rm M}_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$). Conversely, within this same low accretion rate range, jets fail to appear if the prestellar cloud's magnetic field is weak, specifically where the mass-to-flux ratio $\mu_0$ (normalized by the critical value) is approximately 5 to 10. When the accretion rate exceeds $\dot{M}\gtrsim 10^{-3}\,{\rm M}_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$, jets typically form immediately after protostar birth regardless of magnetic strength but quickly weaken and vanish; consequently, they cannot sustain low-velocity outflows if none exist prior to formation. Ultimately, significant mass ejection is absent during early accretion in both weakly magnetized environments and those with very high accretion rates. Therefore, protostars forming under these conditions will follow evolutionary trajectories distinct from the standard star formation process.

Real-world videos often feature complex actions with intrinsic connections between different action categories. This study introduces an attention-driven architecture designed to capture these action relationships for temporal action localization in untrimmed videos. Unlike prior approaches that focus on video-level action co-occurrence, our method differentiates between actions happening simultaneously and those occurring sequentially (i.e., preceding or following one another), categorizing these as action dependencies. To enhance localization accuracy, we propose a novel attention-based Multi-Label Action Dependency (MLAD) layer. This layer comprises two distinct branches: a Co-occurrence Dependency Branch to model simultaneous action relationships and a Temporal Dependency Branch to handle sequential ones. Recognizing that standard multi-label classification metrics fail to explicitly evaluate the modeling of action dependencies, we introduce new metrics that account for both co-occurrence and temporal relationships between action classes. Empirical evaluations and comprehensive analysis demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multi-label action localization benchmarks (MultiTHUMOS and Charades), yielding superior results in f-mAP and our proposed metric.

The globular cluster (GC) systems of low-mass late-type galaxies, exemplified by NGC 2403, have received limited attention. Given NGC 2403's low stellar mass ($M_{\ast}$ = 7 $\times$ 10$^{9}$ M$_{\odot}$), cosmological models anticipate it harbors few, if any, accreted GCs; furthermore, its isolation and remarkably undisturbed HI disk support this view. Utilizing candidates identified in prior literature alongside data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and Hyper Suprime-Cam, we targeted specific GCs for spectroscopic follow-up with the Keck Cosmic Web Imager. Analysis of their radial velocities and other characteristics confirmed eight genuine GCs linked to either the inner halo or the disk of this bulgeless galaxy. Stellar population analysis reveals a broad spectrum of GC ages, spanning from shortly after the Big Bang to the present. All old GCs were found to be metal-poor, with [Fe/H] $\le$ --1. The observed age--metallicity relation indicates formation over multiple Gyr from gas with a low effective yield, comparable to that seen in the SMC, potentially due to outflows of enriched material. With an expected total system of roughly 50 GCs, this study marks the initial phase in comprehensively mapping the star cluster history of NGC 2403 across both space and time.

Networks of weakly coupled oscillators have significantly advanced our comprehension of complex systems. Although such networks were initially defined by pairwise interactions, data-driven model reconstruction reveals that hypernetworks involving triplet and higher-order interactions play a dominant role. This study demonstrates that hypernetworks can arise spontaneously within pairwise nonlinear coupling systems, provided specific triplet frequency resonance conditions are met. These findings are supported by experiments with electrochemical oscillators and simulations of integrate-and-fire neurons. By establishing a comprehensive theoretical framework, we elucidate the mechanism behind emergent hypernetworks by distinguishing between permissible and prohibited frequency resonance conditions. Additionally, we show that microscopic linear (difference) coupling among units generates coupled mean fields with sufficient nonlinearity to enable hypernetwork formation. These insights clarify the widespread presence of hypernetworks and offer a constructive approach for predicting and engineering their emergence.

This research integrates Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) with a whole-body controller to achieve self-collision avoidance for the MIT Humanoid. Current reactive self-collision avoidance controllers fail to ensure collision-free paths because they neglect the robot's complete dynamics, thereby sacrificing kinematic feasibility. In contrast, the proposed CBF-WBC controller can process the robot's underactuated dynamics in real-time to ensure collision-free movement. The approach's efficacy is confirmed through simulations. First, a basic hand-reaching task demonstrates that the CBF-WBC allows the robot's hand to adjust away from an infeasible reference path to prevent self-collision. Second, the CBF-WBC is paired with a linear model predictive controller (LMPC) for dynamic locomotion, where the CBF-WBC tracks the LMPC's predictions. Walking experiments indicate that incorporating CBFs prevents leg self-collisions when footstep placements or swing trajectories from the high-level planner are infeasible for the physical robot, while also producing viable arm movements that enhance disturbance recovery.

Plasmons within nanostructured metals are extensively employed to induce intense light-matter interactions involving quantum light sources. Although the nonclassical characteristics of these quantum emitters (QEs) are well-established in this setting, quantum and surface phenomena within the plasmonic resonator are typically overlooked. In this study, we integrate the Green's tensor method with the Feibelman $d$-parameter framework to theoretically investigate how quantum surface effects in metal-dielectric layered nanostructures impact the relaxation dynamics of a nearby two-level QE. By determining that electron spill-out is the primary quantum effect in jellium-like metals, we concentrate our analysis on sodium. Our findings demonstrate a distinct splitting in the emission spectrum, signaling entry into the strong-coupling regime, and crucially, reveal non-Markovian relaxation behavior in the emitter. These results confirm that the onset of nonclassical surface effects in the metal's optical response does not inhibit strong light-matter coupling.

A density functional theory formulation is developed based on entropic inference principles. This approach applies maximum entropy to inhomogeneous fluids in thermal equilibrium, demonstrating that entropic inference yields the variational principle of DFT when particle density expectations are constrained. This methodology generates a set of trial density matrices parameterized by density, from which the optimal matrix is selected via quantum maximum entropy. Several established approximation schemes within the theory are illustrated to support this framework.

Functional linear regression has recently garnered substantial interest within the field of functional data analysis, particularly when both the response and covariates are functions. Existing literature typically addresses this scenario through either concurrent or nonconcurrent functional models. Concurrent models assume that the response at a specific domain point relies exclusively on the covariate values at that same point, whereas nonconcurrent models posit that covariate values across the entire domain influence the response at every point. To bridge the gap between these two extremes, we introduce a locally sparse functional regression model. This approach permits, though does not enforce, the functional regression coefficient to be exactly zero over certain subsets of its domain. We implement this by utilizing a suitable basis representation of the coefficient and applying an overlapping group-Lasso penalty for estimation. Furthermore, we develop efficient computational strategies grounded in majorization-minimization algorithms and examine key theoretical properties, including model support and estimator consistency. Finally, we demonstrate the method's empirical efficacy through simulation studies and two real-world applications concerning human mortality and energy market bidding.

This study examines how disorder influences topologically nontrivial states within a two-dimensional (2D) mechanical framework. We introduce a quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulator utilizing an out-of-plane spring-mass model and analytically explore the interaction between disorder and topology in both trivial and nontrivial regimes. Using the spin Bott index to characterize topological properties in disordered mechanical systems, we track its evolution as disorder increases to quantitatively demonstrate a disorder-induced transition from a topologically nontrivial QSH insulator to a trivial one. We further corroborate this topological phase transition via transient analysis in discrete lattices. Subsequently, we design a phononic crystal based on the discrete spring-mass model and numerically confirm topologically protected states along the boundary between a trivial insulator and a disordered topological QSH insulator in a continuous system. This research advances the understanding of disorder's role in 2D topological classical systems.

Although normalizing flows offer significant benefits, they are often hindered by drawbacks such as producing unrealistic outputs (like images) and failing to identify out-of-distribution samples. These limitations largely stem from the conventional training approach, which relies exclusively on the maximum likelihood principle. This study introduces a novel training framework utilizing a hybrid objective function that integrates maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) with sliced-Wasserstein distance. Experiments on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world image datasets indicate that this method enhances generative performance, improving both likelihood scores and the visual quality of generated samples. Furthermore, the proposed approach reduces the likelihood of out-of-distribution data, thereby demonstrating superior data fidelity in the resulting flows.

Although superhydrophobic surfaces (SHSs) hold potential for reducing drag, their efficacy is often hindered by trace surfactants that induce Marangoni stresses, thereby increasing drag. This study investigates soluble surfactants within a three-dimensional laminar channel flow featuring periodic SHSs on opposing walls, assuming that strong diffusion minimizes cross-channel concentration gradients. By utilizing a long-wave theory that incorporates rapid transverse Marangoni-driven flow, we develop a one-dimensional model for surfactant evolution, enabling predictions of drag reduction across various parameters. The system displays multiple regimes characterized by the interplay between Marangoni effects, bulk and interfacial diffusion, advection, and shear dispersion. We identify asymptotic regions within the high-dimensional parameter space, deriving specific approximations for drag reduction in each area and validating them against numerical simulations. Ultimately, this atlas of maps offers a comprehensive analytical framework for designing surfactant-contaminated channels with SHSs to optimize drag reduction in practical applications.

The neural tangent kernel (NTK) has recently been employed to elucidate the learning dynamics of neural networks within the large width limit. However, quantitative analyses based on NTK often necessitate network widths that are impractical, resulting in significant time and energy expenditures during both training and deployment. By utilizing a matrix factorization approach, we demonstrate the ability to achieve guarantees comparable to previous analyses while substantially lowering the resource costs for training and inference. The significance of this finding is particularly pronounced when the dimensionality of input points is comparable to the number of input points. More broadly, our work offers a framework for analyzing large width networks where dense linear layers are substituted with low-complexity factorizations, thereby mitigating the heavy reliance on large width.

Using the LHCb detector and a 5.1 fb$^{-1}$ dataset from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, this study searches for a low-mass dimuon resonance, $X$, which may decay promptly or be displaced from the primary collision vertex. To maintain minimal model dependence, event selection criteria and production mechanism assumptions are kept as simple as possible. The search for promptly decaying $X$ bosons covers a mass range starting near the dimuon threshold up to 60 GeV, accounting for non-negligible widths above 20 GeV, while the search for displaced $X \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays extends up to 3 GeV. No signal evidence was found; consequently, 90% confidence-level exclusion limits on the $X \to \mu^+\mu^-$ cross sections were established with minimal reliance on specific models. Furthermore, these findings impose world-leading constraints on GeV-scale bosons within the two-Higgs-doublet and hidden-valley frameworks.

Recent studies attributed a complex Landau spectrum in twisted bilayer graphene (away from the magic angle) to anisotropic hopping within a toy Hofstadter model. Suspecting that this anisotropy stems from unintended uniaxial strain, we have extended the Bistritzer-MacDonald framework to incorporate uniaxial heterostrain. Our findings demonstrate that such strain significantly alters the band structure, splitting the three previously degenerate van Hove points into distinct energy levels. When combined with Boltzmann magnetotransport calculations, this model successfully reproduces the previously unexplained non-saturating $B^2$ magnetoresistance observed across a wide range of densities near fillings $\nu=\pm 2$, while also predicting finer details in the experimental data that were previously overlooked. Unlike the pronounced effects seen in longitudinal resistivity, the Hall coefficient remains largely insensitive to strain, retaining a single sign change on either side of the charge neutrality point—surprisingly, this transition no longer aligns with a van Hove point. Furthermore, the theory forecasts a significant rotation of the principal axes of electrical transport as a function of filling, even when strain and band rigidity are held constant. Consequently, a more rigorous investigation into distinguishing interaction-driven nematic order from strain effects in twisted bilayer graphene appears warranted.

The weighted Tower of Hanoi represents a novel extension of the classic problem, in which the cost of transferring a disc between pegs $i$ and $j$ is defined by a positive real number $w_{ij}\geq 0$. This formulation shifts the objective from minimizing the count of moves to minimizing the aggregate cost of a move sequence. We introduce an optimal dynamic programming algorithm to address this problem, alongside an analysis of its inherent properties and its connection to other variants of the Tower of Hanoi that impose specific move restrictions.

The impact of real-world occurrences on online discourse dynamics and sentiment remains largely unexplored. Specifically, highly polarized communities, which are deeply committed to specific outcomes, typically exhibit divergent emotional sensitivities to external events. This study examines Twitter interactions during the 2018 FIFA World Cup match between Mexico and Germany to assess how live game results influenced conversation patterns and sentiment. Our findings indicate that while exogenous events had a limited effect on conversation volume and virality, they significantly impacted user responsiveness. Notably, we detected a shift in how these external events influenced fans immediately after the single goal was scored. The emotional resilience of the favored team's supporters strengthened following this shock, whereas the disadvantaged team's sentiment became more vulnerable to subsequent external events. These results underscore that the engagement and emotional resilience of online populations with strongly polarized views can be altered by high-stakes external occurrences.

The BOOSTR dataset, titled "Booster Operation Optimization Sequential Time-series for Regression," offers a cycle-by-cycle time series of readings and configurations from the instruments and actuators of Fermilab's 15~Hz Rapid-Cycling Synchrotron (RCS) Booster. This dataset captures time-series data from 55 device parameters that are critical for the high-precision regulation of the Booster's gradient magnet power supply (GMPS). To our knowledge, this represents one of the earliest well-documented public releases of accelerator device parameters. We are making it available with the expectation that it will facilitate research into artificial intelligence applications for advanced control systems, including reinforcement learning and autonomous anomaly detection.

We examine three exactly solvable models of geometric frustration. First, we analyze a one-parameter subset of the 16-vertex model, which can be mapped to a planar Ising model and solved using Fisher-Dub\'{e}at decorations. Next, we explore a one-parameter extension of Villain's fully frustrated model that interpolates between Onsager's 2D Ising model and the Villain model. Finally, we address spin ice models on a tree structure, which admit exact solutions through recursions \textit{a l\'{a} Bethe}.

Software development has benefited from automated functional testing, enabling continuous validation of functionality throughout iterative cycles. In contrast, User eXperience (UX) assessment has traditionally depended almost entirely on real-user testing, a process that is inherently slow and often acts as a bottleneck for interactive system development. To mitigate this limitation, we propose an agent-based framework for automated UX evaluation. Our approach involves developing agents equipped with fundamental problem-solving capabilities and a core affect model, which simulate artificial emotional states as they navigate various game levels. Although this research remains in its early stages, the findings presented here strongly support the potential of utilizing intelligent agents with affective computing models to automate UX testing.

Real-world datasets are often heavily imbalanced, causing significant skew in data-driven deep neural networks and making Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) a formidable challenge. Current LTR approaches rarely train Vision Transformers (ViTs) directly on Long-Tailed (LT) data, and relying on pre-trained ViT weights often results in unfair comparisons. This paper systematically examines ViT performance in LTR contexts and introduces LiVT, a method designed to train ViTs from scratch using exclusively LT data. Noting that ViTs are particularly vulnerable to LTR issues, we employ Masked Generative Pretraining (MGP) to learn generalized features. Substantial evidence indicates that MGP offers greater robustness compared to supervised training methods. Furthermore, while Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) loss performs well with ViTs, it struggles in LTR scenarios; to address this, we propose Balanced BCE (Bal-BCE), supported by strong theoretical foundations. Specifically, we derive an unbiased extension of the Sigmoid function and incorporate additional logit margins to implement it. Bal-BCE facilitates rapid ViT convergence within just a few epochs. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that combining MGP and Bal-BCE, LiVT effectively trains ViTs without requiring extra data and significantly outperforms comparable state-of-the-art methods; for instance, our ViT-B model achieves 81.0% Top-1 accuracy on the iNaturalist 2018 dataset without additional enhancements. The code is accessible at https://github.com/XuZhengzhuo/LiVT.

This work investigates the hyperbolic geometry inherent in the RNS framework of perturbative superstring theory. The objective is to establish a systematic approach for explicitly calculating both on-shell and off-shell closed superstring amplitudes involving any number of external states and loops. By leveraging hyperbolic geometry, we develop off-shell string measures that are compatible with gluing, achieved through the definition of local coordinates near external punctures and a corresponding distribution of picture-changing operators. These amplitudes adhere to the necessary off-shell factorization conditions. Consequently, this formalism enables the explicit computation of string-theory amplitudes once the relevant string measures are formulated using specific coordinates on Teichmüller space, known as Fenchel-Nielsen coordinates.

Semiconductor platforms, such as quantum dot spin qubits, are rising as a promising architecture for quantum information storage and processing, yet they face significant hurdles including charge noise from electron interactions and scalability challenges. This study demonstrates that a magnetic field gradient can be applied to a semiconductor quantum dot array to generate a local quantum coherent dynamical $\ell$-bit, which serves as a potential logical qubit. These dynamical $\ell$-bits drive the system into a many-body localized state. We prove that these states and the associated many-body localization remain protected against various noises, including phonons, for extended durations, provided the electron-phonon interaction is not strictly non-local. Furthermore, we present thermalization-based self-correcting logical gates, representing an advancement beyond the conventional framework of decoherence-free and noiseless subsystems. Consequently, this work establishes a new avenue for passive quantum error correction in semiconductor-based quantum computing.

Deep Neural Networks remain susceptible to minor, adversarially engineered perturbations, with current leading defenses relying on variants of adversarial training. This paper presents a fundamentally distinct approach that trains exclusively on clean data: a sparse coding-based frontend that substantially weakens adversarial attacks before they reach the classifier. Evaluated on the CIFAR-10 dataset across various attack types (including L∞, L2, and L1 bounded attacks), our method demonstrates significant potential as a versatile general-purpose defense strategy.

By leveraging the relationship between pseudogroups and inverse quantal frames, along with the recent characterization of Morita equivalence for these frames via biprincipal bisheaves, we establish a definition of Morita equivalence for pseudogroups and examine its applications. Specifically, two pseudogroups are Morita equivalent if and only if their associated localic étale groupoids are. We also highlight the evident parallels between our proposed definition and the standard concept of strong Morita equivalence for $C^{\ast}$-algebras, which yield several concrete results.

Discrete dissipative coupled systems display intricate phenomena, including chaos, spatiotemporal intermittence, and chimeras. We construct and analyze chimera states, manifesting as both stationary and dynamical confined states within a chain of parametrically driven sites featuring onsite damping and cubic nonlinearity. This system is described by a discrete parametrically driven damped nonlinear Schrödinger equation. In these chimeras, the filled regions exhibit quasi-periodic or chaotic dynamics, characterized by the temporal evolution of the total norm (and its power spectrum) and the largest Lyapunov exponent. Combining systematic numerical simulations with analytical findings, we identify parameter space regions populated by various stable localized states. Furthermore, we detect a phase transition shifting from stationary disorder states to spatially confined dynamical chaotic states. Key system parameters include the forcing strength and detuning, as well as the lattice coupling constant.

Weakly supervised object localization (WSOL) focuses on determining object positions within an image using solely image-level category labels. Standard image classification models face three primary hurdles in localization: (a) they often focus on highly discriminative features, restricting the localization map to a tiny area; (b) the resulting maps are class-agnostic, causing the model to highlight objects from multiple classes simultaneously; and (c) performance is degraded by background noise. To address these issues, we propose ViTOL, which implements two key modifications. First, we utilize a vision-based transformer with self-attention and incorporate a patch-based attention dropout layer (p-ADL) to broaden the localization map's coverage. Second, we employ a gradient attention rollout mechanism to produce class-dependent attention maps. We validate our approach through extensive quantitative, qualitative, and ablation studies on the ImageNet-1K and CUB datasets. ViTOL achieves state-of-the-art MaxBoxAcc-V2 scores of 70.47% and 73.17% on these datasets, respectively. The code is accessible at https://github.com/Saurav-31/ViTOL.

$G$-equivariant convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) constitute a geometric deep learning framework tailored for data residing on homogeneous $G$-spaces $\mathcal{M}$. By inherently respecting the global symmetries within $\mathcal{M}$, GCNNs enhance the learning process. This paper investigates GCNNs defined on homogeneous spaces $\mathcal{M} = G/K$, specifically where $G$ is a unimodular Lie group and $K$ is a compact subgroup. We establish that homogeneous vector bundles provide the appropriate mathematical framework for GCNNs. Furthermore, employing reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, we derive an exact condition for representing $G$-equivariant layers as convolutional layers. This condition is subsequently reformulated as a bandwidth criterion, yielding more robust results for certain groups.

Hadron beauty decays provide a distinctive experimental environment for investigating charmonium and charmonium-like phenomena, including the $\chi_{c1}(3872)$ meson, various exotic states, and the tensor D-wave $\psi_2(3823)$ states. Nevertheless, the fundamental properties of many exotic charmonium-like candidates remain unidentified. This presentation details recent LHCb findings concerning b-hadron transitions to charmonium states, derived from extensive datasets gathered during the Run 1 and Run 2 operational periods. Key outcomes include the most accurate determination of the $\chi_{c1}(3872)$ mass and width via $B^{+} \to J/\psi\pi^{+}\pi^{-}K^{+}$ decays, the detection of a resonant feature labeled X(4740) within the $J/\psi \phi$ mass spectrum from $B^{0}_{s} \to J/\psi\pi^{+}\pi^{-}K^{+}K^{-}$ decays, and a high-precision measurement of the $B^{0}_{s}$ meson mass.

This paper introduces a new computing paradigm known as the \emph{Probe Machine}, which operates as a fully-parallel system unlike the Turing Machine. Instead of processing linearly adjacent data pairs sequentially, the Probe Machine handles multiple data pairs simultaneously. The authors define this model mathematically as a 9-tuple comprising a data library, probe library, data controller, probe controller, probe operation, computing platform, detector, true solution storage, and residue collector. The study analyzes the Probe Machine's computational capabilities, demonstrating that the Turing Machine is merely a special instance of this broader model. Furthermore, the paper revisits two NP-complete problems—Graph Coloring and Hamilton Cycles—and proposes algorithms based on the Probe Machine framework capable of enumerating all solutions for each problem using a single probe operation. The authors also indicate that this model can be realized through nano-DNA probe technologies.
