Given that electronic computers based on the Turing Machine vastly outperform the human brain in computational power, a natural inquiry emerges: can future Probe Machine-based computers surpass human cognitive abilities in additional domains beyond raw processing speed?

This study introduces r2SCAN-D4, a density functional approximation that integrates a regularized, strongly constrained, and appropriately normed semilocal density functional [J. Sun, A. Ruzsinszky, and J. P. Perdew, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 036402 (2015)] with the most recent semi-classical London dispersion correction. While maintaining the computational efficiency of generalized gradient approximations, r2SCAN-D4 achieves accuracy comparable to hybrid functionals for general chemical applications. We validate its numerical robustness through real-world scenarios and benchmarks covering molecular geometries, thermochemistry of main group and organo-metallic systems, and non-covalent interactions in supramolecular complexes and molecular crystals. The method yields bond length errors of only 0.8% for both main group and transition metal systems, matching the performance of hybrid functionals for main group molecules and surpassing them for transition metal complexes. On the extensive GMTKN55 database of chemical properties, r2SCAN-D4 achieves an exceptionally low weighted mean absolute deviation (WTMAD2) of 7.5 kcal/mol, a result that extends to metal-organic reactions with a mean absolute deviation (MAD) of 3.3 kcal/mol. Furthermore, its versatility across organic and metal-organic systems translates to condensed matter applications, where lattice energies of molecular crystals fall within chemical accuracy, with errors under 1 kcal/mol.

Effective filtering of unwanted light signals is essential for neutral atom ensemble-based quantum memories. We present an efficient frequency filter utilizing a $^{85}$Rb vapor cell with a buffer gas, which suppresses both residual laser light and noise photons by nearly two orders of magnitude while incurring minimal loss to the single photons used in our cold $^{87}$Rb quantum memory. This straightforward, passive device delivers an additional 18 dB of attenuation for pump lasers and erroneous spontaneous emissions for every 1 dB of single-photon signal loss. Furthermore, incorporating this frequency filter enhances the non-classical correlations and readout efficiency of our quantum memory by approximately 35%.

We explore the most effective ways to represent mathematical entities using precisely defined symbol sets. Our analysis investigates the insights gained regarding these entities from their chosen syntax and symbols. A central focus of this research is on discrete sets, especially the natural numbers, yielding findings that characterize how these numbers are presented within specific symbolic frameworks and what such presentations reveal about their inherent properties. We will establish limits and restrictions concerning the dimensions and form of these presentations, link established problems from other mathematical domains to issues arising in this context, and demonstrate why this line of inquiry is likely to yield significant and engaging outcomes.

Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging generates high-contrast, detailed visualizations of organs and tissues; however, its lengthy acquisition process renders it susceptible to motion artifacts. To mitigate this, numerous recent methods have been devised to reconstruct fully sampled images from partial measurements, thereby accelerating the imaging process. Nevertheless, the majority of these techniques concentrate on single-modality reconstruction, often overlooking the potential correlations between different imaging modalities. In response, we introduce the Multi-modal Aggregation network for MR Image recOnstruction with auxiliary modality (MARIO). This framework leverages a fully sampled auxiliary modality to uncover complementary representations, which then hierarchically guide the reconstruction of the target modality. By selectively aggregating multi-modal information, MARIO achieves comprehensive, multi-scale, and multi-modal feature fusion, resulting in superior artifact removal. Extensive evaluations on the IXI and fastMRI datasets confirm that our proposed method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in MR image reconstruction.

This study introduces a seizure detection framework that integrates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with factor graphs enhanced by mutual information features derived from a neural network. Specifically, neural mutual information estimation is utilized to quantify correlations across various electroencephalogram (EEG) channels, serving as primary features. Additionally, a 1D-CNN extracts supplementary features directly from the EEG signals, and these combined inputs are used to calculate the probability of seizure occurrence. Finally, learned factor graphs are applied to model temporal dependencies within the signal, where factor nodes are trained using both the neural mutual information and 1D-CNN features. The proposed approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance, validated through 6-fold leave-four-patients-out cross-validation.

This study introduces a co-scaling grid formalism implemented within the Athena++ magnetohydrodynamics code. Leveraging flow symmetries found in astrophysical scenarios characterized by expansion, contraction, and center-of-mass motion, the grid evolves with the same temporal order as the fluid variables. Users define grid evolution laws that may operate independently of fluid dynamics. When applied to standard hydrodynamic benchmarks, this approach yields superior results and enhanced computational efficiency relative to fixed-grid methods.

We establish novel well-posedness results for dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev--Petviashvili I equations on $\mathbb{R}^2$, a family bridging the classical and fifth-order KP-I equations. For sufficiently strong dispersion, we demonstrate global well-posedness within $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$. This achievement relies on integrating resonance and transversality arguments with Strichartz estimates and a nonlinear Loomis--Whitney inequality. Furthermore, we show that in the regime of small dispersion, Picard iteration fails to solve the equations; consequently, we employ an additional frequency-dependent time localization technique.

A graph is considered regularizable if edge weights can be assigned such that every node achieves an identical degree, provided the target degree is non-zero. While literature has extensively examined graphs with positive or non-negative weights, this study introduces and analyzes the concept of arbitrarily regularizable graphs. Specifically, we derive the necessary and sufficient topological conditions for both the graph and its adjacency matrix to be regularizable. Furthermore, we assess the computational complexity of this regularization problem by modeling it as a linear programming framework.

This paper addresses position reconstruction using signals from segmented detectors. A straightforward simulation demonstrates that the centre-of-gravity method yields significant bias when the charge or light distribution width at electrodes or photodetectors is smaller than the read-out pitch. To address this, a new method is introduced that eliminates such bias for events generating signals across two or more read-out channels, thereby enhancing position resolution. Additionally, this approach estimates the position-response function for each event, revealing variations in its width across reconstructed positions that can reach an order of magnitude. A rapid Monte Carlo program is also detailed, simulating signals from silicon pixel detectors traversed by charged particles at various angles. This simulation incorporates local energy-loss fluctuations, position-dependent electric fields, charge carrier diffusion, electronic noise, and clustering charge thresholds. Finally, the simulation is validated through comparison with test-beam data, and its results alongside the centre-of-gravity method are evaluated using the proposed reconstruction technique.

This study employs a computational framework utilizing interface finite elements with Embedded Profiles for Joint Roughness (MPJR) to analyze viscoelastic contact issues involving indenters of arbitrary complex geometries. Building upon MPJR elements originally designed for partial slip scenarios, this work extends their application to accommodate finite sliding displacements. The methodology is demonstrated through a case study of a periodic interaction between a sinusoidal profile and a viscoelastic layer of limited thickness, specifically examining the impact of three rheological models based on Prony series (with one, two, or three arms) used to approximate real polymer behavior. The approach successfully predicts the entire transient phase, spanning from initial normal contact through the progression from full stick to full slip, and finally to gross sliding. A detailed investigation is conducted on how viscoelastic model approximations and sliding velocities influence the results. Ultimately, this proposed method addresses a challenging class of problems that other techniques struggle with, including the analysis of generic indenter profiles, the simulation of transitions from partial to gross slip via finite sliding, and the concurrent assessment of dissipative mechanisms such as viscoelastic dissipation and energy losses from interface friction.

This study demonstrates how unsupervised sense representations can enhance hypernymy extraction. We introduce a technique that identifies disambiguated hypernymy relations by propagating hypernyms to synonym sets (synsets), generating embeddings for these groups, and defining sense-specific connections between corresponding synsets. Assessments on two gold-standard datasets for English and Russian indicate that our approach effectively detects hypernymy relationships that standard Hearst patterns and Wiktionary resources fail to identify in their respective languages.

Symbolic regression uncovers correlations to determine key physical parameters governing material properties through nonlinear analytical formulas. However, the rapid expansion of the expression pool as complexity increases hampers efficiency. We address this issue using a hierarchical strategy where identified expressions serve as inputs for deriving more intricate formulas. This framework notably facilitates knowledge transfer between properties, thereby emphasizing underlying physical connections. We validate this approach by applying the Sure-Independence-Screening-and-Sparsifying-Operator (SISSO) method to find expressions linked to the lattice constant and cohesive energy, which are subsequently employed to model the bulk modulus of ABO3 perovskites.

While art heritage cities attract significant tourism, overcrowding has emerged as a critical challenge for many. This paper tackles the issue of modeling and analytically examining tourist movement through the narrow streets of a historic urban center. We first introduce a mean field game framework that incorporates both continuous and switching decision variables to represent a tourist's location and their chosen point of interest, respectively. We demonstrate the existence of a mean field equilibrium, which functions as a Nash equilibrium when the number of players is infinite. Subsequently, we analyze an optimization problem for an external controller designed to steer the system toward a desirable mean field equilibrium.

This paper investigates the identification of dynamic laws that govern the temporal evolution of time series, providing both finite difference and differential equation representations. Additionally, we explore the imposition of necessary symmetries, such as time reversal, on these laws, and we analyze the compression efficiency of linear laws when applied to audio data.

Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) provide a promising avenue for identifying potential causal genes or disease risk factors by utilizing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as instrumental variables (IVs). Nevertheless, traditional methods often rely on linear causal assumptions, driven by both simplification and the current reliance on GWAS summary statistics. This study introduces a new model for transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) capable of integrating nonlinear relationships among IVs, exposures, and outcomes. The proposed approach remains robust despite violations of standard IV validity assumptions and accommodates the use of summary data. By separating the estimation of marginal causal effects from nonlinear transformations—using sliced inverse regression and sparse instrumental variable regression for the former, and ratio-adjusted inverse regression for the latter—we establish a rigorous inferential framework. Applying this method to ADNI gene expression and IGAP GWAS summary data revealed 18 Alzheimer's disease-associated causal genes, including *APOE* and *TOMM40*, as well as seven additional genes overlooked by two-stage least squares methods restricted to linear models. These results indicate that nonlinear modeling is essential to fully leverage IV regression for detecting potentially nonlinear gene-trait links. We also release an accompanying Python library, nl-causal (https://github.com/nl-causal/nonlinear-causal), which implements the described methodology.

Census 2021 might be the final census in the UK. For population statistics in the years immediately following 2021, the proposed framework involves supplementing existing administrative data with a continuous coverage survey, targeting a yearly sample of approximately 0.5 million addresses, though specific methodological details remain undecided. Concurrently, the ONS is exploring alternative methods to better leverage relevant administrative data. This report presents the core concepts of a rolling approach for providing UK neighbourhood population statistics beyond 2021, situated within the broader context of creating a sustainable future for official statistics that offers faster response times, richer detail, and improved long-term cost efficiency.

Mathematical and numerical modeling, though crucial, is frequently overlooked in biology curricula. Our experience demonstrates that Glowscript effectively facilitates the introduction of computer simulations to students, particularly because its integrated graphics and graphing features offer immediate feedback. As a web-based variant of Python that executes directly in standard browsers, Glowscript also allows learners to seamlessly embed their simulations on external platforms. This article presents several implementations of Glowscript within an undergraduate computational biology course, with the aim of encouraging other science educators to adopt this tool in their classrooms.

Jacobs introduced definitions for (weak, strong, split) generic objects within fibered categories. Leveraging his concept of (split) generic objects, he constructed a variety of significant fibrational structures relevant to categorical logic and computer science, such as higher-order fibrations, polymorphic fibrations, $\lambda$2-fibrations, triposes, and others. We note that a split generic object does not necessarily qualify as a generic object under these specific definitions, and that the rigorous criteria for polymorphic fibrations, triposes, and similar structures exclude certain fundamental cases; for example, the fibered preorder derived from a partial combinatory algebra in realizability fails to constitute a tripos in this framework. Consequently, we suggest a revised terminology alignment that highlights the most prevalent forms of generic objects found in nature, particularly within the study of internal categories, triposes, and the denotational semantics of polymorphism. Furthermore, we introduce a novel class of acyclic generic objects, inspired by recent advances in higher category theory and the semantics of homotopy type theory, which extends the realignment property of universes to arbitrary fibrations.

We introduce a novel framework that extends neural network parameters from standard values to those within $C^*$-algebras. Since $C^*$-algebras generalize the space of complex numbers—exemplified by continuous functions on compact spaces—this approach allows for the continuous combination of multiple models and the application of functional tools like regression and integration. As a result, we can efficiently learn data features and adapt models continuously to various problems. We demonstrate the framework's efficacy in practical tasks such as density estimation and few-shot learning, showing its ability to extract meaningful features even from limited sample sizes. Ultimately, this work underscores the potential of applying $C^*$-algebra theory to broader neural network architectures.

A Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) state represents a localized state within the superconducting gap, created by a magnetic impurity. Recent experiments utilized an STM tip to adjust the exchange interaction between an Fe adatom and the ${\rm FeTe}_{0.55}{\rm Se}_{0.45}$ superconductor, which features a nontrivial $Z_2$ band structure and topological surface states. As the tip approached the isolated Fe adatom, the in-gap state's energy shifted, revealing two anomalous zero-energy crossings that cannot be attributed to the coupling between the magnetic impurity and the superconducting topological surface Dirac cone. In this work, we provide both numerical and analytical investigations of YSR states in superconductors with nontrivial $Z_2$ bands, identifying the origin of these two zero-energy crossings as dependent on the exchange coupling between the magnetic impurity and bulk states. Furthermore, we examine the influence of topological surface states, compare in-gap states to those in systems with trivial $Z_2$ bands, and analyze the spin-polarization of YSR states to guide future experimental measurements.

This study introduces a compact Inverse Compton Light Source (ICLS) design that surpasses both traditional laboratory-scale sources and other compact ICLS configurations by several orders of magnitude in flux and brilliance. The system leverages inverse Compton scattering between a laser pulse with an rms duration of roughly 2/3 picoseconds and an electron beam characterized by extremely low emittance. The accelerator architecture consists of a superconducting radiofrequency (SRF) reentrant gun followed by four double-spoke SRF cavities, with three quadrupole magnets positioned after the linac to focus the electron beam at the interaction point (IP). The total distance from the cathode surface to the IP remains under 6 meters. The cathode generates electron bunches with a length of a few picoseconds and a charge of 10 pC. The incident laser features a 1 MW circulating power, a 1-micron wavelength, and a 3.2-micron spot size at the IP. To ensure high flux despite the relatively low bunch charge, the source operates at a 100 MHz repetition rate. Projected X-ray parameters include an energy of 12 keV, a total flux of $1.4\times10^{14}$ photons per second, a flux of $2.1\times10^{11}$ ph/(s-0.1%BW) within a 0.1% bandwidth, and an average brilliance of $2.2\times10^{15}$ ph/(s-mm$^2$-mrad$^2$-0.1%BW).

Carroll symmetry represents a potent feature of generic null surfaces, effectively substituting the standard Poincaré algebra with a variant characterized by a vanishing speed of light. These symmetries have achieved widespread application in the physics of null manifolds, appearing across diverse contexts from black hole horizons to condensed matter systems where Fermi velocities vanish. This study focuses on fermions residing on two-dimensional ($2d$) null manifolds, systematically investigating the Carroll-invariant structure of their associated field theories. We demonstrate that the free massless versions of these fermions possess $2d$ Conformal Carroll symmetry, which is equivalent to the $3d$ Bondi-Metzner-Sachs (BMS) algebra. Given the manifold's degenerate nature, we identify two distinct classes of Clifford Algebras and establish that two separate fermion actions exist in two dimensions. We analyze the discrete and continuous symmetries of both theories and perform quantization using the highest weight representation of the vacuum. Furthermore, we examine how the symmetries of $2d$ free fermion conformal field theories can be continuously deformed via infinite boosts or degenerate linear coordinate transformations, resulting in the corresponding BMS invariant theory at singular points.

A core challenge in quantum thermodynamics involves extracting energy from a source and depositing it into a suitable battery. These operations—work extraction and charging—function as cyclic Hamiltonian processes applied to individual quantum systems. While passive states exist where energy cannot be reduced via unitary transformations, it is reasonable to assume that a battery not yet fully charged can have its energy increased unitarily. However, different unitaries that raise the average energy by an identical amount can vary significantly in precision, fluctuations, and charging power, and some may be practically unfeasible. Consequently, understanding the capabilities of implementable transformations is critical. This study examines the constraints on battery charging when limited to the family of feasible Gaussian unitaries. We derive optimal protocols for both general unitary operations and the more accessible Gaussian subset. Our results indicate that while practical Gaussian battery charging underperforms compared to theoretical limits, it still achieves asymptotically vanishing relative charge variances and fluctuations.

We introduce a greedy algorithm designed to address binary classification tasks in scenarios where datasets are either too small or unrepresentative, and acquiring additional data is infeasible. This approach is especially valuable for training compact models that struggle with generalization. The method leverages a pre-trained model with relaxed accuracy requirements, employs an iterative hyperparameter pruning strategy, and utilizes a function for data generation. We provide an analysis of the algorithm's correctness and runtime complexity under ideal conditions, along with an extension applicable to deep neural networks. In the ideal case, the asymptotic complexity is bounded by $O\left(|\Theta^2|\left(\log{|\Theta|} + |\theta^2| + T_f\left(| D|\right)\right) + \bar{S}|\Theta||{E}|\right)$, where $|{\Theta}|$ denotes the number of hyperparameters $\theta$ to explore; $|{E}|$ and $|{D}|$ represent the sizes of the evaluation and training sets, respectively; $\bar{S}$ and $\bar{f}$ indicate the inference times for the trained and candidate models; and $T_f({|{D}|})$ is a polynomial function of $|{D}|$ and $\bar{f}$. Under these conditions, the algorithm yields a solution that improves upon simple enumeration and training by a factor of $1 \leq r \leq 2(1 - {2^{-|{\Theta}|}})$. Furthermore, our analysis of the generating function includes a proof that, under specific assumptions, if an open cover of $D$ shares the same homology as the manifold supporting the underlying probability distribution, then $D$ is learnable, and the converse also holds.

This study evaluates the thermodynamic consistency of entropic-force cosmological models, utilizing a generalized entropy that scales with an arbitrary power of the Hubble radius. This framework encompasses the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy (area-proportional) and the nonadditive $S_{\delta=3/2}$-entropy (volume-proportional) as specific instances. A critical requirement for entropic-force cosmology to serve as a viable alternative to standard cosmology is establishing a physical principle that defines the requisite entropy and temperature. We derive the universe's horizon temperature by enforcing the preservation of the Legendre structure in thermodynamics. Furthermore, we assess thermodynamically consistent entropic-force models against supernovae data, deriving constraints to optimize the alternative entropies and temperatures associated with the Hubble screen. Our findings indicate that the resulting temperature deviates from the Hawking temperature.

Robot learning represents a highly promising frontier for advancing automation and machine intelligence, with future systems expected to autonomously master skills, model their surroundings, and engage with them. Although simulation has extensively covered these areas, real-world robot learning research remains constrained by unique challenges such as sensor and actuator noise, the necessity for safe exploration, non-stationary dynamics, difficulties in autonomous environment resetting, and the high costs associated with prolonged experiments. Without scalable solutions to these issues, the vision of learning complex tasks involving intricate hand-eye coordination and rich physical contact will likely remain unattainable outside controlled laboratory settings. We propose dual-arm robotic configurations as a platform to address these limitations. These setups facilitate safe data collection for skill acquisition and perception training through robot supervision, while also streamlining environmental resetting. Additionally, adversarial learning could enhance the generalization of robot learning algorithms by maximizing exploration via game-theoretic objectives while maintaining safety through collaborative task spaces. This paper examines the potential advantages of this configuration alongside the associated challenges and future research directions.

We present ObSynth, an interactive platform that utilizes domain knowledge within large language models (LLMs) to assist users in creating object models from high-level natural language inputs. This approach exemplifies specification reification, transforming abstract or vague descriptions into concrete forms. A user study evaluating ObSynth yielded three primary insights: first, models generated with ObSynth exhibit greater detail, as the system frequently fills in fields users might otherwise overlook. Second, most objects, methods, and fields produced by ObSynth are retained in the final model, underscoring the high quality of the generated components. Third, ObSynth shifted participants' workflows; they focused on verifying the correctness of synthesized parts rather than generating them from scratch, although the tool did not decrease the overall time required to build object models.

Kramers' theorem guarantees double degeneracy in the energy spectra of time-reversal symmetric fermionic systems possessing half-integer total spin. In this study, we extend this analysis beyond closed systems to explore Kramers' degeneracy within open, non-equilibrium environments. We demonstrate that for interacting fermionic systems, Kramers' degeneracy corresponds to the degeneracy of spectra across different spins alongside the vanishing of the inter-spin spectrum. We identify that the violation of Kramers' degeneracy in time-reversal symmetric open quantum systems is intrinsically linked to the system's ability to reach thermal equilibrium. Specifically, following a sudden coupling to an environment that preserves time-reversal symmetry, a Kramers doublet undergoes initial energy splitting followed by a recovery process. Using a concrete model of interacting fermions, we verified both the violation and revival of Kramers' degeneracy, observing that degeneracy is restored once local thermalization occurs. In contrast, for time-reversal symmetry $\tilde{\cal T}$ where $\tilde{\cal T}^2=1$, we find that while spectral degeneracy between different spins exhibits violation and revival, the inter-spin spectral function remains non-zero. Furthermore, we prove that degeneracy in the spectral function protected by unitary symmetry is maintained indefinitely.

Driven by technological progress, intelligent systems are rapidly evolving to analyze complex data relationships for accurate predictions and classifications. AI-based frameworks are fundamentally transforming the healthcare sector. These systems, constructed using robust machine learning and deep learning models, facilitate early disease detection and serve as a valuable supplementary tool for clinical practitioners and surgeons. By leveraging ML and DL, these systems streamline diagnostic processes derived from both clinical records and medical imagery, offering substantial support to clinicians and optimizing workflows. Capable of mimicking human cognition, they can even identify conditions that elude human detection. This paper presents a survey of ML and DL applications across sixteen medical specialties, including Dental medicine, Haematology, Surgery, Cardiology, Pulmonology, Orthopedics, Radiology, Oncology, General medicine, Psychiatry, Endocrinology, Neurology, Dermatology, Hepatology, Nephrology, Ophthalmology, and Drug discovery. Beyond the survey, the paper examines advancements in medical practices driven by these technologies and evaluates their impact on medical professionals.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, individuals turned to digital news outlets for information. To understand how to design these platforms to better support users during a crisis, we conducted a two-week diary study involving 22 participants from across the United States. The participants' news consumption evolved through two distinct phases: the \textbf{seeking} stage, characterized by heightened general consumption driven by three key informational needs—to locate, comprehend, and verify relevant news; and the \textbf{sustaining} stage, where managing the emotional impact of the news became equally critical as the pursuit of information. By gathering design ideas from participants, we identified six themes for creating digital news platforms that offer enhanced informational and emotional support during crises. Consequently, this study contributes a model illustrating how user needs evolve over time regarding crisis news engagement, along with specific design concepts to address those needs in each phase.

This paper introduces a novel, straightforward degree-based estimator designed to approximate the size of the maximum matching in graphs with bounded arboricity. For graphs where the arboricity is at most $\alpha$, this estimator provides an approximation within a factor of $\alpha+2$. Specifically for planar graphs, the method achieves a superior $3.5$-factor approximation. Leveraging this estimator, we derive new results for approximating maximum matching sizes in both streaming and distributed computing frameworks. In the context of vertex-arrival streams, we propose a randomized algorithm requiring $O(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\epsilon^2}\log n)$ space to achieve a $(3.5+\epsilon)$-factor approximation for planar graphs with $n$ vertices. Furthermore, in the vertex-partition model, we present a simultaneous protocol that approximates the matching size within $(3.5+\epsilon)$ using $O(\frac{n^{2/3}}{\epsilon^2}\log n)$ communication per player. Compared to prior estimators, our approach eliminates the need to know the graph's arboricity in advance and offers an improved approximation factor for planar graphs.

We forecast the volume of liquid retrieved from prismatic channels of varying geometries after gas displacement, noting that this recovery factor is heavily influenced by the contact angle where gas-liquid interfaces intersect the channel walls. We demonstrate that normalizing the contact angle by a critical value specific to the channel geometry generates a master curve for the recovery factor. Furthermore, our numerical simulations using the Surface Evolver are corroborated by theoretical analyses of capillary entry pressure in triangular and rectangular channels, as well as the interface configuration in a "scalloped" triangular channel created between three parallel cylinders.

This study employs QCD sum rules to examine the spectra of prospective tetracharm and tetrabottom baryonium, defined as baryon-antibaryon states. Our analysis incorporates non-perturbative contributions up to dimension 10. Numerical findings suggest the existence of four possible tetracharm baryonium states with masses of $(7.33\pm0.12)$, $(7.42\pm0.13)$, $(7.68\pm0.17)$, and $(7.76\pm0.12)$ GeV, corresponding to the quantum numbers $0^{-+}$, $1^{--}$, $0^{++}$, and $1^{++}$, respectively. The associated tetrabottom partners are predicted to lie at $(19.41\pm 0.15)$, $(19.48\pm 0.15)$, $(19.77\pm 0.19)$, and $(19.84\pm 0.19)$ GeV. Furthermore, we analyze the spectra of the $\bar{\Xi}_{bc}\Xi_{bc}$ and $\bar{\Xi}_{cc}\Xi_{bb}$ baryonium states, which fall within the ranges of $13.77-14.40$ GeV and $13.39-14.14$ GeV, respectively. Finally, we investigate potential baryonium decay modes that could be detected in LHC experiments.

Let $H$ represent a graph and $p$ an integer. The edge blow-up $H^p$ is defined as the graph resulting from substituting every edge of $H$ with a distinct copy of the complete graph $K_p$. Denoting $C_k$ and $P_k$ as the cycle and path of length $k$, respectively, this paper establishes sharp upper bounds for $ex(n,K_3,C_3^3)$, derives the exact value for $ex(n,K_3,P_3^3)$, and identifies the specific graphs that achieve these bounds.

We demonstrate that executing ideal projective measurements on quantum systems is unattainable with finite resources. By pinpointing three core characteristics of such measurements, we reveal that resource constraints allow only one of these features to be preserved. While our framework applies universally to any system and measuring device (pointer), we illustrate the concept using an explicit $N$-particle pointer model. For pointers that accurately replicate system statistics, we derive tight analytic formulas for the associated energy cost, which comprises two components: the expense of preparing the pointer in the requisite state and the cost of a global system-pointer interaction to establish correlation. Our findings indicate that even with perfect control over the interaction, achieving flawless correlation demands infinite energy. Furthermore, we outline protocols for attaining optimal correlation under finite resource limitations for the most general system and pointer Hamiltonians, expressing our results as fundamental bounds based on the dimensions of these systems.

This paper introduces a flexible framework for "safe screening," a recently developed technique used in sparse optimization to identify irrelevant variables early in the process. Built upon Fenchel-Rockafellar duality, this framework enables the derivation of a robust safe screening rule tailored for norm-regularized least squares, which we term "dynamic Sasvi." This new rule generalizes the original Sasvi method but eliminates the need to solve a more strongly regularized problem exactly, ensuring its practical reliability. Both theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that dynamic Sasvi can eliminate more features and accelerate solvers compared to existing screening rules.

Love waves, which are antiplane elastic waves traveling along the surface of a heterogeneous medium, are described by a Helmholtz-type scalar equation under time-harmonic conditions. By leveraging the invariance of this governing equation under arbitrary in-plane coordinate transformations, we design broadband cloaks to conceal surface defects. Specifically, using transformation elastodynamics, we calculate the required anisotropic, position-dependent mechanical properties for ideal cloaks capable of hiding triangular and parabolic defects. Both dispersion analysis and time-harmonic numerical simulations confirm the validity of this approach. Furthermore, we develop practical cloaks using layered monoclinic materials whose homogenized properties match those of the ideal designs. Time-harmonic simulations demonstrate that these layered cloaks significantly reduce the scattered fields generated by the defects.

We hypothesize that vigorous convection during the core helium flash of low-mass red giant branch (RGB) stars generates waves traveling into the envelope, depositing enough energy to trigger expansion and brightening. Drawing on research regarding wave excitation by massive star convection prior to core-collapse supernovae, our analysis using the MESA stellar evolution code indicates that this wave energy drives an expansion of tens to hundreds of solar radii within a few years. Although the star brightens significantly, the resulting increase in radius and luminosity is expected to markedly boost mass loss and dust production. This dust shifts the stellar appearance toward the infrared, potentially making the star fainter in visible light and creating the signature of a faint red transient event lasting months to years. Furthermore, we propose that such envelope expansion could cause stars nearing the end of the RGB phase to engulf exoplanets; the enlarged envelope possesses reduced binding energy, enabling planets with several Jupiter masses or more, as well as brown dwarfs, to survive the common envelope phase. This mechanism offers an explanation for the planet orbiting the white dwarf WD1856+534 (TIC 267574918) and the white dwarf–brown dwarf binary system ZTFJ003855.0+203025.5.

Historically, sarcasm arising from numerical elements within text has been cited as a limitation of automated sarcasm detection systems. This paper introduces the first study focused on identifying sarcasm specifically within numbers, illustrated by the example "Love waking up at 4 am." We examine the challenges involved and propose three methodologies—rule-based, machine learning, and deep learning—to detect sarcasm in numeric portions of text. Our deep learning model surpasses four previous sarcasm detection studies, as well as rule-based and machine learning methods, achieving an F1-score of 0.93 on a tweet dataset. These results demonstrate that focusing on text containing numbers can enhance the state-of-the-art in sarcasm detection.

Real-world linear systems often face measurement data contaminated by both significant sparse corruptions and pervasive small-scale noise, which frequently renders standard solvers ineffective. In such scenarios, least squares solutions deviate significantly from the target, and identifying the underlying consistent system becomes challenging. QuantileRK, an iterative projective method within the Kaczmarz family, is known for exponential convergence even in the presence of arbitrarily large sparse corruptions. This paper extends that analysis to scenarios involving both corruptions and noise affecting every data point, proving that QuantileRK maintains its convergence rate up to a specific error threshold. The study provides both theoretical and experimental evidence highlighting the robustness of QuantileRK.

This paper introduces an efficient algorithm for generating point sets suitable for quasi-Monte Carlo integration rules applied to weighted Korobov classes. The proposed method is a reduced fast component-by-component digit-by-digit (CBC-DBD) algorithm, which is particularly effective when the weights within the function space decay rapidly. A key benefit of this approach is that, provided appropriate conditions are met regarding the integrand, the computational cost remains independent of the problem's dimension. Specifically designed for constructing lattice point sets, the resulting lattice rules are applicable across various function spaces. We demonstrate that the integration rules produced by our algorithm achieve error bounds with an almost optimal convergence rate. Additionally, we detail an efficient implementation that significantly accelerates a previously known CBC-DBD algorithm, with these improvements validated through numerical results.

Recent publications have asserted an exact combinatorial solution for a variant of the Marcus-Lushnikov aggregation model. This model begins with a finite collection of monomers, where, at each discrete time step, two aggregates are selected based on size-dependent probabilities and irreversibly merged into a larger mass. The claimed result provides a formula for the complete probability distribution of all possible size configurations using Bell polynomials. In this study, we analyze the asymptotic behavior of this solution to verify if it correctly reproduces the average cluster size distributions derived from the Smoluchowski equations. The findings are complex: for a general arbitrary reaction rate, the agreement is negative, yet for specific "classical" rate kernels—namely constant, additive, and multiplicative—the results align exactly. However, in the case of the multiplicative kernel, a discrepancy emerges between the combinatorial and exact solutions. The underlying reasons for this inconsistent pattern of agreement and disagreement remain unclear, highlighting the need for a deeper understanding of the combinatorial solution's derivation to define its valid scope.

This paper outlines several techniques designed to enhance the generalization of language identification (LID) systems when applied to new speakers and domains. These approaches include Spectral augmentation, which applies masking to spectrograms in frequency or time bands during training, and the utilization of CNN architectures pre-trained on the Imagenet dataset. Additionally, the study introduces a novel Triplet Entropy Loss training method, which combines Cross Entropy and Triplet loss within a single network training process. While all three methods yielded improvements in model generalization, these gains were not statistically significant. Although models trained with Triplet Entropy Loss demonstrated a superior understanding of languages and achieved higher accuracies, evidence suggests they may still be memorizing word patterns in spectrograms rather than capturing finer linguistic nuances. Despite this limitation, the research indicates that Triplet Entropy Loss holds significant potential and warrants further investigation beyond language identification for broader classification applications.

Internet of Things (IoT) innovations depend on a dependable, seamless wireless infrastructure capable of supporting heterogeneous, dynamic Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs). While the Routing Protocol for LLNs (RPL) was engineered to satisfy diverse IoT communication needs, it suffers from load-balancing issues under heavy traffic, leading to degraded performance in packet delivery and latency. This paper addresses load-balancing within RPL networks by employing a reinforcement-learning approach. The suggested method utilizes Q-learning at individual nodes to derive an optimal parent selection strategy based on real-time network dynamics. Each node stores neighbor routing data as Q-values, which encapsulate a composite routing cost derived from congestion levels, link quality, and hop distance. These Q-values are continuously refined by leveraging the current RPL signaling protocol. Extensive simulations evaluate the proposed approach, comparing it against existing solutions to validate its efficacy. The findings indicate that this method significantly enhances network performance regarding packet delivery and average delay, achieving these gains with only a slight increase in signaling frequency.

We demonstrate that every smooth Fano threefold within families 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, and 2.7 exhibits K-stability, and we further establish that smooth Fano threefolds in family 2.5 satisfying a specific, explicit genericity condition are also K-stable.

This paper examines the convex solution $u$ to the Monge–Ampère equation defined on an open, bounded, convex domain of dimension $n \geq 2$, subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions and a nonnegative, bounded right-hand side. For convex functions vanishing on the boundary, the Alexandrov maximum principle $|u(x)| \leq C \operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^\alpha$ holds if and only if the function exhibits uniform Hölder continuity with identical exponent and constant. Furthermore, such convex $\alpha$-Hölder continuous functions belong to the Sobolev space $W^{1,p}$ for all $p < 1/(1-\alpha)$. We establish Hölder continuity with exponent $\alpha=2/n$ when $n \geq 3$, and for any $\alpha \in (0,1)$ when $n=2$, assuming the boundary data satisfy this same Hölder condition; we also demonstrate that these exponent bounds are sharp. The proof relies exclusively on estimating the Hessian determinant of an explicit function on an $n$-dimensional cylinder and applying the comparison principle.

The July 22, 2018 launch of the Micro-X sounding rocket achieved a historic first by deploying Transition-Edge Sensors coupled with SQUID readouts in orbit. This payload integrates an imaging mirror with a microcalorimeter array to capture high-resolution spectra from extended X-ray sources, with Cassiopeia A, a supernova remnant, designated as the initial target. Although a rocket pointing error prevented actual observation of the target, the mission successfully validated the instrument's performance and confirmed the payload's operational viability. Key achievements included maintaining a stable cryogenic environment, executing all planned flight procedures, and detecting X-rays from an on-board calibration source. Comparative analysis showed that the flight environment had no significant impact on detector performance relative to ground testing. Furthermore, the mission provided critical data on how external magnetic fields and specific instrument configurations influence detector behavior. This flight represents a pivotal milestone in the flight readiness of these detector and readout technologies, both of which have been selected for upcoming X-ray observatories.

The lack of accessible Internet of Things (IoT) datasets hinders the development of machine learning-driven security solutions, as static datasets quickly become obsolete due to the rapidly evolving threat environment, and the testbeds used to create them are seldom shared. This paper introduces Gotham, a reproducible and adaptable network security testbed built as middleware on the GNS3 emulator, designed to be easily extended for new emulated devices, services, or attackers. Gotham facilitates an IoT scenario involving 100 emulated devices exchanging data via MQTT, CoAP, and RTSP protocols across a topology of 30 switches and 10 routers. This setup simulates three threat actors, encompassing the full lifecycle of the Mirai botnet alongside red-teaming tools executing Denial of Service (DoS), scanning, and various attacks targeting MQTT and CoAP protocols. The resulting network traffic and application logs can be utilized to generate datasets featuring both legitimate and malicious traces. We aim for researchers to adopt and modify Gotham to incorporate diverse devices and advanced attacks, thereby producing new datasets that mirror the current IoT threat landscape and protocols. The source code required to reproduce this scenario is publicly available.

The swift advancement of wireless communication has led to the widespread deployment of access points (APs) and Internet of Things (IoT) devices, filling our daily environments with diverse wireless signals like Wi-Fi, LoRa, and LTE. Prior studies demonstrate that radio waves are modulated by spatial structures—through reflection, diffraction, and scattering—during propagation, allowing receivers to capture information about the surrounding environment. This phenomenon forms the basis of "wireless sensing," an emerging technology with broad applications including gesture recognition for human-computer interaction, vital sign monitoring for healthcare, and intrusion detection for security. Unlike vision-based or IMU-based methods, wireless sensing offers distinct advantages such as high coverage, ubiquity, low cost, and robustness in challenging lighting or texture conditions. Furthermore, these solutions are lightweight regarding both computational requirements and device size. This tutorial focuses on Wi-Fi sensing, covering theoretical principles alongside code implementations for data collection, signal processing, feature extraction, and model design. It also emphasizes state-of-the-art deep learning architectures, including CNNs, RNNs, and adversarial models, within wireless sensing systems. Ultimately, this guide aims to assist researchers from various fields in entering the wireless sensing domain by providing insights into its theories, designs, and implementation techniques, thereby fostering growth in the research community.

We developed a systematic recipe for computing Feynman integrals with linear propagators via the auxiliary mass flow method. The core strategy involves adding a quadratic term to each linear propagator and subsequently eliminating its impact through differential equations. In practice, we applied this approach to determine all master integrals for vacuum diagrams featuring a gauge link up to four loops, validating the outcomes using nontrivial dimensional recurrence relations.

In silicon quantum dots, the valley degree of freedom introduces significant complexity to low-energy electron dynamics and spin qubit manipulation, primarily due to typically small valley splittings and dot-specific valley-orbit phases. We introduce a four-level model designed to extract tunnel coupling data from silicon double quantum dots (DQDs). This approach utilizes charge sensing measurements on the ground state, adapting a protocol commonly established for GaAs double dots [DiCarlo et al., PRL 92. 226801]. Our theoretical framework enables high-precision determination of both intra- and inter-valley tunnel couplings and remains robust against variations in system parameters, such as individual dot valley splittings.

Endoscopy serves as the primary medical technique for detecting cancer and polyps within hollow organs. However, endoscopic images often suffer from illumination artifacts caused by the orientation of the light source. Sudden changes in the endoscope's lighting pose lead to two critical problems: the creation of overexposed and underexposed tissue regions. These conditions can cause misdiagnoses due to information loss in affected areas or degrade the performance of computer vision algorithms (such as SLAM, structure from motion, and optical flow) utilized during non-invasive exams. This study has a dual objective: first, to introduce a novel synthetic dataset generated using generative adversarial techniques, and second, to investigate both shallow and deep learning-based image enhancement methods under varying lighting conditions. The best quantitative outcomes were achieved by the deep learning-based LMSPEC method, which also maintained a processing speed of approximately 7.6 frames per second.

The busy-forbidden protocol represents a novel readers-writer lock design that eliminates contention among readers, enabling superior performance compared to other locking mechanisms. While the original authors supplied specifications for both the implementation and its simplified external behavior, these were only proven equivalent for a maximum of seven threads. This study introduces a general proof utilizing the cones and foci framework, which translates the question of branching bisimilarity between two specifications into proof obligations concerning the relationships among data objects within the implementation and specification. Furthermore, we extend this framework by defining three additional properties for data objects; when these conditions are met, the two systems are established as divergence-preserving branching bisimilar—a more robust relation than standard branching bisimilarity that also differentiates between livelocks. We demonstrate the soundness of this extension and apply it to provide a comprehensive equivalence proof for the busy-forbidden protocol.

By applying the principle of local detailed balance, we reformulate the Kirchhoff equation for the stationary distribution of Markov jump processes into a physically meaningful tree-ensemble framework. Leveraging this arborification of path-space integration, we derive a McLennan-tree characterization near equilibrium and establish a response formula for the stationary distribution under conditions of large driving forces. This approach yields graphical representations for currents and traffic, facilitating the analysis of diverse asymptotic regimes. Furthermore, we demonstrate how the matrix-forest theorem provides a representation of quasi-potentials, which are instrumental in calculating excess work and heat within nonequilibrium thermal physics. Various examples are provided to clarify these graph-theoretic elements and constructions.

When neutrinos acquire mass via lepton mediators, as proposed in seesaw mechanisms, neutrino appearance probabilities in oscillation experiments are altered by the effective nonunitarity of the lepton mixing matrix. This phenomenon introduces new CP-violating phases and creates ambiguity regarding the standard phase within the three-neutrino framework. We investigate the CP sensitivities of various configurations at the European Spallation Source neutrino super-beam (ESSnuSB) experiment under conditions of nonunitarity, alongside an analysis of its capacity to constrain the related new physics parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining DUNE with ESSnuSB can significantly enhance the sensitivity to these nonunitarity parameters.

This paper introduces a generative adversarial network (GAN) designed to generate 3D sequences of upper-body gestures synchronized with speech and imbued with suitable emotional expressions. The proposed architecture comprises two primary modules: a generator that creates gestures from a joint embedding of speech-derived features and seed poses, and a discriminator tasked with differentiating between synthetic and authentic 3D pose sequences. Within the generator, we utilize separate encoders for Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and text transcripts to capture desired sentiments and their corresponding affective cues. Furthermore, we developed an affective encoder employing multi-scale spatial-temporal graph convolutions to convert 3D pose sequences into latent, pose-based affective representations. This affective encoder is utilized in both the generator to extract emotional features from seed poses for guiding synthesis and in the discriminator to ensure the resulting gestures exhibit appropriate affective alignment with the speech. Extensive evaluations on two benchmark datasets—the TED Gesture Dataset and the GENEA Challenge 2020 Dataset—demonstrate that our method outperforms the best baselines, reducing the mean absolute joint error by 10–33%, the mean acceleration difference by 8–58%, and the Fréchet Gesture Distance by 21–34%. Additionally, a user study reveals that compared to current state-of-the-art baselines, approximately 15.28% of participants found our synthesized gestures more plausible, while 16.32% perceived them as having more speech-aligned affective expressions.

The Galactic Archaeology with HERMES (GALAH) survey's third data release, designated GALAH+ DR3, offers a high-dimensional dataset comprising 678,423 spectra for 588,571 stars, primarily located within 2 kpc (81.2%). This collection integrates precise distances, orbital characteristics, and chemical abundance measurements to investigate Milky Way evolution. The data aggregates observations from GALAH Phase 1 (covering bright, main, and faint surveys, accounting for 70%), K2-HERMES (17%), TESS-HERMES (5%), and ancillary subsets (8%) that include the bulge and over 75 stellar clusters. Stellar parameters—including effective temperature ($T_\text{eff}$), surface gravity ($\log g$), metallicity ([Fe/H]), microturbulence ($v_\text{mic}$), broadening ($v_\text{broad}$), and radial velocity ($v_\text{rad}$)—were derived using a modified version of the SME spectrum synthesis code and 1D MARCS model atmospheres. To resolve spectroscopic degeneracies, the analysis incorporated astrometry from $Gaia$ DR2 and 2MASS photometry. We present abundance ratios [X/Fe] for 30 elements, eleven of which utilize non-LTE computations, spanning five nucleosynthetic pathways. The release includes detailed validation procedures for accuracy and precision, flags for peculiar stars or measurements, and usage recommendations. The stellar sample consists of 65% dwarfs, 34% giants, and 1% other/unclassified types. Analysis of unflagged chemical compositions and ages reveals that 62% are young low-$\alpha$ stars, 9% are young high-$\alpha$, 27% are old high-$\alpha$, and 2% have metallicities $\mathrm{[Fe/H]} \leq -1$. Kinematic data indicate that 4% of the sample belong to the halo. Accompanying this release are several updated Value-Added-Catalogues, including stellar ages and dynamics refined after $Gaia$ eDR3, which facilitate chrono-chemodynamic analyses as demonstrated in this work.

This work investigates the failure of diffusive hydrodynamics in holographic models dual to neutral dilatonic black holes featuring extremal near-horizon geometries conformal to AdS$_2\times$R$^2$. At low temperatures, adjusting the effective infrared gauge coupling causes the lowest non-hydrodynamic mode to collide with the charge diffusive mode, thereby defining the scales where hydrodynamics breaks down; this mode can manifest as either an infrared or a slow mode, leading to distinct scaling behaviors for local equilibrium scales. We verify that the upper bound on the charge diffusion constant remains satisfied by utilizing the pole collision to determine local equilibration velocities and timescales. Furthermore, we analyze hydrodynamic breakdown at arbitrary temperatures, revealing that the convergence radius exhibits a nontrivial dependence on both temperature and the effective gauge coupling constant.

Describing charged particles with spin greater than one moving through a constant electromagnetic field using minimal coupling results in issues like causality violations. Since Regge trajectories in string theory include such states, analyzing them offers a potential solution to these pathologies. This work introduces two specific Lagrangian formulations for the bosonic states at the first massive level of open superstrings in four dimensions; these forms are equivalent under field redefinitions. The first formulation yields the Fierz-Pauli Lagrangian for the spin-2 mode when the electromagnetic field vanishes, while the second provides a more compact representation that streamlines the derivation of the associated Fierz-Pauli equations of motion and constraints.

This work examines random constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) within the unsatisfiable regime. By applying the Guerra-Toninelli interpolation method from statistical physics, we establish a connection between the structural properties of near-optimal solutions in any Max-CSP and those of an associated spin glass defined on the hypercube. Specifically, the noise stability polynomial of the CSP's predicate corresponds, up to a constant factor, to the mixture polynomial of the linked spin glass. Our analysis yields two primary results:

1. We demonstrate that the maximum fraction of satisfiable constraints in a random Max-CSP is directly linked to the ground state energy density of the corresponding spin glass. Leveraging the Parisi formula to compute this energy density, we derive numerical values for several widely studied CSPs.
2. We show that a Max-CSP exhibits generalized versions of the overlap gap property if and only if the associated spin glass does. By transferring findings from Huang et al. [arXiv:2110.07847, 2021], we use this equivalence to rule out algorithms characterized by overlap concentration for a broad class of Max-CSPs, a category that encompasses both local classical and local quantum algorithms.

Over the past few years, machine learning research has increasingly focused on identifying and measuring two key forms of uncertainty: aleatoric and epistemic. This paper examines ensemble-based methods for uncertainty quantification. By distinguishing between various uncertainty-aware learning algorithms, we concentrate on Bayesian techniques and approaches utilizing credal sets, which align naturally with ensemble learning perspectives. For both methodologies, we investigate how to measure aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Finally, an empirical study on classification tasks with a reject option evaluates and compares the effectiveness of these respective measures.

We present quantum sensing protocols designed to detect extremely weak forces using a solitary trapped ion. These schemes leverage spin-motional coupling, generated through laser-ion interactions, to map force information onto the ion's spin states. Consequently, force estimation is achieved by monitoring Ramsey-type oscillations within the spin states. The study examines three distinct quantum probes modeled by the Jaynes-Cummings, quantum Rabi (1D), and Jahn-Teller (2D) frameworks. By applying dynamical decoupling techniques to the Jaynes-Cummings and Jahn-Teller models, the proposed force sensing methods become resilient against spin dephasing arising from thermal and magnetic field fluctuations. In contrast, the quantum Rabi probe features vanishing residual spin-phonon coupling, rendering it inherently robust to thermally induced dephasing. We demonstrate that these techniques enable the detection of both axial and transverse force components with sensitivities surpassing the yN/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ threshold, reaching the xN/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ level (where one xennonewton equals $10^{-27}$ N). Notably, the Jahn-Teller protocol offers the capability to function as a two-channel vector spectrum analyzer for measuring ultra-low voltages.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are frequently deployed to navigate hazardous terrains, yet they remain challenging to operate. Factors such as intricate input-output mappings, restricted perception, complex system dynamics, and the necessity to maintain safe distances create significant hurdles for novice pilots attempting safe landings in cluttered environments. This study introduces a shared autonomy framework designed to help inexperienced pilots execute safe landings on various elevated platforms, achieving performance levels equal to or surpassing those of expert pilots. The proposed system comprises two components: a perceptual module that utilizes a cross-modal variational auto-encoder to compress high-dimensional RGB-D images into latent vectors, and a policy module that delivers assistive control inputs trained via the TD3 reinforcement algorithm. In a user study involving 33 participants who landed a simulated drone with and without assistance, results showed that despite the assistant not knowing the target platform in advance, participants across all skill levels outperformed experienced counterparts when aided by the system.

We numerically examine the three-dimensional flow around a square-back Ahmed body at a Reynolds number of $10^4$. Using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) on a symmetry-enhanced dataset, we characterize and model the flow dynamics. Comparisons with higher Reynolds number experiments in the mid-height near-wake plane reveal that the simulation accurately captures key experimental features, notably the antisymmetric quasi-steady deviation mode. By analyzing 3-D POD modes, we classify physical processes based on their kinetic energy contributions across the full domain. Results indicate that the primary fluctuating mode corresponds to the 3-D quasi-steady wake deviation, with an amplitude well-predicted by 2-D near-wake data. Subsequent energetic fluctuations arise from vortex shedding and bubble pumping mechanisms. Furthermore, we observe a negative correlation between the deviation amplitude and both the spanwise vortex shedding intensity and the suction drag coefficient. Finally, despite the slow convergence of the decomposition, a POD-based low-dimensional model successfully replicates the experimentally observed wake deviation dynamics and the principal characteristics of the global modes identified in the simulation.

GS-14 (GDS J033218.92-275302.7) is a galaxy at redshift $z\sim5.5$ identified via [CII] emission in the ALPINE survey, distinguished by unusual UV spectral features indicative of either a double stellar population or an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Leveraging its extensive multi-wavelength data, we investigated the source of its emission through UV-to-NIR spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, considering scenarios involving single or double stellar populations and/or AGN components. Analysis of the VIMOS spectrum reveals highly-ionized emission lines (Ovi, Nv, and Niv), which were compared against observations from other galaxies and AGN, as well as predictions from radiation transfer models for star-forming regions, AGN, and shocks. SED fitting yields a total stellar mass of $M_*=(4 \pm 1) \times 10^{10} M_\odot$, a main population age of $\sim670$ Myr, and a recent, brief (8 Myr) star formation burst of $\sim 90 M_\odot yr^{-1}$. The Nv line exhibits a characteristic P-Cygni profile, implying a $\sim 3$ Myr old stellar component with a mass of $\sim 5 \times10^{7} M_\odot$, alongside evidence of an additional nebular emission component. While line ratio comparisons with theoretical models could attribute the emission to either star formation or an AGN, the intense radiation field necessary to ionize Ovi strongly suggests AGN activity. Our findings confirm an evolved stellar population existing at $z\sim5.5$ and demonstrate that GS-14 is undergoing a second short star formation burst. Furthermore, the galaxy displays signatures of obscured AGN activity, which may account for its short depletion time, marking GS-14 as one of two ALPINE sources hinting at an active nucleus and a promising candidate for future follow-up observations.

This study introduces nonparametric methods to compare two extrinsic antimeans defined on compact manifolds. Leveraging recent central limit theorems regarding extrinsic sample antimeans relative to an arbitrary embedding of a compact manifold within a Euclidean space, the authors establish an asymptotic chi-square test for assessing the equality of two such antimeans. The paper applies these methods to distributions on the complex projective space $CP^{k-2}$ using the Veronese-Whitney embedding, which serves as a submanifold representation for Kendall planar shape space, and further illustrates their utility through two medical imaging analysis cases.

We investigate the dynamics of entanglement entropy within a bipartition of a quantum XY spin chain, where a dissipative impurity (a spin) is driven by a noisy signal possessing a finite correlation time, analyzed through stochastic quantum trajectories. Our calculations of the noise-averaged entanglement entropy reveal that the rate of entanglement spreading slows down under strong dissipation due to the Zeno effect. We identify the Zeno crossover and demonstrate that noise-averaged entanglement entropy serves as an effective indicator for distinguishing between heating and Zeno regimes. Furthermore, increasing the noise correlation time shifts the Zeno crossover to stronger dissipation levels, thereby expanding the heating regime.

This paper introduces the concept of relative left Bongartz completions for any basic $\tau$-rigid pair $(U,Q)$ within the module category of a finite-dimensional algebra $A$. These completions form a family of basic $\tau$-tilting pairs that include $(U,Q)$ as a direct summand. We demonstrate that relative left Bongartz completions exhibit favorable compatibility with mutations, a property we leverage to investigate the existence of maximal green sequences under $\tau$-tilting reduction. Furthermore, we contextualize our construction and key findings within the framework of silting theory.

This paper investigates automorphisms of Toeplitz subshifts, noting that these groups are abelian, with any finitely generated torsion subgroup being finite and cyclic. When the complexity is non-superlinear, we demonstrate that the automorphism group, modulo a finite cyclic component, is uniquely generated by a root of the shift. In the subquadratic complexity scenario, we establish that the automorphism group modulo torsion is generated by the shift map's roots, proving the non-superlinear result is optimal. Specifically, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we construct minimal Toeplitz subshifts with complexity bounded by $C n^{1+\epsilon}$ whose automorphism groups fail to be finitely generated. Finally, we observe that coalescence imposes no restriction on complexity, as we present a family of coalescent Toeplitz subshifts with positive entropy whose automorphism groups encompass arbitrary finitely generated infinite abelian groups with cyclic torsion subgroups (potentially limited to powers of the shift).

Refactoring is a well-established method for managing technical debt and ensuring software projects remain healthy by adhering to design best practices or addressing design flaws. Earlier surveys indicated that refactoring is predominantly carried out by developers with deep system design knowledge and leadership roles, though these studies were confined to specific projects and organizations. This paper investigates the generalizability of those findings by examining 800 open-source projects. By mining refactoring activities and identifying contributors, we assigned an experience score to each to test hypotheses regarding whether developers with higher scores: (1) execute more refactoring operations, (2) possess distinct motivations for refactoring, or (3) provide better documentation for their changes. Our results show that while refactoring is not exclusive to a specific group, those with higher contribution scores do perform more refactorings. Although experience levels do not correlate with the motivation to refactor, highly contributing developers tend to perform a broader variety of refactoring types regardless of complexity. Conversely, top contributors tend to document their refactoring activities less frequently. A qualitative analysis of three randomly selected projects further confirms that developers responsible for the majority of refactoring typically hold advanced positions within their teams, reflecting their extensive knowledge of system design.

We provide a geometric classification of complex $n$-dimensional $2$-step nilpotent algebras, covering both commutative and anticommutative cases. Specifically, we determine the number of irreducible components and their respective dimensions. As a corollary, this yields a geometric classification of complex $5$-dimensional nilpotent associative algebras. Notably, it is established that this variety consists of $14$ irreducible components and contains $9$ rigid algebras.

Live streaming systems typically rely on a fixed bitrate ladder of resolution-bitrate pairs to eliminate the computational overhead of analyzing every video's complexity to optimize the ladder dynamically. Additionally, live encoders prioritize the fastest available preset to minimize streaming latency, with the expectation that encoding speed matches the video frame rate. However, selecting an optimized encoding preset can enhance Quality of Experience (QoE) and improve CPU utilization efficiency. Addressing this, the paper proposes a Content-Adaptive encoder Preset prediction Scheme (CAPS) tailored for adaptive live video streaming. CAPS determines the encoder preset by leveraging low-complexity spatial and temporal features derived from Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) energy for each video segment, alongside the number of allocated CPU threads and the target encoding speed. Experimental findings indicate that CAPS achieves an overall quality improvement of 0.83 dB PSNR and 3.81 VMAF at the same bitrate compared to the fastest preset used in the HTTP Live Streaming (HLS) bitrate ladder with the x265 HEVC open-source encoder. These gains are realized by sustaining the required encoding speed while minimizing CPU idle time.

The Coherent-Constructible Correspondence maps every $n$-dimensional toric variety $X_\Sigma$ to a Lagrangian skeleton $\Lambda_\Sigma$ within $T^*T^n$, establishing an equivalence between the derived category of coherent sheaves $Coh(X_\Sigma)$ and the wrapped constructible sheaves $Sh^w(T^n, \Lambda_\Sigma)$. This paper extends that correspondence to demonstrate that flips and flops among toric varieties correspond to variations in their Lagrangian skeletons. The central approach involves translating window subcategories arising from variation of GIT into window skeletons.

This study utilizes JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4 to investigate in-medium jet modifications, with a specific focus on uncertainties arising from perturbative scale variations and nuclear parton distribution functions (PDFs), as well as the effects of changes in initial and crossover medium temperatures. We compare our simulations against LHC data concerning the jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor, evaluating how nuclear PDFs interact with various medium parameters. Furthermore, we examine the influence of both nuclear PDFs and medium properties on jet structure through the analysis of the Lund plane.

Consider an analytic Besov type space denoted by $B_p(s)$, its multiplier class $M(B_p(s))$, and the M\"obius invariant subspace $F(p, p-2, s)$ generated by $B_p(s)$. For the range where $0<s<1$ and $\max\{s, 1-s\}<p\leq 1$, this paper provides a complete characterization of interpolating sequences for both $M(B_p(s))$ and $F(p, p-2, s)\cap H^\infty$. Furthermore, we examine specific conditions arising from this characterization through an $L^p$ formulation and the closure of $F(p, p-2, s)$ within the Bloch space.

This study proposes a general deep learning framework designed to synthesize free-viewpoint images of diverse human performers, utilizing only sparse camera inputs and avoiding per-case fine-tuning. The primary challenges in this domain stem from the significant variations in geometry and appearance resulting from articulated body poses, body shapes, and clothing. To address these hurdles, we introduce the Generalizable Neural Performer (GNR), a robust and efficient framework that learns a universal neural representation of human bodies across varying geometries and appearances. Specifically, we compress light fields for novel view rendering into conditional implicit neural radiance fields, incorporating both geometric and appearance dimensions. First, we develop an Implicit Geometric Body Embedding strategy that leverages parametric 3D human models and multi-view image cues to enhance robustness. Furthermore, we propose a Screen-Space Occlusion-Aware Appearance Blending technique that maintains high-quality visuals by interpolating source view appearances into the radiance fields using relaxed yet approximate geometric guidance. For evaluation, we are constructing the GeneBody-1.0 dataset, which features over 360 million frames from 370 subjects captured under multi-view conditions, encompassing a wide range of poses, body types, attire, accessories, and hairstyles. Experiments on GeneBody-1.0 and the ZJU-Mocap dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms recent state-of-the-art generalizable approaches in cross-dataset, unseen subject, and unseen pose scenarios, while also competing effectively with cutting-edge case-specific models. The dataset, source code, and models will be made publicly available.

We introduce a closed bouncing universe model in which the values of coupling constants are determined by the dynamics of a ghost-like dilatonic scalar field. We demonstrate that incorporating a periodic potential for this scalar field results in a cyclic Friedmann universe where coupling values shift randomly between cycles. Although these shuffling adjustments occur during the bounce, the time evolution of couplings within any single cycle remains safely consistent with current observational limits for physically motivated parameter values. This model offers an alternative approach to resolving the fine-tuning problem, distinct from solutions relying on string landscape scenarios.

Oscillons are exceptionally enduring, spatially confined, and temporally periodic field configurations supported by scalar field theories featuring attractive self-interactions. Investigating their longevity is crucial for grasping their cosmological implications. This study examines how gravity influences the decay rate and lifespan of dense oscillons, where self-interactions are comparable to or exceed gravitational effects. We analyze the $\alpha$-attractor T-model of inflation and the axion monodromy model, both of which exhibit potentials flatter than quadratic at large field values beyond a characteristic distance $F$ from the minimum. For oscillons with amplitudes on the order of $F$ and $F\ll 0.1 M_\mathrm{pl}$, their evolution mirrors scenarios neglecting gravity. However, when $F\sim 0.1 M_\mathrm{pl}$, incorporating gravitational interactions results in a modest reduction in lifetime.

The demand for Deep Learning predictions backed by quantifiable confidence is growing, particularly within high-stakes applications. While the Conformal Prediction (CP) framework offers a flexible solution that ensures a bounded error rate, its computational demands often hinder its use on large datasets. This paper introduces a new conformal loss function that condenses the conventional two-step CP process into a single step. By assessing and penalizing deviations from the strict expected CP output distribution, the model can directly learn the mapping between input data and conformal p-values. Our method reduces training time by up to 86% compared to Aggregated Conformal Prediction (ACP), a recognized CP approximation. Through a thorough empirical study on the MNIST dataset for both binary and multi-class classification, we demonstrate that our approach maintains competitive approximate validity and predictive efficiency relative to ACP.

According to the source coding theorem, data compression serves as a fundamental pillar of information theory. Typically, compression leverages statistical redundancies inherent in data based on its prior distribution. However, motivated by scenarios where prior statistics are unavailable but information regarding a subsequent transformation exists, we introduce a novel compression technique termed "reverse compression." This method is designed to function across both classical and quantum information processes and depends solely on the channel to be employed; specifically, all inputs that yield indistinguishable outputs are compressed into an identical state, independent of their prior distribution. Furthermore, this process can be viewed as a higher-order operation within the category of preprocessing. We also examine the application of this method to classical and quantum erasure channels. These examples indicate that noiseless reverse compression is feasible only in trivial scenarios, whereas non-trivial instances of noisy reverse compression may indeed exist.

Standard histopathological analysis of inflammatory cell architecture often discards substantial information present on biopsy slides.
