In the context of autoimmune disorders, critical unresolved issues persist concerning the specific cell types involved in tissue-level inflammation and their intercellular interactions. Although conventional techniques can partially address these queries, artificial intelligence methods for segmentation and classification offer a significantly more efficient pathway to decipher inflammatory architecture in autoimmune diseases, promising new insights. This paper empirically establishes deep learning models utilizing human dermatomyositis biopsy images to identify and detect inflammatory cells. Our methodology enhances classification accuracy by 26% and segmentation performance by 5%. Furthermore, we introduce a novel post-processing autoencoder architecture that yields an additional 3% improvement in segmentation results.

Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) offers a practical solution for individuals facing language impairments. This study introduces PicTalky, an AI-driven AAC platform designed to enhance communication skills and language comprehension in children with developmental language disorders. By integrating a sequence of neural-based natural language processing (NLP) modules, PicTalky achieves more accurate processing of both text and pictograms. The research includes both quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the system's core features. It is anticipated that users with language difficulties will find it easier to articulate their needs and desires, thereby improving their quality of life through this service. The models are freely accessible, accompanied by a demonstration of the web interface. Additionally, this work marks the first implementation of robotics-based AAC, achieved by applying PicTalky to the NAO robot.

Algebraic Quantum Field Theory (AQFT) offers a rigorous examination of the structure underlying relativistic quantum mechanics. This framework is defined by a net of operator algebras indexed across the regions of a Lorentzian manifold, which, in various instances, are represented by a family of von Neumann algebras—specifically, type III factors. Local quantum field logic emerges as a logical system designed to capture the propositional structure inherent within the net's algebras. Within this context, the current work addresses a series of open problems originating in the 1930s concerning the characterization of logical systems that correspond to the lattice of projectors derived from the Murray-von Neumann classification of factors. Specifically, grounded in physical requirements formalized within AQFT, an equational theory capable of characterizing the type III condition in a factor is presented. This equational system inspires the investigation of a diverse range of algebras possessing an underlying orthomodular lattice structure. Furthermore, a Hilbert-style calculus, which is algebraizable within this variety, is introduced, and a corresponding completeness theorem is proven.

This study examines an active reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) integrated into a mobile edge computing (MEC) framework. Unlike passive RIS, the active variant incorporates active reflective amplifiers to effectively mitigate "double path loss." We introduce a joint communication and computing optimization strategy aimed at minimizing maximum computational latency (MCL), adhering to constraints on phase shifts and edge computing capacity. Specifically, the primary problem is decomposed into four subproblems, which are solved using an alternating approach combining block coordinate descent (BCD) and successive convex approximation (SCA). Simulation outcomes demonstrate that, under identical power budgets, active RIS yields significantly superior performance compared to passive RIS.

Payment channels effectively shift transaction volume off-chain, successfully mitigating the scalability constraints inherent in most cryptocurrencies. However, a significant limitation of these channels is the necessity to deposit funds on-chain once a channel's balance is exhausted. Rebalancing was introduced to address this challenge, allowing parties with diminishing channel balances to transfer funds off-chain through a cycle to refill their channels. Existing rebalancing protocols typically offer only local solutions or sacrifice privacy. This work introduces an opt-in rebalancing protocol that ensures both privacy and global optimality, maximizing the total volume of funds rebalanced. By utilizing a linear programming framework and multi-party computation to solve the optimization problem—executed by selected participants to preserve efficiency—we achieve full privacy guarantees. Finally, the rebalancing solution is efficiently decomposed into incentive-compatible cycles that conserve user balances through atomic execution.

Keywords: Payment Channel Networks, Privacy and Rebalancing.

Snake robots, which consist of sequentially linked joint actuators, have recently attracted significant interest in industrial applications, particularly for life detection in confined spaces. These robots navigate complex terrains by coordinating multiple motors along their backbone. However, operating them in unknown environments remains difficult; traditional control methods often result in energy inefficiency or complete navigation failure. To address this, this study develops a snake locomotion gait policy using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for energy-efficient control. Specifically, we employ Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for each joint motor, parameterized by angular velocity, enabling the DRL agent to learn a standard serpenoid curve at every timestep. The simulation and task environment were constructed using PyBullet. Compared to conventional strategies, snake robots controlled by the trained PPO agent demonstrate faster movement and a more energy-efficient locomotion gait. This work illustrates that DRL offers an effective, energy-efficient solution for robot control.

Velocity map imaging (VMI) has long served as a robust method for measuring the 2D momentum distribution of photoelectrons produced by intense laser fields, with ongoing efforts to expand its capabilities into 3D through either direct or reconstructive techniques. Recent research has focused on direct methods, specifically by correlating electron time-of-flight (TOF) with the third momentum component, though this approach demands high timing resolution to distinguish structures within the narrow (< 10 ns) TOF distribution. This study advances VMI lens design and 3D measurement techniques by integrating a plano-convex thick-lens VMI with a TPX3CAM event-driven camera to achieve high-resolution 3D electron momentum data. Simulations indicate that adding a mesh electrode to the thick-lens configuration creates a plano-convex electrostatic field that broadens the detectable electron energy cutoff while maintaining high resolution. Additionally, the thick-lens design extends the electron TOF range, enhancing momentum resolution along this axis. Experimental validation using above-threshold ionization in Xenon demonstrates that the apparatus collects electrons with energies up to ~7 eV and a TOF spread of ~30 ns, representing improvements of approximately 1.4 and 3.75 times, respectively, over prior work. Furthermore, the PCTL-VMI system includes a coincident ion TOF spectrometer capable of isolating distinct 3D momentum distributions for various ionic species in gas mixtures. These methodologies hold promise for advanced applications, especially in systems where electron momentum distributions exhibit complex symmetries requiring high-resolution analysis.

We establish a general, signature-agnostic version of the law of the excluded middle and demonstrate that a logic is semisimple if and only if it adheres to this law, assuming it meets a weakened form of Raftery's inconsistency lemma. Subsequently, we illustrate how this equivalence facilitates straightforward syntactic proofs of the theorems by Kowalski and Kracht, which characterize semisimple varieties of FLew-algebras and Boolean algebras with operators, and further extend these results to FLe-algebras and Heyting algebras with operators. Furthermore, under more stringent conditions, this correspondence holds at the level of individual models: the semisimple models of such a logic are exactly those satisfying an axiomatic formulation of the law of the excluded middle, establishing a Glivenko-like link between the logic and its extension by the excluded middle axiom. This finding encompasses the established Glivenko theorems connecting intuitionistic and classical logic, as well as the modal logics S4 and S5. Consequently, we derive a characterization of the subclassical substructural logics that are Glivenko-related to classical logic.

The CMS collaboration has recently presented a search for electroweak instanton-like events involving anomalous $B+L$ violation, focusing on multi-fermion final states with no bosons. Conversely, numerous theoretical investigations indicate that such anomalous $B+L$ processes could yield a significantly high production rate only if their final states include a substantial number of electroweak gauge bosons. This paper examines the collider signatures of both zero-boson and multi-boson events for anomalous $B+L$ violation at the LHC and establishes an upper limit on the cross-section for the multi-boson process by reanalyzing the CMS results.

Modern data center mission-critical systems are increasingly encountering complex failures, which Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) protocols can mitigate but are seldom adopted due to their complexity and performance overhead. This work introduces a novel strategy for designing high-performance BFT protocols by redefining the ordering responsibilities between the network and the protocol, leveraging a new abstraction from data center network infrastructure. Specifically, we propose an Authenticated Ordered Multicast (AOM) primitive that ensures transferable authentication and non-equivocation. The feasibility of this design is validated through two hardware implementations of AOM on next-generation programmable switches, utilizing either HMAC or public-key cryptography for authentication. Building on this, we co-design a new BFT protocol called Matrix, which exploits AOM's guarantees to remove cross-replica coordination and authentication steps in typical scenarios. Evaluation demonstrates that Matrix significantly surpasses state-of-the-art protocols in both latency and throughput, highlighting the advantages of our proposed network ordering abstraction for BFT systems.

As gravitational waves travel near massive bodies, their trajectories bend, creating gravitational lensing—a phenomenon poised to become a vital tool in astrophysics. When the time delay between distinct paths matches the wave period, lensing generates beating patterns in the waveform, particularly near caustics where these effects are most likely to be detected. However, close to the caustic, the geometrical optics approximation fails because its underlying short-wave asymptotics break down. To accurately model the transition between wave and geometrical optics regimes, alongside the Fresnel number (the ratio of the lens's Schwarzschild diameter to the wavelength), one must also account for the source's angular position relative to the caustic. Using a point mass lens model, we demonstrate that in a two-dimensional parameter space, the nodal and antinodal lines of the transmission factor closely trace hyperbolas across a broad range near the caustic. This insight enables a simple formula for the onset of geometrical-optics oscillations, linking the Fresnel number to the source's angular position normalized by the Einstein angle. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a lens's mass can be determined by analyzing the interference fringes within a specific lensed waveform.

This paper presents a search for new massive resonances decaying into WW, WZ, or ZZ boson pairs within an all-jet final state, utilizing a novel analysis technique. The study utilizes data from the CMS experiment at the LHC, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 77.3 fb$^{-1}$ collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The investigation targets potential resonances with masses exceeding 1.2 TeV, where the decay products of individual W or Z bosons are anticipated to form collimated, large-radius jets. Signal extraction is achieved through a three-dimensional maximum likelihood fit involving two jet masses and the dijet invariant mass, resulting in sensitivity improvements of up to 30% compared to prior methods. No significant excess above the predicted standard model background was observed. Consequently, within a heavy vector triplet model, spin-1 Z' and W' resonances with masses below 3.5 and 3.8 TeV, respectively, are ruled out at the 95% confidence level. For a narrow-width bulk graviton model, cross-section upper limits ranging from 27 to 0.2 fb are established for resonance masses spanning 1.2 to 5.2 TeV. These results represent the most stringent limits to date for the dijet final state.

This study introduces a specific subclass of MD5-algebras and MD5-groups, defined as five-dimensional solvable Lie algebras and Lie groups whose co-adjoint orbits (K-orbits) possess either zero or maximal dimension. The paper's primary achievement is the classification, up to isomorphism, of all MD5-algebras featuring a non-commutative derived ideal. This classification ultimately provides a complete categorization of five-dimensional solvable Lie algebras.

This overview outlines the essential concepts and practical skills required to start applying tensor network methods numerically, specifically designed to assist researchers who already possess a strong theoretical background. The discussion covers fundamental techniques including tensor network contraction, optimal tensor decompositions, and the handling of gauge degrees of freedom. These topics are critical for understanding and implementing widely used algorithms such as DMRG, TEBD, TRG, PEPS, and MERA.

This study examines warm inflation within the framework of holographic cosmology, analyzing both weak and strong dissipative regimes under the slow-roll approximation and the context of intermediate inflation. By selecting a suitable equation of state, we demonstrate that intermediate inflation serves as an exact solution not only in general relativity but also within the specific holographic setup employed here. Several dissipative and physically significant functions are incorporated into this approach, which is subsequently constrained using the most recent Planck observational data. Our findings indicate that three of the evaluated models remain consistent with Planck data across certain parameter ranges, whereas one model is excluded by these observations.

This study tackles the equilibrium between performance and saturation in a specific category of constrained nonlinear systems, featuring two main approaches: balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). To reconcile the tension and conflict between these performance and saturation constraints, a performance safety evaluation (PSE) function is introduced. This function assesses system safety under the influence of destabilizing effect variables (DEVs), such as saturation levels and filter errors, ensuring that the cumulative impacts of these variables are fully leveraged and compensated to restore performance. Notably, the safety region allows for a certain tolerance of DEVs, while compensation mechanisms activate once the system's evaluation indicates a dangerous state. The benefits of this proposed framework are demonstrated through numerical simulations.

A Bayesian reweighting technique, which integrates new data without requiring re-fitting, is utilized to refine the quark Sivers function derived from Semi-Inclusive Deep Inelastic Scattering (SIDIS) measurements. This approach leverages recently released inclusive jet single spin asymmetry data from the STAR Collaboration at RHIC, covering a significantly broader $x$ range than SIDIS data. By extending the reweighting method to accommodate asymmetric uncertainties, the study demonstrates a substantial enhancement in the understanding of the quark Sivers function.

Building upon our previous research regarding the angular distribution of recoil flux from WIMP-target nucleus scattering, this article explores a method to determine the mass of incident halo WIMPs. We propose utilizing or combining "ridge-crater" features found in the angular recoil-energy spectra of various target nuclei within directional direct Dark Matter detection experiments. Our simulations indicate that for WIMP masses in the tens of GeV range, the stereoscopic angular recoil-flux distributions of both light and heavy target nuclei exhibit a longitudinally "ridge-like" pattern. Conversely, when the WIMP mass reaches the hundreds of GeV scale, the angular recoil-flux distributions of heavy target nuclei instead display a latitudinally "crater-like" structure.

Neural network (NN) potentials offer the prospect of highly accurate molecular dynamics (MD) simulations at the computational cost typical of classical force fields. Nevertheless, their predictive reliability diminishes when applied beyond their training domains, thereby highlighting a critical need for Uncertainty Quantification (UQ). While Bayesian modeling offers the necessary mathematical framework for UQ, traditional approaches relying on Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are computationally prohibitive for NN potentials. This study demonstrates that scalable Bayesian UQ using stochastic gradient MCMC (SG-MCMC) produces reliable uncertainty estimates for MD observables when applied to graph NN potentials for coarse-grained systems of liquid water and alanine dipeptide. We illustrate that employing cold posteriors can reduce the amount of training data required and that utilizing multiple Markov chains is essential for robust UQ. Furthermore, we observe that SG-MCMC and the Deep Ensemble method yield comparable results, with the latter requiring less training time and hyperparameter tuning. Both techniques effectively capture aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty; however, they fail to address systematic uncertainty, which must be minimized through proper modeling to ensure accurate credible intervals for MD observables. These findings mark a significant advancement toward accurate UQ, a vital component for trustworthy NN potential-based MD simulations in practical decision-making contexts.

We present the detection of significant (> 4 sigma) point-like gamma-ray emission from the Fermi-LAT instrument in the 300 MeV to 2 TeV range, spatially aligned with the TeV pulsar wind nebula (PWN) HESS J1554-550 inside the supernova remnant (SNR) G327.1-1.1. Following an analysis of this emission, we conducted a comprehensive multiwavelength study to elucidate its origin. Although the central pulsar driving the PWN has not been identified in any spectral band and is likely concealed within the offset X-ray nebula, its contribution via pulsations cannot be assessed due to the emission's faintness. Previous multiwavelength observations characterize this system as an aged SNR (τ ~ 18,000 years) currently experiencing or having recently undergone the interaction between the reverse shock and the PWN. Our results show that the gamma-ray data align exceptionally well with a broadband model previously developed using independent hydrodynamical and semi-analytic simulations of an evolved PWN. Furthermore, we explore the physical implications of this model for the PWN's evolutionary phase, utilizing the new Fermi-LAT data to model distinct particle components through a spatial separation analysis of the displaced PWN counterparts.

This study re-evaluates a specific class of black hole solutions within a global monopole spacetime using an $f(R)$-gravity framework. Our primary focus examines the region near the black hole where the weak field approximation remains applicable. We analyze the black hole's stability through its thermodynamic properties, treating the radial coordinate as a power-law function that serves as the central factor influencing the model's stability. By incorporating both Hawking and local temperatures, we derive explicit expressions for the black hole's thermodynamic quantities as functions of the event horizon. We carefully investigate potential phase transitions within this system, with special attention given to the Hawking-Page transition. Furthermore, we explore a particularly interesting solution where one parameter is associated with the cosmological constant. Our principal finding aims to compare the Hawking and local formalisms for the black hole within this specific $f(R)$-gravity spacetime.

We present a quantum interface designed to facilitate bidirectional entanglement transfer between the orbital angular momentum degree of freedom in free space and the time-energy degree of freedom in optical fibers, offering a new approach to linking remote, heterogeneous quantum nodes. Experimentally, we realized this interface using two interferometric cyclic gates to execute two-way entanglement transfer between these distinct degrees of freedom. The results indicate that the quantum entangled state can be successfully switched back and forth between orbital angular momentum and time-energy domains, maintaining a state fidelity exceeding 90% before and after the transition. This study validates the feasibility and high performance of the proposed interface, establishing a pathway for constructing large-scale quantum communication networks.

This study addresses the challenge of allocating items to platforms subject to group fairness constraints. In our framework, items are categorized into classes, and each platform imposes limits on the number of items it can accept from any specific class, alongside a cap on its total capacity. The primary objective is to assign items to platforms to maximize the total count while adhering to these class-specific and overall limits. When a revenue value is assigned to each match, the goal shifts to maximizing total revenue. This model effectively represents various real-world scenarios, including ad auctions, scheduling, resource allocation, and school choice. Furthermore, we establish a notable link between this problem and computing a generalized maximum independent set on hypergraphs, as well as ranking items under group fairness constraints. We demonstrate that with arbitrary classes, the problem is NP-hard and suffers from strong inapproximability. However, under natural restrictions on classes within both online and offline settings, although the problem remains NP-hard, it allows for approximation algorithms with small factors. We have implemented several of these algorithms, and experimental results indicate they perform efficiently in practice, successfully assigning a high number of items to platforms.

This paper revisits the nonlinear spline primitive in three-dimensional space originally examined by Even Mehlum, specifically the spherical clothoid, defined as a curve on a sphere whose geodesic curvature varies linearly with arc length. We derive its Cartesian coordinate functions in terms of confluent hypergeometric functions (Kummer functions) and its stereographic projection onto the complex plane. Additionally, we introduce new results concerning Humbert series and provide generating function formulas linked to the associated Meixner-Pollaczek polynomials.

Framing entails presenting an argument or issue with a positive or negative tone tailored to the audience and the speaker's objectives (Entman 1983). Variations in lexical framing, which is the central focus of this work, significantly influence public opinion and beliefs. To advance the goal of reframing arguments for beneficial outcomes, we developed a dataset and methodology for this purpose. Leveraging a lexical resource for "connotations," we constructed a parallel corpus and proposed a reframing approach that integrates controllable text generation (ensuring positive connotation) with a post-decoding entailment component (maintaining the same denotation). Our findings demonstrate that this method outperforms strong baselines across dimensions including fluency, meaning preservation, and trustworthiness (specifically fear reduction).

Let $\Gamma$ denote a finitely generated, torsion-free nilpotent group, and let $A^\omega$ represent the space of infinite sequences formed from a finite alphabet $A$. This study examines two categories of self-similar actions of $\Gamma$ on $A^\omega$: those that are faithful with dense orbits and those that are free. Necessary conditions for the existence of self-similar actions of each category are derived. Consequently, two corollaries regarding nilmanifolds are established: the first concerns nilmanifolds equipped with an Anosov diffeomorphism, while the second addresses the presence of an affine structure. Furthermore, the analysis extends to virtual actions of $\Gamma$, defined as actions by a finite-index subgroup $\Gamma'$. A formula incorporating number-theoretic elements is obtained to determine the minimum size of an alphabet $A$ supporting a virtual self-similar action of either type on $A^\omega$.

Forecasting plays a critical role in the design of future experiments by estimating the scientific yield of hypothetical datasets. The Fisher information matrix is a preferred forecasting method because of its computational efficiency and convenient mathematical properties. Nevertheless, the Fisher matrix serves as a reliable approximation of the true likelihood only under specific conditions: when data distributions are nearly Gaussian and observables exhibit near-linear dependence on the parameters of interest. Furthermore, Fisher forecasting methods cannot independently validate their own accuracy. While exhaustive sampling of the exact or mock likelihood can definitively confirm the validity of a Fisher forecast, such sampling is frequently too computationally expensive. We introduce a straightforward test utilizing the Derivative Approximation for LIkelihoods (DALI) technique to evaluate whether the Fisher matrix adequately approximates the exact likelihood. Our analysis reveals that the Fisher matrix fails to approximate the true likelihood in regions where two-dimensional slices of the DALI-derived level surfaces display negative extrinsic curvature. We demonstrate that this method accurately identifies scenarios where the Fisher approximation diverges from the true likelihood across various cosmological models and data configurations, incurring only a modest increase in computational cost relative to standard Fisher forecasts.

While substantial research exists regarding the eigenvalues of high-dimensional sample covariance matrices, most work focuses on Mar\v{c}enko-Pastur (MP) models, where observations are linear transformations of random vectors with independent entries. In contrast, elliptical models, which lack this independence structure and display distinct statistical behaviors, are less understood. Specifically, the applicability of bootstrap methods for inferring spectral statistics in high-dimensional elliptical settings remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we demonstrate how a bootstrap technique previously designed for MP models can be adapted to accommodate the unique characteristics of elliptical models. Our primary theoretical contribution establishes that this adapted method consistently approximates the distributions of linear spectral statistics, which are central to multivariate analysis. Furthermore, empirical evidence indicates that the proposed approach also performs effectively across various nonlinear spectral statistics.

We outline the general requirements for a time-fractional formulation of the Poisson-Nernst-Planck model to ensure that the total current through the sample remains solenoidal, a necessity dictated by Maxwell's equations. Only when this condition is met can the cell's electric impedance be calculated as the ratio of the applied potential difference to the resulting current. Furthermore, we demonstrate that under conditions of anomalous diffusion, the model predicts a constant phase element behavior for the cell's impedance in the low-frequency range. In the parametric plot of reactance against resistance, the slope of the curve corresponds directly to the order of the fractional time derivative.

Sixth-generation wireless communication (6G) is envisioned as an integrated architecture encompassing space, air, ground, and sea. A significant challenge within this framework is underwater information acquisition, which requires transmitting data across the air-water interface. In this context, the Ocean of Things (OoT) plays a pivotal role by acting as a bridge between the Internet of Things (IoT) and the Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT). OoT devices are capable of gathering data via underwater methods and utilizing radio frequencies over the air. While Underwater Acoustic Communications (UWA COMMs) is the most effective medium for OoT devices to exchange information, it frequently suffers from Doppler shifts and synchronization errors. To address these harsh conditions, this paper proposes a deep neural network-based receiver for underwater acoustic chirp communication, termed C-DNN. Furthermore, to enhance deep learning model performance and resolve generalization issues, a novel Federated Meta Learning (FML) enhanced Acoustic Radio Cooperative (ARC) framework, named ARC/FML, is introduced for transfer learning. Specifically, tractable expressions are derived to analyze the convergence rate of FML in wireless environments, considering the impacts of scheduling ratios, local epochs, and single-node data volume. Analysis and simulation results demonstrate that the proposed C-DNN offers superior bit error rate (BER) performance and lower complexity compared to classical matched filters (MF) in underwater acoustic scenarios. Additionally, the ARC/FML framework exhibits robust convergence across diverse channels compared to standard federated learning (FL). In conclusion, the proposed ARC/FML scheme for OoT represents a promising solution for facilitating information exchange across the water-air interface.

Utilizing mass relations derived from Regge phenomenology, we re-examine the mass spectrum of the $1^{3}D_{1}$ meson nonet. We calculate the masses for the kaon and the $s\bar{s}$ member of this nonet, denoted as $1^{3}D_{1}(s\bar{s})$, and compare our findings with values from various theoretical models. Additionally, we analyze the strong decay characteristics of the kaon and $1^{3}D_{1}(s\bar{s})$ within the framework of the $^{3}P_{0}$ model. Based on these results, we propose that the assignment of the $1^{3}D_{1}$ meson nonet requires further experimental verification in the future. Our findings also offer mass constraints to aid in the study of these states.

The exclusive process $pp \to pp (K^{*0} \bar{K}^{*0} \to K^{+}\pi^{-}K^{-}\pi^{+})$ is analyzed in the context of LHC experiments, with reaction amplitudes derived using the tensor-pomeron framework. Two diffractive mechanisms are examined: the $f_{2}(1950)$ $s$-channel exchange, which serves as a candidate for central diffractive tensor glueball production, and the $K^{*0}$-exchange mechanism, representing an irreducible continuum. Comparisons with WA102 experimental data are performed, along with predictions for LHC scenarios. Results indicate that the continuum contribution alone adequately describes the WA102 data. Furthermore, the similar behavior of both continuum and resonance contributions complicates the identification of a broad tensor-glueball state in this reaction.

Machine learning has recently gained significant traction in studying phase transitions and critical phenomena. Specifically, we utilized these methods to uncover physical characteristics within the two-dimensional percolation model. Our process began with Monte Carlo simulations to create a dataset, which was then subjected to various analytical techniques. We employed four distinct Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), along with a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), a convolutional VAE (cVAE), Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and k-means clustering, to determine order parameters, permeability, and critical transition points. The first three CNN variants demonstrated high accuracy in simulating the two order parameters and permeability, exhibiting strong extrapolation capabilities and notable resistance to noise. To verify the robustness of these three CNN models, we used the VAE and cVAE to generate new percolating configurations and introduce perturbations into the original data. Our results showed that physical characteristics could be identified equally effectively using either raw or perturbed configurations, provided the labels were available. In scenarios lacking labels, we turned to unsupervised learning. While PCA performed well in identifying permeability, it failed to deduce the order parameter. Consequently, we applied a fourth type of CNN with varying preset thresholds to successfully identify a new order parameter and the critical transition point. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the efficacy of machine learning in the context of phase transitions and critical phenomena still requires further evaluation.
We present our latest findings on the rigidity and unlockability characteristics of clusters of rigid bodies sliding along the unit sphere.

Phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) refers to the process where the power of a high-frequency oscillation varies in relation to the phase of a low-frequency one. We introduce a model that accounts for the emergence of PAC within two widely recognized neural architectures: a high-frequency oscillation driven by external low-frequency input and two interacting local oscillations with distinct, locally generated frequencies. Additionally, we propose an interconnection framework for brain regions, demonstrating that low-frequency phase synchrony can unify high-frequency activities governed by local PAC and dictate the direction of information flow between distant areas.

Conventional channel estimation (CE) in Internet of Things (IoT) environments faces significant hurdles, including inefficient spectrum usage, excessive power consumption, and obstructed signal paths. While superimposed pilot-based techniques and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) offer partial relief, a comprehensive systematic approach remains underexplored. This paper introduces an RIS-assisted superimposed pilot-based CE framework enhanced by neural networks. At the user equipment (UE), superimposing pilots onto uplink data boosts spectral efficiency and reduces energy usage, while two lightweight networks at the base station (BS) lower computational complexity and processing latency for both CE and symbol detection (SD). These specialized networks are trained cooperatively: conventional methods first extract initial features, which the neural networks (NNs) then refine. This cooperative strategy reduces the amount of training data required. Simulation results indicate that this approach decreases computational load and delay without compromising accuracy, while also improving normalized mean square error (NMSE) and bit error rate (BER) performance at the BS under varying parameter conditions.

Stochastic variance reduction has demonstrated significant success in speeding up first-order algorithms for convex finite-sum optimization problems, including empirical risk minimization. While integrating second-order information has further enhanced the performance of these first-order approaches, there remains limited understanding of how variance reduction can benefit established stochastic second-order techniques like Subsampled Newton. To fill this gap, we introduce Stochastic Variance-Reduced Newton (SVRN), a finite-sum minimization algorithm that combines the advantages of second-order methods—such as simple unit step sizes, parallelizable large-batch operations, and rapid local convergence—with variance reduction to achieve superior convergence rates (per data pass) for smooth, strongly convex problems. Our results indicate that SVRN can accelerate various stochastic second-order methods, including Subsampled Newton and iterative least squares solvers like Iterative Hessian Sketch, and it performs competitively against popular first-order methods equipped with variance reduction.

This work introduces a general framework capable of deriving exact analytical solutions for the time evolution of quantum spin systems subjected to parametric waveforms defined by arbitrary time-dependent functions. The methodology employs the \emph{path-sum} technique, which leverages the algebraic and combinatorial characteristics of graph walks. A comprehensive mathematical exposition of this formalism is provided, alongside a \textsc{Matlab} implementation. By analyzing spin dynamics in monopartite, bipartite, and tripartite systems under chirped pulses as representative examples, the study demonstrates that this approach consistently surpasses traditional numerical techniques, such as ODE integrators and piecewise-constant propagator approximations.

This paper begins with the quantum Hamilton-Jacobi method to demonstrate that the complex pole evolution inherent in the Schrödinger equation is captured by a quantum action formulated through random matrices. Specifically, the wave function corresponds to the probability distribution function of a random matrix, a relationship recognized in the literature as the celebrated Cole-Hopf Transformation.

Merging graphene with other emerging layered materials offers a promising avenue for tailoring the band structure of charge carriers. Given the robust spin-orbit coupling found in BiTeX compounds and the successful creation of a single-layer BiTeI, the experimental realization of a Kane-Mele phase within graphene-based heterostructures appears feasible. This study theoretically investigates how uniaxial in-plane tensile and out-of-plane compressive strain can modulate the topological phase of hybrid systems composed of graphene and BiTeX (where X represents I, Br, or Cl) layers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that structural stress naturally occurring in fabricated samples can trigger a topological phase transition, effectively converting the sample into a novel experimental instance of a time-reversal invariant topological insulator.

This paper offers a comparative evaluation of three deep learning methods designed to detect COVID-19 in chest CT scans. One method utilizes a volumetric strategy with 3D convolutions, whereas the other two initially classify individual slices before aggregating the outcomes at the volume level. Experiments were conducted using the COV19-CT-DB dataset to tackle the challenge posed by the MIA-COV19D Competition at ICCV 2021. On the validation set, our top-performing approach achieved a macro-F1 score of 0.92, representing a significant improvement over the organizers' baseline score of 0.70.

The entropy-based moment method is a widely recognized discretization approach for the velocity variable in kinetic equations, offering significant theoretical advantages but posing implementation challenges with high-order numerical schemes. To address a primary obstacle—the necessity of ensuring numerical solution realizability—the regularized entropy-based moment method was recently proposed. In this study, we employ the relative entropy technique to demonstrate that the regularized method converges to the original method as the regularization parameter vanishes, establishing specific convergence rates. Our analysis relies on the assumptions that the velocity domain is bounded, the original moment solution is Lipschitz continuous in space, and it remains sufficiently distant from the realizability boundary. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm that the derived convergence rates are optimal.

A freestanding crystalline membrane known as a puckered sheet contains an embedded array of bistable buckled units. Recent studies indicate that these units function similarly to spins in a two-dimensional compressible Ising antiferromagnet, distinguished by a coupling to flexural phonons. At finite temperatures, this purely mechanical system exhibits Ising-like phase transitions that result in anomalous thermal expansion. This work demonstrates that geometry can regulate phase behavior: curvature generates a radius-dependent "external field" that promotes alignment between neighboring "spins," thereby disrupting the ordered checkerboard ground state of antialigned neighbors. The strength of this effective field is inversely proportional to the radius of curvature. We theoretically identify this field using both a discrete real-space model and a nonlinear continuum elastic model. Subsequently, we present molecular dynamics simulations of puckered sheets within cylindrical geometries at zero and finite temperatures to investigate how curvature affects configuration stability and phase transitions. Our findings illustrate how curvature and temperature can be leveraged to design and operate responsive, tunable metamaterials at both macroscopic and nanoscopic scales.

Feature selection presents a significant challenge in high-dimensional clustering, particularly in genomics where only a limited number of differentially expressed genes provide meaningful insights into the overall cluster structure. Current methods, including Sparse K-means, often fail to address the issue of identifying features that separate only specific subsets of clusters. In genomic contexts, it is common for a gene to distinguish a single subtype from others or differentiate between just one pair of subtypes. This paper introduces a K-means-based clustering algorithm capable of identifying informative features alongside the specific cluster pairs they can separate. The proposed method functions as an EM algorithm that applies lasso-type constraints to each cluster pair during the M-step and facilitates the E-step by maximizing raw cross-cluster distances rather than minimizing intra-cluster distances. The effectiveness of this approach was validated using both simulated data and a leukemia gene expression dataset.

This study reinterprets Primal Dual Regularized Interior Point Methods (PDR-IPMs) within the Proximal Point Method framework, specifically for Linear and Quadratic Programming. This approach yields the Proximal Stabilized IPM (PS-IPM), which is theoretically robust regarding convergence rates and capable of addressing degenerate problems. The second phase of the research examines the interplay between regularization parameters and the computational cost of linear algebra operations required to solve Newton systems. Notably, when utilizing iterative Krylov methods, we introduce general-purpose preconditioners that leverage regularization and a novel Schur complement rearrangement to remain effective across multiple IPM iterations. Consequently, these preconditioners require recalculation in only a fraction of the total iterations. These regularized second-order methods, permitting infrequent preconditioner updates, offer an alternative approach situated between first- and second-order methodologies.

Although new words frequently enter communities, they do not always remain in the community's vocabulary. While many elements drive lexical evolution, this study examines the underexplored influence of social networks. By analyzing more than 80,000 neologisms across 4,420 online communities over ten years using Poisson regression and survival analysis, we show that network structure significantly impacts lexical change. Beyond sheer size, characteristics such as high connectivity density, the absence of local clustering, and greater external links foster both lexical innovation and retention. Unlike offline groups, these topic-focused communities avoid strong lexical leveling despite heightened contact and instead accommodate more specialized vocabulary. Our findings support the sociolinguistic theory that network structure partially shapes lexical change while also revealing unique patterns specific to online environments.

Network embedding has received extensive research attention and is broadly applied in tasks like link prediction and node classification. Although prior studies have primarily focused on developing new algorithms or adapting to specific problem scenarios, the critical role of initialization strategies during the learning process has often been overlooked. This work tackles that gap, demonstrating that proper initialization can substantially enhance both the effectiveness and efficiency of network embedding algorithms. Specifically, we employ a graph partitioning approach to divide the original graph into disjoint subsets and construct a smaller abstract graph based on these partitions. We derive node embeddings for the entire graph by first computing embeddings on this reduced abstract graph and then propagating them to the nodes in the original graph. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets reveal that our initialization method significantly boosts the performance of state-of-the-art algorithms, improving link prediction accuracy by up to 7.76% and node classification by up to 8.74%. Furthermore, this technique reduces the computational runtime of these algorithms by at least 20%.

This research investigates policy optimization within Markov decision processes (MDPs) featuring multiple reward value functions, aiming to jointly optimize them using criteria like proportional fairness (via smooth concave scalarization), hard constraints (constrained MDPs), and max-min trade-offs. We introduce the Anchor-changing Regularized Natural Policy Gradient (ARNPG) framework, which systematically integrates concepts from high-performing first-order methods to enhance policy optimization algorithms for multi-objective MDPs. Theoretically, algorithms derived from the ARNPG framework achieve $\tilde{O}(1/T)$ global convergence when utilizing exact gradients. Empirically, ARNPG-guided algorithms outperform existing policy gradient-based methods in both exact gradient and sample-based settings.

In 1990, Spie\ss\ established various identities for harmonic numbers, covering sums of the forms $\sum_{\ell=1}^n\ell^k H_\ell$, $\sum_{\ell=1}^n\ell^k H_{n-\ell}$, and $\sum_{\ell=1}^n\ell^k H_\ell H_{n-\ell}$. This paper presents several new formulas involving hyperharmonic numbers, specifically $\sum_{\ell=0}^{n} {\ell}^{p} h_{\ell}^{(r)} h_{n-\ell}^{(s)}$ and $\sum_{\ell=0}^n \ell^{p}(h_{\ell}^{(r)})^{2}$, along with additional results for generalized hyperharmonic numbers.

This paper investigates the global existence of non-Newtonian incompressible fluids governed by equation \eqref{maineq2}. We establish the existence of weak solutions within the anisotropic Besov space $ B^{\alpha, \frac{\alpha}2}_p ({\mathbb R}^n_+ \times (0, \infty)) $ for $ n+2 < p < \infty $ and $ 1 + \frac{n+2}p < \al < 2 $, as well as in the anisotropic Sobolev space $ W^{2, 1}_p ({\mathbb R}^n_+ \times (0, \infty)) $ for $ n+2 < p < \infty $, provided the boundary data are non-zero. Our analysis assumes the extra stress tensor $S$ takes the form $S({\mathbb A}) = {\mathbb F} ( {\mathbb A})$, where ${\mathbb F}(0)$ is a uniformly elliptic matrix and the following condition holds for some $0 < \theta \leq 1$ and $C_0 > 0$:
\begin{align*}
  |\big( {\mathbb F}({\mathbb A}) -{\mathbb F}(0) \big) {\mathbb A} - \big(
{\mathbb F}({\mathbb B})- {\mathbb F}(0) \big){\mathbb B}| \leq A\max (
|{\mathbb A}|^\te, |{\mathbb B}|^\te) |{\mathbb A} -{\mathbb B}|\quad \forall
\,\, |{\mathbb A}|, \,\, |{\mathbb B}| \leq C_0.
\end{align*}
Consequently, the terms $S_1$ and $S_2$ defined in \eqref{0207-1} meet our requirements with $\theta = 1$ for all $d \in {\mathbb R}$, while $S_3$ satisfies the assumption \eqref{assumption} with $\theta = d - 2$ when $2 < d \leq 3$.

A generalized formula is presented to determine the M$_n$/M$_p$ ratio of multipole transition matrix elements within the phenomenological analysis framework. This approach accounts for potential variations between neutron and proton radii and diffuseness, a phenomenon particularly relevant in exotic nuclei. The scope of validity for the original Bernstein formula is examined in the context of proton scattering probes operating at energies of a few tens of MeV. The most significant deviations arise in extremely neutron-rich nuclei (where N/Z$\gtrsim$1.6) or when the electromagnetic deformation parameter exceeds that of the proton scattering probe. Consequently, the anticipated reduction in statistical uncertainties, alongside research into very neutron-rich nuclei at next-generation exotic beam facilities, is expected to enhance the applicability of the generalized Bernstein formula.

Accurately estimating the frequency of natural disasters is crucial for the insurance sector's risk management, yet this task is challenging due to the multitude of influencing factors. This study introduces a Normal approximation method for associated point processes to estimate disaster counts, based on two key assumptions: first, that incident counts in different regions are positively correlated, and second, that this correlation diminishes exponentially with distance beyond a specific local range. Building on these premises, we extend prior findings regarding non-asymptotic $L^1$ bounds for functionals of such processes, originally established by Wiroonsri (2019). We subsequently apply this extended framework to permanental Cox processes, which inherently exhibit positive association. Finally, we utilize our derived Normal approximation results for these processes to analyze fire incident data from Thailand spanning 2007 to 2020, sourced from the Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency of Thailand.

The history of the University of Florence's Institute of Physics spans from the early 20th century, marked by Antonio Garbasso's appointment as Director in 1913, through the 1960s. Leveraging Garbasso's expertise, the Institute secured new facilities on Arcetri hill, adjacent to the existing Astronomical Observatory, and assembled a distinguished cohort of young physicists. This group included Rita Brunetti, Enrico Fermi, Franco Rasetti, Enrico Persico, Bruno Rossi, Gilberto Bernardini, Daria Bocciarelli, Giuseppe Occhialini, and Giulio Racah, who focused on emerging areas such as Quantum Mechanics and Cosmic Rays. Known as the Arcetri School, this collective disbanded in the late 1930s due to the transfer of its members to other universities, alongside the oppressive racial laws and the fascist regime's environment. Following the war, students of this school revived its legacy by establishing research groups in nuclear and elementary particle physics. In the realm of theoretical physics, after the eras of Fermi and Persico, the field experienced renewed growth by the late 1950s with the arrival of Giacomo Morpurgo and, most significantly, Raoul Gatto, who founded the first genuine Italian school of Theoretical Physics at Arcetri.

Many Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) struggle with Link Prediction (LP) tasks, often underperforming simple heuristics due to constraints in expressive power. Specifically, they fail to count triangles—a fundamental component of most LP heuristics—and cannot differentiate between automorphic nodes with identical structural roles. While learning link representations and integrating structural features like triangle counts can mitigate these issues, explicit link representations are typically too costly. Consequently, recent approaches have turned to subgraph-based methods, which achieve state-of-the-art LP results but suffer from inefficiency caused by significant subgraph redundancy. Our analysis of subgraph GNN (SGNN) components led to the development of ELPH (Efficient Link Prediction with Hashing), a novel full-graph GNN that transmits subgraph sketches as messages to approximate essential SGNN functions without constructing explicit subgraphs. ELPH is provably more expressive than Message Passing GNNs (MPNNs), surpassing existing SGNNs on standard benchmarks while offering orders-of-magnitude speed improvements, though it remains limited to datasets that fit within GPU memory. To address this, we introduced BUDDY, a highly scalable model that employs feature precomputation to overcome memory constraints without compromising accuracy. Experimental results confirm that BUDDY exceeds SGNN performance on standard LP benchmarks, combining high scalability with superior speed compared to ELPH.

Knowledge Graphs are now a ubiquitous technology driving search engines, recommender systems, IoT, corporate knowledge management, and Open Data. These systems rely on small information units called triples, which can be combined to create higher-level statements across datasets based on user needs. However, data producers struggle with the high cognitive cost required to reconstruct chains of triples, which prevents them from gaining meaningful overviews of their own data. To address this, we introduce "path outlines," conceptual objects that characterize sequences of triples using descriptive statistics. We interviewed 11 data producers to assess their interest in this approach. We also present Path Outlines, a tool for browsing path-based summaries that utilizes coordinated views and two novel visualizations. In an experiment involving 36 participants, we compared Path Outlines against the current baseline technique. Our results demonstrate that Path Outlines is three times faster, improves task completion, reduces errors, is preferred by users, and makes tasks feel easier.

We employ molecular simulation to derive Ginzburg-Landau free energy functions for molecular fluids. Specifically, we adapt the Expanded Wang-Landau algorithm to compute partition functions, number distributions, and Landau free energies for Argon, carbon dioxide, and water. Subsequently, we parametrize a coarse-grained free energy function based on the density order parameter and evaluate its effectiveness in modeling the onset of criticality within these systems. The derived parameters are directly applicable to hybrid atomistic/continuum simulations, facilitating the connection between microscopic and mesoscopic length scales.

Nonlocality, a fascinating subject within quantum physics, is typically facilitated by distinct quantum states. In this study, we examine a Weyl semimetal slab and discover an unconventional nonlocal correlation phenomenon by positioning two potential wells on its opposing top and bottom surfaces. This correlation stems from the distinctive Weyl orbits inherent to Weyl semimetals and results from the bulk-boundary correspondence principle in topological band theory. Furthermore, we identify a massive nonlocal transport signal and a breakdown of the material body induced by Weyl fermions, which offer experimental signatures to confirm this nonlocal correlation. These findings introduce a novel variant to the family of nonlocality effects and hold promise for the development of innovative electronic devices with advanced functionalities.

We investigate the subgap spectrum of a two-dimensional Abrikosov vortex within an s-wave superconductor, both with and without a point impurity. By solving the Eilenberger equations in the absence of impurities across two vortex models (one being self-consistent), we identify multiple subgap spectral branches. These branches can number arbitrarily high, contingent upon the magnetic field screening length being sufficiently large. The quasiclassical vortex spectrum exhibits a local gap with a width comparable to the bulk gap and a spatial range spanning several coherence lengths; this gap is essential for the emergence of discrete impurity-induced states. Using the Gor'kov equations formalism, we determine that a single impurity can generate up to four discrete quasiparticle states within the vortex. We compute the energies and wavefunctions of these impurity states across various parameters and assert that the majority of these predicted spectral characteristics are detectable via scanning tunnel spectroscopy experiments.

While real-world text data, including DNA sequences, deviates significantly from uniform randomness, average-case string searching algorithms typically outperform worst-case variants in practical applications. This paper investigates the task of determining the longest prefix of every suffix within a string of length $n$ drawn from a constant-sized alphabet that appears elsewhere in the string allowing for $k$ errors. Previously, this issue was examined under the Hamming distance framework. Our primary contribution is an enhancement to the best-known average-case time complexity for non-constant $k$, utilizing only linear space within the Hamming distance model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach extends to the edit distance model, maintaining identical time and space complexities. Specifically, our algorithms operate in $\mathcal{O}(n \log^k n \log \log n)$ average time while consuming $\mathcal{O}(n)$ space. Additionally, we illustrate that these techniques are relevant to various algorithmic challenges in computational biology and other fields.

We introduce a novel approach for retrieving clean CAD models from extensive databases to reconstruct detailed geometries from RGBD scans. Contrary to prior methods that rely on object shape descriptors to index small databases and select the top result, we contend that larger databases benefit from searching within a descriptor's neighborhood to locate more accurate matches. Crucially, we suggest that the lack of distinctiveness in instance-level shape descriptors can be mitigated through geometry-based re-ranking of this neighborhood. Our method first employs learned representations to differentiate model categories and then applies a new robust point set distance metric to re-rank the CAD neighborhood, facilitating fine-grained retrieval in large-scale shape databases. Evaluation on a real-world dataset demonstrates that this conceptually simple, geometry-based re-ranking strategy is highly effective, yielding a substantial improvement in retrieval accuracy over state-of-the-art techniques.

Popular discourse theories like RST and PDTB demonstrate that discourse information significantly enhances numerous downstream NLP tasks, yielding positive synergies and real-world benefits. Although methods for integrating discourse are becoming increasingly sophisticated, current discourse parsers fail to adequately address the demand for robust and general discourse structures. Typically trained on small, domain-limited datasets, these parsers produce noisy and unreliable predictions for arbitrary tasks. Consequently, the scarcity of high-quality, high-volume discourse trees severely hinders further advancement. To mitigate this issue, we propose a task-agnostic, unsupervised strategy for generating tree structures by extending a latent tree induction framework with an auto-encoding objective. This approach is applicable to various tree-structured objectives, including syntactic and discourse parsing. Given the challenging nature of manually annotating discourse trees, we first develop a method to create larger and more diverse discourse treebanks. This paper presents our inference of general tree structures across multiple natural text domains, demonstrating promising results on a diverse range of tasks.

Double-peaked spectral line profiles have been observed for several molecules toward the pre-stellar core L1544. While this morphology in abundant species is attributed to self-absorption, the physical origin of such features in less abundant species remains debated. To investigate the causes of double-peaked spectra in optically thin transitions and their connection to the physical structure of pre-stellar cores, we present high-sensitivity, high-resolution observations of the HC$^{17}$O$^+$ $J=1$-0 transition toward the dust peak in L1544 using the IRAM 30m telescope. Utilizing updated collisional rate coefficients, we modeled the hyperfine structure of this molecular ion for the first time with the radiative transfer code LOC, applying it to the predicted chemical structure of a contracting pre-stellar core alongside a core physical model and the fractional abundance profile of HC$^{17}$O$^+$. We applied an identical analysis to the chemically related C$^{17}$O molecule. Our non-local thermal equilibrium (LTE) radiative transfer model, based on chemical model predictions for a contracting core, successfully reproduced both the observed HC$^{17}$O$^+$(1-0) and C$^{17}$O(1-0) lines. However, reproducing the HC$^{17}$O$^+$(1-0) observations required an upscaled velocity profile by 30%. The double peaks seen in the HC$^{17}$O$^+$(1-0) hyperfine components arise from contraction motions at densities near the critical density of the transition ($\sim$10$^{5}$ cm$^{-3}$), combined with the decrease in HCO$^{+}$ fractional abundance toward the core's center.

Grasping an object through its constituent components is crucial, as it allows for a precise comprehension of the object's geometric structure and improves recognition capabilities when the object appears in unfamiliar orientations or is partially hidden. Nevertheless, manually labeling parts in extensive datasets is both costly and time-intensive. This paper proposes an unsupervised approach to discover object parts, eliminating the need for ground-truth part or keypoint annotations. Our method relies on the premise that objects of the same class in similar poses should exhibit aligned parts at comparable spatial locations. We leverage the fact that neural network features are mostly robust to nuisance variables, with object pose being the primary remaining source of variation within the same object category. Specifically, given a training image, we identify a set of similar images featuring the same object category in the same pose by applying affine alignment to their feature maps. The average of these aligned feature maps acts as pseudo ground-truth for supervised training of the deep network backbone. During inference, part detection is straightforward and efficient, requiring no additional modules or overhead beyond a standard feed-forward neural network. Experiments across various datasets from different domains confirm the method's effectiveness; for instance, we achieve a 37.8 mAP on VehiclePart, outperforming previous methods by at least 4.2 points.

Pyramid schemes are fraudulent investment models where upper-tier members of a hierarchical network generate profits by recruiting and exploiting a growing base of deceived newcomers. Although these schemes have operated for more than a hundred years, their internal dynamics and community structures have remained unstudied due to the opaque nature of participant transactions. This paper offers an empirical investigation of Forsage, a pyramid scheme executed via a smart contract that became one of Ethereum's most resource-intensive applications at its peak. Unlike traditional schemes, Forsage's bytecode and transaction history are fully visible on the blockchain, allowing us to leverage this transparency to examine its operational mechanics, impact on users, and development over time. We measured the multi-million-dollar profits earned by top-level participants alongside the losses suffered by the vast majority of users (approximately 88%). By analyzing the code both manually and through a custom-built transaction simulator, we revealed the scheme's intricate mechanisms. Furthermore, by examining promotional videos and social media activity, we demonstrated how promoters utilized the distinctive capabilities of smart contracts to deceive users with misleading claims of trust and profitability, and how the scheme's activity was concentrated within specific national communities.

We demonstrate why the 1-Wasserstein distance, $W_1$, equals the area between two marginal cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). By initially characterizing the Wasserstein distance through copulas, we establish that $W_1$ under the Euclidean metric is achieved via the $M$ copula. Since random variables linked by the $M$ copula exhibit perfect positive dependence, expressing them in terms of their CDFs reveals that the distance between them corresponds directly to the area separating the two curves.

The surge in mobile data traffic, coupled with rising demands for superior service quality, necessitates the creation of AI-driven algorithms to optimize wireless networks. This study explores how to develop policies that autonomously tune cell configuration parameters in response to fluctuating user demand. Our approach integrates existing offline learning techniques, adapting them systematically to address key challenges inherent to this domain. Empirical findings indicate that our proposed method can deliver significant performance improvements when implemented in live networks, all while adhering to practical constraints regarding computational efficiency.

The emergence of large language models (LLMs)—massive neural networks trained via predictive objectives on extensive natural language corpora—has reignited discussions about whether human-like cognitive abilities can arise in such generic systems with enough data. A key area of focus is their capacity to tackle novel problems without prior specific training, known as zero-shot reasoning, a skill in humans closely linked to analogical thinking. This study directly compared human reasoners with GPT-3 across various analogical tasks, including a new text-based matrix reasoning task inspired by Raven's Progressive Matrices. The findings revealed that GPT-3 possesses a remarkably robust ability to induce abstract patterns, matching or exceeding human performance in most scenarios. Consequently, our results suggest that LLMs like GPT-3 have developed an emergent capability to solve a wide array of analogy problems through zero-shot learning.

Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN) is a networking strategy designed to manage high latency and network interruptions found in various communication systems. These challenges typically arise from partial connectivity in frequently partitioned ad hoc wireless networks, extended propagation times in deep space and inter-planetary links, and frequent link failures caused by node mobility in terrestrial wireless environments. Due to the inherent complexity of these real-world scenarios, it is difficult to experiment with network architectures, protocols, and mobility models directly. Consequently, this document introduces the Urban Delay Tolerant Network Simulator (UDTNSim) version 0.1, a tool capable of simulating urban road networks with DTN-specific features, including routing protocols and mobility models. The mobility models supported in this version are: (i) Stationary Movement, (ii) Simple Random Movement, (iii) Path Type Based Movement, (iv) Path Memory Based Movement, (v) Path Type with Restricted Movement, and (vi) Path Type with Wait Movement. Beyond mobility models, the simulator includes three routing and data hand-off protocols: (i) Epidemic Routing, (ii) Superior Only Handoff, and (iii) Superior Peer Handoff. Built using an object-oriented programming approach, UDTNSim v0.1 offers the flexibility to integrate new features into the DTN environment. It is released as an open-source simulator intended for the research community.

Heavy-ion collisions generate a Quark Gluon Plasma characterized by three conserved quantities: baryon number (B), strangeness (S), and electric charge (Q). This work establishes the Israel-Stewart formalism for BSQ diffusion, incorporating both shear and bulk viscosity, alongside the necessary thermodynamic derivatives for coupling with a BSQ equation of state. We replicate a selection of the ${\mathcal{J}}$ terms found in the DNMR methodology and introduce a method to generate additional terms based on the maximum entropy principle. Furthermore, we conduct a stability analysis designed to constrain transport coefficients within BSQ hydrodynamics.

Multiple implicit approaches to inferring Horizontal Gene Transfer (HGT) concentrate on gene pairs that diverged only after the speciation event separating their host species. This temporal constraint defines the edge set of a "later-divergence-time" (LDT) graph, where vertices represent genes colored according to their species of origin. This study examines LDT graphs within relaxed evolutionary scenarios, which include all standard variants of duplication-transfer-loss models found in literature. We identify LDT graphs as a specific subclass of properly vertex-colored cographs and present both a polynomial-time recognition algorithm and a method to construct a relaxed scenario that explains a given LDT. While every edge in an LDT graph indicates that the corresponding genes are separated by at least one HGT event, the reverse does not hold. We demonstrate that the complete xenology relation is represented by an rs-Fitch graph—a complete multipartite graph adhering to specific vertex coloring constraints—and show that this class of graphs is also recognizable in polynomial time. Finally, using simulations of evolutionary scenarios with diverse duplication, loss, and HGT events, we address how much information regarding total HGT events is captured by LDT graphs. Specifically, we find that a straightforward greedy graph editing scheme can efficiently identify HGT events implicitly encoded within LDT graphs.

Recent research has suggested that quantum complexity—a concept from computer science recently revitalized in black hole physics—can serve as an effective tool for investigating novel phenomena, including quantum chaos and quantum phase transitions. This article bolsters the argument for the latter by employing the 1-dimensional p-wave superconductor, known as the Kitaev chain, as a model system exhibiting a topological phase transition. The Kitaev chain's Hamiltonian features two gapped phases characterized by fermion parity symmetry: a trivial, strongly-coupled phase and a topologically non-trivial, weakly-coupled phase containing Majorana zero-modes. We demonstrate that Krylov-complexity, specifically the associated spread-complexity, can differentiate between these two phases and act as a diagnostic for the quantum critical point dividing them. Furthermore, we address potential ambiguities in current literature regarding how sensitive various complexity measures are to topological phase transitions.

Static Information Flow Control (IFC) systems can restrict data movement within programs, effectively isolating sensitive information or vulnerable components from untrusted data or logic. Although IFC is a proven mechanism for ensuring the confidentiality and integrity essential to computer security, its adoption remains low due to the complexity of its underlying mechanisms, such as security label lattices and the dual concepts of confidentiality and integrity. We introduce a system that departs from prior IFC approaches by reasoning directly about the data developers already handle. This method naturally unifies the traditionally separate concepts of confidentiality and integrity into a single framework, thereby simplifying the reasoning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through two case studies focused on TLS private key management: one for Rocket, a widely used Rust web framework, and another for Conduit, a Rust-based server implementation for the Matrix messaging service.

We define metrics to quantify how much a time series drives interactions among others through synergy or redundancy. We demonstrate that for certain time series classes, early stimuli history generates synergistic effects on these interactions, while later history produces redundancy-dominated effects. These information-theoretic measures are practically easy to calculate, and we support this with simulations on both synthetic data and real-world signals. For instance, applying our metrics to intracranial EEG data reveals that activity from specific deep electrodes triggers synergistic information exchange between distinct brain regions during seizures.

The census of Milky Way globular clusters (GCs) remains an ongoing endeavor. This study investigates 19 new GC candidates within the Galactic bulge by analyzing their near-infrared colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs) derived from the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea Survey (VVV) database. We determined key astrophysical properties for these objects, including reddening, extinction, distance, total luminosity, mean proper motions, metallicity, and age. To identify likely members, we applied a decontamination procedure to the CMDs using vector proper motion diagrams from VIRAC2. The sample exhibits a reddening range of $0.25 \leqslant E(J-K_s) \leqslant 2.0$ mag and extinction of $0.11 \leqslant A_{Ks} \leqslant 0.86$ mag, consistent with bulge expectations. Heliocentric distances span $6.8\leqslant D\leqslant 11.4$ kpc, placing the clusters $0.56$ to $3.25$ kpc from the Galactic centre (assuming $R_{\odot}=8.2$ kpc). Their proper motions align kinematically with the typical Galactic bulge motion, except for VVV-CL160, which displays distinct kinematics. Derived metallicities range from $-1.40 \leqslant$ [Fe/H] $\leqslant 0.0$ dex, with ages estimated at $8-13$ Gyr. Luminosities were calculated in both $K_s$ and V bands, yielding absolute magnitudes of $-3.4 \leqslant M_V \leqslant -7.5$. Additionally, we examined potential RR Lyrae members in the cluster fields. Comparing our findings regarding position, kinematics, metallicity, and age with existing literature, we conclude that 9 candidates are confirmed real GCs, 7 require further observation for confirmation, and 3 are rejected as younger open clusters.

Recent breakthroughs in meta-learning have achieved impressive results across various few-shot learning benchmarks. Nevertheless, these achievements often overlook the relationship between training and testing tasks, leading to potential biases in evaluation. To address this, we introduce a generative method utilizing a variant of Latent Dirichlet Allocation to assess task similarity, thereby optimizing and clarifying meta-learning performance. Our findings demonstrate that this approach offers a valuable evaluation framework for meta-learning algorithms on two few-shot classification benchmarks, aligning with the intuitive principle that greater similarity yields higher performance. Leveraging this similarity metric, we developed a task-selection strategy for meta-learning, which outperforms random task selection by generating more accurate classification outcomes.

It is established that the upper critical dimension for the Ising model is $d_c=4$, beyond which critical phenomena become trivial. Based on extensive simulations within the random-cluster framework, we propose that the Ising model possesses a dual upper critical dimension structure at $(d_c=4, d_p=6)$. For dimensions $d \geq d_p$, critical clusters (excluding the largest) are characterized by percolation universality exponents. We predict diverse geometric characteristics and offer robust evidence across dimensions 4 through 7, as well as on complete graphs. These results substantially deepen our comprehension of the Ising model, a cornerstone system across numerous physics disciplines.

Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) is extensively utilized to extract low-dimensional data representations. However, standard NMF treats all attributes of a data point equally, often resulting in inaccurate representations. For instance, within a human face dataset, if an image features a hat, the algorithm should either disregard the hat or reduce the weight of its corresponding attributes during factorization. This paper introduces Entropy Weighted NMF (EWNMF), a novel variant that assigns an optimizable weight to each attribute of every data point to highlight their significance. This mechanism is implemented by incorporating an entropy regularizer into the cost function and applying the Lagrange multiplier method to resolve the optimization problem. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets confirm the feasibility and efficacy of this approach. The implementation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Poisson-EM/Entropy-weighted-NMF.

HEALPix, or Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization, has established itself as a standard in high-energy and gravitational wave astronomy. While originally designed to enhance the efficiency of all-sky Fourier analyses, it is now also employed for sharing sky localization data. However, when applied to this task, the requirement for a uniform all-sky grid limits its broader adoption within the community. To address this, this work introduces mhealpy, a Python library capable of generating, managing, and analyzing multi-resolution maps. mhealpy offers efficient pixel querying, map arithmetic operations, adaptive mesh refinement, visualization capabilities, and serialization to FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) files. As an extension of HEALPix, it enables the representation of highly resolved regions, providing a convenient common format for exchanging spatial information in joint multi-wavelength and multi-messenger studies.

This study presents a search for new light bosons decaying into muon pairs, utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV recorded by the CMS detector at the CERN LHC. The analysis adopts a model-independent approach, focusing solely on the pair production of a new light boson and its decay into a muon pair. No significant excess over the predicted background is found. Consequently, a model-independent upper limit is established for the product of the production cross section, the branching fraction to dimuons squared, and the acceptance, plotted against the new boson's mass. This limit ranges from 0.15 to 0.39 fb for boson masses between 0.25 and 8.5 GeV. These results are further interpreted within the frameworks of the next-to-minimal supersymmetric standard model and a dark supersymmetry model accommodating non-negligible boson lifetimes, yielding significant improvements over earlier published constraints in both scenarios.

NGC 1266 is a lenticular galaxy (S0) characterized by an active galactic nucleus (AGN) and a significant reservoir of shocked gas. By comparing the ratio of mid-J CO line luminosity to the IR continuum against star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and modeling the CO spectral line energy distribution (SLED), we determined that C-type shocks ($v_{\rm s}$ = 25 km s$^{-1}$, $n_{\rm H}$ = $5\times10^{4}$ cm$^{-3}$) effectively reproduce observations in the mid- and high-J regions ($J_{\rm up}$ = 4--13). Using the {\tt X-CIGALE} code to model the galaxy's spectral energy distribution (SED), we derived physical parameters, including a star formation rate (SFR) of 1.17 $\pm$ 0.47 \emph{M$_{\odot}$}yr$^{-1}$. Additionally, we calculated an SFR of 1.38 $\pm$ 0.14 $M_{\odot}$yr$^{-1}$ based solely on [C\,{\sc ii}] emission from neutral hydrogen regions.
