While previous research has yielded ambiguous results regarding the AGN or starburst nature of NGC 1266's nucleus, our SED modeling indicates an intrinsically low-luminosity hidden AGN, meaning its infrared output falls short of expectations. Furthermore, marginal hard X-ray detections from \emph{NuSTAR} (3--79 keV) argue against an obscured, luminous AGN, suggesting instead that a compact starburst likely dominates the nucleus.

Traditional gene expression analysis relies on clustering algorithms, which partition genes into groups based on similarity within an n-dimensional space to predict biological classifications. This study explores whether network analysis offers superior advantages over these conventional methods. We examined the pros and cons of constructing graphs from time-series gene expression data using either value-based or rank-based approaches. Four community detection algorithms—Clauset-Newman-Moore (greedy), Louvain, Leiden, and Girvan-Newman—were evaluated for their ability to predict five functional gene groups. The quality of these predictions, relative to known biological classifications, was assessed using the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI). Our results demonstrate that the Girvan-Newman algorithm outperforms the three modularity-based methods (greedy, Louvain, and Leiden) across both value-based and rank-based graph constructions. Furthermore, when compared to standard clustering techniques such as K-means, Spectral, Birch, and Agglomerative clustering, Girvan-Newman achieved a higher ARI. Additionally, this research provides a comprehensive tool for graph construction, visualization, and community detection to facilitate further analysis of gene expression data.

Defining time involves tallying the recurrence of periodic events. While past centuries have focused on developing stable and precise oscillators for clock regulation, this work examines a distinct category of clocks founded on stochastic clicking processes. We establish a rigorous statistical framework to analyze the performance of these devices, applying our findings to a single coherently driven two-level atom observed via photodetection as a paradigmatic example of a non-periodic clock. Furthermore, Quantum Jump Monte Carlo simulations and the distribution of photon counting waiting times serve as independent validations of our primary conclusions.

We introduce a new sound localization algorithm designed for non-line-of-sight (NLOS) sources within indoor settings. Our method leverages the diffraction characteristics of sound waves as they bend around obstacles or barriers. By integrating a ray tracing propagation model with a Uniform Theory of Diffraction (UTD) framework, we simulate these bending effects by positioning a virtual sound source on a wedge within the environment. We precompute wedges from a reconstructed mesh of the indoor scene to generate diffraction-based acoustic rays, which are then used to determine the 3D location of the source. A particle filter identifies the convergence region of these rays as the estimated source position. We evaluated the algorithm across various scenarios involving both static and dynamic NLOS sources. In our tests within a 7m x 7m x 3m room, the approach achieved an average localization error of 0.7 meters (L2 distance) between estimated and actual positions. Additionally, we observed a 37% to 130% increase in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods that ignore diffraction, particularly when the sound source is not directly visible to the robot.

This article extends the investigation into the $L^p$-boundedness of the maximal operator $\mathcal M_S$ linked to averages along isotropic dilates of a smooth hypersurface $S$ in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we examine small surface patches near a point $x^0$ that display singularities of type $\mathcal A$ in the sense of Arnol'd, addressing a previously unresolved scenario. By defining $p_c$ as the minimal Lebesgue exponent ensuring $L^p$-boundedness for $p > p_c$, we determine $p_c$ for all analytic surfaces of type $\mathcal A$ (excluding a minor subclass) using metrics derived from associated Newton polyhedra. Beyond the established concept of height at $x^0$, we introduce a novel quantity termed "effective multiplicity," which proves essential to this analysis. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture regarding the determination of the critical exponent $p_c$ through a geometric measure theoretic condition that assesses the order of contact between arbitrary ellipsoids and $S$, applicable to hypersurfaces of any dimension; we demonstrate that this conjecture holds true for all 2-hypersurfaces $S$ where an essentially complete understanding of $\mathcal M_S$ currently exists. Notably, our findings provide a proof of the Iosevich-Sawyer-Seeger conjecture for arbitrary analytic 2-surfaces.

This paper investigates a novel class of neural networks grounded in morphological operators, specifically dilation and erosion. We analyze these networks through the lenses of tropical geometry and mathematical morphology. Our contributions are threefold. First, we investigate training morphological networks using Difference-of-Convex programming and extend binary classifiers to handle multiclass problems. Second, we examine the sparsity of dense morphological networks trained with gradient descent, comparing them to linear models under significant pruning; we demonstrate that morphological networks handle this far more effectively, exhibiting superior compression capabilities, while our approach accounts for the training optimizer to provide both quantitative and qualitative insights. Finally, we explore how architectural design influences shape constraints, particularly monotonicity. Using Maslov Dequantization, we derive a softened variant of an existing architecture, illustrating how this method enhances both training convergence and overall performance.

Lepton scattering serves as a proven, ideal method for investigating the internal structure of small particles, including nucleons and nuclei. As a prospective high-energy nuclear physics initiative, the Electron-Ion Collider in China (EicC) has been proposed. This facility will be built upon the High Intensity heavy-ion Accelerator Facility (HIAF), currently under construction, by adding a new electron ring to the upgraded heavy-ion accelerator. The proposed collider will deliver highly polarized electron beams (approximately 80% polarization) and proton beams (approximately 70% polarization) with tunable center-of-mass energies ranging from 15 to 20 GeV and a luminosity of (2-3) × 10³³ cm⁻² s⁻¹. Additionally, the EicC will offer polarized deuteron and Helium-3 beams, along with unpolarized ion beams spanning from Carbon to Uranium.

The primary scientific objectives of the EicC include precise measurements of nucleon structure in the sea quark region, such as 3D nucleon tomography; the investigation of nuclear partonic structure and parton interactions within the nuclear environment; and the study of exotic states, particularly those containing heavy flavor quarks. Furthermore, the collider will address fundamental questions regarding the origin of mass through measurements of heavy quarkonium near-threshold production. To realize these physics goals, a hermetic detector system incorporating cutting-edge technologies will be developed. This document represents the collective efforts and valuable insights of global experts. The EicC physics program complements current scientific endeavors at the Jefferson Laboratory and the future Electron-Ion Collider project in the United States. Ultimately, the success of this project will significantly advance nuclear and particle physics, as well as accelerator and detector technologies within China.

Quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulators are characterized by topologically protected, spin-polarized edge states that resist backscattering, presenting significant potential for both fundamental research and practical applications. Despite these advantages, identifying suitable materials remains a persistent challenge. Utilizing detailed first-principles theoretical modeling, this study predicts the existence of large bandgap QSH insulators within the recently synthesized bottom-up two-dimensional (2D) MSi$_2$Z$_4$ family (where M = Mo or W, and Z = P or As) adopting a $1T^\prime$ structure. In the $2H$ phase, a structural distortion induces band inversion between the metal ($d$) and P/As ($p$) states, generating spinless Dirac cone states even without spin-orbit coupling. Upon including spin-orbit coupling, a hybridization gap of approximately 204 meV emerges at the band crossings, facilitating spin-polarized conducting edge states with nearly quantized spin Hall conductivity. Furthermore, the inverted band gap demonstrates tunability via a vertical electric field, which can trigger a topological phase transition from a QSH insulator to a trivial insulator exhibiting Rashba-like edge states. Consequently, this research identifies the $1T^\prime$ phase of the 2D MSi$_2$Z$_4$ materials family as promising candidates for large bandgap, tunable QSH insulators featuring protected spin-polarized edge states and substantial spin-Hall conductivity.

This study addresses human motion prediction, which involves forecasting future body poses from past sequences. While current state-of-the-art methods yield strong results, they depend on complex deep learning architectures like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Transformers, or Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), often necessitating multiple training stages and exceeding 2 million parameters. In contrast, this paper demonstrates that by integrating standard practices—specifically Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT), residual joint displacement prediction, and velocity-based auxiliary loss optimization—a lightweight Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with merely 0.14 million parameters can exceed the performance of existing state-of-the-art approaches. Comprehensive evaluations across the Human3.6M, AMASS, and 3DPW datasets confirm that our proposed method, siMLPe, consistently outperforms all competitors. We aim for this straightforward technique to establish a robust baseline for the community and encourage a re-evaluation of human motion prediction. The code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/dulucas/siMLPe}.

Scale-dependent renormalization issues that cannot be addressed perturbatively are pervasive in lattice QCD, playing a crucial role in numerous phenomenological applications. These problems necessitate the non-perturbative solution of renormalization group equations to connect low-energy non-perturbative values of QCD parameters and matrix elements with their high-energy equivalents required for phenomenology. However, bridging the substantial energy gap between the hadronic and perturbative regimes remains an exceptionally challenging endeavor. This contribution specifically examines the QCD coupling constant, critically analyzing the hurdles that current state-of-the-art lattice calculations must overcome to achieve significant improvements. Furthermore, we review a recently proposed strategy for resolving this non-perturbative renormalization issue and explore its implications for future high-precision determinations. This novel approach leverages heavy quark decoupling to match $N_{\rm f}$-flavor QCD with pure Yang-Mills theory, thereby shifting the computation of the non-perturbative coupling evolution to the computationally more tractable pure-gauge sector. We present findings regarding the determination of the $\Lambda$-parameter for $N_{\rm f}=3$-flavor QCD, where this method has been successfully implemented. These results indicate that such techniques hold the potential to achieve unprecedented precision in lattice-based QCD coupling determinations. Moreover, these concepts are broadly applicable and may offer solutions to other non-perturbative renormalization challenges.

Optical isolators are fundamental to photonic systems, yet existing integrated versions suffer from restricted bandwidths caused by strict phase-matching requirements, resonant structures, or material absorption. In this study, we present an ultra-broadband integrated optical isolator based on thin-film lithium niobate photonics. By employing dynamic standing-wave modulation in a tandem setup, we break Lorentz reciprocity to achieve isolation. At a design wavelength of 1550 nm, the device achieves an isolation ratio of 15 dB and an insertion loss under 0.5 dB. Furthermore, experiments confirm that the isolator operates simultaneously at visible and telecom wavelengths with similar performance, delivering isolation bandwidths of approximately 100 nm at both ranges. The device's substantial bandwidth, high flexibility, and real-time tunability promise to facilitate new non-reciprocal functionalities on integrated photonic platforms.

Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) are leading algorithms for modeling discrete and tabular data. Unlike neural networks that rely on millions of trainable parameters, GBDTs optimize the loss function additively with only one parameter per leaf, facilitating efficient high-order optimization. This paper presents a high-order optimization approach for GBDTs grounded in numerical optimization theory, enabling the construction of trees using high-order derivatives of the loss function. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves faster per-iteration convergence, resulting in reduced execution time. The proposed solution is easily parallelizable and can run on GPUs with minimal code overhead. We conclude by exploring future enhancements, such as automatic differentiation for arbitrary loss functions and hybridizing GBDTs with neural networks.

Within neutrino mass models featuring modular flavor symmetries, it has been noted that CP symmetry remains intact at the modulus parameter's fixed point, $\tau = {\rm i}$, but substantial CP violation arises in its vicinity. This study first develops a viable framework based on the modular $A^\prime_5$ symmetry to investigate lepton mass and flavor mixing phenomena. Subsequently, we apply explicit perturbations to the stabilizer at $\tau = {\rm i}$, providing both analytical and numerical insights into why minor deviations from this point generate significant CP violation. Given that low-energy observables are highly sensitive to parameter perturbations, we further illustrate the critical role of renormalization-group running effects in reconciling high-energy theoretical predictions with low-energy experimental data.

Our computations on ferromagnetic spin chains within s-wave superconductors reveal that the energy oscillations of edge states relative to chain length arise from a moiré pattern generated by the interplay of Friedel-like oscillations and the discrete nature of the spin-chain lattice. By adjusting the spin lattice configuration, we can regulate the moiré dispersion of these edge states. Specifically, we demonstrate the ability to engineer non-dispersive edge states that maintain a fixed energy irrespective of the size distribution of the spin chains. This represents a significant advancement in investigating edge states in spin chains subject to specific size variations.

This work derives key solar position formulae for an orbiting planet using a simplified model, including equations for sunrise direction, solar declination, the sunrise equation, daylight duration, solar altitude, and solar azimuth. The derivation employs the concept of effective axial tilt, the Rodrigues Rotation Formula, and orbital quadrant reflections to simplify the general case to that of the winter solstice. Additionally, it presents equations for converting solar time to clock time and calculating sunrise, sunset, and solar noon times, alongside the implementation of an analemma calculator. A comparison between the derived sunrise direction formula and a 304-point dataset of actual Earth sunrise observations yields an average accuracy of 1.25 degrees and estimates Earth's axial tilt at 23.52 degrees, which falls within 0.1 degrees of the accepted value of 23.44 degrees.

Driven by the increasing need for enhanced surveillance in smart cities, new systems are required to equip authorities, resource management agencies, and emergency call centers with superior monitoring tools. This study posits that a complementary solution utilizing a system capable of detecting sound events through Sound Events Recognition (SER) is highly advantageous. To advance the classification of these events, the research evaluated multiple classifiers using the SESA dataset, which includes audio samples from three hazard categories—gunshots, explosions, and sirens—alongside a class of incidental sounds that could be mistaken for hazards. The Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) classifier yielded the best performance, achieving an accuracy of 72.13% with a classification latency of 6.81 ms, thereby confirming the feasibility of this approach.

This study summarizes the key findings from our seismic analysis of B-type main-sequence pulsators, utilizing data from ground-based, MOST, Kepler, and BRITE observations. Our work establishes critical constraints regarding stellar opacities, convective overshooting, and rotation. Across all examined cases, a substantial alteration in the opacity profile at depths corresponding to $\log{T}\in (5.0-5.5)$ is essential to explain the observed pulsational behavior. Specifically, early B-type stellar models require an increase in opacity of at least 200% at the temperature level of $\log T = 5.46$ (known as the "nickel" opacity) to reproduce low-frequency, high-order g modes. Our seismic results indicate that the overshooting parameter, $\alpha_{\rm ov}$, remains below 0.3. Furthermore, for a subset of these stars, the deeper interior regions must rotate more rapidly to sustain g-mode instability throughout the entire observed frequency range.

Open datasets containing personal details remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks even after anonymization. Malicious actors can exploit shared attributes across multiple datasets to perform low-cost joins, thereby breaching individual privacy. However, open data is typically released under a "release-and-forget" paradigm, leaving data custodians unaware of these privacy threats. To bridge this gap, we created a visual analytic tool that empowers data defenders to identify disclosure risks within local, joinable data neighborhoods. This solution emerged from a design study with privacy researchers, involving an initial red-teaming exercise where we simulated ethical data hacking based on various privacy attack scenarios. Leveraging these findings, we developed visual interventions as a defensive strategy and implemented them in PRIVEE, a proactive monitoring workflow for data defenders. PRIVEE integrates risk scores with interactive visualizations, allowing defenders to examine vulnerable joins and assess risks across different levels of data granularity. We validated the tool's ability to emulate attack strategies and diagnose disclosure risks through two case studies conducted with data privacy experts.

This study investigates the settling behavior of falling spheres within Laponite suspensions. Laponite, a synthetic colloidal clay, undergoes physical aging in aqueous environments driven by the spontaneous evolution of inter-particle electrostatic forces. In our experiments, millimeter-sized steel spheres were dropped into Laponite suspensions of varying ages, defined as the time elapsed since sample preparation. Using high-speed imaging, we tracked the trajectories of the spheres to estimate the velocities of their centers of mass. Notably, we found that larger spheres failed to reach terminal velocity throughout the entire observation period. We developed a mathematical model that incorporates rapid structural modifications induced by the falling ball, particularly relevant when the suspension's aging timescale is significantly longer than the ball's fall time. For various sphere sizes and suspension ages, the model accurately predicts the time evolution of the ball's velocity. Additionally, by fitting experimental data to this model, we were able to quantify the rates at which the thixotropic suspensions undergo destructuring in response to the passage of the falling ball.

Destructive interference within a kagome lattice generates topological flat bands (TFBs), characterized by highly degenerate electron states. Although TFBs have been recently identified in various kagome metals such as Fe$_3$Sn$_2$, FeSn, CoSn, and YMn$_6$Sn$_6$, the scarcity of exfoliable and semiconducting kagome materials significantly impedes their practical device implementation. This study demonstrates that Nb$_3$Cl$_8$, featuring a breathing kagome lattice, exhibits a band gap due to the lack of inversion symmetry, yet retains its TFBs through the safeguard of mirror reflection symmetry. Utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations, we directly confirm the existence of these TFBs alongside a moderate band gap in Nb$_3$Cl$_8$. Furthermore, mechanical exfoliation yields stable monolayers of Nb$_3$Cl$_8$ under ambient conditions. Additionally, computational results indicate that monolayer Nb$_3$Cl$_8$ possesses a magnetic ground state, offering a unique platform to investigate the interactions among geometric structure, topology, and magnetism.

Collective flow observables serve as a sensitive probe for extracting insights into the equation of state of nuclear matter from heavy-ion collision data. To achieve more quantitative constraints, it is essential to carefully evaluate other factors influencing collective behavior. This study applies the hadronic transport model SMASH (Simulating Many Accelerated Strongly-interacting Hadrons) to investigate the first four anisotropic flow coefficients in Au+Au collisions at $E_{\rm lab}=1.23A$ GeV, aligning with recent measurements by the HADES collaboration. Given the importance of light nucleus formation in this energy range, two distinct methods are compared: a clustering algorithm based on coalescence and the microscopic formation of deuterons through explicit cross-sections. The analysis further examines how directed and elliptic flow observables respond to the strength of the Skyrme mean field. Additionally, it is shown that the rapidity-odd $v_3$ coefficient is effectively zero in this regime, while the $v_4/v_2^2$ ratio approaches the hydrodynamic expectation of 0.5. This work consolidates the current understanding of collective dynamics within the SMASH framework and provides a foundation for future quantitative constraints on the nuclear matter equation of state using refined mean field calculations.

IRAS23226-3843 has been identified as a changing-look active galactic nucleus (AGN) due to observed variations in its X-ray and optical spectra. Swift data from 2019 indicated a significant rebrightening in both UV and X-ray fluxes compared to 2017 levels. Subsequent observations conducted between 2019 and 2021 utilized Swift, XMM-Newton, and NuSTAR instruments alongside optical spectra obtained from the SALT and SAAO 1.9m telescopes. During 2019, the source experienced a pronounced outburst, with X-ray and optical continuum fluxes varying by factors of 5 and 1.6, respectively, over a two-month period; after accounting for host galaxy contamination, the optical variation corresponded to a factor of 3. Variability amplitudes in Balmer and FeII emission lines were comparable. Notably, the Halpha line profile evolved from blue-peaked shapes in 1997 and 1999 to broad double-peaked profiles in 2017 and 2019, yet these broad profiles remained stable in shape despite the intense flux fluctuations in 2019. By 2020, one year post-outburst, the optical spectral classification shifted to Seyfert type 2. Blue outflow components were detected in both Balmer lines and X-ray Fe bands. A deep broadband spectrum captured during the 2019 peak showed a qualitative resemblance to the 2017 spectrum but with flux levels ten times higher; the soft X-ray band appeared featureless, and the soft excess was effectively modeled using Comptonization. A broadband fit incorporating a power-law continuum, Comptonized soft excess, and Galactic absorption successfully matched the combined EPIC-pn and NuSTAR data, revealing a complex, broadened Fe K emission-line profile. The transition in IRAS23226-3843 is most likely driven by fluctuations in the accretion rate, occurring on timescales ranging from weeks to months.

Lattice mismatch in transition-metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers generates moiré patterns that create flat bands, where interaction effects surpass kinetic energy. At fractional fillings of the flat valence band, long-range electron interactions lead to the formation of Wigner-Mott crystals. This Letter explores the nontrivial electronic phases that emerge away from commensurate fillings. In this regime, competing phases appear: either doped Wigner-Mott charge transfer insulators or a new state featuring frozen charge order alongside conductivity, termed the "electron slush." We suggest that an extremely spatially inhomogeneous local density of states serves as a primary signature of the electron slush.

Driven by recent breakthroughs in machine learning across various fields, data-driven metamaterial design has become a promising approach to realizing the potential of multiscale architectures. However, the current model-centric focus lacks rigorous frameworks for data acquisition, leading to quality issues that negatively impact downstream tasks. Many existing metamaterial datasets are constructed using naive space-filling methods in shape descriptor space, resulting in property distributions that are either highly imbalanced or misaligned with specific design objectives. To address this, we introduce t-METASET, an active-learning framework designed to guide both diverse and task-oriented data generation. Specifically, t-METASET targets a common yet often neglected early-stage scenario in data-driven metamaterial design: when a vast library (~O(10^4)) of shape-only candidates exists without evaluated properties. Our approach utilizes a shape descriptor derived from generative models, employs a sparse regressor as an initial agent, and uses diversity metrics to direct data acquisition toward regions that best support design goals. We validate the framework through three deployment scenarios covering general, task-specific, and customizable applications, demonstrating its efficacy using two large-scale mechanical metamaterial datasets. As t-METASET is applicable to general image-based design representations, it has the potential to accelerate future progress in data-driven design.

This paper presents and analyzes discrete counterparts to Lebesgue and Hausdorff dimensions specifically for graphs. These new measures are found to be intimately connected to established graph properties, such as rank dimension and Prague (or Ne\v{s}et\v{r}il-R\"odl) dimension. This connection enables a formal definition of fractal graphs and allows for the demonstration of fractality within certain graph classes. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between a graph's Hausdorff dimension and its Kolmogorov complexity. Additionally, we highlight the value of this interdisciplinary methodology by uncovering a new characteristic of general compact metric spaces through concepts from hypergraph theory and by deriving an estimate for the Prague dimension of almost all graphs using techniques from algorithmic information theory.

We have conducted a systematic investigation of FRI and FRII radio galaxies using the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT) and MeerKAT. Our primary objective is to determine if the exceptional sensitivity achieved, reaching a few $\mu$Jy between 550 and 1712 MHz at resolutions of approximately $4^{\prime\prime}$ to $7^{\prime\prime}$, uncovers new characteristics in radio emission that could necessitate revisions to the current classification framework for classical radio galaxies. This paper reports findings for an initial set of four galaxies: 4C 12.02, 4C 12.03, CGCG 044-046, and CGCG 021-063. These sources were chosen from the 4C sample based on strict criteria and were imaged using the uGMRT at 550–850 MHz (band 4) and MeerKAT at 856–1712 MHz (L-band). We present full-resolution images for all sources alongside in-band spectral images from MeerKAT. Furthermore, combined uGMRT-MeerKAT spectral images and MeerKAT L-band polarisation maps are provided for CGCG 044-046. Our images reveal extensive morphological features, including filamentary structures within lobe emission, radio emission extending beyond hot-spots in three sources, and misalignments. We also briefly discuss the overall properties of CGCG 044-046 in relation to its local environment and indicate potential restarted activity in 4C 12.03, though this requires confirmation. Ultimately, we conclude that for the sources presented, the traditional FRI/FRII morphological classification remains valid given current enhanced imaging capabilities; however, the abundance of fine details suggests caution when applying automatic classification procedures in surveys with lower sensitivity and angular resolution.

This study examines the evolution of two mutually interacting games, encompassing pairwise interactions and public goods games across various topologies. On 2D square lattices, we demonstrate that game-game interactions consistently enhance cooperation prevalence; notably, as interaction strength increases significantly, phase transitions between cooperation and defection vanish, leading to high levels of cooperation. We developed a mean-field theory that identifies novel dynamical pathways within this framework. Detailed analysis reveals diverse interaction categories in both individual and bulk scenarios—including invasion, neutral, and catalyzed types—whose combination grants cooperators a persistent advantage, thereby boosting cooperation. The robustness of this reciprocity is confirmed through studies of model variants, such as asymmetrical or time-varying interactions, diverse game types, time-scale separations, and different updating rules. Furthermore, structural complexities in the underlying population, including Newman-Watts small-world networks, Erdős–Rényi random networks, and Barabási–Albert networks, do not disrupt the mechanism of dynamical reciprocity. Specifically, as the number of concurrent games increases, the level of cooperation generally improves. Consequently, our work identifies a new class of cooperation mechanisms and highlights significant potential for fostering human cooperation in real-world scenarios where multiple concurrent issues are common.

This study examines how new LHCb fixed-target $p\!+\!^{4}\!He$ data regarding $D^0/{\bar D}^0$ production influence the intrinsic $c \bar c$ component of the nucleon wave function. We find that within our framework, neither the standard gluon-gluon fusion or quark-antiquark annihilation mechanisms—computed via $k_T$-factorization or collinear next-to-leading order methods—can adequately explain the transverse momentum and rapidity distributions of these mesons. First, we analyze $c{\bar c}$-pair production under conventional frameworks, highlighting the critical role of $c \to D$ hadronization at low energies and low transverse momenta, an aspect previously unexamined. Additionally, we incorporate a contribution from the intrinsic $c \bar c$ component in the nucleon wave function, evaluating two symmetric models where $c(x) = \bar c(x)$. To achieve the necessary suppression of the minijet $p_{T}$ spectrum found in phenomenological models used by Monte Carlo generators, the intrinsic charm $g^* c \to g c$ (or $g^* {\bar c} \to g {\bar c}$) contribution must be regularized. We demonstrate that the regularization parameter in our model can be determined by fitting the LHCb fixed-target data. We also address uncertainties in our calculations, including scale, charm quark mass, and fragmentation function variations, and establish limits on the intrinsic charm probability. According to our model, an intrinsic charm probability of $P_{IC} = 1.65\%$ significantly enhances the description of the LHCb data, though this value remains subject to considerable uncertainty.

Over recent years, Electric Vehicle (EV) fleets have grown substantially, driven by a heightened focus on electrifying all transportation sectors. Primarily powered by Lithium-ion battery packs, an EV's operational range depends directly on the total capacity of its Energy Storage System. State of Charge (SOC), defined as the percentage ratio of remaining capacity to total capacity, is essential for accurately determining an EV's real-time range. This paper introduces a novel application of Temporal Convolution Networks (TCNs) for SOC estimation. The model was tested across various drive cycles—including HWFET, LA92, UDDS, and US06—at a 1 C rate and 25°C. Results demonstrate that the TCN architecture achieved an estimation accuracy of 99.1%.

Hand Gesture Recognition (HGR) presents significant challenges due to factors like lighting fluctuations, cluttered backgrounds, and spontaneous data capture. Traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) typically employ a two-stage pipeline to address these issues, including complex signs and background noise; however, existing methods often require expert intervention and auxiliary computations in the first stage to simplify input images. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, compact, end-to-end CNN framework called Fit-Hand (Fine Grained Feature Attentive Network for Hand Gesture Recognition). The proposed architecture comprises two primary components: the FineFeat module and a dilated convolutional layer. The FineFeat module leverages an attention mechanism across multiscale receptive fields to extract fine-grained feature maps, thereby capturing effective features by amplifying the average behavior of multi-scale responses. Concurrently, the dilated convolution layer generates global hand gesture features by expanding the receptive field. Furthermore, an integrated layer combines outputs from both modules to enhance the network's discriminability by synthesizing complementary contextual information regarding hand postures. The efficacy of Fit-Hand is assessed using both subject-dependent (SD) and subject-independent (SI) validation protocols across seven benchmark datasets: MUGD-I through MUGD-V, Finger Spelling, and OUHANDS. Additionally, ten ablation studies were conducted to provide deep insights into the proposed Fit-Hand framework.

Optimizing recommender systems using user interaction data is typically framed as a selection bias issue, with most prior research assuming independence among user interactions. However, real-world feedback often reflects the influence of other users' earlier actions—such as through average ratings, view counts, or sales figures—a phenomenon known as the bandwagon effect. Contrary to existing literature, we contend that the bandwagon effect should not be categorized as a statistical bias; rather, we demonstrate that it leaves both individual interactions and their sample means unbiased. Despite this, we show that it can render estimators inconsistent, creating unique challenges for convergence in relevance estimation. Our theoretical analysis examines the specific conditions under which the bandwagon effect causes consistency problems and investigates various strategies to mitigate them. Ultimately, this work aims to establish the bandwagon effect as an underexplored open problem that is fundamentally distinct from the well-studied selection bias in recommendation systems.

Research has established that preference judgments serve as a superior alternative to graded judgments for evaluating document relevance against queries. Previous studies have confirmed that transitivity holds among preference judgments collected from trained judges, significantly reducing the volume of required judgments. Furthermore, both strict preference judgments and weak preference judgments—which additionally permit judges to indicate equal relevance between two documents for a specific query—are prevalent in the literature. However, it remains uncertain whether transitivity persists when judgments are gathered via crowdsourcing, and if the two types of preference judgments exhibit similar behaviors. In this study, we collect judgments from multiple participants on a crowdsourcing platform and aggregate them to compare strict and weak preference judgments across three dimensions: transitivity, time consumption, and quality. Specifically, we investigate whether aggregated judgments are transitive, the duration required for judges to provide them, and the level of agreement among judges and between crowd-sourced judgments and those from TREC. Our primary findings indicate that only strict preference judgments demonstrate transitivity. Conversely, weak preference judgments differ significantly regarding transitivity, the time required, and the overall quality of the judgments.

The second law of thermodynamics addresses the statistical nature of entropy production, defined by $\langle \Sigma \rangle \geq 0$. In small systems, entropy production behaves as a random variable, allowing for the observation of negative values ($\Sigma < 0$) in certain experiments, a scenario often described as an apparent violation of the second law. To determine the frequency of such violations, we demonstrate that the strong detailed fluctuation theorem, given a specific average $\langle \Sigma \rangle$, establishes a tight lower bound for these apparent breaches. As practical applications, we confirm that this bound holds true for entropy generated during heat exchange between two reservoirs mediated by a bosonic mode under weak coupling, as well as for a levitated nanoparticle and a classical particle confined within a box.

We explore light scalar dark matter within an $L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}$ framework, where the dark matter candidate $\phi_{dm}$ possesses $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ charge but remains a Standard Model singlet. In this scenario, right-handed neutrinos are responsible for both baryon asymmetry and dark matter generation. We posit that dark matter production primarily occurs through scattering involving a pair of right-handed neutrinos; other processes are negligible due to the dark matter's minimal $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ charge, leading to a freeze-in mechanism for the relic density. Analysis of a viable parameter space reveals that the correct dark matter relic abundance can be achieved without disrupting leptogenesis, with the permissible dark matter mass range lying between $10^{-5}$ GeV and 0.1 GeV.

Estimating Lagrangian drift, such as for items lost at sea, is frequently unreliable because of unexplained physical processes within the available data. While introducing stochasticity is a common method to address this uncertainty, it relies on specific modeling assumptions. This study eliminates that dependency by proposing a fully data-driven approach to model probabilistic drift in flexible settings. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is trained to forecast the time-evolution of probability density maps for particle locations from time $t$ to $t+1$, using the velocity field as input. Ground-truth density maps are created using ocean circulation model simulations by introducing uncertainty into the initial positions of particle trajectories. Various loss functions for regressing these predicted density maps are evaluated. Testing the model on unseen velocity data from a different year reveals outputs that align well with numerical simulations, indicating satisfactory generalization across different dynamical scenarios.

The massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system holds great promise for delivering exceptionally high data rates. However, realizing this potential requires the transceiver to possess complete channel state information (CSI) for effective transmit/receive precoding and combining. In practical scenarios, acquiring this information is difficult due to inevitable processing and feedback delays, which severely degrade performance, particularly in high-mobility environments. To address this, we propose a deep learning-based framework that proactively predicts downlink channel state information by analyzing historical channel sequences. The core of this model utilizes a 3-D convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture to efficiently capture the temporal, spatial, and frequency correlations inherent in downlink channel samples, enabling accurate predictions. Simulation results demonstrate that this learning model can effectively extract relevant information and forecast future downlink channels directly from past observations. Consequently, it significantly outperforms the traditional sample-and-hold method and effectively mitigates the adverse effects of dynamic communication environments.

This research examines how extra fermions, charged under the Standard Model's $SU(2)_L \otimes U(1)_Y$ gauge group, influence the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within a type II 2-Higgs-Doublet-Model (2HDM). Our results indicate that the strength of the EWPT can be increased by approximately 40% relative to the standard 2HDM scenario. Consequently, incorporating additional light fermions serves as an effective mechanism to alleviate the conflict between tightening mass limits on BSM scalars and the necessity for extra light scalar degrees of freedom to sustain a strong first-order EWPT. These conclusions hold significant relevance for various non-minimal split supersymmetry frameworks, which inherently introduce new light fermion states.

This study introduces a generalized central limit theorem applicable to nonlinear functionals of the empirical measure derived from i.i.d. random variables, contingent upon specific regularity conditions for the associated linear functional derivative. This extension proves valuable for Monte-Carlo techniques, particularly in scenarios involving nonlinear dependencies on the measure component. Leveraging this finding, the authors address the impact of initial conditions on the convergence of fluctuations between the empirical measure of interacting diffusions and their mean-field limit as particle counts increase, specifically when measure dependence is nonlinear. Additionally, the time-evolution aspect is analyzed via the master equation, a parabolic partial differential equation utilizing L-derivatives with respect to the measure component; this represents a more rigorous form of differentiation that remains intrinsically linked to the linear functional derivative.

This work investigates the dynamics of metrics arising from measure-preserving transformations. We examine a sequence of average metrics and define the associated sequence of $\epsilon$-entropies (termed the {\it scaling sequence}) for the measure relative to these mean metrics. The central finding asserts that the scaling sequences of an automorphism with respect to any {\it admissible metric} are bounded if and only if the automorphism possesses a discrete spectrum. Consequently, this provides a non-spectral method to determine the discreteness of an automorphism's spectrum. While a related result was previously discussed in \cite{Fe}, our methodology differs. This paper is part of a series addressing the asymptotic theory of sequences of metric compacts equipped with measures and their significance in dynamics.

Protoplanetary discs within stellar clusters experience background heating, photo-evaporation, and truncation caused by stellar encounters, with the latter occurring based on stellar density. This truncation diminishes disc masses and characteristic sizes, ultimately inhibiting gas giant formation. This study examines the effects of disc truncation on planet formation using the pebble accretion paradigm, where pebble sizes are calculated from the full grain-size distribution over the disc's lifetime. We adopt a best-case scenario assuming a single embryo and one stellar encounter per disc. Through planet population synthesis, we observe that disc truncation shifts disc mass distributions toward lower values, thereby reducing gas giant occurrence rates. Nevertheless, the resulting encounter models largely resemble those of isolated field stars, maintaining a higher frequency of cold Jupiters compared to hot Jupiters, which aligns with observations. Furthermore, the hot-to-cold Jupiter ratio varies with the periastron distribution of perturbers; a linear periastron distribution yields an enhanced hot-to-cold ratio relative to other models. These findings are valid under our best-case assumptions: a single disc encounter, ambient background heating, and moderate photo-evaporation. Since the combined impact of these factors on gas giant formation remains uncertain, this study aims to motivate quantitative research into how stellar cluster environments specifically influence planet formation.

We introduce the Weil-\'etale complex with compact support for the duals (relative to the Bloch dualizing cycles complex $\mathbb{Z}^c$) of a broad category of $\mathbb{Z}$-constructible sheaves on a proper, integral, one-dimensional arithmetic scheme that is flat over $\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})$. This complex serves as a computational tool for Weil-\'etale homology. For $\mathbb{Z}$-constructible sheaves exhibiting tame ramification, we construct an "additive" complex interpreted as the Lie algebra of the sheaf's dual. The fundamental line is defined as the product of the determinants of this additive complex and the Weil-\'etale complex. We establish a duality theorem demonstrating that the fundamental line admits a natural trivialization, thereby yielding a multiplicative Euler characteristic. Furthermore, we associate a natural $L$-function with the dual of a $\mathbb{Z}$-constructible sheaf; aside from a finite number of factors, this function corresponds to an Artin $L$-function at $s+1$. Our primary theorem provides a formula for the vanishing order of this $L$-function at $s=0$ and asserts that, in the tamely ramified scenario, the special value at $s=0$ equals the Euler characteristic up to sign. This result extends the analytic class number formula, which governs the special value at $s=1$ of the Dedekind zeta function. A version of this theorem for function fields was previously established in arXiv:2009.14504.

The low-lying excited states of the $N=32$ isotope $^{50}$Ar were studied through in-beam $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy conducted at the RIKEN Radioactive Isotope Beam Factory, utilizing techniques such as proton and neutron knockout, multi-nucleon removal, and proton inelastic scattering. While confirming the energies of two transitions previously reported, the study introduces five new states for the first time, notably including a potential $3^-$ candidate. A level scheme constructed from $\gamma\gamma$ coincidences was evaluated against shell-model calculations within the $sd-pf$ space and ab initio predictions derived from chiral two- and three-nucleon interactions. Furthermore, theoretical analyses of proton and neutron knockout cross sections indicate that two of the newly identified transitions likely represent $2^+$ states, and the earlier proposed $4^+$ state may also be a $2^+$ state.

We introduce ANUBIS, a robust machine learning system designed for detecting Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). Our design centers on two key pillars: first, ensuring the system is practical for cyber-response teams by prioritizing prediction explainability; and second, leveraging system provenance graphs to capture causality, which drives superior detection accuracy. Central to ANUBIS's predictive engine is a Bayesian Neural Network capable of quantifying its own confidence in predictions. When evaluated against the DARPA OpTC dataset, ANUBIS demonstrates high accuracy in identifying malicious activities characteristic of APT campaigns. Furthermore, the system learns high-level patterns that enable it to generate explainable narratives for threat analysts. This combination of strong predictive performance and the ability to reconstruct attack stories positions ANUBIS as a powerful asset for enterprise cyber defense.

Imaging through scattering media remains a persistent challenge. While numerous methods exist for focusing light or capturing images in such environments, they are often invasive, limited to static or slowly moving media, or depend on high-resolution cameras and intricate algorithms for image recovery. We propose a computational imaging approach using spatial-temporal encoded patterns (STEP) that overcomes these limitations. This method enables non-invasive imaging through scattering media using only a single-pixel photodetector. Furthermore, the technique demonstrates insensitivity to media motion, and our reconstruction algorithm proves significantly more efficient than traditional correlation-based single-pixel imaging methods, potentially enabling rapid imaging in previously inaccessible scenarios.

Determining the real-time behavior of strongly coupled quantum fields is a primary objective in contemporary nuclear and particle physics, necessitating a deeper understanding of quantum field theory that extends beyond the weak-coupling regime. Although lattice QCD has yielded crucial insights into the non-perturbative static characteristics of quarks and gluons, it obscures their real-time evolution due to an ill-posed inverse problem. In this presentation, I will examine advancements in addressing this inverse problem on the lattice and highlight progress made in directly simulating real-time dynamics.

This study examines stability and stabilization principles for infinite-dimensional linear systems governed by time-fractional differential equations with Caputo derivatives within Hilbert spaces. Initially, utilizing a family of operators derived from strongly continuous semigroups alongside a probability density function, we establish both necessary and sufficient conditions for the exponential stability of these systems. Subsequently, by assuming the system dynamics are symmetric and uniformly elliptic and leveraging properties of the Mittag-Leffler function, we derive sufficient conditions ensuring strong stability. Finally, we identify an explicit feedback control law that achieves strong stabilization for a controlled Caputo time-fractional linear system via a decomposition method. Several examples are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the obtained results.

We introduce a realization of the fracton-elasticity duality formulated entirely through conventional gauge fields, covering standard elasticity alongside incommensurate crystals such as twisted bilayer graphene, quasicrystals, and broader moiré lattices. This framework details all two-dimensional defect types, including disclinations, dislocations, discompressions, and point-like defects, while accounting for body forces and impurities. By partially fixing the gauge, we recover the original tensor gauge field formulation of the duality. We determine how each defect type couples to the dual gauge fields and, leveraging gauge invariance, we derive generalized continuity equations for defect currents and the corresponding mobility constraints inherent to elastic defects.

This study examines the spectrum of linearized excitations within global vortices in $2+1$ dimensions. Following the identification of localized excitation modes, we calculate the decay timescales for the first two modes and compare these findings with numerical evolutions derived from the full non-linear equations. We demonstrate numerically how vortices can be dynamically excited when interacting with external radiation sources or other vortices. Furthermore, we simulate vortex formation during a phase transition and their subsequent interaction with a thermal bath to estimate the resulting mode amplitudes. These numerical experiments reveal that, despite the theoretical capacity of vortices to store significant energy in internal excitations, such dynamic accumulation does not appear to occur in practice. Additionally, we investigate the evolution of a vortex network within an expanding $(2+1)$-dimensional background, specifically a radiation-dominated universe. Our results indicate that while vortices remain excited throughout cosmological evolution, the excitation levels remain minimal; the additional energy stored within the vortices never surpasses $1\%$ of the total core mass.

In optics, coupled solitary waves are termed vector solitons to highlight their particle-like characteristics, which persist even following mutual collisions. These structures emerge from a nonlinear alteration in an optical material's refractive index, driven by light intensity. Our findings reveal that the second harmonic intensity profile produced by Bessel-like beams consists of solitons with diverse geometries encircled by concentric rings; notably, this includes a pair of central solitons of comparable radius intertwined by ellipsoidal rings. We find that their spatial geometry and intensity distribution rely on the topological charge of the incident fundamental Bessel beams. Furthermore, their spatial profile remains invariant during propagation. Their behavior mirrors that of screw dislocations in wave trains, as they collide and rebound at a $90^\circ$ angle relative to the beam's propagation direction. Consequently, we have successfully generated linked, frequency-doubled Bessel-type vector solitons with varying topologies that remain knotted while oscillating along the optical axis during propagation in a laboratory setting.

This paper addresses the critical crowd localization task within crowd analysis. While most regression-based approaches rely on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to generate density maps, they often fail to precisely locate individuals in extremely dense scenes due to two main factors: 1) density maps are composed of blurry Gaussian blobs, and 2) significant overlaps occur in dense areas. To resolve these challenges, we introduce a novel Focal Inverse Distance Transform (FIDT) map designed specifically for crowd localization. Unlike traditional density maps, FIDT maps accurately pinpoint person locations without overlapping in crowded regions. Building on this, we develop a Local-Maxima-Detection-Strategy (LMDS) to effectively extract the center point for each individual. Additionally, we implement an Independent SSIM (I-SSIM) loss function to encourage the model to learn local structural information, thereby improving the recognition of local maxima. Extensive experiments across six crowd datasets and one vehicle dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art localization performance. Furthermore, the proposed approach exhibits superior robustness in negative and extremely dense scenarios, further validating the efficacy of FIDT maps. The source code and models are accessible at https://github.com/dk-liang/FIDTM.

The Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA) is an optimization technique derived from Newton's laws of gravity and dynamics. Since its introduction in 2009, GSA has been adapted into various versions and applied across different fields. However, its effectiveness relies on empirically determined parameter values, which limits its general applicability because parameters optimal for one specific task may not work for another. To address this, this paper introduces the Gravitational Search Algorithm with Normalized Gravitational Constant (GSA-NGC), featuring a novel heuristic for calculating the initial gravitational constant. Rooted in the Brans-Dicke theory of gravitation, this heuristic accounts for the multiple dimensions of the search space. The goal is to enhance solution quality, decrease the number of iterations, and mitigate premature convergence. Experimental validation confirms that GSA-NGC is versatile across various applications and significantly improves the generalizability, performance, and efficiency of the standard GSA.

We report on photometric and spectroscopic data for the nearby Type Ia supernova SN 2019yvq, covering the period from approximately one day post-explosion to roughly 100 days after its peak. This event displays distinct anomalies, particularly an exceptionally bright ultraviolet (UV) excess occurring within the first five days. Swift UV observations reveal that this early emission surpasses the supernova's "peak" brightness, distinguishing SN 2019yvq as more extreme than other known cases with early UV/blue excesses, such as iPTF14atg and SN 2017cbv. Furthermore, the supernova is underluminous ($M_B=-18.4$), exhibits a relatively rapid decline ($\Delta m_{15}(B)=1.35$), and transitions to red colors following an initial blue bump. Spectral characteristics are also unusual, featuring broad-lined, high-velocity silicon absorption. Despite significant differences in peak spectra, we classify SN 2019yvq as a transitional member of the 02es-like subclass based on shared traits like color, peak luminosity, peak titanium, and nebular [Ca II] emission. We tested various published models, including those involving ejecta-companion shock interaction and sub-Chandrasekhar mass white dwarf double detonations. Radio constraints from the VLA establish an upper limit of $(4.5 - 20) \times 10^{-8}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr for the mass-loss rate of a symbiotic progenitor, leaving both red giant and main sequence companions as possibilities. Ultimately, no single model successfully reproduces all observed aspects of the dataset. Additionally, the prevalence of early UV excesses in 02es-like Type Ia supernovae implies a progenitor system capable of generating isotropic UV flux, thereby eliminating certain models for this class.

This study presents a comparative analysis of the existence of fixed points for homomorphisms within a specific class of binary relational systems versus the existence of fixed points for nonexpansive mappings in semimetric spaces.

We present a novel, concise proof of a specific one-scale epsilon regularity criterion by leveraging weak-strong uniqueness for solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations with non-zero boundary conditions, an approach inspired by Struwe's analogous method for the stationary system.

Nonlinear Markov processes constitute measure-valued dynamical systems that maintain positivity. They emerge as the law of large numbers limits of general interacting particle Markov models. In physics, kinetic equations admit Lyapunov functionals such as entropy and free energy, which can be viewed as an inheritance from microscopic master equations. This study investigates nonlinear Markov processes that acquire thermodynamic properties from their underlying microscopic linear counterparts. Furthermore, we develop the thermodynamics of these nonlinear processes and examine the asymptotic assumptions required to ensure this inheritance.

Regional economic disparities play a pivotal role in intensifying spatial heterogeneity. Since income surveys typically yield reliable estimates only at the national or macroregional level, we employ a small area model to calculate microregion-level values for various inequality metrics, including the Gini, Relative Theil, and Atkinson indices. Given that these inequality estimators are bounded within the unit interval and follow skewed, heavy-tailed distributions, we introduce a Bayesian hierarchical model at the area level that incorporates a Beta mixture. We apply this approach to EU-SILC data and conduct a design-based simulation. The results demonstrate that our model surpasses the standard Beta regression model regarding bias, coverage, and error. Additionally, we expand the analysis of inequality estimators by deriving their approximate variance functions.

The newly released Pantheon+ dataset, an updated iteration of Pantheon, holds significant cosmological value. To investigate the source of its enhanced constraining capabilities and internal correlations across various redshifts, we conducted a comprehensive tomographic analysis of Pantheon+ with and without Cepheid host distance calibration. Dividing the data into 10 bins for both scenarios, we identified the first bin ($z\in[0.00122, \, 0.227235]$) as the primary driver of the sample's constraining power, with no observed evolution in the Hubble constant ($H_0$) or matter fraction ($\Omega_m$). Incorporating SH0ES calibration significantly tightens the parameter space for cosmic background dynamics and lowers the constrained $\Omega_m$ values per bin. Notably, the third bin offers a potential local resolution to the current $H_0$ tension, yielding $H_0=71.6\pm4.4$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. Excluding calibration, combining Pantheon+ with cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, cosmic chronometers, galaxy clustering, and weak lensing data produces the tightest $1\,\sigma$ constraint of $H_0=67.88\pm0.42$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$. Conversely, adding the calibration induces a global parameter shift from this combined limit to $H_0=68.66\pm0.42$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, a value inconsistent with Planck-2018 results at approximately the $2\,\sigma$ confidence level.

We demonstrate that the mutual information between a learning machine's representation and the hidden features it extracts from data is lower-bounded by relevance, defined as the entropy of the model's energy distribution. Consequently, models exhibiting maximal relevance—termed Optimal Learning Machines (OLM)—are anticipated to yield maximally informative representations. Investigating this principle across various models, including fully connected Ising models, we reveal that {\em i)} OLMs are characterized by inhomogeneous coupling distributions, and {\em ii)} their learning performance is influenced by sub-extensive features that escape standard thermodynamic analysis. On specific tasks, likelihood maximization is observed in models with maximal relevance. Furthermore, training Restricted Boltzmann Machines on the MNIST dataset indicates that learning corresponds to a broadening of the energy level spectrum, with the hidden layer's internal representation approaching the maximal relevance attainable within a finite dataset. Finally, we examine a Gaussian learning machine to illustrate that learning hidden features is conceptually distinct from parameter estimation.

We introduce a model addressing the strong CP problem through an axion that is parametrically heavier than the conventional one. In this framework, Standard Model quarks are integrated into a larger non-abelian Grand Color group, which, at high energy scales, branches into standard QCD and a new confining sector under which exotic chiral fermions carry charges. Importantly, the axion's vacuum expectation value is naturally driven to zero because the sole renormalizable source of explicit CP violation—excluding topological angles—is found within the Standard Model Yukawa couplings, making it highly suppressed. The axion potential is governed by the scale of this new confining group and is significantly larger than the QCD contribution, thereby reducing its susceptibility to the "axion quality problem." Additionally, potentially detectable corrections to the effective topological angle may emerge in this model and in many other heavy axion scenarios due to non-renormalizable interactions that preserve the Peccei-Quinn symmetry, creating a new "heavy axion quality problem." Our approach features a minimal field content, relies strictly on gauge invariance, and avoids introducing extra symmetries beyond the standard Peccei-Quinn postulate. The resulting phenomenology is diverse and testable through both collider experiments and cosmological observations. Notably, a specific region of parameter space suggests a visible axion with a mass exceeding the GeV scale and a decay constant surpassing a few TeV.

This study introduces a technique for summarizing lengthy scientific papers that leverages the strengths of both extractive and abstractive methods. Prior to generating the summary abstractively, an extractive phase is executed to condition the abstractor module. Both the extractor and abstractor utilize pre-trained transformer-based language models. Our experimental results demonstrate that employing extractive and abstractive models together significantly enhances summarization performance and ROUGE scores.

Iharm3D is an open-source C program designed to simulate black hole accretion systems within arbitrary stationary spacetimes by utilizing ideal general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD). This implementation builds upon the HARM ("High Accuracy Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics") algorithm originally described by Gammie et al. (2003), incorporating subsequent updates detailed in McKinney & Gammie (2004) and Noble et al. (2006). While primarily derived from Ryan et al. (2015), the code excludes the radiative transfer components. HARM operates as a conservative finite-volume method for solving the hyperbolic system of partial differential equations governing ideal GRMHD on a logically Cartesian mesh defined in arbitrary coordinates.

Consider $M_\tau$, the Grauert tube of radius $\tau$ associated with a closed, real analytic manifold $M$. The orthogonal projection from $L^2(\partial M_\tau)$ to $H^2(\partial M_\tau)$, known as the Szeg\H{o} projector $\Pi_\tau$, is linked to the boundary of this tube. Let $D_{\sqrt{\rho}}$ represent the Hamilton vector field of the Grauert tube function $\sqrt{\rho}$ when viewed as a differential operator. This work establishes scaling asymptotics for the spectral localization kernel of the Toeplitz operator $\Pi_\tau D_{\sqrt{\rho}} \Pi_\tau$. Furthermore, it derives scaling asymptotics for the tempered spectral projection kernel $P_{\chi, \lambda}(z,w) = \sum_{\lambda_j \le \lambda} e^{-2\tau\lambda_j} \phi_{\lambda_j}^\mathbb{C}(z) \overline{\phi_{\lambda_j}^\mathbb{C}(w)}$, where $\phi_{\lambda_j}^\mathbb{C}$ denotes the analytic extensions to the Grauert tube of Laplace eigenfunctions defined on $M$.

Functional Distributional Semantics represents a newly introduced framework for acquiring distributional semantics with linguistic interpretability, modeling word meaning as a binary classifier instead of a numerical vector. This study introduces a method for training a Functional Distributional Semantics model using grounded visual data derived from the Visual Genome dataset, which more closely resembles the data encountered during human language acquisition compared to large-scale text corpora. Our model achieves superior performance on four external evaluation datasets relative to prior work on learning semantics from Visual Genome.

Web search frequently generates queries tied to specific events. This paper aims to enhance retrieval effectiveness by utilizing these events, with a specific focus on the task of query expansion. We introduce a technique that expands event-related queries by first identifying associated events and then selecting expansion terms that are semantically linked to both the original query and the detected events. To achieve this, we employ a novel approach that jointly embeds words and events within a shared vector space. Our results demonstrate that leveraging events significantly boosts query expansion performance compared to state-of-the-art methods across various newswire TREC datasets.

This study revisits the generation of lepton masses and mixing angles through the localization of five-dimensional fields within the bulk of Randall-Sundrum models, assuming the Higgs boson is confined to the IR brane. Three distinct mechanisms for neutrino mass generation are examined: (a) the higher-dimensional $L_H L_H$ operator, (b) Dirac masses, and (c) Type I see-saw with bulk Majorana mass terms. In the first two scenarios, neutrino and charged lepton masses and mixing angles are fitted using $\chi^2$ minimization of bulk mass parameters, with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Yukawa couplings varied between 0.1 and 4. Lepton flavor violation (LFV) is analyzed across all three frameworks. The results indicate that the $L_H L_H$ case requires large negative bulk mass parameters for right-handed fields to match experimental data, featuring a heavy Kaluza-Klein (KK) spectrum and relatively mild LFV constraints at leading order; here, charged singlet zero modes are composite, potentially yielding large effective 4-D Yukawa couplings to KK modes. For the Dirac scenario, viable fits exist for bulk mass parameters $c_i$ in the range of 0 to 1, though most optimal regions are excluded by LFV constraints. In the bulk Majorana case, profile equations are solved numerically, providing examples for both normal and inverted neutrino mass hierarchies, which exhibit large LFV rates. Finally, minimal flavor violation (MFV) schemes are discussed for both Dirac and bulk Majorana cases. Under the MFV hypothesis in the Dirac scenario, leptonic masses and mixing angles can be simultaneously fitted while suppressing LFV constraints for KK modes around 3 TeV; similar results are also demonstrated for the Majorana case.

Composite quantum materials serve as prime examples of multifunctional systems capable of hosting multiple novel quantum phenomena simultaneously. This work presents a combined experimental and theoretical investigation demonstrating an exceptionally large exchange bias ranging from 0.8 T to 2.7 T, alongside a fully compensated ferrimagnetic (FCF) state within a specialized cubic alloy of Pt- and Ni-doped Mn$_3$In. In this system, the FCF state arises from oppositely aligned uncompensated moments within two distinct atomic clusters that sum to zero. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal multiple possible ferrimagnetic configurations, identifying the FCF state as the energetically most favorable. The origin of the substantial exchange bias is attributed to the exchange interaction between the FCF background and uncompensated ferrimagnetic clusters, which are stabilized by a negligible energy difference relative to the FCF phase. We employed pulsed magnetic fields up to 60 T and static field magnetization measurements up to 30 T to verify the intrinsic nature of this exchange bias. Furthermore, Hall effect measurements highlight the critical role of uncompensated noncoplanar interfacial moments in achieving large exchange bias. These findings, which establish gigantic exchange bias in a unique compensated ferrimagnetic system, provide a pathway for designing new quantum phenomena with potential technological applications.

Amidst recent outbreaks, false information regarding monkeypox continues to proliferate rapidly online, adversely affecting response strategies and disproportionately harming LGBTQ+ communities in the short term while ultimately weakening public health efforts. To counter this misinformation, we introduce PoxVerifi, an open-source and extensible tool that offers a holistic method for evaluating the accuracy of monkeypox-related claims. By utilizing data from established fact-checking organizations and World Health Organization (WHO) publications, we developed an open-source corpus containing 225 verified monkeypox claims. Furthermore, we trained a specialized, open-source BERT-based machine learning model to classify monkeypox information, achieving 96% accuracy during cross-validation. PoxVerifi operates as a Google Chrome extension designed to help users navigate misinformation directly on any webpage without redirecting them to external sites. It provides a comprehensive toolkit that allows users to view automated accuracy assessments from our trained model, community-voted evaluations, and access similar, vetted claims. In addition to its robust claim-testing capabilities, the platform offers an efficient and accessible way to crowdsource accuracy ratings for monkeypox-related claims, which can be aggregated to generate new labeled datasets on misinformation.

Accurately predicting band offsets at semiconductor heterostructure interfaces presents significant challenges. While density functional theory (DFT) has proven effective for these calculations, there is a need for efficient and precise semilocal functionals to lower computational expenses. Typically, semilocal functionals utilizing the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) substantially underestimate bulk band gaps, leading to inaccurate band offset estimations at heterointerfaces. This study evaluates the performance of various advanced meta-GGA functionals for predicting band offsets in semiconductor heterojunctions. Specifically, we examine r2SCAN (revised strongly-constrained and appropriately-normed functional), rMGGAC (revised semilocal functional based on a cuspless hydrogen model and Pauli kinetic energy density), mTASK (modified Aschebrock and K\"ummel meta-GGA functional), and LMBJ (local modified Becke-Johnson exchange-correlation functional). Our findings indicate that these meta-GGA functionals perform exceptionally well in supercell calculations, particularly when compared to the computationally intensive GW method. Additionally, we report band offsets derived from ionization potentials and electron affinities, as well as band alignments determined via branch point energies. Collectively, our research demonstrates that these meta-GGA functionals can be effectively employed within the DFT framework to estimate band offsets in semiconductor heterostructures with high predictive accuracy.

This paper addresses challenges in Software Defined Networks (SDN), specifically focusing on traffic engineering, failure recovery, fault prevention, and Service Function Chains (SFC) under constraints for reliability and energy efficiency. These scenarios leverage Fog computing as an emerging approach to handle distributed, small-scale traffic flows traversing SDN-enabled switches, potentially Fog Nodes. The primary objective of this integration is to facilitate real-time service delivery, failure recovery, and fault awareness within an SFC framework. Initially, we introduce an architecture named FRFP for Failure Recovery and Fault Prevention. This multi-tier design routes real-time flows through SDN-enabled switches to collectively reduce network side-effects associated with flow rerouting and lower the energy consumption of Fog Nodes. Subsequently, we mathematically define an optimization problem termed the Optimal Fog-Supported Energy-Aware SFC rerouting algorithm (OFES) and develop a near-optimal heuristic, Heuristic OFES (HFES), to resolve this problem in polynomial time. Consequently, the selected paths are optimized for energy usage and reliability, ensuring Quality of Service constraints are satisfied while minimizing network congestion. Although the reliability focus centers on fault prevention, the proposed reallocation technique also functions as a failure recovery mechanism. We evaluate HFES and OFES by comparing their performance regarding power consumption, average path length, fault probability, network side-effects, link utilization, and Fog Node utilization, alongside an analysis of HFES's computational complexity. Using a real-world network topology for simulation, the results demonstrate that the heuristic algorithm is suitable for large-scale networks.

We develop a space-time parallel approach for solving parabolic partial differential equations by integrating the Parareal algorithm temporally with overlapping domain decomposition spatially. This strategy aims to create a discretization of "local" problems suitable for efficient parallel computation, though it necessitates a rigorous evaluation of the resulting significant error sources. By recasting the original Parareal algorithm as a variational method and applying a finite element discretization in space, we facilitate an adjoint-based a posteriori error analysis. Through strategic selection of adjoint problems and residuals, this analysis differentiates between errors caused by temporal and spatial discretizations, as well as those stemming from incomplete Parareal iterations and unfinished domain decomposition solver cycles. Our methodology first establishes an error analysis for the Parareal method on parabolic equations, subsequently refining it for the scenario where spatial subproblems are addressed via overlapping domain decomposition. These frameworks form our Time Parallel Algorithm (TPA) and Space-Time Parallel Algorithm (STPA), respectively. Numerical experiments confirm the accuracy of the error estimator for both algorithms and illustrate the iterations across the distinct error components.

Device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) is widely regarded as the most secure key exchange protocol because it operates safely even with uncharacterized black-box devices. This approach addresses numerous loopholes and side-channels that compromise existing QKD systems. Although implementing DI-QKD remains technically difficult, recent proof-of-principle demonstrations highlight significant advancements in both theoretical frameworks and experimental capabilities. This review introduces DI-QKD, summarizes related experimental efforts, and outlines the necessary theory and analysis techniques for ensuring security. The article concludes with a perspective on future research directions in DI-QKD.

We propose that the splitting of a fuzzy space into two distinct regions can account for the origin of black hole entropy and the apparent validity of a "generalized second law of thermodynamics" in black hole scenarios. By counting the microstates of a black hole modeled as a fuzzy space, we derive the Bekenstein-Hawking formula. This framework yields a discrete area spectrum for the black hole, where the spacing between states increases as the black hole approaches the Planck scale. Consequently, we demonstrate that black hole radiation exhibits decreasing entropy during evaporation, suggesting that certain information regarding the black hole's initial state may be recoverable.

This study aims to offer novel perspectives on the dynamics stemming from resonances caused by the interaction between Earth's oblateness and Solar Radiation Pressure (SRP) for uncontrolled objects with moderate to high area-to-mass ratios. The work presents analytical estimates for the positions of resulting resonant equilibrium points, along with formulas to calculate the maximum amplitude of eccentricity variations based on initial conditions and the object's area-to-mass ratio. Additionally, the periods of eccentricity and inclination fluctuations induced by these resonances are estimated using standard formulas, and a classification system based on the intensity of SRP resonances is introduced. The validity of these estimates is confirmed through numerical simulations, employing Fast Lyapunov Indicators (FLI) to generate phase portraits and bifurcation diagrams. Numerous FLI maps illustrating the location and overlap of SRP resonances are included. The findings suggest that SRP resonances can be effectively modeled within the framework of either the Extended Fundamental Model [1] or the Second Fundamental Model [2].

[1] S. Breiter. Extended fundamental model of resonance. Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy, 85:209-218, 03 (2003). doi: 10.1023/A:1022569419866
