This paper introduces an alternative method that generates autocompletions by extracting anchor texts from a large-scale web crawl, eliminating the dependency on query logs. Evaluation results indicate that while query log-based completions are superior for single-word queries, anchor text-based completions outperform them for queries containing two or more words.

Quantization methods have facilitated rapid and efficient deep neural network inference on devices with limited resources, inspiring researchers to investigate fully quantized training that includes back-propagation. Nevertheless, effectively quantizing gradients remains an unresolved challenge due to their unbounded nature and shifting distributions during training, which necessitate dynamic quantization. However, as we demonstrate, dynamic approaches incur substantial memory overhead and increased data traffic, thereby slowing down the training process. We introduce a straightforward alternative known as in-hindsight range estimation, which utilizes quantization ranges derived from prior iterations to handle current values. This method allows for fast static quantization of both gradients and activations while demanding only minimal hardware support to track output statistics online. Designed as a drop-in replacement for existing range estimation techniques, it complements other advancements in quantized training. We evaluate our approach against current methods in the quantized training literature and validate its efficacy across various architectures, such as MobileNetV2, on image classification benchmarks including Tiny ImageNet and ImageNet.

Many scene text detection approaches have emerged recently, with most claiming state-of-the-art results. However, performance comparisons are often unfair due to inconsistent configurations across training data, backbone networks, multi-scale feature fusion, and evaluation protocols. These disparities obscure the true strengths and weaknesses of the core techniques proposed. This paper meticulously examines these inconsistencies and introduces a unified framework for bottom-up scene text detection methods. Within this framework, non-core modules are standardized to ensure fair comparisons, allowing us to focus on representations for arbitrary-shaped text, such as contour point regression, pixel clustering with auxiliary information, and connected component grouping via learned linkages. Through comprehensive investigation and detailed analysis, this work not only removes barriers to understanding performance differences among existing methods but also clarifies the specific advantages and limitations of previous models under equitable conditions.

This study confirms Lee-Lee's conjecture, which demonstrates that the collection of associated roots for non-self-intersecting curves within an $n$-punctured disc coincides exactly with the set of real Schur roots of acyclic (valued) quivers possessing $n$ vertices.

Recently, there has been growing interest in integrating mathematical morphology into deep neural networks. However, substituting standard convolutional layers with erosion or dilation operations presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiable nature of min and max functions. To address this, p-convolutional layers were introduced as a solution; by leveraging the asymptotic behavior of the counter-harmonic mean, they enable pseudo-dilation or pseudo-erosion depending on an internal parameter $p$, yielding promising outcomes. This paper introduces two novel morphological layers that follow the same foundational principle as p-convolutional layers but overcome their primary limitations, demonstrating their potential utility for future integration into deep convolutional neural network architectures.

We calculate the production rate of axion-like particles within the Earth's core, assuming a temperature of approximately 5000K. By requiring that the core cooling rate remain below 100K/Gyr, consistent with geophysical models, we establish a constraint on thermal geo-axion emission. This analysis leads to a "quasi-vacuum" limit on the axion-electron fine structure constant, $\alpha_a^{QV} < 10^{-18}$, which exceeds current accelerator-based vacuum bounds by four orders of magnitude. Additionally, we explore the potential of using a geoscope to detect geo-axions via photon conversion, offering further opportunities to tighten constraints on $\alpha_a^{QV}$.

Diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) is increasingly viewed as a more accurate, though computationally demanding, alternative to Density Functional Theory (DFT) for predicting the energies of catalytic systems. The primary obstacle to applying DMC in catalysis is the necessity of finite-size extrapolation, which requires simulating progressively larger supercells to mitigate many-body finite-size effects and reach the thermodynamic limit. This study demonstrates that such computational costs can be drastically lowered by exploiting the cancellation of many-body finite-size errors inherent in calculating energy differences, such as binding energies and potential energy surfaces. We validated this error cancellation and convergence using two established adsorbate/slab systems: H2O/LiH(001) and CO/Pt(111). Based on these findings, we propose strategies to achieve thermodynamic-limit binding energies that maximize error cancellation while balancing accuracy and efficiency. Consequently, we correctly predicted the adsorption site preference order on CO/Pt(111)—a task difficult for DFT—recovering the top > bridge > hollow sequence consistent with experimental data. Furthermore, we mapped the potential energy surface for CO diffusion across Pt(111) sites, revealing an L-shaped top-bridge-hollow trajectory with energy barriers that offer additional kinetic support for experimental observations. In summary, this work proves that leveraging error cancellation in energy difference calculations can routinely yield order-of-magnitude improvements in speed and memory usage for DMC simulations, a technique applicable broadly to heterogeneous catalysis and surface chemistry.

Bimonoidal categories, alternatively called rig categories, are structures possessing two monoidal operations where one distributes over the other. We provide a formal definition of sheet diagrams, a graphical system for these categories that Staton previously introduced informally. These diagrams consist of string diagrams situated on a branching surface, which can be conceptualized as an extruded string diagram. Our primary contribution is a standard soundness and completeness theorem for this calculus, demonstrating that sheet diagrams constitute the free bimonoidal category generated by a given signature.

Metasurfaces offer a flexible foundation for creating ultrathin flat optical components suitable for numerous applications. The design workflow typically entails defining or computing the phase profile necessary to achieve a specific optical result. In this work, we introduce an inverse design technique to determine the phase profile required to shape the intensity distribution of a collimated input beam. Drawing upon the principles of optimal transport from non-imaging optics, our model facilitates the redistribution of a collimated beam with any arbitrary intensity pattern into a target output profile. We derive this model from the generalized law of refraction and numerically resolve the resulting differential equation via a finite-difference method. Various examples demonstrate that our approach handles diverse input and output intensity configurations, and we evaluate its viability as a design framework for non-imaging optics.

Resonantly scattered Lyman-$\alpha$ radiation reveals extended neutral hydrogen halos within the circumgalactic medium. We report integral field observations from the Keck Cosmic Web Imager capturing spatially extended, double-peaked Ly$\alpha$ emission in 12 low-mass ($M_{\star} \sim10^9 \, M_{\odot}$) galaxies at $z\sim2$ that exhibit extreme nebular lines. By analyzing individual spaxels, small bins, and radially binned profiles across larger regions, we observe that for most targets, the Ly$\alpha$ blue-to-red peak ratio rises, peak separation shrinks, and the fraction of flux at line center grows with increasing radius. New radiative transfer simulations model each galaxy as a clumpy, multiphase outflow with radially dependent velocities, applying this same velocity structure to low-ionization interstellar absorption features. These models successfully replicate the radial trends in peak ratios, separations, and trough depths, broadly aligning outflow velocities derived from Ly$\alpha$ with those from absorption lines. Our sample is best described by a scenario where neutral, outflowing clumps exist within a hotter, highly ionized inter-clump medium (ICM), whose remaining neutral gas generates absorption at systemic redshift. Specifically, the line-of-sight outflow velocity primarily dictates the peak ratio, HI column density controls peak separation, and residual neutral density in the ICM determines the trough flux fraction. Additionally, azimuthal asymmetries in the line profiles indicate non-radial gas motions at large radii and fluctuations in HI column density within outer halos.

This study addresses monostatic radar sensing using orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) in joint radar-communications (JRC) systems affected by phase noise (PN) arising from oscillator imperfections. We start with a rigorous statistical analysis of PN in the radar receiver across multiple OFDM symbols for both free-running oscillators (FROs) and phase-locked loops (PLLs). Utilizing a delay-dependent PN covariance matrix, we formulate a hybrid maximum-likelihood (ML)/maximum a-posteriori (MAP) estimator for deterministic delay-Doppler parameters and random PN, which creates a difficult high-dimensional nonlinear optimization challenge. To address this nonlinearity, we introduce an iterated small angle approximation (ISAA) algorithm that iteratively refines delay-Doppler-PN estimates using closed-form PN updates dependent on delay-Doppler at each step. Furthermore, diverging from conventional methods that treat PN solely as a nuisance to be mitigated, we propose leveraging PN to resolve range ambiguities by exploiting its delay-dependent statistics (specifically the range correlation effect) through a parametric Toeplitz-block Toeplitz covariance matrix reconstruction approach. Simulation results demonstrate the rapid convergence of ISAA to the hybrid Cramér-Rao bound (CRB) and significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art benchmarks for both FROs and PLLs under diverse conditions, proving that the adverse effects of PN can be transformed into a sensing advantage.

Future Adaptive Optics (AO) systems for large telescopes will demand significant computational power and memory bandwidth, posing challenges with current technology. This work aims to develop a future-proof AO platform based on FPGA architecture that scales with subapertures, pixels per subaperture, and external memory. Using a commercial off-the-shelf FPGA development board, we have created a scalable platform where AO reconstruction time is constrained only by external memory bandwidth. The SPARC design utilizes consistent logic resources regardless of the number of subapertures. This paper targets embedded developers interested in FPGA design and hardware interfaces, focusing on how scalability is integrated across various levels of the FPGA implementation. This work continues Part 1, which detailed the concept, objectives, control scheme, and validation methods for testing the platform.

We describe an atypical class of pressure-driven quantum phase transition in URhSn, characterized by two bicritical points occurring at 6.25 GPa. This distinct transition involves a Fermi surface reconstruction that separates competing ordered phases, which can be effectively modeled using both localized and itinerant descriptions of the magnetic $5f$-electrons. Furthermore, ferromagnetic fluctuations across a broad spectrum of temperatures and pressures within the low-temperature, pressure-induced phase are confirmed by a persistent $T^{5/3}$ resistivity dependence extending up to 11 GPa, indicative of a rare marginal Fermi-liquid state.

Basket trials are increasingly employed to evaluate a novel therapy across multiple patient subgroups under a single protocol. We introduce a Bayesian framework for determining sample sizes in such trials that allows for information borrowing between commensurate subsets. Specifically, we examine a randomized basket design where participants are assigned to either the new treatment or a control within each subtrial. We derive closed-form formulas to ensure each subtrial achieves a predefined probability of correctly determining whether the treatment is superior or not better than the control by a clinically meaningful margin. Subtrial sample sizes are solved simultaneously based on pre-specified levels of pairwise commensurability. When borrowing is disabled, our Bayesian method yields sample sizes comparable to frequentist formulations; however, when borrowing is enabled among commensurate subtrials, the required total sample size is significantly reduced compared to standard non-borrowing approaches. We demonstrate the application of these formulas using two examples drawn from real-world basket trials. Furthermore, a comprehensive simulation study confirms that the proposed methodology maintains true and false positive rates at the desired levels.

Assuming $\eta(1405)$ and $\eta(1475)$ correspond to a single state, we identify $\eta(1295)$ and the $\eta(1405/1475)$ system as the first radial excitations of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons, respectively. This work investigates their production and radiative decays within the $J/\psi\to \gamma\eta_X\to \gamma\gamma V$ channel, where $\eta_X$ represents $\eta(1295)$ and $\eta(1405/1475)$, and $V$ denotes the vector mesons $\rho^0$, $\omega$, and $\phi$. Building on prior research indicating that hadronic decays of these states are significantly influenced by $\bar{K}K^*+c.c.$ meson loops via the triangle singularity mechanism, we demonstrate that similar measurable effects emerge in their radiative decays. Our calculations reveal that the impact of these $\bar{K}K^*+c.c.$ loops on $\eta(1405/1475)$ radiative decays is comparatively minor relative to $\eta(1295)$, due to the latter's substantially stronger coupling to $\bar{K}K^*+c.c.$ However, this same mechanism strongly suppresses the production of $\eta(1295)$ in $J/\psi$ radiative decays. Consequently, the mixing angles extracted from the radiative decays of $\eta(1295)$ and $\eta(1405/1475)$ differ from one another and deviate from values determined in other processes.

Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) using Supervised Learning offers a straightforward and efficient approach for acquiring robotic skills from datasets generated by policies of varying expertise. While it mirrors the simplicity of supervised learning and Behavior Cloning (BC), it additionally utilizes return information. Research indicates that implicit BC can match or surpass explicit BC on datasets derived from policies of comparable skill levels. Despite the advantages of implicit models for learning robotic skills through BC, current offline RL via Supervised Learning methods have been restricted to explicit models. This work demonstrates how implicit models can effectively leverage return information to match or exceed the performance of explicit algorithms when learning from fixed datasets. Moreover, we establish a close connection between our implicit approaches and other established RL via Supervised Learning techniques, thereby creating a unified framework. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our method on high-dimensional manipulation and locomotion tasks.

Detecting and classifying stress through wearable sensor data represents a burgeoning research field with profound implications for physical and mental well-being. This study introduces ADARP, a novel dataset comprising physiological metrics and self-reported results gathered in real-world ambulatory environments from individuals diagnosed with alcohol use disorders. We detail the user study, outline the dataset specifications, confirm the strong correlation between physiological signals and self-reported outcomes, validate stress classification capabilities, and release the dataset publicly to advance future research.

Research indicates that software, akin to natural language, displays "naturalness" measurable via statistical language models. Recently, deep learning has enabled neural language models to represent this software naturalness. This paper presents an experimental assessment of cutting-edge neural language models for source code, specifically comparing RNN-based architectures with Transformer-XL models. Using a large-scale Python code corpus, our experiments demonstrate that the Transformer-XL model surpasses RNN-based approaches, such as LSTM and GRU, in capturing software naturalness while requiring significantly lower computational resources.

This study addresses the problem of enumerating results for similarity-join queries under dynamic conditions. Specifically, given two point sets $A$ and $B$ of size $n$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, a metric $\phi(\cdot)$, and a radius $r > 0$, the task is to identify all pairs $(a, b) \in A \times B$ such that $\phi(a,b) \le r$. The objective is to design a dynamic data structure that maintains these sets and efficiently enumerates all qualifying pairs with a bounded worst-case delay between consecutive outputs, while also supporting fast insertions and deletions. We introduce several efficient structures for low-dimensional settings. For exact similarity joins, we achieve near-linear space complexity with $\log^{O(1)} n$ update and delay times for $\ell_1$ and $\ell_\infty$ metrics, but demonstrate that such structures are infeasible for the $\ell_2$ metric when $d \ge 4$. Regarding approximate similarity joins, where the distance threshold is relaxed, we develop a unified linear-size structure for $\ell_p$ metrics offering $\log^{O(1)} n$ delay and update performance. In high-dimensional spaces, we propose an efficient solution with worst-case delay guarantees based on locality sensitive hashing (LSH).

This study examines the "Relativization Barrier" concerning the Baker-Gill-Solovay oracle Turing machine. It demonstrates that the {\em diagonalization} method constitutes a legitimate mathematical proof technique, provided certain conditions are met when addressing the "relativization barrier."

Sendov's conjecture posits that for any complex polynomial $f$ of degree $n \geq 2$ with all roots contained within the closed unit disk $\{ z: |z| \leq 1 \}$, every root $\lambda_0$ has a corresponding root of the derivative $f'$ within the closed disk $\{ z: |z-\lambda_0| \leq 1 \}$. While this conjecture is established for $n < 9$, results for higher degrees remain incomplete. We demonstrate the existence of a threshold constant $n_0$ such that the conjecture is valid for all $n \geq n_0$. Specifically, we rely on the work of Dégot and Chalebgwa when $\lambda_0$ is distant from both the origin and the unit circle; we refine Miller's earlier approach (supplemented by Chijiwa's results for $\lambda_0$ extremely close to the boundary) when $\lambda_0$ is near the unit circle; and for $\lambda_0$ near the origin, we develop a novel proof utilizing compactness, balayage, and the argument principle.

For a graph class $\mathcal G$, let ${\mathcal G}_n$ represent the collection of graphs in $\mathcal G$ defined on the vertex set $[n]$. When studying specific classes $\mathcal G$, researchers often examine the asymptotic behavior of a graph $R_n$ chosen uniformly at random from ${\mathcal G}_n$. A class $\mathcal G$ is termed "smooth" if the ratio $ n |{\mathcal G}_{n-1}| / |{\mathcal G}_n|$ converges to a limit as $n$ approaches infinity. Establishing the smoothness of a graph class is a crucial preliminary step in analyzing properties of $R_n$, specifically the asymptotic probability of connectivity and the limiting behavior of the components of $R_n$ excluding its largest one. While the composition method by Bender, Canfield, and Richmond demonstrated that surface-embeddable graphs form a smooth class, and minor-closed classes with excluded 2-connected minors also exhibit smoothness, this work extends those findings. Under broad conditions, we prove that our graph classes are smooth and characterize the limiting distribution of the fragment outside the largest component and the size of the core. Furthermore, analogous results are derived for graphs within the class possessing a minimum degree of at least 2.

Recent research (Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 110, 20402 (2013)) introduced 2D-Raman-THz spectroscopy to directly investigate the intermolecular degrees of freedom within liquid water's hydrogen-bond network. Despite its potential, the technique's informational depth remains largely unexplored. Although existing spectroscopic signals can be modeled using molecular dynamics simulations paired with water force fields, linking these spectral signatures to the microscopic details of those force fields remains challenging. This study adopts a distinct approach, beginning with the most fundamental model: a single vibrational mode characterized by electrical and mechanical anharmonicity, enhanced with homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening. An intuitive Feynman diagram framework is constructed to represent all feasible pulse sequences in hybrid 2D-Raman-THz spectroscopy. The results demonstrate that this model accounts for experimental data with high quantitative accuracy using a minimal parameter set, leading to the tentative conclusion that the observed signal stems from the hydrogen-bond stretching vibration near 170 cm$^{-1}$. Additionally, the echo present in the experimental data is quantified through model fitting, with its dominant linewidth attributed to quasi-inhomogeneous broadening under slow-modulation conditions. This broadening, with a correlation time of 370 fs, reflects the lifetime of the hydrogen-bond networks responsible for the absorption band.

This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to calculate statistical equilibrium quantities on a cubic lattice, specifically addressing scenarios involving both energy and statistical temperature. We show that the pivot algorithm, effective in contexts like protein folding for temperatures near the polymeric regime, is ineffective elsewhere. In contrast, our new approach, which relies on localized transformations, performs robustly across all temperature ranges. By accurately approximating equilibrium energy, we also present an efficient method for computing equilibrium entropy at any temperature. We apply these algorithms to model suction or supercritical vortices within tornadic flows, represented as vortex filaments on a cubic lattice. Our findings confirm that supercritical vortices, characterized as smooth and straight, possess the highest energy and correspond to negative temperatures in this framework. Conversely, the lowest-energy states are highly folded and compacted into ball-like structures. These results validate A. Chorin's conclusion that high-energy supercritical vortices in tornadic flows must fold when they extend.

Human red blood cells exhibit consistent sizes, a biological fact we leverage as a prior to classify and detect cells in images where only a sparse set of bounding boxes is available, while the majority are marked with points. This scenario defines a weakly semi-supervised learning task. Our approach substitutes point annotations during training with either stochastic (ST) boxes or predicted bounding boxes. Specifically, our "mean-IOU" ST box strategy maximizes overlap across all boxes in the sample space, guided by a class-specific prior probability distribution of bounding boxes. Unlike existing two-stage methods that train sequentially on boxes then points, our method jointly trains on both box- and point-labeled images. In the most difficult setting, where only 5% of images contain box annotations, our one-stage technique surpasses two-stage methods by 5.56 mAP on a urine dataset. Additionally, we propose a framework to determine the necessary quantity of box-labeled annotations prior to model training.

Following the successful synthesis of low-symmetry penta-PdPSe, which exhibits intrinsic in-plane anisotropy (Li et al., Adv. Mater., 2021), we employed density functional theory to examine its structural, mechanical, electronic, optical, and thermoelectric characteristics. Stability was confirmed through phonon dispersion analysis, molecular dynamics simulations, and cohesive energy calculations, revealing a distinct gap between high- and low-frequency optical branches and a quadratic out-of-plane flexure mode at long wavelengths. The calculated Poisson's ratio indicates that the penta-PdPSe monolayer behaves as a brittle material. Electronic structure analysis identifies it as an indirect semiconductor with bandgaps of 1.40 eV (PBE) and 2.07 eV (HSE06). Optical simulations demonstrate significant absorption across the visible to ultraviolet spectrum, while band alignment studies suggest suitability for water-splitting photocatalysis. Furthermore, the integration of electrical and thermal transport properties indicates a high power factor at room temperature, positioning penta-PdPSe as a promising candidate for thermoelectric devices. Collectively, these results highlight the material's potential for diverse applications in optoelectronics, photocatalysis, and thermoelectrics.

When building econometric or statistical models, we select relevant variables from a large pool of candidates. We utilize a coalitional game to address this selection issue, treating the candidates as players and defining the payoff function based on model performance across various scenarios. Consequently, an irrelevant feature corresponds to a dummy player in the game, offering no value in any modeling context. A feature is deemed irrelevant if a hypothesis test indicates its mean contribution is zero. In our mechanism design, the ultimate objective aligns perfectly with expected model performance by matching the expected sum of individual marginal effects. Within a specific class of noninformative likelihoods, this matching equation assigns a distinct valuation to each feature. Following the estimation of these valuations and their standard deviations, we eliminate any candidate feature whose valuation is not statistically distinguishable from zero. Simulation studies demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly surpasses several widely used practical methods, exhibiting robust accuracy regardless of the chosen payoff function.

Rising industry demands for higher throughput are driving the need for lightweight, high-precision motion systems capable of high acceleration and accurate positioning. However, position-dependent dynamics in these systems significantly restrict the tracking performance achievable through traditional sequential loop closing (SLC) control strategies. This paper introduces a novel extension of the conventional SLC framework tailored for linear-parameter-varying systems, enabling the system to bypass limitations caused by position-dependent effects in high-precision applications. The benefits of this proposed control approach are validated through simulations using a high-fidelity model of a moving-magnet planar actuator, which displays position dependency in both actuation and sensing.

Urn models are fundamental to expressing core concepts in probability theory. This work extends such models by incorporating tubes, where an urn holds colored balls drawn with probabilities proportional to their counts. Each color corresponds to a tube of a specific size. Upon drawing a ball, it is returned to the tube matching its color. We examine two related probability distributions: the first-full distribution, which calculates the probability that a specific tube fills before any others, and the negative distribution, which determines the probability that all tubes become full simultaneously for the first time after exactly $k$ draws. Using multisets, this paper systematically defines both the first-full and negative distributions in a fully multivariate format for the three standard sampling modes: multinomial, hypergeometric, and Polya.

This study experimentally investigates how reputational uncertainty and the speed of social environmental change influence cooperation. Results indicate that reputational uncertainty markedly reduces cooperation, whereas a rapidly changing social environment yields only a second-order qualitative increase. At the individual level, reputational uncertainty promotes greater leniency and forgiveness during network punishment via link proposal and removal, thereby hindering the emergence of cooperative clusters. However, this effect is pronounced solely in fast-changing environments and absent in slow-changing ones. This variation is explained by a substitution pattern between network punishment and action-based punishment (retaliatory defection) across the two social contexts.

High-energy heavy-ion collisions possess vast amounts of angular momentum, $|\vec{J}|$, ranging from $\mathcal{O}(10^3-10^6\hbar)$ across the collision energies $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}}$ explored by the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). A portion of this $\vec{J}$ is transferred to the overlapping collision zone, a factor essential for measuring observables like hadron spin alignment driven by vorticity relative to $\hat{J}$. Experiments infer the orientation of the participant nucleons' angular momentum, $\hat{J}_\mathrm{part}$, within the overlap region by examining the orientation of forward- and backward-moving spectating nucleons, $\hat{J}_\mathrm{spec}$. Through two distinct models, we investigate the decorrelation between $\hat{J}_\mathrm{part}$ and $\hat{J}_\mathrm{spec}$, which arises from angular-momentum conservation, event-by-event fluctuations, and the misalignment between the elliptic overlap region's orientation and $\hat{J}_\mathrm{part}$. Significant decorrelation dependent on $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}}$ is observed in both scenarios, proving substantial enough to serve as a critical corrective factor for experimental observations of phenomena driven by $\vec{J}$.

A computational investigation of the retinal chromophore's photoisomerization within rhodopsin employed a two-state, two-mode framework coupled to thermal reservoirs. Results indicated that steady-state reaction quantum yields (observed at 10 ps and later) differ markedly from transient values, implying a weak link between transient behavior and steady-state dynamics in these systems. Notably, while transient dynamics remained largely insensitive to minor parameter variations, the steady-state quantum yield exhibited high sensitivity to such minute changes. Associating this sensitivity with standard level spacing statistics of the nonadiabatic vibronic system points to quantum chaos as a potential underlying cause. The study further explores the potential for experimentally detecting this phenomenon and its broader implications for condensed-phase photochemistry and biological light detection.

This research investigates kink-antikink collisions within the double sine-Gordon model, considering both scenarios with and without excited vibrational modes. In the presence of a vibrational mode, resonance windows appear only within a restricted parameter range, yet initial excitation allows vibrational energy to convert into translational energy post-collision. This conversion generates one-bounce resonances and a complex array of higher-bounce windows, contingent on whether the wobbling phase is in or out of phase at impact and whether the wobbling amplitude is sufficiently large. When the vibrational mode is excited, the structure of one-bounce windows persists across the entire parameter spectrum, while the interval for higher-bounce resonances expands gradually with increasing wobbling amplitude. We approximated the centers of these one-bounce windows using a simple analytical model for wobbling evolution and demonstrated that the final kink wobbling frequency undergoes Lorentz contraction, a result directly derived from our equations. Furthermore, we observed that the peak energy density remains smoothly behaved throughout all resonance windows.

The Information Bottleneck (IB) method extracts source information relevant to predicting a target variable, typically by optimizing a Lagrangian that balances compression and prediction. However, optimizing this Lagrangian is difficult and often requires multiple trials to tune the multiplier, with our analysis showing that prediction performance strictly degrades as compression increases. In this paper, we approach the IB method through the lens of supervised disentangling by introducing Disentangled Information Bottleneck (DisenIB), which achieves maximum compression without sacrificing target prediction accuracy. Both theoretical and experimental results confirm that our method maintains maximum compression while demonstrating strong generalization, robustness against adversarial attacks, out-of-distribution detection, and supervised disentangling capabilities.

This research investigates nonstochastic bandits and experts within a delayed framework where delays vary based on both time and specific arms. Although prior work has extensively covered scenarios with time-dependent delays, our arm-dependent delay model more accurately reflects real-world complexities, albeit with novel technical hurdles. For the full information (experts) scenario, we introduce an algorithm achieving a first-order regret bound that highlights a distinct trade-off between delays and losses. We establish a comparable first-order regret bound for the bandit setting, provided the learner can observe the count of missing losses; notably, these are the inaugural bounds in delayed settings relying solely on the losses and delays of the optimal arm. Even when the bandit setting offers no information beyond observed losses, we derive a regret bound by adapting the algorithm proposed by Zimmert and Seldin (2020). Our theoretical foundations rest on a new drift bound, which quantifies the performance improvement an algorithm gains from a one-round look-ahead.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have proven effective in process mining, surpassing traditional methods in predictive performance. Building on this foundation, we evaluate four Graph Neural Network (GNN) variants alongside a dropout-enhanced fully connected Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) to forecast the next activity's nature and timestamp. Unlike prior studies, we assess model efficacy across various process stages, segmented by quartiles of event counts and normalized case durations. This approach reveals that model behavior varies significantly throughout a business process. Notably, our experiments indicate that the straightforward MLP frequently outperforms more complex deep-learning architectures in both prediction tasks. Consequently, we emphasize the need for caution when deploying automated prediction techniques at different process phases and advocate for researchers to validate their findings against robust baselines such as simple MLPs.

The controlled production and extraction of high-energy hot carriers in photoexcited metals represent a promising pathway for technological advancements. Although the dynamics of hot carriers in Au-group metals have been extensively studied, there remains a significant gap in the microscopic understanding of these processes within the near-infrared and mid-infrared ranges for Pt-group metals. Given the widespread application of these materials in catalysis and increasingly in plasmonic catalysis, characterizing their microscopic carrier dynamics is essential. This study utilizes *ab initio* many-body perturbation theory to examine hot carrier generation, relaxation times, and mean free paths in bulk Pd and Pt. Our findings indicate that direct optical transitions in these metals predominantly occur in the near-infrared spectrum. Additionally, we observe that the electron-phonon mass enhancement parameter for Pt is 16% greater than that of Pd, a discrepancy that helps clarify various experimental observations of divergent trends. Furthermore, we predict that Pd and Pt hot electrons exhibit total relaxation times of up to 35 fs and 24 fs, respectively, occurring at energies approximately 0.5 eV and 1.0 eV above the Fermi level. Finally, we demonstrate that efficient hot electron generation and extraction can be realized in nanofilms of Pd (110) and Pd (100) under excitation energies between 0.4 and 1.6 eV.

This study presents sequence-to-sequence language resources for Catalan, a moderately under-resourced language, targeting two tasks: Summarization and Machine Translation (MT). We introduce two novel abstractive summarization datasets focused on newswire content and a parallel Catalan-English corpus accompanied by three distinct new test sets. Furthermore, we assess the provided data against competing state-of-the-art models and establish baselines for these tasks using a newly developed Catalan BART. The resulting resources are released under an open license to foster the advancement of Catalan language technology.

Training models using data from randomized experiments is optimal for decision-making; however, due to their high costs, time requirements, risks, infeasibility, or ethical constraints, practitioners often must rely on observational data generated under historical policies. This reliance raises critical questions about which policies perform best in practice and how different data collection methods or variations in problem characteristics—such as delays in observing action-specific rewards—affect policy performance and robustness. This study addresses these issues within the context of optimizing sales channel allocation at LinkedIn, where leads are assigned to one of three channels to maximize conversions over time. A defining feature of this problem is the presence of stochastic delays in outcome observation, which vary by channel and result. To evaluate this, we developed a discrete-time simulation capable of modeling these dynamics to compare three approaches: a historical rule-based policy, a supervised learning policy (XGBoost), and multi-armed bandit (MAB) policies. These were tested across various scenarios involving observational versus randomized training data, different lead conversion patterns, and distinct delay distributions. The simulation results demonstrate that LinUCB, a straightforward MAB policy, consistently surpasses the other methods, delivering an 18% to 47% improvement over the rule-based approach.

The equivalence principle stands as a fundamental pillar of general relativity, yet its validity has only been confirmed within solar system scales for standard matter fields. Consequently, one cannot assume it applies to non-standard matter fields that govern gravitational dynamics across cosmological distances. This study demonstrates a method to test the equivalence principle on cosmological scales for such non-standard fields by analyzing the odd multipoles of the galaxy cross-power spectrum and bispectrum. This approach leverages parity-violating general relativistic distortions of the past light cone imprinted on these statistical measures, under the assumption that galaxies act as test particles composed of baryons and cold dark matter. If the equivalence principle fails between these two components, this framework predicts a non-zero relative velocity between galaxies and baryons. Utilizing the cross-power spectrum from HI intensity mapping and H$\alpha$ galaxy surveys alongside the H$\alpha$ bispectrum, we constrain this relative velocity to be less than 28% of the galaxy velocity.

Causal discovery, the process of automatically building causal models from data, holds significant importance across various scientific fields. Ideally, assessing the performance of these algorithms involves comparing inferred models against ground-truth models on benchmark datasets, which necessitates a defined distance metric between causal models. Although such metrics have been suggested before, they are constrained by focusing solely on the graphical properties of the models. This work overcomes that limitation by defining distances based on the causal distributions generated by the models, rather than just their structural graphs. Drawing on the "ladder of causation" introduced by Pearl and Mackenzie (2018), which categorizes causal model properties into observational, interventional, and counterfactual levels, we propose a corresponding hierarchy of three distances, one for each rung. Our definitions are both intuitively sound and computationally efficient to approximate. We validate these causal distances by benchmarking standard causal discovery systems on both synthetic and real-world datasets with known ground truths. Finally, we illustrate the broader utility of these distances by briefly exploring applications beyond the evaluation of causal discovery methods.

An Archimedean screw functions as a classic pump by leveraging the equivalence between rotation and translation in helical structures. In a similar fashion, a spin spiral texture can transport charge and spin when rotated at a frequency $\omega$. This paper investigates these pumping mechanisms using a microscopic quantum model, employing both perturbation theory and numerical simulations. Within the spiral region, spin polarization and charge current exhibit a linear dependence on $\omega$, while the spin current scales with $\omega^2$ for small frequencies. We demonstrate that the charge current is associated with a mixed momentum-phason Berry phase, representing a novel approximate realization of a Thouless pump. While nearly quantized in spirals with short pitch $\lambda$, this quantization decays as $\lambda^{-1}$ for longer pitches, distinguishing it from true Thouless pumps or Archimedean screws. Furthermore, we examine the transition to non-adiabatic regimes (large $\omega$), the influence of attached magnetic or non-magnetic contacts, and the real-time dynamics of transport observables. Finally, we analyze disorder effects, which surprisingly may enhance the spin current while suppressing the charge current.

The Root-$T \overline{T}$ flow was recently proposed as a universal, classically marginal deformation applicable to any two-dimensional translation-invariant field theory. This flow commutes with the (irrelevant) $T \overline{T}$ flow and admits explicit integration for a broad range of actions, resulting in non-analytic Lagrangians analogous to four-dimensional Modified-Maxwell theory. While it was not initially clear if the Root-$T \overline{T}$ flow preserves integrability—unlike the $T \overline{T}$ flow—we show in this paper that it does for a wide class of classical models by explicitly deriving a deformed Lax connection. Our analysis covers the principal chiral model and non-linear sigma models defined on symmetric and semi-symmetric spaces, both with and without Wess-Zumino terms. Furthermore, we construct Lax connections for two-parameter families of theories deformed by both Root-$T \overline{T}$ and $T \overline{T}$ across all these models.

This paper introduces a geometric framework for non-relativistic quantum mechanics involving mixed states. By leveraging Uhlmann's principal fibre bundle to characterize the space of mixed states, we define a dynamic-dependent metric tensor on the principal manifold as a novel tool. This construction ensures that the projection of geodesic flow onto the base manifold reproduces the temporal evolution dictated by the von Neumann equation. Furthermore, this approach allows us to characterize all conserved quantum observables as Killing vector fields and offers a geometric demonstration of the Poincaré quantum recurrence in systems with finite energy levels.

The presentation details recent findings in soft QCD from the ATLAS, CMS, and TOTEM collaborations at the LHC. Particular emphasis is placed on research concerning diffractive and forward physics, as well as the underlying event, featuring comparisons with earlier data and the introduction of new methodologies.

We investigate site and bond percolation within directed simple random graphs characterized by a specific degree distribution, obtaining formulas for the critical percolation threshold required for the emergence of a giant strongly connected component and the proportion of vertices it contains.

This study tackles two key challenges: (a) developing metrics to measure the utilization of trained artificial intelligence (AI) models, and (b) elucidating how training data is encoded within these models using such metrics. These issues are driven by the need for greater explainability in security and safety-critical domains, exemplified by AI-driven traffic sign classification in autonomous vehicles. Our approach establishes theoretical foundations for measuring AI model utilization and analyzing patterns in how classes are encoded based on utilization, specifically at the levels of computation graphs, subgraphs, and individual nodes. Conceptually, utilization at each node (computation unit) is defined by the count and distribution of unique outputs across the space of all potential tensor-states. We extract these utilization metrics from both clean and poisoned AI models. Unlike clean models, the poisoned models were trained on traffic sign images featuring systematic, physically realizable modifications (triggers) designed to alter correct class labels when present. By examining the class encodings in both model types, we derive conclusions regarding the implications for trojan injection and detection.

The cosmos's maps contain the encoded history of the Universe and the forces that shaped it, offering unique insights into nature that cannot be obtained through other methods. However, the link between fundamental physics and observable cosmic phenomena is frequently the domain of specialists or computational models, rendering these general lessons opaque to many particle theorists. Fortunately, the same core principles that dictate particle interactions—such as locality and causality—also govern the Universe's evolution and the emergence of new physics within data. By concentrating on these principles, we can more intuitively grasp how upcoming cosmic surveys will advance our knowledge of fundamental physics. These lectures will examine this theory-data relationship through three case studies: light relics ($N_{\rm eff}$) and the cosmic microwave background (CMB), neutrino mass alongside CMB gravitational lensing, and primordial non-Gaussianity in relation to galaxy distribution. We will address both the theoretical foundations of these signals and the practical challenges involved in measuring them.

Computational notebooks have become the preferred environment for data science and analytical tasks, facilitating quick iteration and exploration. By storing intermediate states in memory and dividing execution into discrete "cells," these tools enable interactive workflows with immediate feedback. However, as users add, remove, reorder, and re-run cells, an opaque intermediate state accumulates that often diverges from the visible code. This discrepancy complicates the understanding of execution behavior, frequently resulting in errors and reduced reproducibility. We introduce NBSafety, a specialized Jupyter kernel that leverages runtime tracing and static analysis to automatically track lineage for cell execution and global notebook state. NBSafety identifies and mitigates errors arising from unassisted notebook interactions while maintaining the flexibility of standard notebook semantics. Our evaluation of NBSafety's error-prevention capabilities involved replaying and analyzing 666 real-world notebook sessions. The system detected potential safety errors in 117 of these sessions. Furthermore, in the remaining 549 sessions, the cells flagged by NBSafety as resolving safety issues were more than seven times more likely to be selected by users for re-execution compared to a random baseline, even though the users were unaware of NBSafety and thus unaffected by its suggestions.

We present a method for calculating presentations of saturated cluster modular groups. Leveraging this approach, we derive finite presentations for the saturated cluster modular groups of finite mutation type $X_6$ and $X_7$. Furthermore, we confirm that the cluster modular groups associated with finite mutation types $\widetilde{E}_6$, $\widetilde{E}_7$, $\widetilde{E}_8$, $G_2^{(*,*)}$, $X_6$, and $X_7$ are virtually generated by cluster Dehn twists.

Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) offers a robust mechanism for enhancing packet processing capabilities within the Linux kernel. It enables users to develop code in high-level languages like C or Rust and deploy it at designated kernel hooks, such as network drivers. To guarantee safe execution within the kernel, Linux employs an in-kernel static analyzer that permits a program to run only if it can demonstrate crash-free operation, strict memory bounds adherence, and prevention of kernel data leaks. However, BPF programming presents significant challenges. First, even moderately sized programs often exceed the analysis capacity of the kernel checker and are rejected. Second, the checker can occasionally produce false positives, incorrectly flagging safe code as unsafe. Third, achieving even minor performance improvements requires meticulous, expert-level hand-tuning, as traditional optimizing compilers struggle with the safety constraints imposed by the kernel checker. To address these issues, we introduce K2, a program-synthesis-based compiler that automatically optimizes BPF bytecode while ensuring formal correctness and safety. K2 achieves a 6–26% reduction in code size and lowers average packet-processing latency by 1.36% to 55.03% compared to the best clang-compiled results, with throughput gains of up to 4.75%. These results are validated across benchmarks from Cilium, Facebook, and the Linux kernel. Furthermore, K2 integrates specialized domain techniques that accelerate BPF program equivalence checking by six orders of magnitude, making synthesis practical.

We introduce an infinitary labelled sequent calculus for PDL, denoted as G3PDL^{\infty}. From this, we construct a finitarily representable cyclic system, G3PDL^{\omega}. We demonstrate that both systems are sound and complete regarding standard PDL models, with the added property that G3PDL^{\infty} is cut-free complete. Furthermore, we examine proof-search strategies within the cyclic system for the subset of PDL that excludes tests.

Conventional transmission electron microscopy (CTEM) fails to capture half of the wavefunction information because it records only image intensity, omitting phase data. Building on the successful application of deep learning to optical hologram phase recovery, we have developed neural networks to reconstruct phases from CTEM intensities using a dataset of 98,340 exit wavefunctions. These wavefunctions were simulated via clTEM multislice propagation for 12,789 materials sourced from the Crystallography Open Database. Our networks can reconstruct 224x224 wavefunctions in approximately 25 milliseconds across a wide range of physical hyperparameters and materials, with performance improving as the wavefunction distribution becomes more restricted. This deep learning approach to phase recovery surpasses traditional methods by offering live processing, immunity to distortions, no requirement for microscope modifications or multiple images, and applicability to any imaging regime. This paper presents multiple deep learning strategies for CTEM phase recovery to serve as foundational points for future research enhancements. Source code, links to our new datasets, and pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/Jeffrey-Ede/one-shot.

We introduce Partial Registration Network (PRNet), a straightforward, adaptable, and general framework designed for partial-to-partial point cloud registration. Drawing inspiration from recent learning-based registration techniques, we employ deep networks to address the challenges of non-convex alignment and partial correspondence. Unlike prior learning-based approaches that require full shape visibility, PRNet is specifically tailored for partial-to-partial scenarios, demonstrating superior performance over PointNetLK, DCP, and non-learning methods on synthetic datasets. As a self-supervised model, PRNet simultaneously learns a robust geometric representation, a keypoint detector capable of identifying common points between partial views, and the corresponding keypoint-to-keypoint matches. Our results indicate that PRNet consistently predicts keypoints and correspondences across different views and objects. Additionally, the learned representation proves transferable to classification tasks.

Clustering serves as an unsupervised data mining method for segmenting customers, allowing banks to create targeted offers based on specific customer attributes. This study utilizes a real-world financial dataset (Berka, 2000) to group bank customers using an encoder-decoder network and the Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) algorithm. Customer features were derived through four distinct approaches: Dynamic Time Warping, Recency-Frequency-Monetary (RFM) analysis, an LSTM encoder-decoder network, and a proposed hybrid method. After training the LSTM model on transaction data, the encoder automatically generated feature vectors for each customer. Additionally, DTW was employed to calculate distances between transaction amount sequences, while RFM scoring produced another feature vector. The hybrid approach integrated feature vectors from the encoder-decoder output, DTW distances, and demographic information (such as age and gender). These combined vectors were then fed into a k-means clustering algorithm, with results evaluated using Silhouette and Davies-Bouldin indices. The findings indicate that the hybrid approach yields more accurate and meaningful clusters compared to individual techniques. Furthermore, the study observed that the type of neural network layers significantly influences clustering outcomes, and a high network error does not invariably degrade clustering performance.

Transition metal defects within silicon carbide (SiC) create localized electronic states accessible via optical means in the telecommunications band, leveraging a well-established semiconductor infrastructure. Consequently, the spin and optical characteristics of these defects have attracted significant research interest. For defects with a spin of 1/2, the interplay between defect symmetry and robust spin-orbit coupling can limit permissible spin transitions, resulting in long-lived spins that are difficult to control using microwave techniques. This study demonstrates through both analytical and numerical analyses that introducing a central nuclear spin induces a non-trivial mixing of electronic spin states while maintaining the defect's symmetry. Furthermore, the interaction between a weak applied magnetic field and hyperfine coupling generates magnetic microwave transitions that would otherwise be forbidden, facilitating efficient electronic spin manipulation. Additionally, an electric microwave field aligned with the c-axis can control the electronic spin by modulating the relative magnitude of the dipolar hyperfine interaction.

Recently, T. Kim ([8, 9]) introduced the higher-order q-Euler polynomials and multiple q-Euler zeta functions. In this study, we explore the symmetric properties of the multiple q-Euler zeta function and establish several identities regarding the higher-order q-Euler polynomials based on these symmetries.

This article demonstrates that estimator stability is sufficient to establish the validity of leave-one-out cross-validation by deriving concentration bounds within a general framework. Specifically, we present these bounds without relying on Lipschitz continuity assumptions regarding the loss function or the estimator. To achieve our findings, we utilize random variables whose distributions satisfy the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, thereby accommodating a broad and diverse class of distributions. We further validate our approach through several illustrative examples, such as linear regression, kernel density estimation, and stabilized or truncated estimators like stabilized kernel regression.

Code review is an established practice for ensuring software quality, where reviewers examine developer-submitted code to verify its standards. While reviewers and developers often share code snippets during discussions to offer explanations or suggestions, the specific intentions and effects of these snippets remain poorly understood. To address this, we conducted a preliminary study to explore the characteristics and purposes of code snippets within code reviews. We manually collected and analyzed 10,790 review comments from the Nova and Neutron projects in the OpenStack community, ultimately identifying 626 comments containing code snippets for detailed examination. The findings reveal that: (1) code snippets are not commonly used in reviews, with reviewers being the primary contributors; (2) we categorized reviewer-provided snippets into two high-level purposes—Suggestion and Citation—comprising six sub-categories, where Improving Code Implementation is the most frequent objective; (3) for snippets intended as suggestions, approximately 68.1% were accepted by developers. These results point to promising avenues for future research regarding the utilization of code snippets in the review process.

Machine learning algorithms generally rely on the assumption that training and test data consist of independent and identically distributed samples. However, research indicates that high-performance ML classifiers can suffer significant performance drops and produce overconfident, incorrect predictions, especially when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Conditional language models (CLMs), which are primarily trained to predict the next token in a sequence, may experience even more severe degradation on OOD data due to their auto-regressive nature, which involves many sequential prediction steps. Additionally, the potential space for low-quality outputs is vast because the models can generate arbitrary text, making it crucial to determine when to trust the results. We introduce a highly accurate and lightweight OOD detection method tailored for CLMs, demonstrating its efficacy in abstractive summarization and translation tasks. Furthermore, we illustrate how this approach facilitates selective generation under realistic distribution shifts—similar to selective prediction in classification—by automatically abstaining from producing low-quality outputs while generating high-quality ones, thereby enabling safer deployment of generative language models.

Neural networks are widely deployed across numerous domains, many of which involve significant safety and security risks. Consequently, researchers have developed formal verification methods to validate neural network properties. Although prior work has primarily addressed local robustness, this study focuses on a distinct security vulnerability known as data poisoning. In this scenario, an adversary injects a trigger into a portion of the training data such that the trained model misclassifies inputs containing this trigger into a specific target class during testing. We demonstrate that data poisoning checks can be formulated as verifiable properties compatible with existing tools like Marabou and nneum, where counterexamples to these checks serve as the identified triggers. Furthermore, we show that these discovered triggers are transferable from smaller models to larger, more advanced models, enabling the analysis of state-of-the-art image classification systems.

Addressing class imbalance in data mining and machine learning remains a difficult challenge, given that many real-world datasets are inherently skewed. Traditional learning algorithms often optimize for overall accuracy by correctly identifying the majority class while frequently misclassifying the minority class, despite the latter often being more critical in practical applications. Recent literature has addressed this issue using sampling techniques (such as under-sampling the majority and over-sampling the minority), cost-sensitive learning, and ensemble methods. This paper presents a novel clustering-based under-sampling strategy integrated with the AdaBoost algorithm, termed CUSBoost, to improve imbalanced classification. CUSBoost offers an alternative to existing methods like RUSBoost (random under-sampling with AdaBoost) and SMOTEBoost (synthetic minority over-sampling with AdaBoost). The algorithm's performance was evaluated against state-of-the-art ensemble techniques, including AdaBoost, RUSBoost, and SMOTEBoost, across 13 binary and multi-class datasets with varying degrees of imbalance. Experimental results indicate that CUSBoost is a promising and effective solution for handling highly imbalanced datasets.

As overlapping clustering algorithms, especially in social network analysis, gain traction, there is a pressing need for quantitative metrics to evaluate their accuracy. Comparing the true cluster sets against those generated by an algorithm is essential to assess their similarity or difference. A normalized metric is often preferred, typically assigning a score of 0 for completely dissimilar sets and 1 for identical ones. Recently, a normalized mutual information measure [1] has gained popularity, yet it exhibits counterintuitive behaviors that can be rectified through a more traditional normalization approach. We also compare these findings against other metrics, such as the Omega index [2].

The development of next-generation quantum microscopy and spectroscopy relies fundamentally on the creation, control, and detection of coherent electrons. By exploiting and modifying the quantum characteristics of electron beam sources at cryogenic temperatures, their emission capabilities can be significantly improved. This study details electron field emission from a single-crystal, superconducting niobium nanotip operating at 5.9 K. The resulting electron energy spectrum exhibits an exceptionally narrow distribution reaching down to 16 meV, achieved through tunable resonant tunneling field emission via localized band states at the tip's apex, alongside a sharp cutoff determined by the low-temperature Fermi edge. This performance represents a tenfold improvement over conventional field emission sources. The tip's self-focusing geometry produces an emission angle of 3.7 degrees, a brightness of 3.8 x 10^8 A/(m² sr V), and remarkable stability over hours at a 4.1 nA beam current with a 69 meV energy width. Such a source will mitigate lens aberration effects and facilitate novel modes in low-energy electron microscopy, electron energy loss spectroscopy, and high-resolution vibrational spectroscopy.

Advancements in the automatic control of thermal systems and the real-time estimation of heat penetration in living tissue have historically been constrained by the challenges of developing high-fidelity thermodynamic models. In complex thermodynamic environments, estimating thermophysical parameters for processes that vary across space and time is often impractical, necessitating the use of model-free control frameworks. While these frameworks are adopted due to feasibility, they sacrifice robustness guarantees and require extensive empirical testing. However, recent developments in infrared cameras and other thermographic technologies have made real-time, non-invasive sensing of thermal states accessible. This study introduces a novel physics-based method that learns the dynamics of a thermal process directly from real-time thermographic data, specifically focusing on areas of significant thermal activity. We term this technique, applicable to any higher-dimensional scalar field, Attention-Based Noise Robust Averaging (ANRA). By utilizing a partial-differential equation model structure, we demonstrate that ANRA is resilient to noise and can serve to initialize optimization routines for refining parameter estimates. We validate our approach through multiple simulations and by applying it to electrosurgical thermal response data collected from in vivo porcine skin tissue.

We demonstrate that the dominating set problem allows for a constant factor approximation within a constant number of rounds when solved in the LOCAL model on graph classes characterized by bounded expansion. This finding extends the work of Czygrinow et al., which was limited to graphs excluding specific topological minors, to encompass a broader range of uniformly sparse graphs. Furthermore, we illustrate how our general algorithm can be adapted and optimized to achieve an ($11+\epsilon$)-approximation for minimum dominating sets on planar graphs, where $\epsilon > 0$. This result surpasses the prior best-known approximation factor of 52 for planar graphs, a benchmark set by the simple and elegant algorithm proposed by Lenzen et al.

While superposing trajectories—modifying quantum evolution via interferometric path superposition—has improved various quantum communication protocols, its effects within open quantum systems remain poorly understood. Consequently, we investigate this phenomenon through the lens of system-environment interactions. Our findings indicate that superposing multiple trajectories can induce quantum state freezing, a space-time dual to the quantum Zeno effect. Additionally, we demonstrate that non-trivial Dicke-like super(sub)radiance can be generated without relying on multi-atom correlations.

PyPSA (Python for Power System Analysis) is an open-source toolkit designed for simulating and optimizing contemporary electrical power systems across multiple time periods. The software incorporates models for conventional generators with unit commitment, variable renewable energy sources, storage facilities, cross-sector energy coupling, and hybrid alternating and direct current networks. Built to be highly extensible and scalable, PyPSA effectively handles large networks and extensive time series data. This paper outlines the core capabilities of PyPSA, detailing the formulation of complete power flow equations and the multi-period optimization of both operational strategies and investments using linear power flow approximations. PyPSA serves as a bridge within the free software ecosystem, connecting traditional steady-state power flow tools with comprehensive multi-period energy system models. The tool's functionality is validated using two open datasets representing Germany's transmission system (SciGRID) and Europe's (GridKit).

Current summarization models produce fluent text that is frequently factually inaccurate, prompting a proliferation of metrics designed to assess summary factuality. However, the absence of standardized benchmarks prevents meaningful comparisons among these metrics. Furthermore, existing approaches treat factuality as a binary issue, overlooking nuanced insights into the specific types of inconsistencies generated by different systems. To overcome these challenges, we propose a taxonomy of factual errors and leverage it to gather human annotations of summaries from leading models on the CNN/DM and XSum datasets. By analyzing these annotations, we determine the distribution of error categories across various models and evaluate factuality metrics, revealing their correlation with human judgment alongside their distinct advantages and limitations.

Accurately determining the mass of galaxy clusters is a critical challenge in cosmology, as large-scale surveys depend on scaling laws linking cluster observables to their masses. Leveraging high-resolution data from approximately 45 galaxy clusters observed by NIKA2 and XMM-Newton, the NIKA2 SZ Large Program aims to establish a precise scaling relation between the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect and hydrostatic mass. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the hydrostatic mass for CL J1226.9+3332, the highest-redshift cluster within the NIKA2 SZ Large Program at z = 0.89. By combining NIKA2 thermal SZ observations with data from NIKA, Bolocam, and MUSTANG, alongside XMM-Newton X-ray observations, we assess how systematic effects influence mass reconstruction. Our findings indicate that subtle variations in the mass profile shape significantly impact the determination of the integrated mass at R500, underscoring the necessity of robust modeling. Furthermore, we validate the reliability of our hydrostatic mass estimates by demonstrating consistency with existing literature. A crucial parameter for cosmology is the bias inherent in masses derived under the hydrostatic equilibrium assumption. Utilizing lensing convergence maps from the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH), we calculated the lensing mass for CL J1226.9+3332. This allows us to quantify the hydrostatic-to-lensing mass bias for this cluster, which ranges from 1 - bHSE/lens ~ 0.7 to 1, highlighting how different datasets and reconstruction models affect this bias.

The TUCAN (TRIUMF Ultra-Cold Advanced Neutron) collaboration is dedicated to detecting the neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) with exceptional precision. A critical component of this measurement is an ultracold neutron (UCN) polarization analyzer, primarily constructed using a magnetized thin iron film. Researchers deposited several such iron films onto aluminum and silicon substrates, analyzing them via vibrating sample magnetometry and cold-neutron reflectometry. The saturation magnetic field for films on aluminum substrates was found to be approximately 12 kA/m, whereas films on silicon substrates required 6.4 kA/m. Neutron reflectometry estimated the magnetic potential of the iron films on silicon to be 2 T, a performance level deemed sufficient for the UCN polarization analyzer in the nEDM experiment.

This paper presents theoretical proof confirming the existence of the multi-spin-axis magnetic structure in CoO, originally proposed by van Laar in 1964. This tetragonal spin configuration accounts for both the pronounced tetragonal and the less significant monoclinic distortions observed experimentally. The monoclinic distortion is attributed to a "monoclinic-like" rearrangement of oxygen atoms, similar to the rhombohedral-like oxygen distortion recently identified in NiO and MnO. Notably, this oxygen distortion does not affect the tetragonal magnetic structure, which arises from a unique nonadiabatic, atomic-like motion of electrons near the Fermi level. It is argued that this specific electronic motion is the defining characteristic that classifies CoO as a Mott insulator.

This paper introduces a novel, memory-centric approach leveraging CMOS SRAM to accelerate data-intensive applications. The proposed method, termed Augmented Memory Computing, dynamically expands on-chip SRAM storage capacity as needed. It enables SRAM cells to function in two distinct modes: Normal and Augmented. In Normal mode, a cell operates as a standard 6T SRAM, storing one static bit. Conversely, in Augmented mode, each cell can store multiple bits dynamically. We present two new cell designs: an 8T dual-bit augmented cell and a 7T ternary-bit augmented cell. The 8T cell, when in Augmented mode, simultaneously holds one static bit and one dynamic bit (similar to DRAM), effectively doubling its capacity. The 7T cell offers flexibility by storing a single static bit in Normal mode or ternary data (three levels: 00, 01, 10) dynamically in Augmented mode. Consequently, these augmented cells can store either one static bit or multiple dynamic bits depending on the operational mode. We validate the feasibility of these cells through extensive simulations using the GlobalFoundries 22nm FDX node. Furthermore, this augmented memory scheme can be seamlessly integrated with existing in-memory computing techniques to yield additional improvements in energy efficiency and throughput.

We demonstrate that the $\infty$-category of surjections among animated rings is projectively generated and introduce the concept of animated PD-pairs, defined as surjections of animated rings equipped with a "derived" PD-structure. This framework enables the extension of classical results to scenarios that are neither flat nor finitely generated. Leveraging animated PD-pairs, we formulate multiple approaches to derived crystalline cohomology and prove comparison theorems. Specifically, we extend the comparison between derived and classical crystalline cohomology for syntomic (affine) schemes, originally established by Bhatt, to encompass quasisyntomic schemes. Furthermore, we construct a non-completed animated counterpart to prisms and prismatic envelopes. By proving a variant of the Hodge-Tate comparison for animated prismatic envelopes, we derive a result concerning the flat cover of the final object for quasisyntomic schemes, thereby generalizing several existing theorems that were previously restricted to conditions of smoothness and finiteness.

This work reports a single-crystal neutron diffraction investigation of the Shastry-Sutherland lattice compound TbB$_4$ at zero field and under pulsed high magnetic fields reaching 35 T along the crystallographic $c$ axis. Although the findings validate the known magnetic structures at zero field and at the half- and full-magnetization plateaus, they provide novel perspectives on the $\frac{2}{9}$- and $\frac{1}{3}$-magnetization plateaus. A model featuring polarized 4-spin plaquettes arranged in stripes, where stripe density scales with macroscopic magnetization, aligns perfectly with the diffraction data. However, alternative models are also consistent with the observed Bragg peaks, which are inherently constrained by the limitations of pulsed high-field experiments. We examine the distinct intensity distributions in $Q$ space that could differentiate these models in future studies.

Gravitational decoherence (GD) describes how gravity induces the classical behavior of quantum systems. Since these mechanisms intersect general relativity (GR), quantum field theory (QFT), and quantum information, GD holds profound theoretical importance. While numerous GD models exist—many relying on physics that deviates from GR and/or QFT—this overview pursues two primary objectives centered on a unifying theme: (i) to outline GD theories grounded in GR and QFT and examine their experimental implications, and (ii) to evaluate alternative GD models against the standards of GR and QFT, highlighting their distinct theoretical features. Furthermore, we detail how upcoming space-based GD experiments will offer evidence at two levels: (a) distinguishing between competing quantum frameworks and non-GR theories, and (b) determining whether gravity functions as a fundamental or effective theory.

This study examines an attraction-repulsion chemotaxis model involving consumed signals within bounded, smooth domains $\Omega \subset \R^n$ where $n \geq 2$. We establish sufficient conditions on the problem's data that guarantee the existence of global, bounded classical solutions to the associated zero-flux Cauchy problem.

The presence of chiral edge states, linked to a non-trivial bulk-band topology defined by a non-zero topological invariant, along with the control of topological transport through these states, offers promising prospects for topological electronic and spintronic devices. In this work, we predict and propose the practical implementation of spin-gapless valley-filtered chiral edge states, which exhibit topological protection and switching. These states represent a new topological Dirac spin-gapless/half-metal phase found in antiferromagnetic honeycomb structures with zigzag edge terminations. We show that this phenomenon can be realized by applying a perpendicular (transverse) electric field to zigzag nanoribbons featuring antiferromagnetic ordering at the boundaries (or in the bulk), while the Weber-Fechner type nonlinear behavior can be optimized via such electric fields. Furthermore, the existence of these states, their association with non-trivial bulk topology, and the electric-field-induced switching of their spin-polarization—which coincides with a change in bulk-band topology—offer a novel approach to topological spintronics that does not rely on spin-orbit interaction.

To efficiently run dynamically typed languages, many implementations utilize a two-tier architecture. The initial tier ensures low-latency startup by gathering dynamic profiles, such as variable types, while the second tier achieves high throughput via an optimizing compiler that generates code specialized to these recorded types. If the program's behavior shifts and introduces types not previously observed in the specialized code, that code becomes invalid; it is deoptimized, and control reverts to the first tier to begin specialization anew. Conversely, if the behavior becomes more specific (e.g., a polymorphic variable turns monomorphic), no changes occur. Once optimized code is executing, missed optimization opportunities remain undetected.

We propose using a sampling-based profiler to monitor native code without any instrumentation, ensuring zero overhead when the profiler is inactive. We demonstrate an implementation within the \v{R} just-in-time optimizing compiler for the R language. Utilizing these sampled profiles, we detect when native code generated by \v{R} is specialized based on stale type feedback and recompile it to code with more specific types. Our results show that sampling incurs an overhead of less than 3% in most scenarios and up to 9% in rare cases, while reliably identifying stale type feedback within milliseconds.

Although database management systems (DBMSs) are highly optimized, the interface between the programming language (PL) and the DBMS incurs significant costs, even in in-process embedded scenarios. This paper demonstrates that programs interacting with the popular embedded DBMS SQLite can be substantially optimized—achieving a 3.4x speedup in our benchmarks—by inlining across the PL/DBMS boundary. We realized this performance gain by substituting portions of SQLite's C interpreter with RPython code and integrating the resulting meta-tracing virtual machine (VM), named SQPyte, with the PyPy VM. SQPyte maintains standalone SQL performance and outperforms SQLite by 2.2% on the widely adopted TPC-H benchmark suite.

The renowned semiconductor Cd3As2 has regained significant attention owing to its distinctive electronic architecture and quantum transport behaviors as a topological Dirac semimetal. To clarify and regulate these topological quantum states, there is a pressing need for high-quality Cd3As2 thin films.
