The dataset includes ego-vehicle metrics such as waypoints, velocity, and yaw angle, alongside non-ego actor data comprising waypoints, velocity, yaw angle, entry, and exit times. To enhance usability, the framework allows users to incorporate additional actors, sensors, lanes, roads, and obstacles into existing scenarios. A Joint Probabilistic Data Association (JPDA) tracker was employed to identify non-ego vehicles. The authors present preliminary findings and associated applications, with the full dataset slated for release in early 2023.

This study posits that formal language theory and grammatical inference offer essential insights into the capabilities and limitations of deep neural networks regarding long-term dependencies in temporal sequences. Experiments were performed using two RNN architectures—Simple RNNs (s-RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs) of various dimensions—across six formal languages categorized under the Strictly Local (SL) and Strictly Piecewise (SP) classes. These classes represent foundational levels in a mathematically defined hierarchy of subregular classes, encoding local and long-term dependencies, respectively. The Regular Positive and Negative Inference (RPNI) algorithm served as the baseline. While prior research suggested that LSTMs should excel at capturing long-term dependencies and surpass s-RNNs, these findings contradict that assumption. Specifically, LSTMs performed worse on SP tasks than on SL tasks, and s-RNNs not only matched LSTMs on most experiments but also outperformed them on the most complex SP task.

Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) research is increasingly focused on identifying the distinct technological requirements of individuals with dementia to facilitate their independent management of daily tasks. A primary challenge in this domain is accommodating the fluctuating accessibility needs that arise from the specific type of dementia and its progression. Researchers have proposed auto-personalized interfaces, and more recently, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven personalization, as scalable solutions to make commercial technology accessible to users with varying abilities. Despite this, there remains a significant gap in understanding how people with dementia perceive AI as an aid to their everyday technology use and its function within their broader self-management ecosystems, which also encompass non-AI tools and human support. This paper outlines future design directions for AI-based systems tailored to personalize interfaces for various dementia-related memory changes, alongside expectations regarding AI interactions with users.

A. Regev demonstrated that the codimension growth of associative PI-algebras does not exceed an exponential rate. The author previously defined a scale for Lie PI-algebras, encompassing a range of functions situated between exponential and factorial growth. In this work, we demonstrate that this same scale effectively stratifies the standard codimension growth of Poisson PI-algebras that satisfy Lie identities. As a secondary result, we derive a novel upper bound for the codimension growth of Lie PI-algebras using complexity functions. Furthermore, we investigate instances of extremely rapid codimension growth in certain Poisson algebras lacking Lie identities. Our approach primarily relies on techniques involving exponential generating functions and the growth characteristics of associated rapidly increasing entire functions.

Variational autoencoders typically rely on isotropic Gaussian priors and mean-field posteriors, which fails to capture structural relationships or consistency among latent variables. While Gaussian process variational autoencoders address this limitation by incorporating a latent Gaussian process, they incur a cubic inference time complexity. We introduce a more scalable alternative that exploits the independence of auxiliary features common in many datasets. By factorizing the latent kernel across these features within different dimensions, our method achieves substantial speed-ups both theoretically and practically, while empirically matching the performance of existing non-scalable approaches. Furthermore, this approach enables enhanced modeling of global latent information and facilitates broader extrapolation to unseen input combinations.

The core challenge in active learning (AL) lies in determining which data to annotate. While prior research focuses on selecting uncertain or informative samples, the specific impact of these selections on the test performance of the AL model remains underexplored. This study theoretically demonstrates that prioritizing unlabeled data with higher gradient norms minimizes the upper bound of test loss, thereby enhancing performance. Since calculating gradient norms directly for unlabeled data is infeasible without labels, we introduce two solutions: expected-gradnorm, which estimates norms via an expected empirical loss, and entropy-gradnorm, which utilizes an unsupervised entropy-based loss. These approaches are integrated into a unified AL framework. We validate our method on standard image classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, as well as a domain-specific application involving cryo-Electron Tomography subtomogram classification to assess its robustness against noise and practical utility. Experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/xulabs/aitom/blob/master/doc/projects/al_gradnorm.md.

Guided by the Swampland Distance and Emergent String Conjectures in Quantum Gravity, we examine infinite distance degenerations within the complex structure moduli space of elliptic K3 surfaces. Since all K3 surface degenerations are categorized by their associated Kulikov models—Type I (finite distance) or Type II and III (infinite distance)—we provide a detailed characterization of the underlying Weierstrass models for elliptic cases. Building on the two known classes of Type II models, we demonstrate that the more obscure Type III models can also be reduced to two canonical forms. Furthermore, we establish that all infinite distance limits correspond to either Weierstrass models with non-minimal singularities in codimension one or models featuring degenerating generic fibers akin to the Sen limit. We explicitly detail the general structure of the necessary blowups and base changes to eliminate these non-minimal singularities. These findings lay the groundwork for classifying the infinite distance limits of elliptic K3 surfaces as investigated by F-theory in a related study. Notably, Type III limits represent (partial) decompactification limits, indicated by an emergent affine enhancement of the symmetry algebra.

Extensions of the Standard Model that permit Lorentz and CPT violations can be detected through sidereal modulations in neutrino interaction rates. A search for these modulations was conducted using the T2K on-axis near detector, employing two complementary methods that yielded no signal evidence. This study establishes limits on correlated Lorentz and CPT violating terms within the Standard Model Extension for the first time. Consequently, these findings indicate that such symmetry violations are suppressed by a factor exceeding $10^{20}$ at the GeV scale.

Previous research on machine learning fairness has primarily aimed to ensure that classifiers produce predictions with comparable statistical characteristics across different demographic groups. However, existing fairness methods often merely rescale classifier scores to mitigate violations of these properties, neglecting the inherent similarities and differences between group members. We hypothesize that accounting for these inter-group relationships is crucial for accurately measuring unfairness. To test this, we propose Optimal Transport to Fairness (OTF), which defines the degree of fairness constraint violation as the minimum Optimal Transport cost between a probabilistic classifier and a score function that adheres to those constraints. For a specific class of linear fairness constraints, we develop a practical approach to calculate OTF as a differentiable regularizer compatible with standard classification tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that OTF successfully enhances the balance between predictive performance and fairness.

This study introduces a model grounded in Grand Unification theory, incorporating three generations of vector-like fermions, additional Higgs doublets, and an extensive neutrino sector at low energies. Leveraging advanced Deep Learning methods, we conduct the inaugural phenomenological investigation of this framework, specifically targeting new charged vector-like leptons (VLLs) and their potential detection signatures at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Our numerical analysis examines signal events for vector-boson fusion and VLL pair production, both yielding a final state with a pair of charged leptons of distinct flavors and two sterile neutrinos contributing to missing energy. Additionally, we analyze VLL single production, where the final state includes one charged lepton alongside a pair of sterile neutrinos. All computed observables are supplied as datasets for Deep Learning evaluation; a neural network, developed using an evolutionary algorithm, is trained to maximize either the accuracy metric or the Asimov significance across various VLL masses. Considering the three analyzed topologies, we determine that the combined significance for observing new VLLs at the high-luminosity LHC spans from $5.7\sigma$ for a $1.25~\mathrm{TeV}$ mass up to $28\sigma$ for a $200~\mathrm{GeV}$ mass. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a $200~\mathrm{GeV}$ VLL could be excluded by the end of LHC Run-III with a confidence level of $8.8$ standard deviations. These findings indicate that the model is highly testable before the conclusion of LHC operations, offering crucial phenomenological constraints on the energy scale where new gauge symmetries arising from the Grand Unification scenario become apparent.

We examine Chern insulators through the lens of Kähler geometry, which describes smooth manifolds defined by a compatible triplet comprising a symplectic form, an integrable almost complex structure, and a Riemannian metric. The Fermi projector, representing the subspace of occupied bands, establishes a mapping to a Kähler manifold. Within this framework, the quantum metric and Berry curvature of the occupied bands correspond to the Riemannian metric and symplectic form, respectively, on the target space of quantum states. We demonstrate that the minimal volume of a parameter space, measured using the quantum metric, equals $\pi |\mathcal{C}|$, where $\mathcal{C}$ denotes the first Chern number. We also identify the conditions under which this minimal volume is attained in both the Brillouin zone and the twist-angle space. Specifically, if the quantum metric is non-degenerate everywhere, the minimal volume of the Brillouin zone occurs when it inherits a Kähler structure from the space of quantum states. Furthermore, if the quantum volume of the twist-angle torus is minimized, both parameter spaces acquire a Kähler structure inherited from the quantum state space. These findings are linked to the stability of fractional Chern insulators. In two-band systems, the Brillouin zone volume is naturally minimal when the Berry curvature is uniformly non-negative or non-positive; we additionally prove that, due to topological constraints, the latter—which is proportional to the quantum volume form in this context—must possess zeros.

World models improve the sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning (RL) by acquiring behaviors within a latent imagination space. Although applying these models to high-dimensional inputs like pixels has become feasible on standard benchmarks and certain games, their utility in real-world robotics remains unexplored. This paper examines how such agents adapt to real-world autonomous vehicle control scenarios where advanced model-free deep RL methods struggle. Specifically, we deployed an F1TENTH racing robot, equipped with a high-dimensional LiDAR sensor, across a series of time-lapse tasks on test tracks with incrementally increasing complexity. In this continuous-control environment, we demonstrate that model-based agents, which learn via imagination, significantly surpass model-free agents in terms of performance, sample efficiency, task completion success, and generalization. Furthermore, we find that the generalization capabilities of these model-based agents are highly sensitive to the selection of their observation models. Finally, we present extensive empirical evidence supporting the efficacy of world models with sufficient memory horizons in sim-to-real transfer tasks.

This study examines the challenge of creating adversarial malware, where a cyber-attacker strategically alters specific bytes in existing binary files to bypass machine learning-based classifiers. We assessed three recent adversarial generation methods using binary samples from a single public dataset, comparing their efficacy in evading the MalConv classifier. Our findings indicate that the most successful approach involves strategically modifying bytes within the binary header. The paper concludes with a discussion of key takeaways and potential future research avenues in adversarial malware generation.

Black holes represent the universe's most extreme environments, yet they remain completely inaccessible to direct experimentation, and even indirect observation presents formidable technical hurdles. Thermodynamics, through its phenomenological framework, offers a unique pathway to investigate the physical characteristics of such scenarios, thereby inspiring the development of holographic engines. Our analysis demonstrates that an endoreversible Brayton cycle achieves the Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency when fueled by a two-dimensional ideal gas, but surpasses this limit when the working medium is a (2+1)-dimensional BTZ black hole. These insights hold significance not only for unraveling black hole mysteries but also for potential technological advancements involving graphene.

We examine nearest-neighbor weighted random walks on the $d$-dimensional box $[n]^d$, driven by a function $g:[0,1] \to [0,\infty)$. Specifically, when at position $x$, a neighbor $y$ is chosen uniformly, and the walk transitions to $y$ with probability $(1/2)g(n^{-1}y)/(g(n^{-1}y)+g(n^{-1}x))$. We analyze $g$ in the form $f^{m_n}$, where $f$ is analytically well-behaved and $m_n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$. This framework encompasses various significant cases, such as the mean-field Potts model, posterior collapsed Gibbs sampling for Latent Dirichlet allocation, and specific Bayesian posteriors in nuclear physics. Key findings include:
\begin{itemize}
  \item If $f$ is unimodal with a negative definite Hessian at its global maximum, the mixing time of the random walk is $O(n\log n)$.
  \item If $f$ is multimodal, the mixing time is exponential in $n$; however, a simulated annealing scheme governed by $f^K$ for an increasing sequence of $K$ achieves mixing in $O(n^2)$. By employing a step size that decreases with $K$, this can be improved to $O(n\log n)$.
  \item When the process is applied to a general graph instead of the $d$-dimensional box, a simulated annealing scheme defined by the network's conductances yields similar results.
\end{itemize}
Several illustrative examples, including those cited above, are provided.

This paper examines multistage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) as a strategy to mitigate uncertainty regarding the underlying problem ambiguity. Acknowledging that not every realization or scenario path influences the optimal value, we explore how to define and pinpoint critical scenarios within nested multistage DRO frameworks. Our approach generalizes the findings of Rahimian, Bayraksan, and Homem-de-Mello [Math. Program. 173(1--2): 393--430, 2019], which were limited to static or two-stage contexts, by extending them to a full multistage setting. Specifically, we introduce concepts regarding the effectiveness of scenario paths and the conditional effectiveness of realizations along those paths for a broad class of multistage DRO problems. Furthermore, we establish straightforward criteria to determine the effectiveness of scenario paths in multistage environments when distributional ambiguity is characterized by the total variation distance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that these concepts offer valuable insights into the problem's underlying uncertainty.

This paper presents a corpus of cuneiform texts, which served as the source for the dataset utilized in the 2019 Cuneiform Language Identification (CLI) shared task, along with preliminary language identification experiments performed using this corpus. We also outline the CLI dataset and its derivation from the corpus, providing baseline language identification results based on it. To our knowledge, these experiments represent the first application of automatic language identification methods to cuneiform data.

Reproducing natural legged locomotion has long been a primary objective in robotics and computer graphics. Although recent methods have produced encouraging outcomes, they lack the flexibility to adapt to legged systems with varying morphologies. This limitation often stems from their dependence on precise motion capture data or complex learning environments that guarantee natural gait emergence but hinder generalization. This study introduces a versatile framework for achieving realistic locomotion by using the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model to guide the learning process. By capitalizing on the exploratory strengths of Reinforcement Learning (RL), we develop a control policy that bridges the gap between the simplified template model and full-body dynamics necessary for stable, periodic movement. The proposed method is applicable to robots of diverse sizes and shapes, compatible with any RL technique or control architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that, even within a model-free setup utilizing a simple reactive control architecture, the learned policies generate realistic and energy-efficient gaits for both bipedal and quadrupedal robots. Crucially, this is accomplished without relying on motion capture data, imposing strict dynamic or kinematic constraints, or dictating specific limb coordination. Supplemental videos are provided to qualitatively assess the naturalness of the resulting gaits.

This study introduces an entropy regularization term for vector quantization (VQ), derived from an analysis of the persistent homology within VQ embeddings. It demonstrates that increased embedding entropy correlates with improved codebook utilization, thereby reducing overfitting to identity and preventing codebook collapse in VQ-based autoencoders [1]. We establish that homology-constrained regularization effectively boosts the entropy of the VQ process (approximating input entropy) while maintaining the topology of the quantized latent space across mini-batches. Additionally, this work investigates specific patterns observed in the persistent homology diagrams of latents generated by vector quantization. The proposed algorithm is implemented and evaluated as a module within a standard VQ-VAE, with a linked code repository providing a functional implementation of the resulting architecture, termed homology-constrained vector quantization (HC-VQ).

The classical Bertini theorem regarding the generic intersection of an algebraic set with hyperplanes asserts the following: Let $X$ be a nonsingular closed subvariety of $\mathbb{P}^n_k$, where $k$ is an algebraically closed field. Then, there exists a hyperplane $H \subset \mathbb{P}^n_k$ that does not contain $X$ such that the scheme $H \cap X$ is regular at every point. Moreover, the collection of hyperplanes satisfying this condition constitutes an open dense subset of the complete linear system $|H|$, viewed as a projective space. In this work, we demonstrate that it is possible to effectively specify a finite family of hyperplanes $H$ such that at least one of them fulfills the conclusion of the Bertini theorem. As a consequence of the methodology employed in the proof, we provide effective formulas for the multiplicity and the {\L}ojasiewicz exponent of polynomial mappings.

Narrative visualization has recently attracted significant interest. To support its development across diverse scenarios, researchers have established various design spaces. As user demands increase and automation capabilities improve, numerous tools have emerged. This study examines the integration of automation into narrative visualization and design processes by reviewing 122 papers and tools. By analyzing the narrative capabilities and production effort required for different visualizations, we developed a two-dimensional coordinate system to categorize them. The resulting taxonomy maps seven narrative visualization types along the x-axis against four identified automation levels: design space, authoring tool, AI-supported tool, and AI-generator tool. This framework offers a comprehensive overview of current research and development regarding automated narrative visualization tools. Furthermore, we highlight key research challenges within each category and propose new avenues to stimulate future inquiry in this field.

This paper examines the uniqueness of difference polynomials of the form $f^{n}(z)P(f(z))L_c(f)$ and $g^{n}(z)P(g(z))L_c(g)$, where $L_c(f)=f(z+c)+c_0f(z)$ and $P(z)$ is a polynomial with constant coefficients of degree $m$ that shares a small function with the original function. The study utilizes the concepts of weakly weighted sharing and relaxed weighted sharing to derive results that enhance and expand upon recent findings by Sahoo and Biswas (Tamkang J. Math., \textbf{49}(2), 85--97 (2018)).

Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) and interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest regarding the information paradox. Building on this, we extend the concept of reflected entropy to these frameworks. Initially, we define the left-right reflected entropy (LRRE) within BCFT, demonstrating that its holographic counterpart corresponds to the area of the entanglement wedge cross section (EWCS) in AdS/BCFT. We also outline the method for calculating reflected entropy in ICFT. Applying this approach allows us to identify the universal characteristics of the Markov gap in specific scenarios. Additionally, we elucidate the holographic dual of boundary primary correlation functions by leveraging the LRRE/EWCS duality.

Current point-cloud 3D object detectors rely on convolution-like operators that process local neighborhoods using fixed-weight kernels and aggregate global context hierarchically. However, recent advancements in 2D vision, such as self-attention and non-local networks, demonstrate that explicitly modeling long-range interactions yields more robust and competitive models. This paper introduces two self-attention variants for contextual modeling in 3D detection by enhancing convolutional features with self-attention mechanisms. First, we integrate pairwise self-attention into leading BEV, voxel, and point-based detectors, achieving consistent improvements of up to 1.5 3D AP on the KITTI validation set while reducing parameter count and computational cost by 15–80% and 30–50%, respectively. Second, we propose a variant that learns deformations over randomly sampled locations to select the most representative features. This approach enables scalable global contextual modeling for larger point clouds and generates more discriminative feature descriptors. Our method offers flexible integration with most state-of-the-art detectors, boosting accuracy while improving efficiency. We validate these gains across KITTI, nuScenes, and Waymo Open datasets. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/AutoVision-cloud/SA-Det3D.

A defensive alliance in a graph is a vertex set where every member has a majority of its neighbors within the set. Determining the minimum-size defensive alliance is NP-hard, though polynomial-time solutions exist when specific parameters are fixed. While fixed-parameter tractability has been established for structural parameters like the vertex cover number, the status of treewidth remained an open question. This gap is notable given treewidth's prominence and success in other contexts. This work resolves the issue by demonstrating that the problem is W[1]-hard with respect to treewidth, implying no FPT algorithms exist under standard assumptions. This result is counterintuitive, as the problem is FPT when parameterized by solution size, and such "subset problems" typically remain FPT for bounded treewidth. The proof of W[1]-hardness relies on techniques derived from recent hardness results concerning secure sets in graphs.

Tumbling asteroids represent a distinct category of objects characterized by an angular velocity vector that does not align with any of their principal axes of inertia, creating significant challenges for modeling the trajectories of spacecraft intended to orbit them. This study extends previous research on this subject, specifically focusing on asteroid (99942) Apophis during its 2029 close approach to Earth. We examine the orbital dynamics of a spacecraft circling the asteroid during this event, accounting for variations in the spin axis orientation across two distinct sets of initial conditions. By employing three analytical methods—MEGNO, PMap, and Time-Series prediction—we assess the global dynamics of the spacecraft relative to the target. Our findings confirm that no spacecraft maintaining natural orbits can endure the intense perturbations induced by the close encounter with Earth.

Currently, most research on magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) wave diagnostics in magnetic flux tubes relies on pioneering studies that neglect magnetic twist contributions. While other investigations have addressed MHD waves, their derived dispersion relations only cover wave modes with m=0, 1, and 2, omitting the kink mode at m=-1. Consequently, this study aims to provide a comprehensive dispersion relation that incorporates both magnetic twist and the m=-1 wave mode. Similar to the m=+1 mode, the m=-1 mode undergoes a transition from a body to a surface mode at a finite kr0, though its phase speeds are typically lower. In dispersion diagrams, the harmonic curves for m=+1 and m=-1 modes display approximate symmetry around a characteristic velocity, such as the tube velocity in flux tubes. Utilizing this updated dispersion relation, we re-examine spiral wave patterns in sunspots, concluding that, within the framework of linear perturbation analysis, magnetic twist exerts minimal influence on their morphology.

An angular analysis of the $B^0 \rightarrow K^{*0} e^+ e^-$ decay has been conducted using a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 3.0 ${\mbox{fb}^{-1}}$ from the LHCb experiment, gathered during 2011 and 2012 from $pp$ collisions at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. This study marks the first measurement of multiple observables within the dielectron mass squared ($q^2$) range of 0.002 to 1.120${\mathrm{\,Ge\kern -0.1em V^2\!/}c^4}$. The observables $F_{\mathrm{L}}$ and $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$, which correspond to $K^{*0}$ polarisation and lepton forward-backward asymmetry respectively, are determined to be $F_{\mathrm{L}}= 0.16 \pm 0.06 \pm0.03$ and $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = 0.10 \pm 0.18 \pm 0.05$, with the first uncertainty representing statistical error and the second systematic error. Additionally, the observables $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{(2)}$ and $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{Im}}$, which probe photon polarisation in this $q^2$ interval, are measured as $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{(2)} = -0.23 \pm 0.23 \pm 0.05$ and $A_{\mathrm{T}}^{\mathrm{Im}} =0.14 \pm 0.22 \pm 0.05$. All findings align with Standard Model predictions.

This paper utilizes the techniques introduced in [Ti97] and [TZ00] to establish the properness of the log $F$-functional across all conic K\"ahler-Einstein manifolds. As a result, we provide an alternative demonstration of the openness of the continuity method via conic K\"ahler-Einstein metrics.

Integrating Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) with Rate-Splitting Multiple Access (RSMA) offers a promising approach to enhance spectral and energy efficiency in next-generation (B5G and 6G) wireless networks. This paper examines an RS-based transmission strategy within an IRS-assisted network serving both near and cell-edge users. Specifically, we introduce a novel IRS-RS architecture that exploits the synergy between RS and IRS to maximize the weighted sum-rate (WSR). This is achieved by optimizing IRS reflecting coefficients and base station (BS) beamformers, subject to constraints on BS power, user quality of service (QoS), and finite IRS resolution. To address the resulting non-convex WSR maximization problem, we develop an alternating algorithm and evaluate its performance against baseline non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) schemes under both perfect and imperfect channel state information (CSIT) conditions. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed IRS-RS architecture provides superior QoS for cell-edge users compared to the IRS-NOMA transmission scheme.

This paper establishes a theorem on almost global existence for certain abstract nonlinear partial differential equations defined on flat tori, subsequently applying these findings to specific instances: a nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a convolution potential, a beam equation, a quantum hydrodynamical equation, and the stability of plane waves within the NLS framework. The core innovation lies in the abstract result's foundation on a nonresonance condition that is significantly less restrictive than standard conditions; traditional approaches depend on Bourgain's Lemma to partition the "resonant sites" of the Laplace operator on irrational tori, whereas this work bypasses that requirement.

Polarization-dependent near-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XANES) serves as an element-specific tool for investigating the real-space distribution of unoccupied state density in solid-state materials. This study reports on Fe and As $K$-edge measurements of Ba(Fe$_{1-x}$M$_{x}$)$_{2}$As$_{2}$, where M represents Mn, Co, and x takes values of 0.0 and 0.08. The findings indicate a significant polarization dependence in the XANES spectra, characterized primarily by enhanced intensity of electronic transitions when the beam polarization is oriented outside the sample's $ab$ crystallographic plane. These results demonstrate that states with $p_{z}$-orbital character dominate the unoccupied density of states near the Fermi level. Furthermore, partial Fe substitution with Co reduces intensity anisotropy, implying that Co facilitates preferential electronic transfer to $p_{z}$-orbital states. Conversely, Mn substitution increases the $p_{z}$-orbital anisotropy of the spectra, attributed to enhanced local Fe $3d$-$4p$ mixing, which highlights the role of Fe $4p$ states in localizing Fe $3d$ orbitals. Additionally, by comparing our data with prior experiments, we identify the relative mixing between Fe and pnictide $4p_{x,y,z}$ orbitals as a distinct boundary between the electronic properties of iron arsenides and selenides. These conclusions are validated by multiple-scattering theory calculations of the XANES spectra and quantum chemistry analyses of the Fe coordination electronic structure.

We introduce a novel method for optimizing quantum circuits grounded in the ZX-calculus. First, we translate quantum circuits into ZX-diagrams, offering a flexible, low-level graphical framework for representing quantum computations. Subsequently, we apply ZX-calculus rules to develop a simplification strategy for these diagrams, relying on two specific graph transformations: local complementation and pivoting. We demonstrate that the resulting reduced diagram can be converted back into a quantum circuit. Although extracting circuits from arbitrary ZX-diagrams remains largely unexplored, we prove that the graph of our simplified diagrams always possesses a specific graph-theoretic property known as generalized flow, which enables a deterministic circuit extraction process. For Clifford circuits, this procedure generates a new normal form that is asymptotically optimal in size and provides a tighter upper bound on gate depth for nearest-neighbour architectures. Furthermore, for Clifford+T and more general circuits, our technique allows us to bypass gates that disrupt the Clifford structure, resulting in smaller circuits compared to naive 'cut-and-resynthesize' approaches.

LiDAR sensors are a critical component of contemporary autonomous vehicles, offering precise, high-resolution 3D models of their surroundings. Nevertheless, leveraging the growing volume of data from multiple high-resolution LiDAR units poses significant computational challenges. As sensor resolution, point cloud dimensions, and frame rates rise, real-time processing must continue to extract meaningful semantics from these increasingly detailed environmental maps. A key determinant of both the accuracy and runtime efficiency of deep neural networks processing these point clouds lies in the underlying data representation and its computation method. This study investigates the link between computational representations employed in neural networks and their resulting performance traits. Specifically, we introduce a new taxonomy of LiDAR point cloud representations utilized in modern deep learning frameworks for 3D point cloud analysis. Leveraging this framework, we conduct a structured evaluation of various methodological families, revealing shared strengths and weaknesses regarding computational efficiency, memory usage, and representational capacity, with the latter measured via semantic segmentation results. Ultimately, we offer insights and strategic guidance for advancing future neural point cloud processing techniques.

We derive genus $0$ implications from the all-genera quantum HRR formula established in Part IX. This work entails re-proving and broadening the adelic characterization of genus $0$ quantum K-theory previously identified in [Givental A., Tonita V., in Symplectic, Poisson, and Noncommutative Geometry, Math. Sci. Res. Inst. Publ., Vol. 62, Cambridge University Press, New York, 2014, 43-91]. Building upon select findings from Part VIII, we demonstrate the invariance of a specific variety (the "big J-function"), which is constructed from the genus $0$ descendant potential of permutation-equivariant quantum K-theory, under the action of particular finite difference operators in Novikov's variables. We further utilize this property to reconstruct the entire variety from a single point and provide an explicit formulation for the case of a point target space.

Understanding galaxy evolution depends on translating multi-wavelength observations into physical properties, a task facilitated by spectral energy distribution (SED) models that derive parameters from spectrophotometric data. Recent advances in wide, deep multi-waveband surveys have substantially expanded the volume of high-quality data, coinciding with improvements in SED fitting algorithms through enhanced modeling prescriptions, updated templates, and broader wavelength sampling. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of various SED fitting codes, analyzing their methods and outputs to quantify uncertainties arising from modeling assumptions. We applied fourteen widely used codes to CANDELS photometric samples at redshifts of approximately 1 and 3. Our results show consensus on stellar mass but reveal discrepancies regarding star formation rates (SFR) and dust attenuation. To investigate these variations and biases, we examined how specific modeling assumptions—such as star formation histories, nebular, dust, and AGN models—affect derived stellar masses, SFRs, and $A_V$ values. Furthermore, we assessed the divergence among codes concerning the SFR-stellar mass relation and quantified the contribution of modeling choices to uncertainties in stellar mass (~0.1 dex), SFR (~0.3 dex), and dust attenuation (~0.3 mag). Finally, we provide resources outlining best practices for SED fitting.

A Kakeya set $S$ within $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^n$ is defined as a set that contains a line oriented in every possible direction. This work demonstrates that for any square-free integer $N$, the minimum size of such a set in $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^n$ is bounded below by $C_{n,\epsilon} N^{n - \epsilon}$ for any $\epsilon$, thereby confirming a specific instance of the Hickman and Wright conjecture. While similar bounds were previously established only when $N$ is prime, we further prove that determining these bounds for general $N$ can be approached by establishing lower limits on the $\mathbb{F}_p$ rank of the incidence matrix formed by points and hyperplanes over $(\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z})^n$.

Extensive research indicates that numerous classifiers are vulnerable to adversarial examples—minor, strategic alterations to input data that result in incorrect classifications. This study investigates general non-parametric approaches to determine their resilience against such perturbations. We derive broad conditions ensuring that these methods achieve r-consistency, meaning they converge to classifiers that are both optimally robust and accurate as the sample size increases. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that for well-separated data, nearest neighbors and kernel classifiers are r-consistent, whereas histograms are not. Furthermore, for general data distributions, we prove that applying Adversarial Pruning (Yang et al., 2019) to render the data well-separated, followed by nearest neighbor or kernel classification, also guarantees r-consistency.

Our primary objective is to determine the dust mass and grain sizes within the interaction zones between stellar winds and the interstellar medium (ISM) surrounding asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars. By characterizing dust in these regions, we seek to understand the contribution of low-mass evolved stars to galactic dust formation. Utilizing far-infrared images at 70 and 160 microns, we derived dust temperatures and masses for a sample of both carbon-rich and oxygen-rich AGB stars. These parameters were calculated through two methods: first, directly from flux ratios assuming constant 0.1-micron grains; and second, via 3D radiative transfer models spatially constrained by observations to ensure consistency. In these models, grain sizes were varied between 0.01 and 5.0 microns while keeping other parameters constant. Our findings indicate that observed dust masses in wind-ISM interaction regions align with mass accumulated from stellar winds. For carbon-rich sources, incorporating spatial constraints favored larger grain sizes (approximately 2 microns). Conversely, for oxygen-rich sources, spatial constraints led to modeled temperatures that were too high, making it impossible to match observed far-infrared ratios regardless of the grain size, suggesting a complex interaction between grain properties and the stellar radiation field. These results impact our understanding of grain survival during the transition to the ISM and the characteristics of dust particles that seed further growth in the ISM. However, the challenges in modeling oxygen-rich sources demonstrate that deriving dust properties is not straightforward and demands more sophisticated approaches.

**Aims.** Leveraging the recently released database (Trifonov et al. 2020) of radial velocities (RVs) derived from fifteen years of HARPS/ESO observations, we aimed to identify potential exoplanets. **Methods.** For targets with adequate RV data, an automated algorithm was employed to detect significant periodic signals and fit Keplerian models for orbital estimation. Additionally, we examined auxiliary stellar-activity indices and compared our results with prior literature to isolate periodic RV signals lacking corresponding activity variations. The most robust signals underwent manual inspection to flag additional false positives, with a specific focus on long-period (P > 1,000 d) massive candidates orbiting FGK dwarf stars. **Results.** We discovered two Jupiter analogs orbiting the slightly evolved F8V star HD 103891 and the Solar-like star HD 105779. Using nested sampling to determine their orbital parameters, we found periods of 1919 ± 16 d and 2412 ± 54 d, with minimum masses of 1.44 ± 0.02 M_Jup and 0.64 ± 0.06 M_Jup, respectively. While the orbit of HD 103891 b exhibits slight eccentricity (e = 0.31 ± 0.03), the orbit of HD 105779 b is likely circular (e < 0.16). **Conclusions.** With astrometric signatures of 59 and 42 μas, HD 103891 b and HD 105779 b join an expanding list of planets whose precise masses may soon be determined via Gaia astrometry. This discovery underscores the value of long-term RV surveys for investigating planetary occurrence beyond the snow line of Solar-like stars.

It is widely established that shearing causes granular mixtures with variations in size or shape to segregate. Historically, two mechanisms have been suggested to explain this phenomenon, yet their coexistence remains uncertain. To resolve this, we investigated a bidisperse mixture of equal-volume spheroids within a rotating drum, a setup where the two mechanisms are predicted to oppose one another. We provide the first evidence of two distinct segregation mechanisms driven by relative over-stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for non-spherical particles, these mechanisms can act in opposing directions, creating a competitive dynamic. Consequently, segregation intensity fluctuates non-monotonically with the aspect ratio ($AR$), and the segregation direction reverses at specific points for both prolate and oblate spheroids, thereby accounting for previously observed segregation reversals. Aligning with prior findings, we observed that the kinetic mechanism dominates for nearly spherical particles. For moderate aspect ratios, the kinetic mechanism drives spherical particles toward the drum's periphery, with the gravity mechanism playing a minor role. However, at extreme $AR$ values, the gravity mechanism significantly intensifies and surpasses the kinetic counterpart.

Structured tabular data within preclinical and clinical settings holds significant value regarding individual profiles, yet efficiently converting this data into text summaries via automated systems can greatly minimize the manual labor required for report generation. Despite this potential, practical implementation faces substantial hurdles due to limited data availability, sparse information, and the current inability of leading natural language generation models (such as T5, PEGASUS, and GPT-Neo) to generate precise and dependable outputs. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a new table-to-text methodology utilizing a unique two-step architecture that integrates auto-correction, a copy mechanism, and synthetic data augmentation. Our research demonstrates that this approach effectively identifies key biomedical entities and values from structured sources, achieving up to a 0.13 absolute improvement in copying accuracy to produce coherent and reliable text for assay and toxicology validation reports. Furthermore, we show that the system can be adapted to new datasets with minimal effort by fine-tuning using as few as 40% of the training examples. Finally, the model's outputs have been verified by domain experts within a Human-in-the-Loop framework.

We present a new algorithm for future video feature generation and action anticipation based on Recurrent Neural Networks, termed the feature mapping RNN. This innovative architecture integrates three key machine learning principles: parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels, and adversarial training. By leveraging only a few initial video frames, the feature mapping RNN generates future features using a significantly smaller parameter count compared to conventional RNNs. These predicted features are then input into a multi-layer perceptron enhanced with an RBF kernel layer to achieve precise action prediction. Experimental results demonstrate performance gains of 18% on JHMDB-21, 6% on UCF101-24, and 13% on UT-Interaction datasets, surpassing previous state-of-the-art methods in action anticipation.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares have been detected through high-precision, long-baseline, broad-band photometry from missions such as Kepler, K2, and TESS. These data are vital for evaluating biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres and calculating surface UV radiation doses for habitable zone planets orbiting low-mass stars. However, a significant constraint in these evaluations is the scarcity of near-ultraviolet spectral observations of such flares. To encourage further empirical study, we employed a grid of radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, incorporating an updated model for hydrogen line pressure broadening, to forecast the $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ \AA\ continuum flux during the rise and peak of a well-documented superflare from the dM3e star AD Leo. These forecasts rely on semi-empirical combinations of radiative flux spectra, comprising a high-flux electron beam simulation with a substantial low-energy cutoff ($\gtrsim 85$ keV) and a lower-flux simulation with a smaller cutoff ($\lesssim 40$ keV). This two-component framework successfully accounts for hydrogen Balmer line broadening, optical continuum color temperature, Balmer jump magnitude, and the intensity and morphology of the far-ultraviolet continuum during the flare's rise and peak. Furthermore, by integrating spatially resolved analyses of solar flare data from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph with prior radiative-hydrodynamic modeling of the March 29, 2014, X1 solar flare (SOL20140329T17:48), we interpret this two-component electron beam model as depicting the spatial superposition of intense kernels and dimmer ribbons across a broader region.

This work explores an extension of the Standard Model designed to address the muon $g-2$ discrepancy and neutrino masses, with a detailed focus on dark matter phenomenology. The proposed framework incorporates both WIMP and FIMP scalar dark matter candidates, resulting in a two-component dark matter scenario. We analyze various production mechanisms and regimes, highlighting the novel freeze-in semi-production process, and demonstrate that the combined abundance of WIMPs and FIMPs accounts for the observed relic density. The inclusion of additional scalar fields facilitates first-order phase transitions; consequently, we investigate the vacuum evolution and the associated stochastic gravitational wave signals. Furthermore, we indicate that these gravitational wave signatures could be detected by future experiments, offering a complementary method for discovery.

The rise of facial processing technologies (FPT) has sparked growing controversy regarding their potential harms. Although several U.S. states and municipalities have enacted bans on law enforcement and government use of facial recognition, these technologies continue to be developed and deployed across diverse sectors, primarily governed by state biometric privacy statutes. Notably, the 2008 Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) has become a focal point for significant litigation. However, because most BIPA cases settle before technical complexities and legal definitions are thoroughly clarified, considerable uncertainty persists regarding the law's specific application to FPT. Existing litigation reveals a disconnect between technical and legal communities. This paper examines findings from BIPA proceedings concerning FPT to highlight key tensions: instances where the technical implementation of BIPA may foster unintended, negative incentives for FPT development, and scenarios where litigation exposes the inadequacies of relying solely on technical methods to uphold legal privacy principles. These insights are critical for (i) evaluating biometric privacy laws as regulatory frameworks for FPT, (ii) assessing potential FPT harms, and (iii) encouraging strategies to mitigate such harms. By clarifying these issues, we aim to assist courts and legislators in adopting more nuanced regulatory approaches to FPT and enable developers to better comprehend privacy values within the current U.S. legal environment.

We introduce a cosmological framework for the early universe featuring a relaxation mechanism for the potentially large vacuum energy, succeeded by a reheating phase that transitions into the standard hot big bang. By employing a scalar field with a kinetic term scaled by an inverse power of spacetime curvature, the model circumvents the fine-tuning problem of the cosmological constant. Although this mechanism counteracts radiative corrections to dark energy, it would otherwise eliminate both vacuum energy and all other matter components. To finalize this scenario, we utilize a sector that violates the null energy condition, transferring its energy to a reheating sector. We demonstrate this process explicitly, offering a concrete model of the universe's origin that establishes a thermal history with a negligible cosmological constant.

The formation timescales of planets are governed by the coevolution of T Tauri stars and their adjacent protoplanetary disks. This study presents model fits based on magnetospheric accretion and inner disk wall parameters, derived from NUV-NIR spectra of nine classical T Tauri stars within the Orion OB1b region, as part of the ODYSSEUS Survey. By combining NUV-optical data from the Hubble UV Legacy Library of Young Stars as Essential Standards (ULLYSES) Director's Discretionary Program with optical-NIR spectra from the PENELLOPE VLT Large Programme, we determine that these targets exhibit relatively high accretion rates despite the region's intermediate age of 5.0 Myr. The rates span $0.5-17.2 \times 10^{-8}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr, with a median of $1.2\times 10^{-8}$ M$_{\odot}$/yr. Additionally, the near-infrared (NIR) excesses are modeled using inner disk walls situated between 0.05 and 0.10 AU from the host stars, with temperatures ranging from 1200 to 1800 K. We examine how the choice of extinction law influences results, noting that measured accretion rates are highly sensitive to the adopted extinction value. Future work will extend this analysis to the full ULLYSES sample of T Tauri stars to better characterize accretion processes and inner disks across star-forming regions of varying ages and stellar populations.

We investigate the temporal emergence of a universal, uniform distribution of quantum states confined to a finite subsystem, resulting from projective measurements performed on the remainder of the system. Referred to as "deep thermalization," this phenomenon signifies a form of equilibration in quantum many-body systems that is more rigorous than standard thermalization, which merely restricts ensemble-averaged observable values. Although quantum circuit models in one dimension demonstrate this effect exactly, they are unique because deep thermalization coincides precisely with regular thermalization. In this work, we introduce an exactly-solvable model of chaotic dynamics where these two processes unfold on distinct time scales. This model consists of a finite subsystem connected to an infinite random-matrix bath via a narrow constriction, emphasizing the influence of locality and imperfect thermalization on the development of such universal wavefunction distributions. Our analytical predictions are validated against exact numerical simulations, yielding excellent agreement.

"Counting Rocks!" serves as the written companion to an interactive undergraduate introduction to combinatorics, featuring linked videos that explain concepts and illustrate examples. The curriculum covers fundamental counting problems (Chapters 1–4), proof methods (Chapter 5), recurrence relations and generating functions (Chapters 6–7), and an introduction to graph theory (Chapters 8–12). These topics and the accompanying problems align with standard undergraduate combinatorics coursework. Beyond the video resources, most chapters include an investigation section guiding students through deeper explorations of the subject matter. Several sections also demonstrate how to utilize the free, open-source software SAGE for problem-solving. The text is enriched with numerous illustrative figures and concludes each section and chapter with a curated list of exercises ranging from basic to advanced difficulty.

Search engines like Google, Bing, and Yahoo! display suggestions as users type queries to help them locate desired information quickly and uncover relevant topics. These features also assist users who have only a vague concept of what they are looking for. We introduce an algorithm that delivers the top $k$ ranked suggestions from a corpus of $n$ options based on the query prefix entered so far, operating with a time complexity of $O(k \log{n})$ and requiring $O(n)$ additional space.

This paper investigates a natural learning algorithm designed for uniform pacing of advertising budgets, capable of adapting to fluctuating conditions within ad sale platforms. On the demand side, advertisers encounter a core technical hurdle in automating bids to distribute their allocated budgets across a campaign while navigating hidden and potentially dynamic cost functions. This automation must occur in real-time, necessitating low computational costs to match the high frequency of auctions. Furthermore, advertisers are required to exhaust nearly their entire sub-interval budgets (hourly or minutely) to uphold long-term budgeting quotas. To address this, our study examines a straightforward learning algorithm that adapts to the market's latent cost function, learning the optimal average bid value for a short segment of auctions early in the campaign. This enables smooth, real-time budget pacing. We demonstrate that our algorithm is robust to variations in auction mechanisms and converges rapidly to a stable average bidding strategy. The approach not only ensures budgets are almost fully utilized but also paces bidding smoothly to avoid premature campaign exit and the loss of opportunities for high-value impressions later on. Beyond theoretical guarantees, we substantiate the algorithm's effectiveness with experimental results using open-source data from real advertising campaigns.

This study examines the convexity of the range of the Berezin transform. Given a bounded operator $T$ on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H$ defined over a set $X$, the range $B(T)$ is defined as $\{ < Tk_x, k_x >_H : x \in X \}$, where $k_x$ denotes the normalized reproducing kernel at $x \in X$. The primary objective is to characterize the conditions under which this range is convex, specifically for a class of composition operators acting on the Hardy space of the unit disk.

The growing expectations for unmanned air vehicles (UAVs) are driving their operational environments toward confined spaces, necessitating flights in close proximity to objects and subsequent interactions. This proximity introduces variations in UAV dynamics, as propeller thrust and drag coefficients can fluctuate depending on the distance to nearby surfaces. Simultaneously, UAVs must maintain time-based trajectories despite external disturbances. Given these challenging conditions, a standard controller with a fixed structure may be insufficient, requiring parameter adjustments for each specific scenario. Motivated by these factors, this work proposes the practical implementation and evaluation of an autonomous controller for a quadrotor UAV. The system employs a self-adaptive controller utilizing a composite scheme that combines sliding mode control (SMC) with evolving neuro-fuzzy control. The neuro-fuzzy controller's parameter vector is updated adaptively according to the SMC sliding surface. Furthermore, the controller features a novel elastic structure where the count of fuzzy rules dynamically increases or decreases based on a balance between bias and variance. The interaction capabilities of this UAV were experimentally evaluated in real-time, addressing the ground effect, ceiling effect, and flight through strong wind generated by a fan while adhering to time-based trajectories.

Free-space optical (FSO) communication provides significant benefits due to its high directivity, yet it introduces substantial challenges regarding terminal alignment. Specifically, during the link-acquisition phase, also known as coarse pointing, ground stations may fail to establish optical links if pointing errors occur or if information about unmanned aerial vehicle locations is inadequate. To address this, this letter proposes a radio-frequency (RF) lens antenna array designed to enhance coarse pointing performance within hybrid RF/FSO systems. By employing a novel closed-form angle estimator, the proposed algorithm achieves a reduction in minimum outage probability of more than a thousand times compared to conventional approaches.

Detecting objects in Ultra High-Resolution (UHR) images remains a significant challenge in computer vision due to the diverse scales of targets. Specifically, barcode detection faces a dilemma: resizing UHR inputs causes information loss, whereas processing them at full resolution is computationally prohibitive and inefficient. To address this, we introduce a method leveraging semantic segmentation for rapid and precise detection of barcodes across various scales in UHR imagery. Our approach utilizes a modified Region Proposal Network (RPN) tailored for images exceeding 10k×10k pixels, coupled with a novel Y-Net segmentation architecture and a post-processing step to generate bounding boxes around segmented barcode masks. The resulting end-to-end system achieves a latency of 16 milliseconds, making it 2.5 times faster than YOLOv4 and 5.9 times faster than Mask R-CNN. In accuracy tests on a synthetic dataset, our method surpasses YOLOv4 and Mask R-CNN by 5.5% and 47.1% in mean Average Precision (mAP), respectively. The synthetic barcode dataset and associated code are publicly available at http://www.github.com/viplabB/SBD/.

This paper establishes a quantitative spectral inequality for the second Robin eigenvalue within non-compact rank-1 symmetric spaces. Specifically, it demonstrates that for bounded domains in such spaces, the geodesic ball achieves the maximum second Robin eigenvalue among domains of equal volume, provided the Robin parameter is negative and lies within the regime bridging the first nontrivial Neumann and Steklov eigenvalues. This finding extends the research of Freitas and Laugesen in the Euclidean context [FL21] as well as our prior investigation into hyperbolic space [LWW20].

This research investigates the topological complexity of work maps relative to specific subspaces of the configuration space and the workspace, which serves as the target for robot motion. Our primary motivation is to streamline and decrease the quantity of required motion planners, with a specific focus on the set of useful work outcomes. We examine fundamental properties of this targeted complexity, including homotopical invariance, reduction, and the composition of maps. Subsequently, we compare these complexities to derive inequalities that facilitate the reduction in the number of motion planners. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the relative topological complexity of a space pair, as defined by Short, constitutes a specific instance of the targeted complexity of work maps.

Deep Learning (DL) is increasingly being integrated into mobile software applications, referred to here as mobile DL apps. These applications combine DL models trained on extensive datasets with DL programs, which define the model's architecture and the training methodology using specific data. As mobile apps become more reliant on DL, software engineering (SE) for these applications has gained significant importance. However, while current SE research primarily focuses on developing DL models and analyzing faults within the programs themselves, there is a notable lack of study regarding deployment faults—issues that arise when DL models are deployed on mobile devices. Given that billions of users rely on mobile DL apps daily for various tasks, including safety-critical ones, understanding these deployment faults is crucial. To address this gap, this paper offers the first comprehensive investigation into deployment faults within mobile DL apps. By examining real-world faults sourced from Stack Overflow and GitHub, we identified 304 instances. Based on these findings, we developed a fine-grained taxonomy with 23 categories describing fault symptoms and extracted common remediation strategies for different fault types. Additionally, we propose practical implications and future research directions to enhance the deployment of DL models on mobile devices.

Mixture models serve as a valuable instrument for addressing unobserved heterogeneity and form the foundation of numerous model-based clustering techniques. To enhance flexibility, certain parameters can be modeled as functions of auxiliary covariates. Specifically, component weights can be associated with these covariates via a multinomial logistic regression, wherein each weight depends on a linear predictor incorporating one or more covariates. This study extends that framework by substituting the linear predictor with an additive structure, where each component represents a smooth function of the covariates. A Bayesian estimation approach is proposed, utilizing a data augmentation strategy grounded in differenced random utility models. Furthermore, the smoothness of covariate effects is regulated through appropriate prior distributions assigned to spline coefficients. The efficacy of this methodology is evaluated through simulation studies, and its practical utility is demonstrated via an analysis of a novel dataset concerning UK parliamentary votes on Brexit.

Simulating realistic human behavior remains a complex challenge situated at the intersection of social sciences, philosophy, and artificial intelligence. Unlike standard path planning that often ignores environmental context—a factor critical for leisure travel—human movement is driven by intent and surroundings. To address this, two novel algorithms were developed to generate human-like trajectories by incorporating environmental data: the Attraction-Based A* algorithm utilizes environmental features, while the Feature-Based A* algorithm integrates real trajectory data. A human expert evaluated the generated paths for realism, and the study compares the two methods based on efficiency, efficacy, and sensitivity to hyper-parameters. Although the Feature-Based A* algorithm produces trajectories that align more closely with real-world metrics, it suffers from lower time efficiency compared to the Attraction-Based A* algorithm, which limits its practical applicability.

The asymptotic symmetries of Brans-Dicke theory are examined through Penrose's coordinate-independent conformal completion approach, revealing supertranslations and Lorentz transformations in asymptotically flat spacetimes. Employing the Wald-Zoupas formalism, the paper calculates conserved charges and fluxes within the Bondi-Metzner-Sachs algebra. While the scalar degree of freedom influences various fluxes, it contributes exclusively to the Lorentz boost charge. Furthermore, flux-balance laws are utilized to place constraints on displacement, spin, and center-of-mass memory effects.

Structural analysis techniques, such as probing and feature attribution, are becoming vital for examining neural networks. We introduce a novel structural analysis approach based on a formal theory of causal abstraction, offering detailed insights into internal model representations and their influence on input-output dynamics. This method aligns neural representations with variables in interpretable causal models and employs interchange interventions to empirically confirm that these representations possess the causal attributes of their counterparts. We demonstrate this approach through a case study analyzing models trained on the Multiply Quantified Natural Language Inference (MQNLI) corpus, a complex NLI dataset built upon a tree-structured natural logic causal model. Our findings reveal that a high-performing BERT-based model effectively captures portions of the natural logic model's causal structure, while a simpler baseline fails to exhibit any such organization, thereby confirming that BERT representations encode the compositional structure inherent in MQNLI.

The Future Circular Collider's (FCC-ee) electron-positron phase serves as a premier facility for investigating Higgs, top, electroweak, and flavour physics. Situated within a 100 km circular tunnel at CERN, this machine is engineered to function as the initial phase of a future collider capable of $\geq$ 100 TeV proton-proton collisions. Beyond its critical and distinctive Higgs research agenda, the FCC-ee provides robust avenues for uncovering direct or indirect signals of physics extending beyond the Standard Model. Notably, the high-luminosity $Z$ run, expected to generate $5\times 10^{12}$ $Z$ bosons for a two-interaction-point setup, holds exceptional promise for direct searches of long-lived particles. Furthermore, the abundant production of Higgs bosons, $W$ bosons, and top quarks under exceptionally clean experimental conditions may yield further discovery potential at various collision energies. This paper examines three specific scenarios for detecting long-lived signatures at the FCC-ee: heavy neutral leptons (HNLs), axion-like particles (ALPs), and exotic Higgs boson decays. These investigations advocate for innovative optimization of experimental setups and analytical methods, potentially enhancing the sensitivity of other physics searches.

Over the past ten years, online education has become increasingly vital for delivering affordable, high-quality learning to students globally, a trend that accelerated significantly during the global pandemic as learners shifted to digital platforms. Most online educational tasks, such as course and exercise recommendations or automated assessment, rely on monitoring students' knowledge progression, a challenge known in research as \emph{Knowledge Tracing}. Solving this issue necessitates gathering evaluation data that captures how students' understanding evolves. In this paper, we introduce DBE-KT22, a new dataset for knowledge tracing collected from an online exercise system used in a course at the Australian National University. We examine the specific characteristics of the DBE-KT22 dataset and compare it with other existing resources in the field. The dataset is publicly accessible via the Australian Data Archive.

This work addresses the challenge of estimating a $d$-dimensional discrete distribution from samples constrained by a $b$-bit communication limit. Unlike prior studies that primarily analyze global minimax error, we investigate the local behavior of the estimation error, deriving \emph{pointwise} bounds contingent on the target distribution $p$. Specifically, we demonstrate that the $\ell_2$ error diminishes at a rate of $O\left(\frac{\lVert p\rVert_{1/2}}{n2^b}\vee \frac{1}{n}\right)$ for sufficiently large $n$, meaning the error is dictated by the \emph{half-norm} of $p$ rather than the ambient dimension $d$. To achieve this rate uniformly across all $p$, we introduce a two-round sequentially interactive estimation scheme grounded in a novel local refinement strategy: first, a standard global minimax approach localizes $p$, and subsequently, the remaining samples are used to refine the estimate locally. Furthermore, we establish a new local minimax lower bound featuring an (almost) matching $\ell_2$ error, proving that any interactive scheme incurs a $\Omega\left( \frac{\lVert p \rVert_{{(1+\delta)}/{2}}}{n2^b}\right)$ $\ell_2$ error for any $\delta > 0$. This lower bound is obtained by identifying the optimal parametric sub-model containing $p$ and then upper-bounding the quantized Fisher information within that model. Collectively, our upper and lower bounds reveal that $\mathcal{H}_{1/2}(p) = \log(\lVert p \rVert_{{1}/{2}})$ bits of communication—where $\mathcal{H}_{{1}/{2}}(p)$ represents the R\'enyi entropy of order $2$—are both necessary and sufficient to attain optimal centralized performance. Consequently, under $\ell_2$ loss, the appropriate metric for local communication complexity at $p$ is its R\'enyi entropy.

Privacy-preserving publication of event data has gained significant importance in industrial process mining, creating new challenges regarding the balance between data utility and measurable privacy. Current research primarily relies on constructing differentially private trace variants through prefix expansion, yet these methods suffer from practical drawbacks including high computational costs, the generation of artificial variants, the elimination of frequent ones, and restrictions on variant length. This paper proposes a novel approach for directly releasing differentially private trace variants by employing anonymized partition selection strategies to address these limitations. Experiments conducted on real-world event data demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in preserving both raw data utility and the utility of analytical results.

This work introduces both established and novel concepts connecting non-local operators with irregular domains. We examine Cauchy and boundary value problems involving these operators, which manifest anomalous dynamics within the domain's interior and at its boundary. From a macroscopic perspective, this behavior offers a framework for describing regular motion on irregular domains when viewed microscopically.

A hypothetical fifth force interacting with baryon number ($B$) was suggested to explain the observed correlations between acceleration differences ($\Delta a_{ij}$) and baryon-to-mass ratio variations ($\Delta(B/\mu)_{ij}$) in Eötvös experiment samples; however, these findings lack support from contemporary experiments. This study examines the phenomenological consequences of a magnetic analog, $\vec{\mathscr{B}}_5$, to the standard fifth-force electric field, $\vec{\mathscr{E}}_5$, which emerges due to Earth's rotation. We show that if couplings proportional to $\vec{\mathscr{B}}_5$ exist, both the strength and orientation of a potential fifth-force field could deviate significantly from conventional expectations, necessitating further research.

This paper introduces a data-driven approach to accurately simulate the detector response of anti-neutrons interacting within the Electromagnetic Calorimeter (EMC) at BESIII. By utilizing the decay $J/\psi\to p\bar{n}\pi^{-}$ from a BESIII dataset comprising 10 billion $J/\psi$ events, a substantial sample of anti-neutrons is isolated. The simulation evaluates detection efficiency and various observables for anti-neutrons in the EMC, accounting for correlations among the variables. The systematic uncertainty of this data-driven method is established to be below 1% on average, making it a versatile tool for physics processes requiring precise modeling of anti-neutron responses in the EMC.

A pseudoisotopy of $M$ is defined as a diffeomorphism of $M\times I$ that acts as the identity on $M\times 0$. We provide an explicit construction of pseudoisotopies for 4-manifolds that realize specific elements of the "second obstruction to pseudoisotopy." The subsequent paper will present precise formulations of our results regarding 5-manifolds, which were previously announced.

The primary objective is to create a precise and interpretable model for detecting plant diseases via hyperspectral imaging, specifically targeting charcoal rot, a soil-borne fungal pathogen that globally reduces soybean yields. Hyperspectral data were collected across 240 wavelengths spanning 383 to 1032 nm. To address this, we constructed a 3D Convolutional Neural Network capable of identifying charcoal rot with a classification accuracy of 95.73% and an F1 score of 0.87 for the infected class. Using saliency maps, we inferred the trained model to visualize critical pixel locations driving classification decisions and assessed the sensitivity of individual wavelengths. The visualization revealed that 733 nm is the most sensitive wavelength. Given that this falls within the Near Infrared region (700–1000 nm)—a spectrum standard for evaluating plant health—our confidence in the model's predictions is significantly strengthened.

During the current multi-messenger astronomy era, ensuring that data on joint electromagnetic (EM) and gravitational wave (GW) observations of short gamma-ray bursts (sGRBs) remains accessible is crucial. We aim to enable non-experts to rapidly compute joint GW-sGRB detections by integrating a new sGRB model into the existing Gravitational Wave Universe Toolbox. This adaptation involves modifying a generic GRB model into a top-hat jet format suitable for the Toolbox. The study simulates binary neutron star (BNS) populations detectable by user-defined GW instruments to predict resulting sGRB properties and their detectability. Our results provide expected joint detection rates across various combinations of GW detectors and high-energy (HE) instruments. A key finding highlights the transformative impact of the Einstein Telescope (ET), which will detect BNSs at such high rates that nearly all observed sGRBs will have corresponding GW signals. Furthermore, while LIGO's horizon is limited, leveraging HE detector data to search for sub-threshold GW signals at higher redshifts could yield significant success. Conversely, during the ET era, GW data can help identify sub-threshold sGRBs, potentially boosting joint ET-Fermi/GBM observations by approximately 270%. Our initial top-hat jet model underestimated joint detections involving off-axis sGRBs; however, correcting this with a secondary, wider, and weaker jet component reveals that the majority of current-era joint detections will feature off-axis sGRBs, suggesting GRB170817A was less improbable than initially believed. In contrast, during the ET era, most joint detections are expected to involve on-axis sGRBs.

I examine the permissible parameter space and collider potential for various new physics models featuring (broken) Z2 symmetries. I concentrate on the implications of existing constraints and briefly address several future collider possibilities.

The ALICE collaboration at the CERN LHC investigated inclusive J/$\psi$ production in minimum-bias proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}$ = 5.02 TeV. Utilizing a dataset with an integrated luminosity of $L_{\rm int} = 19.4 \pm$ 0.4 nb$^{-1}$, the measurement focused on the dielectron decay channel at mid-rapidity ($|y| < 0.9$) extending down to zero transverse momentum ($p_{\rm T}$). The resulting $p_{\rm T}$-integrated inclusive J/$\psi$ production cross section was determined to be d$\sigma$/d$y$ = 5.64 $\pm$ 0.22 (stat.) $\pm$ 0.33 (syst.) $\pm$ 0.12 (lumi.) $\mu$b. Additionally, the $p_{\rm T}$-differential cross section d$^{2} \sigma$/d$p_{\rm T}$d$y$ was measured across the $p_{\rm T}$ range of 0–10 GeV/$c$ and benchmarked against advanced QCD models. Finally, the extracted values for J/$\psi$ $\langle p_{\rm T} \rangle$ and $\langle p_{\rm T}^{2} \rangle$ were compared with data from collisions at other energies.

This research investigates the operational mechanics and financial returns of contemporary malware designed for cryptocurrency mining. Distinguishing itself from prior work, our analysis encompasses the entire cryptocurrency ecosystem rather than focusing solely on Bitcoin, and extends its scope beyond personal computers to include mobile devices and IoT platforms, all of which have recently become targets for mining attacks. A central inquiry addresses the profitability of these operations, particularly given the current difficulty of mining Bitcoin, to explain why criminals continue to exploit low-end hardware. By examining the primary families of malicious miners active from 2014 to 2017, we detail their functionality, target currencies, and profitability. Our findings reveal that the evolution of the market, characterized by the emergence of new, CPU-minable cryptocurrencies that offer enhanced privacy, has renewed the appeal of mining malware. Consequently, attackers have generated a continuous flow of profits, with some cases reaching into the millions.

A seller engages with a series of short-sighted buyers. Each buyer chooses whether to trust the seller based on the count of actions the seller performed over the most recent K periods, without knowing the sequence in which those actions occurred. The model assumes that seller effort and consumer trust act as strategic complements and that there is a positive probability the seller is a committed type who always exerts maximum effort. I demonstrate that in every equilibrium, the seller maintains a reputation for maximum effort if and only if K falls below a specific threshold. While a larger K enables more buyers to detect opportunism, it simultaneously reduces their incentive to punish such behavior. This dynamic erodes the seller's motivation to maintain a good reputation and decreases consumer welfare. Furthermore, I show that simplifying the summary statistics available to consumers can motivate the seller to uphold his reputation and potentially enhance consumer welfare.

In his 2009 book on configurations and related papers, Branko Gr\"unbaum introduced a sequence of operations for generating new $(n_4)$ configurations from existing ones, a method later termed the "Gr\"unbaum Incidence Calculus." We extend two of these operations to apply to arbitrary $(n_k)$ configurations. By utilizing these generalized operations, we demonstrate that for every $k$, there exists an integer $N_k$ such that a geometric $(n_k)$ configuration exists for all $n \geq N_k$. Furthermore, we refine the upper bound for larger $k$ values by combining empirical findings for $k = 2, 3, 4$ with more detailed analysis.

Heavy flavor physics is generally well-described by the Standard Model, though certain measurements hint at potential new physics. This overview examines the current status and future prospects of the $R(D^{(\ast)})$ and $R(K^{(\ast)})$ anomalies, as well as the persistent discrepancies between exclusive and inclusive determinations of $|V_{cb}|$ and $|V_{ub}|$.

This work introduces a lattice QCD investigation into hidden-charm hexaquarks with the quark composition $usc\bar{d}\bar{s}\bar{c}$, utilizing four sets of gauge configurations produced by the CLQCD Collaboration, where the pion mass spans 220–300 MeV. To probe these hexaquarks, we constructed four operators corresponding to the quantum numbers $0^{++}$, $0^{-+}$, $1^{++}$, and $1^{--}$. Following validation of the spectrum and dispersion relations for standard hadrons, we computed the hexaquark masses, extrapolating the findings to the physical pion mass and the continuum limit.
