Our results indicate that all four hexaquark masses fall below the $\Xi_c \bar \Xi_c$ threshold, with the $0^{-+}$ state situated near the $\eta_c K^+K^-$ threshold. These findings are expected to aid future experimental searches and enhance our comprehension of multiquark state dynamics.

The variational autoencoder (VAE) serves as a widely adopted deep latent variable model for analyzing high-dimensional data by deriving low-dimensional latent representations. It concurrently trains a generative model and an inference network to facilitate approximate posterior inference. Recent adaptations of VAEs designed for temporal and longitudinal data have found utility in healthcare, behavioral analysis, and predictive maintenance; however, these versions fail to address heterogeneous data, which frequently combines continuous and discrete attributes in real-world scenarios. This study introduces the heterogeneous longitudinal VAE (HL-VAE), an extension of existing temporal and longitudinal VAEs specifically tailored for heterogeneous data. HL-VAE ensures efficient inference on high-dimensional datasets by incorporating likelihood models for continuous, count, categorical, and ordinal variables, while also handling missing observations. Validated using both simulated and clinical datasets, the model demonstrates competitive performance in missing value imputation and predictive accuracy.

As visual tracking advances rapidly, current benchmarks are becoming less valuable due to sample redundancy and insufficient differentiation among trackers, rendering comprehensive evaluations excessively time-consuming. Consequently, there is a strong need for a compact yet highly informative benchmark that encompasses all typical challenging scenarios to facilitate efficient performance assessment. In this study, we propose a principled approach to constructing the Informative Tracking Benchmark (ITB), comprising 7% of 1.2 million frames from both existing and newly collected datasets, thereby enabling efficient yet effective evaluation. Specifically, we first establish a quality assessment mechanism to select the most informative sequences from current benchmarks, considering three key factors: the level of challenge, discriminative power, and the density of appearance variations. Additionally, we gather extra sequences to guarantee diversity and balance across tracking scenarios, resulting in a total of 20 sequences per scenario. Through an analysis of 15 state-of-the-art trackers re-trained on this data, we identify effective methods for robust tracking under each scenario and highlight new challenges to guide future research directions in the field.

This study examines the spatial statistics of oxygen abundance in the gas phase across 219 nearby galaxies. To improve the signal-to-noise ratio of faint spectral lines, we develop a novel adaptive binning method, enabling the creation of robust metallicity maps. After eliminating radial gradients, we demonstrate that the resulting two-point correlation functions are largely consistent with a simple injection-diffusion model. By fitting this model, we derive the correlation length ($l_{\rm corr}$), which represents the characteristic scale of interstellar medium mixing. Our findings indicate typical correlation lengths of approximately 1 kpc, showing strong correlations with stellar mass, star formation rate, and effective radius, a weaker link to Hubble type, and notably higher values in interacting or merging systems. We show that the observed trend with star formation rate can be replicated by a simple model of turbulence involving transport and feedback, potentially applicable at low star formation rates if dwarf galaxy winds possess significant mass-loading factors. Additionally, we present the first measurements of the injection width, defining the initial radii where supernova remnants deposit metals; within these radii, the metallicity correlation function deviates from a simple balance of injection and diffusion. We find that this scale is generally less than 60 pc.

Generating images with few-shot learning is a difficult endeavor because it requires creating diverse outputs for unseen categories using only a handful of examples. Current approaches often struggle to balance the trade-off between image quality and diversity. To address this, we introduce Hyperbolic Attribute Editing (HAE), a straightforward and efficient solution. In contrast to methods operating within Euclidean space, HAE leverages data from known categories to model image hierarchies using hyperbolic space. Once trained, HAE can produce images of novel categories by shifting the latent code of an existing image toward any semantic direction within the Poincaré disk while maintaining a fixed radius. Crucially, this hyperbolic framework enables precise control over the semantic diversity of the generated results by adjusting the radius. Comprehensive experiments and visual analyses confirm that HAE not only delivers high-quality and diverse images with minimal data but also ensures a highly controllable and interpretable editing workflow.

This research details a multi-wavelength analysis of the absolute magnitudes and colors of red clump (RC) stars, drawn from a combined APOGEE and GALAH DR2 catalogue, augmented by *Gaia* DR2 astrometry and photometric data from *GALEX* GR6/7, SDSS DR7, *Gaia* DR2, 2MASS, and *WISE*. The study evaluates various distance estimation techniques, including *Gaia* trigonometric parallaxes, the inverse parallax method (1/$\varpi$), and Bayesian statistics, alongside chemical classifications of Galactic disc populations on the [$\alpha$/Fe]$\times$[Fe/H] plane. This investigation addresses the longstanding issue of how population effects influence RC luminosity. Findings reveal that RC stars belonging to chemically defined thin and thick disc populations exhibit distinct absolute magnitudes, whereas their colors remain consistent across all photometric bands. Absolute magnitudes range from -0.12 to +0.13 mag using the 1/$\varpi$ method, with variations shifting based on Galactic population; however, the magnitude differences are more pronounced when using the alternative method. Furthermore, the Besan\c con population synthesis model for 2MASS photometry indicates an absolute magnitude difference between thin and thick disc populations of -0.35 to -0.40 mag. A comparison shows that the model predicts magnitude differences approximately three times larger than those observed. Ultimately, the study confirms that RC absolute magnitudes are dependent on the $\alpha$-element abundances of Galactic populations.

Heckenberger defined the Weyl groupoid for finite-dimensional Nichols algebras of diagonal type. By substituting the braiding matrix with a higher-order tensor, we propose a method to generate additional Weyl groupoids. Furthermore, abelian cohomology theory provides support for the existence of a higher braiding linked to this tensor.

Pooled testing provides an efficient response to the massive testing requirements of the COVID-19 pandemic, though it may involve reduced sensitivity and higher implementation costs in certain contexts. Standard evaluations of this trade-off often rely on the assumption that pooled samples are independent and identically distributed. However, during the pandemic, these assumptions were frequently breached: testing within social networks (such as among roommates, spouses, or colleagues) involves correlated individuals, and infection risks varied significantly across time, location, and people. Ignoring these dependencies and heterogeneities can skew established optimality grids and lead to sub-optimal deployment of the method. Drawing a lesson from this experience, this paper emphasizes the need to combine field sampling data with statistical modeling to optimize pooled testing effectively. Using real-world data, we demonstrate that (a) leveraging natural correlations (non-independence) among samples can yield substantial gains at minimal logistical cost, improving sensitivity and efficiency by up to 30% and 90% respectively; and (b) these improvements remain robust despite significant heterogeneity across pools (non-identical). Our findings complement and expand upon the empirical observations of Barak et al. (2021), who noted sensitivity levels exceeding expectations. Additionally, we offer an interactive tool to determine the optimal pool size based on contextual information.

This study examines the challenge of differentiating functions with bounded second derivatives amidst bounded measurement noise, addressing both continuous-time and sampled-data contexts. It establishes fundamental performance limits for causal differentiators regarding the minimum achievable worst-case differentiation error. A robust exact differentiator is subsequently developed by adapting a single parameter within a linear differentiator. This approach yields a differentiator that surpasses existing continuous-time methods by combining noise robustness with instantaneous convergence to the exact derivative when noise is absent, while also reaching the optimal upper bound on differentiation error under noisy conditions. For sampled-data applications, the notion of "quasi-exactness" is defined to categorize differentiators attaining the lowest possible worst-case error from sampled data in noise-free scenarios. A direct sample-based implementation of the proposed linear adaptive continuous-time differentiator is demonstrated to achieve quasi-exactness within a single sampling step and a theoretically optimal error bound that converges to the continuous-time optimum as the sampling interval diminishes. Numerical simulations are provided to validate these theoretical findings.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of two neural networks—the generator and the discriminator—that are trained together to produce artificial data, like images, from random noise. Recently, the realism of GAN-generated images has advanced to the point where both humans and machines frequently confuse them with authentic examples. However, standard generators struggle to produce images conditioned on specific subcategories of a class. Recent solutions address this *conditional generation* by incorporating prior information, such as text descriptions or image segmentation, before training. Although effective, these methods require predefining subcategories and gathering extensive labeled datasets to train the GAN from scratch. This paper introduces a novel alternative that guides generic non-conditional GANs to function as conditional ones without retraining. Instead, we integrate an encoder network to create high-dimensional random vectors fed into the generator, enabling the creation of images from specific subcategories. Experimental results show that compared to training a conditional GAN from scratch, our guided approach produces images of comparable quality to those from non-conditional GANs after training the encoder on only a few hundred images. This significantly accelerates the process and allows for the seamless addition of new subcategories.

Although recognition-level image understanding has seen significant progress, achieving reliable visual scene understanding necessitates a comprehensive approach that integrates both recognition and cognition levels. This requires leveraging multi-source information, mastering varying degrees of understanding, and incorporating extensive commonsense knowledge. To address this, we introduce the Cognitive Attention Network (CAN), a novel framework designed for visual commonsense reasoning to enable interpretable visual understanding. Our method first employs an image-text fusion module to jointly integrate visual and textual data. Subsequently, a specialized inference module is developed to encode commonsense relationships within the image, query, and response. Extensive experiments conducted on the large-scale Visual Commonsense Reasoning (VCR) benchmark confirm the efficacy of our approach. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/tanjatang/CAN.

This study employs the configuration-operator approach to examine microscopic models of electronic subsystems featuring orbital degeneracy in energy states and non-diagonal electron interaction matrix elements (correlated hopping). Equations are derived for numerically calculating doublon concentration at arbitrary temperatures under integer band filling ($n=1$) across various model density of states distributions. Furthermore, energy spectra derived via the Green function method are analyzed, with particular focus on how correlated hopping influences the transition from itinerant to localized behavior in vanadium Magneli phases (V$_n$O$_{2n-1}$), transition-metal dichalcogenides (NiS$_{2-x}$Se$_x$), and fulleride (A$_n$C$_{60}$) systems.

We present an updated coupled-channel study of eta-meson production, incorporating all recent photoproduction data on the proton. The dip observed in the differential cross sections at center-of-mass energies of $W=1.68$ GeV is attributed to destructive interference between the $S_{11}(1535)$ and $S_{11}(1560)$ states. While the contribution from the $P_{11}(1710)$ resonance is relatively minor, it remains essential for accurately reproducing the shape of the differential cross section. For the $\pi^- N \to \eta N$ scattering process, we propose a reaction mechanism involving the $S_{11}(1535)$, $S_{11}(1560)$, and $P_{11}(1710)$ states. Our findings regarding the significance of these resonances in eta-production reactions align with our earlier conclusions. The analysis yields no strong evidence for a narrow state with a mass of 1680 MeV and a width of 15 MeV. Furthermore, the $\eta N$ scattering length is extracted and examined.

Following Brown[1], we utilize renormalisation group methods combined with dimensional regularisation to build composite operators for the six-dimensional scalar $\phi^3$ theory. We first rewrite bare scalar operators using renormalised composite operators of low dimension, then repeat the process for traceless tensor operators. Next, we express the bare energy-momentum tensor in terms of these renormalised composite operators, noting that some coefficients are divergent. By subtracting these divergences, we derive a manifestly finite energy-momentum tensor. Since the subtracted terms are transverse, this procedure preserves the conservation law of the energy-momentum tensor. The trace of this finite, improved tensor vanishes at the fixed point, signifying conformal invariance. Notably, while the trace is not generally RG-invariant (except at the fixed point), it can be rendered RG-invariant throughout by adding further transverse terms whose coefficients vanish at the fixed point.

We report the acquisition of the first complete solar disk images using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Band 7 (0.86 mm; 347 GHz). Despite a spatial resolution of 21", these observations yielded significant findings. During the observation period, the Sun lacked active regions, and the quiet Sun structures visible on the disk closely resembled those in Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) images at 1600 Å and 304 Å when smoothed to match ALMA's resolution. This similarity was previously noted for Band 6 (1.26 mm) and Band 3 (3 mm) data and also aligns with negative H$\alpha$ images of comparable resolution. However, polar coronal holes, clearly visible in the 304 Å band and small H$\alpha$ filaments, remain undetectable at 0.86 mm. We calculated the center-to-limb variation (CLV) of the brightness temperature ($T_b$) for Band 7, alongside Bands 6 and 3, which were observed during the same campaign, combining them into a unified $T_b(\log\mu_{100})$ curve where $\mu_{100}$ represents the heliocentric angle cosine scaled to 100 GHz. Assuming the absolute calibration of the Band 3 commissioning data is precise, we determined a central disk brightness temperature of 6085 K for Band 7, correcting a previous extrapolation of 5500 K based on Bands 3 and 6. Crucially, the $T_b(\log\mu_{100})$ curve flattens at high $\mu_{100}$ values, a trend mirrored by the corresponding $T_e(\log\tau_{100})$ at large $\tau_{100}$, likely signaling our approach to the temperature minimum.

We define a concept of weak solutions for abstract fractional differential equations, inspired by the formulation of the Caputo derivative. Furthermore, we establish existence theorems for both weak and strong solutions. Additionally, we present two illustrative examples applying our findings: time-fractional wave equations and time-fractional Petrovsky systems.

In blackbox optimization, assessing objective and constraint functions is computationally expensive. While constraint values can sometimes be evaluated independently or sequentially, this study introduces and contrasts two approaches for establishing a hierarchical constraint ordering and terminating the evaluation at a trial point if improvement over the current best solution is deemed impossible. The proposed methods are validated through numerical experiments using a closed-form test problem.

This study introduces a morpheme-based framework for Korean dependency parsing and integrates it into the Universal Dependencies (UD) standard. We provide the linguistic justification for adopting this morpheme-based approach and develop automated scripts to convert between the original UD format and the new format. The efficacy of this format is validated using both statistical and neural models, such as UDPipe and Stanza, alongside our specifically crafted morpheme-based word embeddings for Korean. Results demonstrate that morphUD surpasses existing parsing outcomes across all Korean UD treebanks, supported by comprehensive error analyses.

We introduce and experimentally investigate a technique for implementing frustrated lattice models within a Bose-Einstein condensate trapped in an optical square lattice. Introducing a minor lattice distortion generates an energy gap that divides the lowest band into two. In both bands, nearly flat energy-momentum dispersion occurs along the edges of the first Brillouin zone, while the excited band features a highly degenerate energy minimum. By populating the excited band with ultracold atoms, we construct a classically frustrated $XY$ model representing rotors on a square lattice subject to competing nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor tunneling couplings. Our optical lattice setup allows access to a regime characterized by a fully coherent Bose-Einstein condensate as well as a regime where frustration is anticipated. When adiabatically transitioning from the coherent condensate regime to the frustrated regime, the momentum spectra exhibit a total loss of coherence; however, slowly reverting to the condensate regime largely restores this coherence. The results demonstrate strong agreement with theoretical model calculations.

We present a straightforward yet powerful approach for determining the per-pixel quantum efficiency and temporal resolution of single-photon event cameras, specifically tailored for quantum imaging. By employing photon pairs created via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, this method extracts both individual pixel detection efficiency and system temporal resolution through coincidence measurements. Applying this technique to the TPX3CAM equipped with an appended image intensifier, we measured an average efficiency of 7.4% and a temporal resolution of 7.3 ns. Additionally, the method uncovers significant error mechanisms that may arise during post-processing. We anticipate that this technique, along with its underlying components, will prove valuable for characterizing other quantum imaging systems.

Using the light-cone QCD sum rule approach, we calculated the tensor form factors for the $N(1535) \rightarrow N$ transition by employing both isovector and isoscalar tensor currents. Our numerical analysis utilized the most comprehensive forms of the nucleon interpolating current and the tensor current, incorporating two distinct sets of input parameters for the distribution amplitudes (DAs) of the $N(1535)$ state. The results indicate that the tensor form factors for this transition are highly sensitive to the specific input parameters of the $N(1535)$ DAs. Furthermore, the $Q^2$ dependence of these form factors is accurately described by a p-pole fit function.

A common belief in deep learning is that the network's initial layers handle automatic feature engineering, thereby eliminating the need for data scientists to perform tedious manual feature engineering before training. However, in the context of deep learning for defect prediction, this assumption is incorrect. By preprocessing data using a novel oversampling method known as fuzzy sampling within the GHOST (Goal-oriented Hyper-parameter Optimization for Scalable Training) pipeline, we achieve significantly better performance than previous state-of-the-art deep learning approaches on 14 out of 20 defect datasets. Furthermore, our method produces these state-of-the-art results with much faster deep learning models. These findings provide a strong argument for employing oversampling techniques prior to applying deep learning to software defect prediction datasets.

Sampling equilibrium ensembles for dense polymer mixtures remains a fundamentally difficult challenge in computational physics, even when utilizing lattice-based models. In this work, we introduce a formalism grounded in interacting binary tensors that facilitates addressing this issue via quantum annealing hardware. Our method is broadly applicable because complex features like self-avoidance, branching, and looping can be defined through quadratic tensor interactions. Consequently, microstate configurations for various lattice polymer ensembles are generated by solving appropriate discrete energy-minimization tasks. By leveraging the unique advantages of quantum annealers, we successfully sampled polymer mixtures across a range of densities using the D-Wave quantum computer. This systematic framework provides a promising path for utilizing the rapid advancement of quantum computing to sample discrete models of filamentous soft-matter systems.

In our previous work, "On the Dirac-Frenkel Variational Principle on Tensor Banach Spaces," we offered a geometrical characterization of Tucker-format tensor manifolds with fixed multilinear ranks within tensor Banach spaces, enabling the extension of the Dirac-Frenkel variational principle to topological tensor spaces. This note aims to generalize those findings to broader tensor formats. Specifically, we present a novel geometrical description of tree-based (or hierarchical) format tensors, also referred to as tree tensor networks. These are defined as intersections of Tucker-format tensor manifolds corresponding to various partitions of the dimension set. Our proposed description for tree-based formats is fully compatible with the existing geometrical framework for Tucker-format manifolds.

In the concluding section of *Ontological Promiscuity*, Hobbs (1985) offered a profound insight: since semantics aims to define the relationship between language and reality, assuming a worldview that is isomorphic to our discourse renders semantics almost trivial. This paper seeks to address two critical questions: how we can adjust logical formalisms to achieve this trivialization, and what it means to presuppose a theory of the world within semantic frameworks. We propose that embedding a commonsense theory of the world into semantic formalisms will yield a logical semantics grounded in commonsense metaphysics. Furthermore, we argue that achieving this requires correcting a pivotal oversight in logical semantics: the failure to distinguish between two distinct categories of concepts. These are (i) ontological concepts, akin to Cocchiarella's (2001) first-intension concepts and representing types in a strongly-typed ontology, and (ii) logical concepts (or second-intension concepts), which function as predicates describing properties and relations among objects of various ontological types. Within our proposed framework, termed *ontologik*, we demonstrate how type unification and other operations can resolve the "missing text phenomenon" (MTP)—a central challenge in natural language semantics—by revealing the substantial volume of unstated background knowledge that is implicitly assumed in everyday communication.

Although the concept of a uniform interpolant for quantifier-free formulas from a formula with a specified list of symbols is established in logic, it has remained unfamiliar to the formal methods and automated reasoning communities. This paper precisely defines the concept and introduces two algorithms for computing quantifier-free uniform interpolants within the theory of equality over uninterpreted functions (EUF) given a list of symbols to eliminate. The first algorithm is non-deterministic and produces a uniform interpolant as a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, while the second algorithm yields a compact representation as a conjunction of Horn clauses. Both methods leverage efficient dedicated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) representations for terms. The authors provide correctness and completeness proofs by combining rewrite techniques with model theory arguments.

Current end-to-end speech-to-speech translation (S2ST) systems are typically assessed using text-based metrics, which necessitate automatic transcription of generated speech and create a reliance on the availability and quality of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. To eliminate this dependency, we introduce BLASER, a text-free evaluation metric for S2ST. BLASER utilizes a multilingual multimodal encoder to map source speech, translated output, and reference audio into a shared embedding space, calculating a translation quality score that serves as a proxy for human judgment. We built training and evaluation datasets comprising over 40,000 human annotations across seven language pairs to test this approach. Training BLASER with human rating supervision yielded the best results. At the sentence level, BLASER demonstrated a significantly stronger correlation with human judgments than ASR-dependent metrics—outperforming ASR-SENTBLEU in all directions and ASR-COMET in five. Our analysis indicates that incorporating text alongside speech inputs does not enhance correlation with human scores; instead, using speech alone achieves the highest correlation, validating our research objective. Furthermore, we found that relying on ASR for reference transcripts negatively impacts text-based metrics.

In an earlier study, we derived Cwikel-type estimates on noncommutative tori to establish analogues of the Cwikel-Lieb-Rozenblum (CLR) and Lieb-Thirring inequalities for the negative eigenvalues of fractional Schrödinger operators. The current paper examines "curved" noncommutative tori, where the standard Laplacian is replaced by Laplace-Beltrami operators corresponding to arbitrary Riemannian metrics. We extend the Cwikel-type estimates from our prior work to pseudodifferential operators and powers of these Laplace-Beltrami operators. These extensions yield several applications. First, we derive $L_p$-versions of the standard trace formula for pseudodifferential operators (ΨDOs) on noncommutative tori, specifically for combinations of ΨDOs with $L_p$-position operators. Second, we obtain $L_p$-versions of the noncommutative tori analogues of Connes' trace theorem and integration formula, providing expressions for NC integrals (or Dixmier traces) of products involving $L_p$-position operators, ΨDOs, or powers of Laplace-Beltrami operators. Furthermore, by integrating our Cwikel-type estimates with appropriate variants of the Birman-Schwinger principle, we establish CLR and Lieb-Thirring inequalities for the negative eigenvalues of fractional Schrödinger operators linked to powers of Laplace-Beltrami operators and $L_p$-potentials. Consistent with the original Euclidean context, these Lieb-Thirring inequalities imply a dual Sobolev inequality for orthonormal families. Finally, we address spectral asymptotics and semiclassical Weyl laws for these operator classes on curved noncommutative tori, thereby resolving a conjecture proposed in our previous paper.

This study extends the Luttinger-Tisza-Lyons-Kaplan (LTLK) framework, originally describing classical ground states of Heisenberg-coupled Bravais lattices, to encompass non-Bravais structures. The method involves incorporating specific Lagrange multipliers into the diagonal of the Fourier-transformed coupling matrix, a strategy consistent with previously published general ground state analyses. We demonstrate this approach using a modified honeycomb lattice, which exhibits exclusive three-dimensional ground states and a classical spin-liquid phase depending on two coupling constants. Furthermore, an application to a modified square lattice confirms that the method can also yield incommensurable ground states.

As the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) advances into the 6G era, it aims to achieve super-high data rates, seamless coverage, and ubiquitous AI-driven intelligence. Transfer Learning (TL) holds significant promise for enhancing 6G-enabled IoV applications, such as smart driving, by improving data quality and quantity, accelerating learning, and lowering computational requirements. While TL is already common in wireless fields like spectrum management, its reliability and security within 6G-enabled IoV remain underexplored. A key concern is that malicious vehicles in source domains could propagate untrustworthy models regarding connection availability to target domains, degrading learning performance. Consequently, it is crucial to both select and incentivize trustworthy vehicles for TL participation. This article begins by outlining the integration of TL with 6G-enabled IoV and detailing its specific applications. It then proposes a secure and reliable TL framework that uses reputation metrics to assess pre-trained model reliability and leverages consortium blockchain for efficient, decentralized reputation management. Additionally, a deep learning-based auction mechanism is designed to create a TL model market that motivates high-reputation vehicles to share models. Simulation results confirm that the proposed framework ensures security and reliability while offering well-designed incentives for TL in 6G-enabled IoV.

This study introduces a new, platform-independent risk-aware path planning framework built upon the classical $D^*$ lite algorithm, prioritizing both safety and efficiency. The planner constructs a grid map where occupied, free, and unknown areas are assigned distinct traversal costs; specifically, a penalty cost is applied to unknown voxels adjacent to occupied ones. The implementation further incorporates a dynamic grid map capable of updating and expanding during robotic operations, thereby enhancing mission safety and making the system ideal for exploration and search-and-rescue tasks. On this grid, the $D^*$ lite algorithm generates the safest possible path with minimal traversal cost. The proposed framework supports both 2D and 3D path generation for ground and aerial robots, respectively; in the 3D scenario, a grid with a single voxel height is used to plan 2D paths, which serves as the primary distinction between the two approaches. The effectiveness of this novel scheme is thoroughly validated through extensive simulations and real-world field tests involving both a quadcopter and the Boston Dynamics Spot legged robot.

We report a combined study of the galaxy S04590 at a redshift of $z=8.496$, utilizing Early Release Observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) via NIRSpec, NIRCam, and NIRISS, alongside dedicated Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) detections of the far-infrared [CII] $158\mu$m emission line. By modeling the spectral energy distribution (SED) and analyzing redshifted optical nebular emission lines captured by JWST/NIRSpec, we derived the galaxy's physical characteristics. The best-fitting SED indicates a low-mass system ($M_\star = 10^{7.2}-10^{8}\,M_{\odot}$) with a low oxygen abundance of $12+\log{\rm (O/H)} = 7.16^{+0.10}_{-0.12}$, inferred from strong nebular and auroral lines. Assuming [CII] reliably traces the interstellar medium (ISM), we estimate the total gas mass at $M_{\rm gas} = (8.0\pm 4.0)\times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$, derived from the [CII] luminosity and spatial distribution. This results in an unusually high gas fraction, $f_{\rm gas} = M_{\rm gas}/(M_{\rm gas} + M_\star) \gtrsim 90\%$, which remains consistent with expectations for its low metallicity. Additionally, we calculated the galaxy's metal mass using the gas mass and gas-phase metallicity, finding it aligns with metal production from Type II supernovae. Furthermore, we provide the first constraints on dust-to-gas (DTG) and dust-to-metals (DTM) ratios for galaxies during the reionization epoch ($z\gtrsim 6$), revealing low mass ratios of logDGT $<-3.8$ and logDTM $<-0.5$, yet consistent with local scaling relations and specifically the metal-poor galaxy I Zwicky 18. Our findings underscore the complementary power of ALMA and JWST in characterizing the stellar, gas, and metal content of the earliest galaxies.

Biological functions are facilitated by specialized entities known as motor proteins or molecular motors, which move cellular cargo along linear protein tracks with the ability to bind and unbind reversibly. Motivated by these findings, we constructed a theoretical framework describing the collective behavior of biological molecular motors, incorporating local binding and unbinding events. In this model, particles move along a lattice in a preferred direction, interacting solely through exclusion, while reversible binding occurs at a specific site distant from the boundaries. Treating this binding/unbinding location as a local defect, the inhomogeneous system is modeled as two coupled homogeneous sub-lattices, enabling a complete characterization of the system's stationary dynamics. Results indicate that the quantity and characteristics of steady-state phases are highly sensitive to association and dissociation transition rates. We provide microscopic explanations for these findings along with their biological relevance. Furthermore, our theoretical predictions align closely with extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

Verifying and validating automated driving systems presents significant challenges. Current research and industry efforts focus on scenario-based approaches to reduce testing burdens by defining safety-critical situations. To effectively specify these scenarios within complex real-world design contexts, a structured environmental description is essential. The PEGASUS research project introduced the 6-Layer Model (6LM) for characterizing highway scenarios. This paper refines the 6LM and extends its scope to urban traffic and environments. As defined in PEGASUS, the 6LM offers a framework for categorizing the environment, serving as a structured foundation for subsequent scenario definitions. The model allows for the systematic description and classification of the general environment without embedding specific actor knowledge or anticipating their functions. Furthermore, this paper details various additional applications of the 6LM. The model encompasses descriptions of the road network, traffic guidance elements, roadside structures, temporary modifications, dynamic objects, environmental conditions, and digital information. This work specifies each layer by categorizing its constituent items and establishes guidelines with explanatory examples to standardize the model's application for objective environmental descriptions. Unlike prior publications, the model and its design are presented with considerably greater detail. Finally, the comprehensive overview of the 6LM includes considerations for future work, particularly regarding the expansion of the concept to machine perception.

An exact solution to the Lindblad equation, featuring a quadratic Hamiltonian and linear coupling operators, was originally established using the chord representation, defined as the Fourier transform of the Wigner function. This approach has been extended to multiple components to yield an explicit formula for the reduced density operator of any individual component, alongside moments represented as derivatives of the evolving chord function. Consequently, the Wigner function emerges as the convolution of its direct classical evolution with a broadening multidimensional Gaussian window, which ultimately secures its positivity. Furthermore, the Glauber-Sundarshan P-function also maintains positivity, thereby ensuring the separability of the components. Within the multicomponent framework, a comprehensive dissipation matrix is introduced; its trace, corresponding to twice the previously identified dissipation coefficient, dictates the contraction rate of the phase space volume associated with the Wigner function's argument, while the volume of the chord function expands. The discussion includes examples of Markovian evolution involving a triatomic molecule and an array of harmonic oscillators.

Let $K$ denote the connected sum of knots $K_1, \ldots, K_n$. Since the connected sum allows for bending, the $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$-character variety associated with the exterior of $K$ contains a component of dimension at least 2. We demonstrate a natural method for defining the adjoint Reidemeister torsion on such high-dimensional components and establish that this torsion remains locally constant on subsets of the character variety where the meridian trace is fixed. Furthermore, we prove that if each individual knot $K_i$ satisfies the vanishing identity, then the adjoint Reidemeister torsion of the resulting knot $K$ also satisfies this identity.

Although entanglement serves as a universal resource for quantum networks, entangled photon sources are usually custom-built for specific applications. Achieving versatility through state modulation and tunable temporal properties is essential for flexible network architectures and cryptographic primitives extending beyond quantum key distribution. This study presents a flexible source design capable of generating high-quality entanglement in both continuous-wave and GHz-rate-pulsed modes. By employing readily available optical components, our method utilizes a fiber-based Sagnac loop to produce polarization-entangled photons at telecom wavelengths with high efficiency and fidelities exceeding 0.99. Additionally, phase modulation up to GHz frequencies prior to state generation enables rapid switching of entangled states; we demonstrate 100 MHz phase modulation with an average fidelity of 0.95. Finally, the source's 60 nm spectral bandwidth is fully compatible with reconfigurable, wavelength-multiplexed quantum networks.

This study investigates the phase transitions of RN-AdS black holes at their Davies points using a generalized Ehrenfest classification based on fractional derivatives. Davies points signify locations where heat capacity diverges; under the conventional Ehrenfest framework, these locations mark second-order phase transitions. For RN-AdS black holes, Davies points fall into two categories: the first corresponds to temperature extrema, while the second corresponds to the inflection point (critical point) of the temperature curve. Applying the generalized classification reveals that the transition orders for these two types differ. Specifically, the first type exhibits a $3/2$-order transition, whereas the second type displays a $4/3$-order transition. Consequently, this refined classification distinguishes between phase transitions that would otherwise be grouped together, potentially offering new insights into black hole thermodynamics.

This paper examines the two-dimensional surface quasi-geostrophic equation featuring fractional horizontal dissipation and vertical thermal diffusion, a formulation that generalizes the classical model. We establish the local existence and uniqueness of solutions within the Sobolev space $H^{2-2\alpha}(\mathbb{R}^2)\cap H^{2-2\beta}(\mathbb{R}^2)$, which corresponds to the critical space in the classical context. Additionally, we prove that the solution remains global for sufficiently small initial data. Lastly, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of this global solution as it approaches infinity.

We introduce a molecular simulation technique capable of identifying multiple transition pathways along with their corresponding free-energy profiles simultaneously. This approach, termed multiPMD, builds upon path-metadynamics (PMD) by incorporating multiple paths and repulsive walkers. We demonstrate the application of multiPMD to two C7eq-to-C7ax transitions in Ace-Ala-Nme and six PPII-to-PPII transitions in Ace-(Pro)4-Nme. Furthermore, we describe a method for generating an interpretable "PathMap" that visualizes free-energy ridges separating distinct paths, as well as the branching and merging of these transition channels. Given its flexibility and potential, multiPMD is a highly promising tool for analyzing biomolecular systems—such as proteins and nucleic acids—that feature competing or controversial transition pathways.

Personalized gamification leverages insights about users to customize designs, moving beyond the limitations of a one-size-fits-all approach. This customization must account for both user and contextual factors—such as specific activities and geographic locations—creating multiple opportunities for adaptation and necessitating automated tools. However, critical questions remain regarding which characteristics are most relevant and how to effectively apply this tailoring, alongside a shortage of existing automation solutions. To address these challenges, we employed a two-step approach. Initially, we conducted an exploratory survey to gather participant feedback on the most beneficial game elements across various learning activity types (LAT). Subsequently, we utilized conditional decision trees to model these opinions, thereby formalizing the tailoring process. In the second phase, we developed a recommender system as an output of this research to automate the suggestion of personalized gamification designs. Our findings provide empirical evidence that preferences are influenced by LAT, geographic location, and other user traits; enable the simultaneous creation of designs tailored to both user and contextual features; and offer technological support for designing personalized gamification. Key implications include the necessity of considering demographics, game attributes, geography, LAT, and the interplay between user and contextual data when defining gamification strategies, while our recommender system offers a means to enhance the personalization of these designs.

Amid the proliferation of 5G technology, the escalating need for high data rates has prompted researchers to propose hybrid satellite-terrestrial (HST) networks as an alternative to traditional terrestrial cellular systems. Although HST networks are susceptible to a masking effect, this challenge can be addressed through terrestrial relaying strategies. Consequently, this study investigates wireless multicasting within a hybrid satellite-terrestrial relaying network (HSTRN), where a satellite transmits data to multiple terrestrial nodes via several relays while facing interception attempts from multiple eavesdroppers. The primary objective is to safeguard multicast transmissions by leveraging opportunistic relaying techniques. The model assumes that satellite links experience Shadowed Rician fading, whereas terrestrial links are subject to alpha-mu fading. To evaluate the system's security, we derive closed-form expressions for the probability of non-zero secrecy multicast capacity, ergodic secrecy multicast capacity, and secure outage probability. Utilizing these analytical results, we examine how perfect secrecy can be maintained under adverse channel conditions and explore the trade-offs involving the number of relays, multicast users, and eavesdroppers. Finally, Monte-Carlo simulations are employed to validate the numerical findings.

Although small-scale turbulence is inferred within planets and stars, these natural dynamos successfully produce global-scale magnetic fields, a phenomenon classified as large-scale dynamo action. Typically driven by convection and modulated by rotation, previous numerical investigations into rotating dynamos have often observed that increased flow turbulence weakens the large-scale magnetic field, leaving the physical mechanisms required to sustain such dynamos a subject of debate. This study utilizes a series of numerical simulations to demonstrate that robust large-scale magnetic fields can emerge in rotating convective turbulence if two specific criteria are met: the flow must remain rotationally constrained, and magnetic diffusion must play a significant role at the small convective scale. These results align with earlier asymptotic predictions and indicate that natural dynamos may indeed fulfill these two conditions.
This paper presents a mathematical framework known as the Euclidean Universe, which serves as a foundational basis for Non-Archimedean Mathematics, with specific applications in Nonstandard Analysis.

For a graph $G$, a \textit{$k$-total difference labeling} refers to a total labeling $f$ that assigns values from the set $\{1, 2, \cdots, k\}$ to both edges and vertices, such that for every edge $\{u,v\}$, the condition $f(\{u,v\}) = |f(u) - f(v)|$ holds. The total difference chromatic number, denoted as $\chi_{td}(G)$, represents the smallest integer $k$ for which a $k$-total difference labeling exists where no two adjacent labels are identical. This work expands upon previous research in total difference labeling by establishing a tighter upper bound for $\chi_{td}(K_n)$ and by deriving findings related to infinite regular graphs.

Biomedical research prioritizes efficient, non-invasive methods for delivering cargo to biological cells due to their significant potential in targeted drug therapy. Consequently, considerable effort is dedicated to investigating biocompatible nano-materials that can facilitate this process while maintaining proper self-sealing of the cell membrane. In this study, we employed steered molecular dynamics (SMD) to analyze the effects of indenting and withdrawing a nanospear on a phospholipid membrane. Our findings indicate that the withdrawal phase is directly influenced by the nanocone's initial position; specifically, both the average force and work required are substantially higher when withdrawal begins from a greater depth. This increased resistance is attributed to enhanced hydrophobic interactions between the nanocone and the lipid tails. Additionally, indentations initiated at shallower depths resulted in the removal of several times fewer lipids compared to deeper insertions. Given that selecting the least invasive approach for nanostructure-assisted delivery is critical for medical applications, these results offer valuable insights for achieving efficient and safe drug delivery using nanomaterials.

Graph drawing beyond planarity concerns creating visually effective representations for non-planar graphs defined by specific forbidden edge patterns. A primary metric for evaluating drawing quality is the count of edge crossings. This leads to the inquiry of whether such beyond-planar drawings inherently possess a substantially higher crossing number compared to unrestricted drawings. Chimani et al. [GD'19] established bounds for the ratio between the crossing numbers of three specific classes of beyond-planar graphs and their unrestricted counterparts. The current work generalizes these findings to the primary known classes of beyond-planar graphs characterized by forbidden edge configurations and addresses several unresolved questions posed by the authors.

The decoding algorithm stands as a vital element of an effective language generation pipeline, yet the guiding principles for selecting the appropriate algorithm remain ambiguous. Existing research often evaluates decoding methods within limited contexts, resulting in findings that lack generalizability across different tasks. To address this, we propose a taxonomy that categorizes decoding strategies according to their underlying assumptions regarding the alignment between a model's likelihood and task-specific utility. We contend that this framework offers a comprehensive perspective on the decoding challenge and facilitates generalizable insights by focusing on the relationship between decoding algorithms and likelihood-utility misalignment. Specifically, by examining the correlation between prediction likelihood and utility across a wide range of tasks, we present the first empirical validation of this taxonomy and establish a set of principles to guide algorithm selection. Importantly, our analysis is the inaugural study to connect likelihood-based decoding approaches with methods utilizing external information, such as value-guided techniques and prompting, while encompassing the most diverse array of tasks to date.

Gravitational-wave astronomy involving compact binaries depends on theoretical models predicting the signals emitted during coalescence. These models must not only be precise but also computationally efficient to facilitate the near real-time comparison of millions of signals against detector data. While various regression and interpolation techniques have been utilized to construct efficient waveform models, a systematic comparison of their performance has not yet been conducted. This study addresses that gap by evaluating multiple methods—including polynomial fits, radial basis functions, Gaussian process regression, and artificial neural networks—specifically for gravitational waveform modeling. We apply these techniques to regress analytical models of both non-precessing and precessing binary black hole waveforms, assessing both accuracy and computational speed. Our findings indicate that while most regression methods achieve reasonable accuracy, efficiency considerations often favor the simplest approach. Consequently, sophisticated regression methods are not strictly necessary for standard gravitational-wave modeling applications, although more complex problems may better suit machine-learning techniques, which could also offer additional benefits.

This study examines discrete random walks restricted to the quarter plane, featuring jumps limited to directions $(i,j)$ where $i+j \geq 0$ and small negative steps ($i,j \geq -1$). Known as singular walks, these models have recently been analyzed extensively through combinatorial lenses. We demonstrate the application of the compensation method, originally proposed by Adan, Wessels, and Zijm in the 1990s, to determine positive harmonic functions subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. Specifically, for walks exhibiting drift with positive coordinates, we establish an explicit formula for the escape probability—the likelihood of diverging to infinity without touching the boundary axes. These expressions frequently incorporate well-known recurrent sequences, including the Fibonacci numbers. Subsequently, we offer a probabilistic interpretation of the derived harmonic functions and prove their sufficiency for calculating all positive harmonic functions associated with these singular walks. This is achieved by deriving the asymptotic behavior of Green functions across all directions in the quarter plane and applying Martin boundary theory.

The weight matrix (WM) serves as the program for a neural network (NN). While traditional NNs typically learn their programs via gradient descent on an error function and then remain static, the WM of a self-referential NN can rapidly modify itself during execution. This capability enables recursive self-improvement, allowing the network to meta-learn, meta-meta-learn, and so forth. Although architectures capable of this behavior have been theorized since the 1990s, practical research has been scarce. This work revisits these concepts by leveraging recent advances in fast weight programmers and related linear Transformers. We introduce a scalable self-referential WM (SRWM) that learns to adjust itself using outer products and the delta update rule. We evaluate the SRWM on supervised few-shot learning and multi-task reinforcement learning within procedurally generated game environments. Our results demonstrate both practical utility and competitive performance for this approach, and our code is publicly available.

Statistical challenges in causal inference often revolve around probability distributions distinct from the one generating the observed data, with the target of interest frequently being a marginal quantity within that alternative distribution. This discrepancy introduces significant practical hurdles for statistical inference, even in scenarios where the problem is non-parametrically identified. Specifically, conducting likelihood-based inference or simulating from the model in a general manner becomes particularly difficult. To address this, we propose the "frugal parameterization," which centers the model on the causal effect of interest and constructs the remainder of the model around it. This approach offers a systematic method for creating a regular, non-redundant parameterization based on relevant causal quantities. For discrete variables, odds ratios serve to complete the parameterization, whereas copulas are the natural solution for continuous cases; additional alternatives are also explored. Our methodology enables the construction and simulation of models with parametrically defined causal distributions and allows for fitting these models using likelihood-based techniques, including fully Bayesian frameworks. The proposed parameterizations cover the average causal effect, the effect of treatment on the treated, and other pertinent causal metrics.

High-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy was performed to investigate the electronic structure and superconducting gap in the superconductors K$_{0.68}$Fe$_{1.79}$Se$_{2}$ (T$_c$=32 K) and (Tl$_{0.45}$K$_{0.34}$)Fe$_{1.84}$Se$_{2}$ (T$_c$=28 K). Beyond the electron-like Fermi surface located near the M($\pi$,$\pi$) point, two additional electron-like Fermi pockets were identified around the zone center $\Gamma$(0,0) in K$_{0.68}$Fe$_{1.79}$Se$_{2}$. This finding aligns the Fermi surface topology of K$_{0.68}$Fe$_{1.79}$Se$_{2}$ with that of (Tl,Rb)$_x$Fe$_{2-y}$Se$_{2}$ and (Tl,K)$_x$Fe$_{2-y}$Se$_{2}$ compounds. Furthermore, a nearly isotropic superconducting gap ($\Delta$) was detected along the electron-like Fermi pocket near the M point in both K$_{0.68}$Fe$_{1.79}$Se$_{2}$ ($\Delta\sim$ 9 meV) and (Tl$_{0.45}$K$_{0.34}$)Fe$_{1.84}$Se$_{2}$ ($\Delta\sim$ 8 meV). Establishing a universal framework for the Fermi surface topology and superconducting gap within the A$_x$Fe$_{2-y}$Se$_{2}$ (A=K, Tl, Cs, Rb, etc.) family of superconductors will offer crucial insights into the mechanism of superconductivity in iron-based materials.

MIMO technology facilitates spatial multiple access and enhances system spectral efficiency (SE), yet it introduces drawbacks, particularly the high complexity associated with numerous RF chains. A viable solution involves utilizing reconfigurable antennas (RAs), which can generate diverse radiation patterns to achieve comparable performance with a reduced number of RF chains. Consequently, the system focuses on maximizing SE through optimal beamforming design and RA mode selection. Addressing the non-convex nature of this challenge, we introduce machine learning-based approaches for RA mode selection in both static and dynamic contexts. In static scenarios, we resolve the integer optimization problem inherent to RA mode selection using deep convolutional neural networks (DCNN). For dynamic state selection, we employ a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) framework incorporating offline and online training, which lowers the computational complexity of the optimization problem. Finally, the proposed methods for both scenarios are evaluated against exhaustive search and random selection techniques.

We analyze the deceleration observed in the stochastic dynamics of a ring-exchange model on a square lattice using numerical simulations. Our findings reveal that coarse-grained memory of initial density-wave states persists for surprisingly extended periods. This observation contradicts predictions derived from a low-frequency continuum theory based on mean-field solutions. By examining correlation functions within dynamically active regions, we demonstrate an unconventional transient formation of long-range structure in a direction that was initially featureless, and we argue that the slow melting of this structure is pivotal to the slowing-down mechanism. We anticipate that these results will also apply to the dynamics of quantum ring-exchange processes involving hard-core bosons.

Stock 2 is an open cluster with limited prior study that exhibits an extended main-sequence turnoff (eMSTO). To investigate this feature and characterize the cluster, we conducted high-resolution spectroscopy as part of the Stellar Population Astrophysics (SPA) project. Observations were carried out using the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher in North hemisphere (HARPS-N) spectrograph at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo (TNG), supplemented by additional spectra from the Catania Astrophysical Observatory Spectrograph (CAOS). In total, 46 stars (including dwarfs and giants) were observed, constituting the largest sample gathered for Stock 2 to date. We present stellar parameters, extinction values, radial and projected rotational velocities for the majority of these stars, along with derived chemical abundances for 21 species (atomic numbers up to 56). Our analysis reveals differential reddening within the cluster field, with an average value of 0.27 mag; this appears to be the primary cause of the observed eMSTO, as alternative explanations involving differential rotation, common in other clusters, are ruled out. We estimate the cluster's age at 450$\pm$150 Ma, corresponding to a main-sequence turnoff mass of approximately 2.8 M$_{\odot}$. The mean radial velocity of the cluster is roughly 8.0 km s$^{-1}$. The cluster displays solar-like metallicity, with [Fe/H] = -0.07$\pm$0.06, consistent with its distance from the Galactic center. Chemical abundances in main-sequence stars and giants are consistent within error margins, except for Barium and Strontium, which are significantly overabundant in giants, and Cobalt, which shows marginal overabundance. Ultimately, Stock 2's chemical composition aligns fully with that of other open clusters in the Galactic thin disc.

The LIGO-Virgo collaboration has recently achieved direct detection of intermediate-frequency gravitational waves (ranging from dozens to hundreds of Hertz) using laser interferometers to measure their mechanically induced tidal effects. In contrast, this letter introduces a viable method for actively detecting high-frequency gravitational waves by observing their electromagnetic responses within a high alternating magnetic field. Unlike the original Gertsenshtein-Zeldovich setup, where electromagnetic responses scale with the square of the gravitational wave amplitudes and remain too faint for experimental observation, the responses in this proposed configuration are linearly proportional to the amplitudes, making them detectable with existing weak-light detection technologies. Furthermore, because the wave impedance of the gravitational wave-induced electromagnetic signals differs significantly from that of standard electromagnetic radiation in flat spacetime (approximately 377 Ω), wave-matching techniques can effectively suppress strong background noise lacking gravitational wave information. Since the frequency of the applied alternating magnetic field can be easily tuned, this configuration offers the potential to actively search for gravitational waves across a broad frequency spectrum (e.g., $10^7$ to $10^{12}$ Hz), provided that the required cavity dimensions and magnetic field sweeping frequencies are experimentally feasible.

Utilizing a dataset of $pp$ collisions with an integrated luminosity of 3.0~fb$^{-1}$ recorded by the LHCb detector, we report the inaugural search for the strangeness-changing weak decay $\Xi_b^-\to\Lambda_b^0\pi^-$. This specific $b$-hadron decay mode has not previously been observed. A signal is identified with a statistical significance of 3.2 standard deviations. The measured relative rate is given by
${{f_{\Xi_b^-}}\over{f_{\Lambda_b^0}}}{\cal{B}}(\Xi_b^-\to\Lambda_b^0\pi^-) =
(5.7\pm1.8^{+0.8}_{-0.9})\times10^{-4}$, where $f_{\Xi_b^-}$ and $f_{\Lambda_b^0}$ represent the fragmentation fractions for $b\to\Xi_b^-$ and $b\to\Lambda_b^0$, respectively, and ${\cal{B}}(\Xi_b^-\to\Lambda_b^0\pi^-)$ denotes the branching fraction. Under the assumption that the ratio $f_{\Xi_b^-}/f_{\Lambda_b^0}$ falls between 0.1 and 0.3, the branching fraction ${\cal{B}}(\Xi_b^-\to\Lambda_b^0\pi^-)$ is estimated to lie within the interval of $(0.57\pm0.21)\%$ to $(0.19\pm0.07)\%$.

During the Kepler mission's survey phase, thousands of stars were monitored in short cadence, revealing solar-like oscillations in over 500 main-sequence and sub-giant stars. Subsequently, the Kepler Science Office identified a calibration issue affecting half of this short-cadence data, necessitating a new data release (DR25) with enhanced corrections. We re-examined one month of survey-phase time series to identify additional solar-like oscillations. Our analysis of 99 stars, including 46 with newly reported oscillations, increased the known sample of stars with asteroseismic analysis of short-cadence data by approximately 8%. Using seismic scaling relations, we calculated masses and radii, finding that this new sample consists primarily of massive stars (between 1.2 and 2 solar masses) in the subgiant phase. We also determined granulation parameters and mode amplitudes, which align with established scaling relations. Compared to previously detected main-sequence and subgiant stars, the stars in our study are slightly fainter. Additionally, we investigated surface rotation and magnetic activity; our sample exhibits activity levels similar to the previously known group and comparable to the Sun's range between activity cycle minimum and maximum. For seven stars, we suggest that stellar blends may have previously prevented detection. When comparing radii derived from scaling relations to those from Gaia, we found that Gaia radii are overestimated by an average of 4.4% relative to seismic radii, showing a decreasing trend as the evolutionary stage progresses. Finally, we re-analyzed the DR25 data for main-sequence and sub-giant stars with previously detected solar-like oscillations, providing global seismic parameters for a total of 526 stars.

Natural biological systems have undergone millions of years of evolution to adapt and survive, offering numerous features that can inspire solutions for modern industrial challenges. This inspiration gives rise to a design methodology known as bio-inspired design (BID). While BID has proven effective, a persistent gap between biological and engineering domains often prevents designers from applying it efficiently. To address this, we investigate the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to create a computational bridge between these fields. This paper introduces a generative design framework utilizing pre-trained language models (PLMs) to automatically retrieve biological analogies and generate BID concepts expressed in natural language. We employ the latest generative pre-trained transformer, GPT-3, as the foundational PLM. Three distinct design concept generators were identified and fine-tuned based on the granularity of the problem space representation. Additionally, machine evaluators were fine-tuned to assess the relevance between biological and engineering domains within the generated concepts. The methodology was validated through a case study involving the generation and evaluation of nature-inspired, lightweight flying car concepts. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully produces high-performance BID concepts.

Green hydrogen offers a pathway to decarbonize hard-to-electrify sectors like heavy transport and industry, though its broader impacts on the power grid remain unclear. This study employs an open-source electricity model to examine power sector interactions for three distinct green hydrogen supply chains in Germany by 2030. The analysis compares scenarios where Germany operates as an isolated grid versus an interconnected one, and explores outcomes with and without specific renewable energy capacity limits. Aimed at guiding both modelers and policymakers, the results indicate that large-scale hydrogen storage provides significant grid flexibility, especially in high-renewable environments lacking geographical balancing options. Furthermore, the study finds that green hydrogen's impact on the optimal generation mix is highly sensitive to assumptions about capacity expansion potential. Finally, the analysis highlights a potential distributional impact where green hydrogen production may disadvantage other electricity consumers, a factor policymakers must consider.

Image captioning integrates computer vision and natural language processing to create descriptive narratives for visual content. This dual task demands both precise image comprehension and accurate linguistic analysis, encompassing both syntax and semantics. The rapid expansion of knowledge in this domain makes it challenging to stay current with the latest research. While existing review papers often lack sufficient coverage of these advancements, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of current techniques, datasets, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics. Contemporary research predominantly relies on deep learning, with attention mechanisms, deep reinforcement learning, and adversarial learning leading the field. We examine recent methodologies including UpDown, OSCAR, VIVO, Meta Learning, and a model utilizing conditional generative adversarial networks. Although the GAN-based approach yields the highest scores, UpDown offers a foundational framework for image captioning, while OSCAR and VIVO are particularly valuable for their novel object captioning capabilities. Ultimately, this review serves as a guide for researchers to remain informed about the latest contributions in image caption generation.

For decades, astronomical transients resulting from stellar cataclysms have been modeled as either point-source explosions or central jet engines within spherically symmetric stars. Yet, both observations and theory suggest that many stars possess a slightly flattened, oblate spheroid geometry rather than perfect spherical symmetry. This study introduces axisymmetric two-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations examining the dynamics of point-like explosions originating at the core of massive, aspherical stars with varying degrees of oblateness. We designate these exploding aspherical stars as "ellipsars," a term derived from the elliptical iso-density contours of their progenitors in the two-dimensional axisymmetric framework. Our findings indicate that ellipsars can accelerate expanding rings of relativistic ejecta, potentially giving rise to various astronomical transients, such as low-luminosity gamma-ray bursts, relativistic supernovae, and Fast Blue Optical Transients (FBOTs).

How can image quality from various sub-micrometer (sub$\mu$) CT scans be evaluated and compared? This study utilizes a simple test phantom composed of polymer microbeads to capture projection images and conduct 13 CT scans across multiple commercial and non-commercial scanners. Based on the acquired CT images, signal and noise power spectra are modeled to estimate 3D volume signal-to-noise ratios (3D SNR spectra). Additionally, a time- and shape-independent modulation transfer function (MTF) is calculated for each scan using the same images, accounting for phase contrast and image blur ($\mathrm{MTF_{blur}}$). These 3D SNR spectra and MTF values are then compared against 2D SNR spectra derived from the projection images. Unlike 2D SNR, volume SNR can be normalized relative to the object's power spectrum to produce detection effectiveness (DE), a novel metric that highlights how both technical variations and operator decisions significantly impact scan quality for a fixed measurement duration. Using DE, researchers can assess and compare both source-based and detector-based sub$\mu$ CT scanners. However, future implementation of this approach necessitates a specific scan acquisition protocol capable of measuring 3D signal-to-noise ratios, which would render the current model fit for 3D noise power spectra unnecessary.

Discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) is a prevalent computational technique for investigating mesoscale plasticity by linking dislocation line movements to the macroscopic behavior of crystalline materials. Nevertheless, the high computational expense of DDD simulations constrains their practical application. This work presents a novel DDD-GNN framework where the costly time-integration of dislocation motion is fully replaced by a graph neural network (GNN) trained on existing DDD trajectories. As an initial demonstration, we validate the method's viability and potential using a representative model of a dislocation line moving through a forest of obstacles. Results indicate that the DDD-GNN approach is stable and accurately replicates unseen ground-truth DDD responses across various straining rates and obstacle densities, eliminating the necessity for explicit calculation of nodal forces or dislocation mobilities during time-stepping. This strategy establishes promising new pathways for accelerating DDD simulations and integrating more sophisticated dislocation dynamics.

Community Question Answering (CQA) is a well-established task applicable across various scenarios, including e-commerce and specialized online interest groups. Within these communities, users engage by posting articles, providing comments, and posing or resolving questions. These interactions create heterogeneous information sources, each possessing unique structures and contexts, such as comments linked to articles or answers associated with specific questions. While most existing CQA approaches rely primarily on articles or Wikipedia to extract knowledge, they often fail to fully leverage the diverse range of information available within the community. By incorporating these Multiple Information Sources (MIS), users can access more relevant knowledge. Consequently, we introduce a question-aware heterogeneous graph transformer designed to integrate MIS from user communities for automatic answer generation. To assess our method, we performed experiments on two datasets: $\text{MSM}^{\text{plus}}$, a modified version of the MS-MARCO benchmark, and the AntQA dataset, the first large-scale CQA dataset featuring four types of MIS. Comprehensive results demonstrate that our model surpasses all baselines across every metric.

This study addresses off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning utilizing deep convolutional neural networks. We examine the deep fitted Q-evaluation technique for estimating the expected cumulative reward of a target policy based on data generated by an unknown behavior policy. Our findings demonstrate that by selecting an appropriate network size, one can exploit low-dimensional manifold structures within the Markov decision process to achieve sample efficiency, thereby avoiding the curse of high ambient data dimensionality. Specifically, we derive a precise error bound for fitted Q-evaluation that relies on the intrinsic dimension of the state-action space, the smoothness of the Bellman operator, and a function class-restricted $\chi^2$-divergence. Notably, this restricted $\chi^2$-divergence quantifies the {\it mismatch between behavior and target policies in function space}, which may remain small even when the policies are not proximate in their tabular representations. Furthermore, we introduce a new approximation result concerning convolutional neural networks in the context of Q-function estimation and provide numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings.

We examine a class of one-dimensional Vector Nonlocal Non-linear Schrödinger Equation (VNNLSE) featuring an external complex potential, time-modulated Balanced Loss-Gain (BLG) and Linear Coupling (LC) among the field components, and space-time dependent nonlinear strength. Under specific conditions, this system supports both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian descriptions. We demonstrate that despite the Hamiltonian density being complex-valued, key dynamical variables—including total power, the $\cal{PT}$-symmetric Hamiltonian, wave-packet width, and growth speed—remain real-valued. Furthermore, we investigate the exact solvability of the general VNNLSE, regardless of whether a Hamiltonian formulation exists. In the initial section, we analyze the time-evolution of moments, which correspond to space-integrals of Stokes variables, to derive conditions ensuring solutions remain bounded over time. In the second section, we employ a non-unitary transformation followed by a coordinate transformation to map the VNNLSE into various solvable equations; notably, the coordinate transformation becomes unnecessary when the non-unitary transformation simplifies to a pseudo-unitary one. The resulting exact solutions are time-bounded under the same conditions identified through the moment analysis, and we present several specific exact solutions for the VNNLSE.

Although pre-training has yielded exciting advancements in visual-linguistic (VL) representations, few efforts target small-scale VL models. This paper investigates knowledge distillation (KD) as a method to compress a large, transformer-based VL model into a compact counterpart. A primary obstacle is the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions caused by inconsistent regional visual tokens generated by different detectors in the Teacher and Student models. To overcome this, we retrain and adapt the Teacher using region proposals from the Student's detector while retaining the Teacher's own object detection features. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher can effectively transfer knowledge through intermediate representations. Specifically, we employ mean square error loss to replicate the attention distribution within transformer blocks and introduce a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align hidden states by contrasting them against negative representations stored in a sample queue. Our results demonstrate that this proposed distillation significantly enhances the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. On the COCO captioning benchmark, the model achieves a CIDEr score of 120.8, representing a 5.1-point improvement over its non-distilled version, while attaining 69.8% accuracy on VQA 2.0, a 0.8-point gain from the baseline. Extensive experiments and ablation studies confirm the efficacy of VL distillation across both pre-training and fine-tuning phases.

We demonstrate a variant of Warner's regularity and continuity properties regarding the sub-Riemannian exponential map. The regularity aspect is derived by analyzing sub-Riemannian Jacobi fields, whereas the continuity aspect results from examining the Maslov index of Jacobi curves. Furthermore, we illustrate how these findings establish that the exponential map on the three-dimensional Heisenberg group fails to be injective in any neighborhood surrounding a conjugate vector.

The detection of the Higgs boson confirmed the standard model of particle physics, yet resolving anomalies like dark matter necessitates additional symmetry breaking, suggesting the existence of an undiscovered axial Higgs mode. While the Higgs mode has been identified in condensed matter systems involving magnetism, superconductivity, and charge density waves (CDWs), determining the vector properties of low-energy modes remains difficult, often requiring methods beyond standard spectroscopic or scattering approaches. In this study, we identify an axial Higgs mode within the CDW system RTe₃ by exploiting quantum pathway interference. In RTe₃ (where R is La or Gd), electronic ordering links bands with matching or differing angular momenta. Consequently, the Raman scattering tensor linked to the Higgs mode exhibits both symmetric and antisymmetric parts, excitable through two distinct yet degenerate pathways. This setup generates either constructive or destructive interference based on the polarization of the incident and scattered light. An appropriate tight-binding model incorporating an axial Higgs mode accurately describes the qualitative Raman spectral behavior. By clarifying the antisymmetric component, we offer direct proof that the Higgs mode possesses an axial vector representation (pseudo-angular momentum), implying that the CDW in RTe₃ is unconventional. Furthermore, this work establishes a method for measuring the quantum characteristics of collective modes without relying on extreme experimental conditions.

The variational principle governing safe equilibrium in inhomogeneous elastic bodies containing cracks is established. By applying standard calculus of variations, it is demonstrated that a crack maintains safe equilibrium provided the maximum energy release rate for a hypothetical crack extension remains negative. Crack propagation initiates in the direction of the maximum energy release rate once this rate reaches zero. This energetic condition encompasses the criteria previously proposed by He and Hutchinson (1989). In a practical application, the criterion is employed to forecast the propagation path of an interface crack within a bimaterial system.

The text describes three algebra categories along with morphisms that extend standard algebra homomorphisms. A hom-tensor equivalence, known as the Sweedler product, connects these categories and serves as a tool for computing universal measuring coalgebras in smaller instances. Additionally, a corresponding theory for modules is outlined.

This study presents a theoretical and numerical analysis of scattering dynamics within a finite periodic waveguide network exhibiting parity-time (PT) symmetry. We derive rigorous, exact analytical expressions governing wave propagation, bi-directional reflectionless transmission, and coherent perfect absorption and lasing (CPAL) in such finite periodic optical systems. By leveraging a generalized parametric space—constructed from PT-symmetric transfer matrices, the Lorentz reciprocity theorem, and non-imaginary Bloch phases—we demonstrate that when a unit cell operates in the PT-broken phase or at an exceptional point, propagating modes are guaranteed regardless of the unit cell count or transmission phase. Conversely, in the exact PT-symmetric phase, the existence of propagating waves relies on the unit cell's transmission phase.
