Notably, we identify that bi-directional reflectionless behavior with unity transmittance can be achieved even outside the exceptional point, provided the number of unit cells and specific PT phases are carefully selected. Furthermore, we propose two distinct methods for realizing CPAL: utilizing an odd number of unit cells at the CPAL point, or manipulating a specific broken phase with an appropriate cell count while nullifying the transmission phase. We conclude that this work provides a solid theoretical foundation for exploring extraordinary wave phenomena in PT-symmetric photonics and suggests new pathways for light manipulation.

This work examines a mean field game framework proposed by Chan and Sircar (AMO, 2015) to represent the extraction of a depletable resource. Specifically, we analyze the sensitivity of the solution concerning a parameter $\varepsilon$, which quantifies the interchangeability of producers. We establish that within a specific interval $[0,\varepsilon_0]$ (with $\varepsilon_0 > 0$), the solution possesses infinite differentiability with respect to $\varepsilon$. This finding relies on novel a priori estimates derived for forward-backward systems of linear partial differential equations.

Contemporary datasets frequently contain significant missing data alongside variables of mixed types, posing major hurdles for estimation and inference. Standard complete case analysis often yields severe bias, whereas model-based imputation struggles to handle complex dependencies and diverse data formats. To overcome these issues, we propose a new Bayesian mixture copula designed for nonparametric joint modeling of count, continuous, ordinal, and unordered categorical data, applying it to inference, prediction, and imputation. Distinctively, we present an efficient method for estimating marginal distributions that avoids specifying specific marginal models, yet ensures strong posterior consistency for both the copula parameters and marginal distributions, even under informative missingness (missingness-at-random). Comprehensive simulations show our approach outperforms competing methods in modeling and imputation, particularly regarding mixed data, intricate missingness mechanisms, and nonlinear relationships. Finally, a real-world data analysis illustrates how mishandling missing data can skew statistical results and demonstrates how our proposed solution resolves these distortions.

Nen verbal morphology is exceptionally intricate, with transitive verbs capable of assuming up to 1,740 distinct forms. The intersection of a vast combinatorial space and limited data availability heightens the necessity for NLP tools. Nen morphology employs distributed exponence, representing a complex method for mapping form to meaning. This study seeks to model Nen verbal morphology using state-of-the-art machine learning frameworks for morphological reinflection, while investigating and classifying the error patterns these systems produce. Our findings indicate that model performance is highly sensitive to training data composition; varying distributions of verb types result in different accuracy levels that correlate with E-complexity. Furthermore, we illustrate the patterns inferable from training data through an examination of syncretism.

Following the implementation of the GDPR in May 2018, organizations have adjusted their data handling procedures to meet the law's standards. As the primary mechanism for users to comprehend and manage their privacy, numerous companies revised their privacy policies post-enforcement. Nevertheless, these policies often remain excessively lengthy, laden with jargon, and ambiguously outline data practices and user rights, casting doubt on their actual GDPR compliance. To address this, we compiled a dataset of 1,080 privacy policies annotated with the 18 specific GDPR requirements and developed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model capable of classifying these policies with 89.2% accuracy. Utilizing this model to assess compliance levels, our findings reveal that despite the GDPR's enactment, 97% of websites continue to fail to meet at least one of the required standards.

Large-scale ontologies continue to present significant hurdles for current ontology alignment technologies. This paper introduces a method that integrates neural embedding models with logic-based components to effectively decompose complex ontology matching tasks into smaller, more manageable subtasks. We performed a thorough evaluation using datasets from the Ontology Alignment Evaluation Initiative, yielding encouraging results. These findings indicate that the proposed approach is practically viable and can be incorporated into workflows for systems that struggle to handle very large ontologies.

We report the initial measurement of the two-particle transverse momentum differential correlation function, defined as $P_2\equiv\langle \Delta p_{\rm T} \Delta p_{\rm T} \rangle /\langle p_{\rm T} \rangle^2$, within Pb-Pb collisions occurring at $\sqrt{s_{_{\rm NN}}} =$ 2.76 TeV. The findings for $P_2$ are presented across varying relative pseudorapidity ($\Delta \eta$) and azimuthal angle ($\Delta \varphi$) intervals for multiple collision centralities. It is observed that for $|\Delta \eta| \geq$ 0.9, the dependence on $\Delta \phi$ remains largely consistent regardless of $\Delta \eta$. In the most central 5% of Pb-Pb collisions, the two-particle transverse momentum correlation function displays a distinct double-hump pattern near $\Delta \varphi = \pi$ (the away side), a feature absent in number correlations for the same centrality; this suggests that triangular flow dominates in these collisions. Furthermore, Fourier analyses of $P_2$ conducted across different centralities indicate that correlations where $|\Delta \eta| \geq$ 0.9 are accurately modeled by a flow ansatz, implying that observed momentum correlations are governed by the system's collective motion.

This paper examines fundamental investment concepts through a mathematical lens, with a specific focus on fractional-Kelly portfolios. These portfolios allocate a portion of wealth to a growth-optimal strategy while investing the remainder in a risk-free asset, either earning or paying interest. We develop a unified continuous-parameter time-series framework to analyze these portfolios, clarifying the interconnections among leverage, growth rates, and Sharpe ratios. Our analysis demonstrates that Kelly's criterion yields the same leverage ratios as Markowitz mean-variance optimization. Additionally, for fractional Kelly strategies, we establish a straightforward relationship linking portfolio Sharpe ratios, the fractional coefficient, and log-returns. These findings offer vital insights into realistic growth expectations for diverse investor types, ranging from individual investors to quantitative trading firms. Furthermore, we illustrate these concepts by evaluating the performance of various equity and bond allocations. Finally, we show how these relationships can be utilized via a simple method-of-moments approach to estimate a fund's Sharpe ratio and risk deployment levels based on reported returns.

Small-scale microjets in low-mass young stellar systems can be investigated through forbidden neon emission lines to understand high-energy processes. Using the Hubble Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (HST/STIS) with a spatial resolution of approximately 0".1, we captured spatially resolved [Ne III] spectra of the microjets from the classical T Tauri Star Sz 102. Both the blueshifted and redshifted [Ne III] emissions reach their peak intensity within ~0".1 of the star and diminish gradually as they extend outward to ~0".24. The observed spatial distribution and extent of the [Ne III] microjet align with a scenario where the jet is ionized near its base and subsequently recombines over a timescale longer than the flow duration. Additionally, Ca II H and K lines were detected in the redshifted microjet with a full-width at half-maximum of roughly 170 km/s, matching the widths of other forbidden emission lines, superimposed on a broader stellar component of 300 km/s. Based on observed line centroids and literature values for inclination angles and stellar masses, the launching radius of the Sz 102 jet is estimated to be approximately 0.03 au. This proximity to the star suggests that immediate ionization is possible without significant dilution from circumstellar sources, most likely sustained by keV X-ray flares arising from magnetic reconnection events within the star-disk system, thereby maintaining the observed [Ne III] flux.

We establish a variant of the BKK theorem for the ring of conditions associated with a spherical homogeneous space $G/H$. Furthermore, we define the concept of a ring of complete intersections, initially for spherical homogeneous spaces and subsequently for general varieties. Analogous to how the torus's ring of conditions is described, the ring of complete intersections for $G/H$ can be characterized using the volumes of polytopes.

We introduce a series of experimentally feasible, driven-dissipative protocols designed to control cold atoms within tilted optical lattices. These examples serve as templates illustrating how dissipation can manipulate quantum many-body systems. Specifically, we examine bosonic atoms confined in a tilted optical lattice, submerged in a superfluid bath, and driven by coherent Raman lasers. Utilizing these components, we achieve the controlled transport of atoms and the generation of self-healing quantum states, namely a Mott insulator and the topologically ordered spin-1 AKLT state.

Given the threat of adversarial attacks, ensuring the security of Deep Learning classifiers has become a vital area of research. These attacks typically exploit transferability, meaning an adversarial sample generated for a surrogate model can often deceive a target model with a different architecture, even when both are trained on the same data. While ensemble techniques show promise by reducing the likelihood of misclassification through diverse decision boundaries, recent approaches have either proven vulnerable to advanced adversaries or lack comprehensive end-to-end evaluation. This paper introduces a novel ensemble framework that trains multiple diverse classifiers using a Pairwise Adversarially Robust Loss (PARL) function. By simultaneously leveraging gradients from every layer relative to the input across all classifiers in the ensemble, PARL achieves superior resistance to black-box transfer attacks compared to prior methods, all while maintaining high accuracy on clean data. Furthermore, we assess the system's resilience against white-box attacks, where adversaries utilize the target model's internal parameters. Extensive experiments on standard image classification benchmarks, specifically CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using ResNet20 architectures, demonstrate the proposed methodology's robustness against state-of-the-art adversarial threats.

In 2018, software industry leader Microsoft expanded into the open-source ecosystem by acquiring GitHub, the world's largest open-source platform. This transaction sparked controversy because the free software community values not only the freedom to use software but also its "libre" principles. This study investigates these perceptions among FLOSS developers through a survey targeting traditional communities like Linux and BSD, which gathered 246 responses. The findings indicate that the acquisition prompted some communities to migrate away from GitHub and reignited debates about free and open software within the platform. Ultimately, the research highlights that while GitHub is influential and popular, it does not represent all FLOSS communities.

We investigate both the equilibrium behavior and non-equilibrium dynamics of sparse Boolean networks featuring self-interactions, which evolve under synchronous Glauber dynamics. The equilibrium analysis relies on a novel application of the cavity method to a temperature-dependent pseudo-Hamiltonian describing parallel-dynamics systems. Likewise, the dynamical version of the cavity method is employed to analyze non-equilibrium evolution. However, it is established that direct application of this dynamical approach becomes cumbersome in the presence of self-interactions due to strong memory effects, which hinder explicit analysis beyond a few time steps. To address this, we demonstrate that a system of $N$ variables can be mapped to an equivalent bipartite system of $2N$ variables, enabling the use of the dynamical cavity method under the standard one-time approximation. This significant technical breakthrough facilitates the examination of both transient and long-time behaviors in systems with self-interactions. Furthermore, we examine the dynamics of systems with multi-node interactions, recently utilized to model gene regulatory networks, by mapping them to a bipartite system of Boolean variables with 2-body interactions. We find that when these interactions exhibit a degree of bidirectionality, the systems can sustain a multiplicity of diverse attractors, a critical requirement for gene-regulatory networks to maintain multi-cellular life.

This study presents the initial measurements of elliptic and triangular flow for charged pions, kaons, and anti-protons resulting from lead-lead collisions at 2.76 TeV, utilizing the ALICE detector at the LHC. The observed mass-dependent splitting in differential elliptic flow at LHC energies is compared against RHIC data from lower energies and theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we examine the quark coalescence model by analyzing the quark number scaling of both elliptic and triangular flow.

This article investigates the homogeneous tree $\x$ with degree $q+1$ ($q \geq 2$), introducing symbolic criteria to determine the boundedness of pseudo-differential operators on this structure. We also establish a sufficient condition for weak type $(p, q)$ boundedness. Furthermore, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the symbols $\sigma$ ensuring that the associated pseudo-differential operators $T_\sigma$ map from $L^{p_1}(\x)$ to $L^{p_2}(\x)$ as nuclear operators, for $1 \leq p_1, p_2 < \infty$. We demonstrate that the adjoint of a nuclear operator mapping from $L^{p_2'}(\x)$ to $L^{p_1'}(\x)$ remains nuclear. Finally, explicit formulas are derived for the symbols corresponding to the adjoints and products of these nuclear pseudo-differential operators on $\x$.

In wireless systems like Massive-MIMO, where radio front-ends and back-end processing are linked via a transport network, fulfilling real-time processing demands is crucial to unlock capacity improvements from network scaling. Although basic baseband transport solutions exist, their real-time analysis at large scales remains underdeveloped. To address this, we offer a design, delay, and capacity analysis of baseband transport networks by applying real-time systems principles to wireless processing. We introduce DISTRO, a novel Fat-Tree-based architecture for baseband transport that functions as a real-time network guaranteeing bounded maximum end-to-end delay for every baseband packet. This is accomplished by imposing specific design constraints and limiting queuing delays at each network aggregation point. Furthermore, we characterize wireless capacity using DISTRO and develop an efficient search algorithm to design baseband transport systems that maximize capacity.

Part I examines the accumulating experimental data concerning the structure and origin of the bosonic spectral function \alpha ^{2}F in high-temperature superconducting (HTSC) cuprates near optimal doping. By integrating measurements from optics, neutron scattering, ARPES, and tunnelling, we have extracted key global characteristics of \alpha ^{2}F, including peak positions and counts. These findings provide robust evidence for a strong electron-phonon interaction (EPI) in optimally doped cuprates, with a coupling constant satisfying 1<\lambda \lesssim 3. This analysis supports an Eliashberg-like theoretical framework for HTSC in this regime. Furthermore, we contend that the exclusion of EPI in earlier HTSC studies stemmed from misleading biases regarding EPI strength, alongside physical misconceptions and the erroneous interpretation of experimental data.

We investigate light scattering from a two-dimensional array of atoms excited to Rydberg states. We demonstrate that this system can be mapped onto a generalized waveguide QED model featuring multiple one-dimensional photonic channels (transverse modes), where each channel is directionally coupled to a specific Rydberg surface mode of the array. Under Rydberg blockade conditions, collective excitations of distinct surface modes mutually inhibit one another, generating multi-channel correlated photonic states. By employing an analytical method, we characterize the quantum correlations between channels and clarify the influence of collective two-photon resonances within the array. These findings establish new avenues for exploring multimode many-body physics and quantum information processing with photons in free-space environments.

We introduce a practical experimental approach to demonstrate Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering within non-Gaussian spin states by leveraging its link to quantum metrology. Our proposed criterion relies on quantum Fisher information and utilizes bounds established from generalized spin-squeezing parameters that incorporate higher-order moment measurements. Consequently, we propose the concept of conditional spin-squeezing parameters, which serve to quantify the metrological benefits of conditional states and identify the existence of an EPR paradox.

Learning from limited datasets is difficult because data scarcity often results in poor model generalization. Traditional global pooled representations tend to discard valuable local details. Although recent few-shot learning approaches tackle this issue using deep descriptors and pixel-level metrics, relying on deep descriptors can erase image context, and handling support set classes independently fails to fully leverage discriminative and task-specific embeddings. This paper introduces Sparse Spatial Transformers (SSFormers), a novel Transformer-based architecture designed to isolate task-relevant features while suppressing irrelevant ones. Specifically, input images are segmented into patches of varying sizes to generate dense local features that maintain both local and contextual information. A proposed sparse spatial transformer layer then establishes spatial correspondences between the query image and the entire support set to filter out task-irrelevant patches and retain relevant ones. Finally, an image patch matching module calculates distances between these dense local representations to classify the query image against the support set. Extensive experiments on standard few-shot learning benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results.

Federated learning, a distributed training approach that operates on local devices without central access to raw data, remains susceptible to Byzantine poisoning attacks. We contend that safeguarding the global model requires filtering out malicious clients via the federated aggregation mechanism. To this end, we introduce a dynamic federated aggregation operator capable of identifying and excluding adversarial participants, thereby preventing model corruption. We evaluate this defense strategy using a deep learning classification framework across the Fed-EMNIST Digits, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets within a federated environment. Experimental results demonstrate that dynamically selecting clients for aggregation improves the global model's performance while effectively eliminating both adversarial and low-quality participants.

A detailed thermodynamic examination of complex systems featuring multiple stable configurational states provides insights into the cooperativity of individual transitions. This study introduces a heat capacity decomposition that separates contributions from each distinct configurational state—which collectively form a baseline heat capacity—from those arising from transitions between states. Applying this framework to replica exchange molecular dynamics simulations of linear and 1-1 coarse-grained homo-oligomer models that fold into stable, well-defined molecular knots, we investigate the parameters governing stable and cooperative knot folding. Our findings indicate that a stiff harmonic backbone bending angle potential is essential for generating knots with specific three-dimensional structures. By fine-tuning the backbone equilibrium angle in small steps, various knot topologies ($3_1$, $5_1$, $7_1$, and $8_{19}$) can be produced. Additionally, the temperature-dependent populations of different knotted states can be controlled by adjusting backbone torsion stiffness or incorporating side chain beads. We observe that the sharp total heat capacity peaks observed in homo-oligomer knots are primarily driven by a coil-to-globule transition rather than a cooperative knotting event. However, in certain instances, the cooperativity of both globule-to-knot and coil-to-globule transitions is comparable, implying that highly cooperative folding into knotted structures can be realized through refined model parameters or the introduction of sequence specificity.

The eigenvalues and wave functions for free electron gases within toroidal shells are derived via a basis set expansion tailored to the system's geometry. Significant couplings between poloidal and azimuthal modes emerge at lower ${m_\phi}$ values, altering single-particle density distributions inside the shells. Furthermore, thermodynamic state functions are computed and compared against those of a solid toroidal volume.

Data assimilation (DA) seeks to optimally integrate model predictions with noisy observations. Multi-model DA extends the variational or Bayesian Kalman filter framework, and we demonstrate that it constitutes the minimum variance linear unbiased estimator. Yet, prior implementations failed to estimate model errors, preventing the accurate weighting of individual models and observations. In this work, we present a method for combining multiple models for both forecasting and DA by employing an ensemble Kalman filter with adaptive model error estimation. Applied to the Lorenz96 model, this approach yields substantial error reductions compared to the single best model and an unweighted multi-model ensemble.

Precise automatic segmentation of organs remains a critical but difficult challenge in medical image analysis. The pancreas, characterized by significant anatomical variability within the abdomen, poses particular difficulties for traditional segmentation techniques, often resulting in lower accuracy compared to organs like the liver, heart, or kidneys. This paper introduces a holistic learning framework that combines semantic mid-level features derived from deep learning of organ interiors and boundaries through robust spatial aggregation using random forests. Our approach produces boundary-preserving pixel-wise class labels specifically for pancreas segmentation. Validated on CT scans from 82 patients using 4-fold cross-validation, our method achieves a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient of 78.01% ± 8.2% in testing, representing a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art result of 71.8% ± 10.7% under identical evaluation metrics.

RIS-assisted OFDM systems have garnered significant research attention due to their ability to control the communication environment and mitigate multi-path interference. However, accurate channel estimation in these systems is critically challenged by the increased likelihood of insufficient cyclic prefixes (CP) caused by additional cascaded RIS channels, as well as nonlinear distortions stemming from imperfect hardware. To overcome these challenges, this letter proposes an enhanced extreme learning machine (eELM)-based channel estimation method designed to improve estimation accuracy. Adopting a model-driven approach, least squares (LS) estimation is first utilized to extract initial linear features. Subsequently, an enhanced ELM network is developed to refine these estimates based on the initial features. Specifically, the method guides the network to recognize relevant features and normalizes data post-activation to strengthen the identification of nonlinear factors. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with existing techniques, the proposed approach achieves a significantly lower normalized mean square error (NMSE) under conditions of insufficient CP and hardware imperfections. Furthermore, simulations confirm that the method exhibits robustness against parameter variations.

This research investigates how explicit breaking of spacetime symmetry influences primordial tensor fluctuations through an effective-field theory framework for Lorentz/CPT violation. Our results indicate that while the graviton remains massless, the propagation velocity of tensor modes is altered, leading to a constraint on the symmetry-breaking coefficient of approximately $10^{-15}$ based on recent measurements of the speed of gravity. The symmetry breaking also modifies the de-Sitter phase; consequently, during inflation, the power spectrum exhibits slow oscillations around the general-relativity prediction. Although the primordial tensor power spectrum maintains scale invariance, its amplitude is adjusted. Additionally, modes that enter the subhorizon regime during radiation domination undergo a phase shift proportional to the Lorentz violation coefficient.

This study applies the attention mechanism to autonomous driving for steering angle prediction. We introduce the first model utilizing a recently developed sparse attention mechanism within the visual domain, alongside an aggregated extension of this approach. Our results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority when compared to scenarios without attention and against various other attention types.

In 1989, Witten integrated classical Chern-Simons theory into topology by defining a knot invariant in 3-manifolds through an integral over a specific infinite-dimensional space that remains only partially understood to this day. Despite this, the theory has inspired numerous significant questions and findings within knot theory and low-dimensional topology, alongside the creation of entirely new disciplines. These lecture notes are designed for graduate students and cover Lie groups and Chern-Simons Theory.

When a point P lies within triangle ABC, the cevians originating from P partition the original triangle into six smaller ones. We present theorems concerning the relationship between the inradii of these six resulting triangles.

This paper introduces a Bayesian framework designed to create non-linear, parsimonious, shallow models for multitask regression. The approach leverages the ability of Random Fourier Features (RFFs) to approximate Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernels using an extreme learning machine with a hidden layer composed of RFFs. The core concept involves unifying the dual perspectives of a single model within a Bayesian formulation that generalizes Sparse Bayesian Extreme Learning Machines to multitask scenarios. From the kernel methods standpoint, this formulation allows for the incorporation of prior domain knowledge via RBF kernel parameters. Conversely, from the extreme learning machines perspective, it mitigates overfitting and promotes model parsimony by ensuring that all tasks share a common set of RFFs selected through joint Bayesian optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating the strengths of both kernel methods and extreme learning machines within this unified framework yields significant performance gains compared to each paradigm operating independently.

Rosenbaum (1983) established the concept of the propensity score and highlighted its significance in causal inference for observational data. However, this work created a fundamental conflict with Rubin's (1978) earlier findings, which demonstrated that the propensity score is irrelevant in the Bayesian analysis of unconfounded observational studies when priors for the propensity score and outcome models are independent. Despite extensive efforts to resolve this discrepancy, reconciling these opposing results remains challenging. We propose a straightforward method for integrating the propensity score into Bayesian causal inference using the posterior predictive $p$-value. To illustrate this procedure, we initially consider a model assuming a strong null hypothesis where no causal effects exist for any unit. Computationally, the proposed posterior predictive $p$-value corresponds to the classic $p$-value from a Fisher randomization test, averaged across the posterior predictive distribution of the propensity score. Furthermore, by employing the studentized doubly robust estimator as the test statistic, the resulting $p$-value retains the doubly robust property and remains asymptotically valid for testing the weak null hypothesis of zero average causal effect. Surprisingly, this Bayesian-inspired $p$-value often demonstrates superior frequentist finite-sample performance compared to the frequentist $p$-value derived from asymptotic approximations, particularly when propensity scores exhibit extreme values.

We performed mapping observations of the Class I protostar L1489 IRS using the 7-m array of the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) and the IRAM-30m telescope at the $\mathrm{C^{18}O}$ 2-1 transition to examine gas kinematics spanning 1000 to 10,000 au. The $\mathrm{C^{18}O}$ data reveal a velocity gradient across the protostar oriented nearly perpendicular to the outflow. By analyzing a position-velocity diagram of the $\mathrm{C^{18}O}$ emission along the disk's major axis, we measured the radial profile of the peak velocity. This velocity decreases between radii of $\sim$1400 and 2900 au, whereas it remains nearly constant or increases slightly at $r\gtrsim$2900 au. Comparing disk-and-envelope models against these observations indicates that the radial velocity profile is best described by a scenario where specific angular momentum is constant within 2900 au but rises beyond that radius. We derived the radial profile of specific angular momentum from the observed peak velocities and compared it with analytic core collapse models. These analytic models successfully reproduce the observed angular momentum profile and imply that material from an initial dense core radius of $\sim$4000–6000 au has accreted onto the central protostar. Given that dense cores typically span 10,000–20,000 au and L1489 IRS is nearing the end of its mass accretion phase, our findings suggest that only a fraction of a dense core ultimately forms a star.

Let $p$ denote an odd prime with irregularity index $e_p$. Under the condition $4e_p+8 < \frac{p-1}{2}$, we construct a Galois representation whose image lies within the diagonal torus of $\op{GSp}_4(\Fp)$ and which lifts to a characteristic $0$ representation unramified at all primes $\ell \neq p$, such that its image contains a subgroup of finite index in $\Symp$.

While electrostatic gating is generally preferred over chemical doping for phase engineering in quantum materials due to its ability to reversibly adjust carrier density without altering disorder, this advantage falters in SrTiO$_3$ (STO)-based two-dimensional electron gas field-effect transistors. This anomaly stems from electron trapping induced by external electric fields, though the specific microscopic origins of these trapping centers have remained unclear. This study examines electric field-driven charge trapping and detrapping at the conducting interface between the band insulator $\gamma$-Al$_2$O$_3$ and STO. Transport measurements indicate that under a positive back gate voltage ($V_g$) above STO's tetragonal-to-cubic structural transition temperature ($T_c$), trapping results from both electric field-assisted thermal electron escape from the quantum well and the clustering of oxygen vacancies (OVs). Below $T_c$, an additional trapping mechanism emerges, involving the capture of free carriers at ferroelastic twin walls within the STO. Conversely, applying a negative $V_g$ facilitates charge detrapping, a process that ceases above $T_c$. This behavior underscores the critical influence of structural domain walls on the electrical transport characteristics of STO-based heterostructures. The quantity of trapped or detrapped charges at these twin walls is governed by the wall's net polarity and exhibits complete reversibility with sweeping $V_g$.

We introduce compact formulae for the matrix elements of one- and two-body physical operators, valid for any Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave function, including those describing multi-quasiparticle excitations. Test calculations indicate that applying these formulae can significantly speed up symmetry restoration in heavy nuclear systems.

This paper extends Robinson's order cancellation law for subsets of vector spaces to cases involving unbounded cancellation sets. We define weakly narrow sets within normed spaces, investigate their characteristics, and establish an order cancellation law specifically for such sets. Additionally, we demonstrate the order cancellation law for closed convex subsets in topological vector spaces where the canceled set maintains a bounded Hausdorff-like distance from its recession cone. Furthermore, we topologically embed the semigroup of closed convex sets—those sharing a recession cone with a bounded Hausdorff-like distance from it—into a topological vector space. This finding generalizes the Radstrom theorem as previously expanded by Bielawski and Tabor.

This study theoretically examines minimal search strategies employed by active, self-propelled particles to locate hidden targets within three-dimensional space. Although these particles can detect when a target is nearby—such as through signaling molecules—they lack the ability to determine directional information. We concentrate on composite strategies that alternate between broad outer search phases and focused inner search phases; the latter initiates upon detecting proximity and concludes after a specific duration. In the most basic approach, particles move ballistically during the outer phase but temporarily decrease their directional persistence during the inner phase. A second, adaptive method leverages a dynamic scattering effect by reducing directional persistence exclusively outside a clearly defined target zone. Both strategies demand minimal information processing, utilizing either a single binary or tertiary internal state, yet they significantly enhance the rate of target encounters. Furthermore, the optimal duration for the inner search phase follows a power-law scaling with an exponent of -2/3 relative to target density, illustrating the balance between exploration and exploitation.

Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) function by projecting inputs onto a set of interpretable concepts—the "bottleneck"—which are then used to generate predictions. This architecture enhances interpretability, allowing researchers to analyze which concepts the model identifies in an input and which are considered significant. However, CBMs face practical limitations: they necessitate concept labels during training to learn the bottleneck and fail to utilize robust pretrained models. Additionally, they often lag behind unrestricted neural networks in accuracy, diminishing their appeal for real-world deployment. To overcome these hurdles, we introduce Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck models (PCBMs). Our approach transforms any neural network into a PCBM, maintaining high performance while preserving interpretability. In scenarios where training data lacks concept annotations, PCBMs can transfer concepts from external datasets or natural language descriptions. Furthermore, PCBMs facilitate rapid debugging and updates to mitigate spurious correlations and enhance generalization across new data. A model-editing study demonstrates that refining PCBMs through concept-level feedback yields substantial performance improvements without requiring target domain data or model retraining.

This paper aims to characterize Gaussian-Process optimization when the function domain is significantly larger than the number of allowable evaluations, making it impossible to locate the global optimum. We derive upper bounds on the suboptimality (Bayesian simple regret) for optimization strategies akin to the commonly used Expected Improvement (EI) and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithms. These regret bounds clarify the interplay between the count of evaluations, domain size (defined as the cardinality of finite domains or the Lipschitz constant of the covariance function in continuous settings), and the quality of the retrieved function value. Specifically, we demonstrate that even when the evaluation budget is insufficient to find the global optimum, it is possible to obtain nontrivial function values, such as those achieving a specific ratio relative to the optimal value.

This work investigates the Lie point symmetries and similarity transformations associated with the nonlinear one-dimensional Hall magnetohydrodynamic (HMHD) system, a partial differential equation model. We demonstrate that this 1+1 dimensional system remains invariant under a seven-dimensional Lie algebra. Additionally, we derive a one-dimensional optimal system by utilizing Lie invariants to generate similarity transformations, and we present various types of oscillating solutions.

Anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering plays a pivotal role in the heat conduction of solids. While prior research has established numerous selection rules for these scattering channels—dictated by the conservation of phonon energy and momentum alongside crystal symmetry—most rules derived from symmetry have been developed in an *ad hoc* manner for specific materials. Consequently, a comprehensive formalism capable of encapsulating existing rules and predicting new ones for any crystal structure remains absent. This study introduces a general framework grounded in group theory to determine symmetry-based scattering selection rules for anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions. This approach successfully reproduces established rules and facilitates the identification of novel selection rules between phonon branches dictated by crystal symmetry. By applying this formalism to the in-plane symmetry of graphene, we illustrate the profound effects of symmetry-breaking strain on lattice thermal conductivity. Ultimately, this work quantifies the critical impact of crystal symmetry on thermal transport in solids and proposes pathways for engineering heat conduction through the modulation of crystal symmetry.

Evidence for the hadronic annihilation decay channel $B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi$ has been established with a significance exceeding $3\sigma$. The measured branching fraction and \CP asymmetry are given by \mathcal{B}(B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi) &=& (1.87^{+1.25}_{-0.73}({\rm stat}) \pm 0.19 ({\rm syst}) \pm 0.32 ({\rm norm})) \times 10^{-6} and \mathcal{A}_{CP}(B^{+} \to D_s^{+}\phi) &=& -0.01 \pm 0.41 ({\rm stat}) \pm 0.03 ({\rm syst}), respectively. The final uncertainty in the branching fraction arises from the branching fractions of the $B^+ \to D_s^+ \kern 0.2em\bar{\kern -0.2em D}{}^0$ normalization mode and intermediate resonance decays. Additionally, upper limits have been determined for the branching fractions of associated decay modes $B^{+}_{(c)} \to D^{+}_{(s)} K^{*0}$, $B^{+}_{(c)} \to D^{+}_{(s)} \kern 0.2em\bar{\kern -0.2em K}{}^{*0}$, and ${B_c^{+} \to D^{+}_{s}\phi}$, notably including the constraint ${\mathcal{B}(B^+ \to D^+ K^{*0})} < 1.8 \times 10^{-6}$ at the 90% credibility level.

Let $\Omega$ represent a bounded open domain in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and let $\mathbb{Q}_{+}$ denote the set of all positive rational numbers. In 2017, Chen and Zeng examined the higher-order eigenvalues of the fractional Laplacian $\left.(-\Delta)^{s}\right|_{\Omega}$ for $s>0$ where $s \in \mathbb{Q}_{+}$, deriving a universal inequality of Yang type (see \emph{Universal inequality and upper bounds of eigenvalues for non-integer poly-Laplacian on a bounded domain, Calculus of Variations and Partial Differential Equations, (2017) \textbf{56}:131}). Following the approach established by Chen and Zeng, this work investigates the eigenvalues of the fractional Laplacian and derives an eigenvalue inequality with a lower order under identical conditions. Furthermore, the resulting inequality is universal and extends the eigenvalue inequalities for poly-harmonic operators previously established by Jost et al. (\emph{Universal bounds for eigenvalues of polyharmonic operator. Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. {\bf 363}(4), 1821-1854 (2011)}).

Although semiconductors present a viable foundation for physical qubit implementation, their widespread use is currently restricted by challenges in scalability and the necessity for extremely low operating temperatures. Inspired by nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, our objective is to discover analogous optically active point defects within crystalline silicon, which would offer benefits regarding scalability and integration with classical systems. While transition metal (TM) impurities in silicon are known as common paramagnetic deep defects, there remains a lack of a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the entire 3$d$ series that incorporates generalized Koopmans' condition. By utilizing the HSE06(+U) method to evaluate their potential as optically active spin qubits, we have identified seven TM impurities capable of optically allowed triplet-triplet transitions inside the silicon band gap. These findings mark an initial step toward achieving silicon-based qubits suitable for higher-temperature quantum sensing. Furthermore, such point defects could facilitate spin-photon interfaces in silicon qubits and enable devices for mid-infrared free-space communications.

The modular group $\mbox{PSL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, defined by the presentation $\langle x, \, y \,|\, x^2=y^3=1\rangle$ with generators $x: z\mapsto -1/z$ and $y:z\mapsto (z-1)/z$, contains a proper subgroup $H = \langle y,\,v\,|\, y^3=v^3=1\rangle$, where $v=xyx$. A previous study by M. Ashiq and Q. Mushtaq (Quasigroups and Related Systems, 2006) investigated the action of $H$ on the set $\{\frac{a+\sqrt{-n}}{c}\,|\, a,b=\frac{a^2+n}{c}, c \in \mathbb{Z}, c\neq 0\}$ within the imaginary quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-n})$, for square-free positive integers $n$. The present article identifies and rectifies inaccuracies found in that reference, most notably providing a revised estimate for the number of orbits generated by this action.

Calculating physical quantities in specific quantum field theories, particularly Argyres-Douglas models, presents significant challenges due to the absence of a Lagrangian formulation. This study addresses the issue through two distinct methodologies. First, we employ four-sphere localization to determine two-point correlators and operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients within Argyres-Douglas superconformal theories. Second, we utilize conformal bootstrap techniques to establish rigorous constraints on these coefficients, depending solely on the central charge and the conformal dimensions of the operators. A comparison of outcomes from both approaches reveals strong consistency across all rank-one scenarios and the rank-two Argyres-Douglas theories (A_1,A_4) and (A_1,A_5), specifically within the moduli space of pure SU(5) and SU(6) super Yang-Mills. Furthermore, we leverage our localization findings to derive upper bounds on the scaling dimensions of the lightest neutral unprotected operators in these conformal field theories.

Q-learning is a widely adopted Reinforcement Learning (RL) technique, particularly when paired with function approximation (Mnih et al., 2015). However, theoretical analyses regarding Q-learning remain largely pessimistic. For instance, Baird (1995) demonstrated that Q-learning fails to converge even with linear function approximation in linear MDPs. Additionally, for tabular MDPs utilizing synchronous updates, Q-learning has been found to exhibit sub-optimal sample complexity (Li et al., 2021; Azar et al., 2013). This research aims to reconcile the algorithm's practical efficacy with its disappointing theoretical guarantees. Our investigation begins with the observation that practical implementations of Q-learning typically incorporate two key modifications: (i) the simultaneous use of an online network and a target network, known as online target learning (OTL), and (ii) experience replay (ER) (Mnih et al., 2015). Although these components are known to drive practical success, a comprehensive theoretical explanation of how they enhance convergence remains absent in the literature. By integrating Q-learning with OTL and reverse experience replay (RER)—a variant of ER—we introduce new methodologies named Q-Rex and Q-RexDaRe (Q-Rex augmented with data reuse). We demonstrate that Q-Rex efficiently identifies the optimal policy for linear MDPs, as well as for MDPs characterized by zero inherent Bellman error with linear approximation (ZIBEL), offering the first non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for a Q-learning approach on this class of problems under standard assumptions. Moreover, we show that Q-RexDaRe achieves near-optimal sample complexity in the tabular setting, thereby surpassing the performance of standard Q-learning.

We define explainability through the lens of logic and formula complexity, offering several related definitions within a broad framework. Our primary focus is the special explanation problem, which seeks to justify the truth value of an input formula within a specific input model. This explanation consists of a minimal-sized formula that (1) aligns with the input formula on the given model and (2) globally propagates the associated truth value to the input formula across all models. As a significant case study, we examine propositional logic under this framework, demonstrating that the special explainability problem is complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Furthermore, we present an answer set programming implementation of this problem and analyze its effectiveness in explaining solutions for the n-queens and dominating set problems.

A line driver featuring configurable pre-emphasis has been realized using a 65 nm CMOS process. It employs a three-tap feed-forward equalization (FFE) structure where the relative delays between taps are adjustable in 1/16th UI increments through an 8-stage delay-locked loop (DLL) and digital interpolator. Additionally, output amplitude and source impedance for each tap can be regulated via a programmable array of eight source-series terminated (SST) drivers. The complete circuit operates at 1 Gb/s with a 1.2 V supply, drawing 9 mW of power.

Previous studies indicate that cryptography presents significant challenges for developers. This research seeks to identify the specific cryptographic difficulties developers encounter in real-world scenarios. By clustering 91,954 cryptography-related inquiries from Stack Overflow and manually analyzing a representative sample of 383 questions, we examined the common crypto challenges faced by developers. Our findings reveal that these issues stem from either a fundamental lack of understanding regarding core concepts—such as OpenSSL, public-key cryptography, or password hashing—or the poor usability of cryptographic libraries, which hinders developers' ability to correctly implement cryptographic solutions. These results are concerning and underscore the urgent need for targeted research to enhance the design of cryptographic APIs.

A primary obstacle in applying reinforcement learning practically is the challenge of safe exploration. We introduce a natural safety criterion—uniformly surpassing a conservatively estimated baseline policy, subject to a per-episode exploration limit. Subsequently, we develop an algorithm that employs a UCB-based reinforcement learning strategy for exploration but intervenes to guarantee safety with high probability when necessary. Our experimental evaluation on a sepsis treatment task confirms that our method can effectively learn while maintaining superior performance relative to the baseline policy for every patient.

This work examines the general features of stochastic particle acceleration within a fully developed turbulence spectrum, demonstrating that resonant interactions between particles and high-velocity waves govern the acceleration mechanism. To account for the relativistic electrons suggested by the broadband spectra of several well-observed shell-type supernova remnants under the leptonic TeV emission scenario, fast mode waves must be efficiently generated in the downstream region and dominate the turbulence during the subsonic phase. Strong, collisionless, non-relativistic astrophysical shocks are analyzed assuming a constant Alfvén speed. Results indicate that the energy density of non-thermal electrons is comparable to that of the magnetic field. With plausible parameter choices, this model successfully explains observations of shell-type supernova remnants, though more detailed investigations are needed to fully comprehend the nature of these supernova shocks.

This research examines the computational capabilities of the subtyping engine underlying Kennedy and Pierce's nominal subtyping framework with variance. We illustrate the lattice of fragments within their type system and define their computational strength using regular, context-free, deterministic, and non-deterministic tree languages. Leveraging this theoretical foundation, we introduce Treetop, a generator that produces C# implementations of subtyping machines. This software artifact represents the first practical (though proof-of-concept) fluent API generator capable of supporting context-free API protocols within a decidable type system fragment.

Training cutting-edge Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) systems usually demands large volumes of transcribed audio. This study demonstrates that a joint speech and text model with aligned modalities can be utilized to train a massively multilingual ASR system without any supervised (manually transcribed) speech data for certain languages. By leveraging jointly learned speech and text representations in a real-world, zero-supervised, massively multilingual environment, we aim to expand the linguistic coverage of ASR using only unlabeled speech and text from target languages. Utilizing the FLEURS dataset, we address a task spanning 102 languages, where transcribed speech exists for 52, allowing improvements to end-to-end ASR performance for the remaining 50. First, we illustrate that integrating speech representations with byte-level text representations and language embeddings can significantly lower the Character Error Rate (CER) on languages lacking supervised speech from 64.8% to 30.8%, achieving a 53% relative reduction. Second, by examining a subset of South Asian languages, we show that Maestro-U facilitates knowledge transfer from languages with supervised speech, even when graphemic overlap is minimal or absent. Overall, Maestro-U narrows the gap to oracle performance by 68.5% relative and brings the CER of 19 languages below 15%.

This paper establishes the exact inversion of adjunction formula for quotient singularities and applies this result to demonstrate the semi-continuity of minimal log discrepancies in the context of hyperquotient singularities. Building upon arXiv:2011.07300, we extend prior findings to encompass non-linear group actions.

The LHCb experiment at CERN is being upgraded to prepare for the LHC's Run 3 data collection, which involves transitioning its trigger system to a fully software-based solution operating at the bunch crossing rate. This document evaluates both CPU and GPU implementations of the High Level Trigger's first stage. Following a thorough comparison, both approaches proved viable; however, this summary of their performance and implementation details confirms that the GPU-based option was selected as the baseline.

Prior theoretical research indicates that Population III (Pop3) stars typically emerge within extremely metal-poor gas clouds, roughly $10^5 M_\odot$ in mass, situated inside mini dark matter halos. Through multiple collisions within Pop3 star clusters, very massive stars can develop into intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). This study utilizes star-by-star $N$-body simulations to model the long-term evolution of these clusters. Our findings suggest that if mini dark matter halos persist to the present day, the associated star clusters can evade tidal disruption from the galactic environment and efficiently generate IMBH-black hole mergers across a redshift range of 0 to 20. The estimated average gravitational wave event rate is $0.1-0.8~\mathrm{yr}^{-1} \mathrm{Gpc}^{-3}$, with approximately 40–80% of these mergers occurring at high redshifts ($z>6$). Characteristic strain analysis reveals that while some low-redshift mergers are detectable by LISA, TianQin, and Taiji, the majority fall within the sensitivity ranges of DECIGO and advanced LIGO/VIRGO/Kagra. Additionally, mergers involving pair-instability black holes occur at a rate of roughly $0.01-0.15$~yr$^{-1}$~Gpc$^{-3}$, offering an explanation for events similar to GW190521.

In December 2019, a novel SARS-CoV-2 virus emerged in China and rapidly spread globally as a pandemic. Lacking immediate preventive measures or available vaccines, mathematical modeling offers valuable scientific insights into transmission dynamics and potential drug targets. This study introduces a within-host mathematical model of SARS-CoV-2 infection that accounts for both innate and adaptive immune responses. We analyze the model's equilibrium points and derive an expression for the basic reproduction number, subsequently demonstrating numerically that a transcritical bifurcation occurs. The model is calibrated using real viral load data from two COVID-19 patients. Based on these estimated parameters, we conduct a global sensitivity analysis regarding the peak viral load and evaluate the efficacy of antiviral drugs and vaccination on infection dynamics. Our findings indicate that inhibiting viral production in infected cells reduces viral load more effectively than lowering the infection rate of healthy cells. While vaccination is beneficial, during the vaccine development phase, targeting the blocking of virus production from infected cells represents a promising strategy for antiviral drug development.

Edge computing facilitates low-latency real-time applications by hosting services near end-users, a capability that aligns well with the modern microservices architecture. This architectural shift, which breaks applications into loosely coupled, smaller components, complements the resource-constrained nature of edge infrastructure that often struggles to support monolithic systems. While edge servers can deploy these service components independently, this approach introduces communication overheads. Consequently, simultaneously satisfying application service level objectives and optimizing deployment costs and communication overheads in mobile edge cloud environments remains a complex challenge. This paper introduces and evaluates three dynamic placement strategies: two heuristic methods (a greedy set-cover approximation and an integer programming-based optimization) and one learning-based algorithm. These algorithms aim to meet application constraints, minimize infrastructure costs, and guarantee service availability for all clients and User Equipment (UE) within the network coverage. The proposed solutions are adaptable to various network topologies and microservice-based edge applications. For experimental validation, drone swarm navigation is used as a representative use case. Due to the difficulty of accessing a real-world physical testbed for such scenarios, the study relies on simulation to demonstrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The evaluation compares the approaches based on placement quality, cluster utilization, and determinism. The results indicate that the learning-based algorithm generally yields superior solution quality, though the study also identifies specific conditions under which traditional heuristic algorithms may be more appropriate.
We establish and demonstrate isomorphisms for three combinatorial classes of labeled trees, and additionally provide an alternative proof utilizing generating functions.

Galaxy growth is largely driven by mergers, which disrupt magnetic fields (B-fields) and gas dynamics within the interstellar medium (ISM); however, the specific processes governing the amplification and dissipation of these fields during such events remain uncertain. This study examines the morphology of ordered B-fields in the multi-phase ISM of the Antennae galaxies, the nearest pair of merging spiral galaxies. By comparing polarimetric data from $154~\mu$m thermal dust emission and $11$ cm radio synchrotron radiation, we observe that B-fields at $154~\mu$m are more ordered than those at $11$ cm across the system. Specifically, the ratio of turbulent to ordered B-fields at $154~\mu$m increases in the galaxy cores and star-forming regions. While the relic spiral arm exhibits an ordered spiral pattern in the $154~\mu$m data, the $11$ cm field appears radial. We propose that the $154~\mu$m B-field is primarily shaped by turbulent dynamos fueled by high $^{12}$CO(1-0) velocity dispersion in star-forming areas, whereas the $11$ cm B-field aligns with high HI velocity dispersion caused by the interaction. These findings reveal a dissociation between warm gas, heavily disturbed by the merger, and dense gas that still adheres to the dynamics of the relic spiral arm. Additionally, we identify an $\sim8.9$ kpc scale ordered B-field linking the two galaxies. At the base of the tidal tail, which coincides with HI and $^{12}$CO(1-0) emission, the $154~\mu$m and $11$ cm B-fields are compressed and/or sheared due to the merger. We suggest that amplified B-fields, relative to the rest of the system and other spirals, may facilitate gas flow between the galaxies and along the tidal tail.

Data-driven Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) offer the promise of standardizing and enhancing care through personalized probabilistic guidance. However, the extensive data volume required often mandates collaborative learning across analogous CDSSs, which are frequently unsharable or imperfectly interoperable (IIO) due to non-overlapping feature sets. To address this, we introduce Modular Clinical Decision Support Networks (MoDN), a framework enabling flexible, privacy-preserving learning across IIO datasets while delivering interpretable, continuous predictive feedback to clinicians. MoDN functions as an innovative decision tree comprised of feature-specific neural network modules. It generates dynamic, personalized patient representations and supports multiple, updatable diagnostic predictions throughout a consultation. Furthermore, its modular architecture isolates training updates to specific features, facilitating collaborative learning between IIO datasets without the need to share any data.

The widespread adoption of IoT-enabled nodes has driven a surge in battery-operated devices. Energy harvesters offer a viable alternative by capturing energy to power embedded systems, enabling intermittent computing where tasks run only when sufficient energy is stored in a capacitor. Since harvesters cannot guarantee continuous power, conventional volatile processors—which lose register and cache data during outages—are insufficient. This necessitates Non-Volatile Processors (NVPs) utilizing Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) to preserve critical data during power failures. However, integrating NVM at the cache level often degrades performance and increases energy usage compared to SRAM-based caches. To address this, this paper introduces the Efficient Backup and Restore (eBaRe) hybrid cache architecture, which combines SRAM and STT-RAM in the first-level cache. By implementing specific cache block placement and migration policies, eBaRe minimizes writes to STT-RAM; during power failures, it strategically migrates essential blocks from SRAM to STT-RAM. Compared to baseline architectures, eBaRe reduces STT-RAM writes from 63.35% to 35.93%, achieving a 32.85% performance improvement and a 23.42% reduction in energy consumption. Additionally, the proposed backup strategy cuts backup time by 34.46%.

Recent hypotheses suggest that Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet theory coupled with a scalar field (EGBS) can effectively describe physically viable celestial phenomena, with the scalar field effect remaining active even in standard four dimensions. This study examines static, spherically symmetric configurations of compact stars within the EGBS framework to elucidate its implications for stellar modeling. The evolution of perfect fluid distributions is governed by the condition of pressure isotropy and the requirement that one metric potential be selected from the system of differential equations to fully define the model. In our formulation, given any specific energy density profile $\rho$ for a spherically symmetric configuration and an arbitrary equation of state (EoS), we can construct a model that reproduces that profile. Since the energy density profile determines both the mass $M$ and radius $R_s$ of the compact star, any desired mass-radius relation can be achieved by tuning the scalar potential and the Gauss-Bonnet term coefficient in the EGBS action. This represents a degeneracy between the EoS and the model-defining functions, indicating that the mass-radius relation alone is insufficient to fully constrain the model. As an illustration, we analyze a new class of analytic, spherically symmetric interior solutions using a polytropic EoS. The model is discussed in detail, demonstrating compliance with all necessary physical conditions for realistic compact stars, thereby confirming the consistency of EGBS theory with observational data.

Graph drawing quality is frequently assessed through aesthetics; however, current aesthetic criteria primarily judge adherence to specific rules rather than overall quality. Presently, holistic quality evaluation relies on subjective personal judgments or expensive user studies, both of which have significant drawbacks—lack of reliability and high cost, respectively. Consequently, there is a demand for a direct, objective metric for overall quality that would enable visualization designers to rapidly compare and evaluate drawings during the design phase. To address this gap, we propose a measure that derives overall quality by aggregating individual aesthetic criteria. A user study validates this approach, demonstrating its ability to predict human graph comprehension performance, and the potential implications of this measure for future research are explored.

We investigate a Jarzynski-type equality for work within systems subjected to non-projective unsharp monitoring. Work is defined as the discrepancy between the final expected energy and the measurement outcome $f$ obtained from an energy observation, utilizing the subsequently conditioned normalized state $\hat \rho(t,f)$ evolved to time $t$. The resulting equality relies on the coherences generated during the process, the specific properties of the measurement meter, and the noise it introduces. We examine these factors in detail to clarify their roles. Our analysis reveals that, except for specific instances, the noise does not merely scale the result derived from projective measurements; rather, the meter's unsharpness and resolution create distinct scenarios. Specifically, when the spacing between adjacent energy spectrum elements significantly exceeds the meter's resolution, the outcome resembles the projective case, modified only by a meter-dependent factor. Conversely, when the spectrum is closely spaced such that measurements may become non-informative, a correction to the non-overlapping relation emerges, and we determine the conditions under which this correction vanishes. Furthermore, we evaluate the coherences by assessing the relative entropy of coherence in the evolved post-measurement states. Finally, we validate these findings through an analysis of a two-level system monitored by a basic meter.

This work demonstrates the potency and sophistication of the Bendixson Dulac theorem in deriving upper limits on the number of limit cycles across various families of planar vector fields. In specific instances, we suggest employing a function tied to the curvature of the vector field's orbits as the Dulac function. We establish general findings for Lienard-type equations and rigid planar systems. Additionally, we highlight a significant phenomenon: for every integer $m > 1$, we introduce a straightforward one-parameter differential system where limit cycles exist only for parameter values within a subset of an interval that shrinks exponentially as $m$ increases. A key advantage of these results is that, despite being derived through simple calculations verifiable by hand, they refine and expand upon prior research. Furthermore, for certain systems, determining the number of limit cycles can be reduced to analyzing the geometry of a planar curve and the sign of an associated function in one or two variables.

This work examines the deformation theory of $\mathrm{G}_2$-instantons on nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds. Since nearly parallel $\mathrm{G}_2$ structures correspond bijectively to real Killing spinors, the deformation framework can be expressed using spinors and Dirac operators. We demonstrate that the space of infinitesimal instanton deformations is isomorphic to the kernel of an elliptic operator. Leveraging this approach, we establish the rigidity of abelian instantons. Finally, we apply these findings to characterize the deformation space of the canonical connection on the four normal homogeneous nearly $\mathrm{G}_2$ manifolds.

Identifying and eliminating potentially malicious nodes in networked systems presents a significant challenge, particularly due to inherent detection uncertainties and network connectivity constraints. These factors create indirect costs associated with both erroneously removing benign nodes and failing to detect malicious ones. Although a recent method attempts to address these issues directly, it relies on the unrealistic assumption that the decision-maker possesses precise knowledge of the joint probability of node maliciousness. In reality, such distributions are merely estimates derived from limited data. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a distributionally robust framework for optimal node removal. Despite the problem being NP-Hard, we develop a principled algorithmic solution that approximates the answer using duality combined with Semidefinite Programming relaxation. Comprehensive theoretical and empirical analyses, utilizing both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrate that our approach is highly effective and offers significantly greater robustness compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

We investigate framed links situated within irreducible 3-manifolds that are either $Z$-homology 3-spheres or atoroidal $Q$-homology 3-spheres. We determine the dual of the Kauffman skein module over the ring of two-variable power series with complex coefficients. Furthermore, for links in $S^3$, we present a novel construction of the classical Kauffman polynomial.

The global 2019 Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic, triggered by the rapid spread of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), has caused profound worldwide repercussions, including significant loss of life and severe socio-economic disruption. Digital technologies have emerged as a crucial strategy to combat the crisis, with contact tracing applications playing a central role. Leveraging successful precedents from fighting other infectious diseases, these apps have been deployed to manage the current outbreak. However, their implementation raises substantial privacy concerns due to the storage and processing of data that can reveal user identities, device locations, and behavioral patterns. These issues are particularly acute in nationwide deployments, which risk enabling mass surveillance by authoritarian regimes. Although data protection laws in various countries impose restrictions, uncertainties regarding user privacy remain. This article examines the privacy features of national COVID-19 contact tracing applications by analyzing their inherent characteristics. Using the Brazilian application Coronavírus-SUS as a case study, we provide an in-depth discussion, given Brazil's status as one of the most severely affected nations. Furthermore, anticipating that contact tracing will remain integral to managing current and future pandemics, we outline key research challenges.

An edge-coloring is classified as an interval coloring when the edge labels at any given vertex constitute a sequence of consecutive integers. The interval thickness, denoted as s(G), represents the minimum count of interval-colorable graphs required to edge-decompose a graph G. We establish that for any graph with n vertices, s(G) is o(n), thereby surpassing the prior bound of 2n/5 established by Asratian, Casselgren, and Petrosyan. Although no specific graph with an interval thickness exceeding 2 has been identified, we demonstrate the existence of bipartite graphs featuring an interval spectrum with arbitrarily many large gaps; the interval spectrum comprises all integer values t for which a graph admits an interval coloring using t colors. Furthermore, interval colorings in bipartite graphs model no-wait scheduling scenarios, such as parent-teacher conferences where each interaction duration is uniform. Our findings indicate that any conference involving n participants can be organized within o(n) no-wait periods. Additionally, for any pair of integers t and T where t < T, we construct a set of parent-teacher pairs such that all no-wait schedules are unstable: schedules could theoretically last t hours or T hours, yet no stable schedule exists for any duration x satisfying t < x < T.

The "tipping" model describes a scenario in social networks where an individual adopts a specific behavior or trait once a threshold number of their neighbors already exhibit it. A central challenge in viral marketing is identifying an initial "seed" set capable of triggering network-wide adoption. This paper presents a scalable method for rapidly identifying such seed sets within massive networks, guaranteeing full propagation under the tipping model. Experimental validation across 31 real-world networks demonstrates that our approach frequently identifies seed sets several orders of magnitude smaller than the total population, outperforming traditional nodal centrality metrics in most instances. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits excellent scalability; for instance, it identified a seed set for the Friendster network (5.6 million nodes, 28 million edges) in less than 3.6 hours. Results also show that the method yields compact seed sets even when high-degree nodes are excluded. Finally, our findings indicate that both highly clustered local neighborhoods and dense global community structures tend to inhibit the spread of trends within the tipping model.

Analyzing the system dynamics of micro- and nano-positioning instruments and their controlled operation requires addressing transient hysteresis cycles caused by pre-sliding kinetic friction. This energy dissipation, leading to the convergence of state trajectories, primarily stems from structural hysteresis damping in contact surface asperities during reversals, rather than following exponential (viscous) or finite-time (Coulomb) patterns. This paper examines energy dissipation and convergence within pre-sliding cycles, demonstrating how a piecewise smooth force-displacement hysteresis map influences the energy balance of an unforced second-order system. Furthermore, the Dahl friction model, characterized by a low number of free parameters, is presented alongside this developed analysis.

This work examines the supersymmetric partition function of a two-dimensional linear $\sigma$-model defined on a torus, where the complex structure varies along one worldsheet direction and the Kähler modulus along the other. Motivated by the dimensional reduction of a 4d $\mathcal{N}=4$ $U(1)$ Super-Yang-Mills Janus configuration compactified on a circle times a mapping torus ($T^2$ fibered over $S^1$) with an $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ duality wall, our model features minimal supersymmetry. The partition function relies on two distinct $SL(2,\mathbb{Z})$ elements: one governing the duality twist and the other the mapping torus geometry. Being topological, it can be expressed as a multivariate quadratic Gauss sum. By evaluating this function via two distinct methods, we derive identities connecting various quadratic Gauss sums that extend the {\it Landsberg-Schaar} relation. These results constitute a subset of identities identified by F. Deloup. Each identity includes a phase factor corresponding to an eighth root of unity, which we demonstrate originates as a Berry phase within the supersymmetric Janus-like setup. Furthermore, supersymmetry dictates that the complex structure must vary along a semicircle in the upper half-plane, as established by Gaiotto and Witten in a related context; this semicircle is crucial for generating the correct Berry phase.

This study presents computer simulations of three therapeutic interventions for refractory pulmonary hypertension (RPH), which involve surgically creating an atrial septal defect, a ventricular septal defect, or a patent ductus arteriosus (Potts shunt). The objective across all procedures is to establish a right-to-left shunt that facilitates pressure or volume unloading of the right heart during right ventricular failure without compromising cardiac output. However, this benefit comes at the cost of introducing de-oxygenated blood into systemic circulation, which reduces systemic arterial oxygen saturation. The models utilized in this research are grounded in compartmental representations of human hemodynamics and oxygen transport, with a key variable being the cross-sectional area of the surgically induced defect. Numerical simulations were conducted to evaluate the effects of various interventions and shunt sizes on hemodynamic parameters and oxygen levels. Additionally, an exercise model was developed to analyze exercise tolerance in simulated RPH patients both before and after intervention.

Detecting polyps early in the lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract is crucial for preventing fatal colorectal cancer. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems can enhance detection accuracy and efficiency, thereby reducing the time required by endoscopists. However, a significant hurdle in developing these systems is the scarcity of annotated data. To address the lack of true positive cases, generating synthetic medical data has become an active research focus. Since machine learning (ML) models, which form the backbone of CAD systems, require substantial datasets for effective training, we introduce the PolypConnect pipeline. This pipeline transforms non-polyp images into polyp images to expand training datasets. We present the complete pipeline, supported by quantitative and qualitative evaluations conducted with endoscopists. Models trained on a combination of synthetic and real data achieved a 5.1% increase in mean intersection over union (mIOU) compared to those trained solely on real data. All experimental code is publicly available on GitHub for result reproduction.

Recent online narratives have fueled vaccine hesitancy, substantially undermining the effectiveness of vaccination campaigns, including those for COVID-19. Even though the medical community broadly agrees on the safety and efficacy of current vaccines, many social media users remain exposed to misinformation, leading to indecision or refusal to vaccinate. This study aims to comprehend anti-vaccine sentiment by creating a system that automatically identifies individuals propagating such narratives. We present a publicly accessible Python package designed to analyze Twitter profiles and predict the likelihood of future anti-vaccine sentiment dissemination. Constructed using text embedding techniques, neural networks, and automated dataset generation, and trained on millions of tweets, this model can accurately identify anti-vaccine users up to a year before they post relevant hashtags or keywords. Additionally, we demonstrate how text analysis reveals moral and emotional distinctions between anti-vaccine spreaders and typical users. These findings will assist researchers and policymakers in understanding the drivers of anti-vaccine behavior and the topics discussed on Twitter, enabling the design of more targeted campaigns to debunk harmful myths.

Crosstalk is a prevalent issue in quantum computing systems containing multiple qubits, generating various correlated and non-local errors that pose significant threats to fault-tolerant quantum error correction, which typically assumes errors are local and predictable. Addressing these crosstalk errors demands a thorough understanding, modeling, and detection capability. This paper presents a comprehensive framework and a specific protocol for identifying and localizing such errors. We provide a rigorous definition of crosstalk errors that encompasses a broad spectrum of physical phenomena historically labeled as "crosstalk," alongside a concrete model for crosstalk-free quantum processors; any deviations from this model constitute crosstalk errors. Furthermore, we offer an equivalent, purely operational definition that is independent of any specific model. Leveraging this definition, we develop a protocol to detect a wide range of crosstalk errors in multi-qubit systems by identifying conditional dependencies within observed experimental probabilities. This approach is highly efficient, requiring a number of unique experiments that scales at most cubically, and often quadratically, with the qubit count. We validate the protocol through simulations of 2-qubit and 6-qubit processors.

Determining the central nervous system mechanisms responsible for conscious experience has been a primary focus of cognitive neuroscience. Although classical physics fails to account for causally effective consciousness, the inherent indeterminism of quantum mechanics, along with its distinction between quantum states and observables, offers a promising framework for modeling consciousness. In this study, we apply the Schrödinger equation and the Planck–Einstein energy-frequency relationship to establish the relevant quantum timescale for conscious processes. Additionally, using a simple two-qubit model, we demonstrate that a non-zero interaction Hamiltonian is essential for generating quantum entanglement and producing observable correlations between measurement results.
